docs.title: How spacecraft talk to the ground
docs.text:
One open wiki covers the whole chain, from a bit in an on-board packet to a value on an operator's screen. It explains the CCSDS protocols, the ECSS Packet Utilization Standard, Space Link Extension, ESA's SCOS-2000 mission control system and its Mission Information Base. Every statement cites the document and page it comes from.

Start here Open the MIB Explorer Fly the Solar Orbiter simulator

All information on this site was retrieved from sources publicly available online. See every source →

docs.title: Explore the wiki
docs.text:
• Start here

    The big picture, with step-by-step downlink and uplink walkthroughs and two worked examples built on real Solar Orbiter definitions.

    How it all fits together

  • CCSDS standards

    Space Packet, TM/TC/AOS/USLP transfer frames, channel coding, CLTU, COP-1, SDLS, time codes, CFDP, XTCE and SLE, with every header drawn bit by bit.

    The protocol stack

  • ECSS & PUS

    The Packet Utilization Standard (PUS-C, 2016, and PUS-A, 2003), with a page for every service and a catalogue of all message types.

    Packet Utilization Standard

  • SCOS-2000

    ESA's mission control system: history, architecture, EGSE use, time correlation, EDDS/GDDS/TDRS data dissemination, archives, NCTRS/NIS and EGS-CC.

    SCOS-2000

  • The MIB

    The Mission Information Base explained concept by concept and table by table, from the Database Import ICD.

    The MIB

  • MIB Explorer

    Every parameter, packet, calibration, limit, telecommand and sequence of the public Solar Orbiter MIB, each with its own address.

    Explore

  • Solar Orbiter simulator

    Fly Solar Orbiter on its real trajectory, decode real MIB housekeeping packets, send real telecommands across the light-time delay and inject failures.

    Simulate

  • Missions

    Solar Orbiter in depth, plus Herschel/Planck, Rosetta, Mars Express, Venus Express and other SCOS-2000 users.

    Missions

  • Library & references

    Every source with its summary, contents, reference list, original link and copy time, plus a catalogue of everything those sources cite.

    Library

Independent and sourced

This is a community wiki. It is not affiliated with or endorsed by ESA, CCSDS, ECSS or any mission. Everything here was compiled from publicly available documents, all listed with links back to their originals on Sources & copies. Wiki text and code are MIT-licensed. Read how the pages were produced in Methodology.

docs.title: About this wiki
docs.text:
OPEN-SPACE-INFO is an independent, open wiki that explains how spacecraft and their ground segments exchange data. It covers the CCSDS protocols, the ECSS Packet Utilization Standard, ESA/ESOC's SCOS-2000 mission control system and its ancillary systems, and the SCOS-2000 Mission Information Base (MIB), illustrated with the real, publicly posted Solar Orbiter MIB.

Sourced from public documents

All information on this site was retrieved from sources publicly available online. Every page cites the documents it relies on, and Sources & copies links back to each original with the time we copied it.

docs.title: Who it is for
docs.text: Engineers, students and enthusiasts who want to understand an operational ESA-style ground segment end to end, from a bit in an on-board packet to a value on an operator's display. The wiki also suits anyone who needs to read a real MIB.

docs.title: How to use it
docs.text:
• Start with How it all fits together, then follow the downlink and uplink walkthroughs.
  • Each standard has its own page with field-by-field diagrams, under CCSDS and ECSS & PUS.
  • The MIB section explains the database, and the MIB Explorer shows every item of the Solar Orbiter MIB (2025 and 2020 releases) and of the SWA and STIX instrument databases.
  • The Library and the reference catalogue let you follow any claim back to its source document.

docs.title: License
docs.text: The wiki text, diagrams and code are released under the MIT License. Third-party documents and data keep their owners' copyright and terms and are not covered by that licence; see the third-party notice.

docs.title: Not affiliated
docs.text: This project is not affiliated with or endorsed by ESA, ESOC, CCSDS, ECSS, the Solar Orbiter project, IRAP or any other organisation whose documents are cited. Names of standards, systems and organisations are used only to identify them.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: Corrections and additions are welcome as issues or pull requests on GitHub. Every factual statement must carry a citation (clause and PDF page), as described in the authoring guide. Read how the pages were produced in Methodology.

docs.title: 1. Finding and copying sources
docs.text:
Sources were found by web search and by browsing public archives: ESA mission archives, the CCSDS and ECSS publication sites, conference proceedings, and the Solar Orbiter instrument-team site at IRAP. Only files reachable without login, payment or bypassing access controls were copied. Paywalled papers and HTTP-403 resources were recorded as "not copied" and cited by title only. Each copy was logged with its original URL, the UTC copy time and a SHA-256 checksum. The full list is on Sources & copies.1

The sources were collected in two rounds. The first (5 to 12 November 2026) gathered the core CCSDS, ECSS, SCOS-2000, EDDS and Solar Orbiter documents and the two Solar Orbiter MIB releases. A second round on 12 November 2026 added 78 documents: further CCSDS books (among them RF and modulation, Proximity-1, security, SLE Forward Space Packet and service management), four more ECSS E-50 adoption notices and the E-70 ground systems and operations standards, the four ESA PSS packet standards of 1988 to 1994, Herschel/Planck and Solar Orbiter interface documents, and the SWA 6.5.0 and STIX 2.26.38 instrument databases.124

Two documents found in a public archive print operational login credentials. The wiki cites them and links to their original location, but does not republish the files.5

docs.title: 2. Reading the sources
docs.text: Text was extracted from every PDF with pdftotext, keeping PDF page boundaries so that citations can give exact PDF page numbers. Scanned documents were treated separately: the Alcatel fax of March 2003, which has no text layer, was read from its page images, and the four ESA PSS standards, which are scans, were read from their OCR text (produced with RapidOCR) with every number, field size and code checked against the page images.32 Figures that are pictures (for example the frame drawings of the Solar Orbiter packet ICD) are not in the extracted text; where a page relies on one, its footnote says that the drawing was read in the PDF. The MIB releases and instrument databases were loaded into SQLite databases so that every statistic quoted on the site comes from an explicit SQL query, shown in an "SQL used" box on the page.4

docs.title: 3. Writing and checking the pages
docs.text: The pages were drafted by AI agents (Anthropic's Claude) working from the extracted text under the authoring rules. Every fact must cite a clause and a PDF page, inferences must be labelled as such, and quotations must be short. A separate agent then fact-checked every page: it re-opened each cited page, checked field sizes, values and numbers against the standards and the data, re-ran the SQL, and fixed what was wrong. Further passes compared the pages with each other, so that a header field, a count from the MIB or the date of a standard reads the same everywhere it appears. The library entries, the reference catalogue and the MIB table pages were generated from structured extractions of the documents. The table definitions were cross-checked against the open-source pyscos2000 schema and against the real data.

docs.title: 4. Known limitations
docs.text:
• Errors can survive review. Always check important details against the cited clause, and please report mistakes.
  • Several sources are old issues; the standards map shows which issue each page uses and whether it is current, and the history page explains the ESA PSS standards that preceded them.
  • Many SCOS-2000 documents (SUMs, ADDs, internal ICDs) are not public. The reference catalogue lists them with the public documents that cite them.
  • The Solar Orbiter MIB pages show only two of the 111 posted spacecraft MIB releases (the first and the latest), plus two versions of the SWA instrument database and one of the STIX instrument database.4 See The Solar Orbiter MIB.
  • Some "SQL used" blocks written early in the project query tables such as cvs, cve or dpc with generic column names (COL1, COL2 …) in ICD field order. The local databases were later rebuilt with the ICD field names. The results are the same, but the column names differ.
  • Only Solar Orbiter has a public MIB in the library. For the other missions the wiki describes the interface documents, not parameter-level databases.

  1. This wiki's source registry (data/sources.json), summarised on Sources & copies: original URL, copy time (UTC), SHA-256 checksum and size of each document, and the collection round of the documents added on 12 November 2026. ↩↩

  2. The four scanned ESA PSS standards: PSS-04-106, PSS-04-107, PSS-04-151 and PSS-07-101; how they were read is described on the history page. ↩↩

  3. Alcatel fax: SCOS MIB naming limits, part 2 (March 2003), catalogued from its page images; part 1 (January 2003) has an OCR-quality text layer. ↩

  4. Solar Orbiter MIB release of 16 September 2025 and of 16 April 2020; the SWA instrument database 6.3.4 and 6.5.0; the STIX instrument database v2.26.38. The count of 111 releases comes from the IRAP directory listing https://solarorbiter.irap.omp.eu/MIB/MIBs/ as surveyed on 2026-11-05 (not a library item). ↩↩↩

  5. Herschel/Planck FOP procedures C_GSP_MCS_NCTRS and C_GSP_MCS_SCOS; the reason is recorded in their registry entries. ↩

docs.title: Sources & copies
docs.text:
In one sentence

All information on this site was retrieved from sources publicly available online. This page links back to every one of them.

docs.title: How the information was gathered
docs.text:
Every document and dataset listed below was downloaded from a public web location that needed no login, payment or circumvention of access controls. Each download was logged with its original URL, the UTC time of the copy and a SHA-256 checksum. Three files that had moved were retrieved from Internet Archive snapshots of their original addresses; their entries say so. Text was extracted from the PDFs, and every wiki page cites the clause and PDF page it relies on. Pages that analyse the Solar Orbiter MIB cite the release they queried. The JPL Horizons ephemeris used by the Solar Orbiter simulator consists of API responses, kept unchanged in one zip file together with a manifest of each query URL, download time and checksum.

Copies of the files are kept unchanged in this repository's third-party/ folder, so the citations stay checkable if an original location disappears. They remain the property of their owners and are not covered by the MIT License of the wiki text and code. If you are a rights holder and want a file removed, please open an issue on the repository.

docs.title: Not copied
docs.text:
• Five AIAA SpaceOps papers (SCOS-2000 Release 5, NIS, Data Security, Multi-Spacecraft, Common EGSE/MCS for Herschel/Planck) returned HTTP 403 (paywall). They are cited by title only.
  • The Herschel/Planck spacecraft database zips in the ESA Herschel Science Archive (/hsa/legacy/operations/moc/sdb/data/) returned HTTP 403 on 2026-11-05 and again on 2026-11-12.
  • Two Herschel flight-operations ground-segment procedures (C_GSP_MCS_SCOS and C_GSP_MCS_NCTRS) are cited and listed below, but their PDFs are not hosted here because they print operational login credentials.
  • 109 of the 111 Solar Orbiter MIB releases on the IRAP server: only the first (2020-04-16) and the latest (2025-09-16) were copied, to avoid a long bulk download from a small team server.

docs.title: CCSDS: overview of the protocol stack
docs.text:
The Consultative Committee for Space Data Systems (CCSDS) is a committee set up by the space agencies to solve data-system problems they share. Its member agencies include ESA, NASA, CNES, DLR, ASI, JAXA and others.1 Its results are "Recommended Standards". Endorsing one is voluntary, and a Recommended Standard is reviewed no later than five years after it is issued, as the Space Packet Protocol's statement of intent puts it.2 Together the CCSDS standards define the chain that spacecraft data follows. Telemetry packets are framed by the TM Space Data Link Protocol, protected by channel coding, received by a ground station and, in cross support, delivered to the user over Space Link Extension. Telecommands make the reverse trip as CLTUs, with COP-1 providing retransmission.293948

This page explains how the protocols fit together. It follows two CCSDS reports: the Overview of Space Communications Protocols (CCSDS 130.0-G-4, April 2023) and the Space Data Link Protocols: Summary of Concept and Rationale (CCSDS 130.2-G-3, September 2015).1032 It ends with a map of every layer, the standard that defines it, the copy in this wiki's reference catalogue and the page that explains it.

CCSDS document colours

The protocol itself is specified in a Blue Book (Recommended Standard). Its rationale is explained in a Green Book (Informational Report).10 The reference lists also show Magenta Books (Recommended Practices, such as the SCID code assignment procedures), Yellow Books (CCSDS Records, such as A02.1-Y-4 on CCSDS organization) and retired standards marked "Historical" with an "-S" suffix (for example the SCPS protocols).12

docs.title: From fixed TDM formats to a layered stack
docs.text:
Traditional telemetry used Time Division Multiplexing (TDM). Data items sat in a continuous stream of fixed-length frames according to a fixed multiplexing rule, so every project built its own data system.13 When on-board processors arrived, CCSDS standardized a series of protocols. The timeline shows the sequence described in the 2023 overview:13 ESA's own path, from the PSS-04-106 and PSS-04-107 packet standards to the ECSS adoption notices, is told on From ESA PSS to CCSDS and ECSS.

timeline
  title Evolution of the CCSDS space communications protocols (after CCSDS 130.0-G-4 §2.1)
  Early 1980s : Packet Telemetry with variable-length Source Packets in fixed-length Transfer Frames
              : Telecommand with TC Packets in sporadic variable-length frames, shortly after
  Late 1980s : AOS for the International Space Station, adding audio and video services
  Restructuring : Space Packet Protocol, TM / TC / AOS Space Data Link Protocols, TM / TC Synchronization and Channel Coding
  1990s : SCPS family (network, security, transport, file), all retired except SCPS-TP
  File transfer : CFDP for reliable file transfer over unreliable links
  From July 1998 : Delay Tolerant Networking research, leading to LTP and the Bundle Protocol
  Proximity links : Proximity-1 for short-range links between landers, rovers, orbiters and relays
  2018 : Unified Space Data Link Protocol (USLP)
  Security : SDLS protocol and SDLS Extended Procedures

The 2023 overview expects USLP to become the data link protocol for all future robotic and crewed missions.13 Solar Orbiter, which uses the TC and TM Space Data Link Protocols, is an example of the established configuration (see below).7477

docs.title: The reference model
docs.text:
CCSDS places its protocols in five layers of the OSI model: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport and Application. Session and Presentation layers are rarely used over space links.14 CCSDS does not define programming interfaces. It describes services as abstract primitives (.request, .indication), which can serve as a reference for building an API.14

flowchart TB
  subgraph UPPER["Upper layers (Network, Transport, Application)"]
    direction LR
    SPPapp["SPP"]
    MAL["MO-MAL"]
    CFDP["CFDP"]
    AMS["AMS"]
    BP["Bundle Protocol + CLAs"]
    TCPUDP["TCP / UDP over IP"]
    LTP["LTP"]
    IPOC["IP over CCSDS"]
  end
  SHIM["Either Encapsulation Packet Protocol or Space Packet Protocol"]
  subgraph DLL["Data Link Layer"]
    direction LR
    SDLP["Data Link Protocol Sublayer:<br/>USLP · TM · TC · AOS · Prox-1 · (Ethernet)"]
    SCC["Synchronization and Channel Coding Sublayer:<br/>TM coding · TC coding · Prox-1 coding · SCCC · DVB-S2"]
    SDLP --> SCC
  end
  PHY["Physical Layer: RF and Modulation, optical, wire"]
  UPPER --> SHIM --> DLL --> PHY

Redrawn and simplified after CCSDS 130.0-G-4 figure 2-1, with the two data link sublayers of §2.2.3 shown explicitly.1416

docs.title: The physical layer
docs.text: CCSDS 401.0-B, Radio Frequency and Modulation Systems, is an omnibus standard. It covers the RF signal between spacecraft and ground stations that carries the frames. Proximity-1 has its own physical layer standard.15 ECSS uses ECSS-E-ST-50-05 for the same role, and notes that CCSDS 401.0-B has extra options.61 The library holds CCSDS 401.0-B-32 (October 2021) and ECSS-E-ST-50-05C Rev. 2 (4 October 2011), together with ECSS-E-ST-50-02C on ranging and Doppler tracking; all three are summarised on Radio frequency, modulation and ranging.6768

docs.title: The data link layer
docs.text:
CCSDS divides the OSI data link layer into two sublayers:1634

  • The Data Link Protocol Sublayer moves higher-layer data units over one point-to-point space link inside Transfer Frames. Its protocols are TM, TC, AOS, Proximity-1 and USLP, together called the Space Data Link Protocols. TM, TC, AOS and USLP can carry secured user data through the optional Space Data Link Security (SDLS) protocol. No security requirement exists yet for Proximity-1.16 The wider CCSDS security family (threats, the choice of layer, algorithms and key management) is on Security in CCSDS space links.
  • The Synchronization and Channel Coding Sublayer gets frames across a noisy link. It delimits and synchronizes frames, applies error-correcting coding, and generates and removes bit transitions (pseudo-randomization).2534

The pairing is fixed.1625

Coding standard Used with TM Synchronization and Channel Coding (and the high-rate SCCC and DVB-S2 options) TM, AOS and USLP TC Synchronization and Channel Coding TC and USLP Proximity-1 Coding and Synchronization Proximity-1 and USLP Function TM sync and coding (131.0-B) TC sync and coding (231.0-B) Proximity-1 coding and sync Error correction and frame validation Convolutional + FECF; Reed-Solomon; concatenated; Turbo + FECF; LDPC; SCCC + FECF; DVB-S2 + FECF BCH; BCH + FECF Convolutional + attached CRC; LDPC + attached CRC Pseudo-randomization Cyclic pseudo-noise sequence (optional) Cyclic pseudo-noise sequence (optional) Cyclic pseudo-noise sequence (mandatory with LDPC only) Frame synchronization 32-bit (or longer) Attached Sync Marker, depending on coding 16-bit Start Sequence 24-bit ASM

After CCSDS 130.0-G-4 table 3-3. Only one option of a cell applies at a time, and the TM pseudo-noise sequence differs from the TC and Proximity-1 one.25 Table 3-3 lists only BCH coding for TC, but CCSDS 231.0-B-4 also specifies LDPC codes for the CLTU, with a 64-bit Start Sequence.5859

The two link directions use quite different sync-and-coding data units:

  • On the return link (TM), the unit on the channel is the Channel Access Data Unit (CADU): an Attached Sync Marker followed by a frame, a Reed-Solomon codeblock or a codeword, depending on the coding.53 The 32-bit ASM for uncoded, convolutional, Reed-Solomon and concatenated data is 0x1ACFFC1D.54 The service is for fixed-length frames delivered periodically, and it always delivers validated frames.25
  • On the forward link (TC), the unit is the Communications Link Transmission Unit (CLTU): a Start Sequence, BCH or LDPC codewords, and a Tail Sequence (optional for LDPC).58 The 16-bit BCH Start Sequence is 0b1110101110010000, which is 0xEB90.59 The service is for variable-length frames sent intermittently, and the TC coding delivers non-validated frames to the layer above.25 The TC coding standard also defines the Physical Layer Operations Procedure (PLOP) that switches the channel on and off.58

docs.title: Between the data link and network layers
docs.text: LTP (Licklider Transmission Protocol) adds optional reliability over one link. It usually carries each segment in an Encapsulation Packet. IP over CCSDS is a shim that carries CCSDS-recognized IP datagrams over the Space Data Link Protocols.17

docs.title: The network layer
docs.text:
CCSDS recognizes two network-layer interfaces: CCSDS-recognized IP datagrams and the Bundle Protocol of Delay Tolerant Networking (DTN). The Bundle Protocol builds a store-and-forward "overlay" network that reaches each link through convergence layer adapters (CLAs). DTN is designed for intermittent connectivity, long and variable delays, high error rates and asymmetric or simplex links.18

Between the data link protocols and these network protocols sits the shim position, held by either the Space Packet Protocol or the Encapsulation Packet Protocol.143 The Space Packet itself does forwarding: data moves along a path configured in advance by management, labelled only by its APID. It does not do routing, which the overview defines as choosing paths from origins to destinations in a network.112627

docs.title: Transport and application layers
docs.text:
• Transport: SCPS-TP, which extends TCP and includes UDP by reference. Internet TCP and UDP can run over IP over CCSDS.19
  • Application: AMS, CFDP, lossless, image and multispectral or hyperspectral data compression, the Space Packet Protocol, and the MO MAL Space Packet binding.20 CFDP is a file transfer protocol that also provides transport functions (complete, in-order delivery without duplicates). It can run over SPP (with mission-assigned APIDs), over EPP, over IP or BP, or directly over a Virtual Channel, MAP or Port.21
  • Mission-specific protocols may also run on top. For ESA missions the most important is the ECSS Packet Utilization Standard (PUS). ECSS-E-ST-50C names it as an example of an "application specific source/sink".2061

Time stamps in packets use the CCSDS Time Code Formats (CCSDS 301.0-B), which the Space Packet Protocol cites for its secondary-header time field.4 For describing packet formats, the Space Packet Protocol prefers a CCSDS notation such as XTCE.5

docs.title: Packets and Transfer Frames
docs.text:
Two kinds of data unit run through the whole stack, and keeping them apart is the key to understanding it:

Packet Transfer Frame Defined by Packet protocols: SPP, EPP, others with an authorized PVN Space Data Link Protocols (TM, TC, AOS, USLP, Proximity-1) Scope End to end. Created and used by application processes on board or on the ground. One space link, point to point Length Variable TM, AOS and USLP fixed; TC, Proximity-1 and USLP variable Identified by APID (SPP) or Protocol ID (EPP), with the Packet Version Number Transfer Frame Version Number, Spacecraft ID, Virtual Channel ID (and MAP ID)

Compiled from CCSDS 130.0-G-4 §2.2.7, §3.2.1 and §3.5 and CCSDS 130.2-G-3 §4.1.222040

Fixed-length TM and AOS frames allow simple, robust synchronization on weak, noisy links. Their length must stay constant on a Physical Channel for a Mission Phase and be known to the receiver in advance. Variable-length TC frames let short commands arrive quickly.4022

Every packet that a data link protocol carries directly must have a Packet Version Number (PVN) recognized by CCSDS and recorded by SANA. Other data units travel inside Encapsulation Packets.22 The protocols put packets into frames in different ways:49

  • TM and AOS concatenate packets into the fixed-length data field, split a packet that does not fit across consecutive frames of the same Virtual Channel, and point to the first packet header with the First Header Pointer. Idle Packets fill frames when there is not enough data.
  • TC carries one or more complete packets per frame. It segments long packets only when MAP channels are in use.
  • In both cases the receiver separates packets using each packet's length field, so the data link service provider must know where that field is and what it means.
flowchart LR
  subgraph APP["On-board application process"]
    P1["PUS report"]
  end
  P1 --> SP["Space Packet<br/>6-octet header + data"]
  SP --> TF["TM Transfer Frame<br/>header · data field (packets, First Header Pointer) · OCF · FECF"]
  TF --> CODE["Channel coding<br/>(e.g. Reed-Solomon, convolutional, Turbo, LDPC)"]
  CODE --> CADU["CADU<br/>ASM 0x1ACFFC1D + coded frame"]
  CADU --> RF["RF downlink"]
  RF --> GS["Ground station:<br/>sync, decode, frames"]
  GS --> SLE["SLE RAF / RCF<br/>to control centre"]
  SLE --> MCS["Mission control system<br/>(packets sorted by APID)"]

Downlink nesting as described on this wiki. Elements are linked to their pages above. Frame fields are introduced on the TM Space Data Link Protocol page.495339

See Downlink and Uplink for the complete end-to-end walkthroughs.

docs.title: Channels and identifiers
docs.text:
A key idea in every Space Data Link Protocol is the Virtual Channel (VC). One Physical Channel, a stream of bits in one direction, is shared among several logical streams, each possibly with different service requirements.22 The identifiers form a hierarchy:2342

flowchart TB
  PC["Physical Channel<br/>Physical Channel Name (management only, not in frame headers)"]
  MC["Master Channel (MC)<br/>MCID = TFVN + SCID"]
  VC["Virtual Channel (VC)<br/>VCID; GVCID = MCID + VCID"]
  MAP["MAP Channel (TC and USLP, optional)<br/>MAP ID"]
  PC -->|"one or more"| MC -->|"one or more"| VC -->|"zero or more"| MAP
  • Transfer Frame Version Number (TFVN) separates frame formats. Frames of different Space Data Link Protocols must never be mixed on one Physical Channel.2342 The binary values in the header are 00 for both TC and TM frames (version 1, told apart by management) and 01 for AOS (version 2).43
  • Spacecraft Identifier (SCID) identifies the spacecraft. It is unique only together with the TFVN, which makes the Master Channel Identifier (MCID). TC and TM use 10-bit SCIDs and AOS uses 8-bit ones, so a spacecraft with a TC uplink and an AOS downlink needs two SCIDs. SCIDs are requested through SANA by an agency representative and must be given up for re-use when a spacecraft retires.4445 A Magenta Book (CCSDS 320.0) governs the code assignment, and SANA has replaced the old Space Link Identifiers Blue Book.23 Both documents, and the Solar Orbiter values of every identifier, are described on Space link identifiers.
  • Master Channel (MC): all frames with the same MCID on a Physical Channel. Usually the Physical Channel carries a single MC. When it carries several (for example when one spacecraft relays another, as in an orbiter and lander mission), TM and AOS frames of all of them must have the same length.457
  • Virtual Channel (VC): identified by the VCID within an MC. MCID plus VCID gives the Global Virtual Channel Identifier (GVCID).45
  • MAP channel: TC and USLP can split a VC into MAP channels with a MAP ID. TC uses MAPs to segment packets longer than one frame.4723
Identifier TM TC AOS Proximity-1 USLP TFVN Version 1 Version 1 Version 2 Version 3 Version 4 SCID 0–1023 0–1023 0–255 0–1023 0–65 535 PCID N/A N/A N/A 0–1 N/A VCID 0–7 0–63 0–63 N/A 0–63 MAP ID N/A 0–63 N/A N/A 0–15 Port ID N/A N/A N/A 0–7 N/A

After CCSDS 130.0-G-4 table 3-1.23

The identifiers sit at the very start of every frame header. A receiver can therefore sort frames into Master and Virtual Channels before it looks at anything else. The two layouts used by most ESA missions are shown below. Both headers continue beyond the fields shown, and the full layouts are on the TM and TC pages.

Field positions from the TM and TC Blue Books.5556

Why Virtual Channels? A long, low-priority packet, such as a memory dump, may take several frames on VC 1. If an urgent event report arrives meanwhile, the provider can insert a VC 0 frame between the VC 1 frames, provided it has the buffers for this.41 CCSDS does not standardize the VC multiplexing algorithm, and each project must make sure its own scheme meets its priority and latency needs. The one exception is the SLE Forward Space Packet service, which prescribes the algorithm when it is used.37

docs.title: What the data link protocols offer
docs.text:
Data units TM TC AOS USLP Packets VC Packet MAP Packet, VC Packet VC Packet MAP Packet Fixed-length private data VC Access (none) VC Access MAP Access Variable-length private data (none) MAP Access, VC Access (none) MAP Access Short fixed-length data VC FSH, MC FSH, VC OCF, MC OCF (none) Insert, VC OCF Insert, MC OCF Stream (none) (none) Bitstream Octet Stream Transfer Frames VC Frame, MC Frame VC Frame, MC Frame VC Frame, MC Frame VC Frame, MC Frame

After CCSDS 130.0-G-4 table 3-2. FSH is the Frame Secondary Header and OCF the Operational Control Field. Proximity-1 has no formal service definition.24 USLP issue 3 (June 2024), the issue in the library, adds VC Packet and VC Access services to the USLP column; see USLP.72

The services differ in reliability and timing:

  • TC offers each SDU either the Sequence-Controlled (Type-A) service, a go-back-n ARQ run by COP-1 with reports in the CLCW, or the Expedited (Type-B) service, sent once and used for recovery operations or when a higher layer retransmits.35 COP-1 guarantees complete delivery only over the space link (including SLE), not end to end.48
  • TM and AOS have no retransmission. They keep order on each SAP, may signal gaps, and leave retransmission to higher layers such as LTP.3648
  • TM and AOS services are asynchronous (a queue, every SDU sent once), synchronous (a one-SDU buffer released with frames, so an SDU may be sent several times or not at all) or periodic (synchronous at a constant rate).38

Three combinations are common. Most missions use TC forward with TM return. Missions that need AOS features on the return link use TC with AOS. Missions that need two-way high-rate or audio and video links use AOS in both directions.33

docs.title: Managed parameters
docs.text:
The CCSDS protocols keep long-lived settings out of the data stream. Such managed parameters change rarely, a change usually means a major reconfiguration, and keeping them out of the protocol saves bandwidth. A management system that CCSDS does not specify conveys them to the protocol entities.8 Each data link Blue Book has a section listing its managed parameters. Their settings depend on the mission, the deployment and any SLE provider, and SLE parameters are usually set through CCSDS Service Management. SANA keeps one registry per data-link parameter, giving its format, value range, reserved values and the protocols that use it.51

Typical examples:

Layer Example managed parameters Space Packet Maximum packet length, multiplexing scheme, service type per APID, secondary header contents8 Encapsulation Minimum and maximum data unit length, valid Protocol IDs and extended IDs9 TM packet transfer Valid PVNs, maximum packet length, whether incomplete packets must be delivered57 Data link generally Physical Channel Name, a character string that is also the SAP address of the AOS Insert service46

docs.title: Cross support: Space Link Extension
docs.text:
Space Link Extension (SLE) services give users far from the station access to the space link, in a controlled way. They extend the TM, TC and AOS space link services between ground stations and control centres.39 When Space Packets are forwarded end to end, the ground part of the path is usually an SLE service.29

Direction SLE service Delivers Return Return All Frames (RAF) All TM frames from one space link bit stream Return Return Channel Frames (RCF) One Master Channel or selected Virtual Channels Return Return Operational Control Field (ROCF) MC or VC Operational Control Fields, such as CLCWs Forward Forward CLTU (FCLTU) CLTUs (encoded TC frames) for uplink Forward Forward Space Packet (FSP) Packets from one user, without coordination with other users Forward Enhanced FCLTU (EFCLTU) Uncoded AOS (or TC) frames for uplink

After CCSDS 130.2-G-3 §3.5.39 In the 2023 overview, the FSP specification is listed as "Historical" (CCSDS 912.3-B-3-S).12 See SLE concept, return services, FCLTU, FSP, ISP1 and the SLE API and the cross support reference model and service management.

docs.title: Typical end-to-end configurations
docs.text:
The examples in the 2023 overview show three ways to move user data from an on-board end system through an on-board relay (the spacecraft data handling system) and a ground relay (the station) to a ground end system. Its §4.1 announces five examples, but issue 4 contains only the three in §4.2 to §4.4.28

  1. Space Packets (or Encapsulation Packets) end to end. At each relay, a mechanism that SPP does not specify reads the APID and forwards the packet as instructed. There is no end-point address, and the scheme works by management and agreement.29 PUS telemetry and telecommands, which ECSS-E-ST-70-41C carries in Space Packets, follow this pattern.6
  2. IP over CCSDS. IP datagrams in Encapsulation Packets, routed at each hop by destination address. It suits missions that need Internet integration, where connectivity and round-trip light time allow it.30
  3. Bundle Protocol. Store-and-forward routing of bundles through CLAs, for example over LTP on a CCSDS data link.31

docs.title: Solar Orbiter as an instance
docs.text:
The Solar Orbiter packet ICD (SOL.S.ASTR.TN.00079 issue 7) and the public MIB show the abstract stack as one real configuration:

Element Solar Orbiter setting Protocol combination TC Space Data Link Protocol forward, TM Space Data Link Protocol return7477 Spacecraft ID 0x28A (650), the same on the flight model, ETB and OBC-DM7477 TC frames At most 256 octets. Two TC Virtual Channels, one per on-board TC decoder.74 TC MAP channels MAP 0 for CPDU (high-priority, HPC-1) commands, MAP 1 for normal commands. No segmentation (segment flags 11). Several packets may be aggregated in one segment.73 TM frames Fixed 1115 octets (8920 bits). Data field 1099 octets. Secondary header with a 24-bit VC frame count extension. CLCW in the OCF of every frame. Frame Error Control in every frame.777678 TM Virtual Channels VC4 real-time high priority; VC5 critical event log playback; VC0 real-time; VC1 playback from OBC mass memory; VC2 and VC3 playback from the SSMM; VC7 idle frames only. Priority in that order. VC6 is marked "Not Required".77 Packets Space Packets with PUS version 1 (PUS-A) data field headers; see Space Packet: Solar Orbiter case study75

In the MIB, all 125 commands that use the CPDU header HPC1_TC are flagged high priority (CCF_HIPRI = 'Y') and carry CCF_MAPID = 0, which matches the MAP 0 rule above.79 The SCOS-2000 import ICD uses CCF_MAPID only for high-priority commands and calls it irrelevant otherwise.80 Of the 5318 nominal (NOM_TC) commands, none is high priority. 5113 leave CCF_MAPID blank, 128 set it to 1 and 77 (all on APID 876) set it to 54. By the ICD's rule these values have no effect.7980

Inference

The TM frame length adds up: 6 octets of primary header, 4 of secondary header (1-octet ID plus 3 octets of frame count), 1099 of data field, 4 of OCF and 2 of frame error control give 1115 octets. The ICD gives each component separately and does not show the sum. The TC Virtual Channel identifiers are unclear in the ICD. It calls the suggested values "Zero and One" but then lists them in binary as 000001 and 000010.7478

SQL used 
-- solo-2025-09-16.sqlite (MIB__20250916M25925PFMS001_SOL)
SELECT CCF_PKTID, CCF_HIPRI, CCF_MAPID, COUNT(*) FROM ccf GROUP BY 1, 2, 3;
-- HPC1_TC|Y|0|125 ; NOM_TC|N||5113 ; NOM_TC|N|1|128 ; NOM_TC|N|54|77 ; NOS2KHDR|N||6 ; NO_HDR|Y||5
SELECT CCF_APID, COUNT(*) FROM ccf WHERE CCF_MAPID = '54' GROUP BY 1;   -- 876|77

docs.title: Frequently asked questions
docs.text:
How do the Space Data Link Protocols differ from HDLC? They assume powerful coding, modulation and synchronization below them, and their frames are designed for efficient synchronization and decoding. HDLC was designed for nearly noise-free wire links. The CCSDS frames are also upward-compatible with older TDM frame formats, so existing baseband equipment could be reused.50

Are they secure? TM, TC, AOS and USLP can carry SDLS-protected data (authentication, encryption, or both), but SDLS is optional.5016 See SDLS.

Does COP-1 work for deep space or blind commanding? Yes. For long round-trip times, a shorter retransmission timer or repeated transmission in the coding sublayer keeps the uplink busy. For blind commanding without telemetry, the Expedited service needs no feedback loop.52 See COP-1.
