  B352 -->|"OTAR and key verification algorithms"| B3551
  B3551 -->|"creates, keys, starts and monitors SAs"| B355
  B355 -->|"optional service of"| SDLP
  B3551 -->|"FSR in the OCF; PDUs in packets"| SDLP

The application report (350.0-G-3) is the entry point. It helps a mission planner decide which security services are needed and at which layer to apply them.3 If the answer is the data link layer, the SDLS protocol (355.0-B-2) applies. SDLS fixes no algorithm. The Cryptographic Algorithms standard (352.0-B-2) says which ones to use, and the SDLS annex E baseline is built from them.22064 SDLS defines the parameters of a Security Association but not the services that manage them. Those services are the Extended Procedures (355.1-B-1).221222 The concept and rationale report (350.5-G-2) explains the design of SDLS. Its issue 2 was updated to align with the Extended Procedures and with the current TM, TC, AOS and USLP books.51

Issue cross-references

The documents were published at different times, so their references to each other are not symmetric. The Extended Procedures (February 2020) cite SDLS Issue 1 (355.0-B-1, September 2015) and the draft Symmetric Key Management practice CCSDS 354.0-R-1.150 SDLS Issue 2 (July 2022) cites the Extended Procedures as a normative reference.220 The application report (March 2019) describes SDLS for TM, TC and AOS only, because USLP support arrived with SDLS Issue 2.25219

Several related CCSDS security documents are cited by these five but are not in this wiki's library: Security Threats against Space Missions (350.1-G-2), the Space Missions Key Management Concept (350.6-G-1), the Security Guide for Mission Planners (350.7-G-1), the Information Security Glossary of Terms (350.8-M-2), the cryptographic algorithms Green Book (350.9-G-2), the Security Architecture for Space Data Systems (351.0-M-1), the CCSDS Guide for Secure System Interconnection (350.4-G-1), the Symmetric Key Management draft (354.0-R-1) and the Extended Procedures Green Book, which was still being written.554150151 Statements about these documents are limited to what the five library documents say.

docs.title: What information security covers
docs.text:
The application report names six key elements of information security for a data communications system.6

Element Meaning in CCSDS 350.0-G-3 Access control Limiting system access to specified individuals, groups or processes acting for them Authentication Assurance that the claimed identity of the source of information is not forged Availability Assurance that the system will be available for use Confidentiality Protection against unauthorized disclosure of information Integrity Protection against unauthorized modification of data Accountability Listed, but not defined in the report

Three kinds of thing may need protection in a space mission data system: the information it holds, its services (communications and data processing), and its resources (ground equipment and spacecraft). Security is achieved by placing one or more security services at specific points in the system.6

docs.title: Security policy and threat assessment
docs.text:
The first task is to assess the threats. This is normally part of a System Security Policy (SSP), a formal document that describes the system, its top-level security objectives and the information-security and availability threats against it. The SSP can also give the security standards and evaluation requirements, the rules for access to security-critical systems such as a certificate authority, and, if encryption is used, how keys are distributed and managed.7

The threat assessment looks at the vulnerabilities of the system. For each threat it then estimates the likelihood, the consequences and the cost of realization. A threat matters only if the system is vulnerable to it. Countermeasures are selected per threat, usually through a cost-benefit analysis. What remains is residual risk, which system management must accept before the system goes into production.7

docs.title: Kinds of threat
docs.text:
A threat is any circumstance or event that could harm the system by destroying, disclosing or modifying data, or by denying service. It remains a potential violation until it is shown to be likely to cause harm. It is then reclassified as a vulnerability.8 The report lists five threats to a space mission data system:8

  1. unauthorized destruction of information or resources (spacecraft or ground systems);
  2. unauthorized corruption or modification of information;
  3. theft or loss of information or resources;
  4. disclosure of information to unauthorized entities;
  5. interruption of services.

Threats are accidental (malfunctions, operational errors) or intentional (from casual examination to sophisticated attacks). They are also passive or active. A passive threat leaves the information and the system unchanged. It mainly concerns confidentiality, the only property that can be compromised without leaving a trace. An active threat modifies information or the state of the space or ground segment, so it attacks integrity or availability.8

docs.title: Mission security classes
docs.text:
The report sorts missions into three classes as a guide, not a rule. A real mission may not fit any of them. The classes differ in which services they need and in how much assurance they need that those services work. High-security missions, for example, may need government-approved high-grade algorithms.11

Class Typical missions Telecommand Telemetry Ground data system High Government and military; life-critical crewed missions; some commercial telecommunications missions12 All TC: confidentiality, authentication, access controls, data integrity including anti-replay, availability All TM: confidentiality, data integrity, possibly authentication and access control, availability All data: confidentiality, authentication, data integrity, availability, access controls12 Moderate Commercial communications, meteorological and remote-sensing missions; satellite navigation (possibly high)13 Authentication, data integrity, possibly confidentiality Some or all TM: confidentiality, data integrity Some or all data: authentication, data integrity, possibly access control and confidentiality13 Minimal All other missions14 All TC: authentication, data integrity, possibly confidentiality Some TM: confidentiality, data integrity Some data: confidentiality, data integrity, access control14

High-security missions also need secure access to the spacecraft control system at all times and in all conditions, and protection against detection, interception and exploitation of the data links.12 Even a minimal-security mission is expected to protect its telecommand system against unauthorized access or tampering, whether intentional or not.14

The approach chosen for a mission depends on five factors: the agency's security policy, the mission security requirements, the operational requirements (including cross support and interoperability), the CCSDS standards in use (TC, TM, AOS, SCPS-TP or Proximity-1), and the capability of the on-board systems.10

docs.title: Confidentiality and encryption
docs.text:
Encryption provides confidentiality. A key controls the transformation from plaintext to ciphertext and back, and a new key gives different ciphertext for the same plaintext. Security depends on the strength of the algorithm, the key length and the secrecy of the keys. When the algorithm is public, as AES is, the security of the system is designed to rest on handling the keys: their management, distribution, use and destruction.15

Encryption can be arranged in three ways:15

Arrangement Who can read the data in transit Point-to-point Only the two communicating end points; a link crypto device sits at each end Hop-by-hop Each intermediary decrypts and re-encrypts, so trusted gateways see the plaintext End-to-end Only the final destination; intermediaries can neither decrypt nor examine the data

docs.title: Symmetric and asymmetric keys
docs.text:
In a symmetric system both ends use the same secret key, so a secure key distribution system has to generate, distribute and account for every key. AES is symmetric. In an asymmetric (public-key) system each end has a public key and a private key, and the decryption key cannot in practice be derived from the public one. RSA is the best-known example. In practice it is used in a hybrid scheme: a public-key exchange agrees a session key, and a symmetric algorithm then protects the data. A public key must be securely bound to its owner, normally by a certificate authority that signs it.1716

Cryptographic systems are analysed under worst-case assumptions. The attacker is assumed to know the algorithm completely, to hold a large amount of ciphertext, and to know the plaintext of some of it. Symmetric keys are therefore the main protection of the information and must be distributed and kept securely.17 The report contrasts the old 56-bit-key DES (64-bit blocks, no longer recommended) with AES (128-bit blocks, 128-, 192- or 256-bit keys).17

docs.title: Authentication, integrity, access control and availability
docs.text:
Authentication appends extra information to a message: a digital signature or a message digest. A digital signature, normally made with the sender's private key, proves the origin of the data. A message digest computed over a shared secret also authenticates. Symmetric encryption gives implicit authentication, because the receiver must hold the right key. That protection fails if encrypted data can be captured and replayed without replay protection.18

Data integrity has two parts. For a single data unit an Integrity Check Value (ICV) is appended. A CRC is a simple ICV and SHA-2 a stronger one. Reed-Solomon and Turbo codes also give some integrity through error detection. To protect the integrity of a stream of data units, a sequence number protects against replay, and time stamps give limited replay protection. The ICV is often keyed, or encrypted, for example with AES CMAC.19

Access control keeps resources available only to authorized users or processes. It is a barrier in the intruder's path, not a fundamental technique for confidentiality or integrity. The report recommends good password administration, never sending plaintext passwords over unprotected media, and keeping audit trails.20

Availability is a security concern when an attacker tries to deny access. RF links can be jammed. Jamming the downlink can lose data or, in an emergency, the spacecraft. Jamming the uplink while telemetry still arrives can also lose the spacecraft. Spread spectrum and frequency hopping counter jamming.21

docs.title: Where security can sit in the stack
docs.text:
The report places security at five points of the CCSDS stack. Each has a different scope and a different cost in compatibility.922

flowchart TB
  A["Application layer<br/>TLS, SBSP for DTN bundles,<br/>access control"]
  T["Transport / packet layer<br/>space packet security<br/>(encrypted data field, signature or ICV)"]
  N["Network layer<br/>IPSec (ESP)"]
  D["Data link protocol sublayer<br/>SDLS on TM, TC, AOS (and USLP)"]
  P["Physical layer<br/>bulk encryption and TRANSEC"]
  A --- T --- N --- D --- P

docs.title: Physical layer: bulk encryption and TRANSEC
docs.text:
Bulk encryption, often called link encryption, encrypts the whole physical-layer data structure on a point-to-point basis. On a TC link this covers the CLTU and also the acquisition and idle sequences. On TM or AOS it covers the whole stream of CADUs, including the synchronization marker and any Reed-Solomon check symbols. It gives the highest possible confidentiality. Other services come only implicitly from the encryption.2324 TRANSEC (transmission security) protects the physical layer against jamming. In direct-sequence spread spectrum the signal is spread so that it looks like noise. In frequency hopping the carrier changes over time, and the receiver must stay synchronized with the transmitter.23

The price is high. Bulk encryption denies all cross-support services unless keys are pre-placed at the access points, or public-key technology is used to protect content keys. CCSDS link synchronization cannot work, so the crypto devices must provide synchronization. No error detection and correction information is visible in plaintext, which makes CCSDS channel coding meaningless. It also gives no end-to-end security.40 See TC synchronization and channel coding, TM synchronization and channel coding and RF and modulation for the structures concerned.

docs.title: Data link layer: SDLS
docs.text:
The data link option is SDLS. It adds authentication, confidentiality or both to the contents of transfer frames. It works in the data link protocol sublayer and leaves the synchronization and channel coding sublayer untouched. It does not apply to Proximity-1.25 Its three classes of service are authentication (integrity, source authentication and anti-replay), encryption of the frame data field (or TC segment), and authenticated encryption, which combines both. Frame headers and the error control field are not encrypted. Security can be applied to selected virtual channels, at the cost of more algorithms and more complex key management.2526

Protocol Fully protected services Authentication only Not protected TC MAP Packet, MAP Access, VC Packet, VC Access Some Primary Header fields COP Management control frames; frames from external sources (VC Frame, MC Frame services)27 TM VC Packet, VC Access Some Primary Header and auxiliary fields; the VC Frame Secondary Header VC OCF, MC Frame Secondary Header, MC OCF; frames from external sources28 AOS VC Packet, Bitstream, VC Access Some Primary Header fields VC OCF, Insert service; frames from external sources29

For Proximity-1 the report suggests applying security to the user data above the I/O sublayer. All Proximity-1 protocol handling then works as normal, in a way the report compares to TLS.30

docs.title: Network layer: IPSec
docs.text:
IPSec, from the IETF, protects the payload of IP datagrams end-to-end, including the TCP header. Intermediate systems cannot read the data unless explicitly authorized, so insecure networks can carry sensitive data. IPSec defines a framework and no specific algorithm. Algorithms should come from the CCSDS algorithms standard.31 The ESP structure described in the report has an 8-byte clear header (4-byte SPI and 4-byte sequence number), a variable payload with algorithm-specific data such as an IV, optional padding, a 1-byte pad length, a 1-byte next-header field and an optional variable-length ICV.32 SDLS later borrowed the Security Association concept from IPSec and adapted it to space links (see below).77

Because the lower-layer headers stay in clear for routing, IPSec does not protect against traffic analysis. Encrypted data can still be intercepted in intermediate networks, but it stays confidential.42

docs.title: Packet layer: space packet security
docs.text: Security can also be applied at the space packet level. The packet data field is encrypted, and a digital signature or ICV is added inside it. The optional secondary header may also be encrypted. The primary header and all lower-layer fields stay in plaintext. The report warns that without an authenticated replay counter in the primary header, packets are open to replay, and that fixing this would need a protocol revision. A mission that secures only some packets can use the APID to tell encrypted packets from plaintext ones.33

docs.title: Application layer: TLS, SBSP and access control
docs.text: At the application layer, security for space-packet users looks much like packet security. TLS lets each application secure itself, independently of the rest of the data system. For DTN, the Streamlined Bundle Security Protocol (SBSP) defines a block confidentiality block (BCB) and a block integrity block (BIB).34 Application-layer security needs no investment in the lower layers, but every application has to implement it, which risks duplicated effort and security flaws. The application layer is also where access control naturally sits, for example with access-rights databases and X.509 credentials.3443

docs.title: Combining options
docs.text: Options can be combined. For example, network-layer security can protect data end-to-end across the ground networks while a lower layer protects the space link against traffic analysis. The report's example architecture shows SDLS between the ground TT&C subsystem and the spacecraft and IPSec end-to-end between the end user and an on-board payload, and also marks TLS.35

docs.title: What encryption hides at each layer
docs.text:
Confidentiality has the largest impact on the CCSDS architecture, because it can hide headers that other network and cross-support services need. Authentication and integrity only add a few fields, although those fields can add many bits.36

Security option ASM and EDAC Frame header Frame data field Packet header Packet data field Network layer security Plain Plain Plain Plain Encrypted SDLS Plain Plain Encrypted Encrypted Encrypted Physical (bulk encryption) Encrypted Encrypted Encrypted Encrypted Encrypted

Source: CCSDS 350.0-G-3, table 6-1.36

docs.title: Emergency commanding
docs.text: A tumbling or faulty spacecraft is commanded with short emergency commands. These are sent repeatedly in the hope that one arrives in a brief window, and are typically acted on directly by the hardware command decoder. The report poses a dilemma. Unauthenticated emergency commands open a security hole, so a risk analysis must decide whether they are allowed. Even an unauthorized reset can harm a high-availability mission, or one in the middle of a manoeuvre. But authentication makes the command longer, which may defeat the purpose of a short emergency command.37 The SDLS user requirements return to this point (see below).

docs.title: Impact on SLE cross support
docs.text:
The Space Link Extension services give remote ground systems access to the ground end of the space link. The report rates each SLE service by whether it stays available under each security option. Physical-layer security is left out, because no cross support is possible with it.38

SLE service Data link security, decrypted at the SLE client Data link security, decrypted at the SLE provider Higher-layer security Return Insert, Return All Frames Available Available Available Return MC and VC Frames, MC and VC FSH, MC and VC OCF Available Available Available Return Bitstream, Return Space Packet Not available Available Available Forward CLTU, Forward TC Frame Available Available Available Forward TC VCA, Forward Space Packet Not available Available Available Forward AOS Insert, Coded VCDU, Proto VCDU Available Available Available Forward AOS Bitstream, VCA, Space Packet Not available Available Available

Source: CCSDS 350.0-G-3, figures 6-1 and 6-2.39 In short, frame-level services such as RAF and FCLTU survive data link security. Services that must read inside the frame data field, such as Return Space Packet or Forward Space Packet, stay available under data link security only when it ends at the SLE provider; with higher-layer security they stay available.

docs.title: Comparing and choosing
docs.text:
Option Strength Cost Physical (bulk) Highest confidentiality, full traffic-analysis protection Point-to-point only, no cross support, CCSDS sync and coding lost4044 Data link (SDLS) Compromise: relatively high security while keeping sync and EDAC Protects higher-layer data but not the TC, TM or AOS protocol structures; no traffic-flow protection; hop-by-hop41 Network (IPSec) End-to-end, transparent to applications No traffic-analysis protection42 Packet or application Protects only the application data; a fallback for payloads Many separate implementations, risk of flaws43

The selection guidance in §6.5 says:44

  • Most missions need encryption at one layer only. This keeps the approach simple and the costs and processing load low. Encryption at the network layer or below spares each application its own implementation.
  • Full traffic-analysis protection needs physical-layer encryption, possibly with TRANSEC.
  • High security with some traffic-flow confidentiality that keeps the CCSDS benefits points to data link security. Its protection can be extended into the ground network with low-level SLE services (Return All Frames, Forward CLTU).
  • Per-payload confidentiality on separate virtual channels points to encryption above the frame sublayer, which is the SDLS approach.
  • End-to-end protection points to application-layer or network-layer encryption.
  • Very fine granularity, such as per-application keys or selective fields, needs application-level encryption.
  • High security over RF plus end-to-end protection may need encryption at more than one layer.

Authentication, integrity and access control have less architectural impact. Their fields can sit at the same layer as encryption to keep one "clean" security layer. Access control is likely to be implemented at the application layer.45

docs.title: Agency implementations described by CCSDS
docs.text: Annex A of the application report describes four missions that added security to CCSDS links.46

docs.title: ESA Copernicus Sentinels: telecommand authentication
docs.text:
ESA and industry developed a telecommand authentication system for the Copernicus Sentinel fleet. It was one of the predecessors of SDLS and shares features with it, such as the algorithm of the SDLS telecommand baseline. It has a two-tier key hierarchy. Session (authentication) keys authenticate telecommands and are replenished by Over-The-Air Rekeying (OTAR), similar to the SDLS Extended Procedures. Master keys protect the session keys during OTAR and other critical operations.47

Authentication happens at the segmentation layer, and security associations are distinguished by MAP. An authentication tail identifies the key in use and carries the current value of the Logical Authentication Counter (LAC) and the MAC. Figure A-1 labels the same field "Logical Authentication Channel (LAC)", split into a LAC Id and a LAC Count. ESA's older TC decoder specification also speaks of Logical Authentication Channels with LAC identifiers and LAC counters.4748231 The LAC increments with every telecommand and defeats the replay of an intercepted command. The MAC covers the whole segment except the MAC field itself, and depends on the key and the LAC. The mission control system generates the tail. The on-board security unit checks it, rejects a failing command and reports the reason to the operator.47

Between header and tail sits the segment data field, of 1 to 1016 octets or of 1 to 904 octets as the figure gives it. The whole segment is 1 to 1017 octets.48 OTAR uses a custom PUS service at the application layer, addressed directly to the spacecraft security unit. Keys are generated on the ground in a separate, isolated Key Management Facility (KMF) with a state-of-the-art random-number generator.48

docs.title: International Space Station, STRV-1c/d and ATV
docs.text:
• ISS. The station uses AOS for both links, with the MPDU and Bitstream services. The uplink is encrypted with Triple DES at the VCA sublayer, so the VCDU data zone is encrypted. A 64-bit Insert Zone carries cryptographic synchronization.49
  • STRV-1c/d. These microsatellites put data link security on both links: confidentiality and authentication on telecommand, confidentiality only on telemetry.49
  • ATV. The Automated Transfer Vehicle encrypted its telecommand packets with Triple DES (ANSI X9.52) and added time authentication. The segment data field held a 2-octet key index, an 8-octet IV unique to each message, and the encrypted packet data. Each packet carried a Time Authentication field that the on-board packet processor compared with on-board time, rejecting the packet when the comparison exceeded a threshold.50

docs.title: SDLS concept and rationale (CCSDS 350.5-G-2)
docs.text: The concept and rationale report explains why SDLS is built the way it is. It gives the architecture, the interaction with the data link protocols, the justification of each design choice, the security analyses, and guidance on choosing parameters.52

docs.title: Motivation and target topologies
docs.text:
Before SDLS, a CCSDS mission that needed uplink command authentication or downlink confidentiality had to invent its own solution. SLE already protected the ground leg between control centre and ground station, with identification, authentication and confidentiality, but not the space link. A joint working group of the Space Link and Security areas therefore defined data link security for TM, TC, AOS and USLP without modifying those standards.55

The target is the simple topology. A mission control centre reaches one spacecraft through a ground station, and SLE extends the data link to the control centre (Topology A). Topology B adds a separate payload downlink. Securing the path end to end is split into two tasks: protecting SLE and the ground network, and protecting the data link between the spacecraft and the mission control system, which is SDLS's job. TRANSEC can be added against denial of service and is compatible with SDLS. Secure cross support with another agency's ground station needs a service level agreement.56

SDLS and its Extended Procedures work in a fixed master-slave arrangement with no negotiation. Directives always go from a predetermined master (the Initiator) to a predetermined slave (the Recipient). For space-to-space links a hierarchy between satellites has to be set up, together with a key management scheme. This could be keys per link pair, which becomes impractical as the number of pairs grows, or keys shared across a constellation while keeping key-IV uniqueness for AES-GCM. "Forward" and "return" link then replace "telecommand" and "telemetry". For large constellations the report suggests considering security at a higher layer.57

docs.title: Security objectives and services
docs.text:
Direction Objectives Uplink (TC, AOS, USLP) Command authentication, command integrity, command confidentiality, command anti-replay protection Downlink (TM, AOS, USLP) TM data authentication, integrity, confidentiality, anti-replay protection

Source: CCSDS 350.5-G-2, §2.3.2.58

Three security services meet these objectives: authentication (authentication, integrity and anti-replay, when confidentiality is not needed), encryption (confidentiality only), and authenticated encryption (all of them).58

docs.title: Key requirements
docs.text:
Section 2.4 of the report picks out the main requirements behind SDLS. The full set is the user requirements document of annex C (see below).59

  • Two operational modes for each logical channel on TC, TM, AOS or USLP: a Clear Mode, in which the SDU is left unchanged but the SDLS fields are present, and a Secure Mode with authentication, encryption or authenticated encryption.
  • Independent secure channels, so that clear and secure channels can share one physical channel.
  • Compatibility with three key management schemes: (1) all session keys preloaded for the whole mission; (2) master keys (key encryption keys, KEKs) and some session keys preloaded, with session keys uploaded encrypted by OTAR; (3) session keys generated on board from master keys and an uploaded non-secret seed. Key management itself is specified in the Extended Procedures.
  • Security function control directives handled either in-band, by the security device right after authentication or decryption, or out-of-band, at application level.
  • At most 32 octets of overhead per transfer frame for the complete protocol.
  • No interference between frame verification by SDLS and frame validation by the data link protocol.

docs.title: Which data link services SDLS protects
docs.text:
Services that carry application-layer SDUs, such as packets or variable-length private data, can be protected with any of the three services. The VC Frame Secondary Header is a compromise: it gets authentication only. Services that carry frames or auxiliary data produced elsewhere (Insert data, the MC Frame Secondary Header) are not secured. Their sources can protect them with standard application-layer authentication or encryption.61

Protocol Protected with all three services Authentication only Not protected TM VC Packet, VC Access VC_FSH (also "authentication only" under authenticated encryption) VC_OCF, VC Frame, MC_FSH, MC_OCF, MC Frame TC MAP Packet, MAP Access, VC Packet, VC Access — COP Management (BC frames), VC Frame, MC Frame AOS VC Packet, Bitstream, VC Access — VC_OCF, VC Frame, MC Frame, Insert USLP MAP Packet, MAP Octet Stream, MAP Access — MC_OCF, VC Frame, MC Frame, Insert

Source: CCSDS 350.5-G-2, table 2-2.62 Table 2-1 adds conformance levels. A fully compliant implementation must be able to protect the mandatory services (for TC, MAP Packet and MAP Access). Protection of the TC VC Packet and VC Access services and of the AOS Bitstream service is optional.60

docs.title: Why COP control frames and the OCF stay in clear
docs.text:
The rationale for this is one of the most important passages in the report. SDLS must run before the COP at the sending end and after the COP at the receiving end:70

  • COP-1 is a go-back-N protocol, so it retransmits frames. If FOP-1 ran before SDLS at the sender and SDLS before FARM-1 at the receiver, SDLS would reject every retransmission as a replay and block the link.
  • The MAC detects errors far better than the BCH or short LDPC codes. If SDLS ran before FARM-1, it would discard frames with transmission errors. These would be counted as security events, the CLCW would not report them, and FOP-1 would keep retransmitting frames that FARM-1 never sees.
  • With this order the COP control commands (BC frames) and the Frame Sequence Number, which the FOP sets, cannot be authenticated. The OCF is appended by the Master Channel Generation function after SDLS has run, so it cannot be protected either.

The report accepts the residual risk. An attacker could send false COP directives or OCF contents, but the legitimate operator can always reinitialize the COP, so the denial of service is temporary and not easy to achieve.70 It also warns about mixing frame types. If Type-AD and Type-BD frames share a secured VC, a BD frame accepted after a lost AD frame raises the expected anti-replay number. The AD retransmissions then fail the anti-replay check and are falsely reported as security failures. Mixing AD and BD frames on such a VC while AD frames are pending is therefore not advised.7080

flowchart LR
  subgraph G["Ground (sending end)"]
    direction TB
    g1["1 VC Generation:<br/>frame initialization"] --> g2["2 ApplySecurity:<br/>encrypt data field,<br/>fill header and MAC"] --> g3["3 FOP-1, frame<br/>finalization (sets the<br/>frame sequence number)"] --> g4["4-6 VC mux, MC mux,<br/>All Frames (FECF)"] --> g5["7-8 BCH or LDPC coding,<br/>randomize, modulate"]
  end
  subgraph S["Spacecraft (receiving end)"]
    direction TB
    s1["9-10 demodulate,<br/>decode"] --> s2["11-14 frame validation,<br/>MC and VC demux,<br/>VC Reception"] --> s3["15 FARM-1<br/>(16: CLCW in OCF)"] --> s4["17 ProcessSecurity:<br/>check MAC and ARSN,<br/>decrypt"] --> s5["18 FSR in OCF;<br/>data units to users"]
  end
  g5 -->|"space link"| s1

Source: CCSDS 350.5-G-2, figure 3-3 and table 3-3.81 The other places SDLS leaves alone follow the same logic. In AOS and USLP the Insert Zone is written into the frame on the fly as it goes to the modulator, so it cannot be authenticated. SDLS works only on virtual channels, so Master Channel services (MC_FSH, MC_OCF) cannot be secured. VCs carrying Only Idle Data are not protected: idle frames may be generated somewhere else, their repetitive patterns could help cryptanalysis, and exposing them only leaks activity patterns.71

docs.title: Compatibility with SLE
docs.text: SDLS security sits only at the end points, the spacecraft and the mission control centre, so it should be transparent to SLE processing. The full frame header must stay unaltered. The compatibility goals were F-CLTU and F-TCF for TC, and RAF, RCF and Return OCF for TM, AOS and USLP. Ground station equipment may route frames using fields it has not authenticated. That risk is accepted, because the end processor at mission control detects any manipulation.6375

docs.title: OSI security services, threats and residual risks
docs.text:
SDLS borrows its services from the ISO OSI security architecture. That architecture allows only confidentiality services at the data link layer. SDLS goes further and also authenticates.73

OSI security service SDLS decision Peer entity authentication Not adopted (too complex) Data origin authentication Adopted (TC, TM, AOS, USLP) Access control Not adopted; relevant for TC, residual risk mitigated Connection confidentiality Adopted (TC only) Connectionless confidentiality Adopted (TC, TM, AOS, USLP) Selective field confidentiality; traffic flow confidentiality Not adopted Connection integrity with recovery Adopted (TC only) Connection integrity without recovery; connectionless integrity Adopted (TC, TM, AOS, USLP) Selective field integrity (connection and connectionless) Not adopted Non-repudiation (proof of origin or delivery) Not adopted

Source: CCSDS 350.5-G-2, tables 3-1 and 3-2.74 Annex B justifies each line per protocol, with threats, impact, priority, applicability and residual risk. It gives data origin authentication and connection and connectionless integrity high priority, and traffic flow confidentiality medium priority, as a candidate for a future SDLS extension. It rates non-repudiation as not relevant to space data links.76

The threat analysis assumes trust between CCSDS agencies: protecting against an agency that acts maliciously against another is not a goal. Availability threats, such as jamming or flooding the receiver with unwanted signals, are out of scope and belong to physical-layer measures.72 Traffic analysis protection would mean encrypting every protocol structure, which conflicts with SLE and the data link protocols. It is a residual risk, and missions that need it should consider bulk encryption.75

docs.title: Algorithm agility
docs.text:
SDLS is deliberately algorithm-agnostic, so that it does not have to change when cryptanalysis or brute-force power forces CCSDS to change its recommended algorithms.64 This shapes the fields:

  • Authentication produces a MAC over the SDU and selected header fields. To prove freshness, the data is authenticated together with a time-dependent value. SDLS prefers a counter, the sequence number. Some algorithms need an IV, and block-oriented ones such as GMAC may need padding, so the header can carry both.65
  • Encryption covers only the SDU, for compatibility with SLE and the data link protocols. Most secure modes need an IV. Encryption alone does not protect against manipulation and gives no protection against data substitution. If the plaintext is partly predictable, an attacker may even be able to recover the key. It should be selected only after a threat and risk analysis.66
  • Authenticated encryption follows Encrypt-then-MAC (the other generic compositions are MAC-then-Encrypt and MAC-and-Encrypt). It is the CCSDS-recommended way to obtain both services, and its additional authenticated data (AAD) protects the readable headers.67
  • Separate authentication and encryption algorithms are possible, each with its own key. But SDLS provides only one IV, one sequence counter and one padding field, and the 16-bit SPI limits how key changes can be signalled. CCSDS gives no pairing recommendations, so users need expert advice.68

docs.title: Design of the header and trailer fields
docs.text:
Field Rationale in 350.5-G-2 Security Parameter Index (16 bits) Mandatory. Up to 65,534 SAs per Master Channel, because 0 and 65,535 are reserved. The receiver uses it to find the SA and so the presence and length of the optional fields.83 Initialization Vector (managed) Gives freedom of algorithm. Some IVs must be unique per key, others random. With 128-bit-block algorithms the IV is at most 128 bits, and shorter constructs that partly regenerate the IV at the receiver save overhead at the expense of robustness. Mismanaging the IV can make the security useless.84 Sequence Number (managed) Used with authentication. It may be part of a longer managed counter. Sending it lets the receiver check the MAC and then the counter window as two separate tests, instead of trying every MAC in the window. With GCM-like counters the IV doubles as the transmitted sequence number and the field is omitted.85 Pad Length (1 octet when present) Gives the number of fill bits, 0 to 127. Recommended algorithms need no padding, but the field keeps SDLS algorithm-independent. The report cites ISO Padding Method 2 (a "1" then "0"s, not transmitted), and warns that other padding schemes need careful assessment.86 MAC (trailer) Present with authentication or authenticated encryption. It covers the SDU, selected header fields, any fields between the header and the Security Header, and the Security Header itself.87

Two more design points come from the same section. The MAC is computed last, so placing it after the data it covers suits very high data rates. Using two structures, a header and a trailer, also helps high-rate implementations.8982 On MAC length, the report argues that a MAC needs about twice the key length to resist birthday attacks. With 128- to 256-bit keys that gives 256 to 512 bits, and 512 bits is the SDLS maximum. Shorter MACs are possible with more frequent rekeying. GCM is limited to 128 bits, even when used for authentication only. NIST-style schemes that allow very short MACs by limiting failed attempts are rejected, because locking out a spacecraft after failed attempts is worse than resisting attempts with a long MAC.88

docs.title: Security Associations and the authentication bit mask
docs.text:
The Security Association (SA) comes from IPSec, adapted for space. It is a simplex, stateful session. Both ends must create it, give it keys and activate it before use. SAs can be preloaded or created while others are active. All frames sharing an SA on a physical channel form a Secure Channel.77 IPSec-style parameter negotiation is rejected. Contacts are short and delays long, the ground wants full authority over the spacecraft, and on-board processing is limited. Instead of an IPSec SA database, a simpler Security Association Context (SAC) exists in advance on board and on ground, and maps each SA to its GVCIDs or Global MAP IDs.78

The authentication bit mask zeroes selected header bits before the MAC is computed. The VCID and the TC or USLP Segment Header are always included, because they identify the channel and MAP. The Security Header (except the IV) and the frame data field are also always included. The TM Master Channel Frame Count, the Insert Zone, the OCF, the error control field and the MAC are always excluded. The SCID is not in the default mask, because frame validation has already checked it. Missions can add fields, for example a sensitive VC_FSH, or the SCID when a constellation shares SAs. In cross support the mask must be exchanged out of band.7987

docs.title: Clear Mode and the Recovery SA
docs.text:
Projects often ask for a Clear Mode that bypasses security on an otherwise protected SA. Security experts do not recommend it. A civil mission may still justify it when losing the spacecraft through a telecommand outage is a bigger risk than spoofing, and then on-board FDIR or a ground command may activate it. A Clear Mode SA can use a "no-op" algorithm, for example in testing before the cryptography is integrated. Such an SA can be enabled by a hardware strap and inhibited before flight. The header and trailer can stay present so that throughput does not change. Transitions between secure and clear should go through a separate authenticated SA.90

A TC SA covers one VC only, but several SAs may cover the same VC. Experience with earlier ESA telecommand security led to the Recovery SA, a redundant SA used only as a last resort when the nominal SA has failed. Its context is stored separately at both ends, and its on-board keys should not be erasable, reloadable or revocable.91 The scenario section lists the emergencies it is meant for. If the telemetry link is lost, the ground commands blind, without SDLS reports, and the anti-replay counters may disagree. The programmable key storage may be corrupted. Or anti-replay synchronization may be lost. Recovery SA contexts and keys should be kept in non-erasable, non-volatile memory.110

docs.title: Managed parameters
docs.text:
Parameters that rarely change are managed rather than sent in-line, to save bandwidth. All managed parameters of the underlying data link protocol also apply.92

Group Parameters (350.5-G-2 table 3-4) Static for the mission (per VC or MAP) Presence of Security Header; presence of Security Trailer; Security Header length (the report says up to 42 octets); Security Trailer length (up to 64 octets) Static for the SA SPI; service type; SA context (GVCIDs or Global MAP IDs); transmitted lengths of IV, sequence number, pad length and MAC; authentication algorithm; authentication mask; sequence number window; encryption algorithm Static while the SA is active Authentication key; encryption key (each a value or an index) Dynamic Sequence number (sender's next, receiver's expected); encryption IV (sender's current)

Source: CCSDS 350.5-G-2, table 3-4.93 For bidirectional AOS or USLP links the GVCID does not show direction, so the uplink and downlink should use different SPIs.100

docs.title: Signalling, monitoring and control
docs.text:
Only the SPI, IV, sequence number, pad length and MAC travel in-line. Algorithms, keys and the other managed parameters need a separate, out-of-band logical channel for control and monitoring. The report describes two options:94

  • In-band at the crypto processor. Control messages are multiplexed and demultiplexed at the device that runs SDLS, so the security function stays controllable without the on-board computer. A dedicated VC would need its own FARM-1, COP-1 and CLCW reporting. A reserved MAP avoids that, so MAP IDs should be reserved for security control. On some missions MAPs already route high-priority commands (HPCs) to the command pulse generators.9495
  • Out-of-band through the platform computer. The security processor sits on the avionics bus and exchanges CCSDS packets with the platform computer. It may accept HPCs and software commands, so some commanding survives an OBC outage.95

Monitoring the security function is also vital. Some missions use high-priority telemetry packets that do not need the OBC. The Extended Procedures add a data link solution, the Frame Security Report, an OCF similar to the CLCW (see below).95

SDLS is agnostic about redundancy. It works with VC-based selection of redundant receivers, and with two identical processors running in parallel, which need fully synchronized managed parameters.96 Keys are SA attributes. Switching to another SPI changes the key from one frame to the next, provided the new SA's key is already active.97 SA scope differs by protocol. On TC an SA covers exactly one VC, because SDLS sits before FOP-1. There is no master channel SA, but several MAP-level SAs can share a VC. On TM, AOS and USLP an SA may span several VCs, but never an Only Idle Data VC. If a secured VC also carries idle frames, the idle pattern must be chosen with care to avoid known-plaintext weaknesses.9899

docs.title: Concept of operation
docs.text:
At the sending end the SDU is first encrypted, using the key, the IV and any padding. The Security Header is built from the SA. The mask is applied to give the authentication payload, and the MAC is appended. At the receiving end the order is reversed.102

flowchart LR
  V["Frame validation<br/>by the data link protocol<br/>(CRC, format)"] --> SPI{"SPI matches<br/>a known SA?"}
  SPI -- no --> E1["Error indication"]
  SPI -- yes --> MAC{"MAC verified?"}
  SPI -- yes --> SN{"Sequence number<br/>inside window?"}
  MAC -- no --> R1["Stop and report"]
  SN -- no --> R2["Stop and report"]
  MAC -- yes --> D["Decrypt with the key<br/>identified by the SPI"]
  SN -- yes --> D
  D --> U["Deliver frame data<br/>to the data link protocol"]

The MAC and sequence number checks may run in either order. Both must pass before decryption.103 Three items must stay synchronized between the two ends.104

  • Keys. In-band synchronization typically sends an index into mirrored key tables on ground and on board.
  • IV. For robustness the IV is sent with each message, even though in theory it need not be.
  • Sequence count. TC sequence-controlled service could keep the counters aligned, but TM, AOS and TC expedited service lose frames. A window tolerates gaps and delays, and the Extended Procedures allow the on-board counter to be monitored and set.

docs.title: Baseline modes and the MAC and key length analysis
docs.text:
SDLS annex E defines baseline modes for interoperability testing and operation. The report explains the choices.225105106107

Protocol Service Algorithm Key MAC ARSN or IV Security Header Trailer TC Authentication AES-CMAC 256 bits 128 bits 32-bit sequence number in-line 6 octets (SPI + SN) 16 octets TM Authenticated encryption AES-GCM 256 bits 128 bits 96-bit IV in-line, also the counter 14 octets (SPI + IV) 16 octets AOS, USLP Authenticated encryption AES-GCM 256 bits 128 bits 96-bit IV in-line; mask also excludes the Insert Zone 14 octets (SPI + IV) 16 octets

Sources: CCSDS 355.0-B-2 annex E and CCSDS 350.5-G-2 §4.4 and annex A.225105106107

Why CMAC for TC. Authentication is the key service for protecting control of the spacecraft. CMAC is a NIST algorithm and an ISO standard since 2011. It needs neither an IV nor padding, both of which are delicate to manage. Being cipher-based, it can reuse the AES engine for authentication key encryption and decryption.111

Why GCM for TM, AOS and USLP. Authenticated encryption protects mission products. Encryption alone would not stop forgery. GCM is the CCSDS-recommended AE algorithm, it uses one key for both functions, and its deterministic 96-bit IV construction is recommended. Reusing an IV with the same key leaks information. Research has also found weak GCM keys, so key generation needs care.114106

Sizing the MAC and key. The analysis assumes the worst case for the attacker: telecommands can be sent without limit between two legitimate contacts, with no lockout after failures. The chance of forging a MAC is made comparable to the chance of accepting a telecommand with an undetected channel error. The required length is \(t \ge \mathrm{ld}(\mathrm{MaxInvalids}/\mathrm{Risk})\), where ld is the binary logarithm. The risk categories come from the undetected-frame-error probabilities of ECSS-E-ST-50-04C appendix D for 130 codeblocks at bit error rates of \(10^{-4}\), \(10^{-5}\) and \(10^{-6}\).112

Risk category MAC length (bits) Key length (bits) Medium 78 107 Low 98 127 Lowest 118 147 Conclusion 128 128

Source: CCSDS 350.5-G-2, table A-1.113

Worked example: the attacker budgets (arithmetic by this wiki)

The report assumes 64 telecommands per second for 48 hours, the maximum assumed key validity. That is \(64 \times 172\,800 = 11\,059\,200\) attempts, and \(\mathrm{ld}(11\,059\,200) \approx 23.4\) bits.112 For key search it assumes 60 GIPS for 48 hours, \(1.0368 \times 10^{16}\) instructions, about 53.2 bits. Subtracting these from table A-1 gives about 54.6 bits (MAC) and 53.8 bits (key) for the medium risk, 74.6 and 73.8 for low, and 94.6 and 93.8 for lowest.

Inference

The near-equal differences in the worked example suggest that the analysis used a single risk value per category, about \(2^{-54}\) (some \(10^{-17}\)), \(2^{-74}\) and \(2^{-94}\). This matches the report's statement that both lengths use the same probability of success. The report does not print these risk values. They are back-calculated by this wiki.

The 128-bit values were chosen for margin and convenience, and later research cited by the report says they hold well beyond 2032. Quantum computing changed the key length: Grover's algorithm halves the exponent of a brute-force search, so the baseline key was doubled to 256 bits. The 32-bit anti-replay counter allows about 4 billion uses of a key before it rolls over.113

docs.title: Scenarios
docs.text: In the basic scenario a ground centre sends telecommands over the forward link. Red marks data that needs protection and black marks data that is protected.108 In the complex scenario three on-board elements share a return link, and two of them use separate SAs and keys. A trusted baseband unit does the link-layer security on board. On the ground, separate elements receive their own VC or MC frames and manage their own keys. Because the primary headers stay readable, SLE return services still work. The scenario can represent several missions sharing a channel, or separate housekeeping and payload operations groups.109

docs.title: Telling transmission errors from security events
docs.text:
For FDIR it matters whether a rejected frame was corrupted by noise or by an attacker. A MAC of 64 to 512 bits detects errors far better than a 16-bit CRC, so errors missed by the channel coding could appear as security failures.69 Annex D concludes:

  • TC. The TC requirement is at most one erroneously accepted frame in \(10^{9}\). It is met without a CRC at bit error rates below \(10^{-4}\) (TED mode) or \(10^{-5}\) (SEC mode). ESA's SEC mode with a mandatory CRC reaches below \(10^{-15}\). No extra CRC needs to be mandated when security is applied. The same holds for the short LDPC codes and for USLP uplinks.127
  • TM, AOS, USLP. A CRC is recommended whenever SDLS is used, except with Reed-Solomon \(E=16\) or LDPC codes. Higher integrity can come from the 32-bit USLP CRC or a non-standard longer one.128
Channel coding CRC (FECF) Remark No code; convolutional; Turbo Mandatory — Reed-Solomon (and concatenated) Optional \(E=16\) outperforms a CRC; \(E=8\) is comparable LDPC Optional Outperforms a CRC

Source: CCSDS 350.5-G-2, table D-1.129

docs.title: The user requirements behind SDLS
docs.text:
Annex C reproduces the User Requirements Document (version 3, October 2012) that the working group agreed as the basis for SDLS. Each requirement is marked compliant, partially compliant, not compliant or not applicable.115 Many requirements are only "partially compliant" because SDLS itself defines no management procedures. That gap is what the Extended Procedures fill. Notable entries:

Requirement Content Status noted in the annex SECTMTC_URD_4010 TC objectives, including denial-of-service protection for COP-1 and traffic-analysis protection at APID level Partial: neither is provided116 SECTMTC_URD_5060 Anti-replay counter of at least 32 bits (TBC) Partial: SDLS allows a transmitted counter down to 16 bits118 SECTMTC_URD_6010 / 6020 Baseline algorithms for interoperability testing: HMAC-SHA-256 (authentication), AES-GCM (AE) Compliant119 SECTMTC_URD_10000 Clear Mode and Secure Mode per logical channel Compliant120 SECTMTC_URD_10090 Clear or Secure mode flagged explicitly in the security header or trailer Not compliant: no such flag122 SECTMTC_URD_11020 Key schemes: (1) all session keys preloaded; (2) master keys preloaded, session keys uploaded encrypted (OTAR); (3) session keys derived on board from master keys and an uploaded seed Compliant123 SECTMTC_URD_13010 At most 50 % overhead on the shortest CLTU, so emergency commanding can stay secure Partial: SDLS may exceed this124 SECTMTC_URD_13020 / 13030 / 13040 At least 256 secure channels; non-detection of an invalid TC below \(10^{-20}\); at most 5 % TM overhead Compliant; partial (the minimum 8-octet MAC gives \(5.42 \times 10^{-20}\)); compliant125

The 2012 URD baseline for authentication was HMAC-SHA-256. The published TC baseline uses AES-CMAC, for the reasons given above.119111 The URD also notes that SDLS adds an "Encryption Only" service for the TM link. It is theoretically insecure, but can be secure when authentication is achieved by another channel, and was judged useful for some missions, for example a video channel.117 It also contains the concept of a Reduced Secure Mode after on-board events, with encryption off and a relaxed anti-replay check. SDLS does not define it.121

docs.title: Scope and rationale
docs.text:
The algorithms standard recommends one symmetric encryption algorithm and one mode for all CCSDS missions, plus a choice of authentication and integrity algorithms. It does not say where or when to use them: that is up to mission planners and their risk analysis. Standard, well-known algorithms give high-quality cryptography, economies of scale through off-the-shelf products, and interoperability. The standard also says that using it does not by itself remove every risk, and that an information security risk assessment is still needed.131 It applies to civil missions with confidentiality or authentication requirements, on forward and return links, on ground networks and even for stored data. Security is encouraged for all missions, especially on command links, but a risk analysis may reduce or remove the need. Key management is out of scope.132133

CCSDS does not mandate a layer for encryption. It may sit in an application (TLS), above the network layer (IPSec), at the data link layer (SDLS), at the physical layer (bulk encryption), or at several layers at once.135

docs.title: Normative choices
docs.text:
Topic Requirement Clause Encryption algorithm All CCSDS missions shall use AES (FIPS 197, ISO/IEC 18033-3) §3.1139 Key size Missions planned after Issue 2 shall use 256-bit keys; existing implementations may use 128-bit keys §3.2139 Mode Counter Mode shall be used; other modes are allowed after careful consideration §3.3139 Authenticated encryption When encryption plus integrity and origin authentication is needed, GCM shall be used, with a 128-bit MAC tag §3.4139 Hash-based MAC HMAC (FIPS 198-1) with SHA (FIPS 180-4), normally SHA-256. SHA-224, SHA-384, SHA-512 or RIPEMD-160 may be used if agreed or signalled. SHA-1 shall not be used §4.2.1–4.2.2140 MAC truncation HMAC output should not be truncated; any truncation must be agreed in advance §4.2.3141 Cipher-based MAC CMAC shall be used: AES-256 for new missions; 128, 192 or 256 bits for existing ones. GMAC may replace CMAC when an AE implementation is used for authentication only §4.3142 Digital signatures DSS shall be used; RSA (PKCS #1 v2.1) should be used, with 4096-bit keys for new missions and 2048-bit allowed for existing ones. DSA and ECDSA may be used §4.4143144

"Future" in the key-size clauses means missions whose planning began after the publication of Issue 2.139

docs.title: Concepts behind the choices
docs.text:
• Hash-based and cipher-based MACs. An HMAC runs a hash such as SHA-256 over the data and a shared secret, which gives a MAC of fixed size. A cipher-based MAC uses the secret as the key of a block cipher such as AES. When both confidentiality and authentication are needed it can share one algorithm with encryption, and it is often easier to build in hardware.136
  • Digital signatures. The signer hashes the data and encrypts the hash with its private key. The receiver recovers the hash with the public key, which proves origin, and compares it with its own hash, which proves integrity. Public keys can be sent with the data, cached, or fetched from a key server. A spacecraft that cannot reach a key server can have a key cache preloaded before launch or uploaded later.137144
  • Authenticated encryption (AEAD). Encrypt-then-MAC is secure against adaptive chosen-ciphertext attacks. CCM and GCM are AE modes. GCM is fast in hardware and software, can be parallelized and pipelined, and needs no padding. The standard states that "the use of non-authenticated encryption is highly discouraged for CCSDS missions".138139

docs.title: How SDLS and the Extended Procedures use them
docs.text: The SDLS baselines take their algorithms from this standard: AES-CMAC for TC, AES-GCM for TM, AOS and USLP, all with 256-bit keys and 128-bit MACs.225111 The Extended Procedures baseline uses AES-GCM for OTAR and for key verification, with 256-bit keys, 96-bit IVs and 128-bit MACs.212 CCSDS 355.1-B-1 requires the challenge-related authentication algorithms to come from this standard, and its managed parameters list "AES/Counter Mode, GCM" as the OTAR algorithm choices.162206

docs.title: Security considerations
docs.text: The algorithms standard describes what happens if security is missing. Without confidentiality, sensitive, proprietary or private data such as crew medical information can be disclosed, for example to an RF eavesdropper, a landline tap or an insider. Without authentication, false commands could be injected into a spacecraft's command chain. Without integrity checking, a corrupted command might still be executed, and corrupted telemetry might lead controllers to act on a non-existent problem. The standard adds an availability caution: if on-board security fails and there is no bypass mode, all communication could be lost. SANA takes no action, and the algorithms are in the public domain with no known patents.145146

docs.title: Purpose, scope and roles
docs.text:
The Extended Procedures (EP) define the Key Management, Security Association Management and SDLS Monitoring and Control services needed to run SDLS over a space link. They define the PDUs, the procedures, and the interfaces to SDLS and the data link protocols, including a status report in the OCF. They do not define implementations, the security protocol itself, or any particular algorithm for key generation and management.148 There are two roles:149

  • The Initiator manages the session parameters, provides the resources and always starts a procedure. It is usually the mission operations centre.
  • The Recipient configures itself according to the Initiator's procedures. It is usually the spacecraft.

The Anti-Replay Sequence Number (ARSN) is defined as a counter set to zero when an SA is activated and incremented for each frame sent on that SA.149

docs.title: The three services at a glance
docs.text:
Service Procedures (PICS status: M mandatory, O optional, C conditional) Key Management OTAR (M), Key Activation (M), Key Deactivation (M), Key Destruction (O), Key Verification (M), Key Inventory (M) SA Management Start SA (M), Stop SA (M), Rekey SA (O), Expire SA (C: M if Rekey is supported), Create SA (O), Delete SA (C: M if Create is supported), Set ARSN (O), Set ARSN Window (O), SA Status Request (O), Read ARSN (M) Monitoring and Control Ping (M), Log Status, Dump Log, Erase Log (C: M if a security log exists), Self-Test (M), Alarm Flag Reset (M)

Source: CCSDS 355.1-B-1 §3 and PICS tables A5.1–A5.3.152153 A conforming implementation supports at least one of the three services.154

docs.title: The two-tier key hierarchy
docs.text: The key management service is an SDLS-specific version of the abstract procedures in the CCSDS Symmetric Key Management practice. Initiator and Recipient share the keys for all their links. The baseline is a two-tier symmetric infrastructure. Master keys (also called static keys or key encryption keys) are used for management, with few exceptions. Session keys (traffic protection keys) do the SDLS cryptographic work. OTAR keeps session keys fresh by sending new ones, generated by the Initiator, to the Recipient. OTAR is recommended, but a mission may fly with preloaded keys only.156

docs.title: Key lifecycle
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
  direction LR
  state "Pre-Activation" as Pre
  state "Active" as Act
  state "Deactivated" as Deact
  state "Destroyed" as Dest
  state "Suspended (not used by EP)" as Susp
  state "Compromised (Initiator only, no procedure)" as Comp
  [*] --> Pre : OTAR upload or preload
  Pre --> Act : Key Activation
  Act --> Act : Key Verification
  Act --> Deact : Key Deactivation
  Deact --> Dest : Key Destruction

Source: CCSDS 355.1-B-1, figure 2-1 and §5.4.1.157 A deactivated key can no longer be used for new cryptographic operations, but can still decrypt data encrypted earlier. A destroyed key leaves no record and cannot decrypt anything.160161 Key Inventory reports each key as pre-activation, active, deactivated or destroyed. The size of the key state field is a managed parameter, and its encoding is not stated in the available sources.164206

docs.title: Key management procedures
docs.text:
Procedure Precondition What happens OTAR Initiator has session keys in pre-activation; both ends share an identical master key (pre-active or active) The Initiator activates the master key if needed and applies authenticated encryption under it to the set of (Key ID, key) pairs. It sends an OTAR command PDU. The Recipient authenticates and decrypts, and stores each key under its Key ID in Pre-Active state. How keys are installed and memory slots reused is mission-specific.158 Key Activation Identical pre-active keys at both ends The Initiator moves the listed keys to Active and signals their IDs. The Recipient does the same.159 Key Deactivation Identical active keys Active to Deactivated at both ends (also called revocation).160 Key Destruction Identical deactivated keys Deactivated to Destroyed at both ends; no record is kept.161 Key Verification Identical active keys The Initiator sends a challenge per key. The Recipient returns, per key, an IV, the encrypted challenge and a MAC. The Initiator recomputes and compares, and declares the key verified on a match. The challenge algorithm is out of scope, but must comply with 352.0-B.162 Key Inventory None The Initiator gives a range of Key IDs. The Recipient returns the number of keys in the range and each key's state, so the Initiator can check synchronization and confirm earlier procedures.163 
sequenceDiagram
  participant I as Initiator (MOC)
  participant R as Recipient (spacecraft)
  Note over I: session keys in Pre-Activation
  I->>I: activate master key, AE-encrypt (Key ID, key) set
  I->>R: OTAR command PDU (master Key ID, IV, encrypted keys, MAC)
  R->>R: verify and decrypt, store keys as Pre-Active
  I->>I: Key Activation (Pre-Active to Active)
  I->>R: Key Activation command PDU (Key IDs)
  R->>R: Pre-Active to Active
  I->>R: Key Verification command PDU (Key ID, challenge)
  R-->>I: Key Verification reply PDU (Key ID, IV, encrypted challenge, MAC)
  I->>I: compare, declare keys verified

docs.title: Security Association management
docs.text:
The SA management service sets up the context of an SA for one or more GVCIDs or Global MAP IDs. It supports both simple and complex missions. Simple ones use static SAs with preloaded keys and only choose which SA to use. Long missions may need to rekey or even create SAs on demand.165

stateDiagram-v2
  direction LR
  state "Null, no SA (00)" as Null
  state "Unkeyed, not ready (01)" as Unk
  state "Keyed, dormant (10)" as Key
  state "Operational, in use (11)" as Op
  Null --> Unk : Create SA 0001
  Unk --> Key : Rekey SA 0110
  Key --> Op : Start SA 1011
  Op --> Key : Stop SA 1110
  Key --> Unk : Expire SA 1001
  Unk --> Null : Delete SA 0100

Source: CCSDS 355.1-B-1, figures 2-2 and 5-11.166 The figure splits the transitions into three tiers. Start and Stop apply to every SA, including static SAs with preloaded keys. Rekey and Expire apply where OTAR is supported. Create and Delete apply where SAs can be allocated on demand.165 The 4-bit procedure identifiers of the state-changing directives encode the transition. The left two bits are the state left and the right two bits the state entered, so Start SA, 0b1011, goes from Keyed (10) to Operational (11).167

docs.title: Monitoring and control
docs.text:
The monitoring and control service commands and reads the Recipient Security Function. This may be a separate unit or software applied to one link (TC, TM, AOS or USLP).178

Procedure What it does Ping Checks that the Recipient Security Function is alive; the reply has no data179 Log Status Returns the number of messages in the Security Log and the space left180 Dump Log Sends the whole Security Log to the ground without erasing it; message contents are implementation-specific181 Erase Log Erases the log and returns the count and space after erasure182 Self-Test Runs an implementation-specific self-test; the result is OK (0XXXXXXXb) or not OK (1XXXXXXXb)183 Alarm Flag Reset Clears the FSR Alarm Flag; no reply PDU184

docs.title: Transport over the space link
docs.text:
EP PDUs travel inside packets on the data link services:186

Link Service used for EP PDUs TC MAP Packet service with a dedicated MAP TM VC Packet service AOS (uplink or downlink) VC Packet service USLP (uplink or downlink) MAP Packet service

Several related EP PDUs can be grouped in one packet so that they are transferred together. The APID or MAP number to use is not stated in the available sources.186 Every EP command PDU must travel on an SDLS channel protected by authentication or authenticated encryption. The mission risk analysis decides which.194 The two SPIs that SDLS reserves, 0 and 65535, may carry EP PDUs, and the baseline mode uses them. It is good practice to manage an SA from a different SA, so that control is not lost by accident. At least one SA should be allocated to EP traffic.194210185224

docs.title: PDU format
docs.text:
All EP commands and replies share a Tag, Length, Value (TLV) format with an 8-bit tag, a 16-bit length and a variable value. An implementation that does not recognize a tag can skip the message, which allows proprietary extensions, and TLVs can be nested. The baseline does not use nesting.195210

The data field is optional and octet-aligned, and absent when the length is zero. Where a field is longer than its value, the value is right-justified.196199 The service group distinguishes SA management for SAs that protect Initiator-to-Recipient traffic (01, normally the uplink) from SAs that protect Recipient-to-Initiator traffic (10, normally the downlink).197

Procedure Procedure ID Service group Command tag Reply tag OTAR 0001 00 0x01 — Key Activation 0010 00 0x02 — Key Deactivation 0011 00 0x03 — Key Verification 0100 00 0x04 0x84 Key Destruction 0110 00 0x06 — Key Inventory 0111 00 0x07 0x87 Create SA 0001 01 / 10 0x11 / 0x21 — Rekey SA 0110 01 / 10 0x16 / 0x26 — Start SA 1011 01 / 10 0x1B / 0x2B — Stop SA 1110 01 / 10 0x1E / 0x2E — Expire SA 1001 01 / 10 0x19 / 0x29 — Delete SA 0100 01 / 10 0x14 / 0x24 — Set ARSN 1010 01 / 10 0x1A / 0x2A — Set ARSN Window 0101 01 / 10 0x15 / 0x25 — Read ARSN 0000 01 / 10 0x10 / 0x20 0x90 / 0xA0 SA Status Request 1111 01 / 10 0x1F / 0x2F 0x9F / 0xAF Ping 0001 11 0x31 0xB1 Log Status 0010 11 0x32 0xB2 Dump Log 0011 11 0x33 0xB3 Erase Log 0100 11 0x34 0xB4 Self-Test 0101 11 0x35 0xB5 Alarm Flag Reset 0111 11 0x37 —

Procedure IDs and service groups from CCSDS 355.1-B-1 table 5-1. The hexadecimal tags are computed by this wiki from §5.3.2.2 for CCSDS-defined procedures (User Flag 0). A dash means that no reply PDU is defined.198197

docs.title: PDU layouts
docs.text:
Most field sizes are managed parameters. Annex D fixes them for the baseline. The OTAR command in the baseline uses a 16-bit master Key ID, a 96-bit IV, blocks of a 16-bit Key ID plus a 256-bit session key, and a 128-bit MAC. The Length field is \(N \times 272 + 240\) bits. At most 28 keys fit, so that the PDU stays within 995 octets and the command fits one 1024-octet frame.200213

The Start SA PDU carries a 16-bit SPI and one or more 32-bit GVC/GMAP IDs. How the master channel, VC and MAP values are packed into 32 bits is mission-specific in the normative text. Annex D gives the baseline layout:202216

The Create SA PDU starts with fixed-size fields, followed by pairs of a length and a value: the cipher suite identifiers, the IV, the bit mask, the ARSN and the window. A service type flag set to 1 means the SA provides that service, and authenticated encryption sets both. The meaning of the cipher suite identifiers is mission-specific.204

The other SA PDUs are short. Stop, Expire, Delete, SA Status Request and Read ARSN carry only the 16-bit SPI. Set ARSN and Set ARSN Window add the new value. Rekey SA carries the SPI, the new encryption and authentication Key IDs, the new ARSN and the new IV. For an AE algorithm with a single key, the new authentication Key ID field signals that key. The SA Status reply returns the SPI and an 8-bit field holding the last state-transition procedure ID.205203167 In the baseline the Rekey and Set ARSN PDUs use a 96-bit ARSN field. TC SAs put their 32-bit ARSN in it with the left 64 bits zeroed. TM, AOS and USLP SAs put the 96-bit GCM IV in it, because for AES-GCM the IV is the anti-replay number, so setting the ARSN sets the IV. Read ARSN returns 4 octets for TC and 12 octets for TM and AOS.217218

docs.title: The Frame Security Report
docs.text:
The Frame Security Report (FSR) gives the Initiator systematic, real-time status of frame acceptance by the security function at the receiving end of a secured TC, AOS or USLP link. It is carried in the OCF of TM, AOS or USLP frames, through the MC_OCF or VC_OCF service, and is updated for every SDLS-protected frame received. Other EP messages give on-demand reporting.187

Field Bits Values Meaning Control Word Type 0 1 Tells the FSR apart from the CLCW, whose type is 0188 FSR Version Number 1–3 100 1 marks a CCSDS-defined Type-2 OCF; 00 is Version 1, the only version so far189 Alarm Flag 4 0 / 1 1 once any frame on the link (all VCs and SAs) has been rejected since the last reset. Stays set until an Alarm Flag Reset command190 Bad Sequence Number Flag 5 0 / 1 1 when the last frame's ARSN is outside the window. Not persistent191 Bad MAC Flag 6 0 / 1 1 when the last frame's MAC did not match. Not persistent191 Bad SA Flag 7 0 / 1 1 when the last frame failed SA verification, named an SA not in Operational state, or an Operational SA whose key is not Active. Not persistent191 Last SPI used 8–23 16 bits SPI of the last received frame. The three flags always refer to it192 Sequence Number Value 24–31 8 bits 8 least significant bits of that frame's ARSN192

A frame has only one OCF, so the FSR is multiplexed with the CLCW in a mission-specific pattern. The baseline alternates the two when COP-1 reports on the same virtual channel.193209

Worked example: decoding an FSR (illustrative values)

The 32-bit OCF value 0xCA00012A is constructed for this explanation. It is not from a real mission. The first octet 0xCA is 0b1100_1010. Control Word Type 1 and version 100 make it an FSR, not a CLCW. The Alarm bit is 1: a frame has been rejected since the last reset. Bad SN is 0, Bad MAC is 1 and Bad SA is 0, so the last frame failed its MAC check. The next 16 bits, 0x0001, say that frame used SPI 1, and the last octet, 0x2A, gives the low 8 bits of its ARSN. The Alarm bit stays set until the Initiator sends an Alarm Flag Reset (tag 0x37). The three event flags change with the next frame.190191

docs.title: Baseline implementation mode
docs.text:
Annex D gives a baseline for interoperability testing and operation:209210211212

  • The FSR is an OCF of Type 2 and alternates with the CLCW when COP-1 reports on the same VC.
  • SDLS runs in its own baseline mode, and EP PDUs use the reserved SPIs 0 and 65535. TLV nesting is not used.
  • Key Destruction and Key Inventory are left out of the baseline.
  • OTAR and Key Verification use AES-GCM with 256-bit keys, 96-bit IVs and 128-bit MACs.
  • Key IDs are 16 bits. Values 0–127 are not used to reference session keys in Key Verification.
  • Key Activation and Deactivation handle up to 16 keys per PDU (at most 35 octets, Length = \(N \times 16\)). Key Verification handles up to 21 keys (128-bit challenges; the reply carries per key a 96-bit IV, a 128-bit encrypted challenge and a 128-bit MAC).214215

Inference

The baseline reserves Key IDs 0–127 from session keys and leaves it to implementers to give master keys "a special range". This suggests, but does not state, that 0–127 is meant for master keys.213215

docs.title: Conformance and security considerations
docs.text:
Conformance is claimed by filling in the PICS proforma of annex A.207 The security annex notes that EP PDUs are protected at least by authentication, which gives integrity, and that authentication of the communicating entities relies on SDLS. The protection of especially sensitive PDUs is left to the implementer. Without authentication, unauthorized procedures or software could be uploaded. Without integrity, corrupted procedures could cost the security function or the mission. Without confidentiality, session keys could be disclosed. The standard creates no SANA registries.208

Worked example: a Key Activation command (illustrative bytes)

These bytes are constructed for this explanation. To activate session keys 0x0080 and 0x0081 with baseline 16-bit Key IDs, the PDU is 02 00 20 00 80 00 81. The tag 0x02 means command, CCSDS-defined, key management, Key Activation. The length 0x0020 is \(2 \times 16 = 32\) bits. The data field holds the two Key IDs. This 7-octet PDU travels in a packet on the dedicated TC MAP, inside an SDLS-authenticated frame.201214186194 A matching SA Status reply for SPI 3 after Start SA would be 9F 00 18 00 03 0B. Here 0x9F is the reply tag, the length is 24 bits, the SPI is 0x0003, and 0x0B (1011, right-justified) is Start SA, from Keyed 10 to Operational 11.167196
