docs.title: XTCE: XML Telemetric and Command Exchange (CCSDS 660)
docs.text:
Every mission control system needs a mission database. This is the description, item by item, of every telemetry parameter, packet, calibration, limit, command and verification check that the ground must handle. ESA's SCOS-2000 keeps it in the MIB, a set of ASCII tables. Other control systems have their own formats. Every hand-over between organisations, for example from spacecraft manufacturer to operator or from test system to control centre, has therefore needed a custom translation, more testing and more risk of error.3 XTCE, the XML Telemetric and Command Exchange format, is an open, standard XML Schema for describing such a database. The aim is that TM/TC definitions can be exchanged "without the need for customized import/export, re-validation, or even re-implementation".6

XTCE is an Object Management Group (OMG) specification. CCSDS publishes the OMG text of XTCE 1.2, inside CCSDS front matter, as the Recommended Standard CCSDS 660.0-B-2.21 The CCSDS Informational Report 660.1-G-2 explains every element.26 A second, shorter Informational Report, 660.2-G-2, introduces the concepts and use cases.132 In March 2026 the OMG published XTCE 1.3 (formal/26-06-09) with a new schema. Its specification text differs from 1.2 mostly in wording, as shown below.157 Whether CCSDS will re-issue 660.0 for 1.3 is not stated in the available sources. This page summarises these documents and a NASA tutorial on XTCE 1.1 (2008 or 2009), and records which parts two open implementations, Yamcs and OpenC3 COSMOS, support. It then maps XTCE concepts onto the SCOS-2000 MIB tables, a mapping that the standards themselves do not provide. Each mapping judgement on this page is this wiki's own analysis.

At a glance

Property Value Standard CCSDS 660.0-B-2 (February 2020) = OMG XTCE 1.2, formal/18-10-04 (January 2019)12 Latest OMG version XTCE 1.3, formal/26-06-09 (March 2026), schema XTCE/20250214/SpaceSystem.xsd157158 Normative content the W3C XML Schema SpaceSystem.xsd published by the OMG24 Companions CCSDS 660.1-G-2, XTCE element description (August 2021)26; CCSDS 660.2-G-2, introduction (February 2021)133 Restricted profile OMG XTCE US Govt Satellite Conformance Profile (XUSP, "GovSat")136 Root element SpaceSystem, which can be nested to form a hierarchy9 Main sections TelemetryMetaData, CommandMetaData, ServiceSet922 Scope TM/TC definitions (metadata), not live data transfer6 Out of scope displays, data distribution, protocols, RF, scheduling, orbits, flight software6 Conformance a compliant database is an XML file that validates against the schema7

docs.title: Documents and versions
docs.text:
Document Date Content OMG XTCE 1.0 2005 or 2006 (sources differ, see below) first version, from the OMG Space Domain Task Force27166 OMG XTCE 1.1 2006, 2007 or 2008 (sources differ) revised after a CCSDS review27135166 CCSDS 660.0-G-1 July 2006 original XTCE Informational Report, superseded by 660.2-G-2133 CCSDS 660.0-B-1 October 2007 first CCSDS Blue Book (XTCE 1.1), superseded1166 NASA tutorial (K. Rice, B. Kizzort) March 2008 or 2009 90-slide tutorial for XTCE 1.1; title slide 2008, page footers 2009 (Torrance, California)164. The NTRS record gives the meeting as an "XTCE Training Class" in Torrance starting 23 March 2009, but a publication date of 23 March 2008165 CCSDS 660.1-G-1 May 2012 element description, issue 1134 OMG XTCE 1.2, formal/18-10-04 January 2019 schema XTCE/20180204/SpaceSystem.xsd2 CCSDS 660.0-B-2 February 2020 XTCE 1.2. The CCSDS cover wraps the OMG specification. The normative schema is at the OMG URL124 CCSDS 660.2-G-2 February 2021 high-level introduction: why XTCE, scope, core concepts, schema structure, a usage scenario and the GovSat example, by the CCSDS SM&C working group (MOIMS area)132133 CCSDS 660.1-G-2 August 2021 element-by-element explanation for XTCE 1.2, revising the version for XTCE 1.126 OMG XTCE 1.3, formal/26-06-09 March 2026 schema XTCE/20250214/SpaceSystem.xsd; see What changed in XTCE 1.3157158

The sources disagree on the early dates. 660.1-G-2 says that XTCE 1.0 and 1.1 were both published in 2006, with 1.1 following a CCSDS review.27 660.2-G-2 dates 1.1 to 2008.135 The NASA tutorial says that 1.0 was first published in 2005 by the OMG Space Domain Task Force (active since 2000, with ESA, Boeing, the US Air Force SMC and Lockheed Martin as original submitters, later joined by NASA GSFC and Harris). It says CCSDS published 1.1 as a Blue Book in October 2007 and dates a 1.1 overview Green Book to 2007.166 That last date conflicts with the July 2006 date that 660.2-G-2 gives for 660.0-G-1.133 660.2-G-2 also still cites draft issues of 660.0-B and of itself from 2019 as its references.134 XTCE 1.2 (2019) is largely backward compatible with 1.1 in syntax.27 Its main changes are: a new SpaceSystem namespace; normalised enumeration strings; more ways to state byte order; integer exponents; new rules for string length and float sizes; an updated epoch time/date type; arrays whose dimension sizes are set in the type; XInclude support; time association moved to container entries; a new numeric multi-range alarm and an inside/outside flag for alarms; more places for ancillary data and short descriptions; and argument instance references.27 660.2-G-2 singles out the array change as the largest syntax change. It adds that many schema types were cleaned up to map better onto programming-language classes, and that the command-side types were split off from their telemetry ancestors so that argument references can be used wherever parameter references were allowed.135147

docs.title: What changed in XTCE 1.3
docs.text:
The XTCE 1.3 document (31 pages) has the same structure and section numbers as the OMG text inside 660.0-B-2. It contains no change list, and its normative content is again a separate schema file, now at https://www.omg.org/spec/XTCE/20250214/SpaceSystem.xsd.158 A word-by-word comparison of the two specification texts by this wiki finds these differences:1571591601612369

Topic XTCE 1.2 (660.0-B-2) XTCE 1.3 (formal/26-06-09) Date and schema January 2019; schema 20180204 March 2026; schema 20250214 Copyright holders Boeing, ESOC, Lockheed Martin (2018), OMG (2014–2018) adds Kratos S1 (2025), NASA (2025) and the EDM Council (EDM Association, 2026); Boeing 2018–2025; OMG 2014–2026 Contributors named in the Foreword Lockheed Martin, ESA, Boeing, NASA GSFC, USAF SMC, Harris, Raytheon, SciSys, CSC, GST the same, with "L-3 Harris" for Harris and with Peraton and Kratos S1 added Scope: structures "CCSDS packets and TDM frames" CCSDS packets, TDM frames "and proprietary implementations" Scope: commands command identification, argument specification and validation criteria adds "header and footer parameter definitions" Scope: encodings "parameter and command encoding" "parameter and argument encoding types" Terms Telemetering, Commands Telemetering, Telecommands, and a new term Container: the abstract XTCE word for a partition of the bit stream, used instead of "packet" or "frame" Reserved : in names "reserved for future use" as a selector for data from other SpaceSystems reserved for implementations, to separate names from aliases in alias namespaces Wording "command" "telecommand" in most places

Inference

The comparison covers only the specification texts. The 1.3 schema is not in this wiki's library, so element-level schema changes in 1.3 are not stated in the available sources. The rest of the specification (the SpaceSystem, TelemetryMetaData, CommandMetaData and ServiceSet descriptions, Annex B style notes and the bibliography) differs only by the "telecommand" wording, figure-caption punctuation and corrected typos such as "InputOutputAlgorighm", "Argurments" and "overide". The new use of : fits the alias approach that the mapping below suggests for PCF_PID.

The specification lists Lockheed Martin, ESA, Boeing, NASA GSFC, USAF SMC, Harris, Raytheon, SciSys, CSC and GST as contributors (1.3 adds Peraton and Kratos S1).3159 The European Space Operations Centre is one of the copyright holders of both 1.2 and 1.3.2157 Its bibliography, unchanged in 1.3,163 cites the SCOS-2000 Database Import ICD issue 5.0 (June 2001) and the SCOS-2000 Synthetic Parameters Software User Manual, alongside the CCSDS packet standards, the PUS (draft ECSS-E-70-41 and ESA PSS-07-101), CCSDS time codes and the IRIG-106 TMATS.25 This wiki reads that as a sign that the MIB was among the formats XTCE's authors had in view; the specification does not say how its bibliography was used. See History of the Database Import ICD for the MIB's own evolution.

docs.title: Purpose and scope
docs.text:
XTCE covers the metadata needed to:6

  • define the structure and sequence of CCSDS packets and TDM frames;
  • define how individual data items are packed and unpacked;
  • describe commands: identification, arguments and validation criteria;
  • define parameter and command encoding;
  • define data properties such as default values, validity criteria and dependencies.

It explicitly excludes data distribution mechanisms, command and data protocols, RF and analogue streams, data grouping and coherent data sets, visualisation, scheduling, orbital properties, displays and flight software. It is "a meta-data specification, not a data specification".6

docs.title: Philosophy: neither packets nor frames
docs.text: The industry is split between packet telemetry and TDM (time-division multiplexed) telemetry, and much of the apparent divide is vocabulary. XTCE therefore avoids words such as "minor frame", "major frame" and even "packet" except in examples, and builds in no packet or frame standard. Instead, users build libraries of containers that represent those standards.4 The processing that XTCE metadata supports runs in two directions. Stream processing covers decryption, decoding, frame synchronisation and so on. Parameter processing covers decommutation, de-packetisation, calibration and custom processing. On the command side the corresponding steps are formatting, constraint checking, authentication and verification.5

docs.title: The SpaceSystem model
docs.text:
classDiagram
  class SpaceSystem {
    name, shortDescription
    LongDescription, AliasSet
    Header
  }
  class TelemetryMetaData {
    ParameterTypeSet
    ParameterSet
    ContainerSet
    MessageSet
    StreamSet
    AlgorithmSet
  }
  class CommandMetaData {
    ParameterTypeSet
    ParameterSet
    ArgumentTypeSet
    MetaCommandSet
    CommandContainerSet
    StreamSet
    AlgorithmSet
  }
  class ServiceSet
  SpaceSystem "1" --> "0..1" TelemetryMetaData
  SpaceSystem "1" --> "0..1" CommandMetaData
  SpaceSystem "1" --> "0..1" ServiceSet
  SpaceSystem "1" --> "0..*" SpaceSystem : sub-SpaceSystems

This wiki's summary of 660.0-B-2 §6.1 and 660.1-G-2 §3.2.9111928

The root is called SpaceSystem rather than "Spacecraft", because an operations centre also controls antennas, recorders, ground equipment and RF hardware. Each of these is a SpaceSystem.9 A SpaceSystem can contain sub-SpaceSystems. The standard gives four reasons: fewer name collisions (a dozen identical transponders can each live in their own sub-SpaceSystem), better organisation of databases with thousands of commands and tens of thousands of parameters, the ability to nest spacecraft inside a constellation, and a natural fit to systems of systems.9 The optional Header records the source, version, revision history, notes and classification.10 660.2-G-2 lists its content as date, version, classification and validation status (validated, tested or draft), an author set, a note set and a history set for configuration management.140

660.2-G-2 treats SpaceSystems as namespaces addressed by paths such as /MyMission/SubSystem1/Power/Battery1. A SpaceSystem has no fixed meaning: it can be an instrument, a spacecraft bus, a whole spacecraft, a constellation or a ground station. XTCE 1.2's XInclude support lets each instrument and the spacecraft bus have its own SpaceSystem database, assembled into one large database such as the satellite database.138139 Some organisations keep a single SpaceSystem, others use many.139

Names may contain digits, letters, underscores, hyphens and backslashes, and are case sensitive. The characters / (SpaceSystem path separator), . (member of an aggregate), [ ] (array index) and : are reserved. In 1.2 the : is held for a future selector of data in other SpaceSystems; in 1.3 implementations may use it to separate a name from an alias namespace.9161 Collections are named …Set when unordered and …List when ordered. Meta marks a description (a MetaCommand is a command description), and Ref marks a by-name reference.8

docs.title: References and instances
docs.text: Items refer to each other by NameReference, which is the item's name with an optional Unix-style path through the SpaceSystem hierarchy.29 The NASA tutorial lists absolute, relative and path-less forms. A path-less name is not global: it is looked up in the local SpaceSystem first and then up the tree. Because an XML parser does not resolve these references, every implementation must, and the tutorial counts them among the hardest parts of XTCE to implement.167178 During processing, a ParameterInstanceRef points at a parameter's value. Instance 0 (the default) is the last recorded value, and negative instances go back in time. useCalibratedValue (default true) selects the engineering or raw value.33 Conditions throughout the schema use MatchCriteria: a simple Comparison, a ComparisonList, an arbitrarily complex BooleanExpression, or an escape to a custom algorithm.23 A ContextMatch is a MatchCriteria that selects which calibrator, alarm or significance applies. The Green Book gives mission phases as an example of a context.30

docs.title: Parameter types
docs.text:
A ParameterType is a description of something that can have a value. A Parameter is an instance of it ("a Parameter is not the value itself").1213 The type carries most of the information: data type, description, units, alarm limits, string conversion and, through one of four DataEncodings, the on-the-link form.12 The Green Book describes the processing order. The encoded link value is checked against a valid range and calibrated into the host data type. Alarm checks are then applied to the result.35

XTCE type Typical encoding Notes StringParameterType StringDataEncoding restriction pattern, character width, string alarms5455 EnumeratedParameterType IntegerDataEncoding EnumerationList of label/value pairs. maxValue turns a value into a range. EnumerationAlarm56 BinaryParameterType BinaryDataEncoding data with no type54 BooleanParameterType IntegerDataEncoding, 1 bit oneStringValue / zeroStringValue57 IntegerParameterType IntegerDataEncoding signed, sizeInBits, ValidRange, numeric alarms54 FloatParameterType Float or IntegerDataEncoding (with calibrator) numeric alarms54 RelativeTimeParameterType IntegerDataEncoding (or Binary) units, scale, offset. ReferenceTime by OffsetFrom or Epoch58 AbsoluteTimeParameterType IntegerDataEncoding (or Binary) the same, but no alarms5846 ArrayParameterType via array members in XTCE 1.2 the dimensions and sizes are declared in the type59 AggregateParameterType via members a record ("struct"). Members are referenced as Aggregate.Member60

The Green Book counts ten ParameterTypes in two groups: the scalar types and the complex Array and Aggregate types. Its list of scalar names repeats "String" and leaves out the two time types.54 660.2-G-2 lists all ten with one-line roles (Boolean as "a special case of" enumerated types, Binary as a "blob" catch-all) and distinguishes two forms of ParameterType: one with a DataEncoding, describing a value from the spacecraft, and one without, describing a ground-side value whose Parameter sets dataSource to local.141 It names three common combinations: a FloatParameterType with an IntegerDataEncoding and (typically) a PolynomialCalibrator for a calibrated count, an IntegerParameterType with IntegerDataEncoding, and a FloatParameterType with FloatDataEncoding. For calibrations too complex for the three calibrator kinds it suggests a BinaryDataEncoding with a FromBinaryTransformAlgorithm.142

docs.title: Encodings
docs.text:
• IntegerDataEncoding: encoding is one of unsigned (default), twosComplement, onesComplement, BCD or packedBCD. The default sizeInBits is 8. It can carry calibrators and a changeThreshold.39 The specification body of both 1.2 and 1.3 also lists signMagnitude and spells the complements "twosCompliment" and "onesCompliment".12162 A later Green Book table names "signedMagnitude", and the NASA tutorial warns that the 1.1 schema used the "Compliment" spelling.131168 The GovSat example of 660.2-G-2, which the report states is valid against the 1.2 schema, uses twosComplement.154153 The full list of enumeration strings is that of the schema, which is not in this wiki's library.
  • FloatDataEncoding: IEEE754_1985, IEEE754, MILSTD_1750A, DEC, IBM or TI. The listed sizes are 16, 32, 40, 48, 64, 80 and 128 bits. Not every format supports every size, and a later paragraph of the Green Book mentions only 32, 64 and 128 bits.40 The specification text names only IEEE754_1985 and MILSTD_1750A.12
  • StringDataEncoding: US-ASCII, ISO-8859-1, Windows-1252, UTF-8, UTF-16 (LE/BE) or UTF-32 (LE/BE). The size is either fixed (SizeInBits, optionally ended by a termination character or given by a leading size field, 16 bits by default) or Variable.38
  • BinaryDataEncoding: a size plus optional From/ToBinaryTransformAlgorithms. It is used for data with no type and for exotic formats.41

Every encoding shares a bitOrder (MSB first by default), an optional byte order list for non-big-endian items, and ErrorDetectCorrect (parity, CRC, and a checksum added in 1.2).37 A ParameterType with no encoding describes a local, ground, constant or derived value that never comes from telemetry. Its Parameter should then declare a non-telemetered dataSource.42

docs.title: Calibrators
docs.text:
Integer and float encodings can hold a DefaultCalibrator and any number of ContextCalibrators, each selected by a ContextMatch.43

  • SplineCalibrator: a list of raw-to-calibrated SplinePoints. order 0 gives a step function, 1 linear (the default), 2 quadratic and 3 cubic. extrapolate controls values beyond the end points.44
  • PolynomialCalibrator: Term elements with coefficient and a non-negative integer exponent, for example \(y = 0.5 + 1.5x - 0.045x^2 + 1.25x^3 + 0.0025x^4\).45
  • MathOperationCalibrator: an expression built from MathOperationType, written in postfix (reverse Polish) form.4575

docs.title: Alarms
docs.text:
Every scalar type except AbsoluteTime has a DefaultAlarm and a ContextAlarmList. The first context alarm whose ContextMatch is true is used. Otherwise the default applies, like an if-then chain.4648 All alarms share minViolations (successive violations before the alarm state) and minConformance (successive good samples to leave it).47 The levels are normal, watch, warning, distress, critical and severe.49 The alarm forms are:

Form Applies to Meaning StaticAlarmRanges Integer, Float (and time) nested bands for watch, warning, distress, critical and severe. rangeForm is outside (default: normal in the middle) or inside (normal at the outside)51 ChangeAlarmRanges Integer, Float changePerSample (delta) or changePerSecond (rate), on an absolute or percentage basis, over a span of samples or seconds52 MultiRange Integer, Float any number of ranges (new in 1.2)52 EnumerationAlarm Enumerated alarm level per enumeration label49 StringAlarm String level per matching pattern, with a default level55 AlarmConditions most types a MatchCriteria per level. The most severe true level wins50 CustomAlarm most types algorithm-based47

Boundary semantics

In the Green Book's outside-alarm example, WarningRange minInclusive="-5" maxInclusive="5" makes -5 and 5 themselves warnings: the normal range is -5 < x < 5.51 The "inclusive" values belong to the alarm band. This matters when mapping MIB limits (see below). The NASA tutorial reads its own example the same way. With WatchRange −2000 to 5000 and SevereRange −5000 to 6000, values x ≤ −2000 or x ≥ 5000 are at watch level and x ≤ −5000 or x ≥ 6000 are severe. More severe ranges clip less severe ones, and the colours used for the levels are not part of XTCE.170 The Yamcs manual reads its own example the same way: a value of 40 against a warning range of 10 to 30 raises a warning, which it calls "perhaps a bit counter intuitive". It does not discuss the boundary values themselves.184

For AlarmConditions, the NASA tutorial adds that the condition of each of up to five levels can be a single comparison, several conditions, a Boolean expression or a custom algorithm.171

A ValidRange check applies only to Integer and Float types. It is separate from alarms: an out-of-range value is invalid rather than alarmed.3553 On the telemetry side the tutorial says to ignore the attribute validRangeAppliesToCalibrated. For commands it chooses where the check happens: on the engineering value before calibration (true, the default) or on the encoded value after it (false), but not both.169 Yamcs marks a parameter outside its ValidRange as invalid and skips its limit checks, while a command argument outside its range makes Yamcs reject the command.183190

docs.title: Type inheritance
docs.text: String, Enumerated, Binary, Integer, Float and Boolean types can extend another type of the same kind through @baseType. Loops are illegal. A child can override calibrators, units, the default alarm and ranges, and can prefix context alarms and enumerations. It cannot change the encoding, sizeInBits or signedness.36

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
A Parameter is usually just a name and a parameterTypeRef.61 Its ParameterProperties add:62

  • dataSource: telemetered (the default), derived (computed by an algorithm), constant or local (for example a session variable).
  • readOnly and persistance (spelled this way in XTCE).
  • ValidityCondition: a MatchCriteria that must hold for the value to be valid. The standard's example is a value that is invalid while its subsystem is off.
  • PhysicalAddressSet: hardware addresses, for example on a MIL-STD-1553 bus.
  • TimeAssociation: the offset of the sample from a reference time parameter. In XTCE 1.2 it can also be set per container entry.
  • SystemName: a subsystem name for flat, single-SpaceSystem databases.

One type per parameter? A ParameterType can in theory serve many Parameters. 660.2-G-2 says that this is "not common practice". Most databases give every Parameter its own type, so that a change to an alarm or calibrator cannot spread by accident to other parameters, at the price of a larger file. The same holds for ArgumentTypes.143148 The Yamcs manual makes the same observation from the other side. Many control systems do not separate a parameter from its type, and shared types are mostly generic ones such as uint8 or uint16, or types for a family of identical sensors.182 660.2-G-2 also warns that the dataSource attribute, which defaults to telemetered, "is often overlooked".143

docs.title: Containers
docs.text:
A SequenceContainer describes "a packet, frame, a subframe, or any other grouping". Its EntryList is an ordered list of items.1463 By default the entries are packed back to back, and the container's size is the sum of their encoded sizes.66

Entry Purpose ParameterRefEntry a parameter. Its width comes from the type's encoding66 ParameterSegmentRefEntry part of a parameter (for example a 1 024-bit binary split into 116-bit segments)66 ContainerRefEntry another container, resolved as a unit. Referencing an abstract container triggers dynamic container matching67 ContainerSegmentRefEntry, StreamSegmentEntry parts of containers or streams spread over several containers67 IndirectParameterRefEntry the parameter whose name is held in another parameter's value68 ArrayParameterRefEntry an array, optionally a subset of its dimensions68

Each entry can be modified by three elements:69

  • LocationInContainerInBits sets the position relative to containerStart, containerEnd, the previous entry (the default) or the next entry. The Green Book's XML examples spell the previous-entry value previousEntry.6970
  • RepeatEntry repeats an entry for super-commutated parameters. A Count of 1 means one extra copy, giving two in total. An optional offset sets the gap between copies.69
  • IncludeCondition includes the entry only when a MatchCriteria holds.69

docs.title: Inheritance and identification
docs.text:
The key mechanism is container inheritance. A container names its parent in BaseContainer, and the parent's EntryList is prefixed to the child's. RestrictionCriteria on the BaseContainer state the values that identify the child, such as an APID or a type/subtype. Inheritance can go to any depth, and every RestrictionCriteria along the chain must hold.157172 Only the leaf containers are real packets. Intermediate levels are marked abstract.64

Element Inheritance rule72 @name, @abstract, @idlePattern, descriptions, aliases not inherited EntryList parent's entries prefixed to the child's AncillaryDataSet child's prefixed to parent's DefaultRateInStream, BinaryEncoding/SizeInBits child overrides if present RateInStreamSet child's prefixed; same stream ref overrides RestrictionCriteria scoped to their construction, and apply to inherited entries too 
classDiagram
  class CCSDSPacket {
    <<abstract>>
    Version, Type, SecHdrFlag, APID
    SeqFlags, SeqCount, Length
  }
  class PUSTMHeader {
    <<abstract>>
    PUS version, Service, Subtype, Time...
  }
  class TimeReport {
    S-field, P-field, OBT
  }
  class HKSummary {
    SID, ...
  }
  CCSDSPacket <|-- TimeReport : APID == 0
  CCSDSPacket <|-- PUSTMHeader : SecHdrFlag == 1
  PUSTMHeader <|-- HKSummary : Service == 3, Subtype == 25, SID == 32

This wiki's illustration of the Green Book patterns, not a figure from it.95

The Green Book's telemetry patterns build on this idea. The basic pattern is one abstract "generic packet" header with all packets derived from it, and for many missions one level is enough. Variants add an optional secondary header through an IncludeCondition, a common root container shared by all packets, or a secondary header chosen by dynamic matching, for example when the time-stamp format varies.95 MessageSet is an alternative to inheritance. A Message pairs a container with a MatchCriteria.1673 StreamSet describes fixed-frame, variable-frame or custom streams, and which containers or services they carry.1774

In practice these two are little used. 660.2-G-2 calls MessageSet one of the lesser-used areas, kept for backward compatibility, which "one may want to consider" deprecated. It calls StreamSet under-used and, in the view of many users, too simple to configure front-end processing.145 The NASA tutorial already listed MessageSet, StreamSet, AlgorithmSet and ServiceSet as "the forgotten elements". It noted that StreamSet lacks, for example, Reed-Solomon coding information, and advised describing packets and leaving frame processing to the front end.175 660.2-G-2 likewise recommends defining packets in XTCE and not the framing.144 Arrays changed in 1.2. In 1.1 the number of dimensions sat in the ArrayParameterType and their sizes in the container's ArrayParameterRefEntry. In 1.2 the type can hold both, and the old entry syntax remains for backward compatibility.144

docs.title: Algorithms
docs.text: The AlgorithmSet holds processing that cannot be stated declaratively. A MathAlgorithm is a formula in postfix notation. A CustomAlgorithm (also called SimpleAlgorithm) holds algorithm text and references to external implementations such as Java classes, DLLs or scripts. Input, Input-Output and Input-Output-Trigger algorithms add named inputs, outputs, and periodic or event-driven triggers.1875

docs.title: Commanding
docs.text:
CommandMetaData has the telemetry sets plus an ArgumentTypeSet, a MetaCommandSet and a CommandContainerSet. Parameters are scoped per SpaceSystem, so a telemetry parameter can be used in a command and the other way round.1976 The Green Book draws the line this way. An argument is something an operator (or automation) supplies. A command parameter is part of the command that the system supplies, or that RestrictionCriteria fix.77 On the command side, data flows the other way. The host value is range-checked, then (de)calibrated into the encoding for uplink, and can be range-checked again.78

ArgumentTypes mirror the ParameterTypes but have no alarms. Float and integer argument types carry a ValidRangeSet.2079

660.2-G-2 adds three practical points. Arguments are local to their MetaCommand and cannot be reused by another command, although commands can inherit them through BaseMetaCommand.146 The line between argument and command parameter is not always clear to users. Some see the whole command "load", others only their own arguments, but XTCE has the syntax to separate the two when needed.147 And the CommandContainerSet holds the "pieces/parts" of command containers that several commands share.149 The NASA tutorial describes those shared pieces as "has a" building blocks, for example an optional secondary header included only when the secondary header flag is 1.174 It also lists how a MetaCommand's own CommandContainer differs from a telemetry container. It can hold a FixedValueEntry, for example an opcode, and ArgumentRefEntries, which must cover every argument but need not follow the ArgumentList order. It can extend the parent command's container only through an explicit BaseContainer, its RestrictionCriteria are optional, and it has no abstract attribute of its own. The tutorial encourages simple "parameter == value" restrictions, because they can be processed automatically to tell the system which values it must supply in the named parameters.172173

docs.title: MetaCommand
docs.text:
Element Purpose @abstract a template that is not itself a command. Its CommandContainer is then abstract too80 BaseMetaCommand + ArgumentAssignmentList inherit from another MetaCommand and fix some of its arguments81 ArgumentList the ordered arguments, each referencing an ArgumentType85 CommandContainer the bit layout: ParameterRefEntry, ContainerRefEntry, ArgumentRefEntry, FixedValueEntry (a literal of given sizeInBits). It can extend another container. Its RestrictionCriteria act as assertions that set values8384 TransmissionConstraintList conditions (MatchCriteria) that must hold before release, with a timeOut and an optional suspendable flag8687 DefaultSignificance / ContextSignificanceList a consequenceLevel of none, watch, warning, distress, critical or severe, with spaceSystemAtRisk and reasonForWarning. The level must be confirmed before sending2188 Interlock blocks following commands, within a SpaceSystem scope, until this one reaches verificationToWaitFor (default complete) or a verificationProgressPercentage2189 VerifierSet TransferredToRange, TransferredFromRange, Received, Accepted, Queued, Execution, Complete (several allowed) and Failed2190 ParameterToSetList parameters to set (to a fixed or derived value) once a verification stage is reached, for example a command counter92 ParametersToSuspendAlarmsOnSet suspend alarms on given parameters for a suspenseTime after a stage, to avoid false change alarms2192

Each verifier is one of: a ComparisonList, a ContainerRef (the stage is reached when that container arrives), a ParameterValueChange, a CustomAlgorithm, a BooleanExpression or a single Comparison. A CheckWindow gives timeToStartChecking and timeToStopChecking relative to commandRelease or to the time the last verifier passed.91 MetaCommand inheritance follows rules like those for containers. Argument lists, constraints and verifiers accumulate (with Complete verifiers accrued), and the CommandContainer is inherited only if its BaseContainer explicitly points to the parent's.82 A BlockMetaCommand groups MetaCommand steps with their argument values into one unit. The Green Book's example opens a valve, waits through five NOOPs and closes it.93 The Green Book's command patterns range from a simple MetaCommand whose container is all FixedValueEntries plus arguments, to an abstract mission template with derived concrete commands, to a generic root template shared across missions.96

docs.title: ServiceSet
docs.text: A Service is a named grouping of containers or messages, such as a "memory dump service". Referencing an abstract container includes all its children. The meaning of a grouping is left to the implementation, and services are optional.2294 660.2-G-2 explains that services were introduced "for the European space organizations that deal with services", that is, users of the PUS, and calls the area under-used.150 The NASA tutorial's example groups the containers of each CCSDS virtual channel into one service.176

docs.title: Worked example from 660.2-G-2: the GovSat fragment
docs.text:
Annex A of 660.2-G-2 gives a short, complete XTCE 1.2 file taken from the GovSat example. It has one telemetry packet and one command, and the report states that the assembled fragments are valid against the XTCE 1.2 schema.152153 The definitions below are real (from the source). The diagram is this wiki's rendering of them.

The abstract container CCSDSPacket lists seven unsigned integer parameters whose IntegerDataEncoding sizes add up to the 48-bit Space Packet primary header:154155

Container or command Base RestrictionCriteria Entries CCSDSPacket (abstract) none none the seven header parameters above CCSDSTelemetryPacket (abstract) CCSDSPacket ComparisonList: CCSDSVersion == 0 and CCSDSType == 0 none of its own PowmX0EP_StatusPacket CCSDSTelemetryPacket CCSDSAPID == 47 (useCalibratedValue="true", instance 0) TimeStamp and seven power-module parameters (voltages, currents, PPS source, power state, set point) MetaCommand CCSDSCommand (abstract), container CCSDSCommandPacket CCSDSPacket CCSDSVersion == 0 and CCSDSType == 1 none MetaCommand PM1Enable_Logging, container PM1Enable_LoggingPacket CCSDSCommand / CCSDSCommandPacket CCSDSAPID == 130 four ArgumentRefEntries: message type (8 bits), address (32), port (16), sensor ID (32)

Rows restate Annex A2.2.4 and A2.3.3 of 660.2-G-2.155156

A few details of the example are worth noting:154155156

  • CCSDSSCID and CCSDSVCID have no encoding and dataSource="local". The spacecraft and virtual channel are not in the packet, and the virtual channel of each packet and command is recorded as AncillaryData name="VCID" (6 for the status packet, 27 for the command).
  • The five analogue values (voltage, current, maximum current, bus voltage and set point) are 64-bit FloatParameterTypes on 16-bit twosComplement integer encodings with a PolynomialCalibrator of terms 0.0 and 0.1. Each raw count is therefore 0.1 V or 0.1 A. The PPS source is an unsigned integer on 8 bits.
  • TimeStamp is an AbsoluteTimeParameterType on a 64-bit unsigned encoding, with units="seconds", scale 1.0, offset 0.0 and the epoch TAI. Its short description describes the layout as a 16-bit P-field, 32 bits of seconds and 16 bits of fraction.
  • PowmX0EP_PowerStateType is an EnumeratedParameterType with Off = 1, On = 2, Tripped = 3 and NotWorking = 4, encoded on 8 bits.
  • There is no CommandContainerSet: the command reuses the telemetry header container, "which is legal XTCE".
  • The root element declares the namespace http://www.omg.org/spec/XTCE/20180204, and the Header gives validationStatus="Validated", date 2019-04-04 and version 0.2.

Inference

Compared with the MIB, CCSDSTelemetryPacket plus the APID restriction plays the role of the PID key, and the entries of PowmX0EP_StatusPacket, packed back to back after the inherited header, play the role of PLF offsets. The 64-bit integer encoding of a time stamp whose description mentions a P-field, a seconds field and a fraction field shows a limit of plain integer encodings. Splitting the CUC fields, or honouring a P-field, would need a BinaryDataEncoding with an algorithm or separate parameters (see Time code formats).

docs.title: The usage scenario
docs.text:
660.2-G-2's scenario starts with a spacecraft project manager who receives an XTCE file from each subsystem and payload contractor. The files are merged into one Spacecraft Source Database (SDB), converted to run-time databases for assembly, integration and verification (AIV), and then passed to the mission readiness team. That team includes or translates the database into the operational databases (ODB) of the mission control, flight dynamics, mission planning, procedure generation and simulator systems.151 The report stresses that XTCE is for exchanging database content, not an interface for sending commands or receiving telemetry.151

flowchart LR
    subgraph AIV["Assembly, integration and verification"]
        A["Subsystem A"] -->|XTCE| SDB[("Spacecraft<br/>Source Database")]
        B["Subsystem B"] -->|XTCE| SDB
        C["Payload C"] -->|XTCE| SDB
        D["Payload D"] -->|XTCE| SDB
        SDB -->|XTCE| EGSE["EGSE, editors,<br/>procedure generation"]
    end
    subgraph OPS["Operations"]
        ODB[("Operational<br/>Database")]
        ODB -->|XTCE| MCS["Mission control"]
        ODB -->|XTCE| FDS["Flight dynamics"]
        ODB -->|XTCE| MPS["Mission planning"]
        ODB -->|XTCE| SIM["Simulator"]
        ODB -->|XTCE| PGS["Procedure generation"]
    end
    SDB -->|XTCE| ODB

This wiki's simplified drawing of figure 4-1 of 660.2-G-2.151

This is the same flow that ESA projects implement with MIBs, for example the Herschel/Planck satellite database (see MIB tooling and Operations preparation).

docs.title: Too big and too small: profiles and extensions
docs.text:
660.2-G-2 admits that for many users XTCE has "far more features than are needed". The answer is a trimmed profile, colloquially GovSat, published by the OMG as the XTCE US Govt Satellite Conformance Profile (XUSP). XUSP is not a new schema but a set of executable rules, applied after schema validation. The rules allow only one SpaceSystem, limit the number of polynomial coefficients and the length of mnemonics, and define a standard CCSDS header with its parameters. Organisations may relax rules, for example to allow several SpaceSystems, at a cost in compatibility.136

The same report admits that XTCE can also be too small, when a local "must have" feature is missing, and lists six ways to handle it:137

Option How Trade-off a) AncillaryData name/value pairs, available in many places of the schema easiest; files stay schema-valid b) Modify the schema locally edit the XTCE schema "breaking the standard" c) Modify via an external schema extensions in their own namespace, included at the modification point easier to separate standard and local parts d) External schema and file keep extra information in a second file files stay valid, but two files to manage and software must merge them e) Overload elements reuse an element or attribute for another purpose may break software; "least preferred" f) Change request to the OMG propose a change to the specification "very lengthy", worthwhile for features of broad value

The NASA tutorial approaches the same problem from the exchange side. A full exchange works only between parties that agree in advance on which XTCE features to use. Even partners with different packet formats can exchange part of their data: NASA CCSDS and ESA PUS missions exchanged "the majority of telemetry metadata", with some work.180 Its list of points to agree goes below the CCSDS header: polynomial coefficients, alarm levels, floating-point sizes and formats, and bit and byte order. It suggests writing such constraints in machine-processable form, to configure validators and "builder" tools. 660.2-G-2 later describes the XUSP rules as executable rules for a validation program, which is a similar idea.181136 The tutorial names the GSFC JWST translator, the CNES "Best" suite and ESA CryoSat as exchange implementations, and says that several others exist, mostly on the customer side.180

Inference

For a MIB converter, option a) is the natural home for MIB fields with no XTCE element, such as PCF_DARC, CCF_PLAN or the display tables. Option c) would suit features such as status consistency checks that need structure. Neither 660.2-G-2 nor the tutorial mentions the MIB.

docs.title: Implementing XTCE
docs.text: The tutorial describes four ways to implement XTCE: XSLT and XPath, a DOM or SAX parser, a data-binding "autogenerator" that maps schema types to classes (it used JAXB for the GSFC prototypes, and also mentions Eclipse EMF and XMLSpy), or a mix.177 The order of elements matters and must survive the mapping. A native implementation can configure itself from any valid file, but at the time GSFC's prototype had never decommutated real packet data. A University of Bremen implementation had been demonstrated doing so.179 The hardest parts were name references and their instance syntax, container inheritance with include conditions, type inheritance, and dynamic container matching with NextContainer. Of the last, the authors wrote that it had "never been implemented yet that we are aware of".178

docs.title: Implementations and what they support
docs.text:
Two open implementations document their XTCE coverage element by element. Yamcs reads XTCE into its Mission Database. Its manual says that Yamcs "does not seek full compliance" and reads only the parts that match its own concepts. The reader is deliberately tolerant: it ignores unknown tags and "strives to be backward compatible" with XTCE 1.0 and 1.1, so a file that loads is not thereby valid. The manual points to the xtcetools project for validation.188 OpenC3 COSMOS imports XTCE 1.0 to 1.2, uses .xtce files in a target's cmd_tlm folder in place of its own definition files, and exports one schema-validated XTCE 1.2 file per target with openc3.sh cli xtce_converter.191 See MIB tooling for the licences and the Yamcs SCOS-2000 loader.

XTCE feature Yamcs (server manual) OpenC3 COSMOS (documentation, retrieved 2026-11-12) SpaceSystems hierarchy; several files and sub-loaders one SpaceSystem per file Header version and date only ignored on import Integer, Float, Enumerated, String, Binary types yes yes Boolean type yes, but the string forms are only used in comparisons import only, exported as Enumerated AbsoluteTime type yes not supported (planned) RelativeTime type not supported not supported (planned) Arrays telemetry only, not in commands one dimension only Aggregates yes not listed Float encodings IEEE754_1985, MILSTD_1750A, plus a non-XTCE STRING; DEC, IBM, TI not supported FloatDataEncoding listed as supported; the float formats are not stated Byte order big or little endian only big and little endian String sizes whole bytes only; a 0-bit size tag accepted for arguments (non-XTCE, for SCOS-2000 compatibility) TerminationChar export only Calibrators polynomial, linear spline, MathOperation; contextual calibrators PolynomialCalibrator and DefaultCalibrator; SplineCalibrator not supported (planned) Alarms XTCE alarms incl. context alarms; none for StringParameterType DefaultAlarm with StaticAlarmRanges changeThreshold, ErrorDetectCorrect not supported (checksums handled in the data links) ErrorDetectCorrect ignored, no CRC computed Entry location absolute or relative to the previous entry; not relative to the container end containerStart, containerEnd, previousEntry; nextEntry not supported (planned) ParameterSegmentRefEntry, ContainerSegmentRefEntry, DiscreteLookupList, NextContainer not supported not listed MessageSet, StreamSet not supported (packets arrive from the data links) not listed ParameterProperties PhysicalAddressSet, SystemName, TimeAssociation not supported ParameterProperties listed ArgumentRefEntry with IncludeCondition or RepeatEntry not supported ArgumentRefEntry listed ValidRangeSet one range only ValidRange and ValidRangeSet listed ContextSignificanceList, ParameterToSetList, ParametersToSuspendAlarmsOnSet not supported not listed Several CompleteVerifiers the first to succeed completes the command (XTCE requires all) not listed AncillaryData, AliasSet AncillaryData carries Yamcs-specific options (for example UseAsPacketName); AliasSet is not in the unsupported list, which covers everything that is not supported "one way or another" ignored, except COSMOS-namespace aliases used to restore item names

Yamcs column from §3.1 and §3.7.1.2 of its manual and its TM processing description; COSMOS column from its XTCE documentation page, which is outside this wiki's library.188189185190191 "Not listed" means the COSMOS page names the feature neither as supported nor as unsupported.

Yamcs also works around one XTCE rule. Where the schema requires a DynamicValue, for strings or binaries whose size is not given by another parameter, Yamcs accepts a reference to a dummy parameter _yamcs_ignore, and the manual admits that a file without the element would not validate against the 1.2 XSD.186 Both the Yamcs XTCE compatibility list and its binary-type section mention ToBinaryTransformAlgorithm. The list calls it unsupported, yet §3.1.6 shows it in use for an argument type with a leading-size encoder.188187

Inference: what this means for a MIB converted to XTCE

Using the mapping below and the 2025 Solar Orbiter row counts: the 679 CAF curves would become SplineCalibrators, which COSMOS cannot import today. The 3,796 PTC 9 and 47 PTC 10 telemetry parameters need time types. Yamcs lacks the relative one and COSMOS both. The 1,974 CUR rows need context calibrators, which the COSMOS page does not list. The 512 commands with repeated groups (CDF_GRPSIZE > 0, 569 CDF rows) would need RepeatEntry or arrays on arguments, which the Yamcs XTCE reader does not support. And 22 PRF range sets have more than one range (used by 20 command parameters), while Yamcs keeps only one range per ValidRangeSet. Yamcs' own SCOS-2000 loader bypasses XTCE and may handle these cases differently. Its README lists other gaps (see MIB tooling).130

SQL used 
-- solo-2025-09-16.sqlite
SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(DISTINCT CDF_CNAME) FROM cdf WHERE CAST(CDF_GRPSIZE AS INT) > 0;
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT PRV_NUMBR FROM prv GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(*) > 1);
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM cpc WHERE CPC_PRFREF IN
  (SELECT PRV_NUMBR FROM prv GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(*) > 1);
SELECT PCF_PTC, COUNT(*) FROM pcf WHERE PCF_PTC IN ('9','10') GROUP BY 1;
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM caf; SELECT COUNT(*) FROM cur;

docs.title: XTCE and ECSS-E-ST-70-31C
docs.text:
ECSS-E-ST-70-31C, the European monitoring and control data definition standard, defines what data a supplier must deliver with a product so that the customer can integrate, test and operate it. It leaves out how the data is provided: "spreadsheet data or XML" are both outside its scope.97 It organises the data as a space system model: a hierarchy of system elements, each with activities (telecommands, procedures and other commands), reporting data (parameters and compound parameters with raw and engineering representations) and events.9899 It requires interpretation functions (linear interpolation with an extrapolate/invalid choice, or IFL scripts) selected by ordered conditions. Compound parameters can be records, arrays (fixed or variable) or deduced structures. Limit checks have danger and warning limits, each optionally tied to a corrective activity.100101102

Inference

XTCE could serve as a delivery format for 70-31C data: the SpaceSystem hierarchy for system elements, Parameters and Aggregate/Array types for reporting data, MetaCommands for telecommand activities, ContextCalibrators for ordered interpretation functions, and ContextAlarms for limit sets. Neither document says so. 70-31C does not mention XTCE, and the 70-31C requirements for corrective actions, procedures and events have no direct XTCE element.

docs.title: Mapping XTCE to the SCOS-2000 MIB
docs.text:
The MIB is a relational set of ASCII tables defined by the Database Import ICD. Each table is normalised, with mapping tables instead of many-to-many fields.103 The MIB data model page shows how the tables relate. The mapping below follows the ICD's grouping into monitoring, packets, commanding and verification.

Inference: everything in this section is this wiki's analysis

Neither XTCE, the Green Book nor the ICD defines a mapping between XTCE and the MIB. The correspondences below come from comparing the element definitions in 660.0-B-2/660.1-G-2 with the field definitions in ICD issue 7.0. Many are approximate, and some MIB features have no XTCE counterpart. A real converter would need conventions, for example XTCE AncillaryData, to carry the rest.

docs.title: Table-level map
docs.text: MIB table(s) XTCE concept Fit vdf SpaceSystem/Header (version, date) good pcf Parameter + ParameterType (+ UnitSet) good for raw TM. Synthetic parameters need algorithms cur ContextCalibratorList with a ContextMatch per entry good. Both use first-match-wins order caf / cap SplineCalibrator order 1 good mcf PolynomialCalibrator (terms 0 to 4) exact lgf MathOperationCalibrator possible. No native logarithmic calibrator txf / txp EnumeratedParameterType / EnumerationList (value..maxValue → label) good ocf / ocp DefaultAlarm / ContextAlarmList: StaticAlarmRanges, ChangeAlarmRanges, EnumerationAlarm partial (see below) pid / pic / tpcf concrete SequenceContainer + BaseContainer/RestrictionCriteria on APID, type, subtype, PI1, PI2 good plf ParameterRefEntry + LocationInContainerInBits (containerStart) + RepeatEntry + TimeAssociation good vpd EntryList with counters, RepeatEntry, IncludeCondition, dynamic matching, IndirectParameterRefEntry partial grp / grpa / grpk ServiceSet (packet groups only) weak. XTCE excludes "data grouping" dpf, gpf, spf and their detail tables none: displays are out of XTCE scope none tcp / pcpc / pcdf abstract MetaCommand + CommandContainer (packet header) good ccf concrete MetaCommand good cdf CommandContainer/EntryList: FixedValueEntry, ArgumentRefEntry, ArgumentAssignment good cpc Argument + ArgumentType good cca / ccs SplineCalibrator in an argument encoding (eng → raw) good paf / pas EnumeratedArgumentType good prf / prv ValidRangeSet good for ranges. Discrete value lists are awkward ptv TransmissionConstraintList good cvs / cve / cvp VerifierSet with CheckWindow partial csf / css / sdf / csp BlockMetaCommand (fixed steps only) weak. MIB sequences have formal parameters and timing pst, psv, cps, pvs, psm none. Closest is ArgumentAssignmentList none dst none: command routing is "data distribution" none

docs.title: Parameter types: PTC/PFC to XTCE
docs.text:
The MIB's type system is the PUS PTC/PFC pair, as SCOS-2000 implements it.129 See MIB parameter types and PUS parameter types.

PTC (MIB meaning) XTCE ParameterType DataEncoding 1 Boolean (1 bit) Boolean Integer, unsigned, 1 bit 2 Enumerated (up to 32 bits) Enumerated if textually calibrated, otherwise Integer Integer, unsigned, PFC bits 3 Unsigned integer (4 to 64 bits; 48 and 64 not supported by SCOS-2000) Integer signed="false" Integer, unsigned 4 Signed integer Integer Integer, twosComplement 5 Real: PFC ½ IEEE 32/64 bit, PFC ¾ MIL-STD-1750A 32/48 bit Float Float IEEE754_1985 or MILSTD_1750A 6 Bit string (handled as unsigned integer up to 32 bits) Binary or Integer Binary 7 Octet string Binary Binary 8 Character string String String, US-ASCII 9 Absolute time (CDS, CUC, Unix) AbsoluteTime, ReferenceTime/Epoch Integer with scale (see time codes) 10 Relative time (CUC) RelativeTime Integer, twosComplement, with scale 11 Deduced (none) dynamic container matching or IndirectParameterRefEntry 13 Saved synthetic type of the related synthetic parameter none (derived)

The MIB meanings are those of ICD Appendix A. The XTCE columns are this wiki's choice.12954

docs.title: Monitoring parameters (pcf and calibrations)
docs.text: MIB field XTCE PCF_NAME (8 characters), PCF_DESCR (24) Parameter/@name, @shortDescription. MIB names are case-insensitive for uniqueness, XTCE names case-sensitive1049 PCF_PID (on-board parameter ID) AliasSet alias (for example namespace "PUS") or AncillaryData PCF_UNIT UnitSet/Unit PCF_PTC / PCF_PFC ParameterType class + DataEncoding (table above) PCF_CATEG N / S / T numeric type with numeric calibrator / Enumerated / String106 PCF_NATUR R dataSource="telemetered" PCF_NATUR D, P, H (OL, SPEL or hard-coded synthetic) dataSource="derived" + AlgorithmSet (CustomAlgorithm or InputOutputTriggerAlgorithm)107 PCF_NATUR C + PCF_PARVAL dataSource="constant" + initialValue PCF_NATUR S + PCF_RELATED derived parameter copying another one. No XTCE notion of "saved in synthetic packets" PCF_VALID = PCF_VALPAR ValidityCondition (Comparison). SCOS-2000 also ANDs in the validity of the validity parameter105 PCF_CURTX / CUR (CUR_RLCHK = CUR_VALPAR, by CUR_POS) DefaultCalibrator / ContextCalibrator with ContextMatch. Both use the first match109 CAF_INTER P / F SplineCalibrator/@extrapolate true / false. In the MIB it is a property of the curve, not the parameter110 MCF_POL1..POL5 (\(Y = A_0 + A_1X + \ldots + A_4X^4\)) PolynomialCalibrator, Terms with exponent 0 to 4112 LGF (\(Y = 1/[A_0 + A_1\ln X + \ldots + A_4\ln^4 X]\)) MathOperationCalibrator112 TXP_FROM..TXP_TO → TXP_ALTXT Enumeration/@value, @maxValue, @label11156 PCF_DECIM ToString/NumberFormat (not detailed in the available sources) PCF_CORR / PCF_OBTID ReferenceTime/Epoch or OffsetFrom. XTCE has no notion of time correlation in the available sources108 PCF_USCON (status consistency) none

docs.title: Monitoring checks (ocf and ocp)
docs.text:
MIB XTCE OCF_NBCHCK (consecutive violating samples) @minViolations11347 OCF_INTER U / C (raw or calibrated limits) XTCE numeric ranges apply to the parameter's calibrated (host) value. Raw-value limits would need AlarmConditions with useCalibratedValue="false"11333 OCP_TYPE S (soft) / H (hard) limit pair StaticAlarmRanges: for example WarningRange and SevereRange, following the Green Book's tri-colour recommendation11451 OCP_TYPE S/H for status parameters (expected values) EnumerationAlarmList (levels per label) OCP_TYPE D (delta) ChangeAlarmRanges changeType="changePerSample" changeBasis="absoluteChange" OCP_RLCHK = OCP_VALPAR (applicability) ContextAlarm/ContextMatch OCP_TYPE C (status consistency), E (event generation) none

Inference: limit boundaries differ

In SCOS-2000, "In case the telemetry value matches exactly one of the limit values, this is not considered as an OOL condition."115 In XTCE's outside ranges, the minInclusive and maxInclusive values are themselves in the alarm band.51 A literal copy of OCP_LVALU and OCP_HVALU into minInclusive and maxInclusive would therefore raise alarms at the exact limit values, which SCOS-2000 does not. A converter would need exclusive bounds or adjusted values. The Green Book's StaticAlarmRanges examples use only minInclusive/maxInclusive, but its description of the XTCE 1.2 MultiRange alarm lists both inclusive and exclusive interval forms, so a MultiRange alarm is the likelier way to express SCOS-2000's semantics.32 The attribute names for exclusive bounds are not legible in the available text. SCOS-2000 also stops at the first applicable check (or soft/hard pair) unless configured otherwise, and limit checks always come in low/high pairs.115

docs.title: Telemetry packets (pid, pic, tpcf, plf, vpd)
docs.text:
SCOS-2000 identifies a packet by APID, type and subtype, plus up to two extra identification fields whose position comes from PIC, giving an SPID.116117 In XTCE this is naturally a hierarchy. An abstract CCSDS header container restricts on APID. An abstract PUS header container restricts on service type and subtype. Each concrete SPID container restricts on PI1/PI2 values. The ICD warns that type, subtype and PI fields must sit at the same position in every packet of a given type and subtype.116 XTCE does not impose that constraint, so the mapping from MIB to XTCE is safe, while the reverse may not be.

  • PLF_OFFBY, PLF_OFFBI (octet and bit of the first occurrence, from the start of the source packet header) become LocationInContainerInBits referenceLocation="containerStart" with value 8 × OFFBY + OFFBI.11869
  • PLF_NBOCC, PLF_LGOCC (super-commutation) become RepeatEntry with Count = NBOCC − 1 and offset LGOCC − width. XTCE counts extra copies and measures the gap between them.11869
  • PLF_TIME, PLF_TDOCC (millisecond offsets) become TimeAssociation/@offset (in seconds by default). XTCE has no per-occurrence delta.11862
  • PID_INTER (period of periodic packets, used for expiry) becomes DefaultRateInStream. TPCF_SIZE becomes BinaryEncoding/SizeInBits.11665
  • VPD (variable packets): VPD_GRPSIZE counters become RepeatEntry with a DynamicValue count. VPD_FIXREP becomes a fixed count. VPD_CHOICE becomes dynamic container matching. VPD_PIDREF (deduced parameters by on-board ID) becomes IndirectParameterRefEntry, matching PCF_PID through an alias namespace.1196834

docs.title: Commands (tcp/pcdf, ccf, cdf, cpc)
docs.text: MIB XTCE TCP + PCDF (header layout) abstract MetaCommand whose CommandContainer holds the CCSDS/PUS header fields CCF_TYPE, CCF_STYPE, CCF_APID, CCF_ACK ArgumentAssignments or RestrictionCriteria assertions on the header parameters CCF_CRITICAL Y DefaultSignificance consequenceLevel (for example critical). The ICD leaves extra protection to the mission121 CCF_ILSCOPE (G, L, S, B, F, T, N) / CCF_ILSTAGE (R, U, O, A, C) Interlock with scopeToSpaceSystem / verificationToWaitFor. XTCE has no equivalent of "local source" scope or "only on failure"12189 CCF_PLAN, CCF_EXEC, CCF_HIPRI, CCF_MAPID, CCF_SUBSCHEDID none (AncillaryData) CDF_ELTYPE A (fixed area) FixedValueEntry (value in hex, at most 32 bits)122 CDF_ELTYPE F (fixed parameter) ArgumentAssignment in a derived MetaCommand, or a FixedValueEntry CDF_ELTYPE E (editable) ArgumentRefEntry + Argument CDF_BIT (sort order; elements are packed without gaps) EntryList order. The MIB uses CDF_BIT only to sort122 CDF_GRPSIZE (repeated groups with counter N) RepeatEntry with a DynamicValue count from the counter argument CDF_INTER T + CDF_TMID (dynamic default from TM) none. The closest is an argument initialValue CPC_PTC/PFC, CPC_UNIT, CPC_DISPFMT, CPC_RADIX ArgumentType + encoding + UnitSet (+ AncillaryData) CPC_CATEG C + CPC_CCAREF / T + CPC_PAFREF calibrator in the argument encoding / EnumeratedArgumentType CPC_CATEG A (command ID) / P (parameter ID) none CPC_PRFREF → PRF/PRV ValidRangeSet. The MIB check passes when the value is within or equal to min/max128 PTV (parameter = value, ANDed, validity implied) TransmissionConstraint (ComparisonList)123

docs.title: Verification (cvs, cve, cvp)
docs.text:
MIB XTCE CVS_TYPE A (application acceptance) AcceptedVerifier CVS_TYPE S (start of execution), 0-9 (progress) ExecutionVerifier (with PercentageComplete for progress) CVS_TYPE C (completion) CompleteVerifier CCF_ILSTAGE R, U, O (ground reception, uplink, on-board reception) TransferredToRange, TransferredFromRange, Received (approximate) CVS_SOURCE R (PUS ST[01] report) verifier with ContainerRef to the report container CVS_SOURCE V + CVE (CVE_VAL ± CVE_TOL, ANDed) ComparisonList. A tolerance needs two comparisons CVS_START (seconds after release, or after execution for time-tagged commands, before the window opens) and CVS_INTERVAL (length of the sampling interval used to compute the overall window) CheckWindow timeToStartChecking / timeToStopChecking relative to commandRelease. The stop time has to be derived from CVS_INTERVAL by SCOS-2000's window rule, which the ICD refers to another document for CVE_CHECK B / S (also drives status consistency) none

The MIB meanings are from the ICD.125126121 In the MIB, at most one stage of each type can attach to a command, and SCOS-2000 processes progress reports only for stage 0. In XTCE, a MetaCommand may have several Complete verifiers.12712521

docs.title: What has no XTCE counterpart
docs.text:
• Displays (alphanumeric, graphic and scrolling displays: tables dpf/dpc, gpf/gpc, spf/spc, and printouts ppf/ppc). XTCE excludes displays. SCOS-2000 itself has kept display definitions outside the MIB database since R5.0.6120
  • Command sequences with formal parameters, timing and nesting. From SCOS-2000 R5.0 these are kept as XML files in the FARC. That XML is not XTCE.124 BlockMetaCommand covers only fixed groups.93
  • Parameter sets (PST/PSV/CPS/PVS/PSM), command routing (DST), status consistency checking, event-generating checks, dynamic defaults, and SCOS-2000 configuration hooks such as PCF_DARC or PID_EVENT.
  • Time correlation. The MIB says whether to correlate and with which OBT clock (PCF_CORR, PCF_OBTID). Correlation coefficients are run-time data. See Time correlation in SCOS-2000.

docs.title: Worked example 1: a Solar Orbiter housekeeping parameter
docs.text:
NIH0K31T ("ccT") is defined in the 2025 Solar Orbiter MIB as follows:130

Table Row (abridged) pcf NAME NIH0K31T, DESCR ccT, UNIT degC, PTC 4, PFC 12 (16-bit signed), CATEG N, NATUR R, CURTX CIHP0100TM, DECIM 2 caf CIHP0100TM "Convert raw to degC for IH,HK,IS", ENGFMT R, RAWFMT I, NCURVE 2, INTER blank (ICD default F) cap (−32768 → −327.68), (32767 → 327.67) ocf NBCHCK 2, NBOOL 2, INTER C, CODIN R ocp POS 1 type S: −40 to 40; POS 2 type H: −50 to 65 plf SPID 56316 at octet 66, bit 0 (also SPID 56326) pid / pic / tpcf SPID 56316 "OBC HK Summary Packet (STBY & OBS)": type 3, subtype 25, APID 1316, PI1 32; PIC for (3,25): PI1 at octet 16, 8 bits; TPCF_SIZE 70

A possible XTCE rendering, constructed by this wiki and not validated against the schema, follows the Green Book's syntax examples:445171

<xtce:FloatParameterType name="NIH0K31T_T" shortDescription="ccT">
  <xtce:UnitSet><xtce:Unit>degC</xtce:Unit></xtce:UnitSet>
  <xtce:IntegerDataEncoding sizeInBits="16" encoding="twosComplement">
    <xtce:DefaultCalibrator>
      <!-- CAF/CAP CIHP0100TM; CAF_INTER default 'F' = no extrapolation -->
      <xtce:SplineCalibrator order="1" extrapolate="false">
        <xtce:SplinePoint raw="-32768" calibrated="-327.68"/>
        <xtce:SplinePoint raw="32767"  calibrated="327.67"/>
      </xtce:SplineCalibrator>
    </xtce:DefaultCalibrator>
  </xtce:IntegerDataEncoding>
  <!-- OCF_NBCHCK = 2; OCP soft -40..40, hard -50..65 (calibrated, OCF_INTER = C) -->
  <xtce:DefaultAlarm minViolations="2">
    <xtce:StaticAlarmRanges>
      <xtce:WarningRange minInclusive="-40" maxInclusive="40"/>
      <xtce:SevereRange  minInclusive="-50" maxInclusive="65"/>
    </xtce:StaticAlarmRanges>
  </xtce:DefaultAlarm>
</xtce:FloatParameterType>

<xtce:Parameter name="NIH0K31T" parameterTypeRef="NIH0K31T_T"/>

<xtce:SequenceContainer name="SPID_56316" shortDescription="OBC HK Summary Packet (STBY & OBS)">
  <xtce:EntryList>
    <xtce:ParameterRefEntry parameterRef="NIH0K31T">
      <!-- PLF_OFFBY 66, PLF_OFFBI 0: 66 x 8 = 528 bits from the start of the packet -->
      <xtce:LocationInContainerInBits referenceLocation="containerStart">
        <xtce:FixedValue>528</xtce:FixedValue>
      </xtce:LocationInContainerInBits>
    </xtce:ParameterRefEntry>
  </xtce:EntryList>
  <xtce:BaseContainer containerRef="PUS_TM_3_25">
    <xtce:RestrictionCriteria>
      <xtce:ComparisonList>
        <xtce:Comparison parameterRef="APID" value="1316"/>
        <!-- PIC (3,25): PI1 is the 8-bit field at octet 16 (the SID) -->
        <xtce:Comparison parameterRef="PI1_SID" value="32"/>
      </xtce:ComparisonList>
    </xtce:RestrictionCriteria>
  </xtce:BaseContainer>
</xtce:SequenceContainer>

Inference

RestrictionCriteria is a MatchCriteria, and the Green Book combines several conditions in it with a ComparisonList, in which every Comparison must be true.7131 The example above follows that form. The schema is the normative reference and was not checked. Because containerStart is measured from the start of the concrete container, the container hierarchy must cover the whole packet from the primary header onwards, which matches the MIB's convention that PLF offsets count from the start of the source packet header.118 The soft-to-Warning and hard-to-Severe choice follows the Green Book's tri-colour recommendation. The boundary caveat above also applies: SCOS-2000 does not flag exactly −40 or 40.

docs.title: Worked example 2: a Solar Orbiter telecommand
docs.text:
ZCD00901 "Change Time Report Generation Rate" is PUS TC(9,1) to APID 172. It uses packet header NOM_TC, has acknowledgement flags 9, is non-critical (CCF_CRITICAL N), has no interlock (ILSCOPE N, ILSTAGE C) and one CDF element. That element is the editable parameter PCD09011 "Time Rep Gen rate": 8 bits, PTC 2 PFC 8, CPC_CATEG T with textual de-calibration CCDT0043TX (EVERY_TMFR = 0 … EVERY_256_TMFR = 8), default taken from the CPC entry. Its verification profile (cvp) attaches stages 14001 (type A, report-based, start 0 s, interval 20 s) and 14007 (type C, report-based, 0 s, 20 s).130

<xtce:EnumeratedArgumentType name="PCD09011_T">
  <xtce:IntegerDataEncoding sizeInBits="8"/>
  <xtce:EnumerationList>
    <xtce:Enumeration label="EVERY_TMFR" value="0"/>
    <!-- ... values 1 to 7 ... -->
    <xtce:Enumeration label="EVERY_256_TMFR" value="8"/>
  </xtce:EnumerationList>
</xtce:EnumeratedArgumentType>

<xtce:MetaCommand name="ZCD00901" shortDescription="Change Time Report Generation Rate">
  <xtce:BaseMetaCommand metaCommandRef="NOM_TC">
    <xtce:ArgumentAssignmentList>
      <xtce:ArgumentAssignment argumentName="APID"    argumentValue="172"/>
      <xtce:ArgumentAssignment argumentName="Service" argumentValue="9"/>
      <xtce:ArgumentAssignment argumentName="Subtype" argumentValue="1"/>
      <xtce:ArgumentAssignment argumentName="Ack"     argumentValue="9"/>
    </xtce:ArgumentAssignmentList>
  </xtce:BaseMetaCommand>
  <xtce:ArgumentList>
    <xtce:Argument name="PCD09011" argumentTypeRef="PCD09011_T"/>
  </xtce:ArgumentList>
  <xtce:CommandContainer name="ZCD00901_CC">
    <xtce:EntryList>
      <xtce:ArgumentRefEntry argumentRef="PCD09011"/>
    </xtce:EntryList>
    <xtce:BaseContainer containerRef="NOM_TC_CC"/>
  </xtce:CommandContainer>
  <xtce:VerifierSet>
    <!-- CVS 14001 (A, R) and 14007 (C, R): match the PUS ST[01] acceptance/completion reports;
         window opens 0 s after release, CVS_INTERVAL 20 s -->
  </xtce:VerifierSet>
</xtce:MetaCommand>

This XML was constructed by this wiki following the Green Book's descriptions of BaseMetaCommand, ArgumentAssignment and CommandContainer. The attribute spellings in ArgumentAssignment and the verifier details were not checked against the schema.818391 The header parameters of NOM_TC (APID, service, subtype, ack flags, source ID) are described on the Space Packet page.

docs.title: Scale of a full conversion
docs.text:
Converting the whole 2025 Solar Orbiter MIB (VDF 25925PFM, "20250916-CSW3.1.2_MAS7.33") would involve the following, from this wiki's row counts:130

Item MIB rows XTCE result Monitoring parameters 126 745 pcf Parameters (98 739 numeric raw, 26 328 status raw, 94 text raw; 1 582 synthetic D; 2 saved S) Parameter types by PTC 1: 4 380 · 2: 29 443 · 3: 50 341 · 4: 1 950 · 5: 29 718 · 6: 950 · 7: 5 990 · 8: 120 · 9: 3 796 · 10: 47 · 11: 8 · 13: 2 ParameterTypes (many shareable) Calibrations 679 caf (7 830 points), 229 mcf, 0 lgf, 1 003 txf (35 032 txp), 1 974 cur rows for 907 parameters Spline, Polynomial and Enumeration definitions, ContextCalibrators Checks 5 338 ocf, 7 369 ocp (H 4 153, S 3 096, D 105, C 15) DefaultAlarm/ContextAlarm (C has no equivalent) Packets 11 150 pid, 256 pic, 400 792 plf, 19 863 vpd SequenceContainers and entries Commands 5 454 ccf, 47 609 cdf (A 16 906, F 17 681, E 13 022), 7 155 cpc MetaCommands, entries and Arguments Command calibrations and ranges 99 cca, 624 paf, 565 prf (1 072 prv) argument calibrators, enumerations, ValidRangeSets Verification 206 cvs (A/R 16, C/R 23, C/V 167), 171 cve, 10 697 cvp VerifierSets PTV 5 ptv TransmissionConstraints Sequences 3 404 csf, 13 879 css outside XTCE, apart from simple BlockMetaCommands

How many ParameterTypes the conversion would produce depends on the type policy discussed above. Of the 125 161 raw (PCF_NATUR R) parameters, 90 954 have no calibration (no PCF_CURTX, no CUR row), no unit and no monitoring check. Those 90 954 fall into only 184 distinct PTC/PFC combinations, the most common being 5/1 (28 119), 3/12 (14 237), 3/14 (13 883), ¾ (13 309), 2/1 (3 358) and 1/0 (2 542). Counting all 119 240 raw parameters without checks or CUR rows, there are 1 643 distinct combinations of PTC, PFC, calibration and unit.130

Inference

A converter following 660.2-G-2's common practice would write 126 745 ParameterTypes, one per parameter. One following the generic-type practice that the Yamcs manual describes could share 184 types among the 90 954 plain parameters. Validity conditions are not part of the type, because XTCE puts them in the Parameter's properties.14318262

SQL used 
-- solo-2025-09-16.sqlite (MIB__20250916M25925PFMS001_SOL)
SELECT * FROM vdf;
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM pcf;  -- and likewise for every table in the scale table
SELECT PCF_CATEG, PCF_NATUR, COUNT(*) FROM pcf GROUP BY 1,2;
SELECT PCF_PTC, COUNT(*) FROM pcf GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY CAST(PCF_PTC AS INT);
SELECT OCP_TYPE, COUNT(*) FROM ocp GROUP BY 1;
SELECT COL2 AS CVS_TYPE, COL3 AS CVS_SOURCE, COUNT(*) FROM cvs GROUP BY 1,2;
SELECT CDF_ELTYPE, COUNT(*) FROM cdf GROUP BY 1;
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT CUR_PNAME) FROM cur;
-- worked example 1
SELECT * FROM pcf WHERE PCF_NAME='NIH0K31T';
SELECT * FROM caf WHERE CAF_NUMBR='CIHP0100TM'; SELECT * FROM cap WHERE CAP_NUMBR='CIHP0100TM';
SELECT * FROM ocf WHERE OCF_NAME='NIH0K31T';    SELECT * FROM ocp WHERE OCP_NAME='NIH0K31T';
SELECT l.PLF_SPID, l.PLF_OFFBY, l.PLF_OFFBI, p.* FROM plf l JOIN pid p ON p.PID_SPID=l.PLF_SPID
  WHERE l.PLF_NAME='NIH0K31T';
SELECT * FROM pic WHERE PIC_TYPE='3' AND PIC_STYPE='25'; SELECT * FROM tpcf WHERE TPCF_SPID='56316';
-- worked example 2
SELECT * FROM ccf WHERE CCF_CNAME='ZCD00901'; SELECT * FROM cdf WHERE CDF_CNAME='ZCD00901';
SELECT * FROM cpc WHERE CPC_NAME='PCD09011';  SELECT * FROM pas WHERE PAS_NUMBR='CCDT0043TX';
SELECT * FROM cvp WHERE COL1='ZCD00901';      SELECT * FROM cvs WHERE COL1 IN ('14001','14007');
-- shareable types
SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(DISTINCT PCF_PTC||'/'||PCF_PFC) FROM pcf
 WHERE IFNULL(PCF_CURTX,'')='' AND IFNULL(PCF_UNIT,'')='' AND PCF_NATUR='R'
   AND PCF_NAME NOT IN (SELECT OCF_NAME FROM ocf) AND PCF_NAME NOT IN (SELECT CUR_PNAME FROM cur);
SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(DISTINCT PCF_PTC||'/'||PCF_PFC||'/'||IFNULL(PCF_CURTX,'')||'/'||IFNULL(PCF_UNIT,''))
  FROM pcf WHERE PCF_NATUR='R'
   AND PCF_NAME NOT IN (SELECT OCF_NAME FROM ocf) AND PCF_NAME NOT IN (SELECT CUR_PNAME FROM cur);

docs.title: Space Link Extension (SLE): concept and architecture
docs.text:
Space Link Extension (SLE) is the CCSDS family of ground-to-ground services that carries space link data units (telemetry frames, operational control fields, telecommand CLTUs and packets) between the ground station that terminates the radio link and the mission control centre that actually uses the data. CCSDS defines cross support as one organisation lending part of its space data system to serve another organisation's mission, and SLE is the standard interface where most of that cross support happens: between the tracking stations of one agency and the mission-specific ground systems of another.12137 With SLE, a control centre can bind to a station it does not own, ask for "all frames from this antenna" or "radiate this CLTU at 12:00:03", and receive annotated, time-stamped data over an ordinary terrestrial network, without a mission-specific gateway.3

This page explains the concept and architecture common to all SLE services. The individual services have their own pages: return services RAF, RCF and ROCF, the forward CLTU service, the Forward Space Packet service, and the wire protocol and software interface, ISP1 and the SLE API. The formal architecture model and the management of agreements and service packages are treated in depth on the cross support reference model and service management; this page summarises what every SLE reader needs from them. In the protocol stack, SLE sits above the TM, AOS, USLP and TC data link protocols and their channel coding and CLTU layers; see the CCSDS overview and the standards map.

At a glance

Item Value Concept document CCSDS 910.3-G-3, Cross Support Concept—Part 1: Space Link Extension Services, Green Book, March 20064 Reference model CCSDS 910.4-B-2, Cross Support Reference Model—Part 1: Space Link Extension Services, Blue Book, October 2005, Editorial Correction 1 (July 2007); the library copy carries the CCSDS "Historical Document" banner134133 Transfer service specifications in this library RAF 911.1-B-5, RCF 911.2-B-4, ROCF 911.5-B-4, FCLTU 912.1-B-5 (all July 2023 issues);5678 FSP 912.3-B-3 (August 2016, historical copy)175 Wire protocol ISP1, CCSDS 913.1-B-2 (September 2015): ASN.1 BER over TCP/IP9 Programming interface SLE API core, CCSDS 914.0-M-2 (September 2015), a C++ component API,10 with service-specific books such as the RAF API 915.1-M-2 and the FSP API 916.3-M-2 (both September 2015)166172 Roles Provider = the object closer to the space link (station); user = the object farther away (control centre)11 Directions Return (space to ground, e.g. telemetry) and forward (ground to space, e.g. telecommand)12 Phases Definition phase (service management) and utilization phase (data transfer)13 Provider states 1 'unbound', 2 'ready', 3 'active'14

docs.title: Why SLE exists
docs.text:
The CCSDS space link protocols define how data crosses the radio link. They stop at the ground antenna. A real mission needs the same data units at a control centre, possibly on another continent, possibly hours later, and enriched with facts that only the receiving station knows, such as the reception time. Without standard services, interoperation needs ad hoc gateways designed for each new mission.3 The SLE concept report states the problem plainly: standardising the ground interfaces for transport and management of space data reduces the technical, management and operational cost of cross support.15

The report lists the expected benefits: agencies can cross-support each other more efficiently; station owners can offer standard services to any CCSDS-compliant spacecraft; data users can reach their payloads through a familiar interface over the internet or ISDN; interfaces can be reused mission after mission; a commercial market for TT&C products is stimulated; and a provider only implements the services it actually needs.3 The ECSS communications handbook makes the same point from the European side. Two CCSDS-compliant implementations may still be unable to interoperate because they chose different options, and the handbook says that SLE has "to a great extent" resolved this problem for ground-segment cross support.16

CCSDS divides cross support services into three kinds:17137

Kind Scope CCSDS document part SLE services Extend the CCSDS space link services across the ground Cross Support Concept Part 1 (this page) Ground communications services The communications that underlie the ground element, for example relaying operational data Part 2 (no plans to produce it in 2006) Ground domain services Services that do not use space link data structures: tracking, spacecraft database exchange, mission planning Part 3 (under consideration in 2006)

The part numbers in this table follow the 2006 concept report and the 2005 reference model, which plans Part 2 for ground communications services and Part 3 for ground domain services.137 The 2015 SLE API books, both the core and the RAF book, number them the other way round (Part 2 Ground Domain Services, Part 3 Ground Communications Services).129165

The SLE services themselves have two parts. Data transfer services move space link data units between stations, control centres and end users. Management services schedule and provision the transfer services.13 Management happens mostly in a definition phase; data flows in a utilization phase, either in real time or offline with respect to the pass.13

docs.title: The cross support reference model
docs.text:
The concept report explains SLE. The normative baseline is a separate Recommended Standard, CCSDS 910.4-B-2, Cross Support Reference Model—Part 1: Space Link Extension Services. It provides the common basis and the reference against which every SLE service specification is written and kept consistent.135 Its framework has four parts: the identification of an SLE system and its environment; an architecture model with a functional view and a management (cross support) view; the common characteristics of SLE services together with a template for their specifications; and the identification of the SLE transfer services, each of which is specified in its own Recommended Standard.135 Ground systems that provide services complying with the SLE specifications are called SLE systems.135

The model makes four simplifying assumptions: one space mission, one spacecraft, telemetry and telecommand that comply with the CCSDS space link standards, and ground end users that all belong to one mission management entity. Sharing ground systems between missions is not modelled, but it is not ruled out either. Processing of the contents of packet data fields, services that do not transport CCSDS space link data, and the ground communications underneath SLE are all outside the model.136 It is explicitly not a specification or design of a real SLE system.136

The library copy is issue 2 of October 2005, which added subsections on cross support security and on the time span of agreements and packages to issue 1 of May 1996. Editorial Correction 1 of July 2007 repaired two figures.134 The copy carries the CCSDS "Historical Document" banner, which means the document has either been replaced by a newer issue or withdrawn; which of the two applies is not stated in the available sources.133 The 2015 API books for RAF and FSP still cite issue 2 as a normative reference.167173 The reference model is also older than some of the services it frames. The 2023 RCF and ROCF standards each note that 910.4 defines separate Master Channel and Virtual Channel services, which RCF and ROCF merge, and that a future issue of the reference model is expected to follow.179180
