docs.title: Vocabulary of the model
docs.text:
The architecture model is object oriented. Its objects have ports, through which they provide services to other objects.139140 Many of the terms used throughout the SLE specifications are defined here:

Term Definition in the reference model Port type Ports involved in providing different services are of different types Symmetric / asymmetric ports Symmetric ports each offer all operations of the service; asymmetric ports offer different operations, one acting as consumer and the other as supplier. All SLE services use asymmetric ports. Consumer / supplier Direction of data transfer: from the supplier port to the consumer port Service user / provider The provider offers a service through its ports. Of two objects, the one closer to the space link is the provider, whatever the direction of data flow Invoker / performer One object invokes an operation, the other performs it; most objects do both Binding, initiator, responder Two ports of the same type with an association are bound. The initiator requests the binding and the responder completes it Physical channel The capability to transfer one stream of bits in one direction Space link One forward and/or one return RF carrier, each with one or more physical channels Space link session A continuous period in which an SLE system lets one or more physical channels of a space link be used SL-DU A data structure defined by the space link standards (frame, packet, CLTU, OCF, ...) Space link data channel A uniquely identifiable stream of SL-DUs of one type SLE-SDU An annotated SL-DU and/or control information about processing and transfer. In the forward direction an SLE-SDU may carry control alone, for example a COP directive. For the RF signals the SLE-SDU equals the SL-DU SLE data channel A uniquely identifiable stream of SLE-SDUs of one type, derived from a space link data channel

Sources: definitions, environment and data exchange of the reference model.139140141142 Annex A of the model refines the data units. Data-bearing SLE-SDUs carry data, annotation and, possibly, channel status, which reports changes in the condition of the channel. Separate channel status SLE-SDUs exist for the times when no data unit is available to carry the status. SLE-PDUs are either data-bearing (encapsulating SLE-SDUs) or stand-alone protocol control messages. Annotation and channel status remain valid across several user-provider associations, while protocol control information belongs to one association only.143

docs.title: The cross support environment
docs.text:
A space data system has a space element (the spacecraft, its payloads and operations subsystems) and a ground element, linked by the space link.18 The ground element contains an SLE System, which extends the transfer of forward and return data between the ground termination of the space link and the Mission Data Operation System (MDOS), the mission-dedicated system that sources forward data and sinks return data. In a mission, the MDOS manages the SLE System.19 The SLE System performs RF modulation and demodulation (RF and ranging), ground termination of the space link protocols, annotation of the data, terrestrial networking, and the interfaces to ground-side protocol processing.19

The reference model adds precise roles inside the MDOS. Mission User Entities (MUEs) are the sources of forward data and the sinks of return data; one MUE may receive several transfer service instances. The MDOS holds exactly one SLE Utilization Management (SLE-UM) and one or more MUEs, and it may work with several SLE systems at once, harmonising them itself. The SLE-UM manages only what concerns the SLE system, not the whole MDOS or the spacecraft. It is part of the Mission Management Entity, which coordinates space and ground for the mission. The MDOS is a logical model: its MUEs may be spread over several sites or belong to several agencies.141144 In a multi-spacecraft mission each spacecraft is a separate space element.141

docs.title: Extension over distance, in information and in time
docs.text:
The space link protocols divide one physical channel into logical space data channels (for example virtual channels), each carrying frames or packets. SLE gives ground users access to these channels and extends them in three ways:22

Extension Meaning Example from the concept report Over distance Protocol processing may happen at sites far from the antenna. Each site must forward enough context for the next site to finish processing, because space link protocols are not strictly layered. The APID is only unique within a spacecraft; it is qualified by the SCID in the frame header, so a site that extracts packets far from the frame processing site needs the SCID too.23 In information (annotation) Facts known only at reception are added to each data unit. Earth reception time, receiving location, data unit quality, sequence continuity; also data type, operations mode, and format parameters such as frame size.24 In time Data can be delivered later than they were received, from a brief delay (a reduced ground communication rate) to a long one (temporary storage and later forwarding). Temporary storage at a processing facility followed by later packet extraction.2526

Information that is not tied to a single data unit, such as "loss of frame synchronization", must also be conveyed, and each service specification defines it.23 On the return services page you can see exactly which annotation fields the RAF, RCF and ROCF services carry.

docs.title: Functional groups and SLE complexes
docs.text:
SLE describes processing with SLE Functional Groups (SLE-FGs). An SLE-FG is a building block derived from the layered functionality of channels, frames and packets in the space link protocols. It cannot be decomposed further, and it represents the set of SLE services that a real system can implement at that layer.27 A physical facility that implements a set of functional groups is an SLE Complex. All functions of one functional group must sit in one complex, but different groups can be spread over complexes run by different organisations.20 A complex has a service provision component and a management component, and it is one collection of resources under a single management authority: one station, a network of stations, or, for packet services delivered to payload control centres, a spacecraft control centre.2829

The reference model makes this formal. There are exactly eight SLE-FG types in three categories: three return SLE-FGs, two forward AOS SLE-FGs and three forward telecommand SLE-FGs.145 Each SLE-FG has transfer ports of two kinds, Transfer User (T-U) and Transfer Provider (T-P), and exactly one Function-Management Provider port (FM-P) for set-up and configuration. A T-U port is bound to a T-P port of the same type on another SLE-FG or on the space element. A T-P port is bound to a T-U port of another SLE-FG or of an MUE. Every service instance uses its own pair of port instances.145 At the complex level, an SLE complex exposes at least one user and one provider transfer port, plus a single Complex Management port bound to SLE Utilization Management. A real system that supports several missions exposes one Complex Management port per mission. A complex need not expose every SLE-FG port: for a Return Space Packet service produced from the RF signal, several SLE-FGs are cascaded inside the complex, and only the RF input and the packet output are visible outside.146 Complex Management negotiates service packages with SLE-UM, distributes set-up and configuration parameters to its SLE-FGs, and collects and consolidates their reports.146

A return service instance is produced by a chain of up to three functional groups, and a forward service instance likewise. The table shows what an organisation must implement to offer each kind of service:303132

The dotted arrows matter. The CLCW, carried in the telemetry Operational Control Field, is needed by the CLTU provider to know whether the physical uplink is available, and by the VC and packet provider to decide whether TC frames must be retransmitted under COP-1.33 Some services cannot be separated: Return Insert processing must live in the same functional group as Return All Frames because insert data appear in every frame.34

The concept report's annex C illustrates several real cross support layouts: a station with extensive capability (all return processing up to packet extraction in the station), a station with limited capability (frames sent to separate real-time and offline processing centres), and an SLE System of two complexes in which a ground terminal complex does only space link processing while a remote complex does frame processing, packet extraction, CLTU generation and VC data insertion.35

docs.title: Ports and operation types
docs.text:
In the reference model an SLE service is described by the set of operations that can be invoked and performed through one bound pair of ports of the same type.147 Each SLE service is provided between exactly one port instance of one object and one port instance of another.140 The model names four generic operation types for transfer ports. Who invokes each one depends on the direction, because the roles of supplier and consumer swap:147149150

Operation type Purpose Return port (provider = supplier) Forward port (provider = consumer) Transfer_Data Carries an SLE-SDU with space link data invoked by the provider invoked by the user Transfer_Set Initialises or updates the service attributes and configuration options of the user's instance invoked by the user invoked by the user Transfer_Get Retrieves status and configuration of the instance invoked by the user invoked by the user Transfer_Notification Reports status (periodic or on event) and accounting information invoked by the provider invoked by the provider

Port-type-specific operation names append the type to the port name, for example Rtn-Bit-TransferData or Fwd-Bit-TransferSet.149150 Two further port types face the space element and have no user or provider in this sense: Rtn-RF-Transfer (the space element supplies the RF signal) and Fwd-RF-Transfer (the SLE system supplies it), each with a single ...TransferData operation.150

Inference

The concrete operations of today's specifications fit these types: TRANSFER-DATA (and the RAF transfer buffer) is a Transfer_Data, START and SCHEDULE-STATUS-REPORT are Transfer_Set operations, GET-PARAMETER is a Transfer_Get, and SYNC-NOTIFY, ASYNC-NOTIFY and STATUS-REPORT are Transfer_Notification operations. The reference model does not make this mapping, and it describes binding (BIND, UNBIND) as a relation between ports rather than as one of the four types.

Management ports follow the same pattern. Each SLE-FG supplies one management port, through which Complex Management configures and monitors production. The SLE-FG (supplier) invokes Management_Notification; Complex Management (consumer) invokes Management_Set and Management_Get.151

Source: table 5-3 of the reference model.151 Every SLE service specification must contain the operations with their parameters and ASN.1 definitions, the behaviour of the SLE system in response, the space data channel the service needs, the quality of service required from the underlying communications, and the initialisation and configuration parameters.148 The RAF and FCLTU standards each state that they define their service in conformance with the reference model.156157

Sources: service list and definitions from the concept report,363337 application identifiers from the common BIND types module,38 and the FSP issue from its document control.175

The 2005 reference model names the services slightly differently, and gives each a transfer port type. Reading its tables against the current specifications shows how the catalogue has evolved:155149150152

Reference model service (910.4-B-2) Port type Provider SLE-FG Users named by the model Specification today Return All Frames Rtn-AF-Transfer Return Space Link Processing Return Frame Processing FG, MUE RAF 911.1-B-5 Return Insert (online only)158 Rtn-Insert-Transfer Return Space Link Processing MUE not in this library Return Master Channel Frames; Return Virtual Channel Frames Rtn-MCF-Transfer; Rtn-VCF-Transfer Return Frame Processing MUE (VC frames also feed Return Frame Data Extraction) merged into RCF 911.2-B-4179 Return MC-OCF; Return VC-OCF Rtn-MCOCF-Transfer; Rtn-VCOCF-Transfer Return Frame Processing Forward TC VC Data Insertion FG, Forward TC Space Link Processing FG, MUE merged into ROCF 911.5-B-4180 Return MC-FSH; Return VC-FSH Rtn-MCFSH-Transfer; Rtn-VCFSH-Transfer Return Frame Processing MUE not in this library Return Bitstream; Return Space Packet Rtn-Bit-Transfer; Rtn-SP-Transfer Return Frame Data Extraction MUE not in this library Forward CLTU CLTU-Transfer Forward TC Space Link Processing Forward CLTU Generation FG, MUE FCLTU 912.1-B-5 Forward Telecommand Frame TCFrame-Transfer Forward CLTU Generation Forward TC VC Data Insertion FG, MUE no Recommended Standard yet (2016)178 Forward TC Virtual Channel Access TCVCA-Transfer Forward TC VC Data Insertion MUE not in this library Forward Space Packet (AOS or TC profile) Fwd-SP-Transfer Forward AOS VC Data Insertion or Forward TC VC Data Insertion MUE FSP 912.3-B-3, TC profile only176 Forward Coded Transfer Frame, Forward Proto Transfer Frame, Forward Insert Fwd-Coded Transfer Frame-Transfer, Fwd-Proto Transfer Frame-Transfer, Fwd-Insert-Transfer Forward AOS Space Link Processing MUE (proto frames also from Forward AOS VC Data Insertion) not in this library Forward VCA, Forward Bitstream Fwd-VCA-Transfer, Fwd-Bit-Transfer Forward AOS VC Data Insertion MUE not in this library

The user column matters for cross support inside a station: it is the reference model that names the forward TC functional groups as consumers of the OCF services, which is how the CLCW reaches the uplink equipment.149 A proto Transfer Frame is an AOS frame whose insert zone is not yet filled and which is not yet coded.155 The concept report also mentions future transfer services for non-CCSDS space links and for radiometric, monitoring and return unformatted data.39 ESA's EGS-CC paper describes the Cross-Support Transfer Services (CSTS) as the new generation of SLE, which adds monitoring data from the ground station equipment to the TM and TC services.40

docs.title: Service provision and service production
docs.text:
Every SLE transfer service specification separates two activities:4142

  • Service production transforms the physical channel into the SLE data channel (return), or the SLE data channel into the RF carrier (forward). For RAF this means acquiring the carrier, demodulating, synchronising, decoding and checking frames; for FCLTU it means modulating and radiating CLTUs.
  • Service provision makes the operations available to the user: when service is provided (start and stop times), how (user- or provider-initiated binding), and with which quality of service (for example whether frames with known bit errors are delivered).43

The distinction decides who may change what. Provision parameters affect a single service instance; service management initialises them, and the user may change some of them through service operations. Production parameters such as bit rate, frame length, coding type or modulation index can affect several service instances or the complex's resources, so only service management may change them.4142 One RAF production instance can feed several RAF service instances.43 FCLTU adds a controlled exception: if agreed, the user can ask complex management to change production parameters with the CLTU-THROW-EVENT operation.42

Three kinds of data unit appear in every specification:43

  • the SL-DU (space link data unit), for example a telemetry frame as acquired from the link;
  • the SLE-SDU (SLE service data unit), the SL-DU plus its annotation, or a notification. SLE-SDUs are the parameters of the TRANSFER-DATA and SYNC-NOTIFY operations;
  • the SLE-PDU (SLE protocol data unit), the encoded invocation or return of an operation. Usually one PDU carries one operation, but return services pack many TRANSFER-DATA and SYNC-NOTIFY invocations into one transfer buffer PDU.
flowchart LR
    A["Space link<br/>(RF, symbols)"] -->|"service production:<br/>demodulate, sync,<br/>decode, annotate"| B["SL-DU + annotation<br/>= SLE-SDU"]
    B -->|"service provision:<br/>operations, buffering"| C["SLE-PDU<br/>(e.g. transfer buffer)"]
    C -->|"communications service<br/>(ISP1 over TCP/IP)"| D["Service user<br/>application"]

Diagram based on the RAF production and provision model.43

The specifications deliberately do not define the communications technology. They only require a communications service that delivers invocations and returns in sequence, completely and with integrity, without duplication, with flow control that reports congestion, and with notification when communications are disrupted.44 The approved mapping onto TCP/IP is ISP1.45

docs.title: Delivery modes
docs.text:
The SLE reference model defines online and offline delivery. Within online delivery, the return service specifications distinguish two quality factors, timeliness and completeness, and treat them as separate modes. Each service instance supports exactly one mode, set by service management.41

Mode ASN.1 DeliveryMode Services Behaviour Timely online rtnTimelyOnline (0) RAF, RCF, ROCF Delivery during the pass; frames that cannot be delivered within a set time after acquisition (for example because of a network backlog) are discarded under control, a whole transfer buffer at a time.48 Complete online rtnCompleteOnline (1) RAF, RCF, ROCF Delivery during the pass; a large online frame buffer absorbs network outages so that every frame is delivered in order. Offline rtnOffline (2) RAF, RCF, ROCF Data stored during the pass and delivered later, for any ERT interval the user requests. Forward online fwdOnline (3) FCLTU (and other forward services) CLTUs buffered by the provider and radiated during the space link session. Forward offline fwdOffline (4) — Outside the scope of the current FCLTU specification.

Sources: mode definitions,4146 ASN.1 values.47 The buffering mechanics are explained on the return services page.

In service management terms, each online service instance is tied to one space link session, although it may start before and end after it. Offline instances can exist at any time during the service agreement period and may relate to sessions of other service packages.49 The concept report's glossary defines online as transfer during the associated space link session and offline as transfer at any other time.28

docs.title: Delivery modes in the reference model
docs.text:
The reference model defines the same three modes (complete online, timely online and offline) more abstractly, for both directions. Its definitions differ in detail from what the service specifications later standardised:159

Aspect Reference model 910.4-B-2 (2005) Transfer service specifications Forward online Two qualities: complete and in sequence (routing instructions respected, sequence kept, no ground-induced errors, nothing omitted or duplicated) and expedited (in sequence and without ground-induced errors, but data may be lost). Never extends beyond the end of the space link session. FCLTU and FSP are forward online only.46176 FSP offers the user two transmission modes, sequence-controlled (AD) and expedited (BD).177 Return complete online Delivered in sequence, without ground-induced errors and without omission, even when reception is faster than delivery; may run past the end of the session; needs reserved buffering. A large online frame buffer that keeps filling for the whole provision period (details). Return timely online Two user-settable mechanisms: a notification when the delivery delay exceeds Tdelay-notify (and another when it recovers), and deletion of the queued SLE-SDUs when it exceeds Tdelete, with a notice that says how many were deleted. The user may disable both. One latency-limit set by service management. On backpressure the provider discards a whole transfer buffer and inserts a 'data discarded due to excessive backlog' notification, which carries no count.181182 Forward offline A complete, in-sequence data set whose transfer into the SLE system must be complete before it is transmitted to the spacecraft during the session, at a time defined by SLE management; storage reserved in advance. Outside the FCLTU scope; "the subject of further study" for FSP.46176 Return offline Storage either of all user data of the session (selection deferred until retrieval) or of the service data chosen in advance; the model notes that real systems may not afford the first. Offline frame buffer, ideally one per service agreement; any ERT window (details).

Sources: §3.4.2 of the reference model;159 for the right-hand column, the clauses cited in the cells and the delivery modes table above.

Inference

The two forward qualities of the reference model look like the COP-1 sequence-controlled and expedited services, which FSP exposes as AD and BD transmission modes. The return timely online mechanism of the RAF, RCF and ROCF standards is simpler than the reference model's (one latency limit, no recovery notice, no count). Neither document comments on the difference.

docs.title: Service instances
docs.text:
A service instance is the provision by one SLE complex of the capability to transfer one or more SLE data channels of one type, all related to the same space link session.28144 The provision of RAF from one physical channel to one user is one instance; the same channel served to two users, or several channels served concurrently, are several instances.50 For FCLTU only one instance may exist per physical forward channel at a time.51

Each instance has:

  • a service instance provision period, the time during which it is scheduled to be provided. Reaching its start is the event 'start of service instance provision period' in the state tables;52
  • a binding direction: user-initiated (only the user may invoke BIND) or provider-initiated (only the provider may). Service management decides which, per instance. RAF, RCF and ROCF allow both; FCLTU-BIND is invoked only by the user;5354
  • a delivery mode (above);
  • a responder port identifier, a logical name agreed by both sides in advance and translated locally into technology-specific addresses, for example an IP address and TCP port;45
  • a service instance identifier that is unique within the providing complex.55

docs.title: The service instance identifier
docs.text:
The service instance identifier is a sequence of attribute name/value pairs. In its standard string form, each pair is written name=value and pairs are separated by dots. The attributes, in order, are the service agreement (sagr), the service package (spack), the forward or return functional group (fsl-fg or rsl-fg) and the service name. For return services the service name value starts with onlc, onlt or offl followed by an instance number; for forward services it is the service name plus a number, such as cltu1.56 The standard's own example is sagr=xyz.spack=abcdef.rsl-fg=gfjdy.raf=onlc2.57

Inference

The ASN.1 comments list the prefixes onlc, onlt and offl without expanding them. Reading them as online complete, online timely and offline matches the three delivery modes, and ISP1 Annex B uses onlt1 for "an RCF service instance with timely online delivery mode",59 but the 911.x specifications do not define the prefixes explicitly.

Each attribute is also registered as an ASN.1 object identifier under {iso 3 112 4 3 1 2}: for example raf is arc 22, rcf 46, rocf 49, cltu 7, fsp 10, sagr 52 and spack 53.58

The real Solar Orbiter MIB contains two such identifiers, embedded as default values of the ground commands that open and close links on ESA's network interface system (see below):60

MIB command Service Identifier reconstructed from the three ASCII CDF fields (two fixed 15-character parts and one variable-length part) EGENRTCO / EGENRTCC FCLTU sagr=144.spack=NN11-PERM.fsl-fg=1.cltu=cltu01 EGENRTMO / EGENRTMC RCF sagr=144.spack=NN11-PERM.rsl-fg=1.rcf=onlc0001

Inference

The identifiers follow the 911.x Annex A syntax exactly: service agreement 144, service package NN11-PERM, functional group 1, and service names cltu01 and onlc0001 (an RCF instance, presumably in complete online delivery mode, see the inference above). That NN11 designates an ESA New Norcia antenna and that PERM means a permanently configured package are this wiki's guesses; neither is stated in the available sources.

docs.title: Operations common to all transfer services
docs.text:
All SLE transfer services are built from a small vocabulary of operations. An operation is invoked by one object and performed by the other; a confirmed operation returns a report of its outcome, an unconfirmed one does not.62 The common operations are:63

Operation Invoker Confirmed Purpose BIND initiator (user or provider) yes Establish an association between user and provider UNBIND initiator yes Release the association cleanly PEER-ABORT either no Break the association after a protocol problem START user yes Enter the 'active' state in which data units flow STOP user yes Leave the 'active' state TRANSFER-DATA provider (return) or user (forward) no (return), yes (FCLTU) Carry one data unit SYNC-NOTIFY / ASYNC-NOTIFY provider no Report events in step with (return) or independently of (forward) the data flow SCHEDULE-STATUS-REPORT user yes Request one, periodic, or no further status reports STATUS-REPORT provider no Deliver a status report GET-PARAMETER user yes Read a service parameter of the instance THROW-EVENT user (forward services) yes Forward an event that requires management action INVOKE-DIRECTIVE privileged FSP or TCVCA user yes Invoke TC directives, for example for COP operation

Sources: concept report,63 confirmation and invoker columns from the RAF and FCLTU operation tables.6465

docs.title: Rules that apply to every operation
docs.text:
• Result and diagnostic. Every return carries a result (positive or negative). A negative result carries a diagnostic; the value 'other reason' may only be used when nothing more specific applies. Checks should be done in the order in which the diagnostics are listed, and an implementation that deviates must document its order.66
  • Parameter checking. A parameter is invalid if it is outside the range permitted by service management, conflicts with another parameter of the same invocation (for example a start time after the stop time), or conflicts with the current configuration. Invalid operations are not performed.67
  • Blocking and non-blocking. Every confirmed operation except BIND and UNBIND carries an invoke-ID, an arbitrary 16-bit integer (InvokeId ::= IntUnsignedShort) returned unchanged by the performer. Operations with an invoke-ID are non-blocking: the invoker may issue more invocations before the returns arrive. BIND and UNBIND are blocking. Reusing an invoke-ID that is still awaiting a return is an error; an invoker that wants strictly sequential behaviour can simply use a constant invoke-ID. Effects must be as if operations were performed in the order received.6869
  • Return timeout. If a confirmed operation's return does not arrive within the return-timeout-period (1 to 600 seconds in the ASN.1), the invoker aborts the association with PEER-ABORT 'return timeout'. Returns must therefore never depend on human interaction.7071
  • Protocol errors. An operation not allowed in the current state causes PEER-ABORT 'protocol error'; an undecodable PDU causes PEER-ABORT 'encoding error'; a return with an unknown invoke-ID causes PEER-ABORT 'unsolicited invoke-ID'.72
  • Communications failure. Each bound entity must monitor the health of the communications link, if necessary with a periodic heartbeat, and treat a disruption as a 'protocol abort'. After a protocol abort the provider returns to 'unbound', discards its transfer buffer and resets parameters to their initial values, but keeps the statistics for status reports.73
  • Time. All times are UTC. Return services express the earth receive time in the CCSDS Day Segmented code with a 1958-01-01 epoch and a 16-bit day field, at microsecond or picosecond resolution, accurate to 1 ms; FCLTU times must be precise and accurate to 0.1 s.7475 See time code formats.

docs.title: The generic state machine
docs.text:
Once a service instance exists, the provider is always in one of three states. In state 1 ('unbound') all resources are allocated but no association exists. In state 2 ('ready') an association exists and operations can be exchanged, but data units do not flow. In state 3 ('active') data units flow until the user invokes STOP or either side aborts.14

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Unbound: service instance created<br/>by complex management
    Unbound --> Unbound: BIND rejected
    Unbound --> Ready: BIND accepted
    Ready --> Unbound: UNBIND / PEER-ABORT / protocol abort
    Ready --> Ready: START rejected,<br/>GET-PARAMETER,<br/>SCHEDULE-STATUS-REPORT
    Ready --> Active: START accepted
    Active --> Active: TRANSFER-DATA,<br/>SYNC/ASYNC-NOTIFY,<br/>STOP rejected
    Active --> Ready: STOP accepted
    Active --> Unbound: PEER-ABORT / protocol abort
    Unbound --> [*]: end of provision period<br/>or UNBIND 'end'

Diagram based on the simplified provider state diagrams of the RAF and FCLTU specifications.1476 The full behaviour is defined by a normative state table in section 4 of each specification, with events, predicates, Boolean flags and compound actions. Conformance to the state table is mandatory.7778

docs.title: A typical session
docs.text:
The RAF specification gives a canonical scenario for a user-initiated online instance.79 Complex management creates the instance before its provision period, typically shortly before the pass so that the user can bind in time. The rest of the session looks like this:

sequenceDiagram
    participant U as Service user (control centre)
    participant P as Service provider (station)
    Note over P: state 1 'unbound'<br/>(instance created by complex management)
    U->>P: BIND (initiator-identifier, responder-port-identifier,<br/>service-type, version-number, service-instance-identifier)
    P-->>U: BIND return (positive, version-number)
    Note over P: state 2 'ready'
    U->>P: GET-PARAMETER (e.g. delivery-mode)
    P-->>U: GET-PARAMETER return
    U->>P: SCHEDULE-STATUS-REPORT (periodically, 30 s)
    P-->>U: return (positive)
    U->>P: START (start-time, stop-time, delivery criteria)
    P-->>U: START return (positive)
    Note over P: state 3 'active'
    loop during the pass
        P->>U: transfer buffer (TRANSFER-DATA ... SYNC-NOTIFY ...)
        P->>U: STATUS-REPORT (every reporting cycle)
    end
    P->>U: SYNC-NOTIFY 'end of data'
    U->>P: STOP
    P-->>U: STOP return (positive)
    Note over P: state 2 'ready'
    U->>P: UNBIND (unbind-reason 'end')
    P-->>U: UNBIND return (positive)
    Note over P: state 1, instance may be deleted

Sequence based on the RAF operational scenario; the 30-second reporting cycle is illustrative.79

docs.title: BIND, UNBIND and PEER-ABORT in detail
docs.text:
These three operations are common to all services and share one ASN.1 module (CCSDS-SLE-TRANSFER-SERVICE-BIND-TYPES).80

BIND carries the invoker's credentials, the initiator-identifier (an authority identifier of 3 to 16 visible characters), the responder-port-identifier (a logical port name of 1 to 128 characters), the service-type, the version-number and the service-instance-identifier. The return carries the performer's credentials, the responder-identifier, and either the accepted version number or a diagnostic.8180 The responder port identifier is in the invocation only to help gateways; the responder ignores it when validating the BIND. A wrong value usually makes the BIND fail with no return at all, which ends in a 'return timeout' abort.82 The service type is redundant today, but it anticipates a future generic SLE-BIND.83

Version negotiation works downwards only. The responder either accepts the proposed version or, if it supports negotiation, proposes a lower one; if it supports neither, it rejects the BIND with 'version not supported'. An initiator that cannot accept the lower version unbinds. The 2023 issues of RAF, RCF, ROCF and FCLTU all define version number 6.84858687

BIND diagnostic ASN.1 code Meaning access denied 0 Initiator identifier not recognised by the responder service type not supported 1 Service type not supported by the responder version not supported 2 Requested version not supported and no lower version can be offered no such service instance 3 Instance not defined in any agreed service package already bound 4 Instance already bound via another association service instance not accessible to this initiator 5 Authorised initiator of the instance differs from the requester inconsistent service type 6 Service type does not match the instance invalid time 7 BIND outside the service instance provision period out of service 8 Responder taken out of service by management (production status 'halted') other reason 127 Anything else

Sources: diagnostics,88 codes.80 The responder may be unable to return anything at all for 'no such service instance', 'invalid time' or 'out of service'.88

UNBIND is invoked only by the initiator and only in state 2. Its unbind-reason is 'end' (0), 'suspend' (1), 'version not supported' (2) or 'other' (127). 'End' allows the provider to delete the instance and release its resources, so any later BIND will fail; 'suspend' allows a re-bind before the end of the provision period. The result is always positive: UNBIND is confirmed only so that the initiator knows the association really is released.8980

PEER-ABORT is unconfirmed, valid in states 2 and 3, and carries only a diagnostic code in the range 0 to 255 (ISP1 sends it as a single octet).8091 It deliberately has no credentials: the specification argues that an intruder able to inject an abort could disrupt the link more easily at a lower layer anyway.90

PEER-ABORT diagnostic Code When used access denied 0 Responder identifier in the BIND return not known to the initiator unexpected responder ID 1 Responder identifier does not match the authorised responder operational requirement 2 Local system needs the resources for another purpose protocol error 3 Operation sequencing error communications failure 4 Communications broken on the far side of a gateway encoding error 5 Undecodable operation or parameter return timeout 6 Return not received within the timeout end of service instance provision period 7 Provision period ended while still bound unsolicited invoke-ID 8 Return with an invoke-ID that matches no pending invocation other reason 127 Anything else technology specific 128–255 Reserved for the communications mapping (ISP1 uses 128–199)

Sources: diagnostics,90 codes,80 ISP1 range.91

docs.title: Security: access control and authentication
docs.text:
SLE transfer services build in two security mechanisms, access control and authentication, and leave everything else (confidentiality, integrity, availability, auditing) to the underlying communications or to the mission's own end-to-end measures.9293

Access control works at two levels: the initiator and responder must be registered with each other, and they must be authorised for the specific service instance. Service management specifies the authorised initiator and responder of each instance, and each side presents its identity in the BIND.94 The responder refuses an unknown initiator with 'access denied' and does not even try to authenticate it; a known but unauthorised initiator gets 'service instance not accessible to this initiator'. The initiator, in turn, aborts if the responder identity in the BIND return is unknown ('access denied') or not the expected one ('unexpected responder ID').95

Authentication uses credentials that rely on a secret shared by user and provider. Each instance has one of three authentication levels:9697

Level What carries credentials 'all' Every invocation and return except the PEER-ABORT invocation 'bind' Only the BIND invocation and its return 'none' Nothing; authentication left to the environment

Providers should require 'all' or 'bind'. The two management sides agree the level and the algorithm, and give both ends the passwords or keys.97 In ASN.1, credentials are either unused or an octet string of 8 to 256 octets whose internal structure depends on the algorithm.98 A PDU whose credentials fail authentication is silently ignored, as if it had never arrived.99 The algorithm actually used over TCP/IP is the ISP1 hashed password scheme, described on the ISP1 page.

The concept report models the configuration as entity authentication structures (local and peer entity identifiers, each with an authentication level, method and method parameters) and service instance structures (service instance identifier, initiator identifier, responder identifier, responder port identifier).100

The specifications are frank about the residual risks. Without additional mechanisms an attacker could read telemetry or commands as they cross the wide area network, or replace the data parameter of a PDU. FCLTU adds one integrity check of its own (the monotonically increasing cltu-identification), but the FCLTU standard warns that a hijacked forward service could be used to subvert or destroy a spacecraft.101102 These pages describe the standards' protections; they do not discuss attack techniques.

docs.title: The six security areas of the reference model
docs.text:
Issue 2 of the reference model added a cross support security section. It walks through the six areas that CCSDS requires every Recommended Standard to address, for the transfer services and for service management separately:160

Area SLE transfer services SLE service management Data privacy (confidentiality) Not provided. Left to the mission applications, to the underlying communications, or both; encrypting the SLE PDU is one option. Consider XML encryption. Data integrity Relies on the in-sequence, complete, duplicate-free transfer of the communications service, which does not stop an intermediary altering content. One remedy is for user and provider to agree on credentials computed over the whole PDU. The strict operation sequence makes it hard to inject operations or seize an active service unnoticed. Sequence numbers support integrity. Authentication Credentials carried in the PDUs; the procedure is in the concept report, the algorithms are outside the transfer specifications (for TCP/IP see ISP1). Secret keys must be distributed securely. Digital signatures are recommended. Access control initiator-identifier and responder-identifier in the operations. Unique identification parameters, created by SLE-UM and carried in each message, control access to Complex Management. Availability of resources Not provided; depends on the underlying technology and environment. The configuration files describe the resources Complex Management declares available. Service requests may be rejected if resources are short; denial-of-service protection is left to the network (routers, firewalls). Auditing No requirements; to be agreed bilaterally. Logging access attempts is, however, a standard feature of the SLE API. No requirements; agencies are assumed to keep an audit trail of management messages and of breach attempts.

Source: §2.4 of the reference model.160 The 2015 RAF API book repeats this analysis for RAF and adds that the credential mechanism, and with it the choice between simple and strong protection against masquerading, can be chosen according to the results of a threat analysis.169 Threats and consequences specific to one service are left to that service's specification.160

docs.title: SLE service management
docs.text:
SLE service management collects and exchanges the information needed to agree, schedule, prepare and access SLE services. It is a dialogue between Utilization Management (UM) in the MDOS and Complex Management (CM) in each SLE complex.103 CM presents the complex in a standard way and hides its internal equipment from the user; CCSDS does not define how CM drives that equipment.104 Of the five OSI management functional areas, SLE service management covers configuration, accounting, fault and security management, but not performance management, which stays internal to the provider.105

UM requests provision periods, provides RF, modulation, space link and SLE configuration, provides trajectory predictions and coordinates the mission user entities. CM negotiates service types, numbers of instances and agreement durations, answers requests for space link sessions, and configures and monitors the complex's resources.106

flowchart LR
    R["Registration<br/>(security credentials,<br/>points of contact)"] --> SA["Service Agreement<br/>(T0 − years)"]
    SA --> CP["Configuration Profiles<br/>+ Trajectory Predictions<br/>(T0 − months … days)"]
    CP --> SP["Service Package<br/>submission + scheduling<br/>(T0 − weeks … days)"]
    SP --> EX["Execution T0…T1:<br/>MUE binds to the<br/>transfer service ports"]
    EX --> DB["Post-pass report /<br/>debriefing"]

Diagram based on the nominal interaction timeline and use case of the concept report.107

Management item Content Notes Service Agreement Services to be provided, spacecraft communication characteristics, static and default configuration, nominal contact frequency and duration, nominal trajectory, and the ranges in which later parameters must fall One mission per agreement; negotiated years in advance; a mission may hold several (for example launch, cruise, planetary phases). Registration and agreement establishment were not standardised in 2006.108 Configuration Profile Reusable set of space link and SLE parameters, referenced by any number of service packages Suits spacecraft with a few well-defined TT&C modes.109 Trajectory Prediction Data the TT&C complex uses for antenna pointing and Doppler compensation CCSDS Orbit Parameter Message or Orbit Ephemeris Message (text or XML), or a bilaterally agreed format.110 Service Package Transfer services, provision periods, end users, and configurations for specific space link sessions May hold several forward and return carriers with preferred and acceptable windows, several transfer service instances timed relative to the carriers, alternate scenarios (for example burn/no-burn), and time-sequenced parameter changes.111

A service package goes through a definition phase and a utilization phase, possibly with dormant periods in between, and ends with a debrief from CM to UM.112113 Status reporting during execution and near-real-time service control existed in some providers but were not standardised in 2006.114

docs.title: Agreements, packages and provision periods
docs.text:
The reference model fixes the vocabulary for how long each management object lives:161162163

  • An SLE Service Agreement states which transfer and management services one SLE complex provides to one mission, and on what conditions. Only one agreement is in force between a given complex and a given mission at any time, but a mission may have several over its lifetime. The agreement period often covers the spacecraft's whole operational life, with several packages a day and hundreds or thousands in all; it can also be short, for example launch support, one orbit manoeuvre or an emergency.
  • An SLE Service Package is the set of transfer service instances, with the specification of their production, that one complex provides to one or more users. Its lifetime has a definition phase and a utilization phase. A package has at most one online period, tied to one space link session. Its offline instances may serve that session or sessions of other packages.
  • The service instance provision period is the time during which one instance's capability is provided. Online instances may start before and end after their session.
flowchart LR
    subgraph SA["Service agreement period (one complex, one mission)"]
        direction LR
        P1["Package a<br/>(session 1, online)"] --> P2["Package b<br/>(session 2 online<br/>+ offline)"]
        P2 --> P3["Package c<br/>(offline only)"]
        P3 --> P4["Package d<br/>(session 3)"]
    end
    subgraph PK["Lifetime of one package"]
        direction LR
        D["Definition phase:<br/>SLE-UM creates the<br/>servicePackage managed<br/>object at the complex"] --> DOR["dormant period<br/>(optional)"]
        DOR --> U1["Utilization phase:<br/>online provision period<br/>(one space link session)"]
        U1 --> U2["offline provision<br/>periods, possibly<br/>separated by dormant periods"]
        U2 --> DB["debrief from Complex<br/>Management to SLE-UM"]
    end

Diagram based on figures 4-13 to 4-16 of the reference model.162163

During the definition phase, SLE-UM creates a servicePackage managed object at the complex, together with the lower-level managed objects it contains, and chooses parameter values within the limits of the agreement. The attributes of these objects select the transfer services, identify the interfaces where they are offered and the services that this or other complexes must provide, carry the mission-specific information Complex Management needs to configure production, name the eventual users (MUEs or other complexes), schedule the online and offline instances, and define the reporting from Complex Management to SLE-UM.163 During utilization, provision is controlled in two ways: MUEs invoke control operations on their instances, and SLE-UM invokes management operations. Debrief reports may follow any provision period.163 When a mission uses two complexes, it holds two agreements and negotiates a package with each; each package then specifies only the part of production that its complex performs.161144

What is and is not in this library

The reference model (CCSDS 910.4-B-2) is now in the library and is summarised above. The normative service management specification (CCSDS 910.11), which all SLE documents cite, is not. The newer extensible cross support service management documents and their data formats are described on the cross support reference model and service management.

docs.title: The SLE API and ISP1 in one paragraph
docs.text: The transfer service specifications define operations and ASN.1 types in an abstract way. Two further documents make them implementable. ISP1 (CCSDS 913.1) maps one SLE association to one TCP connection, encodes PDUs with ASN.1 BER, frames them in 8-octet-header TML messages, adds a heartbeat, and defines the hashed-password credentials.115 The SLE API (CCSDS 914.0) defines C++ components (API Proxy, API Service Element, SLE Operations, SLE Utilities) that hide the communications technology and enforce the state tables, so that SLE applications can be written once and products can be exchanged.10116 Service-specific API books add the classes, interfaces and checks of one service each; the RAF book (915.1-M-2), for example, adds the RAF service instance classes and operation objects, and the FSP book (916.3-M-2) adds FOP monitoring for the provider side.170174 Both layers are explained on ISP1 and the SLE API.

docs.title: How ESA's ground segment uses SLE
docs.text:
In ESA's ground segment the mission control system (SCOS-2000) does not talk to stations directly. A 2005 ESOC overview describes the NCTRS (Network Control and TM/TC Router System) as the interface between the mission control system and the ground station network, using SLE for non-ESA stations.117 A 2003 ESOC presentation shows the NCTRS between SCOS-2000 and the stations (Kiruna, Redu, Perth, Villafranca, Kourou, New Norcia, Cebreros and the DSN), labels the link SLE, and lists SLE-conformant ground station interface software among SCOS-2000's enabling technologies.118119 The page on NCTRS, NIS and the ground station interface covers these systems.

flowchart LR
    MCS["SCOS-2000 mission<br/>control system"] -- "NCTRS protocol<br/>(TM, TC, throw events)" --> NIS["NCTRS / NIS<br/>(SLE user)"]
    NIS -- "SLE return: RAF / RCF / ROCF<br/>SLE forward: FCLTU" --- GS["Ground station<br/>(SLE provider)"]
    MCS -- "TM packets, TC history" --> EDDS["EDDS / GDDS<br/>(data dissemination)"]

Diagram based on the ESOC ground segment descriptions.117118120 The 2005 overview mentions SLE specifically for non-ESA stations. Which SLE services are used with which station is mission specific and not stated in the available sources.

Several sources in this library show traces of SLE in ESA's data products and databases:

  • Command verification. The EDDS external user ICD names the first command verification stage 'R', release from SCOS-2000 to "the SLE User (NCTRS/NIS)", and defines 'G' (ground station reception) and 'T' (uplink, also called radiation; for throw event commands it is the execution stage).120 See command verification in the MIB.
  • Packet headers. The Rosetta and Mars Express data delivery ICD defines an 8-bit "SLE Type" field in its 18-octet DDS packet header. It encodes the SLE channel (SLC, MC, VC, bad frames) and the delivery flavour (real-time, real-time flow control, off-line) as values 0 to 11.121 EDDS keeps an 8-bit SleServiceID in its raw packet header "for backward compatibility with the GDDS".122 See EDDS formats.
  • The MIB. The SCOS-2000 database import ICD defines command type CCF_CTYPE = 'T' for SLE throw events, sent to the SLE service provider but not uplinked, and 'N' for NIS throw events, executed by the NIS itself.123 The Solar Orbiter MIB contains six NIS throw events and no SLE throw events (queries below).60
CCF_CNAME Description Event ID SLE service type ESESIONO OPEN SESSION OPEN_SESSION (10) — ESESIONC CLOSE SESSION CLOSE_SESSION (11) — EGENRTCO GENERIC OPEN TC LINK OPEN_LINK (20) FCLTU (4) EGENRTCC GENERIC CLOSE TC LINK CLOSE_LINK (21) FCLTU (4) EGENRTMO GENERIC OPEN TM LINK OPEN_LINK (20) RCF (2) EGENRTMC GENERIC CLOSE TM LINK CLOSE_LINK (21) RCF (2)

The "SLE Service Type" command parameter (ENISTE03, textual calibration CNISX207TC) enumerates RAF (1), RCF (2), ROCF (3), FCLTU (4) and FSP (5), and the "Event ID" parameter (ENISTE02, calibration CNISX205TC) also knows HEARTBEAT_MSG (12), ABORT_LINK (22) and CHANGE_MODE (23).60 The same six commands, with the same service instance identifiers, are present in the April 2020 release.61 The commands are described on the FCLTU page and the return services page.

SQL used 
-- Special command types in the Solar Orbiter MIB (2025-09-16 release)
SELECT CCF_CTYPE, count(*) FROM ccf GROUP BY CCF_CTYPE;
-- -> '' 5443, 'F' 2, 'N' 6, 'R' 3   (no 'T' = SLE throw event)

SELECT CCF_CNAME, CCF_DESCR, CCF_TYPE, CCF_STYPE, CCF_APID
  FROM ccf WHERE CCF_CTYPE = 'N';

-- Service instance identifier pieces: ENISTE35 and ENISTE38 (120 bits, 15 characters each)
-- and ENISTE37 'Service_Instance_End' (CDF_ELLEN 0, variable length)
SELECT CDF_CNAME, CDF_PNAME, CDF_ELLEN, CDF_BIT, CDF_VALUE
  FROM cdf WHERE CDF_CNAME IN ('EGENRTCO','EGENRTMO')
 ORDER BY CDF_CNAME, CAST(CDF_BIT AS INT);

-- Enumerations of the NIS throw event parameters
SELECT CPC_NAME, CPC_DESCR, CPC_PAFREF FROM cpc WHERE CPC_NAME LIKE 'ENISTE%';
SELECT PAS_NUMBR, PAS_ALTXT, PAS_ALVAL FROM pas
 WHERE PAS_NUMBR IN ('CNISX205TC','CNISX207TC') ORDER BY PAS_NUMBR, CAST(PAS_ALVAL AS INT);

Outside ESA's own network, SCOS-2000-based centres reach SLE stations through protocol bridges. At DLR's German Space Operations Center, the SCOS-2000-based GECCOS system speaks the NCTRS protocol to an SLE Switch Board (SSB), which translates it into the standard SLE protocol used by ground stations worldwide.124125 ESA's newer EGS-CC framework includes reference components to talk to a PUS spacecraft via SLE, and plans an extension for CSTS monitoring data.12640 See ancillary systems and EGS-CC. The ECSS communications handbook points to the ESA ground operations software portal, which includes "the ESA SLE Gateway".127 ESA's role in the SLE API is described on the ISP1 and SLE API page.

Two open-source Java implementations are public on GitHub (web sources, not in this library). ESA's SLE Java API (esa/sleapi-j) describes itself as an SLE API package supporting RAF (911.1), RCF (911.2), ROCF (911.5), FCLTU (912.1) and FSP (912.3).183 jsle (yamcs/jsle), from the Yamcs project, implements the user and provider sides of FCLTU, RAF and RCF.184 Their details are on the ISP1 and SLE API page.

In the Solar Orbiter databases of this library, the NIS throw events and the ground-generated packets exist only in the spacecraft MIB. The instrument databases (SWA and STIX) have no throw-event commands at all (every CCF_CTYPE is empty), no commands on APID 1964, which carries the six NIS throw events in the spacecraft MIB, and no packets on APID 1966. In the spacecraft MIB, APID 1966 holds 18 MCS-internal packets, among them good, bad and idle mini transfer frames, bad telemetry packets, time correlation packets and a "TM Packet used by the Releaser G/S response".18660185

SQL used (instrument databases) 
-- swa-idb.sqlite (2021 ASCII set), swa-idb-v6.5.0.sqlite, stix-idb-2.26.38.sqlite
SELECT quote(CCF_CTYPE), count(*) FROM ccf GROUP BY CCF_CTYPE;
-- -> '' 198 (SWA 2021), '' 201 (SWA v6.5.0), '' 100 (STIX 2.26.38)
SELECT count(*) FROM ccf WHERE CCF_APID IN ('1964', '1966');   -- 0 in all three
SELECT count(*) FROM pid WHERE PID_APID = '1966';               -- 0 in all three
-- for comparison, solo-2025-09-16.sqlite: 6 ccf rows on APID 1964 (the NIS throw
-- events) and 18 pid rows on APID 1966
SELECT PID_TYPE, PID_STYPE, PID_SPID, PID_DESCR FROM pid WHERE PID_APID = '1966';
-- -> 18 rows: types 160, 161, 162, 164, 165, 166 and 251; SPIDs 101-103 and 66810-66999

The 2006 concept report references earlier issues of the service standards (for example RAF 911.1-B-2 and FCLTU 912.1-B-2 of December 2004).132 The 2005 reference model in turn references the 2002 issue of the concept report (910.3-G-2) and the 2003 issues of the space link standards.164 The two 2015 API books are built on older service issues than the ones in this library: the RAF API on RAF 911.1-B-3 (January 2010) and the FSP API on FSP 912.3-B-2 (July 2010).167173 Where the concept report describes services that were "not yet defined" in 2006 (the forward AOS services, Return Insert, Return Bitstream), this wiki still has no later source in its library. FSP, which the concept report already lists, now has its own page based on the 2016 issue.

docs.title: SLE forward service: FCLTU
docs.text:
The Forward CLTU (FCLTU) service lets a control centre hand complete Communications Link Transmission Units to a ground station, together with instructions on when to radiate them. The station then radiates each CLTU, bit for bit, on the telecommand uplink and reports back what happened.12 It is the lowest-level forward SLE service. The user does all the telecommand work above the physical layer: packets, segments, TC frames, COP-1 and CLTU encoding. The provider adds the carrier, the acquisition and idle sequences, the timing, and the uplink status that it reads from the spacecraft's CLCWs.3

The higher-level alternative is the Forward Space Packet service (FSP), where the user hands over Space Packets and the provider builds the frames, runs COP-1 and generates the CLTUs before radiating them with the same function that provides FCLTU; the two are compared below.8384 For the concepts shared with the other SLE services (BIND, states, security, service instances) see the SLE overview. The CLTU format itself is on TC synchronization and channel coding, and the frames inside it on TC SDLP and COP-1.

At a glance

Item Value Specification CCSDS 912.1-B-5, July 2023 (adds USLP), with Editorial Change 1, October 20244 Data unit One CLTU per CLTU-TRANSFER-DATA, radiated bit for bit; any octet-aligned bit pattern is accepted2 Produced by Forward TC Space Link Processing SLE-FG3 Reference model names Port type CLTU-Transfer; data channel "CLTU channel", unique identifier "CLTU ID", TC physical channels only9293 Instances Only one FCLTU instance per physical forward channel at a time2 Delivery mode Forward online only (fwdOnline (3))56 Binding User-initiated only; ApplicationIdentifier fwdCltu (16)78 BIND version-number 6 in this issue9 Provider states 1 'unbound', 2 'ready', 3 'active'10 Production status configured, operational, interrupted, halted11 Time precision Radiation times precise and accurate to 0.1 s12

docs.title: What the provider does
docs.text:
The Forward TC Space Link Processing functional group consumes two data channels. One is the CLTU data channel from the user. The other is an OCF data channel, from which it extracts CLCWs to judge whether the physical channel is available (service management may tell it to ignore CLCWs). It then generates the acquisition and idle sequences required by the PLOP in effect, steers the antenna, modulates the CLTUs onto the RF carrier, and radiates them.3

flowchart LR
    MCS["Control centre<br/>(SCOS-2000):<br/>packets → TC frames<br/>→ COP-1 → CLTUs"] -- "CLTU-TRANSFER-DATA<br/>(CLTU + radiation window<br/>+ delay + report flag)" --> BUF
    subgraph FSLP["Forward TC Space Link Processing FG"]
        BUF["CLTU buffer<br/>(octets)"] --> PLOP["PLOP-1 / PLOP-2:<br/>acquisition, idle,<br/>CLTU sequencing"]
        PLOP --> MOD["Modulation<br/>(subcarrier, index)"]
        CLCW["CLCW monitor:<br/>No RF Available,<br/>No Bit Lock"] --> PLOP
    end
    MOD --> ANT(("Antenna → spacecraft"))
    RFP["Return Frame Processing FG<br/>(OCF data channel)"] --> CLCW
    FSLP -- "CLTU-ASYNC-NOTIFY,<br/>STATUS-REPORT" --> MCS

Diagram based on the functional view and operational scenario of the FCLTU specification.313

The reference model describes the same group in terms of ports. To produce FCLTU, the Forward TC Space Link Processing SLE-FG has a consumer CLTU-Transfer port facing the user, a supplier Fwd-RF-Transfer port facing the spacecraft, a supplier management port TCSpLinkProc-Mgmt facing Complex Management, and a consumer Rtn-MCOCF-Transfer or Rtn-VCOCF-Transfer port through which the CLCWs arrive.94 Its functions are to consume the CLTU data channel, consume the OCF channels and judge from the CLCW whether the physical channel is available, generate the acquisition and idle sequences of the PLOP in effect on the asynchronous physical channel, inject the CLTUs, use the antenna steering of the ground element, and modulate and radiate.95 The users that the model names for the CLTU-Transfer port are an MUE and the Forward CLTU Generation SLE-FG, the next group up, which turns TC frames into CLTUs.92

Delivery. In the reference model, forward online delivery happens during the forward space link session and cannot extend beyond it. Forward offline delivery would transfer a complete data set into the SLE system, a transfer that must be finished before the data are transmitted to the spacecraft during the session, at a time set by SLE management.96 FCLTU defines only the online mode; offline is outside the scope of the current specification.5

Production versus provision. Production configuration parameters such as bit rate and modulation index affect complex resources, so only service management may change them. A user may change some provision parameters through operations. If the station and the mission user agree, the user may also change production parameters indirectly, by asking complex management to act through CLTU-THROW-EVENT.14

docs.title: The CLTU being radiated
docs.text:
A CLTU is a start sequence, a series of codewords that hold one or more TC transfer frames (plus fill), and, for BCH coding, a tail sequence.15

Field values from CCSDS 231.0-B-4.151617 With LDPC coding the start sequence is the 64-bit pattern 0x034776C7272895B0, the codewords are 128 or 512 bits, and a tail sequence is optional (128 bits for LDPC (128,64)).151817

Worked example (Solar Orbiter frame limit, illustrative coding). The maximum Solar Orbiter TC frame is 256 octets, or 2,048 bits.19 If BCH coding is used, the frame needs 37 codewords of 56 information bits each (37 × 56 = 2,072 bits, so 24 bits of fill). The CLTU is then 2 + 37 × 8 + 8 = 306 octets. That is well inside FCLTU's maximum-cltu-length range of 12 to 4,096 octets.20 At an illustrative 2,000 bit/s uplink, the CLTU takes 2,448 bits ÷ 2,000 bit/s ≈ 1.22 s to radiate. The coding scheme Solar Orbiter actually uses is not stated in the sections of its ICD consulted here.

docs.title: Carrier modulation modes and the PLOPs
docs.text:
The physical layer operations procedures (PLOPs) of CCSDS 231.0 define how the carrier is modulated around CLTUs (see also TC coding and the CLTU and, for the carrier itself, Radio frequency, modulation and ranging). Missions whose planning began after September 2010 must use PLOP-2.21 There are four carrier modulation modes:22

Mode Carrier is modulated with CMM-1 nothing (unmodulated carrier only) CMM-2 the acquisition sequence (alternating ones and zeros; preferred minimum 16 octets) CMM-3 a CLTU CMM-4 the idle sequence (alternating ones and zeros)

Sources: carrier modulation modes and sequences.2223

FCLTU binds these modes to its own parameters:24

stateDiagram-v2
    direction LR
    state "PLOP-1 (per CLTU)" as P1 {
        [*] --> CMM1a: carrier on,<br/>unmodulated
        CMM1a --> CMM2a: CLTU received
        CMM2a --> CMM4a: acquisition-sequence-length<br/>octets sent
        CMM4a --> CMM3a: plop-1-idle-sequence-length<br/>octets (if > 0)
        CMM3a --> CMM4b: CLTU sent
        CMM4b --> CMM1a: trailing idle (if > 0);<br/>wait delay-time
    }
stateDiagram-v2
    direction LR
    state "PLOP-2 (per session)" as P2 {
        [*] --> CMM1: uplink sweep
        CMM1 --> CMM2: sweep complete
        CMM2 --> CMM4: acquisition sequence sent
        CMM4 --> CMM3: CLTU available and<br/>previous delay-time expired
        CMM3 --> CMM4: CLTU sent;<br/>idle until delay-time expires
    }

Diagrams based on §3.6.2.8 of the FCLTU specification.24

  • PLOP-1: the carrier stays unmodulated (CMM-1) until a CLTU arrives. For each CLTU the provider sends an acquisition sequence of acquisition-sequence-length octets (CMM-2), an optional leading idle sequence of plop-1-idle-sequence-length octets (CMM-4), the CLTU (CMM-3), and an optional trailing idle sequence (CMM-4). The carrier then returns to CMM-1 until the latest of three events: the delay-time expiring (measured from the last bit sent), the next CLTU becoming available, or the end of the session. Both lengths may be set to zero, so that a mission which does not fully follow PLOP-1 can put its own acquisition and idle bits inside the CLTU data.24
  • PLOP-2: after the uplink sweep (CMM-1) the provider sends the acquisition sequence once, then idle (CMM-4) for as long as needed. Each CLTU is sent (CMM-3) as soon as it is available and the previous CLTU's delay-time has expired, with idle in between. PLOP-2 ends with a return to CMM-1, but no standard mechanism decides when.24

The idle sequence lets the spacecraft keep bit synchronisation when no CLTU is being sent. Under PLOP-2, CCSDS 231.0 recommends inserting at least one octet of idle between CLTUs. This avoids a rare synchronisation lockout, where a missed start sequence plus a false start pattern spanning the end of one CLTU would make the receiver miss the start of the next.2325

docs.title: Production status
docs.text:
FCLTU production status has four values. In ASN.1 they are operational (0), configured (1), interrupted (2) and halted (3). Note that the numbering differs from the return services.1126

Value Meaning configured Equipment assigned, but not yet able to radiate CLTUs (initial value) operational Configured, acquisition complete, able to radiate interrupted Stopped by a fault that may be transient halted Taken out of service by management, for example after a non-transient fault or to reassign resources 
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Configured
    Configured --> Operational: sweep done (+ RF available / bit lock if required)<br/>notify 'production operational'
    Operational --> Interrupted: fault, or CLCW shows No RF / No Bit Lock<br/>when required — notify 'production interrupted'
    Interrupted --> Operational: fault cleared — notify 'production operational'
    Configured --> Halted: operator — notify 'production halted'
    Operational --> Halted: operator
    Interrupted --> Halted: operator
    Halted --> Configured: operator restores configuration (no notification)

Diagram based on figure B-1, table B-1 and B2.3–B2.4 of the FCLTU specification.2728

The CLCW drives two optional checks, enabled by rf-available-required and bit-lock-required.

  • PLOP-1: production becomes operational at the end of the uplink sweep. If rf-available-required is 'yes', the CLCW must also show RF available. While the carrier is unmodulated, acquiring, radiating or idling, production drops to 'interrupted' if a required flag shows a problem. For bit lock, this check applies from the end of the acquisition sequence onwards.28
  • PLOP-2: the transition at the end of the sweep requires bit-lock-required to be 'no'. Otherwise production becomes operational during CMM-2 or CMM-4, as soon as a CLCW reports bit lock.29

Uplink status is the provider's summary of the last CLCW it received:3026

uplink-status Code Condition on the last CLCW uplink status not available 0 No CLCW received yet no rf available 1 No RF Available = 1 no bit lock 2 No RF Available = 0, No Bit Lock = 1 nominal 3 Both flags 0

Those two flags are bits 16 and 17 of the CLCW (see the CLCW diagram on the return services page).31 The provider learns which telemetry channel carries the CLCW from the clcw-global-VCID and clcw-physical-channel parameters, either of which may be 'not configured'.3233

The FCLTU GvcId type allows spacecraft identifiers 0 to 65535, but its ASN.1 comment gives 0 to 255 as the range for TM frames.34 The RCF and ROCF modules give 0 to 1023 for TM, which matches the 10-bit TM spacecraft identifier.35 A TM spacecraft such as Solar Orbiter (SCID 650) is therefore encodable in clcw-global-VCID, even though it lies outside the range stated in the FCLTU comment.

Inference

The 0 to 255 TM range in the FCLTU comment looks like an editorial slip copied from the AOS line. The standard does not say so.

Notification mode. A provider may tell the user about an interruption at once ('immediate') or only when it affects a CLTU that is radiating or due ('deferred'). In deferred mode, CLTU-TRANSFER-DATA is accepted until the notification has been sent. The parameter only documents what the implementation does.362937

Production status Operation Effect Diagnostic halted CLTU-BIND, CLTU-START rejected 'out of service' halted CLTU-TRANSFER-DATA rejected 'unable to process' interrupted CLTU-START rejected 'unable to comply' interrupted CLTU-TRANSFER-DATA rejected (in deferred mode, only after notification) 'unable to process' configured, operational all none specified —

Source: table B-2.29

docs.title: Operations
docs.text:
Operation Invoker Confirmed Valid in states ASN.1 tag (invocation / return) CLTU-BIND user only yes 1 [100] / [101] CLTU-UNBIND user yes 2 [102] / [103] CLTU-START user yes 2 [0] / [1] CLTU-STOP user yes 3 [2] / [3] CLTU-TRANSFER-DATA user yes 3 [10] / [11] CLTU-ASYNC-NOTIFY provider no 2, 3 [12] CLTU-SCHEDULE-STATUS-REPORT user yes 2, 3 [4] / [5] CLTU-STATUS-REPORT provider no 2, 3 [13] CLTU-GET-PARAMETER user yes 2, 3 [6] / [7] CLTU-THROW-EVENT user yes 2, 3 [8] / [9] CLTU-PEER-ABORT either no 2, 3 [104]

Sources: operations table,38 states,39404142 PDU tags.4344 Unlike the return services, TRANSFER-DATA is confirmed: every CLTU is individually accepted or rejected.38 BIND, UNBIND and PEER-ABORT follow the common rules on the overview. The BIND service type is 'fwdCltu', and version negotiation in BIND is optional for FCLTU.745

docs.title: CLTU-START
docs.text:
START moves the provider to 'active' and fixes the first CLTU number.39

Parameter Inv. Ret. Meaning invoke-ID M M Echoed first-cltu-identification M The cltu-identification expected in the first CLTU-TRANSFER-DATA start-production-time C If not yet operational, the estimated time radiation can start; otherwise the most recent time production became operational stop-production-time C Estimated stop of radiation, or 'null'; may be after the end of the provision period result, diagnostic M, C

After an 'sldu expired' event the user must STOP and START again. The specification advises choosing a new first-cltu-identification that cannot be confused with a CLTU still being processed, because that CLTU may still produce a notification after the new START.39

START diagnostic Code duplicate invoke-ID common 100 out of service (production 'halted') specific 0 unable to comply (production 'interrupted') specific 1 production time expired specific 2 invalid cltu-ID (lower than a CLTU already buffered) specific 3 other reason common 127

Sources: diagnostics,39 codes.4647

docs.title: CLTU-STOP
docs.text: STOP takes the provider back to 'ready'. Buffered CLTUs that have not started radiating are discarded. A CLTU that is being radiated is completed, and its requested report is still sent as an ASYNC-NOTIFY. Depending on the implementation, one more CLTU may get radiated after the STOP arrives. If STOP is rejected, nothing is discarded.48

docs.title: CLTU-TRANSFER-DATA
docs.text:
Parameter Inv. Ret. Meaning invoke-ID M M Echoed cltu-identification M M Monotonically increasing sequence number; the return holds the next expected value earliest-radiation-time M 'null' or the earliest time the first bit may be radiated latest-radiation-time M 'null' or the latest time radiation may begin delay-time M Minimum gap in µs between this CLTU and the next report M 'produce report' (0) or 'do not produce report' (1): notify when radiation completes data M The CLTU cltu-buffer-available M Remaining buffer, in octets result, diagnostic M, C

Sources: parameter table and definitions,4049 ASN.1 encodings.5047

The rules that make FCLTU deterministic:

  • Sequence numbers. The first CLTU after START must carry first-cltu-identification, and each accepted CLTU increments it. A positive return carries the invocation value plus one. A negative return carries the value the provider still expects.51
  • Radiation window. With a null earliest time, the CLTU is processed as soon as the previous CLTU's delay has elapsed and production is operational. With a null latest time, the CLTU waits as long as the instance is active and production is not halted. If a latest time is given and production is interrupted, processing is deferred until production recovers or the latest time passes; in the second case the CLTU is discarded. Equal earliest and latest times mean "radiate at exactly this time". A CLTU that has not started by its latest time raises 'sldu expired' and is not radiated.52
  • Delay. delay-time is a guard time after the CLTU, and must not be below the managed minimum-delay-time. Its exact effect depends on the PLOP (above).2449
  • Buffering. Accepted CLTUs are buffered and processed in the order received, according to their times and delays. cltu-buffer-available does not include any small extra buffer at the modulator input, which belongs to production.4953
TRANSFER-DATA diagnostic Code Cause duplicate invoke-ID common 100 unable to process specific 0 Production halted; interrupted and notified; blocked after an earlier fault, an expired CLTU, or while a THROW-EVENT is being processed unable to store specific 1 Not enough buffer space out of sequence specific 2 cltu-identification is not the expected value inconsistent time range specific 3 Earliest time later than latest time invalid time specific 4 Window outside scheduled production or the provision period late sldu specific 5 Latest time already past when the invocation arrives invalid delay time specific 6 Below minimum-delay-time CLTU error specific 7 Fails agreed checks, for example longer than the maximum CLTU length other reason common 127

Sources: diagnostics,54 codes.46

Worked example (illustrative). A user STARTs with first-cltu-identification = 100 and sends three CLTUs with null radiation times, a delay time of 100,000 µs, and 'produce report' only on the last one.

sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User (control centre)
    participant P as FCLTU provider
    U->>P: CLTU-START (first-cltu-identification = 100)
    P-->>U: positive, start-production-time = 11:59:40
    U->>P: TRANSFER-DATA id=100, delay 100000 µs, no report
    P-->>U: positive, id=101, buffer-available = 4193998
    U->>P: TRANSFER-DATA id=101, no report
    P-->>U: positive, id=102
    U->>P: TRANSFER-DATA id=103 (skipped 102), produce report
    P-->>U: negative 'out of sequence', id=102
    U->>P: TRANSFER-DATA id=102, produce report
    P-->>U: positive, id=103
    Note over P: radiates 100, 101, 102<br/>≥ 0.1 s apart
    P->>U: ASYNC-NOTIFY 'cltu radiated'<br/>last-processed = 102 (radiated), last-OK = 102
    P->>U: ASYNC-NOTIFY 'buffer empty'

Illustrative sequence built from the rules in §3.4, §3.6 and §3.7.395141 The buffer value assumes the 4,194,304-octet minimum buffer and a 306-octet CLTU.37

docs.title: CLTU-ASYNC-NOTIFY
docs.text:
Notifications travel independently of the CLTU flow, in states 2 and 3.41

notification-type ASN.1 CltuNotification Meaning and effect cltu radiated cltuRadiated [0] The CLTU cltu-last-processed finished radiating (only if its report asked for it) sldu expired slduExpired [1] It did not start by its latest time. Nothing more is radiated, the buffer is discarded, and TRANSFER-DATA is blocked until STOP production interrupted productionInterrupted [2] Immediate or deferred (see above). Same blocking and discarding as above (in state 3) production halted productionHalted [3] Management halted production. Same blocking and discarding (in state 3) production operational productionOperational [4] Ready to radiate (after acquisition or recovery) buffer empty bufferEmpty [5] No more CLTUs buffered; not sent if the buffer was emptied by STOP or by an interruption or halt action list completed actionListCompleted [6] All actions of THROW-EVENT event-thrown-identification succeeded action list not completed actionListNotCompleted [7] At least one action failed event condition evaluated to false eventConditionEvFalse [8] A precondition of the event was false; nothing was done

Sources: notification types and effects,4155 ASN.1.56

Every notification also carries cltu-last-processed (with its radiation start time and status, or 'null'), cltu-last-OK (with its radiation stop time, or 'null'), production-status and uplink-status.5756 The cltu-status values are:5747

cltu-status ForwardDuStatus code Meaning radiated 0 Radiation completed without aborting: guaranteed radiated expired 1 Latest time reached before radiation began: guaranteed not radiated interrupted 2 Radiation started but production became 'interrupted' radiation started 4 (productionStarted) Radiation started, processing not complete radiation not started 5 (productionNotStarted) Could not start because production was 'interrupted'

docs.title: CLTU-SCHEDULE-STATUS-REPORT and CLTU-STATUS-REPORT
docs.text:
Scheduling works as for the return services ('immediately', 'periodically', 'stop'), except that FCLTU has no offline mode.58 A status report contains:59

Field Meaning cltu-last-processed, cltu-last-OK, cltu-status, radiation-start-time, radiation-stop-time As in ASYNC-NOTIFY production-status, uplink-status As above number-of-cltus-received CLTUs checked successfully and buffered during this instance number-of-cltus-processed CLTUs the provider attempted to radiate: radiated, expired, aborted, or being radiated number-of-cltus-radiated CLTUs radiated successfully (not counting one in progress) cltu-buffer-available Octets free; a CLTU leaves the buffer when processing starts

Statistics accumulate over the whole provision period, across associations.6061
