docs.title: SLE over TCP/IP (ISP1) and the SLE API
docs.text:
The SLE transfer service specifications define what is exchanged: operations, parameters and ASN.1 types. They deliberately say nothing about the network. They require only an underlying service that delivers PDUs in sequence, completely and with integrity, without duplication, with flow control, and with notice of disruption.1 Two further CCSDS documents close that gap. The Internet SLE Protocol One (ISP1, CCSDS 913.1-B-2) is a Recommended Standard that maps SLE associations onto TCP connections.2 The SLE Application Program Interface (CCSDS 914.0-M-2) is a Recommended Practice that defines a C++ component architecture, so that SLE user and provider software can be built from interchangeable packages.3 The 2006 concept report already described the API in the same layered way: an API Proxy for the communications technology beneath an API Service Element for the service logic.69

The SLE concepts used here (associations, BIND, PEER-ABORT, credentials) are introduced on the SLE overview. The services carried are described on return services, FCLTU and FSP. Where these documents sit in the SLE documentation tree is shown on the overview.

At a glance

Item ISP1 SLE API Document CCSDS 913.1-B-2, Blue Book, September 20154 CCSDS 914.0-M-2, Magenta Book, September 2015, Technical Corrigendum 1 (August 2016)5 Supersedes 913.1-B-1 (September 2008), now historical 913.1-B-1-S46 914.0-M-1 (October 2008)5 Main change in current issue One-way hash changed from SHA-1 to SHA-2564 Text updated to current service versions; Cor. 1 points to 913.1-B for the hash algorithm5 Layers / components Authentication Layer, Data Encoding Layer, Transport Mapping Layer over TCP/IP7 API Proxy, API Service Element, SLE Operations, SLE Utilities, plus the SLE Application8 Encoding ASN.1 BER (credentials hashed over DER)910 Technology hidden in the Proxy11 One association = one TCP connection7 one Association object in the Proxy11 Service-specific books in this library — RAF API 915.1-M-2 and FSP API 916.3-M-2, both September 20157071

docs.title: ISP1 architecture
docs.text:
ISP1 sits between the "higher layers" and TCP/IP. The higher layers are the SLE transfer service logic: they build and analyse PDUs and run the state tables. ISP1 itself has three sublayers:7

flowchart TB
    HL["Higher layers: SLE transfer service<br/>(RAF / RCF / ROCF / FCLTU state tables)"]
    subgraph ISP1["Internet SLE Protocol Layer"]
        AL["Authentication Layer (AL)<br/>credentials: Protected 1 + SHA-256"]
        DEL["Data Encoding Layer (DEL)<br/>ASN.1 BER encode / decode"]
        TML["Transport Mapping Layer (TML)<br/>messages, heartbeat, connect, abort"]
    end
    TCP["TCP"] --- IP["IP"]
    HL -- "AL-SLE-PDU" --> AL
    AL -- "DEL-SLE-PDU" --> DEL
    DEL -- "TML-SLE-PDU" --> TML
    HL -. "TML association control<br/>(CONNECT, DISCONNECT,<br/>PEER-ABORT, RESET)<br/>and listener interface" .-> TML
    TML --> TCP

Diagram based on figure 2-1 and the interface descriptions of CCSDS 913.1-B-2.712

Two design rules shape the whole protocol:

  • One SLE association uses exactly one TCP connection. Association establishment and release involve only the TML. Once established, every PDU passes through the DEL and the AL.713
  • PEER-ABORT bypasses encoding. The PEER-ABORT invocation is never BER-encoded. The TML sends its one-octet diagnostic as TCP urgent data.1415

ISP1 leaves open how its configuration parameters are defined, agreed, stored and made available to an implementation.7

docs.title: Authentication Layer
docs.text:
The AL adds credentials to outgoing PDUs and checks them on incoming ones, according to the instance's authentication level: 'all' (every invocation and return except the PEER-ABORT invocation), 'bind' (BIND invocation and return only) or 'none'.16 It uses the "Protected 1" simple authentication procedure, with these inputs:10

  • a user name of 3 to 16 characters, identical to the authority identifier in the BIND (initiator-identifier for the initiator, responder-identifier for the responder);
  • a password of 6 to 16 octets;
  • the current time, as an 8-octet CCSDS Day Segmented code without P-field;
  • a random number from 0 to 2,147,483,647.

These four values are DER-encoded as a HashInput and hashed with SHA-256. The result is called "the protected". The credentials carry the time, the random number and the digest, but not the user name, which is already in the BIND.10

HashInput ::= SEQUENCE              -- DER-encoded, then hashed with SHA-256
{ time          OCTET STRING (SIZE(8))      -- CDS, no P-field
, randomNumber  INTEGER (0 .. 2147483647)
, userName      VisibleString
, passWord      OCTET STRING
}

ISP1Credentials ::= SEQUENCE        -- carried inside Credentials 'used' [1] OCTET STRING
{ time          OCTET STRING (SIZE (8))
, randomNumber  INTEGER (0 .. 2147483647)
, theProtected  OCTET STRING (SIZE (20..32))  -- 32 for SHA-256; 20 allowed for SHA-1 peers
}

ASN.1 quoted from figures 3-1 and 3-2 of CCSDS 913.1-B-2.109

The receiver first checks that the credential time is within an acceptable delay of its own clock. This maximum delay is a configuration parameter. It then recomputes the digest using the peer's user name and password, and compares the two.1016 The 20-octet option exists so that implementations can stay compatible with peers built to the SHA-1 based 913.1-B-1.9 If authentication fails, the higher layers apply the transfer service rule: the PDU is ignored, as if it had never arrived.17

Worked example (illustrative values, real algorithm). Take user name MCS-USER, password 01 23 45 67 89 AB CD EF, time 62 40 02 93 2E 7B 01 C8 (2026-11-12 12:00:00.123456 UTC; see return services) and random number 0x12345678. The DER HashInput is:

30 24                                    SEQUENCE, 36 octets
   04 08 62 40 02 93 2E 7B 01 C8         time
   02 04 12 34 56 78                     randomNumber
   1A 08 4D 43 53 2D 55 53 45 52         userName "MCS-USER" (VisibleString)
   04 08 01 23 45 67 89 AB CD EF         passWord

Its SHA-256 digest is C69510D1403E0E97C55A59F4D741C97DE919020E9CE006AC2303046B944C3020. The ISP1Credentials value is 30 32 04 08 62 40 02 93 2E 7B 01 C8 02 04 12 34 56 78 04 20 followed by the 32 digest octets, 52 octets in all. Inside an SLE PDU this becomes Credentials → used [1], encoded 81 34 followed by those 52 octets. This wiki computed these bytes from the ASN.1 definitions. The credentials are invented and are not from any real system.

Inference

The final step assumes the IMPLICIT TAGS encoding of the Credentials CHOICE alternative used [1] OCTET STRING (context-specific primitive tag 1 = 0x81). This follows from the RAF common types module,18 but ISP1 does not print a complete encoded example.

ISP1 is frank about the limits of this scheme. It provides authentication and access control only. Confidentiality, integrity beyond what TCP gives, and strong authentication must come from a secure channel through which ISP1 traffic is tunnelled, or from end-to-end protection of the mission data.1920

docs.title: Data Encoding Layer
docs.text:
The DEL encodes and decodes every SLE PDU except the PEER-ABORT invocation. It uses the ASN.1 types of the applicable service specification and the Basic Encoding Rules.149 The first PDU on a new association must be a BIND invocation. Its service-type and version-number tell the DEL which ASN.1 modules to use for everything that follows on the same association. An unsupported service type or version is reported to the higher layers, which then apply the BIND rules (for example 'service type not supported').149

The top-level CHOICE tags of each service's user-to-provider and provider-to-user PDUs tell the receiver which operation a PDU carries. These tags are listed on the return services and FCLTU pages.

Worked example (illustrative, constructed from the ASN.1). A RAF user sends STOP with invoke-ID 5 and no credentials. rafStopInvocation [2] is a SleStopInvocation, which is a SEQUENCE of invokerCredentials and invokeId.21 With IMPLICIT TAGS, the alternative tag replaces the SEQUENCE tag. Credentials 'unused' is [0] NULL, and the invoke-ID is an INTEGER:

A2 05          [2] constructed (rafStopInvocation), length 5
   80 00       invokerCredentials = unused [0] NULL
   02 01 05    invokeId = 5

Inference

This encoding follows from the RAF ASN.1 modules (tag [2], IMPLICIT TAGS, Credentials CHOICE, InvokeId ::= IntUnsignedShort).211822 The common PDUs module, also under IMPLICIT TAGS, defines SleStopInvocation as a SEQUENCE of invokerCredentials and invokeId only.23 The library has no SLE capture to confirm the bytes.

docs.title: TML messages
docs.text:
TCP carries a byte stream, so the TML frames everything in TML messages: an 8-octet header followed by a body of any length (not necessarily a multiple of four). All integers are big endian.2425

Type ID Message Body 1 SLE PDU message One BER-encoded SLE PDU (never a PEER-ABORT) 2 TML context message 12 octets: protocol ID, version, heartbeat parameters 3 TML heartbeat message Empty (length 0)

Sources: table 3-1 and §3.3.2.2426

Field layout from figure 3-4.24

Worked examples (byte layouts from the standard, parameter values illustrative):

Message Bytes Context, heartbeat 30 s, dead factor 5 02 00 00 00 00 00 00 0C 49 53 50 31 00 00 00 01 00 1E 00 05 Heartbeat 03 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 SLE PDU carrying the RAF STOP above 01 00 00 00 00 00 00 07 A2 05 80 00 02 01 05 PEER-ABORT 'return timeout' one byte 06 sent as TCP urgent data (no TML header)

The PEER-ABORT code 6 is the 'return timeout' value of PeerAbortDiagnostic.2728

docs.title: Heartbeat
docs.text:
TCP cannot tell an idle connection from a dead one. Some TCP implementations offer keep-alive probes, but the Internet host requirements (STD 3, ISP1 reference [E7]) require their default interval to be at least two hours, so ISP1 defines its own heartbeat.29 Two parameters control it. The heartbeat-interval is the longest a TML may stay silent, in seconds. The dead-factor is the number of intervals without any incoming message after which the connection is declared dead. Two timers implement it:30

  • HBT (heartbeat transmit) runs for the heartbeat interval and is restarted on every message sent. When it expires, the TML sends a heartbeat message.
  • HBR (heartbeat receive) runs for the interval × dead factor and is restarted on every message received. When it expires, the TML aborts TCP and reports a protocol abort with diagnostic 'heartbeat receive timeout' (132).

With the illustrative values above, an idle TML sends a heartbeat every 30 s and gives up after 150 s of silence. A heartbeat interval of 0 disables the mechanism.30 The heartbeat is how ISP1 meets the transfer services' requirement to detect communications failure, which they then treat as a 'protocol abort'.31

docs.title: Connection establishment
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant I as Initiating TML (user)
    participant R as Responding TML (provider)
    Note over R: TML-START-LISTEN: passive open on the<br/>socket mapped from the responder port
    I->>R: TCP connect (socket from responder-port-identifier)
    Note over R: start TMS (start-up) timer
    I->>R: TML context message ('ISP1', v1, HB interval, dead factor)
    Note over I: start HBT and HBR;<br/>TML-CONNECT-confirmation
    Note over R: check header, protocol ID, version,<br/>heartbeat ranges, then start HBT;<br/>TML-CONNECT-indication
    I->>R: SLE PDU message: BIND invocation (BER)
    Note over R: first valid SLE PDU: stop TMS, start HBR
    R->>I: SLE PDU message: BIND return
    loop association lifetime
        I-->>R: SLE PDUs / heartbeats
        R-->>I: SLE PDUs / heartbeats
    end

Sequence based on §2.5.3–2.5.4 and §3.3.4 of CCSDS 913.1-B-2.3233

On the responding side, any failed check on the first message ends the connection silently with TCP-ABORT and no TML diagnostic. This happens for a header that does not parse, a first message that is not a context message, the wrong protocol ID or version, or a TMS timeout before the context message and the first SLE PDU arrive.33 If the heartbeat parameters are out of range, §2.5.3 describes a PEER-ABORT with the TML diagnostic 'heartbeat unacceptable' (Annex A code 130, 'heartbeat parameters not acceptable'). The detailed §3.3.4 instead only says that the TML starts its timer "if the values are acceptable", and §2.5.4.2 says it aborts with TCP-ABORT.293233 The start-up timer is ISP1's only defence against unauthenticated users holding resources open.20 If the TMS timer expires after the context message but before a valid SLE PDU, the TML also informs the higher layers with a protocol abort.33

Redundant hosts. A responder port identifier may map to several sockets. The initiator then connects to all of them at once, keeps the first that succeeds, and aborts the others. This relies on only one responding host listening at any time, and the standard leaves open how that is ensured.3435

docs.title: Release and abort
docs.text:
Procedure Trigger What the TML does Orderly release (initiator) TML-DISCONNECT-request after UNBIND Closes the TCP connection36 Orderly release (responder) TML-DISCONNECT-request after UNBIND return Stops HBT, restarts HBR, and waits for the peer to close. Aborts if data arrive or HBR expires36 Peer abort TML-PEER-ABORT-request Sends the diagnostic as one urgent byte, stops HBT and HBR, starts CPA (close after peer abort). Discards incoming data, closes when the peer closes, and aborts TCP if CPA expires28 Receiving an abort TCP urgent data indication Discards data up to the urgent byte and reads it. Codes 0–127 give PEER-ABORT-indication; TML codes give PROTOCOL-ABORT-indication. Then closes28 Simultaneous aborts Urgent data after sending one's own Discards up to and including the urgent byte, closes, and does not report the peer's diagnostic28 Silent abort TML-RESET-request (for example on return timeout) TCP-ABORT, nothing sent28 Protocol abort TCP error, send timeout, or peer close before DISCONNECT or urgent data PROTOCOL-ABORT-indication37

If the TCP API does not support ABORT, ISP1 allows TCP-ABORT to have the same effect as a normal disconnect.28

docs.title: Diagnostic code ranges and TML codes
docs.text:
PEER-ABORT diagnostics are a single octet. Codes 0 to 127 belong to the transfer service specifications, 128 to 199 to ISP1, and 200 to 255 to implementations.38

Code TML diagnostic 128 TML protocol error (for example a context message received after start-up) 129 Badly formatted TML message 130 Heartbeat parameters not acceptable 131 Association establishment timeout 132 Heartbeat receive timeout 133 Unexpected disconnect by peer 134 Premature disconnect during peer abort 135 Timeout during peer abort 199 Other reason

Sources: Annex A and §3.3.7.3940

docs.title: TML state machine
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> S0
    S0: S0 CLOSED
    S1: S1 TML STARTING
    S2: S2 DATA TRANSFER
    S3: S3 PEER ABORTING
    S4: S4 TML CLOSING
    S0 --> S1: CONNECT-request (initiator) /<br/>TCP connect indication (responder)
    S1 --> S2: context message sent (initiator) /<br/>valid context received (responder)
    S1 --> S0: TCP error / TMS timeout / bad first message
    S2 --> S2: SLE PDU / heartbeat (restart HBR)
    S2 --> S3: TCP urgent data indication
    S3 --> S0: diagnostic read, connection closed
    S2 --> S4: DISCONNECT-request / PEER-ABORT-request
    S4 --> S0: peer closed / CPA or HBR timeout → TCP abort
    S2 --> S0: HBR timeout / TCP error / RESET-request

Diagram based on the states, events and predicates of §4.3–4.5; the normative table on PDF pp. 62–65 has many more transitions.4142

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Side Per system Per association Initiator Responder port identifier → one or more (IP address, TCP port) Proposed heartbeat interval, proposed dead factor, CPA timeout Responder Responder port identifier → local socket Acceptable heartbeat interval and dead factor ranges, TML start-up timeout, CPA timeout AL (if level is 'all' or 'bind') — Local identifier and password, peer identifier and password, maximum credential age

Sources: §2.3 and §2.5.8.1643

ISP1 recommends leaving the initiator's local socket unspecified (ephemeral port), and notes that a responder may filter source addresses, for example with a firewall.32

docs.title: ISP1 and its ESA precursor
docs.text:
ISP1 grew out of ESA work. Its precursor was ESA's Specification of an SLE API Proxy for TCP/IP and ASN.1 (SLES-SW-API-0002-TOS-GCI, issue 1.1, February 2001), which took its authentication scheme and service instance identifier from ESA's SLE C++ Application Program Interface for Transfer Services (SLES-SW-API-0001-TOS-GCI, December 2000).4445 When ISP1 was published, all known SLE implementations were based on the ESA proxy specification. Two differences remain:44

  • That generation used draft service specifications with BIND version 1 (RAF 911.1-R-1.7, RCF 911.2-R-1.7, CLTU 912.1-R-1.99h), whose ASN.1 differs. An initiator talking to such a responder must send version 1 and use the old types. The BIND encoding itself did not change.
  • Old service instance identifiers distinguished vcf= and mcf=. The standard uses rcf=, so a timely online RCF instance was vcf=onlt1 or mcf=onlt1 and is now rcf=onlt1.

docs.title: Purpose and scope
docs.text:
The SLE API is a C++ API, independent of the communications technology, for applications that implement SLE services in either the user or the provider role. It also aims to simplify gateways between different technologies. Its goal is that an API package for a platform can be supplied to a new SLE user and integrated with little investment.3 It defines components, their functions, their interfaces and their externally visible behaviour, but not implementations, internal design or the communications technology.46 Service-specific API books complement the core:4647

Book Service In this library CCSDS 915.1-M-2 RAF API yes (library; see RAF with the SLE API) CCSDS 915.2-M-2 RCF API no CCSDS 915.5-M-2 ROCF API no CCSDS 916.1-M-2 FCLTU API no CCSDS 916.3-M-2 FSP API yes (library; see the FSP API)

Two companion Reports belong to the same family: Summary of Concept and Rationale (914.1-G-1, January 2006) and Application Programmer's Guide (914.2-G-2, October 2008), the latter with guidance and source code examples for developers. Neither is in this library.7273

Two optional features of the service standards are deliberately left out. BIND version negotiation is not supported: an unsupported version is simply rejected. Provider-initiated binding is not supported either, although the management parameters for it exist.48

docs.title: Generations of SLE services supported
docs.text:
Generation Services and BIND version Peer TML 1 RAF, RCF, FCLTU version 1 ESOC Specification of a SLE API Proxy for TCP/IP and ASN.1 (SLES-SW-API-0002-TOS-GCI issue 1.1) 2 RAF, RCF, FCLTU version 2; ROCF and FSP version 1 ISP1 (913.1) 3 RAF, RCF, ROCF, FCLTU and FSP version 4 ISP1 (913.1)

Generations 1 and 2 are kept only for backward compatibility and may be dropped. Provisions are marked [Gn:] in the text.49 The service-specific books state which generations they support for their own service, and which issue of the service specification each one follows:

Book Generation 1 Generation 2 Generation 3 Service issue it is written against RAF API 915.1-M-2 version 1 (draft 911.1-R-1.7, ESOC TML) version 2 (911.1-B-2-S) version 4 911.1-B-3, January 20107475 FSP API 916.3-M-2 not valid: FSP first appeared with generation 2 version 1 (912.3-B-1-S) version 4 912.3-B-2, July 20107677

Not covered by the library

The 2023 RAF, RCF, ROCF and FCLTU issues used elsewhere on these pages define BIND version 6 (see the overview), and the 2016 FSP issue defines version 5.78 The 2015 API books list generations only up to version 4. Whether a later API issue covers versions 5 and 6 is not stated in the available sources. For RAF, the return services page lists concrete differences between the API and the 2023 issue.

        P3["PDU Translator<br/>(common + service-specific)"]
    end
    OPS["SLE Operations<br/>(ISLE_Bind, IRAF_TransferData, …)"]
    UT["SLE Utilities<br/>(ISLE_Time, ISLE_SII,<br/>ISLE_Credentials, IMalloc …)"]
    APP <-->|"ISLE_ServiceInitiate /<br/>ISLE_ServiceInform"| S2
    S2 <-->|"ISLE_SrvProxyInitiate /<br/>ISLE_SrvProxyInform"| P2
    P2 --- P3
    P3 --- NET(("network"))
    OPS -.-> APP
    OPS -.-> SE
    OPS -.-> PX
    UT -.-> SE
    UT -.-> PX

Diagram based on figures 2-2 and 2-3 and §2.3 of CCSDS 914.0-M-2.811

  • API Proxy. All technology-specific functions live here, hidden from clients. The Proxy also enforces system-level access control and authenticates peers. ISLE_ProxyAdmin configures it. ISLE_AssocFactory creates Associations, which exchange PDUs through ISLE_SrvProxyInitiate and the client-supplied ISLE_SrvProxyInform. The PDU Translator converts between API operation objects and the transfer encoding; it is the only part of the Proxy that depends on the service type. A Proxy declares its technology with a Protocol ID, and the service element can use several proxies.1150
  • API Service Element. It holds the service instances. A service instance checks that PDUs fit its role, service type and version. For return services, a SI User unpacks each TRANSFER-BUFFER into individual TRANSFER-DATA and SYNC-NOTIFY operations. A SI Provider fills the transfer buffer, runs the release timer, performs the timely online discard, and answers GET-PARAMETER and status reporting itself.5152
  • SLE Operations. These are operation objects for each SLE operation, such as ISLE_Bind, ISLE_Unbind, ISLE_PeerAbort, ISLE_Stop, ISLE_ScheduleStatusReport, ISLE_TransferBuffer and IRAF_TransferData, all derived from ISLE_Operation or ISLE_ConfirmedOperation.53
  • SLE Utilities. Helper objects for time, service instance identifiers, credentials, security attributes and memory (IMalloc, a subset of the COM memory manager).5455
  • SLE Application. Supplied by the user of the API, not part of it. It must provide ISLE_ServiceInform, logging (ISLE_Reporter), optional tracing (ISLE_Trace) and a time source.5657

All interfaces derive from a COM-style IUnknown, so objects are navigated with QueryInterface(). Each interface has a GUID. Compatibility between applications built against different API issues is guaranteed only for interfaces with the same GUID.5859

docs.title: Service-specific extensions: the RAF and FSP books
docs.text:
The core uses placeholders such as I<SRV>_SI User, I<SRV>_SI Provider, I<SRV>_SIAdmin and I<SRV>_SIUpdate. Each service book fills them in. Both books in this library follow the same pattern: the API Service Element and SLE Operations components are extended, and the API Proxy must in addition encode and decode the service's PDUs.7980

Aspect RAF API (915.1-M-2) FSP API (916.3-M-2) User-side class RAF SI User: handles the RAF operation objects, nothing more FSP SI User: same Provider-side configuration IRAF_SIAdmin: delivery mode, transfer buffer size, latency limit, initial production and lock status IFSP_SIAdmin for the FSP configuration, plus IFSP_FOPMonitor for the FOP-1 parameters (the core's I<SRV>_SIAdmin is split in two because there are so many parameters) Provider-side status updates IRAF_SIUpdate: production status and four lock statuses, reported at every change IFSP_SIUpdate: production events such as packet started, radiated, acknowledged, buffer empty, VC aborted, directive completed Done by the provider service instance itself GET-PARAMETER returns, STATUS-REPORT generation, transfer buffer handling, frame counters GET-PARAMETER returns, STATUS-REPORT generation, and optionally the ASYNC-NOTIFY invocations triggered by IFSP_SIUpdate events Service-specific operation objects IRAF_Start, IRAF_TransferData, IRAF_SyncNotify, IRAF_StatusReport, IRAF_GetParameter IFSP_Start, IFSP_TransferData, IFSP_AsyncNotify, IFSP_StatusReport, IFSP_GetParameter, IFSP_ThrowEvent, IFSP_InvokeDirective Core operation objects reused BIND, UNBIND, PEER-ABORT, STOP, SCHEDULE-STATUS-REPORT, transfer buffer BIND, UNBIND, PEER-ABORT, STOP, SCHEDULE-STATUS-REPORT Checks left to the application production status, offline processing latency production status, time windows against the current time, APID, packet version and type

Sources: the package and operation sections of both books.81828380848586 In both books, when the service element makes some of the specification's checks itself, the book documents the resulting split of the diagnostic order between service element and application, because a provider that does not check in the order of the diagnostic codes must document the order it uses (the RAF book attributes this rule to the API core, the FSP book to the FSP specification).8788 For the provider application, the obligations are simple to state: configure every instance through the core and the service SIAdmin interface before ConfigCompleted(), then keep the SIUpdate interface informed for the instance's whole lifetime.8990 The RAF details are on return services and the FSP details on FSP.

docs.title: Flow control and buffering
docs.text:
The API pushes the SLE buffering rules down into the service element and the Proxy, so that applications see only operations:515260

  • Inbound limits. An Association stops reading from the network when more than N1 received PDUs, or N2 ≤ N1 TRANSFER-DATA or TRANSFER-BUFFER PDUs, are waiting for the client. This builds back-pressure on TCP.
  • Outbound queue. A positive transmission request means only "queued". On request, the Association reports actual transmission. It can also remove TRANSFER-BUFFER PDUs that have not started transmission. This is how the timely online discard is implemented: if the previous buffer has not been sent, it is discarded and the next buffer starts with a 'data discarded due to excessive backlog' notification.
  • Application back-pressure. In complete online and offline modes, and for forward services, the service instance returns a code telling the application to suspend data transfer. It calls ResumeDataTransfer() on ISLE_ServiceInform when transfer can continue.
sequenceDiagram
    participant App as Provider application
    participant SI as SI Provider (service element)
    participant As as Association (proxy)
    App->>SI: TRANSFER-DATA (frame n)
    SI->>SI: add to transfer buffer;<br/>start release timer if first
    Note over SI: buffer full or<br/>release timer expired
    SI->>As: TRANSFER-BUFFER invocation
    As-->>SI: queued
    App->>SI: TRANSFER-DATA (frame n+k)
    Note over SI: next buffer due but previous<br/>not yet transmitted (timely online)
    SI->>As: discard queued TRANSFER-BUFFER
    As-->>SI: discarded
    SI->>As: TRANSFER-BUFFER ('data discarded' + new frames)

Illustrative sequence based on §2.3.3.5 of CCSDS 914.0-M-2.52

docs.title: Sequential and concurrent behaviour
docs.text: Every component exposes one of two threading models, through ISLE_Sequential or ISLE_Concurrent. Sequential means only one flow of control passes an interface at a time. The application then has to provide an event loop and timers (ISLE_EventMonitor, ISLE_TimerHandler). Concurrent means several threads may call in at once; the term maps to UML's "concurrent or guarded". A service element can use different models towards the application and towards the proxy. An implementation must support at least one model, and an application must handle the control interface of the model it uses.616257

docs.title: Pass-through mode for gateways
docs.text: As an option, the Proxy supports a pass-through mode for gateways. In this mode it does not insert its own application identifier into BIND invocations and returns, but forwards the identifiers in the operation objects. This keeps end-to-end identification and authentication between the real user and the real provider.63

docs.title: States
docs.text: The Proxy's association state table uses five states: S1 UNBOUND, S2 BIND PEND, S3 BOUND, S4 LOC UNBIND PEND and S5 REM UNBIND PEND.64 The service instance state tables reuse the transfer services' main states ('unbound', 'ready', 'active') and add sub-states that track pending returns between the application and the proxy.65

docs.title: Options and limits
docs.text:
Component Parameter Minimum an implementation must support Proxy Concurrent bound associations per process / per system 1 / 1 Proxy Ports for outgoing BIND per process; ports for incoming BIND per process / per system 1 each Proxy Queued incoming PDUs; queued incoming TRANSFER-DATA or BUFFER (per association / per process) 1/1 each Proxy Queued outgoing PDUs; pending remote returns per association 1 each Proxy Maximum PDU size 100 KB Service element Concurrent service instances, bound instances, proxies, pending remote and local returns 1 each

Sources: Annex E tables E-3 and E-4.66 The service element must support the user role, the provider role, or both (options SEO-1a/b/c), and sequential, concurrent or both flows of control (SEO-2a/b/c).62

Inference

The 100 KB PDU minimum matters for return services. A transfer buffer of 200 RAF TRANSFER-DATA invocations (the RAF conformance minimum67) of 1,115-octet Solar Orbiter frames already holds 223,000 octets of frame data, more than twice the 100 KB minimum, before any annotation or encoding overhead. An implementation built to the minimum would therefore need a smaller transfer-buffer-size for that mission. Real products are expected to support higher limits.66

docs.title: ESA and the SLE API
docs.text:
Both documents record ESA's early role. The ISP1 precursor and the original C++ API specification were ESA documents (SLES-SW-API-0002-TOS-GCI and SLES-SW-API-0001-TOS-GCI). Generation 1 of the CCSDS API keeps interoperability with peers that follow the ESOC TML specification.444549 The ECSS communications handbook points to the ESA ground operations software portal, which includes "the ESA SLE Gateway".68 SCOS-2000 reaches SLE providers through the NCTRS and NIS rather than by embedding an SLE API directly, as described on the SLE overview.

The reference model adds one point about auditing: although the transfer service specifications define no security auditing, logging attempts at access is a standard feature of the SLE API, on top of what firewall logs provide.91

docs.title: Open-source Java implementations
docs.text:
Two SLE implementations in Java are public on GitHub. Neither is in this library, so the facts below come from the repositories themselves, consulted on 2026-11-12.

Item ESA SLE Java API (esa/sleapi-j) jsle (yamcs/jsle) What the repository says it is An "SLE API package" that supports five SLE transfer services A "Java implementation for the CCSDS SLE (Space Link Extension) protocol", plus a stand-alone SLE-to-UDP bridge for testing against a simulator Services RAF (911.1), RCF (911.2), ROCF (911.5), Forward CLTU (912.1), Forward Space Packet (912.3) Forward CLTU, RAF, RCF Roles not stated on the repository page user (client) and provider (server) Dependencies and build Maven; prerequisites listed as OpenJDK 11, Maven 3.8.5 and SUSE Linux Enterprise Server 15 Maven; Netty for networking and the jasn1 library for ASN.1 encoding and decoding Version shown branch 5.1; project version 5.1.8 in the Maven POM master branch; version 1.1.2-SNAPSHOT in the Maven POM Licence European Space Agency Public License (ESA-PL), Weak Copyleft (Type 2), v2.4 (LICENSE file) not stated in the README; the Maven POM declares the GNU Lesser General Public License, linking to version 3 Stated limitations none stated adding automated tests is listed as a to-do; "RCF works effectively as RAF", because the provider does no VCID filtering Context Maven group esa.sle.java, with modules such as esa.sle.java.api.core independent of Yamcs; the separate yamcs-sle package builds Yamcs data links on it

Sources: READMEs, the esa/sleapi-j licence file and both Maven POMs.9293 The jsle bridge sits between a mission control system and a simulator: it offers RAF, RCF or FCLTU on the SLE side, and exchanges CLTUs and AOS or TM frames over UDP on the simulator side.93

Inference

"ESA SLE API" usually refers to an ESA-developed implementation of this Recommended Practice. The esa/sleapi-j repository is an ESA-published implementation in Java, whereas 914.0-M-2 specifies a C++ interface, so it cannot be a literal binding of the C++ headers; how closely its classes follow the CCSDS interfaces is not stated on the repository page. Neither repository states which BIND versions it supports. The version history of ESA's SLE API products, and which implementation the NIS uses, are not stated in the available sources.

docs.title: SLE return services: RAF, RCF and ROCF
docs.text:
The SLE return services carry what a ground station receives from a spacecraft to the users who need it. Return All Frames (RAF) delivers every telemetry frame of one physical channel, including frames that failed decoding if the user asks for them.1 Return Channel Frames (RCF) delivers only the good frames of one Master Channel or one Virtual Channel.2 Return Operational Control Fields (ROCF) delivers only the 4-octet Operational Control Fields (OCFs) of those frames, typically the CLCWs that the spacecraft uses to report the state of its telecommand receiver.3 The three services share the same operations, delivery modes, buffering rules and state machine. They differ in what they select and what they annotate.

This page assumes the concepts on the SLE overview: providers and users, service instances, BIND/UNBIND/PEER-ABORT, and access control. The architecture behind them is on the cross support reference model and service management, and the software side on ISP1 and the SLE API. The frames themselves are described on TM Space Data Link Protocol, AOS and USLP, and the coding that the station undoes on TM synchronization and channel coding.

At a glance

Item RAF RCF ROCF Specification (library issue) CCSDS 911.1-B-5, July 20234 CCSDS 911.2-B-4, July 20235 CCSDS 911.5-B-4, July 20236 Data unit delivered Whole frame (TM, AOS or USLP), good or erred Whole good frame of the selected MC or VC 32-bit OCF of each good frame of the selected MC or VC Produced by Return Space Link Processing FG + Return Frame Processing FG + Return Frame Processing FG Selection at START requested-frame-quality requested-global-VCID GVCID + control-word-type, tc-vcid, update-mode ApplicationIdentifier / service-type rtnAllFrames (0) rtnChFrames (2) rtnChOcf (4) SII service attribute raf (OID arc 22) rcf (46) rocf (49) BIND version-number in this issue 6 6 6 Delivery modes timely online, complete online, offline (one per instance)7 same same

Sources for the SII arcs and application identifiers: the common ASN.1 modules.89

docs.title: Where the services sit in the ground station
docs.text:
All three services start from the same processing chain. The Return Space Link Processing functional group (RSLP-FG) receives the RF signal and produces the RAF data channel: it demodulates the carrier and subcarrier, recovers symbols, synchronises frames, decodes them, and annotates each frame with its earth receive time (ERT), antenna, quality and continuity. The Return Frame Processing functional group (RFP-FG) consumes that RAF data channel. It discards every frame whose quality is not 'good', demultiplexes the rest into Master Channels and Virtual Channels, and, for ROCF, decommutates the OCF from each frame.101112

flowchart LR
    RF(("RF signal")) --> D["Carrier / subcarrier<br/>demodulation,<br/>symbol sync"]
    subgraph RSLP["Return Space Link Processing FG"]
        D --> FS["Frame sync<br/>(ASM or start sequence)"]
        FS --> DEC["Decoding:<br/>RS / LDPC / BCH / FECF check"]
        DEC --> ANN["Annotation:<br/>ERT, antenna-ID,<br/>continuity, quality"]
    end
    ANN -- "RAF data channel<br/>(good + erred +<br/>undetermined)" --> RAF["RAF service<br/>instances"]
    ANN -- "RAF data channel" --> F
    subgraph RFP["Return Frame Processing FG"]
        F["Discard frames<br/>not 'good'"] --> DM["Demultiplex by<br/>MC (TFVN+SCID)<br/>and VC"]
        DM --> OCF["Extract OCF"]
    end
    DM -- "RCF channels" --> RCF["RCF service<br/>instances"]
    OCF -- "ROCF channels" --> ROCF["ROCF service<br/>instances"]

Diagram based on the functional views of the three specifications.101112

The cross support reference model gives the full function lists of the two groups. Real implementations may provide only a subset of a group's services and functions; the service specifications say which functions each service needs.100

Return Space Link Processing SLE-FG Return Frame Processing SLE-FG Uses the ground element's antenna steering and acquires the RF carrier Consumes one RAF data channel Demodulates the carrier into one or more physical channels (symbol streams) Demultiplexes it into Master Channels by MCID (frame version number + SCID) and annotates each MC frame Frame-synchronises and extracts the frames; convolutional decoding may come before or after frame sync Demultiplexes each Master Channel into Virtual Channels by GVCID (MCID + VCID) and annotates each VC frame Error-decodes: optional convolutional decoding, derandomisation, Reed-Solomon decoding and CRC check Decommutates the OCF and the frame secondary header, per MC or per VC Annotates each frame into an RAF SLE-SDU and injects it into the RAF channel of its physical channel Stores enough data for later offline reconstruction, relative either to the source RAF channel or to each product channel Decommutates the AOS insert zone into the Return Insert channel Retrieves stored data and rebuilds the channels for offline instances Stores and later retrieves enough data to rebuild the RAF channel for offline instances

Source: §4.3.2.1.1 and §4.3.2.1.2 of the reference model.100 The model names RAF and the Return VC Frames service as the two return services used for cross support between functional groups; like every service exposed between groups, both are also available to the MDOS.100 The 2005 model lists Master Channel and Virtual Channel frame services, and Master Channel and Virtual Channel OCF services, as four distinct services. RCF and ROCF each merge one pair.23 The model's Master Channel OCF and FSH channels exist only for TM (version 1) master channels, and its VC-FSH channel only for TM virtual channels.101

The services assume a stable physical channel. At any one time all frames on a channel must use the same coding options and, for TM, the same frame length, and the station learns these through service management rather than from the data.1314 The reference model gives the sharpest example: Reed-Solomon coding must be present on all frames of a physical channel or on none, even where the space link standards would allow a mix.100 The concept report puts it from the other side: to offer channel frames, a provider must implement both the frame processing and the space link processing functional groups.15

docs.title: What "good" means
docs.text: The RSLP-FG annotates a frame as good if, after decoding, it consists only of valid Reed-Solomon or LDPC codewords, or, for a frame that uses neither code, if its Frame Error Control Field checks correctly. A USLP frame is good if it passes the USLP frame validation checks (except for the checks of §4.3.10.3.4 c) of the USLP standard). If Reed-Solomon is the outer code of a concatenated scheme, the same rule applies.1617 Erred means that at least one codeword is invalid or the FECF fails. Undetermined means the coding scheme is unknown or unsupported, or the result is not provided, and the exact meaning is implementation dependent.16 The optional Header Error Control field of AOS frames is disregarded when the RAF service reports frame quality.14

docs.title: What exactly is in the data parameter
docs.text:
The RAF specification defines precisely how a frame is trimmed before delivery. RCF and ROCF only ever deliver good frames, so only the first case applies to them.1819

Frame quality and coding What RAF puts in data good, Reed-Solomon Frame with the RS check symbols removed good, LDPC Frame with parity bits and trailing fill bits removed good, BCH Error Control octet of each BCH codeword removed, and fill bits of the last codeword removed erred, convolutional / turbo / LDPC / uncoded Output of the decoder, the same length as a good frame (for an uncoded frame, the frame as acquired) erred, Reed-Solomon The entire candidate codeblock as presented to the RS decoder, unmodified, so offline re-decoding may still succeed erred, BCH The decoder output; fill bits cannot be removed, so the length may differ undetermined A data unit of frame length identified during frame synchronisation; frame or codeblock, in the symbol or bit domain, implementation dependent

The Attached Sync Marker is never included.20 If the frames are protected with the Space Data Link Security protocol, the protection is transparent to the service, and security headers and trailers are left to the applications that consume the frames.20 See SDLS.

The ROCF data parameter is the OCF extracted from the frame, nothing else.21

docs.title: Annotation: what the station adds to each data unit
docs.text:
Each delivered frame or OCF is wrapped in a TRANSFER-DATA invocation that carries the station's annotation.222321

Parameter RAF RCF ROCF Content invoker-credentials M M M Authentication data (or 'unused') earth-receive-time M M M UTC time of the frame's leading edge at the antenna (below) antenna-ID M M M Which antenna acquired the frame: an OID (global form) or 1 to 16 octets (local form); values agreed by CM and UM data-link-continuity M M M −1, 0, or an estimate of missing frames (rules differ per service, below) delivered-frame-quality M — — good (0), erred (1), undetermined (2) private-annotation M M M 'null' or 1 to 128 octets with a meaning agreed in advance data M M M Frame (RAF, RCF) or OCF (ROCF), up to 65,536 octets

Sources: parameter tables,222321 ASN.1 types.242526

docs.title: Earth receive time
docs.text:
The ERT of a frame is the UTC time at which the leading edge of the first bit of the Attached Sync Marker (or, for USLP and other codes delimited that way, of the start sequence) that immediately precedes the frame reached the phase centre of the receiving antenna. The antenna-ID exists precisely to identify that reference point.27 With punctured convolutional codes the number of symbols per information bit varies, so missions must allow for jitter in the ERT.27 The ERT must be accurate to within 1 millisecond of true UTC; this is a mandatory conformance requirement.28

ESA's SCOS-2000 time correlation technical note relies on this definition. It takes its definition of frame reception time from SLE and states that for SLE providers the frame reception time is the ERT, so the ground delay term in the correlation is zero by definition.29 See time correlation.

All SLE times are CCSDS Day Segmented (CDS) codes with an implicit P-field and a 1958-01-01 epoch. The ASN.1 Time type is a CHOICE of two encodings:3031

Worked example (illustrative). A frame whose ASM reached the antenna at 2026-11-12 12:00:00.123456 UTC has day 25,152 (0x6240), millisecond-of-day 43,200,123 (0x02932E7B) and 456 microseconds (0x01C8). In the 8-octet format the ERT is 62 40 02 93 2E 7B 01 C8. In the picosecond format the last four octets become 456,000,000 ps, giving 62 40 02 93 2E 7B 1B 2E 02 00. The arithmetic follows the field definitions above. The CDS code itself is described on the time codes page.

docs.title: Data link continuity
docs.text:
data-link-continuity tells the user whether frames were lost before this one. The encoding is an integer from −1 to 16,777,215.24

  • RAF: −1 means the first frame after production started, 0 means the frame directly follows the last frame acquired, and a positive value is an estimate of the number of frames missed (1 if no better estimate exists). RAF production does not read frame headers to compute it, so this reflects frame synchronisation, not counters.32
  • RCF and ROCF compute it from the frame counters of the selected channel:3334
Selected channel Value First frame after production start, or an AOS or USLP Master Channel (no MC counter) −1 TM Master Channel (MCFCn − MCFCn−1 − 1) mod 256 TM Virtual Channel (VCFCn − VCFCn−1 − 1) mod 256 AOS Virtual Channel (VCFCn − VCFCn−1 − 1) mod 16,777,216 USLP VC, non-truncated header (VCFCn − VCFCn−1 − 1) mod 28 × VC count length USLP VC, truncated header −1

For TM the count is only correct for gaps under 256 frames. Longer gaps must be resolved using the ERT and the nominal frame rate. The AOS VC Frame Count Cycle field is ignored.33

Worked example (illustrative values, real Solar Orbiter frame format). Solar Orbiter TM frames are TFVN 0 frames with 8-bit MC and VC frame counts, modulo 256.35 Suppose the previous VC0 frame delivered by an RCF instance had VCFC 0xFE and the next one has 0x02. The provider reports (2 − 254 − 1) mod 256 = 3, meaning frames 0xFF, 0x00 and 0x01 were lost. Solar Orbiter also extends the VC count by 24 bits in its frame secondary header,36 but RCF does not use that extension: the TM rule above is modulo 256.

Inference

Because RCF ignores the secondary-header extension, a control centre that needs an exact gap count longer than 255 frames for Solar Orbiter would have to compare the 24-bit secondary-header counts itself. The standard's own suggestion is to use the ERT and the nominal frame rate.33 Whether ESA's ground software does this is not stated in the available sources.

docs.title: Delivery modes and buffering
docs.text:
Each return service instance is configured, by service management, for exactly one delivery mode.7 The three modes behave very differently when the ground network cannot keep up. The reference model describes the same three modes in more abstract terms. Its timely online mode uses two user-settable delay thresholds, one for a warning and one for deletion, instead of the single latency limit described below; the two are compared on the overview.102

flowchart LR
    P["RAF/RCF/ROCF<br/>production"] -->|timely online| TB1["Transfer buffer<br/>(transfer-buffer-size<br/>records)"]
    P -->|complete online| OFB["Online frame buffer<br/>(large; whole provision<br/>period)"]
    OFB --> TB2["Transfer buffer"]
    P -->|offline| OFF["Offline frame buffer<br/>(one per service<br/>agreement)"]
    OFF -->|"after RAF-START<br/>(ERT window)"| TB3["Transfer buffer"]
    TB1 -->|"full / release timer /<br/>'end of data'"| PDU1["TransferBuffer PDU<br/>discarded on backpressure"]
    TB2 -->|"full / release timer /<br/>'end of data' / STOP"| PDU2["TransferBuffer PDU<br/>retried until accepted"]
    TB3 -->|"full / 'end of data' /<br/>STOP"| PDU3["TransferBuffer PDU<br/>retried until accepted"]

Diagram based on §3.1.9 of the RAF specification; RCF and ROCF use identical rules.373839

docs.title: The transfer buffer and the release timer
docs.text: In all modes, TRANSFER-DATA and SYNC-NOTIFY invocations are collected in a transfer buffer and sent together as one TransferBuffer PDU, which is a SEQUENCE OF annotated frames and synchronous notifications in insertion order.3724 When the first record goes into an empty buffer, the provider starts the release timer, whose duration is the latency-limit. The buffer is sent when it holds transfer-buffer-size records, when the release timer expires (online modes), or when an 'end of data' notification is inserted.37 Every other operation (returns, status reports) bypasses the buffer and is sent as soon as possible.40 A conforming transfer buffer must hold at least 200 TRANSFER-DATA invocations.28

docs.title: Timely online
docs.text: Timely online mode trades completeness for latency. If the communications service applies backpressure (it will not accept the PDU, or would block the provider), the provider discards the whole TransferBuffer PDU, clears the buffer, inserts a 'data discarded due to excessive backlog' notification, and restarts the release timer. While that notification is in the buffer, the buffer size is temporarily increased by one, so that a buffer of size one still lets some telemetry through instead of carrying only discard notices.40 On RAF-STOP the buffer is flushed immediately. On abort it is cleared.40

docs.title: Complete online
docs.text:
Complete online mode attempts to deliver every frame, in order, with the minimum delay the network allows.38 Frames first go into a large online frame buffer that starts filling as soon as both the provision period and the space link session have started. Filling continues for the whole provision period whether or not a user is bound, and stops only if the association is released with UNBIND 'end'.41 Records move from the online frame buffer to the transfer buffer while the instance is 'active'. A full transfer buffer is retried until the network accepts it.41

Two consequences follow:

  • After a STOP or a lost association, the user can re-bind and issue a new START with a start time in the past to retrieve what was buffered. Frames older than that start time are removed.41
  • A record taken from the online frame buffer cannot be taken again, so data in a transfer buffer that was lost in an abort are gone. The standard deliberately chose this over an application-level acknowledgement, which would hurt throughput, and expects such gaps to be filled offline.41

If the online frame buffer itself overflows (for example during a long outage), the oldest records are discarded (how many is set by service management) and a 'data discarded' notification is queued. A conforming online frame buffer must hold at least 100,000 TRANSFER-DATA invocations. The buffer is emptied at the end of the provision period.4228

docs.title: Offline
docs.text:
Offline mode delivers frames acquired earlier, for an ERT window the user chooses. Frames are kept in an offline frame buffer, ideally one per service agreement, so deleting data affects all offline instances of that agreement and no others.39 Each provider must document the delay before a frame becomes available offline. At START the provider extracts records from the earliest ERT ≥ start-time in original order. Delivery continues until the buffer is full, a frame with ERT > stop-time is found (which generates 'end of data'), the user stops, or the association aborts. Full transfer buffers are retried until accepted.3943 Offline START requires both times to be non-null. stop-time plus the offline processing latency must already be in the past. SYNC-NOTIFY in offline mode only ever reports 'end of data', and SCHEDULE-STATUS-REPORT is rejected.444546 A conforming offline buffer must hold at least 1,000,000 TRANSFER-DATA invocations.28

The reference model explains the storage choice behind offline delivery. An SLE system can store the full user data of a session, so that the MDOS chooses what to retrieve only when it retrieves it, or only the user service data that the MDOS named in advance. The first is more flexible for the user, but its cost grows as the share of data actually retrieved falls, so real systems may restrict or not offer it. The frame processing group's description makes the same choice concrete: storage relative to the source RAF channel needs no advance selection, storage relative to each product channel (MC, VC, OCF or FSH) does, and some implementations can afford only the second. What matters for cross support is what the MDOS and the SLE system agree, not how the system stores internally.102100

Worked example (illustrative numbers). A timely online RAF instance has latency-limit = 1 s and transfer-buffer-size = 200. The spacecraft sends 1115-octet Solar Orbiter frames35 at about 8 frames per second. The release timer, not the size limit, triggers transmission: each TransferBuffer PDU carries about 8 frames and leaves the station about 1 s after its first frame was acquired. If the wide area link stalls for 10 s, roughly ten PDUs are discarded. The user sees one 'data discarded due to excessive backlog' notification at the point of the gap (repeated discards without an intervening delivery produce only one notification45), followed by fresh frames, and data-link-continuity on the first frame after the gap shows the frame-sync view of continuity. The same outage in complete online mode would delay the frames but deliver them all, as long as the online frame buffer did not overflow.

docs.title: Operations
docs.text:
The return services use the operation set described on the overview. The table shows the RAF version. RCF and ROCF are identical apart from the service prefix.47

Operation Invoker Confirmed Valid in states ASN.1 tag (user→provider / provider→user) BIND user or provider (per instance) yes 1 [100] invocation, [101] return UNBIND initiator yes 2 [102], [103] START user yes 2 [0] invocation, [1] return STOP user yes 3 [2] invocation, [3] return TRANSFER-DATA provider no 3 inside [8] TransferBuffer (annotatedFrame [0]) SYNC-NOTIFY provider no 3 inside [8] TransferBuffer (syncNotification [1]) SCHEDULE-STATUS-REPORT user yes 2, 3 [4], [5] STATUS-REPORT provider no 2, 3 [9] GET-PARAMETER user yes 2, 3 [6], [7] PEER-ABORT either no 2, 3 [104]

Sources: operations and states,4722464849 PDU tags.5024

docs.title: START
docs.text:
START moves the provider from 'ready' to 'active' and sets the delivery criteria.51

Parameter RAF RCF ROCF Meaning invoke-ID M M M Echoed in the return start-time M M M ConditionalTime: 'null' (undefined [0]) or a time; only frames with ERT ≥ start-time stop-time M M M 'null' or a time; stop when the next frame's ERT is later requested-frame-quality M — — good frames only (0), erred frames only (1), all frames (2) requested-global-VCID — M M TFVN + SCID + VCID, or VCID 'any' for a Master Channel control-word-type — — M all control words, clcw (with a tc-vcid), not clcw tc-vcid — — C Present only for 'clcw'; a TC VC number, or 'null' for all TC VCs update-mode — — M continuous (0) or change-based (1)

Sources: START tables and parameters.515253

The time rules are the same for all three services.44

  • Online: only frames of this instance's space link session are delivered, whatever the times. A null start time means "from the next frame". A null stop time means "until STOP or the end of the association". A non-null start time must fall within the provision period, and a non-null stop time must not be later than its end.
  • Offline: neither time may be null. The start time must be earlier than the stop time. The stop time plus the offline processing latency must be earlier than the current time. Only frames already acquired when START is invoked can be delivered.
START diagnostic RAF RCF ROCF ASN.1 duplicate Invoke-ID ✓ ✓ ✓ common 100 out of service (production 'halted') ✓ ✓ ✓ specific 0 unable to comply (fault) ✓ ✓ ✓ specific 1 invalid start time ✓ ✓ ✓ specific 2 invalid stop time ✓ ✓ ✓ specific 3 missing time value (offline null time) ✓ ✓ ✓ specific 4 invalid global-VCID — ✓ ✓ specific 5 invalid control word type — — ✓ specific 6 invalid tc-vcid — — ✓ specific 7 invalid update-mode — — ✓ specific 8 other reason ✓ ✓ ✓ common 127

Sources: diagnostics,545556 codes.575826 After 'unable to comply' the user may retry later. If complex management decides the problem is not transient, the provider may abort the association.59

docs.title: STOP
docs.text: STOP takes the provider back to 'ready'. In complete online and offline modes, frames already handed to the communications service are still delivered after the STOP return. The user must not ignore them if it wants complete delivery.41 In timely online mode the transfer buffer is flushed at once.40

docs.title: SYNC-NOTIFY
docs.text:
SYNC-NOTIFY reports events in the same stream as the frames, so the order of notifications and frames reflects the real chronology: an event reported between two frames happened between their ERTs.45

notification-type ASN.1 Notification notification-value Rules loss of frame synchronization lossFrameSync [0] LockStatusReport: time of the in-lock to out-of-lock transition, carrier, subcarrier and symbol-sync lock status At most once per lock status observation period (documented by the provider); no notice for re-lock (the next frame implies it); not in offline mode production status change productionStatusChange [1] running (0), interrupted (1), halted (2) Not in offline mode data discarded due to excessive backlog excessiveDataBacklog [2] none Timely online discard or complete online buffer overflow; one notice per run of discards; not in offline mode end of data endOfData [3] none All modes: session ended, or all frames up to the stop time delivered

Lock statuses use LockStatus: in-lock (0), out-of-lock (1), not in use (2, subcarrier only), unknown (3). Sources: notification rules and values,4560 ASN.1.57

docs.title: SCHEDULE-STATUS-REPORT and STATUS-REPORT
docs.text:
The user can ask for one report 'immediately', for reports 'periodically' every reporting-cycle seconds (a positive response also sends one at once), or for reports to 'stop'. Periodic reporting is off after each BIND. The operation is rejected in offline mode ('not supported in this delivery mode'), with 'already stopped' if a stop is requested while nothing is scheduled, and with 'invalid reporting cycle' if the cycle is outside the agreed range.4661

STATUS-REPORT field RAF RCF ROCF ASN.1 type number-of-error-free-frames-delivered ✓ — — IntUnsignedLong number-of-frames-delivered ✓ ✓ — IntUnsignedLong number-of-frames-processed — — ✓ frames of the requested GVCID examined for OCFs number-of-ocfs-delivered — — ✓ OCFs delivered frame-sync-lock-status ✓ ✓ ✓ in-lock, out-of-lock, unknown symbol-sync-lock-status ✓ ✓ ✓ in-lock, out-of-lock, unknown subcarrier-lock-status ✓ ✓ ✓ in-lock, out-of-lock, not in use, unknown carrier-lock-status ✓ ✓ ✓ in-lock, out-of-lock, unknown production-status ✓ ✓ ✓ running, interrupted, halted

Counters run from the start of the provision period, across associations.48626364 The ROCF frames-processed counter equals the number of frames an RCF instance with the same GVCID would deliver while active.63

docs.title: GET-PARAMETER
docs.text:
GET-PARAMETER reads one configuration parameter. Unknown names are rejected with 'unknown parameter' (specific 0).49 The tables list every readable parameter, the ASN.1 CHOICE tag of the positive result, and the ParameterName code that identifies it in the invocation.

RAF parameter Result tag ParameterName Value transfer-buffer-size parBufferSize [0] bufferSize (4) number of invocations the transfer buffer holds delivery-mode parDeliveryMode [1] deliveryMode (6) rtnTimelyOnline 0, rtnCompleteOnline 1, rtnOffline 2 latency-limit parLatencyLimit [2] latencyLimit (15) seconds (online) or offline [1] NULL reporting-cycle parReportingCycle [3] reportingCycle (26) off, or seconds requested-frame-quality parReqFrameQuality [4] requestedFrameQuality (27) value set by START, else first element of the permitted set return-timeout-period parReturnTimeout [5] returnTimeoutPeriod (29) 1 to 600 s permitted-frame-quality-set parPermittedFrameQuality [6] permittedFrameQuality (302) set of 1 to 3 qualities minimum-reporting-cycle parMinReportingCycle [7] minReportingCycle (301) 1 to 600 s RCF parameter Result tag ParameterName transfer-buffer-size [0] bufferSize (4) delivery-mode [1] deliveryMode (6) latency-limit [2] latencyLimit (15) permitted-global-VCID-set [3] permittedGvcidSet (24) reporting-cycle [4] reportingCycle (26) requested-global-VCID [5] requestedGvcid (28) return-timeout-period [6] returnTimeoutPeriod (29) minimum-reporting-cycle [7] minReportingCycle (301) ROCF parameter Result tag ParameterName transfer-buffer-size [0] bufferSize (4) delivery-mode [1] deliveryMode (6) latency-limit [2] latencyLimit (15) permitted-global-VCID-set [3] permittedGvcidSet (24) permitted-control-word-type-set [4] permittedControlWordTypeSet (101) permitted-tc-vcid-set [5] permittedTcVcidSet (102) permitted-update-mode-set [6] permittedUpdateModeSet (103) reporting-cycle [7] reportingCycle (26) requested-global-VCID [8] requestedGvcid (28) requested-control-word-type [9] requestedControlWordType (104) requested-tc-vcid [10] requestedTcVcid (105) requested-update-mode [11] requestedUpdateMode (106) return-timeout-period [12] returnTimeoutPeriod (29) minimum-reporting-cycle [13] minReportingCycle (301)
