docs.title: State machine and production status
docs.text:
The provider state machine has the three states described on the overview: 'unbound', 'ready' and 'active'. What survives the end of an association matters for return services. Status information from a previous association is lost, with three exceptions: the online frame buffer of a complete online instance (unless the UNBIND reason was 'end'), the offline frame buffer, and the status report statistics, which accumulate over the whole provision period.64

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Unbound
    Unbound --> Ready: BIND (positive)
    Ready --> Active: START (positive)
    Active --> Ready: STOP (positive)
    Ready --> Unbound: UNBIND / PEER-ABORT / protocol abort
    Active --> Unbound: PEER-ABORT / protocol abort
    state Active {
        [*] --> Delivering
        Delivering --> Delivering: TransferBuffer PDU<br/>(TRANSFER-DATA, SYNC-NOTIFY)
        Delivering --> Delivering: STATUS-REPORT (periodic)
    }
    note right of Unbound
        Online frame buffer keeps filling
        (complete online) until end of
        provision period or UNBIND 'end'
    end note

Diagram based on the RAF state diagram and the effects-of-termination rules.736441

Production status describes the return physical channel, independently of any association. It starts as 'halted', because production is not yet configured for the instance. It becomes 'running' when management configures it (antenna at the acquisition point, frequency plan, data rate, decoding), 'interrupted' on a production fault, 'running' again when the fault is fixed, and 'halted' from any state by operator action.74

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Halted: initial value
    Halted --> Running: management configures production
    Running --> Interrupted: production fault detected
    Interrupted --> Running: fault corrected
    Running --> Halted: operator directive
    Interrupted --> Halted: operator directive

Diagram based on figure B-1 and table B-1 of the RAF specification.74

Production status Effect on operations halted BIND and START rejected with 'out of service' running none interrupted none; START is accepted, but no frames flow until production is running again

Source: table B-2 and its note.75

docs.title: Selecting channels: the global VCID
docs.text:
RCF and ROCF select a channel with a global VCID (GVCID): the Transfer Frame Version Number, the spacecraft identifier and a VCID or 'any'. TFVN and SCID together form the Master Channel identifier, so VCID 'any' selects a whole Master Channel.76 The physical channel is not named in START; it comes from the service package, which fixes the RAF data channel feeding the RFP-FG.76

GvcId ::= SEQUENCE
{ spacecraftId   INTEGER (0 .. 65535)   -- TM 0..1023, AOS 0..255, USLP 0..65535
, versionNumber  INTEGER (0 | 1 | 12)   -- TM '00'B, AOS '01'B, USLP '1100'B
, vcId CHOICE { masterChannel [0] NULL, virtualChannel [1] VcId }
}
VcId ::= INTEGER (0 .. 63)              -- TM VCIDs are 0..7

ASN.1 quoted in excerpt from the RCF and ROCF structures modules.7758

Service management defines a permitted-global-VCID-set as a set of MasterChannelComposition entries. Each entry names a Master Channel either alone or with a list of 1 to 8 (TM) or 1 to 64 (AOS, USLP) virtual channels. One instance may permit a single MC, a single VC, a set of VCs, or one MC plus a set of VCs. If the set lists an MC with no VCs, the user cannot ask for one of its VCs.7678

Field layout from the concept report's TM frame figure.79 See TM SDLP for the full header.

Worked example (real Solar Orbiter values). Solar Orbiter's TM frames use TFVN 0b00 and the CCSDS spacecraft identifier 0x28A (650). VC0 carries real-time TM, VC1 to VC3 playback, VC4 high-priority real-time TM, VC5 the critical event log, and VC7 only idle frames.3580 An RCF instance for real-time telemetry would therefore be started with requested-global-VCID = {spacecraftId 650, versionNumber 0, vcId virtualChannel 0}. A Master Channel instance for all VCs would use vcId masterChannel NULL. The values come from the Solar Orbiter ICD, but which instances ESA actually configures is not stated in the available sources.

docs.title: What the OCF carries
docs.text:
A TM, AOS or USLP frame may end with a 32-bit Operational Control Field. Its first bit is the control word type: 0 means the field holds a Communications Link Control Word (CLCW), the report of the spacecraft's COP-1 receiving end (FARM). 1 means some other report. ROCF's 'not clcw' type is the one to use to obtain Frame Security Reports.818283

Field layout from CCSDS 232.0-B-4.84 The semantics of each flag for the FOP-1 machine are explained on the COP-1 page.

docs.title: Selecting OCFs
docs.text:
ROCF START adds three criteria to the GVCID.8185

  • control-word-type: 'all control word types' delivers every OCF. 'clcw' delivers only OCFs with type bit 0. 'not clcw' delivers only those with type bit 1. In ASN.1, ControlWordType is a CHOICE of allControlWords [0] NULL, clcw [1] TcVcid and notClcw [2] NULL. The CLCW choice carries the TC VC selection inside it.58
  • tc-vcid: present only for 'clcw'. It selects CLCWs that report on one telecommand VC, or all of them if 'null' (noTcVC [0] NULL).8586
  • update-mode: 'continuous' delivers every OCF that matches. 'change-based' delivers an OCF only if its content differs from the last one with the same tc-vcid put into the transfer buffer, or if none has been delivered since the last START.85

If filtering suppresses some OCFs, data-link-continuity still reports a discontinuity only when the frame was the first after a gap on the channel. In USLP the OCF may be absent from some frames, so counters can falsely suggest a gap.34

docs.title: How CLCWs reach the control centre
docs.text:
A ground segment can see CLCWs by three routes, and the SLE documents describe all three:

  1. Inside frames delivered by RAF or RCF. The OCF is part of every delivered frame, so the control centre can extract the CLCW itself. Solar Orbiter sets the OCF flag in every frame and always puts a CLCW in it.87
  2. Through ROCF. A user that only needs the command link status, such as a separate commanding facility, can subscribe to the CLCWs of one TC VC without receiving the frames. Change-based mode then delivers a CLCW only when something changes.85
  3. Inside the station. The concept report describes ROCF supplying the CLCW to the forward providers: the CLTU provider needs it to know whether the physical uplink is available, and the VC or packet provider needs it to decide on COP-1 retransmissions.88 The reference model formalises this: the users of its MC-OCF and VC-OCF transfer ports are the Forward TC VC Data Insertion and Forward TC Space Link Processing functional groups as well as MUEs, and the production of Forward CLTU includes a consumer OCF port.103104 The FCLTU production process itself can consume CLCWs from a configured GVCID and physical channel; see FCLTU. With FSP the provider also runs FOP-1, so the station's VC Data Insertion function uses the CLCW to retransmit frames.105
sequenceDiagram
    participant SC as Spacecraft (FARM-1)
    participant GS as Station: RSLP + RFP FGs
    participant MCS as Control centre (FOP-1)
    participant FWD as Station: FCLTU production
    SC->>GS: TM frame, OCF = CLCW (TC VC 1, N(R)=42, Wait=0)
    GS->>MCS: RCF TRANSFER-DATA (whole frame)
    GS->>MCS: ROCF TRANSFER-DATA (CLCW only, change-based)
    GS-->>FWD: CLCW flags (No RF Available, No Bit Lock)
    MCS->>FWD: CLTU-TRANSFER-DATA (next AD frame, N(S)=42)

Illustrative sequence; the values are invented and the internal station path is shown only conceptually.8885

Worked example (Solar Orbiter TC VC numbering, illustrative CLCW). Solar Orbiter uses TC VC 1 for decoder 1 and TC VC 2 for decoder 2, and requires the CLCW TC VC identifiers to match the TC frames.8987 An ROCF instance that follows decoder 1 would therefore use requested-global-VCID = MC 650 (VCID 'any'), control-word-type = clcw with tc-vcid = 1, and update-mode = change-based. A delivered OCF such as 01 04 00 2A would decode as: type 0, version 00, status 000, COP-1 (01), TC VC 1, all flags clear, FARM-B count 0, N(R) = 0x2A = 42. The bytes are invented for illustration.

docs.title: Implementing RAF with the SLE API (CCSDS 915.1-M-2)
docs.text: The SLE API core (914.0-M-2) is generic. A separate Recommended Practice for each service adds what that service needs. For RAF this is CCSDS 915.1-M-2, Space Link Extension—Application Program Interface for Return All Frames Service, issue 2 of September 2015, which replaced issue 1 of October 2008.106 It extends two components, the API Service Element and SLE Operations, and requires the API Proxy to encode and decode the RAF PDUs.107 Its aim is interoperability between applications and API products, and between user and provider applications that both use the API, so that different API products can be exchanged.108 The general API architecture is on ISP1 and the SLE API.

docs.title: Which RAF versions it covers
docs.text:
API generation RAF BIND version-number RAF specification Peer transport mapping Generation 1 1 Draft 911.1-R-1.7 (September 1999) ESOC Specification of a SLE API Proxy for TCP/IP and ASN.1, SLES-SW-API-0002-TOS-GCI issue 1.1 Generation 2 2 911.1-B-2-S (dated December 2004 by the API book, November 2004 by the RAF document control; historical since January 2010) ISP1, 913.1-B-2 Generation 3 4 911.1-B-3 (January 2010) ISP1, 913.1-B-2

Sources: applicability, normative and informative references of 915.1-M-2, and the document control of 911.1-B-5.1091101114 Generations 1 and 2 are kept for backward compatibility for a limited time.109 The RAF issue in this library, 911.1-B-5, defines version 6.112 Which API issue, if any, covers versions 5 and 6 is not stated in the available sources.

docs.title: What the API adds for RAF
docs.text:
The package RAF Service Instances adds two classes. RAF SI User handles the RAF operation objects and adds nothing else to the generic user-side service instance. RAF SI Provider adds two interfaces: IRAF_SIAdmin, through which the provider application sets the RAF configuration, and IRAF_SIUpdate, through which it must report every change of production and lock status.113 The provider-side instance then answers RAF-GET-PARAMETER by itself, generates RAF-STATUS-REPORT by itself, and handles the transfer buffer. The operation factory offered to the application cannot even create status report or transfer buffer objects.113114

Configuration parameter (IRAF_SIAdmin) Used by the service element for delivery-mode Transfer buffer handling (enables or disables discarding), PDU checks, GET-PARAMETER returns latency-limit (online modes only, seconds) Release of the transfer buffer in timely and complete online modes; GET-PARAMETER transfer-buffer-size Number of TRANSFER-DATA and SYNC-NOTIFY invocations per transfer buffer PDU; GET-PARAMETER initial production status, and initial frame-sync, symbol-sync, subcarrier and carrier lock status Initial values of the status report (not needed in offline mode)

Sources: table 2-1, §3.1.1 and A4.1.113115116 The remaining configuration, such as the return timeout period, goes through the generic ISLE_SIAdmin. All parameters must be set before ISLE_SIAdmin::ConfigCompleted() is called; the service element then checks them against the ranges of the RAF specification only, since service management may narrow them further. They cannot be changed afterwards and survive UNBIND, PEER-ABORT and protocol abort.115 Clause 3.1.1.2 calls the buffer size a number of "TRANSFER–BUFFER" and SYNC-NOTIFY invocations, while A4.1 and the GET-PARAMETER method speak of TRANSFER-DATA invocations, which matches the RAF specification.11511665

The service element keeps the status information itself, as table 2-2 and §3.1.2 define:117118

Status parameter How the API maintains it number-of-error-free-frames-delivered Zero at configuration; incremented, when a transfer buffer PDU is actually transmitted, by its TRANSFER-DATA invocations with quality 'good'. Discarded buffers do not count. number-of-frames-delivered Same rule, counting every TRANSFER-DATA invocation. In timely online mode both counts can be lower than the frames the application passed in. requested-frame-quality 'undefined' at configuration; copied from an accepted RAF-START; 'undefined' again after STOP, PEER-ABORT or protocol abort frame-sync, symbol-sync, subcarrier and carrier lock status; production status Set by the application through IRAF_SIUpdate at every change, whatever the state of the instance. In offline mode the application may skip this; the values then stay 'invalid' (production status) and 'unknown' (locks).

Apart from requested-frame-quality, none of these is reset by UNBIND, PEER-ABORT or a protocol abort, which matches the specification's rule that statistics accumulate over the provision period.11764

docs.title: Operation objects and their C++ types
docs.text:
RAF operation Operation object interface Package GUID RAF-BIND, RAF-UNBIND ISLE_Bind, ISLE_Unbind SLE Operations (core) (core) RAF-START IRAF_Start RAF Operations {2F5AEB20-7C28-11d3-9F15-00104B4F22C0} RAF-STOP ISLE_Stop SLE Operations (core) RAF-TRANSFER-DATA IRAF_TransferData RAF Operations {2F5AEB21-…} RAF-SYNC-NOTIFY IRAF_SyncNotify RAF Operations {2F5AEB22-…} transfer buffer (pseudo-operation) ISLE_TransferBuffer SLE Operations (core) RAF-SCHEDULE-STATUS-REPORT ISLE_ScheduleStatusReport SLE Operations (core) RAF-STATUS-REPORT IRAF_StatusReport RAF Operations {2F5AEB23-…} RAF-GET-PARAMETER IRAF_GetParameter RAF Operations {2F5AEB24-…} RAF-PEER-ABORT ISLE_PeerAbort SLE Operations (core) (service instance) IRAF_SIAdmin, IRAF_SIUpdate RAF Service Instances {2F5AEB25-…}, {2F5AEB26-…}

Sources: table 2-3 and the interface headers of annex A; all RAF GUIDs share the suffix -7C28-11d3-9F15-00104B4F22C0.119120 The header file RAF_Types.h mirrors the ASN.1 enumerations and adds a value invalid (−1) to each, returned while a value is unset or not applicable:121

C++ type Values RAF_FrameQuality rafFQ_good 0, rafFQ_erred 1, rafFQ_undetermined 2 RAF_RequestedFrameQuality rafRQ_goodFramesOnly 0, rafRQ_erredFramesOnly 1, rafRQ_allFrames 2 RAF_ParFrameQuality (GET-PARAMETER) the same three, plus rafPQ_undefined 3, reported while the instance is 'ready' RAF_LockStatus rafLS_inLock 0, rafLS_outOfLock 1, rafLS_notInUse 2 (subcarrier only), rafLS_unknown 3 RAF_NotificationType rafNT_lossFrameSync 0, rafNT_productionStatusChange 1, rafNT_excessiveDataBacklog 2, rafNT_endOfData 3 RAF_ProductionStatus rafPS_running 0, rafPS_interrupted 1, rafPS_halted 2 RAF_ParameterName rafPN_bufferSize 4, rafPN_deliveryMode 6, rafPN_latencyLimit 15, rafPN_reportingCycle 26, rafPN_requestedFrameQuality 27, rafPN_returnTimeoutPeriod 29 RAF_AntennaIdFormat rafAF_global 0 (object identifier), rafAF_local 1 (octet string of 1 to 16 octets)122 RAF_DeliveryMode timely online, complete online, offline (the core SLE_DeliveryMode values)

IRAF_TransferData uses −2 for a data link continuity that has not been set, so that the valid values −1, 0 and positive stay distinct. Its invocation checks require an ERT, an antenna ID, a continuity above −2, a frame quality, data, and a private annotation of 1 to 128 octets if present.122

docs.title: Checks split between the API and the application
docs.text:
On the provider side the service element checks a RAF-START before passing it on, and answers it negatively itself if a check fails:123

  • offline mode: the start time must not be null, the stop time must not be null, and the stop time must be earlier than the current time;
  • online mode: a start time, if given, must lie within the scheduled provision period, and a stop time, if given, must not be later than its end;
  • the operation object itself checks that the start time is earlier than the stop time.

The service element does not check production status, because it can change before the application sees the PDU. The offline processing latency check is left to the application too.123 For SYNC-NOTIFY it refuses, in offline mode, the 'loss of frame synchronization', 'production status change' and 'data discarded' types, and in timely online mode the 'data discarded' type.124

Inference

At first sight the timely online rule is surprising, because the RAF specification uses exactly this notification for the timely online discard.45 The API core explains it: in timely online mode the service element itself discards the unsent transfer buffer and starts the next one with the 'data discarded' notification.125 An application-supplied notice would therefore duplicate the API's own. The RAF API book does not give this reason; it only notes that the user side cannot make the check.124

Because the API performs some START checks earlier than the specification's diagnostic order implies, 915.1 documents the split order, as the RAF standard requires of any implementation that deviates:126127

Set by the API service element Set by the application 'duplicate invoke id', 'invalid start time', 'invalid stop time', 'missing time value' 'out of service', 'unable to comply', 'invalid stop time' (offline, when an offline processing latency is used), 'other' 
sequenceDiagram
    participant App as RAF provider application
    participant SE as API Service Element (RAF SI Provider)
    participant Px as API Proxy (ISP1)
    participant U as RAF user
    App->>SE: create RAF instance, provider role (ISLE_SIFactory)
    App->>SE: ISLE_SIAdmin - SII, peer ID, provision period,<br/>BIND initiator, responder port, return timeout
    App->>SE: IRAF_SIAdmin - delivery mode, buffer size,<br/>latency limit, initial production and lock status
    App->>SE: ConfigCompleted() on ISLE_SIAdmin
    SE->>Px: register responder port
    U->>Px: RAF-BIND, then RAF-START
    Px->>SE: START invocation
    SE->>SE: time checks (3.1.3.1)
    SE->>App: START passed on
    App-->>SE: positive return
    loop during the pass
        App->>SE: IRAF_TransferData objects
        SE->>Px: transfer buffer PDU (on size or latency limit)
        App->>SE: IRAF_SIUpdate (lock or production change)
        SE->>Px: RAF-STATUS-REPORT (generated by the SE)
    end
    U->>Px: RAF-GET-PARAMETER
    Px->>SE: answered by the SE, not the application

Illustrative sequence based on the API core configuration rules and the RAF API responsibilities; the API core defines the exact method signatures.128113115129

docs.title: What changed after the issue the API is based on
docs.text:
The 2015 API book follows RAF 911.1-B-3. Comparing it with the 2023 issue in this library shows these differences:

Topic RAF API 915.1-M-2 (based on 911.1-B-3) RAF 911.1-B-5 (2023) BIND version up to 4 (generation 3)109 6112 GET-PARAMETER names six: bufferSize, deliveryMode, latencyLimit, reportingCycle, requestedFrameQuality, returnTimeoutPeriod121 also permittedFrameQuality (302) and minReportingCycle (301)6871 requested-frame-quality before START 'undefined' (rafPQ_undefined 3)121118 the first element of permitted-frame-quality-set; the ASN.1 value range is 0 to 2 only6568 latency-limit in offline mode method returns 0130 'null' (offline [1] NULL)65 reporting-cycle when periodic reporting is off method returns 0130 'null'65

Inference

The two extra GET-PARAMETER names and the "first element of the permitted set" rule are probably additions of a RAF issue later than B-3, which explains why the 2015 API does not know them. The intermediate issue 911.1-B-4 is not in the library to confirm which issue introduced them. The 0 values for 'null' look like a representation choice of the C++ interface.

docs.title: How SCOS-2000 represents received frames
docs.text:
The Solar Orbiter MIB defines internal ground packets on APID 1966 that hold the parts of each received frame other than its data field. Three packet types, "Good", "Bad" and "Idle mini-transfer frame", map naturally onto frame quality and idle frames.90

SPID Type/Subtype Description 66980 161/5 Good mini-transfer frame 66981 161/4 Bad mini-transfer frame 66982 161/3 Idle mini-transfer frame

The good-frame packet lays out the 6-octet TM primary header (TFVN, SCID, VCID, OCF flag, MC and VC counts, data field status), the 4-octet secondary header (ID and 24-bit extension), the CLCW from octet 10 (every field, with separate decoded copies for TC VC 1 and VC 2), the FECF at octet 14, and then "ERT sec", "ERT msec" and "ERT psec" at octets 16, 20 and 24.90

Octet.bit Parameter Description PTC/PFC 0.0 NYG00641 TF Version number 2/2 0.2 NYG00642 Spacecraft Id. 3/6 (10 bits) 1.4 NYG00643 VC Id. ⅔ 2.0, 3.0 NYG00645, NYG00646 MCF Count, VCF Count ¾ 7.0 NYGG0653 TF Secondary Header Data 3/13 (24 bits) 10.0 NYGD0655 Control Word Type 1/0 11.0 NYGD0659 VC Id (of the CLCW) 3/2 (6 bits) 12.0 NYGDA661 VC1 No RF available 2/1, text calibration CYGT0661TM (RF / NO RF) 12.1 NYGDA662 VC1 No Bit Lock 2/1, CYGT0662TM 13.0 NYGD0668 Report Value ¾ (8 bits) 14.0 NYGG0669 Frame Error Cntrl Field 3/12 (16 bits) 16.0, 20.0, 24.0 NYG00538, NYG00539, NYG00540 ERT sec, ERT msec, ERT psec 3/14 each

Offsets are counted from the end of the SCOS-2000 TM header, as for every PLF entry;92 PTC/PFC meanings are on parameter types. See also monitoring in the MIB.

Inference

Octets 0 to 15 are exactly a Solar Orbiter frame (6 + 4 + 1099 + 4 + 2 = 1115 octets35) with its 1099-octet data field removed. "Mini-transfer frame" therefore seems to mean the frame without its data field, plus the reception time. The split into good, bad and idle mirrors the RAF delivered-frame-quality values and the VC7 idle frames. The ERT fields have the same resolution as SLE's picosecond time code. None of this is stated in the available sources, which do not document how the NCTRS builds these packets.

SQL used 
-- Solar Orbiter MIB release 25925PFM (2025-09-16)
SELECT PID_SPID, PID_TYPE, PID_STYPE, PID_APID, PID_DESCR
  FROM pid WHERE PID_SPID IN (66980, 66981, 66982);

SELECT l.PLF_NAME, p.PCF_DESCR, l.PLF_OFFBY, l.PLF_OFFBI,
       p.PCF_PTC, p.PCF_PFC, p.PCF_CURTX
  FROM plf l JOIN pcf p ON p.PCF_NAME = l.PLF_NAME
 WHERE l.PLF_SPID = 66980
 ORDER BY CAST(l.PLF_OFFBY AS INT), CAST(l.PLF_OFFBI AS INT);

docs.title: Opening an RCF link from SCOS-2000
docs.text:
The NIS throw event EGENRTMO ("GENERIC OPEN TM LINK") opens a return link on ESA's network interface system. Its fields mirror RCF-START: a service type, a TFVN, an SCID and a VCID, a channel type that chooses between a virtual channel and a master channel, start and stop times each preceded by a "used" flag, and the service instance identifier.9193

The two 32-bit words after "End Time Used" are labelled "Start time" in the MIB's CDF descriptions, like the two words after "Start Time Used". This page labels them as end time words from their position; the MIB itself does not say so.91

After bit 224 come three ASCII fields, "sagr=144.spack=", "NN11-PERM.rsl-f" (two 15-character fields) and a variable-length "g=1.rcf=onlc0001". Together they spell the RCF service instance identifier sagr=144.spack=NN11-PERM.rsl-fg=1.rcf=onlc0001, valid in the 911.2 Annex A syntax; the onlc prefix presumably denotes a complete online instance (see the overview).9194 The companion command EGENRTMC ("GENERIC CLOSE TM LINK") carries only the event ID CLOSE_LINK (21), the service type and the same identifier. The April 2020 release holds identical definitions.95

Inference

The TFVN, SCID, VCID and channel-type fields correspond one-to-one to the RCF GvcId (with 'MASTER' playing the role of masterChannel). The two "used" flags followed by two 32-bit words look like the two ConditionalTime values of RCF-START. This suggests that the NIS turns this event into an RCF-BIND and RCF-START towards the station. The NIS Throw Events ICD that defines these fields (EGOS-NIS-NIS-ICD-0003, referenced by the SCOS-2000 import ICD96) is not in this library. The meaning of "Mode" and "Link priority" is not stated in the available sources.

SQL used 
SELECT CDF_CNAME, CDF_ELTYPE, CDF_DESCR, CDF_ELLEN, CDF_BIT,
       CDF_PNAME, CDF_INTER, CDF_VALUE
  FROM cdf WHERE CDF_CNAME IN ('EGENRTMO', 'EGENRTMC')
 ORDER BY CDF_CNAME, CAST(CDF_BIT AS INT);

SELECT CPC_NAME, CPC_DESCR, CPC_PTC, CPC_PFC, CPC_CATEG, CPC_PAFREF, CPC_DEFVAL
  FROM cpc WHERE CPC_NAME IN ('ENISTE03','ENISTE06','ENISTE07','ENISTE14',
                              'ENISTE15','ENISTE16','ENISTE18');

SELECT PAS_NUMBR, PAS_ALTXT, PAS_ALVAL FROM pas
 WHERE PAS_NUMBR IN ('CNISX205TC','CNISX207TC','CNISX211TC','CNISX214TC')
 ORDER BY PAS_NUMBR, CAST(PAS_ALVAL AS INT);

The MIB tables involved are documented under CCF, CDF, CPC and PAS. A fuller description of NIS throw events is on the FCLTU page.

docs.title: SLE service identifiers in ESA data products
docs.text:
Telemetry that reaches users through ESA's data distribution still records the SLE channel. The Rosetta and Mars Express data delivery ICD defines an 8-bit "SLE Type" at octet 16 of its DDS packet header:97

SLE Type Real-Time (RT) Real-Time Flow Control (RTFC) Off-Line SLC 0 4 8 MC 1 5 9 VC 2 6 10 Bad Frames 3 7 11

The EDDS raw TM header keeps an 8-bit SleServiceID (field 17) "for backward compatibility with the GDDS", and the GDDS binary packet header carries a one-octet "SLE Service".98 See EDDS formats and GDDS and DDIDs.

Inference

The three columns plausibly correspond to SLE's timely online, complete online ("flow control", meaning no discarding) and offline delivery modes. "MC", "VC" and "Bad Frames" fit RCF master channel, RCF virtual channel and RAF erred frames. "SLC" may mean the whole space link channel (RAF). The ICD does not define these terms.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: The return services use the common access control and authentication rules of the overview. Their specific risk is confidentiality and integrity of the data. The RAF specification relies on unspecified mechanisms above the service (between the spacecraft application and its ground peer), in the underlying communications service, or in bilaterally agreed extras such as encryption of the data parameter. Without them, telemetry crossing the wide area network could be read or substituted without detection. The stated consequences of not applying security are degraded or lost telemetry reception, or altered telemetry.99 SDLS is one such mechanism, applied within the frames themselves.20

docs.title: SLE cross support reference model and service management
docs.text:
Every SLE transfer service runs inside an agreed framework. A mission (the user) and a ground network operator (the provider) agree which services exist, when they exist and how they are configured. Only then can a mission user entity bind to a RAF, FCLTU or FSP instance. This page covers that framework. It starts with the CCSDS Cross Support Reference Model, which defines the vocabulary every SLE book uses. It then follows the service management standards built on that model, from the original SLE service management concept to the extensible Space Communication Cross Support (SCCS) service management suite. It ends with the Monitored Data transfer service used to watch a pass in progress, and with ESA's operational experience at ESTRACK.

At a glance: the documents

Document What it is Status in the library copy CCSDS 910.4-B-2 Cross Support Reference Model—Part 1: SLE Services The SLE architecture: environment, data units and channels, functional groups, complexes, service instances, packages, agreements, ports Issue 2, October 2005, editorial correction 1 July 2007; carries the "Historical Document" banner1 CCSDS 910.3-G-3 Cross Support Concept—Part 1: SLE Services Explains SLE, including the SLE service management concept Green Book, March 20062 CCSDS 902.0-G-1 Extensible SCCS Service Management—Concept The concept and roadmap for the second-generation service management suite Green Book, Issue 1, September 20143 CCSDS 902.4-B-1 Service Package Data Formats (SPDF) XML format that tells a mission which service packages were scheduled Cover dated September 2026, but every page after the cover is headed "Proposed Draft"4 CCSDS 922.1-B-2 CSTS Monitored Data Service (MD-CSTS) Cross Support Transfer Service that reports monitored parameters and events of a service package Issue 2, September 2022; issue 1 April 20175 SpaceOps 2025 paper #16 ESTRACK Deep Space Cross Support using CCSDS Service Management ESOC experience with standard and draft service management formats Conference paper, 20256

docs.title: Part 1: the Cross Support Reference Model (910.4-B-2)
Scope and the three kinds of cross support
docs.text:
Cross support means one agency uses part of another agency's resources to complement its own when operating a spacecraft.7 The reference model names three kinds of cross support service on the ground and planned one part of the reference model for each:7

Kind Content Reference model part SLE services Extend the CCSDS space link services onto the ground Part 1 (this document) Ground communications services Ground communications support, for example relaying operational data Part 2 Ground domain services Services on spacecraft-operations data that does not map onto space link data structures, for example tracking, database exchange and mission planning Part 3

Part 1 makes four assumptions: a single mission, a single spacecraft, CCSDS-compliant TM and TC, and all ground users affiliated with one mission management entity. It does not model the sharing of ground systems between missions, though it does not forbid it. It excludes the processing of packet contents, and it does not model the ground communications that SLE relies on.8 The model is a guideline for agency standards, not the design of a real system.8

docs.title: The environment
docs.text:
Term Definition in the reference model Space element Source of return data and sink of forward data; one spacecraft with its platform and payloads. Each spacecraft of a multi-spacecraft mission is a separate space element. Physical channel The capability to carry one stream of bits in one direction Space link One or both of a forward and a return RF carrier channel, each giving one or more physical channels Space link session A continuous period in which the SLE system makes one or more physical channels of a space link usable Ground element The Mission Data Operation System (MDOS) plus the SLE system (plus components out of scope) SLE system Extends transfer and delivery between the space link ground termination and the MDOS, to specifications issued by the MDOS MDOS Source of forward and sink of return data. It contains one SLE Utilization Management and one or more Mission User Entities (MUEs), and may work with several SLE systems. SLE Utilization Management (SLE-UM) Negotiates the provision of transfer services with the SLE system, and controls and monitors it

Source: SLE system environment.9

SLE services are of two types. Transfer services move SLE data channels between the space element and the MDOS. The management service controls the scheduling and provision of transfer service instances.10 Within one mission, the model speaks of instances of services, and many instances of both types can exist at once.10

docs.title: Data units and data channels
docs.text:
The SLE system exchanges Space Link Data Units (SL-DUs) with the space element. Inside the SLE system and towards the MDOS, it carries SLE Service Data Units (SLE-SDUs). An SLE-SDU wraps an SL-DU with annotation, control information, or both. A control-only SLE-SDU may produce an SL-DU, for example a COP directive that sends an Unlock to the spacecraft, or may matter only on the ground.11 Annotation examples are ground reception time and quality for return data, and requested transmission time and uplink path for forward data.11 A data channel is a uniquely identified stream of data units of one type. SL data channels and SLE data channels have the same types and identifiers, and SLE channels add the annotation.1112

The forward channels that matter for telecommand, from annex A:

Forward SLE data channel SL-DU Unique identifier SLE service Forward physical channel (V1 asynchronous, V2 synchronous) Baseband symbol stream Physical channel ID not exposed CLTU channel (V1 physical channels only) CLTU CLTU ID Forward CLTU TC Transfer Frame channel (V1 VCs) TC Transfer Frame GVCID Forward TC Frame TC-VCA channel (V1 VCs) Frame Data Unit GVCID Forward TC-VCA TC Multiplex channel (V1 VCs) Segment GVCID and MAP identifier not exposed Forward Space Packet channel Space Packet GVCID and APID: 0–2046 for V1 GVCIDs; 0–2031 and 2046 for V2 GVCIDs Forward Space Packet

Source: table A-5.13 The telecommand SL-DU types are CLTU, TC Transfer Frame, Frame Data Unit, Segment and Space Packet. On the return side, the channels run from the physical channel through RAF, Master Channel (MCID) and Virtual Channel (GVCID) down to OCF, FSH, bitstream and space packet channels.1415

docs.title: The baseline transfer services and delivery modes
docs.text:
The reference model lists 20 baseline transfer services. Each one delivers one type of SLE data channel.16

Group Services Return (10) Return All Frames; Return Insert (AOS); Return Master Channel Frames; Return MC-OCF; Return MC-FSH (Packet Telemetry); Return VC Frames; Return VC-OCF; Return VC-FSH (Packet Telemetry); Return Bitstream (AOS); Return Space Packet Forward AOS (6) Forward Bitstream; Forward VCA; Forward Space Packet; Forward Proto Transfer Frame; Forward Insert; Forward Coded Transfer Frame Forward Telecommand (4) TC-VCA; Forward Space Packet; Telecommand Frame; CLTU

Only some of these have their own Recommended Standards. The SLE overview lists the published ones.

Mode Behaviour Forward online During the forward space link session only. Two qualities: complete and in-sequence (follows the routing control instructions, such as the multiplexing scheme, with sequence kept and no ground-induced errors, omissions or duplicates) and expedited (in sequence received, no ground errors, but data may be lost). Cannot extend past the end of the session. Return online, complete In sequence, no ground errors, no omissions, even if data arrives faster than it can be delivered (needs reserved buffering). May extend past the session. Return online, timely Two mechanisms: notification when delivery delay exceeds Tdelay-notify (and again on recovery); deletion of the queue when it exceeds Tdelete. The user can disable both. Forward offline The whole data set must reach the SLE system before it is transmitted to the space element during the session. It is transmitted complete and in sequence at a time set by SLE management. Return offline Delivered during or after the session, as a stored data set. Storage is either user data storage (everything received, with selection later) or user service data storage (only the service data chosen up front).

Source: delivery modes.17 Offline delivery is arranged, like online delivery, through the service package.17

docs.title: Provision, production and ports
docs.text:
Two definitions run through every SLE book:

  • Provision: an SLE system provides a transfer service when it exposes the operations needed to obtain it. Provision is characterised by which data channels are transferred, when, and with what quality of service.18
  • Production: the transformations between the RF carrier and the transferred SLE data channels.18

An SLE system has transfer ports and management ports. A transfer port is either a user port (T-U) or a provider port (T-P), never both. Ports are asymmetric, and each service runs between exactly one pair of ports.18 The ports are named consumer or supplier by the direction of data flow. For return services the provider is the supplier. For forward services the provider is the consumer, because the user supplies the data.19

The model defines four kinds of transfer-port operations. These are the abstract ancestors of the concrete SLE operations:2019

Operation type Invoked by Purpose Concrete examples in the SLE books Transfer_Data The supplier (provider for return, user for forward) Carries an SLE-SDU RAF-TRANSFER-DATA, FSP-TRANSFER-DATA Transfer_Set The user Initialises or updates attributes of the user's instance START parameters, INVOKE-DIRECTIVE Transfer_Get The user Reads status and configuration of the instance GET-PARAMETER Transfer_Notification The provider Status and accounting reports STATUS-REPORT, ASYNC-NOTIFY

Inference

The right-hand column is this page's mapping, not the reference model's. The reference model defines only the abstract types and their naming rule: the port type name plus "Data", "Set", "Get" or "Notification", for example Fwd-SP-TransferData.2019

The forward transfer ports, from table 5-2, show which functional group serves which user:

Port type Service Provider SLE-FG (consumer) User (supplier) CLTU-Transfer Forward CLTU Forward TC Space Link Processing Forward CLTU Generation, MUE TCFrame-Transfer Forward Telecommand Frame Forward CLTU Generation Forward TC VC Data Insertion, MUE TCVCA-Transfer Forward TC VCA Forward TC VC Data Insertion MUE Fwd-SP-Transfer Forward Space Packet Forward AOS VC Data Insertion, Forward TC VC Data Insertion MUE Fwd-Coded Transfer Frame-Transfer Forward Coded Transfer Frame Forward AOS Space Link Processing MUE Fwd-Proto Transfer Frame-Transfer Forward Proto Transfer Frame Forward AOS Space Link Processing Forward AOS VC Data Insertion, MUE Fwd-Insert-Transfer Forward Insert Forward AOS Space Link Processing MUE Fwd-VCA-Transfer Forward VCA Forward AOS VC Data Insertion MUE Fwd-Bit-Transfer Forward Bitstream Forward AOS VC Data Insertion MUE

Source: table 5-2. The TC VC Data Insertion and TC Space Link Processing groups also have OCF consumer ports, through which they receive the CLCWs.21 Two RF-carrier port types (Rtn-RF-Transfer, Fwd-RF-Transfer) face the spacecraft. Each has a single TransferData operation.22

docs.title: Functional groups and their management ports
docs.text:
The functional view breaks an SLE system into eight SLE Functional Groups (SLE-FGs). Each has transfer ports and one Function-Management provider port (FM-P).2324

Category SLE-FG Management port (supplier) Return Return Space Link Processing Rtn-SpLinkProc-Mgmt Return Return Frame Processing Rtn-FrameProc-Mgmt Return Return Frame Data Extraction Rtn-FrameData-Mgmt Forward AOS Forward AOS VC Data Insertion Fwd-AOSData-Mgmt Forward AOS Forward AOS Space Link Processing Fwd-AOSSpLinkProc-Mgmt Forward TC Forward TC VC Data Insertion TCData-Mgmt Forward TC Forward CLTU Generation CLTUGen-Mgmt Forward TC Forward TC Space Link Processing TCSpLinkProc-Mgmt

Sources: tables 4-1 to 4-3 and 5-3.2325 On a management port, the functional group supplies Management_Notification, and Complex Management invokes Management_Set and Management_Get.25 The forward TC group rules that matter for telecommanding (one sequence-controlled service per VC, segmented packets only with sequence control) are on the FSP page. For each service, section 5.6 lists which groups and ports take part. FSP, for example, has an AOS profile and a TC profile.26

docs.title: The cross support view: complexes, packages and agreements
docs.text:
Real SLE systems are built from physical systems run by different agencies or organisations. The cross support view models each of them as an SLE Complex: a set of SLE-FGs under one management authority.27

Concept Definition SLE Complex A set of SLE-FGs under a single management authority, with one established relationship to the MDOS during cross support SLE Utilization Management The single MDOS entity that every complex talks to. It arranges data transfer with the complexes and monitors it, and is part of the Mission Management Entity. SLE Complex Management Negotiates service packages with UM. It also controls and monitors production and provision by the complex's SLE-FGs, distributes set-up parameters to them, and consolidates their reports for UM. SLE transfer service instance The provision by a complex of the capability to transfer one or more SLE data channels of one type, all related to the same space link session SLE Service Package The set of transfer service instances, with the characteristics of their production, that one complex provides to one or more users. Its online services are restricted to one space link session. SLE Service Agreement The transfer and management services a complex provides to an MDOS, and the conditions. Only one is in effect between a given complex and mission at a time.

Sources: cross support view definitions.2728293031

A complex exposes at least one user and one provider transfer port, and exactly one Complex Management port. A real system that serves several missions offers one such port per mission.32 A package only describes the part of production done by the complex that provides it. When a chain of complexes supports a mission, each complex has its own package with UM.29

docs.title: Time spans and phases
docs.text:
The reference model defines three nested periods:34

  • Service agreement period: when a complex lets UM create packages and provides their services. It often covers the whole operational life (several packages a day, hundreds or thousands in total). It can also be short, for example launch support, a manoeuvre or an emergency.
  • Service package lifetime: when the complex provides the services of one package. Its instances exist only during this time.
  • Service instance provision period: when the capability to transfer the instance's channels is provided. Online instances belong to one space link session, but may start before it and end after it. Offline instances can be anywhere in the agreement period.

        D0["Dormant period<br/>(optional)"] --> P1["Online provision periods<br/>(one space link session)"]

        P2 --> DB["Debrief: CM reports<br/>to UM"]

    DEF --> UTIL

During the definition phase, the attributes of the managed objects select:35 (a) the transfer services within the agreement; (b) the interfaces where they are offered; © which services this or other complexes must provide; (d) mission-specific production configuration; (e) the eventual users (MUEs or other complexes); (f) the schedule of online and offline instances; and (g) the reporting by CM to UM. During utilization, provision is controlled two ways: MUEs invoke control operations on their instances, and UM invokes management operations on the complex.36

docs.title: Security in the reference model
docs.text:
Issue 2 added a cross support security section covering six areas:37

Area SLE transfer services SLE service management Data privacy Not provided; to be ensured above or below SLE (for example by encrypting the PDU) XML encryption may be considered Data integrity In-sequence, complete, flow-controlled transfer; strict operation sequence; credentials over the whole PDU can be agreed Sequence numbers Authentication Credentials in the PDUs (procedure in the cross support concept); algorithms out of scope; secure key distribution needed Digital signatures recommended Access control Initiator and responder identifiers Unique identification parameters created by UM and carried in each message to CM Availability Not provided; depends on the underlying network CM may reject requests; denial of service left to routers and firewalls Auditing Not specified; the SLE API logs access attempts Not specified; agencies expected to keep audit trails

Service-specific threats and consequences are left to each service book. For FSP, see the FSP security section. For the wider picture, see security in CCSDS space links.37

docs.title: Part 2: SLE service management in the Cross Support Concept (910.3-G-3)
docs.text:
The Cross Support Concept explains what SLE service management was meant to cover. Of the five OSI management functional areas, it includes four:38

OSI area In SLE service management Configuration The largest part: UM and CM define service packages (input and output channels, processing parameters, storage) Accounting Per-package reports of data received, sent and processed by the complex Fault Notification of faults affecting services; detection and repair inside the complex stay hidden Security Credentials, access control to cross support interfaces, authentication of requests Performance Excluded: an internal matter for the complex's operator

The guiding considerations were these. Mission needs drive the concept. The user is isolated from the provider's internals. Services are presented the same way whatever the provider offers. Reporting gives enough accountability. Automation and low operating cost are design aims. Adoption can be incremental.3839 The SLE overview summarises the services (service agreement, configuration profile, trajectory prediction, service package) and the nominal timeline. The nominal use case runs as follows:

sequenceDiagram
    participant UM as SLE Utilization Management
    participant CM as SLE Complex Management
    participant MUE as Mission User Entity
    Note over UM,CM: Service agreement already in place
    UM->>CM: Trajectory Prediction submission
    CM-->>UM: Trajectory Prediction confirmation
    UM->>CM: Configuration Profile submission
    CM-->>UM: Configuration Profile confirmation
    UM->>CM: Query for available schedule times (outside SLE SM)
    CM-->>UM: Scheduling opportunities
    UM->>CM: Service Package submission (refers to trajectory and profiles, flexible times)
    CM-->>UM: Service Package confirmation / commitment
    UM->>CM: Service Package monitoring
    MUE->>CM: binds to the SLE transfer service ports at the agreed time
    UM->>CM: Service execution configuration request
    CM-->>UM: Service execution configuration response
    CM-->>UM: Post-pass notification / report

Diagram based on figure 5-12 and its description.40 Registration of a user with a provider (credentials, contacts, general bounds) comes before the service agreement, possibly years earlier. The cross support concept states that SLE service management does not cover registration.41

docs.title: Part 3: from SLE service management to SCCS service management
docs.text:
The first standard for this management interface, the SCCS Service Management Service Specification (CCSDS 910.11-B-1, August 2009), and its operations concept (910.14-G-1) are not in this library.42 The 2006 cross support concept cites the same number as a draft, the SLE Service Management Service Specification 910.11-R-1 (Red Book, March 2006).130 The name changed from SLE to SCCS service management with the version-1 specification.45 The extensible concept explains what version 1 covered and why it is being replaced. Version 1 offered the Service Package, Trajectory Prediction, Configuration Profile and Service Agreement management services, using Version-1 information entities.4243 ESTRACK used 910.11-B-1 "whenever possible" for its interfaces.44

Annex B of the extensible concept maps the old terms to the new ones:45

Cross Support Reference Model / SCCS SM version 1 Extensible SCCS SM enterprise model Note Space element (one spacecraft) Space User Node The Space User CSSS may contain several nodes MDOS Earth User CSSS MDOS is only the functional view; the new model adds a physical view of Earth User Nodes SLE-specific transfer service user functions Terrestrial Link Processing, Data Forwarding, Data Store, Application Abstracted SLE Utilization Management Utilization Management (UM) of the Earth User CSSS Essentially the same SLE Complex (renamed SCCS Complex in version 1) Provider CSSS Generalised to all radiometric services SLE Complex Management Provision Management (PM) of the Provider CSSS Essentially the same (implicit) Mission = Earth User CSSS + Space User CSSS Made explicit

The Monitored Data CSTS uses yet another name: its "Cross Support Complex" corresponds to the Earth Space Link Terminal (ESLT) of the SCCS architecture.46

docs.title: Part 4: the extensible SCCS service management concept (902.0-G-1)
Why a new suite
docs.text:
The concept names two groups of shortcomings in version 1. Its scope covered only requesting and scheduling services, not the other management activities over a mission's relationship with a provider. Its structure could not absorb new space communication technologies or new service management techniques.47 SCCS SM covers the physical and data link layer aspects of space link services. In the near term it is focused on single-hop Earth–space links, which the SCCS architecture calls the ABA configuration (Mission A supported by provider B) and which match IOAG Service Catalog 1. The SSI (Solar System Internetwork) configuration adds space–space and space–planet links with internetworking, and matches Service Catalog 2.48 In SSI, data is routed through the provider by internetwork address. The concept says it logically includes SSI, but many SSI details were still undefined, so the SSI configuration is outside the scope of this version and the first standards focus on Service Catalog 1.4849

The enterprise model splits service management between two functions. Utilization Management belongs to the Earth User CSSS, and Provision Management to the Provider CSSS. Each takes part in service catalog consultation, mission telecom analysis, service agreement negotiation and adoption, service planning and scheduling, service package execution, and service accounting.50 The model adds two management functions to the Earth User CSSS. Mission Planning relies on UM to acquire and configure the provider's services, and on Space User Management to configure and control the spacecraft side.51

docs.title: The mission support lifecycle
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    SCC["Service Catalog<br/>Consultation<br/>(usually once)"] --> SAD["Service Agreement<br/>Development:<br/>telecom analyses,<br/>negotiate and adopt"]
    SAD --> SAP
    subgraph SAP["Service Agreement Period (cycles overlap)"]
        PS["Service Planning and Scheduling:<br/>manage configuration profiles,<br/>exchange planning information,<br/>maintain predicted trajectory,<br/>schedule service packages"] --> EX["Service Package Execution:<br/>control (Service Control CSTS),<br/>monitor (MD-CSTS)"]
        EX --> ACC["Service Accounting:<br/>accounting reports"]
        ACC -. "next cycle" .-> PS
    end

Diagram based on figure 4-1 and section 4.525456

Several service agreements may run at once, for example one per mission phase (pre-launch tests, LEOP, cruise, landing), and their periods may overlap.53 Configuration profiles are expected to change rarely, perhaps never after the agreement is adopted.54 Trajectory prediction segments may come from a third party such as a flight dynamics facility, and may even be updated during a pass. They only have to arrive in time to be turned into acquisition data.55 During execution, UM may control well-constrained aspects (bit rate, modulation index, a frequency sweep) through the Service Control CSTS. It monitors through the MD-CSTS (below).56 Within a single transfer service, FSP's throw events cover similar changes: the example events of the FSP book switch command modulation and change the uplink bit rate or modulation index.129

docs.title: Information entities
docs.text:
All management information is exchanged as information entities (IEs), almost all of them in XML.57 The concept defines:

docs.title: Extensibility: abstract service components and functional resources
docs.text:
Each IE has extension points. These are places where technology-specific management information can be inserted, with each extension constrained to a defined type.64 For the service agreement and the configuration profile, the extension points are Abstract Service Components (ASCs). ASCs are layers of space communication functionality whose interfaces stay the same as technologies change. A technology-specific specialisation is a Service Component (SC). For example, an SC for the TM synchronization and channel coding standard carries the Reed-Solomon and turbo decoder parameters.64

Abstract Service Component (figure 6-1) Group Maps to (enterprise model, Provider CSSS) Aperture Space link interface Space Link Processing Forward Physical Channel Transmission Space link interface Space Link Processing Forward Synchronization and Channel Encoding Space link interface Space Link Processing Forward Space Link Protocol Transmission Space link interface Space Link Processing Return Physical Channel Reception Space link interface Space Link Processing Return Synchronization and Channel Decoding Space link interface Space Link Processing Return Space Link Protocol Reception Space link interface Space Link Processing SLS Data Delivery Production Ground link interface Data Forwarding SLS Radiometric Data Production Ground link interface Application Service Offline Data Storage Ground link interface Data Store and Data Forwarding Data Transfer Services (SLE, CSTS, radiometric and file transfer) Ground link interface Data Forwarding Space Internetworking Ground link interface Data Forwarding Service Management Functions (MD-CSTS and the future SC-CSTS) Service management Application Service

Sources: figure 6-1 and its descriptions. The concept itself calls the mappings rough.6566 ASCs carry no parameters of their own. Each SC is made of Functional Resource (FR) Types. Each FR type has configuration parameters, monitored parameters, notifiable events and real-time control directives, and a published identifier. An FR instance is named by its FR Type plus an FR Instance Number. That Functional Resource Name is what MD-CSTS reports against.6667

The concept defines six kinds of configuration for an ESLT: SLS, SLS data delivery, retrieval data delivery, forward offline data delivery, SLS radiometric and retrieval radiometric. Only the SLS configurations include the layered stack of aperture, physical channel, synchronization and coding, and link protocol.68

The telecommand mission example (from the concept)

The mission uses TC on the forward link and TM on the return link. Its service agreement allows each SLS service package up to five SLE FSP instances or one F-CLTU instance, plus one RAF, three RCF, one ROCF, one Tracking Data CSTS and one MD-CSTS. Zero to five instances of the FSP TS Provider FR type feed VC packet requests into one TC Encoding, VC Packet Processing, and VC Generation FR.70 The Earth user sends either packets or CLTUs, but uses only one mode in any one package.69 Configuration profiles then make the choice. One SLS profile has three FSP, one RAF, two RCF, one TD-CSTS and one MD-CSTS instance. Another has one F-CLTU, one RAF, one ROCF, one TD-CSTS and one MD-CSTS instance. A profile also fixes a single initial value for every parameter whose agreement allows a range.7071 Retrieval packages may contain one RAF, three RCF and one TD-CSTS instance.69

docs.title: Service packages and scheduling
docs.text:
There are three kinds of service package. The SLS package covers services that need an active space link. The Retrieval package covers delivery of stored return data, with or without an SLS running. The Forward Offline package covers upload of forward data to the provider before the SLS that will carry it. Version 1 had no Forward Offline package.72 Providers schedule in two ways:73

  • Specific-period scheduling. The mission asks for SLSes at or around given times. The request can be made flexible with a preferred start time plus start-time lead and lag, a preferred and minimum duration, and the relative timing of carriers (for example, the forward carrier for at least n minutes inside the return carrier). Process options are waitlisting (keep trying until a waitlist period expires), improvement after scheduling up to a freeze interval, and service scenarios (nominal plus contingency configurations reserved together, for example for LEOP).
  • Rule-based scheduling, also called generic or standing order scheduling. Mission and provider agree rules, such as "6 return carriers per week, 15–30 min each, 6–30 h apart". PM then generates tentative packages, which UM may delete. The concept names this as the primary mode of the NASA Near Earth Network and ESTRACK. The Recurrent Service Package Request combines the two: rules for a stated horizon, optionally with allowed and forbidden windows.

The extensible SLS Service Package Request keeps what is requested separate from how it may be scheduled. A Space Communication Service Set holds one or more Space Communication Service Requests, each pointing to one configuration profile. A Flexibilities and Constraints component holds rules, each pointing to the requests it applies to. Every provider that adopts the format must support the minimal rule, a fixed start and stop time per request. Providers may add their own rules at this extension point. Trajectory references are another likely extension point, because deep-space packages may need the trajectories of both the spacecraft and a celestial body.74

The planning IEs (Provisional Plan, Communications Geometry, Sustainable Data Rates, RFI, Resource Conflicts, Cost Estimates), the Space Link Event Sequence and the Accounting Report all follow an Event Timeline stereotype. This is a time-ordered series of events. Each event has an identifier unique within the service agreement and an event time. The time is instantaneous or has a duration, carries an uncertainty window, and is absolute or relative. Each event also has an extension point for type-specific data, such as the aperture of a visibility event.75

docs.title: Management services and the roadmap
docs.text:
The concept is to be phased in. First, standard IEs are used inside providers' own management services, which may adapt version-1 operations to carry the new entities. Standard management services follow later, aimed at about 2020.43 The roadmap of 2014 planned these products:

timeline
    title Extensible SCCS SM products as scheduled in 2014 (table 8-1)
    Early 2014 : Concept (Green Book)
    Late 2014 : Simple Schedule Format
    Early 2016 : Planning Data Formats issue 1 : Trajectory Prediction Data Format
    Early 2017 : Service Request and Service Package Data Formats : Service Agreement and Configuration Profile Data Formats
    Early 2018 : Space Link Event Sequence Data Format
    Mid 2019 : Planning Data Formats issue 2
    Late 2019 : Service Catalog
    Mid 2020 : Service Accounting
    Late 2020 : Management Services (Automation)
    To be negotiated : Best Practices (Magenta Book)

Diagram based on table 8-1.76

The 2026 SPDF draft shows how the suite turned out. Its figure 1-1 places SPDF among these books: Concept 902.0-G-1, Simple Schedule Format (SSF) 902.1-B-1, Communications Planning Information Formats (CPIF) 902.2-B-1, SPDF 902.4-B-1, Service Agreement and Configuration Profile Data Formats (SACP) 902.5-B-1, Event Sequence Data Format (EVSQ) 902.6-B-1, Service Catalog (SECA) 902.7-M-1, Service Management Accounting (SMAC) 902.8-B-1, Service Management Utilization Request Formats (SMURF) 902.9-B-1, Service Management Automation Support Handling (SMASH) 902.10-O-1, Best Practices (BPR) 902.11-M-1, Common Data Entities (CDE) 902.12-M-1 and Abstract Event Definition (AED) 902.13-M-1.77 SPDF's reference list confirms some of them: SACP 902.5-B-1 (proposed), CDE 902.12-M-2 (February 2026), EVSQ 902.6-B-1 (proposed), AED 902.13-M-1 Cor. 1 (February 2024), SMURF 902.9-B-1 (forthcoming) and SSF 902.1-B-2 (forthcoming).78

The name-to-number pairs above were checked against the rendered figure, not only the extracted text. The figure gives CDE as 902.12-M-1, while the reference list cites issue 2, 902.12-M-2.7778 The ESOC SpaceOps paper cites the Simple Schedule Format as 902.1-B-1 of May 2018 and the SMURF draft as white book 902.9-W-0.06 of July 2018.118

Inference

The 2014 roadmap's single "Service Request and Service Package" book appears to have become two books, SMURF (requests) and SPDF (packages). No book number for the Trajectory Prediction format appears in the available sources.

docs.title: Part 5: Service Package Data Formats (902.4-B-1)
docs.text:
Status of this document

The library copy is dated September 2026 and labelled Blue Book Issue 1. Every page header says "Proposed Draft". The authority page gives the location as "Not Applicable" and says the statement of authority will be added when the standard is finalised. The document control lists it as the current proposed draft of December 2025.4 Treat its content as a draft.

SPDF tells user missions which requested service packages were scheduled. It covers the apertures, the configuration and the absolute timing that came out of the mission's constraints or the provider's use of the allowed flexibility.79 It covers formats and content only, not how they are exchanged.79 As a feedback message, it closes the loop on Service Package Requests. It can confirm settings, pin down values the request left open, give the times when services will be available and say where they will be provided.80

Type 1 Type 2 Configuration By reference: configuration profile reference, optional trajectory, event sequence and DDOR scan pattern references Contained: full configuration profile contents, plus event sequence and DDOR scan pattern if needed Changed parameters Listed separately (resource, parameter, new value) against the referenced profile or sequence Written directly into the contained data Motivation Compact, like the Simple Schedule Format Migration from legacy systems that send all parameters

Sources: 1.1.2.2, 2.1 and 2.2.3–2.2.4.798182 The two types are functionally equivalent. Provider and user choose one in the service agreement or by other means. An SPDF instance may batch several packages, which should all be of the same type.8183

Sources: figure 3-1 and tables 3-1 to 3-3.848687 Most classes are "fully described" in the Common Data Entities book (902.12-M-2), which is not in this library.7887

The ICS proforma adds two pairs of mutually exclusive conditions. Exactly one of ApertureReference and ApertureCelestialBodyPosition must be present (C1/C2). Exactly one of OnlineSrvPkgType1 and OnlineSrvPkgType2 must be present (C3/C6). A DDORScanPatternWrapper is required whenever the abstract DDOR wrapper is present (C7).85 Unregistered values for the originatingOrganization, spaceUserNode, siteRef and apertureRef parameters are allowed but discouraged. They are prefixed UNR::.88 The normative schema is 902x04b01-SPDF.xsd, which includes 902x12m02-CDE.xsd. Both come from the SANA SCCS-SM XML schema registry, and a GitHub release tagged SANA_Release-20260526 also holds them.89 Security is left to the systems and networks that carry the messages. The document warns that tampering with resource-availability information could, in severe cases, cost the mission.90

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
MD-CSTS is a Cross Support Transfer Service, built on the CSTS Specification Framework (921.1-B-2, not in this library). With it, a mission can receive cyclic or on-change reports of monitored parameters, receive notifications of events, and query current values. All of these relate to the cross support services of a service package.4691 It delivers only current values and stores no history.91 A package may contain several MD-CSTS instances, and each can see every monitored parameter and event of the package, including its own. The MD-CSTS instances are themselves monitored functional resources.9293 Formally, monitoring a package is a UM job, done here with a transfer service rather than a management service. A principal investigator could also use it, for example to correlate instrument data with link status.93

Procedure Version Instances Approach Operations Association Control SFW 2 exactly 1 adopted from the framework BIND, UNBIND, PEER-ABORT (framework) On-Change-Option Cyclic Report (prime) 2 1 or more refined and extended from Cyclic Report START (extended, blocking), STOP (blocking), TRANSFER-DATA (non-blocking) Information Query 2 0 or 1 refined GET (non-blocking) Notification 2 in table 3-1 (text: 1) 0 or more refined START, STOP (blocking), NOTIFY (non-blocking)

docs.title: Naming monitored items
docs.text:
Parameters and events are named by OIDs. A Parameter Name combines a Parameter Identifier (a published OID for the parameter type) with a Functional Resource Name (FR Type OID plus FR Instance Number). Event Names work the same way. FR instance numbers come from scheduling, so they are not fixed in advance.100 The book writes these as text, for example [[{Antenna}: 1]: {antPointingMode}] for the pointing mode of antenna instance 1.101

A cyclic-report START (or a GET, or a Notification START) can select by individual names, by labels (a parameter type for all instances), by a named or default label list agreed by service management, by FR Name (all parameters of one instance) or by FR Type (all instances of a type). Optionally, it can also select procedure configuration parameters. Any unknown item makes the START fail, and the unknown items are returned.102 Several cyclic report instances can run at once with different lists and cycles.102

On-change option. Each START of the cyclic report carries on-change-option. With FALSE, every report contains every subscribed value. With TRUE, the first report is complete, and later reports contain only parameters whose value or qualifier changed since they were last reported. A value that changes and changes back between two reports is not sent.103104

docs.title: Service management parameters and production status
docs.text:
Classifier Sets mdInitiatorId, mdResponderId, mdServiceInstanceId, mdResponderPortId Association Control identifiers mdNamedLabelLists The one set of parameter label lists shared by all cyclic report and query instances; at most one is the default mdMinAllowedDeliveryCycle Shortest allowed reporting cycle mdNamedEventLists Event label lists for Notification; at most one default mdResponseTimeout Service-level response timeout; reportable through cyclic report and query mdProdStat / mdProdStatChange Production status parameter and its change event

Sources: sections 7 and 8.105106 MD-CSTS does not support the framework's "production configuration change" event, because the service itself can report configuration changes.106 Its production status values are refined for monitoring. Configured means set up to reach the package's monitorable resources. Operational means at least one of them can be reached. Interrupted means none can be reached, possibly temporarily. Halted means stopped by management.107

    U->>P: START 3rd cyclic report: FR Name [{Ccsds401SpaceLinkCarrierRcpt}: 2], 10 s
    U->>P: START notification: label {flfSyncDecFrameSyncLockStatChange}
    P-->>U: NOTIFY frame sync locked (S-band, then X-band)
    U->>P: START notifications by FR type: MdCstsProvider, RafTsProvider, FcltuTsProvider
    P-->>U: NOTIFY mdProdStatChange 'operational', fcltu production 'operational'
    U->>P: GET label {antPointingMode} (returns both antennas)
    U->>P: STOP all cyclic report and notification instances
    U->>P: UNBIND

Diagram based on the operational scenario in 2.5.99101111

The example shows MD-CSTS watching an FCLTU service from outside it. The FCLTU instance's state and radiated-CLTU count, and the uplink carrier frequency, are visible to the mission without any FCLTU operation.101109

docs.title: Part 7: ESTRACK in practice (SpaceOps 2025)
docs.text:
The ESOC paper describes the service management interfaces of the ESTRACK Scheduling Office (ESO). The number of ESA spacecraft flying has tripled in twenty years, while ESTRACK capacity stayed stable. Deep-space demand now exceeds the network's capacity at peak periods. ESTRACK therefore acts both as a user of six external providers and as a provider (and broker) to five external partners.644

Planning. The ESTRACK Planning System (EPS) solves all users' standing orders together. Standing orders are planning requirements and constraints from each mission agreement, translated into EPS configuration. The result is a baseline booking covering typically 4 weeks for the LEO network and up to 12 months for deep space. Users then add, modify or delete bookings.112 This is the rule-based scheduling that the extensible concept attributes to ESTRACK.73 Every change request is checked for validity (format, ID, privilege), conflict, technical feasibility (service available on that terminal, visibility) and, for external providers, availability. Valid requests then follow the EMSP request state machine.112 The ESTRACK Management System web Portal (EMSP) handles all external interfaces, both as user and as provider, through the web or system-to-system, using REST or files.112113

Closing the loop. Providers change bookings without warning (LEOP, maintenance, failures), and negotiations for deep space can last months. Immediate per-request confirmation therefore cannot keep two databases consistent. ESTRACK uses the provider's Simple Schedule Format list of everything it has agreed to support.114115 Building inter-network synchronisation correctly took two years for each of two generations of software.116

What every interface has in common. Across 6 agencies and 5 commercial entities, ESTRACK found the same minimal set:117

Item Typical content SC User name, usually the spacecraft code name GS Resource name: site or terminal BOT Start of support (beginning of track) EOT End of support (end of track) Service / Comment A pre-agreed ASCII string, or free text plus Service parameters (for example rates, coding), user ID, provider ID

These map directly onto the SPDF fields above (spaceUserNode, aperture reference, beginningOfTrack, endOfTrack, configuration profile reference, servicePackageID, serviceReqRef).

Inference

That mapping is this page's comparison of the paper's list with 902.4-B-1. The paper does not make it.

Formats and protocols. Since 2017, ESTRACK has used the published SSF and the draft SMURF (white book 0.06) for all new interfaces. It shields its core from partners' variants with XML plus XSL transforms, one independent translator per interface.118119 There are two request styles. The legacy one is replace all: a time range plus a list of supports, which deletes everything else in the range. SMURF's add/modify/delete handles single requests, which suits a yearly deep-space plan where under 1 % changes, but makes the booking system more complex.120

Service definition is the least standardised part. Interfaces use agreed keywords (such as XBand, SBand, Mode1, Mode2), with extra parameters for DDOR, MSPA or complex links. A network operator must still be able to set up the service from instructions read over a voice loop.121 Each ESTRACK service type has a scheduling template of automated tasks. A published catalogue of user scheduled events (absolute-time actions such as starting or stopping the uplink or a recording) has become a de facto standard for occultations and link changes.122

Inference

These user scheduled events play much the same role as the Space Link Event Sequence entity of the extensible concept, which lists planned link changes at absolute or relative times.60 The paper does not make this comparison.

Lessons. Exchange the minimum, and leave complex configuration to documents. Expose only tested configurations. Keep file exchange next to REST, because firewall changes can break live protocols.123 A catalogue of every possible service field proved hard to maintain. The CCSDS functional service levels (online telemetry, uplink, ranging and so on) were awkward, and a single agreed "TTC" service name worked better.123 Individual request confirmation (SPDF) was rated essential when the EPS was designed, but was never used, and only one of ESTRACK's providers supports it.115 The paper expects request formats (format, basic parameters, service-definition parameters) to be standardisable now. Services themselves will stay bilateral, and standing orders are best kept proprietary. The SMURF flexible-request fields (earliest start, latest end, minimum and maximum duration) are not yet implemented anywhere.124 The conclusion names SMAC, SACP and SMASH as the next topics.125

docs.title: Service agreement and package identifiers in the Solar Orbiter MIB
docs.text:
The public Solar Orbiter MIB carries one direct trace of this machinery. The NIS command EGENRTCO "GENERIC OPEN TC LINK" stores the SLE service instance identifier in three fixed-value elements. They join up as sagr=144.spack=NN11-PERM.fsl-fg=1.cltu=cltu01. The TM link commands EGENRTMO and EGENRTMC carry sagr=144.spack=NN11-PERM.rsl-fg=1.rcf=onlc0001. The forward CLTU instance and the return RCF instance therefore name the same agreement and the same package. The values are identical in the 2025-09-16 and 2020-04-16 releases.126127 The first two attributes name the service agreement (sagr) and the service package (spack) defined by the reference model. They are followed by the forward or return functional group and the service instance, using the syntax of the SLE service books.12829 The SLE overview explains the syntax. The FSP page covers the TC link command, and the return services page the RCF instance.

Inference

The -PERM suffix suggests a standing (permanent) package used for every pass, rather than one package per pass. Neither the MIB nor the library documents state this.

SQL used 

-- Fixed-value elements of the TC link opening command (both MIB releases)
SELECT CDF_BIT, CDF_ELLEN, CDF_PNAME, CDF_VALUE
  FROM cdf WHERE CDF_CNAME = 'EGENRTCO' ORDER BY CAST(CDF_BIT AS INT);
-- ENISTE35 'sagr=144.spack=' | ENISTE38 'NN11-PERM.fsl-f' | ENISTE37 'g=1.cltu=cltu01'

-- Joined identifier of all four NIS link commands
SELECT CDF_CNAME, group_concat(CDF_VALUE, '') FROM
  (SELECT CDF_CNAME, CDF_VALUE FROM cdf
    WHERE CDF_CNAME IN ('EGENRTCO','EGENRTCC','EGENRTMO','EGENRTMC')
      AND CDF_PNAME IN ('ENISTE35','ENISTE38','ENISTE37')
    ORDER BY CDF_CNAME, CAST(CDF_BIT AS INT))
 GROUP BY CDF_CNAME;
-- EGENRTCC/EGENRTCO sagr=144.spack=NN11-PERM.fsl-fg=1.cltu=cltu01
-- EGENRTMC/EGENRTMO sagr=144.spack=NN11-PERM.rsl-fg=1.rcf=onlc0001

SELECT CPC_NAME, CPC_DESCR, CPC_PTC, CPC_PFC FROM cpc
 WHERE CPC_NAME IN ('ENISTE35','ENISTE37','ENISTE38');
Tables: cdf, cpc.

docs.title: Notes on the source texts
docs.text:
• 910.4-B-2: the document control lists the current issue as "CCSDS 910.0-B-2".1 The TC profile of FSP (5.6.2.9.2) begins "The production of the TC-VCA service…".26
  • 902.0-G-1 speaks of "Fifteen Abstract Service Components" in 2.4.2 and "twelve" a page later, while figure 6-1 shows thirteen.6465 The Offline Data Storage ASC is also called "Offline Data Delivery Production" in the text.66 5.12 points to deliverable 8.2 c) for the Space Link Event Sequence format, but the roadmap lists that book as 8.2 g).6062
  • 902.4-B-1: the header note in 2.2.2 lists test, provisional and operational uses, but table 3-1 allows INTERFACE-TEST, OPERATIONAL and OTHER.8386 ICS condition C3 refers to OnlineSrvPkgType2 as A2.1.5.13 and C6 to OnlineSrvPkgType1 as A2.1.5.10, but those clauses hold AbstractModCProfParm and AbstractModESeqParm. The ICS also marks apertureRef and eventSequenceRef mandatory where figure 3-1 gives them as [0..1], and it lists no sicfRef.8584 The description of ApertureCelestialBodyPosition repeats that of ApertureReference.87 The expansion of "SICF" is not stated in the available sources.
  • 922.1-B-2: the Notification procedure version is '1' in 3.2.13 but 2 in table 3-1.94 The scenario uses fcltuTsNumberOfCltusRadiated where annex F has fcltuNumberOfCltusRadiated, and fcltuTsProdStatChange where annex F has fcltuProdStatChange. It also reports a RAF production status of 'running', which is not one of the ProdStat values.101111110 Annex F gives the TC PLOP events node as "(1.3.112.4.4.2.¼/2)".109
