docs.title: ECSS: the European space standards system
docs.text:
The European Cooperation for Space Standardization (ECSS) is the body that writes the standards European space projects apply to management, engineering, product assurance and sustainability.12 It is a cooperative effort of the European Space Agency (ESA), national space agencies and European industry associations, and its documents are published by the ESA Requirements and Standards Section at ESTEC in Noordwijk.2 For the subject of this wiki, ECSS matters in three ways: its communications standards (the E-50 series) select and adapt the CCSDS space link protocols; its ground systems and operations standards (the E-70 series) define the Packet Utilization Standard (PUS), the operability requirements a spacecraft must meet, and the monitoring and control data a supplier hands to the operator; and these documents are what a mission control system such as SCOS-2000 and its Mission Information Base are built to serve.

This page explains how ECSS documents are organised, named and produced, and gives a linked map of the documents relevant to telemetry and telecommand. ECSS publishes its own map of the whole system as the ECSS Trees, a set of charts that this wiki holds in its November 2025 edition; each chart carries its own "as of" date, from June 2024 to November 2025.4957 The detailed pages are:

Page What it covers ECSS-E-ST-50C and the CCSDS adoption notices The communications engineering standard (Rev.1 and Rev.2), all six CCSDS adoption notices, the superseded 2008 TM frame and TC standards, the RF and ranging companions and the E-50 handbook ECSS-E-ST-70C The parent ground systems and operations standard: operations and ground segment engineering processes and their documents ECSS-E-ST-70-31C The space system model and the monitoring and control data a supplier delivers, compared with the SCOS-2000 MIB ECSS-E-ST-70-11C Space segment operability: observability, commandability, autonomy, FDIR, time, PUS usage ECSS-E-ST-70-32C PLUTO, the test and operations procedure language ECSS-E-ST-70-01C On-board control procedures (OBCPs) PUS: ECSS-E-ST-70-41C The Packet Utilization Standard: 20 standard service types numbered 1 to 23 (7, 10 and 16 reserved)17 From ESA PSS to CCSDS and ECSS The ESA PSS packet standards of 1988 to 1994 from which the ECSS documents descend

docs.title: What ECSS documents are
docs.text:
ECSS standards open with a near-identical foreword. It says that requirements are stated as what shall be accomplished rather than how the work is organised, and that this lets existing organisations and methods be reused and evolve without rewriting the standards. Its first sentence, which calls each document one of a series meant to be applied together, has changed over time:

Documents in the library Areas named in the opening sentence Issues of 2008 to 2016 (for example ECSS-E-ST-70C, ECSS-E-ST-50-04C, ECSS-E-ST-70-41C) management, engineering and product assurance Issues of 2021 to 2023 (ECSS-E-ST-50C Rev.1, ECSS-E-AS-50-22C to -26C) management, engineering, product assurance and sustainability Issues from December 2024 (ECSS-E-ST-50C Rev.2, ECSS-E-AS-50-21C Rev.2, the PUS Rev.1 draft, ECSS-E-ST-70-11C Rev.1) sentence omitted

Sources: the forewords, PDF p. 2 of each.5823594 Each document is prepared by a dedicated working group (for the adoption notices, the ECSS Space Communications Working Group), reviewed by the ECSS Executive Secretariat and approved by the ECSS Technical Authority.2359

ECSS standards are written to be tailored: each one states that it may be tailored to the characteristics and constraints of a project in conformance with ECSS-S-ST-00.56 The PUS describes itself as a "menu" from which a mission selects services and service levels for each on-board application process.7 ECSS-E-ST-70-11C Rev.1 goes further and says that every mission needs to tailor it, choosing the applicable requirements and adding mission-specific ones.6

docs.title: Branches, disciplines and the system documents
docs.text:
The 2021 to 2023 forewords name four areas: management, engineering, product assurance and sustainability.2 The ECSS Trees of November 2025 show the full structure: two system documents at the top, ECSS-S-ST-00 (system description) and ECSS-S-ST-00-01 (glossary of terms), and below them five branches, each divided into numbered disciplines. The letter after "ECSS-" names the branch, and the Trees file each document under the discipline whose number matches the leading digit of the document number: ECSS-E-ST-50C and ECSS-E-ST-50-04C under E-50, ECSS-E-ST-31C and ECSS-E-ST-32C Rev.1 under E-30 (mechanical engineering).4985

Letter Branch (as named in the Trees) Disciplines Examples S ECSS system (top-level documents) — ECSS-S-ST-00, ECSS-S-ST-00-01 (glossary of terms, the one normative reference of ECSS-E-ST-50C)499 M Space project management M-10 project planning and implementation; M-40 configuration and information management; M-60 cost and schedule management; M-80 risk management ECSS-M-ST-10C Rev.1, ECSS-M-ST-10-01C (organization and conduct of reviews), ECSS-M-ST-40C Rev.1; ECSS-M-ST-00-03C (tailoring) is referenced by E-ST-70-31C5010 Q Space product assurance Q-10 product assurance management; Q-20 quality assurance; Q-30 dependability; Q-40 safety; Q-60 EEE components; Q-70 materials, mechanical parts and processes; Q-80 software product assurance ECSS-Q-ST-80C Rev.2; ECSS-Q-ST-10-09 and ECSS-Q-ST-80 are normative references of ECSS-E-ST-70C; the draft ECSS-Q-80B of 3 April 2000 is cited by the Herschel/Planck EGSE specification546038 E Space engineering E-10 system engineering; E-20 electrical and optical; E-30 mechanical; E-40 software; E-50 communications; E-60 control; E-70 ground systems and operations; E-80 security ECSS-E-ST-10C Rev.1, ECSS-E-ST-50C Rev.2, ECSS-E-ST-70C, ECSS-E-ST-80C (security in space systems lifecycles)52 U Space sustainability U-10 space debris; U-20 planetary protection ECSS-U-AS-10C Rev.2 (adoption notice of ISO 24113, space debris mitigation), ECSS-U-ST-20C55 I Industrialization, production and maintenance I-10 industrialization; I-20 manufacturing; I-30 maintenance, repair and overhaul (MRO) ECSS-I-ST-30-10C (integrated production support)51

Besides the branches, the Trees list the documents that run ECSS itself: discipline P-00 (policy, ECSS-P-00C on standardization objectives, policies and organization) and discipline D-00 (configuration and information management of the documentation: ECSS-D-00B on ECSS processes, the drafting rules and templates for standards, ECSS-D-00-01C, and for handbooks, ECSS-D-00-02A, and ECSS-D-00-11A, the criteria for accepting a draft for public review and for releasing a handbook).57

    S["ECSS-S-ST-00 system description<br/>ECSS-S-ST-00-01 glossary"]
    S --> M["M: project management<br/>M-10, M-40, M-60, M-80"]
    S --> Q["Q: product assurance<br/>Q-10 ... Q-80"]
    S --> E["E: engineering<br/>E-10 ... E-80"]

The ECSS branch structure and the two disciplines this wiki covers, after the ECSS Trees of November 2025.495253

Inference

None of the forewords in the library mentions the industrialization branch, and the 2008 to 2016 forewords do not mention sustainability either. That the branches were added over time is this wiki's reading of the forewords and the Trees; the dates at which ECSS created the U and I branches are not stated in the available sources.

docs.title: Document types
docs.text:
Type Infix Status Example Standard -ST- Normative: "shall" requirements (in recent issues each with a unique identifier) ECSS-E-ST-50C Rev.2, ECSS-E-ST-70-41C Adoption notice -AS- Normative: applies another body's standard "with the following modifications"; in E-50 the six CCSDS notices, elsewhere ISO standards (the adoption of IEC 61025 on fault tree analysis is numbered ECSS-Q-ST-40-12C, with an -ST- infix) ECSS-E-AS-50-21C Rev.2 to ECSS-E-AS-50-26C; ECSS-E-AS-11C (ISO 16290, technology readiness levels) and ECSS-U-AS-10C Rev.2 (ISO 24113) in the Trees Handbook -HB- Informative guidance; not part of the standards, which prevail in any conflict ECSS-E-HB-50A Technical memorandum -TM- Listed with the handbooks; the Trees distinguish a handbook that is "published" from a memorandum that is "made available" ECSS-E-TM-10-20A (product data exchange), ECSS-E-TM-10-23A (space system data repository); none in the library Draft for public review DIR suffix A draft circulated for public review before publication ECSS-E-ST-70-41C Rev.1 DIR1

Sources for the rows: the adoption-notice wording; the handbook disclaimer; the Trees charts of the engineering, sustainability, product assurance and handbook series; the DIR change log.11125255545613 What distinguishes a technical memorandum from a handbook beyond that legend is not stated in the available sources.

Status in the Trees. The legend of each standards chart distinguishes four states: published; affected by the update of another document (M); ongoing (or planned) update of an existing document (U); new document in production (or planned) (N). The handbook charts use "HB published" and "TM made available" with the same U and N marks.525356 In the engineering chart of October 2025, for example, ECSS-E-ST-70-41C is published and its Rev.1 is marked U, and ECSS-E-ST-40-02C (machine learning software engineering) is marked N.52

Normative words. ECSS-E-ST-70-11C Rev.1 spells out the convention shared by the series: "shall" expresses a requirement, "should" a recommendation (which tailoring turns into a requirement or removes), "may" and "need not" express permission, and "can" is descriptive only. Present and past tense state facts.14

Requirement identifiers. In the recent documents of the library every requirement carries a unique label that combines the document number and a running number, for example ECSS-E-ST-50_0970031 (the in-sequence telecommand delivery service of ECSS-E-ST-50C, 2021), ECSS-E-ST-70-11_1670115 (essential telecommands without on-board software, Rev.1 of 2025) or ECSS-E-AS-50-25_1560001 (the clause that applies CCSDS 232.0-B-4, 2023).151611 Labels survive revisions: ECSS-E-ST-50_0970031 is unchanged in Rev.2 of 2024.66 The PUS change log lists "naming each requirement to facilitate tailoring, traceability" among the ECSS drafting rules applied in issue C.18 The 2008 to 2011 issues in the library (ECSS-E-ST-50-01C to -05C, ECSS-E-ST-70C, -70-01C, -70-31C, -70-32C) carry no such labels: their requirements are identified only by clause number and letter (for example 5.1b of ECSS-E-ST-50-03C).37

Inference

The seven digits after the underscore appear to start with a three-digit code per document: 097 for ECSS-E-ST-50, 167 for ECSS-E-ST-70-11, and 152 to 156 for the adoption notices -21 to -25 (ECSS-E-AS-50-21_1520001 up to ECSS-E-AS-50-25_1560001).151679 The sources do not explain the numbering.

docs.title: Issues and revisions
docs.text:
The issue letter and revision appear in the document number. The change logs in the library show a consistent pattern:

Document line Issue A Issue B Issue C Later Communications ECSS-E-50 Part 1A (20 October 2003) and Part 2A (4 July 2005) never issued ECSS-E-ST-50C (31 July 2008) Rev.1, 1 March 2021; Rev.2, 5 December 20241965 TM synchronization and channel coding ECSS-E-50-01A (6 November 2007) never issued ECSS-E-ST-50-01C (31 July 2008) superseded by ECSS-E-AS-50-216774 Ranging and Doppler tracking ECSS-E-50-02A (24 November 2005) never issued ECSS-E-ST-50-02C (31 July 2008) none; still listed as published in May 20256853 TM transfer frame ECSS-E-50-03A (6 November 2007) never issued ECSS-E-ST-50-03C (31 July 2008) superseded by adoption notices2021 TC protocols, synchronization and coding ECSS-E-50-04A (14 November 2007) never issued ECSS-E-ST-50-04C (31 July 2008) superseded by ECSS-E-AS-50-24, -25 and -266976 Radio frequency and modulation ECSS-E-50-05A (14 November 2007) never issued ECSS-E-ST-50-05C (31 July 2008) Rev.1, 6 March 2009; Rev.2, 4 October 201170 CCSDS adoption notices -21 to -26 none none first issues, 1 March 2021 Rev.1 of -21 to -25, 13 January 2023; Rev.2 of -21, 5 December 202474767778 Ground systems and operations ECSS-E-70 Part 1A (25 April 2000) and Part 2A (2 April 2001) never issued ECSS-E-ST-70C (31 July 2008) none in the library71 On-board control procedures never issued never issued ECSS-E-ST-70-01C (16 April 2010), the first issue none in the library72 Operability ECSS-E-70-11A (5 August 2005) never issued ECSS-E-ST-70-11C (31 July 2008) Rev.1, 15 October 202522 M&C data definition ECSS-E-70-31A (9 October 2007) never issued ECSS-E-ST-70-31C (31 July 2008) none in the library23 Procedure language (PLUTO) ECSS-E-70-32A (24 April 2006) never issued ECSS-E-ST-70-32C (31 July 2008), editorial changes none in the library73 PUS ECSS-E-70-41A (30 January 2003) never issued ECSS-E-ST-70-41C (15 April 2016) Rev.1 in public review (DIR1, 11 December 2024), marked as an ongoing update in October 2025181352

The C issues of 2008 were produced by applying the new ECSS template, renumbering the requirements and checking consistency with CCSDS and other ECSS standards.202223 For ECSS-E-ST-70C the change was larger: it merged the two parts of ECSS-E-70A (principles and requirements; document requirements definitions) into one document and replaced the phase-based approach with a process approach that separates operations engineering from ground segment engineering, each with its own customer–supplier relationship.71 ECSS-E-ST-50C Rev.2 changes little: its change log says it was done mainly to stop naming the issues of the adopted CCSDS books, so that the standard need not change when CCSDS updates them, and otherwise lists only the foreword, the deletion of twelve definitions, one typo correction and the bibliography.65

Inference

The A issues are numbered without the ST infix (ECSS-E-70-41A, ECSS-E-70-11A) and the C issues with it (ECSS-E-ST-70-41C, ECSS-E-ST-70-11C). The change logs link the 2008 C issues to the new ECSS template; that the ST infix itself was introduced by that template is this wiki's reading of the numbering, not a statement in the sources. Documents first published after 2008 also start at letter C: ECSS-E-ST-70-01C of 2010 (A and B "never issued") and the adoption notices of 2021, whose change logs call issue C the "First issue".7274 The letter therefore seems to mark the generation of the ECSS document system rather than count the issues of each document; the sources do not say so.

docs.title: How a standard is produced
docs.text:
The PUS gives the most complete record in the library of an ECSS standard's life. In January 2011 the working group for issue C had 190 change requests against issue A. A first draft for public review (DIR1) was reviewed publicly for four months in 2014 and produced 620 discrepancy reports; the status presentation of October 2015 planned delivery of the final draft to ECSS for December 2015, and the standard was published on 15 April 2016.2418 The disposition statistics show 464 review reports from agencies, 156 from industry and 44 from the working group itself.25 The revision now under way follows named steps: Draft for Review (DFR), Draft for public review (DIR, with the public review of ECSS-E-ST-70-41C Rev.1 running from 12 December 2024 to 28 February 2025), draft with implemented review reports, Technical Authority vote for publication, and publication.13 The rules behind these steps are ECSS documents themselves: ECSS-D-00-01C and ECSS-D-00-02A give the drafting rules and templates for standards and handbooks, and ECSS-D-00-11A the criteria for accepting a draft for public review and for releasing a handbook.57 In the Trees of October 2025 the PUS revision is still marked as an ongoing update; its outcome is not stated in the available sources.52

flowchart LR
    CR["Change requests<br/>(e.g. 190 against PUS-A, 2011)"] --> WG["Working group<br/>drafting"]
    WG --> DFR["DFR<br/>Draft for Review"]
    DFR --> DIR["DIR<br/>public review"]
    DIR --> DRR["Discrepancy review<br/>reports dispositioned"]
    DRR --> TA["Technical Authority<br/>vote"]
    TA --> PUB["Publication<br/>(ESA Requirements and<br/>Standards Section)"]
    PUB -->|"lessons learned"| CR

The ECSS document life cycle as recorded for ECSS-E-ST-70-41C and its Rev.1 draft.2413

docs.title: ECSS and CCSDS
docs.text:
The Consultative Committee for Space Data Systems was formed in 1982 by the major space agencies to standardise space data systems for cross support.26 Its Recommended Standards (Blue Books) are not binding on its members: an agency may adopt them, endorse them or write a related standard of its own.27

ESA historically did the last of these. CCSDS recommendations were modified for European needs and republished in the ESA PSS series (Procedures, Specifications and Standards), including or excluding options according to European preferences; all PSS documents have since been withdrawn in favour of ECSS standards or CCSDS Recommended Standards.28 ECSS continued the practice for the core telemetry and telecommand standards (ECSS-E-ST-50-01, -03 and -04 of 2008), with two structural differences from CCSDS: the PUS is an ECSS application-layer protocol with no CCSDS equivalent, and the three CCSDS telecommand books were combined into the single ECSS-E-ST-50-04.29 The handbook announced that this practice was being phased out in favour of direct reuse through adoption notices, which may remove options but otherwise apply the CCSDS text, and that ECSS expected to adopt all new communications-related CCSDS recommendations.2930

That is what happened. ECSS-E-ST-50C lists six adoption notices, ECSS-E-AS-50-21 to -26, which replace ECSS-E-ST-50-01C, -03C and -04C.31 The 2021 Rev.1 named the CCSDS issue each notice was based on; Rev.2 of December 2024 names only the book (for example "CCSDS 131.0-B"), and each notice states which issue applies, so that a new CCSDS issue requires a new revision of the notice but not of ECSS-E-ST-50C.6575

Reference relationships: E-ST-50 follows the ECSS-E-ST-10 process and is complementary to E-ST-70; E-ST-70 references ECSS-E-ST-10 normatively and lists E-ST-70-01, -11, -31, -32 and -41 in its bibliography (dotted where no other link is shown) and defines the space segment operability requirements document by reference to E-ST-70-11; E-ST-70-11 normatively references the adoption notices -24, -25, -26 and the PUS; the PUS satisfies the operability requirements of E-ST-70-11; E-ST-70-01 assumes PUS compliance; E-ST-70-31 assumes E-ST-50, E-ST-70, E-ST-70-41 and E-ST-70-32 and normatively references E-ST-70-01.4360614445634642

The division of labour, in one paragraph (this wiki's summary of the cited scopes): ECSS-E-ST-50 says how to engineer the end-to-end communication system and what it must achieve (for example that commands are delivered in sequence and that every frame identifies its spacecraft); the adoption notices say which protocol does it; ECSS-E-ST-70-11 says what the spacecraft must let the operator see and do; ECSS-E-ST-70-41 says which standard services and packets do that; and ECSS-E-ST-70-31 says what data must be handed over so that a ground system can drive those services, which in ESA's world ends up as the SCOS-2000 MIB.154547

docs.title: How Solar Orbiter used the series
docs.text: The Solar Orbiter TM/TC and packet structure ICD shows how a mission of the 2010s cited ECSS. Its applicable documents include ECSS-E-70-41A (the PUS of 2003), and its reference documents include ECSS-E-ST-50-03C for the TM transfer frame and ECSS-E-ST-50-04C for the telecommand link, both of July 2008 and both since superseded by the adoption notices first issued on 1 March 2021.483174 The SCOS-2000 Database Import ICD (issue 7.0, 2017) in turn references the older ESA PSS standards, the Packet Utilisation Standard ESA PSS-07-101 of May 1994 and the ESA Packet Telecommand Standard, and, as RD-20, ECSS-E-70-41A with the remark that it "will be replaced by ECSS-E-ST-70-41C".3334 Standards therefore live on in missions and ground systems long after ECSS supersedes them, which is why this wiki covers the superseded documents too.

docs.title: ECSS-E-ST-50C communications and the CCSDS adoption notices
docs.text:
ECSS-E-ST-50C ("Space engineering – Communications") is the top-level ECSS standard for the end-to-end data communication system of a spacecraft. It does not define frame formats. It defines the vocabulary, the engineering process with its documents and reviews, and the functional and performance requirements that the chosen protocols must satisfy; the protocols themselves are specified by lower-level ECSS standards, by ECSS adoption notices of CCSDS standards and by the CCSDS books.12 The current issue is Revision 2 of 5 December 2024. It changes no requirement of Revision 1 (1 March 2021) beyond correcting a typing error in requirement 5.2.5.3c: it deletes twelve definitions, fixes that typo and stops naming the issue of each adopted CCSDS book, so that the standard need not be revised every time CCSDS updates one of them.136 This page therefore follows Rev.1 and says where Rev.2 differs. The clause numbers and requirement identifiers are the same in both, but from clause 3.3 onwards each clause sits one PDF page earlier in Rev.2 (see What Rev.2 changed). It also covers all six adoption notices, ECSS-E-AS-50-21 to -26 (for TM coding, the TM, AOS and TC Space Data Link Protocols, TC coding and COP-1), the superseded 2008 standards ECSS-E-ST-50-03C (TM transfer frame) and ECSS-E-ST-50-04C (telecommand), and the communications guidelines handbook ECSS-E-HB-50A. The general ECSS context is on the ECSS overview page, and the PSS standards from which the European choices descend are on the history page.

At a glance

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
The standard specifies requirements for developing the end-to-end data communication system of a spacecraft: the terminology of space communication systems engineering, the activities of the engineering process (following ECSS-E-ST-10), and specific functional and performance requirements. It covers space-to-ground, ground-to-space and space-to-space links used in operations, and the links used during assembly, integration and test (AIT).2 The communication system has three domains, the ground network, the space link and the space network; the standard covers the space link and the space network in detail and the ground network only as far as end-to-end services need it, the rest being left to ECSS-E-ST-70.2 The handbook calls ECSS-E-ST-50 a process-oriented standard, with no options, that should be applied to all missions.8

The standard is explicit that it cannot define a complete link on its own: the complete set of standards for a link is project-dependent, and ECSS-E-HB-50 gives guidance and examples.1

Rev.2 removed twelve definitions on a change request of the ECSS Glossary Task Force (communication service, cross support, downlink, service-provider, service-user, sink, telecommand, telemetry, telemetry link, uplink, user, user application) and renumbered the rest, so its clause 3.2 runs from 3.2.1 "channel" to 3.2.13 "telecommand link".136138 The deleted words are still used in the requirements; the available sources do not say where their definitions now live.

docs.title: Architecture: elements, domains and the protocol stack
docs.text:
The example configuration of the standard has a spacecraft (possibly with a probe or lander on a space-to-space link), a ground station, an operational control centre (OCC) and a mission experiment centre (MEC). Each element has a data handling system that manages its internal links, its external links and the processing between them; the downlink and uplink chains are described as acquisition, formatting, transmission, reception, de-formatting and onward delivery.11

The three domains have very different characteristics:12

Domain Character What the standard focuses on Space network (on-board and inter-spacecraft) On-board networks are varied, often proprietary, conservative and not upgradeable in flight; inter-spacecraft links are intermittent and of variable topology Upper-layer services that leave freedom of on-board data link and physical layers Space link Point-to-point wireless link, inherently unreliable; ground end unconstrained, space end constrained in power, mass and volume; Doppler and variable propagation; must tolerate very high BER Reliable data transfer services Ground network Reliable terrestrial links that can be upgraded during the mission Only the transfer of spacecraft data between ground and space nodes

The standard's figure 4-2 maps the CCSDS and Internet protocols onto the ISO layers, marking which CCSDS standards ECSS formally adopts. In the lower layers the formally adopted ones are the TC, TM and AOS Space Data Link Protocols (each with the optional SDLS protocol, CCSDS 355.0-B) and the TC and TM synchronization and channel coding standards; ECSS-E-50-05 covers radio frequency and modulation. Upper layers include the Space Packet Protocol, the Encapsulation Packet Protocol, CFDP, IP over CCSDS, the Bundle Protocol and LTP, and compression standards. The figure names ECSS-E-ST-70-41C (the PUS) as the example of an application-specific source and sink.13 Its notes add that CCSDS has its own physical layer standard, CCSDS 401.0-B, with more options than ECSS-E-50-05 (see Radio frequency, modulation and ranging), that the Proximity-1 suite is only one possible choice for proximity links, and that the optical communications standards CCSDS 141.0-B and 142.0-B are not shown. Figure 4-2 and its notes are the same in Rev.2.13140

docs.title: Spacecraft control considerations
docs.text: Clause 4.7 explains why the requirements look as they do. Under degraded conditions (on-board failures, bad attitude, tumbling) the minimum goal is to keep some control: in the worst case, commanding in the blind with some certainty of execution, which implies telecommands decoded and executed directly by hardware with minimal on-board functionality; in less extreme cases, receiving critical telemetry acquired by simple and reliable functions that usually do not rely on software. Data unit sizes are chosen to limit the effect of bit errors and drop-outs, and acknowledgements are desirable for critical command functions without preventing blind commanding.14 Control and payload traffic also differ in kind: commands must be delivered in order and may be repeated but not lost, while payload transfer aims at volume, can accept some loss and does not care about order if the data can be reconstituted.15

docs.title: The engineering process and its documents
docs.text:
Clause 5.2 assigns the activities of each engineering phase and the documents they produce. The documents are specified by document requirements definitions (DRDs) in Annexes A to H, and Annex I says at which project review each is first delivered.16

Phase (clause) Who Activities required Outputs (DRD) Requirements engineering (5.2.1) Customer Analyse top-level mission requirements, express communication-specific requirements, formulate new ones CSRD, Annex A Analysis (5.2.2) Supplier Feasibility; data rates, link margins, commandability, Doppler; criticality analysis; top-level architecture; verification plan including compatibility and interoperability tests; candidate solutions; request assignment of globally managed parameters (frequencies, spacecraft identifiers); identify telemetry parameters with their criticality and need for time stamping at source; identify telecommand parameters, data flows and ranging needs Link and Doppler margin and criticality analyses (CSAD, Annex C); CSVP (Annex D) Design and configuration (5.2.3) Supplier Partition into components; assign unique names; component specifications; define manual and automatic procedures (link acquisition, release, synchronization, data rate and frequency negotiation); update link margins CSBD, CSADD, CSDDD, CSPD (Annexes B, E, F, G); configuration item list (CSDDD); simulations (CSAD); procedures (CSOM, Annex H) Implementation (5.2.4) Supplier Procure, manufacture, integrate and test components; interoperability and compatibility tests; manage; update link margins The delivered system; designs, test procedures, simulations, test results and deviations (CSADD, CSDDD, CSVP) Verification (5.2.5) Supplier, accepted by customer Execute agreed tests in a controlled environment; record and analyse results; compliance matrices Verification report (ECSS-E-ST-10-02 Annex F); signed declaration of acceptance; characterization data (CSPD) Operations (5.2.6) Either or both Operate, maintain and reconfigure for mission phases, support troubleshooting, decommission at end of life including stopping transmissions and notifying the ITU-R Periodic utilization and performance reports

Sources: §5.2.1 to §5.2.6.171819202122

DRD Annex Content (paraphrased) First delivery Communication system requirements document (CSRD) A The customer's requirements on ground network, space link and space network SRR, finalised at PDR Communication system baseline definition (CSBD) B The supplier's formal response and technical baseline, with a compliance matrix against the CSRD PDR Communication system analysis document (CSAD) C Full technical analysis leading to frequencies, protocols, options, redundancy and operational concept PDR, finalised at CDR Communication system verification plan (CSVP) D Verification test plan, including tests usable in operations PDR, updated at CDR, QR, AR Communication system architectural design document (CSADD) E Architectural design and relationships with other mission systems PDR Communication system detailed design document (CSDDD) F Detailed design CDR Communication system profile document (CSPD) G Frequency, protocol, option, address, channel and spacecraft identifier assignments, space link and on-board bus bandwidth allocations; the formal statement of compliance to ECSS-E-50 CDR, finalised at AR, ORR and FRR Communication system operations manual (CSOM) H All procedures for operating the communication system, normal (acquisition, loss of signal, hand-over, address initialisation, router configuration) and contingency (uplink-only, downlink-only, unexpected or discontinuous signal) PDR, finalised at CDR, AR, ORR, FRR

Source: Annex I, table I-1.16 The process milestones are the system requirements, preliminary design, critical design, qualification, acceptance, operational readiness and flight readiness reviews (SRR, PDR, CDR, QR, AR, ORR, FRR).23

    SRR([SRR]) --> PDR([PDR]) --> CDR([CDR]) --> QR([QR]) --> AR([AR]) --> ORR([ORR]) --> FRR([FRR])

What a profile looks like in practice

The CSPD records spacecraft identifier, address and channel assignments. For Solar Orbiter the equivalent values are in the TM/TC and packet structure ICD: spacecraft identifier 650 (0x28A), a single 1115-octet frame length and a fixed allocation of data classes to virtual channels.2425

docs.title: Functional and performance requirements
docs.text:
The remaining clauses are short "shall" and "should" statements. They are listed here in full (as paraphrases) because together they explain most protocol features of the CCSDS stack.

5.3 Space communication system. Bandwidth is allocated according to data needs and spacecraft mode, with priority for essential commands and telemetry in emergencies; data must not be lost through congestion (buffering and flow control are suggested); all transmissions must be stoppable by telecommand at any time, which makes those telecommands essential telecommands.26

5.4 Telecommanding.272829

Clause Requirement (paraphrased) Typical realisation 5.4.1 Commandable at all attitudes and anticipated rates Omnidirectional antenna coverage (see ECSS-E-ST-70-11) 5.4.2 A service guaranteeing in-sequence delivery of telecommands COP-1 sequence-controlled service 5.4.3 Probability of accepting an erroneous telecommand below \(10^{-2}/N\), \(N\) = number of telecommands expected over the mission BCH code plus frame error control field 5.4.4 Essential telecommands decodable and distributable when all other systems including the CDMU have failed; list, encoding and effects agreed at PDR; able to switch power to key components and force switch-over to redundancy; for critical operations (e.g. transmitter on/off) not dependent on software Hardware decoder and CPDU (ST[02]) 5.4.5 Only telecommands from authorised sources executed Authentication, possibly SDLS 5.4.6 Encryption when authentication alone cannot meet the security requirement; may be at upper layers or in the protocol sublayer via SDLS in ECSS-E-AS-50-25 SDLS 5.4.7 Commanding in the blind (no telemetry or acknowledgement) possible Expedited service, hardware commands 5.4.8 Telecommand acknowledgements returned to the source CLCW, ST[01] 5.4.9 (new in Rev.1) With several input channels, active-channel selection must not repeatedly select a channel whose lower signal quality causes significant frame rejection Remedy for the "dual lock" issue (see the handbook section below) 5.4.10 (new in Rev.1) Every telecommand carries the identifier of its destination spacecraft Spacecraft Identifier in the TC frame What \(10^{-2}/N\) means (illustrative arithmetic)

A mission that expects to uplink \(N = 10^6\) telecommands must keep the probability of accepting an erroneous one below \(10^{-2}/10^{6} = 10^{-8}\) per telecommand. The standard's note to 5.6.11.7 says that with the BCH coding of ECSS-E-AS-50-24 and the frame error control of ECSS-E-AS-50-25 the undetected frame error probability can be kept below \(10^{-18}\) at the reference BER of \(10^{-5}\), and below \(10^{-8}\) without frame error control.30 The numbers for \(N\) are illustrative.

5.5 Telemetry.313233

Clause Requirement (paraphrased) Typical realisation 5.5.1 Essential telemetry transmissible at all attitudes and rates (notes: may be unachievable on some missions; deep-space missions can use sub-carriers or tones as "semaphores") Low-gain antennas, beacon modes 5.5.2 Essential telemetry acquired from critical points and transmitted even when only one redundant part of other systems including the CDMU works; list, conversions, encodings and formats agreed at PDR; enough to judge overall condition (power state, data handling status, whether TCs are received); should not rely on the space network or on-board software Hardware-generated high priority telemetry 5.5.3 All telemetry identifies its source spacecraft (normally kept as annotation on ground) Spacecraft Identifier in the TM frame 5.5.4 Telemetry in the blind (no uplink signal) possible 5.5.5 All telemetry time-stamped against a common on-board reference so that order can be determined on ground Packet time in the PUS secondary header; time codes 5.5.6 A range of simultaneous source rates with priorities and maximum latencies; the downlink imposes no constraint on individual source rates Virtual channels and packet multiplexing 5.5.7 (new in Rev.1) Telemetry authentication and encryption when security needs it; may be via SDLS of ECSS-E-AS-50-22 and -23 SDLS

5.6 Space link.34353637303839404142

Clause Requirement (paraphrased) 5.6.1 Modulation chosen to minimise bandwidth (ECSS-E-ST-50-05); channel coding chosen to minimise power (ECSS-E-AS-50-21, -24); conformity to the ITU Radio Regulations 5.6.2 Each space link treated as simplex; data integrity mechanisms (ARQ) on contra-flowing links supported 5.6.3 to 5.6.7 Work with short sporadic contacts; interoperability across mission types and ground segments, including receive-only stations; optimised for the orbit; robust to background and burst noise; all mission phases from AIT to end of life 5.6.8 Meaningful commands and status reports within very short acquisition periods 5.6.9, 5.6.10 Isochronous and asynchronous traffic, and housekeeping and payload data, on one link 5.6.11.1 to .4 Worst-case Doppler shift and rate; worst-case tumbling (demonstrated by simulation); worst-case run lengths and transition densities (demonstrated by simulation); adaptable to loss of link, reduced margin and sporadic carrier acquisition 5.6.11.5 Uplink budgets based on a BER of \(10^{-5}\) at the telecommand decoder input 5.6.11.6 At that BER, uplink frame rejection rate below \(10^{-5}\) for 256-octet frames (the note warns that with BCH a 1024-octet frame exceeds \(10^{-5}\), and that LDPC in ECSS-E-AS-50-24 performs better) 5.6.11.7 Probability of accepting a corrupted uplink frame compatible with 5.4.3 5.6.11.8, .9 Downlink frame rejection rate should be below \(10^{-5}\); probability of accepting a corrupted maximum-size downlink frame should be below \(10^{-12}\) 5.6.11.10, .11 Minimise end-to-end delay; downlink rates compatible with all mission phases and with ITU bandwidth allocations 5.6.12 Minimise the number of frequencies; apply to the ITU Radiocommunication Bureau for frequency assignment before SRR; keep unwanted emissions below interference levels (special protection for radio astronomy and deep space bands); respect power flux density limits on the Earth's surface in all phases 5.6.13.1 Frames identify spacecraft and link (the frame version number can identify the link) 5.6.13.2 Formatted data units identify source, destination or both (the identifier need only be unique within the spacecraft, combined with the spacecraft identifier) 5.6.13.3 Formatted data units carry a sequence identifier to detect duplication or omission 5.6.13.4 Error detection in the protocol; undetected error probability is a project item; compatible with 5.6.11 5.6.13.5 ARQ settings verified by end-to-end simulation under all expected conditions, to avoid both loss and excessive retransmission 5.6.14.1 Connection establishment and maintenance (carrier acquisition, configuration, ordered disconnection, possibly rate negotiation) 5.6.14.2, .3 A guaranteed delivery service preserving order; an expedited service that overtakes queued SDUs 5.6.14.4, .5 Isochronous duplex services for voice and video, specified by nominal rate, maximum nominal latency and maximum deviation 5.6.14.6 Time correlation between on-board time and ground time 5.6.14.7 Ranging or Doppler tracking or both (ECSS-E-ST-50-02; PN ranging and Delta-DOR for accurate orbit determination) 5.6.14.8 Telecommand receipt confirmation at the space network gateway (received on board, not necessarily delivered) 5.6.14.9 Exception reporting of all detected errors, which should include corrected errors, undeliverable SDUs, failed deliveries, reconfiguration and unexpected loss of link

The mapping to CCSDS mechanisms is direct: 5.6.13.1 is the Master Channel Identifier, 5.6.13.2 the APID or MAP or VC identifier, 5.6.13.3 the frame and packet counters, 5.6.13.4 the frame error control field and the Reed-Solomon or BCH codes, 5.6.14.2/.3 the AD and BD services of COP-1, 5.6.14.6 the time correlation of ST[09] and the ground time correlation, and 5.6.14.8 the CLCW.

Inference

The mapping in the previous paragraph, and the "Typical realisation" columns of the 5.4 and 5.5 tables, are this wiki's reading. ECSS-E-ST-50C only gives hints in its notes (for example, that the frame version number can identify the link, or that SDLS can provide security).3928

5.7 Space network. The on-board network must be deterministic under all loads, support synchronous command and control of sensors and actuators and asynchronous transfers, give medium access to all nodes, should allow hot redundant nodes, and have lower error rates than the space link. Its services provide reliable delivery (or notification of non-delivery), expedited transfer, network management of routing and configuration tables, redundancy management, exception reporting, telecommand delivery confirmation to the end destination (not execution, which is the application's business) and time distribution. Rev.1 added an inter-spacecraft network subsection with deterministic performance (should), asynchronous transfers, best-effort and reliable qualities of service, expedited transfer, network management, exception reporting and time synchronization.434445

5.8 Ground network. Every data item from the spacecraft is labelled so that parameter name, sampling time and ground reception time can be determined; security prevents unauthorised access to command or acquire data; error rates are much lower than on the space link and network; critical nodes can run hot redundant; the network is available for all scheduled operations.46

Inference

ECSS-E-ST-50C names no ground implementation. That in ESA's ground segment these needs are met by SLE services, by NCTRS/NIS and by the archive annotation of SCOS-2000 is this wiki's reading.

docs.title: What Rev.1 changed
docs.text: Rev.1 (1 March 2021) implements change requests, updates terms (the "space network" of the on-board domain becomes "on-board network"), updates the purpose of the CSDDD and CSPD DRDs and the documentation summary, adds requirements 5.2.5.3c, 5.4.9a, 5.4.10a, 5.5.7a and the inter-spacecraft network clauses 5.7.3 and 5.7.4, modifies some 40 requirements, and deletes 5.4.6b, 5.6.12.4b, 5.7.1.7a and 5.7.2.2a.3

docs.title: What Rev.2 changed
docs.text:
Rev.2 (5 December 2024) was prepared by the same ECSS-E-ST-50C Revision Working Group. Its change log gives one reason for the revision: to stop having to update ECSS-E-ST-50 whenever one of the adopted CCSDS standards is updated.137136 A line-by-line comparison of the two copies held by this wiki finds no other technical change than the ones the change log lists:

Part Rev.1 (1 March 2021) Rev.2 (5 December 2024) Foreword Opens by calling the standard one of a series meant to be applied together for management, engineering, product assurance and sustainability That sentence is gone; the rest is unchanged Clause 3.2 25 terms 13 terms (twelve deleted, see above) Requirement 5.2.5.3c The CSPD DRD is misprinted "(CDPD)" Corrected to "(CSPD)" (the change log calls the typo "CSDP") Table of adoption notices in 4.2 Each notice with the CCSDS issue and date it is based on, e.g. "CCSDS 131.0-B-3 (Sept. 2017)" Book number and title only, e.g. "CCSDS 131.0-B - TM Synchronization and Channel Coding" Bibliography Notices listed with the adopted CCSDS issue Notices listed with the book number only Requirements 5.2 to 5.8, Annexes A to I Baseline Same text and same identifiers, e.g. ECSS-E-ST-50_0970031 for in-sequence telecommand delivery (§5.4.2)

Sources: the change logs, forewords, clause 3.2, §4.2, §5.2.5.3, §5.4.2 and bibliographies of both revisions.136137138139142143141349

Inference

That Rev.2 changes nothing beyond what its change log lists is this wiki's finding, from a normalised text diff of the two extracted copies; ECSS does not state it. The diff also shows the expected side effects: the remaining terms of clause 3.2 are renumbered and the bullet layout of some lists differs.

Because the deleted definitions shorten clause 3, every clause of Rev.2 from 3.3 onwards sits one PDF page earlier than in Rev.1: §5.4.2 is on p. 37 of Rev.1 and p. 36 of Rev.2, requirement 5.2.5.3c on p. 34 and p. 33.144143142 The page numbers in the footnotes of this page are those of Rev.1.

docs.title: Companion standards: radio frequency and ranging
docs.text:
Two clauses of ECSS-E-ST-50C point to companion standards that ECSS did not replace by adoption notices: the overview of 5.6.1 says that suitable modulation schemes are defined in ECSS-E-ST-50-05, and the note to requirement 5.6.14.7a (ranging or Doppler tracking capability) says that suitable methods are defined in ECSS-E-ST-50-02.3442 Both are in the library and are described on Radio frequency, modulation and ranging.

Standard Issues Scope (paraphrased) ECSS-E-ST-50-05C Rev.2, Radio frequency and modulation ECSS-E-50-05A (14 Nov. 2007); B never issued; C (31 July 2008); Rev.1 (6 March 2009); Rev.2 (4 October 2011) Radio techniques between spacecraft and Earth stations in both directions and for orbit-determination tracking: frequency allocation and use, signal requirements such as spectral occupation and power, permissible modulations, the spacecraft–Earth station interface, acquisition and cross-support; for the Space Operation, Space Research and Earth Exploration-Satellite services, not for data-relay satellites ECSS-E-ST-50-02C, Ranging and Doppler tracking ECSS-E-50-02A (24 Nov. 2005); B never issued; C (31 July 2008) Transponder and Earth station requirements for ranging with unprocessed accuracies of 2.5 ns to 30 ns and Doppler of 0.1 mm/s to 1 mm/s; for less demanding projects CCSDS 401.0-B may suffice

Sources: change logs and scopes.194195192193 Rev.2 of ECSS-E-ST-50-05C aligned the standard with CCSDS 401.0-B-20 (April 2009): it removed filtered OQPSK from the 8400–8450 MHz band, dropped FQPSK-B and shaped OQPSK from Annex D.2.2 and corrected the change log, which had called the 2008 and 2009 issues "First issue".194 The library's CCSDS copy is the much later 401.0-B-32 (October 2021).189

docs.title: The adoption notices
docs.text:
An adoption notice applies a CCSDS Recommended Standard as an ECSS standard "with a minimum set of modifications", listed in an applicability table that shows each modified clause with its new wording, a comment and the original CCSDS text.4748 In the 2023 and 2024 notices, clause 4 holds one labelled requirement saying that the CCSDS book applies with the amendments of table 4-1 (ECSS-E-AS-50-21_1520001, -22_1530001, -23_1540001, -24_1550001, -25_1560001) and a second labelled requirement carrying the table; ECSS-E-AS-50-26C of 2021 states the same requirement without a label. All but -23, whose AOS frame had no 2008 ECSS predecessor, close with an informative Annex A listing the remaining differences from the superseded ECSS standard.1491581681754873 ECSS-E-ST-50C lists six notices; the table below adds the revision of each that this wiki holds:49139

Adoption notice Based on (as listed in ECSS-E-ST-50C Rev.1, 2021) Latest revision in the library and the CCSDS issue it adopts Supersedes Wiki page ECSS-E-AS-50-21 CCSDS 131.0-B-3 (Sept. 2017), TM Synchronization and Channel Coding -21C Rev.2 (5 Dec. 2024): 131.0-B-5, Sept. 2023 ECSS-E-ST-50-01C, whole standard TM coding ECSS-E-AS-50-22 CCSDS 132.0-B-2 (Sept. 2015), TM Space Data Link Protocol -22C Rev.1 (13 Jan. 2023): 132.0-B-3, Oct. 2021 ECSS-E-ST-50-03C, "TM Transfer Frame" TM SDLP ECSS-E-AS-50-23 CCSDS 732.0-B-3 (Aug. 2016 per ECSS; the CCSDS document control dates Issue 3 September 2015, see AOS), AOS Space Data Link Protocol -23C Rev.1 (13 Jan. 2023): 732.0-B-4, Oct. 2021 nothing (ECSS-E-ST-50-03 had no AOS frame) AOS ECSS-E-AS-50-24 CCSDS 231.0-B-3 (Sept. 2017), TC Synchronization and Channel Coding -24C Rev.1 (13 Jan. 2023): 231.0-B-4, July 2021 ECSS-E-ST-50-04C clauses 8 and 9 CLTU ECSS-E-AS-50-25 CCSDS 232.0-B-3 (Sept. 2015), TC Space Data Link Protocol -25C Rev.1 (13 Jan. 2023): 232.0-B-4, Oct. 2021 ECSS-E-ST-50-04C clauses 5 and 6 TC SDLP ECSS-E-AS-50-26 CCSDS 232.1-B-2 (Sept. 2010), COP-1 -26C (1 Mar. 2021): 232.1-B-2, Sept. 2010 ECSS-E-ST-50-04C clause 7 COP-1

Sources for the last column: the scope clause of each notice.147156166173515

The adoption notices are revised when CCSDS revises the book, and the applicable CCSDS issue is the one stated in the latest revision of each notice; every notice of 2023 and 2024 repeats this rule under its mapping table, which itself names the books only as "CCSDS 131.0-B-x" and so on. The 2021 ECSS-E-AS-50-26C still lists the issues in its table (for example "CCSDS 232.1-B-2 (Sept. 2010)") and has no such note.4714872 ECSS-E-ST-50C Rev.2 applied the same idea to the parent standard by dropping the issue numbers from its own table.136139 The first issues of -21 to -26 all date from 1 March 2021; -21 to -25 were revised on 13 January 2023 and -21 again on 5 December 2024.1461551651724

The bibliographies cross-check one another. Those of -22C, -23C, -24C and -25C Rev.1 (all January 2023) list -21C Rev.1 as the adoption of CCSDS 131.0-B-4; the bibliography of -21C Rev.2 lists itself as the adoption of 131.0-B-5. The bibliography of -25C Rev.1 lists -23C Rev.1 as an adoption of "CCSDS 232.0-B-4, AOS Space Data Link Protocol"; -23C Rev.1 itself, and the other bibliographies, give 732.0-B-4, so that entry is a typing error.50164166154 All six notices are held in the revisions that the ECSS Trees of May 2025 show as published; the earlier revisions (the first issues of -21 to -25 of 1 March 2021 and ECSS-E-AS-50-21C Rev.1 of 13 January 2023) are not held.145146

Newer CCSDS issues than the adopted ones

The library also holds CCSDS 131.0-B-6 (April 2026), whose document control marks 131.0-B-5 as superseded, and CCSDS 732.0-B-5 (October 2025), which marks 732.0-B-4 as superseded.185186 The latest notices in the library still adopt 131.0-B-5 and 732.0-B-4. Whether ECSS has since revised ECSS-E-AS-50-21 or -23 is not stated in the available sources; by the rule above, the issue named in the latest notice remains the one that applies.

docs.title: ECSS-E-AS-50-21C Rev.2: TM synchronization and channel coding
docs.text:
The notice applies CCSDS 131.0-B-5 (September 2023), which it calls similar to ECSS-E-ST-50-01C, the 2008 telemetry coding standard it supersedes. Its first issue (1 March 2021) replaced ECSS-E-ST-50-01C; Rev.1 (13 January 2023) followed a CCSDS issue that added support for the Unified Space Data Link Protocol and for ground-to-space links; Rev.2 (5 December 2024) follows 131.0-B-5, whose revised pseudo-randomizer avoids spectral spikes on high-rate links, and adds differences from ECSS-E-ST-50-01C (USLP, turbo code rates, attached sync marker patterns) that earlier revisions had missed.146147148 Its table 4-1 modifies five CCSDS clauses (in six rows: 5.1 has one for the requirement and one for a new note):150151

CCSDS clause CCSDS 131.0-B-5 ECSS (ECSS-E-AS-50-21C Rev.2) Effect 3.2.4 Soft-decision decoding with at least 3-bit quantization "should" be used when decoder complexity permits It shall be used for the convolutional decoder No hard-decision convolutional decoding 4.3.1c (new) — Reed-Solomon with E=8 only with 4-dimensional 8PSK trellis-coded modulation (4D-8PSK-TCM) E=8 restricted to one modulation 4.3.5.1 Interleaving depth I = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or 8 E=16: I = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or 8; E=8: I = 8 only Depth tied to the code 4.3.5.2 Depth "normally" fixed on a physical channel for a mission phase Always fixed 5.1 and new note Concatenated codes combine a Reed-Solomon code of section 4 with a convolutional code Only the E=16 Reed-Solomon code; E=8 is never concatenated

Annex A lists what ECSS-E-ST-50-01C lacked compared with CCSDS 131.0-B-5:152153

Topic ECSS-E-ST-50-01C (2008) CCSDS 131.0-B-5 as adopted LDPC codes none several, for a frame or a stream of sync-marked frames Turbo code rates ½ and ¼ ½, ⅓, ¼ and ⅙, with matching ASM patterns Pseudo-randomizer 255-bit sequence 131 071-bit sequence (section 10), the old one only for backward compatibility Frame lengths per code informative (Annex C) normative (section 11) USLP frames not mentioned supported beside TM and AOS frames Managed parameters informative "mission configuration parameters" (Annex G) normative (section 12) Ground-to-space and space-to-space use not covered normative (section 13) Service interface and security discussion none Annexes A and B Coding scheme selection guidance Annex D application profiles none in the book; CCSDS 130.1-G-3 gives performance data

The 2008 standard is in the library as ECSS-E-ST-50-01C: issue A of 6 November 2007, B never issued, C of 31 July 2008, which says it establishes a common implementation of telemetry channel coding without quantifying coding gain.190191 CCSDS has meanwhile issued 131.0-B-6 (April 2026), which adds an interleaver for turbo codewords, allows slicing for all block codes and makes the pseudo-randomizer mandatory.185 Code details are on the TM coding page.

docs.title: ECSS-E-AS-50-22C Rev.1: TM Space Data Link Protocol
docs.text:
The notice applies CCSDS 132.0-B-3 (October 2021). Together with ECSS-E-AS-50-23 it supersedes ECSS-E-ST-50-03C; its Rev.1 change log summarises the new CCSDS issue (support for the SDLS Extended Procedures of CCSDS 355.1-B-1, a normative PICS proforma, and informative options for randomizing the data field of Only Idle Data frames), which, as with -25C Rev.1, are annexes of the CCSDS book, not of the notice.155156157162 Its only modification is an addition: it carries the ESA extended virtual channel frame count of ECSS-E-ST-50-03C over into the CCSDS frame as new clauses 4.1.3.1.7 and 4.1.3.4.159160161

New clause Requirement (paraphrased) 4.1.3.1.7 The Transfer Frame Secondary Header may carry an extended virtual channel frame count 4.1.3.4.2.1 The secondary header is then 32 bits long (Secondary Header Length field = 3) 4.1.3.4.2.2 Its data field holds a 24-bit extension of the Virtual Channel Frame Count 4.1.3.4.2.3 The extension counts the roll-overs of the 8-bit count in the primary header, giving a 32-bit count whose 8 least significant bits stay in the primary header 4.1.3.4.2.4 It is associated with a master channel (every frame carries the count of its own VC) or with one virtual channel (other VCs may omit the secondary header or use it otherwise) 4.1.3.4.2.5 The choice is static on that channel throughout a mission phase

The rules are those of ECSS-E-ST-50-03C §5.3.4; the bit layout is drawn below, where Solar Orbiter's use of the count is shown.8990 Annex A of the notice lists the other differences from the 2008 standard:162163

  • CCSDS 132.0-B-3 specifies service interfaces (section 3) and sending and receiving procedures (4.2, 4.3); ECSS-E-ST-50-03 specified only packet processing and extraction.
  • It provides optional interfaces to SDLS and the SDLS Extended Procedures, including the SDLS Frame Security Report, a new Type-2 Report in the Operational Control Field (4.1.5.5); ECSS-E-ST-50-03 had no SDLS support (see Security).
  • A frame count may not be reset before 255 "unless it is unavoidable" (CCSDS) instead of "unless there is a major system reset" (ECSS-E-ST-50-03).
  • A Synchronization Flag of '1' marks a frame carrying a Virtual Channel Access SDU (CCSDS), while ECSS-E-ST-50-03 used '1' for any frame not meeting the conditions for '0', including frames carrying asynchronously inserted data.
  • Managed parameters (sections 5 and 6.6) and the PICS requirements list (Annex A) are normative; the 2008 standard had informative "mission configuration parameters" and no PICS.
  • The data field of an Only Idle Data frame may be randomized (4.1.4.6.2, with two implementation options in Annex D); the 2008 standard had no such specification.

docs.title: ECSS-E-AS-50-23C Rev.1: AOS Space Data Link Protocol
docs.text:
The notice applies CCSDS 732.0-B-4 (October 2021), which it describes as having a similar purpose to the TM Space Data Link Protocol with some extra features. Because ECSS-E-ST-50-03 covered only the TM frame, it has no annex of differences. Its change log repeats the CCSDS changes listed for -22C Rev.1; its first row labels the first issue "ECSS-E-AS-50-23C Rev.1 ... 13 January 2023", evidently a typing error, since the next row lists the changes of Rev.1 with respect to the issue of 1 March 2021.165166167 Its table 4-1 touches three CCSDS clauses, on two topics, the Replay Flag and the Frame Header Error Control:169170171

CCSDS clause CCSDS 732.0-B-4 ECSS-E-AS-50-23C Rev.1 4.1.2.5.2 The Replay Flag tells the receiver whether a frame is realtime or replayed, so that both kinds can share a virtual channel The Replay Flag shall be '0'; a new note says ECSS does not allow '1' because other means of replaying frames exist and '1' adds processing complexity at the receiving end 4.1.2.5.3 and notes '0' realtime, '1' replay; interpretation (for example a decreasing VC count in reverse playback) negotiated per project Deleted 4.1.2.6.1 One note Existing note numbered 1 (content unchanged); new note 2: the Frame Header Error Control may be restricted to physical channels without an error-correcting code, and with Reed-Solomon coding it brings no benefit and is strongly discouraged

A reversal of the 2008 advice

The 2008 handbook presented the AOS Replay Flag as the way AOS frames handle playback of recorded data.100 The 2023 notice forbids the value '1' in ECSS missions and only says that alternative means of replaying frames exist, without naming them. The newer CCSDS 732.0-B-5 (October 2025) widens the AOS Spacecraft Identifier to 10 bits and the M_PDU First Header Pointer to 16 bits, for frames up to 65 536 octets; no notice in the library adopts it.186 See the AOS page.

docs.title: ECSS-E-AS-50-24C Rev.1: TC synchronization and channel coding
docs.text:
The notice applies CCSDS 231.0-B-4 (July 2021), which it calls similar to clauses 8 and 9 of ECSS-E-ST-50-04C. With -25C and -26C it replaced that standard on 1 March 2021; Rev.1 aligns with 231.0-B-4, which supports USLP frames, and corrects informative notes that still called the randomizer optional with BCH coding.172173174 Most of the European choices that the 2008 handbook explained (see below) reappear here as modifications:176177178179180181182

Topic CCSDS 231.0-B-4 ECSS-E-AS-50-24C Rev.1 Clauses modified Frames per CLTU One or more TC Transfer Frames, or one USLP frame Exactly one TC Transfer Frame, or one USLP frame Note 2 to the definition in 1.6.1.3; Annex A3 BCH decoding mode Error-detecting (Triple Error Detection, TED) or error-correcting (Single Error Correction, SEC), per mission Always SEC: one bit corrected, two detected 2.2.2, 3.5, table 8-2 Frame Error Control Field "may be used", particularly with SEC "is used" (made mandatory by -25C) 2.2.2 Randomization Optional and managed with BCH, always with LDPC Always, with BCH and with LDPC 2.2.4, 3.4.3, note 2 to 5.2.3, table 5-1 state S3, 6.1, note 2 to 6.3.1 deleted, table 8-2 Errors allowed in the CLTU Start Sequence 0 (TED) or 1 (SEC) 1 with BCH Note 1 below table 5-2, table 8-2 Acquisition Sequence Preferred minimum 16 octets Minimum 16 octets (128 bits), alternating ones and zeros 7.2.2 Idle Sequence Unconstrained length At least 8 bits; only the maximum is unconstrained 7.2.4 Idle Sequence between CLTUs with PLOP-2 At least one octet "recommended" At least one octet mandatory, against synchronization lockout 7.5.2 Repetitions parameter of the CLTU service Optional; if above 1, no Type-BD frames Unchanged, apart from the one-frame rule Annex A3

Annex A adds the differences from ECSS-E-ST-50-04C that are not modifications: CCSDS 231.0-B-4 has LDPC codes (section 4) beside the modified BCH code, normative managed parameters (section 8) instead of informative mission configuration parameters, a formal service interface (Annex A) with the optional Repetitions parameter, and USLP support; the performance data of the 2008 Annex D now live in the Green Book CCSDS 230.1-G-3.183184 The coding details are on the CLTU page.

What the ECSS physical layer settings mean in bits (illustrative)

With the minimum values of the notice, a PLOP-2 uplink session starts with at least 128 bits of alternating ones and zeros (16 octets of acquisition), sends a CLTU holding exactly one TC frame, then at least 8 bits of idle sequence before the next CLTU. The receiver searches for the CLTU Start Sequence accepting one bit error and decodes every BCH codeblock in SEC mode.176178179181182 The bit counts are the notice's; the sequence of events is this wiki's illustration.

docs.title: ECSS-E-AS-50-25C Rev.1: TC Space Data Link Protocol
docs.text:
The notice applies CCSDS 232.0-B-4 (October 2021). Its first issue (1 March 2021), together with ECSS-E-AS-50-24C and -26C, replaced ECSS-E-ST-50-04C; Rev.1 follows the new CCSDS issue, which adds corrections and clarifications and a normative protocol implementation conformance statement (PICS) proforma.451 The TC Transfer Frame of the CCSDS book is described as similar to clauses 5 (segmentation sublayer) and 6 (transfer sublayer) of ECSS-E-ST-50-04.47

Where the PICS lives

The change log says Rev.1 adds the PICS proforma "as new normative Annex A"; Annex A of the notice itself is the informative list of differences from ECSS-E-ST-50-04C, and its clause A.2.4 explains that the normative PICS requirements list is Annex A of CCSDS 232.0-B-4.452

The modifications, clause by clause:5354555657

CCSDS clause Change Effect 4.1.1b Data field "up to 1019 or 1017 octets" becomes "up to 1017 octets" Because the FECF is always present 4.1.1c, 4.1.4.1.1 to 4.1.4.1.3 and note Frame Error Control Field becomes mandatory; the "presence established by management" and "every frame of the physical channel" rules and the related note are deleted Every ECSS TC frame ends with the 16-bit CRC 4.1.3.2.1.4 New note 2: with the Packet Assembly Controller a Frame Data Unit can be a MAP Reset command, a segment header with no user data Note 1 to 4.2.1.8.3.1, 4.2.1.8.3.2 to .4 No Bit Lock Flag no longer optional: '0' when at least one demodulator of the physical channel has bit lock, '1' when none has; always the actual status of the physical channel, even in CLCWs reporting an inactive virtual channel; the "permanently 0 if unused" rule is deleted See the CLCW 4.4.1.6, 4.4.2.5 (new) Packet extraction and MAP_SDU reception may use the Packet Assembly Controller 4.4.9 (new) The Packet Assembly Controller Function, see below ESA heritage Table 5-1 "Presence of Frame Error Control: Present, Absent" becomes "Present" Managed parameter fixed Table 5-4 Maximum Frame Data Unit length: up to 1017 (was 1019) Managed parameter narrowed 6.3.7 In a frame with SDLS the FECF always follows the Security Trailer (or the data field) SDLS interplay

A TC frame therefore has a 5-octet primary header, at most 1017 octets of data and a 2-octet FECF: 1024 octets in total at most. The arithmetic is this wiki's; the CCSDS frame format is on the TC SDLP page.

docs.title: The Packet Assembly Controller
docs.text:
The Packet Assembly Controller (PAC) is an ESA feature inherited from the PSS standards. CCSDS 232.0-B does not include it, and the 2008 handbook noted that because of it ECSS segments could be one octet long whereas CCSDS segments had at least two.58 ECSS-E-ST-50-04C had defined it in its segmentation sublayer (§5.5.4) and listed it among its differences from CCSDS.198205 The notice re-introduces it as an optional function used by the MAP Packet Extraction Function (for packets) and by the MAP Reception Function (for MAP_SDUs); despite its name it handles both.59

MAP pairs. Each PAC instance uses two MAP Identifiers: a data MAP with the most significant bit '0' (identifiers 0 to 31) and a control MAP with the same five low bits and the most significant bit '1' (identifiers 32 to 63), so control MAP = data MAP + 32. Segments carrying data use the data MAP; control segments use the control MAP.6061

A control segment is exactly one octet, has Sequence Flags '11' and the identifier of a control MAP; any valid control segment is a MAP Reset command. A Frame Data Unit on a control MAP that breaks these rules is an invalid control segment.6263

Behaviour. On the data MAP the PAC reassembles packets or MAP_SDUs using the Sequence Flags. It keeps a reassembly status flag ('1' while a reassembly is in progress, '0' when complete) and a lockout status flag ('1' in lockout). It enters lockout on an incorrect sequence of Sequence Flags or an invalid control segment; in lockout it neither reconstructs nor delivers, and it stays there until it receives a MAP Reset. A MAP Reset discards any partially reconstructed unit, clears the reassembly flag and exits lockout.64656667

stateDiagram-v2
    Idle: Idle (reassembly flag 0)
    Reassembling: Reassembling (reassembly flag 1)
    Lockout: Lockout (lockout flag 1, nothing delivered)
    Idle --> Idle: 11 no segmentation (deliver)
    Idle --> Reassembling: 01 first segment
    Reassembling --> Reassembling: 00 continuing segment
    Reassembling --> Idle: 10 last segment (deliver)
    Idle --> Lockout: 00 or 10 out of sequence
    Reassembling --> Lockout: 01 or 11 out of sequence
    Idle --> Lockout: invalid control segment
    Reassembling --> Lockout: invalid control segment
    Reassembling --> Idle: MAP Reset (discard partial unit)
    Lockout --> Idle: MAP Reset

PAC states, drawn from requirements 4.4.9.3.1 to 4.4.9.3.9. The state names and the initial state are this wiki's; the notice defines only the two flags and the lockout state.64656667

The eight incorrect transitions listed by the notice are: first followed by first or by no segmentation; continuing followed by first or by no segmentation; last followed by continuing or by last; no segmentation followed by continuing or by last.65

Status report. The PAC reports the data MAP identifier, the reassembly flag and the lockout flag to the sending end. The notice does not specify the format, the transport, or how the sending end reacts (for example by sending a MAP Reset); correct operation depends on the sending end knowing the status.67

Why keep it? The handbook gives the reasons: backward compatibility with the PSS standard and with European decoder hardware, which used the PAC for segmentation, although European missions generally did not use segmentation; it also warned that the one-octet control segment could affect interoperability, for example with SLE forward services (see FCLTU and FSP).58 The notice's own note on MAP Reset gives the operational use: recovery after breaks in the sequence of received frames caused by link problems or by an unplanned end of the transfer service.67

docs.title: Solar Orbiter: one-octet control segments in the real MIB
docs.text:
The Solar Orbiter ICD does not segment packets (Sequence Flags always '11') and uses MAP 0 for CPDU commands and MAP 1 for all other commands.68 The 2025 MIB is close to that but not identical: the 125 CPDU commands force MAP 0, 128 normal commands force MAP 1, 77 commands of APID 876 (all with "SIS_" in their descriptions) force MAP 54, and the other 5 113 normal commands leave CCF_MAPID empty; the ICD's §3.3.1 does not mention MAP 54.70 The Solar Orbiter MIB also defines a PAC reset. Command RESET ("PAC RESET directive") has CCF_CTYPE = 'R' ("Control Segment (a.k.a. Reset Map Command)" in the ICD) and the packet header NO_HDR, so its cdf entries define the frame data field directly.6970 Its layout reproduces the adoption notice exactly:

Bit Length cdf element Value Meaning 0 2 fixed area "RESET 2 Fixed Bit" 0x3 Sequence Flags '11' 2 1 fixed area "RESET 1 Fixed Bit" 0x1 Control MAP (most significant bit '1') 3 5 editable RESETMAP ("MAP ID", PTC 3 / PFC 1; default 1 from CDF_VALUE, while CPC_DEFVAL is 0) 1 Low five bits: the data MAP to reset

With the default value the octet is 0b11100001 = 0xE1, the MAP Reset for control MAP 33, that is for data MAP 1, the "Normal" MAP (the octet value is this wiki's computation from the MIB fields).7068 Fixed areas in cdf are raw hexadecimal values.71

The same MIB has two more one-octet frame data units flagged 'R': TC_ONLY ("CPDU TC_Only", 0b11000110 = MAP 6) and REIN_TTR ("Reinit TTR", 0b11000101 = MAP 5), and the two COP-1 control frames UNLOCK (one octet 0x00) and SETVR (0x8200 followed by an 8-bit V(R)) with CCF_CTYPE = 'F'.70

Inference

TC_ONLY and REIN_TTR have the most significant MAP bit '0', so they are not MAP Reset commands in the sense of the adoption notice. They look like hardware directives to the telecommand decoder or CPDU encoded as segment-header-only frame data units on MAPs 5 and 6. Their on-board meaning is not stated in the available sources.

docs.title: ECSS-E-AS-50-26C: COP-1
docs.text:
The notice applies CCSDS 232.1-B-2 (September 2010) and, together with -24C and -25C, replaces ECSS-E-ST-50-04C, whose clause 7 contained COP-1. It notes that the later CCSDS Technical Corrigendum does not affect the notice.572 It changes one thing:7374

CCSDS 232.1-B-2 §3.3.2 ECSS version A Type-BD frame accepted with no free buffer overwrites the buffer, and an optional "Aborted Indication" may be sent to the higher procedures The buffer content is erased, without the optional signal FARM-1 signals a new FDU with FDU Arrived Indication (GVCID) FDU Arrived Indication (GVCID, FDU aborted indication) (no such parameter) New rule: the FDU aborted indication is set when a Type-BD frame was accepted with no buffer available, and is otherwise not set Note 2: optional Aborted Indication, delivery not specified Note 2: when set, the indication tells the higher procedures that buffered data were erased in favour of the new Type-BD frame

Annex A records one further difference from ECSS-E-ST-50-04C that is not carried over: the old ECSS standard had requirements for a FARM-1 with a single back-end buffer per virtual channel, a case that CCSDS 232.1-B-2 does not include.75 The handbook explains why ECSS had cared: some European on-board hardware had such a FARM-1, in which a newly arrived FDU could overwrite the previous one, so the higher sublayer had to be told; users must know the FARM-1 buffering limits and on-board systems should copy delivered FDUs without delay.76 The full COP-1 machinery is on the COP-1 page.

docs.title: The superseded TM transfer frame standard: ECSS-E-ST-50-03C
docs.text: ECSS-E-ST-50-03C ("Space data links – Telemetry transfer frame protocol", 31 July 2008) defined the TM Transfer Frame as a fixed-length structure sent at a constant frame rate. It was the European counterpart of CCSDS 132.0-B-1 and is now superseded by ECSS-E-AS-50-22 (and, for AOS, -23).777849 It is still worth knowing: Solar Orbiter's frame ICD cites it,79 and it is where the ESA-specific extended virtual channel frame count was first defined in ECSS form, before ECSS-E-AS-50-22C carried it into the CCSDS frame (see above).159

docs.title: Frame and primary header
docs.text:
Field Length (bits) Presence Transfer Frame Primary Header 48 always Transfer Frame Secondary Header 16, 24, ... 512 optional Transfer Frame Data Field variable always Transfer Frame Trailer (Operational Control Field and/or Frame Error Control Field) 16, 32 or 48 optional

The frame is at most 2048 octets, constant in length within a mission phase, sent at a constant rate with the same coding options for all frames of a physical channel, and its length must agree with ECSS-E-ST-50-01 (some codes impose specific lengths). Frames with detected errors need not be delivered; their handling is specified per mission or phase. All frames on a physical channel have the same version number, and a master channel holds one to eight virtual channels.8081

Sources: §5.2.8283848586

Field Bits Values Meaning and rules Transfer Frame Version Number 0–1 0b00 TM frame (value from CCSDS 135.0-B-3) Spacecraft Identifier 2–11 assigned per CCSDS 320.0-B-4 Static in all mission phases; different identifiers may be used for development vehicles and simulated streams Virtual Channel Identifier 12–14 0–7 Frame order across VCs may vary Operational Control Field Flag 15 1 present, 0 absent Static per master or virtual channel in a phase Master Channel Frame Count 16–23 modulo 256 A reset (only at a major system reset) makes completeness undeterminable Virtual Channel Frame Count 24–31 modulo 256 Per-VC accountability; gap detection Secondary Header Flag 32 1 present Static per master or virtual channel Synchronization Flag 33 0 or 1 0: packets or idle data; 1: other data (undefined by the standard); static per VC Packet Order Flag 34 0 when Sync Flag is 0 Reserved; undefined when Sync Flag is 1 Segment Length Identifier 35–36 0b11 when Sync Flag is 0 An obsolete feature; '11' means "not used" First Header Pointer 37–47 offset, 0b11111111111 (no packet starts), 0b11111111110 (only idle data) Ignores the residue of a packet spilling in from the previous frame

docs.title: Secondary header and the extended virtual channel frame count
docs.text:
The secondary header is 2 to 64 octets, fixed-length per master or virtual channel in a phase, and consists of an 8-bit identification (2-bit version '00' and 6-bit length = total length minus one) followed by mission-defined data.8788 ECSS-E-ST-50-03C adds an optional standard use of it: a 4-octet secondary header (length field = 3) whose 24-bit data field counts the roll-overs of the 8-bit Virtual Channel Frame Count, giving a 32-bit count with the 24 most significant bits in the secondary header. The extension is associated with a master channel (present in every frame, carrying the count of the frame's own VC) or with one virtual channel.8990

The handbook explains that this is ESA PSS heritage not specified by CCSDS: it helps sequence frames, resolve ambiguities and detect losses without ground receive time, especially when recorded frames are played back through a real-time virtual channel. It is optional, does not affect frame-level interoperability (SLE RAF/RCF), and excludes any other use of the secondary header on that channel.91

Solar Orbiter uses it. Its frame ICD requires a secondary header in every frame, with identification 0b00000011 and a 3-octet data field holding an additional 24 bits of the virtual channel frame count. The same ICD fixes the frame length at 1115 octets (8920 bits), sets the Synchronization Flag to 0, the Packet Order Flag to 0, the Segment Length Identifier to '11', inserts a CLCW in the OCF of every frame and a frame error control word in every frame, and reserves VC7 for idle frames with First Header Pointer 0b11111111110.929394

docs.title: Data field, idle data and asynchronous insertion
docs.text:
With the Synchronization Flag at 0 the data field carries packets whose Packet Version Number is authorised by CCSDS 135.0-B-3. Packets are placed contiguously per virtual channel, may span frames, may have different version numbers on one VC, and idle packets (an idle Space Packet, at least 7 octets, or a fill Encapsulation Packet) or frames of only idle data fill gaps. The receiver extracts packets with the First Header Pointer and the packet length fields and discards idle data and idle packets.959697

For legacy systems that recorded whole TM frames (for example on a tape recorder), clause 5.4.4 lets recorded frames be played back inside the data field of real-time frames with the Synchronization Flag set to 1, on a dedicated virtual channel, in forward or reverse mode. In forward mode the recorded sync markers must use the alternative pattern 0x352EF853 so that they do not disturb frame synchronization; recorded CLCWs must not be processed by the real-time telecommand system.98 The handbook recommends using this only for legacy support, and notes that AOS frames handle playback with their Replay Flag instead.99100

docs.title: Operational Control Field and Frame Error Control Field
docs.text:
The OCF (4 octets, after the data field) is associated with a master or virtual channel and present in every frame of it in a phase. Bit 0 is the Type Flag: '0' means a Type-1-Report, a CLCW per ECSS-E-ST-50-04 clause 6.3; '1' means a Type-2-Report, whose bit 1 says project-specific ('0') or reserved ('1').101102 The handbook recommends using the OCF only for CLCWs.99

The 16-bit FECF follows the OCF (or the data field). It is mandatory unless the frame is Reed-Solomon encoded, present in every frame of the physical channel in a phase, and is computed as \(\text{FECF} = [X^{16} M(X) + X^{n-16} L(X)] \bmod G(X)\) with \(G(X) = X^{16}+X^{12}+X^5+1\) and the register preset to all ones; the receiver computes a syndrome that is zero for an error-free frame. It detects all odd numbers of bit errors, all patterns of up to two errors and all single bursts of up to 16 bits in blocks under 32 768 bits, and misses a random even-weight (at least 4) error pattern with probability of about \(2^{-15}\). It is never used for correction.103104105

docs.title: Annexes: PSS heritage, CCSDS differences and mission parameters
docs.text:
Annex B lists differences from ESA-PSS-04-106 (Packet Telemetry Standard, January 1988):106107

Annex C lists only two differences from CCSDS 132.0-B-1: the extended VC frame count, and ECSS not using the CCSDS name "OID Transfer Frame" for a frame whose First Header Pointer says "only idle data", because such a frame can still carry useful secondary header and OCF data.10891

Annex D lists the mission configuration parameters, which map naturally onto ground system configuration:109110111

Level Parameters Physical channel Frame length per phase; version number '00'; list of spacecraft identifiers (one per master channel); presence of FECF per phase; handling of frames with detected errors (deliver or discard); multiplexing (out of scope); idle data pattern Master channel Spacecraft identifier; up to eight VC identifiers; secondary header use and length (if associated with the master channel, not with its VCs); OCF presence Virtual channel Spacecraft and VC identifiers; secondary header use and length; Synchronization Flag; OCF presence VC with Synchronization Flag 0 Valid packet version numbers; maximum packet length; handling of incomplete packets (deliver or discard)

docs.title: The superseded telecommand standard: ECSS-E-ST-50-04C
docs.text:
ECSS-E-ST-50-04C ("Space data links – Telecommand protocols synchronization and channel coding", 31 July 2008) specified the data structures and protocols of a telecommand space data link and the physical layer operation procedures, normally from ground to space but usable space to space. Its first issue, ECSS-E-50-04A, dates from 14 November 2007; issue B was never published, and issue C made editorial changes for consistency with CCSDS and other ECSS standards.196197 Where CCSDS splits the telecommand link over three books, this one standard held all of it, which is why three adoption notices were needed to replace it:20819849

Clause of ECSS-E-ST-50-04C Content Replaced by 5 Segmentation sublayer TC Segment, transfer notification, blocking of packets, segmentation with the optional Packet Assembly Controller (5.5.4), MAP multiplexing ECSS-E-AS-50-25 (TC SDLP) 6 Transfer sublayer TC Transfer Frame, CLCW, frame header, error control, delimiting and validation procedures, virtual channel multiplexing ECSS-E-AS-50-25 7 COP-1 Internal variables, interfaces of the sending and receiving ends, control command formats, actions ECSS-E-AS-50-26 (COP-1) 8 Synchronization and channel coding sublayer BCH codeblock, CLTU, randomization, encoding, fill bits, channel logic and decoding at the receiving end ECSS-E-AS-50-24 (CLTU) 9 Physical layer Data structures and procedures, including PLOP-1 and PLOP-2 ECSS-E-AS-50-24 Annexes A to E (informative) Frame error control; changes from ESA PSS-04-107; differences from CCSDS 231.0-B-1, 232.0-B-1 and 232.1-B-1; performance issues; mission configuration parameters Notices' Annex A and the CCSDS books

Its TC Transfer Frame Primary Header is drawn below; compare the CCSDS frame on the TC SDLP page.199200201

docs.text:
Annex B lists, for checking the compatibility of existing systems, the technical differences from ESA PSS-04-107, the ESA Packet Telecommand Standard (issue 2, April 1992), which had a wider scope:202203204
