Because the old 2-bit reserved field held zeros, the standard notes that frames built to the earlier 256-octet definition are still valid under the current one.201 The PSS standard itself is now in the library as ESA PSS-04-107, whose change record says issue 2 only made editorial changes to issue 1 of June 1990; its origins are on the history page.206 Annex C lists the differences from the CCSDS books of the time (231.0-B-1, 232.0-B-1, 232.1-B-1), starting with the same two that the handbook explains below: no assumption about the sublayer below segmentation, and the optional Packet Assembly Controller.205

docs.title: The communications guidelines handbook: ECSS-E-HB-50A
docs.text: ECSS-E-HB-50A (15 November 2008) helps implementers of the E-50 series: it gives an overview of the standards and the related CCSDS books, explains how they combine, discusses questions the standards could not, and advises on options. It is informative; the standards prevail.112113 Some of its content is now historical (it describes ECSS-E-ST-50-01, -03 and -04 of 2008), but its rationale for European choices explains the adoption-notice changes above, and its recommended practices remain relevant.

docs.title: European telecommand choices and their rationale
docs.text:
The handbook lists fourteen differences between ECSS-E-ST-50-04 and the CCSDS TC books. Eleven of them survive in the adoption notices of 2021 and 2023, as the last column notes.11411511611776176177178179180181182

# ECSS-E-ST-50-04 (2008) CCSDS Rationale given 1 Does not assume the adjacent sublayer is the segmentation or transfer sublayer Assumes it Forward compatibility, easy insertion of layers such as security 2 Optional Packet Assembly Controller; minimum segment length 1 octet No PAC; minimum 2 octets Backward compatibility with PSS and European hardware (now in ECSS-E-AS-50-25C Rev.1) 3 Exactly one frame per CLTU Several allowed Fewer BCH codeblocks per CLTU, better performance; European frame delimiting hardware (now in ECSS-E-AS-50-24C Rev.1) 4 FECF always present; minimum frame 8 octets Optional; minimum 6 BCH in correction mode lacks detection power; European hardware always checks the CRC (now in ECSS-E-AS-50-25C Rev.1) 5 CLTU start sequence with one bit error always accepted Optional Fewer CLTU rejections (now in ECSS-E-AS-50-24C Rev.1) 6 Randomization always used Optional Past problems with frames of all zeros, which give codeblocks without transitions (now in ECSS-E-AS-50-24C Rev.1) 7 BCH always decoded in single error correction (SEC) SEC or triple error detection (TED) Fewer CLTU rejections (now in ECSS-E-AS-50-24C Rev.1) 8 Idle sequence of at least 8 bits between CLTUs in PLOP-2 always used Optional Avoids synchronization lockout that can lose the next frame (now in ECSS-E-AS-50-24C Rev.1) 9 Acquisition sequence at least 128 bits 128 bits preferred Adapted to transponder performance (now in ECSS-E-AS-50-24C Rev.1, as 16 octets) 10 Idle sequence at least 8 bits No minimum As 8 (now in ECSS-E-AS-50-24C Rev.1) 11 No Bit Lock Flag defined and always used Optional, mission-specific Observability; used by the PLOP carrier modulation modes (now in ECSS-E-AS-50-25C Rev.1) 12 Names TC Segment, user data unit, Segment Data Field Segment, Service Data Unit, User Data Backward compatibility and clarity 13, 14 FDU Arrived Indication always carries "FDU aborted"; single back-end buffer FARM-1 procedures Optional parameter; case not considered European hardware with single-buffer FARM-1 (the first now in ECSS-E-AS-50-26C)

docs.title: Recommended practice
docs.text:
Telecommand.118119

  • Use the sequence-controlled service for MAPs that use segmentation, because Sequence Flags have no counter and reassembly needs complete, ordered delivery.
  • Assign TC virtual channel identifiers with maximum Hamming distance between them, so that a bit error in an on-board CLCW does not turn one VC into another, and avoid identifiers of all zeros or all ones, which a failed or unpowered decoder can produce.
  • The No RF Available and No Bit Lock flags report the physical channel as a whole, not a single decoder; the CLCW VC field carries the full 6-bit identifier.
  • Near-Earth missions should use the COP-1 sequence-controlled (AD) service and keep the expedited (BD) service for exceptional cases such as recovery; COP-1 retransmission is less efficient for deep space, where an additional mechanism was being studied in 2008.
  • Prefer PLOP-2 to PLOP-1 for its higher throughput.
  • There is no ECSS telecommand decoder specification; the withdrawn ESA PSS-04-151 contained important information, and the PUS has an annex on the CPDU and its interaction with PSS decoders. The PSS specification, issue 1 of September 1992, is now in the library as ESA PSS-04-151.207

The transponder "dual lock" issue. Near-Earth and Lagrange-point spacecraft such as Cryosat-2 combine the uplink from both low-gain antennas with a 3 dB hybrid so that both transponders see the best signal. Without such care, one receiver can run near its threshold (the handbook quotes about −122 dBm) with a poor bit error rate while the other is well above it; the decoder may then select the poor channel and reject telecommands. The handbook recommends the AD service for all near-Earth missions, a realistic pre-launch compatibility test with representative ground station and control system, and mission-specific tuning of COP-1 parameters to the Earth–spacecraft distance.120121 ECSS-E-ST-50C Rev.1 turned the lesson into requirement 5.4.9a.29

Telemetry.99122

  • Use the OCF only for the CLCW; use asynchronously inserted data only for legacy support.
  • Use virtual channels to separate sources with different characteristics (for example an imager with very long packets on its own VC) or different destinations.
  • Choose the maximum packet length with latency in mind: while a long packet is sent, other sources on the VC wait.
  • Do not feed frames with uncorrectable errors to packet extraction, and signal a gap whenever a frame is missing or erroneous, detected with the master, virtual and extended counts.

Channel coding. For telecommand ECSS-E-ST-50-04 left no coding options. For telemetry the handbook tabulates coding gain against bandwidth expansion (frame length 8920 bits, AWGN, BPSK), from Reed-Solomon (255,223) alone (bandwidth ×1.14, about 5.4 dB gain at FER \(10^{-4}\)) through concatenated Reed-Solomon and convolutional codes to turbo rate ¼ (×4, about 11.7 dB). It advises trading coding gain against bandwidth limits, link budget and decoder complexity, noting for example that turbo rate ½ gains about 5 dB over convolutional rate ½ at the same bandwidth but was hard to decode in real time above about 20 Mbit/s.123124 Details are on the TM coding page.

Idle data. TM and AOS channels are synchronous and must fill every frame slot; TC and Proximity-1 are asynchronous and need no idle data in frames (PLOP-2 sends an idle sequence between CLTUs instead). Idle patterns are project-specific; all-zero or periodic patterns can upset bit synchronization, so projects without randomization must choose carefully.125126

TM frame Sync Flag First Header Pointer Data field Only idle data 0 2046 (0b11111111110) Only idle data, pattern a mission parameter; other fields still carry data Packets 0 any other value Packets, possibly idle packets Other data 1 undefined Not specified

Source: handbook table 5-3.125

Packet utilization. The handbook treats ECSS-E-ST-70-41 only where it touches the E-50 protocols: the PUS (issue A at the time) used the older names "telemetry source packet", "telecommand packet" and "data field header"; it reserves APID 2047 for idle packets and APID 0 for the time packet, while CCSDS 135.0-B reserves 2047, 2045–2046 and 2040–2044; and it makes the 16-bit Packet Error Control mandatory on telecommand packets and fixed per APID on telemetry.127128 Solar Orbiter's MIB follows the PUS reservations: the time report TM(9,2) is on APID 0 and the idle packet on APID 2047.129

Security, interoperability and conformance. In 2008 neither ECSS nor CCSDS specified security methods for these protocols; the handbook pointed to CCSDS 350.0-G.130 Today ECSS-E-ST-50C (Rev.1 and Rev.2) points to the SDLS option in the adoption notices, and ECSS-E-AS-50-22C and -23C Rev.1 also open the SDLS Extended Procedures of CCSDS 355.1-B-1 to TM and AOS frames; the CCSDS security books are summarised on the Security page.28155165 Cross support needs agreement on service, physical, communications and enterprise aspects, not just protocols; SLE had largely solved ground-station cross support (the architecture is on cross support reference model and service management), while space-to-space cross support still had to be negotiated case by case.131 Draft PICS proformas for ECSS-E-ST-50-01, -03 and -04 (sending and receiving ends) fill Annexes A to F; a PICS records which options an implementation supports and lets incompatible implementations be spotted early.132

docs.title: Which standard for which link
docs.text: The handbook closes with applicability tables. In short: ECSS-E-ST-50, CCSDS 320.0-B (spacecraft identifiers), CCSDS 135.0-B (space link identifiers), ECSS-E-ST-50-05 and CCSDS 301.0-B (time codes) apply to all missions; the TM frame standard to return links except where AOS applies; AOS to return links with very large data volumes per contact; Proximity-1 to lander–orbiter links; ECSS-E-ST-70-41 to all ESA missions; CFDP to file transfer and reliable return links.133134 It also notes that AOS is sometimes chosen for high-rate downlinks where TM frame counters would roll over during a pass, after the ISS-driven ambitions for symmetric high-rate links faded.135 The identifier books are covered on Space link identifiers: the library holds CCSDS 320.0-M-7 (November 2017), which turned the spacecraft identifier procedures from a Blue Book into a Magenta Book Recommended Practice, and the Space Link Identifiers book 135.0-B-4 (October 2009), whose copy is stamped "Historical".187188 Proximity-1 has its own page.

How some ECSS-E-ST-50C requirements are met by the adoption notices and show up in the Solar Orbiter MIB. The links are this wiki's synthesis of the sources cited above.

SQL used

All queries ran with sqlite3 -readonly on solo-2025-09-16.sqlite (release MIB__20250916M25925PFMS001_SOL).

-- frame-level commands: control segments ('R'), control frames ('F'), NIS throw events ('N')
SELECT CCF_CNAME, CCF_DESCR, CCF_CTYPE, CCF_PKTID, CCF_HIPRI, CCF_MAPID
  FROM ccf WHERE CCF_CTYPE IN ('R','F','S','T','N');
-- their frame data field layout
SELECT * FROM cdf WHERE CDF_CNAME IN ('RESET','TC_ONLY','REIN_TTR','SETVR','UNLOCK')
  ORDER BY CDF_CNAME, cast(CDF_BIT AS int);
SELECT * FROM cpc WHERE CPC_NAME IN ('RESETMAP','VR');
SELECT * FROM tcp;
-- high-priority commands and their MAP
SELECT CCF_HIPRI, CCF_MAPID, CCF_PKTID, count(*) FROM ccf GROUP BY 1, 2, 3;
SELECT CCF_APID, count(*), sum(instr(CCF_DESCR, 'SIS_') > 0) FROM ccf
  WHERE CCF_MAPID = '54' GROUP BY 1;
-- reserved APIDs in use
SELECT PID_TYPE, PID_STYPE, PID_APID, PID_SPID, PID_DESCR FROM pid WHERE PID_APID IN (0, 2047);

docs.title: ECSS-E-ST-70-01C: on-board control procedures
docs.text:
ECSS-E-ST-70-01C ("Space engineering – Spacecraft on-board control procedures", 16 April 2010) standardises the on-board control procedure (OBCP): a program, executed by an interpreter in the on-board software called the OBCP engine, that can be loaded, run and replaced on board without changing the rest of the on-board software (OBSW).12 The standard defines the whole OBCP system: the on-board functions that execute OBCPs, the ground functions that prepare and control them, and the development lifecycle of OBCPs and its relation to the spacecraft and OBSW lifecycles.3

It sits between two other standards. It assumes that the mission also complies with the PUS (ECSS-E-70-41), because several PUS services are invoked to operate OBCPs and to interact with the ground; OBCP operations themselves are initiated with telecommands of the PUS on-board operations procedure service, ST[18].31 It also says it conforms with and extends ECSS-E-ST-70-31, whose data model already knows on-board procedures as a kind of activity.466 PUS-C, in turn, declares its ST[18] to be compliant with and complementary to ECSS-E-ST-70-01.57

At a glance

Item Value Issues ECSS-E-ST-70-01A and B never issued; ECSS-E-ST-70-01C is the first issue (16 April 2010)5 Status (ECSS tree, October 2025) Published; no update shown as ongoing or planned6 Normative references ECSS-S-ST-00-01, ECSS-E-ST-40 (software), ECSS-E-ST-70, ECSS-E-ST-70-31, ECSS-E-70-417 Structure Clause 4 concept; clause 5 capabilities (structure, language, preparation, execution); clause 6 engineering processes8 Two kinds of OBCP On-board application procedure (OBAP), part of the spacecraft design; on-board operations procedure (OBOP), used to operate it16 OBCP states in store (on ground or on board); in engine: inactive, or active (running or held)35 Ground control ECSS-E-70-41 service 18; memory management only for anomaly investigation33 ESA usage ESA's generic operations interface requirements (2019) do not tailor the standard71

docs.title: Why a standard for OBCPs
docs.text:
The introduction notes that OBCPs had been implemented ad hoc on several European missions over about 25 years, which had proved the concept. The standard wants one OBCP concept for any mission that meets the needs of all users (system, on-board software, AIT and operations engineers), gives OBCPs a development lifecycle independent of the rest of the OBSW, and conforms with and extends ECSS-E-70-41 and ECSS-E-ST-70-31.4

The earlier mission documents in this wiki's library show what that ad-hoc state looked like. The Herschel/Planck operations interface requirements of 2003 required that OBCPs be controllable from any command source, access telemetry, issue telecommands and event packets, evaluate simple arithmetic and control structures, run several at once without interference, and be prepared with a simple language and test tools usable by operations engineers rather than software experts; the procedures were to be written in a "Spacecraft Control Language" running in the central data management system.7273

docs.title: Terms
docs.text:
Term (§3.2) Definition (paraphrased) automation Replacing manual operations by computerised mechanisms on-board control procedure (OBCP) A program designed to be executed by an OBCP engine that can easily be loaded, executed and replaced on board; depending on context, the source or the OBCP code OBCP code The complete loadable form of an OBCP, called token code, executable code or bytecode on earlier missions, and "procedure code" in service 18 of ECSS-E-70-41A OBCP engine The OBSW application that handles the execution of OBCPs; OBCP operations are initiated with service 18 telecommands OBCP language The programming language in which humans write OBCP source code OBCP system The whole machinery for creating OBCPs on the ground, uplinking them and handling them on board OBCP step A sequence of source statements forming the smallest operational unit within an OBCP on-board software Software hosted and executed by any programmable on-board computer or processor scheduling Allocating OBSW processor time to OBSW functions (including the engine and OBCPs) by a predefined algorithm survival mode A configuration in which the spacecraft can remain safely without ground intervention for a specified period (also called safe mode)

Source: §3.2.1 Terms such as activity, event, event reporting service, on-board parameter and operations procedure come from ECSS-E-ST-70, ECSS-E-ST-70-31 and ECSS-E-70-41.9 Abbreviations introduced include OBAP (on-board application procedure), OBOP (on-board operations procedure), OBCP, OBSW, CPDU (command pulse distribution unit) and SDE (software development environment).10

docs.title: Stakeholders and domains
docs.text:
Four stakeholder groups use OBCPs - system engineers (spacecraft and payload), on-board software engineers, AIT engineers and operations engineers - and they cooperate throughout the lifecycle; responsibility for the system or software may pass from the prime contractor to the operations organisation some time after launch. The standard therefore classifies OBCP uses by domain rather than by stakeholder:11

Domain Typical uses named by the standard System design (§4.2.2.1) Isolate mission-specific platform functions (thermal or battery control) from the OBSW; one-shot applications deleted after use (deployments, pyrotechnics); a detailed FDIR strategy that is defined late and tuned in system testing (the standard stresses it does not encourage late FDIR definition); equipment delivered late, added, removed or replaced; tuning of configuration sequences of complex equipment; late definition of payload control sequences, monitoring algorithms and recovery actions OBSW design and development (§4.2.2.2) Easier development and validation than OBSW; a more generic, reusable core OBSW; simpler maintenance; OBSW engineers' own test automation, debugging and short-term workarounds AIT (§4.2.2.3) On-ground only: fault injection for robustness tests, long repetitive configuration sequences, temporary test functions Operations and operability (§4.2.2.4) Routine and contingency procedures run on board instead of on the ground: less bandwidth, possibly fewer staff, no ground loop delay, simpler ground procedures, more reliability and autonomy, robustness to station outages (for GEO as well as LEO and deep space); counter unforeseen failures, unpredictable deep-space environments, end-of-life operations such as de-orbiting

Sources: §4.2.2.12131415

docs.title: OBAP and OBOP
docs.text:
From these uses the standard derives two types of OBCP:16

On-board application procedure (OBAP) On-board operations procedure (OBOP) Purpose Implements part of the basic functionality of the spacecraft; an integral part of its design Used to operate the spacecraft Historical name "Application Program", "Flight Application Program" – Qualification Spacecraft qualification needs the complete set of OBAPs (they may still be updated after launch) Not involved in spacecraft qualification Lifecycle Tied to the spacecraft system and the related subsystem or payload, with their engineering processes and reviews Akin to a ground operations procedure; fully decoupled, can be defined after launch without system delta-qualification On-board accommodation Defined rules and a priority scheme for concurrent OBAPs; may request on-board activities not accessible from the ground (for example low-level bus access) Resources independent of the OBAPs and of the number of running OBOPs; the standard's example limits OBOPs to activities accessible from the ground

Sources: §4.3, §5.2.9.2l, §5.4.4.2, §5.4.4.5 and §6.1.1626394246 Both may use the same on-board capabilities and be equally complex; what differs is how they are accommodated and engineered.16

docs.title: The OBCP system
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  subgraph PREP["OBCP preparation environment (ground)"]
    ED["Editors"] --> CHK["Syntax, consistency,<br/>dependency, constraint checks"]
    CHK --> GEN["OBCP code production"]
    VAL["Validation tools<br/>(e.g. simulation)"]
  end
  EDR[("Engineering data repository<br/>system elements, activities (incl. OBCPs),<br/>reporting data, events")]
  GEN --> EDR
  EDR --> CHK
  subgraph EXEC["OBCP execution environment"]
    subgraph GND["Ground part (MCS, EGSE, SDE)"]
      UPL["Uplink, monitoring and control"]
      VIS["Visualisation of the<br/>on-board environment"]
    end
    subgraph OB["On-board part"]
      ST[("OBCP store(s)<br/>optional")] --> ENG["OBCP engine(s)"]
      ENG --> SYS["OBSW, platform, payloads"]
    end
    UPL -- "TC service 18" --> ENG
  end
  EDR --> UPL

The OBCP system, after Figure 4-1 and §4.4.17

The preparation environment belongs to the overall test and operations preparation environment: editors, execution-constraint checks (resource use), consistency checks against the telemetry and telecommand database, configuration management, OBCP code production and validation tools such as a simulator. The standard makes no assumption about whether the OBCP script and the OBCP code are the same thing or whether the script is compiled or turned into pseudo-code.17 All OBCPs are kept in the engineering data repository of ECSS-E-ST-10, whose monitoring and control part (ECSS-E-ST-70-31) holds system elements, activities (telecommands, ground procedures, OBCPs), reporting data and events; its configuration management covers OBCPs.18

The execution environment has a ground part (uplink, monitoring and control services, a view of the on-board environment, constraint and consistency checks) and an on-board part: one or more OBCP engines that offer monitoring and control services towards ground and on-board services, standard services towards the OBSW, platform and payloads, and manage execution, plus optional on-board OBCP stores where OBCPs wait before being loaded. How OBCPs reach a store and how stores are managed is out of scope. Engine and preparation environment are designed together, the split of functions between them may vary, and multiple engines are assumed independent.18

docs.title: OBCP structure (§5.1)
docs.text:
Req. Requirement a Each OBCP has a unique OBCP identifier, assigned by the ground system b Arguments can be defined (values input at initiation); their definition (type, default, range) is in ECSS-E-ST-70-31 §6.7.1.2 c Elements: optional declaration body (declares and initialises variables, declares local functions); optional preconditions body; mandatory main body; optional confirmation body; optional contingency handling body d Nominal execution order: declaration, preconditions, main, confirmation e, f A step construct identifies a block of functionally self-contained statements; steps are unique within an OBCP g, h The confirmation body's result gives the engine the OBCP confirmation status; without it the engine sets an implicit status (for example "success" if all initiated activities succeeded and no exception occurred) i, j A local function construct encapsulates statements with input and output parameters and can be called from anywhere in the OBCP

Source: §5.1.19

flowchart TB
  A(["Activation with arguments"]) --> D["Declaration body<br/>variables (initialised), local functions"]
  D --> P["Preconditions body"]
  P --> M["Main body<br/>steps (unique IDs)"]
  M --> C["Confirmation body<br/>→ confirmation status"]
  M -. "conditions or events" .-> X["Contingency handling body"]
  M -. "call" .-> F["Local functions"]

Elements of an OBCP and their nominal order (§5.1c and d); the dotted paths are not ordered by the standard.19

Compared with the ground language PLUTO (ECSS-E-ST-70-32C), the same four bodies appear, but the watchdog body becomes a contingency handling body, variables are declared and initialised at procedure level rather than per step, and local functions are added.1955

docs.title: OBCP language capabilities (§5.2)
docs.text:
The language lets the user write the OBCP script referring to system elements, activities, reporting data and events fully defined in the engineering data repository.20

Clause Capability (each a "shall" unless noted) 5.2.2 General Syntax formally specified (for example ISO EBNF, ISO/IEC 14977); a comment possible on every source line 5.2.3 Data types The simple data types of ECSS-E-ST-70-31 §5.5; structured types (arrays, records); explicit type casting (implicit conversions not excluded) 5.2.4 Declarations Variables of any type with initial values; constants of any type with values; local functions, unique within the OBCP 5.2.5 Assignments Assign to variables; a variable declared in the declaration body is visible everywhere, including in local functions 5.2.6 Expressions Mathematical, time, string and bitwise operations and functions; array manipulation; expressions over constants, on-board parameters, activity arguments and variables; constants with engineering units, free mixing and automatic conversion of compatible units; parameters referred to by repository name, valued in engineering units or in the raw downlinked form; events and their parameters by repository name 5.2.7 Flow controls If-then-else; multi-way branch on a parameter or variable; loops (count, while, until); nesting 5.2.8 Waits In the main body: until an on-board time, for an interval, until a condition, until an event, until any event from a list; combined conditions; preconditions and confirmations combine the same waits with a condition test; timeouts with defined behaviour 5.2.9.1 Parameters Read any on-board parameter including on-board time; set specific on-board parameters (housekeeping values, values kept between runs, inputs to on-board monitoring) 5.2.9.2 Activities Refer to activities and arguments by repository name; request any on-board activity accessible from the ground unless excluded (for example CPDU commands); choose per activity the verification stages to report; read execution and confirmation status and initiation, start, termination or completion time; initiate and continue (several activities in parallel), initiate and wait for a status, initiate without waiting for completion; an OBCP does not complete while requested verification reporting is outstanding; timeouts on verification waits; an OBAP may request on-board activities not accessible from the ground (for example low-level bus access) 5.2.9.3 Events Raise events with parameters - only existing system events, never new ones; access events raised on board and their parameters 5.2.10 Contingency handling One or more contingency routines triggered by conditions or events (for example a resource exceeded, a parameter out of limits)

Sources: §5.2.2 to §5.2.10.222324252627

Inference

Several capabilities differ from the ground language PLUTO in ways that reflect the on-board setting: raw-value access, bitwise operations, explicit type casts and a "wait for any of these events" construct are added, while PLUTO's user interaction (ask user, inform user) has no on-board counterpart and events cannot be invented by the OBCP. The standard does not define an OBCP language itself, only its required capabilities.2156

docs.title: The preparation environment (§5.3)
docs.text:
Clause Requirement 5.3.1 Script preparation A read-write editor and a read-only viewer; collapse and expand globally or per step; full integration with the engineering data repository, populating OBCPs from context-sensitive menus (for example only objects of the OBCP's parent system element); override of repository defaults (for example a different activity verification profile) 5.3.2 Checking A syntax analyser and consistency, dependency and constraint checker reporting on grammar compliance, consistency with the current repository, inter-OBCP dependencies (execution calls) and constraints: available engine services, memory, maximum code size, CPU use, maximum frequency of parameter sampling or activity invocation; constraints may differ for all OBCPs, OBOPs, OBAPs, sets of them, or per engine 5.3.3 Reports Per OBCP: referenced repository objects (activities including OBCPs, parameters, events), CPU and memory consumption, prerequisites for execution, script quality measures (nesting, loops, ECSS-Q-ST-80 measures); and an activity call tree of all OBCPs 5.3.4 Verification and validation A debugger (should): step-by-step and statement-by-statement execution; step over, into and out of; forced execution paths; setting and viewing internal and external data; event stimulation; simulated activities and responses; simulated interactions with the execution environment (suspend, resume); breakpoints that store all context. A flight-representative V&V environment (shall), with higher fidelity possibly needed for OBAPs (hardware in the loop); test coverage tools for code, branch and decision coverage, identifying missing coverage 5.3.5 Characterisation Static and dynamic memory needs predictable at preparation time (static split between mass memory and local RAM; dynamic including stacks and their persistence); an upper bound of execution duration predictable; the engine provides observability of run-time events and data (for example branching events), with definable and selectable observability levels

Sources: §5.3.2829303132

docs.title: Ground capabilities
docs.text: Before acting on OBCPs, the ground system must check that the requested state transition is allowed (for example "activate" only for a loaded, non-active OBCP), that interdependencies hold (OBCPs that an activated OBCP can call are loaded or scheduled for loading in time), and that resources allocated separately to OBAPs and OBOPs are respected (number of OBCPs loaded or active, CPU, memory). OBCPs are uplinked by telecommand as OBCP code for the target engine. Ground control protocols are based on the ECSS-E-70-41 on-board operations procedure service; the memory management service is reserved for anomaly investigations and for cases where on-board failures prevent the use of other services.33

docs.title: States and operations
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
  state "In store" as Store {
    state "On ground" as OnGround
    state "On board" as OnBoard
    [*] --> OnGround
    OnGround --> OnBoard
    OnBoard --> OnGround
  }
  state "In engine: inactive" as Inactive
  state "In engine: active, running" as Running
  state "In engine: active, held" as Held
  [*] --> Store
  Store --> Inactive: Load (18,1)
  Inactive --> Store: Delete (18,2)

  Running --> Held: Suspend (18,5)
  Held --> Running: Resume (18,6)
  Running --> Inactive: Completion / Stop (18,4) / Abort (18,12)
  Held --> Inactive: Stop (18,4) / Abort (18,12)

OBCP state diagram after Figure 5-1 and §5.4.2.2; numbers are the ECSS-E-70-41 service 18 subtypes that the standard's notes give for each operation. The standard does not prescribe how on-board stores are implemented.343536

The OBCP states are in store (executable form, on board or on the ground) and in engine (in memory the engine can access), the latter either inactive (idle) or active (under engine control), active being running or held.35 The engine performs eight operations, on request by telecommand from the ground or from on-board processes:36

Operation (§5.4.2.3) Transition Service 18 subtype named by the standard PUS-C (ECSS-E-ST-70-41C) counterpart Load in store → inactive 1 TC[18,1] direct-load an OBCP; TC[18,13] load an OBCP by reference; TC[18,19] load by reference and activate an OBCP Activate inactive → running 3 TC[18,3] activate an OBCP; TC[18,14] activate and execute one OBCP step Communicate parameters (active) 7 TC[18,7] communicate parameters to an OBCP Suspend (at end of current statement or of a given step) running → held 5 TC[18,5] suspend an OBCP Resume (from where it was suspended) held → running 6 TC[18,6] resume an OBCP; TC[18,15] resume and execute one OBCP step Stop (at end of current statement or of a given step, or a held OBCP; cannot be resumed) active → inactive 4 TC[18,4] stop an OBCP; TC[18,20] stop and unload an OBCP Abort (immediately) active → inactive 12 TC[18,12] abort an OBCP; TC[18,17] abort all OBCPs and report Delete inactive → in store 2 TC[18,2] unload an OBCP

Sources: §5.4.2.3 of ECSS-E-ST-70-01C and the PUS-C message types of §6.18.4.3664 The subtypes named in the 2010 standard are those of the PUS-A service of 2003, where 1 to 6 and 12 form the minimum capability set and 7 is optional.65 Further rules:36

  • A request inconsistent with the OBCP's state (for example activating an active OBCP) fails with a telecommand verification failure.
  • An OBCP returns autonomously to "inactive" at the end of execution (transition "Completion").
  • The Activate request carries the parameters to pass to the OBCP.
  • A loaded OBCP stays available for reactivation until deleted from the engine.
  • Requests from the ground are reported to their source with telecommand verification reports; requests from on board are reported to the ground with event reports giving the requesting source (an OBSW application or another OBCP), the OBCP identifier and the execution status of the operation.
  • Run-time errors found by the engine are reported with event reports.

docs.title: Integrity
docs.text: A checksum, generated on the ground by the translation process that produced the code from the source, is loaded with every OBCP. It lets the code be verified independently of any uplink protocol protection. The engine verifies it at load time, fails the Load request with a telecommand verification failure if it does not match, and verifies it again whenever the ground asks.37

docs.title: On-board capabilities
docs.text:
Clause Requirement 5.4.4.1 General At most one OBCP engine per on-board application process; the scheduling policy, static and dynamic memory allocation, garbage collection policy, and their observability and controllability from ground are defined 5.4.4.2 Engine services All services needed for the language capabilities (possibly different for OBOPs and OBAPs, for example OBOPs restricted to ground-accessible activities); a global function service of standard functions callable from any OBCP (managed by implementation-dependent means such as patches or extra service 18 subtypes); defined behaviour on a reset or discontinuity of the reference clock used by waits 5.4.4.3 Engine monitoring For each OBCP in the engine: execution status, the step being executed when running, the next step when suspended (reporting configured with ECSS-E-70-41 service 3); engine housekeeping such as free memory, CPU time and I/O slots used; operationally significant events through the event reporting service; detailed data for anomaly investigation (memory management, call stack contents) 5.4.4.4 Loading policy Defined, when OBCPs can sit in more than one store: precedence rules that select the store from which a Load takes the code (for example local RAM, then platform mass memory, then EEPROM); whether the policy is reprogrammable; how resets, reboots, processor switch-over or power loss affect it; definable per OBCP 5.4.4.5 Scheduling A defined OBSW scheduling policy for the engine; a guaranteed minimum processor time over regular intervals (fixed slots, pre-emptive priority scheduling, or a dedicated co-processor are examples); several OBCPs in parallel; OBOP resources independent of OBAP resources; specified maximum numbers of loaded and of active OBOPs; an OBOP's resources independent of how many OBOPs run, so that its designer need not consider the others; defined allocation rules and a priority scheme for concurrent OBAPs 5.4.4.6 Isolation Internal faults do not propagate to the OBSW (CPU and memory faults, engine faults; a wrong value written to a parameter is excluded); the engine never exceeds its allocation; loading and controlling one OBCP does not disturb active ones; OBCPs are isolated from each other and from unauthorised memory 5.4.4.7 Exceptions Every OBCP-internal error (overflow, divide by zero, array bounds) is caught by an OBCP exception handler or by the engine; unhandled errors abort the OBCP; an anomaly event goes to ground for any internal error; a run-time error in an exception handler terminates the OBCP at once; actions are defined for when the engine can no longer support running OBCPs (for example an engine event caught by contingency handlers that set controlled devices to a default state, suspension of all OBCPs, a report to ground) 5.4.4.8 Continuity of service A defined concept, possibly preserving OBCP state in non-volatile memory; a list of OBCPs automatically loaded and activated at engine initialisation (from engine start-up until it accepts an external command)

Sources: §5.4.4.1 to §5.4.4.8.3839404142434445

docs.title: Lifecycles
docs.text:
The concept decouples OBCP development from the spacecraft lifecycle to different degrees: the OBOP lifecycle is fully decoupled from the system and the OBSW (OBOPs can be defined after launch without delta-qualification), while the OBAP lifecycle is only partly decoupled from the OBSW and stays tied to system development (OBAPs are qualified with the system). The engineering process an OBCP needs depends on how well the OBCP system protects the rest of the system against functional and software failures caused by an OBCP, and on quality and risk considerations; "critical" OBCPs deserve special attention to margins and impact.46

Lifecycle line (Figure 6-1) Phases covered Spacecraft A, B (preliminary definition), C (detailed definition), D (qualification and production), E (utilisation), F (disposal) OBSW Prototyping, development, operation and maintenance OBCP software engineering Prototyping, development, operation and maintenance System OBCPs and AIT OBCPs Developed within phases C to D Operations and operability OBOPs From phase D through the end of phase F

Source: Figure 6-1, as read from the drawing.47

docs.title: Management process
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  subgraph N["Collect needs"]
    N1["System design"]
    N2["OBSW"]
    N3["AIT"]
    N4["Operations / operability"]
  end
  N1 & N2 & N3 & N4 --> T["Trade-offs<br/>OBAP vs OBSW<br/>OBOP vs ground procedure<br/>engine capability vs engineering effort"]
  T --> CAP["Capabilities and requirements<br/>engine; preparation and ground execution<br/>environments; engineering processes"]
  T --> SET["Sets of OBCPs (OBAPs, OBOPs)"]
  T --> OBSW["OBSW"]
  T --> OPS["Operations procedures"]

OBCP management overview, after Figure 6-2.48

The OBCP system management process is defined and documented and covers: collecting needs from all stakeholders, the OBSW-versus-OBAP trade-off, and the analysis of future OBOP use cases and engineering-effort benefits leading to requirements on board and on ground. Its output consolidates the required capabilities of the engine, the preparation environment, the ground execution environment and the engineering processes; every requirement traces to one of these four. The output is reviewed at the system requirements review (SRR); engine and preparation environment capabilities are frozen at the software PDR; budgets (OBCPs in parallel, activities invoked by an OBCP) are managed at system level and reviewed at system and OBSW reviews; and OBAP verification and validation is completed before system qualification.48 Figure 6-3 aligns these milestones: the preparation environment becomes available early in the system lifecycle, the OBSW reviews (SRR, PDR, DDR, TRR, CDR, QR) and the OBAP reviews (SRR, PDR, CDR, QR) follow the system ones, and OBAP qualification feeds the system QR (as read from the drawing).49

docs.title: Trade-offs
docs.text:
OBAP vs OBSW (§6.2.2)OBOP vs ground procedure (§6.2.3) In favour of OBAPs In favour of OBSW Variability and flexibility (changing requirements, ageing) Real-time capabilities; execution time (technology-dependent) Programmatic reasons: late definition, reuse (but late selection concentrates validation in a short, critical period) Complex functions, suited to software engineering processes Core system management functions with stable requirements close to subsystem engineering (for example AOCS) Functions that sustain survival modes, which must be fully validated by the end of development Generic parts of a system or product line (for example components supporting ECSS-E-70-41 services); lower schedule risk through early definition In favour of OBOPs In favour of ground procedures Operations during non-visibility or with long signal delays Human response to unforeseen scenarios Safer operations if ground control is lost Less capability and less validation needed on board Fewer operator errors Less engineering effort to develop, validate and update Synchronisation with asynchronous on-board events Simpler configuration management "Coded and up-linked once, used many times" Better overall visibility of operations Atomic operations combined into one block (critical activities) Less need for round-the-clock staff in routine phases

Sources: §6.2.2 and §6.2.3 (the criteria are notes, the trade-offs and their documentation are requirements).5051 The engine itself is traded against engineering effort (§6.2.4): isolation may be relaxed for OBAPs to simplify the engine, at the price of more validation, while for OBOPs a higher level of isolation is mandatory.52

docs.title: Organisation and engineering
docs.text: All stakeholders, their organisation, responsibilities and interactions are identified; each category of stakeholder develops and validates its own OBCPs (OBAPs needing close collaboration of all parties). OBOP execution decisions are approved by one single authority, which checks for example that the maximum number of running OBOPs is not exceeded and that no two OBOPs use the same hardware at once; OBOPs may still be split into sets developed by different teams. Resource allocation between stakeholders follows defined policies (a maximum number of OBOPs per stakeholder, CPU and memory for OBAPs) enforced throughout the project.53 OBAPs follow the software lifecycle of ECSS-E-ST-40 (tailored with adequate documentation and reviews, strict configuration control and adequate validation); OBOPs follow the operations procedure process of ECSS-E-ST-70 (tailored with timely feedback from operations engineers, concurrent documentation maintenance and strict configuration control by developers and test engineers).54

docs.title: How the standard connects to the others
docs.text:
flowchart TB
  E70["ECSS-E-ST-70C<br/>OBCPs are mission operations data;<br/>CFISRD lists them as deliverables"] --> E01["ECSS-E-ST-70-01C<br/>OBCP system"]
  E11["ECSS-E-ST-70-11C Rev.1 §5.8.9<br/>operability: load, parallel, any TC,<br/>any TM, priorities"] --> E01
  E31["ECSS-E-ST-70-31C<br/>onboard procedure activity:<br/>script, preloaded flag, priority"] --> E01
  E01 -- "ground control protocol" --> PUS["ECSS-E-ST-70-41C ST[18]<br/>OBCP management and engine management"]
  E01 -.->|"similar structure"| E32["ECSS-E-ST-70-32C PLUTO<br/>(ground procedures)"]

The OBCP standard among the E-70 standards; arrows show which document places requirements on or supplies data to which.6869676657

  • ECSS-E-ST-70-41C (PUS-C). ST[18] is declared compliant with and complementary to the OBCP standard. Each ECSS-E-ST-70-01 step is represented in the OBCP code by exactly one step identifier; OBCP arguments (values at initiation) and parameters (values during execution) refer to ECSS-E-ST-70-31 and are checked by the OBCP itself, not by the service.5758 One OBCP engine per service and at most one OBCP management subservice per application process echo §5.4.4.1a; the OBCP identifier note points back to requirement 5.1a; loading by reference uses the loading policy of §5.4.4.4a to c; whether the code checksum is verified is a declared option.596063 PUS-C turns the "levels of observability" of §5.3.5.3 into four declared levels - no observability, at procedure level, at step level and at detailed level - reported as events through ST[05], and the states into "inactive", "active and running" and "active and held" (waiting for an event counts as running).6162 PUS-C has no "in store" state: an OBCP is either loaded in the engine or not, and an OBCP loaded by reference comes from an on-board file.63 The full service is described on the ST[18] page.
  • ECSS-E-ST-70-31C. An activity of type "onboard procedure" has a script compliant with ECSS-E-ST-70-01, a "preloaded on board" flag and a priority (high, medium or low) used by the on-board execution system in scheduling conflicts.66
  • ECSS-E-ST-70-11C Rev.1. The operability standard requires that the spacecraft can execute ground-loaded and controlled OBCPs, several at once, that OBCPs can send any command available to the ground and read any engineering telemetry parameter available to it, and that OBCP execution can be prioritised (for example in favour of fault management).67
  • ECSS-E-ST-70C. OBCPs are part of the mission-specific data that populates the monitoring and control databases, and the customer furnished items include "other databases for in-flight operations" such as OBCPs; the OBCP standard in turn requires OBOPs to follow the ECSS-E-ST-70 operations procedure process.686954
  • Generic OIRD. ESA's generic operations interface requirements document (released July 2019) is split into on-board functional requirements based on ECSS-E-ST-70-11C and PUS-C requirements covering ECSS-E-ST-70-41C and ECSS-E-ST-70-01C. It applies no tailoring to the OBCP standard, which it judges to satisfy most ESA needs, and adds a few requirements to its service 18 instead.7071

docs.title: Solar Orbiter: an OBCP system in flight
docs.text:
Solar Orbiter's TM/TC and packet structure ICD describes an OBCP as an interpretable program compiled on the ground with a dedicated compiler and uploaded with service 13 into one of the on-board file partitions; OBCPs are mainly controlled from the ground through service 18 but can also start autonomously, for example on an on-board event.74 The ICD's description lines up with the standard:

ECSS-E-ST-70-01C Solar Orbiter (ICD §5.19) Unique OBCP identifier (5.1a) "OBCP ID", 4 bytes, in every request that addresses one OBCP and in each report entry7477 Steps (5.1e) A "Step ID" set at chosen points of the OBCP design, used to report progress; suspend (TC(18,5)) and stop-and-delete (TC(18,141)) take an optional step ID, with -1 (the default) for immediate and 0 for the end of the current step747579 In store / in engine (5.4.2.2) Stored in file partitions (for example in mass memory), loaded into a RAM "execution slot" of the OBCP interpreter; a limited number of slots, hence an auto-delete option when the OBCP ends74 Inactive, running, held (5.4.2.2) The same three states; the list report adds "loading" (and the MIB calibration a "free" slot)747782 Communicate parameters (5.4.2.3) TC(18,7) with N pairs of parameter ID and value, at start or while running76 Checksum (5.4.3) Reported per OBCP in TM(18,9) and TM(18,144)7781 Engine monitoring (5.4.4.3) TM(18,9) list with state, instruction pointer and last step reached; TC(18,142) enables cyclic TM(18,144) with the current values of the OBCP's parameters, every N cycles of 8 Hz7780 Scheduling and priorities (5.4.4.5) "Normal" or "Emergency" priority chosen at start; only one emergency OBCP runs at a time, further ones are queued7478

The packet carried in every entry of the TM(18,9) OBCP List Report shows the monitoring data of §5.4.4.3 in its real form:

Field sizes and meanings from ICD §5.19.5; parameter names, types and the textual calibration CCDT0124TM from the MIB tables vpd, pcf and txp for SPID 14405.7782 The ICD lists states 1 to 4; the MIB calibration adds 0 "FREE".7782

In the MIB the service has 46 telecommands (32 in 2020): four of the PUS-A subtypes (5 to 8) plus the mission-specific subtypes 140 to 142. The PUS-A subtypes 1 to 4 and 12 (load, delete, start, stop, abort) have no command of their own.828365

Subtype Commands (2025-09-16) Commands (2020-04-16) Meaning (MIB description) 5 1 1 ZCD01205 Suspend an OBCP 6 1 1 ZCD01206 Resume an OBCP 7 3 3 Communicate 1-, 2- or 4-byte parameters to OBCP 8 1 1 ZCD01208 Report list of OBCPs (answered by TM(18,9), SPID 14405, APID 163) 140 38 24 Load and start OBCP: 3 generic (ZCD2Z00R, ZCD2Z00S, ZCD2Z00T) and 35 for named OBCPs 141 1 1 ZCD0128D Stop and delete an OBCP 142 1 1 ZCD0128E Set OBCP HK TM (cyclic TM(18,144), SPID 14406, APID 165) Total 46 32 all 46 addressed to APID 172

The 14 commands added between the two releases are all "load and start" commands ZCPX0001 to ZCPX0015 (no ZCPX0013), for named OBCPs such as SWA6 to SWA8, DMS1, TTC2 and TTC3, the METIS high-voltage door ramps, SSMM1 to SSMM3, MAG2, STR1 and PHI3.8283

Inference

Read against ECSS-E-ST-70-01C, Solar Orbiter has no separate Load, Activate or Delete telecommand: TC(18,140) combines load and activate (like PUS-C TC[18,19]) and TC(18,141) combines stop and delete (like TC[18,20]); abort is not in the MIB. Named "load and start" commands with fixed arguments let the database and its verification profiles describe each OBCP as its own activity, which is how the engineering data repository of §4.4 knows them. This interpretation is the wiki's; the ICD gives no rationale.

SQL used 
-- solo-2025-09-16.sqlite and solo-2020-04-16.sqlite
SELECT CCF_STYPE, count(*) FROM ccf WHERE CCF_TYPE = '18' GROUP BY CCF_STYPE;
SELECT CCF_APID, count(*) FROM ccf WHERE CCF_TYPE = '18' GROUP BY CCF_APID;   -- 172: 46
SELECT PID_TYPE, PID_STYPE, PID_APID, PID_SPID, PID_DESCR FROM pid WHERE PID_TYPE = '18';
-- commands new in 2025
ATTACH 'solo-2020-04-16.sqlite' AS o;
SELECT CCF_CNAME, CCF_DESCR FROM ccf WHERE CCF_TYPE = '18'
   AND CCF_CNAME NOT IN (SELECT CCF_CNAME FROM o.ccf WHERE CCF_TYPE = '18');
-- TM(18,9) layout
SELECT * FROM vpd WHERE VPD_TPSD = (SELECT PID_TPSD FROM pid WHERE PID_SPID = '14405')
 ORDER BY CAST(VPD_POS AS int);
SELECT PCF_NAME, PCF_DESCR, PCF_PTC, PCF_PFC, PCF_CURTX FROM pcf
 WHERE PCF_NAME IN ('NCD12091','NCDB0G90','NCDB0G50','NCD12094','NCDB0GA0','NCDB0GB0');
SELECT * FROM txp WHERE TXP_NUMBR = 'CCDT0124TM';

The 22 command sequences of the 2025 MIB that send a service 18 command are listed on the PLUTO page. Twelve of them contain a TC(18,140) "load and start"; 19 consist of a single service 18 command; all but one name a flight control or contingency recovery procedure document (CSF_DOCNAME) as their source, so that ground procedures trigger and control on-board ones.82

SQL used (sequences) 
-- solo-2025-09-16.sqlite: sequences containing a service 18 command
SELECT f.CSF_NAME, f.CSF_ELEMS, f.CSF_DOCNAME, c.CCF_STYPE
  FROM csf f JOIN css x ON x.CSS_SQNAME = f.CSF_NAME
  JOIN ccf c ON c.CCF_CNAME = x.CSS_ELEMID
 WHERE c.CCF_TYPE = '18';   -- 22 sequences; 12 with subtype 140; 19 with CSF_ELEMS = 1

docs.title: Herschel: an OBCP as fault management
docs.text:
The Herschel/Planck payload management and OBCP note (issue 06, 10 March 2008; see also Herschel/Planck interface documents) specifies, for each instrument, the OBCPs the central data management software needs; most are started by an event report through the event-action table, some by a "mother" OBCP.84 One SPIRE example, paraphrased from its specification:85

Item Value in the note OBCP DB_OBCP_H_SPIRE_DRCU_OFF, ID 0x1102 Triggered by Event 0xC000 from SPIRE nominal or redundant (SPIRE internal FDIR: DRCU power or temperature anomaly) Type, time-out Normal (TBC), 600 s (TBC) OBCP parameters SPIRE_SUBS_ID_CMD (default 370), SPIRE_SUBS_ID_META (default 100) Actions If DB_OBCP_H_SPIRE_OPE_RESUME (0x1107) runs, stop it with TC(18,4); disable four event-action entries with TC(19,5); disable release of the two SPIRE sub-schedules with TC(11,2); switch off the two SPIRE HSFCU power lines (LCL 51 and 52) with TC(8,4,112,3); issue event TM(5,4) 0x1000 "SPIRE DRCU Switched OFF"; re-enable the triggering event-action entries with TC(19,4) Lasting effects Two event-action entries and both sub-schedules left disabled (re-enabling recommended when SPIRE is back on); both LCLs off

Inference

The note predates ECSS-E-ST-70-01C and does not use its vocabulary. In the standard's terms this is a system-design OBCP implementing FDIR (§4.2.2.1), started through the event-action service, using arguments with defaults (§5.1b), initiating activities of services 8, 11, 18 and 19 (§5.2.9.2), raising an existing event (§5.2.9.3) and checking whether another OBCP is running before stopping it. Its interference with DB_OBCP_H_SPIRE_OPE_RESUME is the kind of OBCP interdependency that §5.4.1a asks the ground to check, and that §6.2.5c (written for OBOPs) gives to a single approving authority.
