    SystemElement "1" --> "*" Event
    ReportingData "1" o-- "*" ReportingData : components
    Event --> ReportingData : accompanying data
    ReportingData --> Activity : corrective actions

The SSM entity types and their main relationships, drawn from clauses 4, 6.5, 6.6, 6.7 and 6.8. The diagram form is this wiki's.69111213

The standard's own example is an attitude and orbit control subsystem decomposed into electronics, star trackers, reaction wheels, a sun sensor and a propulsion system, with activities such as "Switch On", events such as "Switch On Failure" and reporting data such as wheel speed or tank pressure attached at the appropriate level.5

docs.title: Naming
docs.text: Because suppliers work in parallel, names that are unique for one supplier may clash at a higher level of integration. The standard therefore uses relative names (one or more words of letters and digits, separated by spaces, such as "Star Tracker") made unique where needed by a reference path after the keyword "of" ("X Thruster of Branch 1", "temperature of XGyro"). Names are case-insensitive. The same scheme names the model itself: "Severity of Event" is the value type Severity of the entity type Event.14

docs.title: Data requirement tables
docs.text: Each entity type is specified as a table of three columns: the value type name, its definition and constraints, and its data type; "List of" and "Ordered list of" mark lower-level entities with arity above one. When a row is conditional, the data is not provided if the condition is false. Language syntax is given with railroad diagrams (non-terminals in rectangles, terminals in rounded boxes, branches for options, return lines for repetitions) and again in ISO/IEC 14977 EBNF in Annex B.151617

docs.title: Simple data types
docs.text:
Type Notes Constant examples from the standard Boolean TRUE, FALSE integer Range mission-dependent; optional engineering units (units per ECSS-E-ST-70-32 Annex B) 23, 5 A, 65536 B unsigned integer Decimal or hexadecimal 2056, 0x2056, 0xFFFF real Range and precision mission-dependent 123, 56e12, 0.1 bit string 0b11001 octet string 0x12AB character string Escape \" and \\ "This is a string." absolute time Calendar or day-of-year form, optional Z 2001-08-18T21:07:43.137468Z, 2001-033T13:21:32.226 relative time Several forms 30 h 10 min, 200 s, -0:00:10:00

Source: §5.5.2.1.181920

PUS types. Two further families come from the PUS. Service type and subtype: standard service types 0–127 and mission-specific 128–255; standard subtypes 0–127, mission-specific subtypes 128–255 within a standard service, or 0–255 within a mission-specific service.21 And the parameter code (PC) = parameter type code (PTC) + parameter format code (PFC):22

PTC Data type PFC range 1 Boolean 0 2 Enumerated 1–16, 24, 32 3 Unsigned integer 0–16 4 Signed integer 0–16 5 Real 1–4 6 Bit-string 0 to any 7 Octet-string 0 to any 8 Character-string 0 to any 9 Absolute time 0–18 10 Relative time 0–16 11 Deduced 0

There is a subtle shift of meaning: in the PUS the PFC defines the size of the encoded value, whereas here it expresses the range of values (PTC 3 PFC 0 is an integer from 0 to 15; PTC 8 PFC 12 a fixed 12-character string). PTC 11 is not used, because every deduced parameter is instantiated as one of the other types. Booleans are 0 (false) and 1 (true) in packets.2223 The SCOS-2000 view of the same codes is on MIB parameter types and PUS parameter types.

User-defined enumerated types. A user can define an enumerated set by name and list of values. When the values are sampled in packets, each element gets a raw correspondence: one raw value (PTC 2) for a one-to-one mapping, or, for many-to-one mappings, a raw type (PTC 3, 4 or 5) with a list of raw intervals per element, plus a default raw value for encoding telecommand arguments. The standard's examples are a battery charge status (trickle 0, full 1, discharge 2) and a filter wheel readout where raw 5–6 means "red", 7–8 "green" and 0–4 or 13–15 "non-operational".2425

Value type sets and value type data types let a data item take any populated value of another item (for example "ID of system element of Type application process", the set of all APIDs) or inherit its type ("same as Data Type of current parameter").26

docs.title: The languages
docs.text:
Complex data items are strings in one of six languages.27

Language Used for Specified in Activity Call Instantiating an activity with argument values or a predefined value set and directives (MAP ID, AD or BD mode, requested verification reports); corrective actions ECSS-E-ST-70-32 Annex A.3.9.28 EXPL (expression language) Validity, selection and pre/post-conditions Annex B.5 IFL (interpretation function language) Raw-to-engineering interpretation and the reverse Annex B.6 SPEL (synthetic parameter expression language) Synthetic parameters Annex B.7 VAL (value language) Default values and value sets Annex B.9 PLUTO Procedures ECSS-E-ST-70-32 (see PLUTO)

Sources: §6.2.2 to §6.2.7 and Annex B.282930

EXPL, IFL and SPEL share an expression grammar: Boolean operators AND, OR, XOR and NOT; relational comparisons, between ... and ... and in (...); + - * / and **; functions from ECSS-E-ST-70-32 Annex C; constants with units; and, in IFL, the keyword raw value. The requirements behind them insist on engineering units on constants, free mixing of compatible units and automatic unit conversion.313228

A glitch in the prose

The prose under the railroad diagrams of B.5, B.6 and B.7 lists the relational operators as "AND, OR, XOR" (a copy of the Boolean operator list). The EBNF of B.7.3 gives the intended set: =, !=, <, >, <=, >=.3133

SPEL adds what a synthetic parameter needs (requirements 6.2.6): a trigger (on update of a reporting data, meaning a new sample rather than a changed value, or on an event, or any combination); a declaration of typed local variables and persistent variables that keep their value between evaluations; if ... then ... else and in case ... is ... or is ... otherwise flow control; a context statement (in the context of ... do ... end context); property requests (get Raw Value of ...; a bare parameter name means its engineering value); bit functions bitand, bitor, bitxor, bitnot, bitshl, bitshr; and an assignment of the result with set ... with ... end with. The result is an engineering value that needs no further calibration.353637383334

synthetic parameter
  trigger
    on update of Bus Voltage of PCDU or on update of Bus Current of PCDU
  end trigger
  declare
    variable Power of type real with units W described by "instantaneous bus power",
    persistent Peak of type real with units W set to 0 W described by "highest power so far"
  end declare
  main
    Power := Bus Voltage of PCDU * Bus Current of PCDU;
    if Power > Peak then
      Peak := Power;
    end if;
    set engineering value with Power end with;
  end main
end synthetic parameter

An illustrative SPEL definition written by this wiki to the EBNF of Annex B.7.3; the parameter names are invented. It is not taken from any mission.3334

VAL writes simple values, records (record ... end record) and arrays (array ... end array), each optionally named after the component it fills, with constants, activity calls, reporting data references or system element references as values.39

docs.title: Data exchange and the data life cycle
Exchange rules
docs.text: The supplier delivers a subset of the model plus product-specific types; the product data schema must be specified, machine-processable and lossless on re-import. The formal languages above should be used, and any other language must be specified in EBNF. The electronic database is under configuration management and is identified by a configuration item ID, a version number, a generation date, a supplier ID and the list of digital files, each with type and checksum; each file is uniquely identified and compressed with a standard tool.4041

docs.title: Product configuration data
docs.text:
Each delivered product is described as either a specification (a theoretical product) or a realization (a real one), and typed as a developed hardware configuration item (CI ID, part, serial and lot numbers, model such as EM, STM or FM, manufacturer), a developed software CI (software identifier, version, release date), a COTS or standard product, or a non-CI product.4243

Versioning. A system element gets a new version when any of its properties change or when any of its activities, reporting data, events or constituent elements are created or deleted; activities, reporting data and events get a new version when any of their properties change (for reporting data, also when sub-components appear or disappear). Every version records number, date, originator, reason and a validation status: not validated, validated by review, by simulation or by testing. The same data is kept for every constituent product, so that knowledge supplied at lower levels or earlier phases stays traceable.4445

docs.title: Population rules
docs.text:
Rule (6.4) Content Language and case All data in English, case-insensitive except engineering units Renaming If an object is renamed during integration, its former names are retained Consistency The data agrees with the product documentation (ICD, user manual) Uniqueness Object names unique within a delivery Life-limited items Accumulated operational cycles or life provided with each delivery Sub-suppliers Provide enough to populate everything the customer needs Domains Domain-specific data (Software, AIV, Operations) identified as such Validation All data validated (review, simulators, real hardware); for operations, with real hardware wherever possible

"Fully populated" is defined precisely. For reporting data it means: everything in the documentation, including dumpable software tables and memory; redundancy links between items conveying the same information; all interpretation functions with their applicability conditions; validity conditions; ground monitoring checks for all reporting data (except those that can take any value); status consistency checks where values depend on activities or events; and corrective actions for violations. For activities: everything in the documentation, all atomic activities, arguments in engineering values with their de-interpretation, pre- and post-conditions, verification conditions for start, progress and completion deduced from low-level telemetry whether or not the PUS verification service is used, redundant and reverse links, criticality, corrective actions, execution profile and resources. For events: all events and their corrective actions.464748

flowchart LR
    U["Unit supplier<br/>SSM of the unit<br/>v1.0, validated by review"] --> S["Subsystem supplier<br/>integrates, renames,<br/>keeps former names"]
    S --> P["Prime contractor<br/>spacecraft SSM<br/>validated by testing"]
    P --> O["Operator<br/>mission database<br/>(for ESA: the MIB)"]
    O -->|"change requests"| P
    P -->|"new versions with<br/>reason and status"| O

The data definition life cycle implied by clauses 6.3 and 6.4. The arrows and roles are this wiki's summary.4446

docs.title: System element data
docs.text:
Every system element has a name unique within the product, a description, a type and a nature (specification or realization), references to the sub-product elements integrated into it, and its redundant elements. The type list is long: system, subsystem, set, equipment, software product, assembly, part, module, element, facility (ground), application process, MAP, VC, any service, function, memory block, memory sub-block, store, CPDU, On/Off device, register load device and sensor.9 Elements that send telecommands or receive telemetry get a PUS source or destination ID; life-limited elements get maximum cycles and duration plus the record of operations.10

Element type Data required (paraphrased) System (6.5.3) ID; ground or space segment; for PUS systems: PFC of the Source ID field and list of TC sources, whether CPDU telecommands have a data field header, maximum TC packet length; PFC of the Destination ID and list of destinations, whether the spacecraft time packet has a data field header, maximum TM packet length Application process (6.5.4) APID (PTC 2 PFC 11, unique in the system); service accesses (commanding path, monitoring path, memory and store management, store access, event report access) with the elements concerned; word length (8, 16, 24, 32 or 64 bits) for padding; PFCs of the length fields of variable bit, octet and character strings; TC checksum type (ISO or CRC); PFC of the TM time field; whether there is a packet sub-counter; TM checksum type Service (6.5.5) Tailoring variables, packet field data types and service-specific configuration, per application process (below) MAP (6.5.6) ID 0–63; mission-specific priority; reachable application processes; whether it is the default MAP for an AP VC (6.5.7) ID; downlink or uplink; packets (AP, service type and subtype) carried Function (6.5.8) Function ID (PTC 8, unique within a service implementation); ordered arguments with ID (the PUS Parameter#), type, arity and default Memory block (6.5.9) Memory ID (PTC 7, unique in the system); read-only or read/write; smallest addressable unit (1, 2, 3, 4 or 8 octets); addressing technique (base plus offset, symbolic reference plus offset, absolute); size Memory sub-block (6.5.10) Symbolic base reference; offset; size; access; reload or patch; content type (object code, dynamic data, data pool, static data); mapped reporting data Store (6.5.11) Store ID; circular or bounded; capacity CPDU (6.5.12) Output lines (name, number PTC 2 PFC 8, description); pulse duration unit 10–15 ms; maximum instructions per packet 12–120 On/Off device (6.5.13) Hardware addresses with the element and ON or OFF type Register load device (6.5.14) Address; independently commandable components with the reporting data echoing each one Sensor (6.5.15) Bi-level, analogue SE or DE, relay, thermistor; address (e.g. RTU); connector

Sources: §6.5.3 to §6.5.15.4950515253545556

docs.title: Service data and PUS tailoring
docs.text:
For each standard PUS service an application process hosts, the supplier provides three things: the tailoring variables (Booleans stating which capabilities are implemented), the data types of the packet fields (the PFC of each field that the tailoring leaves present) and the service-specific configuration data the ground needs to model the service.57 Annex A gives, for each service, a short summary of the PUS service model, a yes/no flowchart whose "yes" branches set tailoring variables, and the packet layouts with semantics, field names, data types and presence conditions.5859

Telecommand verification is the simplest. Three tailoring variables say whether the service verifies start (S1 ST3 and ST4 Provider), progress (S1 ST5 and ST6 Provider) and completion (S1 ST7 and ST8 Provider); the field types are the PFCs of the Code and (if progress is verified) Step Number fields; and the service data is the list of command failure codes valid for all commands, with the stages they apply to and the parameters that accompany them (codes 0 to 5 have a special meaning in the PUS).60

flowchart TD
    Q1{"Can this service verify<br/>start of TC execution?"} -->|Yes| V1["S1 ST3 and ST4 Provider = TRUE"]
    Q1 -->|No| Q2
    V1 --> Q2{"Can it verify<br/>progress of execution?"}
    Q2 -->|Yes| V2["S1 ST5 and ST6 Provider = TRUE"]
    Q2 -->|No| Q3
    V2 --> Q3{"Can it verify<br/>completion of execution?"}
    Q3 -->|Yes| V3["S1 ST7 and ST8 Provider = TRUE"]
    Q3 -->|No| E([End])
    V3 --> E

Tailoring choices for the telecommand verification service (Annex A, figure A-2).59

Housekeeping and diagnostic reporting shows how far this goes: some thirty tailoring variables (whether housekeeping and diagnostic reports exist, whether report control, parameter definition reports, sampling time offset reports and filtered mode exist, whether collection intervals, timeouts and thresholds have defaults...), fourteen field types (SID, collection interval, NPAR1, NFA, NREP, NPAR2, Parameter#, NSID, time offset, timeout, N, threshold type, threshold, mode), service data such as the minimum sampling interval and the absolute and relative sampling accuracies (PUS mission constants <DIAG_MIN_INTERV>, <PARAM_ABS_SAMPL_TIME>, <PARAM_REL_SAMPL_TIME>), and per report a definition with SID, ordered components and their time offsets, whether it is predefined on board, collection interval and filtered parameters.61626364

The services covered follow the service list of the 2003 PUS (ECSS-E-70-41A), with this page linking to the current ECSS-E-ST-70-41C pages:6566

70-31C Annex Service (2003 name) Current page A.2 Telecommand verification ST[01] A.3 Device command distribution ST[02] A.4 Housekeeping and diagnostic data reporting ST[03] A.5 Parameter statistics reporting ST[04] A.6 Event reporting ST[05] A.7 Memory management ST[06] A.8 Function management ST[08] A.9 Time management ST[09] A.10 On-board operations scheduling ST[11] A.11 On-board monitoring ST[12] A.12 Large data transfer ST[13] A.13 Packet forwarding control ST[14] A.14 On-board storage and retrieval ST[15] A.15 Test ST[17] A.16 On-board operations procedure ST[18] A.17 Event/action ST[19]

docs.title: Generic data
docs.text: Every reporting data item names its system element and itself (relative name), describes its purpose, says whether it is a parameter or a compound parameter, lists the domains (AIV, Operations, Software) where it applies, gives per domain a validity condition (an EXPL Boolean expression saying when its interpretation is meaningful), traces back to the sub-product item it came from, and lists redundant reporting data conveying the same information (the standard's example is two boom release sensors).11

docs.title: Parameters and interpretation
docs.text: A parameter has the data type of its engineering value; if it is referenced inside packets it has a Parameter Number (the PUS "Parameter#", never 0, assigned system-wide). If the transported value can be taken directly as the engineering value, only the PFC of the raw value is given. Otherwise an interpretation is defined: the PTC and PFC of the raw value, and per domain an ordered list of interpretation functions, each with an EXPL selection condition; the first function whose condition is true applies. A function is either a linear interpolation between calibration points (raw, engineering), with an extrapolation flag ("extrapolate" from the last two points or declare "invalid" outside the range), or an IFL script. For every interpretation a raw value must give a unique engineering value.676869

docs.title: Compound and synthetic reporting data
docs.text: A compound parameter is a record (ordered components, each with a sampling time offset when in a packet), an array (fixed or variable, minimum and maximum repetitions, components, time offset of the first element, delta time between elements, PFC of the repetition counter of a variable array) or a deduced structure (a list of alternative component lists, each selected by an EXPL condition; more than one can be true).7071 Reporting data computed in the EMCS is synthetic and carries a SPEL script, which can set one or several components of a compound parameter.72

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
Check (6.6.6) Data Selection Limit Upper and lower danger limits and upper and lower warning limits, each with its own corrective activity (independent of the previous check state) Ordered list of limit sets, each with an EXPL validity condition (for example mission phase or unit status); first true applies; per domain Delta Maximum delta (failure if exceeded) and minimum delta (failure if not exceeded) between successive values, each with an activity Ordered lists with validity conditions Expected state List of expected values and a corrective activity Ordered list with validity conditions Status consistency Either a telecommand activity and argument whose last uplinked value the parameter must equal (check suspended during the command's execution window; examples "Set Filter Wheel Position" with "Position = UV", or "Switch LCL1 ON" with "LCL1 Status"), or an EXPL expression for a value set autonomously on board or by a mission event (such as entry into eclipse); plus an activity Per domain

Sources: tables 6-85 to 6-88.73747576

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An activity names its system element and itself, describes its function, has a type (ground procedure, on-board procedure, telecommand, operating system command), domain applicability, traceability references, lists of redundant activities (same effect) and reverse activities (opposite effect), a criticality taken from ECSS-E-ST-70-11 (non critical, locally critical, mission critical) and an ordered, flat list of arguments. Each argument has a name, description, type (any simple type, record or activity call), arity (single value or array, with minimum and maximum repetitions), and a default or fixed value in VAL. Predefined argument value sets can be named and described.127778 ECSS-E-ST-70-11C gives the meaning of the criticality levels.

docs.title: Execution states
docs.text:
Table 6-93 fixes the states an activity passes through and the events marking the transitions, and says which apply to procedures and which to telecommands. For telecommands the stages are reported through the PUS telecommand verification service:7980

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> NotInitiated
    NotInitiated --> Preconditions: activity initiated
    Preconditions --> Routing: preconditions evaluated / PTV passed
    state Routing {
        [*] --> Released: release from EGSE or MCS
        Released --> AtStation: reception by ground station or TC front end
        AtStation --> Uplinking: start of uplink
        Uplinking --> OnBoard: reception on board (AD mode)
        OnBoard --> Accepted: acceptance by destination AP, PUS 1.1 / 1.2
    }
    Routing --> Executing: start, PUS 1.3 / 1.4
    Executing --> Executing: steps, PUS 1.5 / 1.6
    Executing --> Confirmation: confirmation body
    Confirmation --> Completed: PUS 1.7 / 1.8 and end-to-end CEV in telemetry
    Completed --> [*]

Telecommand execution states after table 6-93. The PTV applies to the telecommand itself, not to commands it contains (for example those inside a schedule load); whether station and on-board reception events are reported depends on the ground system and the on-board design.7980

For each activity the supplier gives an execution profile (expected, minimum and maximum duration; earliest and latest start after initiation; resources used and quantities), the steps it consists of (each with its own profile and states, steps within steps for procedures, PUS 1.5/1.6 for telecommand steps), and the failure activities to run if completion fails.818283

docs.title: Telecommands
docs.text:
Data (6.7.4) Content Telecommand data PUS service type and subtype; default application process; whether it may be sent as a high-priority command and, if so, the MAP forced for the uplink (CPDU commands are the example) Array arguments PFC of the repetition number Non-interpreted arguments PFC of the encoded format Interpreted arguments PTC and PFC of the encoded format; per domain an ordered list of de-interpretation functions with selection conditions; each a linear interpolation (values outside the engineering range are invalid) or an IFL script; a unique raw value per engineering value Property arguments PFC for arguments that are system element or reporting data properties (such as an APID) Execution check data Per domain PTV conditions; whether start, progress and completion can be verified with PUS service 1; a start verification condition and a CEV (command execution verification) condition from low-level telemetry, even when service 1 is used; start failure activities; command-specific failure codes (not those reserved by the PUS or defined service-wide) with their parameter components Step check data Per step: number, verification condition, failure activity

Sources: §6.7.4.84858687 The CEV can range from one measurement to comparing every transmitted argument with an "echo" parameter, or comparing a memory dump with the load image.87

docs.title: Procedures
docs.text: Procedures are initiated explicitly (foreground) or run permanently (background) and have earliest and latest validity dates. A ground procedure is a PLUTO script with a default automatic or manual execution mode; an on-board procedure is an ECSS-E-ST-70-01 script with a preloaded flag and a high, medium or low priority for conflicts.88

docs.title: Events
docs.text: An event names its system element and itself, has a description, a type (anomaly report, progress report, information, software error, scheduling event...), domain applicability, references, a severity (normal, low, medium, high, with a pointer to the PUS event reporting service), the reporting data accompanying it with their time offsets from the event time, and per domain the activity to run when it occurs.13

docs.title: How the SCOS-2000 MIB realises the model
docs.text:
The MIB is not an implementation of ECSS-E-ST-70-31C: SCOS-2000's Database Import ICD descends from the PSS era (it still cites ESA PSS-07-101, the 1994 PUS, next to ECSS-E-70-41A) and defines flat, normalised ASCII tables keyed by 8-character names.8911490 Yet almost every concept of the standard has a counterpart. The table below compares them; the third column says where the MIB is narrower.

ECSS-E-ST-70-31C concept SCOS-2000 MIB realisation Difference Electronic database identification (table 6-1) vdf: VDF_NAME, comment, domain, release, issue No file list or checksums in the table Relative names with reference paths Unique alphanumeric names, typically 8 characters, case-insensitively unique, no spaces recommended; descriptions PCF_DESCR (24) and CCF_DESCR (24) / CCF_DESCR2 (64) Flat namespace; hierarchy only through naming conventions and groups System element hierarchy No table; PCF_SUBSYS (future extension), CCF_SUBSYS (numeric subsystem 1–255), monitoring groups grp No SE entity Parameter (reporting data) pcf row Data type of engineering value; raw PTC/PFC PCF_PTC, PCF_PFC; PCF_CATEG N (numerical), S (status), T (text) PTC/PFC give size, as in the PUS Parameter Number (Parameter#) PCF_PID, unique on-board ID Validity condition (EXPL) PCF_VALID = PCF_VALPAR: one integer parameter compared with one raw value; plus automatic expiry when a periodic packet stops No general expressions Ordered interpretation functions with selection conditions PCF_CURTX (single) or cur: CUR_POS order, CUR_RLCHK = CUR_VALPAR, CUR_SELECT; first true applies Conditions limited to parameter = value Linear interpolation with extrapolate/invalid caf / cap; CAF_INTER P (extrapolate) or F (invalid); PCF_INTER is ignored Extrapolation is per calibration, not per parameter IFL script mcf polynomial and lgf logarithmic calibrations Fixed formula families instead of a language User-defined enumerated type with raw intervals txf / txp: TXP_FROM..TXP_TO mapped to TXP_ALTXT Equivalent Record, array, deduced structure Packet layouts: plf (fixed), vpd (variable, with repeat counters); deduced parameters (PCF_PTC 11) with PCF_RELATED Deduced structures not supported; variable packets excluded from full processing Synthetic reporting data (SPEL) PCF_NATUR D (dynamic OL), P (SPEL), H (hard-coded), S (saved); one expression file per parameter SPEL only in the EGSE delivery of SCOS-2000 Limit check: warning and danger, ordered sets with validity conditions ocf / ocp: OCP_TYPE S (soft) and H (hard), OCP_POS order, OCP_RLCHK = OCP_VALPAR; OCF_NBCHCK consecutive violations No per-limit corrective activity; type E checks raise SCOS-2000 events that can trigger system actions Delta check OCP_TYPE D Single min/max delta pair Expected state check Status checks: soft/hard ocp entries listing allowed values for status parameters Status consistency check PCF_USCON = Y plus OCP_TYPE C; reference value maintained from commanding; cve marks affected parameters Limited number of parameters (snapshot packet size) Activity of type telecommand ccf: CCF_TYPE, CCF_STYPE, CCF_APID High priority and forced MAP CCF_HIPRI, CCF_MAPID Equivalent Criticality (three levels) CCF_CRITICAL Y/N ("hazardous"), extra protection mission-specific Two levels Arguments, defaults, fixed values, arrays cdf (editable or fixed elements, CDF_GRPSIZE repeaters), cpc (CPC_DEFVAL) Argument value sets pst, psv, cps, pvs, psm; CCF_DEFSET Equivalent De-interpretation functions cca/ccs numerical, paf/pas textual, referenced by CPC_CCAREF or CPC_PAFREF; range checks prf/prv One de-calibration per command parameter, no selection conditions PTV condition ptv: parameter = value pairs, implicitly ANDed, validity checked No general expressions Execution states and verification CCF_ILSTAGE stages R (ground station), U (uplink), O (on-board reception), A (acceptance), C (completion); cvs CVS_TYPE A, S, 0–9, C with CVS_SOURCE R (PUS reports) or V (parameter checks); cvp profiles Report-based progress only for step 0; failure codes ignored by the verifier CEV condition cve expressions, ANDed per stage Execution profile CVS_START and CVS_INTERVAL (verification window), CVS_UNCERTAINTY No durations or resources Procedures Command sequences csf, css, sdf, csp Not PLUTO; on-board procedures not modelled Event with severity PID_EVENT (N, I info, W warning, A alarm) and PID_EVID generate SCOS-2000 events when a packet arrives Severity is attached to the packet type Service tailoring data Packet headers tcp/pcdf/pcpc, TM packet attributes in pid and tpcf No tailoring variables; services are handled by fixed or mission-specific code

Sources: ICD 7.0 clauses 1.3.1, 3.1 to 3.3 and Appendix C on PUS support.91909210593949596979899100101102103104106107108109110111112

Inference

The rows "System element hierarchy", "Procedures" and "Service tailoring data" compare concepts the ICD never relates to ECSS-E-ST-70-31C; the pairing is this wiki's. The ICD does not cite ECSS-E-ST-70-31C at all.

The ICD also documents what SCOS-2000 does with the PUS services that 70-31C asks suppliers to describe. For example, service 1 reports are matched to commands by the 4 echoed header octets and only the subtype (not the failure code) drives verification; housekeeping packets must be defined in the database before they are enabled on board, with fixed time offsets and collection intervals; service 11 has a ground model of the on-board schedule built around the Rosetta packet structure; services 4 and 12 reports are variable packets and so excluded from full processing.111112113

docs.title: What the Solar Orbiter MIB shows
docs.text:
The release of 16 September 2025 (VDF_NAME 25925PFM, comment "20250916-CSW3.1.2_MAS7.33") gives a measure of how much of the model a real mission populates:115

Model concept MIB measure (2025 release) 2020 release Parameters 126 745 pcf rows: 125 161 raw (R), 1 582 dynamic OL synthetic (D), 2 saved synthetic (S), no SPEL (P) 102 104: 101 714 R, 354 D, 36 hard-coded (H) Parameter Number 19 803 parameters with PCF_PID Validity condition 20 692 parameters with PCF_VALID 8 369 Conditional interpretation 1 974 cur rows for 907 parameters 723 parameters Limit and status checks 5 338 ocf rows (3 199 on calibrated values, 2 139 on raw); 7 369 ocp rows: 3 096 soft (S), 4 153 hard (H), 105 delta (D), 15 status consistency (C) Checks with applicability conditions 859 ocp rows on 563 parameters Telecommands 5 454 ccf rows, 130 high priority, none flagged critical (CCF_CRITICAL 'N' in 5 448 rows, empty in 6) 5 238, 130 high priority, 79 flagged critical (CCF_CRITICAL = 'Y') Verification 206 stages: 16 acceptance by report, 23 completion by report, 167 completion by parameter check; 10 697 cvp links for 5 393 commands Static PTV 5 ptv rows Events Severities in pid: TM(5,1) informative reports raise I, TM(5,2) W, TM(5,3) and TM(5,4) A; TM(1,2) and TM(1,8) failure reports also raise A TM(5,x): 893, 876, 2 189, 1 695 packets

Two examples show the standard's ideas in MIB form. Parameter NIXD0058 (HK_DET_C, mA) has five soft limit sets selected by the status parameter NIXS0002 ("DPU_DET_C criter", values NOT_POWERED, 1Q, 2Q, 3Q, 4Q) and an unconditional hard limit: an ordered list of limit sets with validity conditions, exactly as in table 6-85. Parameter NCAB0EP0 ("CPS A TLV LCL Cur", A) uses calibration CPWP3005TM when NPWZ0000 (PCDU_MODEL) is 10 and CPWP8005TM when it is 11: an ordered list of interpretation functions with selection conditions, as in table 6-77.115

SQL used

All queries ran with sqlite3 -readonly on solo-2025-09-16.sqlite (release MIB__20250916M25925PFMS001_SOL) and, for the last column, on solo-2020-04-16.sqlite (MIB__20200416M10720PFMS001_SOL). In this database cvs and cvp have generic column names: for cvs, COL2 is CVS_TYPE and COL3 is CVS_SOURCE; for cvp, COL1 is CVP_TASK.

SELECT * FROM vdf;
SELECT PCF_NATUR, count(*) FROM pcf GROUP BY 1;
SELECT count(*) FROM pcf WHERE PCF_PID <> '';
SELECT count(*) FROM pcf WHERE PCF_VALID <> '';
SELECT count(*), count(DISTINCT CUR_PNAME) FROM cur;
SELECT OCF_INTER, count(*) FROM ocf GROUP BY 1;
SELECT OCP_TYPE, count(*) FROM ocp GROUP BY 1;
SELECT count(*), count(DISTINCT OCP_NAME) FROM ocp WHERE OCP_RLCHK <> '';
SELECT count(*), sum(CCF_HIPRI = 'Y'), sum(CCF_CRITICAL = 'Y') FROM ccf;
SELECT COL2, COL3, count(*) FROM cvs GROUP BY 1, 2;
SELECT count(*), count(DISTINCT COL1) FROM cvp;
SELECT * FROM ptv;
SELECT PID_TYPE, PID_STYPE, PID_EVENT, count(*) FROM pid
  WHERE PID_EVENT IN ('A','W','I') GROUP BY 1, 2, 3;
-- examples
SELECT * FROM ocp WHERE OCP_NAME = 'NIXD0058';
SELECT * FROM txp WHERE TXP_NUMBR = 'CIXTS002TM';
SELECT * FROM cur WHERE CUR_PNAME = 'NCAB0EP0';
SELECT PCF_NAME, PCF_DESCR, PCF_UNIT FROM pcf
  WHERE PCF_NAME IN ('NIXD0058','NIXS0002','NCAB0EP0','NPWZ0000');

docs.title: Why the standard matters
docs.text:
ECSS-E-ST-70-31C is the reason a supplier's database can be specified contractually: it lists what "complete" means for every parameter, command and event, and it makes ground-side knowledge such as calibration, checks, verification conditions and corrective actions part of the delivery rather than something the operator reconstructs from documents. Its companion requirements in ECSS-E-ST-70-11C (for example that every packet carries what is needed to calibrate and validate its data, or that the same parameter always has the same interpretation) are what make such a model possible on the spacecraft side.46116

Inference

The previous paragraph is this wiki's assessment of the standard's role; the standard itself only states its purpose (defining the data a supplier provides for monitoring and control).2

docs.title: ECSS-E-ST-70-32C: PLUTO test and operations procedure language
docs.text:
ECSS-E-ST-70-32C ("Space engineering – Test and operations procedure language", 31 July 2008) does two things. It lists the capabilities that any language for automated test and operations procedures has to provide, and it defines a reference language that provides them, the Procedure Language for Users in Test and Operations (PLUTO).12 The standard calls the procedure the principal means by which the end user controls the space system, both in functional testing before launch and in operations after launch.1 Its main promise is reuse: a procedure written once for satellite checkout should carry over to mission operations, and the same language should be used from one mission to the next.19

PLUTO is not a stand-alone programming language. It works on top of the space system model (SSM) of ECSS-E-ST-70-31C: a procedure refers to system elements, reporting data, activities and events that the SSM already defines, and it only adds the procedural script.13 This page covers the whole standard, then compares PLUTO with what ESA ground systems actually ran: the Tcl-based TOPE language of the SCOS-2000 EGSE, the command sequences of the SCOS-2000 MIB, and the MOIS procedure tools.

At a glance

Item Value Issues ECSS-E-70-32A (24 April 2006, first issue); B never issued; ECSS-E-ST-70-32C (31 July 2008), which made editorial changes only3 Status (ECSS tree, October 2025) Published; no update shown as ongoing or planned5 Normative references ECSS-S-ST-00-01 (glossary) and ISO/IEC 14977 (extended BNF)4 Normative part Clause 5, requirements on any procedure language (44 lettered requirements: 18 in §5.1, 24 in §5.2, 2 in §5.3)171819 Informative annexes A: the PLUTO language (structure, behaviour, 36 language constructs, EBNF, index); B: engineering units; C: mathematical, time and string functions2 Syntax notation Railroad diagrams plus ISO EBNF for every construct3669 Users of the standard ECSS-E-ST-70-31C requires clause 5 for procedures and names PLUTO as the script type of ground procedures7780

docs.title: Why a common procedure language
docs.text:
The standard places procedures in the life of a space system. The space system consists of a space segment, a ground segment and a launch service segment, whose elements are used at different times: the electrical ground support equipment (EGSE) during development, the launch service segment before and during launch, and the mission control system and ground stations during operations.8

  • Testing. The standard does not prescribe at which integration level automated procedures are used (that is a decision of each mission's verification approach), but notes that they are generally used from subsystem level upwards. Reusing test procedures across integration levels needs standardised EGSE functions; reusing them in operations needs harmonised requirements for EGSE and mission control systems.9
  • Operations. ECSS-E-ST-70 makes procedures the primary mechanism for mission operations and names two kinds of flight control procedure (FCP): nominal procedures, the building blocks of the timelines and schedules of the flight operations plan (FOP), and contingency procedures, which reconfigure the space system after pre-identified anomalies. FCPs were traditionally run by hand; pressure to reduce routine manpower pushes towards automating their execution.10

In this standard the EGSE and the mission control system together are the EMCS (EGSE and mission control system). The procedure language and its development and execution environments are part of the EMCS and have direct access to its other monitoring and control functions.11

FOP and MOP

ECSS-E-ST-70-32C speaks of the flight operations plan (FOP) of ECSS-E-ST-70. The 2008 issue of ECSS-E-ST-70C, published the same day, calls the corresponding document the mission operations plan (MOP) and does not use the abbreviation FOP.1016 ESOC's own plans used the FOP name: its INTEGRAL plan of 2003 is a "Flight Operations Plan" whose mission rules state that the FOP provides the timelines and the nominal and contingency flight procedures (see ECSS-E-ST-70C).107

docs.title: The space system model seen by a procedure
docs.text:
The SSM of ECSS-E-ST-70-31 captures mission knowledge for assembly, integration and verification (AIV) and for operations. Four kinds of SSM object matter to a procedure:1213

SSM object Meaning Examples given by the standard System element A functional element of the space system, from the functional decomposition of the space segment (ECSS-S-ST-00) or of the ground segment (ECSS-E-ST-70) Power subsystem, AOCS, star tracker, optical head; EGSE, MCS, ground station, baseband equipment, telemetry decoder Reporting data Data used to assess the functioning of the space system: parameters (the lowest level of elementary information with a meaning for monitoring) and compound parameters (records of parameters, arrays and sub-records interpreted together, for example a whole telemetry packet or an anomaly report) Temperature, Source Count, Background Count Report, Telemetry Lock Status, Go NoGo Status Activity A space system monitoring and control function: procedures, telecommands to the space or ground segment, and any EMCS function (a printer request, an e-mail, an ftp transfer); missions may add their own activity types Switch On Event The occurrence of a condition or set of conditions during a test session or mission phase, used to trigger a monitoring and control function; associated with system elements, reporting data or activities Undervoltage (of the power subsystem), Switch On Failure (of the star tracker's Switch On activity)

Reporting data can have several representations during its life: an on-board measurement has an encoded value in telemetry and a raw or engineering value on a ground display.12 For any given configuration of the space system (a stand-alone unit test, a partly integrated spacecraft, a ground segment validated against a simulator) only a subset of the SSM is in use, but the model itself is independent of the configuration.13

flowchart TB
  SS["Space system"] --> SEG["Space segment"]
  SS --> GS["Ground segment"]
  GS -.reporting data.-> GNG[/"Go NoGo Status"/]
  SEG --> PWR["Power subsystem"]
  PWR -.event.-> UV(["Undervoltage"])
  SEG --> AOCS["AOCS"]
  AOCS --> STR["Star tracker"]
  STR -.activity.-> SON[["Switch On"]]
  SON -.event.-> SOF(["Switch On Failure"])
  STR -.reporting data.-> BCR[/"Background Count Report"/]
  STR --> OH["Optical head"]
  OH -.reporting data.-> T[/"Temperature"/]
  OH -.reporting data.-> SC[/"Source Count"/]
  GS --> EGSE["EGSE"]
  GS --> MCS["MCS"]
  GS --> STA["Ground station"] --> BB["Baseband equipment"] --> TMD["Telemetry decoder"]
  TMD -.activity.-> SON2[["Switch On"]]
  TMD -.reporting data.-> LOCK[/"Telemetry Lock Status"/]

Example SSM fragment, redrawn after the example of Figure 4-2 of the standard: system elements are boxes, activities double boxes, events rounded, reporting data parallelograms.14

The procedure language refers to system elements, activities, reporting data and events but does not define them; it defines only the procedural script.13 The SSM supplies the common definition of every activity:15

Activity data in the SSM Procedure-specific data in the SSM Name, description, type (procedure, telecommand or operating system call), associated system element Default execution mode (manual or automatic) Version number and configuration history; validation status (testing status) Activation mode (permanently active, or explicitly initiated) Validity period (earliest and latest date of execution); mean, minimum and maximum duration The procedural script Arguments, each with name, description, engineering units, data type and default value; allowed combinations of argument values Planning attributes such as the resource profile (on-board power, downlink bandwidth)

ECSS-E-ST-70-31C turns this into data requirements: every procedure has an initiation mode (background or foreground) and earliest and latest validity dates; a ground procedure adds a script "written according to" PLUTO and a default execution mode (automatic or manual); an onboard procedure adds a script compliant with ECSS-E-ST-70-01, a "preloaded on board" flag and a high, medium or low priority.80 Arguments therefore live outside the script: a procedure receives them at initiation and cannot change them.21

docs.title: Terms
docs.text:
Term (§3.2) Definition (paraphrased) activity A space system monitoring and control function compound parameter A record of any sequence of reporting data, arrays of reporting data and sub-records interpreted together confirmation body Part of a procedure or step that assesses whether its objective has been achieved continuation test Construct that defines how a procedure or step proceeds after a constituent step or activity has executed event A condition or set of conditions that can arise during a test session or mission phase initiation The act of requesting the execution of a step or activity main body Part of a procedure or step dedicated to achieving its objectives parameter The lowest level of elementary information meaningful for monitoring the space system preconditions body Part of a procedure that ensures it executes only if or when predefined initial conditions hold procedure A means of interacting with the space system to achieve an objective or a sequence of objectives reporting data Data used to assess the functioning of the space system (a parameter or a compound parameter) space system model The space system described as system elements, the activities on them, the reporting data that reflects their state and the events raised and handled for their control statement A language element which, with others, implements the goal of a procedure or step step A component of a procedure that achieves a well-defined sub-goal system element A functional element of the space system as represented in the SSM watchdog body Part of a procedure or step that manages contingencies arising during its execution watchdog step A component of the watchdog body that detects one contingency condition and executes corrective actions

Source: §3.2.6 The standard's own abbreviations are AIV, EBNF, EGSE, EMCS, FCP, FOP, MMI (man-machine interface), PLUTO, SCOE (special check-out equipment) and SSM.7

docs.title: Requirements on any procedure language (clause 5)
docs.text: Clause 5 is the normative heart of the standard. It is written for any language, and PLUTO is the one that satisfies it.

docs.title: Procedure structure (§5.1)
docs.text:
Req. Capability a, b Build a high-level, goal-oriented activity (a procedure) from elementary activities (telecommands, operating system calls); a procedure may call other procedures c, d, e Define self-contained sub-goals, each reached by one activity call or a sequence of them; activities can take arguments passed at initiation f A step construct encapsulates complex logic (waiting for a time or a condition, conditional branching) g Sub-goals can run in series or in parallel h, i, j Preconditions (to be fulfilled before start) and confirmation conditions (whether the goal was met) for procedures, and also for steps k–n Contingency actions besides the nominal flow: for a procedure, on space system anomalies, on failure of the nominal path or on other events or conditions; for a step, on failure of its nominal path or on other events or conditions o, p A contingency action should be taken at the level where the failure occurs, and should either fix the anomaly or report it and return control to the nominal flow q If the anomaly cannot be fixed, one of these actions shall be performed: raise an event to flag it at a higher level; reach the goal another way and terminate; abort r While a contingency action runs, the body of the procedure or step is suspended

Source: §5.1.17

docs.title: Language constructs (§5.2)
docs.text:
The 24 requirements of §5.2 list what a procedure must be able to do:18

  • Initiate activities (a–d): request any space system activity; request it and continue at once; or request it and wait for confirmation, then test the result to decide what to do next.
  • Acquire data (e): execution or confirmation status of an activity; initiation, start, termination or completion time of its last execution; the value, validity status, overall or detailed monitoring status (limit, delta, expected-status and status-consistency checks) and sampling time of reporting data; the time of the last occurrence of an event.
  • Replace missing functions (f): when a space system function is not available (for example in an early test phase), set an activity's confirmation status, or a parameter's value, validity status, monitoring statuses or sampling time.
  • Snapshot (g): make a local copy of reporting data so that several properties used by successive statements are sampled at the same instant, avoiding the asynchronous update problem.
  • Generic EMCS access (h): request any operation and read any property of any space system object.
  • Flow control (i): if-then-else, multi-way branching on a parameter or variable, loops (fixed count, while a condition holds, until a condition becomes true), and waits until an absolute time, for an interval, until a condition is true or until an event occurs.
  • Variables and events (j–m): typed local variables, assignment, and local events declared in the procedure or step and raised by it (for example to trigger a contingency action).
  • Expressions and units (n–s): the Annex C functions (should), expressions over constants, parameters from the EMCS, activity arguments and local variables; engineering units on constants, free mixing of compatible units and automatic conversion between them.
  • Comments and users (t–w): comments; messages for user acknowledgement; messages to the procedure execution log; input from the user.
  • Pre- and confirmation conditions (x): any combination of waiting until a time, for an interval, until a condition or until an event, testing a condition, or asking the user for the outcome.

docs.title: Language specification (§5.3)
docs.text: A conforming language shall be formally specified in ISO EBNF (ISO/IEC 14977). PLUTO, with the engineering units and functions of the annexes, should be used for automating procedures in development and exploitation. Using PLUTO ensures conformance with every requirement of the standard and eases the transfer of procedures from functional testing to operations.19

docs.title: The structure of a PLUTO procedure
docs.text:
A procedure has five bodies, in a fixed order; only the main body is mandatory:2044

Body Keyword pair Presence Purpose Execution status while active Declaration declare … end declare optional Declares the procedure's local events (procedure level: events only) – Preconditions preconditions … end preconditions optional Holds the procedure until, or runs it only if, initial conditions are met "preconditions" Main main … end main mandatory Achieves the goal through activities and steps, in sequence or in parallel "executing" Watchdog watchdog … end watchdog optional One or more watchdog steps, all initiated in parallel, each watching for one contingency "executing" Confirmation confirmation … end confirmation optional Decides whether the goal was achieved "confirmation" 
flowchart TB
  subgraph EX["Executing"]
    M["Main body<br/>sub-goals in sequence or in parallel<br/>(steps and activities)"]
    W["Watchdog body<br/>watchdog steps, all in parallel"]
  end
  D["Declaration body<br/>(local events)"] --> P["Preconditions body<br/>(wait / if / ask user)"]
  P --> M
  P --> W
  M --> C["Confirmation body<br/>(wait / if / ask user)"]
  W -- "terminate" --> C

The elements of a procedure, after Figure A-1.20

Preconditions and confirmation bodies accept any combination of: wait until an absolute time, wait for an interval, wait until a condition becomes true, a Boolean if test, and a decision requested from the user; the keyword then chains several conditions.22254563 If an if expression is false, or a wait in the preconditions times out, the procedure (or step) is skipped and its confirmation status becomes "aborted"; a raise-event action after a timeout is not available in a preconditions body, because the watchdog has not started yet.4546 In the confirmation body a false condition or an expired wait gives "not confirmed".63

The procedure main body may contain only seven statement types: set procedure context, initiate in parallel, initiate and confirm step, initiate and confirm activity, initiate activity, inform user, and log. All computation (assignments, loops, waits) therefore happens inside steps.2349

The procedure watchdog body detects and reacts to system-level events such as anomalies, keeps procedure-level invariants true for the whole run, and handles failures that a step's own watchdog could not handle. It need not fix everything itself: it can suspend or abort the procedure while another procedure handles the anomaly. Concurrent watchdog steps watch independent conditions; a triggered watchdog step suspends the main body while the others keep monitoring, so contingencies that interact must be handled within one watchdog step. Error handling after a procedure has ended belongs to the caller.24

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
A step has the same five-body structure, with these differences:2651

  • Its preconditions body is optional for a main-body step but mandatory for a watchdog step, where it is a single wait statement that defines the contingency being watched.2628
  • Watchdog steps have no watchdog body of their own.26
  • A step name is unique within its procedure and can be used to refer to the step.26
  • Step-level declarations add local variables (with an engineering value, a validity status and a sampling time, visible in the step, its lower-level steps and its watchdog steps) and enumerated sets, plus local events that only the step's own watchdog body can use. Before its first assignment a variable's validity status is "not available" according to §A.3.9.14, but "invalid" according to §A.1.7.2.2752
  • A step main body accepts the full statement set (below); a procedure main body only seven.2953
  • The step watchdog body handles failures in the step's main body and keeps step-level invariants; error handling after the step ends belongs to the caller.30
Statement Procedure main body Step main body Clause Set context (in the context of … do … end context) yes yes A.3.9.10, A.3.9.16 Initiate in parallel yes yes A.3.9.11 Initiate and confirm step yes yes A.3.9.12 Initiate and confirm activity yes yes A.3.9.26 Initiate activity yes yes A.3.9.27 Inform user yes yes A.3.9.29 Log yes yes A.3.9.30 Assignment (:=) – yes A.3.9.17 Flow control (if, case, repeat, while, for) – yes A.3.9.18–A.3.9.23 Wait – yes A.3.9.4 Object operation request – yes A.3.9.24 Save context – yes A.3.9.25

Source: §A.1.4, §A.1.7.4, §A.3.9.9 and §A.3.9.15.23294953

docs.title: Behaviour: execution and confirmation status
docs.text:
Every procedure, step and activity carries two statuses that the caller can monitor:31

  • the execution status: "not initiated" (steps and activities), "preconditions", "routing" (telecommands only), "executing", "confirmation" or "completed";3168
  • the confirmation status: "not available" until completion, then "confirmed", "not confirmed" or "aborted".31

docs.title: Procedure
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Preconditions: initiate
  Preconditions --> Executing: preconditions OK
  Preconditions --> Completed: preconditions not OK (aborted)
  state Executing {
    Main --> Watchdog: contingency detected (main suspended)
    Watchdog --> Main: resume
  }
  Executing --> Confirmation: main body completed, or watchdog "terminate"
  Executing --> Completed: abort (aborted)
  Confirmation --> Completed: confirmation completed (confirmed / not confirmed)

Execution states of a procedure, after Figure A-2.31

  1. Preconditions. On initiation the preconditions body runs ("preconditions", "not available"). If they hold, the watchdog body starts (all watchdog-step preconditions are initiated) and then the main body; if not, the procedure completes as "aborted". Without user preconditions both bodies start immediately.31
  2. Main body. Statements run in sequence ("executing", "not available"). Each initiate and confirm statement ends with a continuation test whose outcome is: continue; restart the step or activity from its preconditions; raise a local event for a watchdog step; or abort the procedure.31
  3. Watchdog. If no contingency occurs, the watchdog body ends when the main body ends. If one occurs, the main body is suspended: the atomic statement in progress completes, but its follow-on action is not taken. Every statement except initiate-and-confirm step, initiate activity, initiate-and-confirm activity and initiate in parallel is atomic; inside an initiate-in-parallel, all branches are suspended once their current atomic statements end. The watchdog step then returns one of four continuation actions: resume (main body continues where it stopped and the watchdog step is restarted), terminate (the goal was reached another way; main and watchdog bodies end and confirmation starts), raise event (pass the problem to another watchdog step) or abort.31
  4. Two watchdogs at once. A second watchdog step triggered while the first runs executes in parallel; control returns to the main body only when both have finished; each is restarted when it completes; an "abort" from either aborts the procedure at once.31 If the returned actions differ, the user is asked.62
  5. Confirmation. When every step and activity initiated by the main body has completed (including the remaining branches of an "until one completes" parallel statement), the watchdog body ends and the confirmation body runs, giving "confirmed" or "not confirmed".31
  6. Implicit confirmation. Without a confirmation body: after a watchdog "terminate" the procedure takes the watchdog step's confirmation status; otherwise it is "confirmed" only if every activity and step initiated by the main body was confirmed, and "not confirmed" in all other cases. If an initiated step or activity raised an event in its continuation test, the watchdog step that caught it decides.3163

For a procedure, what happens after it ends is left to the caller; for steps and activities the continuation test inside the calling statement decides.32

docs.title: Step and activity
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> NotInitiated
  NotInitiated --> Precondition: initiate
  Precondition --> Executing: preconditions OK (step)
  Precondition --> Routing: preconditions OK (activity: route)
  Routing --> Executing: execute
  Precondition --> ContinuationTest: preconditions not OK (abort)
  Routing --> ContinuationTest: abort
  Executing --> Confirmation: execution completed / terminated
  Executing --> ContinuationTest: abort
  Confirmation --> ContinuationTest
  ContinuationTest --> Precondition: restart
  ContinuationTest --> Completed: complete

Execution states of a step (Figure A-3) and of an activity (Figure A-4) combined; the "Routing" state applies to activities only.3233

A step runs its preconditions, main and watchdog bodies exactly as a procedure does, then its confirmation body, and finally the continuation test of the statement that initiated it, which maps the confirmation status ("confirmed", "not confirmed" or "aborted") to a continuation action; "restart" sends it back to "preconditions", anything else completes it. Missing preconditions or confirmation use the same defaults as a procedure.32

An activity is executed by the EMCS, not by the procedure. The EMCS reports progress notifications for the state transitions and for type-specific sub-states, such as the routing stages of a telecommand ("released from EMCS", "reception by ground station", "reception on-board"). Initiate activity does not wait; initiate and confirm activity waits and applies a continuation test.33

docs.title: Continuation tests and their defaults
docs.text:
A continuation test holds up to three couplets of confirmation status and continuation action; missing couplets take default actions. The allowed combinations differ between main-body and watchdog statements:3564

Main bodyWatchdog Confirmation status resume abort restart ask user raise event continue terminate confirmed – – – allowed – default – not confirmed – allowed allowed default allowed allowed – aborted – default allowed allowed allowed – – Confirmation status resume abort restart ask user raise event continue terminate confirmed default allowed – allowed – – allowed not confirmed allowed allowed – default allowed – allowed aborted – default – allowed – – –

"–" means forbidden. Read from Figures A-5 and A-6 of the standard.35

Action Meaning resume Watchdog only: resume the suspended main body where it was suspended abort Abort the procedure (or step) restart Main body only: run the initiate-and-confirm statement again; may be bounded by a timeout (relative to the statement's start) or max times, after which an event is raised for a watchdog step or the parent is aborted ask user Ask the user how to proceed; in a main body the user may choose any action except resume, ask user and terminate; in a watchdog any except continue and ask user raise event Raise a local event, caught by a watchdog step; the main body then resumes where it was suspended continue Main body only: carry on with the next statement terminate Watchdog only: end the main body early and start the confirmation body

Source: §A.2.5 and §A.3.9.33.3564 A watchdog initiate and confirm step is re-initiated after it completes unless its action was "abort".35 The allowed combinations may be widened for special tests: a test that checks that a critical command such as "deploy solar array" is rejected can treat "aborted" as success and map it to "continue".35

docs.title: Parallel execution
docs.text: in parallel until all complete (the default) or in parallel until one completes starts all of its steps and activities at once.50 With "until one completes", the first to finish lets the calling body move on; the others keep running and their continuation actions still apply, except "continue", which then does nothing. With "until all complete", each branch's action is handled as it arrives: "abort" aborts the parent and all other branches at once; "restart" restarts that branch (resetting it to "preconditions" and "not available") and the parallel statement cannot end until it finishes again; "raise event" is raised at once and suspends the main body through a watchdog step.34

docs.title: Lexical conventions
docs.text:
• Notation. Each construct is a grammar rule (a non-terminal symbol) defined from non-terminal and terminal symbols, drawn as a railroad diagram (main line mandatory, branch lines optional, return lines repetition, rectangles for non-terminals, rounded boxes for terminals) and repeated in ISO EBNF in clause A.4.3669
  • Case. Only engineering units are case-sensitive; everything else, including keywords, is not. Spaces inside multi-word keywords count as single blanks.3738
  • Comments run from /* to */.37
  • Keywords may be several words ("not confirmed", "execution status", "is contained in"). If an SSM object is named with a keyword, the implementation resolves the ambiguity by grammar precedence, but the standard warns against names that confuse readers.38
  • Identifiers are one or more words separated by spaces; the first word starts with a letter, each word is letters and digits. Switch on Gyro5 in Fine Mode is one identifier. Identifiers are unique in their context (a step name in its procedure); objects elsewhere are reached by an object reference path.39

docs.title: Constants
docs.text:
Constant Form Examples from the standard Boolean TRUE, FALSE – Enumerated Characters in double quotes; \" and \\ escape quote and backslash "red", "not confirmed" Integer Optional sign, digits, optional engineering unit; or hexadecimal 0x followed by 0–9, A–F 23 A, 2056, 0x2056, 0xFFFF Real Optional sign, digits, optional fraction, optional exponent e, optional unit 123.56e12, 0.1, 23E6, 5.3 [kg/m^3] String Characters in double quotes – Absolute time YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ss.f[Z] or YYYY-DDDThh:mm:ss.f[Z] (day of year 001–366; seconds up to 60 in a leap second; any number of fraction digits) 2001-08-18T21:07:43.137468Z, 2001-033T13:21:32.226 Relative time Sum of d, h, min, s components, or [sign]days:hh:mm:ss 30 h 10 min, 200 s, - 0:00:10:00

Source: §A.3.6.40 In the colon form, the railroad diagram shows the fraction of a second introduced by a full stop, while the EBNF rule of clause A.4 writes a colon.4070

docs.title: Types
docs.text:
Predefined type Values Boolean true, false Enumerated set reference A named set of enumerated values, defined system-wide or locally within a procedure (declared in a step declaration body) Signed integer, unsigned integer, real Implementation subsets of those numbers String Character strings Absolute time, relative time Dates (such as 2003-02-15) and intervals (such as 2 s) Property value set The set of all values of a property of an SSM object (for example all APIDs defined for system elements) Property data type The type inherited from a property of an SSM object (for example "real with engineering units V" for a battery voltage)

Source: Table A-1 and §A.3.9.14.4152 In an assignment the two sides must be type-compatible.41

docs.title: Object references
docs.text: Objects are reached with of chains, read from the specific to the general: Temperature of Catalyst Bed of Thruster X of Thruster Main Branch. A reference may start with an explicit object type (variable, predefined value set, activity statement, step, argument, system element, reporting data, parameter, record, array, activity, event).48 When the type is omitted and a name is not unique in the SSM, the 14 precedence levels resolve it, from highest to lowest: variable, local reporting data, local event, activity statement, step, argument, system element, reporting data, parameter, record, array, activity, predefined value set, system event.48 Inside expressions a bare identifier resolves first to a local variable (searched upwards through the step hierarchy), then to a procedure argument, a function name, and finally an object name.65

docs.title: Expressions and operators
docs.text:
The grammar builds expressions as Boolean combinations (AND, OR, XOR) of relational expressions; each relational expression is a term optionally followed by a comparative expression; terms are sums, products and powers of factors.65 Besides the six relational operators (=, !=, <, >, <=, >=), comparative expressions offer between A and B, within C [unit or %] of T and set membership in (T1, T2, ...).65 A factor can be a constant, an argument or variable reference, an object property request, a function call, a parenthesised expression, a signed factor, a NOT factor, or ask user (prompt [default value]) [expect type], which makes the user an input source.6571

Operator (descending precedence) Operand types → result unary -, unary + integer or real → same NOT Boolean → Boolean ** integer**integer → integer; any real operand → real * numbers as usual; relative time × number → relative time / integer / integer → real; relative time / number → relative time + numbers; absolute + relative → absolute; relative + relative → relative; string + anything → string (concatenation) - numbers; absolute − absolute → relative; absolute − relative → absolute; relative − relative → relative =, !=, <, >, <=, >= numbers, strings (case-insensitive), relative times, absolute times → Boolean AND, OR, XOR Boolean → Boolean

Source: Table A-4.66 Boolean expressions are always evaluated completely, without short-circuit: the standard's own warning is that X > 0 AND Y/X = Z still divides by zero when X is 0.66
