docs.text:
The 36 constructs of clause A.3.9 (the two context statements share a row):

Construct Shape (simplified from the EBNF) Notes Clause, PDF p. Procedure Definition procedure [declare] [preconditions] main [watchdog] [confirmation] end procedure Five bodies, main mandatory A.3.9.1, 47 Procedure Declaration Body declare event N [described by "…"], … end declare Events only, used by the procedure watchdog A.3.9.2, 48 Preconditions Body preconditions (if E | Wait) {then (if E | Wait)} end preconditions False or timed out → "aborted" A.3.9.3, 49 Wait Statement wait until E | wait for E | wait for event R, then [save context] [timeout] Until an absolute time or a Boolean; for a relative time or an event A.3.9.4, 50 Save Context save context refer to R by N {, to R by N} Snapshot taken when the wait condition is met A.3.9.5, 51 Timeout timeout E [raise event N] Not allowed with "for a relative time" or "until an absolute time" waits A.3.9.6, 53 Raise Event raise event N Local events only A.3.9.7, 54 Object Reference [type] name {of reference} 14-level precedence A.3.9.8, 55 Procedure Main Body main {statement ;} end main (keywords optional) Seven statement types A.3.9.9, 57 Set Procedure / Step Context in the context of R do {statement ;} end context R is a system element or a (record) compound parameter A.3.9.10/16, 59/69 Initiate In Parallel in parallel [until all complete | until one completes] S ; S ; … end parallel At least two branches A.3.9.11, 60 Initiate And Confirm Step initiate and confirm step N <step definition> end step [continuation test] Waits for the step to finish A.3.9.12, 62 Step Definition [declare] [preconditions] main [watchdog] [confirmation] Same bodies as a procedure A.3.9.13, 63 Step Declaration Body declare enumerated sets, variable V of type T [with units U], events end declare Variables visible downwards A.3.9.14, 64 Step Main Body main {statement ;} end main Twelve statement types A.3.9.15, 67 Assignment V := E Only declared variables A.3.9.17, 70 Flow Control if, case, repeat, while, for – A.3.9.18, 71 If if E then … [else …] end if – A.3.9.19, 72 Case in case E is tag : … {or is tag : …} [otherwise : …] end case First matching tag wins A.3.9.20, 73 Repeat repeat … until E [timeout] Body runs at least once A.3.9.21, 75 While while E [timeout] do … end while Timeout acts at the end of an iteration A.3.9.22, 76 For for V := E to E [by E] do … end for Bounds evaluated once; counter read-only A.3.9.23, 77 Object Operation Request operation [of R] [with [arg :=] E, … end with] set <property> or a non-standard operation A.3.9.24, 79 Save Context Statement save context … as a statement – A.3.9.25, 81 Initiate And Confirm Activity initiate and confirm <activity call> [refer by S] [continuation test] Waits for completion A.3.9.26, 82 Initiate Activity initiate <activity call> [refer by S] Runs in parallel with the caller A.3.9.27, 83 Activity Call A [with arguments … end with | with value set … end with] [with directives … end with] See below A.3.9.28, 84 Inform User inform user E {, E} Does not wait for the acknowledgement A.3.9.29, 88 Log log E {, E} To the procedure execution log A.3.9.30, 89 Watchdog Body watchdog <initiate and confirm step> ; … end watchdog Watchdog steps in parallel A.3.9.31, 90 Confirmation Body confirmation (if E | Wait) {then …} end confirmation False or timed out → "not confirmed" A.3.9.32, 92 Continuation Test in case status : action ; … end case Defaults per Figures A-5/A-6 A.3.9.33, 93 Expression see above – A.3.9.34, 96 Function name ( [E {, E}] ) Annex C or non-standard A.3.9.35, 101 Object Property Request [[get] property of] R [with … end with] Standard and non-standard properties A.3.9.36, 102

Sources: clauses A.3.9.1 to A.3.9.36 and the EBNF of A.4.2.4369 Further rules worth knowing:

  • A case statement compares the in case expression with each tag; the first match runs, and otherwise runs only when nothing matched. Tags may combine comparative expressions with AND/OR/XOR.55
  • A for loop evaluates its three expressions once at the start; the default step is +1; the counter may be read but not assigned.58
  • A while loop whose timeout expires in the middle of a multi-statement iteration completes the iteration first; the timeout acts at the end.57 Repeat and while timeouts either raise an event for a watchdog step or abort the parent step.5657
  • An activity statement named with refer by is the initiation instance of an activity, an EMCS dynamic object that inherits all activity properties and operations; inside a loop it always refers to the latest iteration.60
  • A variable name reused in a lower-level step hides the parent's variable.54
  • A save context creates local reporting data that is "not available" until created, takes all properties of the source when created, and lives only for the current procedure instance.47

docs.title: Activity calls, arguments and directives
docs.text: An activity call names the activity and supplies either explicit arguments or a predefined value set from the operations database, plus optional directives.61 Arguments are simple (an expression, or a reference to an activity, parameter or reporting data, system element or event), records (recursive groups of arguments, as in ECSS-E-70-41) or arrays. Either all arguments are named or none are, in which case their order defines them.61 Directives are specific to an activity type rather than to one activity; for telecommands the standard lists the MAP ID, AD or BD transmission mode, and the verification packets to request.61 Its examples of simple arguments are also PUS-flavoured: a parameter reference for a ST[12] request, a system element (APID) for a ST[14] request, and an activity call as the argument of a ST[11] TC[11,4] insertion into the on-board schedule, where each scheduled command is a record with the telecommand, its release time, sub-schedule and interlock fields.61

docs.title: Standard properties and operations
docs.text:
Two generic mechanisms reach any EMCS service: the object property request (read a property) and the object operation request (do something to an object). "Standard" ones are supported by every EMCS; implementations may add others.42

Object Standard property requests (result) Activity or step execution status; initiation time (when the preconditions check began); start time (start of execution by the destination application process for a telecommand, start of the main body for a procedure or step); termination time; confirmation status; restart number; completion time (end of confirmation for a procedure or step, end of end-to-end verification for a telecommand) Reporting data, variable, argument validity status ("not available", "valid", "invalid"); sampling time; value (engineering values only); monitoring status; status consistency check status; limit check status ("danger high", "warning high", "within limits", "warning low", "danger low"); delta check status; expected check status (each "not available", "nominal" or "failed" unless stated) Event last raise time

Sources: Tables A-5, A-6 and A-7.67 Property requests on an activity refer by default to its last initiation; within a loop only the latest iteration is available; a restart counter is kept.68 Two shorthands keep scripts readable: naming a property alone implies get, and naming a parameter alone implies get value.67 The standard operations mirror the replace-missing-function requirement: set confirmation status for activities and steps; set validity status, set value, set monitoring status, set status consistency check status, set limit check status, set delta check status and set expected check status for reporting data, variables and arguments. Events have none. These operations are meant for configurations in which the spacecraft or the EMCS health monitoring is absent.59

docs.title: Engineering units (Annex B)
docs.text:
PLUTO constants and variables carry units, and §5.2 requires automatic conversion between compatible ones.18 Annex B defines the symbols, based on a 2003 proposal for representing SI units in character strings:72

  • Simple units (Table B-1) include the SI base units, min, h, d, AU, pc, u, L, t, degC, rad, deg, arcmin, arcsec, r (revolution), sr, the derived SI units (Hz … Sv, with Ohm spelled out), bar, eV, dB, Np, bit, B (byte) and Bd.73
  • Prefixes: decimal Y to da and d to y (micro is u); binary Ki to Ei only for bit and B. No prefixes on dB, AU, pc, u, min, h, d; only submultiples on L, Np, deg, arcmin, arcsec, degC, rad, sr; only multiples on t, B, r, Bd; no compound prefixes.73
  • Compound units: multiplication with ., division with / (not repeated outside parentheses), exponent after ^, negative exponents allowed, fractional exponents in parentheses: kg.m^2/s, W/(m^2.K), s^-1.73 Units may be written in square brackets after a number, as in 5.3 [kg/m^3].4074

Missions that need further units should follow the same syntax.73

docs.title: Functions (Annex C)
docs.text:
Group Functions Mathematical (Table C-1) abs, acos, acosec, acosec2, acotan, acotan2, asec, asec2, asin, atan, atan2, average, ceiling, cos, cosec, cosh, cotan, floor, ln, log, max, min, quotient, remainder, round, sec, sin, sinh, sqrt, tan, tanh, truncate, and the constants pi(), e(), G() Time (Table C-2) current time, year, month, day of month, day of week, day of year, hour, minute, second, days, hours, minutes, seconds String (Table C-3) to string (optionally converting to given units), to Boolean, to hex, to integer, to real, capitalize, get from, insert in, is contained in, length of, lower case, omit from, position of, upper case

Sources: Annex C.75 Functions respect units: max (1 V, 100 mV) is 1 V, to string (5 V, mV) is "5000 mV", and hours (2 d 5 h 30 min) is 53.5 h.75

docs.title: A worked example
docs.text:
Illustrative PLUTO procedure

The following procedure was constructed for this page from the grammar of clause A.4; it is not taken from the standard or from a mission. All object names are invented.

procedure
  declare
    event Heater Overcurrent described by "Line current above limit"
  end declare
  preconditions
    wait until Bus Voltage of Power Subsystem > 27 V timeout 2 min
  end preconditions
  main
    initiate and confirm step Warm Up
      declare
        variable Target of type real with units degC
      end declare
      main
        Target := 20 degC;
        initiate and confirm Switch On Heater with arguments Line := 3 end with
          in case not confirmed : restart max times 2; end case;
        wait until Temperature of Camera > Target timeout 30 min;
        log "Camera at ", to string (Temperature of Camera);
      end main
    end step;
    initiate and confirm Switch Off Heater with arguments Line := 3 end with;
  end main
  watchdog
    initiate and confirm step Overcurrent Guard
      preconditions
        wait until Current of Heater Line 3 > 1.5 A
      end preconditions
      main
        initiate and confirm Switch Off Heater with arguments Line := 3 end with;
        inform user "Heater line 3 switched off by watchdog";
      end main
    end step
      in case confirmed : terminate; end case;
  end watchdog
  confirmation
    if Temperature of Camera >= 20 degC
  end confirmation
end procedure

How it runs, following clause A.2:

  1. The procedure enters "preconditions" and waits up to 2 minutes for the bus voltage. On a timeout it completes as "aborted", because no watchdog exists yet to catch an event.46
  2. When the voltage condition holds, the watchdog step Overcurrent Guard starts waiting on its single wait precondition, then the main body starts ("executing").31
  3. In Warm Up, if the heater command is "not confirmed" the explicit couplet restarts it up to twice; "aborted" falls back to the main-body default "abort"; "confirmed" takes the default "continue".6435
  4. If the line current exceeds 1.5 A, the main body is suspended after its current atomic statement, the watchdog step switches the heater off and, when confirmed, returns "terminate": the main and watchdog bodies end and the confirmation body runs.3135
  5. The confirmation body sets "confirmed" only if the camera reached 20 degC; otherwise the procedure ends "not confirmed", and what happens next is up to its caller.6332

docs.title: Observations on the text
docs.text:
Inference

These points come from this wiki's reading of the 2008 text and are not discussed in it:

  • Several examples in the standard declare variables in a short form such as unsigned integer Counter or real AvgeTemp units degC, which does not match the variable … of type … [with units …] rule of the grammar.586752
  • The relative-time colon form ends with a full stop before the fraction in the railroad diagram but with a colon in the EBNF.4070
  • ECSS-E-ST-70-31C points twice to "Table 6 of ECSS-E-ST-70-32" for operator operand types; in ECSS-E-ST-70-32C that table is numbered A-4, which is how a third passage of ECSS-E-ST-70-31C cites it.8166
  • The text of A.2.5 says a user asked in a watchdog may choose any action except continue and ask user, while Figure A-6 forbids "restart" in watchdogs.35

docs.title: PLUTO across the ECSS ground standards
docs.text:
PLUTO is wired into the other E-70 standards:

  • ECSS-E-ST-70-31C assumes conformance to ECSS-E-ST-70-32, requires clause 5 for procedures, uses PLUTO as the data type of procedure definitions, reuses the PLUTO Activity Call syntax (A.3.9.28) for its own Activity Call data type, takes its engineering units from Annex B and its functions from Annex C.767780787981
  • ECSS-E-ST-70C summarises ECSS-E-ST-70-32 in its table of level-3 standards and defines, in Annex I, the human-readable layout of an operations procedure: preconditions, a body of steps (sequential or parallel), an optional contingency element and post-conditions.8283
  • ECSS-E-ST-70-01C (on-board control procedures, 2010) asks for a very similar structure on board: declaration, preconditions, main and confirmation bodies, steps, and a contingency handling body instead of a watchdog.84
Concept ECSS-E-ST-70C Annex I (procedure document) PLUTO (ECSS-E-ST-70-32C) OBCP (ECSS-E-ST-70-01C) Start conditions Pre-conditions (mission phase, ground and space configuration, orbit or environment, other procedures) Preconditions body Preconditions body Body Steps in sequence or parallel; each step with pre-conditions, body, post-conditions Main body of steps and activities, in parallel Main body; steps uniquely identified Contingency Contingency element: restore and resume, reach the goal another way and stop, or abort Watchdog body with resume / terminate / abort Contingency handling body End check Post-conditions; status "success confirmed" or "procedure failed" Confirmation body; "confirmed", "not confirmed", "aborted" Confirmation body; implicit status if absent

Sources: ECSS-E-ST-70C Annex I, ECSS-E-ST-70-32C A.1 and ECSS-E-ST-70-01C §5.1.832084 The three contingency outcomes of Annex I match the "resume", "terminate" and "abort" watchdog actions one for one.8335

docs.title: No PLUTO in SCOS-2000; TOPE instead
docs.text:
None of the SCOS-2000 documents in this wiki's library describes a PLUTO interpreter. The ESTEC user manual of the SCOS-2000-based EMCS (issue 4.0, March 2004) states the situation plainly: ESA had started developing PLUTO software for preparing and executing procedures with SCOS-2000, but since it was not yet available, a Tcl/Tk procedure environment called TOPE (the manual's heading reads "The Test and Operation Procedure Environment") had been delivered to the Herschel/Planck instrument teams.85 TOPE initiates telecommands and SCOE commands, follows their execution through the reports sent back by SCOS-2000, and monitors telemetry and ground parameters.85 Four years earlier, ESA's SCOS-2000 presentation to FIRST/Planck had proposed reusing the TCL/TK procedure automation tool of the PROBA checkout facility, which PROBA used for both AIV and operations.8687 The TOPE language itself is described on SCOS-2000 as EGSE.

The two languages share the same concepts, and the mapping is close:

PLUTO construct Nearest TOPE command (EMCS SUM issue 4.0) initiate <telecommand> tcsend <cmd> … nowait (by default tcsend waits until the ground stage UV_GS_RECEIVE)88 initiate and confirm <telecommand> with a continuation test tcsend <cmd> referby v then waitfor v -until {[getcompleted $v]}, with Tcl logic for the outcome91 Directives (MAP ID, AD/BD, verification packets) tcsend options mapid, vcid, ack {ACCEPT START PROGRESS COMPLETE}, checks, settransfermode AD/BD8889 get value of P, validity and monitoring status fetch P with getengvalue, israwvaluevalid, getoolstate, getsccstate, gettimestamp90 wait until <condition> subscribe P referby v and waitfor v -until {…}91 wait for <relative time> waittime <time>92 Watchdog step watchdog <name> triggeredby <vars> <condition> <action> (not available on TOPE/CCS)93 log putlog, openlog, closelog94

Inference

The mapping in this table is this wiki's comparison. The EMCS manual does not compare TOPE with PLUTO beyond saying that TOPE stands in for PLUTO software that was not yet available. TOPE lacks PLUTO's built-in step state machine, continuation defaults and engineering-unit arithmetic; a TOPE script gets those only through Tcl code written by the user.

docs.title: Command sequences in the MIB
docs.text:
What the SCOS-2000 MIB itself can store is far simpler than PLUTO: command sequences, ordered lists of commands and nested sequences with formal parameters, defined in the tables csf, css, sdf and csp (see sequences). A nested sequence is expanded like a macro when the sequence is loaded; elements carry release and execution delta times (relative to the previous command or to the sequence start), grouping and blocking flags, interlock scope and stage, and flags to override PTV checks or disable CEV checks.959798

Inference

None of the sequence fields defined in the ICD expresses a branch, a loop, a wait for a telemetry condition or a confirmation check. Read in PLUTO terms, a sequence is a main body of initiate statements whose timing is fixed in advance, with interlocks as the only feedback. This comparison is the wiki's; the ICD does not mention PLUTO.

The Solar Orbiter MIB of 16 September 2025 shows how much of the operations material takes this form, and where it comes from:99

Quantity (Solar Orbiter MIB, 2025-09-16) Value Sequences (csf) 3 404, with 13 879 elements (css): 12 629 commands and 1 250 nested sequences Elements timed relative to the previous command / to the sequence start (CSS_RELTYPE) 10 475 / 3 404 Elements with a non-zero release delta (CSS_RELTIME; 3 196 are zero and 44 empty) 10 639 Elements with interlock scope 'N' (no interlock) and stage 'C' 12 494 Elements that disable CEV checks (CSS_CEV = 'Y') 17 Largest sequence / mean size (CSF_ELEMS) 312 / about 4.1 elements Sequences whose source document (CSF_DOCNAME) is an FCP / a CRP / other 2 243 / 1 091 / 70 Sequences that contain a service 18 "load and start OBCP" or other OBCP command 22

The CSF_DOCNAME field records the document from which a sequence was generated.96 In this MIB the names follow a pattern of a two-character prefix (mostly a subsystem code such as DM, AC or SY), FCP or CRP, and a number (for example SY-FCP-010 and IA-CRP-071); a Herschel/Planck naming convention uses the same two families, flight control procedures (FCP) and contingency recovery procedures (CRP).99100 Three real examples, each a single command that starts an on-board control procedure: ASYF010B "Config DST via OBCP v11" (from SY-FCP-010, 18 formal parameters), AITF124B "OBCP_HVdoorRmpUp v02" (from IT-FCP-124, no formal parameters) and AIAC071A "SWA HIS Start HAMMER v02" (from IA-CRP-071, 6 formal parameters). Their single elements are the "Load and start OBCP" commands ZCPX0003 (TTC2), ZCPX0004 (METIS_HVdoorRmpUp) and ZCPX0011 (SWA8), all TC(18,140).99

Inference

That each sequence implements a step or the whole of a written FCP or CRP is deduced from the CSF_DOCNAME values; the MIB does not say how much of each procedure is left to operators. The three sequences above also suggest that, where logic is needed, Solar Orbiter moves it on board: they simply start OBCPs, whose required language capabilities are the subject of ECSS-E-ST-70-01C.

SQL used 
-- Solar Orbiter MIB 2025-09-16 (solo-2025-09-16.sqlite)
SELECT count(*) FROM csf;                                  -- 3404
SELECT CSS_TYPE, count(*) FROM css GROUP BY 1;             -- C 12629, S 1250
SELECT CSS_RELTYPE, count(*) FROM css GROUP BY 1;          -- A 3404, R 10475
SELECT CASE WHEN CSS_RELTIME IS NULL OR CSS_RELTIME = '' THEN 'empty'
            WHEN replace(replace(replace(CSS_RELTIME,'.',''),':',''),'0','') = ''
            THEN 'zero' ELSE 'nonzero' END k, count(*)
  FROM css GROUP BY k;                    -- nonzero 10639, zero 3196, empty 44
SELECT CSS_ILSCOPE, CSS_ILSTAGE, count(*) FROM css GROUP BY 1,2;
SELECT CSS_CEV, count(*) FROM css GROUP BY 1;              -- Y 17
SELECT max(CAST(CSF_ELEMS AS int)), avg(CAST(CSF_ELEMS AS int)) FROM csf;
SELECT CASE WHEN CSF_DOCNAME LIKE '%-FCP-%' THEN 'FCP'
            WHEN CSF_DOCNAME LIKE '%-CRP-%' THEN 'CRP' ELSE 'other' END k, count(*)
  FROM csf GROUP BY k;                                     -- FCP 2243, CRP 1091, other 70
SELECT count(DISTINCT CSS_SQNAME) FROM css JOIN ccf ON CCF_CNAME = CSS_ELEMID
 WHERE CCF_TYPE = '18';                                    -- 22
SELECT CSF_NAME, CSF_DESC, CSF_DOCNAME, CSF_ELEMS, CSF_NFPARS
  FROM csf WHERE CSF_NAME IN ('ASYF010B','AITF124B','AIAC071A');
SELECT CSS_SQNAME, CSS_ENTRY, CSS_TYPE, CSS_ELEMID, CSS_RELTYPE, CSS_RELTIME,
       CSS_ILSCOPE, CSS_ILSTAGE
  FROM css WHERE CSS_SQNAME IN ('ASYF010B','AITF124B','AIAC071A');
SELECT CCF_CNAME, CCF_DESCR, CCF_TYPE, CCF_STYPE FROM ccf
 WHERE CCF_CNAME IN ('ZCPX0003','ZCPX0004','ZCPX0011');   -- 18,140 each

docs.title: MOIS and the procedure tools
docs.text:
Procedures at ESOC are prepared outside the MIB. In 2000 ESA presented a "Winfops / MOIS" system built on MS-Access for procedure preparation, with simple automation in tabular form, among the elements offered to Herschel/Planck.87 By 2023 RHEA described ASTRAL-Prepare as the latest evolution of MOIS (used on more than 100 spacecraft), with editors for OBCP scripts, mission planning rules, PLUTO scripts, Writer procedures and synthetic SCOS-2000 scripts.101102 The same paper lists the executable "operations languages" that such tools export (OBCPs in OL, automation procedures in Tcl/TOPE, SPELL and others) and notes that MOIS has generated them for years through its Writer editor; some ESOC SCOS-2000 missions automated routine operations with Writer procedures and the MOIS Scheduler, starting contingency recovery procedures automatically on known events.103104 ESOC's OPEN preparation environment planned to re-engineer MOIS Writer, its editor for flight operation procedures, as an extension, and the 2025 EGS-CC migration plan keeps MOIS or ProToS for the flight control procedures of missions that stay on a SCOS-2000 MIB, with converters for MOIS and ProToS procedures for missions that move fully to EGS-CC.105106 The tools are described on ancillary systems and EGS-CC and operations preparation.

PLUTO in practice

The available sources show PLUTO scripts as one of several supported procedure formats in a commercial preparation tool, not as the language of ESOC's SCOS-2000 operations. Whether any ESA mission executes PLUTO procedures operationally is not stated in the available sources.

docs.title: ECSS-E-ST-70C: ground systems and operations
docs.text:
ECSS-E-ST-70C ("Space engineering – Ground systems and operations", 31 July 2008) is the top-level ECSS standard of the E-70 discipline. It holds the basic rules, principles and requirements for engineering the ground segment and for preparing and conducting mission operations, and it defines the customer-supplier relationships for both: a customer with a ground segment supplier (GSS) and a customer with an operations supplier (OS).1 It does not cover EGSE and the operations that support space segment verification (that is ECSS-E-ST-10-02) nor the launch segment and its operations.1

Where the other E-70 standards on this wiki describe things - the spacecraft's operability (ECSS-E-ST-70-11), its monitoring and control data (ECSS-E-ST-70-31), procedure languages on the ground (ECSS-E-ST-70-32) and on board (ECSS-E-ST-70-01), and the packet services (ECSS-E-ST-70-41, the PUS) - this standard describes the processes and documents in which those things are produced, validated and used, and it lists the others as its level 3 standards.66

At a glance

Item Value Issues ECSS-E-70 Part 1A "Principles and requirements" (25 April 2000) and Part 2A "Document requirements definition" (2 April 2001); B never issued; ECSS-E-ST-70C (31 July 2008) merges both2 Status (ECSS tree, October 2025) Published; no update shown as ongoing or planned68 Normative references ECSS-S-ST-00-01, ECSS-E-ST-10, -10-02, -10-06, ECSS-E-ST-40, ECSS-M-ST-40, ECSS-M-ST-70, ECSS-Q-ST-10-09, ECSS-Q-ST-803 Structure Clause 4 domain; clause 5 operations engineering (8 processes); clause 6 ground segment engineering (5 processes); clause 7 lifecycle (phases A to F); Annexes A–J normative DRDs; K commonality; L level 3 standards4 Reviews defined CRR, GSSRR, GSPDR, GSCDR, GSQR, COR, ORR, FQR, IOORs, ELR, MCR (plus the space-system reviews of ECSS-M-ST-10)53

docs.title: What changed from the A issues
docs.text: The 2008 issue replaced the phase-based approach of ECSS-E-70A with a process approach: operations engineering and ground segment engineering are separate processes (and disciplines), projected onto the ECSS-M-10 lifecycle model. It identifies separate customer-supplier relationships for operations and for the ground segment and accepts different procurement models (one organisation supplying both, or two). It aligns with ECSS-E-ST-10C system engineering in processes, documents, reviews and terminology, reviews the interfaces with spacecraft design and manufacture (adding the CFISRD), assumes no reference architecture for the ground segment (functions are listed without saying how they are grouped), and brings the document requirements definitions (DRDs) into normative annexes. New DRDs are the mission analysis report (MAR), mission operations plan (MOP), customer furnished items and services requirements document (CFISRD), operations engineering plan (OEP) and ground segment system engineering plan.2

docs.title: Terms
docs.text:
Term (§3.2) Definition (paraphrased) entity A combination of ground systems and the associated personnel or operations organisation ground segment The ground systems needed to prepare or execute mission operations ground segment operations Planning, execution and evaluation of operations of the ground segment or parts of it ground segment customer (GSC) / supplier (GSS) The party procuring / supplying the ground segment ground system An integrated set of ground functions supporting operations preparation or execution incident In service provision, an enquiry, observation or anomaly that relates to, causes or can cause an interruption or quality reduction of the service mission Objectives achieved by a space system, characterised by its expected products (quantity, quality, availability) mission exploitation Planning, generation, use and evaluation of the products of the mission mission information Information on space and ground segments before and after launch: design and operations characteristics, test and operations procedures, TM/TC characteristics; source data from the operations customer and GSS plus data derived by the operations teams mission operations Planning, execution and evaluation of operations of the combined space and ground segments in phases E and F mission operations data The subset of mission information used to execute in-orbit operations: operations procedures, operations rules, monitoring and control databases mission products Products and services delivered by the space system (communications services, science data) operational validation Tests (simulations, rehearsals) establishing that the complete ground segment, its mission operations data and its staff are ready; its completion gives a qualified ground segment operations customer (OC) / supplier (OS) The party procuring / preparing and executing the space and ground segment operations; OC and GSC are usually the same entity space segment operations Planning, execution and evaluation of space segment operations in orbit synthetic parameter A parameter derived from telemetry and other data by an algorithm

Source: §3.2.5 The abbreviation list (§3.3) is long; the ones used most on this page are collected in the glossary.6

docs.title: The domain (clause 4)
docs.text:
The domain of the standard has two components: the ground segment (every ground system used to prepare, conduct and close operations) and the operations organisations (the people). An entity combines an operations organisation with its ground systems, for example a control centre with its mission control team, or a ground station with its operations and maintenance staff.7 Teams typically include operations managers, spacecraft operators (astronauts, operations engineers, spacecraft analysts, spacecraft controllers), payload operators, mission planners, flight dynamics engineers, ground systems operators, mission exploitation staff and ground systems maintenance engineers.8

The ground segment typically consists of four top-level systems, which can be distributed over several centres:9

flowchart LR
  subgraph GS["Ground segment"]
    MOS["Mission operations system"]
    PODS["Payload operations<br/>and data system"]
    GCS["Ground communications system"]
    GSS2["Ground station system<br/>(TT&C stations, payload<br/>downlink stations)"]
    MOS --- GCS
    PODS --- GCS
    GCS --- GSS2
  end
  subgraph SS["Space segment"]
    PF["Platform"]
    PL["Payload"]
  end
  GSS2 <-->|"TT&C"| PF
  PL -- "payload downlink" --> GSS2

Ground segment systems, after Figure 4-2.9

System Functions it typically supports Mission operations system Mission analysis; operations preparation; simulation; mission planning and scheduling; monitoring and control; flight dynamics; on-board software maintenance and management; data archiving; user services; data product delivery; performance analysis and reporting; configuration management (space segment, ground segment, mission information); system maintenance Payload operations and data system Payload operations analysis, preparation, planning and scheduling, control; simulation; payload data processing and archiving; user services; data product delivery; performance analysis; algorithm tuning, development and validation; system maintenance Ground station system TM reception, storage and distribution; TC transmission; tracking, ranging, Doppler and meteorological data; station monitoring and control; time management; network management and scheduling; data distribution; maintenance Ground communications system Data distribution; voice and video; maintenance

Source: §4.3.2 to §4.3.5.9 In ESA's world these map onto systems described elsewhere on this wiki: SCOS-2000 for monitoring and control, its archives and data dissemination, and the NCTRS and ground station interface.

Two engineering disciplines act on this domain: operations engineering (preparing and executing mission operations) and ground segment engineering (defining, designing, producing, integrating, verifying and maintaining the ground segment). They are separate process chains with many links, and both contribute to the space segment requirements and to reviews of the on-board design.10 The standard singles out critical areas for coordination: mission concepts with due weight on ground and operations aspects; spacecraft operability and maintainability; the adequacy of what the operations customer delivers; end-to-end validation; reuse of operations knowledge and data (TM/TC definitions, procedures) from spacecraft design through AIT to operations; commonality between ground services and between AIT and operations; security and safety; and communications design and cost.11

Operations engineering processes and their main products, after Figure 5-1.1213

docs.title: 5.2 Requirements analysis and concept development
docs.text:
The inputs are the operations customer requirements document (OCRD, the "initial technical specification" of ECSS-E-ST-10-06 tailored to operations, written with the end users), the mission description document (mission analysis, system description and operations scenarios for each concept), the space-system trade-off report and the launcher user manual; the first three are phase 0 products.14

  • Mission analysis characterises launcher, ground station, spacecraft, mission-specific (for example station-keeping windows, orbit phasing), payload and data flow constraints, and supplies 13 items: launch window, separation sequence, target orbit, positioning strategy, orbit determination concept, schedule of operational events (nominal and planned contingencies), station coverage, analysis of high-risk sequences, interference risk with flying spacecraft, delta-V budget, environmental impacts (sensor blinding, eclipses), payload operations strategy and data circulation scheme. Output: the MAR.15
  • Operational analysis checks the customer requirements, assesses feasibility, finds the drivers, defines the mission operations concept and derives requirements on operations engineering and the ground segment, and contributes to interface definition. Output: the mission operations concept document (MOCD).16
  • Operational interfaces: space segment operability requirements are compiled in the space segment operability requirements document (SSORD), described as a tailored version of ECSS-E-ST-70-11; on-board mission operations services and their requests and reports are defined with the OC (ECSS-E-ST-70-41 can be tailored for this, or a standalone document or the space-to-ground ICD used); external interfaces go into operational ICDs (contacts, services, data exchange formats and methods) that later join the MOP; and the deliverables and services required from the OC go into the CFISRD.17
  • The operations engineering plan (OEP) gives the schedule for producing and validating mission operations data, the team organisation and the recruitment profile; it exists so that operations manpower can be costed and recruited on time, and may be merged with the GSEP when GSS and OS are one organisation.18
  • User requirements are written for the ground segment and each ground system and for validation, training and simulation tools, covering functionality and performance, automation requirements matching the operations concept and staffing profile, centralisation or decentralisation, user management and human-computer interaction.19
  • The operational validation plan (OVP) covers test preparation, resources, strategies, methods, scenarios, pass/fail criteria and post-test activities.20

The CFISRD items listed in §5.2.2.3f are worth reading in full because they are exactly the interfaces between spacecraft project and operations: space segment documents (SSUM, detailed design, spacecraft monitoring and control database); procedures validated during spacecraft AIT; representative TM/TC samples including payload data; a suitcase for TT&C compatibility tests; access to the spacecraft on ground; the operational simulator and space segment models; on-board software and documentation; data processing tools (mission-specific decommutation, derived-parameter algorithms); the software development environment and validation benches for on-board software maintenance; engineering support during ground segment design and phases E and F; support for in-orbit control in designated phases; and site infrastructure.17

Outputs of §5.2 (Table 5-2) Producer Mission analysis report (MAR) OS Mission operations concept document (MOCD) OS Space segment operability requirements document (SSORD) OS Customer furnished items and services requirements document (CFISRD) OS ICDs for operational interfaces with external entities OS Operations engineering plan (OEP) OS User requirements for the ground segment and ground systems, including validation, training and simulation tools OS Operational validation plan (OVP) OS

Source: Table 5-2.21

Inference

ESA's missions publish an operations interface requirements document (OIRD) for the spacecraft, prepared by ESA and tightly coupled with CCSDS and ECSS standards; since 2019 mission OIRDs start from a generic OIRD built on ECSS-E-ST-70-11C, -70-41C and -70-01C.7778 This plays the role that ECSS-E-ST-70C gives the SSORD. The standard itself does not mention OIRDs.

docs.title: 5.3 Mission operations data production
docs.text:
The inputs are the MAR, MOCD and operational ICDs from the OS; the space segment user manual (SSUM), detailed design documents and space segment monitoring and control database from the OC; and the ground systems user manuals and ground segment monitoring and control database from the GSS.22 The process documents everything needed for in-orbit monitoring and control in the mission operations plan (MOP): organisation, responsibilities, decision making and major mission rules; the sequence of main events of all critical phases (station visibility, major operations); timed operations schedules for every critical operation (each team member's activities, interfaces, external constraints; LEOP, commissioning, fly-bys, orbit insertions); operations procedures for nominal and contingency operations of both segments; and disposal procedures.23 Further rules:23

  • An independently operated entity gets a sub-plan of the MOP (should).
  • Every operations procedure states its required authorisation level, applicability, and execution conditions and constraints before, during and after execution.
  • Space segment procedures are made by expanding the procedures in the SSUM with ground segment specifics.
  • The monitoring and control databases are populated with mission data for space and ground segment processing, which includes mission planning data, OBCPs, TM/TC definitions, display definitions, on-board software images and patches.
  • Mission exploitation data (processing databases, user databases) and a flight dynamics schedule are established.
  • Before delivery, the OC verifies its inputs against representative space segment models, at least the space segment monitoring and control database and the SSUM procedures.

The outputs are the MOP and the space and ground segment monitoring and control databases.24

docs.title: 5.4 Mission operations data validation
docs.text: Mission operations data must be validated to show that it is correct and compatible with the space segment; inspection is enough for some data (parameter descriptions, non-testable procedures). Validation uses tools representative of the space segment design - chiefly the operational simulator - and a flight-representative space segment, exercising all operations procedures and telecommands, all spacecraft modes including non-nominal ones, and all redundancies (within the limits of operating space hardware on the ground). These tests are sometimes called system validation tests (SVTs). Results and the validation status of each data item are recorded.25

docs.title: 5.5 Operations teams build-up and training
docs.text: Operations are carried out by teams; a typical organisation has a mission control team, a flight dynamics team (orbit and attitude determination and prediction, manoeuvre preparation, sensor calibration), ground operations teams (stations, communications, control centre), a mission exploitation team (payload data planning, processing and distribution) and ground segment and space segment support teams of experts. Roles are defined per team member and mission phase; teams are trained before operational validation starts through theory, realistic simulations, rehearsals of operational and contingency scenarios; training is documented in the operations training plan (OTP) and recorded per person.26

docs.title: 5.6 Operational validation
docs.text:
Operational validation takes place in a realistic operational context and demonstrates that the whole ground segment and its interfaces work, that all mission operations data is correct, that all staff are qualified and that the teams can support the mission (for LEOP, the LEOP network and its staff too). It includes:27

Activity Purpose Simulations and rehearsals Teams execute nominal and contingency scenarios of the MOP with the operational simulator in place of the spacecraft Mission readiness tests (MRTs) Validate ground station readiness and train station and network staff Data flow tests (DFTs) Validate TM, TC and tracking interfaces between stations and control centre, and between other ground systems (for example payload data circulation) Tracking campaigns Validate end-to-end ranging and Doppler with missions already flying

It follows the OVP, records unexpected behaviour in the operational validation report, ends with a ground segment acceptance report, is supported by the GSS, and wraps major tests in test readiness and post-test reviews per ECSS-E-ST-10-02. Afterwards, change authority for the ground segment - including shared infrastructure such as LANs, firewalls, power, cabling and buildings - passes to a formal change control board.27

docs.title: 5.7 Operational configuration management
docs.text: Mission operations data and the space segment are kept functional and under configuration control (per ECSS-M-ST-40) through preparation and execution; changes go through the same processes as the original design, development and verification, with definition, implementation, verification, operational validation and formal authorisation. Teams are kept operational; replacement staff are formally trained and exercised in simulations before working autonomously.28

docs.title: 5.8 Operations execution
docs.text:
Operations run from launch to disposal and divide into critical phases (LEOP, commissioning, planetary fly-by or orbit insertion, rendezvous and docking, retrieval) and routine phases (exploitation, cruise, hibernation).29

  • Critical operations are executed per the MOP by staff able to detect and respond to unexpected behaviour in line with the FDIR approach of the SSUM, with managers present for authorisations and facilities augmented as needed.30
  • Routine operations: mission planning from user requests and constraints; detailed schedules produced and executed; each activity's execution verified; health monitoring of both segments; monitoring and control data archived for troubleshooting and performance analysis; performance evaluated; payload data processed, archived and distributed with ancillary data; corrective actions or contingency procedures invoked on anomalies; a new plan and procedures produced, validated and approved for contingencies not covered by the MOP; a revised mission plan agreed with the OC after a major anomaly; and an anomaly review board (also acting as nonconformance review board per ECSS-Q-ST-10-09).31
  • Reporting: periodic operations status reports (for example daily in LEOP, weekly in routine operations), an engineering assessment report after LEOP or critical operations, a commissioning report, performance reports with trend analysis, operations anomaly reports (OARs) tracked to closure for the whole mission, and reports on operations experience, lessons learned, in-orbit performance and end-of-life tests.32

Outputs include the spacecraft in its final orbit configured for exploitation, LEOP, commissioning and routine reports, the mission history archive (telemetry, telecommand history), plans and schedules, performance and trend data, mission products, OARs and mission reports.33

docs.title: 5.9 Space segment disposal operations
docs.text: Disposal operations comprise analyses, development and validation of disposal products and processes, and final de-orbiting, re-entry or retrieval, with disposal or recycling of retrieved elements. The analysis covers storage, dismantling, reuse, recycling or destruction, cost and organisation; rules, procedures and timelines go into a disposal operations plan (part of the MOP) that respects space debris mitigation and launch authority requirements.34

docs.title: Ground segment engineering (clause 6)
docs.text: The five ground segment engineering processes are definition, production, AIT and verification, maintenance and disposal; logistics support activities are included throughout.35

docs.title: 6.2 Ground segment definition
docs.text:
The inputs are the ground segment customer requirements document (GSCRD), the MDD, the MOCD and a draft space-to-ground ICD (SGICD).36 Four sub-processes follow:37

  • Requirements engineering produces the ground segment requirements document (GSRD) from the GSCRD and the operations supplier's user requirements, covering 16 topics: functionality; performance and dependability derived from space system requirements; security; mission safety; operations and logistics support; internal and external interfaces; reuse of generic infrastructure; maintainability; location and site diversity; failure-case operations, recovery and fall-back; system management (user administration, access, equipment configuration, performance monitoring); configuration management; network design and management; commonality; interoperability (for example other agencies' stations).
  • Design engineering records the architecture, down to individual ground systems and including integrated logistics support, in the ground segment design definition file (GSDDF); defines the verification and validation approach; analyses reuse of existing and multi-mission systems; defines internal and external interfaces; identifies critical elements with their reliability, availability, maintainability and safety requirements; justifies the design in the ground segment design justification file (GSDJF); writes the ground segment engineering plan (GSEP) per the ECSS-E-ST-10 system engineering plan; produces the ground segment AIT and verification plans; and contributes RF, voice, video and high-rate data interfaces to the SGICD (pointing to CCSDS 701.0-B-2).
  • Ground systems requirements engineering writes a requirements document for each ground system, with at least functional, performance, interface, design, operational, environment, resource, RAMS, security and verification requirements, applying ECSS-E-ST-40 for software, tracing to the GSRD and generating ICDs for every external interface.
  • Logistics support preparation produces a logistics support plan covering staffing and training, spares, support equipment, software support, packaging, handling, storage and transport, and shared versus mission-procured resources.

docs.title: 6.3 Ground segment production
docs.text: Each ground system follows the ECSS-E-ST-10 system engineering process recursively (definition, production, AIT and verification, maintenance), whether it operates the mission or supports testing, maintenance or training; an operational simulator supplied by the space segment supplier or a third party is treated as a ground system. Reuse of existing systems is analysed; ECSS-E-ST-40 and ECSS-Q-ST-80 apply to software; suppliers support delivery, installation and on-site acceptance; qualification or acceptance tests (possibly including a factory acceptance test) run against the system requirements in the target environment; acceptance reports, user manuals and maintenance manuals and procedures are produced for every system.38

docs.title: 6.4 Ground segment AIT and verification
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  subgraph SUB["Subsystem level"]
    a1["Subsystem AIT"] --> a2["Subsystem verification"] --> a3["Subsystem validation"]
  end
  subgraph SYS["System level"]
    b1["System AIT"] --> b2["System verification"] --> b3["System validation"]
  end
  a3 --> b1
  b3 --> c1["Ground segment AIT"] --> c2["Ground segment verification"] --> c3["Ground segment<br/>operational validation"]

Ground segment AIT and verification, after Figure 6-2; each arrow passes a checkpoint or review. The last box belongs to operations engineering (§5.6).39

AIT uses a preliminary set of mission operations data and proceeds incrementally from low-level subsystems, with a verification test (conformance with design and interfaces) and a validation test (preliminary fitness for use) at each stage. Verification then addresses the ground segment as a whole: conformance to requirements, functional coherence and compatibility of the ground systems, compatibility with the space segment, compatibility with external entities through end-to-end tests, and a first exposure to realistic operational conditions. Any later modification requires non-regression testing.3940

Space segment compatibility testing may use a suitcase representative of the spacecraft TT&C hardware and software, an operational simulator (with emulators or even real spacecraft components in a hybrid simulator), representative TM samples and access to the spacecraft during its AIT and at the launch site. At least two test periods are needed, long enough for the spacecraft's complexity and far enough apart to correct ground problems found in the first; listen-in tests, open-loop routing of AIT telemetry to the control centre, are usually added when possible. Compatibility tests include the mission operations data (databases, procedures, command schedules). Results are reviewed at the ground segment qualification review (GSQR).41

docs.title: 6.5 Maintenance and 6.6 disposal
docs.text: Maintenance keeps the ground segment within its availability and performance requirements and covers obsolescence and migrations (for example when computers or operating systems reach end of service): regular performance monitoring and reports, routine maintenance per procedures with a log, incident management (log incidents and restore service), problem management (diagnose root causes, trend analysis, raise change requests), change management (impact assessment, planning, new releases into operations), configuration management (a configuration database covering hardware, network, software including COTS, documentation, configuration data and mission operations data) and obsolescence management.42 Disposal analyses storage, dismantling, reuse, recycling and destruction, keeps mission data accessible for an agreed duration, and produces a disposal report and data archives with post-mission consolidated data and access tools.43

docs.title: Lifecycle and reviews (clause 7)
docs.text:
The ground segment processes are allocated to ECSS-M-ST-10 phases ending in formal reviews; the ground segment phases are not necessarily aligned with those of the space system, but they are strongly interdependent. GSC, OC, GSS and OS are represented in all ground segment and operations reviews, which should be combined where practical; incremental missions (the standard cites ISS and ATV) repeat the lifecycle per increment.44

docs.title: The document requirements definitions (Annexes A–J)
docs.text:
Annex DRD Called from Purpose and key contents A Customer requirements document (CRD), used as OCRD and GSCRD 5.2.1b, 6.2.1b Top-level assumptions, constraints and operations requirements: mission overview, responsibilities, milestones, constraints (launcher, orbits, operational phases, RF and antenna constraints), operations requirements by function (planning and scheduling, monitoring and control, performance evaluation, flight dynamics, payload operations and data management, on-board software maintenance); for the GSCRD, 11 requirement classes per function from functional to HCI; OCRD and GSCRD may be merged, and a large GSCRD split by entity (for example flight operations segment and payload data segment) B Mission analysis report (MAR) 5.2.2.1c Mission requirements and constraints; overview; launch and early orbit (windows, sequence, eclipses, coverage, injection errors, orbit determination, orbit acquisition strategy); transfer and planetary insertion for interplanetary missions; routine phase (orbit evolution, collision avoidance, eclipses, coverage, payload strategy and constraints, data circulation, occultations, phasing); propellant budgets C Mission operations concept document (MOCD) 5.2.2.2b Requirements and constraints (mission, end users, programmatic constraints, related missions, external dependencies); space segment characteristics (autonomy, data generation, storage and downlink); operations concepts per phase for planning, execution (schedule and procedure execution, manual commanding, pre-transmission validation, command verification, history archiving, health monitoring, FDIR), evaluation, exploitation and support processes; reuse, new developments and trade-offs (for example ground automation versus manual operation) D Operations engineering plan (OEP) 5.2.2.4a.4 Mission overview; lifecycle, reviews and critical path; for each operations engineering process: inputs, manpower and skills, tools, other resources, interrelations, outputs; mission operations teams (structure, roles, reporting and support channels, recruitment profiles); may be merged with the GSEP E Space segment user manual (SSUM) 5.3.1b Mission definition and analysis results; satellite design, system-level autonomy, configurations, budgets (mass, power, thermal, RF links, TM/TC rates, memory, timing, pointing and more), SGICD reference, timelines, modes and transitions, FMEA/FMECA and FTA; per subsystem and payload: design, units, software (design, services cross-referenced to ECSS-E-ST-70-41 as tailored, TM/TC structures, memory maps), performance, TM and TC lists (provided in the space segment monitoring and control database, which formally belongs to the SSUM), failure analysis, modes and nominal and contingency procedures structured in steps, payload data definition F Operational validation plan (OVP) 5.2.2.6c Objectives, schedule, success criteria; management and responsibilities (including simulations officers); ORR procedure; simulations and rehearsals (timetable, briefings, teams, scenarios referenced to the MOP, configurations and versions, tools); ground segment readiness tests (MRTs, DFTs); records and reports (simulation logs and reports, readiness test reports, anomaly and action records) G Mission operations plan (MOP) 5.3.2k Mission management (summary, mission rules from launch hold criteria to mission termination criteria, organisation and charts, briefing and debriefing, reporting and on-call, operational ICDs, configuration control after the pre-launch freeze); per mission phase: events, implementation strategy, timelines (activity, start time, executing position, background activities, procedure references, briefing breakpoints); operations procedures with an applicability and authorisation matrix, organised hierarchically, able to call each other; hand-over procedures between authorities H Operations anomaly report (OAR) 5.8.2.4e Unique mission-level number; context, suspected source, title, time, severity (no impact, minor impact, major impact), originators, authorisation, distribution, version, status and actionee; description and first-occurrence flag; details with supporting TM reports, TC history, logs and mission data; chronicle of actions; operational impact (outages, re-planning, redundancies); recommendations and schedule I Operations procedures 5.3.2l See below J Customer furnished items and services requirements document (CFISRD) 5.2.2.3g Mission information classes to deliver (SSUM, design documents, M&C data including procedures, TM/TC database, other in-flight databases such as OBCPs, synthetic parameter and TM interpretation algorithms, flight dynamics database) with contents, media, format, validation and schedule; suitcase; space segment models for the simulator; on-board software deliveries (sources, images, maps, EEPROM loads) and responsibilities; OBSM facility; pre-launch access (listen-in tests, SVTs); pre-launch technical assistance and post-launch support with response times

Sources: Annexes A to J.54555657585960616263

docs.title: Annex I: what an operations procedure must contain
docs.text:
An operations procedure is the elementary building block of the MOP that achieves one operational objective; it may be called by a mission timeline, an automatically executing schedule or another procedure, or started manually. Each has a unique identification number, and the DRD applies to any human-readable form, on paper or on a display:62

Element Content Preliminary elements Title, version and applicability date, author(s) Introduction (informative, not executable) Objective, execution context, goal and all possible results, figures Required operational authority Special authorisation for manual execution (for example the written authority of the spacecraft operations manager) Expected duration How long execution takes Pre-conditions Conditions that must hold before start, and conditions that prohibit start; referring to mission phase, ground and space segment configuration, orbit position or environment, and the status of other procedures Procedure body Steps executed in sequence or in parallel; each step structured like a procedure (pre-conditions, executable body, post-conditions) with its sequence of activities: uplink a TC, initiate a command stack or predefined sequence, execute a ground command (for example select a display), check telemetry values, wait until a time, for a delta time or while a condition holds, mission-specific activities Contingency element What to do when the system cannot be left as it is (for example a disabled protection, or an aborted orbital manoeuvre): suspend the body, act, then resume; or reach the goal another way and stop; or abort Post conditions How to verify that the goals were met; final status "terminated, success confirmed" or "terminated, failed (with reasons)"

The same structure, made executable, is the PLUTO procedure of ECSS-E-ST-70-32C, whose watchdog actions "resume", "terminate" and "abort" mirror the three contingency outcomes.6275

FCPs, CRPs and the FOP in ESA practice

The standard speaks of the MOP and of nominal and contingency operations procedures. ESA documents use other names for the same products. ECSS-E-ST-70-32C calls nominal and contingency procedures flight control procedures (FCPs) and places them in a "flight operations plan (FOP)".76 The Herschel/Planck OIRD names flight control procedures FCP_<subsystem>_<nnnn> and contingency recovery procedures CRP_<subsystem>_<nnnn>.79 ESOC's preparation environment plans a "FOP Editor" for flight operation procedures maintained by the flight control team, re-engineered from MOIS Writer.80 ESOC's mission plans themselves carried the title "Flight Operations Plan", as the INTEGRAL example below shows.83 In the Solar Orbiter MIB, 2 243 of the 3 404 command sequences name an FCP document as their source and 1 091 a CRP document.8281

SQL used 
-- Solar Orbiter MIB 2025-09-16 (solo-2025-09-16.sqlite)
SELECT count(*) FROM csf;                                   -- 3404
SELECT CASE WHEN CSF_DOCNAME LIKE '%-FCP-%' THEN 'FCP'
            WHEN CSF_DOCNAME LIKE '%-CRP-%' THEN 'CRP' ELSE 'other' END k, count(*)
  FROM csf GROUP BY k;                                      -- FCP 2243, CRP 1091, other 70
SELECT substr(CSF_DOCNAME,1,2), count(*) FROM csf
 WHERE CSF_DOCNAME LIKE '%-FCP-%' OR CSF_DOCNAME LIKE '%-CRP-%'
 GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC;                                -- DM 835, AC 331, ID 218, ...

docs.title: A real flight operations plan: INTEGRAL
docs.text:
ESOC's Flight Operations Plan for INTEGRAL (volume 1 "Mission Management", issue 2, 21 February 2003, written after the launch of 17 October 2002) shows what a MOP looks like in practice, a few years before the 2008 issue of the standard. Volume 1 has five books:83

MOP DRD element (Annex G) INTEGRAL FOP volume 1 <3.1> Introduction: mission, ground segment, operations concept Book 1 "Mission Summary": mission characteristics (highly eccentric orbit, apogee 153 600 km, perigee 9 000 km, 51.6° inclination, 72 h period; stations Redu, Goldstone and Villafranca as back-up), constraints, space and ground segment set-up, objectives; phases LEOP, commissioning (two months, started in parallel with LEOP) and routine (two years, extendable)84 <3.3> Mission operations management Book 2 "Management Set-Up" for the routine phase: tasks split between the operational ground segment (MOC, stations, communications) and the science ground segment (ISOC, ISDC), the organigram and responsibilities; LEOP and commissioning set-ups are in volumes 10 and 1185 <3.2> Mission rules Book 3 "Mission Rules": operational responsibility (the FOP's nominal and contingency flight procedures override all other procedures; deviations need the Flight Director's or spacecraft operations manager's permission); launch hold criteria (ground segment "not fully operational", countdown continues, versus "not operational", countdown stopped at the next check-point); spacecraft and instrument emergencies (loss of attitude, fuel, power or thermal criticality, loss of TM/TC, more than 24 h without station contact) with recovery by the matching contingency procedure or safe mode; redefinition of mission goals; mission termination criteria and run-down86 <3.4> Configuration management and change control Book 4: an overall configuration control board chaired by the Project Scientist plus local boards per centre; only flight procedures in the approved FOP may be used; changes to the FOP, the operational database and on-board software (through the on-board software maintenance system) need the spacecraft operations manager's approval87 Reporting (§5.8.2.4) and OARs (Annex H) Book 5 "Mission Reporting": mission-phase and study reports; routine shift, revolution, weekly, monthly and annual reports; an anomaly notification within one hour, followed by an anomaly report88 <4> Mission phase operations and <5> operations procedures Not in volume 1; mission rule 1.4 states that the FOP provides the timelines and the nominal and contingency flight procedures86

Inference

The column mapping is this wiki's. Only volume 1 of the INTEGRAL FOP is in the library, so how its procedure volumes are structured, and whether they follow the steps-and-contingency layout of Annex I, is not stated in the available sources.

docs.title: Commonality (Annex K)
docs.text: Ground segments are frequently built from existing and multi-mission systems, so the design must consider reuse with customisation and extension. Reuse happens between flight and ground segments (space link elements, mission operations data), between projects (software with the same role, such as monitoring and control, flight dynamics or planning), and in shared middleware and infrastructure. Software commonality should follow the ECSS-Q-ST-80 rules on reuse; the candidate systems are the mission operations system, the payload operations and data system, the EGSE, station monitoring and control and data functions, and simulation, test and training tools; the reusable functions include monitoring, commanding, database management, procedure preparation, management and execution, archiving and distribution, performance evaluation, on-board software maintenance and HCI.64 The EGSE and the ground stations both face the space link and should consider common downlink reception, uplink radiation and downlink and uplink data processing. Mission operations data (monitoring and control definitions, displays) should be reused between manufacturer, checkout and operations, and the monitoring and control systems used in those areas should have compatible databases.65 SCOS-2000 as EGSE and the MIB are ESA's realisation of this recommendation, and ECSS-E-ST-70-31C is the standard for the data that makes it possible.

The level 3 standards point back: ECSS-E-ST-70-31C assumes conformance with ECSS-E-ST-50 and ECSS-E-ST-70 and calls the data it defines part of the product's user manual "see ECSS-E-ST-70", matching the SSUM DRD, in which the space segment monitoring and control database formally belongs to the SSUM.707158 ECSS-E-ST-70-01C requires OBOPs to follow the ECSS-E-ST-70 operations procedure process.74

docs.title: ECSS-E-70 in the document trees (November 2025)
docs.text:
ECSS publishes charts of all its documents. The November 2025 set places the E-70 discipline, ground systems and operations, in the space engineering branch next to E-10 system engineering, E-20 electrical and optical, E-30 mechanical, E-40 software, E-50 communications, E-60 control and E-80 security; the other branches are space project management (M), product assurance (Q), sustainability (U) and industrialization, production and maintenance (I), all under ECSS-S-ST-00 and its glossary ECSS-S-ST-00-01.67

E-70 discipline, engineering branch chart (as of October 2025) Marker ECSS-E-ST-70C Ground systems and operations published ECSS-E-ST-70-01C On-board control procedures published ECSS-E-ST-70-11C Rev.1 Space segment operability published ECSS-E-ST-70-31C Ground systems and operations – Monitoring and control data definition published ECSS-E-ST-70-32C Test and operations procedure language published ECSS-E-ST-70-41C Telemetry and telecommand packet utilization published, with ECSS-E-ST-70-41C Rev.1 marked "U" (ongoing or planned update)

Source: the engineering branch chart.68 The chart legend distinguishes published documents, documents affected by the update of another (M), ongoing or planned updates (U) and new documents in production or planned (N).68 The handbooks and technical memoranda chart (as of November 2024) has an E-70 column with no entries, so the discipline has no published handbook.69 The current state of the PUS revision is described on PUS-A vs PUS-C.

Dates of the charts

Each chart of the November 2025 file carries its own "as of" date: the disciplines overview is as of November 2025, the engineering branch as of October 2025 and the engineering handbooks as of November 2024.676869
