docs.title: PUS: the Packet Utilization Standard
docs.text:
The Packet Utilization Standard (PUS), ECSS-E-ST-70-41C "Telemetry and telecommand packet utilization", defines the application-level interface between a spacecraft and its ground segment. The CCSDS Space Packet Protocol and the ECSS-E-ST-50 communication standards move packets end to end; PUS says what those packets mean: which requests the ground can send, which reports the spacecraft returns, and how both are laid out bit by bit, so that integration, testing and flight operations can rely on a common interface.1 This wiki writes PUS message types as TC[x,y] and TM[x,y], for example TM[3,25] "housekeeping parameter report" or TC[11,4] "insert activities into the time-based schedule".44 The standard did not start in the ECSS system: it began as an ESA standard, ESA PSS-07-101 of May 1994, and many of today's service and subtype numbers were fixed then (see History).7689

At a glance

Item Value Origin ESA PSS-07-101 Packet Utilisation Standard, Issue 1, May 1994, prepared by COES; PUS version number 07685 Current issue ECSS-E-ST-70-41C, 15 April 2016 (656 pages)2 Previous issue ECSS-E-70-41A, 30 January 2003; issue B was never published2 Draft revision ECSS-E-ST-70-41C Rev.1 DIR1, 11 December 2024, public review until 28 February 202552 Scope Use of TC and TM packets for remote monitoring and control of subsystems and payloads, during integration, testing and operations3 Out of scope Mission-specific payload data packets, audio and video, on-board message transport, ground processing35 Standard service types 20 (ST[01] to ST[23], with 7, 10 and 16 reserved)7 Packet version on the wire PUS version number 2 in every TC and TM secondary header8

docs.title: Where PUS sits
docs.text:
PUS complements the space packet and data link standards: it does not move bits, it defines the messages carried by them.1 Requests initiated on the ground travel as telecommand packets to an on-board application process, and reports travel back as telemetry packets; how on-board processes exchange messages among themselves is mission-dependent and outside the standard.5

flowchart LR
  subgraph G["Ground segment"]
    U["Ground application process<br/>(subservice user)<br/>e.g. mission control system"]
  end
  subgraph L["Space link"]
    TC["TC packet<br/>request TC[x,y]"]
    TM["TM packet<br/>report TM[x,y]"]
  end
  subgraph S["Space segment"]
    P["On-board application process (APID)<br/>(subservice provider)<br/>services ST[01] ... ST[23]"]
  end
  U --> TC --> P
  P --> TM --> U

The packets ride in TC transfer frames and TM transfer frames (or AOS frames); on the telemetry side virtual channels separate data streams, and on the telecommand side MAP identifiers create sub-channels inside a virtual channel - up to 64 per virtual channel.6 For the overall chain see downlink and uplink.

docs.title: History
docs.text:
The PUS began as an ESA standard in 1994 and moved into the ECSS system in 2003. The wider story of the ESA packet standards and how they map onto today's CCSDS and ECSS documents is told in From ESA PSS to CCSDS and ECSS; this section follows the PUS itself.

timeline
  title From the ESA PUS to PUS-C Rev.1
  1987 : ESA sets up COES, the Committee for Operations and EGSE Standards
  1992 : PUSV prototype and PUSSAT reference satellite model validate the draft PUS
  1993 : Agency-level review of the PUS
  1994 : ESA PSS-07-101 Packet Utilisation Standard Issue 1, May (PUS version 0)
       : XMM tailors its services from the draft PUS ("missionisation")
  2003 : ECSS-E-70-41A, first ECSS issue (PUS version 1, "PUS-A")
  2010 : ECSS-E-ST-70-01C on-board control procedures, built on service 18
  2011 : 190 change requests collected by January
  2014 : Public review of the PUS-C draft
  2016 : ECSS-E-ST-70-41C published 15 April (PUS version 2, "PUS-C")
       : SAVOIR entrusts ESOC with a Generic OIRD (June)
  2019 : Generic OIRD 1.0 released (July), with one PUS-C tailoring for ESA missions
  2020 : PUSCGen generation toolset, final presentation (15 May)
  2024 : ECSS-E-ST-70-41C Rev.1 DIR1 released for public review (11 December)

The timeline combines the 1994 papers, the standards' title pages and change logs, and the presentations cited below.919495769921005610510912052

docs.title: Before ECSS: the ESA Packet Utilisation Standard (1987-1994)
docs.text:
Satellites used to be monitored and controlled largely at the "hardware" level: telemetry parameters sat at fixed positions in a telemetry format, and commands were fixed-length frames that loaded on-board registers or set switches. Through the 1980s more and more functions moved into on-board software, which still had to be operated with these hardware-oriented techniques - a constraint on its flexibility and on the trend towards on-board autonomy.90 The CCSDS packet recommendations, and the ESA Packet Telemetry Standard (PSS-04-106, January 1988) and Packet Telecommand Standard (PSS-04-107, April 1992) derived from them, opened a flexible end-to-end exchange between ground applications and on-board application processes, each identified by an APID - but they left the internal structure and content of the packets open.9077 (The packet layers themselves are described on Space Packet Protocol.)

In 1987 ESA set up the Committee for Operations and EGSE Standards (COES) to define the functions common to a satellite checkout system (EGSE) and a satellite control system, so that one monitoring and control system could serve pre-launch checkout and post-launch operations, within a project and across projects. Because packets let the same control function be implemented in many different ways, COES found its task feasible only with a clear, packet-based satellite-ground interface, so its first job became a standard defining precisely how telemetry and telecommand packets are used.91

The result was ESA PSS-07-101, Packet Utilisation Standard, Issue 1 (May 1994), prepared by COES and approved by the ESA Inspector General after an Agency-level review during 1993.7695 It defines the application-level interface between ground and space for electrical integration and testing and for flight operations, and it sits in the PSS-07 ground segment documentation tree under the "Mission Data Utilisation Standards" (PSS-07-10), next to standards for orbit and navigation data, station monitoring and control data, and time data (PSS-07-102 to PSS-07-104).77 Its scope already matches today's: monitoring and remote control of subsystems and payloads through packets, but neither the protocols between on-board application processes nor the content of science packets, and no audio or video.78

The 1994 document has two layers. Chapter 3 states operational requirements for nominal and contingency operations, each with a mnemonic and a serial number (for example TC-1: a telecommand packet carries one and only one telecommand function), and writes mission-dependent quantities as "Mission Parameters" in angle brackets, such as <TIME_CORREL_ACCUR>, collected in Appendix B. Chapters 4 to 21 then specify the services that satisfy those requirements, with their telecommand and telemetry packets; chapter 22 summarises every request and report, and chapter 23 defines the parameter types and structure rules.798182 Every packet except CPDU commands and the spacecraft time packet has a data field header carrying a service type and a service subtype, with values 0-127 reserved for the standard and 128-255 for missions, and PUS version number 0.1358592 Seventeen standard services were defined; three of them - task management (7), time reporting (10) and on-board traffic management (16) - were not kept as separate services in the ECSS issues (PUS-A moved the time report into service 9), and PUS-C still reserves their numbers because earlier versions used them.8649757 The 1994 packet headers and the service-by-service lineage are on PUS-A vs PUS-C.

Before approval the standard was validated by a prototyping exercise completed in 1992: a prototype called PUSV, running on one or two SPARC workstations, emulated the on-board behaviour in response to a ground control system and could model different on-board application architectures, while a reference satellite model called PUSSAT served for validation and demonstration.94 The 1994 paper that presented the standard to the community expected it to evolve incrementally as new services matured, and announced that ESOC's distributed mission control infrastructure, SCOS-II, would give full application-level support to PUS missions while COES specified a generic checkout and operations system.95 That ground-system lineage continues on SCOS-2000.

The X-ray observatory XMM gives an early example of tailoring. A 1994 ESOC paper, written while the PUS was still awaiting approval, describes how the project selected services from the draft standard to fit a classical operations concept - real-time control from ESOC through a single ground station with up to 22 hours of contact a day and no bulk on-board storage - and calls this selection and tailoring "missionisation".9697 XMM grouped its services into on-line control, safety management and operations maintenance and numbered them its own way: periodic housekeeping was TM type 1, device commands TC type 2, telecommand verification TM type 3, time-tagged commands type 7 and on-board monitoring of up to 30 parameters type 8. Its requirements came from an XMM Operations Interface Requirements Document (OIRD) and its packets from an XMM Packet Structure Definition.9899

Scanned sources

ESA PSS-07-101 and the two 1994 papers on NTRS are scanned documents. This wiki read them through OCR text, which contains recognition errors and merged words, and checked every number, field size, bit position and subtype quoted on this page and on PUS-A vs PUS-C against the rendered page images.

docs.title: From PUS-A to PUS-C and Rev.1
docs.text:
ECSS-E-70-41A of 30 January 2003 became the first ECSS issue and introduced PUS version number 1; its footnotes record that version 0 "was used by the ESA PUS". ECSS-E-70-41B was never issued.2874 PUS-C still lists PSS-07-101 in its bibliography.9

By January 2011 the working group preparing the third version had 190 change requests asking to remove PUS-A deficiencies, inject lessons learned, meet the needs of future missions, stay consistent with newer ECSS and CCSDS standards, follow the ECSS drafting rules and keep backward compatibility where possible.5654 The working group was convened by ESA with members from Astrium, CNES, DLR, EUMETSAT, Spacebel and TAS.55 The four-month public review of the draft (ECSS-E-ST-70-41C DIR1) ended in December 2014 with 620 discrepancy reports,56 464 of them from agencies and 156 from industry; the working group added 44 of its own in 2015, giving 664 in total, 72 of them major. Of these, 72 concerned the new PUS foundation model alone.59 The reviewers asked, among other things, for more background information, a clearer explanation of how services relate to application processes and packets, a simpler ground segment model, and more tailoring flexibility.60

ECSS-E-ST-70-41C was published on 15 April 2016. Its change log names the main changes: the introduction of the PUS foundation model, used to produce the standard service types and to be used by missions for their own service types and services, and a proper separation of system requirements from interface requirements.2 At the ADCSS 2015 workshop the convenor summarised the result as a new, formally defined vocabulary, a system specification focused on what is expected on board, and a drafting process supported by the foundation model - about 150 generic requirements in clause 5, 2 300 system requirements in clause 6 and 750 interface requirements in clauses 7 and 8.5758

The latest step is ECSS-E-ST-70-41C Rev.1 DIR1 (11 December 2024), a draft distributed for public review from 12 December 2024 to 28 February 2025 that "may not be referred to as an ECSS Standard until published as such".52 It deletes ST[08] and adds ST[24] to ST[27] (see PUS-A vs PUS-C).53

docs.title: The vocabulary
docs.text:
PUS-C defines a precise set of terms; the most important are:

Term Meaning in PUS-C Application process Element of the space system that hosts one or more subservice entities; on board or on ground; implemented in software, firmware or hardware.1110 Service Functional element providing closely related, remotely operable functions; composed of subservices.12 Subservice Elementary part of a service: exactly one subservice provider and its subservice users, interacting through dedicated messages.12 Subservice provider / user The provider executes requests and generates reports; the user initiates requests and processes reports.12 Capability A functionality of a service or subservice, specified as operational requirements.13 Message A request or a report.14 Request / instruction A request is a message of one or more instructions issued by a subservice user for execution by a provider.14 Report / notification A report is a message of one or more notifications; three kinds: verification reports, data reports and event reports.14 Transaction The set of messages related to one capability: request-related, autonomous data reporting, or event reporting.15

Usually the on-board processes host the providers and the ground hosts the users, but the standard allows the reverse: ground equipment can host providers so that a control centre can command it, and a payload can host users, for example to manage a mass memory with file management requests.10

docs.title: The PUS model
docs.text:
PUS-C is organised as a multi-layer model:16

flowchart TB
  F["PUS foundation model<br/>(clause 5): generic concepts and rules"]
  ST["Standard service type model<br/>(clauses 6-8): ST[01] ... ST[23]"]
  MS["Mission-specific service type model<br/>tailored standard types + new types (ID 128-255)"]
  SS["Space system service model<br/>services instantiated in each application process"]
  F --> ST
  F --> MS
  ST --> MS
  MS --> SS
  • The foundation model fixes the generic object types - service type, subservice type, capability type, message, request and report types, transaction types - and the rules that every service type, standard or mission-specific, must obey.1721
  • The standard service type model is the set of service types specified by the standard. Each one has a system specification in clause 6 (semantics: what the service does and how it reacts to requests) and an interface specification in clause 8 (syntax: packet layouts, using the field types of clause 7.3).18
  • The mission-specific service type model is recorded by each mission in a "mission-specific packet utilization definition document" that lists the standard service types it uses, each tailored, plus any mission-specific service types.19
  • The space system service model deploys these types: it says which application process hosts which service instance, with its full tailored specification.20

The 2015 presentation explains why: the foundation model was written with a formal "fact based modelling" technique to remove PUS-A ambiguities, keep all requirements consistent, ease tailoring, and enable the automatic generation of software and documentation.62 A prototype "PUS foundation database" was used to verify the consistency of the message type requirements and to generate parts of clauses 6 and 8 and the message type summary annex.63

docs.title: Tooling built on the foundation model
docs.text:
A study called PUSCGen ("PUS C Gen"; final presentation dated 15 May 2020, slides carrying a Spacebel copyright notice; it started from an ORM model supplied by ESA and reported its findings to ESA) took this idea to a toolset. Its motivation was the size of PUS-C: it wanted to check the standard's internal consistency by producing its content systematically from the foundation model, and to make tailoring easier.120121 The study captured clause 5 in Object Role Modelling (ORM) with the NORMA tool, reviewing and extending the ESA-supplied model, and treated the specification in clauses 6 and 8 as a population of that model. One stated limitation is that the "system objects" a subservice defines or accesses (functions, memories ...) are modelled only generically.122123 The review produced 21 change requests against PUS-C - 7 major (a functional problem), 7 minor (missing internal consistency or not covered by the foundation) and 7 editorial - and a relational database generated from the ORM model.124

On that database the study built three cooperating tools:125126127128

Tool What it does Population Tool defines service, subservice, capability, message, instruction and notification types, and their arguments; tailors them per mission, subject to the dependency and exclusion constraints of the population DOC-GEN regenerates clauses 6 and 8 and Annexes C and D in ECSS-E-ST-70-41C form; a population of the whole standard recreates it "with good fidelity", and in many cases a generated page is "hard to distinguish" from the original ASN1-GEN turns a tailored population into ASN.1/ACN definitions of the TC and TM, which ESA's ASN1SCC compiler converts into data structures, C encoders and decoders (with optional Python bindings) and ICDs

The study observed that almost all PUS-C services follow a very simple, practically stateless template, so it modelled in SDL and MSC only service 1, a "generic PUS C service" template and services 6, 9 and 12; the modelling found that the generation of some ST[01] notifications is not properly defined in the standard.129130 The toolset was validated on a Proba-3 use case, which added a housekeeping-compression subservice to service 3 and a mission-specific reaction-wheel management service numbered 8, and was then adopted by two other ESA activities: an R&D project (not flight software) on CoreSight software-execution tracing, which used services 1 and 6 plus a custom service 192, and a TASTE enhancement project whose MSP430 microcontroller demonstrator used services 1, 2, 3 and a custom service 222, with bare-bones encapsulation instead of CCSDS packets to save memory.131132133 Spacebel was also connecting the ASN.1 output to its SRDB tooling, whose database components can be integrated in SCOS-2000, so that on-board software and ground database are consistent by construction.134 Other database tools are listed on MIB tooling.

docs.title: Identifiers and notation
docs.text:
Names are for humans and identifiers are for the spacecraft; both are unique within their context, and the widest context is the single spacecraft.22

Identifier Range in PUS-C Rule Service type ID 1-255 standard types at most 127, mission-specific types at least 128; withdrawn standard IDs are not reused23 Message subtype ID 1-255 standard subtypes at most 127; mission-specific subtypes in a standard service type at least 12824 Message type ID (service type ID, message subtype ID) uniquely identifies the message type; carried in the packet secondary header24 Application process identifier (APID) 0-2046 identifies an application process that hosts a provider; 2047 reserved for idle packets, 0 for spacecraft time packets32 Application process user identifier 0-65535 identifies an application process that hosts a user; used as source ID of requests and destination ID of reports32

This wiki follows the standard's own notation:

  • ST[xx] - a service type, for example ST[03] housekeeping;7
  • TC[x,y] - a request (telecommand) of service type x and subtype y, for example TC[17,1];
  • TM[x,y] - a report (telemetry), for example TM[1,1] "successful acceptance verification report".45

A request identifier combines the source ID, the destination APID (plus a system identifier) and the sequence count or packet name; a report identifier combines the source APID, the destination ID and the source sequence count. The standard assumes these are unique for the mission but notes that counter wrap-around or testing can repeat them, so timing information may be needed.3841 Where each identifier lives in the packet is shown on packet structures.

docs.title: Messages and transactions
docs.text:
Every message type is either a request type or a report type. A request type defines one or more instruction types and declares whether a request may carry one or several instructions (its "instruction slots"), which instruction types may be combined, and the arguments of each.25 A report type defines exactly one notification type and declares whether one report may hold several notifications.26 Each request type is linked to at most one data report type that serves as its response.29

Three transaction types use these messages:2837

  • a request-related transaction: one request, zero or more verification reports (depending on the acknowledgement flags and the execution checks), and, if the request asks for data, one or more responses;
  • an autonomous data reporting transaction: a data report generated on the provider's own initiative, for example a periodic housekeeping report;
  • an event reporting transaction: one event report (informative, low, medium or high severity), the event being identified by an event definition within the application process.
sequenceDiagram
  participant U as Subservice user (ground)
  participant AR as Acceptance and reporting (on board)
  participant P as Subservice provider
  participant ER as Execution reporting
  U->>AR: TC[x,y] request (ack flags 1111)
  AR-->>U: TM[1,1] successful acceptance (TM[1,2] if failed)
  AR->>P: request distributed for execution
  P->>ER: start of execution notification
  ER-->>U: TM[1,3] success (TM[1,4] failure)
  P->>ER: progress of execution notification (per step)
  ER-->>U: TM[1,5] success (TM[1,6] failure)
  P-->>U: data report (response), if the request type has one
  P->>ER: completion notification
  ER-->>U: TM[1,7] success (TM[1,8] failure)

The diagram combines the request acknowledgement rules of clause 5.4.11.2.2 with the report types of ST[01].3945 Success reports are only sent when the corresponding flag is set; failure reports are always sent. A request whose response would not fit into one telemetry packet of the maximum CCSDS size (65 542 bytes) is rejected; larger transfers are left to file management or mission-specific means.3942

docs.title: Request execution verification
docs.text:
When a provider receives a request, it follows a fixed sequence:40

flowchart TB
  A["Request received by provider"] --> B{"Pre-conditions<br/>fulfilled?"}
  B -- no --> C["Notify failed start of execution<br/>stop processing"]
  B -- yes --> D["Notify successful start"]
  D --> E{"For each step:<br/>execution conditions met?"}
  E -- no --> F["Notify failed progress"]
  E -- yes --> G["Notify successful progress"]
  F --> E
  G --> E
  E -- all steps done --> H{"Any step failed or<br/>post-conditions not met?"}
  H -- yes --> I["Notify failed completion"]
  H -- no --> J["Notify successful completion"]

A successful completion only means that the provider checked every post-condition in the request type's execution verification profile; it does not necessarily mean that the activity achieved its purpose.40 Each profile lists the condition codes and failure notices (code plus parameters) that can be reported at start, progress and completion.30 Whether failed progress is reported in its own TM[1,6] report or folded into the completion report is declared per request type.36

docs.title: Capabilities and applicability constraints
docs.text:
Each subservice type defines at least one capability type, and each capability type carries an applicability constraint that tells a mission whether it must, may or must not provide it:27

Constraint Meaning Example given by the standard minimum every subservice of this type provides the capability the ST[01] verification reports by declaration the mission decides when specifying the subservice enabling periodic housekeeping generation implied by another capability provided automatically if the other one is disabling periodic housekeeping generation by declaration, only if another capability is provided optional, but only on top of another capability register dump on top of register load exclusive-or (on a set) at most one of the set CUC or CDS time reports inclusive-or (on a set) at least one of the set at least one device access capability

Annex C of the standard tags every message type with its constraint ("minimum", "by declaration", "requires TC[x,y]" ...).44 PUS-A instead defined, per service, a "minimum capability set" plus "additional capability sets".48 That scheme comes from PSS-07-101, where the minimum set is the simplest level that is still sensible and coherent and must be part of every implementation of the service, and additional sets are optional.8083 The PUS-C scope clause still uses the capability-set wording to describe service levels, but the requirements themselves work with per-capability applicability constraints.3427

docs.title: Tailoring: the menu approach
docs.text:
The standard says plainly that it is not meant to be applied in full: the services cover a wide range of scenarios, and the mission picks what it needs. PUS should be viewed as a "Menu" from which services and service levels are selected, separately for each application process.34 Early design choices fix the on-board architecture (number, location and role of application processes) and the services each process supports; missions usually record the result in a space-to-ground interface control document.3 All services are optional, and each can be implemented at several levels, the minimum level being the simplest coherent one.4

The idea is as old as the PUS. In 1994 PSS-07-101 asked to be viewed as a "Shopping List"; PUS-A and PUS-C use the word "Menu".80484 The 1994 standard also gave three strong recommendations for the selection: de-select requirements and services from the PUS rather than pick them positively, so that each one is considered and dropped only with a sound technical or operational reason; use the standard service whenever the mission needs its function; and implement each service at one of several levels built from "capability sets", the minimum set being included in every implementation. The outcome of the selection was to be recorded in a mission-specific ground/space ICD.80 Field lengths were already a mission choice: the standard fixes only the type of each field, and "mission-optional" fields that belong to capability sets a mission does not implement can be omitted, so a mission can remain compliant without extra packet overhead.9384

Tailoring the generic level means only adding: mission-specific service types, subservice types, capability types and message types. Reducing the standard capabilities is not recommended because it hampers the reuse of existing hardware and software.31 The standard also assumes that the ground segment implements every standardized capability, so the ground does not constrain tailoring - a point the 2015 presentation repeats: "PUS-C mainly only addresses the on-board capabilities".461

Mandated interdependencies

Even a minimal tailoring must respect the dependencies stated by the standard: request verification is accessible to every service in the same application process; event reporting and large packet transfer are accessible to every service; on-board monitoring and event-action need an event reporting service; and an OBCP service that supports observability levels needs one too.20

Other things a mission must declare include the checksum algorithm used by each provider, the virtual channels used for reports, the on-board memories and their addressing schemes, and the on-board file systems.333435

docs.title: ESA's common tailoring: the Generic OIRD
docs.text:
At ESA the operability requirements that drive this tailoring are written by the Agency, for most missions in a mission-specific Operations Interface Requirements Document (OIRD), an early input to spacecraft development, either stand-alone or inside the system requirements document, and tightly coupled with the CCSDS and ECSS standards.103 (XMM already had one in 1994.99) Mission OIRDs used to be derived from earlier ones, so lessons learnt did not always propagate, differences between missions were not always justified, and the OIRDs had evolved independently of PUS-C and the OBCP standard, partly overlapping them; the resulting variability hampered product-oriented on-board software and mission control systems.104 In June 2016 SAVOIR entrusted ESOC with a Generic OIRD (GOIRD) as the baseline for future missions and for compatible on-board software libraries. GOIRD 1.0 was formally released in July 2019 and had already been used for the Copernicus high-priority candidate missions, ERO/Mars Sample Return and HERA.105109

The GOIRD has two parts, delivered as a PDF document with Excel files (and DOORS modules on request): Part I holds architecture-independent, PUS-agnostic functional requirements traced to the operability standard ECSS-E-ST-70-11C; Part II is a tailoring of PUS-C, written against the PUS-C text in DOORS with a flag (unchanged, modified, deleted or new) and a justification for every change.106107110112 The talk that presented it explains why PUS-C cannot be used as it stands (the GOIRD is also described, with its functional groups and requirement classes, on operations preparation):111

Size of the full PUS-C, as counted in the GOIRD talk Value Service types / subservices 20 / 33, with no mapping to an architecture TC and TM message types if every subservice is implemented 316, of which 88 mandatory "shall be declared when specifying" statements 382

These are the talk's own figures. This wiki's count of the clause 8 message type headings gives 318 message types, 81 of them with "minimum" applicability in Annex C (see the message type catalogue); how the talk arrived at 316 and 88 is not stated in the available sources.11144

Without tailoring two PUS-C implementations would give very different interfaces, and some functions important to ESOC missions were missing (critical event log or system log, file transfer, backup mission timeline).111 The PUS-C part of the GOIRD therefore:113114115116117

  • fixes one common set of services, subservices, capabilities and TC/TM types for all future ESA missions (about 60% of its PUS-C requirements);
  • adds observables to most services, because PUS-C relies heavily on on-demand reports (about 2%);
  • specifies new capabilities at a high level, without TC/TM interfaces - critical event log / system log, parameter extraction from housekeeping, backup mission timeline, file-based operations - to be raised as change requests (about 19%);
  • constrains the avionics architecture: ST[11] is implemented centrally, while services 1, 3, 5, 6 (if applicable) and 17 are required in every packetised unit (under 1%);
  • adds clarifications from earlier missions (about 12%) and changes PUS-C behaviour only minimally, never the defined TC/TM interfaces (under 1%).

A mission OIRD is then produced from the GOIRD - never by copying a previous mission's OIRD - with only mission-specific deltas, mission constants, the sizing of PUS-C services (for example the capacity of the mission timeline) and the de-scoping of what does not apply.105108 The OBCP standard ECSS-E-ST-70-01C is not tailored; a few extra requirements go into service 18.119 The talk also warns that PUS-C leaves key low-level choices open, such as the number of bytes used to encode certain fields, which matters for interoperability between PUS-C units, and calls for coordination among PUS-C library developers.118 How the 2024 draft compares with some of these points is discussed on PUS-A vs PUS-C.

Sources: PUS-C Table 4-1, Annex C and Annex D (page numbers are PDF pages, identical to the printed ones); PUS-A Table 2; PSS-07-101 Table 4-1 and clause 6 (the 1994 document itself uses two names for service 2).74446498682 The reserved identifiers 7, 10 and 16 were used in earlier versions; the standard no longer promotes them but does not forbid reusing existing implementations.7 They are the 1994 task management, time reporting and on-board traffic management services. PUS-A had already marked all three "not used": the time report became subtype 2 of a time reporting subservice inside ST[09], and the traffic management service had never received any subtypes, its specification being left to an Issue 2 of PSS-07-101.49758988 The full list of message types is in the message type catalogue.

Two names for ST[18] and ST[20]

PUS-C itself is not fully consistent: Table 4-1 and clause 6.18 say "on-board control procedure" and Table 4-1 says "parameter management", while the Annex C heading C.2.18 and Annex D say "on-board operations procedure" and clause 8.20 and Annex D say "on-board parameter management".74446

The standard types fall into three families: services with basic functions (for example parameter statistics), services that hold and release requests (the standard's examples are time-based scheduling, position-based scheduling and event-action) and services that offer standard interfaces to devices, to an OBCP engine or to a file system.18

docs.title: How a ground system sees PUS
docs.text:
PUS mainly specifies the spacecraft side, assuming a ground segment that implements every capability.4 In practice the ground knowledge of a mission's PUS tailoring lives in its mission database. In SCOS-2000:

  • incoming telemetry is recognised by APID, service type and subtype - which must sit at the same position in every TM packet of the spacecraft - plus up to two extra identification fields; the combination is looked up in the PID table to find the packet's SPID and structure;64
  • every command definition in CCF carries its service type, subtype, APID and acknowledgement flags, which the header definition copies into the TC packet;65
  • SCOS-2000 decodes and encodes all PUS data types except a few formats (see parameter types), but deduced structures are not supported, and parameters extracted from variable packets cannot feed full TM processing such as limit checks and synthetic parameters, so variable packets should not carry routine housekeeping;6667
  • a few services get ground modelling: service 1 reports drive command verification (using the 4-octet copy of the TC header, and ignoring the failure code), service 9 time reports feed time correlation, and service 11 is modelled with a ground image of the on-board schedule, while most other services get no specific processing.6869 The 4-octet copy is as old as the PUS: the PSS-07-101 verification reports already start with copies of the telecommand's packet ID and packet sequence control, 2 octets each, followed by an optional code and optional parameters.87

Inference: which PUS the ICD appendix cites

Appendix C of the ICD points to "Section 23.5 of [AD-2]" for data types, "Section 23.6" for data structures and "Section 6" to "Section 21 of [AD-5]" for services 1 to 19, although its reference list gives [AD-2] and [AD-5] as SCOS-2000 documents (the Commanding SRD and a displays ICD).666951 Those section numbers match ECSS-E-70-41A, where clause 23.5 is "Simple parameter types", 23.6 "Structured field types", clause 6 the telecommand verification service and clause 14 on-board operations scheduling.50 The appendix therefore appears to have been written against PUS-A. The other candidate, ESA PSS-07-101 (which the ICD lists as RD-6 and cites, for example, for the PID packet type and subtype fields),73 also has "simple parameter types" in clause 23.5 and "structured field types" in clause 23.6, but it specifies telecommand verification in clause 5 and has no services 18 and 19, so the service section numbers fit only PUS-A.82

See also MIB data model, commanding and command verification.

docs.title: PUS on Solar Orbiter
docs.text:
Solar Orbiter is a PUS-A mission: its space-to-ground ICD makes ECSS-E-70-41A its applicable PUS and only allows standard TM/TC within its capability sets unless agreed with ESA and the manufacturer.70 Counting the service types in the September 2025 MIB gives a picture of a real tailoring:72

Service type TM packet definitions (PID) Commands (CCF, nominal header) Notes 0 (no type) 11 0 idle packet (APID 2047), OBC high-priority TM packet (APID 34), three frame pseudo-packets, six ground (LMS) packets on APIDs 2048-2065 1 verification 1 809 0 reports only 2 device 1 1 363 3 housekeeping 397 345 5 events 7 156 35 one definition per event 6 memory 309 221 8 function 1 69 9 time 1 4 the TM(9,2) time report on APID 0 (SPID 9999), keyed as type 9 although it has no data field header 11 scheduling 3 33 12 monitoring 32 254 13 large data 9 28 14 forwarding 4 12 15 storage 7 47 16 0 5 Solar Orbiter "on-board traffic management" 17 test 17 27 18 procedures 2 46 19 event-action 2 48 20 0 17 Solar Orbiter "information distribution" 21 334 33 Solar Orbiter "science data transfer" 22 1 6 Solar Orbiter "context saving" 128-255 (70 types) 1 054 2 725 mission-specific services

Service types 4, 7 and 10 do not occur at all. The command column counts only commands built on the nominal NOM_TC header; the 125 CPDU commands (header HPC1_TC, no service type in CCF), the five frame-level directives and the six NIS throw events are left out.72 Types 16 and 20-22 are numbered in the standard range but carry Solar Orbiter's own mission services as defined in its ICD; PUS-A leaves 16 unused and defines no 20-22, while PUS-C reserves 16 and uses 20-22 for other standard services.7149772 Solar Orbiter's service 16 even carries the name of the 1994 PSS-07-101 service 16, on-board traffic management (see PUS-A vs PUS-C).7186 The details of each service are on How Solar Orbiter uses PUS; individual packets and commands can be browsed in the MIB explorer. The instrument side of the same tailoring is analysed on the STIX instrument database and Solar Orbiter instrument interfaces (the SWA DPU communications ICD) pages.

SQL used 
-- solo-2025-09-16.sqlite (MIB__20250916M25925PFMS001_SOL)
SELECT t, SUM(tm) AS tm_spids, SUM(tc) AS tc_cmds FROM (
  SELECT CAST(PID_TYPE AS INT) t, 1 tm, 0 tc FROM pid
  UNION ALL
  SELECT CAST(CCF_TYPE AS INT), 0, 1 FROM ccf WHERE CCF_PKTID = 'NOM_TC')
GROUP BY t ORDER BY t;
-- aggregated: type 0 / 1-127 / 128-255
SELECT CASE WHEN t = 0 THEN '0' WHEN t < 128 THEN '1-127' ELSE '128-255' END r,
       SUM(tm), SUM(tc), COUNT(DISTINCT t)
  FROM (SELECT CAST(PID_TYPE AS INT) t, 1 tm, 0 tc FROM pid
        UNION ALL SELECT CAST(CCF_TYPE AS INT), 0, 1 FROM ccf WHERE CCF_PKTID = 'NOM_TC')
 GROUP BY r;
-- the packets behind types 0 and 9, and the commands left out
SELECT PID_TYPE, PID_STYPE, PID_APID, PID_SPID, PID_DESCR FROM pid
 WHERE CAST(PID_TYPE AS INT) IN (0, 9);
SELECT CCF_PKTID, CCF_CTYPE, COUNT(*) FROM ccf WHERE CCF_PKTID != 'NOM_TC' GROUP BY 1, 2;

Inference

The large number of service 1 and service 5 packet definitions reflects how SCOS-2000 keys telemetry: PID entries are distinct per APID and per extra identification field (such as an event identifier), so a single report type such as "low severity event" becomes thousands of database packets.

docs.title: Reading the standard
docs.text:
ECSS-E-ST-70-41C is long (656 pages) but regular:47

Part Content Clauses 1-4 scope, references, terms, context and the PUS model Clause 5 the PUS foundation model (generic service type and service deployment levels) Clause 6 system requirements of each service type ST[01]-ST[23] Clause 7 space-to-ground interface: packet field types (7.3) and the Space Packet with PUS headers (7.4) Clause 8 interface requirements: the layout of every TC[x,y] and TM[x,y] Clause 9 the command pulse distribution unit (CPDU) Annexes A-D real number formats, CRC and ISO checksum, summary of all message types with applicability, index of clauses per service

Requirements use "shall", recommendations "should" (to be turned into requirements or tailored out), permissions "may" / "need not", and "can" is descriptive only.43 Clause 6 tells you what a request does; clause 8 tells you how it is encoded, using the PTC/PFC field types of clause 7.3, described on PUS parameter types. The headers of clause 7.4 are described on PUS packet structures, and the differences from the 2003 edition on PUS-A vs PUS-C. The wider ECSS context is on ECSS, ECSS-E-ST-70-11C (space segment operability) and ECSS-E-ST-70-31C (monitoring and control data definition).

One companion standard is tied to a single PUS service. ECSS-E-ST-70-01C (16 April 2010) specifies on-board control procedures (OBCPs) and the engine that runs them; it assumes that missions with OBCPs also comply with ECSS-E-70-41, whose services support OBCP operation and the interaction with the ground (OBCP operations are initiated by service 18 telecommands), and it maps each OBCP operation onto a service 18 subtype (load 1, delete 2, activate 3, stop 4, suspend 5, resume 6, communicate parameters 7, abort 12).101102 See ST[18].

docs.title: PUS message type catalogue
docs.text:
This page is a reference card for the Packet Utilization Standard. The first part lists all 318 standard message types of ECSS-E-ST-70-41C (PUS-C, 15 April 2016): 240 requests (TC) and 78 reports (TM) in 20 service types. It was compiled from the clause 8 interface headings, which name each message type and give its layout, and from Annex C, which summarises every message type with its applicability constraint.12 The second part shows how one real mission database uses the type and subtype numbers: the Solar Orbiter MIB release MIB__20250916M25925PFMS001_SOL (16 September 2025), a PUS-A mission database.2015

At a glance

Item PUS-C (ECSS-E-ST-70-41C) Solar Orbiter MIB, 2025-09-16 release Service types 20 standard types (1-23 without 7, 10 and 16)3 type 0 and types 1 to 22 except 4, 7 and 10, plus 70 types from 128 to 25520 Message types 318 (240 TC, 78 TM) in 33 subservice types1 1 395 distinct (type, subtype) pairs: 227 below type 128, 1 168 from 128 up20 Definitions - 11 150 TM packet definitions (pid), 5 318 nominal TC definitions (ccf)20 Highest subtype 44, TC[3,44]2 255, used once: TC (234,255) "forwardTCthroughSIIS", APID 1164, in the PHI range 231-235; the highest TM subtype is 2532018

docs.title: How a message type is identified
docs.text: A message type is identified by the pair (service type ID, message subtype ID) and carried in the secondary header of every TC and TM packet (see PUS packet structures). Both IDs range from 1 to 255. Standard service types use IDs up to 127 and mission-specific types 128 or above; within a standard service type, the standard subtypes are at most 127 and a mission may add its own from 128 up.45 PUS-A used the same split: types and subtypes 0 to 127 reserved for the standard, 128 to 255 for missions.12 This wiki writes requests as TC[x,y] and reports as TM[x,y], following the standard's own notation.1

docs.title: Applicability constraints
docs.text:
Each message type inherits the applicability constraint of its capability type, which tells a mission whether it must provide it, may provide it, or may provide it only together with another capability.16 Annex C uses these labels:

Label in Annex C Meaning Count in PUS-C minimum always provided by every subservice of that type 81 by declaration provided if the mission says so when specifying the subservice 100 implied by X provided automatically whenever capability X is provided 53 requires X may be declared only if capability X is provided 28 X response the report sent in answer to request X 58 (2 of them also "minimum")

The counts are this wiki's tally of the catalogue below. TM[3,25] and TM[3,26] are counted twice: both are minimum periodic reports and also the responses to the one-shot requests TC[3,27] and TC[3,28].7

docs.title: Rules that span several message types
docs.text:
Some Annex C rows constrain a set of capabilities rather than one message type:8

Printed slips found while compiling

Annex C is informative, and a few of its cells disagree with the normative clauses. Annex C lists the 6.12.3.9.1b alternatives as "TC[12,4], TC[12,5]", while the requirement itself names the delete-all and delete capabilities, TC[12,4] and TC[12,6].910 It gives the third response row of TM[11,10] as "TC[11,10] response" where TC[11,16] is meant. For TM[15,36] it prints "TC[15,36] response" and "6.15.4.5.3" as the interface clause, for TC[15,35] and 8.15.2.33. For TM[17,4] it prints "TC[17,4] response" for TC[17,3], and "TC[15.25]" with a dot.11 The catalogue below uses the corrected values. It also writes the name of TM[5,4] in lower case, as Annex C does; the clause 8.5.2.4 heading capitalises it.2

docs.title: Solar Orbiter: type and subtype usage in the MIB
The release and how it was counted
docs.text:
The figures below come from this wiki's own queries on release MIB__20250916M25925PFMS001_SOL. Its version description record (vdf) has the name 25925PFM, the comment 20250916-CSW3.1.2_MAS7.33, release 25925 and issue 733.20 For each (type, subtype) the page counts:

  • TM definitions: rows of pid with that PID_TYPE and PID_STYPE. SCOS-2000 keys a packet definition on type, subtype, APID and the extra identification fields, so one PUS report type can map to many rows.14
  • TC definitions: rows of ccf with that CCF_TYPE and CCF_STYPE and the nominal packet header NOM_TC. Left out are 125 HPC1_TC high-priority commands and 5 NO_HDR entries, none of which has a type, and 6 NOS2KHDR ground commands of type 251 (open or close TM and TC links and sessions).20

Solar Orbiter follows PUS-A. Its TM/TC ICD tailors the services from the ESA PUS (applicable document AD1, ECSS-E-70-41A) and allows other TM and TC than the standard ones of each capability set only if agreed with ESA and Astrium.15 The comparison therefore uses both editions:

Status Meaning Pairs below type 128 A+C the number is a standard message type of the same kind (TC or TM) in PUS-A Table 43 and in PUS-C 103 A standard in PUS-A only 5 C standard in PUS-C only (the number coincides) 1 M mission-specific subtype (always 128 or above here) in a standard PUS-A service 97 M (own service) a mission service in the standard range that PUS-A does not define (16, 20, 21, 22); any PUS-C name shown belongs to a different service 20 - type 0, packets without a data field header 1

The status compares numbers, not meanings: the PUS-A and PUS-C names are shown so that the reader can judge how close they are. PUS-A Table 43, as transcribed for this page, defines 163 message types (111 TC, 52 TM), and the 2025 MIB uses 108 of them.1320

docs.title: Observations
docs.text:
• Unused services. Types 4, 7 and 10 do not occur, as the ICD states ("not used at all").1920
  • Verification. Only TM(1,1), (1,2), (1,7) and (1,8) appear; there are no start or progress reports (1,3) to (1,6), matching the ICD's service 1 list.1620
  • CPDU numbering. CPDU commands use (2,3), the PUS-A number; PUS-C moved "distribute CPDU commands" to TC[2,4].13220
  • Memory management. Only the absolute-address variants (6,2), (6,5), (6,6), (6,9) and (6,10) are used; PUS-A's base-plus-offset messages (6,1), (6,3), (6,4), (6,7) and (6,8) are absent.1320
  • Large data transfer. Uplink uses PUS-A subtypes (13,9) to (13,11) and (13,13) to (13,16). Of these, (13,13) "Abort Reception of Uplinked Data" and the reports (13,14) and (13,15) exist only in PUS-A, while (13,16) keeps its number in PUS-C as TM[13,16] large packet uplink abortion report. Downlink uses private subtypes from 129 up rather than (13,1) to (13,8). See CFDP and ST[23].2013
  • OBCPs. (18,1) to (18,4) are absent; the mission loads and starts OBCPs with (18,140) and stops and deletes them with (18,141).2017
  • The one "C". (17,3) "Request Connection Test" is not in PUS-A Table 43 but has the number of the PUS-C TC[17,3] "perform an on-board connection test". Whether this is deliberate is not stated in the available sources.13220
  • Own services in the standard range. Type 16 is Solar Orbiter's "On-Board Traffic Management" (MilBus commands), 20 "Information Distribution", 21 "Science Data Transfer" and 22 "Context Saving". PUS-C later gave 20, 21 and 22 different meanings: parameter management, request sequencing and position-based scheduling.18320
  • Extensions. Every mission-specific subtype inside a standard PUS-A service is numbered 128 or higher, as both editions require.12520

Inference

Types 160 to 166 and 170 are not in the ICD's service list. Their MIB entries describe ground-side packets and commands, for example "Time Correlation Report" (164,1), "Bad Telemetry Packets" (162,1) or "PSS Set TC Bit Rate" (170,7), on APIDs 1966 and 1948. They therefore look like ground system definitions rather than spacecraft services. Similarly, types 247, 248 and 251 fall in the SolO-Hi and SPICE ranges, yet their descriptions mention the OBC, the SSMM and "Saved Synthetics". The MIB does not document either point.

docs.title: PUS packet structures: TC and TM headers
docs.text:
Every PUS request travels from ground to spacecraft inside a telecommand (TC) packet, and every PUS report travels back inside a telemetry (TM) packet. Both are CCSDS Space Packets: a 6-octet primary header defined by CCSDS, followed by a packet data field whose first part, the packet secondary header, is defined by the Packet Utilization Standard.1 The secondary header carries the PUS version, the message type (service type and subtype), the acknowledgement flags of a request, the source or destination of the message and, for telemetry, the on-board time stamp. This page dissects these headers bit by bit for ECSS-E-ST-70-41C ("PUS-C", 2016), compares them with ECSS-E-70-41A ("PUS-A", 2003) and the 2024 Rev.1 draft, explains the packet error control algorithms, and shows how the SCOS-2000 Mission Information Base describes the same headers in the real Solar Orbiter database.

Where this page sits

The CCSDS rules for the primary header are covered in depth on Space Packet Protocol. The data types used inside the headers and the user data field (PTC/PFC) are on PUS parameter types. The differences between issues are summarised on PUS-A vs PUS-C. The packets then ride in TC frames and TM frames.

docs.title: 1. The overall layout
docs.text:
PUS-C promotes CCSDS Space Packets for all ground-space messages: a "telecommand packet" carries a request from a ground application process to an on-board one, and a "telemetry packet" carries a report the other way.1 A Space Packet is a primary header of 6 octets followed by a packet data field of 1 to 65 536 octets, so a packet is between 7 and 65 542 octets long.31 PUS-C repeats that the maximum packet size of the Space Packet Protocol is 65 542 bytes and requires a request to be rejected if its response would not fit into one telemetry packet of that size.2

flowchart LR
  subgraph SP["CCSDS Space Packet (7 to 65 542 octets)"]
    direction LR
    PH["Primary header<br/>6 octets<br/>(CCSDS 133.0)"] --> SH["PUS secondary header<br/>TC: 5 octets + spare<br/>TM: 7 octets + time + spare"]
    SH --> UD["User data<br/>application data (TC)<br/>source data (TM)"]
    UD --> SPARE["Spare<br/>(padding)"]
    SPARE --> PEC["Packet error control<br/>16 bits<br/>(mandatory TC, optional TM)"]
  end

The secondary header octet counts in the diagram assume PUS-C field sizes (4 + 4 + 8 + 8 + 16 bits for TC; 4 + 4 + 8 + 8 + 16 + 16 bits plus the time field for TM).1710 Once an application process has generated a packet, nobody may modify it.3

docs.title: 2. The packet primary header
docs.text:
The primary header is defined by CCSDS 133.0-B-2 and reused unchanged by PUS. It has four fields - version (3 bits), packet identification (13 bits), sequence control (16 bits) and data length (16 bits).33 Bit 0 is the first transmitted, most significant bit of a field.32 PUS uses the same left-to-right "Bit 0 first" numbering for every field.4

Field Bits Values Meaning and PUS usage Packet version number 0-2 (3) 0b000 Identifies a CCSDS Space Packet ("version 1 CCSDS packet"). PUS-C sets it to 0.5 Packet type 3 (1) 0 = TM, 1 = TC Distinguishes reporting from requesting packets.33 Secondary header flag 4 (1) 0 / 1 1 when the PUS secondary header is present. All PUS-C TM packets have one except spacecraft time packets; all TC packets have one except CPDU command packets.5 APID 5-15 (11) 0-2047 Names the on-board application process that is the source of a TM packet and the destination of a TC packet. CCSDS reserves only 2047 (all ones) for idle packets; PUS-C adds APID 0 for spacecraft time packets and limits application processes to 0-2046.336 Sequence flags 16-17 (2) 0b11 CCSDS segmentation flags. PUS-C uses 11 (stand-alone) for every packet it defines.5 Packet sequence count or packet name 18-31 (14) 0-16383 TM: incremented by 1 per packet released by the APID, wrapping from 16 383 to 0. TC: a count or a name which, together with the source ID, identifies the packet.5 Packet data length 32-47 (16) 0-65535 Number of octets in the packet data field minus one; the whole packet is 6 octets longer than the data field.5

The primary header fields also carry part of the PUS request identifier and report identifier. A request is identified by its source identifier (in the TC secondary header), its destination (the APID plus a system identifier) and the sequence count or name; a report by its source APID, its destination identifier (in the TM secondary header) and its source sequence count.78 This is why the request verification reports of ST[01] copy the TC packet ID and sequence control fields into their source data: TM[1,1] starts with a "request ID" made of the 3-bit version, the type, the secondary header flag, the APID, the sequence flags and the 14-bit sequence count of the request.9

Why the APID alone is not enough

PUS-C points out that the request ID copied into a verification report cannot identify the request on its own, because it does not contain the source of the request. The source is recovered from the destination ID field in the secondary header of the verification report itself.9

docs.title: 3.1 TC secondary header
docs.text:
In PUS-C every telecommand packet except the CPDU command packet has a TC packet secondary header with the structure below.10

Field Bits Type Values Meaning TC packet PUS version number 4 enumerated 2 Version of the PUS used. 0 was ESA PSS-07-101, 1 is ECSS-E-70-41A, 2 is ECSS-E-ST-70-41C.10 Acknowledgement flags 4 enumerated 0b0000-0b1111 Which successful verification stages the destination must report (table below).11 Service type ID 8 enumerated 1-255 First half of the message type identifier.11 Message subtype ID 8 enumerated 1-255 Second half of the message type identifier.11 Source ID 16 enumerated 0-65535 The application process user identifier of the issuing application process.116 Spare mission fixed-size bit-string all zeros Optional padding of the secondary header to an integral number of words; presence and size declared per application process.1112

The message type ID is the pair (service type ID, message subtype ID). Service types and subtypes run from 1 to 255; the standard ones are at most 127 and mission-specific ones start at 128.13 The notation TC[x,y] used throughout this wiki is exactly this pair.

docs.title: 3.2 The acknowledgement flags
docs.text:
A request carries four flags that ask the destination application process to report the successful acceptance, start, progress and completion of execution.14 Failures do not depend on the flags: failed acceptance, start and completion are always reported, and failed progress is reported either in its own report or within the completion report, as declared for the request type.14

Bit (0 = MSB) Weight Stage reported on success Report generated 0 0b1000 completion of execution TM[1,7] 1 0b0100 progress of execution TM[1,5] 2 0b0010 start of execution TM[1,3] 3 0b0001 acceptance TM[1,1]

The bit assignments come from requirement 7.4.4.1d;11 the report types are the ST[01] successful verification reports.15

Example: 0b1001 (decimal 9) asks for acceptance and completion reports only; 0b0000 suppresses every success report, leaving only failure reports. Solar Orbiter uses 9 for almost all of its commands (see section 9).

docs.title: 3.3 TC user data field
docs.text:
The TC user data field is the application data (whose structure is deduced from the message type), an optional spare field, and a 16-bit packet error control field.16 Each application process declares a telecommand padding word size, and the spare field has the minimum size that makes the total packet length a multiple of it.16 The mission declares whether all TC packets use the ISO 16-bit checksum or the 16-bit CRC; the issuer computes it last, over the complete packet, and the receiving application process verifies it.16

Inference

The bitfield above draws the application data (16 bits) and the spare field (8 bits) with nominal widths chosen by this wiki; both are variable in the standard. Only the 16-bit packet error control field has a fixed size.

docs.title: 4.1 TM secondary header
docs.text:
All PUS-C telemetry packets except the spacecraft time packets of ST[09] carry the TM packet secondary header below.17

Field Bits Type Values Meaning TM packet PUS version number 4 enumerated 2 Version of the PUS (0 = ESA PSS-07-101, 1 = ECSS-E-70-41A, 2 = PUS-C).17 Spacecraft time reference status 4 enumerated mission Status of the on-board time reference used to time-tag this packet. Set to 0 by application processes that do not support the capability.18 Service type ID 8 enumerated 1-255 Message type identifier, first half.18 Message subtype ID 8 enumerated 1-255 Message type identifier, second half.18 Message type counter 16 unsigned integer 0-65535 Counter of generated messages of this type for this destination; 0 if the application process does not count.18 Destination ID 16 enumerated 0-65535 Application process user identifier of the application process addressed by the report.18 Time PFC absolute time mission Time tag of the report. Its PFC is declared when specifying the time service.18 Spare mission fixed-size bit-string zeros Optional padding to an integral number of words, declared per application process.19

Each application process declares three related properties: whether it reports the time reference status, whether it counts messages per destination and type (the two optional capabilities behind these header fields), and whether it time-tags reports before or after collecting their parameter values.6 The meaning of each time reference status value is itself declared by the mission when it specifies the time reporting subservice.20

Why a message type counter?

The 14-bit sequence count in the primary header tells the ground that some packet of an APID is missing. A counter per message type and destination tells it which kind of packet is missing. PUS-A introduced this idea as the 8-bit "packet sub-counter" for exactly this purpose;40 PUS-C widens it to 16 bits and keys it by destination as well.18

docs.title: 4.2 TM user data field
docs.text: The TM user data field contains the source data (deduced from the message type), an optional spare field and an optional 16-bit packet error control field.22 Each application process declares a telemetry padding word size and pads every packet to a multiple of it.22 Whether telemetry is checksummed at all, and with which algorithm (ISO 16-bit checksum or CRC 16-bit), are mission tailoring decisions; if used, the checksum is computed when the packet is complete and is verified by the ground.22

docs.title: 5. Packets without a PUS secondary header
docs.text:
Three kinds of packets in or around PUS have no PUS secondary header:

Packet Primary header settings Data field Source Spacecraft time packet (TM[9,2] CUC or TM[9,3] CDS time report) Secondary header flag 0; APID 0 is reserved for these packets. Optional rate exponential value, spacecraft time, optional time reference status. 5621 CPDU command packet Version 0, type 1, secondary header flag 0, APID of the CPDU, sequence flags 11, sequence count or name 0. Application data only, no spare, then a 16-bit CRC identical to the one of the TC frame error control field. 23 Idle packet APID 11111111111 (2047), secondary header flag 0. Idle data (mission pattern). 3334

The CPDU (command pulse distribution unit) is a simple unit that gives the ground direct access to equipment, for example to reset an S-band transponder in a contingency. Each CPDU request contains one or more command pulse instructions, up to a maximum declared per CPDU that must lie between 12 and 504 (PUS-A allowed at most 120).2341

The pulse duration unit of a CPDU is between 10 ms and 15 ms, and the emitted pulse lasts the unit multiplied by 2 raised to the duration exponential value (0 to 7). A CPDU exposes up to 4096 addressable outputs.23

docs.title: 6. Packet error control
docs.text: The packet error control field detects corruption introduced by lower layers during transmission, processing or storage. PUS offers two 16-bit algorithms, both computed over the whole packet including the primary header but excluding the packet error control field itself.2427

docs.title: 6.1 CRC-16-CCITT
docs.text:
• Generator polynomial \(G(x) = x^{16} + x^{12} + x^{5} + 1\) (0x1021), modulo-2 arithmetic.24
  • The shift register is preset to all ones (0xFFFF) for every packet; the encoding adds \(x^{n-16} L(x)\) to the message polynomial to achieve this preset.25
  • The decoder runs the same register over the data and the received CRC; a zero syndrome means no error was detected.25
  • Detection properties: about \(1.53 \times 10^{-5}\) of all errors go undetected; every odd number of bit errors, every double-bit error no more than 65 535 bits apart and every burst of 16 bits or less are detected.24

docs.title: 6.2 ISO checksum (ISO 8473-1)
docs.text:
• Two running sums modulo 255: \(C_0 = C_0 + B_i\) and \(C_1 = C_1 + C_0\), starting from zero.28
  • The checksum octets are \(CK1 = \lnot(C_0 + C_1)\) and \(CK2 = C_1\), and a value of zero in either octet is replaced by 255.28
  • The decoder runs the sums over the data plus the two checksum octets and accepts the packet if both sums are zero; it rejects immediately if exactly one checksum octet is zero.29
  • It is easy to implement in software (no look-up table, no bit operations), detects every single-bit error and every double-bit error no more than 2 040 bits apart, and leaves about \(1.54 \times 10^{-5}\) of all errors undetected - almost the same as the CRC.27

Inference: a typo in clause B.2.3

The prose of PUS-C clause B.2.3 says "If CK2 = 0, then CK1 = 255". The C code in B.2.6 sets CK2 = 255 instead, and only that reading reproduces the published test vector 00 00 giving FF FF.28 This wiki treats the prose as a typo.

docs.title: 6.3 Test vectors
docs.text:
The standard publishes these test vectors (hexadecimal, most significant digit first). The values were re-computed by this wiki with its own implementation of both algorithms and match.2629

Data CRC-16 ISO checksum 00 00 1D 0F FF FF 00 00 00 CC 9C FF FF AB CD EF 01 04 A2 9C F8 14 56 F8 9A 00 01 7F D5 24 DC

docs.title: 6.4 Worked example (illustrative bytes)
docs.text:
The bytes below are illustrative, constructed by this wiki from the PUS-C field definitions; they are not taken from a real mission. They encode an are-you-alive connection test request, TC[17,1], which has no application data,30 sent to APID 0x064 with sequence count 1, acknowledgement flags 0b1001 and source ID 0x0010.

Octets Value Decoding 0-1 18 64 version 000, type 1 (TC), secondary header flag 1, APID 0x064 2-3 C0 01 sequence flags 11, sequence count 1 4-5 00 06 packet data length 6, so the data field is 7 octets 6 29 PUS version 2 (0010), ack flags 1001 7-8 11 01 service type 17, message subtype 1 9-10 00 10 source ID 16 11-12 07 1D CRC-16 over octets 0-10

Running the CRC decoder over all 13 octets gives a zero syndrome, so the packet is accepted. With the ISO checksum instead of the CRC, the last two octets would be 63 0D.

A matching illustrative report, TM[17,2] (which has no source data),30 from the same APID with sequence count 0x42, message type counter 1, destination ID 16 and a CUC time of 4 coarse and 2 fine octets (PFC 17, see parameter types) is:

08 64 C0 42 00 0E | 20 11 02 00 01 00 10 1E 2C 9A 00 80 00 | B0 4B
primary header    | secondary header (time = 0x1E2C9A00 s + 0x8000/65536 s) | CRC

The first secondary header octet 0x20 is PUS version 2 with time reference status 0; the time field encodes 506 239 488.5 seconds after the mission epoch.

docs.title: 7. PUS-A (2003) equivalents side by side
docs.text:
ECSS-E-70-41A called the secondary header the data field header and built it from smaller, often optional fields whose sizes were fixed by mission constants.3537

TC headerTM headerPrimary header

PUS-A field Bits PUS-C counterpart CCSDS secondary header flag (Boolean, 0) 1 absorbed into the 4-bit PUS version TC packet PUS version number (1) 3 TC packet PUS version number (2), 4 bits Ack 4 Acknowledgement flags, same bit meanings Service type 8 Service type ID Service subtype 8 Message subtype ID Source ID (optional, length known for the mission) n Source ID, 16 bits, always present Spare (optional) n Spare (optional)

In PUS-A the secondary header flag bit was set to 0 to mark a "non-CCSDS defined" secondary header, the version was 1, and the source ID was omitted when the mission had only one TC source.36 The packet error control field was mandatory for all TC packets, with its type fixed per application process by the mission constant <TC_CHECKSUM_TYPE>.36

PUS-A field Bits PUS-C counterpart Spare (former CCSDS secondary header flag) 1 absorbed into the 4-bit PUS version TM source packet PUS version number (1) 3 TM packet PUS version number (2), 4 bits Spare 4 Spacecraft time reference status Service type 8 Service type ID Service subtype 8 Message subtype ID Packet sub-counter (optional) 8 Message type counter, 16 bits Destination ID (optional, length known for the mission) n Destination ID, 16 bits Time (optional, CUC or CDS, per <APPL_TIME_CODE>) n Time (PFC declared by the time service) Spare (optional) n Spare (optional)

The packet sub-counter counted packets of one type and subtype (per destination if the destination ID was used); the destination ID was omitted when the ground was the only destination; and the presence and encoding of the time field were given per application process by <APPL_TIME_CODE>.38 The TM packet error control field was optional, its presence and type set by <TM_CHECKSUM_TYPE>.38

Item PUS-A PUS-C Referenced CCSDS documents CCSDS 102.0-B-5 (TM) and 203.0-B-2 (TC)35 CCSDS 133.0-B-1 Space Packet Protocol1 Sequence flags in TM "grouping flags" 01/00/10/11, standard packets stand-alone38 always 115 Sequence flags in TC 01/00/10/11, standard packets stand-alone36 always 115 TC sequence count one count per TC source and APID36 count or packet name, combined with source ID5 TM source sequence count per APID, and per destination when a destination ID is used; never "short-cycle"38 per APID, wraps at 16 3845 Reserved APIDs 0 time packet, 2047 idle, one APID per CPDU39 0 time packets, 2047 idle, others per SANA6

Mission constants such as <TCPKT_MAX_LENGTH> and <TMPKT_MAX_LENGTH> let a PUS-A mission cap packet sizes below the CCSDS maximum.41 PUS-C replaces mission constants by "declarations" made when tailoring; the Rev.1 draft makes the declaration of both maximum packet sizes an explicit requirement.43

docs.title: 8. What the 2024 Rev.1 draft changes in the headers
docs.text:
ECSS-E-ST-70-41C Rev.1 DIR1 (11 December 2024, a draft for public review) keeps the field sizes of PUS-C but changes the meaning of several fields:42

Item PUS-C (2016) Rev.1 DIR1 (2024 draft) TC secondary header 16-bit field source ID = application process user identifier source APID = the issuer's application process identifier44 TM secondary header 16-bit field destination ID = application process user identifier destination APID = APID of the targeted application process45 Ground application processes identified by user identifiers 0-65535 APIDs 2048-65535, never reused on board; on-board APIDs stay at most 204647 TM packet error control optional field mandatory in the user data field; the checksum calculation is application process dependent46 Maximum packet sizes not stated as requirements TM and TC maximum sizes declared for the mission, not above the CCSDS maximum43 Packets without secondary header time packets, CPDU packets also CFDP PDUs and idle packets (TM), CFDP PDUs and SDLS extended procedure PDUs (TC)48

Inference

Moving source and destination identification into the APID space lets one 16-bit number name both on-board processes (0-2046) and ground processes (2048 and above). The draft is not an approved standard, and missions already flying PUS-C keep the 2016 meaning.

docs.title: 9. Solar Orbiter: the headers in a real MIB
docs.text: The public Solar Orbiter MIB lets us see how a real mission's headers are described to SCOS-2000. Solar Orbiter's space-to-ground ICD makes ECSS-E-70-41A its applicable PUS, so the mission uses PUS-A headers.49

docs.title: 9.1 Telecommand headers (TCP, PCPC, PCDF)
docs.text:
SCOS-2000 builds the first portion of every encoded TC packet from a packet header definition: TCP names the header, PCPC defines header parameters and PCDF lists the elements with their length in bits and their bit offset from the start of the packet.57 Each PCDF element has a type: F fixed value, A APID from CCF_APID, T service type from CCF_TYPE, S subtype from CCF_STYPE, K acknowledgement flags from CCF_ACK, or P a parameter set automatically by the command subsystem, such as the packet length or the sequence counter maintained by the multiplexer for each APID.58

The September 2025 release defines four headers. NOM_TC ("NOM_DH_TC_Packet_Header") is the nominal header:70

PCDF_BIT PCDF_LEN Element PCDF_TYPE Value / parameter 0 3 Version Number F 0 3 1 Type F 1 4 1 DataFieldHeaderFlag F 1 5 11 APID A PH_APID 16 2 Sequence Flag F 3 (11) 18 14 Sequence Count P PH_SSC 32 16 Packet Length P PH_LEN 48 1 Secondary Header Flag F 0 49 3 PUS Version F 1 52 4 Ack K DFH_ACK 56 8 Service Type T DFH_TYPE 64 8 Service Subtype S DFH_STPE 72 8 Source ID O DFH_SRC

This is exactly the PUS-A TC data field header with an 8-bit source ID, 4 octets in total, which the Solar Orbiter ICD confirms: a TC packet data field of at most 242 octets is 4 octets of data field header, 236 of application data and 2 of packet error control.50 The ICD lists reserved ground source IDs (110 mission timeline, 111 TC sequences, 112 recovery actions, 113 back-up mission timeline, 120 direct commands, 121-122 spare) and on-board ones (11 AOCS, 14 system control, 15 OBCP).52

Inference: PCDF_TYPE O

The ICD issues available to this wiki (5.1, 6.9 and 7.0) list only the types F, A, T, S, K and P for PCDF_TYPE.585960 The 2025 release uses O for the source ID, whereas the April 2020 release defined the same element as a fixed (F) area with value 0.74 In ICD 7.0 the letter O appears in this table only as the octal value of PCDF_RADIX, not as a PCDF_TYPE.58 The meaning of O as a type is not stated in the available sources; it plausibly lets the command source set the source ID.

The other headers are HPC1_TC (primary header only, secondary header flag 0), used by 125 commands to APID 44 on MAP ID 0 - the CPDU "HPC-1" commands that the Solar Orbiter ICD sends directly to the command pulse distribution unit on MAP 0 - then NO_HDR (5 directives: two control frames such as UNLOCK and SETVR, three control segments such as RESET) and NOS2KHDR (6 NIS throw events on APID 1964, such as open and close TC link, all with CCF_CTYPE N).7155 SCOS-2000 uses the CCF_CTYPE values R (control segment) and F (control frame) for such directives, whose PCDF/CDF entries define a frame data field rather than a packet, and N for NIS throw events, which the NIS executes without forwarding them to the ground station.61

The acknowledgement flags of each command come from CCF_ACK:71

CCF_ACK Binary Commands Meaning 9 1001 5 225 acceptance and completion reports (empty) - 130 headerless commands and directives 1 0001 78 acceptance report only 0 0000 21 failure reports only (15 NOM_TC commands and the 6 NIS throw events)

This matches the Solar Orbiter ICD, which defines only the acceptance and completion bits and requires the start and progress bits to be zero.51

SQL used (TC headers) 
-- solo-2025-09-16.sqlite (MIB__20250916M25925PFMS001_SOL)
SELECT * FROM tcp;
SELECT * FROM pcpc;
SELECT * FROM pcdf ORDER BY PCDF_TCNAME, CAST(PCDF_BIT AS INT);
SELECT CCF_PKTID, COUNT(*) FROM ccf GROUP BY 1;
SELECT CCF_ACK, COUNT(*) n FROM ccf GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY n DESC;
SELECT CCF_PKTID, CCF_CTYPE, CCF_APID, CCF_MAPID, CCF_ACK, COUNT(*) FROM ccf
 WHERE CCF_PKTID != 'NOM_TC' OR CCF_ACK = '0' GROUP BY 1, 2, 3, 4, 5;
-- solo-2020-04-16.sqlite
SELECT * FROM pcdf WHERE PCDF_TCNAME = 'NOM_TC' ORDER BY CAST(PCDF_BIT AS INT);

A real Solar Orbiter command shows the pieces together: ZCD00B04 "Insert Telecommands in Command Schedule" is TC[11,4] sent to APID 172 with header NOM_TC and CCF_ACK 9.72 APID 172 is 0b0001010_1100: Solar Orbiter splits the APID into a 7-bit process ID (here 10) and a 4-bit packet category that is fixed to 12 for telecommands.54 See it in the explorer and in the TC worked example.

docs.title: 9.2 Telemetry headers (PID_DFHSIZE and friends)
docs.text:
On the telemetry side the MIB does not describe the secondary header field by field. The SCOS-2000 packetiser extracts the APID from the primary header and the type and subtype from a configurable position that must be the same in every packet of the spacecraft; it then looks up the PID table with the key APID, type, subtype and up to two extra identification fields defined in PIC.63 A packet with no data field header is identified by APID alone and gets type and subtype 0.64 Solar Orbiter follows this for its idle and ground packets but not for its time packet: SPID 9999 "Time Report" on APID 0 is keyed as type 9, subtype 2 although the packet has no data field header.7353 Three PID fields then describe the header:

PID field Meaning PID_DFHSIZE Number of octets (0-99) from the start of the source packet to where variable-packet (VPD) processing starts; typically the primary header plus the data field header.65 PID_TIME Y if the packet carries a generation time field, N otherwise.66 PID_CHECK 0 do not check the packet error control field; 1 check it with the CRC.67

In the 2025 Solar Orbiter release these fields take the following combinations:73

PID_DFHSIZE PID_TIME PID_CHECK Packets (SPIDs) Examples 16 Y 0 11 132 almost every spacecraft TM packet 16 N 0 6 non-spacecraft packets (LMS_...) on APIDs 2048-2065, a range the ICD reserves for packets not generated by the spacecraft68 6 Y 0 6 TM[9,2] "Time Report" on APID 0, and five type 160/161 packets on APID 1966 0 Y or N 1 6 frame-level pseudo-packets (good, bad and idle transfer frames, MATIS)

PID_DFHSIZE = 16 is the 6-octet primary header plus a 10-octet data field header. The Solar Orbiter ICD gives the TM packet data field as at most 4 106 octets, made of 4 096 octets of source data and 10 octets of data field header, with the time in CUC format of 4 coarse and 2 fine octets (6 octets).56 Its destination ID field is 8 bits, set to the source ID of the command for solicited telemetry except for several packet categories that are always sent to ground (00000000).53 The time packet TM[9,2] has no data field header, which is why its PID_DFHSIZE is 6.53

Inference: the 10-octet Solar Orbiter TM data field header

The figure of the TM data field header in the Solar Orbiter ICD is not available as text. From the documented sizes (10 octets in total, 6 octets of time, an 8-bit destination ID) and the PUS-A layout, the most likely arrangement is: 1 octet spare/version/spare, 1 octet service type, 1 octet subtype, 1 octet destination ID and 6 octets of time, with no packet sub-counter. The 4 106-octet maximum with no octets left for a packet error control field is consistent with PID_CHECK = 0.

SQL used (TM headers) 
-- solo-2025-09-16.sqlite
SELECT PID_DFHSIZE, PID_TIME, PID_CHECK, COUNT(*) n
  FROM pid GROUP BY 1, 2, 3 ORDER BY n DESC;
SELECT PID_TYPE, PID_STYPE, PID_APID, PID_SPID, PID_DESCR, PID_DFHSIZE, PID_TIME, PID_CHECK
  FROM pid WHERE PID_DFHSIZE != '16' OR PID_TIME != 'Y';
-- first parameter offset per packet (PLF): 16 octets for 9 020 SPIDs
SELECT m, COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT PLF_SPID, MIN(CAST(PLF_OFFBY AS INT)) m
  FROM plf GROUP BY PLF_SPID) GROUP BY m ORDER BY 2 DESC;

The PLF table agrees: in 9 020 of the fixed packets that have PLF entries, the first parameter starts at byte offset 16, immediately after the 16-octet headers.73 PLF_OFFBY counts octets from the end of the SCOS-2000 TM header, which for missions using the SCOS-2000 packetiser is the beginning of the TM source packet - so offsets include the primary and data field headers.69

docs.title: 9.3 How SCOS-2000 assembles a TC packet
docs.text:
flowchart TB
  CCF["CCF record<br/>CCF_PKTID, CCF_APID,<br/>CCF_TYPE, CCF_STYPE, CCF_ACK"] --> HDR
  TCP["TCP / PCDF elements<br/>(bit offsets, lengths, types)"] --> HDR["Header bits<br/>F: fixed  A: APID  T: type<br/>S: subtype  K: ack  P: length, count"]
  CDF["CDF elements + CPC parameters<br/>(PTC/PFC, calibration, defaults)"] --> AD["Application data"]
  HDR --> PKT["Encoded TC packet"]
  AD --> PKT
  PKT --> CRC["Releaser appends 16-bit CRC<br/>(unless CCF_CTYPE = S)"]

The packet length and the sequence counter are set by the command subsystem, not by the operator.58 The releaser appends the 16-bit CRC to standard commands; CCF_CTYPE S marks a command packet without packet error control, typically for EGSE.61 By default SCOS-2000 limits an encoded command to 248 bytes (CMDP_MAX_BLOCK_SIZE), from which the header, the CRC (CMD_CRC_SIZE, default 2 bytes) and any time-tag wrapper are subtracted.62 The data that follows the header is described on Commanding in the MIB and in the MIB data model.
