docs.title: PUS parameter types (PTC/PFC)
docs.text: Every field of a PUS packet - a housekeeping value, a command argument, a time tag, even the spare bits - has a type that is identified by two small numbers: the packet field type code (PTC), which says what kind of value the field holds (Boolean, unsigned integer, real, absolute time ...), and the packet field format code (PFC), which says how that value is encoded (how many bits, which floating-point format, which time code).1 The pair is the common vocabulary between the on-board software, the space-to-ground ICD and ground systems such as SCOS-2000, whose MIB stores a PTC and a PFC for every monitoring parameter (PCF) and every command parameter (CPC).5153 This page lists every type and format defined by ECSS-E-ST-70-41C ("PUS-C"), compares them with ECSS-E-70-41A ("PUS-A") and the 2024 Rev.1 draft, and shows what the SCOS-2000 import ICD and the Solar Orbiter database actually use. The MIB-specific view continues on MIB parameter types.

docs.title: Why a type code system
docs.text:
PUS-A explains the motivation: the standard does not fix a length or encoding for each field of each packet; instead a mission selects, field by field, the length and encoding that best suit it, and records the choice as a parameter code.22 The tabular notation is a simple alternative to ASN.1, and the encoding rules deliberately differ from the ASN.1 Basic Encoding Rules, mainly because of the limited space-link bandwidth.22 PUS-C keeps the idea but renames the codes: a "packet field code" is the combination of a PTC and a PFC, and the meaning of a PFC depends only on its PTC.1 The scheme is older than ECSS: the ESA PUS of 1994, PSS-07-101, already combined a "Parameter Type Code" and a "Parameter Format Code" into a parameter code, valid for both telecommand and telemetry data (see the history page).33

Tailoring therefore happens at two moments:1

  • when a mission defines a new message type, it declares the PTC of each of its fields;
  • when a standard message type leaves a format open (for example the length of a parameter identifier), the mission declares the PFC when specifying the application process that uses that message type.

PUS-A describes four scopes at which such a choice can be made: mission defined (one format everywhere), application process defined, service instance defined, or request/report defined (the format is deduced from preceding fields, possibly together with mission constants).24

docs.title: Conventions used in packet structure diagrams
docs.text:
PUS specifies packet contents with structure diagrams: the first row names each field and the second row gives its type. A field marked "optional" is present or absent at mission, application process or service-instance level, and its omission can mean that both ends already know the value (a fixed value, a "current value" set by other means, or a look-up table indexed by earlier fields).2 A group of fields marked "repeated N times" is an array; for a variable-length array, N is carried explicitly in front of the entries, while for a fixed-length array N is a mission constant.2 The Rev.1 draft adds that N is 0 when the array is empty.43

Bits are numbered from the left: the first, most significant bit of an n-bit field is "Bit 0" and the last is "Bit N-1"; 8 adjacent bits form an octet.3 This is the same convention as CCSDS (see Space Packet Protocol).

docs.title: The twelve packet field types
docs.text:
PTC PUS-C type Formats (PFC) Also in PUS-A? Section 1 Boolean 0 = 1 bit, n > 1 = n bits yes, PFC 0 only PTC 1 2 enumerated 1 to 64 bits yes, PFC 1-16, 24, 32 PTC 2 3 unsigned integer PFC 0-19 yes, PFC 0-16 PTC 3 4 signed integer PFC 0-16 yes, PFC 0-16 PTC 4 5 real PFC 1-4 yes, PFC 1-4 PTC 5 6 bit-string 0 = variable, n = n bits yes PTC 6 7 octet-string 0 = variable, n = n octets yes PTC 7 8 character-string 0 = variable, n = n characters yes PTC 8 9 absolute time PFC 0-46 yes, PFC 0-18 PTC 9 10 relative time PFC 2-18 yes, PFC 0-16 (different numbering) PTC 10 11 deduced 0 yes PTC 11 12 packet 0 = TM packet, 1 = TC packet no PTC ("Any TM", "Any TC") PTC 12

The PTC column is Table 7-1 of PUS-C;1 the PUS-A column summarises clause 23.5 and the "Any TC"/"Any TM" abbreviations of clause 5.2.2542

docs.title: Boolean (PTC 1)
docs.text: A Boolean field is PTC 1. A value greater than 0 means TRUE and 0 means FALSE. PFC 0 is a 1-bit Boolean; any PFC n > 1 is an n-bit Boolean (for example PFC 8 is an 8-bit Boolean).4 PUS-A defined only the 1-bit form (PFC 0), with 1 = TRUE and 0 = FALSE.26

docs.title: Enumerated (PTC 2)
docs.text:
An enumerated value is an unsigned integer that may appear in logical and comparative expressions but not in arithmetic: each value stands for a text meaning, an error code being the typical example (0 "unchecked", 3 "invalid").5 The PFC is simply the length in bits, from 1 to 64.5 PUS-A allowed only the lengths 1-16, 24 and 32 bits.27

Enumerated is the type of every identifier in the PUS headers: PUS version, acknowledgement flags, service type, message subtype, source ID and destination ID are all enumerated fields (see packet structures).21

docs.title: Unsigned integer (PTC 3)
docs.text:
Unsigned integers are encoded with Bit 0 as the most significant bit.6

PFC Size Range Notes 0 4 bits 0-15 PFC 0-12 are (PFC + 4) bits 1 5 bits 0-31 2 6 bits 0-63 3 7 bits 0-127 4 8 bits 0-255 one octet 5 9 bits 0-511 6 10 bits 0-1 023 7 11 bits 0-2 047 e.g. an APID 8 12 bits 0-4 095 9 13 bits 0-8 191 10 14 bits 0-16 383 e.g. a sequence count 11 15 bits 0-32 767 12 16 bits 0-65 535 two octets 13 3 octets 0 to \(2^{24}-1\) (16 777 215) 14 4 octets 0 to \(2^{32}-1\) 15 6 octets 0 to \(2^{48}-1\) 16 8 octets 0 to \(2^{64}-1\) 17 1 bit 0-1 new in PUS-C 18 2 bits 0-3 new in PUS-C 19 3 bits 0-7 new in PUS-C

PFC 0-16 are identical in PUS-A; PFC 17-19 (1 to 3 bits) appear only in PUS-C.628 The "e.g." notes are this wiki's illustrations of where such widths occur in packet headers.

docs.title: Signed integer (PTC 4)
docs.text:
Bit 0 is the sign (0 positive, 1 negative) and negative values are the two's complement of the absolute value.7

PFC Size Range 0-12 (PFC + 4) bits \(-2^{PFC+3}\) to \(2^{PFC+3}-1\) (from -8..7 for PFC 0 up to -32 768..32 767 for PFC 12) 13 3 octets -8 388 608 to 8 388 607 14 4 octets \(-2^{31}\) to \(2^{31}-1\) 15 6 octets \(-2^{47}\) to \(2^{47}-1\) 16 8 octets \(-2^{63}\) to \(2^{63}-1\)

The signed formats are the same in PUS-A and PUS-C; unlike PTC 3, PTC 4 has no 1-3 bit formats.729

docs.title: Real (PTC 5)
docs.text:
PFC Format Size 1 IEEE 754 single precision 4 octets 2 IEEE 754 double precision 8 octets 3 MIL-STD-1750A single precision 4 octets 4 MIL-STD-1750A extended precision 6 octets

The four formats are the same in PUS-A and PUS-C.830

IEEE single (PFC 1)IEEE double (PFC 2)MIL-STD-1750A (PFC 3 and 4)

Normal values are \((-1)^{sign} \times 2^{exponent-127} \times 1.fraction\); exponent 255 encodes infinities (fraction 0) and NaN (fraction not 0); exponent 0 encodes zero and denormalized values. Range about \(1.12 \times 10^{-38}\) to \(3.40 \times 10^{38}\) with a precision of about \(1.15 \times 10^{-7}\).9

Exponent 2 047 encodes infinities and NaN; range about \(2.22 \times 10^{-308}\) to \(1.79 \times 10^{308}\), precision about \(2.22 \times 10^{-16}\).9

The 1750A formats are a normalized fractional two's-complement mantissa times 2 to the power of a two's-complement exponent: 24-bit mantissa plus 8-bit exponent for single precision, and a 40-bit mantissa split around the 8-bit exponent for extended precision. Zero is all zeros. Real example from the standard: 40 00 00 7F is \(0.5 \times 2^{127}\) and 80 00 00 00 is \(-1.0\).1031

docs.title: Bit-string (PTC 6)
docs.text:
A bit-string carries bits whose meaning is application process specific. PFC 0 is a variable-length bit-string; PFC n > 0 is a fixed-length bit-string of n bits.11

The length field is an unsigned integer whose own PFC is declared per application process.11 Two rules make PTC 6 special:11

  • every spare field of a TM or TC packet is a fixed-length PTC 6 field, and all its bits are zero;
  • the length of a fixed-length bit-string may be deduced, but only from preceding fields of the same packet, from mission constants, or both - never from later fields.

Inference

The widths in the diagram above (8-bit length, 24-bit data) are illustrative. The standard leaves the length-field size to the application process declaration.

docs.title: Octet-string (PTC 7)
docs.text: PFC 0 is a variable-length octet-string with the same "length then data" structure as the variable bit-string, the length counting octets; PFC n > 0 is a fixed string of n octets.12 The length-field PFC is declared per application process, and a deduced fixed length may only depend on preceding fields or mission constants.12 As with bit-strings, the meaning of the octets is application process specific;12 the Solar Orbiter examples below show octet strings carrying whole tables, science blocks and embedded commands.

docs.title: Character-string (PTC 8)
docs.text: Character strings hold visible characters, each encoded as its ASCII code on one octet. PFC 0 is variable length (length then characters), PFC n > 0 is a fixed string of n characters.13 The Rev.1 draft makes "visible" precise - the space 0x20 plus the printable characters 0x21 to 0x7E - and requires shorter values to be padded at the end with spaces up to the PFC length.44

docs.title: Absolute time (PTC 9)
docs.text:
An absolute time is a positive number of seconds and fractions of a second from an epoch. With CUC, the epoch is either the CCSDS epoch of 1 January 1958 or an agency-defined epoch - in the latter case the field is effectively a free-running counter that the ground converts with time correlation coefficients. CDS always uses the 1958 epoch.14 Both codes are defined in CCSDS 301.0-B-4 (see time code formats); PUS-C notes that CCSDS allows 1-7 octets of coarse time and 1-10 octets of fine time, of which PUS implements coarse time of 1-4 octets and fine time of 1-10 octets.14

PFC Encoding Length 0 explicit format, P-field included (CUC or CDS) variable 1 CDS, 2-octet day, no microseconds 6 octets 2 CDS, 2-octet day, with microseconds 8 octets 3-18 CUC: coarse = (PFC + 1) div 4 octets, fine = (PFC + 1) mod 4 octets; implicit P-field 1-7 octets 19-46 CUC: coarse = (PFC - 12) div 7 octets, fine = 4 + (PFC - 12) mod 7 octets; implicit P-field 5-14 octets

The rows paraphrase PUS-C Table 7-10.15 PUS-A had PFC 0-18 with the same meanings; PFC 19-46 (fine time of 4-10 octets) are new in PUS-C.32

For PFC 18 the time is \(t = C_1 256^3 + C_2 256^2 + C_3 256 + C_4 + F_1 256^{-1} + F_2 256^{-2} + F_3 256^{-3}\) seconds from the epoch.15

docs.title: CUC PFC table
docs.text:
The table below expands the two formulas. The resolution (\(2^{-8f}\) s for f fine octets) and the range before wrap-around (\(2^{8c}\) s for c coarse octets) are computed by this wiki from the formula above; they are not printed in the standard.

PFC Coarse Fine Octets Resolution Range 3 1 0 1 1 s 256 s 4 1 1 2 3.9 ms 256 s 5 1 2 3 15.3 µs 256 s 6 1 3 4 59.6 ns 256 s 7 2 0 2 1 s 18.2 h 8 2 1 3 3.9 ms 18.2 h 9 2 2 4 15.3 µs 18.2 h 10 2 3 5 59.6 ns 18.2 h 11 3 0 3 1 s 194 days 12 3 1 4 3.9 ms 194 days 13 3 2 5 15.3 µs 194 days 14 3 3 6 59.6 ns 194 days 15 4 0 4 1 s 136 years 16 4 1 5 3.9 ms 136 years 17 4 2 6 15.3 µs 136 years 18 4 3 7 59.6 ns 136 years 19-25 1 4-10 5-11 0.23 ns and finer 256 s 26-32 2 4-10 6-12 0.23 ns and finer 18.2 h 33-39 3 4-10 7-13 0.23 ns and finer 194 days 40-46 4 4-10 8-14 0.23 ns and finer 136 years

PFC 17 - 4 octets of seconds and 2 octets of fraction - is the format Solar Orbiter uses for its packet time stamps ("CUC 9/17").56

Decoding a CUC value (illustrative bytes)

The six octets 1E 2C 9A 00 80 00 read as PTC 9, PFC 17 give coarse time 0x1E2C9A00 = 506 239 488 s and fine time 0x8000 / 65 536 = 0.5 s, so the value is 506 239 488.5 s after the mission epoch. The bytes are invented for illustration.

docs.title: Relative time (PTC 10)
docs.text:
A relative time is a positive or negative offset in seconds and fractions from an event identified by other fields, or the difference between two absolute times. Negative offsets are the two's complement of the positive offset.16

PFC PUS-A (2003) PUS-C (2016) Rev.1 DIR1 (2024 draft) 0 explicit CUC, P-field included - - 1 CUC 1 coarse, 0 fine - CDS without microseconds, 6 octets 2 CUC 1 coarse, 1 fine CDS with microseconds, 8 octets CDS with microseconds, 8 octets 1-16 (PUS-A) coarse = (PFC + 3) div 4, fine = (PFC + 3) mod 4 - - 3-18 (PUS-A meanings continue up to 16) CUC, coarse = (PFC + 1) div 4, fine = (PFC + 1) mod 4 same as PUS-C

Sources: PUS-A clause 23.5.10, PUS-C Table 7-11 and Rev.1 DIR1 Table 7-11.351645 In the full 7-octet CUC form, a positive offset has C1 in the range 0-127, leaving the sign bit free.16

Inference: the relative-time renumbering

The two formulas mean that a PUS-A relative-time format n equals the PUS-C format n + 2: PUS-A PFC 1 (1 coarse octet) is PUS-C PFC 3, and PUS-A PFC 16 (4 + 3 octets) is PUS-C PFC 18. PUS-C thereby aligns the relative-time CUC numbering with the absolute-time numbering. Anyone converting a PUS-A interface document into a ground database must therefore not copy relative-time PFC values blindly.

docs.title: Deduced (PTC 11)
docs.text: A deduced field (PTC 11, PFC 0) has a structure and format that is worked out from preceding fields of the same packet, from mission constants, or both; the rule must be declared when the field is specified.17 PUS-A illustrates it with a pair "Parameter#" (enumerated) followed by "Parameter Value" (deduced): the value field changes type from packet to packet according to the parameter identifier in front of it.36 Ground databases use the same idea for generic reports that carry values of arbitrary parameters, for instance the value of a parameter that failed an ST[12] monitoring check (see the Solar Orbiter examples below).

docs.title: Packet (PTC 12)
docs.text: PTC 12 carries a whole packet inside a field: PFC 0 is a CCSDS telemetry packet and PFC 1 a CCSDS telecommand packet, both compliant with PUS.18 For example, TC[11,4] "insert activities into the time-based schedule" of ST[11] carries an optional sub-schedule ID and a count N, followed by N instructions, each an optional group ID, a release time (absolute time) and the request itself as a "TC packet" field,19 and TC[21,1] of ST[21] loads a sequence of "TC packet" fields each followed by a relative-time delay.20 PUS-A had no PTC for this; its structure diagrams simply used the abbreviations "Any TC" and "Any TM".42

docs.title: Structured fields
docs.text:
Simple types are combined into structures. PUS-A formalised this as structure rules set #1:37

  • a record is a fixed sequence of distinct components (simple or structured);
  • an array repeats one component; a fixed array repeats it an implicit number of times, a variable array is preceded by an unsigned integer D giving the number of entries;
  • a deduced structure is one component whose type is chosen by "determining parameters" (preceding fields or mission constants), which may only be Boolean, enumerated, integer or character-string values, or themselves deduced.

PUS-A added six nesting and identification rules (NIR1-NIR6): fields outside any array are at level 1 and array components one level deeper; a concrete parameter may be named only once, at level 1 or 2, unless each extra occurrence has a specialised meaning (NIR5); and the last determining parameter must sit at the level of the structure it determines or one level above, the first one at level 1 or 2.39 Encoded fields are packed bit-aligned one after the other, with optional zero padding to reach a mission word boundary.4024

flowchart TB
  R["Record Ra (level 1)"] --> P1["Records Rb, Rc<br/>Pa .. Pd"]
  R --> FA["Fixed array FAa<br/>n entries known implicitly"]
  R --> VA["Variable array VAa<br/>D entries, D given explicitly"]
  R --> RD["Record Rd<br/>Ph, Pi"]
  FA --> RE["Record Re (level 2)<br/>Pe, Pf"]
  VA --> RF["Record Rf (level 2)<br/>Pg"]
  R -.-> DS["Deduced structure S<br/>type chosen by determining parameter P"]

The solid part of the diagram follows the second example of PUS-A clause 23.6.5; the dashed deduced structure S is added from the example of clause 23.6.4, where S is a variable array, a record A or a record B depending on a preceding parameter P.4140 PUS-C expresses the same ideas with "repeated N times" arrays and PTC 11 deduced fields instead of a separate set of structure rules.217

docs.title: Differences between issues at a glance
docs.text:

docs.title: Key element sizes in the Rev.1 draft
docs.text:
The 2024 draft adds a requirement that fixes the size of common elements "to ensure inter-operability of PUS-C implementations from different providers".46 Its Table 7-13:

Key element Size Number of instructions in a request 2 bytes Boolean 1 byte (1 bit in the secondary header) Collection interval 4 bytes Parameter ID, event ID 4 bytes each Housekeeping report structure ID 2 bytes Memory ID 2 bytes Memory start address, register address, memory bit-mask 4 bytes Sub-schedule ID, group ID 2 bytes each PMON ID, FMON ID 2 bytes each APID 2 bytes (11 bits in the primary header) Packet store ID 2 bytes OBCP ID 2 bytes CPDU ID 1 byte CFDP entity ID 2 bytes CFDP transaction sequence number 4 bytes Data source ID 2 bytes

The rows restate DIR1 Table 7-13.46 Until the revision is published, these sizes are a proposal; PUS-C (2016) leaves them to each mission.

docs.title: PTC/PFC in SCOS-2000
docs.text:
The SCOS-2000 Database Import ICD lists, in its Appendix A, every PTC/PFC combination the importer accepts and how it is held internally. It refers to the original ESA PUS, ESA PSS-07-101 (1994), as its PUS reference.4750 Monitoring parameters store their type in PCF_PTC (range 1-13) and PCF_PFC, command parameters in CPC_PTC and CPC_PFC.5153

PTC PFC accepted by SCOS-2000 Internal type Restrictions and extensions 1 0 unsigned integer, 1 bit - 2 1-32 unsigned integer only limit is 32 bits 3 0-14 unsigned integer PFC 15 and 16 (48 and 64 bits) not supported 4 0-14 signed integer PFC 15 and 16 not supported 5 1, 2, 3, 4 real PFC 4 (1750A extended) only for command parameters, from R3.0 6 1-32 unsigned integer PFC 0 not supported; monitoring side only 7 0, n octet string PFC 0 only for command/sequence parameters 8 0, n ASCII string PFC 0 only for command/sequence parameters 9 1, 2, 3-18, 30 absolute time PFC 0 not supported; PFC 1 from R5.0; PFC 2 only for commands; PFC 30 = Unix time (SCOS-2000 extension) 10 3-18 relative time CUC only 11 0, n > 0 deduced PFC > 0 forces a fixed width, command parameters only 13 0 saved synthetic parameter SCOS-2000 extension, characteristics taken from PCF_RELATED

Sources: ICD 7.0 Appendix A, Table 4, the PCF/CPC field descriptions, and the summary of exceptions in Appendix C.4748515349 The bold values are not defined by the PUS. The PCF_WIDTH field lets a monitoring parameter occupy a padded slot wider than its PTC/PFC implies, which matters for variable packets and deduced parameters.52

Inference: where SCOS-2000 and PUS-C disagree

  • PTC 9 PFC 30: SCOS-2000 uses it for Unix time (4 octets of seconds since 1970 plus 4 octets of microseconds), described as "Not defined in PUS".48 The ICD's PUS reference is ESA PSS-07-101,50 which, like PUS-A, defines absolute-time PFCs only up to 18 (in PSS-07-101: 0 a full definition with P-field, 1 and 2 CDS, the higher codes CUC),3432 but PUS-C assigns PFC 30 to a CUC code of 2 coarse and 8 fine octets.15 A PUS-C mission that needs that CUC format cannot express it with this code in an ICD 7.0-compliant SCOS-2000 database.
  • PTC 3 PFC 17-19, PTC 9 PFC 19-46, PTC 12 are absent from the ICD 7.0 table. Whether later SCOS-2000 releases accept them is not stated in the available sources.
  • PTC 10: SCOS-2000 numbers relative CUC times with the absolute-time formula (PFC 3-18), i.e. the PUS-C numbering, not the PUS-A one (see the relative-time inference above).

SCOS-2000 also defines special command parameter types that build PUS requests more easily: Command ID parameters (CPC_CATEG = A, PTC 7 PFC 0) are filled with the raw encoding of another command; Parameter ID parameters (CPC_CATEG = P, PTC 3) receive the on-board identifier of a telemetry parameter; and Deduced command parameters (PTC 11) inherit type, width and calibration from the TM parameter named by the preceding Parameter ID.54 Configuration variables must be 32-bit signed integers (PTC 4, PFC 14), double-precision reals (PTC 5, PFC 2) or character strings (PTC 8).55

docs.title: The Solar Orbiter MIB in numbers
docs.text:
The September 2025 Solar Orbiter release defines 126 745 monitoring parameters and 7 155 command parameters. Their PTC distribution:5758

PTC Type PCF (monitoring) Distinct PFC in PCF CPC (command) Distinct PFC in CPC 1 Boolean 4 380 1 (0) 225 1 (0) 2 enumerated 29 443 23 (1-32) 1 552 13 (1-32) 3 unsigned integer 50 341 15 (0-14) 4 349 15 (0-14) 4 signed integer 1 950 8 (0-14) 178 6 (2-14) 5 real 29 718 2 (1, 2) 702 2 (1, 2) 6 bit-string 950 12 (1-20) 0 - 7 octet-string 5 990 104 (1-6448) 84 22 (0-236) 8 character-string 120 17 (1-70) 6 5 (0-32) 9 absolute time 3 796 4 (2, 15, 17, 30) 58 2 (15, 17) 10 relative time 47 3 (6, 15, 17) 1 1 (17) 11 deduced 8 1 (0) 0 - 13 saved synthetic 2 1 (0) 0 -

Observations from the same queries:5758

  • Reals are almost all IEEE single precision: 28 316 of the 29 718 real monitoring parameters are PTC 5 PFC 1, and 630 of 702 real command parameters. No MIL-STD-1750A format is used.
  • Time: 2 116 absolute-time parameters are PFC 15 (4-octet CUC seconds) and 1 677 are PFC 17 (4 + 2 octets, the packet time stamp format). Two parameters of the "Time Correlation Report" packet (SPID 66840, type 164, APID 1966) use the SCOS-2000 Unix format PFC 30 (NYG02101 "Period From" and NYG02102 "Period To"), and one uses CDS with microseconds, NYG02204 "GS Acceptance Time" (see the inference box below).
  • No PTC 12 and no PFC beyond the ICD 7.0 table appear: unsigned integers stop at PFC 14, absolute CUC times at PFC 17.
  • Deduced parameters are the value fields of generic on-board reports, for example NCD0C0B5 "OBCHP_S12_Par value", whose type follows the parameter identifier NCD0C095 given in PCF_RELATED. It is placed in eight fixed event packets (SPIDs 66652-66659, TM(5,3) "RW Mom Lvl Check" reports on APIDs 1964 and 1973) and in 1 431 variable-packet (VPD) structures.
  • Saved synthetic parameters (PTC 13): NTTSS030 and NTTSS031 ("Last C_Lock DST-½"), derived from the synthetic parameters NTTSX030 and NTTSX031. The April 2020 release had none (it had 102 104 PCF records and no PTC 13).60 See synthetic parameters.
  • Variable-length strings appear only on the command side: 13 command parameters are PTC 7 PFC 0 and one is PTC 8 PFC 0, as the ICD requires.48
  • Long fixed octet strings (up to PFC 6448, i.e. 6 448 octets) hold whole tables and science blocks as single parameters, for example NCAMBP00 "SSE segments" (6 448 octets) and NIM02004 "1920 Science" (4 048 octets).

Inference

NYG02204 is a monitoring parameter (PCF_NATUR = R) of type PTC 9 PFC 2, a combination that ICD 7.0 says is supported only for command parameters.48 It belongs to a packet that, judging by its description, is produced by the ground segment; whether the SCOS-2000 release used by Solar Orbiter accepts it for monitoring is not stated in the available sources. The packet is SPID 66850, "TM Packet used by the Releaser G/S response" (type 165, subtype 1, APID 1966). APID 1966 also carries packets described as "MISC_PACKET", "Saved Synthetics", "Time Correlation Report" and "TCO Time_Couples", so the PFC 30 and PFC 2 time parameters most likely belong to packets generated by SCOS-2000 on ground rather than to spacecraft telemetry.

docs.title: A real command: time-tagging with PTC 9 and PTC 7
docs.text:
The command ZCD00B04, TC[11,4] "Insert Telecommands in Command Schedule", shows four types working together. Its application data, as defined in the CDF and CPC tables, is:59

CDF_BIT Parameter Description PTC/PFC Size 0 PCD0B041 Sub_schedule Identifier ¾ 8 bits 8 PCD0B042 Nb TCs to add in Sub-Sch (repeat counter, group size 2) ¾ 8 bits 16 PCD0B043 Time Tag 9/17 48 bits (CUC 4 + 2) 64 PCD0B044 Complete TC packet (Command ID, CPC_CATEG = A) 7/0 variable

The repeated group (time tag plus embedded packet) is the PUS-A equivalent of a "repeated N times" array, and the embedded command is a variable octet string filled by SCOS-2000 with the encoding of another command - the role PTC 12 plays in PUS-C. Event-action definitions such as ZCS01301 (TC[19,1]) use the same Command ID mechanism with PCD13013 "TC to send upon event".59 Explore it in the MIB explorer.

SQL used 
-- solo-2025-09-16.sqlite (MIB__20250916M25925PFMS001_SOL)
SELECT PCF_PTC, COUNT(*) n, COUNT(DISTINCT PCF_PFC),
       MIN(CAST(PCF_PFC AS INT)), MAX(CAST(PCF_PFC AS INT))
  FROM pcf GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY CAST(PCF_PTC AS INT);
SELECT PCF_PTC, PCF_PFC, COUNT(*) FROM pcf GROUP BY 1, 2;
SELECT CPC_PTC, COUNT(*), COUNT(DISTINCT CPC_PFC), GROUP_CONCAT(DISTINCT CPC_PFC)
  FROM cpc GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY CAST(CPC_PTC AS INT);
SELECT PCF_NAME, PCF_DESCR, PCF_PTC, PCF_PFC, PCF_NATUR, PCF_RELATED FROM pcf
 WHERE (PCF_PTC = '9' AND PCF_PFC IN ('2', '30')) OR PCF_PTC IN ('11', '13');
SELECT CPC_NAME, CPC_DESCR, CPC_PTC, CPC_PFC, CPC_CATEG FROM cpc WHERE CPC_CATEG = 'A';
SELECT d.CDF_BIT, d.CDF_PNAME, d.CDF_ELLEN, d.CDF_GRPSIZE
  FROM cdf d WHERE d.CDF_CNAME = 'ZCD00B04' ORDER BY CAST(d.CDF_BIT AS INT);
SELECT l.PLF_NAME, p.PID_SPID, p.PID_TYPE, p.PID_STYPE, p.PID_APID, p.PID_DESCR
  FROM plf l JOIN pid p ON p.PID_SPID = l.PLF_SPID
 WHERE l.PLF_NAME IN ('NYG02204', 'NYG02101', 'NYG02102', 'NCD0C0B5');
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT VPD_TPSD) FROM vpd WHERE VPD_NAME = 'NCD0C0B5';
SELECT PID_TYPE, PID_STYPE, PID_SPID, PID_DESCR FROM pid WHERE PID_APID = '1966';
-- solo-2020-04-16.sqlite
SELECT PCF_PTC, COUNT(*) FROM pcf GROUP BY 1;

docs.title: PUS-A vs PUS-C (and the 2024 Rev.1 draft)
docs.text:
Three generations of the Packet Utilization Standard are in use or in preparation today: PUS-A (ECSS-E-70-41A, 30 January 2003), flown by many ESA missions of the 2000s and 2010s; PUS-C (ECSS-E-ST-70-41C, 15 April 2016), the current standard; and Rev.1 DIR1 (ECSS-E-ST-70-41C Rev.1, 11 December 2024), a draft distributed for public review.153 Behind them stands the ESA PUS, ESA PSS-07-101 Issue 1 of May 1994, whose packets carry PUS version number 0 and from which PUS-A inherited most of its structure and numbering.114111 A ground segment often has to support more than one of these, so the differences matter in practice: the same service number can mean different things, the same field can have a different size, and the same PFC value can encode a different time format. This page compares the documents clause by clause. The bit-level PUS-A and PUS-C header details are on PUS packet structures, the data types on PUS parameter types, and the wider history of the ESA packet standards on From ESA PSS to CCSDS and ECSS.

ESA PUS PUS-A PUS-C Rev.1 DIR1 Document ESA PSS-07-101 Issue 1 ECSS-E-70-41A ECSS-E-ST-70-41C ECSS-E-ST-70-41C Rev.1 DIR1 Date May 1994 30 January 2003 15 April 2016 11 December 2024 Status ESA standard, prepared by COES, approved by the ESA Inspector General first ECSS issue second issue, in force draft for public review (12 December 2024 - 28 February 2025) PUS version number in packets 0 1 2 2 Length (PDF pages) 225 (scan) 228 656 733 Standard service types 17 (1-17) 16 (1-19 with 7, 10, 16 unused) 20 (1-23 with 7, 10, 16 reserved) 23 (1-27 with 7, 8, 10, 16 reserved)

Sources: the title pages, change logs and cover pages, PSS-07-101 Table 4-1, PUS-A Table 2, PUS-C Table 4-1 and DIR1 Table 4.2-1.11412512815354472563 Page counts are those of the copies in this wiki's library.

docs.title: Before PUS-A: ESA PSS-07-101 (1994)
docs.text:
PUS-A did not start from a blank page. Its direct ancestor, ESA PSS-07-101 Packet Utilisation Standard, Issue 1 (May 1994), was prepared by ESA's Committee for Operations and EGSE Standards (COES), set up in 1987 to define a monitoring and control system common to satellite checkout and mission control, and it was approved by the ESA Inspector General after an Agency-level review in 1993.114139142 Why it was written, how a prototype validated it and how XMM tailored it first are told on the PUS overview. This section compares its content with its successors.

Source note: a scanned standard

PSS-07-101 exists here only as a scanned PDF. This wiki read it through OCR text, which contains recognition errors, merged words and scrambled table layouts, and checked every field size, bit position, value and subtype number quoted on this page against the rendered page images. The same applies to the two 1994 conference papers on NTRS.

docs.title: Concepts in 1994
docs.text:
The 1994 vocabulary is already close to PUS-A's. A Service is a set of on-board functions with conceptually related capabilities that a ground system controls and monitors through Service Requests and Service Reports; a report that only returns requested data is a Service Response, every other report a Service Indication. The Service Provider is the on-board application process that executes the service, the Service User is the ground system, and a Supporting Service is one used only in the context of another service.121122 Three criteria selected the standard services: commonality (functions many missions need), coherence (strongly related capabilities with an unambiguous scope and minimal interaction with other services) and implementation independence (no assumed on-board architecture).120 One rule differs from today's model: a service cannot be split across application processes, although one process may host several services and, where permitted, several processes may host distinct instances of a service.121 PUS-C instead deploys services subservice by subservice: each subservice has exactly one provider, each subservice entity is hosted by an application process on board or on ground, and an application process hosts at most one provider of a given subservice type.106

The 1994 document puts operational requirements first (chapter 3, each with a mnemonic such as TC-1 or TRAFF-1 and with mission parameters in angle brackets) and then one chapter per service with its scope, concept, requests and reports and capability sets; it ends with the summary of requests and reports in chapter 22 and the parameter types in chapter 23 - the same clause numbers that PUS-A kept.11711911639

docs.title: The 1994 packet headers
docs.text:
PSS-07-101 takes the packet header from the ESA packet telemetry (PSS-04-106) and telecommand (PSS-04-107) standards and standardises the start of the packet data field, the data field header. In both directions it has the same 24-bit core; telemetry adds an optional time field. The 1994 paper presenting the standard prints the same two layouts.124125127140

Field Size Meaning in PSS-07-101 PUS version number 3 bits Only version 0; a new version was foreseen for telemetry packets carrying more than one service data unit.125127 Checksum type 1 bit Selects the packet error control algorithm: ISO 16-bit checksum (0) or CRC (1). In telemetry, 0 can also mean that no check is included.125127 Ack (TC only) 4 bits Which success reports the application process sends, one bit per stage; failure reports are always sent. 1111 means at least four verification steps are expected.125 Spare (TM only) 4 bits Reserved.127 Service type, subtype 8 + 8 bits Unique across all application processes; on ground their combination may set the processing priority (TM).125127 Time (TM only) variable On-board reference time in CUC or CDS, chosen per application process by the mission parameter <APPL_TIME_CODE>, possibly absent; CDS uses the CCSDS epoch of 1 January 1958; the time is any well-defined time before the sampling of the packet's data.127

The packet header around this core also differs from later practice:124126

  • telecommand packets have version number 0, but telemetry source packets have "version 2", coded as the value 4 (0b100); PUS-A and PUS-C use 0 for both;46109
  • the 14-bit telecommand sequence count is split: its <NUM_SOURCE_BITS> most significant bits carry a source ID (for example, one per ground control centre; zero bits if there is a single source) and the rest a sequence count kept per source and per APID - PUS-A moved the source ID into an optional data field header field, PUS-C made it a 16-bit field;454
  • telecommand sequence flags are always 11 for ESA missions and telemetry "segmentation flags" are always 11 (unsegmented);
  • the telecommand packet error control field (16 bits) is mandatory, and the largest telecommand packet is 65 542 octets; the telemetry error control field is optional.124127

The CRC of Appendix A.2 is the one still used today: generator polynomial \(x^{16} + x^{12} + x^5 + 1\), encoder and decoder initialised to all ones, computed over the whole packet except the error control field; PUS-C Annex B specifies the same CRC-16-CCITT.137110 For the PUS-A and PUS-C fields see Packet header changes below and PUS packet structures.

Inference: reading the first four bits

In PSS-07-101 the first data-field-header bits are the 3-bit version 000 followed by the checksum-type bit; PUS-A starts with a 0 flag bit followed by the 3-bit version 001; PUS-C has a 4-bit version 0010.125454 Read as one 4-bit number, a PSS-07-101 telecommand using a CRC therefore shows the same value (1) as a PUS-A packet. A decoder that must tell the ESA PUS from PUS-A cannot rely on these bits alone and needs mission knowledge. The multi-SDU telemetry version foreseen in 1994 (and again in PUS-A) does not appear in PUS-C, whose version 2 simply identifies ECSS-E-ST-70-41C.

docs.title: Service lineage: 1994 to 2016
docs.text:
The 1994 summary table (Table 22-1) fixes subtype numbers that are still in use. The table follows each service through the three issues; the PUS-C column restates the comparisons made further down this page.1325023

minimum set: acceptance reports (1,1), (1,2) unchanged TM[1,1]-TM[1,8] kept; TM[1,10] added 2 Device-level commanding (clause 6: device command distribution): on/off (2,1), register load (2,2), CPDU (2,3), "distribute command in TC segment" (2,4) (2,4) dropped CPDU moved to TC[2,4]; TC[5,7], TM[5,8] added 6 Memory management: load, dump, check, by base plus offsets or absolute addresses, (6,1)-(6,10) unchanged same numbers, now object and raw memory 7 Task management: start, stop, suspend, resume, abort task, perform activity within task, (7,1)-(7,6) not used reserved 8 Function management: activate (8,1), de-activate (8,2), perform activity of function (8,3) only (8,1) "perform function" TC[8,1] (deleted in Rev.1 DIR1) 9 Time management: change time report generation rate (9,1) time report added as (9,2) TM[9,2] CUC or TM[9,3] CDS 10 Time reporting: the time report (10,1) merged into service 9 reserved 11 Onboard scheduling: enable, disable, reset, insert (1-4), delete (5, 6), time-shift (7, 8), detailed reports (9, 11 with report 10), summary reports (12, 14 with report 13) requests 9, 11, 12, 14 now report a subset of the schedule; 15-19 added (time-shift all, full detailed and summary reports, schedule status request and report) 1-4, TM[11,10], TM[11,13] kept 12 Onboard monitoring: (12,1)-(12,11), out-of-limit report (12,12) (12,12) becomes "check transition report" 1-12 kept, renamed 13 Large data transfer: downlink (13,1)-(13,8), uplink (13,9)-(13,16) unchanged only 1-3, 9-11 and 16 kept 14 Packet transmission control: enable, disable and report transmission of packets, housekeeping, diagnostic and event reports, (14,1)-(14,16) renamed "forwarding", same 16 subtypes remodelled as forward-control configurations 15 Onboard storage and retrieval: packet selection (15,1)-(15,6), storage and retrieval (15,7)-(15,11) catalogue report (15,12), (15,13) added redefined around packet stores 16 Onboard traffic management: no subtypes; specification left to an Issue 2 not used reserved 17 Test: perform connection test (17,1), connection test report (17,2) unchanged kept; on-board connection test added 18, 19 - on-board operations procedure; event-action (new) kept, extended

The 1994 time report is the spacecraft time source packet, the one telemetry packet without a data field header.126130 The reserved numbers 7, 10 and 16 of PUS-C are therefore the 1994 task management, time reporting and on-board traffic management services; PUS-A had already marked them "not used".247 Several names also predate ECSS: "telecommand verification" and the "Normal/Progress" and "Error/Anomaly" event reports were PSS-07-101 names that PUS-A kept and PUS-C replaced.1325027

Inference

Because of this continuity, a decoder written for PUS-A and keyed on (type, subtype) would find the same message types in a mission built to the 1994 PUS for services 1, 4, 5, 6, 13 and 17 and for most of services 3 and 12. The differences that matter are the sampling-time-offset, masked/unfiltered and out-of-limit/check-transition subtypes of services 3 and 12, services 2, 7-11 and 14-16, and the headers above.

docs.title: Parameter types in 1994
docs.text:
PSS-07-101 already uses the parameter code made of a parameter type code (PTC) and a parameter format code (PFC), with eleven PTCs: Boolean (1), enumerated (2), unsigned (3) and signed (4) integer, real (5), bit string (6), octet string (7), character string (8), absolute time (9), relative time (10) and deduced (11). Packet structures follow a single "structure rules set number 1" of records, fixed and variable arrays and "choice structures" (whose type is deduced from preceding fields, a deduced parameter being a special case), and each mission selects the physical format of each field by giving its parameter code.133134136 Notable details:

  • enumerated parameters may be 1, 2, 4, 8, 12, 16, 24 or 32 bits long (PUS-A: 1-16, 24, 32; PUS-C: 1-64), and unsigned integers use PFC 0-16 as in PUS-A;13451
  • absolute and relative time share one format table: PFC 0 is an explicit format with P-field, PFC 1 and 2 are CDS without and with microseconds (absolute time only), and PFC 3-18 are CUC with (PFC + 1) div 4 octets of coarse time and (PFC + 1) mod 4 octets of fine time;135
  • the time code reference is the CCSDS time code format CCSDS 301.0-B-1 together with a planned ESA time code standard, PSS-04-202, "not available before mid 1995".115

Inference: where SCOS-2000 got its relative-time numbering

PUS-A renumbered relative time (PFC 1-16 with (PFC + 3) div 4 coarse octets), and PUS-C went back to PFC 3-18 with (PFC + 1).11322 The SCOS-2000 Database Import ICD 7.0 lists ESA PSS-07-101 as its PUS reference (RD-6) and numbers relative CUC times like PSS-07-101: PTC 10 PFC 4 is 1 coarse plus 1 fine octet.106158 SCOS-2000's relative-time numbering is therefore most likely inherited from the 1994 standard rather than borrowed from PUS-C. See parameter types.

docs.title: Why PUS-C was written
docs.text:
The PUS-C change log gives five reasons for replacing issue A: remove its deficiencies and inject lessons learned, meet the needs of future missions, acknowledge newer ECSS and CCSDS standards, apply the ECSS drafting rules (for example naming every requirement for tailoring and traceability), and keep backward compatibility when possible.1 By January 2011 the working group had collected 190 change requests.92 At the 2014 SAVOIR Mass Memory Day the convenor listed the planned service types, still showing large data transfer (ST13) and a new "large packet transfer" (ST24) as "TBC", and the options under study for transferring data larger than one packet.8788 The final standard kept number 13 for a simplified "large packet transfer" that only moves packets of up to about 65 KB, without retransmission.98

docs.title: Service-by-service changes from PUS-A to PUS-C
docs.text: The message names below are those of PUS-A clause 22 and PUS-C Annex C and clause 8.5023 Where PUS-C kept a subtype number, the meaning is usually close; where a number disappears, the function was redesigned.

docs.title: ST[01] request verification
docs.text:
Subtype PUS-A PUS-C 1-8 TC acceptance, execution started, execution progress and execution completed reports, each success and failure successful/failed acceptance, start, progress and completion of execution verification reports 10 - failed routing verification report

PUS-C adds a routing and reporting subservice for the on-board routing of requests and its failure report TM[1,10].2417 PUS-A listed standard acceptance failure codes (0 illegal APID, 1 invalid length, 2 incorrect checksum, 3 illegal type, 4 illegal subtype, 5 illegal or inconsistent application data);48 PUS-C instead asks each request type to declare an execution verification profile with its own codes and failure parameters.13 See ST[01].

docs.title: ST[02] device access
docs.text: PUS-A had three requests: distribute on-off commands (2,1), register load commands (2,2) and CPDU commands (2,3).50 PSS-07-101 had a fourth, (2,4) "distribute command in TC segment", for hardware commands carried at telecommand segment level that need no software to execute, for example to unblock or reset the on-board packet assembly controller; PUS-A dropped it.132141 PUS-C keeps (2,1) and (2,2), moves CPDU commands to TC[2,4], and adds register dumps (TC[2,5], TM[2,6]) and physical and logical device commanding and data acquisition (TC[2,7]-TM[2,12]); subtype 3 is no longer used.25 The 2015 presentation lists these as new capabilities for register acquisition, software-distributed CPDU commands and low-level device commands.95 See ST[02].

docs.title: ST[03] housekeeping
docs.text:
Subtypes PUS-A PUS-C 1-4 define new / clear HK and diagnostic report definitions create / delete HK and diagnostic parameter report structures 5-8 enable / disable HK and diagnostic report generation enable / disable the periodic generation of HK and diagnostic reports 9-12 report the definitions, definition reports report the structures, structure reports 13-24 sampling-time offsets, periodic / filtered generation modes, unfiltered parameter reports not used 25, 26 housekeeping / diagnostic parameter report housekeeping / diagnostic parameter report 27-36 - one-shot reports, append parameters, modify collection interval, report periodic generation properties 37-44 - parameter functional reporting configuration subservice

Sources: PUS-A clause 22 and PUS-C Annex C.2.3.5026 PUS-A's optional filtered mode generated a housekeeping packet only when its parameters changed beyond ground-set thresholds, with a long timeout as a fallback;49 it has no counterpart in PUS-C ST[03]. The new functional reporting subservice operates on sets of HK and diagnostic reports, reducing the number of requests needed to change the telemetry plan.96 See ST[03].

docs.title: ST[04] parameter statistics and ST[05] event reporting
docs.text: ST[04] keeps subtypes 1-9 (report, reset, enable/disable periodic reporting, add, delete and report the list - now called "parameter statistics definitions"); PUS-A subtype 10 "Clear Parameter Statistics List" is gone.5027 ST[05] keeps the four event report subtypes, renaming PUS-A's "Normal/Progress Report" and "Error/Anomaly Report" into "informative event report" and "low/medium/high severity anomaly report", and adds TC[5,7] and TM[5,8] to report the list of disabled event definitions.5027 See ST[04] and ST[05].

docs.title: ST[06] memory management
docs.text:
Subtypes PUS-A PUS-C 1, 3, 4, 7, 8 load / dump / check memory using base plus offsets, and reports load / dump / check object memory data, and reports 2, 5, 6, 9, 10 load / dump / check memory using absolute addresses, and reports load / dump / check raw memory data, and reports 11-22 - atomic raw load, abort all dumps, scrubbing, write protection, object checks, load/dump by reference and to files

Sources: PUS-A clause 22 and PUS-C Annex C.2.6.5028 PUS-C splits the service into raw data, structured data, common and memory configuration subservices,28 and extends the base plus offset idea to memory objects such as files; the 2014 working-group draft still showed only the first three subservices.8991

Inference

The subtype numbers line up: PUS-A's base-plus-offset messages (1, 3, 4, 7, 8) became PUS-C's object memory messages and its absolute-address messages (2, 5, 6, 9, 10) became raw memory messages. A ground system decoding by subtype number alone would still find the right report family, but the field layouts of clause 8.6 differ from PUS-A clause 11.

docs.title: ST[08] function management and ST[09] time management
docs.text: ST[08] is unchanged in substance: PUS-A "Perform Function" (8,1) and PUS-C TC[8,1] "perform a function".5029 ST[09] keeps TC[9,1] (change / set the time report generation rate) but splits PUS-A's single time report (9,2) into TM[9,2] "CUC time report" and TM[9,3] "CDS time report", of which a mission provides exactly one.502921 Both services were larger in 1994: PSS-07-101 function management had "activate", "de-activate" and "perform activity of function" (8,1)-(8,3), and the time report was a separate service 10, so service 9 only changed the time report generation rate.132 See ST[08] and ST[09].

docs.title: ST[11], ST[21] and ST[22]: scheduling split in three
docs.text: The PUS-A "on-board operations scheduling service" was "completely re-assessed" into three service types: time-based scheduling (ST[11]), telecommand - later "request" - sequencing (ST[21]) and orbit-position-based scheduling (ST[22]).97 ST[11] keeps the first four subtypes (enable, disable, reset, insert) and the detail and summary reports TM[11,10] and TM[11,13], adds sub-schedules and groups (subtypes 18-27), and reuses subtype 19 for a sub-schedule status report where PUS-A had a "Command Schedule Status Report".5030 The report numbers 10 (detailed) and 13 (summary) and the first four request subtypes already had these roles in the 1994 "onboard scheduling service", which also allowed a command to be interlocked to the success or failure of an earlier one.132141 See ST[11], ST[21] and ST[22].

docs.title: ST[12] on-board monitoring
docs.text:
Subtypes PUS-A PUS-C 1, 2 enable / disable monitoring of parameters enable / disable parameter monitoring definitions 3 change maximum reporting delay change the maximum transition reporting delay 4-7 clear list, add, delete parameters, modify checking information delete all, add, delete, modify parameter monitoring definitions 8, 9 report current monitoring list, list report report parameter monitoring definitions, definition report 10, 11 report current out-of-limit list, list report report the out-of-limits, out-of-limits report 12 check transition report check transition report 13-16 - status of each definition, enable / disable the monitoring function 17-28 - functional monitoring subservice

Sources: PUS-A clause 22, PUS-C Annex C.2.12.5031 ST[12] is the most backward compatible of the redesigned services; its big addition is functional monitoring. See ST[12].

docs.title: ST[13] large packet transfer
docs.text: PUS-A had a data downlink operation with acknowledgement and repetition (subtypes 1-8) and an uplink operation with acceptance, repeated parts and reception reports (9-16).50 PUS-C keeps only the first, intermediate and last part reports TM[13,1]-TM[13,3], the uplink parts TC[13,9]-TC[13,11] and the uplink abortion report TM[13,16].32 The 2015 presentation describes it as a simplification limited to packets of up to 65 KB, without retransmission.98 See ST[13].

docs.title: ST[14] forwarding and ST[15] storage
docs.text: PUS-A ST[14] enabled and disabled the forwarding of whole packet classes (TM source, housekeeping, diagnostic, event report packets).50 PUS-C ST[14] manages forward-control configurations: add or delete report types per application process, housekeeping and diagnostic structure identifiers, and event definitions to block.33 The 2015 presentation says the service was "completely remodelled" to keep service types independent.100 PUS-C ST[15] keeps the two subservices (packet selection, storage and retrieval) but redefines them around packet stores that can be created, deleted, resized and copied, with open and by-time-range retrieval.5034 See ST[14] and ST[15].

docs.title: ST[17], ST[18], ST[19]
docs.text:
• ST[17]: PUS-A "Perform Connection Test" (17,1) and its report (17,2) become the "are-you-alive connection test" TC[17,1] / TM[17,2]; PUS-C adds an on-board connection test TC[17,3] / TM[17,4] towards another, declared application process.503519
  • ST[18]: subtypes 1-7 and 12 keep their roles (load, delete/unload, start/activate, stop, suspend, resume, communicate parameters, abort); PUS-C replaces the two list reports with an execution status report (TC[18,8], TM[18,9]) and adds loading by reference, step-by-step execution, observability levels and an OBCP engine management subservice.5036 The OBCP standard ECSS-E-ST-70-01C (2010), written when PUS-A was in force, maps its OBCP operations onto exactly the subtypes PUS-C kept: load 1, delete 2, activate 3, stop 4, suspend 5, resume 6, communicate parameters 7 and abort 12; it notes that PUS-A calls OBCP code "procedure code".146145
  • ST[19]: PUS-A's event detection list becomes a set of event-action definitions; PUS-C adds enabling and disabling of the whole event-action function (TC[19,8], TC[19,9]) and a definition report (TC[19,10], TM[19,11]).5037

See ST[17], ST[18] and ST[19].

docs.title: New in PUS-C: ST[20] and ST[23]
docs.text: ST[20] parameter management reads and sets on-board parameter values and maintains parameter definitions - identifier, memory address and PTC/PFC - with an optional capability to create new parameters by associating a new memory location or field code with a predefined identifier.18 ST[23] file management handles flat or structured on-board file systems through a file handling subservice and a file copy subservice, without imposing a file delivery protocol such as CFDP.2090 See ST[20] and ST[23].

docs.title: Reserved numbers and mission-specific collisions
docs.text:
PUS-C reserves service types 7, 10 and 16 because they were used in earlier versions of the standard, while allowing existing implementations to be reused.2 The earlier version is PSS-07-101: 7 was task management (start, stop, suspend, resume and abort on-board software tasks, in many missions only for contingencies), 10 the time reporting service carrying the spacecraft time packet, and 16 on-board traffic management, meant for on-board routing (for example APID to MAP mapping), packet assembly controller reports, packet bus load and retransmission statistics, and ground control of traffic problems, but never given any subtypes.128132131141 PUS-A already listed all three as "not used".47 Missions designed to PUS-A sometimes used numbers in the standard range for their own services. Solar Orbiter, whose applicable PUS is ECSS-E-70-41A, defines:103104

Service type Solar Orbiter meaning (PUS-A based) PUS-C meaning 16 On-board traffic management (MilBus configuration) (reserved) 20 Information distribution (incl. TC(20,128) inter-instrument communication) parameter management 21 Science data transfer request sequencing 22 Context saving position-based scheduling

All four are present in the 2025 Solar Orbiter MIB: 5, 17, 33 and 6 commands, and 0, 0, 334 and 1 telemetry packet definitions respectively.108 Solar Orbiter also numbers its CPDU command as TC(2,3), the PUS-A subtype, where PUS-C uses TC[2,4].10525

The practice continues with PUS-C: the PUSCGen study's Proba-3 use case defines a mission-specific "reaction wheels management" service numbered 8, a number that PUS-C assigns to function management.1572

Inference

A ground system that serves several missions cannot interpret a service type number without knowing the mission's PUS edition and tailoring. The 4-bit PUS version field (1 for PUS-A, 2 for PUS-C) identifies the edition, but not the mission-specific use of standard-range numbers. Solar Orbiter's service 16 also carries the name of the 1994 service 16, "Onboard Traffic Management", and its requests TC(16,1)-TC(16,5) set the MilBus configuration and switch the bus and its remote-terminal channels between nominal and redundant, close to the 1994 scope of on-board routing and bus control. This suggests that the mission or its platform reused the PSS-07-101 number and name for a function PUS-A had dropped, but no source in this library says so.159131

docs.title: What the 2024 Rev.1 draft proposes
docs.text:
ECSS-E-ST-70-41C Rev.1 DIR1 is a draft for public review (12 December 2024 to 28 February 2025) and "may not be referred to as an ECSS Standard until published as such".53 Its change log repeats the PUS-C goals - remove deficiencies, meet future missions' needs, stay consistent with ECSS and CCSDS, apply drafting rules - and adds consistency with the foundation model. It lists the main changes:54

  • evolution of the request verification approach (ST[01]);
  • evolution of housekeeping reporting (ST[03]);
  • deletion of a service not used in current and future missions: ST[08] function management;
  • standardization of services used in current and future missions: ST[26] parameter extraction and ST[27] critical packet log management;
  • standardization of services for file based operations: ST[24] file transfer and ST[25] file data storage;
  • configuration policies formalised as requirements for the applicable services.

docs.title: New services
docs.text:
ST Name Subservices Purpose 24 file transfer file transaction; file downlink manager Manages file transmission and reception through CFDP entities (CCSDS 727.0-B-5) and automates the downlink of files generated on board with "downlink managers".7076 25 file data storage data storage control; PUS report-type data source control Stores data from on-board sources into files in directories for later downlink; a data source maps to at most one directory and has a recording status.71 26 parameter extraction parameter extraction Extracts parameters from other application processes' telemetry so that central autonomy functions (FDIR, OBCPs) can use them.72 27 critical packet log management critical packet log management Keeps critical packets (events of mission-specified severity and negative TC acknowledgements) in a bounded on-board log that can only be cleared once downlinked; exactly one per space system.73

The file transfer service's requests include opening and closing file transmission and reception opportunities (TC[24,1]-TC[24,4]), suspending, resuming and cancelling transactions, configuring remote CFDP entities, and starting, suspending and stopping downlink managers (TC[24,18]-TC[24,20]).74 File data storage adds directory attributes, data-source mapping and recording control (TC[25,1]-TM[25,16]).75 Parameter extraction has add, delete and report requests TC[26,1]-TC[26,3] with the definition report TM[26,4], and critical packet log management has two requests, TC[27,1] "downlink critical packet log" and TC[27,2] to clear the packets already downlinked.69 See CFDP for the underlying protocol.

docs.title: Changes to existing services
docs.text: Service Change in DIR1 ST[01] Observables are now defined (numbers of requests whose routing or acceptance verification succeeded or failed), and the execution reports are renamed "... of request execution ...".<sup>58</sup> ST[03] The diagnostic reporting subservice is gone; reports belong to six housekeeping categories, signalled by the message type: TM[3,25], TM[3,26], TM[3,50], TM[3,51], TM[3,52], TM[3,53]. The periodic generation properties report moves from TM[3,35] to TM[3,34].<sup>59</sup><sup>60</sup> ST[05] New request TC[5,9] "generate event report".<sup>61</sup> ST[08] Deleted; 8 becomes a reserved identifier.<sup>56</sup> ST[09] New time control and time distribution subservices: TC[9,4] / TC[9,5] set the reference time with absolute or relative time, TC[9,6] / TC[9,7] start and stop time distribution to on-board users.<sup>62</sup><sup>76</sup> ST[12] TC[12,10] / TM[12,11] become "current out-of-limits"; new TC[12,29] / TC[12,30] enable and disable check transition list logging.<sup>63</sup> ST[14] With the diagnostic subservice gone, the diagnostic parameter report forward-control messages (PUS-C TC[14,9]-TM[14,12]) disappear; clause 8.14 keeps the application process, housekeeping and event report blocking forward-control messages.<sup>65</sup><sup>33</sup> ST[15] The diagnostic storage-control messages (PUS-C TC[15,31], TC[15,32], TC[15,37], TM[15,38]) disappear; new TC[15,10] aborts all requests to copy the packets of a packet store selected by time window, and TC[15,41] changes the default retrieval priority of a packet store.<sup>66</sup> ST[17] New variable-size are-you-alive test TC[17,5] / TM[17,6].<sup>64</sup> ST[21] New TC[21,15] "change request sequence directory attributes" and TC[21,16] / TM[21,17] to report the attributes of the request sequence directory.<sup>67</sup> ST[23] New TC[23,25] "checksum a file" with its checksum report (printed as "TC[23,26]" in the clause heading), and TC[23,27] / TC[23,28] to enable and disable directory protection.<sup>68</sup>

docs.title: Changes to the space-to-ground interface
docs.text:
Clause 7.4 of the draft keeps the PUS-C secondary header field sizes; the changes are in meaning and in the declarations required:77

Item Change in DIR1 Source / destination TC "source APID" and TM "destination APID" replace the user identifiers; ground application processes get APIDs 2048-65535.828057 TM packet error control the field becomes mandatory in the TM user data field.81 Maximum packet sizes must be declared for TM and TC.79 Packets without secondary header CFDP PDUs, idle packets and SDLS extended procedure PDUs are acknowledged.83 Relative time PFC 1 (CDS without microseconds) added.84 Character strings visible characters defined as 0x20-0x7E, padding with spaces.85 Key element sizes Table 7-13 fixes sizes such as 4-byte parameter and event IDs and 2-byte APID fields.86

Inference: the draft and ESA's Generic OIRD

Several DIR1 changes answer gaps that ESA's Generic OIRD (2019) listed for PUS-C. The GOIRD added, as high-level "new capabilities" to be raised as change requests, a critical event log or system log, parameter extraction from housekeeping, a backup mission timeline and file-based operations, and it complained that PUS-C leaves the number of bytes of key fields open.152153 DIR1 adds critical packet log management (ST[27]), parameter extraction (ST[26]) and file transfer and file data storage (ST[24], ST[25]), and its Table 7-13 fixes key element sizes.5486 The DIR1 change log describes ST[26] and ST[27] as services "used in current and future missions"; no source in this library states that the GOIRD change requests were their origin, and a backup mission timeline does not appear among the DIR1 main changes.

Inference: state of the draft

The DIR1 text still contains drafting artefacts that a reviewer will notice: unresolved cross-references printed as "Error! Reference source not found." (for example in clauses 7.4.3.2 and 7.4.4.1), and a change log whose "current step" line names ECSS-E-ST-32-02C Rev.2 and whose description refers to "ECSS-E-70-41C (15 April 2026)".5478 Such details, and the content itself, may change before publication.

docs.title: PUS-C in practice: tailoring and tooling
docs.text:
Two ESA activities give a practitioner's view of the PUS-A to PUS-C step. The Generic OIRD talk of 2019 calls PUS-C "a major step forward compared to PUS-A": a solid foundation model, clear and extensive system requirements in which the behaviour of each service type and its requests is (almost) unambiguous, an interface definition separated from the system requirements, and new service types and subservices such as file management and housekeeping functional reporting.149 The same talk counts what that thoroughness costs - 20 service types, 33 subservices, 316 message types of which 88 are mandatory (this wiki's own count of the clause 8 headings is 318, 81 of them "minimum" in Annex C; see the message type catalogue),23 and 382 "shall be declared" options - and concludes that ESA missions need one common PUS-C tailoring, which the GOIRD provides.150151 The 2020 PUSCGen study, which rebuilt PUS-C from its foundation model in a database, raised 21 change requests (7 major) and showed that the standard can be regenerated and tailored automatically and turned into ASN.1/ACN definitions from which ESA's ASN1SCC compiler generates encoders and decoders.154155156 Both are described on the PUS overview, under the Generic OIRD and tooling built on the foundation model.

The contrast with the 1990s is instructive. In 1994 XMM selected services from the draft PUS and gave them its own type numbers (periodic housekeeping as TM type 1, telecommand verification as TM type 3, time-tagged commands as type 7), a process its author called "missionisation".143144 Twenty-five years later the GOIRD aims for the opposite: a single selection of services, subtypes and capabilities shared by all new ESA missions, with mission OIRDs limited to deltas, constants and sizing.151148

docs.title: Practical consequences
docs.text:
Inference

  • Ground databases are edition-specific. Header sizes (PID_DFHSIZE and the PCDF header definitions), service numbering and PFC values all change between PUS-A and PUS-C. Solar Orbiter's MIB, for example, defines a 4-octet PUS-A TC data field header and a 10-octet TM data field header (see packet structures).
  • SCOS-2000 documentation predates PUS-C. The Database Import ICD 7.0 (2017) still refers to the ESA PUS PSS-07-101 for data types and quotes PUS-A section numbers for service support, and it uses PTC 9 PFC 30 for Unix time where PUS-C defines a CUC format (see parameter types).106107 Reading PSS-07-101 alongside the ICD explains some SCOS-2000 conventions, such as its relative-time PFC numbering and the 4-octet telecommand identification at the start of verification reports, which the 1994 standard already defines (see above).135129
  • Migrating to PUS-C or Rev.1 is less about new services than about identifiers: the 16-bit source and destination fields, the message type counter, the time reference status and, in Rev.1, APID-based addressing all have to be reflected in the MIB and in on-board routing.
