docs.title: ST[01] Request verification
docs.text:
When a ground operator sends a telecommand, the first question is always the same: did it arrive, was it accepted, and did it do what it should? Service type 1 of the Packet Utilization Standard answers that question. It defines a family of telemetry reports, TM[1,1] to TM[1,10], with which the on-board software tells the request's originator that a request passed or failed each stage of its life: routing, acceptance, start of execution, each progress step, and completion. The service has no requests of its own; it is a supporting service for the requests of every other standard and mission-specific service.135 This page explains the model behind the reports, every report layout, the acknowledgement flags that select which success reports are sent, the capability sets, the differences between PUS-A (2003), PUS-C (2016) and the 2024 Rev.1 draft, and how the SCOS-2000 MIB and the real Solar Orbiter database turn these reports into command verification.

Where this page sits

The packet headers that carry the acknowledgement flags and the request identifier are dissected on PUS packet structures. The ground-side tables that consume the reports (cvs, cve, cvp) are covered in depth on Command verification in the MIB. The lower-layer acknowledgement of telecommand frames by COP-1 is a separate mechanism that works below the packet level.

docs.title: 1. At a glance
docs.text:
Item Value Service type 1 (all its packets are of service type 1)31 PUS-C name ST[01] request verification1 PUS-A name Telecommand verification service35 Subservice types routing and reporting; acceptance and reporting; execution reporting1 Requests (TC) none Reports (TM) TM[1,1] to TM[1,8] and TM[1,10]; subtype 9 is not defined34 Minimum capability (PUS-C) every report type of a subservice that is present34 Minimum capability (PUS-A) (1,1) and (1,2)41 Message type Name in ECSS-E-ST-70-41C Generated Subservice Clauses TM[1,1] successful acceptance verification report only if requested by the acknowledgement flags acceptance and reporting 6.1.4.2, 8.1.2.1 TM[1,2] failed acceptance verification report always acceptance and reporting 6.1.4.3, 8.1.2.2 TM[1,3] successful start of execution verification report only if requested execution reporting 6.1.5.1.1, 8.1.2.3 TM[1,4] failed start of execution verification report always execution reporting 6.1.5.1.2, 8.1.2.4 TM[1,5] successful progress of execution verification report only if requested execution reporting 6.1.5.2.1, 8.1.2.5 TM[1,6] failed progress of execution verification report if the reporting policy says so execution reporting 6.1.5.2.2, 8.1.2.6 TM[1,7] successful completion of execution verification report only if requested execution reporting 6.1.5.3.1, 8.1.2.7 TM[1,8] failed completion of execution verification report always execution reporting 6.1.5.3.2, 8.1.2.8 TM[1,10] failed routing verification report always routing and reporting 6.1.3.3, 8.1.2.9

3424

The success/failure split into separate subtypes is deliberate: PUS-A explains that the difference is operationally so important that each outcome gets its own subtype, so that failure reports can be selected by type alone, for example for priority routing or storage on board or on the ground.36 The PUS message type catalogue lists these types next to those of all other services.

docs.title: 2. The model: requests, verification stages and reports
2.1 Who generates what
docs.text:
PUS-C describes the service in terms of the entities of its service model. A request is generated by a subservice user (for a telecommand, a ground application process) and addressed to exactly one subservice provider in an on-board application process.22 Along the way three kinds of on-board functions look at the request, and each is a different ST[01] subservice:

  • the routing and reporting subservice, hosted by every application process that routes requests on board (for example a central computer forwarding a packet to an instrument), checks that the routing can continue and reports routing failures;27
  • the acceptance and reporting subservice, hosted exactly once by every application process that executes requests, checks a request before handing it to the service it addresses;38
  • the execution reporting subservice, hosted at most once by such an application process, turns the execution notifications of the subservice providers into verification reports on their behalf.48

A request verification service contains at least one of these subservices; PUS-C explicitly allows the routing reports of one request to come from the subservices of different request verification services, for example one attached to the platform and one to a payload.5 Acceptance and execution reports can only come from the application process that executes the request.5 Whether an application process implements the execution reporting subservice is not its own choice: it follows from the operational needs of the services it hosts.8

Every verification report is addressed to the application process that hosts the subservice user that generated the request; in packet terms the report's destination is the request's source identifier.6 The Rev.1 draft turns this into an interface rule: the destination ID field of every service 1 telemetry packet carries the value of the source ID field of the related telecommand packet.47

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant G as Ground (subservice user)
    participant R as Routing AP<br/>(routing and reporting)
    participant D as Destination AP<br/>(acceptance and reporting)
    participant P as Subservice provider<br/>(e.g. ST[03])
    participant E as Execution reporting<br/>(same AP as D)
    G->>R: TC packet (request + ack flags)
    alt routing checks fail
        R-->>G: TM[1,10] failed routing (request discarded)
    end
    R->>D: forward request
    alt acceptance checks fail
        D-->>G: TM[1,2] failed acceptance (request discarded)
    else accepted
        D-->>G: TM[1,1] if acceptance ack flag set
        D->>P: distribute request
        P->>E: start / progress / completion notifications
        E-->>G: TM[1,3]/[1,4], TM[1,5]/[1,6], TM[1,7]/[1,8]
    end

The diagram is this wiki's rendering of clauses 6.1.3 to 6.1.5 of ECSS-E-ST-70-41C.91115

docs.title: 2.2 Identifying the request: the request ID
docs.text:
A PUS-C request is uniquely identified by three things: the source identifier of the application process that generated it, the destination identifier (the APID of the executing application process plus the identifier of the system that hosts it) and a sequence count or request name produced by the source.22 In a CCSDS telecommand packet the APID goes into the Space Packet primary header, the count or name into the packet sequence control field, and the source identifier into the TC secondary header.22

Every ST[01] report therefore starts with a request ID field that is a copy of the first 32 bits of the telecommand's primary header: the packet ID (version, type, secondary header flag, APID) and the packet sequence control (sequence flags and count).32 The request ID alone is not unique: the standard points out that the missing source identifier is carried in the destination identifier of the report's own telemetry secondary header.32 PUS-C also admits that identifiers repeat in practice, for example during tests or when the 14-bit counter wraps around, so a ground system may need timing information to keep requests apart over a whole mission.22

Field Bits PUS-C type Meaning Packet version number 3 enumerated Copied from the verified TC. Packet type 1 enumerated Copied (always 1 for a TC). Secondary header flag 1 Boolean Copied. Application process ID 11 enumerated APID of the destination of the TC. Sequence flags 2 enumerated Copied. Packet sequence count 14 unsigned integer Sequence count or packet name of the TC.

32

PUS-A describes the same 4 octets more loosely, as a 2-octet "Telecommand Packet ID" and a 2-octet "Packet Sequence Control", both copies of the telecommand header fields.38 It also requires each telecommand source to keep a separate sequence count per APID, so that each packet can be traced through the end-to-end telecommand system, and it states that the packet sequence control is copied into the acknowledgement as the identifier of the acknowledged packet.44

docs.title: 2.3 The stages of execution
docs.text:
PUS-C defines an execution verification profile for every request type: the pre-conditions checked before execution starts, the conditions checked during each step, the post-conditions checked at the end, and the codes to report for each successful or failed condition.20 The subservice provider executes each request in a fixed order:25

flowchart TB
  A[Request received by subservice provider] --> B{Pre-conditions<br/>fulfilled?}
  B -- no --> B1[Notify failed start of execution<br/>stop processing] --> X([TM 1,4])
  B -- yes --> B2[Notify successful start] --> S{Steps left?}
  S -- yes --> C{Step execution<br/>conditions fulfilled?}
  C -- no --> C1[Notify failed progress of that step] --> S
  C -- yes --> C2[Notify successful progress of that step] --> S
  S -- no --> D{Any step failed, or<br/>post-conditions not met?}
  D -- yes --> D1[Notify failed completion<br/>stop processing] --> Y([TM 1,8])
  D -- no --> D2[Notify successful completion] --> Z([TM 1,7 if requested])

25

Two subtleties matter for operations:

  • A successful completion only means that the provider checked all post-conditions in the profile; it does not necessarily mean that the request achieved its purpose. What "success" means depends on the profile.25
  • A failed progress does not stop the request: the provider records it and continues with the next step, and the request then ends with a failed completion.25 Each progress notification must identify the step or instruction it refers to.20

PUS-A uses the same four stages and gives the operational motivation. Acceptance includes the checksum check and the check that the application process supports the requested service and subservice; start of execution covers feasibility and validity checks of the parameters against the current state; progress steps are telecommand-specific; completion closes the profile.36 Its overview table shows which reports suit which kind of command, with 10 s of execution time as the example threshold:42

Command Short execution (under 10 s) Long execution (over 10 s) Immediate A + Et, or Et alone A + Es + Ep + Et, or Es + Ep + Et Delayed execution A + Et A + Es + Ep + Et

A = acceptance, Es = execution start, Ep = execution progress (one or more), Et = execution complete.42 For an immediate command a separate acceptance report is not needed, and a short command may only need a single execution report.42

PUS-A also limits the scope of the service: it covers telecommands that originate from the ground, including those stored in an on-board schedule for later release, but not commands generated autonomously on board, whose invocation is reported through event reporting instead.43

docs.title: 3.1 PUS-C
docs.text:
Every PUS-C request carries four flags that say which successful stages the destination application process must report: acceptance, start of execution, progress of execution and completion of execution.24 Failures are not optional: failed acceptance, failed start and failed completion are always reported, and failed progress follows the reporting policy described below.24 In a telecommand packet the four flags form the 4-bit acknowledgement flags field of the TC secondary header, after the 4-bit TC packet PUS version number (2 for PUS-C).29

Bit of the flags field Requests the report of Report generated if set Clause 0 (first transmitted, most significant) successful completion of execution TM[1,7] 7.4.4.1d.4 1 successful progress of execution TM[1,5] 7.4.4.1d.3 2 successful start of execution TM[1,3] 7.4.4.1d.2 3 (last transmitted, least significant) successful acceptance TM[1,1] 7.4.4.1d.1

30

Read as a 4-bit unsigned number, the field is therefore 8 for "completion only", 1 for "acceptance only", 9 (0b1001) for both, and 15 (0b1111) for all four. This numeric reading is what the SCOS-2000 CCF_ACK field stores (see section 7).52

docs.title: 3.2 PUS-A
docs.text:
In PUS-A the "Ack" field has the same four bits and the same bit numbering: bit 3 asks for acceptance, bit 2 for start, bit 1 for progress and bit 0 for completion, and all zeros means that no success acknowledgements are sent.45 PUS-A points out a ground-side benefit of the flags: because the ground knows which stages it asked for, it can report "packets uplinked but not yet verified".45 It also notes that acknowledgement packets go only to the source of the original telecommand, so the ground never receives acknowledgements for commands generated on board.46 The PUS-A data field header differs around the flags: it starts with a 1-bit CCSDS secondary header flag (set to 0) and a 3-bit PUS version number (set to 1), and its source ID field has a mission-defined length or is omitted.45

Why the success reports are selectable

PUS-A ties the choice of success reports to the operational scenario of each command instance, for example whether there is ground coverage when it executes, and requires the ground system to be configured so that it only asks for stages that a given command can actually verify.43

docs.title: 4.1 Routing and reporting
docs.text: The application processes that a routing and reporting subservice serves, and the list of routing checks it performs, are declared when the spacecraft architecture and the subservice are specified. Typical checks are that the request is not corrupted, that the destination exists, that it is ready (for example that the unit that hosts it is switched on) and that routing can continue.9 For each request that fails, the subservice generates exactly one failed routing notification, carried in one TM[1,10] report, and discards the request.10 The failure codes, and the auxiliary data attached to each code, are declared per subservice and are common to all requests it routes.10 There is no successful routing report, and the standard leaves the routing architecture itself unspecified.2

docs.title: 4.2 Acceptance and reporting
docs.text:
The acceptance checks are declared when specifying the subservice; the standard's examples are the integrity check and the availability of the addressed service.12 A request that passes generates one TM[1,1] report, but only when its acceptance flag asks for it; a request that fails generates one TM[1,2] report and is discarded.1314 The failure codes for failed acceptance are declared per subservice and do not depend on the request.14

PUS-A fixes six standard acceptance failure codes and leaves all other values to the application process or to the individual command:39

Code Meaning (PUS-A) 0 illegal APID (PAC error) 1 incomplete or invalid length packet 2 incorrect checksum 3 illegal packet type 4 illegal packet subtype 5 illegal or inconsistent application data

PUS-C does not carry this list over: it only requires that each acceptance subservice declares its own failure codes.14 PUS-A also states that failure codes for the later stages are always mission-specific.43

docs.title: 4.3 Execution reporting
docs.text:
The execution reporting subservice does not check anything itself. It receives the notifications that the subservice providers raise while executing the request (see 2.3) and wraps each of them into a report:415

  • a successful start, progress or completion notification becomes a TM[1,3], TM[1,5] or TM[1,7] report only if the corresponding acknowledgement flag is set;15
  • a failed start or failed completion notification always becomes a TM[1,4] or TM[1,8] report;1517
  • a failed progress notification becomes a TM[1,6] report only if the application process is configured to do so for that request type; otherwise it is folded into the failed completion notification.1617

That last policy is declared per request type of each subservice, including the standard request types of clause 6 that do not specify it themselves.18 ST[02] gives an example of the folded form: a request to distribute physical device commands produces one failed completion report containing the first failed progress notification of the request.27

docs.title: 4.4 Requests with several instructions
docs.text: Many PUS-C requests contain an ordered list of instructions (for example "enable the periodic generation of" several housekeeping reports in one packet).23 Each request type declares whether all instructions are checked before execution starts; if so, one unsuitable instruction fails the start of the whole request.21 Requests whose instructions are independent are instead processed instruction by instruction: the faulty ones produce a failed start of execution notification for that instruction while the valid ones are executed.2126 For the ground this means that a TM[1,4] for one instruction does not prove that nothing happened.

docs.title: 5. Report layouts
docs.text:
All ST[01] reports are telemetry packets of service type 1 whose source data field starts with the request ID of section 2.2.3132 The field types (enumerated, Boolean, unsigned integer, deduced) are the PUS types described on PUS parameter types; a mission declares the format code, and hence the size, of each field whose size the standard does not fix.28

Report Source data field (in order) Fixed sizes TM[1,1], TM[1,3], TM[1,7] request ID 32 bits TM[1,2], TM[1,4], TM[1,8], TM[1,10] request ID, failure notice (code, data) request ID only TM[1,5] request ID, step ID request ID only TM[1,6] request ID, step ID, failure notice (code, data) request ID only

3233

Field PUS-C type Size Meaning request ID see 2.2 32 bits Identifies the verified request together with the report's destination ID. step ID enumerated declared by the mission Identifies the step (or instruction) whose progress is reported; values are request-specific. failure notice: code enumerated declared by the mission The reason for the failure, from the list declared for the subservice or request type. failure notice: data deduced deduced from the code Auxiliary data "used to explain the reason"; its presence and structure are deduced from the code.

323310

The failure notice illustrates the PUS "deduced" mechanism: the code determines what follows. PUS-A expresses the same idea as a "Parameters" field of any structure that conforms to its structure rules and is identified by the code.39 The PUS-A step field of TM(1,5) and TM(1,6) is called "Step Number" and indicates which intermediate step of the execution profile has completed.40

A worked example with illustrative bytes shows how compact the reports are. Suppose the ground sends a request to APID 172 with sequence count 291 (0x123). Its first 32 bits are 0x18AC (version 0, type 1, secondary header flag 1, APID 172) and 0xC123 (stand-alone flags 11, count 291). A TM[1,1] for that request carries exactly the 4 source data octets 18 AC C1 23; a failed completion report carries the same 4 octets followed by the failure code and its data.32

docs.title: 6. Capability sets and the 2016 and 2024 changes
6.1 Applicability in PUS-C
docs.text: In PUS-C every capability type, and through it every message type, has an applicability constraint; the values used in Annex C are minimum, by declaration, implied by, requires and response.1934 For ST[01] all report types are minimum within their subservice: if a mission includes an execution reporting subservice, it supports all six execution reports, and an acceptance subservice supports both TM[1,1] and TM[1,2].34 What is tailored is which subservices exist (6.1.2.1) and, through the acknowledgement flags and the execution verification profile, which reports a given request actually produces.520

docs.title: 6.2 Capability sets in PUS-A
docs.text:
PUS-A organised the same choice as capability sets:41

Set Subtypes Rule Minimum 1 (acceptance success), 2 (acceptance failure) always implemented Additional 3 and 4 (execution started) each requires the other Additional 5 and 6 (execution progress) each requires the other Additional 7 and 8 (execution completed) each requires the other

The additional capabilities can be chosen per telecommand.41 PUS-A had no routing report: TM(1,10) and the routing and reporting subservice are new in PUS-C, as is the formal execution verification profile.372

docs.title: 6.3 Differences between issues
docs.text:
Aspect PUS-A (ECSS-E-70-41A, 2003) PUS-C (ECSS-E-ST-70-41C, 2016) Rev.1 DIR1 draft (2024) Service name Telecommand verification Request verification Request verification Reports (1,1) to (1,8) TM[1,1] to TM[1,8], TM[1,10] unchanged; execution reports renamed "... of request execution verification report" Routing failure not defined TM[1,10] TM[1,10] Standard failure codes 0 to 5 for acceptance none; declared per subservice none Ack field position after a 1-bit secondary header flag and a 3-bit PUS version (1) after a 4-bit PUS version (2) same as PUS-C Report destination to the TC source to the application process of the request source the destination ID must equal the TC source ID Failed reports in a critical log not defined not defined may be stored in the ST[27] critical packet log, by declaration

3639453429474849

The full comparison of the two issues is on PUS-A vs PUS-C.

docs.title: 7.1 The verifier
docs.text:
SCOS-2000's verifier uses the incoming type 1 reports to close the report-based verification stages of released commands. It extracts the 4 octets that echo the telecommand packet ID and sequence control from each service 1 report and uses them to find the command instance the report refers to.50 The ICD lists the constraints this imposes on a mission:50

  • the 4 echo octets must sit at the same position in every type 1 packet;
  • the mapping from subtypes to verification stages is a static configuration that applies to every command of the mission (typically subtype 1 closes the acceptance stage successfully);
  • progress reports TM(1,5) and TM(1,6) are processed, but only for progress stage 0; further progress stages can only be verified through telemetry parameters;
  • the failure code in negative reports is ignored: only the subtype decides that the stage failed.
flowchart LR
  TM["TM(1,x) received"] --> K["Extract 4 echo octets<br/>(TC packet ID + sequence control)"]
  K --> M{"Matching released<br/>command?"}
  M -- no --> N[Not used for verification]
  M -- yes --> S["Map subtype to stage<br/>(static, mission-wide)"]
  S --> P{"Success or<br/>failure subtype?"}
  P -- success --> OK["Stage PASSED"]
  P -- failure --> KO["Stage FAILED<br/>(failure code ignored)"]

The flowchart is this wiki's summary of ICD 7.0 Appendix C §3.1.50 The section numbers that the appendix quotes for the PUS services (section 6 for service 1, 7 for service 2, 8 for service 3) match the clause numbers of these services in ECSS-E-70-41A, although the appendix cites them as "[AD-5]", which the ICD's own list of applicable documents assigns to a different document.503551

docs.title: 7.2 The database side
docs.text:
Three groups of MIB fields drive this behaviour:

Item Table / field Role Ack flags of a command ccf.CCF_ACK Default value 0 to 15 of the complete Ack field; can be changed when loading a command (from SCOS-2000 R4.0).52 Position of the Ack field pcdf element of type K Header element whose value is taken from CCF_ACK.53 Verification stages cvs CVS_TYPE A (acceptance), S (start), 0-9 (progress step), C (completion); CVS_SOURCE R (report) or V (parameter values).54 Stage window cvs.CVS_START, CVS_INTERVAL, CVS_UNCERTAINTY Delay in seconds after release (or execution, for time-tagged commands) before the window opens; length in seconds of the sampling interval used to calculate the overall window; optional specific window that replaces the TC SPACON default (-1 keeps the default).55 Parameter checks cve Expected value and tolerance of monitoring parameters for V stages.56 Profile cvp Associates commands with stages, at most one stage of each type per command.57

A report-based progress stage can only be of type 0, which is how the verifier limitation shows up in the data.55 Unsetting an acknowledgement flag when loading a command disables the matching report stage, but it cannot add a stage that is not in cvp; every command for which the spacecraft generates service 1 reports must therefore be given the corresponding stages in the database.57 The stage statuses, the window arithmetic and interlocks are explained on Command verification in the MIB.

docs.title: 8.1 The tailoring
docs.text:
Solar Orbiter's TM/TC ICD applies PUS-A (ECSS-E-70-41A is its applicable document AD1)61 and restricts service 1 to two stages, acceptance and completion. Only four Ack values are allowed: 0000 (no success reports), 0001 (acceptance success or failure, TM(1,1) or (1,2)), 1000 (execution success or failure, TM(1,7) or (1,8)) and 1001 (both). The start and progress bits are "not used" and set to zero; the value for each command is coded in the spacecraft database.5860 (The ICD text introduces these bit settings with the words "defined for BepiColombo", although the document is the Solar Orbiter ICD.)60 The mission's service list contains only subtypes 1, 2, 7 and 8 for service 1, all four marked "M", i.e. part of the minimum capability set that every user must implement.63

The central software (CSW) applies two groups of checks to every incoming packet, whatever its Ack flags:59

Group Checks Failure report Static acceptance checks constant header fields (version, type, data field header flag, sequence flags, PUS version); packet length field between 5 and 241; length against received bytes; packet error control; process ID against the allocation; packet category 12 for TCs; service type and subtype supported by the addressed process TM(1,2) Consistency checks (addressed process only) actual length against the length expected for the type and subtype; parameters defined, in range and of the expected type TM(1,8)

Consistency checks only start after all static checks pass, and execution only starts after all consistency checks pass; type-specific success checks (for example reading back written hardware data) may follow before the completion report.59 All four Solar Orbiter report layouts start with the 2-octet TC packet ID and the 2-octet TC packet sequence control; the failure reports add a 2-octet Failure ID and optional parameters of any size.62

Annex 9 of the ICD allocates the standard Failure IDs used by the CSW (and optionally by other software) together with their parameters:65

Failure ID Meaning Parameters 0 illegal APID type, subtype of the received TC (1 octet each) 1 incomplete or invalid length type, subtype 2 incorrect checksum (CRC) type, subtype, received checksum (2 octets), computed checksum (2 octets) 3 illegal packet type type, subtype 4 illegal packet subtype type, subtype 5 illegal or inconsistent application data field type, subtype, position of the first inconsistent parameter (1 octet), its received value (1 octet) 6 illegal segment sequence flag type, subtype, two application-specific 2-octet values 7 illegal MAP ID type, subtype

Codes 0 to 5 are the PUS-A acceptance codes, extended by two link-layer codes.6539 The type and subtype parameters are set to zero when they were not received.65 Table 14.3-1 reserves 0 to 500 for standard codes and gives each user a range: 1000-1999 SSMM, 2000-2999 star trackers, 4000-9999 OBCPs, 10000-39999 CSW (10000-19999 command and control, 20000-29999 AOCS, 30000-39999 other CSW processes), 40000-59999 payload (one block of 1,000 codes per instrument: EPD 40000, MAG 41000, RPW 42000, SWA 43000, SPICE 44000, PHI 45000, EUI 46000, METIS 47000, STIX 48000, SoloHI 49000; 50000-59999 spare) and 60000-64999 the ground (60000-63999 SCOEs, 64000-64999 the ESOC mission control system).66

docs.title: 8.2 What the MIB contains
docs.text:
The September 2025 Solar Orbiter MIB defines service 1 reports for 29 APIDs, all of packet category 1 (the low 4 bits of the APID), which the ICD reserves for service 1 acknowledgements:6867

Report Packets in pid APIDs Additional identification (pic) TM(1,1) acceptance success 29 29 none TM(1,2) acceptance failure 274 29 Failure ID: byte offset 20, 16 bits TM(1,7) completion success 29 29 none TM(1,8) completion failure 1,477 29 Failure ID: byte offset 20, 16 bits

68

Byte 20 is where the Failure ID sits: 16 octets of PUS-A TM headers, then the 4 echo octets. Because of this pic entry the SCOS-2000 packetiser treats every failure code as a separate packet with its own SPID and description, while the verifier itself still ignores the code (section 7.1).6850 The April 2020 release had the same structure with 273 TM(1,2) and 1,457 TM(1,8) packets.72 The SWA instrument database follows the same convention for its own reports, with the same pic entries for (1,2) and (1,8) at offset 20.73

For the central software's DMS application (APID 161, process ID 10) the codes are grouped in a way that suggests one block per service:68

Code (hex) Report Example description in pid 256 (0x0100) to 271 (0x010F) TM(1,2) 256 "Illegal CCSDS packet version number", 259 "Unknown Process Identifier", 268 "Unknown service type", 271 "Calculated checksum not equal to received checksum" 262, 264 (0x0106, 0x0108) TM(1,8) "Number of parameters is out of the allowed range", "The actual TC length is different from the expected TC length" 512 (0x0200) to 520 TM(1,8) "At least one CPDU command failed", "Wrong MilBus 1553 bus ID or bus coupler ID" 768 (0x0300) to 785 TM(1,8) 768 "SID is out of the allowed range", 778 "SID is not defined", 781 "HK/Diagnostic structure exceeds TM size" 1280 (0x0500) to 1300 TM(1,8) "Selected EID does not exist", "A CEL dump is still ongoing"

Inference

The high octet of the CSW codes matches the service whose requests they refer to (0x01 generic packet checks, 0x02 device commands, 0x03 housekeeping, 0x05 event reporting, and so on, for example 0x12 OBCP loading and 0x13 event-action detection lists; high octets from 0x80 = 128 upwards appear to belong to private services). This is deduced from the descriptions in pid; the ICD does not describe the scheme. As a result, of the 289 distinct CSW codes in the MIB (256 to 37,000 across the six CSW report APIDs), 194 lie below 10000, outside the 10000-39999 CSW range of ICD Table 14.3-1, and the 95 that fall inside it (32769 = 0x8001 and above) follow the same high-octet pattern rather than the table's sub-ranges. By contrast, every code above 500 of the SSMM, star tracker and instrument APIDs lies in its allocated range (the EGSE APID 1937 uses 64997 to 64999, in the ground range). A reviewer should treat the table as a design intent for the CSW rather than a description of its codes.

A real report from the MIB shows the layout of a failure packet. SPID 14028, TM(1,2) code 271 "Calculated checksum not equal to received checksum" on APID 161, is decoded through the plf table as the TC packet ID at byte 16, the TC sequence control at byte 18 (both PTC 3, PFC 12), the Failure ID at byte 20 (PTC 2, PFC 16) and two 32-bit fields "Received Checksum" and "Calculated Checksum" at bytes 22 and 26.69 This differs from the parameters that Annex 9 lists for the standard code 2 (1-octet type and subtype, then 2-octet received and computed checksums): the DMS application defines no code 2 in the MIB (its TM(1,2) codes are 256 to 271) and reports a checksum error as code 271 with this different layout.656869 Success packets such as SPID 14181 contain only the two echo fields.69 See the APID 161 page of the explorer for the full list.

docs.title: 8.3 Verification profiles of the commands
docs.text:
Because service 1 has no requests, no command in ccf has CCF_TYPE = 1, in the 2025 and 2020 releases and in the SWA database alike.707273 The command definitions agree with the tailoring. Grouping the 5,454 commands of ccf by their default Ack value and by the stages attached to them in cvp gives:70

CCF_ACK Meaning Stages (CVS_TYPE/CVS_SOURCE) Commands 9 (0b1001) acceptance + completion reports A/R + C/R 5,225 1 (0b0001) acceptance report only A/R + C/V 78 null no PUS data field header C/V only (89) or none (41) 130 0 no success reports none 21

70

The 78 commands with Ack 1 are all TC(2,128) MIL-STD-1553 commands to the two PCDUs (39 each for PCDU A and B, names starting ZPW0 and ZPW1), whose completion is verified by checking a telemetry parameter rather than by a TM(1,7) (ST[02] has a worked example). The commands with a null Ack are the 125 CPDU commands of header HPC1_TC and the five commands of header NO_HDR ("FARM UNLOCK directive", "SETV( R ) Directive", "PAC RESET directive", "Reinit TTR" and "CPDU TC_Only").70 Only acceptance and completion stages exist in the whole cvs table: 16 report-based acceptance stages, 23 report-based completion stages and 167 parameter-based completion stages.70

docs.title: 8.4 Worked example: enabling a housekeeping report
docs.text:
The command ZCD00305 "Enable HK Para Rpt Gen" is TC(3,5) to APID 172 (process ID 10, category 12) with one 8-bit parameter, the housekeeping SID. Its CCF_ACK is 9 and its profile is stage 14001 (acceptance, report-based, CVS_START 0 s, CVS_INTERVAL 20 s) plus stage 14007 (completion, report-based, same timing), both without a specific CVS_UNCERTAINTY window.7155

  1. SCOS-2000 builds the header NOM_TC, whose pcdf definition places a 4-bit K element at bit 52, and fills it with 9 (0b1001).7153
  2. On board, the DMS application checks the packet. If, for example, the checksum is wrong, it sends TM(1,2) with Failure ID 271 from APID 161; the verifier sets stage 14001 to failed, and the packetiser files the report as SPID 14028 with its own description.6850
  3. Otherwise it sends TM(1,1) (SPID 14181) because bit 3 is set, and stage 14001 passes.6858
  4. If the SID is unknown, execution fails and a TM(1,8) with code 778 "SID is not defined" (SPID 14149) closes stage 14007 as failed; otherwise TM(1,7) (SPID 14182) closes it as passed.68

With the illustrative header of section 5 (sequence count 291), the TM(1,1) source data would be 18 AC C1 23 and the TM(1,8) source data 18 AC C1 23 03 0A, followed by any parameters of code 778. The bytes are constructed for this explanation; the codes and SPIDs are real MIB entries.68

SQL used 
-- solo-2025-09-16.sqlite (MIB__20250916M25925PFMS001_SOL)
-- service 1 packets per subtype and APID count
SELECT PID_STYPE, COUNT(*), COUNT(DISTINCT PID_APID) FROM pid
 WHERE PID_TYPE = '1' GROUP BY PID_STYPE;
SELECT DISTINCT CAST(PID_APID AS INT) % 16 FROM pid WHERE PID_TYPE = '1';  -- packet category
SELECT * FROM pic WHERE PIC_TYPE = '1';
-- failure codes of the DMS application
SELECT PID_STYPE, PID_PI1_VAL, PID_SPID, PID_DESCR FROM pid
 WHERE PID_TYPE = '1' AND PID_APID = '161' ORDER BY CAST(PID_PI1_VAL AS INT);
SELECT PID_APID, PID_STYPE, MIN(CAST(PID_PI1_VAL AS INT)), MAX(CAST(PID_PI1_VAL AS INT))
  FROM pid WHERE PID_TYPE = '1' AND PID_STYPE IN ('2','8') GROUP BY 1, 2;
-- layout of a failure report
SELECT p.PLF_NAME, p.PLF_OFFBY, c.PCF_DESCR, c.PCF_PTC, c.PCF_PFC
  FROM plf p JOIN pcf c ON c.PCF_NAME = p.PLF_NAME WHERE p.PLF_SPID = '14028';
-- Ack values and verification profiles (cvs/cvp columns are COL1..COLn in ICD order)
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ccf WHERE CCF_TYPE = '1';  -- 0 in all three databases
SELECT CCF_ACK, COUNT(*) FROM ccf GROUP BY 1;
SELECT IFNULL(c.CCF_ACK,'NULL'), prof, COUNT(*) FROM (
  SELECT c.*, (SELECT GROUP_CONCAT(t,'+') FROM (SELECT s.COL2||s.COL3 t FROM cvp v
          JOIN cvs s ON s.COL1 = v.COL3 WHERE v.COL1 = c.CCF_CNAME ORDER BY 1)) prof
    FROM ccf c) c GROUP BY 1, 2;
SELECT COL2, COL3, COUNT(*) FROM cvs GROUP BY 1, 2;
SELECT * FROM pcdf WHERE PCDF_TCNAME = 'NOM_TC' ORDER BY CAST(PCDF_BIT AS INT);
-- the worked example
SELECT CCF_CNAME, CCF_TYPE, CCF_STYPE, CCF_APID, CCF_ACK FROM ccf WHERE CCF_CNAME = 'ZCD00305';
SELECT s.* FROM cvp v JOIN cvs s ON s.COL1 = v.COL3 WHERE v.COL1 = 'ZCD00305';
-- solo-2020-04-16.sqlite and swa-idb.sqlite: same pid and pic queries

docs.title: 9. Design notes and pitfalls
docs.text:
• Verification is end to end, not link level. COP-1 confirms that a TC frame reached the on-board decoder; only ST[01] says what the application process did with the packet. A command can be "transferred" at frame level and still fail acceptance.1
  • The request ID needs context. Two requests from different sources can carry the same 32-bit request ID; the source is in the report's secondary header destination ID.32 The Solar Orbiter ICD likewise keeps the TC sequence counter per APID and source ID.64
  • Absence of a success report is not a failure. Success reports exist only if they were requested; a ground system has to know the Ack value of each instance, which is why SCOS-2000 disables the report stages whose flags were unset at load time.2457
  • Failure codes are mission data. PUS-C defines no standard codes, so their meaning lives in the mission ICD and in the MIB. On Solar Orbiter they become separate packet definitions.1468

Inference

Defining one SPID per failure code, as Solar Orbiter does, gives operators a readable reason for each failure in the packet history even though the SCOS-2000 verifier ignores the code. The cost is a large number of near-identical packet definitions (1,751 of the 1,809 service 1 packets in the 2025 release are failure packets). This trade-off is this wiki's reading of the data; no source discusses it.

docs.title: ST[02] Device access
docs.text:
Most of the time a spacecraft is operated through high-level functions: "switch the instrument to science mode", "load this schedule". Underneath, every such function ends in a handful of elementary actions on hardware: a relay pulse, a register write, a message on a data bus. Service type 2 of the Packet Utilization Standard gives the ground direct access to those elementary actions. It exists for contingencies and troubleshooting, when the nominal on-board function may itself be the problem, and for assembly, integration and test, when the basic communication with a unit must be validated before any software runs on it.137 This page describes the device model of ECSS-E-ST-70-41C, every request and report with its data field, the command pulse distribution unit (CPDU) of clause 9, the capability rules, the much smaller PUS-A service, and the way Solar Orbiter implements the service with CPDU pulses, MIL-STD-1553 bus commands and SpaceWire packets in its MIB.

Related pages

The CPDU packet is the one standard telecommand packet without a PUS secondary header; its header rules are on PUS packet structures. CPDU packets travel over the lowest layers of the telecommand chain, the TC Space Data Link Protocol and the CLTU. Memory loads, which some missions use instead of register loads, belong to ST[06] Memory management.

docs.title: 2. Why the service exists
docs.text:
PUS-A explains the motivation in its telecommanding concept. A spacecraft design contains many elementary control actions implemented in hardware or software, such as switching a relay, loading a hardware register or starting a software task; higher-level commands end up triggering one or more of them. Although routine operations do not use them, the ground system must have direct access to all elementary control actions, so that it can bypass a malfunctioning on-board function during contingencies.37 One group of these actions, the device commands, is executed by hardware: hard wired pulse commands, on-off commands and register loads.38

PUS-A lists three ways to route device commands: embedded directly in a telecommand segment and routed by the decoder to the device (bypassing software, for example when the processor has failed); through a CPDU inside the telecommand decoder; or inside a telecommand packet to an application process that extracts and forwards them. It also recommends that commands of the same type can be packed into one packet so that a multi-command function is executed completely or not at all.38

PUS-C keeps the purpose but generalises the devices. A device is any on-board entity that can be configured by commands or that generates data, including actuators, sensors, transponders and units with no PUS support of their own. Device commands bypass the nominal functions of the on-board software, so the service performs only a minimum of verification on board.1

docs.title: 3. The device model
docs.text:
ECSS-E-ST-70-41C defines five kinds of addressable object for this service. All of them are declared when the subservice (or, for CPDUs, the spacecraft architecture) is specified; none is created by telecommand.4691114

Object Declared properties Requests On/off device the list of devices and, per device, the hardware addresses used to command it (for example switch on, switch off, cold or warm reset, open or close a valve) TC[2,1] Register hardware address, the register fields, and the "register consistency checks" applied when loading it; the sets of loadable and dumpable registers may differ TC[2,2], TC[2,5] CPDU the CPDUs managed by the subservice (see section 6) TC[2,4] Physical device device identifier, communication links (for example a MIL-STD-1553B bus and a SpaceWire link) and, per link, the protocols for commanding and for receiving data TC[2,7], TC[2,8] Logical device logical device identifier, supported commands and their arguments, and the parameter identifiers usable for data acquisition TC[2,10], TC[2,11]

4691114

The physical/logical distinction is explained with a MIL-STD-1553B remote terminal. Commanded as a physical device, the request contains the bus command word itself: address, transmission direction, subaddress and data word count. Commanded as a logical device, the request contains only a logical device identifier, a command identifier and its parameters, and the on-board software maps them onto the right link and protocol.1

flowchart LR
  G["Ground TC packet"] --> AP["Application process with<br/>device access subservice"]
  G -.->|"VC + MAP to CPDU (no software)"| CPDU
  AP -->|"TC 2,1"| ONOFF["On/off device<br/>hardware address"]
  AP -->|"TC 2,2 / 2,5"| REG["Register"]
  AP -->|"TC 2,4: rebuilt CPDU request"| CPDU["CPDU<br/>(own APID)"]
  AP -->|"TC 2,7 / 2,8: link + protocol data"| PHY["Physical device<br/>e.g. 1553 RT, SpW node"]
  AP -->|"TC 2,10 / 2,11: mapped by software"| LOG["Logical device"] --> PHY
  CPDU --> PULSE["Pulse on output line"]

The flowchart is this wiki's summary of clauses 6.2 and 9.1.130

docs.title: 4.1 TC[2,1] distribute on/off device commands
docs.text:
A request contains an ordered list of one or more instructions; each instruction holds a single device address. The delay applied between consecutive instructions depends on the spacecraft architecture.5 The request is rejected as a whole, with a failed start of execution notification, if any instruction names an unknown address; otherwise the instructions are executed in the order in which they appear.5

Field PUS-C type Repetition Meaning N unsigned integer once number of instructions on/off device address enumerated N times hardware address to which the on/off command is sent

19

docs.title: 4.2 TC[2,2] distribute register load commands
docs.text:
Each instruction holds a register address and the data for the register fields. The whole request is rejected if any instruction names an unknown register or fails its register consistency checks, because, as the standard notes, a partial load can leave a device in an unknown or inconsistent state.7 Valid requests are executed in order.7

Field PUS-C type Repetition Meaning N unsigned integer once number of instructions register address enumerated N times hardware address of the register register data deduced N times values of the register fields; structure deduced from the address

20

docs.title: 4.3 TC[2,5] distribute register dump commands and TM[2,6] register dump report
docs.text:
Register dumps are processed differently from loads. Each instruction (a register address) is checked on its own: an unknown address produces a failed start of execution notification for that instruction, and the valid instructions are processed regardless. For each valid instruction the subservice distributes the dump command and builds a register dump notification (address plus the value of each register field); all notifications of one request go into a single TM[2,6] report.8 Dumping requires the load capability.8

Field (TM[2,6]) PUS-C type Repetition Meaning N unsigned integer once number of dumped registers register address enumerated N times address of the dumped register register data deduced N times value of each register field

2223

Request-level versus instruction-level rejection

All "distribute" requests of ST[02] (on/off, register load, CPDU, physical and logical commands, and both acquisition requests) are rejected as a whole when one instruction is invalid, and their instructions are executed in order. Only the register dump request is checked instruction by instruction.57810 The consequences for verification reports are described on ST[01] Request verification.

docs.title: 5.1 TC[2,7] distribute physical device commands
docs.text:
Each instruction contains a physical device identifier, protocol-specific data and command data. For a MIL-STD-1553B remote terminal the standard's example maps them to the terminal address (which also selects the bus), the transfer direction, subaddress or mode code indicator and word count or mode code, and up to 32 sixteen-bit data words.12 Instructions for the same device are sent in order at the maximum rate the protocol allows; no ordering can be assumed between instructions for different devices.12

The request is rejected if any instruction names an unknown device or contains invalid protocol data. During execution the subservice checks the result of each transmission. A failed transmission produces a failed execution notification with the instruction index, the transmission return code and any auxiliary data, and the request then ends with a single failed completion of execution report containing the first of these notifications.12

Field PUS-C type Repetition Meaning N unsigned integer once number of instructions physical device ID enumerated N times device (and implicitly link) to address protocol-specific data deduced N times for example the 1553 direction, subaddress and word count command data deduced N times the data to transmit

24

docs.title: 5.2 TC[2,8] acquire data from physical devices and TM[2,9]
docs.text:
The acquisition request is the read counterpart. Each instruction carries a transaction ID, chosen by the requester to recognise the answer, the device ID and the protocol data that select the data to report. For each successful acquisition the subservice generates one TM[2,9] report; a failed acquisition produces a failed execution notification with the transaction ID and the transaction execution status, and the request ends with one failed completion report containing the first such notification.13 The data acquisition return codes and their auxiliary data are declared per device and link.13

Field (TC[2,8]) PUS-C type Repetition N unsigned integer once transaction ID unsigned integer N times physical device ID enumerated N times protocol-specific data deduced N times Field (TM[2,9]) PUS-C type Meaning transaction ID unsigned integer copied from the instruction data acquisition return code enumerated part of the transaction execution status auxiliary data deduced, deduced presence detail for the return code, if any data block deduced the acquired data

2526

docs.title: 5.3 TC[2,10] and TC[2,11]: logical devices and TM[2,12]
docs.text:
A logical device command names the logical device, a command ID and the command arguments, with no reference to the physical link or protocol. The subservice maps the logical device to a physical device, link and protocol, maps the command ID to protocol-specific data, formats the arguments as command data, transmits and checks the result, reporting failures as for physical commands.15 The standard's stated benefit is that the same request can be used during on-board software development and in flight, even though the physical access to the device differs.15

A logical acquisition names the logical device and a parameter ID; the subservice maps the parameter to protocol data, acquires it, and returns one TM[2,12] report per successful acquisition with the acquired parameter value.16 Logical commanding requires physical commanding, and logical acquisition is implied by logical commanding.35

Message Fields in order TC[2,10] N (unsigned integer); repeated N times: logical device ID (enumerated), command ID (deduced), command arguments (deduced) TC[2,11] N (unsigned integer); repeated N times: transaction ID (unsigned integer), logical device ID (enumerated), parameter ID (enumerated) TM[2,12] transaction ID (unsigned integer), data acquisition return code (enumerated), auxiliary data (deduced, deduced presence), parameter value (deduced)

272829

docs.title: 6.1 Concept
docs.text: Clause 9 of ECSS-E-ST-70-41C defines the CPDU: a simple unit that gives the ground direct access to equipment, for example to reset a transponder or a sensor during a contingency. Each CPDU is logically an application process with its own APID. It can be reached directly, through a virtual channel and a multiplexer access point (MAP) that is physically linked to it, or indirectly, through an application process that hosts a device access subservice and receives TC[2,4].30 A CPDU request is a list of command pulse instructions, each naming an addressable output and the duration of the pulse.30

docs.title: 6.2 Rules
docs.text:
Property Rule (PUS-C) Pulse duration unit declared per CPDU, from 10 ms to 15 ms Addressable outputs declared per CPDU; up to 2^12 (4,096), identified by values 0 to 2^12 - 1; only some are equipped with output lines Instructions per request maximum declared per CPDU, at least 12 and at most 504, constrained by the TC segment size Duration exponential value 0 to 7 Pulse length pulse duration unit × 2^(duration exponential value) Access APID, MAPs physically linked to the CPDU and the VC used for each MAP declared in the spacecraft architecture; MAP 0 is usual for a CPDU behind a decoder without cross-coupling Connected outputs each physically connected output has a declared minimum and maximum pulse duration

313233

With the allowed range of the unit, the eight duration codes span from 10 ms (unit 10 ms, code 0) to 1.92 s (unit 15 ms, code 7):

Code Factor Unit 10 ms Unit 15 ms 0 1 10 ms 15 ms 1 2 20 ms 30 ms 2 4 40 ms 60 ms 3 8 80 ms 120 ms 4 16 160 ms 240 ms 5 32 320 ms 480 ms 6 64 640 ms 960 ms 7 128 1.28 s 1.92 s

The table is computed from the formula in requirement 9.2.3c.33 PUS-A gives the same end point, 128 × D "between 1,28 and 1,92 seconds".52

docs.title: 6.3 The CPDU packet
docs.text:
A CPDU request travels in a CCSDS Space Packet with version 0, type 1, secondary header flag 0, the CPDU's APID, sequence flags 11 and sequence count or name 0. Its data field has no secondary header and no spare, only the application data and a 16-bit CRC identical to the frame error control field of the TC data link.34

3433

When a device access subservice receives TC[2,4], it rebuilds the CPDU request in the format the CPDU expects and distributes it; the standard imposes no delay between consecutive CPDU requests.10 The TC[2,4] data field wraps the instructions in two levels of repetition:

Field PUS-C type Repetition Meaning N1 unsigned integer once (optional) number of CPDU instructions CPDU ID enumerated N1 times (optional) which CPDU, if the subservice manages several N2 unsigned integer N1 times number of command pulse instructions output line ID enumerated, 12 bits N2 times output to pulse reserved bit-string, 1 bit N2 times - duration exponential value unsigned integer, 3 bits N2 times pulse length code

2110

Inference

The upper limit of 504 instructions matches the largest CCSDS TC frame. A TC transfer frame is at most 1,024 octets, of which 5 are the primary header, 2 the frame error control field and 1 the segment header, leaving 1,016 octets for one packet.53545556 A CPDU packet of 6 header octets, 504 two-octet instructions and a 2-octet CRC is exactly 6 + 1,008 + 2 = 1,016 octets. PUS-C only says that the limit is constrained by the segment size.31 The same arithmetic links the PUS-A maximum of 120 instructions to its maximum CPDU packet length of 248 octets (6 + 240 + 2).4151

docs.title: 7. Capability rules and verification
docs.text:
PUS-C requires at least one of four capabilities: on/off commands, register commands, software CPDU commands, or physical device commanding.3 The remaining message types depend on them (section 1). Each of the "distribute" and "acquire" requests reports a rejected request with a failed start of execution notification. Execution checks are defined only for the physical and logical device requests: there, a failed transmission or acquisition produces a single failed completion report built from the first failed notification.512131516 The device access subservice defines no observables.17

Device commands bypass the nominal on-board functions and get only a minimum of on-board verification.1 The confirmation that a relay actually switched therefore has to come from telemetry: Solar Orbiter verifies the completion of its PCDU power commands with parameter checks rather than with a completion report (section 10.4).71

docs.title: 8. Rev.1 draft
docs.text: The December 2024 draft for public review keeps the same eleven message types with the same subtypes, TC[2,1] to TM[2,12], and the same clause structure.36

docs.title: 9. PUS-A: the device command distribution service
docs.text:
PUS-A's service 2 is much smaller. It distributes on/off and register load commands and CPDU commands for the reconfiguration of vital spacecraft functions, and it defines no reports.3942

PUS-A request Application data Notes (2,1) Distribute On-Off Commands N (unsigned integer, optional), then N addresses (enumerated) N is omitted if the service handles one command at a time (2,2) Distribute Register Load Commands N (optional), then N × (register address, register data) the data structure is known from the address and follows structure rule set 1 (2,3) Distribute CPDU Commands a CPDU packet: N × (output line ID, 1 octet; duration, 1 octet) no data field header; processed by the CPDU itself

434445

On reception, the application process unpacks the commands, reformats them for the internal bus or device driver (the address structure is mission-dependent and may contain subfields) and distributes them in packet order. Annex A.3 of PUS-A gives an example with a 24-bit OBDH command.40

The PUS-A CPDU is described in more detail than in PUS-C, in Annex D, which is transcribed from ESA PSS-04-151 (the telecommand decoder specification, issue 1, which PUS-A dates September 1993; the cover of the document itself says September 1992 and its inner pages September 1993, see the history page):414849

  • a CPDU is solely accessible from the ground, has up to 256 output lines and a dedicated APID, and receives one complete packet per telecommand segment, in practice on MAP 0 (MAP 1 is a likely second interface when CPDUs are cross-coupled);4150
  • the packet is 10 to 248 octets long, always an even number, ends with the frame CRC, and is checked to be "CLEAN" (length and CRC) and then "LEGAL" (version 0, type 1, data field header flag 0, programmed APID, sequence flags 11); a packet failing a check is erased;51
  • each instruction is two octets: the first selects one of 256 outputs, and in the second the 5 most significant bits are reserved and ignored and the 3 least significant bits select a duration of 1 × D to 128 × D, with D between 10 and 15 ms;52
  • once a packet is accepted, the CPDU ignores further segments until all its pulses are issued; there is no "abort", and an instruction for an output that is not physically implemented is processed as if the output existed, without any anomaly report;5052
  • the mission constants <CPDU_DURATION_UNIT> (10 to 15 ms) and <CPDU_MAX_INSTR> (12 to 120 instructions) characterise each CPDU.47

52

A small inconsistency in PUS-A

The text of request (2,3) describes the duration as "a value between 0 and 8", while Annex D defines a 3-bit field with values 000 to 111, i.e. 0 to 7.4552 PUS-C settles the range at 0 to 7.33

The capability sets of PUS-A require either (2,3), because a CPDU is a dedicated application process, or one of (2,1) and (2,2); a service without CPDU commands may add the other of the two.46

Aspect PUS-A PUS-C CPDU request (2,3), sent to the CPDU APID TC[2,4] to a software subservice; the direct CPDU packet is defined in clause 9 CPDU outputs, instruction size 256, 2 octets (8 + 5 + 3 bits) up to 2^12, 2 octets (12 + 1 + 3 bits) Max instructions 12 to 120 12 to 504 Register dump not defined TC[2,5] / TM[2,6] Physical and logical devices not defined TC[2,7] to TM[2,12] Reports none TM[2,6], TM[2,9], TM[2,12]

45473135

docs.title: 10.1 What the ICD defines
docs.text:
Solar Orbiter's TM/TC ICD, based on PUS-A, describes service 2 as the distribution of CPDU commands for the reconfiguration of vital unit functions, of MIL-STD-1553 bus command messages and of SpaceWire command messages. It distinguishes two CPDU paths: packets received by the CPDU TC decoder on MAP 0, with no software involved and a non-PUS structure, and the software-distributed TC(2,3), which the central software (CSW) receives on MAP 1 and routes to the CPDU. If the processing of a CPDU packet is not complete, new commands are ignored. No register load commands exist, because all OBC registers are mapped in memory and reachable through service 6.59

The ICD names three kinds of CPDU pulse command. HPC-1 commands are sent from the ground directly to the CPDU inside the on-board computer, without the central software; HPC-2 commands use the same command lines but are issued by the on-board computer's reconfiguration module; HPC-3 commands are generated by the CSW writing dedicated CPDU registers.64 The ICD's acronym list expands HPC as "High Power Command".65 Its MAP assignments are not fully consistent: the segment header clause gives MAP 0 ("CPDU") for "CPDU command (i.e. TC(2,3))" and MAP 1 for all other commanding, whereas the TC(2,3) clause says that the CSW receives TC(2,3) on MAP 1.6459 In the MIB, only the 125 HPC-1 commands carry CCF_MAPID = 0, while the TC(2,3) commands leave CCF_MAPID empty (section 10.2).67

Request / report Content Verification TC(2,3) CSW-distributed CPDU commands (HPC3) command number (1 octet), filler (5 bits), pulse length (3 bits) TM(1,2) for static check failures, TM(1,8) as defined in a referenced document TC(2,128) Distribute MilBus 1553 Commands bus, bus coupler, N command words, then per command the 1553 command word fields and M data words same TM(2,129) MilBus 1553 Commands Answer bus, echoed command word, bus coupler and its status word, RT status word, N and the returned data words - TC(2,130) Distribute SpaceWire Commands SpW link (1 octet), coupler (1 octet), N (2 octets), raw SpW packet same

59606162

These four are the only service 2 entries in the mission's service list.63 The TC(2,3) layout is the PUS-A Annex D instruction; TC(2,128) is a mission-specific implementation of what PUS-C calls physical device commanding, with the 1553 command word fields given explicitly; TC(2,130) carries a complete SpaceWire packet, whose data is a PUS command plus a 4-octet SpaceWire header.596212

docs.title: 10.2 What the MIB contains
docs.text:
The September 2025 MIB holds 1,363 service 2 commands and one service 2 report, plus 125 CPDU commands without a PUS header:67

Kind Header (CCF_PKTID) APID Commands CCF_ACK Verification profile Direct CPDU (HPC-1), MAP 0 HPC1_TC 44 125 null parameter check or none TC(2,3) software CPDU (HPC-3) NOM_TC 172 105 9 acceptance + completion reports TC(2,128) MIL-STD-1553 NOM_TC 172 1,257 9 (1,179) or 1 (78) reports, or acceptance report + parameter check TC(2,130) SpaceWire NOM_TC 172 1 9 acceptance + completion reports TM(2,129) 1553 command report - 161 SPID 14002 - variable packet (VPD)

6768

APID 44 is process ID 2 (OBC hardware, high-priority TC functions to the CPDU on MAP 0) with packet category 12; APID 172 is process ID 10, the CSW data management application.6667 The single report, TM(2,129), is defined on APID 161, i.e. process ID 10 with packet category 1, although the ICD gives TM(2,129) packet category 2 and Annex 8 reserves category 1 for service 1 acknowledgements.686166 The April 2020 release had the same counts for TC(2,3), (2,128) and (2,130).73 No TC(2,1), (2,2) or (2,4) exists in either release, which matches the ICD.6759

The pcdf definition of HPC1_TC is the CPDU packet header of PUS: fixed version 0, type 1, data field header flag 0, the APID from CCF_APID, sequence flags 0b11, and the sequence count and length set by the commanding system. It has no secondary header elements at all.69

69

All 125 HPC-1 commands carry exactly one instruction: two 8-bit fixed areas, an output line (values 2 to 215 in the MIB) and a pulse length code. Code 2 is used 81 times and code 1 38 times; one series of "Dummy commands" (ZBC04100 to ZBC04107) uses each of the eight codes 0 to 7 once.69 Since fixed areas in cdf are hexadecimal raw values, the pulse code octet holds the 3-bit duration code in its least significant bits, as in the PUS-A instruction.5852

docs.title: 10.3 Worked example: two CPDU commands
docs.text:
HPC-1 (direct) HPC-3 (through the CSW) Command ZBC04001 "Select PM A EEPROM Image 1" ZCSXZ600 "HPC-3 IMU 1 Channel 1 On" Packet HPC1_TC, APID 44, MAP 0, no secondary header NOM_TC, TC(2,3), APID 172 Application data 02 01: output line 2, code 1 10 02: output line 0x10 = 16, code 2 Pulse length 2 × D 4 × D Ack / verification no Ack field; completion stage 9000: parameter NCDD05GE "PM A Image select status" must read IMAGE_1 Ack 9; acceptance and completion reports (stages 11 and 17)

7052

The application data bytes are real (fixed areas from the MIB). The pulse unit D of the Solar Orbiter CPDU is not stated in the available sources; the ICD refers to the unit documentation for the pulse length.59

docs.title: 10.4 Worked example: a PCDU switch-off over MIL-STD-1553
docs.text:
ZPW04800 "PCDU A APR1_C1 SwitchOFF" is a TC(2,128) with Ack 1 (acceptance report only). Its cdf entries fill the generic 1553 layout of ZCD00280 "Distribute 1553 commands" with fixed values:71

Bits Element Value in the MIB Meaning 0-7 Bus ID (PCD02801, textual calibration) BUS_1 (engineering) MIL bus 1 8-15 Bus Coupler ID (PCD02802) BUSCPLR_DEF (editable) default coupler 16-23 number of bus commands 0001 one 1553 message 24-39 command word 2281 (hex) see the bit field below 40-47 number of data words 1 one data word 48-63 data word RPW04800 "APR1_APR1_OFF" default 8401 (hex) the PCDU command itself

7160

The bit split (5 + 1 + 5 + 5 bits) is the one defined by the generic command ZCD00280 (RT address, transmit/receive flag, subaddress or mode, number of data words or mode code), and the word count of 1 agrees with the separate data word count field.71 The command's completion is verified by stage 40: telemetry parameter NPWD0764 "IFA_APR1_Conv1_ST" must read raw 0 (tolerance 0) with a CVS_INTERVAL of 60 s.71 The hex values and the field layout are real MIB data; the assignment of remote terminal 4 to PCDU A is not stated in the available sources beyond the command description.

The answer path uses TM(2,129) (SPID 14002), defined as a variable packet in vpd: the bus ID, the 16-bit command word decoded again into its four fields by negative offsets, the bus coupler status, the RT status word with its individual flags (message error, instrumentation, service request, busy, terminal flag and others), and a counted list of data words.68

SQL used 
-- solo-2025-09-16.sqlite (MIB__20250916M25925PFMS001_SOL)
SELECT CCF_TYPE, CCF_STYPE, CCF_PKTID, COUNT(*), GROUP_CONCAT(DISTINCT CCF_APID),
       GROUP_CONCAT(DISTINCT CCF_ACK), GROUP_CONCAT(DISTINCT CCF_MAPID)
  FROM ccf WHERE CCF_TYPE = '2' OR CCF_PKTID = 'HPC1_TC' GROUP BY 1, 2, 3;
SELECT CCF_STYPE, CCF_ACK, COUNT(*) FROM ccf WHERE CCF_TYPE = '2' GROUP BY 1, 2;
SELECT * FROM pid WHERE PID_TYPE = '2';
SELECT * FROM pcdf WHERE PCDF_TCNAME = 'HPC1_TC' ORDER BY CAST(PCDF_BIT AS INT);
SELECT CDF_VALUE, COUNT(*) FROM cdf WHERE CDF_DESCR = 'HPC_PULSE_LENGTH' GROUP BY 1;
SELECT * FROM cdf WHERE CDF_CNAME IN ('ZBC04001','ZCSXZ600','ZCD00280','ZCD00282','ZPW04800')
 ORDER BY CDF_CNAME, CAST(CDF_BIT AS INT);
SELECT CPC_NAME, CPC_DESCR, CPC_PTC, CPC_PFC, CPC_RADIX, CPC_CATEG, CPC_DEFVAL
  FROM cpc WHERE CPC_NAME IN ('RPW04800','PCD02801','PCD02802','PCD02803');
-- verification (cvs/cvp/cve use COL1..COLn in ICD order)
SELECT v.COL1, s.* FROM cvp v JOIN cvs s ON s.COL1 = v.COL3
 WHERE v.COL1 IN ('ZBC04001','ZCSXZ600','ZPW04800');
SELECT * FROM cve WHERE COL1 IN ('9000','40');
SELECT * FROM vpd WHERE VPD_TPSD = '14002' ORDER BY CAST(VPD_POS AS INT);
-- grouping of TC(2,128) by name prefix
SELECT SUBSTR(CCF_CNAME,1,4), COUNT(*), MIN(CCF_DESCR) FROM ccf
 WHERE CCF_TYPE = '2' AND CCF_STYPE = '128' GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC;

docs.title: 10.5 What the 1,257 bus commands are
docs.text:
Grouping the TC(2,128) commands by the first four characters of their names shows which units are commanded directly over the bus. The descriptions quoted are the alphabetically first and last of each group:72

Prefix Commands Example descriptions ZCSX 468 "TCS BEA-MEA_Group_1_Grp_LCL_OFF" ... "TCS Module_4_Group_6_Htr_192_LCL_ON" ZPW0, ZPW1 248 + 248 "PCDU A APR1_C1 SwitchOFF" ... "PCDU_A DPL2_CH2_FIRE_TK_060SEC" (and the same for PCDU B) ZDSG 38 "DST A Coherence ON-OFF" ... "Dst-Tx B Set RF Power (DST-B FM1)" ZAMG, ZAMK, ZAHG, ZAHK 4 × 24 "H-APME_A Clear Alarms" ... "MAPME_B Set Thresholds" ZMU0, ZMU1, ZMUG, ZMUK 16 + 16 + 8 + 8 "IMU_11 Enable/Disable critical mode" ... "IMU_24 Pump diode current" ZRUG, ZRUK, ZRU0, ZRU1 15 + 15 + 12 + 12 "RIU BIT Start" ... "RIU TLV Open Red" ZDMG, ZDMK 15 + 15 "DEU A Arm Pinpuller" ... "DEU B Switches ST Info" ZSDG, ZSDK, ZSD0, ZSD1 8 + 8 + 1 + 1 "SADE A MY Motor Config" ... "SADE B System Mode Set" ZRWG 4 "RW_1 Torque Command" ... "RW_4 Torque Command" ZPWG, ZPWK 2 + 2 "PCDUA SNAPSHOT_CMD", "PCDU_B TEST_CMD" ZCD0 1 the generic "Distribute 1553 commands" ZCD00280

Inference

The unit names are read from the command descriptions, and the group boundaries from a naming convention that is not documented in the available sources. The picture they give is that Solar Orbiter implements the PUS idea of "physical device commanding" mainly for power distribution, heaters and RF equipment, with each useful bus message stored in the MIB as a fully defined command, rather than with on/off or register commands.

docs.title: 11. How SCOS-2000 handles service 2
docs.text:
The SCOS-2000 import ICD states that the mission control system does no specific processing of service 2 packets. It can aggregate several packets into one TC segment, and so into one frame and CLTU, but it cannot dynamically pack several command definitions into one TC packet. A TC(2,3) therefore either holds one pulse instruction or has several instructions defined in the database, in which case it is handled as a single command for history and verification. CPDU commands can be defined so that they may not be inserted into a time-tagged TC(11,4) or aggregated with other commands in the same segment.57

Where the bits are defined

Because SCOS-2000 has no service-specific logic here, everything about a device command lives in the MIB: the header in tcp and pcdf, the command in ccf, its elements in cdf and cpc, and the check of its effect in cvs and cve. See Commanding in the MIB and Command verification in the MIB.

docs.title: ST[03] Housekeeping
docs.text:
Housekeeping telemetry is the steady stream of temperatures, voltages, currents, modes, counters and status flags that tells the ground what state the spacecraft is in. Service type 3 of the Packet Utilization Standard defines how an on-board application process assembles such on-board parameters into periodic reports, how the ground creates, changes, enables and disables those report definitions, and how it asks for one-shot snapshots. A second, parallel set of reports, the diagnostic reports, serves anomaly investigation with fast, temporary sampling. PUS-C adds a third layer, parameter functional reporting, that switches whole sets of reports at once on mode changes.123 This page covers every concept, request and report of ECSS-E-ST-70-41C, the very different PUS-A service with its filtered mode and sampling-time offsets, the categories of the 2024 Rev.1 draft, and the full decoding chain in SCOS-2000, with real Solar Orbiter packets from the MIB.

Where this page sits

The packet headers around a housekeeping report are on PUS packet structures; the parameter encodings are on PUS parameter types. How SCOS-2000 describes parameters and packets in general is on Monitoring in the MIB. Whether a generated report actually reaches the ground is decided by ST[14] Real-time forwarding control and, for stored data, ST[15] On-board storage and retrieval.

docs.title: 2.1 Report structures and their identifier
docs.text:
A housekeeping parameter report structure is the on-board definition of one kind of report. It consists of an identifier, a collection interval, an ordered list of simply commutated parameters, an ordered list of super commutated parameter sets and, if the subservice can enable and disable reports, a periodic generation action status.5 The structure is identified by the combination of the hosting application process and the structure identifier,5 traditionally called the SID (structure identification) in PUS-A, where the ground uses it together with the APID and the report's nature (housekeeping or diagnostic) to interpret the content.54 A diagnostic parameter report structure has the same elements, except that its status field is always present.17

erDiagram

    APPLICATION_PROCESS ||--o{ DIAG_REPORT_STRUCTURE : hosts
    HK_REPORT_STRUCTURE ||--o{ SIMPLY_COMMUTATED_PARAMETER : "ordered list"
    HK_REPORT_STRUCTURE ||--o{ SUPER_COMMUTATED_SET : "ordered list"
    SUPER_COMMUTATED_SET ||--|{ SET_PARAMETER : "ordered list"
    FUNCTIONAL_REPORTING_DEFINITION ||--|{ REPORTING_ENTRY : contains
    REPORTING_ENTRY }o--|| HK_REPORT_STRUCTURE : "or diagnostic"

        enum structure_id
        uint collection_interval
        enum periodic_generation_action_status
    }
    SUPER_COMMUTATED_SET {

    }

The entity diagram is this wiki's rendering of requirements 6.3.3.2c, 6.3.4.2c and 6.3.5.2.51721

The on-board resources available for structures (how many, how many parameters) and for evaluating them at the same time are declared when the subservice is specified.5 Structures may be predefined on board or created on request, and the standard assumes that all of them, including predefined ones, can be deleted, appended to and re-timed.191213

docs.title: 2.2 Collection interval and sampling interval
docs.text: The collection interval of a structure is the interval at which its parameters are collected and one report is generated. It is expressed in units of the minimum sampling interval of the on-board parameters.25 Each on-board parameter has a spacecraft-wide unique identifier and is associated with exactly one minimum sampling interval; all parameters accessed by one application process share the same interval, and different subsystems may use different ones (the standard's example is 125 ms for the platform and 500 ms for a payload).30 The sampling interval of a parameter, by contrast, belongs to the application process that acquires or computes its value.2

docs.title: 2.3 Simply and super commutated parameters
docs.text:
A simply commutated parameter contributes one sampled value per report. A super commutated parameter contributes several values, sampled at a sub-period equal to the collection interval divided by the super commutated sample repetition number. Each parameter appears only once in a structure, in one of the two forms.2 Super commutated parameters come in sets, and the samples are interleaved by set: for a set of A and B with two samples, the report contains A1, B1, A2, B2.6 If the sub-period is shorter than the update period of the on-board value, some samples are identical.6

For a real example of the timing, see the Solar Orbiter AOCS diagnostic report in section 9.7: a 2 s collection interval with 16 samples, so one sample every 125 ms.97

docs.title: 2.4 Periodic generation and its status
docs.text:
When the periodic generation of a structure is enabled, the subservice generates one report per collection interval, collecting one value of each simply commutated parameter and all samples of each super commutated parameter during that interval.6 A newly created structure always starts disabled.8 If a housekeeping subservice offers no enable/disable capability, its reports are always enabled.5 Clause 6.3 of PUS-C does not state whether predefined structures start enabled or disabled; the Rev.1 draft makes the start and restart configuration policy a declaration of the subservice.49

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Disabled: TC 3,1 create (status set to disabled)
    Disabled --> Enabled: TC 3,5 enable
    Enabled --> Disabled: TC 3,6 disable
    Disabled --> Disabled: TC 3,29 append, TC 3,31 modify interval
    Enabled --> Enabled: TM 3,25 every collection interval, TC 3,31 modify interval
    Disabled --> [*]: TC 3,3 delete
    note right of Enabled
        TC 3,3 delete and TC 3,29 append
        are rejected while enabled
    end note

The state diagram is this wiki's summary of clauses 6.3.3.4 to 6.3.3.9; one-shot reports (TC[3,27]) can be requested in either state.7891213

docs.title: 2.5 Housekeeping versus diagnostic
docs.text: The two reporting subservices provide "similar functions": housekeeping for nominal operations, diagnostic for contingency operations. A diagnostic report type can be enabled when a particular anomaly occurs and disabled at other times.2 PUS-A calls the scenario "diagnostic mode", a selected set of parameters sampled at a higher rate than normal, and says it was previously known as "dwell mode" or "oversampling mode".69 It also explains why the reports are distinct even though they work the same way: the different subtypes let them be routed, stored and processed separately.5769

docs.title: 2.6 Parameter functional reporting
docs.text: The parameter functional reporting configuration subservice controls the reports of the housekeeping and diagnostic subservices of its own service, for example on mode transitions.320 A parameter functional reporting definition has an identifier and a list of entries; each entry names a report structure (by optional APID when the service is distributed over several application processes, by its nature as housekeeping or diagnostic, and by its identifier) together with the status and collection interval to apply.21 Applying a definition can be exclusive: all reports of the service are disabled first.322

docs.title: 3. The housekeeping reporting subservice
docs.text:
Every request of the subservice follows the same pattern. Rejected instructions (or, for single-instruction requests, rejected requests) produce a failed start of execution notification, which reaches the ground as a TM[1,4], and the valid instructions of a multi-instruction request are executed regardless of the faulty ones.79

Capability Request Instructions Rejected if Effect Create TC[3,1] exactly one the identifier is in use; a parameter appears twice; resources exceeded structure created, status disabled Delete TC[3,3] one or more unknown identifier; status enabled structure deleted Enable TC[3,5] one or more unknown identifier status enabled Disable TC[3,6] one or more unknown identifier status disabled Report structures TC[3,9] one or more unknown identifier one TM[3,10] per valid instruction One-shot TC[3,27] one or more unknown identifier one TM[3,25] per valid instruction Append TC[3,29] exactly one status enabled; unknown structure or parameter; simply commutated parameters added to a structure that has super commutated ones; parameter already present; resources exceeded parameters added at the end: simply commutated first, then sets Modify interval TC[3,31] one or more unknown identifier new collection interval Report generation properties TC[3,33] one or more unknown identifier one TM[3,35] holding all notifications

7891011121314

Three details are easy to miss:

  • Report structures answers each instruction with its own TM[3,10], while report generation properties puts all answers into a single TM[3,35].1014
  • One-shot reports of structures with super commutated parameters are not specified: the content of the super commutated part is implementation dependent.11
  • Append to a structure that already has super commutated sets may only add further sets, which keeps the simple parameters in front of the arrays.12

TC[3,5] and TC[3,6] are mandatory when the service includes a parameter functional reporting configuration subservice, since that subservice works by enabling and disabling reports.7

docs.title: 4. The diagnostic reporting subservice
docs.text:
The diagnostic subservice mirrors the housekeeping one: TC[3,2], [3,4], [3,7], [3,8], [3,11], [3,28], [3,30], [3,32] and [3,34] correspond to TC[3,1], [3,3], [3,5], [3,6], [3,9], [3,27], [3,29], [3,31] and [3,33], with TM[3,26], [3,12] and [3,36] as reports.16 The differences are:

Aspect Housekeeping Diagnostic Create, delete, enable, disable by declaration minimum (always provided) Status in the structure only if enable/disable is provided always present One-shot report generates one report generates one report "independently" of the periodic generation status Number per service at least one subservice zero or more subservices

4717184

docs.title: 5. The parameter functional reporting configuration subservice
5.1 Applying configurations: TC[3,37]
docs.text:
A TC[3,37] carries a configuration execution flag and one or more definition identifiers. The whole request is rejected if the flag is invalid; unknown definitions are rejected individually. If at least one instruction is valid and the flag is "exclusive", every enabled housekeeping and diagnostic report of the service is first disabled. Then, for each valid definition, each referenced report structure is told to take the entry's collection interval and to enable or disable its periodic generation; entries pointing at structures that do not exist produce a failed execution notification.22

flowchart TB

  F -- no --> X["Reject request<br/>failed start of execution"]
  F -- yes --> V{"At least one known<br/>definition?"}
  V -- no --> Y["Failed start for each<br/>unknown definition"]
  V -- yes --> E{"Exclusive?"}
  E -- yes --> D["Disable every enabled HK and<br/>diagnostic report of the service"] --> L
  E -- no --> L["For each valid definition and entry"]
  L --> S{"Structure exists?"}
  S -- yes --> A["Set collection interval<br/>enable or disable generation"]
  S -- no --> N["Failed execution notification"]

The flowchart is this wiki's reading of requirement 6.3.5.3.22

docs.text: ECSS-E-ST-70-41C gives the types of the ST[03] fields but not their sizes: the format code of each field is declared by the mission.31 The tables below give the fields in transmission order.
