docs.title: ST[05] Event reporting
docs.text:
The event reporting service, service type 5 of the Packet Utilization Standard, is how a spacecraft tells the ground that something happened: a failure or anomaly detected on board (including by FDIR - failure detection, isolation and recovery), the start, progress or end of an activity initiated from ground or autonomously, a built-in test result, or a normal payload event.1 Each report carries a severity (informative, low, medium or high), encoded in the message subtype to make ground detection and routing easier, and an event definition identifier that, together with the APID of the reporting application process, tells the ground exactly which event occurred and how to read the auxiliary data that follows.2

Events are also an on-board currency. They feed the event-action service ST[19], on-board control procedures (ST[18]), the on-board monitoring service ST[12] raises them, and the forwarding and storage services can block them per event definition.7202425 This page covers the PUS-C definition (clauses 6.5 and 8.5), the PUS-A one (clause 10), the tailoring data of ECSS-E-ST-70-31C, the 2024 draft, the SCOS-2000 event packet mechanism of the MIB, and a data-driven tour of the 7 156 service 5 packet definitions of the public Solar Orbiter MIB.

At a glance

Item Value Service type 5, "event reporting"11 Subservice types exactly one: the event reporting subservice1 Providers per application process at most one3 Event reports TM[5,1] informative, TM[5,2] low, TM[5,3] medium, TM[5,4] high severity5 Control requests TC[5,5] enable, TC[5,6] disable, TC[5,7] report disabled list, TM[5,8]15 Minimum capability the four event reports15 2024 draft addition TC[5,9] generate event report39 SCOS-2000 no specific processing; any TM packet can raise an operator event (PID_EVENT)4344 Solar Orbiter MIB (Sept 2025) 7 142 event report definitions on 43 APIDs, plus 14 private table reports73

docs.title: 1.1 Events, event definitions and event reports
docs.text:
PUS-C defines an event report simply as a report related to the occurrence of an event, generated by a subservice provider; it is one of three report kinds, next to verification reports and data reports.18 The service exists to report information of operational significance that the provider-initiated reports of other services do not already carry.1

The standard separates three notions:

Notion What it is Identified by Event report type one of four, by severity; all low-severity reports share TM[5,2], and so on message subtype16 Event definition one detectable event, its severity, its identifier and its auxiliary data event definition system identifier = APID of the hosting application process + event definition identifier, unique within that APID4 Event notification one occurrence: the event definition identifier plus the auxiliary data, if any carried in exactly one event report of the definition's severity5

The note to clause 5.3.5.4 explains the design: since all reports of one severity share one message type, the message type cannot say which event happened, so the standard adds event definitions, each tied to a single event and a single event report type.16

docs.title: 1.2 Severity levels
docs.text:
Subtype PUS-C name PUS-A name Typical meaning 1 informative event report Normal/Progress Report normal progress, autonomous action not related to a fault 2 low severity anomaly report Error/Anomaly Report - Low Severity anomaly of low severity 3 medium severity anomaly report Error/Anomaly Report - Medium Severity anomaly of medium severity 4 high severity anomaly report Error/Anomaly Report - High Severity anomaly of high severity

Names from PUS-C clause 6.5.4 and PUS-A clause 10.2-10.3.52829 Neither standard defines what each level implies operationally; missions do. Solar Orbiter, for example, uses "low" for warnings needing no recovery action, "medium" for anomalies requiring ground recovery action, and "high" for anomalies requiring on-board recovery action (section 8.1).56

PUS-A explains why severity sits in the header: event reports are infrequent and often unexpected, so they should be unambiguous, by flagging the severity in the data field header to ease ground detection and routing, and by including auxiliary data so that the ground understands context and cause.26

docs.title: 1.3 Who raises and who consumes events
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  subgraph AP["On-board application process (APID)"]
    FDIR["FDIR, mode logic,<br/>device drivers, payload SW"]
    MON["ST[12] on-board monitoring<br/>(check transitions)"]
    ER["ST[05] event reporting<br/>subservice provider"]
    FDIR -- "event occurrence" --> ER
    MON -- "raise event (if an event<br/>definition is attached)" --> ER
  end
  ER -- "TM[5,1..4]" --> EA["ST[19] event-action:<br/>release an action request"]
  ER -- "TM[5,1..4]" --> OBCP["ST[18] OBCP engines"]
  ER -- "TM[5,1..4]" --> FWD["ST[14] real-time forwarding<br/>(event report blocking)"]
  ER -- "TM[5,1..4]" --> STO["ST[15] packet stores<br/>(event report blocking)"]
  FWD --> GND["Ground: MCS alarms,<br/>archive, operators"]
  STO -. "later dump" .-> GND
  • Every on-board monitoring service is associated with exactly one event reporting subservice, which catches the events it raises; a check definition can name an event definition for each kind of violation (below low limit, above high limit, unexpected value, delta thresholds), raised when the new checking status is established.202122
  • The event-action subservice is associated with at least one event reporting subservice and must be able to react to all of its event reports.23
  • The real-time forwarding control service keeps an "event report blocking forward-control" definition per application process, listing event definition identifiers whose reports are not forwarded to ground; the storage and retrieval service has the equivalent per packet store.2425
  • PUS-C notes that event reports are used by the ground but also by on-board functions such as event-action services and OBCP engines, which is why disabling an event definition also stops those on-board reactions (section 4.3).78

docs.title: 2. Declarations a mission must make
docs.text:
Declaration Clause List of events the subservice can detect 6.5.3a4 For each event: event definition, severity level, event definition identifier, auxiliary data 6.5.3b4 Destination of the event reports (one destination for all reports of a subservice) 6.5.4b5 For each event: initial event report generation status (enabled or disabled) 6.5.5.1b6 Whether TC[5,5]/TC[5,6] are provided 6.5.5.2a7 Whether TC[5,7]/TM[5,8] are provided 6.5.5.4a9

The event definition identifier is an enumerated field and the auxiliary data a deduced field whose presence and structure follow from the definition; their sizes are mission choices.1219

docs.title: 3. Message types and capability sets
docs.text:
Message type Name Requirement / interface clause Applicability TM[5,1] informative event report 6.5.4 / 8.5.2.1 minimum TM[5,2] low severity anomaly report 6.5.4 / 8.5.2.2 minimum TM[5,3] medium severity anomaly report 6.5.4 / 8.5.2.3 minimum TM[5,4] high severity anomaly report 6.5.4 / 8.5.2.4 minimum TC[5,5] enable the report generation of event definitions 6.5.5.2 / 8.5.2.5 by declaration TC[5,6] disable the report generation of event definitions 6.5.5.3 / 8.5.2.6 implied by TC[5,5] TC[5,7] report the list of disabled event definitions 6.5.5.4 / 8.5.2.7 requires TC[5,5] TM[5,8] disabled event definitions list report 6.5.5.4 / 8.5.2.8 response to TC[5,7]

Source: Annex C, Table C-9.15 The applicability terms are explained in clause 5.3.4.17 Every packet of the service has service type 5.11

docs.title: 4.1 TM[5,1] to TM[5,4]: the event reports
docs.text:
All four reports have the same source data field:12

Field Type Presence Meaning event definition ID enumerated always Together with the APID, identifies the event definition - and therefore the presence and structure of the auxiliary data.12 auxiliary data deduced deduced presence Context and cause of the occurrence, as declared for that event definition.124

A subservice that supports enabling and disabling generates an event notification for an occurrence only if the definition is enabled; one that does not support it reports every occurrence. Each notification goes into one event report of the definition's severity.5

Inference: the time of an event

The PUS-C event report has no time field of its own.12 This wiki reads that as relying on the time stamp of the TM packet secondary header, unless a mission adds a time to the auxiliary data. PUS-C does not say whether that time stamp is the occurrence time or the report generation time; Solar Orbiter's ICD defines the packet time as the time "when the generation of the packet was started".52

docs.title: 4.2 TC[5,5] enable and TC[5,6] disable the report generation
docs.text:
Both requests have the same application data:13

Field Type Meaning N unsigned integer Number of instructions. event definition ID enumerated, repeated N times Event definition to enable or disable.

The subservice keeps, for each detectable event, an event report generation status (enabled or disabled).6 Processing is per instruction: an instruction naming an unknown event definition is rejected with a failed start of execution notification, and the valid instructions of the same request are executed regardless.78 Valid instructions set the status to "enabled" or "disabled".78

docs.title: 4.3 What "disabled" really means
docs.text:
PUS-C is explicit: disabling the report generation of an event definition means the ground is no longer told about occurrences and the on-board services configured to react to those event reports are not triggered either. It does not prevent on-board software from catching the occurrence directly, without going through event reports.8 The standard gives the reduction of on-board processing load as an example reason to disable reporting.8

stateDiagram-v2
  direction LR
  state "ENABLED - each occurrence gives a TM[5,x]" as EN
  state "DISABLED - not reported, no ST[19] or OBCP reaction" as DIS
  [*] --> EN: initial status declared enabled
  [*] --> DIS: initial status declared disabled
  EN --> DIS: TC[5,6] instruction
  DIS --> EN: TC[5,5] instruction
  EN --> EN: TC[5,5] (no change)
  DIS --> DIS: TC[5,6] (no change)

State per event definition, from clauses 6.5.5.1-6.5.5.3.678

docs.title: 4.4 TC[5,7] report the list of disabled event definitions and TM[5,8]
docs.text:
TC[5,7] has no application data. The response TM[5,8] lists every event definition whose status is "disabled":149

Field Type Meaning N unsigned integer Number of disabled event definitions. event definition ID enumerated, repeated N times A disabled event definition.

docs.title: 4.5 Observables
docs.text:
For each severity level the subservice must expose: the accumulated number of detected occurrences, the number of disabled definitions, the accumulated number of generated reports, the event definition identifier of the last report, and the generation time of the last report.10 These are typically made available as on-board parameters that housekeeping can sample.

Inference

The last sentence is this wiki's reading: PUS-C defines the observables but does not prescribe how they reach the ground.

docs.title: 5. PUS-A (ECSS-E-70-41A) differences
docs.text:
Aspect PUS-A (2003) PUS-C (2016) Report identifier RID (Report ID), enumerated; with the APID it implicitly defines the parameters field29 event definition ID, enumerated; with the APID it identifies the event definition12 Auxiliary data "Parameters", type Any, optional, following structure rules set #1 with standard data types2932 "auxiliary data", deduced, deduced presence12 Enable/disable data NRID (unsigned integer, omitted if only one RID per request) + RID repeated30 N always present + event definition ID repeated13 Disabled list report none TC[5,7] / TM[5,8]15 Initial status, destination, observables not specified declared / defined6510 Instances any number of application processes, one instance each27 at most one provider per application process3

PUS-A capability sets: the minimum set is the four reports (subtypes 1-4); the additional set is subtypes 5 and 6, each requiring the other.31 PUS-A's scope lists three families of events (failures or anomalies detected on board, autonomous on-board actions, normal progress of operations), noting that one report can combine several, for example a unit switched off because a temperature exceeded its limit.27 PUS-C's list is similar but has four items, adding FDIR detections explicitly, hardware built-in test results and normal payload events.1 The motivation PUS-A gives for disabling reports is also processing load.28

docs.title: 5.1 Tailoring data in ECSS-E-ST-70-31C
docs.text:
ECSS-E-ST-70-31C, which models the PUS-A service, asks a mission database for:3435

Item Type Meaning S5 ST5 and ST6 Provider Boolean event reports can be enabled and disabled S5 Multiple RIDs Boolean several RIDs per enable/disable request (if the above is TRUE) S5 RID PFC of PTC 2 size of the report identifier field S5 NRID PFC of PTC 3 size of the repetition counter (if multiple RIDs) RID (per event) PTC 2 the unique identifier of each event raised by the service

docs.title: 6. Changes in the 2024 Rev.1 draft
docs.text:
ECSS-E-ST-70-41C Rev.1 DIR1 (11 December 2024) changes the service in five ways:

  1. New TC[5,9] "generate event report", by declaration: one instruction carrying an event APID, an event severity, an event definition identifier and optional event data (a variable-length octet string); it is rejected for an invalid APID, severity or identifier, and otherwise generates the requested event report packet.394142
  2. The event list must include at least all asynchronous error conditions that any subservice can raise and that request verification does not report, for example a telecommand not dispatched on time by time-based scheduling or data lost on file swapping by file data storage.36
  3. Instead of an initial status per event, a configuration policy for start and restart of the subservice is declared, which includes the initial statuses.37
  4. TC[5,5] and TC[5,6] carry an ordered list of instructions and are rejected as a whole if any instruction names an unknown event definition; otherwise the instructions are executed in order.38
  5. TM[5,8] reports an empty list with N = 0.40

Editorial loose ends in the draft

In DIR1 the interface clause of TC[5,9] refers to system clause 6.5.5.4 and to "Figure 8.5-5", while the system requirement is 6.5.5.5 and the figure is numbered 8.5-8. In the Annex C table (Table C-8 in the draft) the rows for TC[5,5] and TC[5,9] both show "b" in the system-clause column, and the TC[5,9] row gives 8.5.2.5 instead of 8.5.2.9 as its interface clause.4142 These are draft-stage inconsistencies, not technical changes.

docs.title: 7.1 No special service 5 processing - but a general event mechanism
docs.text:
The SCOS-2000 Database Import ICD states that SCOS-2000 has no specific processing of service 5 packets. Instead it can associate the generation of an event of a given severity and text message with any received TM packet; these events are stored (visible in retrieval) and distributed live to operators, with configurable severity depending on their role.43

"Events & Actions (EVAC)" is one of the SCOS-2000 functions listed in a 2003 ESA Bulletin description of the system.50 The association between a TM packet and an event is made per packet in the PID table:4445

PID field Type Meaning PID_DESCR Char(64) Packet description; also the message text of the SCOS-2000 event packet. PID_EVENT Char(1) N no event (default), I event of severity Info, W Warning, A Alarm. PID_EVID Char(17) Optional event number; the full event ID becomes TPKT_OBE::nnnn. The ICD suggests 1-9999, because other SCOS-2000 events use 5-digit numbers from 10000.

Because the on-board event definition identifier is a field inside the packet, the MIB needs an extra identification rule to tell event definitions apart: the PIC table gives, per type/subtype (and optionally APID), the offset and width of up to two additional identification fields, and the packetiser then looks up PID with APID, type, subtype, PI1 and PI2 to find the packet's SPID.4746 An APID-specific PIC entry takes precedence over a type/subtype-only one.47

sequenceDiagram
  participant S as Spacecraft
  participant P as SCOS-2000 TM packetiser
  participant D as MIB (PIC, PID, PLF/VPD)
  participant E as Event and alarm handling
  participant A as Archive
  S->>P: TM[5,4] APID 215, event ID 0xE389 + auxiliary data
  P->>D: PIC(5,4,215)? none - use PIC(5,4): PI1 at octet 16, 16 bits
  P->>D: PID(type 5, subtype 4, APID 215, PI1 58249, PI2 0)
  D-->>P: SPID 27318, PID_EVENT = A, PID_DESCR = "REC_PCDU3 - FMON_PCDU3_A PCDU A Failure"
  P->>A: file TM packet (SPID 27318)
  P->>E: SCOS-2000 event packet, severity Alarm, message = PID_DESCR
  P->>P: extract parameters (PLF) for displays

The flow combines the ICD rules with real rows of the Solar Orbiter MIB.474474

docs.title: 7.2 Other SCOS-2000 event sources
docs.text: Events can also be generated on ground from telemetry values: a monitoring check of type E in OCP raises an event with full ID BEHV::<parameter> when the parameter leaves the specified range, which can trigger system actions such as an e-mail or a script; such checks are not shown as out-of-limits.48 The Solar Orbiter MIB defines no check of type E (it uses only C, D, H and S checks).77 Archived events can later be retrieved from the archive; the EDDS user manual, for instance, lists "Packet Ev" requests returning raw event packets and "Event Record Report" requests returning events with their ID, category, time stamp, severity and message.51

docs.title: 8. Solar Orbiter: the space-to-ground ICD
docs.text: Solar Orbiter uses PUS-A (ECSS-E-70-41A) as its applicable standard (see PUS packet structures).53 Its ICD extends service 5 considerably.

docs.title: 8.1 Categories, size and routing
docs.text:
• Four categories: TM(5,1) normal progress; TM(5,2) low criticality (warning, no recovery action required); TM(5,3) medium criticality (ground recovery action required); TM(5,4) high criticality (on-board recovery action required). Typically "low" events are just stored for downlink, while "high" events always have a predefined recovery response by the central software.56
  • Event reports are one of the prime means of controlling day-to-day operations.56
  • The source data field must not exceed 40 bytes (exceptions agreed with ESA); the event ID is 2 bytes, Enumerated, and the parameters field at most 38 bytes, its structure defined by the combination of event ID and APID.5758
  • Event IDs are unique per process ID (PID).57
  • A generated event can be recorded in the Safe Guard Memory (SGM) Critical Event Log (CEL) for medium and high levels, forwarded to ground, recorded in the OBC mass memory (OMM), and/or forwarded to service 19.57
  • Event packets use packet category 7, "Event generation", which is exclusive to service 5 and to TM(17,2).68

docs.title: 8.2 The Critical Event Log
docs.text: The CEL combines a linear buffer holding the first m events and a circular buffer holding the last n; in a burst, the first m and last n events survive. An occurrence counter per event ID keeps track of history even when the buffers overflow. One TC reads the buffers and the occurrence table (possibly producing several TM packets) and one TC clears all three together to keep them consistent.57

docs.title: 8.3 Messages
docs.text:
Message Name in the ICD Application / source data Notes TM(5,1)-(5,4) Nominal/Progress, Error/Anomaly Low/Medium/High Event ID (2 bytes) + parameters (n bytes) Packet category 7.58 TC(5,5) Enable Event Packet Generation NEID (1 byte, 1..TBD) + EID (2 bytes) x NEID Intended for ground testing, not recommended in flight.59 TC(5,6) Disable Event Packet Generation same as TC(5,5) Same remark.59 TC(5,128) Clear Critical Event Log NoOfEntries (2 bytes); a number at least the log size clears everything CSW only; clears both SGMs.60 TC(5,129) Downlink Critical Event Log SGM ID (1 byte): 01 SGM A, 10 SGM B, 11 A or B CSW only; events replayed into real-time TM "as recorded", so packets with past time stamps appear; also triggers TM(5,130).61 TM(5,130) Critical Event Log Occurrence Table Report SGM ID, NEID, then PID, EID, occurrence count per entry Occurrences since the last clear.62 TC(5,131) / TM(5,132) Report Enabled EID / Enabled EID Report none / NEID (2 bytes) + EID (2 bytes) x NEID 63 TC(5,133) / TM(5,134) Report Disabled EID / Disabled EID Report none / NEID (2 bytes) + EID (2 bytes) x NEID 64

Inference

TC(5,133)/TM(5,134) play the role that PUS-C standardises as TC[5,7]/TM[5,8]. On Solar Orbiter they are a mission-specific extension of PUS-A, which has no such report.3315

docs.title: 8.4 Event ID allocation: severity in the top two bits
docs.text:
For the central software (CSW), and optionally for other software, Annex 9 of the ICD allocates event IDs so that the two most significant bits equal the subtype minus one, and the remaining 14 bits are split into functional ranges:65

Range (14 low bits) TM(5,1) TM(5,2) TM(5,3) TM(5,4) Use 0x0000 0x0000 0x4000 0x8000 0xC000 reserved 0x0001-0x001F 0x0001- 0x4001- 0x8001- 0xC001- Boot SW events 0x0020-0x041F 0x0020- 0x4020- 0x8020- 0xC020- General application SW events 0x0420-0x141F 0x0420- 0x4420- 0x8420- 0xC420- Specific application SW events 0x1420-0x149F 0x1420- 0x5420- 0x9420- 0xD420- Events from unexpected SW and HW errors 0x14A0-0x349F 0x14A0- 0x54A0- 0x94A0- 0xD4A0- Monitoring events (0x2700-0x27FF reserved for CDHS) 0x34A0-0x3EFF 0x34A0- 0x74A0- 0xB4A0- 0xF4A0- OBCP events 0x3F00-0x3FFE 0x3F00- 0x7F00- 0xBF00- 0xFF00- ESOC 0x3FFF 0x3FFF 0x7FFF 0xBFFF 0xFFFF reserved

Annex 9 also gives decimal ranges per user for failure IDs of TM(1,2)/TM(1,8), "Failure and Event ID allocation across APID": for example SSMM 1000-1999, STR 2000-2999, OBCP 4000-9999, CSW 10000-39999 and payloads 40000-59999 (EPD 40000, MAG 41000, RPW 42000, SWA 43000, SPICE 44000, PHI 45000, EUI 46000, METIS 47000, STIX 48000, SoloHI 49000, each a block of 1000).66 TC(3,139) "Request Snapshot HK Parameter Anomaly Report" relies on the severity bits: it makes the software generate one TM(5,x) whose subtype is deduced from the given event ID and whose parameters are those of the HK packet named by the SID.67

docs.title: 9. Solar Orbiter: what the MIB contains
docs.text: All statements in this section come from this wiki's queries of the September 2025 release MIB__20250916M25925PFMS001_SOL unless the April 2020 release is named.73

docs.title: 9.1 How many events, and where
docs.text:
APID group (process ID) Event packets TM(5,1) TM(5,2) TM(5,3) TM(5,4) Private 5,13x CSW (PID 10-16) 2 321 397 167 278 1 466 13 SSMM (PID 30-32) 49 4 17 20 8 0 Star trackers (PID 40-41) 84 2 20 34 28 0 Payload (PID 50-104) 3 237 876 951 1 213 196 1 EGSE range (PID 112-127) 1 465 95 4 1 366 0 0 Total 7 156 1 374 1 159 2 911 1 698 14

The "CSW" row groups process IDs 10-16. Strictly, the ICD calls processes 10-14 "OBC CSW" and 15-16 (OBCP and thermal control) "OBC SW". The MIB defines no event packet for process 15, while process 16 (APIDs 259 and 263) has 701.6973

The April 2020 release had 5 667 type 5 packet definitions (CSW 2 130, payload 1 993); payload event definitions grew by about 60 % in five years.78 Process IDs follow the ICD's allocation (10 DMS, 11 AOCS, 12 payload application, 13 platform, 14 system control, 16 thermal control, 30-32 SSMM, 40-41 STR, 50-104 instruments, 112-127 EGSE).69

Inference: the EGSE-range APIDs

1 465 event packets sit on APIDs 1954-1991 (process IDs 122-124), a range the ICD allocates to EGSE.69 Most of them share a single event ID per APID (for example 33537, 33538 or 33539) and are told apart by an 8-bit second identification field at octet 18; their descriptions (for example "S_TCS2 TCL 13 Temperature Level 2_LO", "S_MAG12_LO") look like monitoring transition messages. Their exact role is not stated in the available sources.

docs.title: 9.2 How SCOS-2000 recognises them
docs.text:
PIC has one generic rule per event subtype - first identification field at octet 16, 16 bits wide, no second field - which is exactly the 2-byte event ID right after the 16 octets of packet headers (a 6-octet primary header and the 10-octet Solar Orbiter TM data field header).7354 Twenty-five APID-specific PIC rules, all on the EGSE-range APIDs 1954-1991, add a second field at octet 18 or 19 (8, 16 or 32 bits) for APIDs that reuse one event ID for several packet layouts.73 The same rule (octet 16, 16 bits) appears in the SWA instrument database, and a 2001 packet ICD for the HIFI test-equipment interfaces (TEI) of Herschel places its 16-bit "Event ID" at the same byte position 16-17 of TM(5,4).7980

The mapping to SCOS-2000 severities is uniform:73

On-board report PID_EVENT SCOS-2000 event severity TM(5,1) I (1 374) Info TM(5,2) W (1 159) Warning TM(5,3) A (2 911) Alarm TM(5,4) A (1 698) Alarm TM(5,130/132/134) empty (default N); N for the PHI TM(5,134) none

PID_EVID is empty for every packet in the database, so all events get the default event ID. Service 1 failure reports TM(1,2) and TM(1,8) are also mapped to A (274 and 1 477 packet definitions) - see ST[01].73

The SWA instrument database delivered by the instrument team defines the same 248 SWA event packets with PID_EVENT = 'N'; in the spacecraft MIB they carry I/W/A.7973

Inference

The severity mapping is therefore applied when instrument databases are merged into the spacecraft MIB, not by the instrument teams.

docs.title: 9.3 Does the MIB follow the event ID convention?
docs.text:
Software Event packets (subtypes 1-4) Top two bits = subtype - 1 CSW, APIDs 167, 183, 199, 215, 231, 263 2 308 2 308 (100 %) EGSE range, APIDs 1954-1991 1 465 1 465 (100 %) SSMM, star trackers and instruments 3 369 1 726 (51 %)

For the CSW the convention holds without exception. Classifying the CSW event IDs by the 14-bit ranges of Annex 9 gives 897 monitoring events, 707 general application events, 647 specific application events and 57 in the ESOC range (for example the on-board monitoring messages S12_Lower_Limit_Exceeded_(DMS)_W).73 Several instruments instead number their events in their decimal block of the APID allocation table: EUI 46000-46619, PHI 45100-45476, RPW 42101-42729, SWA 43501-43999.7366

docs.title: 9.4 Examples of event definitions
docs.text:
Severity APID Event ID SPID Description (PID_DESCR) TM(5,1) 215 0x0F1E 27284 Recovery_Action_1_Started TM(5,1) 199 0x0BA9 32028 METIS-A_PowerDown_Started-(LCL-RSA_status) TM(5,1) 167 0x0B41 14323 OMM_Activate_End TM(5,2) 167 0x4902 14012 TC_Segment_Error_occurred TM(5,2) 183 0x4425 20136 RW_Direct_Command_Failed_(TM_ 5-2) TM(5,2) 1591 0xAA0A 58430 SWA_E_PAS_MISS_SCI_PKT TM(5,3) 167 0x85C4 14214 1553_BUS1_RT5_Error TM(5,3) 231 0x8AC8 10195 LEOP_AS_Step_9_SASM-P_Not_Reached TM(5,3) 1207 0xA553 55116 LFR permanent error (too many RMAP errors). TM(5,4) 215 0xE389 27318 REC_PCDU3 - FMON_PCDU3_A PCDU A Failure TM(5,4) 263 0xC1D1 27559 SMON_TCS1 TCL 73 Low TM(5,4) 215 0xD1D3 27499 This event is when Configure Coms cannot detect the separation

Real rows of PID.74 All but one of the 2 308 CSW event packets decode the event ID with parameter NCD05011 "OBCHP_PTM_EID" (PTC 2, PFC 16): 2 239 in fixed layouts (PLF) and 68 in variable ones (VPD); the exception, SPID 64610 "REC_SYS1 Ops Alarm Ground Cmd", uses a twin parameter, NCDX0950, with the same description. NCD05011 appears in 2 322 PLF layouts in all (83 of them on EGSE-range APIDs) and is calibrated by the textual calibration CCDT0004TX "Event ID list" with 1 419 entries (for example 58249 = FMON_09, 34244 = BMERR_B1_R5).74 The commands TC(5,5) and TC(5,6) use a command alias set of the same name for their EID parameter.75

Events can be large. In TPCF, 398 event packets have a declared size that implies more than 40 octets of source data. 364 of them have "Snapshot" in their description, which matches the events TC(3,139) produces, whose parameters are a whole HK packet.7367

Inference: TPCF_SIZE in this MIB

The ICD recommends that TPCF_SIZE include the SCOS-2000 packet header (64 or 76 bytes).49 In this MIB the values match the bare source packet instead (18 octets for an event with only an event ID, 36 for packet 27318 below), so this wiki subtracts the 16-octet headers to estimate the source data length.

docs.title: 9.5 Commands
10.1 Decoding a high-severity event (real layout, illustrative values)
docs.text:
The layout below is the real one of SPID 27318 in the MIB PLF table; the byte values are illustrative, constructed for explanation.74

Octets Bytes (illustrative) Parameter Decoded 0-5 08 D7 C0 05 00 1D primary header TM, APID 215 (0b0001101_0111: process 13 platform, category 7 events), stand-alone, count 5, data length 29 6-15 (10 octets) data field header type 5, subtype 4, time (CUC, 4 + 2 octets)54 16-17 E3 89 NCD05011 EID 58249 = FMON_09; 0b11... = high severity 18-21 00 00 00 09 NCD8E093 FMON ID 9 22-23 00 03 NCD8E098 Nb of cycles 3 24 01 NCD8E099 logic type AND 25-28 00 00 00 2A NCD8E09B SMon ID 42 29 06 NCAB0UJ0 current check status OUT_OF_LIMIT 30-35 3B 9A CA 00 80 00 NCAB0UM0 time stamp coarse 1 000 000 000 s + 0.5 s

The packet is 36 octets, matching TPCF_SIZE = 36. Its data field is 30 octets, so the Space Packet data length field holds 30 - 1 = 29 (0x001D). Its 20 octets of source data respect the ICD limit of 40 octets of source data.57 The auxiliary data come from Solar Orbiter's private service 142 "Functional Monitoring" (two of the parameter descriptions begin with "OBCHP_S142_"), which serves FDIR by grouping service 12 monitors into a Functional Monitor (FMON) evaluated with AND/OR logic.71 The event therefore says which FMON triggered, after how many cycles and with which logic, then - judging by the description of NCD8E09B, OBCHP_SMon_Mon_ID, an inference - which service 12 monitoring ID was involved, its check status, and when.

docs.title: 10.2 Building a disable request (real layout, illustrative values)
docs.text:
Disable two DMS events, 0x4902 "TC_Segment_Error_occurred" and 0x85C4 "1553_BUS1_RT5_Error", with ZCD00506 to APID 172 (process 10, category 12). The sequence count is illustrative; the CRC is computed with the CCITT polynomial initialised to all ones, as the Solar Orbiter ICD prescribes for the packet error control.72

Octets Bytes Field 0-1 18 AC version 0, type TC, secondary header flag 1, APID 172 2-3 C0 02 stand-alone, sequence count 2 (illustrative) 4-5 00 0A packet data length = 11 - 1 6 19 secondary header flag 0, PUS version 1, ack 1001 (CCF_ACK = 9) 7-8 05 06 service type 5, subtype 6 9 78 source ID 120 "direct commands"70 10 02 NEID = 2 11-12 49 02 EID 18690 13-14 85 C4 EID 34244 15-16 7C E2 packet error control (CRC-16)

The header layout is that of the MIB's NOM_TC definition, explained on PUS packet structures; the ICD gives the TC data field header a length of 4 octets (secondary header flag 0, PUS version 1, the 4 acknowledgement bits, service type, subtype and the source ID) and sets the sequence flags to 11 (stand-alone).5570 The ICD's remark applies: such commands are meant for ground testing, not for flight.59

docs.title: 11. Other missions
docs.text: The Herschel/Planck Operations Interface Requirements Document (2003) asks for three event packet types - normal events, progress reports and warnings; exceptions requiring on-board action; errors and anomalies requiring ground action - and requires that anomaly reports carry a unique identification, the time of occurrence and the data relevant to the detection. To save bandwidth, only transitions to and from an anomaly state are reported, with a minimum period before the same event can be reported again, and the two anomaly types are also stored in a Critical Events Log that can be read and cleared by dedicated telecommands.81 The same CEL idea reappears in Solar Orbiter (section 8.2). See Herschel and Planck.

docs.title: ST[06] Memory management
docs.text:
The memory management service, service type 6 of the Packet Utilization Standard, lets the ground load data into on-board memories, dump their contents to ground and ask the spacecraft to check an area by computing a checksum on board.1 It is the low-level tool behind on-board software maintenance: patching code, uploading tables, reading back registers and logs, and verifying that memory has not been corrupted. PUS-A described it as an "off-line" activity for troubleshooting and software maintenance rather than routine operations, and asked that any on-board memory be readable and any RAM area loadable from ground.56

PUS-C (ECSS-E-ST-70-41C, 2016) turned the PUS-A service into four subservices: raw data memory management (absolute addresses), structured data memory management (memory objects such as files or on-board control procedures, addressed by a base plus an offset), a common subservice (abort all dumps) and a memory configuration subservice (scrubbing and write protection).1 This page covers all 22 message types, the declarations each mission must make, the checksum algorithms, the PUS-A original (clause 11), the tailoring data of ECSS-E-ST-70-31C, the 2024 draft, the ground side in SCOS-2000, and the real memory map and commands of Solar Orbiter as described in its ICD and MIB.

At a glance

Item Value Service type 6, "memory management"28 Subservices raw data, structured data (at least one of the two), common, memory configuration (at most one of each)4 Hosting all memory management subservice providers in one application process (a note in PUS-C, a requirement in the 2024 draft; see section 9)465 Message types (PUS-C) 22: subtypes 1-2243 Minimum capability raw: TC[6,2], TC[6,5]/TM[6,6]; structured: TC[6,1], TC[6,3]/TM[6,4]; common: TC[6,12]43 Checksum field 16-bit bit-string; algorithm (ISO or CRC) declared per spacecraft3050 PUS-A equivalent clause 11, subtypes 1-10 (base plus offset: ⅓/4/⅞; absolute: ⅖/6/9/10)64 Solar Orbiter absolute addressing only; TC(6,2), (6,5), (6,9) plus private 6,128-6,131 and 6,140; 221 commands in the MIB84103

docs.title: 1.1 The memory as a system object
docs.text:
In PUS-C an on-board memory is a logical memory space; the mapping onto physical memories, possibly managed by different processors, is out of the standard's scope.4648 Each memory has exactly one memory identifier, unique across the spacecraft at any time - although the same identifier may serve several physical memories that cannot be accessed at the same time, as in cold redundancy.48 For each memory the mission declares:48

Characteristic Values Memory access alignment constraint minimum number of bytes the services use to address the memory Memory size in bytes Allowed operations "read only", "read and write" or "write only" Addressing scheme absolute and/or base plus offset exposed to ground Scrubbing supported yes / no Write protection supported yes / no

Behind the alignment constraint sits the physical smallest addressable unit, the minimum number of bytes a physical memory can address.48 With absolute addressing, addresses and offsets are in bytes. With base plus offset addressing, addresses are byte offsets from a base reference that gives the "byte-zero" address - an explicit address, or a symbolic one such as a table, a parameter set or a file whose absolute address is known on board.49

docs.title: 1.2 Raw and structured data
docs.text:
Subservice Memory content Addressing Examples given by PUS-C Raw data memory management type not implicitly known absolute: start address = offset from the start of the memory none specific; memories in general are "e.g. RAM, mass memory unit" Structured data memory management type implicitly known base (the object) + offset within the object files, OBCPs, static configuration tables

Definitions and examples from clauses 6.6.1.1-6.6.1.3 and 6.6.4.3.1216 The base of a structured memory is declared per memory: for a file store it can be the file identifier used by file management (repository path plus file name); for the OBCP store it can be the OBCP identifier.16 Bases are either static (declared in advance, each with a maximum size, such as a list of configuration tables) or dynamic (created at run time, for example when a file is uploaded), and a dynamic base is identified either by a "base address" or by a "memory object identifier".16

flowchart TB
  subgraph SVC["ST[06] memory management service (one application process)"]
    RAW["Raw data memory management<br/>TC[6,2] load, TC[6,11] atomic load<br/>TC[6,5]/TM[6,6] dump, TC[6,9]/TM[6,10] check<br/>TC[6,19] load by reference, TC[6,20] dump to file"]
    STR["Structured data memory management<br/>TC[6,1] load, TC[6,3]/TM[6,4] dump<br/>TC[6,7]/TM[6,8] check data, TC[6,17]/TM[6,18] check object<br/>TC[6,21] load by reference, TC[6,22] dump to file"]
    COM["Common memory management<br/>TC[6,12] abort all memory dumps"]
    CFG["Memory configuration<br/>TC[6,13]/[6,14] scrubbing<br/>TC[6,15]/[6,16] write protection"]
  end
  RAW --- M1[("Memory ID A<br/>absolute addressing")]
  STR --- M2[("Memory ID B<br/>base + offset<br/>(files, OBCPs, tables)")]
  CFG --- M1
  CFG --- M2
  COM -. aborts dumps of .-> RAW
  COM -. aborts dumps of .-> STR
  STR -. file paths .- FM["ST[23] file management"]
  RAW -. file paths .- FM

The 2014 draft of PUS-C presented three subservices (raw, structured, and a common one that also handled scrubbing and write protection);73 the published standard separates the memory configuration subservice, which manages each memory "as a whole", independently of content and addressing scheme.374 With 44 discrepancy review reports (DRRs), ST[06] was the second most discussed service type of the review, after ST[12] with 58 (the foundation model of clause 5 drew 72).75

docs.title: 1.3 Checksums
docs.text:
Whether the raw and the structured subservices checksum their data is declared per subservice.514 PUS-C does not fix the algorithm in the service: for each checksum algorithm used on board, the spacecraft architecture declares which subservice providers use it, so that every service checksumming the same object (for example an OBCP stored in a file, checked by both the OBCP service and the memory service) uses the same algorithm; the algorithm implies the type (ISO or CRC) and the size.50 In the packets the checksum is always a 16-bit bit-string.30 The two candidate algorithms are those of Annex B: the CRC-16-CCITT (polynomial \(x^{16}+x^{12}+x^5+1\), encoder and decoder initialised to all ones) and the ISO 8473-1 checksum, which Annex B says can be used to check memory areas through the memory management service.5455

PUS-A was more prescriptive: memory management uses the 16-bit ISO checksum, computed over all octets of the memory area.63

docs.title: 2. Message types and capability sets
docs.text:
Message type Name Subservice Applicability TC[6,1] load object memory data structured minimum TC[6,2] load raw memory data areas raw minimum TC[6,3] dump object memory data structured minimum TM[6,4] dumped object memory data report structured response to TC[6,3] TC[6,5] dump raw memory data raw minimum TM[6,6] dumped raw memory data report raw response to TC[6,5] TC[6,7] check object memory data structured by declaration TM[6,8] checked object memory data report structured response to TC[6,7] TC[6,9] check raw memory data raw by declaration TM[6,10] checked raw memory data report raw response to TC[6,9] TC[6,11] load a raw memory atomic data area in a non-interruptible transaction raw by declaration TC[6,12] abort all memory dumps common minimum TC[6,13] / TC[6,14] enable / disable the scrubbing of a memory configuration implied by "scrubbing memories support" (by declaration) TC[6,15] / TC[6,16] enable / disable the write protection of a memory configuration implied by "write protecting memories support" (by declaration) TC[6,17] check an object memory object structured by declaration TM[6,18] checked object memory object report structured response to TC[6,17] TC[6,19] load raw memory data areas by reference raw by declaration TC[6,20] dump raw memory data areas to file raw by declaration TC[6,21] load object memory data areas by reference structured by declaration TC[6,22] dump object memory data areas to file structured by declaration

Source: Annex C, Tables C-10 to C-13.43 "Minimum" applies to the subservices that the service actually contains; the applicability vocabulary is explained in clause 5.3.4.44 Every packet has service type 6, and whether multiple instructions per request are supported is declared for the service.28

A subtype typo in the standard

Clause 8.6.2.22 of PUS-C says that TC[6,22] "shall be of message subtype 20"; the heading, clause 6.6.4.9 and Annex C all give 22. The 2024 draft repeats the slip.424372

docs.title: 3. Request processing: why loads and dumps behave differently
docs.text:
PUS requests are made of instructions (for example one memory area each) and produce notifications inside reports.47 Clause 5.3.5.2.3 lets each request type declare whether all instructions must be suitable before execution starts; PUS-C names the raw memory load as an example of a request that can only execute if all its instructions are suitable.45 ST[06] applies two regimes:

flowchart TB
  subgraph LOAD["Loads: TC[6,1], [6,2], [6,19], [6,21]"]
    L1["Check the whole request:<br/>memory ID, write access, write protection,<br/>addresses, alignment, lengths, sizes"] -->|any problem| LR["Reject request:<br/>failed start of execution"]
    L1 -->|all valid| L2["Execute instructions in order"]
    L2 --> L3["Write data"]
    L3 -->|write error| LA["Abort request:<br/>failed execution notification<br/>+ failed completion report"]
    L3 --> L4{"checksumming?"}
    L4 -->|yes, mismatch| LA
    L4 -->|ok / no| L5{"more?"}
    L5 -->|yes| L2
    L5 -->|no| LC["Completion of execution<br/>(always in the verification profile)"]
  end
  subgraph DUMP["Dumps and checks: TC[6,3], [6,5], [6,7], [6,9], [6,20], [6,22]"]
    D1["Check request-level conditions<br/>(memory, read access, packet size)"] -->|fail| DR["Reject request"]
    D1 -->|ok| D2["Check each instruction"]
    D2 -->|faulty| D3["Failed start for that instruction"]
    D2 -->|valid| D4["Extract / checksum, one notification"]
    D3 --> D5["Continue with the others"]
    D4 --> D5
    D5 --> D6["One report with all notifications"]
  end

Sources: clauses 6.6.3.3-6.6.3.7 and 6.6.4.4-6.6.4.9.79101718 For every load the execution verification profile must include the completion of execution, so the ground always learns whether the whole load succeeded.717 PUS-C notes that checking the instructions that follow a faulty one is optional for loads: if for instance a variable-length data field does not match its length, the rest of the request can no longer be parsed.7

docs.title: 4. Raw data memory management
docs.text: The raw subservice declares the list of memories it manages (all with absolute addressing), uses memory identifiers if it manages more than one, and declares its write access per writeable memory.6 In all raw messages the memory ID field is omitted when the subservice manages a single memory.630

docs.title: 4.1 TC[6,2] load raw memory data areas
docs.text:
Field Type Presence Meaning memory ID enumerated optional Target memory.30 N unsigned integer always Number of instructions (areas).30 repeated N times: start address unsigned integer always Byte pointer aligned on the access alignment constraint.307 data to load variable octet-string (length + data) always The PFC of the length field is declared per application process (requirement 7.3.8d).3053 checksum bit-string (16 bits) optional Present if the subservice checksums; verified after writing.307

The request is rejected (failed start of execution) for an invalid memory ID, no write access, a write-protected memory, a start address beyond the memory size or misaligned, a load length that is not a multiple of the alignment constraint, or data running past the end of the memory.7 Otherwise instructions run in order; a write error, or a checksum mismatch after writing, aborts the request immediately with a failed execution notification and a failed completion of execution report.7

docs.title: 4.2 TC[6,11] load a raw memory atomic data area in a non-interruptible transaction
docs.text:
This request changes selected bits of one aligned memory word without touching the others, in a single non-interruptible transaction; it holds exactly one instruction.8

Field Type Presence Meaning memory ID enumerated optional Target memory.35 start address unsigned integer always Aligned byte pointer.35 bit mask fixed octet-string, deduced size always Selects the bits to change; size = access alignment constraint of the memory.358 data to load fixed octet-string, deduced size always New values for the selected bits; same size.358

The subservice reads the current value of the addressed word, replaces the bits selected by the mask with the corresponding bits of the data, and writes the result:8

\[\text{new} = (\text{old} \land \lnot\,\text{mask}) \lor (\text{data} \land \text{mask})\]

It needs both read and write access and rejects an unknown or write-protected memory, an address beyond the memory or misaligned, and a request whose size does not match the deduced mask and data sizes. Its verification profile includes completion of execution.8

docs.title: 4.3 TC[6,5] dump raw memory data and TM[6,6]
docs.text:
TC[6,5] field Type Presence memory ID enumerated optional N unsigned integer always start address unsigned integer repeated N times length unsigned integer repeated N times TM[6,6] field Type Presence memory ID enumerated optional N unsigned integer always start address unsigned integer repeated N times dumped data variable octet-string (length + data) repeated N times checksum bit-string (16 bits) repeated, optional

Layouts from Figures 8-70 and 8-71.32 The request is rejected as a whole for an invalid memory ID, no read access, or a response that would exceed the maximum CCSDS packet size of 65 542 octets.952 Each instruction is then checked (address in range and aligned, length within the memory and a multiple of the alignment); faulty instructions get their own failed start notification and the valid ones are dumped anyway. Each valid instruction yields one notification with the start address, the data and, if the subservice checksums, the checksum of the dumped area; all go into a single TM[6,6].9 Because a response may not exceed one packet, PUS-C foresees file management for data larger than a packet; other mechanisms are mission-specific.52 The 2024 draft replaces the rejection by splitting the response over several packets (section 9).70

docs.title: 4.4 TC[6,9] check raw memory data and TM[6,10]
docs.text: Same request layout as the dump; the report carries, per instruction, the start address, the length and the 16-bit checksum.34 Checking on board and comparing the checksum on ground avoids downlinking memory suspected to be faulty.10 The capability is "by declaration".43

docs.title: 4.5 TC[6,19] load raw memory data areas by reference
docs.text:
The data to load are not in the telecommand but in an on-board file (see ST[23] file management):1139

Field Type Presence memory ID enumerated optional repository path variable character-string always file name variable character-string always N unsigned integer always start address unsigned integer repeated N times offset in file unsigned integer repeated N times length unsigned integer repeated N times checksum bit-string (16 bits) repeated, optional

Rejection adds two file conditions to those of TC[6,2]: the file does not exist, or is not recognised as a file containing memory data; an offset beyond the file size is also an error.11 Execution reads each area from the file and writes it, with the same abort rules as TC[6,2].11 An object path is the combination of a repository path and an object name.51

docs.title: 4.6 TC[6,20] dump raw memory data areas to file
docs.text:
Field Type Presence memory ID enumerated optional repository path, file name variable character-strings always N unsigned integer always start address, length unsigned integers repeated N times

The request is rejected if the destination file already exists. The subservice creates the file and appends each dumped area; the standard does not specify the formatting of the data in the file (raw bytes or with headers).1240 The raw subservice defines no observables.13

docs.title: 5. Structured data memory management
docs.text:
The structured subservice manages memories with base plus offset addressing; write access is declared per memory.15 All its requests carry, after the optional memory ID, a base field of type deduced: its format depends on the memory (a base address or a memory object identifier).2916

Message Fields (after memory ID, base) Notes TC[6,1] load object memory data N; offset (unsigned integer), data to load (variable octet-string), checksum (optional) x N Also called scatter load when N > 1. Rejected additionally for an unknown or write-protected memory object.1729 TC[6,3] dump object memory data N; offset, length x N Rejected for unknown object, no read access, or response too large.1831 TM[6,4] dumped object memory data report memory ID, base, N; offset, dumped data (variable octet-string), checksum (optional) x N One notification per valid instruction.1831 TC[6,7] check object memory data N; offset, length x N By declaration.1933 TM[6,8] checked object memory data report memory ID, base, N; offset, length, checksum x N 1933 TC[6,17] check an object memory object (memory ID, base only) Checksums the whole object; rejected if its length cannot be determined. Example: the checksum of a file.2038 TM[6,18] checked object memory object report memory ID, base, length, checksum 2038 TC[6,21] load object memory data areas by reference repository path, file name, N; destination offset, offset in file, length, checksum (optional) x N 2141 TC[6,22] dump object memory data areas to file repository path, file name, N; offset, length x N File must not exist.2242

Offsets are byte offsets within the object identified by the base, independent of how the object is physically stored.49 The structured subservice defines no observables.23

docs.title: 6. Common memory management: TC[6,12]
docs.text: TC[6,12] "abort all memory dumps" has no application data.36 It aborts every dump request under execution by the raw subservice and by the structured subservice - including dumps to file. The subservice exposes one observable: a flag saying that at least one dump is in progress.24

docs.title: 7. Memory configuration: scrubbing and write protection
docs.text:
For scrubbing, PUS-C does not specify the mechanism, which is memory dependent and can be hardware or software; the service only keeps a memory scrubbing status per memory, which is used to trigger the scrubbing.25 Write protection can likewise be hardware or software; its status is the memory write protection status.26 For each, the mission declares support, the list of memories concerned, and (for scrubbing) the initial status.2526

Request Application data Effect Rejected if TC[6,13] enable the scrubbing of a memory memory ID (optional) status "enabled" memory cannot be scrubbed2537 TC[6,14] disable the scrubbing of a memory memory ID (optional) status "disabled" memory cannot be scrubbed2537 TC[6,15] enable the write protection of a memory memory ID (optional) "write protected" memory cannot be write protected2637 TC[6,16] disable the write protection of a memory memory ID (optional) "write unprotected" memory cannot be write protected2637 
stateDiagram-v2
  direction LR
  state "Scrubbing ENABLED" as SE
  state "Scrubbing DISABLED" as SD
  state "WRITE PROTECTED" as WP
  state "WRITE UNPROTECTED" as WU
  SE --> SD: TC[6,14]
  SD --> SE: TC[6,13]
  WU --> WP: TC[6,15]
  WP --> WU: TC[6,16]
  note right of WP: loads to this memory are rejected

Each request holds exactly one instruction.2526 The observables are the scrubbing status and the write protection status of each controllable memory.27 A load is rejected if it targets a write-protected memory (section 4.1), and a write that fails because hardware protection appears during the load aborts it.7

docs.title: 8. PUS-A (ECSS-E-70-41A) differences
docs.text:
PUS-A's memory management "provides basic dump, load and check facilities without the maintenance of service state information" and need not know which areas are changeable, the block sizes or what they contain.57

Aspect PUS-A (2003) PUS-C (2016) Structure one service, two addressing techniques57 four subservices1 Memory ID fixed octet-string, may be read as characters; omitted if only one memory block58 enumerated, optional30 Base deduced: unsigned integer or symbolic fixed-length character string58 deduced; base address or memory object identifier2916 Units SAU (smallest addressable unit: 16, 24, 32 or 64-bit word possible), counts from zero5758 bytes, aligned on the access alignment constraint49 Offset signed integer58 unsigned integer29 Length / data Length (SAUs) + Data (variable octet string)58 data to load as variable octet-string (length in octets)30 N omitted if only one area per request58 always present30 Checksum ISO 16-bit, computed over the data words only, optional58 16-bit, algorithm declared3050 Load verification compare uplinked checksum before writing; 11.2 says the data are loaded only if the checksums match, while the note in 11.3.1 makes skipping the write a design option; if completion is reported, re-read and compare5758 write, then checksum the loaded data; abort on mismatch7 Large dumps may use the large data transfer service (ST[13])57 response limited to one packet; files for larger data52 Subtypes 11-22 - atomic load, abort, scrubbing, write protection, object checks, by-reference and file operations43

PUS-A message names: (6,1) Load Memory using Base plus Offsets; (6,2) Load Memory using Absolute Addresses; (6,3) Dump Memory using Base plus Offsets; (6,4) Memory Dump using Base plus Offsets Report; (6,5) Dump Memory using Absolute Addresses; (6,6) Memory Dump using Absolute Addresses Report; (6,7) Check Memory using Base plus Offsets; (6,8) Memory Check using Base plus Offsets Report; (6,9)/(6,10) the same with absolute addresses.58596061 Its minimum capability set is one load-and-dump family matching the memory's addressing: (6,1), (6,3), (6,4) or (6,2), (6,5), (6,6); Table 18 then lists the dependencies (each load requires its dump and report, each check its report) and the optional support of symbolic base references.62 The concept clause adds scatter loads and dumps, optional checksum protection of loads, end-to-end verification by reading back, and checking memory without dumping it.56 More on the transition: PUS-A vs PUS-C.

docs.title: 8.1 Tailoring data in ECSS-E-ST-70-31C
docs.text:
ECSS-E-ST-70-31C models the PUS-A service. Its tailoring data (Table 6-33) are Booleans per addressing technique:76

Item Meaning S6 ST1 ST3 and ST4 Provider a managed memory uses base plus offset S6 Symbolic Base References, S6 Base Multiple Memory Blocks, S6 Base Data Level Checksum, S6 Base Scatter Load, S6 Base Scatter Dump options of base plus offset S6 ST7 and ST8 Provider, S6 Base Scatter Check on-board checking (base plus offset) S6 ST2 ST5 and ST6 Provider a managed memory uses absolute addressing (forced TRUE if base plus offset is FALSE) S6 Absolute Multiple Memory Blocks, S6 Absolute Data Level Checksum, S6 Absolute Scatter Load, S6 Absolute Scatter Dump options of absolute addressing S6 ST9 and ST10 Provider, S6 Absolute Scatter Check on-board checking (absolute)

The field sizes it asks for (Table 6-34 to 6-36) are: memory ID (PTC 7, PFC > 0), N (PTC 3), offset (PTC 4, signed), length (PTC 3), start address (PTC 3), and the base as either PTC 8 (symbolic) or PTC 3 (unsigned integer).77 The standard also models the memories themselves: a memory block has an ID (PTC 7), accessibility ("read-only" or "read and write"), smallest addressable unit (1, 2, 3, 4 or 8 bytes, the PUS constant <SMALLEST_ADDRESSABLE_UNIT>), addressing technique and size; a memory sub-block adds a symbolic base reference, an offset, a loading instruction ("reload" or "patch"), a type ("object code", "dynamic data", "data pool", "static data") and the reporting data it maps to.78

docs.title: 9. Changes in the 2024 Rev.1 draft
docs.text:
ECSS-E-ST-70-41C Rev.1 DIR1 (11 December 2024) keeps the 22 message types and makes these changes:

  • Dumps and checks become all-or-nothing. TC[6,3], TC[6,5], TC[6,7], TC[6,9], TC[6,20] and TC[6,22] carry an ordered list of instructions; the whole request is rejected if any instruction is invalid, and otherwise instructions execute in order. In PUS-C faulty instructions were rejected individually.666769
  • Large dumps are split instead of rejected. The general rule of clause 5.4.11.3.2 changes: a response too long for one packet of the maximum size is split into several self-contained PUS telemetry packets, with splitting criteria declared per subservice and the group marked by the primary header sequence flags (01 first, 00 continuation, 10 last, 11 stand-alone); the draft names memory dumps as a typical case. Accordingly the TC[6,5] and TC[6,3] rejection lists no longer contain the packet-size condition.706667
  • The note allowing loads to skip checking the instructions that follow a faulty one, present in four PUS-C load clauses, no longer appears.771
  • Hosting is reworded. In PUS-C, 6.6.2.2a says each subservice provider is hosted by exactly one application process, only a note adds that all of them are therefore in a single application process, and 6.6.2.2b allows at most one memory management subservice provider per application process. DIR1 makes the single hosting application process a requirement and limits each application process to the subservice providers of at most one memory management service.465
  • Scrubbing and write protection statuses are maintained by the memory configuration subservice (PUS-C said "the memory management service").6825

docs.title: 10. Ground segment: SCOS-2000 and on-board software maintenance
docs.text:
SCOS-2000's function list includes On-board Software Maintenance (OBSM).82 The Database Import ICD describes its role for service 6: OBSM generates memory load (patch) commands from memory images and processes dump packets to update memory images. The exact structure of the service 6 packets and the generation of patch and dump commands are left to mission-specific implementations, and the ICD recommends reusing a structure already used by a previous SCOS-2000 mission so that existing OBSM functions can be reused.79 Two general SCOS-2000 limits matter here: variable-length octet strings are supported for encoding TC parameters but not for decoding TM, which therefore needs special processing "e.g. memory dump processing"; and parameter values from variable TM packets do not take part in full TM processing.8081

sequenceDiagram
  participant O as OBSM (ground)
  participant M as MCS / TC chain
  participant S as On-board AP (ST[06])
  O->>O: compare new image with reference image
  O->>M: generate TC(6,2) patches (data from image)
  M->>S: TC(6,2) load
  S-->>M: TM(1,1) acceptance, TM(1,7) completion
  M->>S: TC(6,9) check same area
  S-->>M: TM(6,10) checksum
  M->>O: compare with checksum of the image
  opt full verification
    M->>S: TC(6,5) dump
    S-->>M: TM(6,6) x n packets
    M->>O: rebuild and compare image
  end

Inference

The sequence is this wiki's composition of the OBSM role in the ICD with the PUS-A end-to-end verification concept (load, then read back or checksum and compare).7956 It is not a procedure taken from a mission document.

docs.title: 11.1 Service description
docs.text:
Solar Orbiter's ICD (PUS-A based)83 defines service 6 for loading, dumping and checking a contiguous area of RAM, PROM, EEPROM, safeguard memory (SGM) or mass memory, identified by a memory ID:84

  • Only absolute addressing is used; addresses are expressed in single addressable units (SAU) of the selected memory.84
  • TC(6,2) and TC(6,5) contain one block each. A scatter patch is obtained with TC(6,128), which applies a set of patches pre-loaded with TC(6,2).84
  • TM(6,6) is not limited in length: the application generates as many dump packets as needed for the commanded area.84
  • TC(6,9) requests a check whose result TM(6,10) is sent via real-time telemetry.84
  • The memory ID is 2 bytes. Units A and B nominally use the same memory IDs, the unit being selected by APID; for cross-access between redundant units, unit A memories use 1-255 and unit B memories 257-511 (most significant byte 1 plus the unit A ID).86
  • The SAU can be 8, 16 or 32 bits; the address multiplier (MUL) is the address increment from one SAU to the next.86

Restated from the ICD table, which also flags the patch/dump/check operations allowed per memory.85

docs.title: 11.3 Messages
docs.text:
Message Name Data (sizes) Notes TC(6,2) Load Memory (patch) Memory ID (2, enumerated), Start Address (4), Length (4), Data (n) Start address + length - 1 must stay inside the physical memory.88 TC(6,5) Dump Memory Memory ID (2), Start Address (4), Length (4) Must not cross memory ID boundaries; if it does, a warning event is raised and the dump stops at the boundary. Not limited by the TM packet size.89 TM(6,6) Memory Dump Report Memory ID (2), Start Address (4), Length (4), Data (n) Each packet self-contained and contiguous (split at page boundaries); multi-packet dumps flagged with the segmentation flags of the primary header; destination always ground; packet category 9.90 TC(6,9) Check Memory Memory ID (2), Start Address (4), Length (4) Checksum is the CRC 16 of Annex 6, computed on the memory's basic word length.91 TM(6,10) Memory Check Report Memory ID (2), Start Address (4), Length (4), Checksum (2) Destination always ground.92 TC(6,128) Apply Pre-loaded Set of RAM Patches Pre-Loaded Patches Number (4), 1..30 CSW only (section 11.4).93 TC(6,129) Abort Dump none SSMM software only; rejected if no dump is ongoing.94 TC(6,130) / (6,131) Enable / Disable EEPROM Patch none SSMM only; powers the SSMM EEPROM banks on and enables patches, or the reverse.95 TC(6,140) Load Memory with Mask Memory ID (2), Start Address (4), Data (4), Mask (4) CSW only; loads single or multiple bits.96

Inference: Solar Orbiter anticipates the 2024 rule

Splitting a long dump into self-contained TM(6,6) packets grouped by the segmentation flags is what the 2024 draft makes the general PUS rule (section 9), whereas PUS-C would reject such a dump request and PUS-A suggested the large data transfer service.90705257

The dump category 9 is "Exclusive for Service 6 (6,x) telemetry", and dump packets are among the categories whose destination ID is always zero (ground).98100 Solar Orbiter's service 8 functions live in PM RAM at fixed addresses and can be modified or added by service 6 patches, which shows how ST[06] underpins ST[08] function management.97

docs.title: 11.4 The RAM patch mechanism (TC(6,128))
docs.text:
The patching buffer is a RAM area with a patch table of up to 30 descriptors (number of bytes, source address in the pre-loading area, destination address) and a pre-loading area holding the patch bytes. The ground loads both with TC(6,2), checks their content and consistency, then sends TC(6,128) with the number of descriptors to apply (the first n entries); after execution the buffer is erased.93

Inference

The mechanism makes a scatter patch atomic from the software's point of view: the patches are staged harmlessly and then applied in one step, instead of a series of TC(6,2) loads that would leave running code half-patched between packets. The ICD calls it a "safe loading/patching" of different RAM addresses but does not give the rationale.87

docs.title: 11.5 Masked load: Solar Orbiter and PUS-C compared
docs.text: The ICD rule is (existing data AND inverse mask) OR (loaded data AND mask), the same formula as PUS-C's TC[6,11] (section 4.2), but with data before mask in the packet.968 In the MIB, ZCD0068C "Load Memory With Mask" has exactly these four fields with a 32-bit word to load.103

docs.text: All figures below come from this wiki's queries of the September 2025 release MIB__20250916M25925PFMS001_SOL.103104

docs.text:
Subtype Commands APIDs Examples 2 91 20 ZCD00602 "Load Memory Using Absolute Address", ZSM00025 "SSMM Load Mem Absolute Addresses", ZST16200 "STR1 Load Mem RAM" 5 82 20 ZCD00605 "Dump Memory Using Absolute Address", ZIP06054 "dumpRAM" (PHI) 9 29 20 ZCD00609 "Check Memory Using Absolute Address" 128 2 172, 812 ZCD00680 "Apply Pre-loaded Set of RAM Patches", ZID52542 (EPD) 129 5 492, 508, 524, 924, 1532 ZSM00040 "SSMM Abort Dump", ZIU51000 "EUI_AbortDump", ZIA58056 "SWA_TC_MEM_DUMP_ABORT" 130 / 131 3 / 3 492, 508, 524 ZSM00014 "SSMM Enable EEPROM Patch", ZSM00017 "SSMM Disable EEPROM Patch" 140 6 172, 1020 ZCD0068C "Load Memory With Mask", ZIM00614 (MAG)

The 20 APIDs of subtypes 2, 5 and 9 are the OBC (172), the three SSMM processes (492, 508, 524), both star trackers (652, 668) and fourteen instrument processes. All 221 commands have CCF_ACK = 9 (acceptance and completion reports), which satisfies PUS-C's requirement that loads always report completion, and none is flagged critical.1037

The OBC memory ID parameter PCD06021 uses the alias set CCDT0037TX "Memory ID", whose 38 entries reproduce the OBC part of the ICD memory map one-to-one (19 memories for each of units A and B; the SSMM, star-tracker and payload memory IDs are not in it): A_PM_PROM = 3, A_TTR_PROM = 5, A_PM_EEPROM = 19, A_PM_RAM = 35, ..., A_CROME_REG = 101, and the unit B twins 259-357 (0x0103-0x0165).10385

docs.title: 12.2 Three ways to model a load
docs.text:
The 91 TC(6,2) definitions show how a MIB copes with PUS variable data in SCOS-2000:103

Style Definitions How the data is modelled Example Group repeater 30 Length (32-bit) is a repeat counter (CDF_GRPSIZE = 1) over one data element of the SAU size: 8-bit (PTC 3 PFC 4), 16-bit (PFC 12) or 32-bit (PFC 14) ZCD00602: data block of N 32-bit words Octet string ("(OBSM)" variants) 10 Length is a plain 32-bit value; the data is one variable octet string (PTC 7, PFC 0) to be filled from a memory image ZCDX0602 "DMS Load Memory by Absolu address (OBSM)", ZSTX1620 "STR1 Load Mem RAM (OBSM)" Fixed layout 51 no repeat counter and no octet string: a fixed set of fields, often with the memory ID, address and length preset, followed by named values (a register, a table such as an FSS look-up table) ZCDX0100 "Load RMH_ATPTR_CROME_REG_A": memory A_CROME_REG, start address 5642, length 1, then the register value

Inference: start addresses count SAUs

ZCDX0100 loads the CROME register area (A_CROME_REG, mapped at 0x0700 0000-0x0701 FFFF, 128 kB) at start address 5642, so addresses are counted from the start of each memory, not on the absolute bus map. Whether the count is in octets or in 32-bit SAUs is not settled by the sources: the TC(6,2), (6,5) and (6,9) parameter definitions say "in single addressable unit, with count starting from zero", while the memory map gives every OBC memory an address multiplier of 4, the "address increment" from one SAU to the next.888586 The MIB favours SAUs: the preset start addresses of the ten consecutive registers RMH_ATCNT 0 to RMH_ATCNT 9 are 5792 to 5801 (step 1), and values such as 5642, 5779 or 8961 are not multiples of 4, as 32-bit-aligned byte offsets would be.103 In SAUs, 5642 corresponds to byte offset 5642 x 4 = 22 568 (0x5828).

Dumps follow the same pattern: of the 82 TC(6,5) definitions, 12 have no preset value and 70 preset at least one field (a fixed or default value in CDF_VALUE); on the OBC alone, ZCD00605 sits next to 46 dedicated dumps of reconfiguration-module registers, FSS look-up tables, boot reports and HPTM registers, such as ZCDX0200 "Dump RMH_ATPTR_CROME_REG_A" (memory 101, address 5642, length 1).103

docs.title: 12.3 Reports and how SCOS-2000 identifies them
13. Worked example: a memory check round trip (real layout, illustrative values)
docs.text:
Check 256 SAUs of processor RAM A_PM_RAM (memory ID 35) on the OBC with ZCD00609 - 1 KiB if, as inferred in section 12.2, lengths count 32-bit SAUs. The layout is real; the sequence count and start address are illustrative; the header follows the ICD's TC packet definition;102 the CRC is computed with the Solar Orbiter ICD algorithm (CCITT polynomial, initial value all ones).101

Octets Bytes Field 0-1 18 AC TC, secondary header flag 1, APID 172 (process 10, category 12) 2-3 C0 01 stand-alone, sequence count 1 4-5 00 0F packet data length = 16 - 1 6-9 19 06 09 78 PUS version 1, ack 1001; service 6, subtype 9; source ID 120 10-11 00 23 memory ID 35 A_PM_RAM 12-15 00 00 00 00 start address 0 (illustrative) 16-19 00 00 01 00 length 256 SAU 20-21 38 6E packet error control (CRC-16)

The answer is a TM(6,10) on APID 169 laid out as in SPID 14170: memory ID 00 23, the same start address and length, and the 16-bit CRC of the area. The ground compares it with the CRC of its reference memory image; a match shows, with the error-detection strength of a 16-bit CRC, that the area is intact without dumping it.9110101

Checksum test vectors

To validate a ground implementation, the standards give test vectors (hexadecimal). This wiki's implementation reproduces all of them.

Data ISO checksum (PUS-A Annex A.2) CRC (Solar Orbiter Annex 6) 00 00 FF FF 1D 0F 00 00 00 FF FF CC 9C AB CD EF 01 9C F8 04 A2 14 56 F8 9A 00 01 24 DC 7F D5

Sources: PUS-A A.2.5 and the Solar Orbiter CRC compliance table.63101 The ISO algorithm keeps two running sums modulo 255, \(C_0 = C_0 + B_i\) and \(C_1 = C_1 + C_0\), then sets \(CK_1 = -(C_0 + C_1)\) and \(CK_2 = C_1\), replacing a zero by 255.63

docs.title: 14. Other missions: Herschel and Planck
docs.text: The Herschel/Planck Operations Interface Requirements Document asks that memory areas be split into code, fixed data and variables; that the ground can load any changeable area, with a contiguous area per telecommand; that each load packet be self-consistent (not dependent on earlier packets, and re-sendable alone); that the destination detect corrupted loads (for example by checksums); that end-to-end verification confirm the data in memory, possibly by dumping; that any memory, including non-volatile and mass memories, be dumpable with a single request even if several TM packets are needed; and that a checksum check over a start address and length be available.107 It also requires that on-board software can be modified, by changing the non-volatile image or patching the working copy, while the unit is operational.108 See Herschel and Planck.
