docs.title: ST[08] Function management
docs.text:
The function management service (service type 8) is the PUS "escape hatch" for on-board software functions that are not modelled by any other standard service. A single request, TC[8,1] perform a function, names a function by its identifier and optionally passes it a list of arguments; what the function does is entirely up to the mission.17 The service is already part of the first ECSS edition of the Packet Utilization Standard (ECSS-E-70-41A, "PUS-A", 2003), survives in ECSS-E-ST-70-41C ("PUS-C", 2016) only "for backward compatibility reasons", and is deleted in the 2024 Rev.1 draft.120 This page describes the service in full, compares the editions, explains what the SCOS-2000 ground system does (and does not do) with it, and shows from the real Solar Orbiter MIB how one mission uses service 8 to trigger its on-board recovery functions.

At a glance

Item Value Service type 87 Subservice types one: the function management subservice1 Message types (PUS-C) TC[8,1] perform a function, the only one, capability "minimum"8 Reports none defined; outcome reported only through ST[01] request verification418 Observables none defined5 PUS-A name Perform Function (8,1), clause 1218 2024 Rev.1 draft ST[08] deleted; service type 8 becomes "(reserved)"2021 SCOS-2000 no specific processing, no specific limitation23 Solar Orbiter 64 TC(8,1) commands plus private subtypes 140 to 145 in the 2025 MIB45

docs.title: 1. Why the service exists
docs.text:
An on-board application process usually has a specialised role, for example controlling a payload instrument or the attitude and orbit control subsystem, and that role comes with functions the ground wants to invoke. PUS does not constrain what these functions are: they can cover any nominal operation of a subsystem or payload, including predefined mode changes.1 PUS-A presents the service as the realisation of its "software management" concept: functions can be implemented as mission-specific services with their own request and report structures, or through a generic, high-level function service in which "the function itself is specialized ... but the associated packet structure is standardized".14 PUS-A also insists that ground and on-board software talk through packets designed for the purpose, and not through general memory load and dump packets.15

By 2016 the editors preferred the first route. PUS-C encourages missions to define mission-specific service types, or mission-specific subservice types of standard services, "instead of using the function management service type", and keeps ST[08] only for backward compatibility.1 The 2024 Rev.1 draft completes the move: its change log lists the "deletion of service not used in current and future missions: ST[8] function management", and clause 6.8 now reads "ST[08] (reserved)", with a note repeating the advice to replace it by mission-specific service or subservice types.2120

Inference

The standards do not explain the technical drawback, but the structure of TC[8,1] suggests it: the meaning of a function and the format of its arguments are hidden behind an opaque identifier, so a ground system cannot validate or model the request generically. A mission-specific subservice type, by contrast, is specified with the same foundation-model rules (request types, instruction types, reports, observables) as every standard service.

docs.title: 2. Service model
docs.text: The PUS-C service model is small. Each function management service contains at least one function management subservice, and each application process hosts at most one function management subservice provider.2 The service therefore lives inside the application process whose functions it exposes: a request is addressed to that process by its APID in the packet primary header (see PUS packet structures).

docs.title: 2.1 Accessibility: the declared function list
docs.text:
The subservice can only access functions that are declared. When a mission specifies a function management subservice it must declare:3

Declaration Clause Content List of functions 6.8.3.1a the functions the subservice can perform Argument list per function 6.8.3.1b for each function that uses arguments, the arguments and their definition Argument supply policy per function 6.8.3.1c either (1) a value is supplied for every argument, or (2) only the arguments to update are supplied and the others keep their current values

The supply policy is fixed per function, not per request. PUS-A said the same thing in other words: the option is chosen "at Function ID-level, rather than at packet instance".318 The second policy means that a function keeps a persistent set of argument values on board, which a request can partially overwrite.

docs.title: 2.2 Processing a perform-a-function request
docs.text:
Each request to perform a function carries exactly one instruction, and the instruction contains the function identifier and, if the function uses arguments, the list of arguments and their values.4 The subservice rejects the request if the instruction refers to an unknown function or an unknown argument, or if an argument value does not comply with the function's argument definition. A rejected request produces a failed start of execution notification, which the request verification service turns into a TM[1,4] report.46 For a valid instruction the subservice "initiate[s] the execution of the function"; nothing more is specified, and no observables are defined.5

flowchart TD
  A["TC[8,1] arrives at the destination application process"] --> B{"Function ID known?"}
  B -- no --> R["Reject: failed start of execution notification<br/>(TM[1,4] via ST[01])"]
  B -- yes --> C{"Every argument ID known?"}
  C -- no --> R
  C -- yes --> D{"Every value complies with the<br/>function's argument definition?"}
  D -- no --> R
  D -- yes --> E["Initiate the execution of the function"]
  E --> F["Mission-specific behaviour,<br/>progress and completion reporting per ST[01] if requested"]

The diagram follows clause 6.8.4d to f.45 Because the standard says only that execution is initiated, the meaning of a successful completion report (TM[1,7]) for a function is a mission decision.

docs.title: 3. TC[8,1] perform a function
docs.text:
Every packet of the service has service type 8; a perform-a-function request has message subtype 1. Its application data field has the structure of PUS-C Figure 8-87:7

Field PUS-C type Presence Meaning function ID fixed character-string always identifier of the function to perform N unsigned integer optional number of (argument ID, argument value) pairs that follow argument ID enumerated repeated N times identifies the argument argument value deduced repeated N times the value; its type is deduced from the argument ID

The field types are the PUS packet field type codes (PTC) of PUS parameter types: fixed character-string is PTC 8, unsigned integer PTC 3, enumerated PTC 2 and deduced PTC 11.10 A deduced field must get its structure only from preceding fields of the same packet, from mission constants, or both; here the preceding argument ID tells the receiver how to read the value.11 Below the argument part, Figure 8-87 carries the annotations optional and deduced presence: in PUS structure diagrams, an optional field is one whose presence is fixed at the level of the mission, application process or service instance, and here the presence of arguments follows from the function's declaration (6.8.3.1b).7123

Inference

PUS-C fixes the field types but none of the field lengths in Figure 8-87. The widths in the diagram above (32, 8, 8 and 16 bits) are chosen by this wiki for illustration. The real Solar Orbiter layout in section 7 uses a 1-octet unsigned function ID instead.

PUS-A defines the same request with two variants, one for each supply policy:18

PUS-A, subset of parameters loadedPUS-A, full set of parameters loaded Field Type Presence Meaning Function ID Fixed CharString always together with the APID, implicitly defines the presence and structure of the fields that follow; its internal structure is "beyond the scope" of PUS-A N Unsigned Integer optional number of (Parameter#, Value) pairs Parameter# Enumerated repeated N times which parameter the following value belongs to Value Deduced repeated N times type deduced from Parameter#; parameters not loaded keep their current values Field Type Presence Meaning Function ID Fixed CharString always as above Parameters Any optional a data structure of parameter values following structure rules set #1 (PUS-A subclause 23.6.2), whose structure is known implicitly

PUS-A states that the length of the Function ID character string may be defined per mission or per application process, and that the Function ID is assigned "at the level of the individual controls", for example load manoeuvre parameters, start manoeuvre or configure an instrument to a mode.1718

docs.title: 4. Capability sets
docs.text:
PUS-C classifies each message type by an applicability constraint: "minimum" means every subservice of that type provides it, "by declaration" means the mission decides, and "implied by" or "requires" link capabilities together.9 For ST[08] the summary is trivial:8

Edition Message Capability Notes PUS-C (2016) TC[8,1] perform a function minimum the only message type of the service PUS-A (2003) (8,1) Perform Function minimum capability set (Table 19) "There are no additional capability sets"19 Rev.1 DIR1 (2024) - - service type 8 reserved20

PUS-A adds that any number of on-board application processes may each provide a single instance of the service, and that "There are currently no service reports defined".1618

docs.title: 5. Edition differences
docs.text:
Aspect PUS-A (ECSS-E-70-41A) PUS-C (ECSS-E-ST-70-41C) Rev.1 DIR1 (2024 draft) Status standard service, clause 12 kept for backward compatibility, clause 6.8 / 8.8 deleted, type 8 reserved Request Perform Function (8,1) TC[8,1] perform a function - Argument naming Parameter#, Value argument ID, argument value - Supply policies subset (array of pairs) or full set (implicit structure "Any") supply all arguments, or only those to update; declared per function - Rejection rules not specified unknown function, unknown argument, non-compliant value; failed start of execution - Reports none none; no observables -

The table is assembled from the clauses cited in sections 2 to 4.183420 The wider picture of the editions is on PUS-A vs PUS-C.

What replaces it

The Rev.1 draft gives no direct successor. Its note points missions to mission-specific service types or mission-specific subservice types of standardized services.20 In PUS-C, request-driven behaviour that is close to "perform a function" is also available through ST[18] on-board operations procedures and ST[21] request sequencing, which have full models with status reports.

docs.title: 6. Ground side: SCOS-2000
docs.text:
SCOS-2000 decodes and encodes every PUS type and subtype through its database, and only some services get extra ground processing, such as report-based verification or a model of the on-board scheduler.22 For service 8 the Database Import ICD is explicit: "There is no specific processing of Service 8 TM/TC packets in SCOS-2000", and no specific limitation applies.23

A TC[8,1] is therefore defined in the MIB like any other command, with one ccf record and a cdf layout (see Commanding in the MIB). A cdf element can be a fixed area (CDF_ELTYPE = A), whose value is a raw unsigned integer written in hexadecimal and never visible as a command parameter in the command history.2829

Inference

The ICD's PUS appendix labels its references "Section 12 of [AD-5]" for service 8 and "Section 13" and "Section 14" for services 9 and 11. In the ICD's own reference list, AD-5 is a display ICD, so the label is a slip. The numbers match the clauses of ECSS-E-70-41A for every service in the appendix (verification 6, device commanding 7, housekeeping 8, ..., function management 12, time management 13, scheduling 14, test 19), and so do the subclauses it cites (13.3.1 for the rate change, 14.3.4 for time-shifting), so the appendix most likely refers to PUS-A.262427 The ICD's reference list itself cites the PUS only as RD-6, ESA PSS-07-101 (May 1994).25 The clause numbering of that older standard is not available here, so it cannot be ruled out as the intended reference.

docs.title: 7. Solar Orbiter: service 8 for FDIR recovery functions
docs.text: Solar Orbiter's packet structure ICD (SOL.S.ASTR.TN.00079, Airbus Defence and Space) tailors its TM/TC services from the ESA PUS, which its applicable document AD1 identifies as ECSS-E-70-41A, and from the ESA operations interface requirements, and it refers to the ECSS-E-70-41A capability sets.3130 In its service table, service 8 carries the mnemonic O (a user may choose to implement the service), and every service 8 message is marked X, "shall be implemented", for the central software (CSW) of the on-board computer. TC(8,1) and TC(8,140) to TC(8,143) are also marked O (optional) in the payload software column; the SSMM and star tracker columns are empty.3033

docs.title: 7.1 What the functions are
docs.text:
The ICD gives service 8 one objective: to support the FDIR recovery actions that are not implemented on board through standard services.34 The design is described as follows:34

  • The functions (recovery actions) sit in the processor module RAM (PM-RAM) at fixed addresses for a given CSW release, and can be modified by service 6 memory patches without recompiling the CSW.
  • The service maps each function ID to the start address of the function code. Two spare function IDs point to a non-operational (NOP) function, so up to two new functions can be added by patching new code and re-pointing the spare IDs.
  • A function can be removed by patching its mapping to the NOP function, or by disabling it with a dedicated service 8 command.
  • A function is typically a sequence of commands with branching logic (for example IF and WHILE) and stop steps; it reads and writes the system datapool and can generate events and TM snapshots.
flowchart LR
  G["Ground or on-board event-action<br/>TC(8,1) FID = n"] --> T["Service 8 table<br/>FID to start address"]
  T -->|enabled| F["Function code in PM-RAM<br/>(commands, IF / WHILE, stop steps)"]
  T -->|"spare FID"| N["NOP function"]
  F --> DP["System datapool<br/>read / write"]
  F --> EV["Events (ST[05])<br/>and TM snapshots"]
  P["Service 6 patch"] -. "modify code or<br/>re-point FID" .-> T
  P -.-> F

The diagram restates the ICD description.34

docs.title: 7.2 TC(8,1) Start Function and the private subtypes
docs.text:
Solar Orbiter names TC(8,1) "Start Function" in its detailed definition ("Perform Function" in the summary table). The function runs only if its execution is currently enabled. The application data are a 1-octet unsigned function ID (range 1 to 255) followed by 0 to m octets of function-specific parameters "of any Type".3533 This departs from both PUS editions, where the function ID is a fixed character-string.187

The mission adds five private telecommands and one private report to manage the function table:33363738

Message Name Application / source data TC(8,140) Enable Function Execution NFID (1 octet), then NFID × FID (1 octet). NFID = 0 enables at service level, keeping the individual statuses TC(8,141) Disable Function Execution same layout; NFID = 0 disables at service level TC(8,142) Enable Autoreset of Execution Enable Flag same layout; sets autoreset "Enabled" and the execution status "Disabled" TC(8,143) Disable Autoreset of Execution Enable Flag same layout; execution status unaffected TC(8,144) Report Function Status N (1 octet; 0 = all functions), then N × Function ID TM(8,145) Function Status Report N, then N × (Function ID, Execution status, Autoreset status), 1 octet each; statuses 0 = Disabled, 1 = Enabled

The autoreset mechanism makes a function one-shot: once autoreset is enabled, the function must be explicitly enabled before it can run, and after it has run its status returns to "Disabled" automatically. With autoreset disabled, the execution status stays at whatever TC(8,140) or TC(8,141) last set.37

stateDiagram-v2
  direction LR
  EN: Enabled, autoreset off
  DIS: Disabled, autoreset off
  ARM: Enabled, autoreset on (armed)
  DAR: Disabled, autoreset on
  [*] --> EN
  EN --> DIS: TC(8,141)
  DIS --> EN: TC(8,140)
  EN --> DAR: TC(8,142)
  DIS --> DAR: TC(8,142)
  DAR --> ARM: TC(8,140)
  ARM --> DAR: TC(8,1) runs the function once, or TC(8,141)
  DAR --> DIS: TC(8,143)
  ARM --> EN: TC(8,143)
  note right of EN
    TC(8,1) may run the function
    any number of times
  end note

Inference

The state diagram is this wiki's reading of the TC(8,140) to TC(8,143) descriptions.3637 The initial state drawn (enabled, autoreset off) is arbitrary: the initial state of each function, and how the service-level enable flag (NFID = 0) combines with the per-function status, are not stated in the available sources.

All these telecommands are verified with the mission's standard rule: a TM(1,2) acceptance failure if a service 1 static check fails, and a TM(1,8) completion failure in the cases listed in a reference document not available here.35

docs.title: 7.3 Service 8 in the 2025 MIB
docs.text:
The MIB release MIB__20250916M25925PFMS001_SOL defines 64 TC(8,1) commands and one command for each private subtype. All of them go to APID 236; the status report TM(8,145) comes from APID 227.45 On Solar Orbiter the upper 7 bits of the APID are the process ID and the lower 4 bits the packet category (12 for every telecommand), so both APIDs belong to process ID 14, the CSW System Control Application in charge of system modes, configuration, FDIR and autonomy.3940 APID 227 carries packet category 3, which the ICD's category table reserves for variable-length tabular reports.32

Inference: a packet category slip in the ICD

The ICD's own definition of TM(8,145) gives "Packet Cat: 12", the value of its telecommand definitions, although category 12 is reserved for service 21 telemetry and for telecommands.3832 The MIB's APID 227 (category 3, tabular report) fits the variable-length status report, so the "12" is most likely copied from the TC template. The available sources do not confirm this.

Subtype MIB command(s) Parameters Explorer 1 ZCSF0002 to ZCSF1016 (64 commands) function ID as a fixed area, plus 0 to 6 parameters ZCSF0003 140 ZCS0088C Enable Function Execution PCD088C1 "Number of function" (repeater), PCD08011 "FID" ZCS0088C 141 ZCS0088D Disable Function Execution same ZCS0088D 142 ZCS0088E Enable Autoreset Execution Enable Flag same ZCS0088E 143 ZCS0088F Disable Autoreset Execution Enable Flag same ZCS0088F 144 ZCS00890 Report Function Status same ZCS00890 TM 145 SPID 10096 Function Status Report variable packet: NCD08911 count, then NCD08912 FID, NCD08913 execution status, NCD08914 autoreset SPID 10096

The function ID never appears as an editable parameter of a TC(8,1): it is a fixed area of 8 bits in the cdf, so each on-board function is a separate MIB command. The 64 commands use 63 distinct function IDs between 0x02 and 0x54 (2 to 84); ZCSF0016 and ZCSF1016 share 0x16. The same 63 values, with names such as RCV_TTR_TMEOBT (3) or REC_SYS_1 (16), form the textual calibration CCDT0048TC of the FID parameter of the private subtypes.45 The status values in TM(8,145) are calibrated by CCDT0003TX (0 = DISABLED, 1 = ENABLED).45

The arguments of the 64 functions follow a clear pattern:45

Argument pattern Commands Example no argument (function ID only) 9 ZCSF0003 "TME / OBT Failure Recovery"; ZCSF0005 and ZCSF0006 "Spare function 1" and "2" HK SID (PCD03011, 8 bits) and EID (PCD038B1, 16 bits); the last two arguments in all but ZCSF0049, which appends a second SID and an EID (PCSB0090, PCSB0141) 55 ZCSF0010 "System Failure Recovery: PM reset" of which also a textually calibrated unit or channel selector 34 ZCSF0040 "STR Execute Recovery Action 1 Function" (STR unit identifier) of which also an FMON Id (PCD8E012, 32 bits) 17 ZCSF0022 "PCDU Execute Recovery Action 1 Function"

The two spare functions match the two spare function IDs of the ICD.3445

Inference

The ICD says functions "will be able to generate events and TM snapshots".34 The trailing HK SID and EID arguments of 55 functions very probably select which housekeeping snapshot and which event the function emits; one fixed instance (ZCSF1016, below) supplies EID SNAP_EUI_OFF, which supports that reading. Their exact semantics are not stated in the available sources. Likewise "FMON Id" suggests a functional-monitoring identifier.

Between the April 2020 release (61 TC(8,1) commands) and the September 2025 release, three TC(8,1) commands were added: ZCSF000D "EPS Execute Recovery Action 4 Function", ZCSF000E "SADE Execute Recovery Action 2 Function" and ZCSF1016 "Start REC_SpW2 for EUI".4546

docs.title: 7.4 How the functions are triggered
docs.text:
Service 8 commands appear in only seven command sequences, which wrap the management subtypes (for example ADMC081A "Enable Function Exec", which sends TC(8,140) followed by TC(8,144)) and one direct use, ADMC401A "Trigger RM OPS Alarm", which sends ZCSF0010 with HK SID 192 and EID GND_OPS_ALARM.45 The more typical trigger is on board. Sequence AIUC900A "EUI DefineSwOffFdir" loads three event-action definitions with TC(19,1) ZCS01301 "Add Event to the Detection List": for the EUI events 46397, 46398 and 46399, the action to release is ZCSF1016.45 ZCSF1016 is FID 0x16 (the same function as ZCSF0016 "PL/SPW Execute Recovery Action 2 Functio", a description truncated to 40 characters in the MIB) with all three arguments frozen as fixed values: payload type PL_EUI, HK SID 192 and EID SNAP_EUI_OFF.45

sequenceDiagram
  participant EUI as EUI instrument
  participant EV as ST05 event reporting
  participant EA as ST19 event-action
  participant S8 as ST08 service (APID 236)
  participant F as Recovery function 0x16
  EUI->>EV: anomaly, event 46397/46398/46399
  EV->>EA: event matches a detection-list entry
  EA->>S8: release ZCSF1016 = TC(8,1) FID 0x16 (PL_EUI, SID 192, EID SNAP_EUI_OFF)
  S8->>F: function enabled? then start
  F-->>EV: event SNAP_EUI_OFF and TM snapshot (inferred)

The last arrow is inferred, as explained above; the rest of the chain is MIB data.45

docs.title: 7.5 Worked example: encoding ZCSF1016
docs.text:
The bytes below build the complete TC packet for ZCSF1016. The application data are real: they follow from the MIB cdf definition and the raw values of the calibrations (PL_EUI = 1 in CCDT0282TX, SNAP_EUI_OFF = 65281 in CCDT0004TX). The sequence count, the source ID and therefore the CRC are illustrative.45

18 EC  C0 03  00 0A   19 08 01 78   16 01 C0 FF 01   5B E7
|----primary----|     |---DFH---|   |-app data--|    |CRC|
Octets Field Value Source 18 EC version 0, type 1 (TC), data field header flag 1, APID 236 header NOM_TC MIB tcp/pcdf45 C0 03 sequence flags 0b11 (stand-alone), sequence count 3 count illustrative Solar Orbiter ICD41 00 0A packet data length C = 10 (11 octets follow) computed 19 secondary header flag 0, PUS version 1, ack 0b1001 (acceptance and completion) CCF_ACK = 9 MIB4542 08 01 service type 8, subtype 1 78 source ID 120 ("Direct commands") illustrative choice Solar Orbiter ICD43 16 function ID 0x16 fixed area MIB cdf45 01 payload type PL_EUI fixed value MIB cdf, pas45 C0 HK SID 192 fixed value MIB cdf45 FF 01 EID SNAP_EUI_OFF = 65281 fixed value MIB cdf, pas45 5B E7 packet error control, CRC-16 (polynomial \(x^{16}+x^{12}+x^5+1\), preset all ones) over the 15 preceding octets computed by this wiki Solar Orbiter ICD Annex 644

docs.title: ST[09] Time management
docs.text:
Every spacecraft keeps a spacecraft time reference (an on-board clock), and every PUS telemetry report is time-tagged with it. The ground, however, works in UTC. The time management service (service type 9) closes that gap: it periodically samples the on-board clock at a precisely defined instant, the start of a particular telemetry transfer frame, and sends the sample to the ground in a time report. The ground, which also time-stamps the reception of that frame, can then pair the two times and maintain a correlation between on-board time and UTC, and from it reconstruct when every other reported event happened.1 This page covers the PUS-C service (ECSS-E-ST-70-41C, 2016) in full, compares it with PUS-A (2003) and the 2024 Rev.1 draft, explains how SCOS-2000 turns time reports into time correlation coefficients, and shows Solar Orbiter's real time packet and time commands from its MIB.

At a glance

Item Value Service type 911 Subservices (PUS-C) time reporting (exactly one); time reporting control (at most one)3 Message types (PUS-C) TC[9,1] set the time report generation rate; TM[9,2] CUC time report; TM[9,3] CDS time report13 Where the reports come from application process APID 0, in packets without a secondary header311 Sampling trigger leading edge of the first bit of the attached synchronization marker of selected VC 0 frames9 Generation rate every 1, 2, 4, ... 256 VC 0 frames, set as a rate exponential value 0 to 8410 Added in the 2024 Rev.1 draft TC[9,4] to TC[9,7]: set the reference time, distribute time to on-board users39 Ground counterpart time correlation (SCOS-2000 TCO)40 Solar Orbiter SPID 9999 "Time Report", OBT in CUC 4+2, private TC(9,128) to TC(9,131)5261

docs.title: 1.1 Spacecraft time, time codes and correlation
docs.text:
PUS-C does not say how the on-board clock is built: it may be a free-running counter or a clock synchronized to a GPS receiver.4 What it fixes is how the clock is reported. The time in a time report uses one of two CCSDS time code formats:2

  • CUC (CCSDS unsegmented time code), consecutive bits of a binary counter, suited to spacecraft time measurement;
  • CDS (CCSDS day segmented time code), typically used when the on-board time is synchronized with a ground reference such as TAI or UTC.

Both consist of a preamble field (P-field), which says how to read the time, and a time specification field (T-field), which carries the value.2 In CCSDS 301.0-B-4 the CUC T-field is a count of basic time units (normally seconds) since an epoch plus an optional binary fraction, and the first P-field octet encodes the epoch type (001 for 1958 January 1, 010 for an agency-defined epoch), the number of coarse octets minus one, and the number of fine octets.21 The CDS T-field is a day count, milliseconds of day and an optional submillisecond field; its P-field identifies the code (100), the epoch, the day-segment width and the submillisecond resolution.22

A time reporting subservice supports exactly one of the two formats.25 PUS-C uses this choice as its own example of an "exclusive-or" capability constraint.6

The correlation itself is a ground function. PUS-A summarises why it matters: once the correlation is known, the ground can reconstruct the on-board time of every event or parameter sample, whether the sample is explicitly time-stamped or deduced from implicit time offsets relative to the packet time. PUS-A leaves on-board time distribution and GPS-based schemes out of scope.25

docs.title: 1.2 What the operability standard requires
docs.text:
ECSS-E-ST-70-11C Rev.1 (space segment operability, October 2025) states the system-level requirements that ST[09] serves. Among them:24

Requirement Content (paraphrased) 5.4a the space segment provides timing information that lets the ground keep the OBT-UTC correlation better than <TIME_CORREL_ACCUR> over <TIME_CORREL_PERIOD> 5.4b the ground can set the on-board time by telecommand 5.4c on-board time increases monotonically in all modes, including standby and survival 5.4d all on-board timing derives from a single Central Time Reference 5.4e to g engineering telemetry shows whether an application process has achieved time synchronization 5.4h, j no on-board clock, and no telemetered on-board time, wraps around during the mission 5.4i every TM source packet should carry its on-board generation time 5.4o, w the on-board time system's contribution to correlation error is bounded (<ONBOARD_STABILITY> ms/day) and every on-board delay is documented

The angle-bracket items are mission parameters to be filled in during tailoring.24

docs.title: 2. Service layout
docs.text:
PUS-C constrains where the two subservices live:3

Rule Clause Content One service per spacecraft 6.9.2.1a each spacecraft contains exactly one time management service One time reporting subservice 6.9.2.2.1a exactly one per time management service Optional rate control 6.9.2.2.2a at most one time reporting control subservice APID 0 6.9.2.3a the time reporting subservice provider is hosted by the application process with APID 0 One control provider per process 6.9.2.3b each application process hosts at most one time reporting control subservice provider; the note adds that the two subservices may be hosted by different application processes No reports from APID 0 other than time reports 6.9.2.3c if the control subservice can generate reports, it must not be hosted by the APID 0 process

The last rule exists because APID 0 packets have no secondary header: a report of any other type sent from APID 0 could not be identified.3 PUS-C reserves APID 0 for spacecraft time packets (and APID 2047 for idle packets) in its general application process rules.14

docs.title: 3. Spacecraft time reference and its declared parameters
docs.text:
PUS-C leaves several properties for the mission to declare. Together they are the "managed parameters" of the service:4578

Declaration Clause Notes default time report generation rate 6.9.3b used until TC[9,1] changes it supported generation rates 6.9.3c a subset of 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256; counted in VC 0 transfer frames sampling accuracy of the time reference 6.9.3d declared at spacecraft architecture level; contributes to correlation accuracy accuracy of the time between frame transmission and the reported sample 6.9.3e PUS-C does not require the time packet to go down in the frame that triggered it format: CUC or CDS 6.9.4.1a exactly one time reference status reported? and its meaning 6.9.4.1b, c optional field of the time report generation rate included in the report? 6.9.4.1d optional field of the time report P-field explicit or implicit, and the implicit value 6.9.4.2b, c / 6.9.4.3b, c an omitted P-field is "considered implicit"

The service also supplies the synchronized time that all services use to time-stamp their reports (6.9.3f).4 Each on-board application process time-tags every report with the on-board reference time, declares whether it time-tags before or after collecting the parameter values, and declares whether it can report the status of the time reference.15 That status travels in the 4-bit spacecraft time reference status field of every PUS-C TM secondary header; an application process that does not support it sets the field to 0. The PFC of the TM header time field is declared when specifying the time service.1617 See PUS packet structures for the header itself.

Inference

PUS-C defines no values for the spacecraft time reference status; requirement 6.9.4.1c leaves its meaning to the mission.5 A typical use would be to flag an unsynchronized or freshly reset clock, as the operability requirements 5.4e to g ask for, but that pairing is this wiki's reading.24

docs.title: 4. The time report generation process
docs.text:
This is the heart of the service. The time reporting subservice:9

  1. samples the spacecraft time reference once for each telemetry transfer frame on virtual channel 0 whose virtual channel frame count modulo the generation rate equals 0;
  2. takes the sample at the instant of the leading edge of the first bit of the attached synchronization marker (ASM) of that frame;
  3. generates the time report at the required rate, with the T-field set to the sampled value formatted in the chosen time code;
  4. applies a new rate immediately to determine the next frame that triggers sampling.
sequenceDiagram
  participant TFG as TM frame generator (VC 0)
  participant CLK as Spacecraft time reference
  participant TR as Time reporting (APID 0)
  participant GS as Ground station
  participant MCS as Ground (SCOS-2000)
  Note over TFG: VC frame count mod rate = 0
  TFG->>CLK: first ASM bit of the frame leaves (trigger)
  CLK->>TR: sampled time value
  TFG->>GS: the trigger frame (ERT stamped on reception)
  TR->>TFG: time packet TM[9,2] / TM[9,3]
  TFG->>GS: a later frame carries the time packet
  GS->>MCS: frames with ERT
  MCS->>MCS: pair the sample with the trigger frame's ERT minus delays = time couple

The on-board part of the diagram follows PUS-C clause 6.9.4.4; the ground part follows the SCOS-2000 time correlation note (section 9).944

The VC frame count is an 8-bit, modulo-256 counter in bits 24 to 31 of the TM transfer frame primary header.23 A rate of \(2^n\) frames, \(n\) = 0 to 8, therefore divides the 256-frame counter cycle exactly: with rate 32 the frames with counts 0, 32, 64, ..., 224 trigger a sample, 8 per counter cycle; with rate 256 only count 0 does.1023 PUS-A's annex C gives the reason for the upper limit: the sample taken at frame count 0 must be telemetered before the VC 0 frame counter has counted 255 more frames, "so as to avoid ambiguity"; for a higher sampling rate it must be sent before the selected number of frames has elapsed.32

Which frames trigger a sample? (illustrative)

Rate exponential value 5, so rate \(2^5 = 32\). VC 0 frames are numbered by their VC frame count.

VC 0 frame count 30 31 32 33 ... 63 64 ... 255 0 triggers sampling? no no yes no no yes no yes

If TC[9,1] sets the exponent to 8 while the count is 40, the next trigger is the frame with count 0 (the next multiple of 256), because the new rate applies immediately.9

docs.title: 5. Spacecraft time packets: TM[9,2] and TM[9,3]
5.1 The packet
docs.text:
Time reports are spacecraft time packets. They have no packet secondary header, so their secondary header flag is 0, and their APID is 0. They therefore carry no service type or subtype on the wire. PUS-C still associates the message types TM[9,2] and TM[9,3] with them, so that other services can refer to them, for example ST[14] real-time forwarding control.11 PUS-C's TM secondary header rule makes the same exception.16

The fixed values are those of PUS-C clause 8.9.1; the field sizes are those of the Space Packet primary header.1118

docs.title: 5.2 Source data
docs.text:
TM[9,2] (CUC) and TM[9,3] (CDS) have the same structure:12

Field PUS-C type Presence Meaning rate exponential value unsigned integer optional (6.9.4.1d) \(n\) such that the report rate is \(2^n\) VC 0 frames, 0 to 8 spacecraft time absolute time always the sampled time reference, CUC (TM[9,2]) or CDS (TM[9,3]) per CCSDS 301.0-B-4 spacecraft time reference status deduced optional (6.9.4.1b) mission-defined status of the time reference

Each report contains a single time notification with these items.78 PUS-C does not fix the width of the rate field; PUS-A makes it one octet.1227

Inference: a copy-paste slip

Requirement 6.9.4.3e.2 says the subservice generates "a single CDS time report containing the CUC time notification". In the CDS clause this can only mean the CDS notification of item 1; the wording repeats the CUC clause.8

docs.title: 5.3 The time field: PTC 9
docs.text:
An absolute time in a PUS-C packet is of PTC 9, a positive offset in seconds and fractions of a second from an epoch. CUC may use the CCSDS 1958 epoch or an agency epoch, in which case the value is a free-running counter converted on ground with the time correlation coefficients; CDS must use the 1958 epoch.19 The PFC selects the format:20

PFC Format Length 0 explicit: P-field included (CUC or CDS) variable 1 CDS, 2-octet day, no µs 6 octets 2 CDS, 2-octet day, with µs (day, ms of day, µs of ms) 8 octets 3 to 18 CUC, implicit P-field: coarse octets = (PFC + 1) div 4, fine octets = (PFC + 1) mod 4 1 to 7 octets 19 to 46 CUC, implicit P-field: coarse octets = (PFC - 12) div 7, fine octets = 4 + (PFC - 12) mod 7 up to 14 octets

A note of clause 7.3.10 says PUS-C implements CUC with 1 to 4 coarse octets and 1 to 10 fine octets, where CCSDS 301.0-B-4 allows up to 7 coarse octets.19 PFC 17, for example, is 4 coarse and 2 fine octets, the format Solar Orbiter uses (section 10). The full catalogue is on PUS parameter types.

docs.title: 6. TC[9,1] set the time report generation rate
docs.text:
The time reporting control subservice exists for missions whose time correlation accuracy needs vary.2 Its single request:1012

  • contains exactly one instruction, with one argument: the rate exponential value, where rate = \(2^{\text{rate exponential value}}\);
  • is rejected, with a failed start of execution notification, if the rate is invalid (not one of the supported rates);
  • otherwise sets the rate used by the time reporting subservice.

The subservice's only observable is the current time report generation rate.10

Field PUS-C type Meaning rate exponential value unsigned integer 0 to 8 (1 to 256 frames), limited to the declared supported rates

PUS-A calls the request "Change Time Report Generation Rate (9,1)" and fixes the field as a 1-octet unsigned integer in the range 0 to 8.27

docs.title: 7. Capability sets
docs.text:
Edition Message Capability PUS-C TM[9,2] CUC time report exactly one of TM[9,2] / TM[9,3] is "minimum"; each is "by declaration"13 PUS-C TM[9,3] CDS time report (see above)13 PUS-C TC[9,1] set the time report generation rate minimum for the time reporting control subservice13 PUS-A (9,2) Time Report minimum capability set of the time reporting sub-service, provided only by APID 0 (Table 21)28 PUS-A (9,1) Change Time Report Generation Rate minimum set of the optional rate control sub-service, which requires time reporting (Table 20)28

PUS-A adds that sending the time packet to the ground is enabled and disabled with the packet forwarding control service, and that there are no additional capability sets.28

docs.title: 8. Edition differences
docs.text:
PUS-A (2003) and annex CPUS-C (2016)Rev.1 DIR1 (2024 draft)

PUS-A clause 13 defines the two sub-services. The rate control sub-service maintains one of the rates 1 to 256 and passes it to the time reporting sub-service, which samples the "satellite time reference" (a free-running counter from a given epoch) at VC 0 frame count 0 and every frame where the count modulo the rate is 0, downlinks it before the next sample, and applies a new rate from the next qualifying frame.26 The Time Report (9,2) holds an optional 1-octet Rate (omitted if the rate is fixed), the Satellite Time in CUC only, with an implicit or explicit P-field (implicit value: the mission constant <MISSION_TIME_CODE>), and an optional Status whose type and values are not specified.27

Annex C, transcribed from ESA PSS-04-106, details the older ESA scheme:29303132

  • the on-board reference is "Spacecraft Elapsed Time", a free-running counter from an arbitrary epoch, in TAI seconds, coded CUC with 1 to 4 coarse and 0 to 3 fine octets (P-field 0010 followed by the octet counts);
  • the standard time source packet has APID all zeros and no data field header; its first data octet carries the sampling rate in bits 4 to 7 (0000 = 1 frame to 1000 = 256 frames), then the P-field and T-field, then mission-defined time-system parameters such as fixed on-board delays;
  • the ground time-tags, in CDS-coded UTC, the reception of the first ASM bit of the VC 0 frame with count 0, extracts the CUC sample from the time packet, and thereby correlates elapsed time with UTC.

PUS-C keeps the frame-count sampling rule and the APID 0 packet, and adds:24512

  • the CDS report TM[9,3] next to the CUC report TM[9,2];
  • the rate as an explicit rate exponential value in TC[9,1] and, optionally, in the report;
  • the spacecraft time reference status, optional in the report and present in every TM secondary header;
  • declared sampling and timing accuracies;
  • formal rejection of TC[9,1] with a failed start of execution notification.

The draft grows ST[09] to four subservices:3334

  • time reporting and time reporting control, as in PUS-C; the time reporting subservice is now described as hosted by the application that provides the spacecraft time reference from the on-board clock (still APID 0);
  • time control: at least one per service, hosted by the process maintaining the reference time and by every on-board user that receives distributed time. TC[9,4] sets the reference time to an absolute time, TC[9,5] adds a signed relative offset; both may carry an optional time reference status whose processing is application-specific;3739
  • time distribution: at most one per service. TC[9,6] starts a one-shot (interval 0) or periodic (interval in seconds) distribution to N application processes; TC[9,7] stops it. The distributed time can travel in a TC[9,4] packet or any other on-board means; the observable is each periodic distribution's period.3839

It also requires the time reference and its status to be accessible on board by all services (6.9.3g).36 The draft "may not be referred to as an ECSS Standard until published as such" (see PUS-A vs PUS-C).35

docs.title: 9.1 What SCOS-2000 does with time reports
docs.text:
The SCOS-2000 Database Import ICD lists service 9 among the services with specific ground processing: time report packets feed the time correlation function, which builds time couples (an on-board time and the corresponding UTC). Support for both free-running and synchronized clocks is available from SCOS-2000 R5.2; before that, time correlation was a mission-specific function. One limitation matters operationally: SCOS-2000 does not automatically update its ground parameters when a TC(9,1) succeeds.40

Inference

Because the ground's frame-matching rule depends on the rate (section 9.2), a rate change by TC(9,1) presumably has to be mirrored in the ground configuration by the operators. The ICD states only the absence of the automatic update.4049

docs.title: 9.2 From a time report to a time couple
docs.text:
The SCOS-2000 time correlation technical note (EGOS-MCS-S2K-TN-1030) describes the mechanism. The spacecraft samples its clock when a frame whose counter is a multiple of \(N\) (a power of 2 from 1 to 256) is transmitted, and sends the sample in a later frame; knowing \(N\), the ground identifies the triggering frame and takes its Earth reception time (ERT) from the NIS header.44 It then removes the delays:4447

\[ \text{FTT} = \text{ERT} - \text{ground delay} - \text{propagation delay} - \text{on-board processing (radiation) delay} \] \[ \text{OLT} = \text{FTT} + \text{on-board latching delay} \]

FTT is the frame transmission time, when the frame generator starts the frame and requests the clock sample; OLT is the OBT latching time, when the sample is actually latched. The pair (OBT in the time report, OLT in UTC) is the time couple. For SLE service providers the ground delay is zero by definition, because the provider already corrects the ERT.47 Because the time packet arrives in a later frame, the packetiser opens a configurable window after each triggering frame; a time packet outside the window is ignored (the "plausibility check", bounded by the MISCdynamic variables TCO_FAR_FTT_PLAUSIBILITY_LIMIT and TCO_CLOSE_FTT_PLAUSIBILITY_LIMIT).4449

A time couple (illustrative numbers)

Quantity Value ERT of the triggering VC 0 frame 12:10:00.250 000 UTC ground delay 0.000 120 s propagation delay (one-way light time) 480.000 000 s on-board frame radiation delay 0.000 050 s on-board latching delay 0.000 010 s FTT = ERT - 0.000 120 - 480 - 0.000 050 12:02:00.249 830 UTC OLT = FTT + 0.000 010 12:02:00.249 840 UTC OBT in the time report 811 339 200.5 s (CUC)

The couple is (811 339 200.5, 12:02:00.249 840). The formulas are from TN-1030; the numbers are invented by this wiki.44

docs.title: 9.3 Coefficients, accuracy and validity
docs.text:
From the couples the time correlation server computes the coefficients of a linear OBT-to-UTC relation, expressed relative to the last couple used (\(\text{UTC}_N\), \(\text{OBT}_N\)) for resolution:4543

Clock type Method Relation free-running least-squares fit over a set of couples (gradient and offset) \(\text{UTC(OBT)} = \text{UTC}_N + \text{Gradient}\,(\text{OBT} - \text{OBT}_N) + \text{Offset}\) synchronized (e.g. GPS) difference, one couple suffices (gradient 1) \(\text{UTC(OBT)} = \text{UTC}_N + \text{OBT} - \text{OBT}_N - \text{Offset}\)

The two methods can be switched at run time.48 Every new couple is checked: the deviation is the difference between the couple's UTC and the UTC computed from its OBT with the current coefficients. Against two configurable limits (accuracy, the tighter, and validity) the coefficients are "valid and accurate", "valid and inaccurate" or "invalid and inaccurate". For synchronized clocks a separate synchronization status compares the computed offset with the expected offset of the time source (for example the GPS-UTC leap-second offset).4448

stateDiagram-v2
  VA: Valid, accurate
  VI: Valid, inaccurate
  II: Invalid, inaccurate
  VA --> VI: couple with deviation above the accuracy limit
  VA --> II: deviation above the validity limit, or reset
  VI --> II: deviation above the validity limit, or reset
  VI --> VA: new coefficients computed and committed
  II --> VA: new coefficients computed and committed

The state machine is TN-1030 Figure 6.48 In automatic mode the system recalculates the coefficients from the latest couples when the deviation grows, and after a configurable number of consecutive invalid deviations (TCO_AUTORESET_INVALID_DEVIATIONS) it resets: the couple buffer is emptied and a new correlation is computed once two new time reports have been received.49

Inference: two triggers for the automatic update

TN-1030 states the automatic recalculation trigger in two ways. Section 4, section 6.2 and the summary at the end of the engine description say it happens when the deviation exceeds half the accuracy limit (section 6.2 writes "accuracy" for "deviation"). Step 6 of the engine description states the condition as a deviation within the validity interval but above the accuracy interval.444849 The available sources do not say which one the software implements.

The full SCOS-2000 design (TCO engine, client library, coefficient packets) is on Time correlation in SCOS-2000.

docs.title: 10.1 The on-board time
docs.text: In Solar Orbiter's packet structure ICD, service 9 carries the mnemonic M: a user must implement the service.5051 The on-board computer (OBC) maintains the On Board Time (OBT), normally synchronized with a controlled oscillator, from which clock signals and a PPS (pulse per second) signal are distributed. The mission's zero time reference is 00:00 on 1 January 2000. The OBT is CUC with 4 coarse octets and 2 fine octets; it starts at 0 at OBC power-up, is set to real time with the private TC(9,128) "Set OBT", and is maintained in the OBC processor module and in two TTR boards.52 Every TM data field header carries the packet time in the same CUC 4+2 format (PTC 9, PFC 17).57

docs.title: 10.2 The time packet
docs.text:
The standard spacecraft time source packet has the name and layout of PUS-A annex C: APID 0, no data field header, 8 octets of data (packet length C = 7), and a T-field referred to the first ASM bit of the VC 0 frame with frame count 0. The annex does not restate the other multiples of the rate; TC(9,1) sets the rate.5853 The TM(9,2) definition gives process ID 0 and packet category 0, the category that the ICD reserves for the service 9 time packet.5360

The layout is from the ICD (annex 4 and TM(9,2), where the Rate is a 1-octet enumerated "S-field" and the OBT is 6 octets).5853 In the MIB the packet is SPID 9999 "Time Report": type 9, subtype 2, APID 0, PID_TPSD = -1 (a fixed packet), PID_DFHSIZE = 6 and PID_TIME = Y; the tpcf record names it YCD00902 with a size of 14 octets. Its plf entries extract three parameters:61

Octet Parameter Description PTC/PFC Calibration 6 NCD09021 OBCHP_Time Rep S-Field 2/8 textual CCDT0043TX: 0 = EVERY_TMFR ... 8 = EVERY_256_TMFR 7 NCD09022 OBCHP_Time Rep P-Field ¾ none 8 NCD09023 OBCHP_OBT 9/17 none; PCF_CORR blank, so the ICD default Y (correlate) applies

Inference

The S-field occupies a whole octet but its upper 4 bits are always zero, so reading it as an 8-bit enumerated value gives the same 0 to 8 as the PUS-A bit 4-7 code. PID_DFHSIZE = 6 equals the 6-octet primary header, consistent with a packet without a data field header, but the ICD says the field is irrelevant for fixed packets (PID_TPSD = -1). What locates the parameters is plf: its offsets count from the start of the packet header, so octet 6 is the first data octet.614142

Decoding a complete Solar Orbiter time packet (illustrative bytes)

00 00 C3 4A 00 07 05 2E 30 5C 0D C0 80 00

Octets Field Value 00 00 version 0, type 0, no secondary header, APID 0 time packet C3 4A sequence flags 0b11, count 842 (illustrative) 00 07 data length C = 7 8 data octets 05 S-field: rate code 5 every 32 VC 0 frames (EVERY_32_TMFR) 2E P-field 0 010 11 10 CUC, agency epoch, 4 coarse, 2 fine 30 5C 0D C0 coarse 811 339 200 s 80 00 fine 0.5 s

The OBT is 811 339 200.5 s after the zero reference, nominally 2025-09-16 12:00:00.5. That is not UTC: SCOS-2000 applies the correlation of section 9 to obtain it. The bytes are constructed by this wiki.5852

docs.title: 10.3 Commands, then and now
docs.text:
The ICD defines one standard and four private telecommands:5153545556

Message Name Application data TC(9,1) Change Time Report Generation Rate Rate, 1-octet unsigned, 0 to 8: once every \(2^{\text{Rate}}\) VC 0 frames TC(9,128) Set OBT Action (1 octet: 0 = set absolute value, 1 = add delta, 2 = subtract delta), OBT seconds (4 octets), OBT subseconds (2 octets, "n/a if action = 0") TC(9,129) Accept Time Synchronisation OBT at the next synchronization signal, CUC, 6 octets with the fine part zero TC(9,130) Start Time Synchronisation to User PID of the user (1 octet; SSMM, STR or payload), Period (1 octet: 0 = one-shot, 1 to 255 s) TC(9,131) Stop Time Synchronisation to User PID (1 octet)

TC(9,129) is the interesting one. The CSW does not execute it: it generates it and sends it to other packet terminals (for example the solid-state mass memory) at the frequency set by TC(9,130). The time it carries is that of the next synchronization signal the addressee will see: the PPS, the MIL-STD-1553 bus major frame synchronization, or a SpaceWire time code.55 It is the only service 9 message with an entry in all four software columns of the summary table: X (shall be implemented) for the CSW, SSMM and STR software, and M for payload software.5051

Inference

Solar Orbiter's private TC(9,128), TC(9,129)/(9,130) and TC(9,131) cover the same ground as the time control (TC[9,4], TC[9,5]) and time distribution (TC[9,6], TC[9,7]) subservices that the 2024 Rev.1 draft standardizes: a one-shot or periodic distribution to named application processes, with interval 0 meaning one-shot.3955 The available sources do not say whether the draft was inspired by such mission practice.

The two MIB releases differ markedly here:6162

Subtype 2020-04-16 release 2025-09-16 release 1 ZCD00901 ZCD00901 (APID 172, parameter PCD09011, 2/8, calibration CCDT0043TX) 128 ZCD00980 "Set OBT" (action + 9/17 time), ZCD2Z01R add and ZCD2Z01S subtract (fixed action + 10/17 relative time), ZCD2Z01T absolute (32-bit seconds + 16-bit fixed zero) none 129 11 commands, one per user: ZSM00045/46/47 (SSMM), ZIX09129 (STIX), ZIA58057 (SWA), ... none 130 ZCD00982, ZCD2Z00U ("to SSMM": fixed PID OP_SSMM, period 0) unchanged 131 ZCD00983 unchanged

The PID parameter of TC(9,130) and TC(9,131) (PCD09821, calibration CCDT0130TC) lists the 7-bit process IDs of the ICD's APID annex: OP_SSMM = 30, SSMM_DEBUG_A/B = 31/32, STAR_TRACKER_A/B = 40/41, PLOAD_BCAST = 49 and the payload process IDs 50 to 104.6159 The SWA instrument database still contains its own TC(9,129) "SWA_TC_ACC_TIME" with the time split into COARSE_TIME (PTC 9, PFC 15) and FINE_TIME (PTC 3, PFC 12).63

Inference

Why the 2025 release drops TC(9,128) and all TC(9,129) commands is not stated in the available sources. One fact points to a deliberate removal of the command definitions only: the 2025 release still contains the TC(9,128) command parameters PCD09801, PCD09802 and PCD2Z05D and the action calibration CCDT0044TC, but no ccf, cdf or sequence entry uses them.61 For TC(9,129) a plausible reason is that the CSW, not the ground, generates it. For TC(9,128) the definitions may have moved to a restricted database, but this is speculation.

docs.title: 10.4 Ground-generated time correlation packets
docs.text:
The Solar Orbiter MIB also describes the packets SCOS-2000 itself generates for time correlation, on APID 1966 with service type 164:61

SPID Description Main fields (offset in octets) 66840 Time Correlation Report period from/to (PTC 9, PFC 30, Unix time), packets received, bit rate, offset, gradient, standard deviation and error, deviation 66841 TCO Time_Couples OBT OBT (16), OBT latching time (24), frame transmission time (36), Earth reception time (48), light time delay (60), on-board frame radiation delay (68), ground station delay (76), ground station ID (84), deviation (88), frame counters (96, 97), OBT size (98), raw OBT 9/17 (99) 66842 TCO_Coefficients OBT validity (16), accuracy (17), gradient (18), offset (26), OBT_N (34), UTC_N (42), standard deviation (50), standard error (58)

The time couple packet carries most of the quantities of the TN-1030 time couple packet (OBT, OLT, FTT, ERT, light time delay, radiation delay, ground station delay and ID, deviation), plus frame counters and the raw OBT. TN-1030's Table 1 also has an 8-octet OBT latching delay between the radiation delay and the ground station delay. The Solar Orbiter definition has no such field: its ground station delay starts at octet 76, which is where the latching delay would be (TN-1030 offset 60 plus the 16 octets that the MIB offsets of SPIDs 66840 to 66842 start from, PID_DFHSIZE = 16).4661

docs.title: ST[11] Time-based scheduling
docs.text:
A spacecraft is not always reachable from the ground: a low Earth orbiter sees a ground station only part of the time, and a deep-space probe suffers long signal propagation delays. The time-based scheduling service (service type 11) lets the ground load telecommands in advance, each with a release time, into an on-board time-based schedule; the service releases each request to its destination application process when its time comes.143 ESA ground systems call these execution time-tagged commands, and the Solar Orbiter project calls its schedule the Mission Timeline (MTL).7084 This page describes the PUS-C service (ECSS-E-ST-70-41C, 2016) in full: its model, every one of its 27 message types, the filters and the capability sets. It then covers the PUS-A predecessor ("on-board operations scheduling", with interlocks and relative times), the 2024 Rev.1 draft, how SCOS-2000 builds and models TC(11,4) commands, and how Solar Orbiter uses the service, with data from its real MIB.

At a glance

docs.title: 1.1 The scheduled activity
docs.text: The schedule holds scheduled activities. Each consists of scheduling data (the release time and, if supported, a sub-schedule identifier and a group identifier) and the request to release later. An activity is identified by the identifier of its request.2 A PUS request identifier combines the source identifier of the issuer, the destination (APID of the executing process plus a system identifier) and the packet sequence count; in a TC packet these are the source ID field of the secondary header and the APID and sequence count of the primary header.37

docs.title: 1.2 An extension of ground control
docs.text: PUS-C describes the service as an extension of ground monitoring and control. A released request is executed as if it had come straight from its original source: the executing process sends its verification reports, if any, to the source identified in the request, not to the scheduler. The release of a request does not depend on the success or failure of earlier released requests.24 The schedule is therefore open-loop. This differs from PUS-A, whose optional interlocks let a release depend on the outcome of an earlier command (section 7).43

docs.title: 1.3 Sub-schedules and groups
docs.text:
Two optional grouping concepts organise the schedule:2

Sub-schedule Group Purpose one coherent on-board operation a spacecraft entity, for example one instrument or a software item Creation automatically, when an insert request names an unknown sub-schedule (created disabled) explicitly, by TC[11,22], with an initial status Deletion automatically, when its last activity is released or deleted; also by reset explicitly, by TC[11,23], only when empty Can exist empty? no yes Control enable or disable by TC[11,20] / TC[11,21] enable or disable by TC[11,24] / TC[11,25] Status report TC[11,18] gives TM[11,19] TC[11,26] gives TM[11,27]

Groups let operations disable, for example, all activities of one instrument when the conditions for their execution are not met, independently of the application processes and sub-schedules the activities belong to.2 The PUS-C working group presented the service with exactly these two concepts at ADCSS 2015, as one of three services resulting from a complete re-assessment of the PUS-A scheduling service. The other two were then called "telecommand sequencing" (ST21) and "orbit-based scheduling" (ST22); PUS-C publishes them as ST[21] request sequencing and ST[22] position-based scheduling.6942

docs.title: 1.4 Operational requirements behind the service
docs.text:
The space segment operability standard ECSS-E-ST-70-11C Rev.1 defines an on-board operations schedule as an on-board facility that stores and releases telecommands loaded in advance, and asks, among others, that:6768

  • any telecommand can be loaded into the schedule (5.8.5a);
  • the schedule content can be changed both while the execution function is enabled and while it is disabled (5.8.5b, c);
  • its capacity covers at least the autonomy period (5.8.5d);
  • the transfer delay to the destination process is predictable, and transfer errors are reported to the ground and to the schedule service (5.8.5e to g);
  • a telecommand with the same release tag as one already loaded is not rejected but released immediately after it (5.8.5h);
  • telecommands that "elapsed" while their schedule, sub-schedule or application process was disabled are not released when it is re-enabled (5.8.5i).

docs.title: 2. Service layout and accessibility
docs.text: Each time-based scheduling service contains at least one subservice, and each application process hosts at most one provider.3 The mission declares the list of application processes the subservice may release requests to; all requests of an addressable process can be scheduled, and the hosting process is addressable by nature. A released request is processed by the service named by its service type in the destination process.4

The subservice must expose four observables: the execution function status, the current number of scheduled activities, and, if supported, the current numbers of sub-schedules and of groups.27

docs.title: 4.1 The three statuses
docs.text: The subservice keeps a time-based schedule execution function status (enabled or disabled), set to "disabled" when the subservice starts; one sub-schedule status per sub-schedule; and one group status per group.71316

docs.title: 4.2 Releasing activities
docs.text:
The execution process handles activities in the order of their release times. An activity is disabled if the execution function is disabled, or its sub-schedule is disabled, or its group is disabled. When an activity's release time is reached, the process, in sequence: releases the request if the activity is not disabled; deletes the activity; and deletes the sub-schedule if that was its last activity.12

flowchart TD
  T["Release time of the next activity reached"] --> D{"Execution function enabled<br/>AND sub-schedule enabled (if any)<br/>AND group enabled (if any)?"}
  D -- yes --> R["Release the request to its destination<br/>(verification reports go to the original source)"]
  D -- no --> X["Do not release"]
  R --> DEL["Delete the scheduled activity"]
  X --> DEL
  DEL --> L{"Last activity of its sub-schedule?"}
  L -- yes --> DS["Delete the sub-schedule"]
  L -- no --> N["Next activity"]
  DS --> N

The flowchart restates clause 6.11.4.6.12 Three consequences are worth spelling out. First, a disabled activity is lost, not postponed: disabling the schedule over a release time discards what falls due. Second, PUS-C prescribes no notification to the ground when an activity is deleted without release. Third, PUS-C does not prescribe the release order of activities with exactly the same time.12 The operability standard and the 2024 draft both fill that last gap with "insertion order" (sections 1.4 and 9).6864

docs.title: 5.2 Controlling the schedule: TC[11,1], TC[11,2], TC[11,3]
docs.text: These three requests have no application data.28 Enable and disable set the execution function status; neither depends on whether the schedule contains activities.8 Reset is accepted whatever the execution status, and in sequence sets the status to "disabled", deletes all activities, deletes all sub-schedules (if supported) and enables all groups (if supported).9

docs.title: 5.3 Inserting: TC[11,4]
docs.text:
Field Type Presence Meaning sub-schedule ID enumerated if sub-schedules are supported one sub-schedule for the whole request N unsigned integer always number of instructions group ID enumerated repeated N times; if groups are supported group of this activity release time absolute time repeated N times when to release request TC packet repeated N times the complete telecommand packet to release

The layout is PUS-C Figure 8-91.28 The processing rules are:1011

  • The request is rejected as a whole (failed start of execution) only if it would create a new sub-schedule while the maximum number of sub-schedules is already reached.
  • Each instruction is rejected individually, with its own failed start of execution notification, if the schedule is full, if its release time is earlier than now + time margin, if it names an unknown group, or if the embedded request fails the declared verification checks.
  • Valid instructions are processed regardless of faulty ones in the same request.
  • If the named sub-schedule is unknown, it is created with status "disabled"; each valid instruction then creates an activity with its request, release time, sub-schedule and group.

Inference

PUS-C fixes the field types of Figure 8-91, not their widths. The 8, 8, 8 and 40-bit widths and the 64-bit placeholder for the embedded packet are illustrative. Section 11 shows the real Solar Orbiter layout.

The filter semantics differ subtly: an unknown sub-schedule is silently ignored by delete and report filters, but makes a time-shift filter fail.2325 A reasonable reading is that a time-shift that silently skips a mistyped sub-schedule would leave the schedule inconsistent, whereas deleting or reporting nothing is harmless; the standard gives no rationale.
