docs.title: ST[13] Large packet transfer
docs.text:
A space packet may be up to 65 542 octets long, but real spacecraft impose much smaller limits on the packets they exchange with the ground.1 Some requests (a large memory load, a file) and some reports (a big table dump) do not fit. The large packet transfer service type, ST[13] of the Packet Utilization Standard, splits such a "large packet" into smaller parts, carries each part in an ordinary TM or TC packet, and rebuilds the large packet at the other end. The services that produce and consume the large packets need not know that this happened.2 Abbreviations are expanded in the glossary.

At a glance

Item Value Service type 134 Subservices (PUS-C) large packet downlink, large packet uplink; at least one, at most one of each5 Messages (PUS-C) TM[13,1]-[13,3] downlink parts, TC[13,9]-[13,11] uplink parts, TM[13,16] uplink abortion report - all "minimum"18 Size limit packets up to the CCSDS maximum (about 65 KB); no retransmission23 Accessible from any other service (like event reporting)6 PUS-A (2003) clause 16 "Large data transfer service", subtypes 1-16, with acknowledgement, sliding window and retransmission24 Solar Orbiter service 13 used as a file transfer: uplink to CSW partitions (subtypes 9-11, 13-16 and 128; no 12), downlink from the SSMM (subtypes 129-153)34

docs.title: Why the service exists
docs.text: Ground-to-space protocols usually cap the TM and TC packet lengths below the CCSDS maximum, so a large request can exceed the mission's maximum telecommand packet length and a large report the maximum telemetry packet length.2 Solar Orbiter is a concrete case: a telecommand packet data field holds at most 242 octets (236 of application data) and a telemetry packet at most 4 112 octets.3536 By principle, the sources and destinations of large packets are not supposed to know about these link constraints.2

docs.title: From PUS-A to PUS-C
docs.text:
PUS-A had a complete transfer protocol (described below). During the PUS-C revision the working group weighed standardising PUS-A service 13 with or without its "extended packets", a new service 24 limited to 65 KB packets with or without retransmission, both, or leaving the problem to the lower layers.22 The final standard kept number 13 for what the 2015 status presentation calls a simplification of PUS-A large data transfer that only uploads and downloads CCSDS packets of at most 65 KB, without retransmission.23 Recovering lost parts is left to the space link (for example COP-1 on the uplink); bulk file movement belongs to ST[23] file management and CFDP.

Inference

The pointers to COP-1, ST[23] and CFDP are this wiki's reading of where the removed functions now live; clause 6.13 itself does not name them.

docs.title: Service layout
docs.text:
• Each large packet transfer service contains at least one of the two subservices and at most one of each.5
  • Each provider is hosted by exactly one application process, and an application process hosts at most one provider; when both subservices exist, the on-board downlink sending entity and the on-board uplink receiving entity live in the same application process.5
  • The foundation model makes large packet transfer, like event reporting, accessible to every other service.6

Each subservice has two entities, one on board and one on the ground:

Subservice Sending entity Receiving entity Large packet downlink on board: splits the large packet, wraps each part in a "downlink part report", downlinks them ground: collects the part reports, rebuilds the packet, delivers it to its destination Large packet uplink ground: splits the large packet, wraps each part in an "uplink part request", uplinks them on board: collects the part requests, rebuilds the packet, delivers it to its destination

Source: §6.13.1.2-6.13.1.3.23

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Item Meaning Maximum concurrent downlinks how many large packets can be in transit at once Downlink maximum part size size of each part; bounded by the packet data field of a maximum-length TM packet Downlink reception timeout longest wait allowed between two successive part reports at the receiving end Resources resources given to the sending entity, declared with the spacecraft architecture

Sources: §6.13.3.1-6.13.3.2.7

docs.title: Sending: splitting into part reports
docs.text: For each large packet the on-board sending entity assigns a unique large message transaction identifier, splits the packet into parts, numbers the parts with a part sequence number starting at 1, and wraps each part in one report: TM[13,1] for the first part, TM[13,2] for intermediate parts and TM[13,3] for the last part. All parts have the downlink maximum part size except the last, which may be shorter. Part reports go out in increasing sequence number at the highest frequency the operational constraints allow, to a ground application process declared in the space-to-ground architecture.8 The standard assumes large packets are not duplicated on board and leaves the hand-over between the source service and ST[13] out of scope.8

docs.title: Receiving: reconstruction on the ground
docs.text:
The ground receiving entity starts a downlink operation on the first part, restarts a reception timer after every successful first or intermediate part, adds each part to the reconstruction, and ends the operation with the last part. If the timer reaches the reception timeout the operation is aborted. When all parts arrived, the large packet is generated for routing to its destination; the receiving entity does not check the large packet's checksum. If the operation was aborted or completed with parts missing, the ground monitoring and control system is notified of the abortion and the missing parts, and the packet and its parts are discarded.9

sequenceDiagram
    participant SRC as On-board source service
    participant S13 as ST[13] downlink sending entity
    participant G as Ground receiving entity
    participant DST as Ground destination
    SRC->>S13: large packet (L octets)
    S13->>S13: transaction ID t, parts 1..n of size P (last <= P)
    S13->>G: TM[13,1] (t, 1, part 1)
    Note over G: start reception timer
    loop parts 2 .. n-1
        S13->>G: TM[13,2] (t, k, part k)
        Note over G: restart timer
    end
    S13->>G: TM[13,3] (t, n, last part)
    G->>DST: rebuilt large packet
    Note over G: on timeout or missing parts, notify the monitoring and control system and discard

The diagram restates §6.13.3.3.89 The observables of the on-board downlink subservice are the number of on-going downlinks and the list of their transaction identifiers.10

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: The uplink mirrors the downlink: a declared maximum number of concurrent uplinks, an uplink maximum part size (the user data space of a maximum-length TC packet), an uplink reception timeout between two part requests, and declared on-board resources.11

docs.title: Sending: uplink part requests
docs.text: The ground sending entity assigns a transaction identifier, numbers the parts from 1, wraps them in TC[13,9] (first), TC[13,10] (intermediate) and TC[13,11] (last) and sends them in increasing order to the on-board application process that hosts the receiving entity.12

docs.title: Receiving: on-board reconstruction and abortion
docs.text:
The on-board receiving entity starts the uplink operation on the first part, restarts its timer after the first and each intermediate part, ends on the last part, and aborts on timeout or when it detects a discontinuity in the sequence. A successful uplink generates the large packet for routing to its destination (again without checking its checksum). An aborted uplink produces one large packet uplink abortion notification with the reason, reported in a TM[13,16] large packet uplink abortion report, and the packet and its parts are discarded.1314 The observables are the number of on-going uplinks and their transaction identifiers.15

stateDiagram-v2
  state "idle" as IDLE
  state "receiving (timer running)" as RX
  [*] --> IDLE
  IDLE --> RX : TC[13,9] first part
  RX --> RX : TC[13,10] next part in sequence (restart timer)
  RX --> IDLE : TC[13,11] last part - rebuild and route the large packet
  RX --> IDLE : timeout - TM[13,16], discard
  RX --> IDLE : sequence discontinuity - TM[13,16], discard

One state machine runs per transaction identifier, up to the declared number of concurrent uplinks.1113

Inference

The standard does not say what the receiving entity does with a TC[13,10] or TC[13,11] whose transaction identifier is unknown, nor how a duplicated part is treated; a repeated sequence number is presumably a "discontinuity".

docs.title: Message types and data fields (PUS-C)
docs.text:
Message Name Fields TM[13,1] first downlink part report large message transaction identifier (unsigned integer), part sequence number (unsigned integer), part (fixed octet-string) TM[13,2] intermediate downlink part report same as TM[13,1] TM[13,3] last downlink part report same, but the part is a fixed octet-string of deduced size (from the packet length) TC[13,9] uplink the first part transaction identifier, part sequence number, part (fixed octet-string) TC[13,10] uplink an intermediate part same as TC[13,9] TC[13,11] uplink the last part same, last part of deduced size TM[13,16] large packet uplink abortion report transaction identifier (unsigned integer), failure reason (enumerated)

Sources: §8.13.2, Figures 8-140 to 8-146.1617 The widths of the identifier and sequence number fields, and the values of the failure reason, are not stated in the available sources; they are left to the mission. Every message type is "minimum" for its subservice in Annex C.18

Worked example (illustrative values)

A mission whose largest TM packet leaves 1 000 octets for the part (the downlink maximum part size P) has to downlink a 9 500-octet large packet. It needs \(n = \lceil 9500 / 1000 \rceil = 10\) parts: TM[13,1] with sequence number 1, TM[13,2] with 2 to 9, and TM[13,3] with 10 carrying the remaining 500 octets. The receiving entity knows the last part's size from the TM packet length.816

docs.title: The 2024 Rev.1 draft
docs.text: A comparison by this wiki of clause 6.13 and of §8.13 in the Rev.1 DIR1 draft with the 2016 issue found no change other than renumbered figures (8.13-1 to 8.13-7); Annex C lists the same message types with the same "minimum" applicability.192021

docs.title: PUS-A (ECSS-E-70-41A, 2003)
docs.text: The PUS-A large data transfer service was a supporting service, used by the ground or other services to move large service data units in a controlled way, avoiding service-specific solutions. Its examples were reporting a command schedule bigger than one packet and loading a large memory area with size-limited telecommands.24 It aimed at three properties: knowing when a transfer is complete, re-transmitting only the lost or erroneous parts, and delivering the parts in order and without duplicates.24

docs.title: The service data unit
docs.text:
The unit passed to the service was a TM or TC packet or an extended packet, whose data field could exceed the 65 535-octet limit; an extended packet had the same structure but its packet length field set to 0.26

Field Type Meaning Unit Type enumerated 0 = standard packet, 1 = extended packet Packet Header 6 octets standard primary header (length 0 if extended) Data Field Header deduced TM or TC data field header Packet Data any source data of a large report or application data of a large request

A Large Data Unit ID distinguished overlapping transfers from or to the same application process. Parts had a fixed part size, smaller than the maximum data field, except possibly the last.2526

docs.title: The protocol
docs.text:
• Sliding window (optional): the sender may run ahead of the last acknowledged part by at most "window size" parts; several window sizes may be used, for example a large one for memory management. Without a window, parts are sent at the highest rate allowed.27
  • The receiver tracks the last successfully received part (no gaps before it) and acknowledges it at the window boundary, or only at the end without a window; the final acknowledgement is sent only once the destination has the whole unit.27
  • Acknowledgement timer at the sender after the last part of a window or of the unit, and a reception timer at the receiver after each first or intermediate part; expiry on either side fails the transfer.27
  • Erroneous or missing parts form the set of failed parts, reported to the sender (at the window boundary when a window is used) and re-transmitted with the same sequence number.27
  • Either end, or the ground, may abort at any time.27
Subtype Direction Name Role (13,1) / (13,2) / (13,3) TM First / Intermediate / Last Downlink Part Report downlink parts (13,4) TM Downlink Abort Report sender (on board) aborted (13,5) TC Downlink Reception Acknowledgement ground acknowledges up to a part (13,6) TC Repeat Parts ground lists failed parts (13,7) TM Repeated Part Report re-sent part (13,8) TC Abort Downlink receiver (ground) aborts (13,9) / (13,10) / (13,11) TC Accept First / Intermediate / Last Uplink Part uplink parts (13,12) TC Accept Repeated Part re-sent part (13,13) TC Abort Reception of Uplinked Data sender (ground) aborts (13,14) TM Uplink Reception Acknowledgement Report on board acknowledges up to a part (13,15) TM Unsuccessfully Received Parts Report on board lists failed parts (13,16) TM Reception Abort Report receiver (on board) aborted

Sources: §16.3.28293031 Every downlink request has an uplink report of identical structure and vice versa.28 The part messages carry an optional Large Data Unit ID (omitted when only one transfer at a time is supported), a sequence number starting at 1 and the part; the abort messages carry the unit ID and a mission-specific reason code; the acknowledgement carries the unit ID and a sequence number; the failed-parts messages carry the unit ID, N and N sequence numbers.283031

Capability sets: the downlink minimum was (13,1)-(13,5) and (13,8); the uplink minimum (13,9)-(13,11), (13,13), (13,14) and (13,16). Selective repeat, (13,6)/(13,7) on the downlink and (13,12)/(13,15) on the uplink, and the sliding window were additional capabilities.3233

Aspect PUS-A large data transfer PUS-C large packet transfer Unit packet or extended packet (beyond 65 535 octets) CCSDS packet only Acknowledgement (13,5) / (13,14) none Retransmission optional selective repeat, sliding window none Aborts both ends, both directions: (13,4), (13,8), (13,13), (13,16) on-board uplink abortion report TM[13,16] only; ground downlink aborts are local Subtypes kept - 1, 2, 3, 9, 10, 11, 16 (same numbers)

Sources: PUS-A clause 16 and PUS-C clause 6.13 and Annex C.262791418

docs.title: Solar Orbiter
docs.text: Solar Orbiter (see How Solar Orbiter uses PUS) uses service 13 to transfer files. The uplink goes from the ground to the Central Software (CSW) of the on-board computer, which stores files in "partitions" of the OBC mass memory or the SafeGuard Memory (SGM). The downlink goes from the Solid State Mass Memory (SSMM) to the ground, with structures specified in the SSMM software TM/TC ICD (SOL.A.TAS.ICD.00001, not in this library).3837

docs.title: Uplink: files into CSW partitions
docs.text:
An uplinked file is split into a first part carrying the SDU header (file characteristics) and the first data, intermediate parts carrying data, and a last part carrying the last data and a checksum (the ICD's overview calls it a CRC). The ICD states that the reception of all parts can be confirmed at the end of a transfer and that retransmission of the relevant parts can be requested after an unsuccessful one, without saying here which side does what.38 Each file has an attribute:39

Attribute Meaning 1 OBCP (on-board control procedure) 2 TC sequence, delayed 3 TC sequence, immediate 4, 5 unused 6 other 7 FAT, internal software use only

Typical uploads are TC files, profiles and ephemerides, and OBCPs; typical downloads are SSMM data files such as science files.39

The rules: the SDU length of TC(13,9) (header plus data) fixes the length of every TC(13,10) SDU; the last part is shorter; and if the data and the 4-octet checksum do not fit, the checksum may go into another TC(13,11). When the attribute is "TC sequence - immediate", the CSW executes the file as a TC sequence once TC(13,11) completes, creating a TC(134,1) with sequence identifier 1 and an execution rate of 1 Hz.404142

Message Content (sizes in octets) Purpose TC(13,13) Abort Reception of Uplinked Data unit ID (1) aborts a session or confirms an on-board autonomous abort reported by TM(13,16) TM(13,14) Uplink Reception Acknowledgement Report unit ID (1), sequence number (2) all parts up to that number received; also reports completion of upload and storage TM(13,15) Unsuccessfully Received Parts Report unit ID (1), N (2), N x sequence number (2) sent after TC(13,11) when parts are missing TM(13,16) Reception Abort Report unit ID (1), reason (4): 0 file manager storage error, 1 checksum error, 2 file transfer time-out session aborted TC(13,128) Change File Transfer Time-out value time-out (4), in seconds private subtype

Sources: §5.14.4-5.14.8.434445

Worked example (derived from the ICD limits)

With the full 236 octets of application data, TC(13,9) has 3 octets of unit ID and sequence number, 13 of SDU header and 220 of file data, so its SDU is 233 octets and every TC(13,10) carries 233 octets of file data. A 10 000-octet file then needs 1 first part (220 octets), 41 intermediate parts (9 553 octets) and 1 last part with the remaining 227 octets plus the 4-octet checksum: 43 telecommands with sequence numbers 1 to 43. This arithmetic is this wiki's, assuming maximum-length commands.354042

Compared with PUS-C, Solar Orbiter keeps the PUS-A uplink half: acknowledgement (13,14), the failed-parts report (13,15) and abort on both sides, with a file header added inside the first part.3431 It does not, however, define PUS-A's TC(13,12) Accept Repeated Part, which PUS-A Table 30 pairs with (13,15); neither the ICD service table nor the MIB has a subtype 12.343353 How the parts listed in a TM(13,15) are re-sent is not stated in the available sources. The ICD service table also lists subtype 128 as a TM ("Change Timeout value"), whereas §5.14.8 and the MIB (ZCD00D80) define it as a telecommand.344553

docs.title: Downlink: SSMM file transfer sessions
docs.text:
The downlink subtypes are all private and implemented only in the SSMM software: start, suspend, resume, terminate and abort a file transfer session (TC(13,129) and 13,131-134), change session parameters, end-of-file-transfer timeout, downlink virtual channel and retransmission limit (13,135-138), report the parameters (13,139/140), and control low-level file transfers (enable/disable, start, suspend, resume, abort, repeat parts, confirm reception, request the end-of-transfer report: 13,141-148), with reports 13,130 and 13,149-153.4634

In the 2025 MIB the SSMM commands (APID 492) show the mechanism: an LLFT is appended or replaced by time window or data volume with a packet store index (ZSM00075, ZSMX0075, ZSMX1075, ZSM00105), and TC(13,146) "SSMM Repeat LLFT Parts" asks for blocks between a start and an end ID - a selective repeat. The reports are SSMM LLFT start and end-of-file-transfer reports, a retransmission-limit report and an EOFT timeout on APID 490, an FTS parameters report on APID 483 and TM(13,152) "SSMM FDU Layout" carrying the session ID, an FDU counter and packet store data words on APID 493.5354 With the ICD's allocation, 490 is the SSMM (PID 30) with category 10, "file transfer, exclusive for service 13 telemetry", and 493 is category 13, listed as spare.47

Inference: FDUs and naming differences

"FDU" is not expanded in the available Solar Orbiter sources; "file data unit" is the ICD title of TM(13,153). The MIB, however, has no TM(13,153): it uses subtype 153 for the TC "SSMM Reset FTS Queue" and carries the FDUs in TM(13,152), which the ICD names "Low-level file transfer abort report". Two other MIB names differ from the ICD titles: subtype 135 is "SSMM Append LLFT" in the MIB but "Change file transfer session parameters" in the ICD, and subtype 142 is "SSMM Replace LLFT" in the MIB but "Start low-level file transfer" in the ICD.46345354 The SSMM ICD (RD9) would settle this.

On the ground the downlinked files become TM files in the mission file archive (FARC), served by EDDS as plain concatenations of TM packets; extracting the packets into the packet archive is not part of the baseline. Event packets with SPID 4000 record each transfer: transaction ID, packet store ID, status (ACTIVE, COMPLETED, INCOMPLETE, INJECTED, ABORTED and others), FDUs received and expected, retransmissions, times and file name.4849

docs.title: Service 13 in the MIB
docs.text:
Commands APID Content ZCD00D09, ZCD00D0A, ZCD00D0B, ZCD00D0D, ZCD00D80 172 (DMS, CSW) TC(13,9), (13,10), (13,11), (13,13), (13,128) 23 SSMM commands, subtypes 129-153 492 (SSMM) file transfer session and LLFT control

Source: ccf; 28 service 13 commands and 9 service 13 packets in both the 2025 and the April 2020 release.5354

The TC(13,9) definition ZCD00D09 fixes the sequence number to 0x0001 and makes the partition and file attribute selectable through text aliases; the file content is a single variable-length octet string (PTC 7, PFC 0), and TC(13,10)/(13,11) have no separate checksum field, so the checksum must be appended to the octet string by whoever builds the commands.55 The ranges allow session IDs 1-255 and sequence numbers 2-65 535 for later parts.55 The reports TM(13,14)-(13,16) are SPIDs 14166-14168 on APID 170, the DMS with category 10, and TM(13,16) decodes the reason through the calibration LDT_FMS_STOR / LDT_CHECKSUM / LDT_TIME_OUT.54

Partition alias (CCDT0192TX) Value Partition alias Value OMM_TC_FILES_A 161 OMM_TC_FILES_B 177 OMM_OBCPS_A 162 OMM_OBCPS_B 178 OMM_S_FILES_A 163 OMM_S_FILES_B 179 OMM_PAYLOAD_A 164 OMM_PAYLOAD_B 180 SGMA_TC_FILES 193 SGM_OBCPS 194 SGMB_TC_FILES 195 File type alias (CCDT0082TX) Value FT_INVALID, FT_OBCP, FT_DEL_TCSEQ, FT_IMM_TCSEQ 0, 1, 2, 3 FT_PL_CTX, FT_PS, FT_PLAIN, FT_FAT 4, 5, 6, 7

Source: paf and pas.55

docs.title: The s13a, s13p and s13t tables
docs.text:
The 2025 MIB release contains three files that are not MIB tables of the SCOS-2000 import ICD: s13a.dat (7 rows), s13p.dat (11 rows) and s13t.dat (12 rows). They are absent from the April 2020 release. No document in this library mentions them; the column names below are therefore generic.5657

s13a (7 rows)s13p (11 rows)s13t (12 rows) COL1 COL2 COL3 COL4 COL5 COL6 PLAIN N 0 0 PAYLOAD PLAIN OBCP O 1 1 OBCP OBCP DEL D 2 2 DEL DELAYED TC IMM I 3 3 IMM IMMEDIATE TC PAYLOAD N 4 4 PAYLOAD PAYLOAD CONTEXT INVALID N 5 5 INVALID INVALID OTHER N 6 6 OTHER OTHER COL1 COL2 COL3 COL4 COL5 COL6 TCFA M 161 161 TCFA OMM TC Files (A) OBCA M 162 162 OBCA OMM OBCPs (A) SYSA B 163 163 SYSA OMM System Files (A) SPRA M 164 164 SPRA OMM Spare (A) TCFB M 177 177 TCFB OMM TC Files (B) OBCB M 178 178 OBCB OMM OBCPs (B) SYSB B 179 179 SYSB OMM System Files (B) SPRB M 180 180 SPRB OMM Spare (B) CSWA N 193 193 CSWA SGM-EEPROM CSW TC Files (A) OBCS N 194 194 OBCS SGM-EEPROM Default OBCPs CSWB N 195 195 CSWB SGM-EEPROM CSW TC Files (B) COL1 COL2 COL3 COL4 COL5 COL6 COL7 UNKNOWN C -2 UNKNOWN Plain file OTHER SYSA OBCP C -1 OBCP OBCP OBCP OBCA SCOS0 - SCOS3 C 0 - 3 UNKNOWN SCOS stack file CSF1 C 4 CSF1 TC sequence (CSF type 1) TCFA CSF2 C 5 CSF2 Time tagged TC sequence (CSF type 2) TCFA CSF3 C 6 CSF3 Backup MTL (CSF type 3) SYSA CSF0 C 7 CSF0 Mixed TC sequence (CSF type 0) TCFA PLAIN W 8 BINARY Plain file ALL W 9 UNKNOWN UNKNOWN

(The four SCOS0-SCOS3 rows, codes 0 to 3, are merged here.)

Inference: what the s13 tables appear to contain

  • s13a = file attributes. COL3 (always equal to COL4) gives the numeric attribute: OBCP 1, delayed TC 2 and immediate TC 3 agree with the ICD's attribute table and with the MIB alias set CCDT0082TX, and payload context 4 agrees with CCDT0082TX.3955 The mnemonics PLAIN, OBCP, DEL, IMM and PAYLOAD match the five values the Solar Orbiter DDID gives for the command-history field s13ObFileAttribute (PLAIN, OBCP, TC_DELAYED, TC_IMMEDIATE, PAYLOAD_CONTEXT).50 The codes for 0, 5 and 6 do not agree: s13a says 0 PLAIN, 5 INVALID, 6 OTHER; CCDT0082TX says 0 FT_INVALID, 5 FT_PS, 6 FT_PLAIN; the ICD says 4-5 unused and 6 other.
  • s13p = destination partitions. COL3 equals the partition values of the TC(13,9) alias set CCDT0192TX, and the descriptions name the OBC mass memory (OMM) sides A and B and the SGM EEPROM.55 The values read naturally in hexadecimal: 0xA1-0xA4 for OMM side A, 0xB1-0xB4 for side B, 0xC1-0xC3 for the SGM.
  • s13t = ground file types. Each row maps a file type to a format tag (COL4), optionally a default attribute (COL6, an s13a COL1 value) and a default partition (COL7, an s13p COL1 value): OBCP files go to OBCA, TC sequence files (CSF types 0-2) to TCFA, the backup MTL (mission timeline) to SYSA.
  • The one-letter codes (s13a COL2 N/O/D/I, s13p COL2 M/B/N, s13t COL2 C/W) and the negative codes in s13t COL3 are not explained by any available source.
  • Taken together, the tables look like configuration for a ground tool that turns files (OBCPs, command sequences, SCOS-2000 command stack files) into service 13 uplinks.

docs.title: Service 13 elsewhere on the ground
docs.text:
The SCOS-2000 import ICD states that SCOS-2000 has no specific support for service 13; a mission-specific uplink implementation exists from Rosetta, and other missions need their own implementation to generate service 13 data units and process the reports.52 The Rosetta, Mars Express and Venus Express data delivery ICD shows the trace this leaves in the command history: a column flags commands encapsulated in a service 13 packet, and commands of an aborted transfer are shown as "ABORTED".51 For Solar Orbiter, the EDDS packet TC report carries s13ObFileId (the file a command was uplinked in) and s13ObFileAttribute.50

SQL used 
-- solo-2025-09-16.sqlite (MIB__20250916M25925PFMS001_SOL)
SELECT CCF_CNAME, CCF_DESCR, CCF_STYPE, CCF_APID, CCF_NPARS
  FROM ccf WHERE CCF_TYPE = '13' ORDER BY CAST(CCF_STYPE AS INT);
SELECT PID_TYPE, PID_STYPE, PID_APID, PID_SPID, PID_DESCR, PID_TPSD
  FROM pid WHERE PID_TYPE = '13';
SELECT c.CDF_ELTYPE, c.CDF_DESCR, c.CDF_ELLEN, c.CDF_BIT, c.CDF_PNAME, c.CDF_VALUE,
       p.CPC_PTC, p.CPC_PFC, p.CPC_CATEG, p.CPC_PAFREF, p.CPC_PRFREF
  FROM cdf c LEFT JOIN cpc p ON p.CPC_NAME = c.CDF_PNAME
 WHERE c.CDF_CNAME IN ('ZCD00D09','ZCD00D0A','ZCD00D0B','ZSM00075','ZSM00125')
 ORDER BY c.CDF_CNAME, CAST(c.CDF_BIT AS INT);
SELECT * FROM pas WHERE PAS_NUMBR IN ('CCDT0192TX','CCDT0082TX');
SELECT * FROM prv WHERE PRV_NUMBR IN ('VCD00176','VCD00248');
SELECT l.PLF_NAME, l.PLF_OFFBY, p.PCF_DESCR, p.PCF_PTC, p.PCF_PFC, p.PCF_CURTX
  FROM plf l JOIN pcf p ON p.PCF_NAME = l.PLF_NAME
 WHERE l.PLF_SPID IN ('14166','14168','80012','80014','80018');
SELECT * FROM txp WHERE TXP_NUMBR = 'CCDT0027TM';
SELECT * FROM s13a; SELECT * FROM s13p; SELECT * FROM s13t;
-- solo-2020-04-16.sqlite (MIB__20200416M10720PFMS001_SOL)
SELECT CCF_TYPE, COUNT(*) FROM ccf WHERE CCF_TYPE = '13' GROUP BY 1;
SELECT PID_TYPE, COUNT(*) FROM pid WHERE PID_TYPE = '13' GROUP BY 1;
SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE name LIKE 's13%';   -- returns nothing

docs.title: ST[14] Real-time forwarding control
docs.text:
Every report an on-board service generates - a verification report, a housekeeping packet, an event - costs processing, on-board network capacity and downlink bandwidth. The real-time forwarding control service type, ST[14] of the Packet Utilization Standard, lets the ground decide which of those reports actually leave the spacecraft in the real-time telemetry channel, per application process, per service type, per report type and, optionally, per housekeeping or diagnostic structure and per event definition.1 Whether the same reports are stored on board is a separate matter, handled by ST[15] on-board storage and retrieval.29 Abbreviations are expanded in the glossary; the PUS-A and PUS-C issues are compared in PUS-A vs PUS-C.

At a glance

Item Value Service type 142 Subservice real-time forwarding control (one), hosted at most once per application process3 Configurations application process forward-control (always); housekeeping, diagnostic and event-blocking forward-control (each by declaration)5 Messages (PUS-C) TC[14,1]-[14,3], [14,5]-[14,7], [14,9]-[14,11], [14,13]-[14,15]; TM[14,4], [14,8], [14,12], [14,16]28 Minimum capability TC[14,1] and TC[14,2]28 Observables none defined23 PUS-A (2003) clause 17 "Packet forwarding control service", subtypes 1-16, enable/disable flags34 Solar Orbiter PUS-A based, hosted by the CSW Data Management System application, real-time VC only, everything enabled by default4252

docs.title: Generation versus forwarding
docs.text:
PUS-A set out the principle: generating telemetry is controlled inside each originating service (for example ST[03] enables or disables a housekeeping structure), but forwarding is a higher-level control, done either by the originating application process (a packet may be generated but not forwarded) or by a centralised application process that receives all packets bound for the ground and routes the downlink.33 PUS-C keeps the idea: a subservice controls reports of its own application process and of the other application processes declared for it, and it knows those application processes but not which service and report types they can produce, so keeping the configuration meaningful is a ground responsibility.46

flowchart LR
  subgraph AP1["Application process A"]
    S3["ST[03] housekeeping<br/>(generation control)"]
    S5["ST[05] events"]
    S1["ST[01] verification"]
  end
  subgraph AP2["Application process B"]
    X["its services"]
  end
  S3 --> F
  S5 --> F
  S1 --> F
  X --> F
  F{"ST[14] real-time<br/>forwarding control"} -->|forwarded| RT["real-time telemetry<br/>(virtual channel to ground)"]
  F -->|blocked| N["not sent in real time"]
  S3 -.-> S15["ST[15] packet selection<br/>(storage, independent)"]

The figure combines PUS-A §4.12 and PUS-C §6.14.1; the independence of ST[15] is stated explicitly in the 2024 draft.33129

docs.title: Service layout and accessibility
docs.text:
• Each real-time forwarding control service contains at least one subservice, and each application process hosts at most one subservice provider.3
  • The list of controlled application processes is declared; the hosting application process is always included, and the subservice must be able to handle all reports from all of them at any time.4

docs.title: The four forward-control configurations
docs.text:
Capabilities declared per mission decide which configurations exist: per housekeeping structure, per diagnostic structure, per event definition, and, if either structure-level control exists, whether a subsampling rate can be attached to a structure.5

Configuration One definition per controlled AP contains Empty configuration means Present Application process forward-control AP ID; 0..n service type definitions, each with 0..n report type (message subtype) definitions block all reports always Housekeeping parameter report forward-control AP ID; 0..n housekeeping structure IDs (each with a subsampling rate if supported) block all housekeeping reports by declaration Diagnostic parameter report forward-control AP ID; 0..n diagnostic structure IDs (each with a subsampling rate if supported) block all diagnostic reports by declaration Event report blocking forward-control AP ID; 0..n event definition IDs block nothing by declaration

Sources: §6.14.3.2.2-6.14.3.2.5.68910 The maximum number of definitions in each configuration equals the number of controlled application processes (that can produce that kind of report); the maximum numbers of service types per AP, report types per service type, structure IDs per definition and event IDs per definition are declared.68910

Inside a definition an empty list means "all": an AP definition without service types forwards every report of the AP, a service type definition without report types forwards the whole service type, a housekeeping definition without structure IDs forwards all its housekeeping reports - and an event-blocking definition without event IDs blocks all events of the AP.6810 The first three configurations are therefore allow-lists and the last a block-list.

flowchart TD
  CFG["Application process forward-control configuration"] --> APA["AP 0x064<br/>(no service types = all reports)"]
  CFG --> APB["AP 0x065"]
  APB --> ST1["service type 1<br/>(no report types = all of ST[01])"]
  APB --> ST3["service type 3"]
  ST3 --> RT25["report type 25"]
  APB --> ST5["service type 5"]
  ST5 --> RT2["report type 2"]
  ST5 --> RT4["report type 4"]

Illustrative content (constructed for explanation, not from a source): every report of AP 0x064, all ST[01] reports of AP 0x065, its TM[3,25] reports and its TM[5,2] and TM[5,4] events are allowed in real time.

docs.title: Forwarding control processing logic
docs.text:
A report is blocked as soon as one applicable configuration blocks it.11

flowchart TD
  R["Report from AP a, type (s, t)"] --> A{"AP definition<br/>for a?"}
  A -- no --> B["BLOCK"]
  A -- yes --> S{"AP definition has<br/>service types?"}
  S -- no --> K["passes AP level"]
  S -- yes --> S2{"definition for s?"}
  S2 -- no --> B
  S2 -- yes --> T{"s definition has<br/>report types?"}
  T -- no --> K
  T -- yes --> T2{"t listed?"}
  T2 -- no --> B
  T2 -- yes --> K
  K --> H{"HK report and HK<br/>control declared?"}
  H -- yes --> H1{"HK definition for a,<br/>and SID listed or list empty?"}
  H1 -- no --> B
  H1 -- yes --> E
  H -- no --> E{"event report and event<br/>control declared?"}
  E -- yes --> E1{"blocking definition for a<br/>with empty list, or EID listed?"}
  E1 -- yes --> B
  E1 -- no --> FWD["FORWARD"]
  E -- no --> FWD

The decision tree restates requirements 6.14.3.3a-i; diagnostic reports follow the same branch as housekeeping reports with the diagnostic configuration.11 If none of the optional capabilities is provided, only the application process configuration applies.7

docs.title: Managing the configurations: requests
docs.text: Each instruction rejected in a request produces a failed start of execution notification (ST[01]); the valid instructions of the same request are still executed.13

docs.title: Application process forward-control
docs.text:
TC[14,1] add report types carries any mix of three instructions: add a report type (AP ID, service type, message subtype), add all report types of a service type (AP ID, service type), and add all report types of an AP (AP ID). It creates the AP and service type definitions as needed; adding a whole service type deletes its report type list, and adding a whole AP deletes its service type list - turning the definition into "all".1213 Instructions are rejected when:1213

  • the AP is not controlled by the subservice;
  • a new service type definition would exceed the maximum per AP, or a new report type would exceed the maximum per service type;
  • the instruction is meaningless because the whole AP (empty service type list) or the whole service type (empty report type list) is already forwarded.

TC[14,2] delete report types carries either any mix of "delete a report type", "delete a service type" and "delete an AP", or one "empty the configuration" instruction. Unknown items are rejected. Deletions cascade: removing the last report type of a service type removes that service type definition, and removing the last service type of an AP removes the AP definition.14

Inference: why the deletions cascade

Without the cascade, deleting the last listed report type would leave an empty list, which means "forward everything" - the opposite of the intention. Deleting the emptied definition instead makes the report types (or service types) fall back to "blocked". The standard states the rule but not this rationale.

TC[14,3] (requires TC[14,1]) asks for TM[14,4], one notification per AP definition with its service types and their report types.15

docs.title: Housekeeping and diagnostic parameter report forward-control
docs.text:
TC[14,5] adds housekeeping structure IDs (AP ID, SID and, if supported, a subsampling rate) or "all structure IDs" of an AP (which empties the list); it is rejected for an uncontrolled AP, when the maximum number of SIDs is reached, or when the AP already forwards all its SIDs.16 TC[14,6] deletes SIDs, whole APs, or empties the configuration, with the same cascade (an emptied definition is deleted, so that AP's housekeeping becomes blocked); deleting a SID also deletes its subsampling rate.17 TC[14,7] (requires TC[14,5]) returns TM[14,8] with each AP, its SIDs and their subsampling rates.18 TC[14,9] to TC[14,11] and TM[14,12] do the same for diagnostic structures.19

Subsampling rate

The standard lets missions declare a subsampling rate per structure but does not define its meaning (for example "forward one report in N"); that is not stated in the available sources.516

docs.title: Event report blocking forward-control
docs.text: TC[14,14] adds event definition IDs to block (AP ID, event ID) or blocks all events of an AP (empty list); it is rejected for an uncontrolled AP, when the maximum is reached, or when the AP already blocks all events.21 TC[14,13] deletes event IDs, whole APs, or empties the configuration; an emptied definition is deleted, which un-blocks that AP's events.20 TC[14,15] (requires TC[14,14]) returns TM[14,16].22

docs.title: Message types and data fields (PUS-C)
docs.text:
Message Fields Conventions TC[14,1] add / TC[14,2] delete report types, TM[14,4] content report N1; N1 x (AP ID; N2; N2 x (service type; N3; N3 x message subtype)) add: N2 = 0 all of AP, N3 = 0 all of service type; delete: N1 = 0 empty, N2 = 0 delete AP, N3 = 0 delete service type; report: N1 = 0 empty, N2/N3 = 0 nothing listed TC[14,5] add HK SIDs, TM[14,8] HK content report N1; N1 x (AP ID; N2; N2 x (HK structure ID; optional subsampling rate)) add: N2 = 0 all SIDs; report: N1 = 0 empty, N2 = 0 none TC[14,6] delete HK SIDs N1; N1 x (AP ID; N2; N2 x HK structure ID) N1 = 0 empty, N2 = 0 delete AP TC[14,9], TC[14,10], TM[14,12] as TC[14,5], TC[14,6], TM[14,8] with diagnostic structure IDs same TC[14,13] delete / TC[14,14] add event IDs, TM[14,16] content report N1; N1 x (AP ID; N2; N2 x event definition ID) delete: N2 = 0 delete AP; add: N2 = 0 all; report: N1 = 0 empty, N2 = 0 none TC[14,3], TC[14,7], TC[14,11], TC[14,15] no application data

Sources: §8.14.2, Figures 8-147 to 8-158.24252627 The counters N1, N2 and N3 and the subsampling rate are unsigned integers; the AP, service type, subtype, structure and event IDs are enumerated; widths are mission-defined.2425

Not stated

For TC[14,6] and TC[14,10] the interface clause defines N1 = 0 as "empty the configuration"; for TC[14,13] it defines only N2 = 0 ("delete an application process"). How the "empty the event report blocking configuration" instruction of §6.14.3.7.1 is encoded is not stated in the available sources.2720

Message Applicability (Annex C) TC[14,1], TC[14,2] minimum TC[14,3] / TM[14,4] requires TC[14,1] / response HK per-structure capability by declaration; TC[14,5], TC[14,6] implied; TC[14,7] requires TC[14,5]; TM[14,8] response diagnostic per-structure capability by declaration; TC[14,9], TC[14,10] implied; TC[14,11] requires TC[14,9]; TM[14,12] response event per-definition capability by declaration; TC[14,13], TC[14,14] implied; TC[14,15] requires TC[14,14]; TM[14,16] response

Source: Table C-22.28

Worked example (illustrative values)

Starting from an empty configuration on a subservice that controls AP 0x065 and supports housekeeping and event control:

Step Request Effect 1 TC[14,1]: AP 0x065, N2 = 2: service type 1 (N3 = 0), service type 5 (N3 = 2: subtypes 2, 4) all ST[01] reports and TM[5,2], TM[5,4] pass the AP level 2 TC[14,1]: AP 0x065, service type 3, subtype 25 TM[3,25] passes the AP level 3 TC[14,5]: AP 0x065, SID 7 only housekeeping structure 7 passes the HK level 4 TC[14,14]: AP 0x065, event ID 0x0201 that event is blocked; other TM[5,2]/TM[5,4] still pass 5 TC[14,2]: AP 0x065, service type 5, subtypes 2 and 4 the emptied service type 5 definition is deleted: events of AP 0x065 are blocked again

Each step follows the requirements quoted above.12162114

docs.title: The 2024 Rev.1 draft
docs.text: The Rev.1 DIR1 draft adds that the configuration policy applied when the subservice starts and restarts must be declared, keeps only the housekeeping and event capabilities (its Annex C no longer lists TC[14,9]-[14,12] for diagnostic structures), and says explicitly that ST[14] is fully independent of ST[15].302931 The 2015 status presentation records that the service was "completely remodelled" during the PUS-C review to keep service types independent of each other.32

docs.title: PUS-A (ECSS-E-70-41A, 2003)
docs.text:
The PUS-A packet forwarding control service kept, per application process, sets of enabled types, enabled subtypes per type, and enabled housekeeping, diagnostic and event report definitions (SID and RID). A packet was forwarded only if its type and its subtype were enabled and, for housekeeping, diagnostic and event packets, also its SID or RID - three independent attributes that all had to be "enabled".35 The service could sit in the originating application process (then N1 and the APID were omitted from the requests) or in a centralised one.3536

Subtype PUS-A request or report Data (14,1) / (14,2) Enable / Disable Forwarding of Telemetry Source Packets N1, APID, N2, type, N3, subtype (14,3) / (14,4) Report Enabled Telemetry Source Packets / report same layout (14,5) / (14,6) Enable / Disable Forwarding of Housekeeping Packets N1, APID, N2, SID (14,7) / (14,8) Report Enabled Housekeeping Packets / report same layout (14,9) - (14,12) the same for diagnostic packets N1, APID, N2, SID (14,13) - (14,16) the same for event report packets N1, APID, N2, RID

Sources: §17.3.3637383940 For (14,1)/(14,2), N2 = 0 enabled all types of the AP, or disabled them and cleared their subtype sets; N3 = 0 added or removed the listed types (removing also cleared their subtypes); N3 > 0 added or removed subtypes of a type. These requests did not touch the SID/RID level, and an unknown type or subtype was an error that did not stop the rest of the request.36 The minimum capability set was (14,1) and (14,2); the rest were additional, and control of a kind of definition was offered only if the AP generated it.41

Inference

Read literally, PUS-A enabling a type with N3 = 0 adds the type but no subtype, and the report (14,4) says that N3 = 0 means none of its subtypes is enabled; yet the forwarding rule needs both. Solar Orbiter's private status report instead uses N3 = 0 to mean that the status applies to all subtypes of the type (see below).3748

Aspect PUS-A packet forwarding control PUS-C real-time forwarding control Model enable/disable flags at type, subtype, SID/RID level add/delete definitions in four configurations Default meaning of "nothing defined" not stated AP and HK/diagnostic: blocked; events: not blocked Events enable list (RID) block list (event definition ID) Subsampling none optional per HK/diagnostic structure Status reports (14,3)/(14,4), (14,7)/(14,8), (14,11)/(14,12), (14,15)/(14,16) TC[14,3]/TM[14,4], TC[14,7]/TM[14,8], TC[14,11]/TM[14,12], TC[14,15]/TM[14,16]

Sources: PUS-A clause 17 and PUS-C clause 6.14.356105

docs.title: Solar Orbiter
docs.text:
In Solar Orbiter's TM/TC ICD (see also How Solar Orbiter uses PUS), service 14 applies only to the real-time virtual channel; the service keeps, per process ID, which packets may be transmitted, and by default every packet of every on-board process ID is enabled. The forwarding rule is PUS-A's: type and subtype, plus the SID or EID for housekeeping, diagnostic and event packets, must all be enabled.42 The ICD's service table marks every service 14 message for the CSW only, with no entry for the SSMM, star tracker or payload software.43 Instead of PUS-A subtypes ¾ and 15/16, Solar Orbiter defines private reports: TC(14,128)/TM(14,129) for TM source packets and TC(14,130)/TM(14,131) for event packets.43

Solar Orbiter addresses applications by their 7-bit process ID (the high bits of the APID); the ICD shows it as a 1-bit filler and a 7-bit PRID.4450

Sources: §5.15.1-5.15.12.444546

Printed typo

§5.15.8 of the ICD gives TC(14,10) "Disable Forwarding of Diagnostic Packets" the service subtype 6; its heading, the service summary and the MIB (ZCD00E0A) all use subtype 10.454352

The status reports carry a forwarding status FSTAT (0 disabled, 1 enabled) at each level. TM(14,8) and TM(14,12) list, per PRID, the SIDs with their FSTAT (SID 0 meaning all); TM(14,131) lists EIDs (2 octets, 0 meaning all) with FSTAT; TM(14,129) gives an FSTAT for the process ID, each type and each subtype, where N2 = 0 applies the status to all types, N3 = 0 to all subtypes of a type, and type or subtype 0 means "all".474849

docs.title: Service 14 in the MIB
docs.text:
The 2025 Solar Orbiter MIB has 12 service 14 commands and 4 service 14 packets, the same as in April 2020, all on the DMS application: commands on APID 172 (PID 10, category 12) and reports on APID 163 (category 3).525350

Command Subtype Name in the MIB ZCD00E01 / ZCD00E02 1 / 2 Enable / Disable Forwarding TM Source Pkts ZCD00E05 / ZCD00E06 / ZCD00E07 5 / 6 / 7 Enable / Disable Forwarding HK Pkts, Report Housekeeping Packets Forwarding S (description truncated in the MIB) ZCD00E09 / ZCD00E0A / ZCD00E0B 9 / 10 / 11 Enable / Disable Forwarding of Diagnostic Packets, Report Diagnostic Packets Forwarding Sta (truncated) ZCD00E0D / ZCD00E0E 13 / 14 Enable / Disable Forwarding RID Pkts ZCD00E80 / ZCD00E82 128 / 130 Rpt TM Source Pkt / RID Pkt Forwarding Status

Source: ccf.52

The three nested repeat groups of TC(14,1) are encoded with cdf group sizes: "Number of Process IDs" (bit 0) repeats the next 5 parameters, "Number of PUS Types" (bit 16) the next 3 and "Number of PUS Subtypes" (bit 32) the next 1 - the same technique the SCOS-2000 import ICD illustrates with a two-level (14,2) example.5456 The process ID is an 8-bit enumerated parameter with a 70-value text alias set CCDT0018TX (TIME 0, DMS 10, AOCS 11, PAYLOAD 12, PLATFORM 13, SYSTEM 14, OBCP 15, THERMAL 16, OBDB 17, OP_SSMM 30, SSMM_DEBUG_A/B 31/32, SSMM_HK_SOURCE 33, STR1/STR2 40/41, then the instrument process IDs from EPD_0 50 to SPICE_8 104, for example SWA_0 95 to SWA_4 99), and the event IDs of TC(14,13) are 16-bit unsigned integers.54 The reports are variable packets: SPID 14160 decodes TM(14,129) with a status parameter after the PID, each type and each subtype, matching the ICD.5548

Command Counter ranges in prv TC(14,1) N1 1-117, N2 0-116, N3 0-231 TC(14,5) N1 1-78, N2 1-233, SID 1-192 TC(14,13) N1 1-58, N2 1-116, EID 1-65 535

Source: prf and prv.54

Inference: where the ranges come from

The maxima are exactly what fits in Solar Orbiter's 236 octets of TC application data: for TC(14,13) with one process ID, 3 octets of N1, PRID and N2 leave room for 116 two-octet event IDs; with one event each (4 octets per process ID) 58 process IDs fit after N1. TC(14,5) and TC(14,1) give 233, 78, 117, 116 and 231 the same way. The MIB does not state the derivation.5154 The minimum of 1 for N2 in TC(14,5) also means that the MIB offers no N2 = 0 ("all structures") form there; neither PUS-A §17.3.3 nor the Solar Orbiter ICD defines one for (14,5) - only PUS-C TC[14,5] does.384525

The Herschel/Planck Operations Interface Requirements Document asked for the same control on that mission - per APID, all packets, types and subtypes, housekeeping, diagnostic and report packets - and classified these commands as hazardous; each application also had to report, on request, which packets were enabled and their generation frequency.58 SCOS-2000 itself does no specific processing of service 14 packets.57

docs.title: ST[15] On-board storage and retrieval
docs.text:
A spacecraft is out of contact with the ground for most of its life, yet the operators want to see everything it did while nobody was listening. Service type 15 of the Packet Utilization Standard provides that memory. It selects reports generated by the other on-board services, writes them into named packet stores in on-board memory, and lets the ground manage those stores and ask for their contents to be sent down later.1 The retrieved data are called playback (also "deferred" telemetry, or a packet store "dump"), as opposed to the real-time telemetry generated during a pass.578183 This page covers the ECSS-E-ST-70-41C ("PUS-C", 2016) service completely - both subservices, the three status variables of a packet store and the rules that link them, the packet selection logic, and all 37 message types with their data fields - then compares it with the very different ECSS-E-70-41A ("PUS-A", 2003) service and the 2024 Rev.1 draft. It ends with the ground view: virtual channels, how SCOS-2000 handles playback, and the two real implementations described in the public Solar Orbiter MIB.

Where this page sits

The reports that end up in packet stores come from services such as ST[01] request verification, ST[03] housekeeping and ST[05] event reporting. The sister service that controls which reports go directly to the ground is ST[14] real-time forwarding control; its filtering model is the same as the packet selection subservice described here. Retrieved packets leave the spacecraft on a TM virtual channel. File-based storage is handled by ST[23] file management and CFDP.

docs.title: 1. At a glance
docs.text: Item Value Service type 15 (every message of the service is of service type 15)<sup>42</sup> PUS-C name ST[15] on-board storage and retrieval<sup>1</sup> PUS-A name On-board storage and retrieval service (clause 18)<sup>59</sup> Subservice types storage and retrieval (exactly one per service); packet selection (one or more)<sup>4</sup> System object the packet store, identified by a packet store identifier<sup>5</sup><sup>6</sup> Store types circular (oldest packets overwritten) and bounded (storage stops when full)<sup>2</sup> Retrieval modes open retrieval (everything newer than the last packet sent) and by-time-range retrieval (between two dates)<sup>2</sup> PUS-C message types 30 requests and 7 reports, subtypes 1-6, 9 and 11-40<sup>55</sup> PUS-C minimum capability TC[15,1], TC[15,2], TC[15,14], TC[15,15] (and so TC[15,16]), TC[15,3], TC[15,4]<sup>55</sup> PUS-A minimum capability (15,1), (15,2) and one downlink option, (15,7) and/or (15,9) into a dedicated VC or via (15,8)<sup>70</sup>

docs.title: 2. Why spacecraft store telemetry
docs.text:
PUS-C gives two reasons for storing telemetry packets on board and dumping them on request. The first is intermittent coverage or limited real-time bandwidth: the store is sized to hold every packet generated for spacecraft monitoring and control for at least the longest gap between ground station passes plus a mission-dependent margin, and the packets are retrieved in later passes in an order based on their operational significance. The second is recovery of lost packets on missions with continuous coverage: the spacecraft keeps the most recent set of packets, whose size is a mission configuration parameter, so that the ground can fetch again what the space link lost.1

PUS-A said the same and named the two sizing constants: <PKT_STORAGE_TIME>, the margin added to the longest non-coverage period, and <PKTS_NUM_STORED>, the number of recent one-shot packets kept for loss recovery, "typically the last 100". It gives the classic example of selective retrieval - anomaly reports are needed on the ground sooner than routine status packets - and adds a rule that the 2025 operability standard repeats: storage must not be interrupted when the ground asks for a retrieval or a deletion.5880

The 2025 space segment operability standard ECSS-E-ST-70-11C turns this into design requirements. The storage function must be able to store any packetised data generated on board, be sized to hold all engineering telemetry for the specified autonomy period, be able to put the same packet in more than one store, keep stored data retrievable through the standard services after a reconfiguration or cold restart of the managing application process, offer priorities for parallel retrievals from different stores, keep storing while a retrieval or reset is in progress, and manage separate storage devices (for example engineering and science mass memories) independently.80 Storage configuration and contents must survive safe mode and a reconfiguration of the storage unit, and stay accessible through the standard storage and retrieval subservices afterwards, without ground intervention.83

Mission requirements documents read the same way. The Herschel/Planck operations interface requirements ask for a single centralised storage function in the data management computer, storage of all packets independent of whether they are also sent to the ground, packet stores selectable by APID and packet type, 48 hours of capacity, and retrieval by store, APID and packet time - with the note that the obvious use is to dump the event and telecommand verification packets first at the start of each visibility period.84

docs.title: 3. Architecture: two subservices
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  subgraph GEN["Report generators (any application process)"]
    HK["ST[03] housekeeping reports"]
    EV["ST[05] event reports"]
    VR["ST[01] verification reports"]
    OT["other reports"]
  end
  subgraph PS["Packet selection subservice(s)"]
    SC["storage-control configuration<br/>per packet store"]
  end
  subgraph SR["Storage and retrieval subservice"]
    direction TB
    ST1[("packet store A<br/>circular")]
    ST2[("packet store B<br/>bounded")]
    RET["open retrieval /<br/>by-time-range retrieval"]
  end
  HK & EV & VR & OT --> SC
  SC -- "time-stamp, then store<br/>if storage enabled" --> ST1
  SC -- "time-stamp, then store<br/>if storage enabled" --> ST2
  ST1 --> RET
  ST2 --> RET
  RET -- "routed to the store's<br/>virtual channel" --> VC["TM virtual channel<br/>(playback)"]
  GND["Ground"] -. "TC[15,x]" .-> SC
  GND -. "TC[15,x]" .-> SR
  VC --> GND

PUS-C splits the service into a storage and retrieval subservice, which stores telemetry packets in packet stores and retrieves them later on ground request, and a packet selection subservice, which decides which reports of which application process may enter which store. A service contains exactly one storage and retrieval subservice and at least one packet selection subservice; how they talk to each other is left out of the standard.14 Each application process hosts at most one provider of each subservice.4 The packet selection subservice can live in the application process that generates the reports, in a process that routes them, or in the process that hosts the storage and retrieval subservice.3 PUS-A described the same choice as a decentralised design, where each generating process selects its own packets, or a centralised one in which one process that sees all telemetry does selection, storage and retrieval.6078 The diagram above is this wiki's summary of that structure.

docs.title: 4. Packet stores
docs.text: The packet store is one of the system objects of PUS-C: an object defined and maintained within the scope of a service.5 Within a storage and retrieval subservice each store has a unique packet store identifier; its meaning and internal structure are outside the standard, and the standard suggests the name of an object in memory as an example.6 On the wire the identifier is a fixed character-string in every PUS-C message.42 PUS-A called it the "Store ID", a character string that may for example point to a physical recorder or a file.62

docs.title: 4.1 What a mission must declare
docs.text:
PUS-C does not fix any of the numbers; it lists what each mission must declare when it specifies its storage and retrieval subservice (requirement letters of clause 6.15.3.1):6

Req. Declaration Why it matters a Maximum number of packet stores maintained at the same time bounds TC[15,20] create packet stores b List of pre-defined packet stores stores that exist without being created c (rule) each store is managed by exactly one storage and retrieval subservice one owner per store d, e Whether circular stores and whether bounded stores are supported decides whether a store type field is needed f Type (circular or bounded) of each store per-store property g Virtual channels usable by the subservice limits TC[15,28] and TC[15,20] h Virtual channel used to transmit packets retrieved from each store routing of playback i, j Whether concurrent retrievals are supported, and how many the maximum covers open and by-time-range retrievals together; per store at most one of each runs at a time k, l Whether pending retrieval requests are queued, and the queuing policy m, n Whether retrievals are prioritised, and the priority policy adds a retrieval priority field to TC[15,9] and TC[15,15]

docs.title: 4.2 Circular and bounded stores
docs.text: A circular store overwrites its oldest packets when it is full, so it always holds the most recent packets; a bounded store stops storing (new packets are discarded) when it is full.26 In packet fields the type is an enumerated value with raw value 0 for "circular type" and 1 for "bounded type".54 PUS-A added operational detail that PUS-C dropped: a store used for lost-packet recovery must be circular; a bounded store must be explicitly emptied (at least its oldest part) before it can store again; when a circular store is being downlinked and new packets arrive faster than they can be sent, the downlink wins and "the overwriting pointer shall always stay behind the retrieval pointer"; and the service need not record gaps caused by packets it could not store, because the ground can detect them afterwards.61

docs.title: 4.3 Time-stamping
docs.text:
Every packet is time-stamped when it is stored, and retrieval works on these storage time tags. Each subservice declares its time-stamping method; PUS-C gives two examples: storage based (the time the packet was stored) and packet based (the on-board time already in the packet's secondary header).78 PUS-A made storage time-stamping optional and only then allowed retrieval by time.60

Inference

With packet-based time-stamping, "retrieve from 10:00 to 11:00" means "packets generated between 10:00 and 11:00"; with storage-based time-stamping it means "packets that arrived in the store in that hour". The two differ for packets that waited in an on-board queue, for example reports relayed from an instrument. The standard only names the two methods and leaves the consequence to the mission.

docs.title: 5. The three status variables
docs.text:
The storage and retrieval subservice keeps three statuses for every packet store. They are the key to the whole service, because almost every request is accepted or rejected according to them.

Status (PUS-C name) Values (raw) Changed by packet store storage status "enabled" / "disabled" (raw values not stated in the available sources) TC[15,1], TC[15,2]8 packet store open retrieval status "suspended" (0) / "in progress" (1) TC[15,15], TC[15,16], end of a resume-all retrieval1054 packet store by-time-range retrieval status "disabled" (0) / "enabled" (1) TC[15,9], TC[15,17], reaching the end time1454

A store created by TC[15,20] starts with storage disabled, by-time-range retrieval disabled and open retrieval suspended.19 The two retrieval statuses behave as follows (diagram drawn by this wiki from clauses 6.15.3.4 and 6.15.3.5):12131516

stateDiagram-v2
  direction LR
  state "Open retrieval" as OR {
    [*] --> Suspended
    Suspended --> InProgress: TC[15,15] resume
    InProgress --> Suspended: TC[15,16] suspend
    InProgress --> Suspended: resume-all reached the last packet stored before the request
    Suspended --> Suspended: TC[15,14] change start time tag
  }
  state "By-time-range retrieval" as BTR {
    [*] --> Disabled
    Disabled --> Enabled: TC[15,9] start (window from-to)
    Enabled --> Disabled: TC[15,17] abort
    Enabled --> Disabled: end retrieval time reached
  }

Most management requests require the store to be idle. The table collects the conditions that cause an instruction (or, where noted, the whole request) to be rejected:

Request Storage must be disabled Open retrieval must be suspended By-time-range retrieval must be disabled Other rejection conditions TC[15,14] change open retrieval start time tag - yes - start time tag in the future (whole request)11 TC[15,15] resume open retrieval - - only if concurrent retrievals are not supported unknown store12 TC[15,9] start by-time-range retrieval - only if concurrent retrievals are not supported yes start later than end; window fully in the past with no packet in it15 TC[15,11] delete content up to a time - yes yes unknown store18 TC[15,21] delete packet stores yes yes yes unknown store; "delete all" silently skips busy stores20 TC[15,25] resize yes yes yes size incompatible with memory availability23 TC[15,26] / TC[15,27] change type yes yes yes (whole request)24 TC[15,28] change virtual channel - yes yes invalid VC (whole request)25

The pattern is consistent: storage may continue while a store is being read, but nothing may change a store's shape (size, type) or its contents while a retrieval is running.

docs.title: 6. The storage and retrieval subservice, request by request
docs.text: Most PUS-C requests carry a list of instructions, one per packet store. Unless the standard says the whole request is rejected, each faulty instruction gets its own failed start of execution notification while the valid ones are still executed.9 Those notifications become ST[01] failed start of execution reports. The usual encoding is a count N followed by N store identifiers; N = 0 means "all packet stores".42

docs.title: 6.1 Controlling storage: TC[15,1] and TC[15,2]
docs.text:
For every packet it receives, the subservice time-stamps it and writes it into every enabled store whose storage selection criteria it matches.8 TC[15,1] "enable the storage function of packet stores" and TC[15,2] "disable the storage function of packet stores" set the storage status of the listed stores, or of all stores; an instruction naming a store that does not exist is rejected.9

Field Type Meaning N unsigned integer number of stores that follow; 0 = all stores packet store ID (repeated N times) fixed character-string store to enable (TC[15,1]) or disable (TC[15,2])

42

docs.title: 6.2 Open retrieval: TC[15,14], TC[15,15] and TC[15,16]
docs.text:
Open retrieval is the routine "send me what I have not seen yet" mode. While a store's open retrieval status is "in progress", the subservice reads its packets in storage time-tag order, starting from the store's open retrieval start time tag, and routes them to the store's virtual channel (in priority order if priorities are supported). Suspending and resuming must not create a gap or an overlap in the retrieved sequence.10

  • TC[15,14] change the open retrieval start time tag of packet stores moves the start point. The request carries one time tag and a list of stores (N = 0: all). A time tag in the future rejects the whole request; an instruction for an unknown store or for a store whose open retrieval is in progress is rejected; the "all stores" form changes only the stores that are suspended.11
  • TC[15,15] resume the open retrieval of packet stores sets the status to "in progress" and, if priorities are supported, sets the retrieval priority. If the subservice does not support concurrent retrievals, it rejects a resume for a store whose by-time-range retrieval is enabled. For the "all stores" form the standard adds that each store returns to "suspended" once the last packet stored before the request started executing has been retrieved.12
  • TC[15,16] suspend the open retrieval of packet stores sets the status back to "suspended".13
Message Fields (in order) TC[15,14] open retrieval start time tag (absolute time); N (unsigned integer, 0 = all); packet store ID (fixed character-string) x N TC[15,15] N (0 = all); then N x TC[15,16] N (0 = all); packet store ID x N

46

Inference

The no-gap, no-overlap rule is what lets operators split a long dump over several passes (suspend before loss of signal, resume at the next acquisition), and TC[15,14] lets them move the start point back to fetch data again. These uses are this wiki's illustration; the standard states only the mechanisms.

PUS-C states the "suspend at the end" rule only for the resume-all form of TC[15,15]; for an individual resume it does not say when an open retrieval stops by itself. The 2024 Rev.1 draft resolves this with an explicit per-store open retrieval policy ("suspend" or "stay open", see section 10), which suggests that the 2016 text was found incomplete on this point.

docs.title: 6.3 By-time-range retrieval: TC[15,9] and TC[15,17]
docs.text:
The by-time-range mode is meant to recover packets lost in the downlink: the ground names a window and the spacecraft re-sends the packets whose storage time tags fall inside it, then switches the by-time-range status back to "disabled" by itself when it reaches the end time.214 Support for this mode is optional and declared per subservice.14

TC[15,9] "start the by-time-range retrieval of packet stores" carries one or more instructions, each with a store, an optional retrieval priority and the window. An instruction is rejected if the store does not exist; if concurrent retrievals are unsupported and the store's open retrieval is in progress; if the start time is later than the end time; if the window is entirely in the past and the store holds no packet in it; or if a by-time-range retrieval of that store is already enabled.15 TC[15,17] "abort the by-time-range retrieval of packet stores" disables it for the listed stores or for all stores.16

The field order and types are those of Figure 8-165; the widths are illustrative because PUS-C leaves the integer, character-string and time formats to the mission (see PUS parameter types).44 The real Solar Orbiter layouts are in section 12.

docs.title: 6.4 Reporting the status: TC[15,18] and TM[15,19]
docs.text:
TC[15,18] "report the status of each packet store" has no application data. The response, TM[15,19] "packet store status report", lists for every store its identifier, storage status, open retrieval status and - if by-time-range retrieval is supported - its by-time-range status.1747

Field Type N unsigned integer packet store ID fixed character-string (repeated N times) packet store storage status enumerated packet store open retrieval status enumerated packet store by-time-range retrieval status enumerated, optional

docs.title: 6.5 Deleting contents: TC[15,11]
docs.text: TC[15,11] "delete the content of packet stores up to the specified time" carries a storage time followed by N store identifiers (N = 0: all stores). For each store it deletes everything from the oldest packet up to and including the last packet time-stamped at or before that time. It refuses stores that are being retrieved by either mode.1845 PUS-A explains why such a request is needed: a full bounded store must be explicitly emptied, at least its oldest part, before it can store new packets again.61

docs.title: 6.6 Creating, deleting, reporting and copying stores: TC[15,20] to TC[15,24]
docs.text:
PUS-C standardises what PUS-A left to the missions: the life cycle of the stores themselves.

  • TC[15,20] create packet stores (optional capability) carries one instruction per new store: identifier, size in bytes, type (only if both types are supported) and virtual channel (only if more than one VC is supported). The whole request is rejected if one instruction names an existing store or if two instructions name the same store; an individual instruction is rejected if the maximum number of stores is reached, if memory is insufficient (the criteria are not specified) or if the VC is invalid. A new store starts idle: storage disabled, by-time-range retrieval disabled, open retrieval suspended.19
  • TC[15,21] delete packet stores is mandatory when creation is provided. Only idle stores can be deleted (storage disabled, no retrieval running); the "delete all" form simply deletes every store that is idle.20
  • TC[15,22] report the configuration of each packet store (no application data) returns TM[15,23] packet store configuration report with, for each store, identifier, size in bytes, type and VC (the last two only when they can vary).21
  • TC[15,24] copy the packets contained in a packet store selected by time window copies, from a source store to an empty destination store, the packets selected by one of three filters: from time tag to time tag (inclusive), at and after a time tag, or at and before a time tag. The request is rejected if either store is unknown, if the window is invalid or if the destination is not empty.22
Message Fields (in order) TC[15,20] N; then N x TC[15,21] N (0 = all); packet store ID x N TM[15,23] same structure as TC[15,20] TC[15,24] time window type (enumerated); time tag 1 (absolute time, deduced presence); time tag 2 (absolute time, deduced presence); from packet store ID; to packet store ID

4849

The enumeration values of the time window type are not listed in clause 8.15.3, which only defines the store type and the two retrieval statuses.54

docs.title: 6.7 Changing store properties: TC[15,25] to TC[15,28]
docs.text: TC[15,25] resize packet stores gives a new size in bytes per store; the time and conditions for the change to take effect are implementation dependent. When resizing is provided, the subservice must also offer TC[15,26] change a packet store type to circular, TC[15,27] change a packet store type to bounded and TC[15,28] change the virtual channel used by a packet store. The two type changes carry one store identifier each; the standard says explicitly that it does not define what happens to the stored packets when the type changes. TC[15,28] carries a store identifier and the new VC (enumerated).23242550

docs.title: 6.8 Summarising the contents: TC[15,12] and TM[15,13]
docs.text:
TC[15,12] "summary-report the content of packet stores" (N store IDs, N = 0 for each store) returns TM[15,13] packet store content summary report. For each store it gives the storage time tags of the oldest and of the newest packet, the current open retrieval start time tag, the percentage of the store that is filled, and the percentage filled by packets between the open retrieval start time tag and the newest packet - which, the standard notes, is the amount of data still to transfer to the ground.26

The report starts with N (unsigned integer) and repeats this entry N times (Figure 8-168).45

docs.title: 6.9 Observables
docs.text: PUS-C requires the following values to be observable for each store: open retrieval status, by-time-range retrieval status (if supported), current open retrieval start time tag, filling percentage, time stamp of the last packet stored, and the filling percentage between the open retrieval start time tag and the newest packet.27

docs.title: 7. The packet selection subservice
docs.text: The packet selection subservice decides, per packet store, which reports may be stored. It always controls the reports of the application process that hosts it, can be declared to control others, must be able to handle all reports of the processes it controls, and must always have access to the stores of its storage and retrieval subservice.28

docs.title: 7.1 The storage-control configuration
docs.text:
For each store the subservice keeps an application process storage-control configuration: a set of definitions, one per controlled application process, each holding zero or more service type storage-control definitions, each holding zero or more report type storage-control definitions (a message subtype).30 An empty level means "everything below": an application process definition with no service types stores every report of that process; a service type definition with no report types stores every report of that service. An empty configuration - no definition at all - blocks every report from that store.303 The subservice knows the application processes it controls but not which service and report types they can generate, so it may accept definitions that mean nothing; keeping them consistent is left to the ground.30 The mission declares the maximum numbers of service type definitions per process and of report type definitions per service type.30

Three optional, finer controls can be declared on top of this:29

Configuration Granularity Empty configuration means Extra housekeeping parameter report storage-control HK report structure ID per application process no HK report is stored optional subsampling rate per structure diagnostic parameter report storage-control diagnostic report structure ID per application process no diagnostic report is stored optional subsampling rate per structure event report blocking storage-control event definition ID per application process every event report is stored (it is a blocking list) -

313233

The meaning and unit of the subsampling rate are not stated in the available sources; the same optional field appears in ST[14] forwarding control.29

docs.text:
Clause 6.15.4.3 spells out when a report is blocked from a store. The flowchart is this wiki's drawing of those requirements.34

docs.title: 7.3 Managing the application process configuration: TC[15,3] to TM[15,6]
docs.text:
TC[15,3] add report types to the application process storage-control configuration and TC[15,4] delete report types from the application process storage-control configuration share one nested layout (Figures 8-161 and 8-162):43

  • In TC[15,3], N2 = 0 adds all report types of the process and N3 = 0 adds all report types of the service type. Adding at a coarse level deletes the finer definitions beneath it (adding a whole service type removes its report type list). An instruction is rejected if the process is not controlled, if a maximum is reached, or if it tries to add a report type under a service type (or a service type under a process) that is already stored in full - the standard calls such an addition "meaningless".3543
  • In TC[15,4], N1 = 0 empties the whole configuration, N2 = 0 deletes a process and N3 = 0 deletes a service type. Deleting the last report type of a service type deletes the service type definition, and deleting the last service type deletes the process definition, so the hierarchy never keeps empty levels that would silently mean "everything".3643
  • TC[15,5] report the content of the application process storage-control configuration (one packet store ID) returns TM[15,6] application process storage-control configuration content report with the same nested layout.3743

Inference: why the cascade matters

Because an empty service type definition means "all report types", a naive delete that left an empty definition behind would turn "stop storing TM[3,25]" into "store every service 3 report". The cascading deletion in requirement 6.15.4.4.2o avoids exactly that.

docs.text:

383940515253

Note the reversed numbering in the event group: subtype 33 deletes and 34 adds, whereas for the housekeeping and diagnostic groups the lower subtype adds.52 The packet selection subservice has no observables of its own.41

docs.title: 7.5 Worked example (illustrative)
docs.text:
Suppose a mission has one store "EVTS" for operationally important reports, and the application process with APID 100 must put there all its ST[05] reports and its TM[1,2] and TM[1,8] failure reports, but not its routine events with event definition ID 7. With the service of this page the ground would send (field lists, not bytes; the values are invented for the explanation):

  1. TC[15,3]: store "EVTS", N1 = 1, APID 100, N2 = 2, {service type 5, N3 = 0}, {service type 1, N3 = 2, subtypes 2 and 8}.
  2. TC[15,34]: store "EVTS", N1 = 1, APID 100, N2 = 1, event definition ID 7 (only if event-level blocking is declared).
  3. TC[15,1]: N = 1, store "EVTS".
  4. Later, TC[15,5] for "EVTS" to check the result in TM[15,6].
