docs.title: 2.1 Layout and accessibility
docs.text:
Each event-action service contains at least one event-action subservice, and an application process hosts at most one event-action subservice provider.7 The specification of a subservice must declare two lists:5

  • The event reporting subservices it listens to. There is at least one, and the event-action subservice must be able to detect and react to every event report that they generate. PUS-C also states, as a deployment rule, that the on-board monitoring and the event-action services both require the presence of an event reporting service.8
  • The application processes it may address when releasing requests. The hosting application process is always in that list, and PUS-C assumes that all requests of an addressable application process may be used as actions.5

The released request is processed by the executing service named by its service type and application process identifier, and that service produces the execution verification reports. The request is regarded as generated not by the event-action subservice but by the source that sent the add request, the original source.5 The verification reports therefore go to the source identifier written inside the stored request.1

Inference

Because the stored request keeps the source identifier that the ground wrote into it, the ground can tell an autonomous recovery command from a normal one by its source identifier alone. Solar Orbiter reserves source ID 112 for "Recovery Action commands (Service 19 Event Action List)" (see section 8.2). PUS-C does not mandate such a convention.

docs.title: 2.2 The event-action definition
docs.text:
The maximum number of definitions that a subservice can evaluate at the same time is a mission declaration. Each event-action definition contains two things:9

  1. The event definition system identifier. If the subservice listens to more than one event reporting subservice, this is the identifier of the application process that hosts the event reporting subservice, plus the event definition identifier. Otherwise it is the event definition identifier alone.
  2. The action: the request to release when the event report is detected.

The term comes from ST[05]. An event definition is unique within the application process that reports it, so the pair (application process ID, event definition ID) is unique across the spacecraft. PUS-C calls this pair the "event definition system identifier".10 The definition identifier is therefore the event, not a separate key. A subservice holds at most one definition per event, and adding a definition for an event that already has one replaces its action (see TC[19,1] below).11

docs.title: 2.3 Statuses and action initiation
docs.text:
The subservice maintains two kinds of status, both with the values "disabled" (raw 0) and "enabled" (raw 1):1213

  • the event-action function status, one for the whole subservice;
  • the event-action status, one per definition.

The processing logic is short. If the function is disabled, no action is triggered at all. If the function is enabled and an event used by an enabled definition occurs, the subservice "shall immediately trigger the related action", that is, release the request. Triggering does not change the definition's status: it stays enabled and fires again on the next occurrence of the same event.6

stateDiagram-v2
  direction LR
  [*] --> Disabled : TC(19,1) add (new event)
  Disabled --> Disabled : TC(19,1) add again (action replaced)
  Disabled --> Enabled : TC(19,4) enable
  Enabled --> Disabled : TC(19,5) disable
  Enabled --> Enabled : event occurs and function enabled / release request
  Disabled --> [*] : TC(19,2) delete
  Disabled --> [*] : TC(19,3) delete all
  Enabled --> [*] : TC(19,3) delete all

The state machine above is drawn from clauses 6.19.5 to 6.19.8. Adding a definition creates it disabled. Adding or deleting is rejected while the definition is enabled. Delete-all removes every definition whatever its status.6111415 The function status has a separate, two-state machine: TC[19,8] sets it to enabled, and TC[19,9] and TC[19,3] set it to disabled. TC[19,8] and TC[19,9] leave the per-definition statuses unchanged, while TC[19,3] also deletes every definition.1615

Inference

Two rules work together. Definitions are always created disabled, and an enabled definition can be neither modified nor deleted. The result is a two-step "arm" procedure: load and verify the definition (for example with TC[19,10]), then enable it explicitly. A stored action can also never change under a live trigger. The standard states the rules but not this rationale.

docs.title: 2.4 Observables
docs.text: PUS-C requires two observables for the subservice: the event-action function status and the number of event-action definitions.17 In PUS-C terms, observables are on-board parameters provided by the subservice, so the ground can sample them like any other parameter, for example in housekeeping.18

docs.title: 3. Requests and reports
docs.text:
All requests of the service follow the PUS instruction model. A request contains one or more instructions. For example, TC[19,4] carries either a single "enable all" instruction or one or more "enable an event-action definition" instructions. PUS-C itself uses this case as its example of a request with several instruction slots.19 For every multi-instruction request of ST[19], PUS-C 2016 rejects faulty instructions one by one, with a failed start of execution notification per instruction (reported as TM[1,4]), and still processes the valid ones.2022

The packet field structures below use the PUS-C structure-diagram conventions. A field marked optional is present or absent for the whole mission, application process or service instance, not packet by packet. N gives the number of repetitions of the group that follows.23 The PFC, and so the width, of each enumerated or unsigned-integer field is a mission choice, declared when the application process is specified.24 The "TC packet" type is PTC 12 PFC 1: a complete PUS-C telecommand packet, primary header included.25

docs.title: 3.1 TC[19,1] add event-action definitions
docs.text:
Each request carries one or more instructions. Each instruction gives an event definition system identifier and the action to release.11 The packet layout is:26

Field Type Presence Meaning N unsigned integer always number of instructions that follow application process ID enumerated optional (repeated) APID hosting the event reporting subservice; present when the event-action subservice listens to more than one event definition ID enumerated repeated the event to react to request TC packet repeated the complete telecommand to release

The mission declares the list of verification checks to run on the embedded request. An instruction is rejected if:11

  1. it refers to an event-action definition that is enabled;
  2. the maximum number of definitions that can be evaluated at the same time is already reached;
  3. the embedded request fails any of the declared verification checks.

For a valid instruction there are two cases. If no definition exists for the event, a new one is created with status "disabled". If one exists, its action is replaced by the new one.11

A hypothetical byte layout helps to see the nesting. Assume a mission with 8-bit N, a 16-bit APID field and a 16-bit event definition ID:

Inference

PUS-C gives no separate length field for the request. A parser can find the end of the embedded packet only from the packet data length field of its own primary header. This is this wiki's reading of how a "TC packet" field is delimited, not a statement of the standard.

docs.title: 3.2 TC[19,2] delete event-action definitions
docs.text: This capability exists only if declared.14 Each instruction gives an event definition system identifier, and the layout is the same as TC[19,1] without the request field: N, then for each instruction an optional APID and an event definition ID.27 An instruction is rejected if the definition is enabled or unknown. A valid instruction deletes the definition.14

docs.title: 3.3 TC[19,3] delete all event-action definitions
docs.text: This request also exists only if declared, and has no application data.1528 It first sets the event-action function status to "disabled" and then deletes every definition, "without regard to" its enabled or disabled status.15 Since TC[19,2] rejects enabled definitions, TC[19,3] is the only request that removes a definition while it is enabled.

docs.title: 3.4 TC[19,4] / TC[19,5] enable and disable event-action definitions
docs.text:
Both requests are minimum capabilities. Each carries either one or more instructions naming a definition, or exactly one "all" instruction without argument.2021 The packet layout is N followed by N groups of an optional APID and an event definition ID.2930 An instruction naming an unknown definition is rejected. A valid instruction sets that definition's status to enabled (TC[19,4]) or disabled (TC[19,5]). A valid "all" instruction does the same for every definition.2021

How is 'all' encoded?

PUS-C 2016 gives the packet layout of TC[19,4] and TC[19,5] but does not say how the "enable all" or "disable all" instruction appears in it.29 For TC[19,10] it says explicitly that N = 0 means "report all".31 The 2024 Rev.1 draft adds the same N = 0 rule to TC[19,4] and TC[19,5].48

Two editorial slips in the 2016 text: in 6.19.7.1, NOTE 2 points to clause 6.19.6.2 (disable the function) where the disable-definitions clause is 6.19.7.2.20 In 8.19.2.11a, the subtype 11 packet is called an "event-action status report", although clause 6.19.8.6 calls it an event-action definition report.32

docs.title: 3.5 TC[19,6] and TM[19,7]: status of each definition
docs.text:
TC[19,6] exists only if declared and has no application data.3334 The response is a single TM[19,7] event-action status report, with one notification per definition: the event definition system identifier and the event-action status.33

Field Type Presence Meaning N unsigned integer always number of definitions reported application process ID enumerated optional (repeated) part of the event definition system ID event definition ID enumerated repeated part of the event definition system ID event-action status enumerated repeated 0 = disabled, 1 = enabled

Source: Figure 8-216 and Table 8-20.3513

docs.title: 3.6 TC[19,8] / TC[19,9]: enable and disable the function
docs.text: Both requests are minimum capabilities and have no application data. Each carries exactly one instruction without argument.163637 TC[19,8] sets the function status to "enabled" and TC[19,9] sets it to "disabled". Neither changes the status of any definition.16 With the function disabled the service "does not react to any event reports".6

docs.title: 3.7 TC[19,10] and TM[19,11]: report the definitions
docs.text:
This capability exists only if declared, and it requires TC[19,1].38 The request carries one or more instructions naming definitions, or one "report all" instruction, which is N = 0 in the packet.31 Unknown definitions are rejected one by one. The single TM[19,11] report contains, for each reported definition, its system identifier, its status and its action, that is the full stored request:3832

Field Type Presence Meaning N unsigned integer always number of definitions reported application process ID enumerated optional (repeated) part of the event definition system ID event definition ID enumerated repeated part of the event definition system ID event-action status enumerated repeated 0 = disabled, 1 = enabled request TC packet repeated the stored action

Within ST[19], TM[19,11] is the only report that returns the stored action itself.38

Inference

A ground system can compare the returned request byte for byte with the TC[19,1] it sent. This catches a definition that was silently replaced, since TC[19,1] overwrites the action of an existing disabled definition. This is this wiki's suggestion of use. The standard only defines the report.

docs.title: 3.8 Enumerations
docs.text: Enumeration Engineering value Raw value Source event-action function status "disabled" / "enabled" 0 / 1 Table 8-19<sup>13</sup> event-action status "disabled" / "enabled" 0 / 1 Table 8-20<sup>13</sup>

docs.title: 4. Worked example: arming an action
docs.text:
The sequence below shows the life of one definition, using the standard message types. The application process numbers are illustrative.

sequenceDiagram
  participant G as Ground (source ID s)
  participant EA as Event-action subservice (APID a)
  participant EV as Event reporting (APID b)
  participant X as Executing service (APID c)
  G->>EA: TC[19,1] add (b, event 0x0123, request R to APID c, source ID s)
  Note over EA: definition created, status disabled
  G->>EA: TC[19,10] report definition (b, 0x0123)
  EA-->>G: TM[19,11] (b, 0x0123, disabled, R)
  G->>EA: TC[19,4] enable (b, 0x0123)
  G->>EA: TC[19,8] enable the function (if not already enabled)
  EV-->>G: TM[5,x] event 0x0123 (also seen on-board)
  EA->>X: release R immediately
  X-->>G: TM[1,x] verification of R, sent to source ID s
  Note over EA: definition stays enabled

The message flow follows clauses 6.19.3, 6.19.5.2, 6.19.7.1 and 6.19.8.562011 The event number 0x0123 is illustrative.

docs.title: 5. PUS-A (2003) compared
docs.text:
PUS-A specifies the same service type 19 in its clause 21. The concept is the same: actions are attached to events that also give rise to an event report, and the action can be any standard or mission-specific telecommand.3940 PUS-A sees the action as directly reconfiguring hardware, starting an on-board operations procedure, or starting a command sub-schedule "which can contain a predefined command sequence". There was no request sequencing service yet.40

PUS-A maintains an event detection list whose entries hold an optional application process ID, an event report ID (RID), the action (a telecommand packet) and an optional enabled/disabled action status.41 The requests are:42

Subtype PUS-A name PUS-A behaviour PUS-C counterpart (19,1) Add Events to the Detection List New entries are disabled. An existing entry's action is replaced only if it is disabled, otherwise the request to replace it "shall be ignored". TC[19,1], with rejection (failed start of execution) instead of silent ignore (19,2) Delete Events from the Detection List Deletion is ignored for an enabled entry. An unknown entry is flagged as an error, and the rest of the request is still processed. TC[19,2] (19,3) Clear the Event Detection List Clears all entries. TC[19,3], which also disables the function (19,4) / (19,5) Enable Actions / Disable Actions Enables or disables the listed actions. Unknown events are flagged. TC[19,4] / TC[19,5] (19,6) / (19,7) Report the Event Detection List / Event Detection List Report Reports APID, RID and action status, not the telecommand. TC[19,6] / TM[19,7] - - - TC[19,8] / TC[19,9] function enable and disable (new) - - - TC[19,10] / TM[19,11] definition report including the request (new)

In PUS-A, N and the APID are "systematically omitted" when the service can handle only one event per request or listens to only one application process.42 The PUS-A minimum capability set is (19,1), (19,4) and (19,5), plus one of (19,2) or (19,3). Subtypes (19,6) and (19,7) are additional capabilities that require each other.43 PUS-C keeps the subtype numbers 1 to 7, adds the function-level control as a new minimum capability, adds observables, and formalises the "original source" of released requests.3517

docs.title: 6. The 2024 Rev.1 draft
docs.text:
The ECSS-E-ST-70-41C Rev.1 draft (DIR1, public review December 2024 to February 2025) keeps all eleven message types and their layouts. This wiki compared the clause texts word by word and found these changes:44

  • Start-up configuration. The configuration policy applied when the subservice starts or restarts must be declared, covering the function status and each definition status. At start the function status is set to "enabled".44
  • Timing. The maximum action generation time, the time from detecting the event to generating the action, must be declared.45
  • All-or-nothing requests. A request that contains an invalid instruction is now rejected as a whole, with one failed start of execution notification. A request with only valid instructions is executed in the order of its instructions.4647
  • N = 0 for enable/disable all in TC[19,4] and TC[19,5].48
  • Three more observables: the number of actions triggered by event detections, and the numbers of enabled and of disabled definitions.49

docs.title: 7. Modelling ST[19] in SCOS-2000
docs.text:
The hard part of TC[19,1] for a ground system is the embedded telecommand. The SCOS-2000 Database Import ICD handles it with a special command parameter type. A parameter of type Command ID (CPC_CATEG = 'A' in cpc, which must be PTC 7 PFC 0, a variable-length octet string) takes the name of another command as its value. SCOS-2000 then encodes it as the raw packet of that command, "with configurable values for the main packet header fields".5051 Appendix C of the ICD gives TC(19,1) as its example of a telecommand containing TC data that this type simplifies. It also warns that the embedded TC is encoded with fixed values for header fields such as the sequence counter. Apart from this, SCOS-2000 does no specific processing of Service 19 packets.52 More on command parameter types is on Commanding in the MIB.

Inference

With a fixed sequence counter, every autonomous release of the same action carries the same packet sequence count. Its verification reports cannot be told apart by sequence count from those of an earlier release. The time of the report, or the event that triggered it, has to do that. The ICD gives the caveat. This consequence is this wiki's reading.

docs.title: 8.1 Which PUS?
docs.text:
Solar Orbiter's packet structure ICD (SOL.S.ASTR.TN.00079, issue 7) has ECSS-E-70-41A as applicable document AD1. It forbids non-standard use of the standard services and puts mission extensions in private services or private subtypes.5354 Its service 19 therefore follows PUS-A, with the event detection list terminology, plus one private pair of subtypes. Table 5.1-1 marks Service 19 as optional for payload instruments. An instrument that implements it must provide (19,1), (19,4) and (19,5), and the others are optional. The central software (CSW) of the on-board computer implements all nine message types.55

Reading Table 5.1-1

The extracted text of Table 5.1-1 does not keep its column layout. This wiki checked the rendered PDF page 37: every "X" of the service 19 rows is in the CSW column, and every "M" or "O" is in the payload (P/L SW) column. The legend on PDF page 31 defines these marks.55

docs.title: 8.2 The Solar Orbiter tailoring
docs.text:
The CSW service keeps, for each event, the process ID that generates the event report, the event report ID, the action telecommand packet and the action status. It reacts to event reports TM(5,1) to TM(5,4) from one or more application processes.56 Solar Orbiter identifies an application process by a 7-bit process ID (PID) and a packet category. Event-action entries name the PID, preceded by a one-bit filler that completes the octet.5758

The fixed part above is followed by TC, "a complete stand alone TC packet" whose length the ICD gives as TBD. A newly created entry is disabled. Errors give TM(1,2) acceptance failure or TM(1,8) completion failure reports.58 TC(19,2) carries the same filler, PID and EID without the packet.59 TC(19,3) has no application data and clears the list.60

Enable and disable use one layout with a repetition count:

Solar Orbiter gives N = 0 a particular meaning. With N = 0 "the Event/Action status shall be changed on Service level", and the individual entries are left unchanged.61 Read this way, TC(19,4) and TC(19,5) with N = 0 act as a service-level switch, the role of PUS-C's TC[19,8] and TC[19,9], while TC(19,4) with N > 0 corresponds to PUS-C's TC[19,4]. The ICD does not use the PUS-C terms "event-action function" or "function status".

Inference

PUS-C 2016 does not say how "enable all definitions" is encoded, and Rev.1 later chose N = 0 for it (section 6). The same packet, TC(19,4) with N = 0, therefore means "enable the function" on Solar Orbiter but "enable all definitions" in Rev.1. Ground software that serves both conventions must keep them apart.

The list report TM(19,7) returns, for each entry, a copy of the PID, the EID, the action status and the first ten octets of the stored telecommand (packet header plus data field header). The full packet is not returned.62

The split of the 10-octet TC header into sub-fields comes from the MIB definition of the report (SPID 10001, below). The ICD gives only "TC Header, 10 bytes".6267 Solar Orbiter adds a private pair. TC(19,130) requests the entry for one PID and EID, and TM(19,131) returns that entry's action status and complete TC packet. These play the role of PUS-C's TC[19,10] and TM[19,11] for a single definition.63

Two further conventions matter for event-action:

  • Source ID 112, set by the ground, marks "Recovery Action commands (Service 19 Event Action List)". Other reserved ground sources are 110 (mission timeline), 111 (TC sequences), 113 (back-up mission timeline) and 120 (direct commands).64
  • Event ID ranges. Every severity (TM(5,1) to TM(5,4)) has a block of EIDs reserved for ESOC: 0x3F00-0x3FFE, 0x7F00-0x7FFE, 0xBF00-0xBFFE and 0xFF00-0xFFFE.65

docs.title: 8.3 Event-action definitions in the Solar Orbiter MIB
docs.text:
The 2025 MIB release has 48 service 19 commands and 2 service 19 report definitions.67 The CSW commands are addressed to APID 236 (PID 14 "System Control", category 12). The two reports come from APID 227 (PID 14, category 3, "table generation").6757

Command Subtype Description (MIB) Parameters ZCS01301 1 Add Event to the Detection List PCD0E012 Process ID (8 bits), PCS13012 EID (16 bits), PCD13013 "TC to send upon event" (Command ID) ZCS01302 2 Delete an Event from the Detection List Process ID, EID ZCS01303 3 Clear the Event Detection List none ZCS01304 4 Enable Actions PCD13041 "Nb Actions to process" (8 bits) repeating 2 elements ZCS01305 5 Disable Actions as subtype 4 ZCS01306 6 Report the Event Detection List none ZCS01382 130 Report Single Event Detection Entry Process ID, EID

The MIB merges the filler and the 7-bit PID into one 8-bit enumerated parameter (PTC 2 PFC 8). Its command textual calibration CCDT0018TX (tables paf/pas) maps 70 values, the same as the monitoring textual calibration of the same name (CCDT0018TX, tables txf/txp), from 0 "TIME", 10 "DMS", 11 "AOCS", 13 "PLATFORM" and 14 "SYSTEM" to the instrument process IDs such as 50 "EPD_0" and 99 "SWA_4".67 PCD13013 is the Command ID parameter of section 7: CPC_CATEG A, PTC 7, PFC 0.6751

On the telemetry side, SPID 10001 (TM(19,7)) is a variable packet. Its counter NCD13071 repeats a group of 16 parameters per entry: PID, EID, status, TC packet ID, sequence control and length, a 32-bit data field header, and the same 32 bits decoded again (VPD_OFFSET = -32) as secondary header flag, PUS version, four ack flags, type, subtype and source ID.67 SPID 10000 (TM(19,131)) decodes PID, EID, status and header fields, then a data byte NCD0B0A9 repeated by the value of the packet length field NCD0B0A8, then one final byte NCD0B0AA.67

Inference

The TM(19,131) definition is a neat trick. A CCSDS packet data length field holds "number of octets minus one", so repeating one byte length times and then reading one more byte consumes exactly the embedded packet's data field. The MIB does not explain this. It is deduced from the structure.

Predefined definitions. Of the 25 TC(19,1) commands in the 2025 MIB, four are editable (the generic ZCS01301, the test command ZCSXN001 "Add S19 Entry RAW NOTFLIGHT", and the EPD and METIS commands described below). The other 21 have every value fixed (CDF_ELTYPE = 'F'). The table pairs each one's trigger event with its action command. The EID column also gives the event name from the EID calibration (CCDT0004TX) or the event packet description.67

Definition command Event source PID Trigger EID Action command Action ZCSX0031-ZCSX0040 (10 commands) SYSTEM "EPD scvTM OFF" 48896 (0xBF00) ... "SWA scvTM OFF" 48905 (0xBF09) ZCSX0021-ZCSX0030 (one per instrument, for example ZCSX0023 for EPD) TC(11,2) "P_OFF_instrument SSID" ZCSX0042 SYSTEM "MAG scvTM OFF" 48898 ZCPX0009 TC(18,140) "Load and start OBCP (MAG2)" ZCSX0047-ZCSX0054 (8 commands) SWA_4 SWA events such as "Eas1OffEvent" 43655, "PasDetOffNmOFF" 43652 ZCSX0043-ZCSX0046 TC(11,2) "P_OFF_SWA EAS1/EAS2/PAS/HIS SSID" ZCSX1301 "Define Loss-of-UL FDIR Event-Action" PLATFORM 48912 (0xBF10, "Unexp_loss_UL" in CCDT0004TX), the TM(5,3) of APID 215 "REC_DST_E1 Unexpected Loss Of UL" ZCDX8605 TC(134,5) "Execute Loss-of-UL FDIR TC File" ZCSX1302 "Define SNAFU FDIR Event-Action" AOCS 3201 (0x0C81, "STR_AC_START" in CCDT0004TX), the only event with this EID in pid: a TM(5,1) of APID 183 described as "STR_Activate_Function_Started_(Pre-Power_On_Of_SCV_Units)" ZCDX8606 TC(134,5) "Execute SNAFU FDIR TC File"

The P_OFF actions are TC(11,2) "Disable Release of TCs" commands built as fixed areas. For example, ZCSX0023 "P_OFF_EPD SSID" holds the hexadecimal octets 04, 67, 00, 7B, 00, 8F, 00, A3, 00.67 Under the Solar Orbiter TC(11,1)/(11,2) layout (N1 sub-schedule IDs, each followed by a count N2 of process IDs) this reads as four sub-schedules, 103, 123, 143 and 163, each with no process ID.66 The FDIR actions start on-board TC files through private service 134 (see ST[21] Request sequencing).67

The whole P_OFF mechanism is installed by one ground sequence, ADMF730A "Define P_OFF S12 S19 v04" (procedure DM-FCP-730, issue 4, 07/11/2024). It has 44 elements:67

  1. report the current ST[12] monitoring list and the ST[19] event detection list;
  2. twenty TC(12,5) commands ZCSX0001-ZCSX0020, "Define EPD_A_OFF S12" to "Define SWA_B_OFF S12", which add on-board parameter monitors. ZCSX0001, for example, applies an expected-value check (mask 12, expected value 8) to the parameter NCSG3JN0 "EPD A SCV Status" and raises EID "EPD scvTM OFF";
  3. eighteen TC(19,1) definitions: the P_OFF entries of the table above, except that for MAG the sequence loads ZCSX0042 (start OBCP MAG2) and not ZCSX0033 (the TC(11,2) action), so ZCSX0033 is defined in the MIB but not used by this sequence;
  4. two TC(19,4) commands that enable the ten SYSTEM entries (EIDs 48896-48905) and the eight SWA_4 entries;
  5. the two reports again.
sequenceDiagram
  participant MON as CSW ST[12] monitor (SYSTEM)
  participant EV as CSW event reporting
  participant EA as CSW ST[19] (APID 236)
  participant MTL as CSW ST[11] mission timeline
  MON->>MON: expected-value check on NCSG3JN0 (EPD A SCV Status) fails
  MON->>EV: raise EID 0xBF00 (EPD scvTM OFF)
  EV-->>EA: TM(5,3) seen on-board
  EA->>MTL: release ZCSX0023, a TC(11,2) disabling sub-schedules 103, 123, 143, 163
  Note over MTL: time-tagged TCs of those sub-schedules are no longer released

The flow is drawn from the MIB definitions above and the Solar Orbiter definitions of services 11, 12 and 19.675666

Inference

The trigger EIDs 0xBF00-0xBF10 lie in the "ESOC" block of the TM(5,3) range, so these monitors and event-actions are most likely defined by the mission control centre rather than by the CSW supplier. The same block also holds OBCP-generated events in the MIB, for example 48917 "OBCP_STR1: STR Recovered" at APID 183. The SNAFU trigger 3201 is not in an ESOC block: it falls in the TM(5,1) range 0x0420-0x141F of "Specific Application SW Events".65 The reading of the P_OFF chain is also an inference from names and structures. When an instrument's secondary-voltage telemetry unexpectedly reports OFF, the timeline sub-schedules that command that instrument are disabled, so that queued commands are not sent to a switched-off unit. Neither purpose is stated in the available sources. The meaning of "SNAFU" is not stated either.

Instrument implementations. Two instruments define their own service 19 in the MIB:67

  • EPD (APID 812): ZID52514 "TC 19,1 Add Action" carries a 16-bit RID, a 2-bit "Action SensorID", a 6-bit "Action Code" and an 8-bit parameter instead of an embedded telecommand. Its delete, enable and disable commands carry one RID.
  • METIS (APID 1084): ZIT01901 "Add Event" follows the ICD layout (1-bit filler, 7-bit PID fixed to 67, 16-bit EVENT_ID, raw packet as an octet string). The MIB provides canned enable/disable commands for 1, 2, 3, 5 and 9 actions, plus ZIT019A4 "Enable EVENT ACTION SRV", which is TC(19,4) with N fixed to 0, the service-level switch.

Growth. The April 2020 release had 14 TC(19,1) commands, and the September 2025 release has 25. The additions are the two FDIR definitions ZCSX1301 and ZCSX1302, the MAG2 OBCP variant ZCSX0042 and the eight SWA sub-unit definitions ZCSX0047-ZCSX0054.6768

SQL used 
-- service 19 commands and packets (solo-2025-09-16.sqlite)
SELECT CCF_STYPE, count(*) FROM ccf WHERE CCF_TYPE='19' GROUP BY 1;        -- 1:25 2:2 3:1 4:9 5:9 6:1 130:1
SELECT PID_STYPE, PID_APID, PID_SPID, PID_DESCR FROM pid WHERE PID_TYPE='19';
-- parameter layout of the CSW commands
SELECT c.CDF_CNAME, c.CDF_BIT, c.CDF_ELLEN, c.CDF_GRPSIZE, c.CDF_PNAME, p.CPC_DESCR, p.CPC_PTC, p.CPC_PFC, p.CPC_CATEG
  FROM cdf c LEFT JOIN cpc p ON p.CPC_NAME=c.CDF_PNAME
 WHERE c.CDF_CNAME IN ('ZCS01301','ZCS01304','ZCS01382') ORDER BY 1, CAST(c.CDF_BIT AS INT);
-- predefined definitions: trigger and action
SELECT f.CCF_CNAME,
       (SELECT CDF_VALUE FROM cdf WHERE CDF_CNAME=f.CCF_CNAME AND CDF_BIT='0')  AS pid,
       (SELECT CDF_VALUE FROM cdf WHERE CDF_CNAME=f.CCF_CNAME AND CDF_BIT='8')  AS eid,
       (SELECT CDF_VALUE FROM cdf WHERE CDF_CNAME=f.CCF_CNAME AND CDF_BIT='24') AS action
  FROM ccf f WHERE f.CCF_TYPE='19' AND f.CCF_STYPE='1' AND f.CCF_APID='236';
SELECT PAS_ALTXT, PAS_ALVAL FROM pas WHERE PAS_NUMBR='CCDT0004TX' AND PAS_ALTXT LIKE '%scvTM%';
SELECT PID_TYPE, PID_STYPE, PID_APID, PID_PI1_VAL, PID_DESCR FROM pid
 WHERE PID_TYPE='5' AND PID_PI1_VAL IN ('48896','48905','48912','3201');
-- the report layouts
SELECT VPD_TPSD, VPD_POS, VPD_NAME, VPD_GRPSIZE, VPD_OFFSET FROM vpd WHERE VPD_TPSD IN ('10000','10001');
-- the ground sequence that installs the P_OFF chain
SELECT CSS_ENTRY, CSS_ELEMID FROM css WHERE CSS_SQNAME='ADMF730A' ORDER BY CAST(CSS_ENTRY AS INT);
SELECT SDF_ENTRY, SDF_POS, SDF_PNAME, SDF_VALUE FROM sdf WHERE SDF_SQNAME='ADMF730A' AND SDF_ENTRY IN ('41','42');
-- 2020 release for comparison (solo-2020-04-16.sqlite)
SELECT count(*) FROM ccf WHERE CCF_TYPE='19' AND CCF_STYPE='1';           -- 14

docs.title: 8.4 Heritage
docs.text: The ESA Operations Interface Requirements Document of Herschel/Planck (2003) already states the service as requirements on the CDMS, the spacecraft command and data management system. EVNT-1 to EVNT-4 ask it to respond to an event packet by issuing a telecommand, conditioned on the source APID and the event report identifier, and to maintain an action list that can be added to, deleted from, enabled, disabled, cleared and reported. Herschel/Planck marks the service "Not Applicable" for instruments.69

docs.title: ST[20] On-board parameter management
docs.text:
The parameter management service (service type 20) gives the ground direct access to on-board parameters: it can read their current values, set new values and, optionally, redefine where a parameter lives in memory and how it is encoded.1 Each parameter definition binds a spacecraft-wide parameter identifier to a memory location and a packet field code (PTC and PFC). A predefined identifier can be pointed at a new memory location or field code, for example to make a parameter for an OBCP, or to export an internal software variable as a parameter for housekeeping or monitoring.2 ST[20] is new in PUS-C (ECSS-E-ST-70-41C, 2016): the PUS-A list of standard services stops at service 19.3434

The service is small, with seven message types and no observables, but it touches the foundations of the standard: the on-board parameter, the on-board memory and the packet field code. This page covers each clause, then the 2024 Rev.1 draft. It then turns to Solar Orbiter, whose PUS-A based design uses the number 20 for something else entirely and puts its parameter management in private service 139.

Two names

Clause 6.20 and Table 4-1 call the service "parameter management", and clause 8.20 calls it "on-board parameter management".153 This wiki uses the planned page title "On-board parameter management" and treats both names as the same service.

docs.title: 1. The service at a glance
docs.text:
Message type Name Capability (Annex C) System / interface clause TC[20,1] report parameter values minimum 6.20.4.1 / 8.20.2.1 TM[20,2] parameter value report response to TC[20,1] 6.20.4.1 / 8.20.2.2 TC[20,3] set parameter values by declaration 6.20.4.2 / 8.20.2.3 TC[20,4] change raw memory parameter definitions by declaration 6.20.5.2 / 8.20.2.4 TC[20,5] change object memory parameter definitions by declaration 6.20.5.3 / 8.20.2.5 TC[20,6] report parameter definitions requires TC[20,4] or TC[20,5] 6.20.5.4 / 8.20.2.6 TM[20,7] parameter definition report response to TC[20,6] 6.20.5.4 / 8.20.2.7

Source: Annex C.2.20, Table C-29.6 The only mandatory capability is reading values. Writing values, redefining parameters and reading definitions back are each declared per mission.

flowchart LR
  G["Ground"] -->|"TC[20,1] report values"| PM["ST[20] parameter management subservice"]
  PM -->|"TM[20,2] values"| G
  G -->|"TC[20,3] set values"| PM
  G -->|"TC[20,4] / TC[20,5] change definitions"| PM
  G -->|"TC[20,6] report definitions"| PM
  PM -->|"TM[20,7] definitions"| G
  PM <-->|"read / write via definition"| MEM[("on-board memory<br/>(memory ID, address, PTC/PFC)")]
  MEM -.->|"same parameter ID"| USERS["ST[03] housekeeping, ST[04] statistics,<br/>ST[12] monitoring, ST[18] OBCPs ..."]

The diagram combines clauses 6.20.1 to 6.20.5. The dashed link reflects NOTE 2 of 6.20.5.1: changing a parameter definition "affects any service that makes use of that parameter".17

docs.title: 2.1 On-board parameters
docs.text:
PUS-C defines the on-board parameter as a system object in its generic service model. Each parameter has exactly one identifier, unique across the whole spacecraft. It can be a sensor measurement or a software variable held in memory, and services read it as part of their routine work, for example to monitor it or to compute another value.8 The baseline parameter set comes from the spacecraft design. The standard foresees defining new parameters in orbit, changing an existing definition, or setting a value through ST[20]. NOTE 3 of 5.4.3.2 adds that this is naturally limited to software parameters in memory, and that the on-board software may protect essential parameters against being overwritten.8

Every parameter is also associated with one minimum sampling interval. The interval is the unit in which services such as housekeeping and monitoring express their time intervals, and all parameters accessed by one application process share it. The standard's example is 125 ms for the platform and 500 ms for a payload.8

docs.title: 2.2 On-board memories and addressing
docs.text:
A parameter definition points into an on-board memory, a logical memory identified by a memory ID. For each memory the mission declares its access alignment constraint, its size in bytes, the allowed operations ("read only", "read and write" or "write only"), and whether scrubbing and write protection are supported.9 Two addressing schemes can be exposed in the space-ground interface:10

  • Absolute addressing: addresses and offsets are in bytes from the start of the memory.
  • Base plus offset: a byte offset from a base reference. The base can be an absolute address or a symbolic one, "e.g. the name of a table, a parameter set or a file", whose address is known on board.

The base-plus-offset scheme is what makes TC[20,5] useful. Offsets count from the first byte of the referenced object "independently of the actual physical storage", so a parameter can be defined inside a table or a file without the ground knowing where the object physically sits.10 The 2014 ECSS status presentation says the same of ST[6]: the base-plus-offset concept "has been extended to access memory objects such as files", and it lists for ST[20] the "dynamic creation (!) of new parameters based on raw or structured data memory access".34

docs.title: 2.3 The parameter definition
docs.text:
The mission declares the parameter identifiers whose definitions the subservice manages. Each parameter definition consists of:11

  1. the on-board parameter identifier, unique in the spacecraft;
  2. a memory ID, if the subservice manages more than one memory;
  3. an address: base plus offset for a base-plus-offset memory, or a byte offset from the start for an absolute-addressed memory;
  4. the packet field code (PTC and PFC) of the memory field used to read or write the value.

The packet field code tells the software how to read or write the value at the address. The value fields of TM[20,2] and TC[20,3] are "deduced" from the parameter ID, so in this wiki's reading the same code also fixes how the value appears in those messages.21 See PUS parameter types for the PTC/PFC table and MIB parameter types for its SCOS-2000 form.

docs.title: 2.4 Layout and accessibility
docs.text:
Each parameter management service contains at least one parameter management subservice. An application process hosts at most one provider.12 For the definition-changing capabilities, the mission declares two lists:7

  • the parameters whose definitions may be changed;
  • the memories that may be used for parameter definitions, which, the note says, "allows restricting the memories on which new parameters can be mapped".

PUS-C defines no observables for this subservice.13

docs.title: 3. Requests and reports
docs.text: All ST[20] requests are multi-instruction requests. In PUS-C 2016, an invalid instruction gets its own failed start of execution notification (reported as TM[1,4]), and the valid instructions of the same request are still processed.1415 The field types follow the PUS-C conventions. "Enumerated" and "unsigned integer" widths are mission choices. "Deduced" (PTC 11 PFC 0) means that the structure and format follow from preceding fields or mission constants, here from the parameter ID.1619

docs.title: 3.1 TC[20,1] report parameter values / TM[20,2] parameter value report
docs.text:
This is the only mandatory capability. Each instruction names one parameter. An unknown parameter is rejected. Each valid instruction yields one parameter value notification (identifier and value), and the request yields one TM[20,2] with all of them.14

Message Field Type Meaning TC[20,1] N unsigned integer number of parameters parameter ID enumerated repeated N times TM[20,2] N unsigned integer number of values reported parameter ID enumerated repeated value deduced format specific to that parameter ID

Source: Figures 8-219 and 8-220.2021

docs.title: 3.2 TC[20,3] set parameter values
docs.text:
This capability exists if declared. Each instruction gives a parameter ID and its new value, with the same layout as TM[20,2]: N, then N pairs of parameter ID and deduced value. An unknown parameter is rejected. Otherwise the parameter is set to the new value.2223

Inference

The only rejection criterion that PUS-C 2016 lists for TC[20,3] is "unknown parameter". It names no range check, read-only check or memory-protection check. The protections that NOTE 3 of 5.4.3.2 mentions would therefore be implementation checks beyond the standard, or go into the list of parameters that the mission declares as manageable. The standard does not say which.

docs.title: 3.3 TC[20,4] change raw memory parameter definitions
docs.text:
This capability exists if declared. Each instruction gives the definition to change (by its parameter identifier), the memory ID if there is more than one memory, the start address as a byte offset, and the new PTC and PFC.24

Field Type Presence Meaning N unsigned integer always number of instructions parameter ID enumerated repeated the definition to change memory ID enumerated optional (repeated) when more than one memory is managed absolute address unsigned integer repeated byte offset of the new location PTC enumerated repeated new packet field type code PFC enumerated repeated new packet field format code

Source: Figure 8-222.25 An instruction is rejected if:24

  1. the parameter definition identifier is unknown;
  2. the memory ID is not allowed for parameter definitions;
  3. the memory address is invalid;
  4. the packet field code is not compatible with the memory alignment constraint;
  5. the packet field code is invalid.

A valid instruction installs the new definition.

docs.title: 3.4 TC[20,5] change object memory parameter definitions
docs.text:
This capability exists if declared. It is the same as TC[20,4], except that the address is a base plus an offset inside an object memory, and the base field is "deduced". Its form depends on the memory and can be an address or a symbolic reference.2627 The five rejection conditions are those of TC[20,4].26

Field Type Presence N unsigned integer always parameter ID enumerated repeated memory ID enumerated optional (repeated) base deduced repeated offset unsigned integer repeated PTC, PFC enumerated, enumerated repeated

Source: Figure 8-223. Clause 8.20.2.5b cites "Figure 8-222", but the figure printed under it is Figure 8-223, so this is an editorial slip in the 2016 text.27 The Rev.1 draft keeps the slip: its 8.20.2.5b cites Figure 8.20-4 (raw memory) above Figure 8.20-5.33

docs.title: 3.5 TC[20,6] report parameter definitions / TM[20,7] parameter definition report
docs.text:
This capability exists if declared, and only if at least one of TC[20,4] and TC[20,5] is provided.28 Each instruction names a parameter. Unknown parameters are rejected. Each valid instruction yields a parameter definition notification containing the parameter ID, the memory ID (if several memories), the addressing scheme (if any memory uses base plus offset), the absolute or base-plus-offset address, and the PTC/PFC.28

Field Type Presence Meaning N unsigned integer always number of definitions parameter ID enumerated repeated memory ID enumerated optional when several memories are managed addressing scheme enumerated optional 0 = absolute, 1 = base plus offset addressing scheme dependent address see below repeated absolute: one unsigned integer; base plus offset: deduced base and unsigned offset PTC, PFC enumerated repeated

Source: Figures 8-224 to 8-227 and Table 8-21.293031

docs.title: 3.6 Enumeration
docs.text:
Addressing scheme (Table 8-21) Raw value "absolute addressing scheme" 0 "base plus offset addressing scheme" 1

Source: §8.20.3.31

docs.title: 3.7 A redefinition, step by step
docs.text:
The next diagram shows how the ground could turn a spare identifier into a new housekeeping parameter. The parameter number and the subsequent ST[03] step are illustrative.

sequenceDiagram
  participant G as Ground
  participant PM as ST[20] subservice
  participant HK as ST[03] housekeeping
  G->>PM: TC[20,6] report definition of parameter P (spare)
  PM-->>G: TM[20,7] P: memory m, address a0, PTC/PFC f0
  G->>PM: TC[20,4] redefine P as memory m, byte offset a1, PTC 3 PFC 12
  Note over PM: checks: P known, m allowed, a1 valid, alignment and PFC valid
  G->>PM: TC[20,6] report definition of P
  PM-->>G: TM[20,7] P: memory m, address a1, PTC 3 PFC 12
  G->>HK: add P to a housekeeping structure (ST[03])
  HK-->>G: housekeeping reports now carry the 16-bit value at a1

The rules come from clauses 6.20.5.2 and 6.20.5.4.2428 PTC 3 PFC 12 is a 16-bit unsigned integer.17

docs.title: 4. The 2024 Rev.1 draft
docs.text: A word-by-word comparison of clauses 6.20 and 8.20 of the Rev.1 public-review draft with the 2016 text, made by this wiki, finds a single substantive change. A request that contains an invalid instruction is now rejected as a whole, with one failed start of execution notification. A request with only valid instructions is executed in instruction order. This is the same change Rev.1 makes across the standard.32 The message types and packet layouts are unchanged.33

docs.title: 5. Relations to other services
docs.text:
• ST[06] memory management loads and dumps memory areas. ST[20] works one level higher, on named, typed parameters. The base-plus-offset addressing is shared.1034
  • ST[03], ST[04], ST[12] sample parameters by identifier. Redefining a parameter changes what they all see.7
  • ST[18] OBCPs are the standard's own example of a user of new parameters.2
  • ST[23] file management: a base-plus-offset base may be a file, so a parameter can live inside an on-board file.10

docs.title: 6.1 Service type 20 is "information distribution"
docs.text:
Solar Orbiter's packet structure ICD follows ECSS-E-70-41A and lists the mission's Operations Interface Requirements Document (OIRD, SO-ESC-RS-05001) as a reference document.35 The same mission-level numbering appears earlier in ESA's Herschel/Planck OIRD (2003), which lists service 20 as "Information Distribution CDMS - User", 21 as "Science Data Transfer" and 22 as "Context Saving". Services 20 and 22 are marked "Not used" there, and only 21 is mandatory for instruments.36 PUS-C later gave these three numbers to new standard services. On Solar Orbiter, service 20 is Information Distribution. Its packets go from the OBC to the payload instruments, both as an OBC heartbeat (so that instruments can switch down in a controlled way if the spacecraft enters Survival Mode) and to distribute inter-instrument communication data.37 It has nothing to do with PUS-C's ST[20].

Message Direction Content TC(20,1) Start Information Distribution for User ground to CSW instrument ID (1 octet), period (2 octets: 0 = one shot, otherwise a number of 125 ms software cycles) TC(20,2) Stop Information Distribution for User ground to CSW instrument ID (1 octet) TC(20,128) Inter-Instruments Communication CSW to all instruments 236 octets: 36 octets of platform data and 200 octets of instrument data

Source: §5.21.3839 Table 5.1-1 makes the service optional for payloads. The CSW implements TC(20,1) and TC(20,2), and TC(20,128) is optional for the payload.40

The ICD fixes the TC(20,128) packet itself. APID 796 is process ID 49 ("Payload broadcast") with category 12. The sequence count increments at 8 Hz and wraps every 2048 s. The acknowledgement flags are 0, so payloads generate no TM(1,1)/TM(1,7) for it, and the source ID is 14 (System Control). The CSW fills it from the system data pool. Each instrument's share comes from a dedicated TM(3,25), extracted by the TM extraction service. An instrument served at less than 8 Hz sees gaps in the sequence count.39

The layout above is that of SOL-SGS-TN-0007 issue 2.0, §6.3.41 The issue 7 ICD flags differ: bit 1 is a "science data outage" flag and bits 2 to 15 are commandable flags whose content is TBC, with no solar array steering flag.39 The rest of the platform section holds roll rate and roll angle (4-octet floats), four reaction wheel speeds (4-octet floats, rad/s), four validity flags and a spare.4142 The SGS note (2016) records how the Science Operations Working Group split the 200 instrument octets. Each instrument opens its block with a 4-octet heartbeat copied from the on-board time coarse field. Spare octets were allocated in advance, including all 14 of SPICE's, because SPICE did not then plan to take part.4344

Block Octets (SGS TN §6.2) EPD ZID52530 STIX ZIXX0128 "Aligned" STIX ZIX20128 PHI ZIP14800 Spacecraft 1-36 36 36 36 36 EPD 37-66 30 30 30 20 EUI 67-89 23 23 23 20 MAG 90-109 20 20 20 20 METIS 110-129 20 20 20 20 PHI 130-143 14 14 14 20 RPW 144-176 33 33 33 20 SOLOHI 177-190 14 14 14 20 STIX 191-206 16 (bit 1520) 16 (bit 1520) 16 (bit 1632) 20 (bit 1568) SWA 207-222 16 (bit 1648) 16 (bit 1648) 16 (bit 1760) 20 (bit 1728) SPICE 223-236 14 (bit 1776, last) 14 (bit 1776, last) 14 (bit 1520, before STIX) 20 (bit 1408, before STIX)

The 2025 MIB contains five TC(20,128) definitions at APID 796, all from instrument databases: EPD's ZID52530, MAG's ZIM02028 (one undivided 1888-bit, that is 236-octet, block), PHI's ZIP14800, and two from STIX, ZIX20128 and ZIXX0128 "STIX Information Distribution Aligned". The CCF_DESCR2 text of ZIXX0128 is cut off after "Duplicated from ZIX201". ZIXX0128 is new in 2025, and the 2020 release has the other four.5859 EPD's ZID52530 and STIX's ZIXX0128 follow the SGS note's sizes and order.45 STIX's older ZIX20128 has the SGS sizes but puts SPICE before STIX and SWA. PHI's ZIP14800 uses an even 20 octets per instrument, in the same order as ZIX20128. That is the layout of the issue 7 ICD, which lists the instruments alphabetically (EPD, EUI, MAG, METIS, PHI, RPW, SoloHI, SPICE, STIX, SWA) at 20 octets each, with a remark that deviations must be agreed between the PIs and ESA.39

Inference

The orders cannot all describe the same on-board packet. The "Aligned" STIX copy reads as a later correction of ZIX20128 to the SGS allocation. ZIX20128 and ZIP14800 then look like definitions left over from the ICD's even split. Which definition matches the flight CSW is not stated in the available sources.

The agreed cadences are 1 Hz generation for most instruments' TM(3,25) (MAG 8 Hz, SWA 0.25 Hz, SPICE none) and 1 Hz distribution of TC(20,128) (SWA 8 Hz). Delays are at most 250 ms in each direction, so 500 ms in total.4647 In the 2025 MIB, eleven TC(20,1) commands (ZCD01401 plus one canned command per instrument, ZCD2Z010-ZCD2Z019) and one TC(20,2) are addressed to APID 172 (process ID 10, DMS). Ground sequences use them 90 and 58 times respectively.58 The instrument reactions to service 20 data are still "To be written" in the SGS note.48

docs.title: 6.2 The real counterpart: private service 139
docs.text:
Solar Orbiter's equivalent of ST[20] is service 139. The service clause heads it "Parameter Management service" and Table 5.1-1 lists it as "Datapool Management Service", reserved for the CSW.4940 It "allows the ground to manage on board data", software variables or equipment acquisitions, by reading or changing values. There are two kinds of data:49

  • Variables, used by housekeeping (service 3) and monitoring (service 12);
  • Updatable constants, "system level tuneable parameters" used in algorithms such as the AOCS, for which service 139 is a more convenient interface than memory management (service 6).

Parameters are addressed by a 32-bit Parameter ID defined in the SRDB (the ICD uses the acronym without expanding it). The ID is made of a process ID, a read-only/read-write flag and a local ID. The SRDB and the CSW map each ID to a start address, a length and a parameter type. The set is "frozen for a given CSW release", but new parameters can be defined with TC(139,4).49

Solar Orbiter Purpose PUS-C ST[20] analogue TC(139,1) Change Value of onboard Parameters NPAR (1 octet), then NPAR pairs of parameter ID (4 octets) and value (deduced). Not usable for "Byte Array" parameters. TC[20,3] TC(139,2) Get Value of On-board Parameters NPAR (1 octet), NPAR parameter IDs (4 octets) TC[20,1] TM(139,3) On-board Parameters Value Report NPAR, then ID and value pairs TM[20,2] TC(139,4) Define Onboard Parameters NPAR (1-18), then ID (4), RAM address (4), length (1), type (4). Maps a predefined "spare" ID to a RAM location. TC[20,4] - no definition report TC[20,6] / TM[20,7]

Source: §5.29.1 to §5.29.4.5051

The ICD lists the type codes: 0x00020008/10/20 for 8-, 16- and 32-bit enumerations, 0x00030004, 0x0003000C and 0x0003000E for UINT8, UINT16 and UINT32, 0x00040004, 0x0004000C and 0x0004000E for INT8, INT16 and INT32, and 0x00050001, 0x00050002 and 0x00050003 for single, double and "double read as single" floats.51 The MIB calibration CCDT0017TC holds the same values in decimal, plus BYTE_ARRAY = 0.58

Inference

Eleven of the twelve listed codes read as a PUS PTC in the upper 16 bits and the matching PFC in the lower 16 bits: 0x0003000E is PTC 3 PFC 14 (4-octet unsigned), 0x00020010 is PTC 2 PFC 16 (16-bit enumerated), 0x00050002 is PTC 5 PFC 2 (IEEE double precision).1718 The exception is 0x00050003, "Float Double Precision read as Float Single Precision", whereas PTC 5 PFC 3 is the 4-octet MIL-STD simple precision format.18 Solar Orbiter's TC(139,4) therefore carries in effect a packet field code, as PUS-C's TC[20,4] does, with one mission-specific value. The ICD does not state this encoding rule. It is deduced from the values.

The parameter ID. Annex 11 of the ICD defines the common 32-bit structure for system data pool parameters: a 1-bit filler (0), the 7-bit process ID of Annex 8, a read/write flag (0 = read and write, 1 = read only, "not modifiable via service 132") and a 23-bit local ID. The local ID is a 3-bit filler (0b010), an 8-bit unit ID (for example CSW or IMU) and a 12-bit counter, a free-running number whose last 4 bits give the functional type for CSW parameters.52 The bit widths are in a figure that the text extraction misses. This wiki read them from the rendered PDF page.

In the MIB, all but one of the 19,803 on-board parameter IDs (PCF_PID) have a most significant octet between 10 and 17: 12,178 with 17, 3,140 with 11 (AOCS), 1,176 with 14 (SYSTEM), 1,138 with 13 (PLATFORM), 1,000 with 16 (THERMAL), 598 with 10 (DMS), 529 with 12 (PAYLOAD) and 43 with 15 (OBCP). The exception is DUMMYVAL "ALWAYS_VALID" with ID 0. Process IDs 10 to 16 are the OBC software processes of Annex 8. Annex 8 lists 17 as a spare, but the MIB's process ID calibration CCDT0018TX names it "OBDB".5853 The read/write bit is 0 in all 19,803 IDs. The 3-bit filler is 0b000 in 15,433 IDs, 0b001 in 1,778 and 0b010 in only 2,592, so the MIB does not follow the Annex's fixed filler value.58

Inference

The text's reference to service 132 (SGM management in the same ICD) may be meant for service 139, since service 139 is the one that changes data pool values. The meaning of process ID 17 "OBDB" and of the varying filler bits is not stated in the available sources.

docs.title: 6.3 Service 139 in the MIB
docs.text:
The 2025 MIB has 217 TC(139,1), 10 TC(139,2) and 7 TC(139,4) definitions, none of them flagged critical, and 26 TM(139,3) packet definitions.58

APID Process TC(139,1) TC(139,2) TC(139,4) 172 10 DMS 8 2 1 188 11 AOCS 29 2 2 204 12 PAYLOAD 3 1 1 220 13 PLATFORM 8 3 1 236 14 SYSTEM 161 1 1 268 16 THERMAL 8 1 1

Most TC(139,1) commands are canned settings with fixed parameter IDs, for example "Set DST RX A SCV Health", "Set TWTA SCV Presel = A", "Set GFE Gyro Biases" and "Update SC Mass CSWv3_0". The generic forms are ZCD2Z004/5/6 "Set value of (½/4-byte integer) parameters".58 Ground sequences use TC(139,1) 358 times (in 270 sequences), TC(139,2) 64 times and TC(139,4) 9 times.58

In the generic commands, and in all TC(139,2) and TC(139,4) definitions, the parameter ID fields are of the SCOS-2000 type Parameter ID (CPC_CATEG = 'P', PTC 3 PFC 14). The operator gives a telemetry parameter name and SCOS-2000 encodes its on-board identifier PCF_PID.5558 The same command parameter, PCD03014 "Datapool parameter ID" (unsigned, 32 bits), appears in 49 service 139 commands, 114 service 12 commands, 24 service 3 commands and 2 service 130 commands.58 Most canned TC(139,1) commands do it differently: 173 of the 217 have no Parameter ID field at all, and 163 of these carry the identifier as a 32-bit fixed area. "Set DST RX A SCV Health" (ZCS2Z03T), for example, holds the fixed areas 0x01 (NPAR) and 0x0E0C83B0, which is the PCF_PID of NCST3H20 "DST-RX A SCV Health", followed by an editable 8-bit value.58

Reading values back. The generic TM(139,3), for example SPID 10114 from APID 227, is a variable packet. A count NCD8B031 repeats a pair made of NCD0C095 "Monitored Par ID" (32 bits, with VPD_PIDREF = 'Y') and NCD8B033, a value of PTC 11, deduced.58 In SCOS-2000, VPD_PIDREF = 'Y' means that the value is an on-board parameter ID, which is compared with the PCF_PID values to find the telemetry parameter.56 The deduced value then takes that parameter's type: NCD8B033 has PCF_RELATED = NCD0C095, the field that names the parameter whose value supplies the on-board parameter ID for a deduced parameter.5758 This is the ground half of PUS-C's "deduced" value field. Twenty more TM(139,3) definitions at APID 1953 decode particular reports with fixed layouts, keyed on the first parameter ID (pic: offset 17, width 32), for example SPID 65908 "TC Link Mon Params Report".58

Inference

APID 1953 falls in the EGSE process ID range (process ID 122).53 In the mission-specific dup file, three of the generic TM(139,3) SPIDs are paired with APID 1953: 14177 (APID 163, DMS), 20131 (APID 179, AOCS) and 27108 (APID 211, PLATFORM). The first parameter IDs that key the twenty fixed-layout definitions all have 10, 11 or 13 in their top octet, which are exactly these three processes. This suggests that the MOC maps the real reports onto this APID to apply the fixed-layout definitions. This is not documented in the ICD or the TN.

docs.title: 6.4 Worked example: a real redefinition
docs.text:
ZCAX8B04 "Define SPARE RWAB THR 3.1.2" is a TC(139,4) to the AOCS application (APID 188) with every value fixed in the MIB:58

# Parameter (name, PCF_PID) RAM address (raw CDF_VALUE) Length Type 1 NCAT2PB0 "RW1_GgHtr_MON__GgHtr_MMH", 185118745 = 0x0B08B019 40077920 4 UINT32 (0x0003000E) 2 NCAT2PC0 "RW2_WDE_2_URP__GgHtr_MMH", 0x0B08B01A 40077940 4 UINT32 3 NCAT2PD0 "RW3_GgHtr_MON__WDE_3_URP", 0x0B08B01B 40077960 4 UINT32

The three IDs are consecutive AOCS spares (top octet 0x0B = 11). Their entries in the mission file ASW_sw_para.dat (next section) are HKA_SPARE_PARAM26-28, "Reserved parameter 26 [27, 28] in the AOCS application".58 TC(139,4) gives these spare identifiers a memory location and a type. The MIB parameter descriptions, such as "RW1_GgHtr_MON__GgHtr_MMH", give them their new meaning, which from the names relates to the reaction wheels. This is the PUS-C TC[20,4] use case, "exporting an existing internal variable as a parameter for housekeeping or monitoring".2

The RAM addresses are given as printed. Their command parameter has CPC_RADIX = 'D'.58 Read as decimal, 40077920, 40077940 and 40077960 are 0x02638A60, 0x02638A74 and 0x02638A88, 20 bytes apart. All three fall inside the OBC "Processor RAM" range 0x0200 0000 to 0x027F FFFF of the ICD's memory ID allocation (Figure 5.7-1).54 Read as hexadecimal, 0x40077920 would fall in none of the listed RAM ranges. The two other fixed RAM addresses found in the MIB's ground sequences, 40111920 and 40116648 (sequences AACF612A and AACF613A), also fall in that range when read as decimal.58

Inference

The memory map therefore supports the declared decimal radix, and the encoded RAM address field of the first definition would be 02 63 8A 60. The ICD does not say which memory a TC(139,4) address refers to beyond "PM-RAM", so this remains a consistency check, not a statement of the sources.

A request that needs no such interpretation is a TC(139,2) reading the first parameter back. This octet string is illustrative: it is built from the real MIB layout of ZCA08B02 and the real PCF_PID, but it was not captured from the spacecraft:58

TC(139,2) application data: 01 0B 08 B0 19
  01           NPAR = 1
  0B 08 B0 19  Parameter ID = PCF_PID of NCAT2PB0 (185118745)

docs.title: 6.5 The ASW_sw_para table and its possible relation to ST[20]
docs.text:
The 2025 release contains a file that the ICD does not define, ASW_sw_para.dat, loaded into this wiki's database as table asw_sw_para with three columns. The first column holds MIB names and the second on-board software symbol names. The third holds a description, empty in 15,662 of the 105,222 rows.58 The MIB overview lists it among the mission-specific files and gives first statistics.

First column matches Rows Example (column 1, column 2) pcf.PCF_NAME (monitoring parameters, prefix N) 77,565 NCAP0001, OBDB_ACCSETPARAMS_ACCUNITA_ACCAXIS1_COEFPOLYTACCBIAS_0 ... of which have an on-board ID PCF_PID 19,397 NCAT2PB0, HKA_SPARE_PARAM26 cpc.CPC_NAME (command parameters, prefix P) 3,676 PCA8B021, PTC_GET_N_PARAM ccf.CCF_CNAME (commands, prefix Z) 2,221 ZAHG0001 tpcf.TPCF_NAME (telemetry packet names, prefix Y) 7,665 YCA00101, TMA_TCACK_ACC_SUCCESS calibration tables txf, caf, paf, cca, mcf, lgf (prefix C) 260 CCDT0001TX, AOCS_PROFILE_ID prf.PRF_NUMBR (value range sets, prefix V) 77 VCD00147, Z_IDINT0TO1 no MIB table (prefix B) 13,727 BCAY0000, SSEA_SEGMENTS_END_TIME_C

Source: this wiki's queries.58 Of the 19,803 pcf entries with an on-board ID, all but 406 appear in asw_sw_para. The 2020 release has 85,430 rows.5859

Inference

ASW_sw_para looks like an export of the on-board software's view of the database. Each MIB item (parameter, packet, command, command parameter, calibration, value range, and B-prefixed items that match no MIB table) is paired with the symbol of the application software (ASW) that implements it. The relation to ST[20]-style parameter management is that the 19,397 parameters with an on-board ID are the data pool parameters that service 139 (and services 3 and 12) address by Parameter ID. ASW_sw_para then tells which software variable each identifier is bound to, including the "spare" variables that TC(139,4) can map. This matches the ICD's statement that the parameter definitions come from the SRDB and are frozen per CSW release.49 The file's purpose and origin, and the nature of the B-prefixed items, are not stated in the available sources.

SQL used 
-- solo-2025-09-16.sqlite
SELECT CCF_APID, CCF_STYPE, count(*) FROM ccf WHERE CCF_TYPE='139' GROUP BY 1,2;
SELECT CCF_STYPE, count(*) FROM ccf WHERE CCF_TYPE='20' GROUP BY 1;              -- 1:11 2:1 128:5
SELECT c.CDF_CNAME, c.CDF_BIT, c.CDF_ELLEN, c.CDF_PNAME, p.CPC_DESCR, p.CPC_CATEG, c.CDF_VALUE
  FROM cdf c LEFT JOIN cpc p ON p.CPC_NAME=c.CDF_PNAME
 WHERE c.CDF_CNAME IN ('ZCD08B02','ZCD08B04','ZCAX8B04','ZID52530','ZIX20128','ZIXX0128','ZIP14800','ZIM02028','ZCS2Z03T')
 ORDER BY 1, CAST(c.CDF_BIT AS INT);
SELECT CCF_CNAME, CCF_DESCR, CCF_DESCR2 FROM ccf WHERE CCF_TYPE='20' AND CCF_STYPE='128';
-- TC(139,x) with / without a Parameter ID (CPC_CATEG='P') field
SELECT CCF_STYPE, count(*), sum(EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM cdf c JOIN cpc p ON p.CPC_NAME=c.CDF_PNAME
       WHERE c.CDF_CNAME=f.CCF_CNAME AND p.CPC_CATEG='P')) FROM ccf f WHERE CCF_TYPE='139' GROUP BY 1;  -- 1:217/44 2:10/10 4:7/7
-- Parameter ID bit fields
SELECT (CAST(PCF_PID AS INT)>>23)&1 AS rw, (CAST(PCF_PID AS INT)>>20)&7 AS filler, count(*)
  FROM pcf WHERE PCF_PID<>'' GROUP BY 1,2;                                           -- 0|0:15433 0|1:1778 0|2:2592
-- RAM addresses used in sequences
SELECT s.SDF_SQNAME, s.SDF_VALUE FROM sdf s JOIN cpc p ON p.CPC_NAME=s.SDF_PNAME WHERE p.CPC_DESCR='RAM address';

 WHERE c.CDF_PNAME='PCD03014' GROUP BY 1;                                          -- 3:24 12:114 130:2 139:49

-- asw_sw_para (an indexed in-memory copy was used for speed)

SELECT count(*) FROM asw_sw_para a JOIN pcf p ON p.PCF_NAME=a.COL1;                -- 77565

docs.title: ST[21] Request sequencing
docs.text:
The request sequencing service (service type 21) stores on board an ordered list of telecommand requests and releases them one by one, with a specified delay between one release and the next. Several such request sequences can run in parallel. A sequence can be loaded directly from the ground, with the requests inside the load request, or from a file already stored on board.1 PUS-C presents it, like event-action, as an extension of ground monitoring and control. The executing application process sends the verification reports of each released request to the source named in that request. Releases do not depend on whether earlier requests of the sequence succeeded.1

Request sequencing is new in ECSS-E-ST-70-41C (2016). It is one of three services into which the PUS-A on-board operations scheduling service was split, together with time-based scheduling and position-based scheduling.2 This page covers the service clause by clause, compares it with its neighbours and with the 2024 Rev.1 draft, and shows how Solar Orbiter, designed to PUS-A, does the same job with a private "TC Sequencer" service 134, while its own service type 21 carries science data.

Where this page sits

Packet headers are on PUS packet structures, field types on PUS parameter types. On-board files belong to ST[23] File management. Ground-side command sequences, which SCOS-2000 expands into individual commands before uplink, are a different thing, described on Command sequences in the MIB.

docs.title: 1. The service at a glance
docs.text:
