Source: Annex C.2.21, Table C-30. Clause 6.21.5.1a adds a minimum rule: at least one of TC[21,1], TC[21,2] and TC[21,8] must be provided.7

docs.title: 2. Origins
docs.text: PUS-A (2003) had no request sequencing service. In its concept clause, a telecommand attached to an on-board event could start a command sub-schedule of the scheduling service, and such a sub-schedule "can contain a predefined command sequence".5 During the preparation of PUS-C, the PUS-A scheduling service was "completely re-assessed resulting in 3 proposed new service types": ST[11] time-based scheduling, ST[21] then called "telecommand sequencing", and ST[22] orbit-based scheduling.2 The 2015 status presentation describes ST[21] in terms close to the final text: it releases "one by one" the telecommands of an on-board sequence, with specified delays, several sequences running in parallel, loaded from an on-board file or from the ground.3 The 2014 presentation lists "load a request sequence by reference" among the standard requests that operate on files.4 The published standard uses the more general word "request".6

docs.title: 3.1 Layout and accessibility
docs.text: Each request sequencing service contains at least one request sequencing subservice. An application process hosts at most one provider.8 The mission declares the application processes that the subservice may address. The hosting process is always one of them, and all their requests are assumed usable.9 As with ST[19], a released request is executed by the service that its service type and APID designate. The request counts as generated by the original source, the subservice that sent the load request, and not by the sequencer.9

docs.title: 3.2 The request sequence
docs.text:
For each subservice the mission declares:10

  • the maximum number of request sequences that can be processed at the same time;
  • the total resources available for storing request sequences;
  • the verification checks applied to the requests contained in sequences.

Each request sequence has a request sequence identifier, unique within the service. If the sequence is loaded from a file, the identifier "can be used by the loading policy". The sequence contains an ordered list of request entries, and PUS-C sets no maximum on their number. Each entry contains:10

  1. a single request;
  2. a time interval: the delay between the release of this request and the release of the next. For the last entry, it is the delay between the last release and the completion of the sequence.

For each loaded sequence the subservice keeps a request sequence execution status, "inactive" (raw value 0) or "under execution" (raw value 1).1011

stateDiagram-v2
  direction LR
  [*] --> Inactive : TC(21,1) direct-load / TC(21,2) load by reference
  [*] --> UnderExecution : TC(21,8) load by reference and activate
  Inactive --> UnderExecution : TC(21,4) activate
  UnderExecution --> Inactive : last release + its interval elapsed
  UnderExecution --> Inactive : TC(21,5) abort / TC(21,13) abort all
  Inactive --> [*] : TC(21,3) unload

The state machine is drawn from clauses 6.21.5.2 to 6.21.5.8.13141516171819 "UnderExecution" stands for "under execution". Sequences are persistent. They stay loaded after completion, and to remove one automatically "the last request in the sequence can be the request to unload the request sequence".16

docs.title: 3.3 Timing: a worked example
docs.text:
The interval semantics are easiest to see with numbers. The sequence below is illustrative: three entries with intervals of 10 s, 0 s and 5 s, activated at t0.

Entry Request Interval Released at Note 1 R1 10 s t0 released on activation 2 R2 0 s t0 + 10 s 10 s after R1 3 R3 5 s t0 + 10 s together with R2 (interval 0) - - - t0 + 15 s status returns to "inactive"

The rules applied are 6.21.4g and 6.21.5.5f.1016 Each interval runs from a release, not from the completion of execution. R2 is released 10 s after R1 whether R1 succeeded, failed or is still executing.1

docs.title: 3.4 Loading capabilities
docs.text:
A subservice must offer at least one of three ways to get a sequence on board:12

  • direct load (TC[21,1]): the request itself contains the requests of the sequence;
  • load by reference (TC[21,2]): the sequence already exists on board in a file, and the request names that file;
  • load by reference and activate (TC[21,8]).

If load by reference is offered, the mission declares whether a loading policy is supported. With a policy, the policy, rather than an explicit file path, determines which file holds the sequence.1214 ST[21] does not define the policy itself. The equivalent ST[18] clause for OBCPs refers to ECSS-E-ST-70-01, clauses 5.4.4.4a to c.20

docs.title: 4. Requests and reports
docs.text:
Every ST[21] request carries exactly one instruction, so a rule violation rejects the whole request with one failed start of execution notification (TM[1,4]). This differs from the per-instruction rejection of ST[19] and ST[20] in the 2016 text.1324 The field types are the PUS-C types:252627

  • the request sequence ID is a fixed character-string (PTC 8, PFC n > 0: n visible ASCII characters, one octet each);
  • file path parts are variable character-strings (PTC 8 PFC 0: a length field followed by that many characters; the PFC of the length field is declared per application process);
  • request is a TC packet (PTC 12 PFC 1), a complete PUS-C telecommand;
  • delay is a relative time (PTC 10), a CUC or CDS offset whose PFC is chosen by the mission.

docs.title: 4.1 TC[21,1] direct-load a request sequence
docs.text:
The instruction carries the sequence identifier and its ordered list of entries.13

Field Type Meaning request sequence ID fixed character-string identifier of the new sequence N unsigned integer number of entries request TC packet repeated N times: the request to release delay relative time repeated N times: the interval after that request

Source: Figure 8-228.28 The request is rejected if the identifier is already loaded, if resources are insufficient, or if any contained request fails the declared verification checks. Otherwise the sequence is loaded with status "inactive".13

The delay field width depends on the mission's choice of PFC. As an illustration, PFC 17 in the relative time table is CUC with (17 + 1) div 4 = 4 octets of coarse time and (17 + 1) mod 4 = 2 octets of fine time:26

A 10 s delay in this format is 00 00 00 0A 00 00, an illustrative encoding computed from the formula of Table 7-11.26

docs.title: 4.2 TC[21,2] load a request sequence by reference
docs.text:
The instruction carries the identifier and, unless the loading policy is used, the file path of the on-board file.14

Field Type Presence request sequence ID fixed character-string always repository path variable character-string optional (absent when the loading policy applies) file name variable character-string optional

Source: Figure 8-229.29 A file path is the combination of a repository path and an object name, as for any on-board file system.30 Besides the TC[21,1] conditions, the request is rejected if the file does not exist or is not recognised as a request sequence file. A valid request loads the sequence with status "inactive".14 PUS-C names the request sequencing subservice as an example of a service that accesses the file system without going through ST[23].31

docs.title: 4.3 TC[21,3] unload a request sequence
docs.text: This request is provided if either load capability is. It carries the sequence ID (Figure 8-230). It is rejected if the sequence is not loaded or is "under execution". Otherwise the sequence is unloaded.1532

docs.title: 4.4 TC[21,4] activate a request sequence
docs.text: This is a minimum capability, and it carries the sequence ID (Figure 8-231). It is rejected if the sequence is not loaded, if resources are insufficient, or if the sequence is already under execution. A valid request sets the status to "under execution" and starts releasing. After the last release and the elapse of its interval, the status returns to "inactive".1633 Re-activating a running sequence is therefore an error, not a restart.

docs.title: 4.5 TC[21,8] load by reference and activate a request sequence
docs.text: This capability exists if declared. It has the same fields as TC[21,2] (Figure 8-234) and combines the load and the activation in one request.1734 The rejection list is that of TC[21,2] plus activation. In the 2016 text, the lack of resources appears twice, as items 2 and 5.17 The loaded sequence remains loaded (persistent) after completion.17

docs.title: 4.6 TC[21,5] abort a request sequence
docs.text: This is a minimum capability, and it carries the sequence ID (Figure 8-232). It is rejected if the sequence is not loaded or is "inactive". A valid request sets it to "inactive" and stops releasing.1835

docs.title: 4.7 TC[21,13] / TM[21,14] abort all request sequences and report
docs.text: This capability exists if declared. TC[21,13] has no application data.1936 For each sequence under execution, releasing stops and the status becomes "inactive". One TM[21,14] lists the aborted identifiers: N (unsigned integer), then N request sequence IDs (fixed character-strings).1937

docs.title: 4.8 TC[21,6] / TM[21,7] execution status of each sequence
docs.text:
This capability exists if declared. TC[21,6] has no application data. TM[21,7] contains one entry for each loaded sequence:383940

Field Type Meaning N unsigned integer number of loaded sequences request sequence ID fixed character-string repeated execution status enumerated 0 = inactive, 1 = under execution

docs.title: 4.9 TC[21,9] / TM[21,10] checksum a request sequence
docs.text: This capability exists if declared. TC[21,9] carries one sequence ID and is rejected if the sequence is not loaded. TM[21,10] returns the ID and the calculated checksum, a 16-bit bit-string, the only field of the service whose size the standard fixes.414243 The algorithm is one of the spacecraft's declared checksum algorithms. PUS-C asks the mission to declare, for each checksum algorithm, the subservice providers that use it, so that all providers that checksum the same data object use the same algorithm. The algorithm also fixes the checksum type (ISO or CRC) and size.44

docs.title: 4.10 TC[21,11] / TM[21,12] report the content of a sequence
docs.text: This capability exists if declared. TC[21,11] carries one ID and is rejected if the sequence is not loaded. TM[21,12] returns the ID and the ordered entries in the same layout as TC[21,1]: N, then N pairs of request and delay.454647 Figure 8-238 carries a note pointing to the execution status enumeration, although the report has no status field. This looks like a copy-over from Figure 8-233.47

docs.title: 4.11 Observables and enumeration
docs.text: The subservice must expose the list of loaded sequence identifiers and their execution status, as an array sized for the maximum number of sequences that can be loaded at once.48 The status enumeration (Table 8-22) is "inactive" = 0 and "under execution" = 1.11

docs.title: 5. ST[21] among its neighbours
docs.text:
Service What triggers a release What is stored on board ST[21] request sequencing activation, then the delay of each entry; not conditional on earlier results1 ordered lists of (request, delay), loaded directly or from a file12 ST[11] time-based scheduling the due on-board time2 activities inserted by TC[11,4]22 ST[22] position-based scheduling the spacecraft reaching an orbit position position-tagged requests, with sub-schedules and groups23 ST[18] OBCP the procedure's own logic OBCP code, loaded directly (TC[18,1]) or by reference (TC[18,13])2021 ST[19] event-action an event occurrence one request per event definition49

The relation to ST[19] is explicit in the standard: an event-action can "start a request sequence".49

Inference

The design rationale is this wiki's reading. ST[21] is the light-weight option: it needs no procedure engine and no time-tag arithmetic, and a single TC[21,8] stored as the action of an event-action definition can fire a recovery of any length. The standard does not discuss these trade-offs.

docs.title: 6. The 2024 Rev.1 draft
docs.text:
The Rev.1 public-review draft (DIR1, December 2024) changes ST[21] more than ST[19] or ST[20]. This wiki's word-by-word comparison found:

  • Directories. A new clause 6.21.5 "Usage of directories" lets the mission declare the maximum number of request sequence directories. Each directory has two attributes: immediate execution of request sequence files after creation, and immediate deletion of request sequence files after execution. A file is "created" in a directory when it is uploaded there or moved or copied into it.50
  • Three new message types: TC[21,15] change request sequence directory attributes, TC[21,16] report the attributes of a request sequence directory, and TM[21,17] request sequence directory attributes report. TC[21,15] and TM[21,17] carry a directory path (variable character-string) and two Booleans, and TC[21,16] carries the path only.5152
  • Identifier type. The request sequence ID changes from a fixed character-string to an enumerated field in every message.53
  • TC[21,8] unloads after completion. Load-and-activate now sets the status to "inactive" and unloads the sequence after the last interval. A reserved identifier value requests "the next free identifier".5455
  • Timing declaration. If TC[21,8] is provided, the mission declares the time needed to activate a sequence and release its first request.56
  • Clarifications. Aborting does not unload a sequence. The duplicated lack-of-resources item is removed. The observables add "reference of the request if activated".5758

The draft has visible editing residue. Clause 6.21.10 d to f speaks of "the storage and retrieval subservice". Requirement 8.21.2.8c sets "N" to 0 although TC[21,8] has no N field. Clause 8.21.2.15b cites "Figure 8.15-7", 8.21.2.16b and 8.21.2.17b cite Figures 8.21-10 and 8.21-11 (the figures printed under them are 8.21-14 and 8.21-15), and their notes refer to a clause "6.21.911". The stray execution-status note of the 2016 Figure 8-238 is gone from its Rev.1 counterpart, Figure 8.21-11.51555253

Inference

The directory attributes standardise a pattern that missions already used. Solar Orbiter's file attribute "TC sequence - immediate" (section 7.2) executes an uplinked TC file as soon as the upload completes. That Rev.1 was influenced by such missions is not stated in the available sources.

docs.title: 7.1 Service type 21 is "science data transfer"
docs.text:
Solar Orbiter follows ECSS-E-70-41A. Like the earlier Herschel/Planck interface requirements, which state that "Science data Packets shall be type 21", it uses service type 21 for Science Data Transfer between the payload and the solid state mass memory (SSMM). The number has nothing to do with PUS-C's ST[21].596061 Packet category 12 is "PRIVATE-SCIENCE or TELECOMMAND", described as exclusive for service 21 telemetry and for telecommands.62 In the 2025 MIB, all 334 service 21 packet definitions and the APIDs of all 5,449 commands that have one (for example APID 236 of the CSW system control process) use category 12.71 Table 5.1-1 makes the service mandatory for payloads.63

Message Content (SOL.S.ASTR.TN.00079 §5.22) TC(21,1) / TC(21,2) enable/start and disable/stop science transfer to the SSMM, as defined by each instrument; at least one pair is required TM(21,3) fixed length, with a 1-octet structure ID (SSID, 0-255) selecting the parameter list TM(21,4) fixed length, no SSID TM(21,5) variable-length "anonymous data stream": SSID (1 octet), N (2 octets), then N data words TM(21,6) variable length with fixed start and end parameter blocks around a repeated block of N1 entries TC(21,128) Reset Output Buffer (listed in Table 5.1-1 only)

Source: §5.22.1 to §5.22.6 and Table 5.1-1.6163

The 2025 MIB holds 334 service 21 packet definitions and 33 commands.71

Instrument TM(21,3) TM(21,5) TM(21,6) TM(21,7) Total EPD 8 36 12 0 56 EUI 0 36 0 0 36 MAG 19 0 0 0 19 METIS 0 0 30 0 30 PHI 0 0 2 0 2 RPW 18 0 47 0 65 SOLOHI 6 0 0 0 6 SPICE 0 0 0 6 6 STIX 0 0 18 0 18 SWA 54 0 42 0 96

The instrument is identified from the process ID of the APID (APID div 16) using the allocation of Annex 8.7164 SPICE's six TM(21,7) packets ("SPICE Detector Science Uncompressed" and similar) use a subtype that the issue 7 ICD does not define. For TM(21,3), (21,5) and (21,6), the MIB identifies the SSID as the 8-bit field at octet 16 (pic).71

docs.title: 7.2 The real counterpart: private service 134 "TC Sequencer"
docs.text:
What PUS-C calls request sequencing, Solar Orbiter's CSW provides as service 134, TC Sequencer. The service is reserved for the CSW. It manages "TC Sequences (also called TC Files)": files of telecommand packets uploaded beforehand with service 13, which Solar Orbiter calls "Large Data Transfer" (the PUS-C counterpart is ST[13] large packet transfer). Execution reads the packets in order and releases them "at a given rate, with potentially some delays between chosen consecutive TCs".6563

  • The upload attribute selects TC File - Delayed, executed on request by TC(134,1), or **TC File
  • Immediate**, executed automatically after a successful upload, "the intended mechanism for MTL uploading".65 For an immediate file the CSW creates a TC(134,1) itself, with TC sequence identifier 1 and a rate of 1 Hz.66
  • Sequences are controlled by a logical TcSeq ID. Per ID there can be at most one queued sequence, waiting while another sequence with the same ID runs.65
  • At software initialisation, service 134 executes the selected back-up timeline file in the safeguard memory and so loads the mission timeline queue with back-up time-tagged TCs. At least two file placeholders allow one to be updated safely.67
  • Among the source IDs that the ground sets, 111 is "TC Sequences", next to 110 for the mission timeline and 112 for event-action recovery commands.68
Message Fields PUS-C analogue TC(134,1) Start TC Sequence TcSeq ID (1), Partition ID (1), File ID (4), TC Exec Rate (4, float) TC[21,8] load by reference and activate TC(134,2) Abort TC Sequence TcSeq ID, Partition ID, File ID TC[21,5] TC(134,3) TC Sequence Wait Delay Delay (2 octets, multiples of 125 ms); used only inside a sequence the per-entry delay TC(134,4) TC Sequence Set Frequency TC Exec Rate (4, float); used only inside a sequence (no analogue)

Source: §5.28.1 to §5.28.4.6970 The receiving functions must be able to keep up with the selected rate.69

The two models of time differ. PUS-C puts a delay in every entry. Solar Orbiter releases at a base rate and inserts TC(134,3) "wait" commands, which may only appear inside a sequence, where a longer gap is needed. A 16-bit count of 125 ms steps allows gaps of up to 65,535 × 0.125 s = 8,191.875 s, about 2 h 16 min. This figure is arithmetic on the field definition, not stated in the source.70 Neither the TN service list nor the MIB has telemetry of type 134, so Solar Orbiter has no equivalent of TM[21,7], TM[21,10] or TM[21,12].6371

Inference

With no service 134 reports, the ground presumably follows TC file execution through the verification reports of the released TCs (source ID 111) and through CSW housekeeping. The sources do not describe how sequence status is monitored.

docs.title: 7.3 Service 134 in the MIB
docs.text:
Both MIB releases contain TC(134,1) to TC(134,4) (ZCD08601-ZCD08604) and two subtypes absent from the issue 7 ICD: TC(134,5) "Start Two Part Id TC Sequence" (ZCD08605, shortened to "Start Two Part Id TC SEQ" in 2025) and TC(134,6) "Abort Two Part Id TC Sequence" (ZCD08606). These add a "Storage Partition ID" octet between the partition ID and the file ID. TC(134,6) has no rate field.7172 All are addressed to APID 172 (process ID 10, DMS). Both partition parameters use the calibration CCDT0192TX, with values such as OMM_TC_FILES_A = 161, OMM_TC_FILES_B = 177, SGMA_TC_FILES = 193 and SGMB_TC_FILES = 195.71

The 2025 release adds seven canned TC(134,5) commands that start FDIR TC files. The 2020 release has only the generic ZCD08605:7172

Command Description TcSeq ID File ID (hex) Rate (Hz) ZCDX8605 Execute Loss-of-UL FDIR TC File 58 00840010 1 ZCDX8606 Execute SNAFU FDIR TC File 54 00440010 1 ZCDX8607 Execute REC_SpW3_SpW OL FDIR TC File 53 00340010 10 ZCDX8608 Execute REC_SSMM1 A FDIR TC File 53 00340020 10 ZCDX8609 Execute REC_SSMM1 B FDIR TC File 53 00340030 10 ZCDX8610 Execute REC_SSMM2 A FDIR TC File 53 00340040 10 ZCDX8611 Execute REC_SSMM2 B FDIR TC File 53 00340050 10

All seven use partition OMM_TC_FILES_A with storage partition OMM_TC_FILES_B.71 The first two are the actions of the event-action definitions ZCSX1301 and ZCSX1302. On an unexpected loss of uplink, or on the AOCS event chosen for "SNAFU", the CSW's event-action service starts the corresponding TC file, which is exactly PUS-C's "event-action starts a request sequence" pattern.7149

Inference

"Two Part Id" plausibly means that the file is identified by a pair of partitions, here the A and B copies of the OMM TC-file area, so that the sequencer can fall back to the other copy. The five SpaceWire and SSMM recovery files (ZCDX8607 to ZCDX8611) share TcSeq ID 53, so under the rule of at most one queued sequence per ID they cannot run in parallel: while one runs, only one other can wait. Neither reading is stated in the available sources.

In ground sequences, TC(134,1), TC(134,2) and TC(134,6) are used once each and TC(134,5) twice.71

SQL used 
-- solo-2025-09-16.sqlite
SELECT CCF_CNAME, CCF_DESCR, CCF_STYPE, CCF_APID FROM ccf WHERE CCF_TYPE='134' ORDER BY CAST(CCF_STYPE AS INT);

  FROM cdf c LEFT JOIN cpc p ON p.CPC_NAME=c.CDF_PNAME
 WHERE c.CDF_CNAME LIKE 'ZCD0860%' OR c.CDF_CNAME LIKE 'ZCDX86%' ORDER BY 1, CAST(c.CDF_BIT AS INT);
SELECT PAS_ALTXT, PAS_ALVAL FROM pas WHERE PAS_NUMBR='CCDT0192TX';
SELECT count(*) FROM pid WHERE PID_TYPE='134';                                  -- 0
-- service 21 science data per instrument (process ID = APID / 16)

SELECT CCF_STYPE, count(*) FROM ccf WHERE CCF_TYPE='21' GROUP BY 1;             -- 1:14 2:14 128:5
SELECT * FROM pic WHERE PIC_TYPE='21';
-- use in ground sequences
SELECT c.CCF_TYPE, c.CCF_STYPE, count(*) FROM css s JOIN ccf c ON c.CCF_CNAME=s.CSS_ELEMID
 WHERE s.CSS_TYPE='C' AND c.CCF_TYPE='134' GROUP BY 1,2;

SELECT CCF_CNAME, CCF_DESCR FROM ccf WHERE CCF_TYPE='134';                      -- ZCD08601..ZCD08606 only

docs.title: ST[22] Position-based scheduling
docs.text:
ST[22] position-based scheduling is the PUS-C service type that keeps telecommands on board and releases each one when the spacecraft reaches a chosen point on its orbit, instead of at a chosen time. It is the orbit-position counterpart of ST[11] time-based scheduling: the ground loads requests together with a position tag (an orbit number plus a position on that orbit), and the on-board subservice releases them when that position comes round. The standard does not say how the spacecraft knows where it is; that is left to the mission.1 Because an orbit position comes back on every revolution, ST[22] also offers something ST[11] does not: persistent activities that stay in the schedule and fire again on a later orbit.26

At a glance

Item Value Defined in ECSS-E-ST-70-41C (15 April 2016): system clause 6.22, interface clause 8.22, summary in Annex C Table C-3112746 Previous edition none: PUS-A (2003) lists no service 22; its standard services stop at 1956 Subservice types exactly one, the position-based scheduling subservice; at most one provider per application process3 Message types 28: 24 requests (TC) and 4 reports (TM), subtypes 1 to 28 with no gaps46 Minimum capability TC[22,1], TC[22,2], TC[22,3], TC[22,4]; everything else is "by declaration" or implied46 Optional concepts persistent scheduling, sub-schedules, groups, identification by request ID, position-window filters672324 Draft revision ECSS-E-ST-70-41C Rev.1 DIR1 (11 December 2024) changes several rules; see below58 Solar Orbiter does not implement it; its service type 22 is a mission "Context Saving" service66

docs.title: Why schedule by position?
docs.text:
PUS-C groups ST[22] with ST[11] and ST[19] event-action as service types that hold requests and release them when something happens: a time, an orbit position, or an event.50 Position-based scheduling extends ground monitoring and control. The application process that executes a released request sends its verification reports directly to the source named in the request, that is, the ground application that loaded it. The release of a request does not depend on whether earlier released requests succeeded or failed.2 The released request is not generated by the scheduling subservice: it remains a request of the original source.4

The two scheduling services are built from the same template. Subtypes 1 to 27 have the same numbers and the same names, with "time" replaced by "position", and every capability of ST[11] has a positional twin:4647

Aspect ST[11] time-based ST[22] position-based Release tag in TC[x,4] release time, an absolute time field49 position tag, a "deduced" field whose structure the mission declares2927 Insertion guard time margin: release time must be at least current time + margin48 position margin: release position must be at least current position + margin8 Release accuracy maximum delta time between tag and real release, declared48 maximum delta position between tag and real release, declared8 Shifting time-shift: TC[11,7], TC[11,8], TC[11,15]47 position-shift: TC[22,7], TC[22,8], TC[22,15]46 Repeating activities not offered: Table C-17 ends at TM[11,27] with no persistency fields4749 optional persistent activities with a periodicity in orbits6 Extra request - TC[22,28] set the orbit number10

docs.title: Position tag: orbit number plus angle
docs.text:
Every position tag has two parts: the orbit number and the position on that orbit. The orbit number never wraps round during a mission, while the position within the orbit is cyclic. The orbit number increases on board by itself, and the ground can set it with TC[22,28].5 The position is an angle measured in the plane of the osculating inertial orbit, starting from its intersection with the Earth-fixed equatorial plane. The 2016 standard goes no further: the algorithm and the accuracy used to compute the angle are mission-specific.5

\[ \text{position tag} = (n, \theta), \qquad n \in \mathbb{N} \text{ (orbit number, never wraps)}, \qquad \theta \text{ (angle on the orbit, cyclic)} \]

The bit layout of a position tag, and of the delta position used to shift activities, is not fixed by the standard either: both must be declared when the subservice is specified, which is why clause 8 types them as "deduced".27 A deduced field (PTC 11, PFC 0) has a structure that follows from preceding fields of the same packet or from mission constants.54

Inference

The standard compares positions ("earlier than", "greater than", "in the order of their release positions") without spelling out the ordering. Since the orbit number is monotonic and the angle is cyclic, the natural order is lexicographic: first by orbit number, then by angle. This wiki uses that reading in its examples.

docs.title: Scheduled activities
docs.text:
The schedule is a set of scheduled activities. Each one holds the request to be released and its scheduling data:82

Element Present when Meaning Request always the telecommand packet to release later Position tag always release position (orbit number, position on orbit) Activity persistency status persistent scheduling supported persistent or non-persistent Persistent activity periodicity persistent scheduling supported (and status persistent, on the wire) an integer number of orbits Sub-schedule ID sub-schedules supported the sub-schedule the activity belongs to Group ID groups supported the group the activity belongs to

A scheduled activity is identified by the request identifier of the request it contains. PUS-C builds that identifier from the source ID (the application process user identifier of the originator), the destination (APID plus system identifier), and the packet sequence count or request name.852 On the wire, ST[22] reports and requests carry it as three fields: source ID, application process ID and sequence count.2030

erDiagram
  SCHEDULE ||--o{ SCHEDULED_ACTIVITY : contains
  SUB_SCHEDULE ||--o{ SCHEDULED_ACTIVITY : "groups (optional)"
  GROUP ||--o{ SCHEDULED_ACTIVITY : "groups (optional)"
  SCHEDULED_ACTIVITY ||--|| REQUEST : wraps
  SCHEDULED_ACTIVITY {
    tag position "orbit number + angle"
    enum persistency "persistent / non-persistent"
    uint periodicity "orbits"
  }
  REQUEST {
    enum sourceID
    enum APID
    uint sequenceCount
  }
  SUB_SCHEDULE {
    enum id
    enum status "enabled / disabled"
  }
  GROUP {
    enum id
    enum status "enabled / disabled"
  }

The diagram restates clauses 6.22.1.2, 6.22.6.2, 6.22.7.1 and 6.22.8.1.281417 Position-based sub-schedules and groups are among the system objects that the standard says a service maintains.51

docs.title: Persistent scheduling
docs.text: By default an entry is deleted once its request is released. If the subservice supports persistent scheduling, each activity carries an activity persistency status. A non-persistent activity is deleted after release; a persistent one stays in the schedule and can be released again or deleted later.6 When a persistent activity's release position is reached, the subservice adds its persistent activity periodicity (an integer number of orbits) to its orbit number. The activity therefore comes back every k orbits at the same angle.138

docs.title: Sub-schedules
docs.text: A sub-schedule is a sequence of position-tagged requests that together perform one coherent on-board operation. Sub-schedules are created automatically when an insert request names an unknown one, and they are deleted when they become empty. A new sub-schedule starts in the disabled state.212 Each sub-schedule has a status, enabled or disabled, and the mission declares the maximum number that can exist at the same time.14

docs.title: Groups
docs.text: A group is a second, independent way to switch requests on and off. It works regardless of the destination application process and of the sub-schedule. Groups typically map to spacecraft entities such as a unit or a piece of software, and the standard's example is an instrument whose requests are held back while its conditions are not met. Unlike sub-schedules, groups are created and deleted by explicit request and may exist while empty.217 A group that still has activities cannot be deleted.18

docs.title: The margins
docs.text:
Two declared quantities protect the schedule:8

  • the position margin: an activity can only be inserted or shifted if its release position is at least the current position plus the margin. This keeps the schedule consistent at all times;
  • the maximum delta position: the largest allowed gap between the release position in a scheduled activity and the position at which the request is really released.

docs.title: What a mission must declare
docs.text:
PUS-C leaves many ST[22] properties to the mission's own specification of the subservice. A mission that implements ST[22] has to state at least the following:

Declaration Clause Note Application processes the subservice can release requests to 6.22.3.1a4 the hosting process is always addressable Whether persistent scheduling is provided 6.22.5a6 Whether sub-schedules are supported 6.22.6.1a7 Whether groups are supported 6.22.6.1b7 Maximum number of scheduled activities 6.22.6.2c8 resources assumed sufficient whatever the request sizes Position margin 6.22.6.2d8 Maximum delta position 6.22.6.2e8 Capability to set the orbit number (TC[22,28]) 6.22.6.4a10 Verification checks applied to a request being inserted 6.22.6.6f12 Maximum number of sub-schedules 6.22.7.1a14 Maximum number of groups 6.22.8.1a17 Identification of activities by request identifier 6.22.11.1a23 needed by TC[22,5], [22,7], [22,9], [22,12] Position-window filtering 6.22.12.1a24 needed by TC[22,6], [22,8], [22,11], [22,14] Structure and format of position tags and of delta positions 8.22.1b, 8.22.1c27 the "deduced" fields of clause 8 Each "by declaration" capability (Annex C) Table C-3146 see the message table below

docs.title: The execution function
docs.text:
The whole schedule has an on/off switch, the position-based schedule execution function status. It is disabled when the subservice starts. TC[22,1] enables it and TC[22,2] disables it, whether or not the schedule contains activities. TC[22,3] resets the schedule: it disables the function, deletes every activity, deletes all sub-schedules (if supported) and re-enables all groups (if supported).911

stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Disabled : subservice start
  Disabled --> Enabled : TC[22,1]
  Enabled --> Disabled : TC[22,2]
  Enabled --> Disabled : TC[22,3] reset (schedule emptied)
  Disabled --> Disabled : TC[22,3] reset (schedule emptied)

docs.title: Release logic
docs.text:
The execution process handles activities in order of release position. An activity counts as disabled if the execution function is disabled, if its sub-schedule is disabled, or if its group is disabled. When an activity's release position is reached, the process runs these steps in order:13

flowchart TB
  R["Release position of an activity reached"] --> D{"Disabled?<br/>(function, sub-schedule<br/>or group disabled)"}
  D -- no --> REL["Release the request to its<br/>destination application process"]
  D -- yes --> SKIP["Request not released"]
  REL --> P{"Persistent scheduling<br/>supported?"}
  SKIP --> P
  P -- no --> DEL["Delete the activity"]
  P -- yes --> PS{"Activity<br/>persistent?"}
  PS -- no --> DEL
  PS -- yes --> INC["Orbit number += periodicity<br/>(activity stays in the schedule)"]
  DEL --> E{"Sub-schedule<br/>now empty?"}
  E -- yes --> DSS["Delete the sub-schedule"]
  E -- no --> END["Done"]
  INC --> END
  DSS --> END

Three consequences are worth spelling out, because they are easy to get wrong in an implementation or a ground model:13

  • A disabled activity is not kept for later. When its position passes, it is deleted (or, if persistent, moved on by its periodicity) exactly as if it had been released.
  • The standard prescribes no notification to the ground when a request is deleted without having been released.
  • The release order of activities with exactly the same position is not prescribed.

A small inconsistency in Annex C

The system clause says the capability to report sub-schedule status (TC[22,18]) requires the capability to enable sub-schedules.16 Annex C nevertheless marks TC[22,18] "by declaration", whereas its ST[11] twin TC[11,18] is marked "requires TC[11,20]".4647

docs.title: Data fields, message by message
docs.text: The structure diagrams of clause 8 give field names and PUS field types but no sizes: the enumerated and unsigned integer widths are chosen by the mission, and position fields are "deduced". Fields marked optional are present or absent at mission, application process or service level (for example, the sub-schedule ID exists only if sub-schedules are supported). A "repeated N times" block is an array: for a variable-length array the count N is sent first, for a fixed-length one N is known implicitly. Every ST[22] array is of the first kind, with an explicit N field.53 See PUS parameter types for the field types.

docs.title: Requests without application data
docs.text: TC[22,1], TC[22,2], TC[22,3], TC[22,16], TC[22,17], TC[22,18] and TC[22,26] have no application data field at all.284043

docs.title: TC[22,4] insert activities into the position-based schedule
docs.text:
Field Type Presence Meaning sub-schedule ID enumerated optional (sub-schedules supported) sub-schedule for all activities in this request; created (disabled) if unknown N unsigned integer always number of activities that follow repeated N times: group ID enumerated optional (groups supported) group of this activity position tag deduced always release position; structure declared by the mission activity persistency status enumerated optional (persistent scheduling supported) non-persistent = 0, persistent = 1 persistent activity periodicity unsigned integer deduced presence: only when the status is persistent period in orbits request TC packet always the complete telecommand packet to release

This is Figure 8-240.29 The sub-schedule ID is per request, while group, position and persistency are per instruction, mirroring the system requirements.12 The embedded request is a full PUS telecommand packet, which PUS-C types as PTC 12, PFC 1.55

Checks. The whole request fails its start of execution if it would create a sub-schedule beyond the declared maximum. Each instruction is then checked on its own and rejected if the schedule is full, if it names an unknown group, if its position is inconsistent with the planned orbit, if it is non-persistent and earlier than current position plus margin, or if the embedded request fails the declared verification checks. Valid instructions are executed even when others in the same request fail.12

Effect. For each valid instruction a new scheduled activity is created with the given request, position tag, persistency status, sub-schedule and group. A persistent activity whose position is already below current position plus margin is moved forward by its periodicity as many times as needed, rather than rejected.12

docs.title: Requests that identify activities by request ID
docs.text:
TC[22,5] (delete), TC[22,9] (detail-report) and TC[22,12] (summary-report) all carry a list of request identifiers; TC[22,7] (position-shift) puts one delta position in front of the list, and that delta applies to every listed activity.3032343723

Field Type Present in Meaning delta position deduced TC[22,7] only shift to apply; format declared by the mission N unsigned integer all four number of request IDs repeated N times: source ID enumerated all four originator of the scheduled request application process ID enumerated all four destination APID of the scheduled request sequence count unsigned integer all four packet sequence count of the scheduled request

An unknown request identifier makes only its own instruction fail (failed start of execution); the others are still processed. Deleting the last activity of a sub-schedule deletes the sub-schedule too.23

docs.title: Requests that select activities with a filter
docs.text:
TC[22,6] (delete), TC[22,11] (detail-report) and TC[22,14] (summary-report) carry one filter; TC[22,8] (position-shift) carries a delta position followed by the same filter.31333639

Field Type Presence Meaning delta position deduced TC[22,8] only shift to apply position window: type enumerated always 0 all, 1 between 2 position tags, 2 from position tag, 3 to position tag tag 1 deduced deduced presence (types 1 and 2) the "from" position tag tag 2 deduced deduced presence (types 1 and 3) the "to" position tag N1 + N1 × sub-schedule ID unsigned integer + enumerated optional (sub-schedules supported) zero or more sub-schedules N2 + N2 × group ID unsigned integer + enumerated optional (groups supported) zero or more groups

The window types and their raw values come from Table 8-25.45 The filter semantics are in Filtering below. A request fails as a whole if the window type is invalid or if the "from" tag is greater than the "to" tag.25

docs.title: TC[22,15] position-shift all scheduled activities
docs.text: The only field is the delta position (deduced).40 The request is rejected, and nothing is shifted, if the earliest non-persistent activity would end up before current position plus margin. Otherwise every activity moves by the delta, and persistent activities that would fall below the margin are pushed forward by whole periodicities.22

docs.text:
Field Type Presence Meaning N (printed "enumerated", see note) always number of activities reported repeated N times: sub-schedule ID enumerated optional group ID enumerated optional position tag deduced always scheduled release position activity persistency status enumerated optional 0 non-persistent, 1 persistent persistent activity periodicity unsigned integer deduced presence (persistent only) orbits request TC packet always the complete stored request

Entries are ordered by release position.3521 The detail report returns the complete stored request, usually as a telecommand packet, whereas the summary report gives only its identifier.21

Printed type of N

Figure 8-246 types the counter N as "enumerated", while every other ST[22] array counter, including the one of the summary report, is an unsigned integer.3538 This looks like an editorial slip in the 2016 issue; it is not discussed in the available sources.

docs.title: Sub-schedule and group management
docs.text:
Message Fields Notes TC[22,20] enable / TC[22,21] disable position-based sub-schedules N (unsigned integer), N × sub-schedule ID (enumerated) N = 0 means "all sub-schedules"; unknown IDs are rejected one by one4215 TM[22,19] position-based sub-schedule status report N, N × (sub-schedule ID, sub-schedule status) status: 0 disabled, 1 enabled4145 TC[22,22] create position-based scheduling groups N, N × (group ID, group status) the initial status is given at creation; rejected if the group exists or the maximum is reached4218 TC[22,23] delete position-based scheduling groups N, N × group ID N = 0 deletes all groups; a group with activities cannot be deleted4218 TC[22,24] enable / TC[22,25] disable position-based scheduling groups N, N × group ID N = 0 means all groups4219 TM[22,27] position-based scheduling group status report N, N × (group ID, group status) status: 0 disabled, 1 enabled4345

The "delete all groups" variant has a twist: every group is deleted, and a failed execution notification is raised for each group that still had activities.18

Inference

Requirement 6.22.8.2.2h deletes the identifier of every group, yet 6.22.8.2.2d forbids deleting a group that has activities. Read together, the failure notification for such groups probably means those groups survive, but the text does not say so explicitly.

docs.title: TC[22,28] set the orbit number
docs.text: One field: the orbit number (unsigned integer). The new number takes effect at the end of the current orbit, not immediately. How the counter increments on board is left open.4410

docs.title: Enumerations
docs.text:
Table Field Raw value: meaning 8-23 sub-schedule status 0 disabled, 1 enabled 8-24 group status 0 disabled, 1 enabled 8-25 position window type 0 all, 1 between 2 position tags, 2 from position tag, 3 to position tag 8-26 activity persistency status 0 non-persistent, 1 persistent

All four come from clause 8.22.3.45

docs.title: Filtering
docs.text:
When the position-window filtering function is declared, a filter combines a position window with optional lists of sub-schedules and groups:24

  • from tag to tag: activities between the two tags, both included;
  • from tag: activities at or after the tag;
  • to tag: activities before or at the tag;
  • all (window type 0 in Table 8-25).45

The sub-schedule part selects every activity of the listed sub-schedules and silently ignores unknown sub-schedules. The group part selects every activity of the listed groups. When more than one part is present, the result is the intersection: (window) ∩ (union of the listed sub-schedules) ∩ (union of the listed groups).24

Inference

The standard says unknown sub-schedules are ignored in a filter, but is silent about unknown groups. Whether an unknown group in a filter is an error is not stated in the available sources.

docs.title: Position-shifting rules
docs.text:
All three shift requests (TC[22,7], TC[22,8], TC[22,15]) follow the same pattern:222325

  1. All or nothing for non-persistent activities. If adding the delta to the earliest non-persistent activity selected would put it before current position plus margin, the whole request fails at start of execution and nothing moves.
  2. Persistent activities never fail. A persistent activity that would fall below the margin is moved forward by its periodicity, as many times as needed, so a shifted persistent activity can never end up with a past tag.

docs.title: Worked example (illustrative)
docs.text:
The numbers below are invented for explanation; the standard fixes neither the units nor the encoding of positions and deltas.

Shifting a persistent activity

Assumptions: current position (orbit 1000, 90°); position margin 10°, so the earliest acceptable position is (1000, 100°); a persistent activity at (1000, 120°) with a periodicity of 1 orbit; no non-persistent activities are selected.

  1. TC[22,7] asks for a delta of −30°. The new tag would be (1000, 90°), below (1000, 100°).
  2. Because the activity is persistent, the request is not rejected: the orbit number is incremented by the periodicity until the tag clears the margin, giving (1001, 90°).23
  3. Had the activity been non-persistent, the same request would have been rejected with a failed start of execution and no activity would have moved.23

docs.title: Observables
docs.text: The subservice must publish five observables: the current orbit number; the execution function status; the number of scheduled activities; and, when supported, the number of sub-schedules and the number of groups.26 The standard lists them as observables of the subservice; how a mission reports them to the ground (for example as housekeeping parameters) is not stated in the available sources.

docs.title: A complete transaction
docs.text:
The sequence below follows one persistent activity from loading to its second release. It combines the insertion rules, the release logic and the ST[01] reporting rule that a released request reports to its original source.12132

sequenceDiagram
  participant G as Ground (source ID s)
  participant P as ST[22] provider (APID p)
  participant D as Destination process (APID d)
  G->>P: TC[22,4] sub-schedule 3, N=1, group 2, tag (orbit n, θ), persistent, period k, request R
  P-->>G: TM[1,1] / TM[1,7] for the TC[22,4] itself (if requested)
  G->>P: TC[22,20] enable sub-schedule 3 (new sub-schedules start disabled)
  G->>P: TC[22,1] enable the execution function
  Note over P: orbit n, angle θ reached
  P->>D: release R (still identified as a request of source s)
  D-->>G: TM[1,x] verification of R, sent to source s
  Note over P: R persistent: tag becomes (n+k, θ)
  Note over P: orbit n+k, angle θ reached
  P->>D: release R again
  D-->>G: TM[1,x] verification of R

docs.title: Illustrative encoding of TC[22,4]
docs.text:
The diagram shows one possible tailoring, with field widths invented for this example (the standard leaves all of them to the mission): 8-bit identifiers and counter, a position tag made of a 32-bit orbit number and a 32-bit angle in units of 360°/2^32, an 8-bit persistency status and a 16-bit periodicity. Only the start of the embedded request (its 6-octet Space Packet primary header) is drawn.

With these assumptions the first 14 octets would be 03 01 02 00 00 30 39 40 00 00 00 01 00 0F, followed by the embedded telecommand. These bytes are illustrative, not taken from any mission.

docs.title: What the 2024 Rev.1 draft changes
docs.text:
ECSS-E-ST-70-41C Rev.1 DIR1 is a public-review draft and not yet a standard.57 For ST[22] it keeps the same 28 message types60 but rewrites several rules:

Topic 2016 issue Rev.1 DIR1 draft (2024) Angle measured in the osculating orbit plane from the Earth-fixed equatorial plane; nothing more5 positive in the flight direction, measured from the ascending intersection with the equator, in degrees 0 to 360; angle accuracy must be declared58 Delta position format declared by the mission27 two parts: a signed orbit-number shift and a position shift in degrees58 New declarations - position resolution; configuration policy at start and restart (for example, whether a sub-schedule or group is disabled after its last activity)59 Reset (TC[22,3]) deletes all sub-schedules11 enables all sub-schedules61 Unknown sub-schedule on insert created automatically, disabled12 rejected62 Faulty instructions other instructions still processed12 the request is rejected as a whole; valid requests execute in order62 Same release position order not prescribed13 insertion order, although the copied NOTE 3 still says "not prescribed"63 Late release no rule an event report if an activity cannot be released within the maximum delta position63 Observables five26 adds first/last entry positions and the counts of persistent and non-persistent activities64

docs.title: Solar Orbiter: a different "service 22"
docs.text:
Solar Orbiter's space-to-ground ICD tailors its services from the ESA PUS, which for this mission is ECSS-E-70-41A (PUS-A), plus an ESA operations requirements document.65 PUS-A has no position-based scheduling, and the ICD uses type 22 for its own Context Saving Service instead.6656 The service lets a payload instrument save its operational context as a file in the OBC Mass Memory (OMM) before switch-off and get it back later:67

Subtype Direction Meaning in the Solar Orbiter ICD (22,1) TC, CSW to instrument request the user to report its context (22,2) TM, instrument to CSW context report from the user (context data up to 4094 octets) (22,3) TC, CSW to instrument accept the requested context: 2-byte segment counter N (1 to 18) and up to 234 octets of context data, sent at 1 Hz (22,4) TC, ground to CSW request the CSW to restore the stored context to an instrument (1-byte instrument PID) (22,5) TC, ground to CSW request the CSW to perform context saving for an instrument (1-byte instrument PID)

The OBC central software (CSW) stores the received TM(22,2) as a file in the OMM, where the ground can reach it with the private file management service 133 (see ST[23] file management).6769 The ICD prints both "up to 234 octets" and "236 octets" as the per-telecommand maximum; the MIB definition discussed below uses 234.6874

docs.title: What the MIB contains
docs.text:
The September 2025 Solar Orbiter MIB (MIB__20250916M25925PFMS001_SOL) has six commands and one telemetry packet of type 22, and no command or packet of type 22 with a position-based meaning:74

Name / SPID Type, subtype APID Description in the MIB Parameters ZIP16010 TC (22,1) 1164 requestContextReport none ZIX22001 TC (22,1) 1452 STIX Request User to Report Context none 54331 TM (22,2) 1451 STIX Context Report from User - ZIP16030 TC (22,3) 1164 acceptContextReport 16-bit segment counter (PTC 3, PFC 12), 1872-bit context data (PTC 7, PFC 234, i.e. 234 octets) ZIX22003 TC (22,3) 1452 STIX Accept Context 16-bit "N - Context Data Struct" (PTC 3, PFC 12), defined as a group repeater (CDF_GRPSIZE 1) over the 8-bit "Context Octet" (PTC 3, PFC 4) ZCD01604 TC (22,4) 172 Request CSW to restore context. 8-bit Process Identifier (PTC 2, PFC 8) ZCD01605 TC (22,5) 172 Request CSW to perform context saving fr... 8-bit Process Identifier (PTC 2, PFC 8)

The two TC(22,3) definitions differ. ZIP16030, whose parameters are named PHI_CONTEXT_segment and PHI_CONTEXT_data, follows the ICD layout, a segment counter followed by a fixed 234-octet block. STIX's ZIX22003 makes its 16-bit N a repeat count for the octet that follows, so in the database N gives the number of context octets, not the segment number that the ICD describes.747268

The Process Identifier parameter of ZCD01604 and ZCD01605 is decoded by the textual calibration CCDT0202TC, which lists 55 instrument process IDs from EPD_0_PID (50) to SPICE_8_PID (104). The April 2020 release had a second TM(22,2) packet, SPID 53091 "PHI_contextData" on APID 1163, which is no longer present in 2025.7475 The tables queried are ccf, cdf, cpc, pas and pid.

SQL used 
-- solo-2025-09-16.sqlite (MIB__20250916M25925PFMS001_SOL); same queries on solo-2020-04-16.sqlite
SELECT CCF_CNAME, CCF_DESCR, CCF_TYPE, CCF_STYPE, CCF_APID, CCF_NPARS
  FROM ccf WHERE CCF_TYPE = '22' ORDER BY CAST(CCF_STYPE AS INT);
SELECT PID_TYPE, PID_STYPE, PID_APID, PID_SPID, PID_DESCR FROM pid WHERE PID_TYPE = '22';
SELECT d.CDF_CNAME, d.CDF_ELLEN, d.CDF_BIT, d.CDF_PNAME, c.CPC_DESCR, c.CPC_PTC, c.CPC_PFC
  FROM cdf d LEFT JOIN cpc c ON c.CPC_NAME = d.CDF_PNAME
 WHERE d.CDF_CNAME IN ('ZIP16030','ZIX22003','ZCD01604','ZCD01605')
 ORDER BY 1, CAST(d.CDF_BIT AS INT);
SELECT PAS_ALTXT, PAS_ALVAL FROM pas WHERE PAS_NUMBR = 'CCDT0202TC';

docs.title: Scheduling support in the SCOS-2000 database
docs.text:
The SCOS-2000 MIB has explicit support for time-based on-board scheduling. The ICD requires the command that loads execution-time-tagged telecommands, the "(11,4)" insert command, to be defined in the database (both ccf and cdf). SCOS-2000 wraps time-tagged commands in it, and the wrapper's name, type, subtype and parameters are configured through SCOS-2000 MISCconfig variables (CMD_LOAD_TT*); the wrapper also reduces the space left for command parameters.70 Each command can also name a default on-board sub-schedule in CCF_SUBSCHEDID.71 Solar Orbiter's MIB defines that wrapper as INSERTTT, type 11 subtype 4 on APID 172.74

Inference

The ICD (issue 7.0) describes no equivalent for orbit-position tags. A mission flying ST[22] with SCOS-2000 would most likely define TC[22,4] as an ordinary ccf command whose last element carries the embedded packet, and build the position tag fields as normal command parameters. This is not documented in the available sources.

docs.title: ST[23] File management
docs.text:
ST[23] file management is the PUS-C service type that lets the ground manage on-board file systems: create, delete, lock and inspect files, manage directories, search for files, and copy or move files between file systems, including between the spacecraft and the ground.56 The user need not be on the ground: the standard's own example of an on-board subservice user is a payload controlling a solid-state mass memory through file management subservices.1 It is an interface service: it does not care what is inside a file, and it sits on top of an on-board file handling system that does the real work.54 For moving files across the space link it assumes a separate file transfer layer, for example the CCSDS File Delivery Protocol (CFDP), but it does not standardise that layer.6

At a glance

Item Value Defined in ECSS-E-ST-70-41C (15 April 2016): system clause 6.23, interface clause 8.23, Annex C Tables C-32 and C-3353851 Previous edition none: PUS-A (2003) has no file management service61 Subservice types file handling (exactly one per service) and file copy (at most one); if both exist they are hosted by the same application process7 Message types 24: 20 requests (TC) and 4 reports (TM)51 Minimum capability TC[23,1] create, TC[23,2] delete, TC[23,3]/TM[23,4] report attributes; TC[23,14] copy a file when the optional file copy subservice exists517 Related protocol CFDP (CCSDS 727.0-B-5) as a possible underlying file transfer layer662 Draft revision Rev.1 DIR1 (2024) adds checksum and directory protection, a new ST[24] file transfer service built on CFDP and a new ST[25] file data storage service7778 Solar Orbiter no ST[23]; files are managed with private service 133 and SSMM extensions of services 13 and 158086

docs.title: Files, repositories and paths
docs.text:
PUS-C defines a small vocabulary for file systems:235

Term Definition On-board file system a system that controls data organised in files; each one has exactly one identifier, unique across the whole spacecraft Object a file or a directory Repository path the logical path to where an object is located: a physical path such as a directory, or a logical path such as a mounted device (the standard's examples are /mm1 for a mass memory and /mm1/dir1) Object name the identifier of an object within its repository Object path repository path + object name (a file path or directory path); unique at mission level Flat / structured a flat file system has no directories; a structured one stores files in directories

For each file system the mission declares whether files may have unbounded size (limited only by the physical memory), which attributes exist (for example type or creation date), and whether files can be locked. A file system may be accessed by only one file management service.3 The service must always be able to read the size in bytes of any file, and, where locking exists, its lock status; the readable and settable attribute sets are declared per file system.11 Each file system also declares the wildcard characters it recognises.10

flowchart LR
  subgraph GROUND["Ground segment"]
    U["Subservice user<br/>(mission control system)"]
    GFS[("Ground file system<br/>(remote file system)")]
  end
  subgraph SC["Spacecraft"]
    subgraph AP["Application process hosting ST[23]"]
      FH["File handling<br/>subservice"]
      FC["File copy<br/>subservice"]
    end
    FHS["On-board file<br/>handling system"]
    FTH["File transfer handler<br/>(e.g. CFDP entity, or local copy)"]
    FS1[("File system A<br/>e.g. /mm1")]
    FS2[("File system B")]
    OTHER["Other services<br/>(ST[06], ST[18], ST[21])"]
  end
  U -- "TC[23,x]" --> FH
  U -- "TC[23,x]" --> FC
  FH -- "TM[23,4/8/13]" --> U
  FC -- "TM[23,23]" --> U
  FH --> FHS
  FHS --> FS1
  FHS --> FS2
  FC --> FTH
  FTH --> FS1
  FTH <-. "file transfer layer" .-> GFS
  OTHER -. "read/write files" .-> FHS

The diagram combines clauses 6.23.1 to 6.23.3 and 6.23.5: the file handling subservice talks to the on-board file handling system, the file copy subservice uses an underlying file transfer handler, and other services may use the same file systems, because ST[23] has no exclusive access.6825

docs.title: Who detects which error
docs.text:
The standard deliberately leaves argument checking to be shared between the service and the file handling system, and defines only the outcome:8

Error found by Example Reported as the file management service an invalid object path, a wildcard where none is allowed failed start of execution the on-board file handling system creating a file that already exists, deleting a missing or protected file failed completion of execution

Both appear as ST[01] request verification reports (TM[1,4] and TM[1,8]).58

docs.title: What a mission must declare
docs.text: Declaration Clause File systems accessed by the service 6.23.3.2.1a<sup>9</sup> For each file system: unbounded file size supported; supported attributes; locking supported 5.4.5c-e<sup>3</sup> Wildcard characters recognised by each file system 6.23.3.3a<sup>10</sup> Readable and settable file attributes per file system 6.23.3.4.1<sup>11</sup> Wildcards supported in find patterns; extent of the search (one directory or recursive) 6.23.4.4c-d<sup>17</sup> Type of directory deletion (empty only, no sub-directories, recursive, ...) 6.23.4.5.2b<sup>19</sup> Whether directory renaming is supported 6.23.4.5.3b<sup>20</sup> File systems usable by the copy subservice as source, destination or both 6.23.5.1a<sup>23</sup> Whether file copy status reports include a progress indicator 6.23.5.5.1a<sup>33</sup> Each "by declaration" capability of Annex C Tables C-32, C-33<sup>51</sup>
