The table follows Annex C, which lists TM[23,23] as a response to TC[23,22] even though the report is generated periodically after that request, not once.5136 Every packet of the service carries service type 23.38 All rows also appear in the PUS message type catalogue.

docs.title: Field types used by ST[23]
docs.text: Almost every ST[23] request is built from variable-length character strings (PTC 8, PFC 0): an unsigned integer length followed by that many characters. The characters must be visible ASCII characters, one octet each, and the width of the length field is declared per application process.53 Paths are always split into two strings, repository path and object name, except in the found-files report, which returns whole matching paths.3943 Other types used are Boolean (PTC 1; PFC 0 is one bit, PFC n > 1 is n bits) for the lock status, unsigned integer for sizes, counters and operation IDs, enumerated for object type and operation status, relative time (PTC 10) for the reporting interval, and deduced (PTC 11) for the mission-defined additional attributes.525556 See PUS parameter types for the full PTC/PFC rules.

docs.title: TC[23,1] create a file
docs.text:
Instruction content: the object path; the maximum size in bytes (if the file system does not support unbounded files); the lock status (if locking is supported); and any additional attributes that can be set at creation. The request is rejected (failed start) for an invalid path or an invalid maximum size; if the file system then fails to create the file, a failed completion is reported.12

Field Type Presence Meaning repository path variable character-string always where to create the file file name variable character-string always name of the new file maximum size unsigned integer always on the wire size limit in bytes; 0 means unbounded file locked status Boolean optional (locking supported) create the file locked or unlocked additional file attributes deduced optional mission-defined attributes

This is Figure 8-261, together with rule 8.23.2.1c on the value 0.39

A dangling \"repeated N times\"

Figures 8-261 and 8-264 print a "repeated N times" label above the additional file attributes field, but neither figure contains an N field.3941 The available sources do not explain how the number of additional attributes is encoded; presumably it is part of the mission-defined (deduced) structure.

docs.title: TC[23,2] delete a file
docs.text: One instruction with the object path (Figure 8-262: repository path + file name). Rejected if the path is invalid or contains wildcard characters that the file system recognises: one request deletes exactly one file. A locked file cannot be deleted.1340

docs.title: TC[23,3] report the attributes of a file and TM[23,4] file attribute report
docs.text:
The request carries one object path (Figure 8-263).40 If the file system returns the attributes, the service sends one TM[23,4] with:1441

Field Type Presence repository path variable character-string always file name variable character-string always file size unsigned integer always (the minimum capability) file locked status Boolean optional (locking supported) additional file attributes deduced optional

docs.title: TC[23,5] lock a file and TC[23,6] unlock a file
docs.text: Locking a file makes it read-only: the file handling system must write-protect it and refuse to delete or move it, and the only change allowed on a locked file is unlocking it. File systems usually also protect files while they are open. Both requests carry one object path (Figures 8-265 and 8-266) and reject wildcards. Unlock exists whenever lock is declared.151642

docs.title: TC[23,7] find files and TM[23,8] found files report
docs.text: The request carries a repository path and a search pattern (Figure 8-267). Wildcards are allowed in the pattern only, never in the repository path, so one request cannot search several repositories. Whether the search covers only the given directory or descends recursively is declared by the mission.1742 The report repeats the repository path and the pattern, followed by N (unsigned integer) and N matching file paths, each a single variable character string (Figure 8-268). Finding nothing is not an error; the list is then empty.1743

docs.title: TC[23,9] create, TC[23,10] delete and TC[23,11] rename a directory
docs.text:
Directory operations belong to structured file systems, and the three requests come as a set: delete and rename are implied by create.851

  • Create a directory: one directory path (repository path + directory name; Figure 8-269).1844
  • Delete a directory: one directory path (Figure 8-270), no wildcards. The kind of deletion depends on the file handling system and is declared: only empty directories, only directories without sub-directories, or recursive deletion. A locked file anywhere below the directory prevents its deletion.1944
  • Rename a directory: repository path, old directory name and new directory name (three strings, Figure 8-271). Support must be declared, and a locked file below the directory also prevents renaming.2044

docs.title: TC[23,12] summary-report the content of a repository and TM[23,13]
docs.text: The request carries one repository path, without wildcards (Figure 8-272). The report lists only the direct children of that repository, never recursively. TM[23,13] contains the repository path, N, and for each object its object type (enumerated: 0 file, 1 directory) and object name (Figure 8-273). An empty repository gives an empty list, not an error.214550

docs.title: File handling observable
docs.text: For each file system, the subservice exposes the available unallocated memory.22

docs.title: File systems and operations
docs.text: The copy subservice works across the file systems declared for it, as source, destination or both. They include on-board file systems and remote ones such as the ground. A file on a remote file system is identified by a remote file path (repository path + file name).23 Each copy or move is a file copy operation with an operation ID that is unique for the operation's lifetime. The requester (usually the ground) puts the ID in the copy or move request; the ID is then used to suspend, resume or abort the operation and appears in its status reports.2425

docs.title: TC[23,14] copy a file and TC[23,15] move a file
docs.text:
Both requests have the same layout (Figures 8-274 and 8-275):46

Field Type Meaning operation ID unsigned integer identifier of the new file copy operation source file path: repository path variable character-string where the source file is source file path: file name variable character-string source file name target file path: repository path variable character-string destination repository target file path: file name variable character-string destination file name

Rejection (failed start): the operation ID is already used by an ongoing operation; the source or target path is invalid; or both source and target are on a remote file system, because remote-to-remote copies are not allowed.2526

Execution: the subservice picks the underlying file transfer handler from the two paths. That handler may be a file transfer layer or a capability of a local file system; the choice is implementation-dependent. The subservice then processes the handler's execution notifications and turns each one into an ST[01] execution verification report: successful ones only if the acknowledgement flags asked for them, failed ones always. For example, a lack of space on the target file system makes the handler fail and produces a failed execution report.2526 The attributes of the created target file, such as permissions, depend on the file system and the implementation.25

Inference

Because the copy request is verified through the handler's notifications, a single TC[23,14] can produce progress or completion reports long after it was accepted, for example when a CFDP transfer spans several passes. The standard does not define how many progress steps there are; that follows from the request's execution verification profile.

docs.title: Suspending, resuming and aborting
docs.text:
Request Fields Behaviour TC[23,16] suspend file copy operations N, N × operation ID each unknown ID is rejected on its own; the handler is asked to suspend each valid one2747 TC[23,17] resume file copy operations N, N × operation ID mirror of TC[23,16]2847 TC[23,18] abort file copy operations N, N × operation ID the handler is asked to abort each valid operation3147 TC[23,19] suspend all file copy operations involving a repository path repository path suspends every ongoing operation whose source or destination lies within the path2948 TC[23,20] resume all file copy operations involving a repository path repository path resumes operations that are on hold3048 TC[23,21] abort all file copy operations involving a repository path repository path rejected if no operation is ongoing; otherwise aborts ongoing operations3248

The standard suggests using the repository path variants with the logical path that represents the ground, to act on every transfer to or from the ground at once, or with the root path to act on all transfers.2932 All six requests apply equally to operations started by TC[23,14] and TC[23,15].27

As printed

Only the suspend all requirement (6.23.5.3.3d) states the repository-path condition. The resume all (6.23.5.3.4d) and abort all (6.23.5.4.2f) requirements, read literally, act on every operation that is on hold or ongoing.3032 The caption of Figure 8-281, the layout of TC[23,21] abort all, also says "Suspend all".48 Both look like editorial slips.

docs.title: Periodic file copy status reporting
docs.text:
TC[23,22] enables periodic status reports with a reporting interval (relative time, Figure 8-282); an invalid interval is rejected. TC[23,24], with no data, disables them.343549 While enabled, the subservice sends exactly one TM[23,23] file copy status report at the end of every interval, with one entry per ongoing operation:3649

Field Type Presence Meaning N unsigned integer always number of ongoing operations repeated N times: operation ID unsigned integer always the operation operation status enumerated always Table 8-27: 0 "pending", 1 "in progress" progress indicator unsigned integer optional (declared) percentage of completion

Three states, two codes

The system requirement lists three operation states: in progress, pending (waiting for on-board resources) and on hold.36 Table 8-27 encodes only "pending" (0) and "in progress" (1), so the on-hold state of a suspended operation has no raw value.50 Figure 8-283 also labels its array "repeated N2 times" while the counter is called N; the 2024 draft prints "repeated N times".4977

stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Pending : TC[23,14] or TC[23,15] accepted
  Pending --> InProgress : resources available
  InProgress --> OnHold : TC[23,16] / TC[23,19]
  Pending --> OnHold : TC[23,16] / TC[23,19]
  OnHold --> InProgress : TC[23,17] / TC[23,20]
  InProgress --> [*] : completed (TM[1,7] or TM[1,8])
  Pending --> [*] : TC[23,18] / TC[23,21] abort
  InProgress --> [*] : TC[23,18] / TC[23,21] abort
  OnHold --> [*] : TC[23,18] / TC[23,21] abort

Inference

The three state names come from requirement 6.23.5.5.4c; the transitions are this wiki's reading of the suspend, resume and abort requirements. PUS-C does not draw a state machine for file copy operations.

docs.title: File copy observables
docs.text: Three flags: at least one operation in progress, at least one operation on hold, and whether status reporting is enabled.37

docs.title: Worked example: creating a file (illustrative)
docs.text:
The bytes below are constructed for explanation: the field widths are a possible tailoring, not values from the standard or from a mission. They assume 8-bit length fields for the character strings, a 32-bit maximum size and an 8-bit Boolean (PFC 8), and use the standard's own example repository /mm1.55352

The application data would be 04 2F 6D 6D 31 07 63 74 78 2E 62 69 6E 00 01 00 00 00 (18 octets). If the name were already taken, the service would pass the request on and the file handling system would refuse it, producing a failed completion of execution (TM[1,8]).812

docs.title: What the standards say
docs.text:
PUS-C states that it assumes a dedicated file transfer layer, CFDP being the example, to copy files between ground and space, and that it does not standardise that protocol.6 CFDP (CCSDS 727.0-B-5) moves a file from one filestore to another, typically across a space link. The unit it moves is a file delivery unit (FDU): the file plus metadata such as file names, filestore requests or messages to the user. Each end-to-end delivery is a transaction between a sending and a receiving entity, run in unacknowledged or acknowledged mode.62 Its user interface consists of the request primitives Put, Report, Cancel, Suspend and Resume, plus a set of indications.66 A transaction ID combines the source entity ID with a sequence number specific to that entity.67 See the CFDP page for the protocol itself.

CFDP also manipulates files. It assumes a virtual filestore that can at least create, delete, rename, append to and replace files, create and remove directories, and list directories.64 These actions travel as filestore requests inside a transaction and are executed by the destination when the data transfer is complete, in the order submitted.68 On the wire each request is a Filestore Request TLV (type 0x00) with a 4-bit action code:70

CFDP action code Action Second file name Closest ST[23] request (Inference) 0b0000 Create File no TC[23,1] create a file 0b0001 Delete File no TC[23,2] delete a file 0b0010 Rename File yes none (ST[23] renames directories only, TC[23,11]); TC[23,15] move a file is the nearest 0b0011 Append File yes none 0b0100 Replace File yes none 0b0101 Create Directory no TC[23,9] create a directory 0b0110 Remove Directory no TC[23,10] delete a directory 0b0111 Deny File (delete if present) no none 0b1000 Deny Directory (remove if present) no none (directory listing user operation) list directory - TC[23,12] / TM[23,13], TC[23,7] / TM[23,8] - - - TC[23,5] / TC[23,6] lock and unlock have no CFDP counterpart

CFDP returns directory listings through its directory operations, not through filestore responses.6863

Inference: one way to stack them

The right-hand column and the mapping below are this wiki's reading; neither PUS-C nor CFDP defines a mapping between the two.

  • TC[23,14] copy a file from an on-board path to a ground path would make the on-board file copy subservice issue a CFDP Put.request to the ground entity. A copy from the ground to the spacecraft would need the ground CFDP entity to send the file, for example through a CFDP proxy operation, which CFDP describes as a way to make a remote entity deliver a file.6369
  • TC[23,16], TC[23,17] and TC[23,18] correspond to CFDP Suspend, Resume and Cancel requests on the transaction behind the operation; TM[23,23] corresponds to what a Report.request returns.66
  • The ST[23] operation ID is chosen by the requester, while a CFDP transaction ID is allocated by the source entity, so an implementation has to keep a table linking the two.2467
sequenceDiagram
  participant G as Ground MCS (ST[23] user)
  participant FC as On-board file copy subservice
  participant CE as On-board CFDP entity
  participant GE as Ground CFDP entity
  G->>FC: TC[23,14] op 42, /mm1/sci.dat to /ground/sci.dat
  FC-->>G: TM[1,1] accepted, TM[1,3] started (if requested)
  FC->>CE: Put.request (destination = ground entity)
  CE->>GE: Metadata PDU, file data PDUs, EOF PDU
  GE-->>CE: NAKs / Finished PDU (acknowledged mode)
  CE-->>FC: Transaction-Finished.indication
  FC-->>G: TM[1,7] completed (or TM[1,8] on failure)
  Note over G,FC: meanwhile TM[23,23] reports op 42 "in progress" each interval

The diagram is illustrative: it combines the ST[23] copy rules with CFDP's copy procedure (metadata, file data, EOF and, in acknowledged mode, NAK and Finished PDUs) and its indications.25366566

docs.title: The 2024 draft: ST[24] file transfer and ST[25] file data storage
docs.text: The Rev.1 DIR1 draft fills the gap. It introduces File Based Operations (FBO) built from communication links, file management systems (ST[23]), file transaction entities using CFDP, downlink managers and data sources. Two new services carry it: ST[24] file transfer, with a CFDP file transaction subservice and a file downlink manager subservice, and ST[25] file data storage, which stores on-board data into files. These subservices need a file management system on board, which implies at least one ST[23] file handling subservice.78

docs.title: Files elsewhere in PUS-C
docs.text:
Several other services read or write the files that ST[23] manages:

Service Requests Use of files ST[06] memory management TC[6,19], TC[6,21] load ... by reference; TC[6,20], TC[6,22] dump ... to file memory loads read data from a file (path + offset + length); dumps create a file at the given object path57 ST[18] on-board operations procedure TC[18,13] load an OBCP by reference; TC[18,19] load by reference and activate the OBCP code is already on board in a file59 ST[21] request sequencing TC[21,2] load a request sequence by reference; TC[21,8] load by reference and activate the sequence is already on board in a file60

The standard notes this explicitly: the file management service has no exclusive access, and request sequencing can, for example, load a sequence from an on-board file.8

docs.title: What the 2024 Rev.1 draft changes in ST[23]
docs.text:
The draft is under public review and is not yet a standard.71 For ST[23] it proposes:

  • Wildcards in delete: the delete-a-file request may delete several files when wildcards are used in the file name inside one directory, and a locked file is an explicit rejection reason.72
  • Checksum a file: new TC[23,25] checksum a file and report subtype 26, checksum report of a file, with a 16-bit bit-string checksum; the checksum type is mission-specific. The draft's clause 8 heading prints the report as "TC[23,26]" although its text describes a telemetry packet.7377
  • Directory protection: new TC[23,27] and TC[23,28] enable and disable protection, so that a directory cannot be deleted, moved or renamed.7477
  • Repository report: TC[23,12] and TM[23,13] lose the word "summary", and each file entry now carries its attributes.7577
  • Copy and move with wildcards: source file names may contain wildcards; the target name is then ignored.76
  • Atomic requests: suspend, resume and similar multi-instruction requests are rejected as a whole if one instruction is invalid, and valid ones execute in order.76

docs.title: Solar Orbiter: file management without ST[23]
docs.text: Solar Orbiter is a PUS-A mission and has no ST[23]; neither the 2020 nor the 2025 MIB contains any packet or command of type 23.798687 Files exist on board all the same, and the mission handles them with private services.

docs.title: Service 133 "File Management" (OBC)
docs.text:
The ICD reserves service 133 for the OBC central software. It manages files in the OBC local storage areas, the OBC Mass Memory (OMM), the Safe Guard Memory (SGM) RAM and the SGM EEPROM. Files carry uplinked command material (OBCPs, TC files, the back-up MTL), profiles and ephemerides, or software patch data; the service manages the files but not the use of their contents.8182 Files are named by a partition ID (1 byte) and a 32-bit file ID instead of character-string paths:81

Subtype ICD name Application or source data (ICD) TC(133,6) Copy File source partition ID, source file ID, destination partition ID, destination file ID TC(133,7) Delete File partition ID, file ID TC(133,8) Modify File Attributes partition ID, file ID, type, protection TC(133,9) Request File Information partition ID, file ID TM(133,10) File Information Report partition ID, file ID, address, size, type, protection, mode (closed/open), creation time TC(133,11) Request Partition Mapping partition ID TM(133,12) Partition Mapping Report partition ID, N, then N × (file ID, address, size) TC(133,128) Verify File Checksum partition ID, file ID, expected checksum

For Copy File the ICD lists the accepted combinations: same name to another partition, new name in the same partition, or new name in another partition. A second list, also headed "accepted" as printed, names the remaining case, same name in the same partition.81

Both layouts are real: the field order and sizes come from the ICD, and the MIB definitions match them bit for bit. ZCD08506 places its four parameters at bits 0, 8, 40 and 48, and SPID 14319, a 47-byte packet, places its parameters from byte 16 to byte 41, the 6-octet creation time filling the last bytes.8186 Under the PUS-C rule for absolute time, PFC 17 means 4 octets of coarse and 2 of fine time, which agrees with that layout.54

The MIB calibrations give the actual values:86

Calibration Used by Values (raw: text) CCDT0192TX "Partition" partition IDs 161 OMM_TC_FILES_A, 162 OMM_OBCPS_A, 163 OMM_S_FILES_A, 164 OMM_PAYLOAD_A, 177 OMM_TC_FILES_B, 178 OMM_OBCPS_B, 179 OMM_S_FILES_B, 180 OMM_PAYLOAD_B, 193 SGMA_TC_FILES, 194 SGM_OBCPS, 195 SGMB_TC_FILES CCDT0082TX "File types" file type 0 FT_INVALID, 1 FT_OBCP, 2 FT_DEL_TCSEQ, 3 FT_IMM_TCSEQ, 4 FT_PL_CTX, 5 FT_PS, 6 FT_PLAIN, 7 FT_FAT CCDT0003TX "Disabled/Enabled status" file protection 0 DISABLED, 1 ENABLED CCDT0080TM "Closed_Open" file mode 0 CLOSED, 1 OPEN

Protection polarity

The ICD describes the protection field as "0 = Delete Enabled, 1 = Delete Disabled" for TC(133,8) but as "0 = Delete Disabled, 1 = Delete Enabled" for TM(133,10). The MIB simply labels both 0 DISABLED and 1 ENABLED.8186 Which polarity the software implements is not stated in the available sources.

The MIB holds six service 133 commands, all on APID 172, and two reports on APID 163:86

MIB entry Subtype Description ZCD08506 TC(133,6) Copy File ZCD08507 TC(133,7) Delete File ZCD08508 TC(133,8) Modify File Attributes ZCD08509 TC(133,9) Request File Information ZCD0850B TC(133,11) Request Partition Mapping ZCD08580 TC(133,128) Verify File Checksum 14319 TM(133,10) File Information Report (fixed layout, 47 bytes) 14320 TM(133,12) Partition Mapping Report (variable layout: partition ID, file count NCD850C2 with a 3-parameter repeated group)

Inference

The file type value FT_PL_CTX ("payload context") fits the Solar Orbiter context-saving service, whose instrument contexts the CSW stores as files in the OMM, reachable through service 133 (see ST[22]).83 Likewise FT_OBCP, FT_DEL_TCSEQ and FT_IMM_TCSEQ fit the OBCP and TC-file uses named in the ICD. The MIB does not document these meanings.

docs.title: SSMM packet stores as files (service 15) and file transfer (service 13)
docs.text:
On the Solid State Mass Memory (SSMM) side, the ICD lists private service 15 subtypes 129 to 133 to create, resize, delete, rename and list packet stores on the SSMM, and TM(15,134), the SSMM packet stores list report. The MIB names the same commands "SSMM Create File", "SSMM Resize File", "SSMM Delete File", "SSMM Rename File" and "SSMM List Files" (ZSM00190 to ZSM00210, APID 492) and the report "SSMM List File Report" (SPID 80021, APID 483).8486 Files are moved across the link with private service 13 subtypes. The ICD calls them file transfer sessions and low-level file transfers, with an "End Of File Transfer" timeout; the MIB names the same subtypes with the abbreviations FTS, LLFT and EOFT. The CFDP page describes them.8586

Inference

Matching the ICD subtype names with the MIB descriptions suggests that, on Solar Orbiter, FTS stands for "file transfer session", LLFT for "low-level file transfer" and EOFT for "end of file transfer". The MIB itself does not spell out these abbreviations.

SQL used 
-- solo-2025-09-16.sqlite (MIB__20250916M25925PFMS001_SOL)
SELECT CCF_TYPE, CCF_STYPE, COUNT(*) FROM ccf WHERE CCF_TYPE IN ('23','133') GROUP BY 1, 2;
SELECT PID_TYPE, PID_STYPE, PID_APID, PID_SPID, PID_DESCR, PID_TPSD
  FROM pid WHERE PID_TYPE IN ('23','133');                     -- no type 23 rows
SELECT d.CDF_CNAME, d.CDF_ELLEN, d.CDF_BIT, d.CDF_PNAME, c.CPC_DESCR, c.CPC_PTC, c.CPC_PFC, c.CPC_PAFREF
  FROM cdf d LEFT JOIN cpc c ON c.CPC_NAME = d.CDF_PNAME
 WHERE d.CDF_CNAME LIKE 'ZCD085%' ORDER BY 1, CAST(d.CDF_BIT AS INT);
SELECT l.PLF_NAME, l.PLF_OFFBY, p.PCF_DESCR, p.PCF_PTC, p.PCF_PFC, p.PCF_CURTX
  FROM plf l JOIN pcf p ON p.PCF_NAME = l.PLF_NAME
 WHERE l.PLF_SPID = '14319' ORDER BY CAST(l.PLF_OFFBY AS INT);
SELECT TPCF_SPID, TPCF_SIZE FROM tpcf WHERE TPCF_SPID IN ('14319','14320');
SELECT VPD_POS, VPD_NAME, VPD_GRPSIZE FROM vpd WHERE VPD_TPSD = '14320' ORDER BY CAST(VPD_POS AS INT);

docs.title: MIB Explorer
docs.text:
Browse the real Solar Orbiter Mission Information Base, the SCOS-2000 database that tells the ground segment how to decode every telemetry packet and encode every telecommand. Every parameter, packet, APID, calibration curve, limit set, telecommand, verification stage and command sequence has its own shareable address. Use the selector to switch between the Solar Orbiter spacecraft MIB (releases of 2025-09-16 and 2020-04-16) and two instrument databases: SWA (2021 set and v6.5.0) and STIX (v2.26.38). Field names link to the MIB table reference, and the concepts are explained in The MIB.

The explorer needs JavaScript. The underlying data are plain JSON files under explorer/data/.

Where these data come from

The spacecraft MIB and SWA tables come from releases posted publicly by the Solar Orbiter SWA/PAS team at IRAP (https://solarorbiter.irap.omp.eu/MIB/), copied on 2026-11-05 (SWA v6.5.0 on 2026-11-12). The STIX tables come from the STIX team's open directory at FHNW (https://pub099.cs.technik.fhnw.ch/data/idb/), copied on 2026-11-12. The banner above the results shows the exact release, original URL and copy time. See Sources & copies and the library entries for the 2025-09-16 release, the 2020-04-16 release, the SWA instrument database, SWA v6.5.0 and STIX v2.26.38. The data are presented as published. This wiki is not affiliated with ESA, the Solar Orbiter project, IRAP or FHNW.

docs.title: Library
docs.text: The library holds 200 sources used to write this wiki: standards, interface control documents, manuals, papers, presentations and MIB databases. Every entry has a summary, its table of contents, the documents it references, the wiki pages that cite it, a link to its original location, the UTC time it was copied, and a SHA-256 checksum of the copy kept in this repository. See Sources & copies for the provenance policy, and the reference catalogue for every document these sources cite.

docs.title: Provenance
docs.text: Original locationhttps://indico.esa.int/event/93/contributions/3555/attachments/2828/3285/02.SESP_2015-From_HPSDB_to_EGS-CC_Presentation.pdfCopied (UTC)2026-11-12T17:49:15ZSHA-256863636f8f3040e4cba98de2c7f9be7525fefa106ac14c54c8350ab2be722d765Size370.8 KBOur copy02.SESP_2015-From_HPSDB_to_EGS-CC_Presentation.pdf (unchanged third-party file, not MIT; see the notice)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A 16-slide Thales Alenia Space presentation on the lineage of its industrial system reference database. HPSDB (Herschel/Planck System Data Base) became SRDB for Meteosat Third Generation (MTG), and the slides look ahead to adapting SRDB to EGS-CC based systems. HPSDB was specified around two ESA requirements: 'commonality' between the two spacecraft and between database users, met by physical instantiation and category flags, and 'smooth transition' of validated data from AIT to operations, met by logical instantiation and category flags.

Most slides explain the data model with a reaction-wheel example. Objects (equipment, subsystem, model) contain items (TM packets, TM parameters, curves, synthetic parameters, groups, constants), and identifiers are built from a core part (Axxx packets, Cxxxx curves, Dxxx synthetics, Gxxx groups, Kxxx constants, Mxxx TM parameters) prefixed by a position code such as A101. Category flags (AIT, OPS, SW) give each user a consistent view of an object. Physical instantiation separates the 'defined' from the 'realized' part, for example a serial-numbered unit with modified curves. Logical instantiation attaches lower-level objects at positions inside higher-level objects. Further slides cover generic objects, working, reference and archive areas with check-out and check-in, object versioning by environment counter or label, a configurable number of levels, resource parameters that make one parameter's validity depend on another's state, groups, and full versus flat XML export views.

The mapping slide and the conclusion state that the SRDB high-level model should map onto the EGS-CC product structure, while the low-level items and pseudo-items still need conversion algorithms. For an engineer, it explains the identifier scheme seen in Herschel/Planck MIB exports.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• HPSDB was specified for two ESA requirements: 'commonality' (between the two spacecraft and between database users), achieved via physical instantiation and category flags, and 'smooth transition' (re-use of validated data up to operations), achieved via logical instantiation and category flags. (PDF p. 2)
  • SRDB is an adaptation of HPSDB for MTG; the one major concept change is the ability to attach a former version of an object, whereas HPSDB can attach only the most recent version. (PDF p. 2)
  • Item core identifiers: Axxx TM packet, Cxxxx curve, Dxxx synthetic parameter, Gxxx group, Kxxx constant, Mxxx TM parameter; an instantiation part such as a position code (A101) is prefixed, giving identifiers like A101M001. (PDF p. 3)
  • Category flags (for example AIT, OPS, SW) select per-user views of an object, with the main constraint that every object view is consistent. (PDF p. 4)
  • Physical instantiation distinguishes the defined part (object type) from realized parts (serial-numbered units) that may physically delete, modify or add items such as a unit-specific curve. (PDF p. 5)
  • Logical instantiation attaches lower-level objects at positions (for example two reaction wheels at A101 and A102, a gyro at A200) and lets the higher-level object add synthetic parameters such as D001 = A101M002 + A102M002 in a pseudo-position (AZZZ). (PDF p. 6)
  • Data live in a working area, a reference area and an archive area, with check-out, modification, check-in and archive steps. (PDF p. 9)
  • A 'resource' parameter lets a parameter's validity depend on another parameter's state, for example A101M001 valid only if the PCDU relay status A200M001 is 'closed' in the exported operations files. (PDF p. 12)
  • The SRDB high-level data model is expected to map to the EGS-CC product structure package; the low-level items and pseudo-items need conversion algorithms to EGS-CC aspects. (PDF p. 13)
  • SRDB exports full XML views (generic, element and subsystem objects with attachment lists) and flat XML views (fully instantiated identifiers per object). (PDF p. 15)
  • Conclusion: the Herschel/Planck experience validated the HPSDB concept; MTG integrated that feedback plus new requirements (resource, owner flag, list of aliases); EGS-CC compatibility was still to be implemented. (PDF p. 16)

docs.title: Provenance
docs.text: Original locationhttps://explorers.larc.nasa.gov/PDF_FILES/12_3-SolarOrbiter_EID-A_Issue_1-0_2007-10-09.pdfCopied (UTC)2026-11-12T17:52:05ZSHA-2561b654610c282f217acb80ff846fbf19036dce1008731beabc58239fa051bfbf1Size1.3 MBOur copy12_3-SolarOrbiter_EID-A_Issue_1-0_2007-10-09.pdf (unchanged third-party file, not MIT; see the notice)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The first issue of Part A of the Solar Orbiter Experiment Interface Document (EID-A), released by ESA/ESTEC with the instrument Announcement of Opportunity in 2007. EID-A states the technical and programmatic requirements that every Principal Investigator's instrument must meet. Part B, written by each PI, answers it and becomes the binding agreement, and both parts become applicable to the prime contractor.

The document begins with programme background (Cosmic Vision, the joint mission with NASA's Inner Heliospheric Sentinels), the project document tree and the ESA contacts. Section 3 describes the spacecraft as then conceived: perihelion down to 0.22 AU, a heat shield, X-band and Ka-band communications through a steerable HGA, New Norcia as baseline ground station, payload allocations of 180 kg, 180 W and 100 kbps, and a table of candidate instruments (SWA, RPW, MAG, EPD, DPD, VIM, EUS, EUI, COR, STIX, HI/WFC) with their mass, power and data rate. It also covers thermal control and the data handling architecture, in which a data management system is the instruments' gateway to ground over dual cold-redundant SpaceWire links.

Section 4 holds the instrument interface requirements: labelling, lifetime, coordinates, alignment, mechanical, thermal, electrical, SpaceWire data handling (including reception of SpaceWire time codes), 18 software design rules (boot software in PROM, memory areas, event reports on resets and errors, single-TC enabling of uploaded software), EMC, handling and environment. Sections 5 to 8 cover operations (mostly TBW), verification and testing, product assurance and management. Section 9 lists normative ECSS/PSS and informative references. For telemetry and telecommand engineers its value is historical: it shows the Solar Orbiter instrument data interface before PUS and MIB details were defined.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The EID has two parts: EID-A gives the Solar Orbiter technical and programmatic requirements all PIs must comply with; EID-B is the PI's response and the sole binding agreement between the ESA project office and each PI. Both go under formal configuration control once signed and become applicable to the prime contractor. (PDF p. 11)
  • In 2007 the mission was planned for a 2015 launch, with an ESA-NASA joint mission combining Solar Orbiter and NASA's Inner Heliospheric Sentinels; the Call for Letters of Intent drew 23 responses. (PDF p. 10)
  • The near-Sun phase brings the spacecraft as close as 0.22 AU. (PDF p. 14)
  • Communications assumption: X-band and Ka-band transponders with parallel telemetry downlink via a 2-degree-of-freedom steerable HGA, X-band LGA for LEOP, New Norcia as baseline ground station and Cebreros as backup. (PDF p. 18)
  • Remote sensing instruments operate in three 10-day windows per orbit (around perihelion and at highest northern and southern latitudes), while in situ instruments operate continuously. (PDF p. 18)
  • Payload allocations: 180 kg mass, 180 W power and 100 kbps data rate. (PDF p. 20)
  • Candidate instrument data rates in the 2007 table include SWA 14 000 bps, RPW 5 000 bps, MAG 800 bps, EPD 3 100 bps, STIX 200 bps and EUI 20 000 bps, for a total of 106 100 bps that exceeds the allocation. (PDF p. 21)
  • The data management system provides instrument command and control, command timeline management, packetised science data acquisition, mass memory storage and transmission to ground, and health monitoring of instruments that are off. (PDF p. 30)
  • Instruments interface with the spacecraft data handling system through a dual cold-redundant SpaceWire interface (ECSS-E-50-12) for TM transmission and TC reception. (PDF p. 30)
  • Instruments shall be able to receive SpaceWire time codes (ECSS-E-50-12), and each instrument shall support 2 independent SpaceWire lines routed separately to the spacecraft DHS. (PDF p. 70)
  • On-board software shall comply with ECSS-E-40, keep a minimum boot software in PROM from which all functions are accessible, use separate memory areas for code, constants and variables, and allow uploaded software to be checked before it is enabled by a single telecommand. (PDF p. 71)
  • Any communication between ground and an on-board software function shall use purpose-designed TC and TM source packets, and the software shall generate event reports before forced resets and on overload, arithmetic overflow, illegal instruction, data bus error, EDAC memory corruption and checksum error. (PDF p. 71)
  • The MOC supplies PIs in near real time with raw instrument data plus spacecraft HK and auxiliary data, performs out-of-limit checks on a set of payload parameters and notifies anomalies to the SOC and PIs; inputs to the satellite database are still 'TBW'. (PDF p. 88)

docs.title: Provenance
docs.text: Original locationhttps://indico.esa.int/event/180/contributions/1369/attachments/1263/1488/1400_Trifin_-_Paper.pdfCopied (UTC)2026-11-12T17:48:38ZSHA-2569f416e252d0e20df81ed7b3eea54361f13c7c1187f80c5ce588d8a12058052d0Size84.4 KBOur copy1400_Trifin_-_Paper.pdf (unchanged third-party file, not MIT; see the notice)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A short SESP 2017 workshop paper introducing OPEN (Operations Preparation Environment), ESOC's planned single framework for preparing the tailoring data of mission operations data systems. Examples of such data are monitoring and control definitions, procedures and display definitions. The authors observe that each data system and mission has its own preparation tool, with no coherent overall solution and no synergy between spacecraft and ground-station operators. OPEN is therefore a light, data-type-agnostic framework of generic services (access and version control, reporting, comparison and merging, consistency checking, import/export, baselines), extended by plug-ins for specific data types.

OPEN-CC is the variant that is aware of EGS-CC data types. It is the basis for three preparation environments: MICONYS-CC (spacecraft operations, including a re-engineered MOIS Writer as the FOP editor), GSMC-CC (ground station monitoring and control) and the operational simulators (SIMULUS). A secondary objective is the transition from SCOS-2000 to EGS-CC. OPEN-CC will import tailoring data in the legacy SCOS-2000 MIB format, both to migrate missions and to let external organisations keep delivering MIBs for MICONYS-CC-controlled systems. Table 1 maps the planned data definitions (M&C model, TM/TC packets, PUS services, user-defined displays, synthetic parameters, scripts, automation procedures, mission planning rules, etc.) to the three environments.

OPEN is implemented in Java on OSGi and the Eclipse Rich Client Platform. Data is held as EMF models in a distributed version control system, and editing works offline or online. See operations preparation.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• ESOC data systems need a wide variety of tailoring data (M&C data definitions, procedures, user-defined displays) prepared by the Phase E operations teams. EGSE and AIT teams prepare equivalent products in phases C/D. (PDF p. 1)
  • OPEN's objectives are to streamline operations tailoring and reduce operator effort, host all preparation applications in one consistent environment, harmonise spacecraft and ground-station operations tools, and extend configuration management to all operations artefacts. (PDF p. 1)
  • A secondary objective is supporting the transition from SCOS-2000 to the EGS-CC based infrastructure. The framework and some extensions are foreseen to be released under an ESA open source or community licence. (PDF p. 2)
  • OPEN is mostly agnostic to EGS-CC data types. OPEN-CC adds EGS-CC-aware framework extensions, and EGS-CC-specific extensions can only extend OPEN-CC. (PDF p. 2)
  • The MICONYS-CC preparation environment will import tailoring data in the legacy SCOS MIB format, to migrate missions from SCOS-2000 to EGS-CC and to let external organisations deliver SCOS-2000 MIBs for systems controlled by MICONYS-CC. (PDF p. 2)
  • The foreseen FOP editor is a re-engineering of the current FOP editor, MOIS Writer, as an OPEN-CC extension. (PDF p. 2)
  • GSMC-CC will import ground station sub-system databases and ground station MIBs to configure the EGS-CC monitoring and control model and to generate displays and low-level automation procedures. (PDF p. 2)
  • Table 1 lists the planned data definitions with their target environments (MICONYS-CC, GSMC-CC, SIMULUS). Examples are the M&C Model, TM/TC packets for the EGS-CC packet encoder/decoder, PUS-based on-board M&C services, user-defined displays, synthetic (derived) parameters, scripts, Java and DSL automation procedures and mission planning rules. (PDF p. 3)
  • OPEN functions fall into Managed Data, Data Management Services and Data Editors and Browsers. Data models follow the EGS-CC Conceptual Data Model (CDM). Imports such as an S2K MIB are provided by dedicated extensions. (PDF p. 4)
  • OPEN is built in Java on OSGi and the Eclipse Rich Client Platform. It runs on desktop operating systems including Windows, offline or online, and stores managed data as Eclipse Modelling Framework (EMF) models in a distributed version control system. (PDF p. 5)
  • OPEN is intended to ultimately become the preparation environment of all ESA missions operated at ESOC. (PDF p. 5)

docs.title: Provenance
docs.text: Original locationhttps://indico.esa.int/event/323/contributions/5027/attachments/3732/5186/15.05_-_Generic_OIRD.pdfCopied (UTC)2026-11-12T17:49:13ZSHA-25675dd11ab885265f40c67187f95fbf3bfae569592b2d5f7f34a0d40c0db9969caSize552.9 KBOur copy15.05_-_Generic_OIRD.pdf (unchanged third-party file, not MIT; see the notice)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A talk on ESA's Generic Operations Interface Requirements Document (GOIRD). An OIRD is the ESA-prepared document that sets the space segment's operability requirements, the functions the spacecraft and payload must offer so that the mission can be operated, as an early input to spacecraft development. Mission OIRDs used to be derived from earlier ones, so lessons learnt were not always propagated, differences between missions were not always justified, the OIRDs had evolved independently of PUS-C and the OBCP standard, and this variability hampered product-oriented on-board software and mission control systems.

In June 2016 SAVOIR asked ESOC to create a Generic OIRD as the baseline for future missions and for compatible OBSW libraries. Mission OIRDs are then produced from the GOIRD, with only mission-specific deltas, mission constants, PUS-C service sizing and de-scoping. GOIRD 1.0 was released in July 2019 and was already used for the Copernicus high-priority candidate missions, ERO/Mars Sample Return and HERA.

The GOIRD is a PDF document with Excel/DOORS content in two parts:

  • Part I, functional requirements: architecture-independent and PUS-agnostic operability requirements traced to ECSS-E-ST-70-11C, grouped by topic (modes, telecommands, telemetry, timing, autonomy, FDIR, safe mode, subsystems);
  • Part II, a PUS-C tailoring of ECSS-E-ST-70-41C: one common set of services, subservices and capabilities for all ESA missions. The talk quantifies the full standard (20 services, 33 subservices, 316 TC/TM types of which 88 are mandatory, and 382 'shall be declared' options). It describes added observables, new capabilities (critical event/system log, parameter extraction from HK, backup MTL, file-based operations), architecture rules (service 11 centralized; services 1, 3, 5, 6 and 17 in every packetized unit) and minimal changes to the standard.

OBCPs (ECSS-E-ST-70-01C) are not tailored. The talk notes that PUS-C leaves low-level encoding choices open, hurting interoperability, and calls for PUS-C library developers to coordinate.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• For most ESA missions the operability requirements are captured in a mission-specific OIRD (Operations Interface Requirements Document), prepared by ESA, standalone or integrated in the System Requirements Document, and tightly coupled with CCSDS and ECSS standards. (PDF p. 3)
  • Problems with per-mission OIRDs: derived from previous OIRDs, lessons learnt not propagated, differences not always justified, evolution independent of PUS-C and OBCP standards, and partial overlap between OIRD and PUS requirements. (PDF p. 4)
  • SAVOIR entrusted ESOC in June 2016 with establishing a Generic OIRD, to be the baseline specification for future missions and to allow compatible OBSW libraries. (PDF p. 5)
  • The GOIRD has Part I, on-board functional requirements (space segment operability, ECSS-E-ST-70-11C), and Part II, PUS-C requirements (ECSS-E-ST-70-41C) and OBCP (ECSS-E-ST-70-01C). (PDF p. 7)
  • The GOIRD is delivered as a PDF with three attached Excel files (functional requirements, PUS-C requirements, changelog); its scope is limited to robotic missions with an avionics-like subsystem in mind. (PDF p. 8)
  • The GOIRD does not replace mission OIRDs: missions start from all GOIRD requirements and trace only truly mission-specific changes (mission constants, PUS-C service sizing, de-scoping), with no copy and paste from previous mission OIRDs. (PDF p. 10)
  • Generic OIRD 1.0 was formally released in July 2019 and used to build the OIRDs of the Copernicus high-priority candidate missions, ERO / Mars Sample Return and HERA. (PDF p. 12)
  • Functional requirements are kept in DOORS with ID, text and notes, relationship to ECSS-E-ST-70-11C (unchanged, new or modified) and clause, justification, and a mission-family flag (interplanetary, astronomy, Earth Observation); TC authentication requirements apply only to Earth Observation missions. (PDF p. 16)
  • PUS-C is described as a major step forward from PUS-A: a solid foundation model, clear system requirements, interface definition separated from requirements, and new service types (e.g. file management). (PDF p. 19)
  • PUS-C as is defines 20 services with 33 subservices, 316 TCs and TM reports if all subservices are implemented (only 88 mandatory) and 382 'shall be declared when specifying' statements, so two untailored implementations would have very different interfaces. (PDF p. 20)
  • The GOIRD PUS-C tailoring fixes a common set of services, subservices, TC/TM types and capabilities for all future ESA missions (about 60% of the GOIRD PUS-C requirements). (PDF p. 23)
  • New capabilities not in PUS-C (critical event log/system log, parameter extraction from HK, backup MTL, file-based operations) are added as high-level requirements without defined TC/TM interfaces (about 19%), to be raised as change requests. (PDF p. 25)
  • Architecture rules: some services must be centralized, e.g. service 11 (Mission Timeline); services 1, 3, 5, 6 (if applicable) and 17 must be implemented in all packetized units. (PDF p. 26)
  • Changes to PUS-C behaviour are kept to under 1% of the requirements, with no modification of defined TC and TM interfaces; clarifications from lessons learnt make up about 12%. (PDF p. 27)
  • PUS-C leaves key low-level aspects unstandardized, such as the number of bytes used to encode certain packet fields, which matters for interoperability of PUS-C units. (PDF p. 28)
  • The ECSS OBCP standard is not tailored in the GOIRD; a few extra requirements are added to PUS-C service 18. (PDF p. 29)

docs.text: Original locationhttps://indico.esa.int/event/93/contributions/3576/attachments/2798/3255/1530_Armitage.pdfCopied (UTC)2026-11-12T17:52:38ZSHA-2566abac3c01fdda0db4733dce7b39ce339b2cfdf7973d7765de551979ad0c91b44Size387.4 KBOur copy1530_Armitage.pdf (unchanged third-party file, not MIT; see the notice)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
An eight-page conference paper by two Terma B.V. engineers on how a ground system should verify telecommands when the spacecraft itself stores, repeats or generates commands. It first summarises how SCOS-2000 verifies commands from the MIB: by an expected telemetry parameter value inside a time window, by PUS service 1 reports (TM(1,x)) and by status consistency checks, with a 'superseded' state for overlapping commands. It then lists the limitations seen in missions: only one verification type per stage (missions borrow the last progress stage to combine a TM(1,7)/TM(1,8) report with a parameter check), a verifier hard-coded in C++ and CORBA that is expensive to customise, and on-board time-line manipulations (PUS service 11) that every mission implements differently.

The core of the paper describes Terma's CCS5 checkout system. CCS5 keeps most of the SCOS-2000 verifier behaviour in C++ but exposes its in-memory telecommand cache to the Tcl-based TOPE procedure language. Each command carries properties (id, raw, apid, executionTime, subscheduleId, timeTagged, cyclicRepeats, isModelled) that scripts read and change with commands such as tcprop, tcsubscribe, updatecommand and the mtl* time-line helpers. This supports ground tracking of time-line edits, cyclic commands (for example triggered by orbit position) and 'modelled' commands sent by another party, which helps in system validation tests, hot-redundant CCS servers and EGSE front ends; options for modelling OBCP and event-action behaviour are tabulated. The paper ends with cautions about imperfect ground models and accumulated timer drift, and with critical remarks on PUS tailoring, CCSDS MO and the EGS-CC.
tags: Tools, MIB editors and related standards

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• SCOS2000 TC verification is defined in the MIB; global settings and environment variables add space-link propagation delay and permitted time jitter on top of the verification windows. (PDF p. 1)
  • Verification by TM parameter expected value checks the first parameter sample after the time window opens; it works even for non-PUS spacecraft but has no explicit reference to the command. (PDF p. 1)
  • Verification by PUS service 1 reports (TM1,x) is practically unambiguous, but the Source Sequence Counter wraps round to zero; the paper reports that this caused ambiguous reports on one major science mission with a reduced SSC range. (PDF p. 1)
  • SCOS2000 also offers status consistency checks (SCC, called 'change on command only' or COCOMO elsewhere) and a 'superseded' status when a second command expecting a different value is sent while the first is still pending. (PDF p. 2)
  • The MIB data model allows only one verification type per stage; several missions borrow the last progress stage to check a TM parameter in addition to TM(1,7)/TM(1,8) completion reports. (PDF p. 2)
  • Customising the SCOS2000 verifier requires C++ and CORBA changes, recompilation and reinstallation, which makes mission adaptation costly; for PUS service 11 time-tagged commands SCOS2000 moves the verification timeouts to the execution time given in the MTL loading command. (PDF p. 2)
  • The authors state they know of no ESA mission that has followed the PUS standard exactly for on-board time-line modification. (PDF p. 2)
  • TOPE, the TCL-based test procedure language previously used in SCOS2000-based CCS, was re-implemented for CCS5; mission-specific verification behaviour is scripted in TOPE rather than coded in C++. (PDF p. 2)
  • Required TC cache size is (verification timeout + propagation delay) x commanding rate, e.g. (30 + 10) . 100 = 4000 commands; the cache grows with a warning rather than dropping incomplete commands. (PDF p. 3)
  • CCS5 command IDs are unique across the system, with the workstation ID in the upper 4 bits; all properties of all commands are archived at every verification stage, and a subset is indexed for SQL queries. (PDF p. 3)
  • Time-line commands from TOPE: tcsubscribe filters sent commands by properties (e.g. {type 11}); ::utope::mtldelete, mtldisablerelease, mtlenablerelease, mtlreset and timeshift update the ground model of the mission time line, and the TC verifier follows the modified execution times. (PDF p. 4)
  • Cyclic commands use the cyclicRepeats property (a count, or -1 for infinite) decremented on each repetition; updatecommand <id> <stage> <state> set to IDLE and then PENDING re-opens a verification window. (PDF p. 4)
  • A modelled command (isModelled = true) is verified and archived like a real one but discarded at the point of transmission; use cases are system validation tests (MCS commanding while CCS listens), hot redundancy and command tracking within the EGSE. (PDF p. 5)
  • Table 2 weighs options for modelling command sequencing, on-board control procedures (generic XML representation, external tools such as MOIS or APEX, or an operational simulator) and the event-action service. (PDF p. 6)
  • Ground models must avoid timers whose drift accumulates over repeated cycles (for example a TC sequence modelled with a fixed inter-command delay). (PDF p. 7)
  • The authors call PUS too loosely defined and over-tailorable, and warn that an EGS-CC primarily supporting PUS may prolong its use; with hindsight they would have implemented the verifier fully in scripts. (PDF p. 7)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A six-page conference paper by Petro Kazmirchuk of Terma B.V. describing DYNHK, the 'dynamic housekeeping' feature of Terma's CCS5 central checkout software. On-board software can define new housekeeping or diagnostic report packets at run time through PUS service 3 telecommands, but a checkout system only recognises packets already described in its spacecraft reference database, so AIT engineers have had to hand-craft static definitions. DYNHK instead watches the uplinked TC(3,1)/TC(3,2) definition requests and TC(3,3)/TC(3,4) clear requests and creates or disables the matching SCOS-2000 MIB entries in memory, without interrupting the running test session.

The paper summarises the PUS-A service 3 sub-services and the content of their application data (SID, collection interval, parameter identifiers, NFA and supercommutated groups), and explains the CCS5 architecture: server and client consoles, the interface manager IFMGR, Tcl-based TOPE scripts, and in-memory MIBs that can be merged from several suppliers with a 'Source' column. It walks through the packet identification chain shared with SCOS-2000 (APID, type and subtype, PIC, PID, then PLF/VPD) and lists exactly which PID and VPD columns are filled for a new definition: PID_TPSD equal to the allocated SPID, PID_INTER from the collection interval, VPD positions from the parameter list and a REPEATER row for supercommutated groups. It also names the configuration that generic PUS leaves open (a scheduling rate in milliseconds, a TC-to-TM APID mapping and predefined PIC rows). For an engineer it is a concise worked mapping of PUS service 3 onto MIB tables.
tags: Tools, MIB editors and related standards

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Sub-services used: TC(3,1) Define New Housekeeping Parameter Report, TC(3,2) Define New Diagnostic Parameter Report, TC(3,3)/TC(3,4) Clear HK/Diagnostic Parameter Report Definitions, and the reports TM(3,25) and TM(3,26). (PDF p. 1)
  • TC(3,1)/(3,2) application data hold the SID, a collection interval in units of the default HK scheduling rate (DIAG_MIN_INTERV) and the list of on-board parameter IDs with counters; SID together with APID and sub-service uniquely identifies a TM packet definition. (PDF p. 2)
  • CCS5 loads MIB tables into memory where TOPE can read all tables and write some; multiple MIBs (e.g. from different suppliers) can be merged, with a special field 'Source' recording each MIB's origin. (PDF p. 2)
  • DYNHK runs as the TOPE script DynHkMonitor.tcl on the CCS Server Console; after a TC(3,1)/(3,2) is verified it derives a definition, assigns a unique SPID and publishes it atomically to the server, all client consoles and IFMGR with CCS5::remote. (PDF p. 2)
  • Redefining an existing SID disables the old definition and adds a new one with a new SPID, so SPID and TPSD are never reused within a session; packets for a cleared definition are archived as unknown. (PDF p. 3)
  • Dynamic entries are tagged Source = 'DYNHK' and can optionally be saved as separate MIB files and reloaded in a later session, depending on whether the on-board software keeps its definitions across reboots. (PDF p. 3)
  • Identification follows SCOS2000: APID from the CCSDS header, service type/subtype from the data field header, PI1/PI2 locations from PIC, SPID from PID, then packet contents from PLF and/or VPD. (PDF p. 4)
  • VPD rather than PLF is used because TC(3,x) lists parameter IDs without offsets; VPD also allows variable-length strings, and CCS5 archives all VPD samples so retrieval does not depend on when a packet was (re-)defined. (PDF p. 4)
  • Users must configure a 'schedulingRate' (to convert the collection interval to milliseconds for parameter expiry) and a TC-APID-to-TM-APID mapping, and must predefine PIC records because the SID is not directly referenced in the MIB ICD. (PDF p. 4)
  • PID rows created: PID_TYPE 3, PID_STYPE 25 or 26, PID_APID from settings, PID_PI1_VAL/PID_PI2_VAL from the SID, PID_SPID from a user-configurable offset, PID_TPSD = SPID, PID_TIME = Y, PID_INTER from the collection interval, PID_CHECK = 1; clearing sets PID_VALID to false. (PDF p. 5)
  • VPD rows: VPD_TPSD = PID_TPSD, VPD_POS 1..NPAR, VPD_NAME = the PCF_NAME whose PCF_PID equals the parameter ID; if NFA = 1 a REPEATER row is added with VPD_GRPSIZE = NPAR2 and VPD_FIXREP = NREP. (PDF p. 5)
  • Planned next steps: a dedicated MMI to pick parameters and send TC(3,1)/(3,2) and TC(3,5), and support for the new service 3 sub-services of ECSS-E-ST-70-41C. (PDF p. 6)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A seven-page conference paper from Vitrociset (Rome) presenting the Health Monitoring System (HM), a plug-in that lets a SCOS-2000-based EGSE or mission control system watch its own computers and links. The HM collects operating-system resources (disk usage, memory, CPU load), the status of processes, point-to-point TCP connections between hosts and the state of time synchronisation on every EGSE machine. Its key design choice is to report all of these as ordinary telemetry parameters defined in the SCOS-2000 MIB and carried in dedicated TM packets, so that they can be shown on standard SCOS-2000 displays, limit-checked and used by watchdogs in test procedures.

The architecture follows the three levels of Java Management Extensions (JMX): an instrumentation level of MBean plug-ins, one per kind of managed resource; an agent level with an MBean server and an RMI connector on each host; and a manager level. An HM Agent runs as a service on each subsystem, and a single HM Manager, started with the normal SCOS-2000 start-up and optionally with a GUI, packs the collected values into configurable TM packets and injects them into the SCOS-2000 telemetry chain through the CORBA-based EXIF interface; a port to the newer SMF module is planned. Configuration is XML-based: an agent file lists the managed objects in containers, and a manager file maps each monitored object identifier to a MIB parameter name. The paper shows mimic displays and the complete mapping table (HM_* parameters) for the VEGA launcher EGSE, where the system was in use on three servers and three clients.
tags: Tools, MIB editors and related standards

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The HM is conceived as a Central Checkout System (CCS) component with a client-server structure, potentially extensible as a topological graph over the whole EGSE. (PDF p. 1)
  • Monitored items: OS resources (disk usage, memory, CPU load), status of processes, point-to-point connections between hosts, and the status of the time synchronisation process. (PDF p. 2)
  • Driving factor: model every monitored entity as a TM parameter defined in the SCOS-2000 MIB, contained in ad-hoc defined TM packets, so it can be shown on a SCOS-2000 display. (PDF p. 2)
  • The architecture uses JMX MBean technology with instrumentation, agent and manager levels; agents run on the same machine as the resources they control, or in a mediation/concentrator element when no JVM is available. (PDF p. 3)
  • The HM Manager is installed on one EGSE machine as central collector and is normally launched within the standard SCOS-2000 startup process, optionally with a GUI showing the flow of data from agents to SCOS-2000. (PDF p. 4)
  • The HM Manager inserts the collected information into a configurable set of TM packets and injects them regularly into the SCOS-2000 telemetry chain through the CORBA EXIF interface; a porting to the new SMF module is foreseen. (PDF p. 4)
  • Mapping EGSE status to TM parameters makes it visible at display and procedure level, so dedicated watchdogs can react to anomalies; mimic displays of the VEGA EGSE status are shown. (PDF p. 5)
  • Each agent mounts its plug-ins at start-up from an XML file organised in containers of managed objects (ClassType and Name attributes, e.g. Sampler, TCPMonitor, disk, process, connection, ntp). (PDF p. 6)
  • A second XML file for the HM Manager associates monitored object Ids with SCOS-2000 TM parameter names as defined in the MIB; the VEGA example maps hosts CL1-CL3, PAR, MCK and CMD to parameters named HM_32_xx, HM_16_xx, HM_FL_xx and HM_1_xx. (PDF p. 7)
  • At the time of writing the HM was in use on the VEGA launcher EGSE, monitoring three servers and three clients plus the connection status and status words of various SCOEs; it can be adopted on any SCOS-2000 MCS or EGSE by writing the XML configuration and populating the MIB. (PDF p. 7)

docs.text: Original locationhttps://gsaw.org/wp-content/uploads/2014/03/2014s12b_schutz.pdfCopied (UTC)2026-11-12T17:52:54ZSHA-256c22ad08be63d032a4c3af3c31822a74b4ec19d0eefcf68d8e7a541ceabd82ffbSize2.4 MBOur copy2014s12b_schutz.pdf (unchanged third-party file, not MIT; see the notice)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A 22-slide GSAW 2014 presentation on the EGOS User Desktop (EUD). EUD is ESA's Java and Eclipse RCP framework for building rich-client graphical user interfaces for ground data systems, and the basis for the new generation of GUIs at ESOC. It was in mission operations from 2013. The presentation frames EUD as part of ESA's modernisation of its ground data systems infrastructure, driven by obsolescence, removal of COTS dependencies, re-use, open-source technology, Linux/Windows independence and a harmonised look and feel.

The slides describe EUD as a pluggable integration platform. A 'Display' is an Eclipse RCP view or editor plug-in, so standard RCP views run unchanged. EUD provides 11 generic displays, among them the familiar SCOS-2000 types AND (alphanumeric), GRD (graphic), mimic and matrix displays, scrolling parameter, XY graph, live and history message displays. It also offers an extended widget library and standard data-provision interfaces (parameter, message, scripting, system control, persistent storage and session services), connected to each back-end system through adapters.

The status slides list systems with EUD-based GUIs: SCOS-2000, SIMSAT, NIS and FARC as replacement GUIs; ARES, GSMC, FIDES, GSSC and MPSF as new developments; MATIS and SPMON ongoing; GFTS, DARC and DABYS planned. They also show screenshots of the EUD Telemetry Desktop in operation for Gaia, ARES and the Offline Display Development Environment (ODDE). The listed benefits include display definition files that work across ODDE, the MCS, SIMSAT, ARES and GSMC, and no licence cost. Future plans are Web-EUD on Eclipse RAP, more display types and use in EGS-CC. It is useful context for ancillary systems and displays.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• EUD is a framework for rich-client GUIs and an integration platform for GUI components, aimed mainly at ground data systems. It is described as ESA's foundation for new-generation GUIs at ESOC and in mission operation since 2013. (PDF p. 2)
  • The motivations for modernising ESA's ground data systems infrastructure are obsolescence of existing implementations, removing COTS dependencies and cost reduction through re-use. The objectives are open-source technology, Linux/Windows independence, shared implementations and a harmonised look and feel. (PDF p. 3)
  • EUD is implemented in Java on Eclipse RCP, uses only open-source software and runs on multiple platforms. (PDF p. 4)
  • The pluggable UI unit is a 'Display', technically an Eclipse RCP View or Editor plug-in. RCP-compliant views run in EUD without modification, and an extended EUD view base class can replace AbstractViewPart. (PDF p. 5)
  • EUD provides 11 common displays, among them GRD, AND, MIMIC and MATRIX. (PDF p. 6)
  • The architecture layers EUD generic displays (Alphanumeric, MIMIC, Graph, Scrolling Param, Matrix, XY Graph, Live and History Message) and EUD core services over interfaces such as IEudParameter, IEudMessage, IEudScriptEngine, IEudSystemControl, IPersistentStorage and ISessionManager. These are bound to back-end services through application-specific adapters, on top of Eclipse RCP, EMF, GEF, GMF and BIRT. (PDF p. 10)
  • The framework was mature since 2011, and most ground system GUIs were EUD-based. It replaced the GUIs of SCOS-2000, SIMSAT, NIS and FARC, and was used for new developments ARES, GSMC, FIDES, GSSC and MPSF. (PDF p. 11)
  • Ongoing EUD developments were MATIS and SPMON. GFTS, DARC and DABYS were planned. (PDF p. 12)
  • The EUD Telemetry Desktop (EUD-TMD) was in operation for Gaia. (PDF p. 13)
  • Display definition files are cross-compatible across ODDE, the MCS, SIMSAT, ARES and GSMC, and EUD has no licence cost. (PDF p. 18)
  • Future plans: Web-EUD, running EUD in a browser via Eclipse RAP with minor code changes, more generic displays (density distribution, spectral analysis, 3D graphs) and use in more systems such as EGS-CC. (PDF p. 19)
  • Lessons learned: consolidating functionality across domains took much initial effort, an agile approach was crucial, and adapters for legacy systems can be tedious. (PDF p. 21)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A conference paper from DLR's German Space Operations Center (GSOC) on how to operate New Space small satellites inside a multi-mission environment built on CCSDS and ECSS standards. It first describes the GSOC set-up: GECCOS, a SCOS-2000-based mission control system, connects through the NCTRS protocol to an SLE Switch Board and from there to a worldwide ground station network over SLE. Procedures are prepared and run with ProToS, and telemetry is monitored with SATMON. Under this approach the spacecraft manufacturer has to deliver a MIB and operations procedures.

The case study is CubeL, a 3U CubeSat launched in early 2021 that uses the CubeSat Space Protocol (CSP) rather than CCSDS packets and PUS, and came without a MIB. Integrating it took custom work on both the space and ground segments: a patched modem firmware, a new S-band commanding tool, an auxiliary MIB and a new offline-processing tool.

The proposed alternative uses EGS-CC, the planned replacement for GECCOS. Its domain-agnostic kernel is adapted to a mission by an exchangeable Reference Implementation (RI) and by the Tailoring Data Model (TDM). The authors define a CSP RI in which an EGS-CC activity processor calls the manufacturer's CSP C API through SWIG-generated Java/JNI bindings packaged as Karaf bundles. A prototype commanded CubeL in January 2024. The paper ends with an outlook on multiple RIs side by side, a project-specific software modem at the ground-station interface, and how requirements on manufacturers might change (exposing an API instead of delivering a MIB).

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• GSOC's core mission operations systems and ground station equipment are stated to rely on CCSDS 132.0-B-3, CCSDS 232.0-B-4, CCSDS 133.0-B-2 and ECSS E-ST-70-41C. (PDF p. 1)
  • GECCOS, the SCOS-2000-based MCS at GSOC, uses the NCTRS protocol to connect to an SLE Switch Board (SSB), which gives access to a worldwide ground station network via SLE. (PDF p. 3)
  • The two elements described as central to TM/TC communications are the MIB, in which each TM/TC is precisely defined, and the procedures that fix the order in which TCs are sent. (PDF p. 3)
  • Procedures are prepared and executed with GSOC's ProToS tool suite through the GECCOS API; telemetry is monitored with SATMON, also accessible outside the control centre as SATMON@home. (PDF p. 4)
  • The paper calls it an 'industry standard' that the manufacturer provides a MIB and the procedures so that SCOS-2000-based systems such as GECCOS can operate the spacecraft. (PDF p. 4)
  • CubeL (3U CubeSat, launched early 2021) was the first small satellite operated at GSOC; its manufacturer toolkit uses CSP packets over ZMQ with a command-line tool, CSP-Term. (PDF p. 5)
  • CubeL had no MIB; integrating it required patching the on-board modem firmware, a new S-band commanding tool, an auxiliary MIB for telemetry parsing, a new offline-processing tool and mission-planning changes. (PDF p. 6)
  • EGS-CC is set to replace GECCOS as the central MCS component at GSOC; its kernel is domain-agnostic and is adapted to an application by a Reference Implementation (RI). (PDF p. 7)
  • The Tailoring Data Model (TDM) tailors the kernel's abstract Monitoring and Control Model (MCM) into a hierarchy of monitoring and control elements with parameters, events and activities. (PDF p. 8)
  • In the CSP RI, an activity is routed through the MCA and MCM kernel components to an activity processor that calls the manufacturer's CSP API; the API's return value is mapped to the activity result. (PDF p. 8)
  • The CSP component is an Apache Maven project with three modules (csp-library, csp-terminal, csp-feature); SWIG generates Java bindings and JNI glue code for the C CSP libraries, deployed in EGS-CC's Apache Karaf OSGi runtime. (PDF p. 9)
  • A prototype EGS-CC system with a CSP RI commanded CubeL in an experimental pass in January 2024 (pings to the on-board computer and requested housekeeping TM). (PDF p. 11)
  • For non-CCSDS links the paper proposes routing the RF signal to a project-specific software modem at the operations centre, since the SLE-based ground-station interface and CORTEX hardware rely on CCSDS 401.0, 131.0 and 231.0. (PDF p. 13)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The Herschel/Planck Packet Structure Interface Control Document (PS-ICD) is the mission-specific application-layer definition of every telemetry and telecommand packet exchanged between ground and the Herschel and Planck on-board units, subsystems and instruments. It complements ESA PSS-04-106/107. Being tailored for the mission, it states that it supersedes the Packet Utilisation Standard (ECSS-E-70-41A), and requirement 1000-GEN allows only the type/subtype combinations and data field layouts it defines.

After the operations scenario, Table 2-1 lists which of the 22 service types are used by the CDMS, the ACMS and the instruments. Chapters 3 and 4 fix the TC and TM packet headers: 3-bit command source codes in the TC sequence count, the Ack flags, a maximum TC packet of 248 octets (228 usable inside an MTL command), a maximum TM packet of 1024 octets, a 48-bit CUC time in the TM data field header, and on-board consistency checks of TM packets. Chapter 5 specifies the packet data fields of each service: verification, device commands, housekeeping and diagnostic reporting, events, memory management, function management, time, on-board scheduling (mission timeline with sub-schedules), monitoring, packet transmission control, storage and retrieval, test, OBCPs, event/action and science data transfer.

Appendices cover bit and field conventions, the type/subtype usage matrix per unit, the APID allocation with base address and offset per packet category, the virtual channel mapping, the CRC-16 checksum with test vectors, parameter types (PTC/PFC), and the time and idle packets. Appendix 9 is a self-contained MIL-STD-1553B Satellite Data Bus Protocol specification. It is the key reference for anyone reading Herschel or Planck MIBs or raw packets.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The PS-ICD complements PSS-04-106/107 with all mission-specific details of data transfer between ground and on-board applications and, being tailored for Herschel/Planck, supersedes the PUS (ECSS-E-70-41A); requirement 1000-GEN allows only the services and data structures it defines. (PDF p. 39)
  • Service usage (Table 2-1): services 4, 7, 10, 13, 20 and 22 are not used; service 11 (scheduling), 15 (storage) and 16 (traffic management) are CDMS-only; service 21 (science data transfer) is instruments-only; 8, 12 and 18 are optional for instruments. (PDF p. 45)
  • TC sequence count source codes (3 MSBs): 0b000 ground high priority, 0b001 CDMU FDIR, 0b010 mission time line, 0b011 OBCPs, 0b100 ground low priority, 0b101 ACC FDIR, 0b110 other CDMU sources, 0b111 other ACMS sources; applications must not check sequence count monotony. (PDF p. 47)
  • Maximum TC packet data field is 242 octets (maximum TC packet 248 octets), but TCs encapsulated in MTL commands are limited to an overall 228 octets; packet length must be an integer number of 16-bit words. (PDF p. 47)
  • TC data field header: CCSDS secondary header flag 0, PUS version 0 only, 4-bit Ack (acceptance, start, progress, completion), type, subtype and a spare octet; failure reports are always generated, and Ack bit 3 = 0 suppresses only TM(1,1). (PDF p. 48)
  • All commands except the 'Standard Distribute CPDU command' TC(2,3) carry a data field header; because the type and subtype sit in that header, (2,3) is not indicated in the CPDU command packet itself. (PDF p. 46)
  • The mandatory 16-bit Packet Error Control field lets the receiving application verify the whole TC packet; its type is fixed for the mission and defined in Appendix 4. (PDF p. 49)
  • Maximum TM packet is 1024 octets (data field at most 1018 octets); segmentation flags are 0b11, except that TM(21,x) science packets may use them for packet grouping, which neither the on-board system nor the ESA ground system supports specially. (PDF p. 51)
  • The TM data field header holds spare bits, PUS version 0, type, subtype, a spare octet and a 48-bit CUC time; a user unable to provide time synchronised with the central time reference sets the MSB of the time field to 1. (PDF p. 52)
  • TM packets used on board by the CDMU or ACC are checked for APID, length, PEC, type and subtype (failure codes 0 to 4); on failure an event report TM(5,x) is raised, and unidentifiable packets go to ground on VC4. (PDF p. 53)
  • APID structure: the upper bits are a base address per unit and the 4 LSBs encode packet category and prime/redundant unit, for example CDMS 16 (0x10), ACMS 512 (0x200), HIFI 1024 (0x400), PACS 1152 (0x480), SPIRE 1280 (0x500), HFI 1408 (0x580), LFI 1536 (0x600), SCS 1664 (0x680); APIDs 2016-2046 are reserved for SCOE/EGSE and 2047 for idle packets. (PDF p. 158)
  • Packet category mapping: verification, events, essential HK TM(3,25) and most reports use base address + 0 (or + 1 for a redundant instrument) on VC0; non-essential HK TM(3,25) and diagnostic TM(3,26) use base + 2 (+ 3) on VC4; science TM(21,x) uses VC1; stored packets go out on the VC of their packet store (VC3 recommended for science, VC2 for others). (PDF p. 164)
  • The PEC is a CRC-16 with generator polynomial X^16 + X^12 + X^5 + 1, initialised to all ones; test vectors include 00 00 -> 0x1D0F and AB CD EF 01 -> 0x04A2. (PDF p. 166)
  • Parameter types: PTC 1 Boolean, 2 Enumerated, 3 Unsigned, 4 Signed, 5 Real, 6 Bit-string, 7 Octet-string, 8 Character-string (on-board use limited to software version identification), 9 Absolute time, 10 Relative time (not used), 11 Deduced. (PDF p. 172)
  • Absolute time is PTC 9, PFC 17: 6 octets CUC (4 coarse, 2 fine) of spacecraft elapsed time without P-field, synchronised to TAI after the on-board time is set. (PDF p. 178)
  • The Standard Spacecraft Time Source Packet uses APID 0 (all zeros) and carries spacecraft elapsed time for ground time correlation with UTC. (PDF p. 180)
  • The time packet's P-field is 0b00101110, meaning 4 coarse and 2 fine time octets. (PDF p. 181)
  • Idle packets, which fill transfer frames when no data is ready, use APID 0x7FF (all ones). (PDF p. 182)
  • Appendix 9 specifies the MIL-STD-1553B Satellite Data Bus Protocol (physical, data link and transfer layers) for units connected to the data management subsystem; its transfer layer uses a 1-second frame divided into 64 subframes, and instrument TM packets must fit subframe boundaries. (PDF p. 217)
