docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A Thales Alenia Space technical note that specifies the on-board control procedures (OBCPs) the Herschel/Planck CDMS on-board software runs on behalf of the scientific instruments. It also defines the Event/Action Table (EAT) entries that tie instrument or platform event reports to those OBCPs. OBCPs that ground needs for nominal payload operations are out of scope.

Section 3 sets the framework. It covers instrument-internal FDIR (the instrument raises a PUS service 5 event and the CDMS starts an OBCP through an EAT entry), spacecraft FDIR that affects the payload (1553B bus DLL, TFL TC and TFL TM failures, science data monitoring through the service 12 monitoring table, and Class B heater-loop failures), and the five spacecraft modes. On any transition to Sun or Earth Acquisition Mode the CDMS starts one 'mother' OBCP per spacecraft (DB_H_PL_SC_MODE_OBCP or DB_P_PL_SC_MODE_OBCP), which calls the instrument OBCPs.

Sections 4 (Herschel: SPIRE, PACS, HIFI) and 5 (Planck: HFI, LFI, sorption cooler SCE) repeat the same structure per instrument. Each gives the triggering event reports with APIDs and event IDs, the EAT entries (APID, event ID, TC(18,3) start-OBCP packet, action handling ID, parameter-passing and action status), and a specification table per OBCP. That table gives its ID, trigger, time-out and parameters, and the PUS telecommands it sends, such as TC(18,4) stop procedure, TC(19,5) disable actions, TC(11,2) disable sub-schedule release and TC(8,4,112,3) PCDU unit off. Section 6 lists the data-pool IDs the OBCPs use, and section 7 lists open issues on verification reports, TC rate and FDIR hierarchy. For an engineer it is a detailed real example of PUS services 5, 11, 12, 18 and 19 working together for payload FDIR.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Purpose: specify the OBCPs needed for Herschel/Planck payload management in the CDMS OBSW and the Event/Action Table entries linking payload event reports to nominal or recovery actions. (PDF p. 10)
  • EAT entries for instrument-internal FDIR use Action Handling ID 0b01 (disabled in AFS, enabled in AFO), action status enabled by default and parameter passing usually disabled; an instrument with separate nominal and redundant APIDs needs two EAT entries per failure case. (PDF p. 12)
  • EAT entries for spacecraft 1553B bus FDIR (DLL, TFL TC, TFL TM events generated by the CDMU BSW) use Action Handling ID 0b11, enabled in both AFS and AFO; the OBCP to start is HPSDB- and flight-configurable through the EAT. (PDF p. 13)
  • The hard-coded TFL TM FDIR triggers when the CDMU receives no more than 1 TM packet from an instrument in 90 s (SDB_FDIR_TFL_TM_PERIOD_<Instrument>VALUE = 90 s, SDB_FDIR_TFL_TM_MIN<Instrument>_VALUE = 1); the service 12 monitoring-table-based science data monitoring allows thresholds to be changed in flight. (PDF p. 13)
  • A Class B heater loop failure generates event TM(5,4,114,5) and a switch to redundant heaters; only HIFI uses Class B loops and requests no extra action. (PDF p. 14)
  • There are five spacecraft modes: Launch, Sun Acquisition (SAM), Earth Acquisition (EAM), Nominal (NOM) and Survival (SM); transitions are commanded by ground (direct TC, MTL or OBCP) or autonomously on separation or CDMS/ACMS level ¾ alarms. (PDF p. 14)
  • Because only one OBCP is started during a mode transition, a 'mother' payload OBCP per spacecraft (DB_H/P_PL_SC_MODE_OBCP) calls the instrument OBCPs; the survival-mode OBCP is a placeholder because instruments are switched off by the reconfiguration module after a level 4 alarm. (PDF p. 18)
  • SPIRE event reports use APIDs 0x0500 (prime) and 0x0501 (redundant), so each SPIRE failure case needs two EAT entries. (PDF p. 21)
  • Spacecraft 1553B bus FDIR events (for example 152 DLL, 171 TFL TC, 185 TFL TM for SPIRE) come from CDMS APID 0x0010. (PDF p. 23)
  • PACS event reports use APIDs 0x0480 (prime) and 0x0481 (redundant). (PDF p. 40)
  • LFI event reports use a single APID, 0x0600, for prime and redundant. (PDF p. 97)
  • SCE event reports use APIDs 0x0680 (prime) and 0x0681 (redundant). (PDF p. 109)
  • SPIRE internal FDIR events (TM(5,2)) 0xC000 (DRCU anomaly), 0xC010 (DPU power anomaly), 0xC100 (operations anomaly) and 0xC110 (operations resume) start the DRCU_OFF, OFF, OPE_STOP and OPE_RESUME OBCPs via TC(18,3). (PDF p. 21)
  • Example OBCP DB_OBCP_H_SPIRE_DRCU_OFF (ID 0x1102, time-out 600 s TBC) stops conflicting OBCPs with TC(18,4), disables EAT entries with TC(19,5), disables SPIRE sub-schedule releases with TC(11,2), and switches off the SPIRE HSFCU LCLs with TC(8,4,112,3). (PDF p. 27)
  • OBCP IDs are grouped by instrument, for example SPIRE 0x1102-0x1107, PACS 0x1208-0x120C and HIFI 0x130D-0x130E; the Herschel mode-transition mother OBCP DB_H_PL_SC_MODE_OBCP has ID 0x0001. (PDF p. 81)
  • Planck OBCP IDs continue the scheme: HFI 0x2102-0x2103, LFI 0x2204-0x2205, SCE 0x2306-0x2308, and DB_P_PL_SC_MODE_OBCP is also 0x0001 (time-out 30 s TBC; all Planck instruments 'do nothing'). (PDF p. 122)
  • HIFI requests no CDMS support for internal failures; for 1553B bus FDIR events 151, 170 and 184 it requests a reset (DB_OBCP_H_HIFI_RESET). (PDF p. 71)
  • Section 6 maps the OBCP parameters (sub-schedule IDs, payload side, restart indices, temporary outputs) to data pool IDs DID_OBCP_32_OFFSET_000 to _110. (PDF p. 123)
  • Open issues: which verification reports OBCP-generated TCs should request (including TM(1,9)), and a suggested limit of one TC per second per OBCP to reduce TM(1,x) load. (PDF p. 123)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A short GMV paper from the 2019 SESP workshop. It describes how legacy TOPE test procedures were kept running when ESTEC's Avionics Test Bench Real-Time Bench (ATB-RTB) moved from SCOS-2000 to the EGS-CC monitoring and control infrastructure. TOPE (Test procedure, preparation and execution) is a Tcl extension with AIV commands such as parameter fetch, packet and parameter subscription and tcsend. It runs inside the TSEQ subsystem (TOPE interpreter, TSVR server, TEXEC execution tools and TPREP preparation tools) and talks to the SCOS-2000 kernel through EXIF, its CORBA-based external interface. EXIF offers injection services (events, parameters, commands) and provision services (telemetry, packets, events, command history) as separate CORBA servers.

The paper outlines EGS-CC's Monitoring and Control Model (MCM): a hierarchy of monitoring and control elements holding activities, events and parameters. It then presents the TOPE Adaptation Layer (TAL), developed in the ERFEC activity. TAL replaces EXIF by implementing CORBA servers (JacORB) that conform to the existing TSEQ/SCOS-2000 IDL, so TSEQ needs no changes. TAL consumes EGS-CC M&C Access, M&C Definition Management, Messaging and System Configuration services. It also contains a MIB-to-MCM conversion: TAL loads the ASCII MIB files (the EagleEye mission MIB in the ATB) and a mapping file, generates the EGS-CC configuration data, and translates TOPE commands, parameters and events into MCM activities, parameters and events. Definitions created only in the MCM cannot be written back to the ASCII MIB. TAL is delivered as OSGi bundles that run inside an EGS-CC session.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• ESA used two flavours of SCOS: SCOS-2000 for operations at ESOC and SCOS-EGSE for EGSE applications at ESTEC; the latter includes TOPE for automation procedures. (PDF p. 1)
  • GMV's adapters allow existing MIB databases to be migrated to EGS-CC and existing TOPE scripts to run on EGS-CC; they were deployed with a development version of EGS-CC in ESTEC's Avionics Test Bench (ATB). (PDF p. 1)
  • TOPE extends Tcl with AIV commands grouped by interaction pattern: synchronous (fetch, syslog, database patch commands), asynchronous subscription (TM packets and parameters), synchronous with asynchronous progress (tcsend, callasync) and local helper commands. (PDF p. 2)
  • In ATB-RTB, TOPE runs in the TSEQ subsystem, made of the TOPE interpreter (one instance per sequence), TSVR (coordination server), TEXEC (execution GUI and debugger) and TPREP (editor and consistency checker). (PDF p. 2)
  • EXIF is the CORBA-based external interface extension module of SCOS-2000; it allows telemetry acquisition, command sending, raising events or alarms and retrieving historical data, and is internally several CORBA servers reached via the CORBA naming service. (PDF p. 3)
  • The EGS-CC Monitoring and Control Model separates the abstract M&C view from processing specific to the data units exchanged with controlled systems, so one kernel can control spacecraft, EGSE and ground station equipment. (PDF p. 4)
  • TAL (TOPE Adaptation Layer), developed in the ERFEC activity, replaces the SCOS-2000 EXIF and implements CORBA servers compliant with the existing TSEQ/SCOS-2000 IDL files. (PDF p. 4)
  • TAL loads ASCII MIB files and a MIB-to-MCM mapping file, generates the EGS-CC CDM from the MIB, and creates or extracts MCM parameters, activities and events upon CORBA requests. (PDF p. 6)
  • ASCII MIB files must always be provided (the EagleEye mission was used in the ATB), and new TM/TC defined only in MCM definitions cannot be converted back into ASCII MIB definitions. (PDF p. 6)
  • TAL is written in Java using JacORB, delivered as OSGi bundles running as a single instance inside an EGS-CC system session, and validated with the EGS-CC Component Test Framework and Test Management System. (PDF p. 7)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
An ESOC paper from SESP 2019 on EGOS-CC, the ESOC initiative to adopt the European Ground Systems Common Core (EGS-CC) as the base of its next generation of monitoring and control infrastructure. EGOS-CC replaces SCOS-2000 for mission control and STC2 for ground station network operations, both expected to face obsolescence in the following decade. The paper lists the strategic objectives (lower cost of ownership, a modern operations environment, cross-fertilisation between mission and network operations). It then breaks the infrastructure down into a development environment (the EGS-CC SDE), a preparation environment based on the OPEN framework, the SLES12 platform baseline, EGS-CC itself used unmodified, extension components, adapter components and external ancillary applications.

The main products are M4C (Mission Control Core based on Common Core, the SCOS-2000 successor) and GSMC-CC (the STC2 successor), with OPEN-M and OPEN-S as the preparation tools for missions and ground stations. Legacy cross-domain applications such as data distribution and long-term archiving stay outside the EGS-CC runtime and are adapted to it. Three tables list the planned extension and adapter components, among them a CSTS Monitoring Data provider, an ESTRACK schedule interface, file-based operations, OBSW patch/dump management, TM file ingestion, command request file management, a mission propagation delay (OWLT) extension to time correlation, and a PUS-C service 11 replacing the PUS-A reference implementation. The paper also covers the engineering approach (black-box use of EGS-CC, a top-down hierarchical functional model and gap analysis) and the programmatics: incremental delivery, a pilot Juice MCS as first target, a pilot GSMC-CC, and validation against the BepiColombo simulator.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• At ESOC, SCOS-2000 is the basis for mission control systems and STC2 for ground station network operations; both are expected to face significant obsolescence problems in the next decade, which EGOS-CC addresses. (PDF p. 1)
  • The EGOS-CC infrastructure is decomposed into Development Environment (EGS-CC SDE), Preparation Environment, Platform Baseline, EGS-CC, Extension Components, Adapter Components and External Ancillary Applications. (PDF p. 2)
  • The Tailoring Environment at ESOC is to be based on the OPEN framework; the platform baseline is SLES12; EGS-CC is to be adopted without modifications. (PDF p. 3)
  • Design drivers for mission control systems include many dozens of parallel users in LEOP, off-line operations with short passes or long propagation delays, and processing of real-time and deferred data. (PDF p. 3)
  • M4C (Mission Control Core based on Common Core) and GSMC-CC have functional scopes very similar to SCOS-2000 and STC2 respectively; M4C can be extended per mission, GSMC-CC is not mission specific. (PDF p. 4)
  • Cross domain applications such as data distribution and long-term archiving run outside the EGS-CC runtime and are being adapted to integrate with both M4C/GSMC-CC and the current S2K and GSMC infrastructure. (PDF p. 4)
  • OPEN (Operations Preparation Environment for EGS-CC based systems) is extended by OPEN-M for mission operations and OPEN-S for ground stations, to be available under the ESA Software Community License. (PDF p. 5)
  • Cross-domain components include a REALS alert adapter, a CSTS Monitoring Data provider/adapter and a Ground Schedule Increment loader; ground-station components include a Ground Station M&C interface, ESTRACK schedule interface and STDM interface. (PDF p. 5)
  • Mission-operations components include File Based Operations, OBSW Management, TM Files Ingestion, Command Request Management (CRF files), a TM Packet Interface Adapter for flight dynamics, Mission Propagation Delay (OWLT) and PUS-C Service 11. (PDF p. 6)
  • Engineering principles: black-box use of EGS-CC (no source-code modifications of kernel or reference implementation), adoption of the EGS-CC SDE and product requirements for all extensions, and a top-down hierarchical functional model used for a functional gap analysis. (PDF p. 6)
  • Development of OPEN and EGOS-CC extensions started in 2017; the Juice MCS (J-MCS) is the first target MCS, with a pilot J-MCS before a commitment in September 2019, and a pilot GSMC-CC with a decision at the end of 2019. (PDF p. 7)
  • Parallel EGS-CC sessions allow simultaneous connection to the EGS-CC RTF Simulator and the BepiColombo mission simulator for familiarisation and regression testing. (PDF p. 7)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A two-page fax sent on 27 March 2003 by the Alcatel Space Industries Herschel/Planck project office in Cannes to the five Herschel and Planck instrument teams (HIFI, SPIRE, PACS, HFI and LFI), with copies to ESTEC and ESOC. It follows up the January 2003 fax on the same subject (its REF3, library item alc-scos-fax-2003-01-27) and adds two further constraints that the instrument teams must respect when they build their SCOS-2000 Mission Information Base (MIB) files, so that instrument-level databases can be carried forward to module-level testing (the 'smooth transition').

The first rule concerns the pid table: each packet's PID_SPID must equal its PID_TPSD. The stated reason is the mapping between the Herschel/Planck System Database (HPSDB) and the SCOS 'bridge' files: different SCOS packets (SPIDs) will no longer be able to address the same variable packet structure definition (VPSD). The second rule concerns the pcf table: the width field (printed 'PCF-WIDTH') must not be null, because it is considered indirectly redundant with VPD_OFFSET and the HPSDB will only support VPD_OFFSET.

For an engineer the fax is a compact, real example of how a prime contractor tailored the generic SCOS-2000 Database Import ICD (issue 5.1, REF1) and the project naming convention (REF2) for a multi-instrument programme, and of the constraints that a central system database imposes on instrument MIBs. It asks the teams to report if the new requirements are incompatible with their implementation.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Purpose: support the 'smooth transition' from instrument test level to module test level; the requirements are additional to those listed in REF3 (H-P-ASP-LT-2607). (PDF p. 1)
  • Requirement 5: in table 'pid' the fields PID_SPID and PID_TPSD shall be such that PID_SPID = PID_TPSD. (PDF p. 1)
  • Justification 5: only to facilitate the mapping between HPSDB and the SCOS bridge files; different SCOS packets (SPID) will no longer be able to address the same variable packet structure definition (VPSD). (PDF p. 2)
  • Requirement 6: in table 'pcf' the field 'PCF-WIDTH' shall not be set to 'Null'. (PDF p. 1)
  • Justification 6: the field (printed 'PCF_WIDFT') is (indirectly) redundant with VPD_OFFSET, and HPSDB will only support VPD_OFFSET. (PDF p. 2)
  • REF1 is the SCOS-2000 Data base import ICD S2K-MCS-ICD-0001-TOS-GCI issue 5.1; REF2 is the naming convention specification H-P-1-ASPI-SP-0141 issue 01/02. (PDF p. 1)
  • Addressed to HIFI (K. Wafelbakker), SPIRE (K. King), PACS (O. Bauer), HFI (J. Charra) and LFI (C. Butler), with external copies to ESTEC and ESOC. (PDF p. 1)
  • Document impact: REF2 will be updated accordingly. (PDF p. 2)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A fax of 27 January 2003 (three pages, the third carrying only the letterhead) from the Alcatel Space Industries Herschel/Planck project office in Cannes to the HIFI, SPIRE, PACS, HFI and LFI instrument teams, copied to ESTEC and ESOC. Its subject is the limits that the Herschel/Planck naming convention places on identifiers in the SCOS-2000 Mission Information Base (MIB), so that instrument test databases can move to module-level testing without renaming (the 'smooth transition').

It sets five requirements. Calibration-curve and range-set identifiers are limited to Number(3) and command-verification-stage identifiers to Number(4), one digit fewer than the SCOS-2000 Database Import ICD issue 5.1 (REF1) supports, because the naming convention (REF2) defines these identifiers at theoretical element level as 'IDIN03F' and 'IDIN04F'. Dynamic UDC definitions inside the single SCOS 'constant packet', allocated in the plf table, are partitioned into ranges of 100 between System, SVM, PLM and each instrument, with 0600-1023 kept spare for allocation by ASP, and the SPID of the constant packet must support 1024 octets. The justification is that the constant packet is unique, so allocations would overlap when databases are integrated, and that all test levels generate the same archive file format; the fax concedes that a lot of disk space is lost at instrument level.

The document shows concretely how a prime contractor constrained the generic MIB for a multi-instrument programme. It is REF3 of the follow-up fax of March 2003 (library item alc-scos-2003-03-27).

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Requirement 1: limit the 'curve' identifier to Number(3); justification: REF1 supports Number(4) and REF2 defines a curve identifier as 'IDIN03F'. (PDF p. 1)
  • Requirement 2: limit the 'range set' identifier to Number(3); REF1 supports Number(4), REF2 defines it as 'IDIN03F'. (PDF p. 1)
  • Requirement 3: limit the 'command verification stage' identifier to Number(4); REF1 supports Number(5), REF2 defines it as 'IDIN04F'. (PDF p. 1)
  • Requirement 4: dynamic UDC allocation inside the 'constant packet' in table 'plf': System 0000-0099, SVM 0100-0199 and PLM 0200-0299 for both satellites; HIFI (Herschel) and HFI (Planck) 0300-0399; PACS (Herschel) and LFI (Planck) 0400-0499; 0500-0599 printed as HIFI for Herschel and not used for Planck ('Sorbtion cooler ?'). (PDF p. 2)
  • Requirement 5: the SPID corresponding to the 'constant packet' shall support 1024 octets; spare range 0600-1023 to be allocated by ASP according to needs. (PDF p. 2)
  • Justification 4: the dynamic UDC is allocated to a dedicated SCOS packet (part of the reserved SPIDs), the unique 'constant packet', so allocation is needed to prevent overlapping at integration time. (PDF p. 2)
  • Justification 5: all levels generate the same archiving file format, so system level can access instrument- and module-level archives for the constant packet; drawback: a lot of disk space is lost, mainly at instrument level. (PDF p. 2)
  • REF1 is the SCOS-2000 Data base import ICD S2K-MCS-ICD-0001-TOS-GCI issue 5.1; REF2 is the naming convention specification H-P-1-ASPI-SP-0141 issue 01/02. (PDF p. 1)

docs.title: Provenance
docs.text: Original locationhttps://arxiv.org/pdf/1001.4730Copied (UTC)2026-11-05T14:06:56ZSHA-25668442bd2e3c1a14b13580b2fdba8d6ec7198464d09673d0fc6cae0e261bb26d6Size535.5 KBOur copyarxiv-1001.4730-planck-lfi-tm.pdf (unchanged third-party file, not MIT; see the notice)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A peer-reviewed paper (JINST, December 2009; arXiv preprint January 2010) by the Planck Low Frequency Instrument (LFI) Data Processing Centre team describing the 'Level 1' ground software that receives and first processes LFI telemetry. It first explains the on-board chain: 22 radiometers, the 14-bit ADC of the data acquisition electronics, and the seven processing types (raw, co-added, mixed and requantised, and losslessly compressed variants) that keep LFI within a 53.5 kbit/s telemetry budget. It then describes the packets: ESA packet telemetry and CCSDS packets with a PUS data field header, a structure identifier (SID) after the headers, a 16-bit CRC, a 48-bit CUC on-board time, an extra tertiary header in science packets, and essential, fast (supercommutated) and slow housekeeping packets.

The second half covers the three Level 1 subsystems. A Real-Time Assessment system based on SCOS-2000 monitors housekeeping, sends telecommands and acts as a telemetry gateway; the paper explains how the instrument was described in the SCOS Mission Information Base (PID keyed by APID, type, subtype and SID; PCF; PLF with offsets and occurrences for supercommutation) and how SCOS 2.3e, and later the HPCCS with its PIPE protocol, were used. A Telemetry Handler reused from INTEGRAL/ISDC software archives raw packets as FITS files, unscrambles them and produces calibrated Time Ordered Information (TOI). A ROOT-based Quick-Look system displays the data. The last section gives the ground formulas for decompression, dequantisation, demixing, conversion to volts and on-board-time reconstruction.

For this wiki it is a real, citable example of PUS packet design, MIB population and SCOS-2000 used as instrument EGSE and real-time assessment tool.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Level 1 consists of a Real-Time Assessment system (RTA, based on SCOS 2000), a Telemetry Handler (TMH) and a Telemetry Quick-Look system (TQL). (PDF p. 4)
  • LFI has 22 radiometers fed by 11 feedhorns at 30, 44 and 70 GHz; each radiometer output is digitised by a 14-bit ADC in the DAE and stored as a 16-bit unsigned integer (quantisation step 0.30518 mV). (PDF p. 4)
  • The LFI telemetry budget must not exceed 53.5 Kbps because a whole day of packets is stored on board and downlinked during the Daily Tele-Communication Period; the REBA offers 7 processing types (PType 0-6) to reduce the data rate. (PDF p. 6)
  • Nominally all 44 detectors use PType 5, and every 15 minutes one detector in turn is also processed with PType 1 to calibrate the gain modulation factors and second quantisation. (PDF p. 7)
  • Packets follow the ESA Packet Telemetry and Telecommand standards, CCSDS packet telemetry and the ESA PUS: two fixed-length headers, a variable data segment and a 16-bit CRC whose specification and C reference implementation are in the PUS. (PDF p. 7)
  • The packet sequence counter counts modulo 16384 per application process; the OBT is a 48-bit CUC field as specified in the PUS. (PDF p. 8)
  • Most Planck TM packets carry a Structure ID (SID); the set (APID, Type, Subtype, SID) identifies the data segment structure, and Planck defined additional custom services for scientific telemetry. (PDF p. 8)
  • The data segment of each SCI packet is filled up to a maximum of 980 bytes; the tertiary header holds detector, phase-switch status, processing type, REBA parameters and number of samples. (PDF p. 9)
  • Essential HK packets are sent every 32 s, fast HK is sampled once per second (some packets supercommutated into four sub-fields and delivered every 4 s), and slow HK every 64 s. (PDF p. 9)
  • SCOS 2000 cannot process the compressed scientific telemetry, so it is used mainly as EGSE during ground tests and for HK monitoring in flight; it also acts as a telemetry gateway via its TCP/IP and CORBA interfaces. (PDF p. 11)
  • Configuring SCOS means defining the MIB: PID holds APID, Type, Subtype and SID as each packet's 'primary key', PCF describes each monitored parameter and its calibration curve, and PLF places parameters in packets by offset and number of occurrences. (PDF p. 12)
  • For LFI-only tests the EGSE was SCOS 2.3e with a modified Telemetry Receiver (TMR) replaying simulated telemetry and a tailored Flight Dynamics Interface (FDIF) client; from the Planck integration tests the HPCCS with the PIPE protocol and an LFIGateway were used. (PDF p. 12)
  • The TMU groups HK packets by APID, Type, Subtype and SID and stores unscrambled telemetry as FITS files in one-hour chunks; TM2TOI writes one FITS file per HK parameter with calibration applied. (PDF p. 13)
  • Conversion to volts uses the DSA, BTI, DGI and DOI values, inverting Vout = GDAE(Vin + ODAE) + ZDAE; PType ⅖ data are dequantised and demixed with GMF1 and GMF2. (PDF p. 15)

docs.title: Provenance

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
An eight-page ESA Bulletin article (May 2007) by ESOC's Ground System Engineering and Mission Operations departments explaining how ESA reduced the cost and risk of mission control systems (MCS) and operational simulators. It summarises the lineage of ESOC infrastructure software, from the Multi-Satellite Support System (1970s) through the first SCOS (mid-1980s) to SCOS-2000 (late 1990s) and the SIMSAT simulator kernel, now gathered in the ESA Ground Operations Software (EGOS), and describes what an MCS and an operational simulator do.

The core idea is the 'mission family': missions with common platforms or operational profiles (interplanetary, Earth observation, observatory, navigation). Ground software is built in layers, each defined only by its differences ('deltas') from the layer below: generic infrastructure software, a family kernel, and a thin mission-specific layer. Requirements documents shrink to delta requirements. The interplanetary family (Rosetta, Mars Express, Venus Express, with BepiColombo and Solar Orbiter to join) used a two-layer MCS, one system reconfigured for the three missions; the Earth observation family (CryoSat, GOCE, Aeolus) added a self-standing Earth Observation Mission Kernel. The article reports quick migrations of the Rosetta and Mars Express systems to a new kernel, combined maintenance by one team, reuse of simulator models through the Simulator Model Portability (SMP) standard, and charts of falling development costs.

For an engineer it explains why SCOS-2000-based missions share so much configuration and code, and it places Solar Orbiter in the interplanetary family from the start.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• ESOC's first reusable infrastructure software was the Multi-Satellite Support System (MSSS), developed in the 1970s and used for over 20 years; the first SCOS generation followed in the mid-1980s and SCOS-2000 in the late 1990s. (PDF p. 3)
  • EGOS (ESA Ground Operations Software) covers mission control, simulator infrastructure and ground station back-end software, with SIMSAT and SCOS-2000 as cornerstones; Linux is the operating system of choice for simulators and MCS. (PDF p. 3)
  • The MCS verification and validation extends to the operational data that configure it, including the database describing the spacecraft telemetry and command data. (PDF p. 4)
  • Mission families in use at ESOC: interplanetary, Earth observation, observatory and navigation. (PDF p. 4)
  • The interplanetary family comprises Rosetta, Mars Express and Venus Express; BepiColombo (launch in 2013) and Solar Orbiter (launch in 2015) were under preparation to join it. (PDF p. 5)
  • Interplanetary operations need allowance for long signal delays in telecommand verification and telemetry time-stamping, file-transfer commanding protocols, and parallel real-time and playback telemetry streams. (PDF p. 5)
  • Within the Earth observation family on-board time is managed differently: CryoSat uses DORIS beacons, GOCE a simple counter synchronised by ground, and Aeolus a GPS receiver in addition to its counter. (PDF p. 5)
  • The delta approach uses three layers: infrastructure software reused across families, a family kernel reused within a family, and a mission-specific layer; requirements migrate downwards under a control board. (PDF p. 6)
  • The interplanetary MCS used a two-layer approach, giving a single system usable for the three missions by reconfiguration; the Earth observation MCS used three layers with an Earth Observation Mission Kernel. (PDF p. 7)
  • Venus Express was based on SCOS-2000 version 3.1 while Rosetta and Mars Express stayed on the previous version; Rosetta then migrated to the new interplanetary kernel in a few months and Mars Express in a few weeks. (PDF p. 8)
  • Common tools for spacecraft checkout and operations preparation promote a seamless transition from manufacture to operations, as exploited by Herschel and Planck. (PDF p. 7)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A single ground-segment procedure from the Herschel/Planck Flight Operations Plan (FOP, PT-HMOC-OPS-FOP-6001-OPS-OAH). It uses the standard FOP layout: a summary sheet, a flowchart page (an image, not extracted) and six numbered steps. It covers starting and stopping the mission-specific instances of the NCTRS (Network Control and TM/TC Router System) on the two NCTRS machines of MCS chains A and B. NCTRS is the ESOC gateway between ground stations and the mission control system; see NCTRS, NIS and the ground station interface.

The procedure is built around one constraint: only one NCTRS instance per mission may run on each chain, so at most one Herschel and one Planck NCTRS exist on NCTRS-A and NCTRS-B. For the same reason, the NCTRS OVERVIEW task must never be started there, because it would allow an instance to be started on a machine of the other mission. The operator opens a terminal on a DCR client, enables X display forwarding, and connects to the NCTRS host by telnet. The operator then runs the stop command for the mission (repeated, because clean-up is sometimes incomplete), checks the process list, and runs the start command, after which the NCTRS MMI appears on the client. A final step logs in to the NCTRS MMI. Troubleshooting notes cover an instance that is still running and the missing X display permission.

This is a rare public, concrete example of how NCTRS was operated at ESOC for a SCOS-2000 based mission. It gives no protocol or interface detail.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The objective is starting or stopping NCTRS-A and NCTRS-B. The procedure ensures there is only one NCTRS instance per mission, i.e. one Herschel and one Planck NCTRS per MCS chain (A and B). (PDF p. 1)
  • The NCTRS OVERVIEW task is not started (and is stopped with 'NCTRSstop OVERVIEW') because it would allow another instance to be started on a machine of the other mission. (PDF p. 3)
  • The operator works from a DCR client terminal, runs 'xhost +' and connects to the NCTRS host by telnet. The NCTRS MMI then appears on the DCR client's display. (PDF p. 3)
  • The mission instance is stopped with NCTRSstop Herschel or NCTRSstop Planck. The procedure says to run the command three times because clean-up is sometimes incomplete, and to check with 'ps -ef' that no Herschel or Planck tasks remain. (PDF p. 3)
  • The mission instance is started with NCTRSstart Herschel or NCTRSstart Planck, after which the NCTRS MMI should appear on the DCR client. (PDF p. 4)
  • Troubleshooting: if NCTRS does not start, it is probably still running and must be stopped first. If it cannot create displays, the 'xhost +' was probably forgotten before the telnet session. (PDF p. 4)
  • The last step is a login on the NCTRS MMI. The source prints the host and MMI credentials, which are deliberately not reproduced here. (PDF p. 4)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A one-procedure extract from the Herschel/Planck Flight Operations Plan (FOP), document PT-HMOC-OPS-FOP-6001-OPS-OAH, in the ground-segment procedure group (prefix C_GSP_MCS). It is the standard ESOC FOP procedure layout: a summary sheet (objectives, constraints, spacecraft configuration, reference files, referenced displays and a configuration-control table), a flowchart page whose graphic did not survive text extraction, and numbered steps with branch targets.

The procedure tells a Herschel or Planck operator how to use a SCOS-2000 client workstation of the Herschel/Planck mission control system (HPMCS): log in to the workstation with the mission-specific operations account, start the SCOS client with a start script, log in to the client under one of the operational user roles, stop the client cleanly (close the task-launcher applications, log the user out, exit the desktop), switch the client to another MCS chain (A, B or C) with a switch script, and change mission by logging out and logging back in under the other mission's account.

For an engineer, it is a concrete example of how ESOC packages ground-segment operations as FOP procedures. It also shows that the Herschel and Planck MCS ran as redundant server chains, with clients bound to one chain at a time, on both Sun Unix and Linux workstations. The architecture and Herschel/Planck interface pages put it in context. It contains no telemetry or telecommand definitions.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The procedure has four objectives: log in and out on a H/P workstation, start and stop a H/P SCOS client, change the MCS chain, and change the mission between Herschel and Planck. Its only constraint is that the workstation is switched on. (PDF p. 1)
  • Herschel and Planck use separate workstation operations accounts, with different password schemes for the Unix and Linux workstations. The credentials are printed in the source and are deliberately not reproduced here. (PDF p. 3)
  • To stop a SCOS client, the operator closes all client applications from the task launcher (Telemetry, Commanding and Others tabs, Stop, Select all), logs the SCOS user out via the desktop Login button, then presses the red Exit button on the desktop. (PDF p. 3)
  • A client is moved to another MCS chain by running the switch_client command in a terminal and choosing client type A, B or C. The choice is case sensitive, and the terminal must be closed afterwards. (PDF p. 4)
  • The SCOS client is started with the hpmcs.start command. The user then logs in with the Login button on the top SCOS taskbar. (PDF p. 4)
  • The client user accounts listed are FCT, OD, PST, PROJECT, PISA, OBSM, MPS, SIM and SWS. (PDF p. 4)
  • To change a workstation from Herschel to Planck (or back), the operator logs out and restarts the procedure from step 1 with the other mission's login. (PDF p. 4)
  • The configuration-control table runs from creation on 27/02/08 to version 4 on 09/04/09. The intermediate changes added Linux clients (04/12/08), client selection (10/02/09) and MCS-chain selection (16/02/09). (PDF p. 1)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A three-page technical note dated 12 February 2003 by Erich Wiezorrek, archived by SPIRE as SPIRE-PAC-NOT-001542, proposing how the Herschel/Planck Central Checkout System (CCS) could execute a predefined test script holding the complete telecommand sequence during system tests, while letting an instrument EGSE (IEGSE) provide the actual telecommand parameter values, telecommand IDs and waiting times.

The concept is a request/response exchange over the PIPE protocol. The CCS sends a TC packet to the IEGSE requesting the parameters for a named observation; the IEGSE uses the HCSS (in particular its CUS) to instantiate the observation and returns the delta times, telecommand IDs and parameter values coded in IEGSE housekeeping (HK) telemetry packets. The delivered test script contains the request, a wait for all HK packets, the retrieval of the values from those packets, and a final sequence that sends each telecommand with its external request ID and waits the specified time. The approach was prototyped on the PACS instrument-level-test EGSE built on SCOS-2000: MIB files describing the IEGSE TC and TM packets were ingested, the script ran in TOPE, and the result was checked in the SCOS-2000 telecommand history.

The note lists the deliveries (one common IEGSE MIB for all three instrument teams and a test script per test) and open points: conversion from TOPE syntax to the CCS format, support of the TCrequestID argument of TCsend (known since SCOS 2000 version 2.3e), naming conventions not yet followed by the prototype MIB, a 242-character limit on the observation request, and how parameters are passed to scripts. Page 3 holds an example TOPE (Tcl) test script.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The CCS sends a TC packet via the PIPE protocol to the IEGSE requesting the TC parameters for a named observation; the IEGSE instantiates the observation with the HCSS (CUS) and returns delta times, TC IDs and parameter values in IEGSE HK TM packets. (PDF p. 1)
  • All CCS-IEGSE communication steps are part of the delivered test script: the TC request, a wait for all IEGSE HK packets, and retrieval of the TC parameters, IDs and delta times. (PDF p. 1)
  • Prototype: MIB files describing the IEGSE TC and TM packets were ingested into the PACS ILT EGSE SCOS 2000 system; the test script ran in the TOPE subsystem and the resulting TC sequence was checked with the SCOS 2000 telecommand history application. (PDF p. 2)
  • The instrument teams deliver a MIB describing the IEGSE TC and TM packets, identical for all three instrument teams, plus a test script per test containing the TC sequence and all TOPE commands for CCS-IEGSE communication. (PDF p. 2)
  • The TCrequestID argument of TCsend transfers the external TC ID to SCOS 2000 (known since SCOS 2000 version 2.3e). (PDF p. 2)
  • The prototype MIB does not yet follow the naming conventions, and the observation-requesting IEGSE TC is limited to 242 characters by the Herschel telecommand length limitation. (PDF p. 2)
  • The example script uses TOPE statements such as TCsend, Subscribe ... ReferBy ... Whenever UPDATE_raw, vwait, Fetch ... into and WaitTime, with MIB names prefixed ZC (commands) and ZM (parameters). (PDF p. 3)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A CCSDS Green Book (informational, non-normative) that gives an architectural tour of every space communications protocol CCSDS recommends and shows how they combine in a mission data system. It is the natural starting point before reading any of the individual Blue Books: it contains no protocol specifications, only the map.

Section 2 recounts the history, from early fixed-format TDM telemetry through the 1980s Packet Telemetry, Telecommand and AOS standards, which were later restructured into the Space Packet Protocol, the TM, TC and AOS Space Data Link Protocols and the TM and TC synchronization and channel coding books. It also covers SCPS, CFDP, DTN (LTP and Bundle Protocol), data compression, Proximity-1, USLP and SDLS. It then places all of them in a five-layer reference model (Physical, Data Link with its two sublayers, Network, Transport, Application).

Section 3 is the most useful part for a telemetry and telecommand engineer. It explains Virtual Channels, Master Channels (MCID = TFVN + SCID) and MAP channels, and tabulates the identifier ranges of each data link protocol (Table 3-1), the services each one offers (Table 3-2) and the coding, randomisation and synchronisation options of each coding standard (Table 3-3). It also explains where COP-1 retransmission applies and how Encapsulation Packets carry IP or DTN traffic. Section 4 gives example end-to-end protocol stacks: Space Packet or Encapsulation Packet forwarding, IP over CCSDS and BP-based routing. A 61-entry reference list catalogues the CCSDS books as they stood in 2023.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The report is a top-level overview only: protocol specifications are in CCSDS Blue Books and their rationale is in accompanying Green Books. (PDF p. 9)
  • Packet Telemetry, Telecommand and AOS were restructured into the Space Packet Protocol, the TM, TC and AOS Space Data Link Protocols, and TM and TC Synchronization and Channel Coding. (PDF p. 16)
  • CCSDS has retired all SCPS protocols except SCPS-TP. (PDF p. 17)
  • USLP was released in 2018 and is envisioned as the data link layer protocol for all future robotic and crewed missions. (PDF p. 18)
  • The CCSDS Data Link Layer has two sublayers: the Data Link Protocol Sublayer (Transfer Frames) and the Synchronization and Channel Coding Sublayer. (PDF p. 20)
  • SDLS can add authentication and confidentiality to TM, AOS, TC and USLP Transfer Frames; its use is optional, and no security requirements exist for Proximity-1. (PDF p. 20)
  • TM, AOS and USLP use fixed-length Transfer Frames for robust synchronisation; TC, Proximity-1 and USLP use variable-length frames for telecommand. (PDF p. 25)
  • A Master Channel is the set of frames with the same MCID (TFVN + SCID) on a Physical Channel and consists of one or more Virtual Channels. (PDF p. 25)
  • Only TC and USLP (COP-1) and Proximity-1 and USLP (COP-P) have link-level retransmission; TM and AOS rely on higher layers for complete delivery. (PDF p. 25)
  • Identifier ranges (Table 3-1): TFVN is version 1 for TM and TC, 2 for AOS, 3 for Proximity-1 and 4 for USLP; SCID 0-1023 (TM, TC, Prox-1), 0-255 (AOS), 0-65535 (USLP); VCID 0-7 (TM), 0-63 (TC, AOS, USLP); MAP ID 0-63 (TC), 0-15 (USLP). (PDF p. 28)
  • Table 3-2 maps data types to services: VC Packet / MAP Packet services for packets, VC/MAP Access services for private data, FSH/OCF/Insert services for short fixed-length data, Bitstream/Octet Stream for streams, and VC/MC Frame services for frames. (PDF p. 29)
  • Table 3-3: TM coding options are convolutional, Reed-Solomon, concatenated, turbo, LDPC, SCCC and DVB-S2 with a 32-bit or longer ASM; TC uses BCH (optionally with FECF) or LDPC with a 16-bit Start Sequence; Proximity-1 uses a 24-bit ASM. (PDF p. 31)
  • The TM pseudo-noise randomisation sequence differs from the one used by TC and Proximity-1. (PDF p. 31)
  • Handling of APIDs along managed data paths is set by management agreement and is not formally part of the Space Packet Protocol; SPP gives no reliability, ordering or duplicate-suppression guarantees. (PDF p. 35)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The CCSDS Green Book that explains the concepts behind the TM Synchronization and Channel Coding Blue Book and the rationale for its choices. It is a tutorial and performance reference, not a specification. Section 2 places channel coding in the layered CCSDS telemetry model: packets go into fixed-length TM Transfer Frames, an Attached Sync Marker precedes each frame or codeblock, and coding protects the frames. Section 3 introduces the recommended code families and the BER, WER and FER performance measures on the AWGN channel, with Shannon capacity and sphere-packing bounds for comparison.

One chapter covers each code family:

  • Convolutional codes: the (7,½) code, its punctured rates (⅔, ¾, ⅚, ⅞), Viterbi decoding, soft quantisation and truncation length.
  • Reed-Solomon codes: the (255,223) E=16 and (255,239) E=8 codes over GF(2^8), symbol interleaving, virtual fill and shortening, and hard algebraic decoding.
  • Concatenated RS + convolutional coding, including frame lengths for each interleaving depth.
  • Turbo codes: the encoder, the iterative decoder, performance for rates ½ to ⅙, error floors and burst erasures.
  • LDPC codes: the near-Earth C2 code and the deep-space AR4JA family, their encoders and decoders.

Chapter 9 covers the ancillary functions an implementer of a ground decoder or frame synchroniser needs: the pseudo-randomiser (h(x) = x8+x7+x5+x3+1) and its spectral problems at high data rates, frame synchronisation for each code, the CCSDS CRC-16 used as the FECF, code transparency and NRZ-L/NRZ-M conversion. Annexes give a glossary, soft-decision quantisation strategies and the rationale for the turbo-code parameters. The 72-entry bibliography is the classic coding literature behind the standard.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The report is informational only; in case of conflict the TM Synchronization and Channel Coding Recommended Standard (CCSDS 131.0-B-3, its reference [3]) prevails. (PDF p. 13)
  • The TM Transfer Frame is fixed-length to ease synchronisation on weak space-ground signals and to suit block-oriented codes; an Attached Synchronization Marker signals the start of each frame. (PDF p. 23)
  • Recommended codes: the constraint-length-7 rate-½ convolutional code and its punctured versions; the (255,223) and (255,239) Reed-Solomon codes and their shortenings; RS+convolutional concatenations; and families of Turbo and LDPC codes. (PDF p. 26)
  • Code performance is reported on the AWGN channel against Eb/N0 using three measures: BER, WER (codeword error rate) and FER. (PDF p. 27)
  • The (7,½) convolutional code achieves free distance dfree = 10, which no other rate-½ code with K <= 7 matches. (PDF p. 32)
  • Both RS codes use the field generator polynomial F(x) = x8+x7+x^2+x+1; their code generator polynomials are self-reciprocal, which simplifies the encoder. (PDF p. 47)
  • Frame lengths for RS interleaving depths I = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 8 are 1784 to 14272 bits for E=16 and 1912 to 15296 bits for E=8 (Table 6-1). (PDF p. 58)
  • Turbo-code performance is shown for rates ½, ⅓, ¼ and ⅙ with information block lengths 1784, 3568, 7136 and 8920 bits (10 decoder iterations). (PDF p. 74)
  • Two LDPC sets were chosen: a quasi-cyclic high-rate code (C2, a modified regular (4,32) code) for near-Earth links and nine AR4JA codes (rates ½, ⅔, ⅘; k = 1024, 4096, 16384) for deep space. (PDF p. 84)
  • The pseudo-randomiser uses h(x) = x8+x7+x5+x3+1, repeats every 255 bits and is reset to all ones at the start of each codeblock, codeword or frame; its first 40 bits are 1111 1111 0100 1000 0000 1110 1100 0000 1001 1010. (PDF p. 98)
  • At high data rates, the short (N = 255) standard randomiser applied to zero-filled idle frames can produce spectral spurs that break ITU power-flux-density limits, so a longer LFSR may be needed. (PDF p. 98)
  • The CCSDS CRC-16 used for the Frame Error Control Field has generator polynomial G(X) = X^16 + X^12 + X^5 + 1. (PDF p. 111)
  • Optional NRZ-L to NRZ-M conversion at the transmitter (and its inverse at the receiver) resolves phase ambiguity: NRZ-M represents a '1' by a change of level. (PDF p. 116)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The CCSDS Green Book that explains the concept and rationale of the three classic Space Data Link Protocols: the TC, TM and AOS Space Data Link Protocols, plus the COP-1 retransmission procedure that goes with TC. Proximity-1 is left to its own report. It is short and readable, and it is the best place to learn why the link layer looks as it does before tackling the Blue Books.

Section 2 sets out the design goals (several qualities of service with simple on-board algorithms, upward compatibility with older TDM formats) and the usual protocol pairings: TC up with TM down, TC with AOS, or AOS both ways. It also places the Data Link Protocol Sublayer above the TM and TC synchronization and channel coding sublayer. Section 3 takes the user's view. It covers unidirectional services, the Sequence-Controlled (Type-A) and Expedited (Type-B) TC services, the absence of delivery guarantees in TM and AOS, the asynchronous, synchronous and periodic timing models, and a table of every service (packet, encapsulation, VC/MAP access, FSH, OCF, insert, bitstream, frame).

Section 4 takes the implementer's view. It covers variable-length TC frames versus fixed-length TM/AOS frames, Virtual Channel multiplexing for priority, the identifier hierarchy (TFVN, SCID, MCID, GVCID, Physical Channel Name, MAP ID), how COP-1 works (FOP-1, FARM-1, CLCW, go-back-n), and how packets are segmented (TC MAPs) or packed with a First Header Pointer (TM/AOS). A short FAQ compares the protocols with HDLC, mentions SDLS security, managed parameters in SANA, and COP-1 for deep-space and blind commanding.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Only TC-SDLP, TM-SDLP and AOS-SDLP are covered; Proximity-1 has its own rationale report (CCSDS 210.0-G-2). (PDF p. 8)
  • Only one Space Data Link Protocol may be used on a given Physical Channel; TC usually gets its feedback through TM or AOS on the reverse Physical Channel. (PDF p. 14)
  • The three common pairings are TC forward with TM return (used by most missions), TC with AOS, and AOS in both directions (for example for piloted missions or high-rate two-way links). (PDF p. 14)
  • The TC Type-A (Sequence-Controlled) service uses go-back-n ARQ to give complete, in-sequence delivery at a single SAP; Type-B (Expedited) sends each SDU once, typically for recovery operations or when a higher layer retransmits. (PDF p. 20)
  • TM and AOS give no completeness guarantee and no delivery confirmation, but preserve the order of SDUs at a single SAP. (PDF p. 21)
  • CCSDS recommends no standard Virtual Channel multiplexing algorithm, except that SLE Forward Space Packet (912.3-B-2) imposes its own algorithm when it is used. (PDF p. 22)
  • TM and AOS offer asynchronous (queue, each SDU sent once), synchronous (single buffer, an SDU may be sent several times or not at all) and periodic (constant rate) service types. (PDF p. 23)
  • TM and AOS frame length is fixed on a Physical Channel during a Mission Phase and must be known to the receiver through management. (PDF p. 32)
  • TFVN values: TC and TM are version 1 (binary '00'), AOS is version 2 ('01'); TC and TM frames are told apart by management. SCIDs are 10 bits for TFVN 1 and 8 bits for AOS. (PDF p. 35)
  • A spacecraft using TC forward and AOS return needs two SCIDs; MCID = TFVN + SCID, and MCID + VCID = GVCID. (PDF p. 35)
  • COP-1 is a pair of per-VC procedures: FOP-1 at the sender and FARM-1 at the receiver, with status returned in CLCWs; FARM-1 rejects Type-A frames after the first sequence error until the expected sequence number arrives. (PDF p. 37)
  • In TM and AOS, packets are concatenated into frames and may span frames; the First Header Pointer marks the first packet header, and an Idle Packet fills frames when no data is available. (PDF p. 39)
  • For deep-space commanding, performance improves by lowering the COP-1 timer or by multiple frame transmission in the coding sublayer; for blind commanding the Expedited service can be used. (PDF p. 41)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A short CCSDS Green Book that explains, from the user's point of view, the two CCSDS packet protocols: the Space Packet Protocol (SPP, 133.0-B-2) and the Encapsulation Packet Protocol (EPP, 133.1-B-3). It specifies nothing itself; it gives the concepts, the rationale and guidance on when to use one, the other or both.

Section 2 presents the SPP as a self-delimited carrier whose only addressing feature is the Application Process Identifier (APID). It stresses that the SPP defines no routing or network service: packets flow along managed data paths configured by management, and the APID naming domain (usually one spacecraft) is allocated by the project. The service is preconfigured, one-way, asynchronous, unconfirmed, incomplete and not sequence-preserving. A worked example shows an instrument that uses three managed data paths: images to the ground, commands to the instrument and status back to the control system, with store-and-forward handled transparently.

Section 3 describes the EPP as a 'shim' that carries protocol data units (PDUs) without an authorised Packet Version Number over the Space Data Link Protocols (TM, TC, AOS, Proximity-1, USLP). The Encapsulated Protocol Identifier, registered in SANA, identifies the user. An example shows CFDP over EPP.

Section 4 is a FAQ. It covers layering, coexistence with IP and DTN (IP over CCSDS), reliability (COP-1, COP-P, CFDP, LTP or the application itself), real-time traffic (priority Virtual Channels, the AOS/USLP Insert Zone), segmentation of large data with the Sequence Flags, extending the APID domain through the secondary header, and the SPP versus EPP trade-off: header size, ancillary data and maximum length.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The Report defines both the SPP and the EPP as protocols that are 'not a Network Layer protocol'; the SPP can act as an Application Layer protocol or as a 'shim' between upper-layer protocols and the Space Data Link Layer. (PDF p. 9)
  • The SPP defines no path, network or routing functionality; aside from the APID it defines none of the mechanisms of a managed data path, which is configured by design or by a management system before data transfer. (PDF p. 13)
  • APIDs are unique only within one naming domain, which usually corresponds to a spacecraft; the space project that owns the domain allocates the APIDs. CCSDS defines no standard APID domain naming service; missions sub-allocate the domain or extend it with mission-specific secondary-header fields. (PDF p. 14)
  • SPP services are preconfigured, unidirectional, asynchronous, unconfirmed, incomplete and non-sequence-preserving; two-way exchanges need two managed data paths, one per direction. (PDF p. 15)
  • The SPP gives no delivery confirmation and no retransmission; reliability is left to the user application or to higher-layer protocols such as LTP or CFDP, or to the Data Link Layer. (PDF p. 17)
  • The nominal example uses three managed data paths for one instrument: preprocessed images to the ground analysis system, commands from the ground to the instrument, and periodic status back to the control system. (PDF p. 19)
  • The main purpose of the EPP is to carry PDUs that have no authorised Packet Version Number over the Space Data Link Protocols, using their VC, MAP or Proximity-1 Packet Services. (PDF p. 21)
  • The EPP carries exactly one user data unit per Encapsulation Packet, unchanged; the maximum data unit length is 4,294,967,287 octets. Unlike the SPP service, the EPP service is sequence-preserving, and the provider may signal gaps. (PDF p. 22)
  • An EPP user is identified by the Encapsulated Protocol Identifier (EPI), registered in SANA; a SAP is the combination of a PVN, an EPI and an SDLP channel. (PDF p. 23)
  • IP over CCSDS (CCSDS 702.1-B-1) carries IP PDUs one-for-one in Encapsulation Packets, using the Internet Protocol Extension (IPE) convention. (PDF p. 25)
  • Point-to-point reliability for packets can come from COP-1 (telecommand frames) or COP-P (Proximity-1 frames); isochronous data can use the Insert Zone of AOS or USLP. (PDF p. 25)
  • The maximum Space Packet is 65536 octets; larger data units are segmented by the source application, and the primary-header Sequence Flags mark the first and last segments, with the secondary header available for a segment number. (PDF p. 26)
  • Trade-off: the Encapsulation Packet header is configurable from 1 to 8 octets against the fixed 6-octet Space Packet primary header, but it has no field for ancillary data such as time or for extending the naming domain. (PDF p. 27)

docs.text: Original locationhttps://ccsds.org/Pubs/131x0b5.pdfCopied (UTC)2026-11-12T14:10:34ZSHA-25646e42acff79265c9e6b7b295cafcad77fcc3d142ea507feb257dbd043db370b0Size1.2 MBOur copyccsds-131.0-131x0b5.pdf (unchanged third-party file, not MIT; see the notice)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The CCSDS Recommended Standard for the Synchronization and Channel Coding Sublayer on return (and optionally forward) links that carry fixed-length TM, AOS or USLP Transfer Frames. It sits between the data link protocol and the RF and modulation layer, and it defines three functions: error-control coding with frame validation, synchronization, and pseudo-randomization. This is the document a ground-station or decoder engineer uses to turn a stream of coded symbols back into Transfer Frames. The rationale is in the companion Green Book 130.1-G-3.

The coding sections specify:

  • the rate-½, K=7 convolutional code (G1 = 171 octal, G2 = 133 octal, G2 inverted) and its punctured rates ⅔ to ⅞;
  • the (255,223) E=16 and (255,239) E=8 Reed-Solomon codes in Berlekamp dual-basis representation, with interleaving depths 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 8 and virtual fill;
  • concatenated RS outer and convolutional inner coding;
  • Turbo codes (rates ½ to ⅙, information blocks of 1784 to 8920 bits);
  • LDPC coding of a Transfer Frame: the (8160,7136) rate-223/255 code and the AR4JA family with rates ½, ⅔ and ⅘ and k = 1024, 4096 or 16384;
  • LDPC coding of a stream of Sync-Marked Transfer Frames, with Code Sync Markers.

Section 9 defines the Attached Sync Marker (0x1ACFFC1D, plus longer markers for turbo and LDPC) and the CADU. Section 10 makes the new 131071-bit randomizer (h(x) = x17+x14+1) the default and keeps the legacy 255-bit sequence for backward compatibility. Section 11 fixes the allowed frame lengths for each coding option, section 12 tabulates the managed parameters, and section 13 covers use on ground-to-space and space-to-space links. Annexes give the ChannelAccess service primitives, patent notices, the LDPC generator circulants and the Berlekamp-to-conventional RS transformation.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Issue 5 (September 2023) replaces issue 4 (April 2022); its substantive change is a revised pseudo-randomizer to avoid spectral spikes on high-data-rate links. (PDF p. 7)
  • Scope: synchronization and channel coding for TM, AOS and USLP Transfer Frames over the CCSDS RF physical layer (401.0-B), on space-to-ground, space-to-space or ground-to-space links. (PDF p. 13)
  • Bit numbering: Bit 0 is the first transmitted bit and the MSB of any binary field. (PDF p. 19)
  • Frame validation uses the RS or LDPC decoder's own decision; if neither code is used, the TM/AOS/USLP Frame Error Control Field must be present. (PDF p. 23)
  • Basic convolutional code: non-systematic, rate ½, K = 7, connection vectors G1 = 1111001 (171 octal) and G2 = 1011011 (133 octal), with inversion on the G2 output; punctured rates ⅔, ¾, ⅚ and ⅞ use no inversion. (PDF p. 27)
  • Reed-Solomon E=16 gives the (255,223) code and E=8 the (255,239) code; allowable interleaving depths are I = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 8, normally fixed on a Physical Channel for a Mission Phase. (PDF p. 32)
  • The 32-bit ASM 0x1ACFFC1D is used for uncoded, convolutional, RS, concatenated, rate-⅞ LDPC and SMTF-stream LDPC data; 64-bit 0x034776C7272895B0 for rate-½ turbo and rate-½, ⅔, ⅘ LDPC; longer markers for rate-⅓, ¼ and ⅙ turbo. (PDF p. 66)
  • The embedded-data-stream ASM (for example frames played back inside another stream) is 0x352EF853. (PDF p. 68)
  • The ASM is never presented to the RS, turbo or LDPC encoder or decoder, and it is not randomized. (PDF p. 68)
  • Randomization is required unless the designer verifies proper operation without it; its presence is fixed per Physical Channel and known a priori by the receiver. (PDF p. 69)
  • The default pseudo-random sequence is 131071 bits long, generated by h(x) = x^17 + x^14 + 1 and seeded with '11000111000111000'; the legacy 255-bit sequence h(x) = x^8+x^7+x^5+x^3+1 (all-ones seed) may still be used for backward compatibility. (PDF p. 70)
  • Frame lengths: uncoded or convolutional-only frames may be any number of octets up to 2048 (TM/AOS) or 65536 (USLP); RS frames are L = (255-2E-q)*I octets; turbo frames are 223, 446, 892 or 1115 octets; rate-⅞ LDPC frames are 892 octets and rate-½, ⅔, ⅘ LDPC frames 128, 512 or 2048 octets. (PDF p. 73)
  • All managed parameters are fixed for all Transfer Frames on a Physical Channel during a Mission Phase. (PDF p. 76)
  • The service (Annex A) is ChannelAccess.request/indication; the receiving end gets a Quality Indicator (uncorrectable error) and a Sequence Indicator (frames lost through loss of frame sync). (PDF p. 83)
  • The turbo-code patent (US 5,446,747, France Telecom/TDF) expired in 2012; the rate-½, ⅔ and ⅘ LDPC codes are covered by US Patent 7,343,539 (Caltech). (PDF p. 86)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Issue 6 of the CCSDS Recommended Standard for the Synchronization and Channel Coding Sublayer under fixed-length TM, AOS and USLP Transfer Frames. It supersedes the library's issue 5 and is the reference for anyone building or configuring a telemetry encoder, decoder or frame synchroniser. The rationale is in the Green Book 130.1-G-3.

The sublayer now has four functions: error-control coding with frame validation, Transfer Frame slicing, synchronization and pseudo-randomization. The new section 3 is the main change. With Reed-Solomon, Turbo or LDPC coding, each frame may get a 32-bit Attached Sync Marker (ASM). The stream of Sync-Marked Transfer Frames is then cut into Information Blocks of the code's length, and each randomized codeword carries its own Code Sync Marker (CSM). Without slicing, one frame fills one codeword, and ASM and CSM are the same marker.

The codes themselves are unchanged from issue 5:

  • the rate-½, K=7 convolutional code (171/133 octal) and its punctured rates;
  • (255,223) and (255,239) Reed-Solomon with interleaving depths 1 to 8;
  • concatenated coding;
  • Turbo codes with rates ½ to ⅙;
  • the (8160,7136) and AR4JA-family LDPC codes.

Turbo coding gains an optional row-column channel interleaver of depth 4 against burst errors. Section 9, 'Codeword Synchronization', tabulates the CSM patterns and the CADU. Randomization is now mandatory: the 131071-bit sequence is the default and the 255-bit one remains for legacy systems. Sections 11 and 12 give the allowed frame lengths and the managed parameters with and without slicing. Section 13 covers uplink and space-to-space use. The annexes give the ChannelAccess service, patents, LDPC circulants and the Berlekamp transformation.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Issue 6 (April 2026) replaces issue 5 (September 2023): it adds a channel interleaver for Turbo codewords, allows slicing with all block codes and makes the pseudo-randomizer mandatory; Editorial Correction 1 is dated May 2026. (PDF p. 7)
  • The sublayer provides four functions: error-control coding including frame validation, Transfer Frame slicing, synchronization, and pseudo-randomizing. (PDF p. 20)
  • Transfer Frame slicing is optional with R-S, Turbo or LDPC coding, fixed for a mission phase, and must not be used with uncoded data or convolutional coding alone. (PDF p. 28)
  • With slicing, each M-bit Transfer Frame is prefixed with the 32-bit ASM 0x1ACFFC1D to form an SMTF; the SMTF stream is cut into k-bit Information Blocks, encoded, randomized (mandatory) and given CSMs. The ASM cannot be confused with the identical 32-bit CSM because the ASM is randomized. (PDF p. 28)
  • Without slicing each Transfer Frame is one Information Block, there is a single level of synchronization, and the terms CSM and ASM are interchangeable. (PDF p. 29)
  • With no coding, convolutional coding or Turbo coding the FECF is mandatory for frame validation; with R-S, concatenated or LDPC coding the decoder may validate, and with slicing a frame is invalid if any part of it lies in an invalid Information Block. (PDF p. 30)
  • Basic convolutional code: non-systematic, r = ½, K = 7, G1 = 1111001 (171 octal), G2 = 1011011 (133 octal), with symbol inversion on the G2 output path; puncturing gives one of the rates ⅔, ¾, ⅚ or ⅞. (PDF p. 32)
  • Reed-Solomon: E = 16 gives the (255,223) code and E = 8 the (255,239) code; allowable interleaving depths are I = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 8. (PDF p. 36)
  • Turbo channel interleaver (7.3.12): a row-column interleaver of depth 4 with Nc = 4/r = 8, 12, 16 or 24 columns, external to the Turbo encoder's own bit permutation; its use is a managed parameter and it is highly recommended for tumbling spacecraft or solar scintillation. (PDF p. 51)
  • The CADU is the CSM plus the randomized Transfer Frame, R-S codeblock, Turbo codeword or LDPC codeword, formed before any convolutional encoding. (PDF p. 65)
  • CSM patterns: 0x1ACFFC1D (uncoded, convolutional, R-S, concatenated, rate-⅞ LDPC); 0x034776C7272895B0 (rate-½ Turbo and rate-½, ⅔, ⅘ LDPC); 96-, 128- and 192-bit markers for rate-⅓, ¼ and ⅙ Turbo. (PDF p. 67)
  • The CSM is never presented to the R-S, Turbo or LDPC encoder or decoder; it is attached directly to the codeword or codeblock. (PDF p. 68)
  • The CSM synchronizes the pseudo-randomizer; the sequence starts at the first bit after the CSM, and the CSM itself is not randomized. (PDF p. 70)
  • The pseudo-randomizer is mandatory for all combinations of CCSDS modulation and coding; the note records telemetry link problems on missions that did not use it. (PDF p. 69)
  • The pseudo-random sequence is 131071 bits long, h(x) = x^17 + x^14 + 1, seeded with '11000111000111000'; the legacy 255-bit sequence h(x) = x^8 + x^7 + x^5 + x^3 + 1 (all-ones seed) may be used for backward compatibility but may cause spectral lines at 1/255 of the symbol rate. (PDF p. 70)
  • No frame-length constraint applies when slicing is used, when data are uncoded or with convolutional coding alone (maximum 2048 octets for TM, 65536 for AOS and USLP); without slicing R-S frames are L = (255-2E-q)I octets, Turbo frames 223, 446, 892 or 1115 octets, rate-⅞ LDPC frames 892 octets and rate-½, ⅔, ⅘ LDPC frames 128, 512 or 2048 octets. (PDF p. 73)
  • Managed parameters now include Randomizer (Long 131071 bits or Short 255 bits), Slicing (Present/Absent) for R-S, Turbo and LDPC, and Channel Interleaver (Present/Absent) for Turbo; all are fixed on a Physical Channel for a Mission Phase. (PDF p. 77)
  • Turbo codes suit power-constrained links beyond low-Earth orbit; LDPC codes suit high-data-rate, bandwidth-limited links; either may be selected for AOS or USLP ground-to-space links. (PDF p. 79)
  • The service (Annex A) is ChannelAccess.request(Frame) and ChannelAccess.indication(Frame, Quality Indicator, Sequence Indicator); only one user may use the service on a Physical Channel. (PDF p. 81)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The CCSDS Recommended Standard for the TM Space Data Link Protocol, the data link protocol that carries telemetry on almost every ESA and NASA science mission. It defines the fixed-length TM Transfer Frame and the services built on it. The frame is cut into Virtual Channels and Master Channels, and it carries Space Packets or Encapsulation Packets. Each frame is coded and synchronised by the TM Synchronization and Channel Coding sublayer below it.

Section 2 explains the concepts: Physical, Master and Virtual Channels, GVCID addressing, and the asynchronous, synchronous and periodic service types. Its tables summarise the eight services (VCP, VCA, VC_FSH, VC_OCF, VCF, MC_FSH, MC_OCF, MCF) and the SDLS protection each one can get. Section 3 defines each service's parameters and primitives.

Section 4 is the core for anyone writing a frame decoder. It defines the 6-octet primary header (version '00', 10-bit SCID, 3-bit VCID, OCF flag, 8-bit MC and VC frame counts, and the data field status with the secondary-header flag, sync flag, packet order flag, segment length ID and 11-bit First Header Pointer). It also covers the optional secondary header of up to 64 octets, packet packing and spanning across frames, Only Idle Data frames filled with a 32-bit LFSR pattern, the 4-octet Operational Control Field (Type-1 for the COP-1 CLCW, Type-2 for project use or SDLS Frame Security Reports) and the CRC-16 Frame Error Control Field. The sending-end and receiving-end functions are modelled as packet processing, VC generation and multiplexing, MC generation and multiplexing, and all-frames generation. Section 5 lists the managed parameters per Physical Channel, Master Channel, Virtual Channel and packet transfer. Section 6 specifies the frame with SDLS security header and trailer, and the annexes give the PICS proforma and the OID randomizer logic.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Issue 3 (October 2021) adds support for the SDLS Extended Procedures (355.1-B-1), a normative PICS proforma (annex A) and informative OID randomization options (annex D). (PDF p. 7)
  • TM Transfer Frames are fixed-length on a Physical Channel during a Mission Phase, which keeps synchronization simple and robust on weak, noisy links. (PDF p. 18)
  • Eight services: VCP (asynchronous, SAP = GVCID + PVN), VCA, VC_FSH, VC_OCF, VCF, MC_FSH, MC_OCF and MCF; the MC services are addressed by MCID, the VC services by GVCID (Table 2-1). (PDF p. 23)
  • Frame structure: Primary Header (6 octets), optional Secondary Header (up to 64 octets), Data Field, optional Operational Control Field (4 octets) and optional Frame Error Control Field (2 octets). (PDF p. 60)
  • Primary header layout: Version (2 bits, '00'), SCID (10 bits), VCID (3 bits), OCF Flag (1 bit), MC Frame Count (8 bits), VC Frame Count (8 bits) and Transfer Frame Data Field Status (16 bits). (PDF p. 61)
  • TM and TC frames share version number '00' and are told apart by the ASM (TM) or the Start Sequence (TC). (PDF p. 62)
  • MC and VC Frame Counts are modulo-256 counts that should not be reset before reaching 255 unless unavoidable; a reset makes the completeness of the frame sequence undeterminable. (PDF p. 63)
  • Data Field Status: Secondary Header Flag, Synchronization Flag ('0' for packets or idle data, '1' for a VCA_SDU), Packet Order Flag, Segment Length Identifier (set to '11' when the sync flag is '0') and an 11-bit First Header Pointer. (PDF p. 64)
  • First Header Pointer: offset of the first packet that starts in the data field; '11111111111' if no packet starts in the frame; '11111111110' for an Only Idle Data (OID) frame. (PDF p. 66)
  • OID frame data fields are filled with a PN sequence from a 32-cell LFSR, D0 + D1 + D2 + D22 + D32, that is never restarted; the first bytes are FF FF FF FF 6D B6 D8 61 45 1F. (PDF p. 69)
  • OCF Type Flag (bit 0): '0' means a Type-1 report holding a CLCW; '1' means a Type-2 report, where bit 1 selects project-specific content ('0') or an SDLS Frame Security Report ('1'). (PDF p. 71)
  • The FECF is a 16-bit CRC appended as the last 16 bits of the frame; its presence is set by management for the whole Physical Channel during a Mission Phase. (PDF p. 71)
  • Managed parameters per Physical Channel include the frame length, TFVN (1), valid SCIDs, MC multiplexing scheme and FECF presence; valid VCIDs are 0 to 7 and MC_FSH length is 2 to 64 octets. (PDF p. 88)
  • With SDLS, a Security Header and Security Trailer surround the Data Field on Virtual Channels where a managed parameter says SDLS is in use; the primary and secondary headers are unchanged. (PDF p. 91)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The CCSDS Recommended Standard for the Space Packet Protocol (SPP), which defines the Space Packet. This is the variable-length, self-delimiting data unit that on-board applications use for telemetry and telecommand, and that PUS builds on. The Space Packet is the unit that SCOS-2000 and its MIB identify by APID. It travels in the packet services of the TM, TC, AOS, Proximity-1 and USLP data link protocols, or over the DTN Bundle Protocol.

Section 2 explains the concept. The APID names a managed data path inside one naming domain (usually one spacecraft). The protocol itself does no routing, segmentation, retransmission or flow control, and its services are preconfigured, unidirectional, asynchronous, unconfirmed, incomplete and not sequence-preserving. There are two services: the Packet Service (the user supplies ready-made packets) and the Octet String Service (the provider wraps user octets into packets). Section 3 gives their parameters and primitives.

Section 4 specifies the packet bit by bit. The 6-octet primary header holds a 3-bit version ('000'), Packet Type (0 = telemetry, 1 = telecommand), Secondary Header Flag, 11-bit APID (all ones = Idle Packet), 2-bit Sequence Flags, a 14-bit Packet Sequence Count (or Packet Name for telecommand) and the 16-bit Packet Data Length (data field length minus one). The packet data field may hold an optional secondary header (a CCSDS time code, ancillary data, or both) and user data, giving packets of 7 to 65542 octets. Section 5 lists the managed parameters. The annexes contain the PICS proforma, the new APID and Secondary Header Format SANA registries, and the informative references.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Issue 2 (June 2020) removes the networking-type terminology and implied functionality of issue 1 (2003); EC 2 (September 2024) changes the page size to A4. (PDF p. 7)
  • SPP itself defines no path, network or routing functionality; the APID names a managed data path whose meaning and configuration are entirely mission-specific. (PDF p. 16)
  • Missions with several processors or spacecraft must sub-allocate the single APID naming domain or extend it with mission-specific secondary-header fields. (PDF p. 17)
  • SPP services are preconfigured, unidirectional, asynchronous, unconfirmed, incomplete and non-sequence-preserving; the protocol does no segmentation, retransmission or flow control. (PDF p. 19)
  • Two services, both addressed by APID: the Packet Service (user-formatted Space Packets) and the Octet String Service (the provider formats octet strings into packets). (PDF p. 20)
  • A Space Packet is a 6-octet Primary Header plus a 1 to 65536-octet Packet Data Field, so 7 to 65542 octets in total. (PDF p. 31)
  • Primary header: Packet Version Number (3 bits, '000'), Packet Type (1 bit), Secondary Header Flag (1 bit), APID (11 bits), Sequence Flags (2 bits), Packet Sequence Count or Packet Name (14 bits) and Packet Data Length (16 bits). (PDF p. 32)
  • Packet Type is '0' for telemetry (reporting) and '1' for telecommand (requesting); the Secondary Header Flag is static per APID and is '0' for Idle Packets. (PDF p. 33)
  • The Idle Packet APID is all ones ('11111111111', 2047); the reserved APIDs for CFDP and LTP of issue 1 were removed, so it is now the only reserved value. (PDF p. 34)
  • Sequence Flags: '00' continuation segment, '01' first segment, '10' last segment, '11' unsegmented; they must be '11' when the Octet String service is used. (PDF p. 34)
  • The Packet Sequence Count is per APID and modulo-16384; the Packet Name alternative is allowed only in telecommand packets. (PDF p. 35)
  • Packet Data Length C = number of octets in the Packet Data Field minus 1. (PDF p. 36)
  • The optional secondary header is a Time Code Field (a CCSDS time code from 301.0-B-4), an Ancillary Data Field, or both, and stays fixed for a managed data path; it is mandatory if there is no User Data Field. (PDF p. 37)
  • Managed parameters: Maximum Packet Length, Packet Multiplexing Scheme, Service Type per APID, and Packet Secondary Header Contents. (PDF p. 42)
  • SANA APID registry policy: 0-2046 unmanaged, 2047 reserved by the CCSDS Blue Book; a new registry records Secondary Header Format documents. (PDF p. 48)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The CCSDS Recommended Standard for the Encapsulation Packet Protocol (EPP). EPP is a thin 'shim' protocol that lets the TM, TC, AOS, Proximity-1 and USLP data link protocols carry data units that have no CCSDS-authorised Packet Version Number. Examples are IP datagrams (through IP over CCSDS), DTN/LTP traffic and private mission data. Each user data unit goes unchanged into one Encapsulation Packet (Packet Version Number '111', 'Version 8 CCSDS Packet'), which then travels in a VC, MAP or Proximity-1 packet service. Earlier issues (called 'Encapsulation Service') could also wrap data in a Space Packet; issue 3 removes that option.

Section 2 gives the concept and features: one-way, asynchronous, unconfirmed and order-preserving delivery with possible gaps. Users are addressed by the Encapsulation Protocol Identifier (EPI), and a SAP combines PVN, EPI and the SDLP channel (GVCID, GMAP ID and so on). Section 3 defines the ENCAPSULATION.request and ENCAPSULATION.indication primitives.

Section 4 specifies the packet. The variable header is 1, 2, 4 or 8 octets: version, 3-bit EPI, 2-bit Length of Length, then (for the longer headers) a 4-bit User Defined field, a 4-bit EPI Extension, a 2-octet CCSDS Defined field and a 1, 2 or 4-octet Packet Length that counts the whole packet. Table 4-2 gives the resulting size limits, from a 1-octet idle packet to 4,294,967,295 octets. The section also covers Encapsulation Idle Packets (EPI '000'), the extended-ID escape ('110') and private data ('111'). Section 5 lists the managed parameters, and the annexes note that EPP has no security of its own (SDLS or BPSec provide it) and rename the two SANA protocol-ID registries.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Issue 3 removes the Space Packet as an encapsulation format, renames the standard from 'Encapsulation Service' to 'Encapsulation Packet Protocol' and adds USLP support. (PDF p. 7)
  • EPP carries CCSDS-recognised protocol data units that lack an authorised Packet Version Number over the packet services of the Space Data Link Protocols. (PDF p. 16)
  • One user data unit goes unchanged into one Encapsulation Packet; delivery is one-way and unconfirmed, preserves order, and may have gaps. (PDF p. 17)
  • A SAP is identified by PVN + EPI + SDLP channel; the channel is the GVCID for VCP services and the GMAP ID for TC and USLP MAP Packet services. (PDF p. 19)
  • An Encapsulation Packet is 1 to 4,294,967,295 octets: a 1 to 8-octet header plus 0 to 4,294,967,287 octets of encapsulated data. (PDF p. 23)
  • Header fields: Packet Version Number (3 bits, '111'), EPI (3 bits), Length of Length (2 bits), then optionally User Defined (4 bits), EPI Extension (4 bits), CCSDS Defined (2 octets) and Packet Length (1, 2 or 4 octets). (PDF p. 24)
  • EPI '000' marks an Encapsulation Idle Packet (usable as the idle packet of TM, AOS and USLP), '110' means the EPI Extension field identifies the protocol, and '111' means mission-specific private data. (PDF p. 25)
  • Length of Length '00', '01', '10', '11' gives a Packet Length field of 0, 1, 2 or 4 octets; '00' is allowed only for a one-octet idle packet. (PDF p. 25)
  • The Packet Length field holds the total packet length in octets, header included (unlike the Space Packet's length-minus-one). (PDF p. 26)
  • Maximum packet sizes for 2, 4 and 8-octet headers are 255, 65,535 and 4,294,967,295 octets (Table 4-2); the 4-octet length accommodates IPv6 jumbograms. (PDF p. 27)
  • Managed parameters: minimum and maximum data unit length, and the valid (and valid extended) Encapsulation Protocol Identifiers from SANA. (PDF p. 30)
  • EPP provides no security; SDLS (355.0-B, 355.1-B) at the data link layer or the Bundle Security Protocol at the network layer can be used. (PDF p. 31)
