docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A historical (Silver Book) issue of the CCSDS Recommended Standard that catalogues the identifiers used by the CCSDS space link protocols, says how each is managed, and lists the values CCSDS has defined or reserved. Its stated goal is to manage identifier values independently of the protocol specifications. It is the ancestor of the registries now held by SANA and a handy one-stop reference for older missions; see space link identifiers.

Section 2 introduces three management methods. Values may be defined by CCSDS in the protocol specification, assigned by CCSDS on request through a separate procedure (for example Spacecraft IDs under CCSDS 320.0), or managed by projects, with some values reserved. Sections 3 to 7 then tabulate the identifiers protocol by protocol:

  • CFDP Entity ID and the SCPS-TP Connection Identifier, both managed by projects;
  • the Space Packet APID, with reserved values 2040 to 2047 (2045 CFDP, 2046 ISO 8473, 2047 Idle Packet);
  • the SCPS-NP identifiers;
  • the data link identifiers: Transfer Frame Version Number, SCID, VCID (AOS VCID 63 reserved for idle frames), TM Frame Secondary Header Version, MAP ID, Proximity-1 Port ID, CLCW Version, Packet Version Number (Space Packet 000, SCPS-NP 001, Encapsulation Packet 111) and the Encapsulation Protocol Identifier with its extension mechanism.

Annex A (normative) specifies the IP Extension (IPE) header. This is a variable-length, odd-valued shim after the Encapsulation Packet header that identifies IPv4 (33), IPv6 (87) and the IP header-compression formats. Annex D gives the bit position and meaning of the length field of each CCSDS packet type, which the data link protocols use to extract packets from frames.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The document is a CCSDS Historical Document: no longer current, either replaced by a newer issue or withdrawn as obsolete. (PDF p. 1)
  • Issue 4 (October 2009) added the IPE specification (annex A) and direct multiplexing of IPv4 in transfer frames; issue 2 added Proximity-1 Port IDs and issue 3 the security subsection and the IPv4/Encapsulation Protocol IDs. (PDF p. 8)
  • Lossless Data Compression, SCPS-FP and the TM and TC Synchronization and Channel Coding standards are left out because they use no identifiers. (PDF p. 15)
  • Each identifier is managed in one of three ways: defined by CCSDS in the protocol specification, assigned by CCSDS on Agency request under a separate procedure, or managed by individual projects (possibly with CCSDS-reserved values). (PDF p. 15)
  • The CFDP Entity ID and the SCPS-TP Connection Identifier are managed by projects, with no reserved values. (PDF p. 18)
  • The APID is managed by projects; CCSDS reserves APIDs 2040-2044 for future use, 2045 for CFDP, 2046 for ISO 8473 and 2047 for the Idle Packet. (PDF p. 20)
  • The SCPS-NP Domain Identifier is 'Assigned by CCSDS' but no assignment procedure exists; one must be developed if SCPS-NP is used globally. (PDF p. 21)
  • The SCID is assigned by CCSDS (procedure in CCSDS 320.0-B-5); the VCID and the TC MAP ID are managed by projects; the Transfer Frame, Frame Secondary Header, CLCW and Packet version numbers and the Proximity-1 Port ID are defined by CCSDS. (PDF p. 22)
  • Transfer Frame Version Numbers: TM and TC frames are both version 1 (binary 00), distinguished by the ASM or the CLTU Start Sequence; AOS is version 2 (01); Proximity-1 is version 3 (10). (PDF p. 23)
  • Only one VCID is reserved: binary 111111 (63) for AOS Idle Transfer Frames; no VCID is reserved for the other data link protocols. (PDF p. 23)
  • Packet Version Numbers: 1 (000) Space Packet, 2 (001) SCPS-NP, 8 (111) Encapsulation Packet; the binary-encoded value goes in the packet header. (PDF p. 25)
  • Encapsulation Protocol IDs (3 bits): 000 Fill, 010 IPE, 011 CFDP, 110 Extended Protocol ID (4-bit field, all 16 values reserved), 111 arbitrary aggregations of octets; 001, 100 and 101 are reserved. (PDF p. 26)
  • Proximity-1 Port IDs: 000 Bitstream and 010 Packets on both links; 001 Hardware Commands on the forward link only; all other values are reserved. (PDF p. 27)
  • The IPE header is one or more octets after the Encapsulation Packet header; the LSB of every octet except the last is 0 and the last octet's LSB is 1, so all valid values are odd. (PDF p. 31)
  • IPE header values include 33 for IPv4, 35 for Frame Relay IP Header Compression Control Protocol, 87 for IPv6, and 97 to 113 for RFC 2507/2508 compressed-header formats. (PDF p. 32)
  • Packet length fields: Space Packet bits 32-47 (data field octets minus 1, add 7 for the total); SCPS-NP bits 3-16 (total octets); Encapsulation Packet bits 8-15, 16-31 or 32-63 (total octets including header). (PDF p. 37)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The CCSDS Recommended Standard for the Data Link Layer of Proximity-1. Proximity-1 is the bi-directional protocol for short-range links among landers, rovers, orbiters and relays, characterised by short delays, moderate signals and short, independent sessions. The C&S sublayer (211.2-B) and the Physical Layer (211.1-B) are specified in separate books. This book defines the Frame, Medium Access Control (MAC), Data Services and Input/Output sublayers, the timing services and the COP-P reliability procedure.

Section 3 specifies the Version-3 Transfer Frame: a 5-octet header plus up to 2043 octets of data. The header fields are the Version Number 10, QoS indicator, PDU Type ID, Data Field Construction ID, 10-bit SCID, PCID, Port ID, Source-or-Destination ID, Frame Length and Frame Sequence Number. U-frames carry user data and P-frames carry supervisory PDUs (directives, the PLCW, time distribution and status reports). Issue 6 lets the Version-4 (USLP) frame replace it. Section 4 describes the sublayers: MAC persistence (hailing, COMM_CHANGE, resynchronisation), the Sequence Controlled (go-back-n ARQ) and Expedited qualities of service, and port-based delivery. Section 5 specifies time-tag recording at the ASM trailing edge and the transfer of time to a remote asset. Section 6 gives the full-duplex, half-duplex and simplex state tables. Section 7 gives the FOP-P and FARM-P with their modulo-256 variables. Section 8 covers I/O operations.

The annexes contain:

  • a PICS proforma;
  • the SPDU directive formats (SET TRANSMITTER/CONTROL/RECEIVER PARAMETERS, SET V(R) and others);
  • the Management Information Base parameters;
  • the vehicle-controller notifications;
  • security and SANA notes;
  • Mars Odyssey and MRO (Electra) compatibility notes;
  • a data-format hierarchy.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Issue 6 (July 2020) adds the use of the Version-4 (USLP) Transfer Frame; Editorial Change 1 (September 2024) fixes heading numbering in sections 2 and 6. (PDF p. 7)
  • Proximity links are short-range, bi-directional, fixed or mobile radio links among probes, landers, rovers, orbiting constellations and relays, with short delays, moderate signals and short, independent sessions. (PDF p. 12)
  • The Data Link Layer has five sublayers: Coding and Synchronization (specified in 211.2-B), Frame, Medium Access Control, Data Services (which contains COP-P) and Input/Output. (PDF p. 22)
  • Addressing uses a triad: the SCID (source or destination, according to the Source-or-Destination Identifier), the PCID (selects one of two redundant receivers) and the Port ID (routes user data to logical or physical ports, including hardware command decoders). (PDF p. 25)
  • The PLTU uses a 24-bit ASM and a CRC-32; idle data between variable-length PLTUs maintains symbol synchronisation. (PDF p. 25)
  • Two data transfer services exist: packet delivery (packets with a CCSDS-authorised PVN, segmented and reassembled if needed) and user-defined data delivery (octets, not reassembled), plus timing services. (PDF p. 26)
  • Sequence Controlled service is a go-back-n ARQ using the PLCW report and guarantees no loss, duplication or misordering within a session; Expedited service has no ARQ and suits upper layers with their own retransmission or spacecraft recovery. (PDF p. 27)
  • A Version-3 Transfer Frame is a 5-octet header plus a data field of up to 2043 octets; the header holds Version (2 bits, value '10'), QoS (1), PDU Type ID (1), DFC ID (2), SCID (10), PCID (1), Port ID (3), Source-or-Destination ID (1), Frame Length (11) and Frame Sequence Number (8). (PDF p. 30)
  • QoS '0' marks Sequence Controlled and '1' Expedited frames; PDU Type '0' is a U-frame (user data) and '1' a P-frame (SPDUs). (PDF p. 32)
  • U-frame DFC ID: '00' integer number of unsegmented packets, '01' segment data, '10' reserved, '11' user-defined data. (PDF p. 33)
  • Segmented packets carry an 8-bit segment header: 2 sequence flags ('01' first, '00' continuing, '10' last, '11' unsegmented) and a 6-bit pseudo packet ID; only complete packets are delivered. (PDF p. 38)
  • SPDU types: Type 1 (directives, reports, PLCW), Type 2 (time distribution), Type 3 (enterprise-specific status reports of 0 to 15 octets). (PDF p. 43)
  • The Version-4 (USLP) Transfer Frame may replace the Version-3 frame over the Proximity-1 C&S sublayer, with USLP taking over the Frame Sublayer functions. (PDF p. 44)
  • MAC persistent activities (hailing, COMM_CHANGE and resynchronisation) repeat a directive until the expected RESPONSE arrives within a WAITING_PERIOD; their parameters come from the MIB. (PDF p. 47)
  • Time tags are recorded at the trailing edge of the last ASM bit of every incoming and outgoing frame; collection is triggered by a SET CONTROL PARAMETERS directive, and time correlation itself is outside the standard's scope. (PDF p. 55)
  • COP-P uses modulo-256 single-octet variables, with FOP-P variables VE(S), V(S), VV(S), N(R) and NN(R), and a SYNCH_TIMER that triggers resynchronisation when no valid PLCW arrives. (PDF p. 96)
  • A Type 1 SPDU holds up to seven 16-bit self-identifying directives (Directive Type in bits 13-15, kept for compatibility with Mars Odyssey). (PDF p. 119)
  • Annex C lists the Management Information Base parameters (for example Hail_Lifetime, Carrier_Only_Duration, Comm_Change_Waiting_Period) with the sublayer that uses each. (PDF p. 141)
  • Security is left to layers above or below; SANA action is not required, and no patents are known to apply. (PDF p. 148)
  • Mars Odyssey's convolutional code lacks the G2 inversion; its UHF CW beacon frequencies are 437.1000, 440.7425, 444.3850 and 448.0275 MHz, with 401.585625 MHz for the lander. (PDF p. 149)
  • For symbol rates above 512 ks/s, projects interoperating with MRO's Electra radio should consider NRZ-L instead of Bi-Phase-L. (PDF p. 157)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The CCSDS Green Book that explains and justifies the TC Synchronization and Channel Coding Recommended Standard (231.0-B-4). That standard is the sublayer that turns variable-length TC or USLP Transfer Frames into CLTUs (Communications Link Transmission Units) for the uplink, and back again on board. It is the most practical companion to the Blue Book, for spacecraft telecommand-decoder designers and for ground engineers who build CLTUs (for example behind an SLE FCLTU service).

Section 2 lists what the sublayer does at each end. Section 3 explains the (63,56) BCH code: 56 information bits, 7 inverted parity bits and a filler bit per 64-bit codeword, frames split seven octets at a time, 0x55 fill, and why the older 40, 48 and 56-bit codewords were dropped. Section 4 explains how the short-blocklength (128,64) and (512,256) LDPC codes were chosen. Sections 5 and 6 give the CLTU format for BCH (start sequence 0xEB90, tail C5 C5 C5 C5 C5 C5 C5 79) and for LDPC (64-bit start sequence, optional tail). Section 7 covers the Physical Layer Operations Procedures PLOP-1 and PLOP-2. Section 8 walks through the on-board CLTU reception state machine (Inactive, Search, Decode). Section 9 covers the TC pseudo-randomizer, section 10 systematic retransmission for deep-space links, and section 11 gives extensive performance data: frame rejection and undetected-error rates, and LDPC decoders such as layered BP and most-reliable-basis.

The annexes give the theory behind the randomizer and tail sequences, performance of obsolete features, a go-back-n analysis with multiple copies, BCH undetected-error calculations and, most usefully, worked hexadecimal examples of real TC Transfer Frames and CLTUs with and without randomization.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The report is informational; CCSDS 231.0-B-4 (July 2021) is the controlling Recommended Standard. (PDF p. 13)
  • TC Synchronization and Channel Coding is used below the TC Space Data Link Protocol or USLP for variable-length frames; TM Synchronization and Channel Coding handles fixed-length frames. (PDF p. 17)
  • The sending-end sublayer adds error protection, delimits data units, lets the receiver resolve bit ambiguity, and (through the PLOPs) controls acquisition and idle bit patterns. (PDF p. 18)
  • A CLTU carrying one maximum-length (1024-octet) TC Transfer Frame has 147 BCH codewords and is 1186 octets long. (PDF p. 24)
  • A BCH codeword is 56 information bits, 7 complemented parity bits and one filler bit (always 0); I0 is transmitted first. (PDF p. 24)
  • Codeword lengths of 40, 48 and 56 bits were dropped in June 2000 in favour of the 64-bit codeword, which has 14% bandwidth overhead (25% for the old 40-bit option). (PDF p. 25)
  • Frame data go into BCH codewords seven octets at a time regardless of frame boundaries; the last codeword is padded with alternating 0/1 fill (0x55), up to six octets. (PDF p. 25)
  • Uplink uses are grouped into four modes (emergency, command/ARQ, file upload, human support); the (128,64) and (512,256) LDPC codes target the first two and can replace BCH with little impact elsewhere. (PDF p. 28)
  • With BCH coding, the CLTU Start Sequence is 0xEB90 and the 64-bit Tail Sequence is C5 C5 C5 C5 C5 C5 C5 79. (PDF p. 35)
  • With LDPC coding, the Start Sequence is the 64-bit pattern 0347 76C7 2728 95B0; the tail sequence is optional with the (128,64) code. (PDF p. 38)
  • PLOP-2 is required for missions whose planning began after September 2010; PLOP-1 sends an acquisition sequence before every CLTU, costing throughput but avoiding missed CLTU boundaries. (PDF p. 45)
  • The TC randomizer (Bit Transition Generator) is an 8-bit LFSR, h(x) = x^8 + x^6 + x^4 + x^3 + x^2 + x + 1, initialised to all ones; with BCH it randomizes the 56-bit information fields (not the parity, start or tail sequences), and with LDPC it is reset for each codeword after encoding. (PDF p. 63)
  • Annex F gives worked hexadecimal examples of TC Transfer Frames (with FECF) and the resulting BCH- and LDPC-coded CLTUs, with and without randomization. (PDF p. 134)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The CCSDS Recommended Standard for the TC Synchronization and Channel Coding Sublayer, the uplink counterpart of TM coding. It takes variable-length TC or USLP Transfer Frames, protects them with error-control coding, wraps them in a Communications Link Transmission Unit (CLTU) and hands them to the Physical Layer through a Physical Layer Operations Procedure (PLOP). It is the specification behind every telecommand decoder on board and behind the CLTUs a ground station radiates, including those delivered through SLE FCLTU. The rationale and worked examples are in 230.1-G-3.

Section 2 lists four functions: error-control coding, synchronization, optional pseudo-randomizing and optional repeated transmissions. Section 3 defines the modified (63,56) BCH code with generator g(x) = x7+x6+x^2+1, which gives 64-bit codewords of 56 information bits, 7 inverted parity bits and a zero filler bit, padded with alternating-bit fill. It can be decoded in error-detecting or error-correcting mode. Section 4 defines the rate-½ (128,64) and (512,256) LDPC codes through their parity-check and circulant generator matrices. Section 5 defines the CLTU: Start Sequence (16-bit 0xEB90 for BCH, 64-bit 0x034776C7272895B0 for LDPC), codewords and Tail Sequence (C5C5 C5C5 C5C5 C579 for BCH, an optional 128-bit pattern for LDPC (128,64), none for (512,256)). It also gives the receiver state machine with states S1 Inactive, S2 Search and S3 Decode and events E1 to E5. Section 6 specifies the Bit Transition Generator randomizer, h(x) = x8+x6+x4+x3+x^2+x+1, which is optional with BCH and mandatory with LDPC. Section 7 specifies the carrier modulation modes CMM-1 to CMM-4 and PLOP-1 and PLOP-2, and section 8 the managed parameters. Annex A gives the ChannelAccess service with its optional Repetitions parameter.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Issue 4 (July 2021) clarifies the short-LDPC procedures and adds USLP support; EC 1 (October 2024) fixes the table of contents and moves to A4. (PDF p. 7)
  • Four sublayer functions: error-control coding, synchronization, pseudo-randomizing (optional) and repeated transmissions (optional). (PDF p. 18)
  • The modified BCH code can be decoded in error-detecting or error-correcting mode; the FECF of the TC or USLP frame can lower the undetected-error probability, especially in error-correcting mode. (PDF p. 19)
  • Repeated transmission is requested with an optional Repetitions parameter in the service primitive; how the repetitions are performed is not specified. (PDF p. 20)
  • BCH codeword: 56 information bits plus 7 parity bits from g(x) = x^7 + x^6 + x^2 + 1 plus a filler bit that is always zero, 64 bits (8 octets) in total. (PDF p. 24)
  • Two rate-½ LDPC codes are specified, (n=128, k=64) and (n=512, k=256), built from M x M circulant submatrices with M = k/4. (PDF p. 27)
  • CLTU = Start Sequence + encoded codewords + Tail Sequence. For BCH, the Start Sequence is 16 bits (0xEB90) and the Tail Sequence is 64 bits (C5C5 C5C5 C5C5 C579). (PDF p. 30)
  • For LDPC, the Start Sequence is 64 bits (0347 76C7 2728 95B0); an optional 128-bit Tail Sequence (5555 5556 AAAA AAAA 5555 5555 5555 5555) applies only to LDPC (128,64), and no tail is used with (512,256). (PDF p. 31)
  • CLTU reception states are S1 INACTIVE, S2 SEARCH and S3 DECODE; events E1 to E5 are channel activation, channel deactivation, start sequence found, codeword rejection and (for LDPC 128,64) tail sequence detected. (PDF p. 33)
  • The randomizer polynomial is h(x) = x^8 + x^6 + x^4 + x^3 + x^2 + x + 1, starting from all ones; randomization is always applied with LDPC and required with BCH unless proper operation without it is verified. (PDF p. 36)
  • With BCH the BTG is preset at the start of the Transfer Frame(s); with LDPC it is preset at the start of each codeword and reset after each codeword. (PDF p. 37)
  • PLOP-2 shall be used for missions whose planning begins after September 2010; the preferred minimum Acquisition Sequence length is 16 octets. (PDF p. 39)
  • Carrier Modulation Modes: CMM-1 unmodulated carrier, CMM-2 carrier with acquisition sequence, CMM-3 carrier with CLTU, CMM-4 carrier with idle sequence. (PDF p. 40)
  • Managed parameters: code type (BCH or LDPC), maximum CLTU length, maximum Repetitions, PLOP-1 or PLOP-2; for BCH also the decoding mode, allowed errors in the Start Sequence (0 or 1) and randomizer use; for LDPC the code length and use of the tail sequence. (PDF p. 44)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
This version of the CCSDS Recommended Standard for the TC Synchronization and Channel Coding Sublayer incorporates Technical Corrigendum 1 (July 2026). The sublayer sits below the TC and USLP data link protocols. It protects variable-length Transfer Frames with error-control coding, delimits them in a Communications Link Transmission Unit (CLTU) and drives the Physical Layer through a Physical Layer Operations Procedure (PLOP). The technical content is that of the library's Issue 4 with EC 1, except for the new LDPC tail sequence. It is the uplink counterpart of TM coding and the format behind SLE FCLTU and the CLTU page.

The standard specifies:

  • four sublayer functions: error-control coding, synchronization, pseudo-randomizing and optional repeated transmissions (section 2);
  • the modified (63,56) BCH code with g(x) = x7+x6+x^2+1, giving 64-bit codewords that can be decoded in error-detecting or error-correcting mode (section 3);
  • the rate-½ (128,64) and (512,256) LDPC codes (section 4);
  • the CLTU (section 5): the 16-bit 0xEB90 Start Sequence and C5C5C5C5C5C5C579 Tail Sequence for BCH, the 64-bit 0x034776C7272895B0 Start Sequence for LDPC, an optional 128-bit Tail Sequence for LDPC (128,64), and the S1/S2/S3 receiver state machine;
  • the 255-bit Bit Transition Generator randomizer, required with LDPC (section 6);
  • the carrier modulation modes CMM-1 to CMM-4, PLOP-1 and PLOP-2 (section 7), and the managed parameters (section 8).

The corrigendum replaces the LDPC (128,64) Tail Sequence with 63A1ED72C6AC79E25555555555555555. The pattern stops a decoder with probability of about 1-10^-4. A new note gives its derandomized form, which is what an LDPC decoder actually sees.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Technical Corrigendum 1 (July 2026) changes only 5.2.4.2: a revised LDPC (128,64) Tail Sequence, a new note 3 and decoding-probability details in the requirement and note 2. (PDF p. 7)
  • The modified BCH code can be decoded in error-detecting or error-correcting mode, depending on mission requirements. (PDF p. 19)
  • Repeated transmission is requested through an optional Repetitions parameter of the service primitive. (PDF p. 20)
  • BCH codeword: 56 information bits, 7 parity bits from g(x) = x^7 + x^6 + x^2 + 1 and a final Filler Bit that is always zero, 64 bits (8 octets) in total. (PDF p. 23)
  • Two rate-½ LDPC codes are specified, (n=128, k=64) and (n=512, k=256), with parity-check matrices built from M x M submatrices, M = k/4 = n/8. (PDF p. 26)
  • The CLTU is Start Sequence + codewords + Tail Sequence; for BCH the Start Sequence is the 16-bit pattern 1110 1011 1001 0000 (0xEB90) and for LDPC the 64-bit pattern 0347 76C7 2728 95B0. (PDF p. 30)
  • The BCH Tail Sequence is the 64-bit non-correctable pattern C5C5 C5C5 C5C5 C579, which stops the decoding process. (PDF p. 30)
  • Corrigendum: the optional 128-bit LDPC (128,64) Tail Sequence is now 63A1 ED72 C6AC 79E2 5555 5555 5555 5555 and stops the decoder with probability of roughly 1-10^-4; its derandomized form, which the decoder fails on, is 9C987328 AE457F17 39DC7AF4 640B5D95. (PDF p. 31)
  • No Tail Sequence is used with LDPC (512,256); a conventional decoder reliably fails to decode when it over-runs the end of the CLTU. (PDF p. 31)
  • CLTU reception states are S1 INACTIVE, S2 SEARCH and S3 DECODE; events are E1 channel activation, E2 channel deactivation, E3 start sequence found, E4 codeword rejection and E5 tail sequence found (optional, LDPC 128,64). (PDF p. 33)
  • In S2, no Start Sequence error is allowed in BCH error-detecting mode and one error in error-correcting mode. (PDF p. 33)
  • Randomizer h(x) = x^8 + x^6 + x^4 + x^3 + x^2 + x + 1 (255-bit period, first bits 1111 1111 0011 1001 ...); always applied with LDPC, and required with BCH unless the designer verifies operation without it. (PDF p. 35)
  • With BCH the BTG is preset to all ones at the start of the Transfer Frame(s); with LDPC it is preset at the start of each codeword and reset to all ones after each codeword. (PDF p. 36)
  • PLOP-2 shall be used for missions whose planning began after September 2010; the preferred minimum Acquisition Sequence is 16 octets. (PDF p. 38)
  • Carrier Modulation Modes: CMM-1 unmodulated carrier, CMM-2 carrier modulated with the acquisition sequence, CMM-3 carrier modulated with CLTUs, CMM-4 carrier modulated with the idle sequence. (PDF p. 39)
  • Managed parameters: code type, maximum CLTU length, maximum Repetitions, PLOP-1 or PLOP-2; for BCH the decoding mode, allowed Start Sequence errors (0 or 1) and randomizer use; for LDPC the code length and use of the tail sequence. A maximum Repetitions value of 1 means repeated transmission is not available. (PDF p. 42)
  • The service primitive is ChannelAccess.request (Frame(s), Repetitions); support for Repetitions is optional. (PDF p. 45)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The CCSDS Recommended Standard for the TC Space Data Link Protocol, the telecommand data link protocol used on the uplink of most ESA missions. It defines the variable-length TC Transfer Frame, the Communications Link Control Word (CLCW) that reports acceptance status back to the ground, and the services for sending Space Packets and private data units on Virtual Channels and MAP channels. Retransmission is handled by COP-1 (CCSDS 232.1), and frames are coded into CLTUs by TC Synchronization and Channel Coding.

Section 2 covers the channel tree (Physical, Master, Virtual and MAP channels), the Type-A (sequence-controlled) and Type-B (expedited) service types, and six data services: MAP Packet, VC Packet, MAP Access, VC Access, VC Frame and MC Frame. A COP Management service controls the FOP. Section 3 gives each service's primitives.

Section 4 specifies the PDUs. The 5-octet primary header holds the version ('00'), Bypass Flag, Control Command Flag, 2 spare bits, 10-bit SCID, 6-bit VCID, 10-bit Frame Length (total length minus one, so at most 1024 octets) and 8-bit Frame Sequence Number. The flag combinations give Type-AD, Type-BD and Type-BC frames. The optional Segment Header holds Sequence Flags and a 6-bit MAP ID for segmentation. The section also defines the Unlock and Set V(R) control commands and the CRC-16 FECF. The 32-bit CLCW carries COP in Effect, VCID, the No RF Available, No Bit Lock, Lockout, Wait and Retransmit flags, the FARM-B counter and the Report Value N(R). Section 4 then models the sending functions (MAP packet processing, MAP generation and multiplexing, VC generation and multiplexing, MC multiplexing, all-frames generation) and the matching receiving functions. Section 5 lists the managed parameters, and section 6 adds the SDLS security header and trailer and the order of processing between TC, COP-1 and SDLS.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Technical Corrigendum 1 (October 2023) expands and clarifies 6.5.2, the order of processing between TC, COP-1 and SDLS; this copy includes it. (PDF p. 7)
  • Six data transfer services: MAP Packet (SAP = GMAP ID + PVN), VC Packet (GVCID + PVN), MAP Access, VC Access (all Type-A or Type-B), VC Frame and MC Frame; a COP Management service controls COP retransmission per Virtual Channel. (PDF p. 24)
  • TC Transfer Frame = 5-octet Primary Header + Data Field (up to 1019 octets, or 1017 with FECF) + optional 2-octet Frame Error Control Field. (PDF p. 69)
  • Primary header: Version (2 bits), Bypass Flag (1), Control Command Flag (1), Reserved Spare (2), SCID (10), VCID (6), Frame Length (10) and Frame Sequence Number (8). (PDF p. 70)
  • Bypass/Control Command flags 0/0 = Type-AD (sequence-controlled data), 1/0 = Type-BD (expedited data), 1/1 = Type-BC (control commands); 0/1 is reserved. (PDF p. 72)
  • Frame Length holds total frame octets minus one; the 10-bit field limits a TC frame to 1024 octets. (PDF p. 73)
  • The Segment Header (Sequence Flags 2 bits + MAP ID 6 bits) is required on any VC with more than one MAP or carrying SDUs larger than one frame; it must not be present in frames carrying control commands. (PDF p. 74)
  • Control commands: Unlock is a single all-zero octet; Set V(R) is three octets 10000010 00000000 followed by the new V(R) value. (PDF p. 77)
  • The CLCW is 32 bits: Control Word Type '0', Version '00', Status Field (3), COP in Effect ('01' for COP-1), VCID (6), spare (2), the No RF Available, No Bit Lock, Lockout, Wait and Retransmit flags, FARM-B Counter (2), spare (1) and Report Value (8). (PDF p. 81)
  • The CLCW is the only reporting mechanism of the protocol and is usually carried in the OCF of TM or AOS frames; each Virtual Channel in use has its own CLCW reporting. (PDF p. 80)
  • Physical Channel managed parameters include the maximum frame length, TFVN 1, valid SCIDs, FECF presence, maximum frames per coding-sublayer data unit, maximum bit rate and maximum Repetitions. (PDF p. 107)
  • Virtual Channel managed parameters include VCID 0 to 63, COP in Effect, CLCW reporting rate, Segment Header presence, valid MAP IDs 0 to 63, blocking, and the Repetitions values for Type-A data and for COP control commands. (PDF p. 109)
  • At the receiving end with SDLS, FARM-1 runs first, then SDLS ProcessSecurity, then the rest of the Virtual Channel Reception Function (6.5.2, as amended by Cor. 1). (PDF p. 120)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The CCSDS Recommended Standard for COP-1, the closed-loop go-back-n retransmission procedure that gives the TC Space Data Link Protocol (and, since Cor. 1, USLP) complete, in-order, duplicate-free delivery of telecommand frame data units on each Virtual Channel. It is the specification behind the 'AD mode' and 'BD mode' of every ESA mission control system: the ground runs the FOP-1 (Frame Operation Procedure) and the spacecraft runs the FARM-1 (Frame Acceptance and Reporting Mechanism). The FARM-1 reports its state in the CLCW, which is returned in the OCF of TM or AOS frames.

Section 2 explains the concept. Type-AD frames carry sequence-controlled data numbered N(S); Type-BC frames carry the Unlock and Set V(R) control commands; Type-BD frames carry expedited data that is sent once. The section also introduces the key variables V(S), V(R), N(R) and N(S), the Wait flow control and the Lockout mechanism. Section 3 defines the interfaces between COP-1 and the higher procedures and frame generation and reception procedures at each end. Section 4 defines the directive request and notification, asynchronous notification and transfer notification primitives (Initiate AD Service variants, Terminate, Resume, Set V(S), Set FOP sliding window, Set T1_Initial, Set Transmission_Limit, Set Timeout_Type and others).

Section 5 specifies FOP-1 (Revision B). It covers its variables (V(S), NN(R), the Sent_Queue and Wait_Queue, timers, Transmission_Count, Suspend_State and so on), its actions, and the state table over six states: Active, Retransmit without Wait, Retransmit with Wait, Initializing without BC Frame, Initializing with BC Frame, and Initial. Section 6 specifies FARM-1 with its states Open, Wait and Lockout, the sliding window (W, PW, NW), the Type-B counter and its state table. Section 7 lists the managed parameters. Annex D records the changes from the historical Telecommand Part 2.1 recommendation.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Cor. 1 (April 2019) extends COP-1 to USLP and clarifies the FARM window widths depending on whether Type-AD frame retransmission is allowed. (PDF p. 7)
  • In case of conflict with the TC SDLP or USLP books, this Recommended Standard takes precedence. (PDF p. 10)
  • COP-1 is a go-back-n ARQ: a FOP-1 at the sender and a FARM-1 at the receiver per Virtual Channel, with acceptance status returned in CLCWs. (PDF p. 15)
  • Valid Type-B frames are always accepted by FARM-1 and only increment the CLCW Type-B counter; Type-B frames also carry the control commands. (PDF p. 15)
  • The AD Service ensures no FDU is lost, duplicated or delivered out of sequence on one VC; it uses Type-AD frames for data and Type-BC frames for the Unlock and Set V(R) control commands; four 'Initiate AD Service' directives exist. (PDF p. 16)
  • Key variables: V(S) at the sender, V(R) at the receiver, N(S) in the frame header and N(R) in the CLCW; a 'Wait' mechanism gives flow control. (PDF p. 17)
  • Directive types (Table 4-1): Initiate AD Service without CLCW check, with CLCW check, with Unlock, or with Set V(R); Terminate AD Service; Resume AD Service; and the setup directives Set V(S) to V*(S), Set FOP_Sliding_Window_Width, Set T1_Initial, Set Transmission_Limit and Set Timeout_Type. (PDF p. 28)
  • BD (Expedited) frames are sent once with no delivery guarantee, typically for recovery or when a higher layer retransmits; 'Expedited' does not mean faster, and AD mode is recommended when a reliable link exists. (PDF p. 17)
  • Systematic retransmission can optionally be provided outside COP-1 for Type-AD or Type-BC frames and has no effect on FOP-1 behaviour. (PDF p. 41)
  • FOP-1 states: Active (S1), Retransmit without Wait (S2), Retransmit with Wait (S3), Initializing without BC Frame (S4), Initializing with BC Frame (S5) and Initial (S6). (PDF p. 37)
  • The FOP-1 specified here is Revision B (FOP-1B) from issue 2 of the historical Command Operation Procedures; Revision A came from issue 1. (PDF p. 49)
  • FARM-1 states: Open (S1), Wait (S2) and Lockout (S3). (PDF p. 61)
  • FOP-1 managed parameters: T1_Initial, Transmission_Limit, FOP_Sliding_Window_Width K (1 to 255, K <= PW) and Timeout_Type (0 or 1). (PDF p. 72)
  • FARM-1 managed parameters: W (1 to 256), PW (1 to 256), NW (0 to 127) and the CLCW reporting period; with the 6.1.8.3.1 operation W is an even number from 2 to 254 and PW = NW = W/2, while the 6.1.8.3.2 operation allows PW > NW down to NW = 0, PW = W. (PDF p. 73)
  • Terminology changed from the historical book: 'Command Link Control Word' became 'Communications Link Control Word' and 'Command Operation Procedure' became 'Communications Operation Procedure'. (PDF p. 79)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The CCSDS Recommended Standard that defines the standard binary and ASCII time code formats used to time-tag data in space data systems. Its formats appear everywhere in telemetry and telecommand: in the Space Packet secondary header, in the PUS packet time fields (SCOS-2000 TM packets usually carry a CUC on-board time), in time correlation and in ground files. The standard defines formats only, not timing accuracy or stability.

Section 1 defines four levels of interpretability: Level 1 is fully self-defined with a CCSDS epoch, Level 2 has an agency-defined epoch, Level 3 only guarantees monotonic increase and Level 4 only gives the length. It also sets the CCSDS bit numbering, where bit 0 is transmitted first and is the MSB. Section 2 (new in issue 4) discusses security: time codes can be critical, so integrity, authentication or confidentiality must come from other layers.

Section 3 is the specification. Each code is an optional P-field (preamble: extension flag, 3-bit code ID, detail bits) followed by a T-field:

  • CUC: a binary count of seconds and binary fractions from 1958 January 1 TAI (ID '001') or an agency epoch (ID '010'), with 1 to 4 coarse and 0 to 3 fine octets, and more through the new second P-field octet. It is not UTC-based.
  • CDS: a day count (16 or 24 bits) plus milliseconds of day (32 bits) plus optional microseconds or picoseconds. It is UTC-based.
  • CCS: a BCD calendar code in month/day or day-of-year form with up to 10^-12 s resolution.
  • ASCII A and B: YYYY-MM-DDThhss.d...Z and YYYY-DDDThhss.d...Z.
  • Agency-defined codes (ID '110').

The annexes give the counter ranges (normative), the rationale and comparison of the codes, a glossary of time terms, the TAI-UTC leap-second relation and table, and NASA PB-5J as an example of an agency-defined code.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Issue 4 (November 2010) defines a second P-field octet for CUC, adds a new section on security and updates editorial elements; EC 1 (February 2014) corrects page v. (PDF p. 7)
  • Four recommended codes (one unsegmented, three segmented) use the SI second; each is a P-field (preamble, explicit or implicit) plus a T-field (time). (PDF p. 9)
  • Four levels: Level 1 complete unambiguous interpretation (CCSDS epoch), Level 2 partial (agency epoch), Level 3 only monotonic increase, Level 4 only code length. (PDF p. 9)
  • Security services for critical time codes (integrity, authentication, confidentiality) are out of scope and must come from other OSI layers. (PDF p. 12)
  • P-field octet 1: bit 0 extension flag, bits 1-3 time code identification, bits 4-7 code-specific detail; IDs 000, 011 and 111 are reserved. ASCII codes have no P-field. (PDF p. 14)
  • CUC: binary count from 1958 January 1 TAI (ID '001', Level 1) or an agency-defined epoch (ID '010', Level 2); P-field bits 4-5 give coarse octets minus one, bits 6-7 the fine octets; it is not UTC-based and leap seconds do not apply. (PDF p. 15)
  • The optional CUC P-field octet 2 adds up to 3 more coarse octets (bits 1-2) and up to 7 more fine octets (bits 3-5); bits 6-7 are reserved for mission definition. (PDF p. 15)
  • CDS (ID '100'): a 16 or 24-bit day count from 1958 January 1 (or an agency epoch), 32-bit milliseconds of day and optional 16-bit microseconds or 32-bit picoseconds; it is UTC-based and needs leap-second correction. (PDF p. 16)
  • CCS (ID '101'): BCD calendar code, 16-bit year plus month/day or day-of-year, then hour, minute and second, with up to six optional subsecond segments down to 10^-12 s. (PDF p. 17)
  • ASCII Time Code A is YYYY-MM-DDThhss.d...Z and Code B is YYYY-DDDThhss.d...Z; the 'Z' terminator is optional; example 1988-01-18T17:20:43.123456Z. (PDF p. 19)
  • Agency-defined codes use ID '110'; P-field bits 4-7 give the T-field length minus one (1 to 16 octets); a monotonic code is Level 3, otherwise Level 4. (PDF p. 22)
  • Comparison: CUC is computer-efficient but not UTC-compatible; CDS is UTC-compatible and computer-efficient; CCS and ASCII are UTC-compatible and human-readable (Table B-1). (PDF p. 26)
  • The CCSDS epoch 1958 January 1 is Julian date 2436203.5 and lies exactly 2922.0 days after 1950 January 1. (PDF p. 29)
  • TAI = UTC + accumulated leap seconds; the table in Annex D runs from 10 s (1972) to 34 s (from 2009 January 1). (PDF p. 39)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The CCSDS procedure for requesting, assigning and relinquishing Spacecraft Identifiers (SCIDs), the field that names a spacecraft in TM, TC, AOS, Proximity-1 and USLP transfer frames. It matters to any project that needs a registered SCID and to anyone reading the SCID field on the space link identifiers page.

The key idea of issue 7 is the Qualified SCID: Q-SCID = frequency band . Transfer Frame Version Number (TFVN) . SCID. Each TFVN and each ITU frequency band forms a separate namespace, so one spacecraft may hold several Q-SCIDs. SANA tries to give it the same number in all of them. Table 1-1 gives the SCID size per frame version: 10 bits for TM/TC (version 1), 8 bits for AOS (version 2), 10 bits for Proximity-1 (version 3) and 16 bits for USLP (version 4, TFVN 1100). Table 2-1 maps ITU near-Earth and deep-space downlink allocations to SANA frequency band designators such as S-NE, X-DS and Ka-DS.

Section 3 sets out the roles of the CCSDS Secretariat, the Agency Heads of Delegation, the Agency Representatives (ARs) and SANA, the assignment manager. Requests go through the online SANA form. SANA does not reserve blocks of numbers or assign SCIDs to simulators. Every assignment also returns a permanent ISO Object Identifier (OID), because SCIDs are reused. Archived data should be labelled with the OID rather than the SCID. ARs must relinquish Q-SCIDs within two months of the end of operations, and freed numbers go to the bottom of the stack. Annex A describes the SANA Spacecraft Identifier registry columns and its registration rules.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Issue 7 changed the document from a Recommended Standard (Blue Book) to a Recommended Practice (Magenta Book) and introduced the frequency band as a qualifier of the SCID. (PDF p. 7)
  • Technical Corrigendum 1 (July 2019) adds USLP (version-4) transfer frames and ITU-defined frequency ranges. (PDF p. 8)
  • The procedures must be followed by every organisation that needs a SCID to use CCSDS space communication protocols, and by SANA, which registers the identifiers. (PDF p. 10)
  • GSCID = TFVN . SCID and Q-SCID = FB . TFVN . SCID ('.' is concatenation); the OID is a permanent ISO identifier, whereas the SCID is valid only for the mission's operational lifetime. (PDF p. 11)
  • SCID sizes by TFVN: version 1 (00, TM and TC) 10 bits, 0-1,023; version 2 (01, AOS) 8 bits, 0-255; version 3 (10, Proximity-1) 10 bits, 0-1,023; version 4 (1100, USLP) 16 bits, 0-65535. (PDF p. 12)
  • Each TFVN needs its own SCID assignment table and each frequency band per TFVN its own Q-SCID table; SANA attempts, without guarantee, to assign the same SCID in every domain. (PDF p. 14)
  • SANA no longer assigns SCIDs for simulation, testing or ground simulators, which do not radiate; missions may self-assign such SCIDs internally. (PDF p. 15)
  • Table 2-1 maps ITU bands to SANA frequency band designators, for example S-NE (2.200-2.290 GHz) and S-DS (2.290-2.300 GHz), X-NE (8.025-8.400 GHz) and X-DS (8.400-8.450 GHz), and Ka-DS (31.8-32.3 GHz); only downlink allocations are shown. (PDF p. 16)
  • The management system has four elements: the CCSDS Secretariat, the Agency Heads of Delegation, the Agency Representatives and SANA. (PDF p. 18)
  • ARs must relinquish all Q-SCIDs no later than two months after the end of the spacecraft's operational phase. (PDF p. 19)
  • After telemetry is received, the SCID should be replaced by the OID as the permanent label of the data, because SCIDs are reused and identifying archived data by SCID is problematic. (PDF p. 20)
  • Requests are submitted by the designated AR through the online SANA form, stating the TFVN and the uplink and downlink frequency bands; one form per Q-SCID request. (PDF p. 21)
  • SANA assigns codes on availability; specific numbers are honoured only exceptionally; each Q-SCID is unique within its TFVN and frequency band during its assignment period. (PDF p. 21)
  • Every Q-SCID request also returns a unique persistent OID; reservation of blocks of IDs for unspecified spacecraft is not accepted, and protoflight models or simulators may get OIDs but not separate SCIDs. (PDF p. 22)
  • Relinquished SCIDs are placed at the bottom of the available stack to maximise the time before reuse. (PDF p. 23)
  • The SANA Spacecraft Identifier registry records spacecraft name, channel, version number, SCID, GSCID, OID (1.3.112.4.7...), requestor, status, transmit and receive frequency bands, and expected launch and end dates. (PDF p. 24)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A CCSDS Green Book that guides mission planners on where and how to add security to a mission built on CCSDS protocols, and on what that costs in interoperability. It is the overview behind the security in CCSDS space links page and puts SDLS in context.

Section 2 introduces the vocabulary: confidentiality, integrity, authentication, access control and availability, the System Security Policy, threat assessment, and accidental versus intentional and passive versus active threats. Section 3 maps five implementation points onto the CCSDS stack (Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport and Application). It sketches the likely requirements for high-, moderate- and minimal-security missions; even minimal-security missions are expected to authenticate telecommands. Section 4 explains the mechanisms: symmetric and asymmetric encryption, key management, digital signatures and message digests, integrity check values, anti-replay sequence numbers, access control, and RF jamming as an availability threat.

Section 5 compares five options:

  • Physical Layer bulk encryption with TRANSEC;
  • Data Link security with SDLS, showing which TC, TM and AOS services it protects or leaves unprotected (SDLS does not apply to Proximity-1);
  • IPSec at the Network Layer;
  • Space Packet security, with the packet header left in clear and a replay weakness;
  • Application Layer security (TLS, the DTN Streamlined Bundle Security Protocol).

Section 6 analyses the effect of each option on visible fields, on emergency commanding (whether hardware-decoded emergency commands should be authenticated) and on SLE return and forward services. It gives selection guidance: usually encrypt at one layer only. Annex A summarises real implementations: the ESA Copernicus Sentinel telecommand authentication (MAP-based, with a Logical Authentication Counter, a 128-bit MAC and OTAR through a custom PUS service), ISS AOS uplink 3DES, STRV-1c/d and the ESA ATV.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Issue 3 renames the report from 'The Application of CCSDS Protocols to Secure Systems' (issues 1 and 2, 1999 and 2006) to 'The Application of Security to CCSDS Protocols'. (PDF p. 6)
  • The report mainly addresses security of the space-ground and ground-space data link; ground systems are assumed to use off-the-shelf solutions such as IPSec, and risk-assessment methods are out of scope. (PDF p. 9)
  • Passive threats compromise only confidentiality and leave no trace; active threats modify information or system state, violating integrity or availability. (PDF p. 14)
  • Security implementation points on the CCSDS stack are the Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport and Application Layers; the choice depends on agency policy, mission security and operational requirements, the CCSDS standards used and on-board capability. (PDF p. 15)
  • Missions are grouped as high, moderate or minimal security; even minimal-security missions are expected to need authentication and integrity of all telecommand data. (PDF p. 18)
  • Integrity of individual data units uses an Integrity Check Value (CRC, SHA-2, or a keyed hash or AES CMAC); integrity of a stream uses sequence numbers or time stamps against replay. (PDF p. 22)
  • RF jamming threatens availability; spread spectrum and frequency hopping (TRANSEC) are the counter-techniques. (PDF p. 23)
  • Bulk encryption at the Physical Layer encrypts the whole CLTU with acquisition and idle sequences on the uplink, and the whole CADU stream on TM or AOS. (PDF p. 25)
  • SDLS (355.0-B) provides authentication, encryption or authenticated encryption for TM, TC and AOS frame data fields, inserting a Security Header and optional Trailer; it can be applied per Virtual Channel and is not applicable to Proximity-1. (PDF p. 27)
  • For TC, SDLS fully protects the MAP Packet, MAP Access, VC Packet and VC Access services, authenticates some primary-header fields, and does not protect COP control frames or frames inserted through the VC Frame or Master Channel Frame services. (PDF p. 29)
  • For TM, SDLS does not protect the VC and MC Operational Control Fields or the MC Frame Secondary Header; for AOS, it does not protect the OCF or the Insert service. (PDF p. 29)
  • IPSec ESP adds an 8-byte clear header (4-byte SPI and 4-byte sequence number), padding, pad-length and next-header fields and an optional ICV. (PDF p. 31)
  • Space packet security encrypts the packet data field (optionally the secondary header) and keeps the primary header in clear; without an authenticated replay counter in the header, packets are open to replay. (PDF p. 31)
  • Confidentiality impact: Network Layer security leaves everything except the packet data field in clear; SDLS encrypts the frame data field including packet headers; bulk encryption hides everything, including ASM and EDAC. (PDF p. 34)
  • Emergency commands acted on directly by the hardware command decoder pose a trade-off: no authentication opens a security hole, while authentication lengthens commands that must be very short. (PDF p. 34)
  • In figures 6-1 and 6-2, frame-level SLE services (RAF, RCF, FCLTU, OCF and FSH services and others) are marked 'V' for all options, while services that extract frame contents (Return Bitstream, Return Space Packet, Forward TC VCA, Forward Space Packet, Forward Bitstream, Forward VCA) are marked 'U' when Data Link security ends at the SLE client; the 'V'/'U' legend is not explained in the text. (PDF p. 36)
  • Bulk encryption denies all cross-support services unless keys are pre-placed at the access points, and it makes CCSDS synchronisation and channel coding ineffective. (PDF p. 37)
  • Most missions should encrypt at only one layer; full traffic-analysis protection needs Physical Layer encryption, and Data Link security lets RAF and FCLTU extend the secure link into the ground network. (PDF p. 39)
  • The ESA Copernicus Sentinel telecommand authentication works at the TC segmentation layer, with a Logical Authentication Counter and a 128-bit MAC in an authentication trailer, master and session keys, and Over-The-Air Rekeying through a custom PUS service. (PDF p. 41)
  • The ISS encrypts its AOS uplink with 3DES at the VCA sublayer, using a 64-bit insert zone for cryptographic synchronisation; the ATV used 3DES encryption plus a Time Authentication field in TC packets. (PDF p. 42)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The CCSDS Green Book that explains the concept, design rationale and operation of the Space Data Link Security (SDLS) protocol (CCSDS 355.0-B-2). SDLS adds authentication, encryption or authenticated encryption to the frames of the TC, TM, AOS and USLP data link protocols without changing those protocols. Read it next to the Blue Book to understand why SDLS looks the way it does.

Section 2 gives the motivation. SLE already protects the ground leg, so SDLS secures the remaining end-to-end link between mission control system and spacecraft, without breaking SLE frame services (FCLTU, RAF, RCF, ROCF). Hence frame headers stay in clear. Table 2-2 lists, service by service, what SDLS can protect. OCFs, Insert Zone data, VC and MC Frame services and COP-1 control (BC) frames are never protected, and the VC Frame Secondary Header is authenticated only. The section also covers Encrypt-then-MAC, the danger of encryption without authentication, the three key-management schemes (preloaded keys, OTAR, on-board key derivation) and the 32-octet overhead limit.

Section 3 explains several design choices:

  • why SDLS sits between the frame functions and COP-1 (it is applied before the FOP at the sending end and after the FARM at the receiving end, so that COP retransmissions are not rejected as replays);
  • how it plugs into TC, TM, AOS and USLP;
  • the Security Header (16-bit SPI, optional IV, sequence number and pad length) and the Trailer (MAC);
  • managed parameters and Clear Mode.

Section 4 walks through Security Associations, sending and receiving processing, sequence-counter windows and the baseline modes: TC authentication with AES-CMAC, and TM, AOS and USLP authenticated encryption with AES-GCM. Both use 256-bit keys and 128-bit MACs, as derived in Annex A. The other annexes map ISO security services to each protocol, reproduce the 2012 User Requirements Document and analyse error-detection performance.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Issue 2 (January 2024) replaces issue 1 (June 2018) and aligns the report with the SDLS Extended Procedures and the current TC, TM, AOS and USLP Blue Books. (PDF p. 6)
  • SDLS protects the SDUs carried by the space data link protocols and selected protocol data structures, within the constraints of compatibility with the data link and SLE services. (PDF p. 13)
  • Target topology: a mission control centre and a spacecraft linked through a ground station; SLE security protects the ground network, and SDLS protects the end-to-end data link between the mission control system and the spacecraft. (PDF p. 16)
  • For space-to-space links, SDLS works master-slave with no negotiation: directives always flow from a predetermined Initiator to a predetermined Recipient. (PDF p. 17)
  • TC MAP Packet and MAP Access, TM and AOS VC Packet and VCA, and USLP MAP Packet, MAP Access and MAP Octet Stream protection is mandatory; TC VC Packet and VCA and AOS Bitstream are optional; Insert, MC_OCF, VC Frame and MC Frame are not supported. (PDF p. 18)
  • Three security services: authentication (integrity, source authentication, anti-replay), encryption (confidentiality only) and authenticated encryption (all of these). (PDF p. 19)
  • VC Frame Secondary Header data can only be authenticated; OCF services, VC and MC Frame services, the Insert service and COP Management (BC frames) are not protected. (PDF p. 21)
  • SLE compatibility requires FCLTU, Forward TC Frames, RAF, RCF and Return OCF to keep working, which is possible only if the full frame header is left unaltered. (PDF p. 22)
  • Encryption without authentication gives no protection against data substitution and can give a false sense of security. (PDF p. 23)
  • SDLS assumes Encrypt-then-MAC composition; authenticated encryption is the CCSDS-recommended way to provide both authentication and confidentiality. (PDF p. 24)
  • Requirements: Clear and Secure modes per logical channel, coexisting clear and secure channels, compatibility with three key-management schemes (all keys preloaded, OTAR of session keys, on-board derivation from master keys), and at most 32 octets of overhead per Transfer Frame. (PDF p. 26)
  • SDLS is applied before the COP at the sending end and after it at the receiving end; otherwise COP-1 go-back-N retransmissions would be discarded as replays and the MAC would reject frames that the FARM should handle. (PDF p. 27)
  • The Security Header starts with a mandatory 2-octet Security Parameter Index; up to 65534 Security Associations per Master Channel are possible, with SPI values 0 and 65535 reserved. (PDF p. 46)
  • With GCM-type algorithms that use an incrementing counter as IV, the transmitted IV also serves as the sequence number, and the separate Sequence Number field is omitted. (PDF p. 47)
  • A Clear Mode on a protected SA is not recommended, but civilian missions may justify it; it can be realised as a 'no-op' algorithm SA, keeping header and trailer to avoid throughput changes. (PDF p. 51)
  • Because TM, AOS and expedited TC cannot guarantee in-sequence delivery, the receiver accepts sequence numbers within a window, so gaps do not block the link. (PDF p. 66)
  • TC baseline: authentication with AES-CMAC over VC ID and frame data, 32-bit anti-replay sequence number sent in-line, 256-bit key, 128-bit MAC. (PDF p. 66)
  • TM baseline: authenticated encryption with GCM over VC ID and frame data, 32-bit anti-replay sequence number, 256-bit key, 128-bit MAC and 96-bit IV. (PDF p. 67)
  • In the TM baseline, the IV is an incrementing counter, so the separate Sequence Number field is not needed; GCM needs no padding, and a single key serves both authentication and encryption. (PDF p. 68)
  • Annex A's analysis gives MAC/key lengths of 78/107, 98/127 and 118/147 bits for medium, low and lowest risk and selects 128 bits for both; the baseline key length was later doubled to 256 bits against Grover's algorithm. (PDF p. 78)
  • Annex D: the TC requirement of at most one undetected-error frame in 10^9 is met without a mandatory CRC (BER < 10^-4 in TED mode, < 10^-5 in SEC mode); ESA's SEC mode with mandatory CRC achieves below 10^-15. (PDF p. 130)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The short CCSDS Recommended Standard that fixes which cryptographic algorithms CCSDS missions use for confidentiality, authentication and authenticated encryption. It does not say where in the stack to apply them; that is left to mission planners and to documents such as 350.0-G-3 and the SDLS Blue Book (355.0-B-2). Its choices are the algorithms behind SDLS baseline modes and many CCSDS security designs.

Section 2 gives the background: why civilian missions now need security, symmetric hash-based and cipher-based MACs, digital signatures and authenticated encryption (AEAD). It stresses that encryption without authentication is dangerous and highly discouraged.

The normative sections 3 and 4 make these choices:

  • Encryption: AES for all missions, a 256-bit key for missions planned after this issue (128-bit allowed for existing implementations), and Counter Mode.
  • Authenticated encryption: GCM with a 128-bit MAC.
  • Hash-based MAC: HMAC (FIPS 198-1) with SHA-256 normally; SHA-224/384/512 or RIPEMD-160 by prior agreement; SHA-1 forbidden; truncation discouraged and only by agreement.
  • Cipher-based MAC: AES-CMAC (256-bit key for new missions), with GMAC allowed when a GCM implementation is used for authentication only.
  • Digital signatures: DSS, preferably RSA (PKCS #1 v2.1) with 4096-bit keys for new missions (2048-bit for existing), with DSA or ECDSA allowed.

Annex A discusses the threats and consequences of omitting confidentiality or authentication. It notes that all the algorithms are public domain with no known patents.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• One symmetric encryption algorithm and one mode are recommended for all CCSDS missions; several alternative authentication/integrity algorithms are offered; how, when and where to apply them is left to mission planners. (PDF p. 9)
  • Key management is outside the scope of the standard (see the Space Missions Key Management Concept, 350.6-G-1). (PDF p. 9)
  • Applicable to all civilian missions needing confidentiality, authentication or authenticated confidentiality; security is encouraged especially on command links, subject to a risk analysis. (PDF p. 10)
  • The use of encryption without authentication is highly discouraged for CCSDS missions. (PDF p. 16)
  • All CCSDS missions shall use AES (FIPS 197, ISO/IEC 18033-3) for encryption; missions planned after issue 2 shall use 256-bit keys, while existing implementations may use 128-bit keys. (PDF p. 17)
  • The mode of operation shall be Counter Mode; when encryption with integrity and origin authentication is needed, GCM shall be used with a 128-bit MAC. (PDF p. 17)
  • HMAC (FIPS 198-1) with SHA (FIPS 180-4), normally SHA-256; SHA-224, SHA-384, SHA-512 or RIPEMD-160 may be used by prior agreement, and SHA-1 shall not be used. (PDF p. 18)
  • HMAC output should not be truncated; any truncation must be agreed a priori by the communicating entities. (PDF p. 19)
  • A cipher-based MAC shall be CMAC with AES (256-bit key for new missions; 128, 192 or 256 bits for existing ones); GMAC may replace CMAC when an authenticated-encryption implementation is used for authentication only. (PDF p. 19)
  • Digital signatures shall follow DSS (FIPS 186-3), preferably RSA (PKCS #1 v2.1) with 4096-bit keys for new missions and 2048-bit for existing ones; DSA and ECDSA are also allowed. (PDF p. 19)
  • Spacecraft without access to a key server can carry a pre-loaded public key cache or receive public keys by upload after launch. (PDF p. 20)
  • If on-board security services fail and there is no bypass mode, communications may be lost entirely. (PDF p. 22)
  • All referenced algorithms are in the public domain, and no patents are known to apply; no SANA action is required. (PDF p. 23)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The CCSDS Recommended Standard for the Space Data Link Security (SDLS) Protocol, an optional security sublayer inside the Data Link Layer that adds authentication, encryption or authenticated encryption to the frames of the TM, TC, AOS and (new in issue 2) USLP Space Data Link Protocols. It does not apply to Proximity-1, and it does not mandate any cryptographic algorithm: CCSDS 352.0 lists the recommended ones.

Section 2 explains the concept. A Security Association (SA) is a one-way, stateful cryptographic session bound to one or more Global Virtual Channels (GVCIDs) or, for TC and USLP, GMAP_IDs. Authentication uses a MAC over a masked part of the frame, with anti-replay sequence numbers checked against a window. Section 3 defines two abstract functions. ApplySecurity runs at the sending end. ProcessSecurity runs at the receiving end and returns a verification status code: invalid SPI, MAC failure, anti-replay failure or padding error. The section also lists the parameters of the SA database. Section 4 specifies the PDUs. The Security Header carries a 16-bit Security Parameter Index (SPI), followed by an optional Initialization Vector, Sequence Number and Pad Length, up to 64 octets in all. The Security Trailer carries the MAC. Section 4 also gives the SA management, sending and receiving procedures. Section 5 shows where the header and trailer sit in each frame type, and Table 5-1 says which data link services are protected. Section 6 (Table 6-1) lists the managed parameters, for example SPI 1-65534, IV 1-32 octets and MAC 8-64 octets. Annex A is the PICS proforma, Annex B covers security considerations (no key management, COP directives and the CLCW are unprotected) and Annex E gives baseline modes: AES-GCM for TM, AOS and USLP, and AES-CMAC for TC.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Issue 2 (July 2022) adds USLP support and a normative reference to the SDLS Extended Procedures (CCSDS 355.1-B-1); issue 1 (September 2015) is superseded. (PDF p. 7)
  • The Security Protocol works only at the Data Link Layer (OSI layer 2), with the TM, TC, AOS and USLP Space Data Link Protocols. It is not applicable to Proximity-1. (PDF p. 14)
  • The standard mandates no cryptographic algorithm; CCSDS 352.0-B-2 lists the recommended algorithms, and Annex E gives non-normative baseline implementations. (PDF p. 10)
  • The Security Header is a mandatory 16-bit Security Parameter Index (SPI), followed by an optional Initialization Vector, Sequence Number and Pad Length (each fixed-length for the life of the SA). The whole header is at most 64 octets. (PDF p. 35)
  • SPI values 0 (all zeros) and 65535 (all ones) are reserved by CCSDS; the managed-parameter range is 1-65534. (PDF p. 35)
  • The Security Trailer, when present, holds only a fixed-length MAC; it is present whenever authentication or authenticated encryption is applied. (PDF p. 37)
  • Every SA specifies exactly one service type: authentication, encryption, or authenticated encryption. A 'clear mode' SA with a no-op algorithm is possible for testing but not recommended in operations. (PDF p. 39)
  • At the sending end, only one SA at a time can be active on a given GVCID or GMAP_ID. SAs are not created for Virtual Channels that carry Only Idle Data frames. (PDF p. 38)
  • ProcessSecurity must at least distinguish these failure codes: no failure, invalid SPI, MAC verification failure, anti-replay sequence number failure, and padding error. (PDF p. 30)
  • In a TM frame only the Frame Data is encrypted. The MAC covers the Primary Header, Secondary Header, Security Header and Frame Data, but not the ASM, OCF or ECF. (PDF p. 47)
  • For TC, each SA must be associated with exactly one VC. The COP Management, VCF and MCF services are not protected. (PDF p. 47)
  • Table 5-1 shows that the TM VC_FSH can be authenticated but not encrypted, and that the OCF-based services (VC_OCF, MC_OCF) are never protected. (PDF p. 50)
  • Managed transmitted lengths: IV 1-32 octets, Sequence Number 2-8 octets, Pad Length 1-2 octets, MAC 8-64 octets. Authentication algorithms are HMAC, CMAC, GMAC, GCM or agency-specific; encryption algorithms are AES/Counter Mode, GCM or agency-specific. (PDF p. 52)
  • The protocol gives no protection against jamming, traffic-flow analysis or false COP directives/CLCW contents, and it provides no key management. (PDF p. 64)
  • The TM baseline is AES-GCM authenticated encryption with a 256-bit key, a 96-bit IV sent in-line and a 128-bit MAC, giving a 14-octet Security Header and a 16-octet Security Trailer. (PDF p. 70)
  • The TC baseline is AES-CMAC authentication with a 256-bit key, a 32-bit anti-replay sequence number and a 128-bit MAC, giving a 6-octet Security Header and a 16-octet Security Trailer. (PDF p. 71)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The CCSDS Recommended Standard for the auxiliary procedures needed to operate SDLS over a space link. The SDLS Blue Book defines how frames are protected; this one defines how keys and Security Associations (SAs) are managed and how the on-board security function is monitored. The model is an Initiator, usually the mission operations centre, commanding a Recipient, usually the spacecraft.

Section 2 outlines three services:

  • Key Management: a two-tier symmetric scheme of master keys and session keys, a key lifecycle from pre-activation through active and deactivated to destroyed, and Over-The-Air Rekeying (OTAR), which is recommended but optional for missions with pre-loaded keys.
  • SA Management: a state model Null, Unkeyed, Keyed and Operational, with Create, Rekey, Start, Stop, Expire and Delete transitions, plus setting and reading the anti-replay sequence number (ARSN) and its window.
  • Monitoring and Control: Ping, security log status, dump and erase, Self-Test and Alarm Flag Reset.

Section 3 defines each procedure. Section 4 covers interfaces. EP PDUs travel as packets on a dedicated TC MAP, a TM or AOS VC packet service or a USLP MAP, and they must be protected by SDLS authentication or authenticated encryption. Section 4 also defines the 32-bit Frame Security Report (FSR), a new Type-2 OCF carried in TM, AOS or USLP frames and alternated with the CLCW. Section 5 gives the PDU formats: a TLV-based EP PDU with an 8-bit tag (command or reply, CCSDS or user, service group, procedure ID) and a 16-bit length. Sections 6 and 7 cover managed parameters and conformance. Annex D gives a baseline implementation: AES-GCM with 256-bit keys, 96-bit IV and 128-bit MAC for OTAR and key verification, at most 28 keys per OTAR command so that it fits a 1024-octet frame, and the reserved SPIs 0 and 65535 for EP traffic.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The standard defines the Key Management, SA Management and SDLS Monitoring and Control services, their data structures and their interfaces with the SDL and SDLS protocols; it does not mandate cryptographic algorithms for key generation and management. (PDF p. 11)
  • A goal is a new telemetry OCF type, the Frame Security Report, fully compatible with TM, AOS and USLP. (PDF p. 12)
  • Initiator (usually the MOC) and Recipient (usually the spacecraft) are the two peers; the ARSN starts at zero when an SA is activated and increments for every frame sent on it. (PDF p. 13)
  • Key management is a two-tier symmetric infrastructure: master keys (key-encryption keys) for management and session keys (traffic keys) for SDLS operations, refreshed by OTAR; OTAR is recommended but not required if a mission flies with pre-loaded keys only. (PDF p. 17)
  • Key lifecycle states are Pre-Activation, Active, Deactivated and Destroyed, with Key Activation, Deactivation, Destruction and Verification transitions; the Suspended state of the Symmetric Key Management practice is not used. (PDF p. 17)
  • SA state model: Null -(Create SA)-> Unkeyed -(Rekey SA)-> Keyed -(Start SA)-> Operational, reversed by Stop SA, Expire SA and Delete SA; static missions need only Start and Stop with pre-loaded SAs. (PDF p. 18)
  • Because an OCF can hold only one control word, the FSR is multiplexed with the CLCW in a mission-specific pattern. (PDF p. 19)
  • EP PDUs use a dedicated MAP of the TC MAP packet service, the TM or AOS VC packet service, or the USLP MAP packet service. (PDF p. 63)
  • The 32-bit FSR holds Control Word Type '1' (1 bit; a CLCW is '0'), FSR Version Number '100' (3 bits), Alarm flag (1), Bad SN, Bad MAC and Bad SA flags (1 bit each), Last SPI (16) and the 8 LSBs of the ARSN (8), and it is sampled for each received SDLS-protected frame. (PDF p. 64)
  • The FSR Alarm Flag latches at '1' once any frame has been rejected by the Recipient Security Function and stays set until reset by a dedicated command; the other flags reflect only the last frame. (PDF p. 65)
  • All EP command PDUs must be sent over an SDLS channel protected by authentication or authenticated encryption; the reserved SPIs 0 and 65535 may be used for EP traffic, and using a different SA from the one being affected is good practice. (PDF p. 67)
  • EP commands and replies use a TLV format: an 8-bit Tag (Procedure Type, User Flag, 2-bit Service Group, 4-bit Procedure ID) and a 16-bit Data Field Length in bits. (PDF p. 69)
  • Service Group values: 00 Key Management, 01 SA Management for Initiator-to-Recipient SAs, 10 SA Management for Recipient-to-Initiator SAs, 11 Security Monitoring and Control; Table 5-1 assigns procedure IDs (for example OTAR 0001, Start SA 1011, Ping 0001). (PDF p. 71)
  • SA management managed parameters include SPI 1-65534, service type, Security Header IV (1-32 octets), SN (2-8 octets), PL (1-2 octets) and Trailer MAC (8-64 octets) lengths, the authentication bit mask, ARSN and ARSN window. (PDF p. 102)
  • Baseline mode: FSR as OCF Type 2 alternating with the CLCW when COP-1 reports on the same VC, no TLV nesting, and the two reserved SPIs for EP PDUs. (PDF p. 120)
  • Baseline OTAR and Key Verification use AES-GCM with 256-bit keys, a 96-bit IV and a 128-bit MAC; Key Destruction and Key Inventory are not in the baseline. (PDF p. 121)
  • A baseline OTAR command carries a 16-bit master key ID, a 96-bit IV, N encrypted key blocks of 272 bits (16-bit key ID plus 256-bit key) and a 128-bit MAC, with N <= 28 so that the PDU (at most 995 octets) fits a 1024-octet frame. (PDF p. 122)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The CCSDS Physical Layer book: a loose-leaf collection of individual recommendations, in the CCIR 'considering / recommends' style, for the RF and modulation systems of Earth stations and spacecraft. It is the basis of the radio frequency, modulation and ranging page and sits below the TM and TC coding standards, which cite it normatively. Part 1 covers conventional near-Earth and deep-space missions; a Part 2 for data relay satellites is foreseen. Each recommendation is tagged Category A (missions closer than 2 million km) or Category B (deep space), or applies to both when it has no suffix.

Section 2 (technical) covers six areas:

  • Earth-to-space RF: phase modulation on a residual carrier, sweep ranges and rates, multiple uplink carriers;
  • telecommand: 8 or 16 kHz PSK sine-wave subcarriers with NRZ-L/M, low rates of 4000/2^n symbol/s, medium-rate PCM/PM/bi-phase-L, and BPSK up to 2.048 Msymbol/s;
  • space-to-Earth RF;
  • telemetry: PCM formats, symbol transition density, QPSK conventions, modulator imbalances, spurious emissions, and the high-rate bandwidth-efficient modulations (GMSK, filtered OQPSK, SRRC-8PSK, 4D-8PSK TCM, APSK) for the 2, 8, 26 and 32 GHz bands;
  • radio metric: group delay calibration and stability, PN ranging, telemetry ranging, Delta-DOR;
  • spacecraft: transponder turnaround ratios such as 221/240 and 749/880, plus new ratios for multiple spacecraft per aperture and lunar inter-satellite links.

Section 3 (policy) covers frequency utilisation (including the Category B channel plan and multiple spacecraft per aperture), uplink power limits, ranging waveforms, charged-particle calibration, the spacecraft and Earth station compatibility tests, and interference. Section 4 (procedural) gives the link Design Control Table with its statistics and the occupied-bandwidth algorithms, and section 5 the terminology and glossary.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Issue 32 updates recommendations 2.4.18 and 2.4.23 and adds 2.6.13 and 2.6.15. (PDF p. 11)
  • Part 1 targets conventional near-Earth and deep-space missions with moderate communications requirements; Part 2 is to cover data relay satellites. (PDF p. 5)
  • Newer recommendations follow the nomenclature of the CCSDS Publications Manual (A20.0-Y-4); older ones keep the conventions of the original Blue Book. (PDF p. 13)
  • Recommendations are grouped as technical (section 2), policy (section 3) and procedural (section 4); a page label such as 2.5.3A-1 encodes section, subsection, position, mission category and page. (PDF p. 26)
  • Category A missions are at an altitude below 2.0 x 10^6 km and Category B missions at or beyond it, matching the Deep Space boundary set by WARC ORB-88 and effective on 16 March 1990; a recommendation without an A or B suffix applies to both. (PDF p. 27)
  • Agencies shall support phase modulation with a residual carrier on Earth-to-space links. (PDF p. 36)
  • Telecommand subcarriers are PSK-modulated sine waves of 8 kHz or 16 kHz. (PDF p. 49)
  • Telecommand data use NRZ-L or NRZ-M on PSK subcarriers, with attention to the symbol transition density. (PDF p. 50)
  • Low-rate telecommand coded symbol rates are 4000/2^n symbol/s (n = 0 to 9), with symbol and subcarrier transitions coinciding; 4000 symbol/s only with the 16 kHz subcarrier. (PDF p. 51)
  • Medium-rate telecommand uses PCM/PM/bi-phase-L directly on the carrier at 4000 x 2^n coded symbol/s (n = 1 to 6). (PDF p. 54)
  • When a residual-carrier system is insufficient, telecommand uses BPSK up to 2.048 coded Msymbol/s at 1000 x 2^n coded symbol/s (n = 0 to 11). (PDF p. 55)
  • Space-to-Earth links: at most 64 consecutive identical coded symbols; at least 125 (Category A) or 275 (Category B) transitions per 1000 coded symbols; pseudo-randomizer use as in the TM Synchronization and Channel Coding standard. (PDF p. 76)
  • Above 2 coded Msymbol/s, Category A space research downlinks use GMSK (BTs = 0.25, precoded), baseband-filtered OQPSK or SRRC-8PSK to meet the SFCG spectrum mask; SFCG limits the 8450-8500 MHz band to 10 MHz per mission. (PDF p. 99)
  • EES 8 GHz high-rate downlinks use SRRC-filtered 4D-8PSK TCM, QPSK, OQPSK, 8PSK, 16/32/64APSK or filtered OQPSK to meet the SFCG mask and protect the adjacent deep-space band above 8400 MHz. (PDF p. 110)
  • Telemetry ranging records the uplink PN range-code phase and the frame counter of a TM or AOS frame on board; it can reach 1 m standard deviation at 200 ksymbol/s or more and costs up to 4 percent of telemetry throughput. (PDF p. 165)
  • The transponder turnaround frequency ratio for the 2025-2120/2200-2300 MHz bands is 221/240, needed only for missions requiring cross support and coherent two-way links. (PDF p. 184)
  • The 7145-7235/8400-8500 MHz ratio is 749/880. (PDF p. 185)
  • New in issue 32: flexible turnaround ratios with '749' in the numerator for multiple spacecraft per aperture in the ⅞ GHz bands (2.6.13). (PDF p. 199)
  • New in issue 32: 2407/2800 and 2407/2816 ratios for coherent 23.15-23.55 GHz forward and 27.0-27.5 GHz return inter-satellite links, for example lunar orbit-surface proximity links (2.6.15). (PDF p. 202)
  • Category B missions in the 2, 7, 8, 32 and 34 GHz bands select frequencies from the channel frequency plan of table 3.1.6B-1, coordinated through an organisation such as the SFCG. (PDF p. 219)
  • All relevant spacecraft-Earth station compatibility tests of table 3.5.1-1 shall be performed before cross support. (PDF p. 236)
  • The uniform link Design Control Table is used to exchange link budgets between agencies, with 3-sigma tolerances for telecommand and 2-sigma for all other systems. (PDF p. 249)
  • Uncertain link parameters are modelled with uniform, triangular or truncated Gaussian probability density functions, with default assignments per budget line. (PDF p. 282)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The CCSDS Recommended Standard that adopts the Object Management Group's XML Telemetric and Command Exchange (XTCE) specification, version 1.2 (OMG formal/18-10-04, January 2019) as the CCSDS exchange format for telemetry and telecommand definitions. The CCSDS wrapper adds only front matter (authority, statement of intent, document control) to the OMG text. The normative content is the XML schema SpaceSystem.xsd, which OMG publishes as a machine-readable file and which is not printed here. See XTCE.

XTCE is a metadata format. It describes how telemetry and commands are structured, encoded, calibrated, constrained and verified, so that a spacecraft manufacturer, a test facility, a simulator and a control centre can exchange a TM/TC database without writing custom import/export tools. The specification avoids both packet and TDM nomenclature. It does not cover live data transfer, displays, protocols or flight software. The root object is the hierarchical SpaceSystem. It contains an optional Header, nested sub-SpaceSystems, TelemetryMetaData (ParameterTypeSet, ParameterSet, ContainerSet, MessageSet, StreamSet, AlgorithmSet) and CommandMetaData (which adds ArgumentTypeSet and MetaCommandSet). The document explains the four data encodings (integer, float, string, binary) and container inheritance, where a BaseContainer with RestrictionCriteria identifies a packet subtype. For commands it describes transmission constraints, significance levels, alarm suspension, interlocks and the eight verifier stages. The bibliography cites the SCOS-2000 Database Import ICD and the ESA PUS, so XTCE is the natural counterpart of the SCOS-2000 MIB.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• 660.0-B-2 (February 2020) is the current issue; 660.0-B-1 (October 2007) is superseded. (PDF p. 7)
  • The CCSDS book embeds the OMG publication XML Telemetric and Command Exchange Version 1.2, OMG Document Number formal/18-10-04, released January 2019. Its normative machine-consumable file is https://www.omg.org/spec/XTCE/20180204/SpaceSystem.xsd. (PDF p. 9)
  • Copyright holders of the specification text: Boeing Satellite Systems, the European Space Operations Centre, Lockheed Martin – Integrated Systems & Solutions (all 2018), and the Object Management Group (2014-2018). (PDF p. 10)
  • XTCE deliberately avoids both packet and TDM terminology ('minor frame', 'major frame', 'packet' appear only in examples) and does not itself use CCSDS or IRIG-106 formats, though such containers can be modelled with it. (PDF p. 16)
  • Out of scope: data distribution, command and data protocols, RF characterisation, data grouping, visualisation, scheduling, orbital properties, displays and flight software. XTCE is a metadata specification, not a specification for transferring live or historical TM/TC data. (PDF p. 19)
  • Conformance: the schema (.xsd) in Annex A is normative, and a compliant database is an XML file that validates against it. (PDF p. 19)
  • Names may contain only digits, a-z letters, underscores, hyphens or backslashes and are case sensitive. '/', '.', '[', ']' and ':' are reserved; '/' separates SpaceSystems in a hierarchical path. (PDF p. 23)
  • There are four parameter encodings. IntegerDataEncoding: unsigned, signMagnitude, twosCompliment, onesCompliment, BCD, packedBCD. FloatDataEncoding: IEEE754_1985 or MILSTD_1750A. StringEncoding: UTF-8 or UTF-16, fixed or terminated/size-prefixed. BinaryDataEncoding. (PDF p. 25)
  • SequenceContainers may inherit from a BaseContainer, and RestrictionCriteria (a MatchCriteria) distinguish a subtype. This is how XTCE identifies packets, for example 'minor frame counter equals 20'. (PDF p. 27)
  • MetaCommands carry an ArgumentList, CommandContainer, TransmissionConstraintList, significance (none, watch, warning, distress, critical, severe), ParametersToSuspendAlarmsOn, Interlock, Verifiers and ParameterToSetList. (PDF p. 32)
  • There are eight command verifier stages: TransferredToRange, TransferredFromRange, Received, Accepted, Queued, Execution, Complete and Failed. A command may have several 'Complete' verifiers. (PDF p. 33)
  • The bibliography lists the SCOS-2000 Database Import ICD Issue 5.0 (S2K-MCS-ICD-0001-TOS-GCI) and the SCOS-2000 Synthetic Parameters SUM as inputs to XTCE. (PDF p. 39)
