docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A 270-page CCSDS Green Book that explains, element by element, how to use the XTCE 1.2 XML schema adopted by CCSDS 660.0-B-2. It expands the terse annotations of the OMG schema without contradicting them, and it is the companion of the high-level introduction CCSDS 660.2-G-2. The page XTCE uses it.

Section 2 describes what an XTCE mission database holds: parameters and their ParameterTypes (link encoding, alarms, calibration), containers built by inheritance, and commands with arguments. It also lists the changes from XTCE 1.1 to 1.2, such as local array dimension sizes, byte-order options, a new numeric alarm, XInclude and time association in container entries. Section 3 covers the core mechanics: NameReference path rules, NameDescriptionType, comparisons, BooleanExpression, MatchCriteria, ParameterInstanceRef and size-related elements. Section 4 is the reference body. It goes through SpaceSystem and Header, then the ten ParameterTypes (string, enumerated, binary, boolean, integer, float, absolute/relative time, array, aggregate) with their encodings, calibrators and alarms, with recommended encoding tables for IEEE754 and MIL-STD-1750A. It then covers ParameterSet, SequenceContainer EntryList and BaseContainer inheritance, Message/Stream/Algorithm sets, MetaCommand (arguments, CommandContainer, constraints, verifiers) and ServiceSet. Sections 5-7 give advanced topics and patterns: abstract and concrete containers, dynamic matching, MetaCommand inheritance, pseudo-parameters, and packet and command patterns with optional secondary headers. Section 8 is a JAXB data-binding case study, and section 9 and Annex A give a complete telemetry and command example. For SCOS-2000 users, the closest equivalents are the MIB data model and its packet identification.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Issue 2 (August 2021) is current and supersedes 660.1-G-1 (May 2012). It updates the report from XTCE 1.1 to XTCE 1.2 and accompanies the introduction CCSDS 660.2-G-2. (PDF p. 6)
  • XTCE 1.0 was published in 2006 and XTCE 1.1 later in 2006, after a CCSDS review; XTCE 1.2 followed in 2019. (PDF p. 19)
  • In XTCE 1.2, array dimensions and their sizes are declared in the ArrayParameterType. In 1.1, only the number of dimensions was declared there, and the sizes were given where the array was used in a container. (PDF p. 19)
  • Other changes in 1.2 include new byte-order options, integer exponents, a revised string length specification, a new numeric alarm, an inside/outside alarm flag, XInclude support, and time association moved to the container entry. (PDF p. 19)
  • The top-level structure is SpaceSystem, containing TelemetryMetaData, CommandMetaData and optional recursive child SpaceSystems. (PDF p. 21)
  • A NameReference without a path looks in the local SpaceSystem first and then in each ancestor SpaceSystem. A qualified NameReference uses a Unix-like SpaceSystem path. (PDF p. 22)
  • There are ten ParameterTypes: the scalar String, Enumerated, Binary, Boolean, Integer, Float and time types, and the complex Array and Aggregate ('struct') types. (PDF p. 109)
  • Members of an aggregate are referenced as 'AggregateName.MemberName'. (PDF p. 154)
  • FloatDataEncoding supports the IEEE754_1985 and MILSTD_1750A formats. The recommendation tables show how to encode 32-, 64- and 128-bit values. (PDF p. 157)
  • The basic telemetry pattern is one abstract 'Generic Packet' header container with every specific packet derived from it through RestrictionCriteria. An optional secondary header can be added through a container entry reference (printed 'ContainerEntryRef') with an IncludeCondition. (PDF p. 259)
  • There are three command patterns. In the simple one, the MetaCommand's CommandContainer uses FixedValueEntry for opcodes. In the complex one, an abstract mission command template is specialised. In the generic one, there is an extra level of template inheritance. (PDF p. 262)
  • Annex B gives corrected schema keys that enforce XTCE 1.2's @name uniqueness policy. Many of the XTCE 1.1 keys were broken. (PDF p. 284)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A short (42-page) CCSDS Green Book that introduces the XML Telemetric and Command Exchange (XTCE) format at a high level. It is the entry point of the three CCSDS XTCE books: the Blue Book CCSDS 660.0-B-2 adopts the OMG schema, and the Element Description Green Book CCSDS 660.1-G-2 explains each element in detail. The wiki page is XTCE.

Section 2 explains why a non-proprietary telemetry and telecommand database format is useful (exchange between spacecraft and instrument manufacturers, simulators, control, planning and trending systems), gives the version history (XTCE 1.0 in 2006, 1.1 in 2008, 1.2 in 2019) and lists the main changes in 1.2. It also covers the GovSat/XUSP conformance profile for users who find XTCE too large, and six ways to handle features XTCE lacks, from AncillaryData name/value pairs to OMG change requests. Section 3 walks through the schema: the SpaceSystem hierarchy and Header; TelemetryMetaData with its ten ParameterTypes, four DataEncodings, calibrators, ParameterSet, SequenceContainer inheritance, MessageSet, StreamSet and AlgorithmSet; CommandMetaData with ArgumentTypes, MetaCommand inheritance, CommandContainer, transmission constraints, significance, interlocks and the eight verifier stages; and ServiceSet, which was added for European PUS-style services. Section 4 shows XTCE as the exchange format between subsystem suppliers, the spacecraft Source Database and the operational databases. Annex A is a small GovSat example with a CCSDS packet header, one telemetry packet and one command. For SCOS-2000 readers, the counterpart is the MIB data model.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• XTCE 1.0 was published in 2006, XTCE 1.1 in 2008 after a CCSDS review, and XTCE 1.2 in 2019. The OMG manages the associated schema. This report pertains to all versions but specifically to 1.2. (PDF p. 10)
  • XTCE 1.2 is largely backwards compatible with 1.1. The biggest syntax change is that array dimension sizes can be defined in the ArrayParameterType itself. Other changes include a new SpaceSystem namespace, normalised enumeration strings, changed byte order, integer exponents and updated float encoding sizes. (PDF p. 10)
  • XTCE is not tied to a particular telemetry format such as CCSDS Space Packets or major/minor frames. (PDF p. 11)
  • Several SpaceSystems can be defined in separate files and combined with XInclude, for example one database per instrument plus one for the spacecraft bus. (PDF p. 13)
  • GovSat, published by the OMG as the XTCE US Govt Satellite Conformance Profile (XUSP), is not a new schema but a set of executable rules that restrict XTCE, for example to a single SpaceSystem. (PDF p. 14)
  • For missing features the report lists six options, from AncillaryData name/value pairs (the easiest, and schema-compatible) to local schema changes, external schemas, overloading elements (least preferred) and OMG change requests. (PDF p. 15)
  • XTCE defines ten ParameterTypes: Integer, Float, Enumerated, String, Boolean, Binary, RelativeTime, AbsoluteTime, Array and Aggregate. A ParameterType without a DataEncoding describes a ground-side value, and its Parameter should set dataSource to 'local'. (PDF p. 20)
  • All ParameterTypes except Array and Aggregate use one of four DataEncodings: Integer, Float, String or Binary. The numeric encodings support spline, polynomial and MathOperation calibrators. (PDF p. 21)
  • It is common practice for each Parameter to have its own ParameterType, so that changing alarms or calibrators in a shared type cannot propagate by mistake. (PDF p. 22)
  • Container inheritance is the preferred way to define packets. The report recommends defining packets, not framing information, in XTCE. (PDF p. 22)
  • MessageSet ('has a' construction) is kept only for backwards compatibility and may be considered deprecated. StreamSet is seen by many as too simple for front-end configuration. (PDF p. 23)
  • Derived or pseudo parameters are typically Parameters without a DataEncoding, with dataSource set to 'derived' and an algorithm in AlgorithmSet that names them in its OutputSet. (PDF p. 25)
  • Command Arguments are local to a MetaCommand and cannot be reused, but MetaCommands can inherit through BaseMetaCommand. ArgumentTypes have no alarm definitions. (PDF p. 14)
  • Significance levels are none, watch, warning, distress, critical and severe. There are eight verifier stages: Transferred to range, Transferred from range, Received, Accepted, Queued, Execution, Complete and Failed. (PDF p. 29)
  • ServiceSet was introduced for European organisations that use services as in the ECSS Packet Utilization Standard (ECSS-E-ST-70-41C). (PDF p. 30)
  • XTCE is meant for exchanging database information, not as the direct interface for sending commands or receiving telemetry. (PDF p. 31)
  • The Annex A example defines an abstract CCSDSPacket container with the seven primary header fields (3-bit version, 1-bit type, 1-bit secondary header flag, 11-bit APID, 2-bit flags, 14-bit count, 16-bit length) and a status packet restricted to APID 47. (PDF p. 38)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The CCSDS Recommended Standard for the CCSDS File Delivery Protocol (CFDP). CFDP transfers files between filestores on spacecraft and on the ground, and between spacecraft. It runs over any packet delivery service, which the standard abstracts as the Unitdata Transfer (UT) layer. That layer can be CCSDS TC and TM packet services, AOS, Space Packets, Encapsulation packets, the Bundle Protocol or ground networks. CFDP is described on the wiki page CFDP. For on-board file handling in PUS, see also ST[23] File management; this standard itself does not mention PUS.

Issue 5 restructures the protocol. It removes the Extended Procedures and the service classes 3 and 4. It moves Store and Forward Overlay operations to normative Annex B. It adds large files (64-bit offsets), multi-segment records with per-segment metadata, and a choice of checksum algorithm from a SANA registry. Section 2 gives the architecture: entities, users, transactions, the virtual filestore and the Copy, Put and Proxy-Put interaction sequences. Section 3 defines the service primitives, such as Put.request and the indications. Section 4 specifies the procedures: the optional PDU CRC (the TC CRC), the 32-bit file checksum (modular, null or registry algorithms), Copy File procedures with NAKs, positive acknowledgement, fault handling, filestore actions, inactivity monitoring and link-state changes. Section 5 gives the bit-exact PDU formats: the fixed header, the file directive PDUs (EOF, Finished, ACK, Metadata, NAK, Prompt, Keep Alive), File Data PDUs and the TLV parameters. Section 6 defines user operations carried in reserved messages: proxy, directory listing, remote status report, suspend and resume. Section 7 defines Class 1 (unreliable) and Class 2 (reliable) transfer. Section 8 lists the CFDP Management Information Base, which is not the SCOS-2000 MIB. Annex A is the PICS and Annex F works a modular checksum example.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Issue 5 (July 2020) moves Store and Forward Overlay to normative Annex B, removes the Extended Procedures, adds large files, multi-segment records and per-segment metadata, and adds a choice of checksum from a new SANA registry. EC 1 (September 2024) fixes the heading numbering under 7.2.3. (PDF p. 7)
  • CFDP is intended for CCSDS packet telecommand, packet telemetry and the AOS Path service, and also for ground networks. It works space-to-ground, ground-to-space and space-to-space. Service classes 3 and 4 have been deleted together with the Extended Procedures. (PDF p. 12)
  • The fixed PDU header has these fields: Version (3 bits, '001' for the second protocol version), PDU type (directive/data), Direction, Transmission Mode (acknowledged/unacknowledged), CRC flag, Large File flag, PDU Data field length (16 bits), Segmentation control, Length of entity IDs (3 bits, octets minus one), Segment metadata flag, Length of Transaction sequence number (3 bits), then the variable-length source entity ID, transaction sequence number and destination entity ID. (PDF p. 75)
  • A transaction is uniquely identified by the source entity ID together with the transaction sequence number. (PDF p. 75)
  • File-Size Sensitive (FSS) fields, such as offsets and file size, are 32 bits when the Large File flag is 0 and 64 bits when it is 1. Files whose size cannot be held in an unsigned 32-bit integer, and all files of unbounded size, must be flagged 'large'. (PDF p. 77)
  • Directive codes (hex): 04 EOF, 05 Finished, 06 ACK, 07 Metadata, 08 NAK, 09 Prompt, 0C Keep Alive; 00-03 and 0D-FF are reserved. (PDF p. 78)
  • The 4-bit condition codes include 0000 No error, 0001 Positive ACK limit reached, 0101 File checksum failure, 0111 NAK limit reached, 1000 Inactivity detected, 1011 Unsupported checksum type, 1110 Suspend.request received and 1111 Cancel.request received. (PDF p. 79)
  • The optional PDU CRC uses the standard CCSDS Telecommand CRC algorithm of the TC Space Data Link Protocol and covers the PDU from the first header octet up to the CRC. (PDF p. 49)
  • Every file carries a 32-bit checksum. The modular checksum (type 0) and the null checksum (type 15) are mandatory; types 1-14 from the SANA Checksum Identifiers registry are optional. If the preferred type is unsupported, an Unsupported Checksum Type fault is raised. (PDF p. 50)
  • There are two service classes: Class 1, Unreliable Transfer, and Class 2, Reliable Transfer. The state tables are in the CFDP Implementers Guide (720.2-G). (PDF p. 108)
  • The CFDP MIB holds the local entity configuration (entity ID, which indications are required, default fault handlers) and, per remote entity, items such as the UT address, ACK/NAK/keep-alive timers, the default transmission mode, the check limit, the default checksum type, the maximum file segment length and the inactivity limit. (PDF p. 116)
  • CFDP has no security mechanisms of its own; the UT-layer stack must provide them. The initial SANA checksum registry has 0 Modular, 1 Proximity-1 CRC32, 2 CRC-32c, 3 IEEE 802.3 FCS and 15 NULL. (PDF p. 145)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The CCSDS Recommended Standard for the Advanced Orbiting Systems (AOS) Space Data Link Protocol. AOS is a Data Link Layer protocol with fixed-length frames that carries packets, bitstreams and other data over space-to-ground, ground-to-space and space-to-space links, mostly for high-rate return links. It sits beside the TM and TC protocols and below the Space Packet and Encapsulation protocols. Frame length and synchronisation come from the TM Synchronization and Channel Coding sublayer (or FACM or DVB-S2). The wiki page is AOS.

Section 2 gives an overview of the protocol: Physical, Master and Virtual Channels, the services and the functions. Section 3 defines the seven services: Virtual Channel Packet (VCP), Bitstream, Virtual Channel Access (VCA), VC Operational Control Field (VC_OCF), Virtual Channel Frame (VCF), Master Channel Frame (MCF) and Insert. Section 4 specifies the AOS Version 2 Transfer Frame. Its 6- or 8-octet Primary Header carries a 2-bit Version '01', an 8-bit SCID, a 6-bit VCID, a 24-bit VC Frame Count, a Signaling Field (Replay Flag, VC Frame Count Cycle) and an optional RS(10,6) Frame Header Error Control. The frame also has an optional Insert Zone, a Data Field holding an M_PDU (11-bit First Header Pointer), a B_PDU (14-bit Bitstream Data Pointer) or a VCA_SDU, an optional 4-octet OCF and an optional 2-octet FECF. Section 4 then gives the sending and receiving procedures (multiplexing, idle data, OID frames on VCID 63). Section 5 tabulates the managed parameters, and section 6 restates the frame, procedures and parameters with the SDLS Security Header and Trailer.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The protocol provides seven services: Virtual Channel Packet, Bitstream, Virtual Channel Access, VC_OCF, Virtual Channel Frame, Master Channel Frame and Insert. (PDF p. 22)
  • Issue 4 (October 2021) is current. It adds support for the SDLS Extended Procedures, a PICS proforma (Annex A) and OID frame randomization examples (Annex D). Issues B-1 (2003), B-2 (2006) and B-3 (2015) are superseded. (PDF p. 7)
  • An AOS Transfer Frame consists of a Primary Header (6 or 8 octets), an optional Insert Zone, the Data Field, an optional 4-octet Operational Control Field and an optional 2-octet Frame Error Control Field. Its length is constant for a mission phase on a Physical Channel. (PDF p. 56)
  • The Primary Header holds the Master Channel ID (2-bit Transfer Frame Version Number plus 8-bit Spacecraft ID), a 6-bit VCID, a 24-bit VC Frame Count, an 8-bit Signaling Field and an optional 2-octet Frame Header Error Control. (PDF p. 57)
  • The Transfer Frame Version Number is '01', which denotes the AOS Version 2 Transfer Frame. SANA assigns the 8-bit Spacecraft ID according to CCSDS 320.0-M. (PDF p. 58)
  • VCID 'all ones' (63) is reserved for Only Idle Data (OID) Transfer Frames. The valid user VCIDs are 0-62 and need not be consecutive. (PDF p. 58)
  • The VC Frame Count is a 24-bit sequential count, modulo 16,777,216, of frames on each Virtual Channel. It must not be reset early unless that is unavoidable. (PDF p. 59)
  • In the Signaling Field, the Replay Flag (bit 40) is 0 for realtime and 1 for replay frames. The VC Frame Count Cycle Use Flag and the 4-bit VC Frame Count Cycle extend the frame count. (PDF p. 60)
  • The optional Frame Header Error Control (bits 48-63) is a shortened Reed-Solomon (10,6) code with 4-bit symbols and E=2 symbol-correction capability that can protect the 10-bit MCID, the 6-bit VCID and the 8-bit Signaling Field. (PDF p. 62)
  • M_PDU header: bits 0-4 are a reserved spare and bits 5-15 are the First Header Pointer. 'All ones' means no packet starts in the frame, and 'all ones minus one' means idle data only. (PDF p. 66)
  • B_PDU header: bits 0-1 are a reserved spare and bits 2-15 are the Bitstream Data Pointer. 'All ones' means the frame is full of valid data, and 'all ones minus one' means idle data only. (PDF p. 68)
  • Managed parameters of a Physical Channel include the Transfer Frame Length, Version Number 2, the valid SCIDs, the MC multiplexing scheme, and the presence of FHEC, Insert Zone (with its length) and FECF. (PDF p. 88)
  • The Data Field Content of each Virtual Channel is managed as one of M_PDU, B_PDU, VCA_SDU or Idle Data. The presence of the VC_OCF is also managed per Virtual Channel. (PDF p. 89)
  • With SDLS, a managed parameter per Virtual Channel indicates the presence of the Security Header. The Security Header and Trailer surround the Data Field and shorten it. (PDF p. 91)
  • The OID randomizer LFSR (Fibonacci or Galois form) is initialised only at device start-up, not per frame, and generates the pattern FF FF FF FF 6D B6 D8 61 45 1F ... (PDF p. 112)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Issue 5 (October 2025, with Editorial Change 1) of the CCSDS Recommended Standard for the AOS Space Data Link Protocol. AOS is a Data Link Layer protocol with fixed-length frames for space-to-ground, ground-to-space and space-to-space links. It carries packets, bitstreams and other data. The wiki page is AOS. The structure is the same as issue 4 (CCSDS 732.0-B-4): an overview (Physical, Master and Virtual Channels, addressing by TFVN + SCID + VCID); seven services (Virtual Channel Packet, Bitstream, Virtual Channel Access, VC_OCF, Virtual Channel Frame, Master Channel Frame and Insert); the Transfer Frame and its sending and receiving procedures; managed parameters; the SDLS variant; a PICS proforma; and OID randomizer examples.

An engineer will look here mainly for what changed in issue 5, because the changes break bit-level compatibility with older decoders. The Spacecraft ID grows from 8 to 10 bits. Its two new most significant bits go in bits 42-43 of the Primary Header, which were the reserved spare of the Signaling Field in issue 4, so the MCID becomes 12 bits. The M_PDU header loses its 5-bit spare, and the First Header Pointer becomes a full 16 bits, which allows frames of up to 65,536 octets. The optional Frame Header Error Control moves from RS(10,6) to a shortened RS(15,11) code over GF(2^4), which also protects the SCID MSBs and the VC Frame Count Cycle. The Bitstream Data Pointer stays at 14 bits, so frames carrying B_PDUs are still limited to 16,384 bits. VCID 63 remains reserved for Only Idle Data frames. For identifiers and SANA registries see space link identifiers.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Issue 5 extends the SCID field in the Transfer Frame Primary Header to 10 bits and the First Header Pointer in the M_PDU header to 16 bits, to accommodate frames of up to 65,536 octets. Editorial Change 1 changes the Frame Header Error Control to a Reed-Solomon (15,11) code. (PDF p. 7)
  • The addressing identifiers are TFVN, SCID and VCID: MCID = TFVN + SCID, and GVCID = MCID + VCID. A Physical Channel may carry several Master Channels with the same TFVN. (PDF p. 18)
  • An AOS Transfer Frame consists of a Primary Header (6 or 8 octets), an optional Insert Zone, the Data Field, an optional 4-octet OCF and an optional 2-octet Frame Error Control Field. Its length is constant for a Mission Phase on a Physical Channel. (PDF p. 54)
  • The 12-bit MCID is made of three non-contiguous fields: the 2-bit Transfer Frame Version Number, the 2 SCID MSBs and the 8 SCID LSBs. It occupies bits 0-9 and 42-43 of the Primary Header. (PDF p. 55)
  • Bits 0-1 hold the Transfer Frame Version Number '01' (AOS Version 2 frame). Bits 2-9 hold the 8 SCID LSBs, and bits 42-43 hold the 2 SCID MSBs. Missions using issue 4 or earlier have an 8-bit SCID and set bits 42-43 to '00'. (PDF p. 57)
  • Bits 10-15 hold the VCID. 'All ones' (63) is reserved for Only Idle Data frames, and VCIDs need not be consecutive. (PDF p. 57)
  • The VC Frame Count (bits 16-39) is a 24-bit count modulo 16,777,216 per Virtual Channel. When used, the 4-bit VC Frame Count Cycle (bits 44-47) extends it to 28 bits. (PDF p. 58)
  • The Signaling Field is now 2 bits (bits 40-41): the Replay Flag (0 = realtime, 1 = replay) and the VC Frame Count Cycle Use Flag. (PDF p. 59)
  • The optional Frame Header Error Control (bits 48-63) is a Reed-Solomon (15,11) code over GF(2^4), shortened by 5 symbols to a binary (40,24) code with E=2. It protects the 12-bit MCID, 6-bit VCID, 2-bit Signaling Field and 4-bit VC Frame Count Cycle, but not the VC Frame Count. (PDF p. 60)
  • OID Transfer Frames are filled with a pseudo-noise sequence from a 32-cell LFSR with polynomial D0 + D1 + D2 + D22 + D32. The LFSR is initialised only at device start-up and is never restarted. (PDF p. 64)
  • The M_PDU header is now just the 16-bit First Header Pointer, with no spare bits. 'All ones' means no packet starts in the frame, and 'all ones minus one' means idle data only. (PDF p. 64)
  • The B_PDU header keeps a 2-bit spare and a 14-bit Bitstream Data Pointer, so the frame size with the Bitstream Service is limited to 16,384 bits. (PDF p. 68)
  • The OCF Type Flag (bit 0) is '0' for a Type-1 report (CLCW) and '1' for a Type-2 report. In a Type-2 report, bit 1 = '1' means an SDLS Frame Security Report. (PDF p. 68)
  • The FECF is a CRC with generator X^16 + X^12 + X^5 + 1 and the shift register preset to all ones. (PDF p. 70)
  • Valid user VCIDs are 0-62, with 63 always valid for OID frames. Data Field Content per VC is managed as M_PDU, B_PDU, VCA_SDU or Idle Data. (PDF p. 88)
  • The PICS adds item AOS-47.1 'SCID Length' (4.1.2.2.3) as a mandatory feature. (PDF p. 103)
  • The OID data pattern starts FF FF FF FF 6D B6 D8 61 45 1F 11 F1 97 16 72 3C BE 7E 00 B1 for both the Fibonacci and the Galois LFSR forms. (PDF p. 110)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The CCSDS Recommended Standard for the Unified Space Data Link Protocol (USLP). USLP is a single Data Link Layer protocol for space-to-ground, ground-to-space and space-to-space links. It defines the Version-4 Transfer Frame (TFVN '1100'), and its frames can be fixed or variable length, up to 65,536 octets. It can run over TM, TC or Proximity-1 synchronisation and coding, FACM or DVB-S2. USLP unifies what the TM, TC, AOS and Proximity-1 protocols do separately. The wiki page is USLP.

Section 2 gives an overview of the protocol: Physical Channel, Master Channel (identified by the 20-bit MCID), Virtual Channel and MAP channel, the services and the functions. Section 3 defines ten services: MAP Packet, VC Packet, MAP Access, VC Access, MAP Octet Stream, USLP MC_OCF, VC Frame, MC Frame, Insert and COPs Management. Section 4 specifies the frame. The Primary Header has 13 fields, 4 to 14 octets in all: TFVN, a 16-bit SCID, the Source-or-Destination ID, a 6-bit VCID, a 4-bit MAP ID, the End of Frame Primary Header Flag, a 16-bit Frame Length, the Bypass/Sequence Control and Protocol Control Command flags, the OCF Flag, and a VCF Count of variable length (0-56 bits). It is followed by an optional Insert Zone, the Transfer Frame Data Field (a 1-3 octet header with the TFDZ Construction Rule, the UPID and the First Header/Last Valid Octet Pointer), an optional OCF and an optional CRC-16 FECF. Section 4 also gives the sending and receiving procedures, including COP-1 and COP-P interaction. Section 5 lists the managed parameters per channel and section 6 adds SDLS. The annexes contain the PICS, the FECF CRC, the Proximity-1 relationship, the 4-octet truncated frame for short telecommands, the SANA registries (UPID, SCID range C0000-CFFFF) and OID randomization.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Issue 3 (June 2024) adds the VC Packet and VC Access services, raises the maximum number of frames per CLTU from one to more than one (matching TC), and adds a table, diagram and text on the order of COP and SDLS. EC 1 (October 2024) is editorial only. (PDF p. 7)
  • Out of scope: the COP-1 and COP-P procedures themselves, the SDLS security services, flow control, implementations, and management activities. (PDF p. 13)
  • A USLP Transfer Frame consists of a Primary Header (4-14 octets), an optional Insert Zone, the Transfer Frame Data Field (TFDF header of 1-3 octets plus the TFDZ), an optional 4-octet OCF and an optional 2-octet FECF. (PDF p. 89)
  • The non-truncated Primary Header has 13 fields: TFVN (4 bits), SCID (16), Source-or-Destination ID (1), VCID (6), MAP ID (4), End of Frame Primary Header Flag (1), Frame Length (16), Bypass/Sequence Control Flag (1), Protocol Control Command Flag (1), Reserve Spares (2), OCF Flag (1), VCF Count Length (3) and VCF Count (0-56 bits). (PDF p. 90)
  • The TFVN is '1100' binary, the USLP Version-4 Transfer Frame. The MCID is bits 0-19 (TFVN plus SCID). (PDF p. 91)
  • The Frame Length field holds the total octets minus one, so a frame is limited to 65536 octets. Frames can be fixed or variable length; if the Physical Channel is fixed length, the subordinate MCs and VCs are fixed length too. (PDF p. 93)
  • End of Frame Primary Header Flag = 1 marks a truncated Primary Header containing only the first six fields. It is intended for short forward-link or direct-from-Earth telecommands. (PDF p. 93)
  • Bypass/Sequence Control Flag: 0 means a Sequence-Controlled frame, subject to the FARM acceptance checks; 1 means an Expedited frame, which bypasses them. It is equivalent to the Proximity-1 QoS Indicator. (PDF p. 94)
  • VCID 63 is the only VC used for Only Idle Data (OID) frames. OID frames carry a randomized idle pattern from an LFSR initialised only at device start-up. (PDF p. 99)
  • The TFDF Header has a 3-bit TFDZ Construction Rule, a 5-bit USLP Protocol Identifier (UPID, registered with SANA) and an optional 16-bit First Header/Last Valid Octet Pointer. There are eight construction rules; for example, '000' means fixed-length TFDZ packets spanning frames, with an FHP. (PDF p. 100)
  • The FECF, if present, occupies the last 16 bits of every frame and is computed with the CRC-16 procedure of Annex B. (PDF p. 107)
  • A truncated frame has a 4-octet header plus the TFDF only, with no Insert Zone, OCF or FECF. It is allowed only on variable-length VCs. SDLS on truncated frames needs a Truncated Transfer Frame Length of at least 28 octets. (PDF p. 186)
  • SANA: the new UPID registry; for Version 4 the SCID range is 0x0000-0xFFFF and the GSCID (= MCID) range is C0000-CFFFF; MAP IDs are '0000'-'1111'. (PDF p. 191)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A CCSDS Green Book that sets out the concept for the extensible Space Communication Cross Support Service Management (SCCS SM). SCCS SM covers the processes and information that a mission (user) and a ground-station network (provider) exchange to agree, configure, schedule, execute and account for space link and ground data transfer services, such as the SLE services used by ESA ground stations. The report explains why the first-generation SM standard (CCSDS 910.11-B-1) was too narrow: it covered scheduling only and could not take new technologies. The new concept defines standard XML Information Entities with built-in extension points.

Section 2 is a summary. Section 3 describes the SCCS SM Enterprise Model: the Mission (Earth User and Space User CSSS) and the Provider CSSS, the Utilization Management and Provision Management functions, and functional and physical views, including Delta-DOR and three-way tracking examples. Section 4 gives the mission support lifecycle: Service Catalog Consultation, Service Agreement Development, and a Service Agreement Period with repeating planning/scheduling, execution and accounting stages. Section 5 describes 19 Information Entities, from Service Catalog, Service Agreement and Configuration Profile to Trajectory Prediction, Service Package Request, Schedule of Services and Accounting Report. Section 6 shows how extensibility works through Abstract Service Components, technology-specific Service Components and Functional Resources, using a telecommand mission and an AOS mission as examples. Sections 7 and 8 cover management services and the roadmap of follow-on Blue Books, including the Simple Schedule Format (CCSDS 902.1). Annex B maps the model onto the SLE Cross Support Reference Model (CCSDS 910.4-B-2). See SLE service management.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• SCCS SM is the set of processes for collecting and exchanging the information needed to negotiate, configure, schedule, prepare, access and report on SCCS services. The Mission and the SCCS service provider carry them out together. (PDF p. 11)
  • The Version-1 SCCS SM standard (CCSDS 910.11-B-1) focused on requesting and scheduling services and could not gracefully accommodate new technologies. The extensible concept was developed to remove these shortcomings. (PDF p. 21)
  • The near-term scope is the single-hop Earth-space link (the 'ABA' configuration) and the IOAG Service Catalog #1 services. The Solar System Internetwork is left for later. (PDF p. 13)
  • The Mission consists of an Earth User CSSS and a Space User CSSS. The Provider CSSS transports Data Link Layer data units between them and tracks the spacecraft. Utilization Management (mission side) and Provision Management (provider side) exchange the service management information. (PDF p. 22)
  • The mission support lifecycle has three phases: Service Catalog Consultation, Service Agreement Development, and the Service Agreement Period. In the last phase, planning and scheduling, Service Package execution and accounting stages repeat cyclically. (PDF p. 42)
  • Several Service Agreements, each for a different mission phase (for example LEOP or cruise), may exist concurrently and overlap. (PDF p. 43)
  • Almost all SCCS SM Information Entities are formatted in W3C XML. (PDF p. 48)
  • An extensible Information Entity has fixed core parameters and abstract extension points. A valid Information Entity has one extension for every extension point, and provider-unique capabilities can be added as extensions. (PDF p. 66)
  • Abstract Service Components (ASCs) are the extension points of the Service Agreement and Configuration Profile. They are specialised into technology-specific Service Components, whose management parameters are represented by Functional Resources. (PDF p. 67)
  • There are six basic ESLT configurations: SLS, SLS data delivery, retrieval data delivery, forward offline data delivery, SLS radiometric and retrieval radiometric. (PDF p. 68)
  • The layered model used for the ASCs comprises aperture, physical channel, channel synchronization and coding, and space data link protocols. Data stores, such as the Offline Frame Buffer of SLE RAF/RCF, buffer data between sessions. (PDF p. 68)
  • Standard SCCS Management Services were expected around 2020. Until then, the standard Information Entities can be carried by provider-specific management services. (PDF p. 101)
  • Streaming, low-latency management services are expected to be built on the CCSDS CSTS Specification Framework. (PDF p. 102)
  • The roadmap orders the follow-on Blue Books: Simple Schedule Format first, then Planning Data Formats, Trajectory Prediction, Service Request and Service Package, Service Agreement and Configuration Profile, Space Link Event Sequence, Service Catalog, Service Accounting, Management Services, and a Best Practices Magenta Book. (PDF p. 103)
  • Table 8-1 estimated the Simple Schedule Format Blue Book for late 2014 and the Management Services (Automation) Blue Book for late 2020. (PDF p. 107)
  • The SCCS SM Enterprise Model evolves from the SLE Cross Support Reference Model. The CSRM SLE Complex became the SCCS Complex (now the Provider CSSS), and the MDOS corresponds to the Earth User CSSS. (PDF p. 111)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A short CCSDS Blue Book in the 902 family of Space Communication Cross Support Service Management (SCCS-SM) standards, which grew out of the concept in CCSDS 902.0-G-1. It defines the Service Package Data Format (SPDF). This is the XML message a TT&C service provider (a ground-station or relay network) sends back to a mission to report which requested service packages were scheduled. The message gives the scheduled times, the antenna (aperture) and the configuration that apply. It closes the loop on a Service Package Request made with the SMURF format (CCSDS 902.9-B-1). The concepts of online services and service packages come from the SLE Cross Support Reference Model (CCSDS 910.4-B-2). The wiki page is SLE service management.

Section 1 places the SPDF among the other 902 books (Simple Schedule Format, Service Catalog, Service Agreement and Configuration Profile, Event Sequence, Common Data Entities, and others) and gives the mission-planning use case. Section 2 explains the two equivalent encodings. Type 1 is compact: it references configuration profiles, trajectories, event sequences and Delta-DOR scan patterns, and lists only the parameters that were modified. Type 2 embeds the complete configuration profile, event sequence and DDOR scan pattern contents. Section 3 specifies the UML classes, most of which inherit from the Common Data Entities (CCSDS 902.12-M-2). These are the header with its servicePkgUsage enumeration, the body with spaceUserNode and serviceReqRef, and the ServicePkg with its ID, beginning/end of track in CCSDS ASCII Time Code B and an optional status. Section 3 also covers aperture location and the Type 1/Type 2 online-package classes. Annex A is the ICS proforma, Annex B covers security and the SANA registries (with the 'UNR::' prefix for unregistered values), and Annex C points to the normative XSD '902x04b01-SPDF.xsd'.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The SPDF expresses a package of one or more services (typically telecommand, telemetry and tracking) from a service provider to a mission user. It tells spacecraft operators which ground-station or relay resources are scheduled for them and how they are configured. (PDF p. 9)
  • Service package data can be sent in a 'Type 1' or a 'Type 2' format. They differ only in how much is conveyed directly and how much is referenced: Type 1 references the Service Configuration Profiles, and Type 2 includes them in full. (PDF p. 10)
  • The standard covers only the data format and content, not the protocols or methods used to exchange it. (PDF p. 10)
  • The Service Package is sent by the Provider CSSS to the Mission when the source Service Package Request has been scheduled, in reply to later queries, and to document later modifications. (PDF p. 15)
  • Parameter extensions are outside the scope of the standard. They should be documented in an ICD agreed by the parties and registered with SANA. (PDF p. 16)
  • One SPDF instance can carry several ServicePkg elements. All of them should use the same type (all Type 1 or all Type 2). (PDF p. 16)
  • A Type 1 online package holds a configuration profile reference, optional trajectory, event sequence and DDOR scan pattern references, and a list of modified parameters (resource, parameter, value). (PDF p. 17)
  • The normative XML Schema mapping is a 'virtual annex' published as separate schema files. (PDF p. 17)
  • servicePkgUsage is a mandatory enumeration with the values INTERFACE-TEST, OPERATIONAL and OTHER. When the header startTime and endTime are present, they must span the earliest start and latest end of the contained services. (PDF p. 20)
  • ServicePkgBody carries the mandatory spaceUserNode (a SANA-registered spacecraft name) and serviceReqRef (for example the ServiceReqID of the SMURF request). (PDF p. 21)
  • ServicePkg carries servicePackageID, beginningOfTrack and endOfTrack (CCSDS ASCII Time Code B) and an optional servicePackageStatus. The recommended status values are CREATED, SCHEDULED, DELETED, ARCHIVED, EXECUTING and ABORTED. (PDF p. 22)
  • In a Type 1 package, one concrete AbstractModCProfParm (or AbstractModESeqParm) instance is required for each configuration-profile (or event-sequence) parameter that differs from the referenced profile. (PDF p. 29)
  • Only SANA-registered values should be used for originatingOrganization, spaceUserNode, siteRef and apertureRef. Unregistered values should be prefixed with 'UNR::'. (PDF p. 48)
  • The schema file is '902x04b01-SPDF.xsd', which includes '902x12m02-CDE.xsd'. Both are distributed through the SANA service-management XML schema registry and a CCSDS-CSSM GitHub release (SANA_Release-20260526). (PDF p. 50)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The Cross Support Reference Model (CSRM), Part 1 is the root document of the CCSDS Space Link Extension (SLE) family. It defines the concepts and vocabulary that the SLE transfer service specifications (RAF, RCF, ROCF, FCLTU, FSP) and the SLE service management standards build on (for the ESA ground-station side, see NCTRS and NIS). The reference model assumes a single mission and a single spacecraft whose telemetry and telecommand follow the CCSDS space link standards.

Section 2 defines cross support (one agency using another agency's resources) and sets out the SLE documentation tree. It also covers the six security areas SLE must address: privacy, integrity, authentication, access control, availability and auditing. Section 3 describes the space mission data system: space element, SLE system and the Mission Data Operation System (MDOS). It describes the data units involved (SL-DUs, SLE-SDUs, data channels) and the full baseline of return, forward AOS and forward telecommand transfer services, with the online (complete and timely) and offline delivery modes. Section 4 gives the architecture model. In the functional view there are eight SLE Functional Groups, from Return Space Link Processing to Forward CLTU Generation. In the cross-support view, SLE Complexes are managed by SLE Utilization Management, and the Service Agreement, Service Package and transfer service instance concepts are defined, along with their time spans. Section 5 is the template for SLE service specifications, with its ports and service production. Annex A tabulates the Packet Telemetry, Telecommand and AOS data units and the return and forward SLE channel trees. The later SCCS service management concept (CCSDS 902.0-G-1) generalises this model. See also SLE service management.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• SLE services are of two kinds. SLE transfer services move data within the ground data system or between it and the ground sources and sinks. SLE management services control the scheduling and provision of those transfer services. (PDF p. 12)
  • The model assumes a single mission and a single spacecraft with CCSDS-compliant TM and TC, and ground users affiliated with a single mission management entity. Processing the contents of source packets is out of scope. (PDF p. 13)
  • Cross support services on the ground are of three kinds: SLE services, ground communications services and ground domain services (for example tracking or exchanging spacecraft databases). Part 1 of the reference model covers SLE. (PDF p. 20)
  • The SLE data transfer specifications do not define data privacy capabilities. Privacy is left to the mission applications, the underlying communication service, or both. (PDF p. 22)
  • Authentication uses credentials carried in the transfer service data units, and access control uses the initiator-identifier and responder-identifier parameters. The algorithms are out of scope. (PDF p. 23)
  • The baseline return SLE transfer services are RAF, Return Insert, Return MC Frame, MC-OCF, MC-FSH, VC Frame, VC-OCF, VC-FSH, Return Bitstream and Return Space Packet. (PDF p. 32)
  • The forward AOS services are Bitstream, VCA, Space Packet, Proto Transfer Frame, Insert and Coded Transfer Frame. The forward telecommand services are TC-VCA, Forward Space Packet, Telecommand Frame and CLTU. (PDF p. 33)
  • There are three delivery modes: complete online, timely online and offline. Return online delivery may extend beyond the end of the Space Link session, and forward online delivery may not. (PDF p. 33)
  • Timely online return delivery gives the user two controls: a delay-notification threshold (Tdelay-notify) and a deletion threshold (Tdelete), above which the queued SLE-SDUs are discarded and the user is told how many. (PDF p. 34)
  • SLE-FGs are of eight types in three categories. The return ones are Return Space Link Processing, Return Frame Processing and Return Frame Data Extraction. The forward AOS ones are VC Data Insertion and Space Link Processing. The forward TC ones are VC Data Insert, CLTU Generation and Space Link Processing. (PDF p. 42)
  • The Forward TC Space Link Processing SLE-FG uses CLCWs from MC-OCF or VC-OCF channels to decide whether the physical channel is available. It generates acquisition and idle sequences according to the PLOP in effect and radiates the CLTUs. (PDF p. 55)
  • An SLE Complex is a set of SLE-FGs under a single management authority. All SLE Complexes interface to a single SLE Utilization Management within the MDOS. (PDF p. 55)
  • An SLE Service Package is the set of SLE transfer service instances, with their production characteristics, provided by one SLE Complex. Its online services are restricted to one Space Link Session. (PDF p. 57)
  • The SLE Service Agreement period often covers the whole operational life of a spacecraft and may involve several service packages per day. Shorter agreements can cover only launch support, a manoeuvre or emergency operations. (PDF p. 63)
  • Annex A maps SL-DUs to their sources. Packet Telemetry has frames, FSH, OCF, VCA_SDU and source packets. Telecommand has CLTU, TC frames, frame data units, segments and packets. AOS has coded frames, insert zone, proto frames, OCF, VCA-SDU, bitstream PDU and space packets. (PDF p. 84)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
CCSDS Green Book (informational report) that explains the concept behind the Space Link Extension (SLE) services. Cross support means one organisation provides part of its space data system to serve another organisation's mission. SLE services make this possible by extending the CCSDS space link services (TM, TC, AOS) across the ground between ground stations, control centres and users. The report summarises the Cross Support Reference Model (910.4-B-2), the draft Service Management specification (910.11-R-1) and the transfer service specifications. It assumes a single mission and spacecraft that use CCSDS TM/TC or AOS.

The report describes extension of the space link in distance (processing at remote sites), information (annotation such as reception time) and time (offline delivery). It then lists the transfer services and maps them to SLE Functional Groups. Return services are RAF, RCF, RFSH, ROCF and RSP (return services); forward TC services are FSP, FTCVCA, FTCF and CLTU; forward AOS services were still undefined at the time. Functional Groups are grouped into SLE Complexes. The report also covers the operations common to all services (BIND, UNBIND, PEER-ABORT, START, STOP, TRANSFER-DATA, notifications, status reports, GET-PARAMETER, plus THROW-EVENT and INVOKE-DIRECTIVE), a simplified state diagram, an RCF-START example table with ASN.1, and the two-layer SLE API (API Proxy and API Service Element).

Section 5 introduces SLE Service Management: Utilization Management in the MDOS and Complex Management in the provider negotiate Service Agreements, Configuration Profiles, Trajectory Predictions and Service Packages across definition and utilization phases. The annexes give a glossary, cross-support scenarios, antenna-pointing management scenarios and the SLE security mechanisms (credentials with 'all', 'bind' or 'none' authentication levels, and access control).

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Issue history: 910.3-G-1 (May 1995) and 910.3-G-2 (April 2002) are marked superseded; 910.3-G-3 (March 2006) is the current issue. (PDF p. 5)
  • The report assumes a single mission and a single spacecraft whose TM/TC systems comply with the CCSDS TM recommendations and either the TC recommendations or the AOS recommendation, with all ground end-users affiliated to one mission manager. (PDF p. 9)
  • Cross Support services are of three kinds: SLE services, Ground Communications services and Ground Domain services (for example tracking, exchanging spacecraft databases, mission planning). Only Part 1 (SLE) of the Cross Support Concept exists; Part 2 is not planned and Part 3 is under consideration. (PDF p. 10)
  • SLE services comprise data transfer services and management services, and operate in a definition phase (management) and a utilization phase (data transfer, in real time or off-line). (PDF p. 15)
  • The SLE system extends space link services in distance, in information (annotation, e.g. reception conditions) and in time; for example, the SCID from the frame must accompany packets processed remotely because APIDs are only unique within a spacecraft. (PDF p. 20)
  • Return SLE services: Return All Frames (RAF), Return Channel Frames (RCF, master or virtual channel), Return Frame Secondary Header (RFSH), Return Operational Control Field (ROCF) and Return Space Packet (RSP, selected by APID from one VC); R-Insert and R-Bitstream were not yet defined. (PDF p. 24)
  • Providing a return packet service requires three SLE Functional Groups: Return Space Link Processing, Return Frame Processing and Return Frame Data Extraction. (PDF p. 27)
  • Forward TC SLE services: Forward Space Packet (FSP), Forward TC Virtual Channel Access (FTCVCA), Forward TC Frame (FTCF) and Forward CLTU; the ROCF service supplies the CLCW needed for link availability and COP-1 retransmission decisions. (PDF p. 28)
  • Forward AOS SLE services (F-AOSSP, F-AOSVCA, F-Bitstream, F-pVCDU, F-cVCDU, F-VCDU, F-Insert) were not yet defined by CCSDS and are planned in two Functional Groups. (PDF p. 31)
  • All functions of a Functional Group must be implemented within a single SLE Complex; one or more Functional Groups can be implemented in SLE Complexes operated by different organisations. (PDF p. 32)
  • Operations common to all SLE transfer services: BIND, UNBIND, PEER-ABORT, START, STOP, TRANSFER-DATA, SYNC-NOTIFY/ASYNC-NOTIFY, SCHEDULE-STATUS-REPORT, STATUS-REPORT and GET-PARAMETER; some services add THROW-EVENT and INVOKE-DIRECTIVE. (PDF p. 34)
  • The RCF-START operation table carries invoker-credentials, performer-credentials, invoke-ID, start-time, stop-time and global-VCID in the invocation, with result and a conditional diagnostic in the return; each operation has an ASN.1 definition. (PDF p. 37)
  • The SLE API has two layers: the API Proxy (technology-independent interface to the communications system) and the API Service Element (enforces CCSDS state tables and checks operation parameters). (PDF p. 38)
  • SLE Service Management exchanges Service Agreements, Configuration Profiles, Service Packages and Trajectory Predictions between Utilization Management (user/MDOS side) and Complex Management (provider side). (PDF p. 39)
  • Of the five OSI management functional areas, SLE Service Management covers configuration, accounting, fault and security management, but not performance management. (PDF p. 41)
  • SLE transfer service instances have one of three authentication levels: 'all' (every invocation and return carries credentials), 'bind' (only BIND and its return) or 'none'; access control allows only one specified user to initiate each service instance. (PDF p. 75)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The CCSDS Recommended Standard that defines the Return All Frames (RAF) service of the Space Link Extension. RAF is the SLE transfer service a ground station uses to deliver every telemetry frame of the selected quality from one space link physical channel to a mission user. The frames can be TM, AOS or, new in issue 5, USLP transfer frames. Each frame travels in an SLE-SDU annotated with Earth receive time, antenna ID, data-link continuity, delivered frame quality ('good' or 'erred', judged from Reed-Solomon/LDPC decoding or the FECF) and an optional private annotation.

Section 2 places RAF in the SLE Reference Model. It explains how service production (the Return Space Link Processing functional group) differs from service provision, how service management sets user- or provider-initiated binding and the delivery mode (timely online, complete online or offline), and how buffering works (transfer buffer, online and offline frame buffers). It also covers security concerns. Section 3 specifies each operation with its parameter table, effects and diagnostics: RAF-BIND (with version negotiation; this issue is version '6'), UNBIND, START (time window and requested frame quality), STOP, TRANSFER-DATA, SYNC-NOTIFY (loss of frame sync, production status change, data discarded due to excessive backlog, end of data), SCHEDULE-STATUS-REPORT, STATUS-REPORT, GET-PARAMETER and PEER-ABORT, together with access control and the 'all'/'bind'/'none' authentication levels. Section 4 gives the provider state machine (unbound, ready, active). The annexes contain the normative ASN.1 modules, the production-status model (running, interrupted, halted) and a conformance matrix. This is the service through which ground stations hand frames to control systems such as SCOS-2000 via NCTRS/NIS.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Issue 5 (July 2023) adds support for USLP Transfer Frames; issues B-1 (2002), B-2 (2004), B-3 (2010) and B-4 (2016) are superseded; Editorial Change 1 (October 2024) only corrects a figure font. (PDF p. 6)
  • The RAF service delivers to a mission user all telemetry frames of the selected frame quality from one space link physical channel. (PDF p. 9)
  • The underlying communications service must deliver invocations and returns in sequence, completely and with integrity, without duplication, with flow control and with notification of disruption. (PDF p. 9)
  • Multiplexing Reed-Solomon coded and uncoded frames on one physical channel, allowed by the historical AOS architecture (701.0-B-3), is no longer allowed by the recommendations in force. (PDF p. 10)
  • A telemetry frame is a TM, AOS or USLP Transfer Frame; each acquired frame is wrapped in an SLE-SDU with annotation such as the ERT. (PDF p. 23)
  • Delivery modes are timely online (controlled discarding allowed after a latency limit), complete online and offline; each service instance supports exactly one mode and either user or provider initiation, both set by service management. (PDF p. 25)
  • For a 'good' Reed-Solomon encoded frame the RS check symbols are removed before delivery; an 'erred' RS frame is delivered complete with check symbols. (PDF p. 27)
  • RAF operations: BIND and UNBIND (user or provider), START, STOP, SCHEDULE-STATUS-REPORT and GET-PARAMETER (user, confirmed), TRANSFER-DATA, SYNC-NOTIFY and STATUS-REPORT (provider, unconfirmed), and PEER-ABORT. (PDF p. 32)
  • The version-number value for the RAF service defined by this issue is '6'; a responder may propose a lower version during BIND negotiation. (PDF p. 63)
  • requested-frame-quality in RAF-START is one of 'good frames only', 'erred frames only' or 'all frames'. (PDF p. 73)
  • RAF-TRANSFER-DATA carries invoker-credentials, earth-receive-time, antenna-ID, data-link-continuity, delivered-frame-quality, private-annotation and data. (PDF p. 77)
  • earth-receive-time is the UTC time at which the leading edge of the first bit of the Attached Sync Marker preceding the frame was at the phase centre of the receiving antenna. (PDF p. 78)
  • data-link-continuity is -1 for the first frame after the start of production, 0 for a direct successor, and a positive estimate of missed frames otherwise (1 if no better estimate). (PDF p. 79)
  • RAF-SYNC-NOTIFY notification types: 'loss of frame synchronization', 'production status change' (running, halted or interrupted), 'data discarded due to excessive backlog' and 'end of data'. (PDF p. 83)
  • GET-PARAMETER parameters include delivery-mode, latency-limit, minimum-reporting-cycle, permitted-frame-quality-set, reporting-cycle, requested-frame-quality, return-timeout-period and transfer-buffer-size. (PDF p. 95)
  • Annex A defines the ASN.1 modules CCSDS-SLE-TRANSFER-SERVICE-COMMON-TYPES, -BIND-TYPES, -COMMON-PDUS, -SERVICE-INSTANCE-ID, -RAF-STRUCTURES, -RAF-INCOMING-PDUS and -RAF-OUTGOING-PDUS. (PDF p. 115)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The CCSDS Recommended Standard for the Return Channel Frames (RCF) service of the Space Link Extension. RCF delivers to a mission user the telemetry frames of one Master Channel or one Virtual Channel, selected by a global VCID made of TFVN, SCID and VCID. The frames can be TM (TFVN '00'), AOS ('01') or, new in this issue, USLP ('1100'). RCF replaces the separate 'Return MC Frames' and 'Return VC Frames' services of the SLE Reference Model. It is the companion of RAF and is described on SLE return services.

Section 2 describes production. The Return Frame Processing functional group (RFP-FG) consumes a RAF data channel, discards every frame whose quality is not 'good' (Reed-Solomon/LDPC codewords valid, or FECF correct, or the USLP validation checks passed), demultiplexes by MC and VC, and annotates each SLE-SDU with the ERT, the antenna ID, the data-link continuity and an optional private annotation. Section 2 also covers service management, the timely online, complete online and offline delivery modes, buffering and security. Section 3 specifies the operations with their parameter tables and diagnostics: RCF-BIND (version number '6' for this issue, with version negotiation), UNBIND, START (start and stop time, requested-global-VCID), STOP, TRANSFER-DATA, SYNC-NOTIFY (loss of frame synchronization, production status change, data discarded due to excessive backlog, end of data), SCHEDULE-STATUS-REPORT, STATUS-REPORT, GET-PARAMETER and PEER-ABORT. Section 4 gives the provider state machine (unbound, ready, active). Annex A holds the seven ASN.1 modules, Annex B the production-status model and Annex C the conformance matrix. See NCTRS/NIS for how ESA's control centres connect to ground stations; this document does not name any ESA system.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Issue 4 (July 2023) adds support for USLP Transfer Frames; issues B-1 (2004), B-2 (2010) and B-3 (2016) are superseded; EC 1 (October 2024) repairs figure 2-3. (PDF p. 6)
  • RCF delivers to a mission user all telemetry frames from one Master Channel or one Virtual Channel. It replaces the separate Return MC Frames and Return VC Frames services defined in the SLE Reference Model. (PDF p. 9)
  • The communications service underneath RCF must deliver invocations and returns in sequence, complete, with integrity, without duplication, with flow control, and with notification of disruption. (PDF p. 10)
  • The RFP-FG consumes one RAF data channel, discards every frame whose quality is not 'good', demultiplexes it into Master and Virtual Channels, and can store data for offline delivery. (PDF p. 28)
  • A frame is 'good' if it contains only valid Reed-Solomon or LDPC codewords or, for uncoded frames, if its FECF decodes successfully. A USLP frame is 'good' if it passes the USLP Frame Validation Check Procedure, apart from the checks in 4.3.10.3.4 c). (PDF p. 29)
  • Delivery modes: timely online, complete online or offline. Each service instance supports only one mode, which service management sets. (PDF p. 27)
  • The version-number value for the RCF service defined by this issue is '6'. A responder that supports version negotiation may propose a lower version; otherwise the diagnostic is 'version not supported'. (PDF p. 64)
  • The RCF-START parameters are invoker-credentials, performer-credentials, invoke-ID, start-time, stop-time and requested-global-VCID, plus result and diagnostic in the return. (PDF p. 72)
  • requested-global-VCID is made of TFVN, SCID and VCID. The valid TFVNs are '00' (TM), '01' (AOS) and '1100' (USLP). The physical channel is selected through the service package, not through RCF. (PDF p. 73)
  • RCF-TRANSFER-DATA carries invoker-credentials, earth-receive-time, antenna-ID, data-link-continuity, private-annotation and data. Unlike RAF, it has no delivered-frame-quality parameter. (PDF p. 79)
  • earth-receive-time is the UTC time at which the leading edge of the first bit of the start sequence preceding the frame was at the phase centre of the receiving antenna. (PDF p. 80)
  • SYNC-NOTIFY 'loss of frame synchronization' is sent once per lock-status observation period. There is no explicit notification when lock is regained, and it is never sent in offline mode. (PDF p. 84)
  • The parameters readable by GET-PARAMETER are delivery-mode, latency-limit, minimum-reporting-cycle, permitted-global-VCID-set, reporting-cycle, requested-global-VCID, return-timeout-period and transfer-buffer-size. (PDF p. 96)
  • Annex A defines seven ASN.1 modules: CCSDS-SLE-TRANSFER-SERVICE-COMMON-TYPES, -BIND-TYPES, -COMMON-PDUS, -SERVICE-INSTANCE-ID, -RCF-STRUCTURES, -RCF-INCOMING-PDUS and -RCF-OUTGOING-PDUS. (PDF p. 115)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The CCSDS Recommended Standard for the Return Operational Control Fields (ROCF) service of the Space Link Extension. ROCF delivers to a mission user the 4-octet Operational Control Fields (OCFs) extracted from the good-quality frames of one Master Channel or one Virtual Channel of a TM, AOS or USLP return link. The document notes that the most common OCF payload is the CLCW of the Communications Operation Procedure (see COP-1). It can also deliver other control-word types such as the SDLS Frame Security Report. ROCF replaces the separate Rtn MC-OCF and Rtn VC-OCF services of the SLE Reference Model. It is described with RAF and RCF on SLE return services.

Section 2 explains production: the RFP-FG takes a RAF data channel, keeps only 'good' frames, and demultiplexes by MC and VC. It also covers service management, the delivery modes (timely online, complete online, offline), buffering and security. Section 3 defines the operations. ROCF-BIND carries version number '6'. ROCF-START takes start/stop time, requested-global-VCID, control-word-type ('all control word types', 'clcw' or 'not clcw'), tc-vcid (only for 'clcw': pick the CLCWs that report on one TC Virtual Channel, or 'null' for all of them) and update-mode ('continuous', or 'change-based', which delivers an OCF only when its content changes). The other operations are UNBIND, STOP, TRANSFER-DATA (ERT, antenna-ID, data-link-continuity, private-annotation, OCF data), SYNC-NOTIFY, SCHEDULE-STATUS-REPORT, STATUS-REPORT, GET-PARAMETER and PEER-ABORT. Section 4 gives the provider state machine. The annexes hold the ASN.1 modules, the production status model, the conformance matrix, an index and acronyms.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Issue 4 (July 2023) adds support for USLP Transfer Frames plus clarifications and corrections. EC 1 (October 2024) repairs figure 2-3. (PDF p. 6)
  • ROCF delivers to a mission user all operational control fields from one Master Channel or one Virtual Channel. It merges the Rtn MC-OCF and Rtn VC-OCF services of the SLE Reference Model into one. (PDF p. 9)
  • The ROCF delivery criteria are: ERT within the start/stop window, SCID and VCID matching the requested global VCID, a matching control word type, and, for CLCWs (control word type '0'), a matching telecommand VC. For 'not clcw' OCFs, the Frame Security Report can be delivered. (PDF p. 17)
  • The most common OCF payload is the CLCW of the COP, which has no confidentiality protection, so the confidentiality of ROCF data usually depends entirely on the underlying communications service. (PDF p. 46)
  • Only frames annotated 'good' feed ROCF production: valid Reed-Solomon or LDPC codewords, or a correct FECF for uncoded frames. (PDF p. 30)
  • The version-number value for the ROCF service defined by this issue is '6'. (PDF p. 66)
  • The ROCF-START invocation carries invoker-credentials, start-time, stop-time, requested-global-VCID, control-word-type, a conditional tc-vcid and update-mode. The return carries performer-credentials, result and diagnostic. (PDF p. 74)
  • control-word-type is 'all control word types', 'clcw' (type '0') or 'not clcw'; 'not clcw' is the type to use to obtain FSRs. tc-vcid is present only for 'clcw', and 'null' selects CLCWs for every TC VC. (PDF p. 77)
  • In update-mode 'continuous' every matching OCF is delivered. In 'change-based' an OCF is delivered only if its content differs from the last one delivered for the same tc-vcid, or if none has been delivered since the most recent START. (PDF p. 78)
  • ROCF-TRANSFER-DATA carries invoker-credentials, earth-receive-time, antenna-ID, data-link-continuity, private-annotation and the OCF data. (PDF p. 83)
  • GET-PARAMETER exposes delivery-mode, latency-limit, minimum-reporting-cycle, permitted-global-VCID-set, permitted-control-word-type-set, permitted-tc-vcid-set, permitted-update-mode-set, reporting-cycle, requested-control-word-type, requested-global-VCID, requested-tc-vcid, requested-update-mode, return-timeout-period and transfer-buffer-size. (PDF p. 100)
  • Annex A defines the common SLE ASN.1 modules plus CCSDS-SLE-TRANSFER-SERVICE-ROCF-STRUCTURES, -ROCF-INCOMING-PDUS and -ROCF-OUTGOING-PDUS. (PDF p. 119)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The CCSDS Recommended Standard that defines the Return All Frames (RAF) service of the Space Link Extension. RAF is the SLE transfer service a ground station uses to deliver every telemetry frame of the selected quality from one space link physical channel to a mission user. The frames can be TM, AOS or, new in issue 5, USLP transfer frames. Each frame travels in an SLE-SDU annotated with Earth receive time, antenna ID, data-link continuity, delivered frame quality ('good' or 'erred', judged from Reed-Solomon/LDPC decoding or the FECF) and an optional private annotation.

Section 2 places RAF in the SLE Reference Model. It explains how service production (the Return Space Link Processing functional group) differs from service provision, how service management sets user- or provider-initiated binding and the delivery mode (timely online, complete online or offline), and how buffering works (transfer buffer, online and offline frame buffers). It also covers security concerns. Section 3 specifies each operation with its parameter table, effects and diagnostics: RAF-BIND (with version negotiation; this issue is version '6'), UNBIND, START (time window and requested frame quality), STOP, TRANSFER-DATA, SYNC-NOTIFY (loss of frame sync, production status change, data discarded due to excessive backlog, end of data), SCHEDULE-STATUS-REPORT, STATUS-REPORT, GET-PARAMETER and PEER-ABORT, together with access control and the 'all'/'bind'/'none' authentication levels. Section 4 gives the provider state machine (unbound, ready, active). The annexes contain the normative ASN.1 modules, the production-status model (running, interrupted, halted) and a conformance matrix. This is the service through which ground stations hand frames to control systems such as SCOS-2000 via NCTRS/NIS.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Issue 5 (July 2023) adds support for USLP Transfer Frames; issues B-1 (2002), B-2 (2004), B-3 (2010) and B-4 (2016) are superseded; Editorial Change 1 (October 2024) only corrects a figure font. (PDF p. 6)
  • The RAF service delivers to a mission user all telemetry frames of the selected frame quality from one space link physical channel. (PDF p. 9)
  • The underlying communications service must deliver invocations and returns in sequence, completely and with integrity, without duplication, with flow control and with notification of disruption. (PDF p. 9)
  • Multiplexing Reed-Solomon coded and uncoded frames on one physical channel, allowed by the historical AOS architecture (701.0-B-3), is no longer allowed by the recommendations in force. (PDF p. 10)
  • A telemetry frame is a TM, AOS or USLP Transfer Frame; each acquired frame is wrapped in an SLE-SDU with annotation such as the ERT. (PDF p. 23)
  • Delivery modes are timely online (controlled discarding allowed after a latency limit), complete online and offline; each service instance supports exactly one mode and either user or provider initiation, both set by service management. (PDF p. 25)
  • For a 'good' Reed-Solomon encoded frame the RS check symbols are removed before delivery; an 'erred' RS frame is delivered complete with check symbols. (PDF p. 27)
  • RAF operations: BIND and UNBIND (user or provider), START, STOP, SCHEDULE-STATUS-REPORT and GET-PARAMETER (user, confirmed), TRANSFER-DATA, SYNC-NOTIFY and STATUS-REPORT (provider, unconfirmed), and PEER-ABORT. (PDF p. 32)
  • The version-number value for the RAF service defined by this issue is '6'; a responder may propose a lower version during BIND negotiation. (PDF p. 63)
  • requested-frame-quality in RAF-START is one of 'good frames only', 'erred frames only' or 'all frames'. (PDF p. 73)
  • RAF-TRANSFER-DATA carries invoker-credentials, earth-receive-time, antenna-ID, data-link-continuity, delivered-frame-quality, private-annotation and data. (PDF p. 77)
  • earth-receive-time is the UTC time at which the leading edge of the first bit of the Attached Sync Marker preceding the frame was at the phase centre of the receiving antenna. (PDF p. 78)
  • data-link-continuity is -1 for the first frame after the start of production, 0 for a direct successor, and a positive estimate of missed frames otherwise (1 if no better estimate). (PDF p. 79)
  • RAF-SYNC-NOTIFY notification types: 'loss of frame synchronization', 'production status change' (running, halted or interrupted), 'data discarded due to excessive backlog' and 'end of data'. (PDF p. 83)
  • GET-PARAMETER parameters include delivery-mode, latency-limit, minimum-reporting-cycle, permitted-frame-quality-set, reporting-cycle, requested-frame-quality, return-timeout-period and transfer-buffer-size. (PDF p. 95)
  • Annex A defines the ASN.1 modules CCSDS-SLE-TRANSFER-SERVICE-COMMON-TYPES, -BIND-TYPES, -COMMON-PDUS, -SERVICE-INSTANCE-ID, -RAF-STRUCTURES, -RAF-INCOMING-PDUS and -RAF-OUTGOING-PDUS. (PDF p. 115)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The CCSDS Recommended Standard for the Forward Communications Link Transmission Unit (FCLTU) service, the Space Link Extension transfer service through which a mission control centre sends CLTUs to a ground station for radiation to a spacecraft. The provider radiates each CLTU bit for bit in the order submitted. It may check the length but never interprets the content, so any octet-aligned bit pattern can be uplinked. The service is online-only. The wiki page is SLE forward service: FCLTU.

Section 2 describes the model. The Forward TC Space Link Processing SLE Functional Group in the SLE Complex extracts the CLTUs and radiates them, production status moves through configured, operational, interrupted and halted, and the CLCW from a return channel (clcw-global-VCID, clcw-physical-channel) can gate radiation through the bit-lock and RF-available flags. The section also covers buffering and security. Section 3 specifies the operations with parameter tables and diagnostics: CLTU-BIND (version number '6'), UNBIND, START (first-cltu-identification, start/stop production time), STOP, TRANSFER-DATA (monotonically increasing cltu-identification, earliest and latest radiation time, delay-time, report request, data; the return gives cltu-buffer-available), ASYNC-NOTIFY ('cltu radiated', 'sldu expired', production interrupted/halted/operational, 'buffer empty', action-list results), SCHEDULE-STATUS-REPORT, STATUS-REPORT, GET-PARAMETER (for example plop-in-effect PLOP-1/PLOP-2, maximum-cltu-length, modulation index and frequency, acquisition and idle sequence lengths), THROW-EVENT (management events such as an uplink bit-rate change) and PEER-ABORT. Section 4 gives the provider state machine. Annex A has the ASN.1 modules, Annex B the production status model, and Annex F example throw events for low-rate commanding.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Issue 5 (July 2023) adds support for USLP Transfer Frames. Issues B-1 (2002), B-2 (2004), B-3 (2010) and B-4 (2016) are superseded. EC 1 (October 2024) corrects a figure font. (PDF p. 6)
  • FCLTU is an SLE transfer service that enables a mission to send CLTUs to a spacecraft. (PDF p. 10)
  • The provider transmits CLTUs in submission order and bit for bit. It may check constraints such as the maximum length but never interprets or modifies the content, so any octet-aligned bit pattern can be uplinked. The service exists only in the online delivery mode. (PDF p. 23)
  • The version-number value of the FCLTU service defined by this issue is '6'. (PDF p. 53)
  • The CLTU-START invocation carries first-cltu-identification. The return carries the conditional start-production-time and stop-production-time. (PDF p. 59)
  • The CLTU-TRANSFER-DATA invocation carries invoker-credentials, invoke-ID, cltu-identification, earliest-radiation-time, latest-radiation-time, delay-time, report and data. The return carries performer-credentials, cltu-identification, cltu-buffer-available, result and diagnostic. (PDF p. 66)
  • cltu-identification is a monotonically increasing sequence number. The return carries the value expected in the next invocation: one more than the accepted value, or the expected value after a rejection. (PDF p. 67)
  • The CLTU-ASYNC-NOTIFY types are 'cltu radiated', 'sldu expired', 'production interrupted', 'production halted', 'production operational', 'buffer empty', 'action list completed', 'action list not completed' and 'event condition evaluated to false'. (PDF p. 74)
  • Configuration parameters readable through GET-PARAMETER include acquisition-sequence-length, bit-lock-required, clcw-global-VCID, clcw-physical-channel, delivery-mode ('fwd online'), maximum-cltu-length, minimum-delay-time, modulation-frequency, modulation-index, notification-mode, plop-1-idle-sequence-length, plop-in-effect ('PLOP-1' or 'PLOP-2'), protocol-abort-mode, rf-available-required and subcarrier-to-bit-rate-ratio. (PDF p. 92)
  • CLTU-THROW-EVENT forwards an event to SLE Complex Management, for example an uplink bit-rate change after the spacecraft has been commanded to the new rate. Its outcome is reported later through CLTU-ASYNC-NOTIFY. (PDF p. 95)
  • Production status transitions run between Configured, Operational, Interrupted and Halted. Reaching 'operational' typically involves the uplink sweep and the acquisition sequence, and it can optionally require bit lock and/or RF available. (PDF p. 141)
  • The example throw events assume low-rate commanding on a 16 kHz subcarrier (maximum 4000 bit/s): Set Mod on/off, Change Rate (7.8125-4000 bit/s), Change Index (1-1570 mrad) and Change Rate/Index. (PDF p. 152)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The CCSDS Recommended Standard for the SLE Forward Space Packet (FSP) service. This SLE transfer service lets a mission control centre hand individual Space Packets to a ground station's SLE provider. The provider segments them into TC frames, runs COP-1 (FOP-1) on the virtual channel, and radiates them in sequence-controlled (AD) or expedited (BD) mode. The wiki page is SLE FSP. This issue only covers Space Packets sent through the telecommand stack (TC SDLP, COP-1, CLTU coding). The AOS forward use foreseen in the reference model is out of scope, and only online delivery is defined.

Section 2 places FSP in the forward telecommand functional groups. TC VC Data Insertion builds and buffers TC frames and acts on CLCWs. CLTU Generation randomises, BCH-encodes and adds start and tail sequences. TC Space Link Processing radiates the result. Section 2 also covers scheduling and configuration through service packages, the three provider states (unbound, ready, active) and the security aspects. Section 3 specifies the thirteen operations: BIND, UNBIND, START, STOP, TRANSFER-DATA (with packet-identification, production time window, transmission mode, MAP-identifier, blocking and radiated or acknowledged notifications), ASYNC-NOTIFY, SCHEDULE-STATUS-REPORT, STATUS-REPORT, GET-PARAMETER, THROW-EVENT, INVOKE-DIRECTIVE (the COP-1 directives such as Initiate AD Service or Set V(S)) and PEER-ABORT. Section 4 gives the provider state tables. The normative annexes define the ASN.1 data types, the queue and MAP/VC multiplexing model (FIFO, absolute priority, polling vector), production status and the conformance matrix. For context see SLE and the ESA ground-station interface in NCTRS and NIS.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• FSP is an SLE transfer service that lets a mission send Space Packets to a spacecraft in sequence-controlled or expedited mode. (PDF p. 12)
  • This version handles only Space Packets (CCSDS 133.0-B) sent through the telecommand stack. Use with the AOS stack is out of scope, and only the online delivery mode is defined (offline is for further study). (PDF p. 12)
  • The underlying communications service must deliver invocations and returns in sequence, completely, without duplication, with flow control that signals backpressure, and with notification of disruptions. (PDF p. 13)
  • No Forward TC Frame Recommended Standard exists, so the Forward CLTU Generation and Forward TC VC Data Insertion functional groups must be in the same Complex. (PDF p. 30)
  • The Forward TC VC Data Insertion SLE-FG blocks or segments packets into TC frames. For sequence-controlled frames it sets the Frame Sequence Number and keeps a copy, then retransmits or deletes the copy according to the CLCW from Type-0 OCF channels. (PDF p. 31)
  • This version does not support applying SDLS to the TC frames, because a user generally does not want to disclose its security configuration to the FSP provider. (PDF p. 31)
  • Service packages set the production parameters: the TC VC, the MAP and frame multiplexing schemes, maximum packet and TC frame lengths, and the CLTU and space link processing configuration. (PDF p. 35)
  • There are thirteen operations, from FSP-BIND to FSP-PEER-ABORT. ASYNC-NOTIFY, STATUS-REPORT and PEER-ABORT are unconfirmed, and all the others are confirmed. (PDF p. 36)
  • The provider states are 1 'unbound', 2 'ready' and 3 'active'. Packets may be transferred only in state 3, and FSP-STOP discards packets not yet passed to the segment queues. (PDF p. 37)
  • After an association ends, accounting information, notification references and COP parameters set by directives persist for the service instance provision period. (PDF p. 38)
  • FSP-TRANSFER-DATA carries packet-identification, earliest and latest production time, delay-time, transmission-mode, MAP-identifier, blocking, three notification flags and the data. Its return reports packet-buffer-available. (PDF p. 75)
  • packet-identification is a monotonically increasing sequence number that starts at the first-packet-identification given in FSP-START. The provider returns the value it expects next. (PDF p. 74)
  • At most one FSP service instance per TC VC may invoke directives. The supported directives are Initiate AD Service (without CLCW check, with CLCW check, with Unlock, with Set V(R)), Terminate AD, Resume AD, Set V(S) to V*(S), Set FOP_Sliding_Window_Width, Set T1_Initial, Set Transmission_Limit, Set Timeout_Type and Abort VC. (PDF p. 124)
  • Two levels of multiplexing are defined: MAP multiplexing of Frame Data Units and VC multiplexing of TC frames. Each can use FIFO, absolute priority or a polling vector, and only one service type (FSP or TC VCA) is allowed on a VC. (PDF p. 173)
  • The queue model has an FSP requests queue per service instance, a packets queue per instance (or per permitted MAP), a segments queue per packets queue, and at most one directives queue per VC. (PDF p. 174)
