docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The CCSDS Recommended Standard for the Internet SLE Protocol One (ISP1), the wire protocol that carries the SLE transfer-service PDUs of RAF, RCF, ROCF, FCLTU and FSP over TCP/IP. The service specifications define the operations but deliberately leave out communications, and this document fills that gap. It is the subject of SLE over TCP/IP (ISP1) and the SLE API.

Section 2 gives a layered model. The Authentication Layer (AL) generates and checks credentials. The Data Encoding Layer (DEL) encodes the service's ASN.1 types with BER. The Transport Mapping Layer (TML) maps one SLE association onto exactly one TCP connection. Section 2 also defines the primitives of each interface (AL, DEL, TML data transfer, association control and listener) and the use of TCP, and covers security. Section 3 specifies the messages and procedures. Authentication follows the ISO/IEC 9594-8 'Protected 1' simple scheme: a DER-encoded HashInput (CCSDS CDS time, random number, user name of 3-16 characters, password of 6-16 octets) is hashed with SHA-256, and the time, random number and digest travel in the ISP1Credentials. The authentication level per service instance is 'all', 'bind' or 'none'. TML messages have an 8-octet header (type 1 SLE PDU, 2 Context, 3 Heartbeat; 3 reserved octets; a 4-octet length) and are big-endian. The 12-octet context message carries 'ISP1', version 1, the heartbeat-interval and the dead-factor. The section also covers heartbeat timers, connection establishment and release, and PEER-ABORT sent as one octet of TCP urgent data. Section 4 is the TML state table (S0 Closed to S4 TML Closing), Annex A lists the TML diagnostic codes, and Annex B covers interoperability with the earlier ESA 'SLE API Proxy' specification, from which ISP1 derives.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Issue 2 (September 2015) changes the recommended one-way hash function from SHA-1 to SHA-256 and updates references. Issue 1 (September 2008) is superseded. (PDF p. 7)
  • ISP1 transfers the SLE PDUs defined in the SLE transfer service standards over TCP and IP, using ASN.1 for data encoding. (PDF p. 10)
  • The architecture has three layers above TCP/IP: the Authentication Layer (AL), the Data Encoding Layer (DEL) and the Transport Mapping Layer (TML), plus a TML association-control interface and a listener interface. (PDF p. 19)
  • The user name is 3-16 characters and equals the authority identifier used in BIND. The password is 6-16 octets. The authentication level is 'all' (every PDU except PEER-ABORT), 'bind' (only BIND invocation and return) or 'none'. (PDF p. 44)
  • Credentials follow the 'Protected 1' simple authentication procedure of ISO/IEC 9594-8. A DER-encoded HashInput holds the time as an 8-octet CCSDS CDS code without P-field, a random number (0..2147483647), the user name and the password. (PDF p. 44)
  • The hash function is SHA-256 (FIPS 180-4). ISP1Credentials carries the time, the random number and 'theProtected' (20..32 octets; 20 octets keeps compatibility with SHA-1 implementations). (PDF p. 46)
  • The DEL encodes SLE PDUs with the ASN.1 types of the applicable service specification and version, using BER. The first PDU on an association must be the BIND invocation. (PDF p. 46)
  • The TML maps one SLE association to exactly one TCP connection and uses three message types: 1 SLE PDU, 2 TML Context and 3 TML Heartbeat. Each message has an 8-octet header: a 1-octet type, 3 reserved octets and a 4-octet body length. (PDF p. 47)
  • The TML context message body is 12 octets: 'ISP1' (hex 49 53 50 31), 3 reserved octets, protocol version 1, a 2-octet heartbeat-interval and a 2-octet dead-factor. The heartbeat message body is empty. All integers are big-endian. (PDF p. 48)
  • Heartbeat: the HBT timer (heartbeat-interval) triggers a heartbeat message when the link is idle. When the HBR timer (heartbeat-interval × dead-factor) expires, the TML issues TCP-ABORT with the diagnostic 'heartbeat timeout'. An interval of 0 disables the mechanism. (PDF p. 49)
  • PEER-ABORT sends its diagnostic as one byte of TCP urgent data. The receiver discards buffered data up to the urgent pointer and then reads the diagnostic. (PDF p. 27)
  • The TML states are S0 CLOSED, S1 TML STARTING, S2 DATA TRANSFER, S3 PEER ABORTING and S4 TML CLOSING. (PDF p. 58)
  • ISP1's precursor is ESA's 'Specification of a SLE API Proxy for TCP/IP and ASN.1' (SLES-SW-API-0002-TOS-GCI). Its authentication scheme and service instance identifier come from ESA's SLE C++ API (SLES-SW-API-0001-TOS-GCI). (PDF p. 67)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The CCSDS Recommended Practice that defines a C++ Application Program Interface for SLE transfer services. It is a component-based API, independent of the communications technology, that SLE user applications (such as a mission control system) and provider applications (ground station equipment) can link against, so that SLE software packages can be exchanged and reused. It also eases gateways between different technologies. This core document covers what is common to all services; the service-specific parts are in the companion books 915.1/915.2/915.5 (RAF, RCF, ROCF) and 916.1/916.3 (FCLTU, FSP). See SLE over TCP/IP (ISP1) and the SLE API.

The API supports three generations of service specifications, identified by the BIND version number. It deliberately omits BIND version negotiation and provider-initiated binding. Section 2 is a UML logical model with six packages: API Proxy (technology-specific communication, the PDU translator, access control and peer authentication), API Service Element (it creates and configures service instances, handles BIND/UNBIND and enforces the SLE state tables), Common Control Interfaces, SLE Application (interfaces the application must supply, for example ISLE_Reporter, ISLE_Trace and ISLE_TimeSource), SLE Operations (operation objects such as ISLE_Bind and ISLE_TransferBuffer) and SLE Utilities (time, credentials, service instance identifiers). Section 3 specifies each component, including the 'Protected 1' credential generation with a DER-encoded HashInput, which Cor. 1 points to CCSDS 913.1-B for the hash algorithm, and the handling of threads and events. Section 4 gives the state tables for associations and service instances. Annex A is the normative C++ interface specification. Annex B defines COM-style HRESULT result codes, Annex C the service instance identifier for version-1 services, Annex D a COM-like 'simple component model' (IUnknown-style interfaces with reference counting), and Annex E the conformance options.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Issue 2 (September 2015) supersedes issue 1 (October 2008). Technical Corrigendum 1 (August 2016) makes the one-way hash function refer to CCSDS 913.1-B and removes the reference to the Secure Hash Algorithm standard. (PDF p. 7)
  • The Recommended Practice defines a C++ API for SLE transfer services that is independent of the communications technology. The API can be configured for user or provider applications and simplifies gateways. (PDF p. 11)
  • Only the parts common to all SLE services are defined here. The service-specific APIs are in CCSDS 915.1-M-2 (RAF), 915.2-M-2 (RCF), 915.5-M-2 (ROCF), 916.1-M-2 (FCLTU) and 916.3-M-2 (FSP). (PDF p. 11)
  • Exceptions to SLE conformance: BIND version-number negotiation is not supported (an unsupported version is rejected with 'version number not supported'), and provider-initiated binding for return services is not included. (PDF p. 12)
  • Three generations are supported. G1: RAF, RCF and FCLTU with BIND version 1. G2: RAF, RCF and FCLTU version 2, plus ROCF and FSP version 1. G3: RAF, RCF, ROCF, FCLTU and FSP with BIND version 4, as printed. (PDF p. 12)
  • G1 interoperates with peers that follow the TML of ESOC's 'Specification of a SLE API Proxy for TCP/IP and ASN.1' (SLES-SW-API-0002-TOS-GCI, Issue 1.1, February 2001). G2 and G3 interoperate with peers that follow ISP1 (CCSDS 913.1-B-2). (PDF p. 13)
  • The API is decomposed into the packages API Proxy, API Service Element, Common Control Interfaces, SLE Application, SLE Operations and SLE Utilities. (PDF p. 29)
  • The API Proxy hides all technology-specific aspects and performs system-level access control and peer authentication. Its PDU Translator is the only proxy element that depends on the SLE service type. (PDF p. 30)
  • Credentials are generated and checked with the 'Protected 1' procedure of ISO/IEC 9594-8, applied to a DER-encoded HashInput (time, random number, user name, password). Cor. 1 points to 913.1-B for the hash function. (PDF p. 143)
  • Result codes follow the COM HRESULT layout: a 1-bit severity, 2 reserved bits, a facility and a 16-bit code. SLE-specific codes are in facility ITF (4), above hex 0200. (PDF p. 312)
  • The API defines its own minimal COM-like component model, because COM itself needs a special run-time and registry that are not available on all platforms. (PDF p. 321)
  • Conformance allows limited implementations, such as a 'lightweight' user-only API or a provider-only API, through defined optional features of the Proxy and the Service Element. (PDF p. 330)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A short CCSDS Magenta Book that adds the Return All Frames (RAF)-specific part of the SLE Application Program Interface. The generic C++ API (component model, service instances, operation objects, proxies) is defined in the API core specification CCSDS 914.0-M-2. This book adds only the RAF-specific classes, interfaces, checks and status handling needed to build RAF users and providers on top of it. The service itself is specified in the RAF Blue Book, cited here as issue 3 (the library holds issue 5). The wiki pages are SLE over TCP/IP and the SLE API and SLE return services.

Section 1 states that the API supports three RAF generations, identified by BIND version numbers 1, 2 and 4. Generation 1 interoperates through ESOC's earlier TCP/IP proxy specification, and Generations 2 and 3 through the ISP1 transport mapping (CCSDS 913.1-B-2). Section 2 extends the API model. RAF SI User and RAF SI Provider classes are added, and the provider exports the IRAF_SIAdmin (configuration: delivery-mode, latency-limit, transfer-buffer-size) and IRAF_SIUpdate (lock statuses, production status) interfaces. Five RAF operation objects are added (START, TRANSFER-DATA, SYNC-NOTIFY, STATUS-REPORT, GET-PARAMETER), and a security section covers privacy, integrity, authentication levels and threats. Section 3 gives the normative behaviour: configuration rules, how frame counters and requested-frame-quality are maintained, the START time-window checks per delivery mode, and SYNC-NOTIFY restrictions. Annex A gives the C++ type definitions and interfaces.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The API core specification (CCSDS 914.0-M-2) defines a C++ API for SLE transfer services at a generic level. Each service needs a supplementary Recommended Practice, and this one covers RAF. (PDF p. 9)
  • The API supports three RAF generations: Generation 1 (BIND version 1, draft RAF 911.1-R-1.7), Generation 2 (version 2, RAF B-2) and Generation 3 (version 4, RAF B-3). Support for Generations 1 and 2 is for backward compatibility for a limited time. (PDF p. 10)
  • Generation 1 implementations interoperate with peers that follow ESOC's 'Specification of a SLE API Proxy for TCP/IP and ASN.1' (SLES-SW-API-0002-TOS-GCI, Issue 1.1, February 2001). Generations 2 and 3 use the ISP1 transport mapping layer. (PDF p. 10)
  • The RAF SI Provider class exports IRAF_SIAdmin for RAF configuration parameters and IRAF_SIUpdate for dynamic status. It answers RAF-GET-PARAMETER and generates RAF-STATUS-REPORT autonomously. (PDF p. 17)
  • The RAF configuration parameters are delivery-mode, latency-limit (for the timely and complete online modes) and transfer-buffer-size, which is the maximum number of TRANSFER-DATA and SYNC-NOTIFY invocations per transfer buffer PDU. (PDF p. 28)
  • The status information comprises number-of-error-free-frames-delivered, number-of-frames-delivered, requested-frame-quality, the frame-sync, symbol-sync, subcarrier and carrier lock statuses, and the production-status. (PDF p. 21)
  • RAF-specific operation objects are IRAF_Start, IRAF_TransferData, IRAF_SyncNotify, IRAF_StatusReport and IRAF_GetParameter. BIND, UNBIND, STOP, SCHEDULE-STATUS-REPORT, PEER-ABORT and the TRANSFER-BUFFER pseudo-operation use the common SLE operation objects. (PDF p. 22)
  • SLE transfer authentication can be set to one of three levels: every invocation and return, only BIND, or none. (PDF p. 25)
  • Frame counters are incremented when a TRANSFER-BUFFER PDU is sent to the user. Frames in a discarded buffer are not counted. (PDF p. 30)
  • For RAF-START in offline mode, the start and stop times must not be null and the stop time must be in the past. In online mode, the times must lie within the scheduled provision period. (PDF p. 32)
  • In offline mode, RAF-SYNC-NOTIFY may not report loss of frame sync, a production status change or data discarded for excessive backlog. In timely online mode, data discard for excessive backlog is not allowed. (PDF p. 33)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A CCSDS Magenta Book that adds the Forward Space Packet (FSP)-specific part of the SLE Application Program Interface. The generic C++ API (component model, service instances, operation objects, proxies) is defined in the API core specification CCSDS 914.0-M-2. This book adds what an implementation needs to provide or use the SLE FSP service, which carries telecommand Space Packets to a ground station that runs COP-1 on its behalf. It is the FSP counterpart of the RAF API book CCSDS 915.1-M-2. See also SLE over TCP/IP and the SLE API.

Section 1 states that two FSP generations are supported: Generation 2 (BIND version 1, FSP B-1) and Generation 3 (BIND version 4, FSP B-2). There is no Generation 1. Section 2 extends the API model with FSP SI User and FSP SI Provider classes. The provider exports three interfaces. IFSP_SIAdmin holds the configuration (APID list, MAP list, virtual channel, maximum frame and packet length, blocking and multiplexing settings, packet buffer size). IFSP_FOPMonitor holds the FOP-1 parameters (sliding window, timer, transmission limit, V(S), FOP state). IFSP_SIUpdate receives the production events (packet started, radiated or acknowledged, buffer empty, production status change, VC aborted, directive completed). Table 2-1 maps each event to the status parameters it updates and the FSP-ASYNC-NOTIFY it triggers. A long subsection explains which checks are left to the application in multi-threaded designs: production status, blocked state, time windows, and APID/version/type checks on the opaque packet data. It also explains the special return handling for TRANSFER-DATA, INVOKE-DIRECTIVE and THROW-EVENT. Section 3 gives the normative component behaviour and diagnostic ordering, and Annex A (about 90 pages) gives the C++ types, operation objects and service instance interfaces.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The book specifies only the FSP-specific extensions to the SLE API core: functionality, interfaces and externally visible behaviour. It does not cover implementations, internal design or communications technology. (PDF p. 10)
  • Two FSP generations are supported: Generation 2 (BIND version 1, FSP 912.3-B-1) and Generation 3 (BIND version 4, FSP 912.3-B-2). Generation 1 does not apply because the first FSP issue was written as part of Generation 2. Generation 2 support is for backward compatibility for a limited time. (PDF p. 11)
  • The FSP SI Provider exports IFSP_SIAdmin (configuration), IFSP_FOPMonitor (FOP parameters, used only to answer GET-PARAMETER) and IFSP_SIUpdate (production events). The application must keep the FOP parameters updated, whatever the service instance state. (PDF p. 20)
  • IFSP_SIUpdate methods are PacketStarted, PacketRadiated, PacketAcknowledged, BufferEmpty, PacketNotStarted, ProductionStatusChange, VCAborted, NoDirectiveCapability, DirectiveCapabilityOnline, DirectiveCompleted and EventProcCompleted. Each updates status parameters and may trigger an FSP-ASYNC-NOTIFY. (PDF p. 22)
  • Configuration parameters include apid-list, blocking-timeout-period, blocking-usage, directive-invocation-enabled, map-list, maximum-frame-length, maximum-packet-length, segment-header, VC multiplexing control and scheme, virtual-channel and maximum-packet-buffer-size. Generation 3 adds bit-lock-required and rf-available-required. (PDF p. 26)
  • The FOP parameters handled are fop-sliding-window, timeout-type, timer-initial, transmission-limit, transmitter-frame-sequence-number, fop-state, and MAP multiplexing control and scheme. (PDF p. 27)
  • Status counters are kept separately for AD (sequence-controlled) and BD (expedited) packets received, processed and radiated, plus number-of-packets-acknowledged and packet-buffer-available. (PDF p. 28)
  • Production status 'halted' rejects both BIND and START. 'Interrupted' accepts BIND but rejects START. 'Configured' and 'operational' accept both. (PDF p. 30)
  • Several TRANSFER-DATA invocations can be in transit. When a check fails, the service element may therefore pass the operation to the application, which inserts the next expected packet identification and buffer size. INVOKE-DIRECTIVE and THROW-EVENT are handled the same way. (PDF p. 31)
  • When a packet cannot be processed (non-operational production or expired latest start time), the service instance becomes blocked until the user sends FSP-STOP and then FSP-START. A blocked AD mode is cleared by a TRANSFER-DATA with mode 'sequence controlled and unblock AD'. (PDF p. 32)
  • The API treats packets as opaque, so the service element is not required to check APID, packet version or packet type. These checks are left to the application. (PDF p. 33)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The CCSDS Recommended Standard for the Monitored Data Cross Support Transfer Service (MD-CSTS). CSTS is the family of cross support transfer services documented alongside the SLE transfer services. Through MD-CSTS, a mission can watch the ground station that is supporting it. The mission can receive cyclic or on-change reports of monitored parameters, query current values, and receive notifications of events for everything in a service package: antennas, RF carriers, frame decoders, and the SLE and CSTS provider instances. The service delivers only current values, not history. It is built from procedures of the CSTS Specification Framework (CCSDS 921.1-B-2, not in the library) and uses the SANA Functional Resource registry to name parameters and events. The relevant wiki pages are SLE service management and SLE over TCP/IP and the SLE API, since MD-CSTS PDUs are carried by ISP1.

Section 2 explains production and provision and the naming scheme. A Parameter Name combines a Parameter Identifier (an OID on the CCSDS registration tree) with a Functional Resource Name (type OID plus instance number), and Event Names are built the same way. Section 2 then gives a long operational scenario. Section 3 composes the service from four procedures: one Association Control; the prime On-Change-Option Cyclic Report (1..); an optional Information Query (0..1); and Notification (0..). Section 4 specifies the on-change extension to the framework Cyclic Report. Sections 5-7 refine Information Query and Notification and set the inherited configuration parameters. Sections 8-9 define the service-level functional resource items mdResponseTimeout, mdProdStat and mdProdStatChange. The annexes give the ICS proforma, the ASN.1 OIDs and PDUs, the production-process requirements, security and SANA considerations, and an informative example Functional Resource set (antenna, CCSDS 401 carriers, FCLTU and RAF providers).

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• MD-CSTS lets a mission receive cyclic reports on, and query current values of, the parameters of the cross support services provided by a Cross Support Complex (an Earth Space Link Terminal), and receive event notifications. (PDF p. 12)
  • The standard does not define which parameters are reported or which events are notified, nor how they are measured. (PDF p. 13)
  • The service delivers only current parameter values. It cannot deliver stored values from earlier times. (PDF p. 25)
  • A service package may contain several MD-CSTS instances. Each instance can report all monitored parameters and events of the package, including RF links and SLE transfer service instances. (PDF p. 26)
  • Implementations must use the SANA Functional Resource Registry as the normative source of Functional Resource Types, parameters and events. Annex F is only an example. (PDF p. 28)
  • A Parameter Name combines a Parameter Identifier (a Published Identifier OID, for example ccsds-401-carrier-xmit-actual-carrier-freq) with a Functional Resource Name (Functional Resource Type OID plus a positive Functional Resource Instance Number assigned at scheduling). (PDF p. 29)
  • The On-Change-Option Cyclic Report procedure lets the user choose a parameter list, a delivery cycle, and whether to report every value or only changed values. Several instances can run concurrently. (PDF p. 30)
  • The service consists of Association Control (exactly 1), On-Change-Option Cyclic Report as prime procedure (1..), Information Query (0..1) and Notification (0..). (PDF p. 50)
  • With the on-change option, a parameter whose value changes and changes back between two cycles is not reported. (PDF p. 51)
  • Cyclic reporting of procedure configuration parameters is optional, because those parameters are static for the life of an MD service instance. (PDF p. 52)
  • MD-CSTS supports the framework's response-timeout and production-status parameters (mdResponseTimeout, mdProdStat) and the production status change event (mdProdStatChange). It does not support the production configuration change event. (PDF p. 65)
  • The Monitored Data Production Process must keep each monitored parameter's value until a new one is available. It delivers values as QualifiedParameter and events as [eventName: eventValue] pairs. (PDF p. 98)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A journal-style preprint describing the whole ground segment of CHEOPS, ESA's first small-class (S-class) mission, launched 18 December 2019 into a 690 km Sun-synchronous orbit. Unusually for ESA, all operations are the responsibility of the consortium. The Mission Operations Center (MOC) at INTA's CEIT near Madrid and the Science Operations Center (SOC) at the University of Geneva were built from scratch to ECSS standards or by reusing existing systems, on a 50 M€ ESA budget and a 4-year development.

The paper follows the weekly operational chain. Users submit observation requests through PHT2. Flight dynamics (GMV Focus/Autofocus) produces orbits and ground-station contacts. A Deimos-built MPS with a genetic-algorithm Schedule Solver produces the XML Activity Plan. At the MOC the Activity Plan is checked against constraints such as the Sun Exclusion Angle and converted into telecommands. The mission control system is SCOS-2000 version 5.4.2, configured through its MIB and driven by a Python automation library under GMV's Flyplan. Its CommandBuilder maps activities to TCs in SSF stack files. During the 4-6 daily passes, Auto Stacks uplink TCs in AD mode. SMON retrieves parameters from the packet archive (PARC, MySQL), and the external interface supports automatic commanding. SCOS-2000 time correlation handles the free-running on-board oscillator. Post-pass tools (TM Processor, TM Replayer, RGTgenerator, HKTMreporter) split virtual channels, detect frame-counter gaps and produce TC, event and out-of-limits reports.

The SOC pipeline (monitor4cheops, Preprocessing using the MIB, Quick Look, Data Reduction), the archive, MUST/WebMUST trending from RAPID files, the Simulus/SIMSAT simulator with SLE, and the hardware architecture complete the picture. The automation keeps staffing at 3-4 people for the SOC and 5 for the MOC.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• CHEOPS launched on 18 December 2019 on Soyuz VS23 into a nadir-locked Sun-synchronous orbit at 690 km, with a 98.7 min period, and is visible from the ground station about 4-6 times a day. All mission operations are the responsibility of the consortium rather than ESA. (PDF p. 1)
  • The S-class status capped ESA's contribution at 50 M€ (including launch) with a 4-year development. The consortium matched it, for a total of 105 M€ covering the nominal mission, which ended in 2023. (PDF p. 2)
  • The SOC's MPS (Java, Eclipse RCP client, RESTful services, PostgreSQL) builds a weekly Activity Plan starting on Saturday. A genetic-algorithm 'Schedule Solver' written in C optimises a merit function of guaranteed-time to guest-observer ratio, priority and fill factor. (PDF p. 4)
  • At the MOC, GFTS (Generic File Transfer System) receives the Activity Plan and StarMaps. Flyplan (GMV) orchestrates the automation, and its monitorCHEOPS activity watches configured paths to trigger processing, making operations data-driven as well as time-driven. (PDF p. 5)
  • CONCHECK verifies that every slew respects the Sun Exclusion Angle, initially 120 degrees and relaxed to 117 degrees from February 2025. (PDF p. 6)
  • The CHEOPS MCS is based on SCOS-2000 version 5.4.2, configured through environment variables and the MIB. The CommandBuilder maps each Activity Plan activity to one or more TCs using a rule file, and writes them to an SSF file, an ASCII file readable by any standard SCOS-2000 using the MIB. (PDF p. 6)
  • Received TM is converted into packets and stored in the SCOS-2000 packet archive (PARC), which archives TM, TC and event data in a MySQL database. (PDF p. 6)
  • Two Auto Stack instances are reserved for automated operations. SMON provides TM parameter values from the PARC (latest, past, or next sample). TCs are uplinked in AD mode with acknowledgement stages for ground station and on-board reception and execution. (PDF p. 7)
  • CHEOPS time comes from a free-running local oscillator rather than GPS. A SCOS-2000 time correlation feature uses a linear approximation and updates the coefficients whenever the monitored accuracy falls below the requirement. (PDF p. 7)
  • Post-pass: the SCOS-2000 TM Processor splits ground-station files into one TM file per virtual channel (real-time HK, recorded HK, science). TM Replayer ingests recorded HK into the PARC. Gaps are detected from jumps in the transfer frame virtual channel frame counter, and RGTgenerator produces the TCReport for the MPS. (PDF p. 8)
  • The SOC Preprocessing chain decodes and reformats the TM according to the spacecraft's MIB, checks for missing packets, time-tags data with the OBT-UTC correlation and converts packets to FITS. (PDF p. 10)
  • ESA's MUST and WebMUST are used for TM visualisation and trend analysis as alternatives to SCOS-2000. The MUST database is updated with RAPID files generated by SCOS-2000, and the Python MUSTLink API serves periodic trending. (PDF p. 12)
  • The spacecraft simulator is based on ESA's Simulus 5.4 and SIMSAT, and communicates with ground stations via the Space Link Extension protocol. Automation keeps routine staffing at 3-4 people for the SOC and 5 for the MOC. (PDF p. 12)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The EDDS Configuration and Installation Guide (CIG) tells ESOC system administrators and EDDS developers how to build, deploy, configure and run the EGOS Data Dissemination System release v2.3.0. EDDS gives external users web-service and MMI access to data held by the SCOS-2000 packet archive (PARC), the DARC data archive and the FARC file archive (archives).

Section 3 lists the platform (SLES 12, Java 8, Tomcat, MariaDB, ActiveMQ, OpenLDAP, Pure-FTPd), explains the Ant/Maven build and the long edds-deploy.properties file, and describes deploying the separate components: Archiver, Delivery Manager, Web Service, MMI (standalone or web), EDDS Server, Request Submitter, Stream Client, Performance Processor and Migrator. It also covers firewall ports, HTTPS, logging, SFTP and SFT transfer of response files, and serving several missions from one Delivery Manager.

Section 4 is the most useful part for understanding data handling. It gives the full EDDS Server property table and explains how to enable services per mission, XSL transformations of results, and which SCOS-2000 MIB files each mission domain must supply: pid.dat (SPID to APID conversion), tpcf.dat (packet descriptions), command subsystem and host files, MISCbase.ids and MISCcontext_SHARED.sta, plus mapping files for command source types and on-board-queue request status. Appendix A explains how EDDS decodes raw packet headers and the hexadecimal TC history records it receives over CORBA from the PARC, using XML structure files with field offsets, lengths, verification-stage positions and mission custom fields. The remaining appendices cover the SMON server, ActiveMQ, FARC subscriptions, RSA keys, backups and LDAP.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Intended readers are ESOC system administrators and EDDS developers; the guide covers build, deployment and mission-specific configuration of EDDS v2.3.0. (PDF p. 8)
  • Prerequisites start with SLES 12, JDK 8 (1.8.0_72) for compiling and JRE 8 for running, Apache Tomcat with the manager application, and MariaDB, versions per the SLES 12 baseline. (PDF p. 10)
  • Further prerequisites: MariaDB max_allowed_packet raised to 50M, Maven, Ant, ActiveMQ, OpenLDAP and Pure-FTPd; GFTS is recommended when the EDDS Server and Delivery Manager run on different machines. (PDF p. 11)
  • When the EDDS Server and Delivery Manager are on separate machines, SFT 'Sender' and 'Receiver' instances move response files into the 'edds-server-completed' folder; one Delivery Manager can serve multiple missions. (PDF p. 57)
  • Each EDDS Server is configured for one SCOS-2000 mission; missing properties fall back to defaults with a warning in the log. (PDF p. 58)
  • The services offered per mission are set with SUPPORTED_BATCH_REQUESTS and SUPPORTED_STREAM_REQUESTS, listing request types from the DataAccessDataElement type in common.xsd; batch and stream requests are routed through ActiveMQ queues with a MISSION_NAME selector. (PDF p. 69)
  • EDDS needs MIB files per mission domain under MIB_FILES_LOCATION: pid.dat converts SPIDs into APIDs and tpcf.dat gives TM packet descriptions; without them filters such as an APID search for TM packets fail. (PDF p. 72)
  • CMD_SUBSYSTEM_FILE, CMD_HOST_FILE and MISCbase.ids map subsystem, source and domain IDs in TC history packets to names for the TC report; MISCcontext_SHARED.sta maps domains and data streams for the data provision services. (PDF p. 72)
  • CMDsourceTypeMapping.properties maps the command source type number (MANUAL_STACK, AUTO_STACK, EXT_SOURCE, TC_SPACON, OBQM_DISP, SMF_SOURCE) to long and short descriptions in the Packet TC report. (PDF p. 73)
  • CMD_ttRqstObqStatusMapping.properties maps 16 on-board-queue request status values (TT_EXECUTED to TT_UNKNOWN) and must exist under config/MIB/0 or TC packet decoding may fail. (PDF p. 74)
  • Raw TM, TC and EV header layouts written to raw output files are defined by XML files based on RawPktHeaders.xsd (for example fields 'Apid' and 'Type', or 'ServiceType' and 'ServiceSubType'). (PDF p. 79)
  • Because the PARC returns TC history records hex-encoded over CORBA, EDDS decodes them with a TCPacketStructure XML file giving offset, length, type and occurrence of each field, the verification-stage positions (verStates sized by CMD_NUM_VER_STAGES) and optional mission CustomFields. (PDF p. 80)
  • TC_PKT_CMD_LEN_PAR_INFO, the length of the INFO field in bytes, must be 3 for SCOS-2000 6.2.0 and later and 2 for earlier versions. (PDF p. 80)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
This is issue 25.0 (2025) of the EDDS Configuration and Installation Guide, covering release v3.6.1 of the EGOS Data Dissemination System. It keeps the structure of the 2018 issue (library item cig-i14r0) but documents the modernised platform and the integration with the European Ground Systems Common Core (EGS-CC).

Section 3 describes prerequisites (SLES 15, OpenJDK/JRE 11, Tomcat 9, MariaDB, ActiveMQ, OpenLDAP, Pure-FTPd), the build and the large edds-deploy.properties table, and deploying the Archiver, Delivery Manager, Web Service, MMI, EDDS Server and optional tools. The property tables now include EGS-CC settings: a REST data-access endpoint, an HTTP or Kafka retrieval mode and a batch size. They also add Egscc* request types (parameters, parameter definitions, TM and TC packet reports, raw TM, activity reports) next to the classic SCOS-2000 ones, and a list of data sources ('DARC', 'PARC', 'HARC').

Section 4 adds a short subsection on EGS-CC missions, which only need an EDDS domain named after the mission's dataspace in the HBase cluster. It keeps the SCOS-2000 mission configuration: server properties, enabling services, retrying failed requests, XSL transformations and the MIB files each domain must supply (pid.dat, tpcf.dat, command subsystem and host files, MISCbase.ids, MISCcontext_SHARED.sta, source-type and OBQ-status mappings). Appendix A explains how raw packet headers and PARC TC history records are decoded, and adds XML custom-field definitions for TC records obtained from the SCOS-2000 data provision service. A new Appendix L describes the GitLab DevOps pipeline and the per-mission configuration directories.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Issue 25.0 corresponds to EDDS v3.6.1i1; the change log runs from issue 1.0 (2010-05-28) to 25.0 (2025-03-07), with issues 15.0 to 24.0 covering EDDS v2.4.0 to v3.6.0. (PDF p. 3)
  • The only DCR entry for this issue is EDDS-1396, upgrading Tomcat to 9.0.100. (PDF p. 3)
  • Prerequisites: SLES 15 (baseline SLES15-064-ESOCL01-i3r1), OpenJDK 11 (11.0.20+9) for compilation and JRE 11 for running, plus Tomcat and MariaDB from the SLES 15 baseline. (PDF p. 10)
  • edds.server.supported.batch.requests lists request types such as Param, ParamStatistics, ParamDefinition, PktTm, PktTc, PktEvRaw, PktTmRaw, PktTmGapReport, ArchiveFile, OolRecordReport and EGS-CC variants (EgsccParam, EgsccPktTm, EgsccPktTmRaw, EgsccActivityReport); edds.server.supported_data_sources takes 'DARC','PARC','HARC'. (PDF p. 17)
  • Stream request types are ParamStream, PktTmStream, PktTcStream, PktEvStream and OolStream; edds.server.enable.egscc turns on the EGS-CC integration. (PDF p. 18)
  • EGS-CC data are retrieved from a REST data-access endpoint (edds.egscc.rest.dataaccess.url) using HTTP or Kafka retrieval modes, with a default batch size of 5000. (PDF p. 34)
  • EGS-CC missions need no mission-specific configuration beyond a domain named after the mission dataspace in the HBase cluster; their configuration files are under config/HARC. (PDF p. 61)
  • As in earlier issues, pid.dat (SPID to APID) and tpcf.dat (TM packet descriptions) from each SCOS-2000 domain must be copied to the EDDS MIB location. (PDF p. 76)
  • TC records from the SCOS-2000 data provision service are decoded with DataProvisionCustomField XML files whose FieldPath follows the CHIScommandRecord.idl structure, for example command.record.releaseInf.subsystemName. (PDF p. 86)
  • TC_PKT_CMD_LEN_PAR_INFO is 3 for SCOS-2000 6.2.0 and later and 2 for earlier versions. (PDF p. 87)
  • Appendix L: EDDS DevOps pipelines run from the ESA GitLab project, and deployment is per mission, using a directory per mission under edds/edds-mission-config holding server and delivery-manager configuration. (PDF p. 118)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A one-page table, published on ESA's Cosmos web site, that lists the documents of the common Herschel EGSE effort: the shared electrical ground support equipment for the Herschel instruments' tests. The page carries no title, date or author; the title used here comes from the file name, and the PDF metadata name Luc Dubbeldam as author of a file converted from an Excel sheet in November 2014.

Each row gives a category (EGSE, CDMS simulator, router, test-equipment interface (TEI), test control, MIB, on-board software maintenance facility), a document type (terms of reference, URD, plan, specification, SSD, SOW, ICD, SUM, report), the title, the document identifier, an issue or draft status and the responsible party (HIFI, PACS, SPIRE or ESA). Nineteen documents are listed, twelve of them under HIFI. They include the Herschel EGSE integration plan, the EGSE-ILT user requirements document, the real-time analysis URD, the CDMS simulator requirements and interface test specification, the router SOW and packet router ICD, ESA's EGSE Gateway ICD, the TEI specification, SOW and URD, the test-control SOW, the TTA-2000 test-technology SUM, the MIB-editor requirements and evaluation report, and the on-board software maintenance facility URD.

For this wiki it is a map of the early Herschel instrument EGSE document tree, useful to trace documents cited elsewhere: the integration plan (library item cosmos-herschel-egse-integration-plan), its reference documents, and the EGSE Gateway ICD that the EMCS user manual (emcs-sum-4-0) lists as applicable document [A1].

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• 19 documents are listed in 7 categories: EGSE (5), CDMSsim (3), Router (3), TEI (3), Test control (2), MIB (2) and OBSMF (1). (PDF p. 1)
  • HIFI is responsible for 12 of the 19 documents, PACS for 2, SPIRE for 1 and ESA for 2; two rows name no owner. (PDF p. 1)
  • The MIB category contains the MIB-editor requirements (SRON-U/HIFI/SP/2000-002) and the MIB-editor evaluation report (SRON-U/HIFI/RP/2001-001, status 2). (PDF p. 1)
  • ESA supplies the EGSEGateway ICD (TOS-GCE/98.015/PSH) and the test technology activities TTA-2000 SUM (SCO-TTA-SUM-0001). (PDF p. 1)
  • Three documents have no identifier ('none'): the EGSE working group terms of reference, the CDMS simulator software specification and the on-board SW maintenance facility URD. (PDF p. 1)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Issue 1 (identical to draft 4) of the plan, dated 6 November 2001 and prepared by Luc Dubbeldam and Erich Wiezorrek, that specifies the activities and responsibilities for integrating the EGSE for Instrument Level Tests (EGSE-ILT) of the three Herschel instruments. It lists the EGSE-ILT building blocks and who delivers each: SCOS-2000 (ESA), the SCOS gateway (ESTeC), the test-equipment interface and the TM-TC router (HIFI), test control (PACS), the CDMS simulator (SPIRE), and OBSM and the MIB editor (ESA). A block diagram shows the instrument, the 1553B CDMS simulator, the router, a test client, the TEI, the EGSE and SCOS gateways, the HCSS, test control, SCOS-2000 and the MIB.

The plan is a sequence of incremental integration tests, each with a configuration figure, the functions to be demonstrated, test prerequisites and numbered steps: the router (TM packets from a test client to SCOS 2000 and TC packets back, plus throughput), the test-equipment interface, the CDMS simulator (routing, its command interface and a time packet protocol still to be confirmed), test control (retrieving housekeeping values from SCOS 2000, uplinking telecommands, test procedures, command mnemonic sequences and autonomy procedures), and the interface between test control and the HCSS. Every SCOS-based test starts by importing or loading a test MIB that describes the TM and TC packets used; the router test also starts ESA's TTA-2000. On-board software maintenance (OBSM) is left as an open item.

It is short, but it shows how SCOS-2000 and its MIB sat at the centre of the Herschel instrument EGSE from 2001. The EGSE version of SCOS-2000 later supplied to the instrument teams is described in the EMCS user manual (library item emcs-sum-4-0).

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Purpose: specify the activities and responsibilities required for the integration of the EGSE-ILT for the three Herschel instruments. (PDF p. 3)
  • Deliveries: SCOS-2000 by ESA, SCOS gateway by ESTeC, test-equipment interface and TM-TC router by HIFI, test control by PACS, CDMS-simulator by SPIRE, OBSM and MIB editor by ESA. (PDF p. 3)
  • Router test: demonstrate routing of TM packets from a test client to SCOS 2000, routing of TC packets from SCOS 2000 to the test client, and throughput; steps include importing the test MIB into SCOS 2000 and starting TTA-2000, the router, the EGSE gateway and the SCOS gateway. (PDF p. 5)
  • Each test configuration requires a MIB describing the TM and TC packets used. (PDF p. 5)
  • The TEI is very likely a LabView interface, so a PC running LabView may suffice as test equipment. (PDF p. 8)
  • CDMS-simulator tests follow RD.1 (section 4.8); handling of the time packet protocol is TBC and how to test it is an open question. (PDF p. 9)
  • Test-control test: retrieve actual HK parameter values from SCOS 2000, uplink TCs from test control, and exercise test procedures, command mnemonic sequences and autonomy procedures defined in RD.2 sections 3.3.1-3.3.3. (PDF p. 11)
  • Section 4 (OPEN ITEM: OBSM) has a heading but no content. (PDF p. 13)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The Herschel/Planck Operations Interface Requirements Document (OIRD), issue 2.2 of 2003, prepared at ESOC by S. J. Dodsworth and S. Matussi. It identifies the requirements on the Herschel and Planck spacecraft and their payloads that are needed to conduct mission operations, and the operational data and documentation that industry and the instrument teams must deliver to the Mission Operations Centre (MOC).

Section 2 gives operability and autonomy requirements: no need for ground reactions faster than 3 minutes, two independent telecommands for hazardous functions, self-contained telemetry values in contiguous bits, contributing parameters of synthetic parameters in the same packet, one on-board central time reference with on-ground correlation to UTC, and 48 hours of operation without ground contact. Section 3, derived from the draft ECSS Packet Utilisation Standard, begins with a table of PUS services mandatory, optional or not applicable to the instruments and then states requirements per service: APID and SID allocation rules, telecommand verification, device commanding, housekeeping, event reporting with a critical events log, memory management, function and time management, the on-board mission timeline, on-board monitoring, packet transmission control, packet stores, test, OBCP management and science data transfer. Requirements marked P apply to spacecraft and payloads, PO to the spacecraft with possible relevance to payloads.

Section 4 and the annexes define the Satellite Users Manual, the Satellite Database (complying with the SCOS-2000 Database Import ICD issue 5.1, with configuration-control and spacecraft-configuration files and versioned deliveries up to launch), the Flight Dynamics Database, on-board software deliveries, and naming conventions for procedures and timelines.

For this wiki it links PUS, the SCOS-2000 MIB and the Herschel/Planck operations concept.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Section 3 is derived from the ECSS Packet Utilisation Standard [AD-1]; the Space/Ground ICD [AD-2] and the Packet Structure ICD (PSICD) [AD-5] contain the full TM/TC frame and packet details. (PDF p. 10)
  • Requirements marked 'P' apply to the spacecraft and the payloads, 'PO' to the spacecraft with possible (non-mandatory) relevance to payloads; unmarked requirements apply to the spacecraft only. (PDF p. 10)
  • In routine science operations ground contact lasts a few hours per day, during which about 24 hours of stored telemetry are downlinked and the next schedule uplinked; operations use the same TM/TC database as the EGSE. (PDF p. 11)
  • A specific telecommand instance is identified by the application ID and sequence control fields; its meaning by type and subtype in the data field header; an acknowledgement field selects the verification reports required. (PDF p. 11)
  • On-board monitoring reports limit or expected-status transitions with event packets, which the document notes is not in accordance with the PUS transition reporting list. (PDF p. 13)
  • CTRL-1: in no mission phase shall the MOC need to send telecommands with a response time of less than 3 minutes. (PDF p. 15)
  • TC-1: execution of hazardous functions is implemented by means of two independent telecommands. (PDF p. 15)
  • TC-4: a telecommand packet contains one and only one telecommand function; TC-9/TC-10: on-board data changes and readouts use dedicated telecommands, not multi-purpose software load/dump commands. (PDF p. 16)
  • TM-12: a parameter value is transmitted in contiguous bits within one packet; TM-16: all contributing parameters of a synthetic parameter should be in the same packet; TM-17: all packets include the time field in the data field header. (PDF p. 18)
  • TIM-1: all on-board timing (TC time-tagging, application software, TM time-stamping) is synchronised with a single on-board Central Time Reference. (PDF p. 18)
  • TIM-2/TIM-4: telemetry timing allows on-ground correlation of on-board time with UTC, and after switch-on or reset a unit flags in each timed packet that its time is not yet synchronised. (PDF p. 19)
  • AUT-1: the spacecraft operates 48 hours without ground contact without interrupting mission product generation, and survives 7 days in safe mode without ground intervention. (PDF p. 19)
  • Applicable PUS services for instruments: mandatory 1, 3, 5, 6, 9, 14, 17, 21; optional 8 and 18; not applicable 2, 11, 12, 15, 16, 19; 4, 7, 10, 13, 20 and 22 not used. (PDF p. 24)
  • PACK-¾/6/7: the location of an HK parameter is derivable from APID, type/subtype and SID; SIDs are unique within an APID; subcommutation is not used; supercommutation is allowed under regular sampling conditions. (PDF p. 25)
  • TCV-6: telecommand verification packets indicate the TC source (ground, mission timeline, OBCP), encoded in the packet sequence control field per the PSICD. (PDF p. 26)
  • EVRP-1 defines three event report types (normal/progress, exceptions needing on-board action, errors needing ground action); EVRP-9 stores types 2 and 3 in a Critical Events Log accessible regardless of SSMM state. (PDF p. 28)
  • MTL-12: mission timeline execution accuracy is 1 s; MTL-13: commands with the same execution time execute in uplink order. (PDF p. 33)
  • OBSR-2.⅓/4: telemetry storage uses packet stores selectable by APID and packet type, circular or linear, sized for at least 48 hours of packets. (PDF p. 34)
  • SDBC-½: the prime contractor and instrument developers deliver one common Satellite Database for system engineering, AIV and operations; SDBC-4: its content complies with AD-8 (SCOS-2000 Database Import ICD). (PDF p. 40)
  • SDBD-⅕: SDB deliveries are versions 0 to 4 plus a pre-launch update at L-1 month, delivered as a set of ORACLE data files with field-level configuration control files. (PDF p. 41)
  • Annex A2: the spacecraft database is delivered according to AD-8 with a Configuration Control File and a Spacecraft Configuration File. (PDF p. 60)
  • Annex A4: database naming follows RD 1 (H-P-1-ASPI-SP-0141); flight control procedures are named FCP_<subsystem>_nnnn (e.g. FCP_AOC_0001) and timelines TDoyFfNn. (PDF p. 70)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A 20-page interface control document (issue 1.0, 19 December 2001) by Luc Dubbeldam of the HIFI instrument team that defines the PUS-style telecommand and telemetry packets exchanged with the HIFI test equipment interfaces (TEIs) used in instrument-level testing. Its stated purpose is to describe the packet structure of the telecommand packets; it also defines the telemetry.

Section 3 defines the packet headers with byte positions: the TC source packet (version 000, type 1, secondary header flag 1, 11-bit APID, sequence flags 11, a sequence count split into a 3-bit source field (always 000) and an 11-bit counter, packet length = data field octets minus 1) followed by a 4-octet data field header (CCSDS secondary header flag 0, PUS version 0, 4-bit acknowledge flags for acceptance, start, progress and completion, type, subtype, spare); and the TM source packet with a 10-octet data field header (PUS version, type, subtype, spare, 32-bit coarse and 16-bit fine on-board time). Both packets end with a 16-bit packet error control field.

Section 4 lists services per TEI on APIDs 2016 to 2023: commands accepted by all TEIs (function management type 8,4 'Set OBS-ID' and 'Set BB-ID', connection test 17,1), common telemetry (acceptance reports 1,1 and 1,2 with error codes, error/alarm 5,4, link connection report 17,2), and device-specific command and housekeeping (3,25), event (5,x) and science (21,1) packets for the power distribution unit (PDU, APID 2016), focal-plane unit test equipment (FPU, 2017), scanner (2019), sources (SRC, 2020) and vector network analyser (VNA, 2021); the LOU section is still to be done. It is a compact, real example of a PUS-A-era instrument EGSE packet ICD of the kind that is turned into MIB tables.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The TC source packet header has version 000, type 1, header flag 1 and an 11-bit APID; sequence flags are 11 and the 14-bit sequence count is split into a 3-bit source (always 000) and an 11-bit counter maintained per source and APID. (PDF p. 4)
  • The TC data field header is 4 octets: CCSDS secondary header flag (0), PUS version (0), a 4-bit ACK field (bit 3 acceptance, bit 2 start of execution, bit 1 progress, bit 0 completion), packet type, packet subtype and a spare octet. (PDF p. 4)
  • The TM data field header is 10 octets: spare bit, PUS version (0), spare, type, subtype, spare octet, a 32-bit coarse on-board time in seconds and a 16-bit fine time in sub-seconds; the packet length C is always odd. (PDF p. 5)
  • Commands accepted by all TEIs (APIDs 2016-2023) include 'Set OBS-ID' and 'Set BB-ID' as function-management TC(8,4) with Function ID 1 and Activity IDs 1 and 2, and the connection test TC(17,1). (PDF p. 6)
  • Acceptance failure reports TM(1,2) carry error codes 0 illegal APID, 1 incomplete or illegal length, 2 incorrect checksum, 3 illegal type, 4 illegal subtype and 5 illegal or inconsistent application data. (PDF p. 7)
  • TEI-specific APIDs: PDU 2016, FPU 2017, scanner 2019, SRC 2020 and VNA 2021; housekeeping uses TM(3,25), and scanner and VNA measurement reports use TM(21,1). (PDF p. 8)
  • The TEI-SRC safety report defines 1-bit flags telling SCOS when it must not release a command that increases a bias. (PDF p. 17)

Ground systems and operations — Telemetry and telecommand packet utilization

Document IDECSS-E-70-41ADate2003-01-30OrganisationECSS Secretariat, ESA-ESTEC Requirements & Standards Division (prepared by the ECSS Working Group for Ground Systems and Operations; published by ESA Publications Division)AuthorsECSS Working Group for Ground Systems and OperationsTypeStandardStatusPublished 30 January 2003 as ECSS-E-70-41A ('PUS-A'). The document has no change log and states no issue number beyond the 'A' letter. Its successor is ECSS-E-ST-70-41C, the second issue of 15 April 2016 (library item ecss-e-st-70-41c-15april2016). Its change log lists ECSS-E-70-41A as the first issue and ECSS-E-70-41B as never issued (PUS-C p. 3). Footnotes on pp. 44 and 48 note that PUS version 0 was used by the earlier ESA PUS.Pages228

docs.title: Provenance
docs.text: Original locationhttps://redmine.oas.inaf.it/attachments/download/416/ECSS-E-70-41A(30Jan2003)-PUS.pdfCopied (UTC)2026-11-12T14:11:05ZSHA-256ca5ecf050941deeab4a693fc15a167ec13b2fce7f9bc7bd81e912eeeaf32fd0dSize2.0 MBOur copyECSS-E-70-41A-30Jan2003-PUS.pdf (unchanged third-party file, not MIT; see the notice)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The first ECSS Packet Utilization Standard (PUS-A). It defines the application-level interface between ground and spacecraft that sits on top of the CCSDS packet telemetry and telecommand recommendations (CCSDS 102.0 and 203.0). The scope (clause 1) frames PUS as a menu: every service is optional, it comes as a minimum capability set plus additional ones, and each mission tailors it per application process and documents the result in a space-ground ICD.

The document covers:

  • Operations concepts (clause 4): APID allocation (APID 0 reserved for the time packet, 2047 for idle packets, and one APID per CPDU), packet routing and size, the telecommand execution profile and verification, telemetry reporting, scheduling, monitoring, storage and diagnostic mode;
  • Packet structures (clause 5): the TC data field header (PUS version, 4-bit Ack, service type and subtype, optional source ID) and the TM data field header (PUS version, type and subtype, optional packet sub-counter, destination ID and time), plus the 16-bit packet error control;
  • 16 standard services (clauses 6-21), each with a concept, requests and reports, and capability sets: 1 TC verification, 2 device command distribution, 3 housekeeping and diagnostic reporting, 4 parameter statistics, 5 events, 6 memory management, 8 function management, 9 time management, 11 scheduling, 12 on-board monitoring, 13 large data transfer, 14 packet forwarding control, 15 storage and retrieval, 17 test, 18 on-board operations procedures and 19 event-action. Clause 22 summarises all the requests and reports;
  • Parameter types (clause 23): PTC 1-11 with their PFC formats and the structure rules for repeated groups. This is the origin of the PTC/PFC scheme that the SCOS-2000 MIB uses.

Normative annexes give the CRC and ISO checksum, the mission constants, the spacecraft time packet and time correlation (taken from ESA PSS-04-106), and the CPDU (taken from ESA PSS-04-151).

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• PUS complements ECSS-E-50 and the CCSDS packet TM/TC recommendations by defining the application-level ground-space interface for integration, testing and flight operations. (PDF p. 5)
  • All services are optional; each has a minimum capability set and optional additional capability sets, and PUS is a 'menu' tailored per application process and recorded in a space-ground interface control document (SGICD). (PDF p. 14)
  • APID 2047 (all ones) is reserved by CCSDS for idle packets; PUS reserves APID 0 for the standard spacecraft time packet and requires a dedicated APID for each CPDU. (PDF p. 24)
  • Missions may define <TCPKT_MAX_LENGTH> and <TMPKT_MAX_LENGTH> below the CCSDS 65K-octet maximum; data exceeding them use the large data transfer service with acknowledgement and retransmission. (PDF p. 25)
  • TC packets follow CCSDS 203.0-B-2: version 0, type 1, data field header flag 1 (mandatory except for CPDU telecommands), 11-bit APID, sequence flags (11 = stand-alone), 14-bit sequence count per source and APID, packet length = data field octets - 1; maximum TC packet 65 542 octets. (PDF p. 43)
  • TC data field header: CCSDS secondary header flag (0), TC packet PUS version number (1), Ack (4 bits: acceptance, start, progress, completion), service type (8 bits), service subtype (8 bits), optional source ID, spare; a 16-bit Packet Error Control is mandatory for TCs and its type is set by <TC_CHECKSUM_TYPE>. (PDF p. 44)
  • Service types and subtypes 0-127 are reserved for the standard and 128-255 are mission-specific; within mission-specific services all subtypes 0-255 are free. (PDF p. 45)
  • TM source packets follow CCSDS 102.0-B-5: type 0, data field header mandatory except for the time packet, grouping flags, 14-bit source sequence count per APID that wraps from 2^14-1 to 0 and must never 'short-cycle'. (PDF p. 47)
  • TM data field header: spare bit, PUS version (1), spare, service type, service subtype, optional packet sub-counter, optional destination ID, optional time (CUC or CDS per <APPL_TIME_CODE>), spare; the optional 16-bit PEC is set by <TM_CHECKSUM_TYPE>. (PDF p. 48)
  • Table 2 lists the standard service types: 1-6, 8, 9, 11-15 and 17-19; types 7, 10 and 16 are not used. (PDF p. 50)
  • Service 1 reports: (1,1)/(1,2) acceptance success/failure, (1,3)/(1,4) execution started, (1,5)/(1,6) progress, (1,7)/(1,8) execution completed success/failure; service 2 requests: (2,1) on-off, (2,2) register load, (2,3) CPDU commands. (PDF p. 183)
  • A parameter code is the pair PTC (parameter type code) and PFC (parameter format code); missions adopt the standard formats and may add mission-specific PFCs. (PDF p. 190)
  • The simple parameter types are PTC 1 Boolean, 2 Enumerated, 3 Unsigned integer, 4 Signed integer, 5 Real, 6 Bit-string, 7 Octet-string, 8 Character-string, 9 Absolute time, 10 Relative time and 11 Deduced. (PDF p. 192)
  • The packet CRC uses g(x) = x^16 + x^12 + x^5 + 1 with encoder and decoder initialised to all ones, computed over the whole packet except the PEC field. (PDF p. 207)
  • Annex B mission constants include <APPL_TIME_CODE>, <CPDU_DURATION_UNIT> (10 to 15 ms), <CPDU_MAX_INSTR> (12 to 120), <MONLIST_MAX_PARAMS>, <SMALLEST_ADDRESSABLE_UNIT>, <TCPKT_MAX_LENGTH>, <TC_CHECKSUM_TYPE> and <TM_CHECKSUM_TYPE>. (PDF p. 215)
  • Spacecraft elapsed time is a CUC count of TAI seconds from an arbitrary epoch; P-field bits 0-3 = 0010, bits 4-5 = coarse octets minus one (1-4), bits 6-7 = fine octets (0-3). (PDF p. 218)
  • The time packet (APID 0, no data field header) carries a rate octet, then the P- and T-field time sample. The clock is sampled at the leading edge of the ASM of the VC 0 frame with VC frame count 0 (every 256 VC0 frames by default, or 128 down to 1). (PDF p. 219)
  • A CPDU telecommand packet is 10 to 248 octets long, with an even number of octets, ends with a 16-bit CRC, and is carried in a single TC segment and frame (normally on MAP 0). (PDF p. 222)

Adoption Notice of CCSDS 131.0-B-5, TM Synchronization and Channel Coding

It follows ECSS-E-AS-50-21C (1 March 2021, first issue, which superseded ECSS-E-ST-50-01C of 31 July 2008) and ECSS-E-AS-50-21C Rev.1 (13 January 2023) (change log, p. 3). The context clause states that ECSS-E-ST-50-01C is superseded by ECSS-E-AS-50-21 (latest version) (p. 6). Whether a later revision exists is not stated in the document.Pages12

docs.title: Provenance
docs.text: Original locationhttps://ecss.nl/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/ECSS-E-AS-50-21C-Rev.2(5December2024).pdfCopied (UTC)2026-11-12T17:52:08ZSHA-2565a79cc6745e7ac4352c6dcfa8215fa00611c11d6d1ef9b35552b0635bfa51f0cSize346.3 KBOur copyECSS-E-AS-50-21C-Rev.2-5December2024-.pdf (unchanged third-party file, not MIT; see the notice)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
An ECSS Adoption Notice for telemetry synchronization and channel coding. Instead of keeping its own coding standard, ECSS makes the CCSDS Blue Book CCSDS 131.0-B-5, TM Synchronization and Channel Coding (Issue 5, September 2023) applicable as written, apart from a short list of amendments. It is the current ECSS replacement for the 2008 stand-alone standard ECSS-E-ST-50-01C, and page 6 repeats the ECSS mapping table from the superseded ECSS-E-ST-50-01C/-03C/-04C to the six adoption notices ECSS-E-AS-50-21 to -26 and their CCSDS base books.

Clause 4 (Table 4-1) holds the normative changes:

  • soft-decision decoding with at least 3-bit quantization becomes mandatory for the convolutional decoder (CCSDS only recommends it);
  • the Reed-Solomon E=8 code may only be used with 4D-8PSK trellis-coded modulation, only with interleaving depth I=8, and it is never concatenated with a convolutional code. E=16 keeps I=1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 8;
  • the interleaving depth is fixed on a physical channel for a mission phase (the word 'normally' is deleted).

Informative Annex A lists what changed compared with ECSS-E-ST-50-01C. CCSDS 131.0-B-5 adds LDPC codes, turbo rates ⅓ and ⅙, the matching ASM patterns, a 131071-bit pseudo-randomizer for high-rate links (the 255-bit one stays for legacy use), normative frame lengths and managed parameters, USLP frames, ground-to-space use, formal service interfaces and security considerations. The old application-profile annex has no equivalent in the CCSDS book. Rev. 2 updates the notice to the CCSDS issue with the new randomizer and adds the differences that earlier revisions missed. An engineer uses this notice to see which CCSDS TM coding options an ECSS project may use.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Requirement ECSS-E-AS-50-21_1520001 makes CCSDS 131.0-B-5, TM Synchronization and Channel Coding, Issue 5 (September 2023) applicable as written with the amendments of Table 4-1. (PDF p. 8)
  • Rev. 2 updates the notice to the CCSDS issue that adds a revised pseudo-randomizer for high-data-rate links, and adds previously missed differences concerning USLP, turbo code rates and ASM bit patterns; Rev.1 (13 January 2023) had added USLP and ground-to-space support. (PDF p. 3)
  • Mapping of superseded standards: ECSS-E-ST-50-01C maps to ECSS-E-AS-50-21 (CCSDS 131.0-B-x); ECSS-E-ST-50-03C to -22 (132.0-B-x) and -23 (732.0-B-x); ECSS-E-ST-50-04C to -24 (231.0-B-x), -25 (232.0-B-x) and -26 (232.1-B-x). (PDF p. 6)
  • Clause 3.2.4 is modified: soft bit decisions with at least three-bit quantization shall be used for the decoder of the convolutional code (CCSDS says 'should ... whenever constraints permit'). (PDF p. 8)
  • New requirement 4.3.1c: the Reed-Solomon code with E=8 shall not be used unless the modulation is 4D-8PSK-TCM. (PDF p. 9)
  • Clause 4.3.5.1 is modified: interleaving depth I = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or 8 when E=16, and I = 8 only when E=8; clause 4.3.5.2 makes the interleaving depth fixed on a Physical Channel for a Mission Phase. (PDF p. 9)
  • Clause 5.1 is modified so that concatenated codes use only the E=16 Reed-Solomon code with a convolutional code; a new NOTE states that E=8 is not concatenated with a convolutional code. (PDF p. 9)
  • CCSDS 131.0-B-5 specifies turbo rates ½, ⅓, ¼ and ⅙, whereas ECSS-E-ST-50-01 had only ½ and ¼; it also adds LDPC codes, which ECSS-E-ST-50-01 did not include. (PDF p. 10)
  • Section 10 of CCSDS 131.0-B-5 specifies a 131071-bit pseudo-randomizer that replaces the 255-bit randomizer of ECSS-E-ST-50-01 unless backward compatibility with legacy systems requires the latter. (PDF p. 10)
  • CCSDS 131.0-B-5 supports TM, AOS and USLP (CCSDS 732.1-B-3) frames and also ground-to-space and space-to-space links (Section 13); ECSS-E-ST-50-01 covered neither USLP nor such use. (PDF p. 11)
  • The mission configuration parameters of ECSS-E-ST-50-01 Annex G become normative managed parameters in Section 12 of CCSDS 131.0-B-5; the application profiles of ECSS-E-ST-50-01 Annex D have no equivalent (guidance is in CCSDS 131.4-M-1-S and CCSDS 130.1-G-3). (PDF p. 11)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
An ECSS Adoption Notice that makes the CCSDS Blue Book CCSDS 132.0-B-3, TM Space Data Link Protocol (Issue 3, October 2021) applicable to ECSS projects with a minimum set of changes. Together with ECSS-E-AS-50-23C (AOS), it replaces the 2008 ECSS standard ECSS-E-ST-50-03C, Telemetry transfer frame protocol. Page 6 gives the ECSS mapping from each superseded ECSS-E-ST-50-0x standard to its adoption notice and CCSDS base book.

The only normative change (Table 4-1) is an addition. ECSS keeps its own extended virtual channel frame count, which was already in ECSS-E-ST-50-03C and is not in the CCSDS book. When it is used, the Transfer Frame Secondary Header is 32 bits long (so its length field holds 3) and carries a 24-bit count of the roll-overs of the 8-bit Virtual Channel Frame Count. This gives a 32-bit frame count. Its use is tied to a master channel or to a single virtual channel and stays static for a mission phase.

Informative Annex A lists what CCSDS 132.0-B-3 adds or changes compared with ECSS-E-ST-50-03C: formal service interfaces and protocol procedures, optional SDLS and SDLS Extended Procedures interfaces (including the new Type-2 Frame Security Report in the OCF), different wording on frame-count resets, the Synchronization Flag now tied to the VCA service rather than to asynchronously inserted data, normative managed parameters, a PICS and Only Idle Data frame randomization. An engineer uses this notice with CCSDS 132.0-B-3 to configure an ECSS-compliant TM frame generator or decoder.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Requirement ECSS-E-AS-50-22_1530001 makes CCSDS 132.0-B-3, TM Space Data Link Protocol, Issue 3, October 2021 applicable with the amendments of Table 4-1. (PDF p. 8)
  • Rev.1 updates the notice to the new CCSDS issue, adding clarifications and support for the SDLS Extended Procedures (CCSDS 355.1-B-1), a PICS proforma and Only Idle Data frame randomization options. (PDF p. 3)
  • New requirement 4.1.3.1.7 allows the Transfer Frame Secondary Header to carry an extended virtual channel frame count, specified in the new section 4.1.3.4. (PDF p. 8)
  • With the extended count the Transfer Frame Secondary Header is 32 bits (4 octets), so the Secondary Header Length field contains 3, and its data field holds the 24-bit extension. (PDF p. 9)
  • The extension is a binary count of roll-overs of the 8-bit Virtual Channel Frame Count, giving a 32-bit count: the 24 most significant bits in the secondary header and the 8 least significant bits in the primary header. (PDF p. 9)
  • Use of the extended count is associated with either a master channel (every frame carries it, with the value of its own virtual channel) or a single virtual channel, and is static throughout a mission phase. (PDF p. 10)
  • CCSDS 132.0-B-3 adds optional SDLS and SDLS Extended Procedures interfaces for TM frames, including the SDLS Frame Security Report (FSR) as a new Type-2 Report (subsection 4.1.5.5); ECSS-E-ST-50-03 had no SDLS support. (PDF p. 11)
  • Frame counts (modulo 256): CCSDS 132.0-B-3 forbids resetting them before 255 'unless it is unavoidable', where ECSS-E-ST-50-03 said 'unless there is a major system reset'. (PDF p. 12)
  • In CCSDS 132.0-B-3 a Synchronization Flag of '1' means the frame carries a VCA-SDU; ECSS-E-ST-50-03 had used flag '1' also for legacy asynchronously inserted data. (PDF p. 12)
  • Subsection 4.1.4.6.2 of CCSDS 132.0-B-3 specifies randomization of the data field of Only Idle Data (OID) frames, with two implementation options in its informative Annex D; ECSS-E-ST-50-03 had no such specification. (PDF p. 12)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
An ECSS Adoption Notice that makes the CCSDS Blue Book CCSDS 732.0-B-4, AOS Space Data Link Protocol (Issue 4, October 2021) applicable to ECSS projects with a minimum set of changes. AOS (Advanced Orbiting Systems) frames do the same job as TM frames and add some features of their own. The ECSS standard ECSS-E-ST-50-03C, which this notice and ECSS-E-AS-50-22C supersede, covered only the TM Transfer Frame and had no AOS frame, so the notice has no 'differences' annex. Page 6 gives the ECSS mapping from each superseded ECSS-E-ST-50-0x standard to its adoption notice and CCSDS base book.

The normative changes in Table 4-1 are few:

  • the Replay Flag of the AOS primary header must always be '0' (realtime). CCSDS allows '1' for replayed frames, but ECSS forbids it because other ways of replaying frames exist and because the flag makes processing at the receiving end more complex. The CCSDS interpretation requirement and its notes are deleted;
  • a new note to the Frame Header Error Control clause says that this optional field may be restricted to physical channels whose frames are not protected by an error-correcting code. With Reed-Solomon coding, for example, it brings no benefit and is strongly discouraged.

The change log says that Rev.1 follows the new CCSDS issue, with SDLS Extended Procedures support, a PICS proforma and Only Idle Data randomization options, all of which are in the CCSDS book. An engineer uses this notice to know how an ECSS mission may use AOS framing, for example on high-rate payload downlinks.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Requirement ECSS-E-AS-50-23_1540001 makes CCSDS 732.0-B-4, AOS Space Data Link Protocol, Issue 4, October 2021 applicable with the amendments of Table 4-1. (PDF p. 8)
  • The AOS protocol of CCSDS 732.0-B-4 has a similar purpose to the TM Space Data Link Protocol (CCSDS 132.0-B-3) and supports some features not available in it; ECSS-E-ST-50-03 was limited to the TM Transfer Frame and did not include the AOS Transfer Frame. (PDF p. 6)
  • Clause 4.1.2.5.2 is modified: the Replay Flag shall be set to '0'. (PDF p. 8)
  • A new NOTE explains that '0' indicates a Realtime Transfer Frame and that ECSS does not allow the CCSDS value '1' (Replay Transfer Frame), because there are alternative means of replaying frames and processing at the receiving end becomes more complex; CCSDS requirement 4.1.2.5.3 and its notes are deleted. (PDF p. 9)
  • New NOTE 2 to clause 4.1.2.6.1: Frame Header Error Control may be restricted to physical channels where the AOS frames are not protected by an error-correcting code; with e.g. Reed-Solomon coding it brings no benefit and is strongly discouraged. (PDF p. 10)
  • Rev.1 adds clarifications and support for SDLS Extended Procedures (CCSDS 355.1-B-1), a PICS proforma and Only Idle Data frame randomization options, following the new CCSDS issue. (PDF p. 3)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
An ECSS Adoption Notice that makes the CCSDS Blue Book CCSDS 231.0-B-4, TC Synchronization and Channel Coding (Issue 4, July 2021) applicable to ECSS projects. It covers the uplink coding layer: BCH and LDPC codewords, the CLTU, the randomizer, the acquisition and idle sequences and the Physical Layer Operations Procedures (PLOP). It replaces clauses 8 (synchronization and coding sublayer) and 9 (physical layer) of the 2008 ECSS-E-ST-50-04C, whose frame and COP-1 parts went to ECSS-E-AS-50-25C and -26C.

Table 4-1 makes the CCSDS options stricter in several ways:

  • a CLTU carries exactly one TC Transfer Frame or a single USLP frame (CCSDS allows several TC frames);
  • the modified BCH code is always decoded in error-correcting (SEC) mode: it corrects one bit and detects two. The error-detecting (TED) option is removed, so one error in the Start Sequence is accepted;
  • the randomizer is mandatory for BCH as well as for LDPC, and the FECF is always used;
  • the Acquisition Sequence is at least 16 octets of alternating ones and zeros, and the Idle Sequence is at least 8 bits;
  • with PLOP-2, at least one octet of Idle Sequence shall separate consecutive CLTUs, to avoid a synchronization lockout that a false start pattern could cause;
  • the managed-parameter Table 8-2 is restricted to match.

Informative Annex A lists further differences from ECSS-E-ST-50-04C: LDPC coding, normative managed parameters, formal service interfaces, the optional CLTU Repetitions parameter and USLP support. The performance annex now lives in CCSDS 230.1-G-3. Rev.1 aligns the notice with CCSDS 231.0-B-4 and USLP and corrects notes that showed the randomizer as optional for BCH. An engineer uses this notice to build or verify an ECSS-compliant spacecraft command decoder or ground CLTU generator.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Requirement ECSS-E-AS-50-24_1550001 makes CCSDS 231.0-B-4, TC Synchronization and Channel Coding, Issue 4, July 2021 applicable with the modifications of Table 4-1. (PDF p. 8)
  • CCSDS 231.0-B-4 corresponds to clauses 8 (Synchronization and coding sublayer) and 9 (Physical layer) of ECSS-E-ST-50-04. (PDF p. 6)
  • Modified Note 2 to the Transfer Frame definition: the service data unit of the Coding & Synchronization sublayer is one TC Transfer Frame or a single USLP Transfer Frame (CCSDS allows one or more TC frames); Annex A3 of CCSDS is changed in the same way. (PDF p. 8)
  • Clause 2.2.2 is changed so that the modified BCH code is decoded in error-correcting mode and the FECF is used to reduce the probability of undetected errors. (PDF p. 9)
  • Randomization is not optional for either BCH or LDPC: clauses 2.2.4, 3.4.3, Note 2 of 5.2.3, Table 5-1 and 6.1 are modified, Note 2 of 6.3.1 is deleted, and the Table 8-2 Randomizer row allows only 'Used'. (PDF p. 9)
  • Clause 3.5 is modified: BCH codewords shall be decoded in Single Error Correction (SEC) mode, correcting one bit and detecting two; the Triple Error Detection (TED) option is deleted. (PDF p. 10)
  • With BCH coding, the search for the Start Sequence in State 2 accepts a Start Sequence containing one error; Table 8-2 allows only 'Error-Correcting' decoding and '1' error in the Start Sequence. (PDF p. 11)
  • Clause 7.2.2 is modified: the Acquisition Sequence minimum length shall be 16 octets (CCSDS: preferred minimum), with alternating ones and zeros. (PDF p. 13)
  • Clause 7.2.4 is modified: the Idle Sequence shall be at least 8 bits long; its maximum length is unconstrained. (PDF p. 13)
  • Clause 7.5.2 is modified: with PLOP-2 a minimum Idle Sequence of one octet shall be inserted between each CLTU, to prevent a lockout when a CLTU start pattern is missed and a false start pattern spans the last BCH codeword and the Tail Sequence. (PDF p. 14)
  • Annex A: CCSDS 231.0-B-4 adds LDPC coding (ECSS-E-ST-50-04 had only the modified BCH code), normative managed parameters (formerly informative Annex E), formal service interfaces and the optional Repetitions parameter for CLTU transfer. (PDF p. 17)
  • ECSS-E-ST-50-04 Annex D (frame rejection and undetected error rates) has no equivalent in CCSDS 231.0-B-4; similar data is in CCSDS 230.1-G-3. CCSDS 231.0-B-4 supports both TC SDLP and USLP frames. (PDF p. 18)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
An ECSS Adoption Notice: rather than rewriting the TC data link protocol, ECSS adopts the CCSDS Blue Book CCSDS 232.0-B-4, TC Space Data Link Protocol (Issue 4, October 2021) and lists only the clauses it changes for use in ECSS projects. Together with the notices for TC synchronization and channel coding (ECSS-E-AS-50-24C) and COP-1 (ECSS-E-AS-50-26C), it supersedes the older stand-alone ECSS-E-ST-50-04C telecommand standard, and page 6 gives a mapping table from each superseded ECSS-E-ST-50-0x standard to its replacement notice and CCSDS base document.

The core is Table 4-1, a clause-by-clause applicability table that shows the ECSS text, a comment and the original CCSDS wording. The main ECSS tailorings are:

  • the Transfer Frame Data Field is capped at 1017 octets, and the Frame Error Control Field is mandatory (the CCSDS options for 1019 octets and for no FECF are removed, also in the SDLS clause 6.3.7 and the managed-parameter tables 5-1 and 5-4);
  • the CLCW No Bit Lock Flag becomes a mandatory, real report of the spacecraft demodulators' bit lock;
  • a new clause 4.4.9, Packet Assembly Controller Function, inherited from ECSS-E-ST-50-04, is added. It reassembles Packets or MAP_SDUs from segmented Frame Data Units, enters a lockout state on bad segment sequences, and is released by a one-octet MAP Reset control segment sent on a paired control MAP (data MAP ID + 32).

Informative Annex A lists further differences from ECSS-E-ST-50-04C: formal service interfaces, optional SDLS support, normative managed parameters and a PICS. An engineer uses this notice to know exactly which CCSDS TC frame options an ECSS-compliant spacecraft must support.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Requirement ECSS-E-AS-50-25_1560001 makes CCSDS 232.0-B-4, TC Space Data Link Protocol, Issue 4, October 2021 applicable with the modifications of Table 4-1. (PDF p. 8)
  • The superseded ECSS-E-ST-50-01C, -50-03C and -50-04C (31 July 2008) map to Adoption Notices ECSS-E-AS-50-21 (CCSDS 131.0), -22 (132.0), -23 (732.0), -24 (231.0), -25 (232.0) and -26 (232.1). (PDF p. 6)
  • Clause 4.1.1b is modified so that the Transfer Frame Data Field is up to 1017 octets (the CCSDS option of 1019 octets is deleted). (PDF p. 8)
  • The Frame Error Control Field (2 octets) is made mandatory: 4.1.1c is changed from optional to mandatory and 4.1.4.1.1 and 4.1.4.1.3 are deleted. (PDF p. 9)
  • The CLCW No Bit Lock Flag is no longer optional: '0' when at least one spacecraft demodulation unit for the physical channel has bit lock, '1' when none has; it always reports the actual physical channel status. (PDF p. 10)
  • New clause 4.4.9 adds the Packet Assembly Controller Function, usable by MAP Packet Extraction and MAP Reception to reassemble Packets or MAP_SDUs; the name is inherited from earlier standards. (PDF p. 12)
  • Each Packet Assembly Controller instance uses a pair of 6-bit MAP Identifiers: a data MAP (MSB 0, range 0 to 31) and a control MAP equal to the data MAP + 32. (PDF p. 13)
  • The function keeps a reassembly status flag ('1' while reconstruction is in progress) and enters a lockout state on an incorrect sequence of Sequence Flags or an invalid control segment; eight illegal sequence-flag transitions are listed. (PDF p. 15)
  • The function reports the data MAP ID, reassembly status flag and lockout status flag to the sending end, but the format and transport of that status are not specified. (PDF p. 17)
  • A control segment is one octet long (Segment Header only) with Sequence Flags '11' and a control-MAP identifier; a valid control segment is a MAP Reset command, which discards a partial packet and exits lockout. (PDF p. 18)
  • Managed-parameter Table 5-1 (Presence of Frame Error Control: Present only) and Table 5-4 (Maximum Frame Data Unit Length: up to 1017) are modified accordingly. (PDF p. 19)
  • Clause 6.3.7 (SDLS) is modified so that the FECF always follows the Security Trailer, or the Data Field when there is no trailer. (PDF p. 20)
  • Annex A notes that, unlike ECSS-E-ST-50-04C, CCSDS 232.0-B-4 offers formal service interfaces, optional SDLS, normative managed parameters (formerly 'mission configuration parameters' in Annex E of ECSS-E-ST-50-04) and a normative PICS. (PDF p. 21)
