docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A short ECSS Adoption Notice that makes the CCSDS Blue Book CCSDS 232.1-B-2, Communications Operation Procedure-1 (Issue 2, September 2010) applicable to ECSS projects with one targeted modification. COP-1 is the retransmission protocol used with the TC Space Data Link Protocol. The sending end (FOP-1) and the receiving end (FARM-1) cooperate, through the CLCW report, to deliver telecommand frames in order, without gaps or duplicates. COP-1 was previously specified in clause 7 of ECSS-E-ST-50-04C, which this notice supersedes jointly with ECSS-E-AS-50-24C (TC coding) and ECSS-E-AS-50-25C (TC data link). Page 6 tabulates each superseded ECSS-E-ST-50-0x standard against its adoption notice and the CCSDS issue it was based on in 2021.

The single normative change (Table 4-1, clause 3.3.2) concerns Type-BD (bypass) frames arriving when no FARM-1 back-end buffer is free. CCSDS lets the buffer contents be erased and an optional 'Aborted Indication' be sent. ECSS instead makes this explicit: the FDU Arrived Indication gains a parameter, the FDU aborted indication. It is set only when a Type-BD frame was accepted with no buffer available, which tells the higher procedures that buffered data was overwritten.

Informative Annex A records the one other difference from ECSS-E-ST-50-04C: that standard had special requirements for a FARM-1 with a single back-end buffer per virtual channel, which CCSDS 232.1-B-2 does not include. The bibliography lists the full family of ECSS-E-AS-50-2x notices, the superseded 2008 standards and the CCSDS TC coding Green Book.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• CCSDS 232.1-B-2, Communications Operation Procedure-1, Issue 2, September 2010 applies with the modifications in Table 4-1. (PDF p. 8)
  • A recently published technical corrigendum to CCSDS 232.1-B-2 does not affect the Adoption Notice. (PDF p. 5)
  • COP-1 is used with the TC Space Data Link Protocol to deliver frames in sequence and without gaps or duplication; it was previously clause 7 of ECSS-E-ST-50-04. (PDF p. 6)
  • In 2021 the adoption notices were based on CCSDS 131.0-B-3 (Sept. 2017), 132.0-B-2 (Sept. 2015), 732.0-B-3 (August 2016), 231.0-B-3 (Sept. 2017), 232.0-B-3 (Sept. 2015) and 232.1-B-2 (Sept. 2010). (PDF p. 6)
  • Clause 3.3.2 is modified: when a Type-BD frame is accepted by FARM-1 with no buffer available, the buffer data is erased and the FDU Arrived Indication carries a new 'FDU aborted indication' parameter (GVCID, FDU aborted indication). (PDF p. 9)
  • The FDU aborted indication is set only when a Type-BD Transfer Frame is accepted by FARM-1 and there is no buffer available; the optional CCSDS 'Aborted Indication' signal is removed. (PDF p. 10)
  • ECSS-E-ST-50-04 had requirements for a FARM-1 with only one back-end buffer per virtual channel; this special case is not in CCSDS 232.1-B-2. (PDF p. 11)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The informative ECSS communications handbook, the companion to ECSS-E-ST-50 and its Level-3 data-link, coding, RF and on-board bus standards. It explains how the ECSS E-50 standards and the related CCSDS Recommended Standards fit together into a coherent protocol stack, evaluates issues that the standards cannot discuss, and gives guidance on option selection.

Section 3 is a primer on CCSDS document colours (Blue, Green, Magenta, Orange, Yellow, Silver), the withdrawal of ESA PSS standards, and ECSS's then-policy of re-publishing modified CCSDS books, which was being replaced by adoption notices. Tables 3-1 and 3-2 list each covered standard with its 2008 issue and date, and an OSI-layer map shows where each one sits.

Section 4 has one chapter per standard, each giving purpose, description, differences from CCSDS, options and recommended practice. It covers ECSS-E-ST-50, ranging/Doppler, RF and modulation (including the 'transponder dual lock' issue), TM coding, the TM transfer frame, the TC protocols (14 documented differences from CCSDS 231/232, e.g. the Packet Assembly Controller and one frame per CLTU), AOS, Proximity-1, Space Packet and Encapsulation, IPv4/IPv6, PUS (field usage and reserved APIDs 0 and 2047), CFDP, SCIDs, compression, time codes, SpaceWire, MIL-1553 and discrete interfaces.

Section 5 covers cross-cutting topics such as channel coding options, playback of recorded frames, idle data, security, interoperability and PICS. Section 6 recounts the history of CCSDS (TC/TM, AOS, Proximity-1, CFDP, DTN, SOIS) and gives applicability tables. Annexes A-F are draft PICS proformas for the sending and receiving ends of ECSS-E-ST-50-01, -03 and -04, and Annex G gives false-decoding probabilities for RS E=8 with 4D-8PSK-TCM. This is a good map of the European space-link protocol landscape around 2008.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The handbook is informative best practice and is not binding; in case of conflict the ECSS standards prevail. (PDF p. 17)
  • The E-50 series covers the space link and space network in detail and the ground network only as needed for end-to-end services; other ground aspects belong to the ECSS E-70 series. (PDF p. 24)
  • CCSDS publication categories: Blue Books (Recommended Standards), Green (Informational Reports), Magenta (Recommended Practices), Orange (Experimental), Yellow (Record) and Silver (Historical, with '-S' appended to the number). (PDF p. 25)
  • ESA PSS communication standards were modified versions of CCSDS recommendations; all PSS documents have been withdrawn in favour of ECSS or CCSDS standards. (PDF p. 25)
  • ECSS differs from CCSDS in having the ESA-developed PUS (ECSS-E-ST-70-41) as an application layer and in combining the TC protocols into the single ECSS-E-ST-50-04. Modifying CCSDS books was being phased out in favour of adoption notices. (PDF p. 26)
  • In 2008 the covered issues were the 'C' editions of 31 July 2008 for E-ST-50, -01, -02, -03, -04, -05, -12 and -14 and 15 Nov 2008 for -13, with -11 (SpaceWire protocols) to be published; ECSS-E-ST-70-41 was issue A of 30 Jan 2003. (PDF p. 27)
  • Other covered standards and issues: CCSDS 133.0-B-1 (Sep 2003), 133.1-B-1 (Jun 2006), 135.0-B-3 (Oct 2006), 301.0-B-3 (Jan 2002), 320.0-B-5 (Sep 2007), 727.0-B-4 (Jan 2007) and 732.0-B-2 (Jul 2006); for AOS there was no ECSS standard, only CCSDS 732.0-B. (PDF p. 28)
  • The space link protocols are mapped onto five OSI layers (physical, data link, network, transport, application); CFDP spans transport and application, and Proximity-1 spans data link and physical. (PDF p. 29)
  • 'Transponder dual lock': when both receivers lock, one near its threshold (about -122 dBm), telecommands can be rejected; Cryosat-2 combines both LGA signals with a 3 dB hybrid; see report TEC-ETC/2008.66/PMcM. (PDF p. 44)
  • ECSS-E-ST-50-04 includes the optional Packet Assembly Controller, inherited from PSS, so its minimum TC segment is one octet (CCSDS: two). European hardware uses the PAC, but European missions generally do not use segmentation. (PDF p. 69)
  • In CCSDS several TC frames may share one CLTU; in ECSS-E-ST-50-04 a CLTU contains exactly one frame, for reliability and compatibility with European hardware. (PDF p. 69)
  • ECSS-E-ST-70-41 (2003) still calls the packets 'telemetry source packet' and 'telecommand packet' and the secondary header the 'Data Field Header'; it reserves APID 2047 (idle) and APID 0 (time), while CCSDS 135.0-B also reserves 2045-2046 and 2040-2044. (PDF p. 95)
  • PUS makes the 16-bit Packet Error Control field mandatory on TC packets and optional (fixed per APID) on TM; it was not yet in CCSDS 133.0-B-1. (PDF p. 95)
  • Playback of recorded TM frames by asynchronous insertion uses a dedicated VC; in forward mode recorded ASMs must use the alternative pattern 0x352EF853, and recorded CLCWs must not be processed by the real-time TC system. (PDF p. 127)
  • Applicability guidance: ECSS-E-ST-50-05 and CCSDS 301.0-B for all missions; AOS for very large return data volumes; Proximity-1 for inter-spacecraft links; ECSS-E-ST-70-41 for all ESA missions. (PDF p. 141)
  • For ground components the handbook points to the EGOS portal (SCOS-2000, SIMSAT, ground station systems, ESA SLE Gateway). (PDF p. 142)
  • Annexes A-F are draft PICS proformas for the sending and receiving ends of ECSS-E-ST-50-01, ECSS-E-ST-50-03 and ECSS-E-ST-50-04. (PDF p. 144)
  • For the R-S E=8 code (interleaving I=8) concatenated with 4D-8PSK-TCM, the false decoding probability stays below 1e-19 when the mean BER is below 1e-9 or the FER below 5e-7, which is negligible. (PDF p. 256)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The 2008 ECSS standard for telemetry synchronization and channel coding: how the downlink stream of TM or AOS transfer frames is protected with error-correcting codes, framed with a sync marker and randomized. It closely follows CCSDS 131.0-B-1, whose codes it subsets, in 'shall' requirement form, and Annex E compares it with the 1989 ESA-PSS-04-103 Telemetry channel coding standard. ECSS has since superseded it with the adoption notice ECSS-E-AS-50-21.

Clause 4 gives an overview of the coding concepts. The normative clauses then specify:

  • the convolutional code (clause 5): rate ½, constraint length 7, connection vectors 171/133 octal with inversion of G2, Viterbi decoding with soft decisions of at least 3 bits, and punctured rates ⅔, ¾, ⅚ and ⅞;
  • the Reed-Solomon (255,223) code with E=16 (clause 6): field and code generator polynomials, interleaving depth I=1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or 8, virtual fill, the dual-basis representation, and E=8 (255,239) restricted to 4D-8PSK-TCM with I=8;
  • turbo codes of rates ½ and ¼ (clause 7) for information blocks of 1784, 3568, 7136 and 8920 bits;
  • frame synchronization with the attached sync marker (clause 8): 0x1ACFFC1D, longer turbo ASMs and the embedded ASM 0x352EF853;
  • the 255-bit pseudo-randomizer h(x) = x8+x7+x5+x3+1 (clause 9).

The informative annexes give the Berlekamp/conventional transformation, Reed-Solomon coefficient expansions, compatible frame lengths (for example 1115 octets at I=5), application profiles with coding gains, the changes from ESA-PSS-04-103, the differences from CCSDS 131.0-B-1, the mission configuration parameters and a turbo code patent notice. It remains a compact reference for downlinks designed to the 2008 ECSS profile.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Category A spacecraft are those at an altitude above the Earth's surface of less than 2 × 10^6 km; category B at or above 2 × 10^6 km. (PDF p. 10)
  • Bit numbering: the first transmitted bit of an N-bit field is bit 0 and is the most significant bit. (PDF p. 11)
  • The basic convolutional code is rate ½, constraint length 7, with connection vectors G1 = 1111001 (171 octal) and G2 = 1011011 (133 octal) and symbol inversion on the G2 output path; the punctured versions (rates ⅔, ¾, ⅚, ⅞) have no inversion. (PDF p. 18)
  • Soft bit decisions with at least 3-bit quantization shall be used for the convolutional decoder; if NRZ-L to NRZ-M conversion is used it should be done at the encoder input and reversed at the decoder output. (PDF p. 17)
  • Decoding failures of the Viterbi decoder are not signalled and produce error bursts, so ECSS-E-ST-50-03 requires a CRC on TM frames unless Reed-Solomon coding is used. (PDF p. 17)
  • Reed-Solomon code: J = 8 bits per symbol, E = 16, n = 255, 32 parity symbols and k = 223 information symbols per codeword; field generator polynomial F(x) = x^8 + x^7 + x^2 + x + 1. (PDF p. 22)
  • The Reed-Solomon interleaving depth I shall be 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or 8 (I=1 means no interleaving), and shall be fixed on a physical channel for a mission phase; maximum codeblock length is 255I symbols. (PDF p. 23)
  • The E=8 (255,239) Reed-Solomon code shall only be used with 4D-8PSK-TCM modulation, shall not be concatenated with a convolutional code and shall use interleaving depth I=8. (PDF p. 28)
  • Turbo information block lengths are 1784, 3568, 7136 and 8920 bits (223 × 1, 2, 4 and 5 octets), with codeblock lengths of 3576/7152 bits for 1784 at rates ½ and ¼. (PDF p. 31)
  • The ASM is 1ACFFC1D for non-turbo-coded data, 034776C7 272895B0 for rate-½ turbo and 034776C7 272895B0 FCB88938 D8D76A4F for rate-¼ turbo coded data. (PDF p. 38)
  • The ASM immediately precedes each codeblock or frame with no intervening bits, and is never presented to the Reed-Solomon or turbo encoder or decoder. (PDF p. 38)
  • A recorded frame stream embedded in real-time frames shall use the embedded ASM 352EF853; it shall not be used with turbo-coded frames. (PDF p. 39)
  • Presence or absence of pseudo-randomization is fixed for a physical channel and is not signalled in the telemetry: the receiver knows it a priori. (PDF p. 40)
  • The pseudo-random sequence is generated by h(x) = x^8 + x^7 + x^5 + x^3 + 1, repeats after 255 bits, and is never exclusive-ORed with the ASM. (PDF p. 42)
  • Maximum TM frame lengths with E=16 Reed-Solomon: 223, 446, 669, 892, 1115 and 1784 octets for I = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 8; with E=8 and I=8, 1912 octets. (PDF p. 55)
  • Compared with ESA-PSS-04-103 (1989), the standard adds punctured convolutional codes, RS E=8 restricted to 4D-8PSK-TCM and turbo codes, and drops the PSS restriction on using the randomizer with convolutional coding under BPSK. (PDF p. 62)
  • The codes are a subset of CCSDS 131.0-B-1: the CCSDS recommendations also have turbo rates ⅓ and ⅙ and unrestricted E=8 Reed-Solomon codes. (PDF p. 63)
  • Mission configuration parameters of a physical channel: channel coding scheme, frame length, pseudo-randomization, embedded-stream ASM use, convolutional code rate, interleaving depth, virtual fill length, turbo code rate and turbo information block length. (PDF p. 64)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The 2008 ECSS standard for ranging and Doppler tracking: how a ground station measures the distance (range) and radial velocity (range rate) of a spacecraft through its transponder, and what the transponder and the station must do so that the measurements are accurate. It covers direct Earth-station links for the Space Operation, Space Research and Earth Exploration Satellite services, for unprocessed ranging accuracies of 2.5 to 30 ns and Doppler accuracies of 0.1 to 1 mm/s. Data-relay and meteorological missions are out of scope.

Clause 4 sets out the requirements:

  • the five functions of the system (Earth-to-Space link, transponder, Space-to-Earth link, link control and data acquisition, which includes integrated Doppler, ranging and meteo);
  • frequency assignment and phase modulation. The ranging signal is a sine tone (100 kHz to 1.5 MHz) phase-modulated by a series of square-wave ambiguity-resolution codes Cn = Q1 xor Q2 xor ... Qn. Rules cover sharing the carrier with telecommand and telemetry and choosing the tone to avoid interference;
  • carrier frequency stability, given as Allan variance curves;
  • Earth-station uplink and downlink parameters such as modulation indices, phase noise and group-delay stability (category A versus category B, that is, closer or farther than 2 million km);
  • the spacecraft transponder: coherent turn-around for two-way Doppler, coherent and ranging on/off modes selected by telecommand, group-delay constancy and calibration, telemetered monitoring and technological loss;
  • end-to-end error budgets for Doppler and ranging, and meteo and station-location measurements.

Clause 5 lists the RF compatibility tests between transponder and station. The annexes compare the standard with CCSDS 401.0-B tone-ranging assumptions, define the ranging technological loss and explain integrated Doppler measurement. It is the ECSS reference for the radiometric tracking side of the TT&C link.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Scope: spacecraft ranged or Doppler-tracked over direct links to Earth stations (not via data relay satellites) in the Space Operation, Space Research and Earth Exploration Satellite services, with unprocessed ranging accuracies of 2,5 ns to 30 ns and Doppler accuracies of 0,1 mm/s to 1 mm/s. (PDF p. 7)
  • Category A spacecraft are less than 2 × 10^6 km above the Earth's surface; category B are at or beyond that altitude. (PDF p. 9)
  • The transponder is assumed to carry telecommand and telemetry on the same RF carriers as ranging; the system has five functions: Earth-to-Space link, transponder, Space-to-Earth link, link control and data acquisition. (PDF p. 11)
  • Ranging modulation on both links shall be phase modulation (PM); the baseband ranging signal is a sine tone phase-modulated by codes Cn = Q1 ⊕ Q2 ⊕ ... ⊕ Qn, where Qi are square waves at 2^-i × ft, with code transitions at tone phase 90°. (PDF p. 17)
  • Suppressed-carrier telemetry is not compatible with simultaneous ranging; orbit determination then uses time sharing between telemetry and ranging or a separate ranging transponder. (PDF p. 17)
  • Code acquisition sequence: tone alone, then tone modulated with the sequence of codes, then tone with the final code; deep-space missions may restart the code sequence continuously for faster re-acquisition at reduced accuracy. (PDF p. 15)
  • Earth-to-Space link: tone frequency selectable 100 kHz – 1,5 MHz, code period 2^n/ft with n = 0 to 20, tone modulation index 45° or 22,5°, group delay variation 20 ns/12 h pp (category A) or 2 ns/12 h pp (category B). (PDF p. 25)
  • For deep space and two-way Doppler the transponder shall be coherent (downlink carrier derived from the uplink carrier by the turn-around ratio); coherent/non-coherent and ranging on/off shall be selectable by telecommand. (PDF p. 28)
  • With on-board digital synthesis, the deviation from the ideal turn-around ratio shall not cause a Doppler bias above 0,1 mm/s averaged over 1 s. (PDF p. 29)
  • For ambiguity resolution the ranging channel group delay shall be constant within ± 1/(5 ft) over 0,3 ft to 1,7 ft; for the measurement itself, constant within ± 30 ns at the tone frequency, as seen from the diplexer interface. (PDF p. 29)
  • Typical on-board delay calibration accuracies are ± 5 ns for category A and ± 2,5 ns for category B missions. (PDF p. 30)
  • Ranging measurement quantization shall be at most 1/65536 of the tone period, and station ranging accuracy 1 ns or 1/1000 of the tone period, whichever is larger; Doppler quantization shall be below 1/1000 of the carrier period. (PDF p. 34)
  • For tropospheric correction the station measures pressure (± 1 hPa), temperature (± 1 °C) and relative humidity (±1%); the antenna phase centre location shall be known better than 0,5 m. (PDF p. 34)
  • Compatibility tests use at least engineering qualification models of spacecraft equipment, often in a portable compatibility test unit ('suitcase'). (PDF p. 36)
  • Integrated Doppler measures the continuous carrier phase rather than independent velocity samples, giving a high-resolution change in range up to an unknown constant; it can be two-way (coherent) or one-way (non-coherent). (PDF p. 41)

Space data links - Telemetry transfer frame protocol

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The 2008 ECSS standard for the Telemetry (TM) Transfer Frame, the fixed-length data link layer container in which spacecraft downlink packets. It is essentially the ECSS version of CCSDS 132.0-B-1 (TM Space Data Link Protocol), written in ECSS 'shall' requirement form, and it replaces the frame part of the older ESA-PSS-04-106 Packet Telemetry Standard. ECSS later superseded it with adoption notices of the CCSDS TM and AOS books.

Clause 4 explains physical channels, master channels (Transfer Frame Version Number plus Spacecraft Identifier) and up to eight virtual channels. Clause 5 specifies the frame field by field:

  • the 48-bit Primary Header: 2-bit version '00', 10-bit SCID, 3-bit VCID, OCF flag, 8-bit master and virtual channel frame counts, and the 16-bit Data Field Status with secondary header flag, synchronization flag, packet order flag, segment length identifier '11' and the 11-bit First Header Pointer (all ones = no packet start, '11111111110' = idle data only);
  • the optional Secondary Header (2 to 64 octets), including an ECSS-specific 24-bit extended virtual channel frame count;
  • the Data Field with packet processing and extraction functions, idle packets and asynchronously inserted data;
  • the 4-octet Operational Control Field (Type-1 report = CLCW);
  • the 16-bit CRC Frame Error Control Field, mandatory unless the frame is Reed-Solomon encoded. Annex A shows shift-register encoder and decoder sketches.

Informative annexes compare the standard with ESA-PSS-04-106 (Annex B) and with CCSDS 132.0-B-1 (Annex C), and list every mission configuration parameter of physical, master and virtual channels (Annex D). This is a good map for configuring a TM frame decoder or a mission TM profile.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• A TM Transfer Frame is fixed-length: Primary Header 48 bits, optional Secondary Header 16 to 512 bits, Data Field, optional trailer 16, 32 or 48 bits; maximum frame length 2048 octets, constant per mission phase and sent at a constant rate. (PDF p. 12)
  • A master channel consists of one to eight virtual channels; all frames on a physical channel share the same Transfer Frame Version Number. (PDF p. 13)
  • Primary Header fields: Master Channel Identifier 12 bits, Virtual Channel Identifier 3 bits, OCF Flag 1 bit, Master Channel Frame Count 8 bits, Virtual Channel Frame Count 8 bits, Transfer Frame Data Field Status 16 bits. (PDF p. 14)
  • The Master Channel Identifier is the 2-bit Transfer Frame Version Number (set to '00') plus the 10-bit Spacecraft Identifier (bits 2-11), which is assigned by the CCSDS Secretariat per CCSDS 320.0-B-4 and is static through all mission phases. (PDF p. 15)
  • With Synchronization Flag '0', the Packet Order Flag is '0' and the Segment Length Identifier is '11' (an obsolete feature marked as not used). (PDF p. 19)
  • First Header Pointer (bits 37-47): offset of the first packet starting in the data field; '11111111111' if no packet starts in the frame; '11111111110' if the data field contains only idle data. (PDF p. 20)
  • The Secondary Header is 2 to 64 octets: 8-bit identification (2-bit version '00' and 6-bit length = total length minus one) followed by 8 to 504 bits of mission data. (PDF p. 21)
  • Extended virtual channel frame count: a 32-bit secondary header (length field = 3) whose 24-bit data field counts roll-overs of the 8-bit VC frame count, giving a 32-bit count. This is not in the CCSDS recommendations. (PDF p. 22)
  • The Operational Control Field is 4 octets after the data field; Type Flag '0' = Type-1-Report containing a CLCW per ECSS-E-ST-50-04 clause 6.3; Type Flag '1' = Type-2-Report (bit 1 '0' project-specific, '1' reserved). (PDF p. 28)
  • The Frame Error Control Field (2 octets) is mandatory unless the frame is Reed-Solomon encoded; it uses G(X) = X^16 + X^12 + X^5 + 1 with the shift register preset to all ones. (PDF p. 30)
  • Compared with ESA-PSS-04-106: PSS allowed 892, 1115 or 1784 octets with RS coding or 128 to 2040 octets without, fixed for the whole mission; this standard allows up to 2048 octets, constant per mission phase. (PDF p. 34)
  • ESA-PSS-04-106 defined only a 32-bit secondary header and reserved all Type-2 reports; this standard allows 16 to 512 bits and project-specific Type-2 reports. (PDF p. 35)
  • CCSDS 132.0-B-1 calls a frame with First Header Pointer '11111111110' an OID (Only Idle Data) Transfer Frame; ECSS keeps the meaning but not the term. (PDF p. 37)
  • Annex D lists the mission configuration parameters: frame length, version number, SCID list, FECF presence, error-frame handling, idle pattern, VCIDs, secondary header and OCF association, synchronization flag, valid packet version numbers, maximum packet length and incomplete-packet handling. (PDF p. 38)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The 2008 ECSS standard for the whole telecommand (TC) uplink data link, from the segment to the radiated carrier. It closely follows CCSDS 231.0-B-1, 232.0-B-1 and 232.1-B-1, and Annex B compares it with the 1992 ESA Packet telecommand standard ESA-PSS-04-107. ECSS has since replaced it with three adoption notices.

Its clauses follow the protocol stack:

  • Segmentation sublayer (clause 5): the TC Segment, a one-octet header with 2-bit Sequence Flags and a 6-bit MAP Identifier, plus blocking of several packets into one frame, segmentation and reassembly, MAP multiplexing and the optional Packet Assembly Controller with lockout and MAP reset;
  • Transfer sublayer (clause 6): the variable-length TC Transfer Frame (5-octet primary header with version, Bypass and Control Command flags, 10-bit SCID, 6-bit VCID and 10-bit Frame Length; up to 1024 octets; mandatory 16-bit FECF), the 4-octet CLCW carried in the TM OCF, and the frame procedures and VC multiplexing;
  • COP-1 (clause 7): FOP-1 and FARM-1 variables, the sliding window, the service interfaces, the Unlock and Set V(R) control commands and complete state tables;
  • Synchronization and channel coding (clause 8): the (63,56) modified BCH codeblock, the CLTU with Start Sequence 0xEB90 and Tail Sequence 0xC5C5C5C5C5C5C579, the mandatory randomizer, fill, and SEC-only decoding;
  • Physical layer (clause 9): acquisition and idle sequences, carrier modulation modes CMM-1 to CMM-4, and PLOP-1/PLOP-2.

The annexes give the FECF algorithm, the changes from ESA-PSS-04-107 (for example frames of 1024 instead of 256 octets, and COP-1B instead of COP-1A), the differences from CCSDS (one frame per CLTU, mandatory FECF and randomizer), frame rejection and undetected-error performance, and the mission configuration parameters. It remains a compact, complete reference for ESA telecommand chains of that generation.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Scope: data structures and protocols for a telecommand space data link and the physical layer operation procedure; normally ground-to-space, but usable for space-to-space links. (PDF p. 12)
  • The stack comprises the segmentation sublayer, the transfer sublayer (with COP-1) and the synchronization and channel coding sublayer of the data link layer, plus the physical layer procedures at the sending end; security sublayers may be inserted by tailoring. (PDF p. 17)
  • The TC Segment Header holds 2-bit Sequence Flags (bits 0-1) and a 6-bit MAP Identifier (bits 2-7), allowing up to 64 MAPs per virtual channel. (PDF p. 23)
  • The optional Packet Assembly Controller pairs a data MAP (MAP ID MSB '0') with a control MAP (same ID with MSB '1'); on an exception it enters lockout until a MAP reset control segment is received. (PDF p. 30)
  • A TC Transfer Frame consists of a 5-octet Primary Header, the Data Field and a 2-octet Frame Error Control Field, all always present; its length never exceeds 1024 octets and is at least 8 octets. (PDF p. 38)
  • TC Primary Header fields: Transfer Frame Version Number 2 bits, Bypass Flag 1, Control Command Flag 1, Reserved Spare 2, Spacecraft Identifier 10, Virtual Channel Identifier 6, Frame Length 10 (bits 22-31), Frame Sequence Number 8. (PDF p. 38)
  • The CLCW is 4 octets, conveyed in the Operational Control Field of a telemetry transfer frame; the No Bit Lock Flag is bit 17. (PDF p. 45)
  • COP-1 control commands are carried in type-BC frames: Unlock is a single all-zeros octet; Set V(R) is three octets, '10000010', all zeros, then the new V(R) value. (PDF p. 89)
  • A BCH codeblock is 8 octets: 56 information bits, 7 complemented parity bits from the (63,56) modified BCH code with g(x) = x^7 + x^6 + x^2 + 1, and a filler bit always '0'. (PDF p. 118)
  • A CLTU is a 16-bit Start Sequence (EB90), Encoded Data (one or more BCH codeblocks carrying exactly one TC Transfer Frame) and an 8-octet Tail Sequence of seven C5 octets followed by 79. (PDF p. 115)
  • The randomizer is used in all CLTUs, with h(x) = x^8 + x^6 + x^4 + x^3 + x^2 + x + 1 (period 255 bits); the bit transition generator stays all-ones until the Start Sequence is detected. (PDF p. 117)
  • Codeblocks shall be decoded in error-correcting (SEC) mode: one bit in error is corrected and two are detected. (PDF p. 122)
  • The acquisition sequence shall be at least 128 bits of alternating ones and zeros. (PDF p. 123)
  • The idle sequence shall be at least 8 bits of alternating ones and zeros. (PDF p. 124)
  • Carrier modulation modes: CMM-1 unmodulated carrier, CMM-2 acquisition sequence, CMM-3 telecommand data (CLTU), CMM-4 idle sequence. (PDF p. 125)
  • PLOP-2 should be used in preference to PLOP-1 because it supports a higher data throughput; with PLOP-2 a minimum idle sequence of one octet is inserted between CLTUs. (PDF p. 126)
  • Changes from ESA-PSS-04-107: blocking of packets, VCs without segments, no authentication or Segment Trailer, maximum frame length 1024 instead of 256 octets, COP-1B instead of COP-1A, a different Tail Sequence, randomization added, only 64-bit codeblocks and PLOP-1 added. (PDF p. 132)
  • Differences from CCSDS: the PAC (so segments can be one octet), exactly one frame per CLTU, mandatory FECF (minimum frame 8 instead of 6 octets), always accepting a one-bit error in the Start Sequence, mandatory randomization and SEC, mandatory idle between CLTUs in PLOP-2 and a defined No Bit Lock Flag. (PDF p. 135)
  • Annex D gives frame rejection and undetected error performance for channel bit error rates of 10^-4, 10^-5 and 10^-6, assuming PLOP-2 on an AWGN binary symmetric channel. (PDF p. 137)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The ECSS standard for the radio-frequency and modulation layer of the TT&C link. It covers the radio techniques used for telemetry, telecommand and tracking between spacecraft and Earth stations in the Space Operation, Space Research and Earth Exploration-Satellite services (including meteorological satellites, but not data-relay links), and it aligns them with the ITU Radio Regulations and with CCSDS 401.0-B-20.

What an engineer finds in it:

  • frequency allocations (Table 4-1) from S-band (2025-2110 MHz up, 2200-2290 MHz down) to X, K and Ka bands, with deep-space sub-bands, special conditions per band, and the assignment and ITU coordination procedure;
  • transmitted signal rules: coherent turnaround ratios such as 221/240 (S/S) and 749/880 (X/X), frequency stability, polarization, occupied bandwidth limits, spurious emissions, power-flux-density limits and radio-astronomy protection;
  • residual-carrier phase modulation (clause 6.1): NRZ-L/NRZ-M/SP-L waveforms and symbol rates (telecommand 4000/2^n sps), 8 or 16 kHz telecommand subcarriers, telemetry subcarriers, a minimum data transition density (with the ECSS-E-ST-50-01 randomizer as fallback), modulation index limits and phase noise;
  • suppressed-carrier modulation (clause 6.2): BPSK, QPSK, UQPSK, OQPSK, filtered OQPSK, GMSK and 8PSK TCM, mandatory above 1 Msps and restricted to the bandwidth-efficient schemes above 2 Msps;
  • link acquisition (clause 7): downlink switched on by on-board automation, uplink carrier sweep values (for example ±150 kHz at 32 kHz/s), and transponder lock reported in the CLCW;
  • the RF interface control process (spacecraft-Earth station ICD, link budget tables, compatibility tests), and the GMSK and 4D-8PSK-TCM formats in detail (clause 9).

Annexes give the ICD DRD, cross-support notes (NASA DSN), Ariane-5 RF constraints, the differences from CCSDS 401 and tailoring guidance.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Rev. 2 removes filtered-OQPSK from the 8 400 MHz - 8 450 MHz band and aligns Annex D.2.2 and the bibliography with CCSDS 401.0-B-20 (April 2009) instead of 401.0-B-17. (PDF p. 3)
  • Scope: radio communication techniques for spacecraft-Earth station links in both directions and for tracking; applicable to spacecraft supported by Earth stations (not by data relay satellites) in the Space Operation, Space Research and Earth Exploration-Satellite services, the latter including Meteorological Satellite. (PDF p. 9)
  • Category A: altitude less than 2 × 10^6 km; category B and 'deep space': 2 × 10^6 km or more [ITU/RR/1.177]. (PDF p. 11)
  • Primary allocations include 2 025–2 110 MHz (SR, SO, EES, Earth-space), 2 200–2 290 MHz (SR, SO, EES, space-Earth), 7 145–7 190 MHz and 8 400–8 450 MHz (deep space), 8 025–8 400 MHz (EES space-Earth) and 31 800–32 300 / 34 200–34 700 MHz (deep space). (PDF p. 17)
  • Coherent turnaround ratios (fup/fdown) include 221/240 for S-band up/S-band down and 749/880 for X-band up/X-band down; band pairs should come from Table 5-1, otherwise Table 5-2 shall be used. The ratios derive from CCSDS 401.0-B-20. (PDF p. 24)
  • Telecommand PCM symbol rates are 4 000/2^n sps (n = 0..9, NRZ-L or NRZ-M on a subcarrier) or 4 000 × 2^n sps (n = 1..6, SP-L); NRZ-M is not used for category B, and 4 ksps only with the 16 kHz subcarrier. (PDF p. 38)
  • SP-L shall only be used for direct modulation of the RF carrier (no subcarrier), and NRZ waveforms only on a subcarrier; SP-L is also known as bi-phase or Manchester encoding. (PDF p. 39)
  • Telecommand subcarriers are 8 or 16 kHz sine waves; above 4 ksps telecommand symbols are SP-L encoded directly on the carrier. (PDF p. 40)
  • For NRZ telemetry above 60 ksps no subcarrier is used: SP-L direct modulation up to 1 Msps at S and X band, or suppressed-carrier modulation per clause 6.2. (PDF p. 41)
  • Data transition density shall be at least 125 (category A) or 275 (category B) per 1 000 consecutive symbols, with runs of ones or zeros limited to 64 symbols; otherwise the ECSS-E-ST-50-01 clause 9 pseudo-randomizer shall be used. (PDF p. 42)
  • Peak modulation index limits: telecommand NRZ 0,2-1,4 rad, telecommand SP-L 0,2-1,0 rad, telemetry sine subcarrier max 1,5 rad, ranging Earth-space 0,1-1,4 rad, ranging space-Earth 0,01-0,7 rad; combined Earth-space index should not exceed 1,75 rad. (PDF p. 43)
  • Residual carrier power shall exceed -15 dBc (space-Earth) and -10 dBc (Earth-space). (PDF p. 44)
  • Suppressed-carrier modulation shall be used for telemetry above 1 Msps; above 2 Msps (bands below 8 500 MHz) or 20 Msps (31,8-32,3 GHz) only TCM 8PSK, filtered OQPSK or GMSK shall be used. (PDF p. 45)
  • If the ground network can resolve phase ambiguity from the sync marker, no differential encoding is used for BPSK/QPSK/OQPSK/UQPSK; otherwise differential encoding shall be performed. (PDF p. 46)
  • Uplink acquisition at 2 025-2 110 MHz (category A): unmodulated carrier swept with a symmetrical triangular waveform; recommended max sweep rate 32 kHz/s, max discontinuity 10 Hz, max sweep range ±150 kHz for a 2BL = 800 Hz transponder PLL; transponder lock reported in telemetry (CLCW). (PDF p. 55)
  • The spacecraft-Earth station ICD is drafted in Phase B and follows the normative DRD of Annex A (stations, equipment configuration, performances, applicable TT&C standards and waivers, link parameter choices, TT&C operational modes). (PDF p. 72)
  • Annex D: unlike CCSDS 401 (2.2.3), only NRZ-L is recommended for category B telecommand; filtered OQPSK is restricted to specific filters, and SRRC-4D 8PSK TCM only to 2,0 and 2,5 b/s/Hz. (PDF p. 77)
  • ITU Radio Regulations cannot be tailored; tailoring should be supported by the frequency coordinator. (PDF p. 79)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The top-level ECSS standard for space communications. It covers the end-to-end data communication system between spacecraft, ground stations and control centres, and between spacecraft. It is mainly a process standard, framed within ECSS-E-ST-10 systems engineering. It defines the terminology and the engineering activities, and sets top-level functional and performance requirements. The protocol details are left to Level-3 ECSS standards, to the ECSS Adoption Notices of CCSDS books (ECSS-E-AS-50-21 to -26) and to CCSDS standards directly. The ground segment itself is left to ECSS-E-ST-70.

Clause 4 explains the principles: the three domains (space network, space link and ground network), the communication engineering activities and review milestones (SRR to FRR), and spacecraft-control considerations such as commanding in the blind. Its Figure 4-2 maps CCSDS and Internet protocols onto the OSI layers, and a table shows which adoption notice supersedes which part of ECSS-E-ST-50-01/-03/-04.

Clause 5 holds the numbered requirements:

  • telecommanding: in-sequence delivery, an erroneous-TC acceptance probability below 10^-2/N, hardware-decoded essential telecommands, authentication and encryption, TC destination identification;
  • telemetry: essential telemetry, source identification, time-stamping, authentication and encryption;
  • space link: uplink BER of 10^-5, frame rejection and undetected-error targets, ITU frequency filing before SRR, identifiers, error detection, ARQ verification, guaranteed and expedited delivery, time correlation, ranging/Doppler, TC receipt confirmation, exception reporting;
  • on-board and inter-spacecraft networks and the ground network.

Normative Annexes A to H define the eight communication-system DRDs (CSRD, CSBD, CSAD, CSVP, CSADD, CSDDD, CSPD and CSOM), and Annex I maps them to project reviews.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The standard covers space-ground and space-to-space links and the AIT links to the spacecraft; it details the space link and space network domains and covers the ground network only as needed for end-to-end services (other ground aspects are in ECSS-E-ST-70). (PDF p. 9)
  • For control operations the objective is guaranteed, in-order delivery of commands (commands may be repeated, never lost); for payload data the goal is to move as much data as possible, accepting some loss. (PDF p. 16)
  • Table in clause 4.2: ECSS-E-AS-50-21 (CCSDS 131.0-B-3) supersedes ECSS-E-ST-50-01C; -22 (132.0-B-2) the TM Transfer Frame of ECSS-E-ST-50-03C; -23 (732.0-B-3) adds AOS; -24 (231.0-B-3), -25 (232.0-B-3) and -26 (232.1-B-2) replace clauses 8-9, 5-6 and 7 of ECSS-E-ST-50-04C. (PDF p. 20)
  • Figure 4-2 places CCSDS and Internet protocols on the OSI layers (CFDP, BP/LTP, IP over CCSDS, Space Packet and Encapsulation, TC/TM/AOS/USLP/Proximity-1 data links, coding sublayers, RF) and cites ECSS-E-ST-70-41C as an example of an application-specific source/sink. (PDF p. 21)
  • The communication engineering milestones are SRR, PDR, CDR, QR, AR, ORR and FRR, following the ECSS-E-ST-10 process. (PDF p. 27)
  • A service guaranteeing in-sequence delivery of telecommands is required (5.4.2), and the probability of accepting an erroneous telecommand must be below 10^-2/N, N being the number of TCs expected over the mission (5.4.3). (PDF p. 37)
  • Essential telecommands must be decodable and distributed even when all other systems, including the CDMU, are non-operational; for critical operations they must not depend on software, and their list is agreed at PDR. (PDF p. 37)
  • TC encryption is required when authentication alone cannot meet the security requirements; SDLS in ECSS-E-AS-50-25 is cited as a data-link option. (PDF p. 38)
  • New in Rev.1: hot-redundant TC chains must avoid repeatedly selecting the channel with lower signal quality (dual-lock issue, see ECSS-E-HB-50 clause 4.4.5.2), and all telecommands must carry a destination spacecraft identifier. (PDF p. 39)
  • All telemetry must carry a source spacecraft identifier and be time-stamped against a common on-board reference time; telemetry-in-the-blind must be supported. (PDF p. 40)
  • Uplink budgets assume a BER of 10^-5 at the TC decoder input; at that BER the uplink frame rejection rate for 256-octet frames must be below 10^-5. (PDF p. 45)
  • With BCH coding, the probability of undetected uplink frame error can be below 10^-18 with frame error control and below 10^-8 without; downlink frame rejection should be below 10^-5 and acceptance of corrupted maximum-size frames below 10^-12. (PDF p. 46)
  • An application for frequency assignment must be made to the ITU Radiocommunication Bureau before SRR. (PDF p. 47)
  • Space link frames must identify the spacecraft and link; data units must carry a source/destination identifier and a sequence identifier, and the protocol must include error detection. (PDF p. 48)
  • The space link must provide guaranteed and expedited delivery, time correlation of on-board time with ground time, ranging and/or Doppler tracking, TC receipt confirmation at the space network gateway, and exception reporting. (PDF p. 50)
  • Eight DRDs are defined (CSRD, CSBD, CSAD, CSVP, CSADD, CSDDD, CSPD, CSOM). The CSPD records frequency, protocol, address, channel and SCID assignments and is the formal statement of compliance to ECSS-E-50. (PDF p. 88)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The top-level ECSS standard for space communications, in its December 2024 revision. It sets the requirements for developing the end-to-end data communication system of a spacecraft: space-ground and space-to-space links in operations, and the links used during assembly, integration and test. It is a process and top-level requirements standard in the ECSS-E-ST-10 framework. The protocol details sit in the Level-3 ECSS-E-ST-50-xx standards, in the ECSS Adoption Notices of CCSDS books and in CCSDS standards, and the ground segment is mostly left to ECSS-E-ST-70.

Rev.2 is a small maintenance revision. It removes the issue numbers and dates of the adopted CCSDS books (in the clause 4.2 table and the bibliography), so that ECSS-E-ST-50 need not be reissued whenever CCSDS updates a book. It also deletes twelve generic terms from clause 3.2 at the request of the Glossary Task Force, and fixes the 'CSDP' typo in 5.2.5.3c.

Content an engineer finds:

  • clause 4: the principles (guaranteed in-order delivery for control, best effort for payload data), the table of which adoption notice (ECSS-E-AS-50-21 to -26) replaces which part of ECSS-E-ST-50-01C/-03C/-04C, Figure 4-2 mapping CCSDS and Internet protocols onto OSI layers, the three domains (space network, space link, ground network) and the review milestones;
  • clause 5: numbered requirements (ECSS-E-ST-50_09700xx) on telecommanding (in-sequence delivery, erroneous-TC acceptance below 10^-2/N, hardware essential telecommands, authentication and encryption, destination identifiers), telemetry, space link performance (uplink BER 10^-5, frame rejection and undetected-error targets), ITU frequency filing, link services, on-board and inter-spacecraft networks and the ground network;
  • normative Annexes A to H, which define the eight communication-system DRDs (CSRD to CSOM, including the CSPD compliance profile), and Annex I, which maps them to reviews.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Rev.2 removes the issue identifier and date of the adopted CCSDS documents, so that ECSS-E-ST-50 does not need updating whenever an adopted CCSDS standard is updated; it also deletes 12 terms from clause 3.2 (communication service, cross support, downlink, service-provider, service-user, sink, telecommand, telemetry, telemetry link, uplink, user, user application). (PDF p. 3)
  • The standard covers space-ground and space-to-space links in operations and the links used in AIT; it details the space link and space network domains and covers only the ground network aspects needed for end-to-end services (others are in ECSS-E-ST-70). (PDF p. 9)
  • For control operations the objective is guaranteed delivery of commands in transmission order (commands can be repeated but not lost); for payload data the aim is to transfer as much data as possible, accepting some loss. (PDF p. 15)
  • Table in clause 4.2: ECSS-E-AS-50-21 (CCSDS 131.0-B) supersedes the whole of ECSS-E-ST-50-01C; -22 (132.0-B) the TM Transfer Frame of ECSS-E-ST-50-03C; -23 (732.0-B) adds AOS; -24 (231.0-B), -25 (232.0-B) and -26 (232.1-B) replace clauses 8-9, 5-6 and 7 of ECSS-E-ST-50-04C. (PDF p. 19)
  • Figure 4-2 maps CCSDS and Internet protocols onto the data link, coding and physical layers and upper layers, marks which CCSDS books are formally adopted by ECSS, and gives ECSS-E-ST-70-41C as an example of an application-specific source/sink. (PDF p. 20)
  • Communication engineering milestones include SRR, PDR, CDR, QR, AR, ORR and FRR. (PDF p. 26)
  • Requirement 5.4.2 demands a service guaranteeing in-sequence delivery of telecommands; 5.4.3 requires the probability of accepting an erroneous telecommand to be below 10^-2/N, N being the number of telecommands expected over the mission. (PDF p. 36)
  • Essential telecommands must be decodable and distributed even when all other systems, including the CDMU, are non-operational; their list is agreed at PDR and, for critical operations, they must not depend on software. (PDF p. 36)
  • Telecommand encryption is required when authentication alone cannot meet the security requirements; the SDLS option of ECSS-E-AS-50-25 is cited as a data-link-layer means. (PDF p. 37)
  • Hot-redundant TC chains must not repeatedly select the input channel with lower signal quality (dual-lock issue, ECSS-E-HB-50 clause 4.4.5.2), and all telecommands must carry a destination spacecraft identifier. (PDF p. 38)
  • Uplink budgets are based on a BER of 10^-5 at the telecommand decoder input; at that BER the uplink frame rejection rate for 256-octet frames shall be below 10^-5. (PDF p. 44)
  • Downlink frame rejection should be below 10^-5 and the probability of accepting corrupted maximum-sized downlink frames below 10^-12; with BCH, undetected uplink frame error can be below 10^-18 with frame error control and 10^-8 without. (PDF p. 45)
  • An application for frequency assignment shall be made to the Radio Communication Bureau of the ITU for the selected space communication frequencies. (PDF p. 46)
  • Formatted space link data units shall carry a sequence identifier giving their position in the stream (5.6.13.3), and the space link protocol shall include an error detection capability (5.6.13.4). (PDF p. 47)
  • The space link shall provide a guaranteed delivery service and an expedited delivery service for SDUs (5.6.14.2, 5.6.14.3). (PDF p. 49)
  • The space link provides telecommand receipt confirmation and exception reporting; ranging/Doppler methods are referred to ECSS-E-ST-50-02. (PDF p. 50)
  • The CSPD (Annex G) is the supplier's formal statement of compliance with ECSS-E-ST-50, listing frequencies, protocols and options, address, channel and spacecraft identifier assignments and bandwidth allocations; first version at CDR, final at FRR. (PDF p. 80)

docs.text: Original locationhttps://ecss.nl/wp-content/uploads/standards/ecss-e/ECSS-E-ST-70-01C16April2010.pdfCopied (UTC)2026-11-12T17:48:20ZSHA-256f4992c6902cbf380aa10a31b20bfd47307594905d48f9c1942fdd0863d3407acSize952.8 KBOur copyECSS-E-ST-70-01C16April2010.pdf (unchanged third-party file, not MIT; see the notice)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The ECSS standard for on-board control procedures (OBCPs): small programs that an OBCP engine in the on-board software executes and that can be loaded, run and replaced without changing the rest of the flight software. It sets out a mission-independent OBCP concept that serves system, software, AIT and operations engineers. It gives OBCPs a lifecycle independent of the main OBSW, and it builds on the PUS (ECSS-E-70-41, especially service 18, the on-board operations procedure service) and on ECSS-E-ST-70-31 monitoring and control data.

What it contains:

  • Concept (clause 4): stakeholders and uses, such as platform and payload functions, late FDIR tuning, one-shot deployments, test automation, fault injection in AIT and on-board execution of operations procedures for autonomy. It distinguishes OBAPs (on-board application procedures, part of the qualified spacecraft design) from OBOPs (on-board operations procedures, used to operate it). It also describes the OBCP system: a ground preparation environment, a ground execution environment and the on-board engines.
  • Capabilities (clause 5): OBCP structure (identifier, arguments, declaration, preconditions, main, confirmation and contingency bodies, steps, local functions), the required language features (formal EBNF syntax, data types, engineering units, waits, parameter and activity access with verification stages, events), preparation tools (editor, checkers, reports, step-by-step debugging, flight-representative validation, worst-case memory and timing), the state model (in store, inactive, running, held) with Load/Activate/Suspend/Resume/Stop/Abort/Delete mapped to service 18 subtypes, a code checksum, and on-board housekeeping, loading policy and scheduling.
  • Engineering processes (clause 6): OBAP versus OBSW and OBOP versus ground trade-offs, management milestones (SRR, software PDR, qualification), and ECSS-E-ST-40 or ECSS-E-ST-70 processes for OBAPs and OBOPs respectively.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• OBCPs had been implemented ad hoc on several European missions over the previous 25 years; the standard defines a mission-independent concept that conforms with and extends ECSS-E-70-41 and ECSS-E-ST-70-31. (PDF p. 6)
  • Missions implementing OBCPs are assumed to be compliant with ECSS-E-70-41, whose services support OBCP operation and ground interaction. (PDF p. 7)
  • An OBCP is a software program executed by an OBCP engine that can easily be loaded, executed and replaced on board; OBCP code is the loadable form (historically token code, executable code or bytecode), called procedure code in service 18 of ECSS-E-70-41A. (PDF p. 9)
  • OBCP operations are initiated by ECSS-E-70-41 Service 18 telecommands. (PDF p. 10)
  • Two types: On-board Application Procedures (OBAP), part of the basic spacecraft functionality and qualified with it (historically 'Application Program' or 'Flight Application Program'), and On-Board Operations Procedures (OBOP), used to operate the spacecraft and not part of its qualification. (PDF p. 14)
  • The OBCP system has a ground preparation environment, a ground execution environment and on-board OBCP engines (optionally with OBCP stores); OBCPs live in the engineering data repository defined by ECSS-E-ST-70-31. (PDF p. 17)
  • Each OBCP has a unique OBCP Identifier assigned by the ground and may have arguments; it consists of optional declaration, preconditions, confirmation and contingency handling bodies and a mandatory main body, executed in the order declaration, preconditions, main, confirmation. (PDF p. 18)
  • The OBCP language syntax shall be formally specified, for example with ISO EBNF (ISO/IEC 14977). (PDF p. 19)
  • The ground system uplinks OBCPs by telecommand as OBCP code; OBCP management and operation telecommands are based on the ECSS-E-70-41 on-board operations procedure service, while the memory management service is reserved for anomaly investigation and exceptional cases. (PDF p. 26)
  • OBCP execution states: in store; in engine, either inactive or active (running or held). (PDF p. 27)
  • Engine operations map to service 18 subtypes: Load (1), Delete (2), Activate (3), Stop (4), Suspend (5), Resume (6), Communicate Parameters (7), Abort (12); a stopped OBCP cannot be resumed from that point. (PDF p. 28)
  • A ground-generated checksum is loaded with the OBCP code and verified at load time; on failure the engine fails the Load request with a telecommand verification failure. Runtime errors and on-board-commanded OBCP requests are reported by event reports. (PDF p. 29)
  • A given on-board application process shall implement at most one OBCP engine. (PDF p. 29)
  • The OBCP management process output is reviewed at the system requirements review (SRR); OBCP engine and preparation environment capabilities are frozen at the software PDR; OBAP validation is completed before system qualification. (PDF p. 36)
  • OBAPs follow the ECSS-E-ST-40 software lifecycle; OBOPs follow the ECSS-E-ST-70 operations procedure engineering process. (PDF p. 41)

Space segment operability

Document IDECSS-E-ST-70-11C Rev.1Issue / versionSecond issue, Revision 1Date2025-10-15OrganisationECSS Secretariat, ESA-ESTEC Standards Section (prepared by the ECSS-E-ST-70-11C Rev.1 Working Group)AuthorsECSS-E-ST-70-11C Rev.1 Working GroupTypeStandardStatusSecond issue, Revision 1, dated 15 October 2025, the newest ECSS standard in the library. It revises ECSS-E-ST-70-11C (31 July 2008), which followed ECSS-E-70-11A (5 August 2005); ECSS-E-70-11B was never issued (change log, p. 3). The change log notes that a new DOORS module, not linked to the previous version, was created because of the number of changes.Pages84

docs.title: Provenance
docs.text: Original locationhttps://ecss.nl/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/ECSS-E-ST-70-11C-Rev.1-(15October2025).pdfCopied (UTC)2026-11-12T14:11:10ZSHA-2566d957991230614a6eddd34405eadb62f931212f0fe6c3518df8242de9655b728Size775.2 KBOur copyECSS-E-ST-70-11C-Rev.1-15October2025.pdf (unchanged third-party file, not MIT; see the notice)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
ECSS-E-ST-70-11C Rev.1 is the ECSS space segment operability standard. It lists the on-board functions an unmanned spacecraft must provide so that it can be operated safely and cost-effectively from the ground in any nominal or predefined contingency situation. Each mission tailors it by selecting requirements and adding its own, and mission-specific values are left as mission constants in angle brackets (e.g. <TC_VERIF_DELAY>, summarised in Annex A). The 2025 revision updates the 2008 text with modern operations experience and ESA's generic operations interface requirements. It also aligns the standard with ECSS-E-ST-70-41 (PUS) to remove overlap, and it drops the old tailoring annex.

Clause 3 defines the six operability categories (observability, commandability, compatibility, deactivation, flexibility, testability) and the criticality terms: essential and critical telecommands, high priority command and telemetry, mission-critical function. Clause 4 states one-line general requirements per category. Clause 5 gives the detailed requirements, grouped by function:

  • virtual channel allocation;
  • telemetry design rules: self-contained values, no sub-commutation in HK packets, same APID order within a VC, HPTM, a dedicated VC for idle frames;
  • diagnostic mode;
  • datation, including OBT/UTC correlation, no clock wrap-around and GNSS time;
  • telecommand rules: one function per TC, arm/fire for critical functions, verification of every stage, COP-1 windows;
  • modes and reconfiguration;
  • autonomy levels E1-E4 and D1-D2, and FDIR/safe mode;
  • PUS-specific operability (APIDs, memory management, scheduling, monitoring, large packets, storage, OBCPs, event-action, files);
  • subsystem rules for processors, power, TT&C, AOCS, mechanisms, thermal, payload and file systems.

This is the requirements baseline behind many PUS and MIB design choices.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Rev.1 aligns the scope of ECSS-E-ST-70-11 with ECSS-E-ST-70-41 to avoid overlap, rewrites clause 5.8 as complementary PUS operability requirements, updates the Annex A mission constants and removes the former Annex B tailoring guide. (PDF p. 3)
  • Six operability categories are defined: commandability, compatibility, deactivation, flexibility, observability and testability. (PDF p. 10)
  • An essential telecommand is distributed without on-board software; a high priority command is a pulse command routed to hardware by a CPDU; high priority telemetry reports mission-critical equipment status under all circumstances. (PDF p. 11)
  • Mission-dependent quantities are 'mission constants' written in angle brackets, e.g. <TC_VERIF_DELAY>, and summarised in Annex A. (PDF p. 16)
  • No telecommand executed at the wrong time or configuration may lead to loss of the mission; mission-critical functions can be protected with two independent telecommands (e.g. ARM and FIRE). (PDF p. 19)
  • Security: implementing CCSDS 355.0-B SDLS (Baseline Mode for TC Authentication) and CCSDS 355.1-B Extended Procedures is recommended. (PDF p. 24)
  • Different data classes get different downlink bandwidth through physical and virtual channels; the VC-to-data-class assignment does not change during the mission, but the bandwidth allocation can. (PDF p. 25)
  • Telemetered values must be self-contained (no delta or change-only telemetry), and fast-changing critical parameters such as pyro currents must be latched and the latched value telemetered. (PDF p. 26)
  • A telemetry parameter keeps the same structure and interpretation in every packet; super-commutated parameters are sampled regularly; housekeeping packets do not use sub-commutation; packets of one APID on one VC are delivered in generation order. (PDF p. 28)
  • Idle frames go on a dedicated virtual channel; idle packets only complete a frame that already holds a meaningful packet; all packets except idle, time and HPTM packets are available for on-board storage. (PDF p. 30)
  • On-board time must be settable by TC, monotonically increasing in all modes and never wrap around; all telemetry source packets should carry an on-board generation time in their header. (PDF p. 32)
  • The sampling time of a parameter in a non-variable packet must be derivable from the packet generation time by an implicitly known offset; GNSS-based OBT must report the GNSS/OBT correlation and handle leap seconds autonomously. (PDF p. 33)
  • A telecommand contains one and only one on-board function, keeps the same action definition for the whole mission (no flip/flop commands) and must not cause permanent loss of commanding. (PDF p. 35)
  • With COP-1 and the AD service, the sliding window must be configured for in-orbit conditions so as not to limit the uplink rate artificially. (PDF p. 38)
  • Mission-critical functions need at least two separate command actions (arm/enable then execute); critical register loads need a separate execute command. (PDF p. 38)
  • Every TC except pure hardware (CPDU) commands gets acceptance-stage verification; invalid TCs (wrong length, CRC or APID) fail at acceptance; success reports can be disabled; register loads are echoed by dedicated telemetry parameters. (PDF p. 40)
  • Autonomy levels: E1 (ground control) to E4 (goal-oriented on-board re-planning) for mission execution, and D1 (essential data storage) to D2 (all mission data) for data management. (PDF p. 49)
  • PUS operability: one or more application processes per subsystem; APID assignment fixed for the mission; APID + type + subtype (plus further fields) uniquely identify packet structure; HK packets have fixed content and fixed sample-time offsets; parameter IDs are unique across the spacecraft. (PDF p. 60)
  • Time-tagged TCs with equal release times are not rejected but released one after the other; TCs that 'elapsed' while a schedule was disabled are not released when it is re-enabled. (PDF p. 62)
  • A mission must be able to define maximum TC and TM packet lengths below the CCSDS maxima, and must support large-packet uplink and downlink by splitting. (PDF p. 63)
  • TT&C: at least two receivers on different antennas are always active; TCs with repetitive bit patterns must be processed without error (CCSDS 231.0-B randomisation is suggested); a ground-configurable <NO_TC_TIMEOUT> triggers on-board contingency recovery. (PDF p. 71)
  • Annex A defines 23 mission constants, e.g. <TIME_CORREL_ACCUR>, <TC_VERIF_DELAY>, <SAFE_TIME>, <NO_TC_TIMEOUT>, <MIN_DATA_RATE_SM> and <CEL_DUMP_TIME>. (PDF p. 82)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
ECSS-E-ST-70-31C (31 July 2008) is the ECSS standard that defines the monitoring and control data a supplier delivers with a product (a unit, subsystem, instrument or whole spacecraft) so that the customer can integrate, test and operate it. It defines what data is delivered, not how (spreadsheets, XML or databases are out of scope), and assumes missions follow ECSS-E-ST-50, ECSS-E-ST-70, the PUS (ECSS-E-ST-70-41) and PLUTO (ECSS-E-ST-70-32). In ESA practice it is the standard-level counterpart of mission databases such as the SCOS-2000 MIB.

The standard introduces the space system model (SSM): a hierarchy of system elements, each with activities (telecommands and procedures), reporting data (parameters and compound parameters) and events. Chapter 5 sets conventions: railroad diagrams, naming, and simple data types, including the conventional types and the PUS PTC/PFC types, enumerations, value-type sets and complex types defined by languages. Chapter 6 gives the requirements as data tables (Table 6-1 to 6-111): exchange and configuration control of the electronic database, complex types (activity calls, expressions, interpretation functions, procedures, synthetic parameters, value sets), product configuration, system element data (system, application processes, the PUS service tailoring variables, MAPs, VCs, functions, memories, stores, CPDU and devices), reporting data (parameter numbers, raw PTC/PFC, interpretation/calibration, compound parameters, synthetic reporting data, limit, status and delta checks), activities (arguments, execution and verification data, telecommands with service type and subtype, MAP and priority, procedures) and events.

Annex A (informative) summarises, for each PUS-A-era standard service from TC verification to event/action, the service model, a tailoring flowchart and packet structures. Annex B gives EBNF grammars for the data types and the languages EXPL (expressions), IFL (interpretation functions), SPEL (synthetic parameters, with trigger, declaration and main bodies), PLUTO and VAL.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The standard defines the monitoring and control data that a supplier delivers with a product so that the customer can perform integration, testing and mission operations; how the data is provided (e.g. spreadsheets or XML) is outside its scope. (PDF p. 10)
  • It assumes missions conform to ECSS-E-ST-50, ECSS-E-ST-70, ECSS-E-ST-70-41 (PUS) and ECSS-E-ST-70-32 (PLUTO). (PDF p. 10)
  • A parameter is defined as the lowest level of elementary information that has a meaning for monitoring the space system; a synthetic parameter is reporting data generated within the monitoring and control system by an expression. (PDF p. 13)
  • The space system model (SSM) is a hierarchy of system elements mirroring the functional breakdown (system, subsystem, set, equipment, assembly, part or module), each carrying activities, reporting data and events. (PDF p. 15)
  • Simple data types include Boolean, integer, unsigned integer, real, bit, octet and character strings, absolute and relative time, and the PUS types identified by PTC and PFC (e.g. PTC 1 PFC 0 is Boolean with TRUE = 1). (PDF p. 24)
  • The product data schema must be computer-processable and lossless on re-import, the electronic database must be under configuration management with identification data (ID, version, date, supplier, files and checksums), and each digital file must be compressed with a standard tool. (PDF p. 38)
  • Synthetic parameter evaluations return engineering values directly, can be triggered on update of reporting data or on events, and support conditional branching, typed local variables and persistent variables. (PDF p. 41)
  • For packet parameters, the 'Parameter Number' (PUS Parameter#) is delivered, with value 0 not used and numbers assigned system-wide; raw values are described by PTC and PFC and translated by an interpretation function. (PDF p. 101)
  • Limit-check data consist of an ordered list of limit sets, each with a validity condition (the first TRUE one applies), upper and lower danger and warning limits, and an activity call as corrective action for each limit. (PDF p. 108)
  • Telecommand data include the PUS service type and subtype, the default application process, and a priority flag that forces a MAP ID for high-priority (e.g. CPDU) commands. (PDF p. 119)
  • Annex A presents, for each standard PUS service, the service model, a yes/no tailoring flowchart with Boolean tailoring variables, and the packet structures with field data types. (PDF p. 127)
  • SPEL definitions have the form 'synthetic parameter [Trigger Body] [Declaration Body] Main Body end synthetic parameter', with triggers 'on event' or 'on update of'. (PDF p. 236)

docs.text: Original locationhttps://ecss.nl/wp-content/uploads/standards/ecss-e/ECSS-E-ST-70-32C31July2008.pdfCopied (UTC)2026-11-12T17:48:18ZSHA-25696fa8029c6c91cc51f4f3a319e7f90031b1f6c32299937ed24ea6a2b2ce8f4faSize1.4 MBOur copyECSS-E-ST-70-32C31July2008.pdf (unchanged third-party file, not MIT; see the notice)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The ECSS standard for automated test and operations procedures. It does two things. First, it sets the requirements that any language for writing spacecraft test procedures (EGSE, AIV) and flight control procedures (mission control) must meet. Second, it defines a reference language that meets them, PLUTO (Procedure Language for Users in Test and Operations). The aim is to reuse procedures from functional testing in mission operations, and to use one common procedure language across missions.

Clause 4 places procedures in the EMCS (EGSE and mission control system). They refer to, but never define, the objects of the ECSS-E-ST-70-31 space system model: system elements, reporting data (parameters and compound parameters), activities (procedures, telecommands, operating-system calls) and events. Clause 5 holds the normative requirements: goal-oriented procedures built from steps, run in series or in parallel, with preconditions, confirmation and contingency actions; initiating activities with or without waiting for confirmation; reading execution and confirmation status, parameter values, validity and monitoring status; overriding missing functions in early tests; local copies of reporting data; flow control and waits; engineering units; user interaction and logging. Any compliant language must be formally specified in ISO EBNF.

The informative but extensive Annex A specifies PLUTO itself. A procedure has declaration, preconditions, main, watchdog and confirmation bodies, and steps have the same structure. Execution and confirmation status models apply to procedures, steps and activities, with continuation tests after 'initiate and confirm' statements. The annex then defines the lexical rules, constants and types and every language construct with railroad diagrams, a full EBNF grammar and an index. Annex B lists the SI-based engineering units and their syntax, and Annex C the mathematical, time and string functions. Many constructs come with a short worked PLUTO example script, for instance an 'Activate Freon Loop' procedure.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The procedure is the principal mechanism used to control the space system in pre-launch functional testing and in-orbit operations; the standard sets requirements for any procedure language and defines the reference language PLUTO (procedure language for users in test and operations). (PDF p. 7)
  • ECSS-E-ST-70 defines two types of flight control procedure (FCP): nominal procedures, the building blocks of the flight operations plan timelines, and contingency procedures for recovery after pre-identified anomalies. (PDF p. 15)
  • EMCS is the joint term for the EGSE and the mission control system; the procedure language and its development and execution environments are an integral part of any EMCS. (PDF p. 15)
  • Procedures refer to the space system model of ECSS-E-ST-70-31 (system elements, reporting data, activities, events) but do not define these objects; an activity is a procedure, a telecommand or any EMCS function such as a file transfer. (PDF p. 16)
  • For procedures the SSM also holds the default execution mode (manual or automatic), the activation mode (permanently active or explicitly initiated) and the procedural script. (PDF p. 18)
  • Procedure sub-goals can run in series or in parallel; preconditions and confirmation conditions may be specified for procedures and steps, and contingency actions should be taken at the level where the failure occurs. (PDF p. 19)
  • If an anomaly cannot be rectified, the procedure (or step) raises an event to a higher level, achieves the goal by other means and terminates, or aborts; the body is suspended while a contingency action runs. (PDF p. 20)
  • Procedures must be able to read an activity's execution or confirmation status and times, reporting data values and sampling time, parameter validity and monitoring status (limit, delta, expected status, status consistency), and the last occurrence time of an event. (PDF p. 20)
  • When a space system function is unavailable (e.g. in an early test phase), a procedure must be able to replace it by setting an activity's confirmation status or a parameter's value, validity, monitoring status or sampling time; local copies of reporting data avoid inconsistent samples. (PDF p. 21)
  • Any compliant language shall be formally specified in ISO EBNF (ISO/IEC 14977); PLUTO, its engineering units and functions should be used for automating procedures in development and exploitation phases. (PDF p. 23)
  • A PLUTO procedure has an optional declaration body (local events), optional preconditions body, mandatory main body, optional watchdog body (watchdog steps all initiated in parallel) and optional confirmation body; arguments are defined externally and cannot be changed in the procedure. (PDF p. 24)
  • Main body statements: set procedure context, initiate in parallel, initiate and confirm step, initiate and confirm activity, initiate activity, inform user and log; a parallel set ends when any one or when all of its members have ended. (PDF p. 26)
  • Execution status of a procedure goes through 'preconditions', 'executing', 'confirmation' and 'completed'; confirmation status ends as 'confirmed', 'not confirmed' or 'aborted' and is 'not available' before completion. (PDF p. 29)
  • Only engineering units are case sensitive in PLUTO; all other words, including keywords, are not. (PDF p. 39)
  • Table A-1 lists the predefined PLUTO types; Tables A-2 to A-7 list the operation and property requests available on activities, steps, reporting data, variables, arguments and events, and Table A-4 the predefined operators. (PDF p. 6)

docs.title: Provenance
docs.text: Original locationhttps://ecss.nl/wp-content/uploads/2016/06/ECSS-E-ST-70-41C15April2016.pdfCopied (UTC)2026-11-12T14:11:03ZSHA-256fed627dae2aa2a1e9dbfb873861002fbee40a37a3883019d6701af34852ea51dSize4.9 MBOur copyECSS-E-ST-70-41C-15April2016.pdf (unchanged third-party file, not MIT; see the notice)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
PUS-C, the second issue of the ECSS Packet Utilization Standard, is the reference for the application-level ground-space interface of most current ESA missions. It sits above the CCSDS Space Packet Protocol and the ECSS-E-ST-50 data link standards. It defines a menu of optional service types, each a set of request and report message types carried in CCSDS space packets, tailored per application process. Compared with PUS-A, it was rebuilt on a formal PUS foundation model (clause 5), which gives generic rules for service, subservice, capability, message and transaction types and for their deployment onto application processes, on-board parameters, memories, virtual channels and file systems. It also separates semantics (clause 6, system requirements) strictly from syntax (clause 8, interface requirements).

Clause 7 defines the packet field types: PTC/PFC codes for Boolean, enumerated, integers, reals, strings, absolute and relative time and deduced and packet fields. It also defines the PUS use of the space packet: the TM secondary header (PUS version 2, time reference status, service type and subtype, message counter, destination ID, time) and the TC secondary header (PUS version 2, acknowledgement flags, service type and subtype, source ID), padding and the CRC/ISO checksum.

The standard service types are ST[01] request verification, [02] device access, [03] housekeeping, [04] parameter statistics, [05] events, [06] memory management, [08] function management, [09] time management, [11] time-based scheduling, [12] on-board monitoring, [13] large packet transfer, [14] real-time forwarding control, [15] on-board storage and retrieval, [17] test, [18] OBCPs, [19] event-action, [20] parameter management, [21] request sequencing, [22] position-based scheduling and [23] file management. Each has clause 6 and clause 8 sections, and Annex C summarises every message type with its tailoring rule. Clause 9 covers the CPDU, and the annexes give real-number formats and checksums.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The update from ECSS-E-70-41A introduced the PUS foundation model (used to produce the standard and the mission-specific service types and the mission services) and a proper separation of system and interface requirements. (PDF p. 3)
  • All services are optional and implemented at distinct capability levels; PUS is a 'menu' selected per application process. The standard mainly addresses the spacecraft, and it assumes the ground segment implements all standardized capabilities. (PDF p. 10)
  • Normative references include ECSS-E-ST-70-01 (OBCPs), ECSS-E-ST-70-11 (operability), ECSS-E-ST-70-31 (monitoring and control data definition), CCSDS 133.0-B-1 (Space Packet Protocol, September 2003) and CCSDS 301.0-B-4 (Time Code Formats, November 2010). (PDF p. 11)
  • Messages from a subservice user to a provider are requests, made of instructions; messages back are reports, made of notifications, and come as verification, data and event reports. (PDF p. 19)
  • Standard service type IDs (Table 4-1): 1 request verification, 2 device access, 3 housekeeping, 4 parameter statistics reporting, 5 event reporting, 6 memory management, 8 function management, 9 time management, 11 time-based scheduling, 12 on-board monitoring, 13 large packet transfer, 14 real-time forwarding control, 15 on-board storage and retrieval, 17 test, 18 OBCP, 19 event-action, 20 parameter management, 21 request sequencing, 22 position-based scheduling, 23 file management; 7, 10 and 16 are reserved. (PDF p. 22)
  • Service interdependencies: request verification is accessible to any service in the same application process; event reporting and large packet transfer are accessible to any service; on-board monitoring and event-action require an event reporting service. (PDF p. 24)
  • Service type IDs are 1-255, with standard ones at most 127 and mission-specific ones at least 128; message subtype IDs are 1-255, with standard ones at most 127 and mission-specific subtypes in a standard service at least 128. A removed standard service type's ID is not reused. (PDF p. 26)
  • APIDs are unsigned integers up to 2046: APID 2047 is reserved for idle packets, APID 0 for spacecraft time packets, and other values are reserved per the SANA registry. (PDF p. 39)
  • Absolute time values are offsets from an epoch: CUC may use the CCSDS 1958 epoch or an agency epoch (free-running counter), while CDS must use 1958 January 1; PUS supports CUC coarse time of 1 to 4 octets and fine time of 1 to 10 octets. (PDF p. 435)
  • Absolute time (PTC 9) PFCs: 0 explicit P-field, 1 CDS without µs (6 octets), 2 CDS with µs (8 octets), 3-18 CUC with coarse octets = (PFC+1) div 4 and fine octets = (PFC+1) mod 4, and 19-46 CUC with longer fine time. (PDF p. 436)
  • Deduced fields are PTC 11 PFC 0, and their structure may depend only on preceding fields of the same packet and/or mission constants; packet fields are PTC 12 (PFC 0 TM packet, PFC 1 TC packet). (PDF p. 437)
  • All PUS packets are stand-alone space packets (sequence flags '11'); the TM packet sequence count wraps from 2^14-1 to 0; TC packets carry a sequence count or packet name that, with the source ID, identifies the packet. (PDF p. 438)
  • TM secondary header: PUS version number (4 bits, set to 2), spacecraft time reference status (4 bits), service type ID (8), message subtype ID (8), message type counter (16), destination ID (16), time (absolute time), optional spare. Version 0 was the ESA PUS (ESA PSS-07-101) and version 1 was ECSS-E-70-41A. (PDF p. 439)
  • Whether TM packets carry a packet error control field, and whether it is the ISO 16-bit checksum or the 16-bit CRC, is declared at mission tailoring. (PDF p. 441)
  • TC secondary header: PUS version number (4 bits, 2), acknowledgement flags (4 bits), service type ID (8), message subtype ID (8), source ID (16), optional spare. Ack bit 3 requests success reports for acceptance, bit 2 for start, bit 1 for progress and bit 0 for completion of execution. (PDF p. 442)
  • Every TC packet carries a checksum (ISO or CRC 16-bit, declared at mission tailoring), computed when all other fields are complete and verified on-board. (PDF p. 444)
  • A CPDU is a simple unit giving ground direct access to equipment (e.g. resetting a transponder). It has its own APID, a pulse duration unit of 10-15 ms, up to 2^12 addressable outputs and 12 to 504 pulse instructions per request; pulse duration = unit x 2^n with n = 0 to 7. (PDF p. 606)
  • ST[01] reports: TM[1,1]/[1,2] acceptance success/failure, TM[1,3]/[1,4] start, TM[1,5]/[1,6] progress, TM[1,7]/[1,8] completion, and TM[1,10] failed routing verification. (PDF p. 628)
  • Examples of message types in Annex C: TM[3,25] housekeeping parameter report, TM[5,1] informative event report, TC[6,2] load raw memory data areas, TC[8,1] perform a function, TM[9,2]/TM[9,3] CUC/CDS time reports, TC[17,1] are-you-alive test, TC[23,1] create a file. (PDF p. 630)
  • Annex D indexes each service type to its system (clause 6) and interface (clause 8) pages, e.g. ST[03] housekeeping at pp. 78 and 456 and ST[12] on-board monitoring at pp. 198 and 508. (PDF p. 655)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The public-review draft (DIR1, 11 December 2024) of revision 1 of ECSS-E-ST-70-41C, the ECSS Packet Utilization Standard (PUS). It defines the application-level interface between ground and space: a set of standard services for remote monitoring and control of spacecraft subsystems and payloads, and the structure of the telecommand packets carrying requests and the telemetry packets carrying reports. Missions tailor it as a 'menu' of services and capability sets.

The change log gives the aims of the revision: remove deficiencies of issue C, add lessons learned, align with newer ECSS and CCSDS standards and the ECSS drafting rules, and make the PUS foundation model consistent. Main changes: a reworked ST[01] request verification and ST[03] housekeeping, deletion of ST[08] function management (service type 8 is now reserved), new standard services ST[24] file transfer (based on CFDP), ST[25] file data storage, ST[26] parameter extraction and ST[27] critical packet log management, and configuration policies formalised as requirements.

The structure follows the 2016 issue. Chapter 4 gives context and modelling; chapter 5 the PUS foundation model (generic service type and deployment abstraction levels); chapter 6 the system requirements for service types ST[01] to ST[27], with 7, 8, 10 and 16 reserved; chapter 7 the space-to-ground interface, including packet field type codes (Boolean to deduced, absolute and relative time) and the CCSDS space packet with the PUS TM and TC secondary headers (PUS version number 2, time reference status, message type ID, message type counter, destination or source APID, spare and padding, and packet error control by CRC or ISO checksum); chapter 8 the request and report layouts for every service; chapter 9 the CPDU. Annexes cover IEEE and MIL-STD-1750A real formats, CRC and ISO checksums, a summary of all requests and reports, and a specification index.
