docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• This is an ECSS Draft Standard for Public Review (12 December 2024 to 28 February 2025) and may not be referred to as an ECSS Standard until published. (PDF p. 1)
  • Main changes of Rev.1: evolved ST[1] request verification and ST[3] housekeeping, deletion of ST[8] function management, standardisation of ST[26] parameter extraction and ST[27] critical packet log management, ST[24] file transfer and ST[25] file data storage for file-based operations, and configuration policies formalised as requirements. (PDF p. 3)
  • The PUS defines the application-level interface between ground and space; all services are optional, each can be implemented at several capability-set levels, and the mission tailoring is usually documented in a space-to-ground ICD. (PDF p. 10)
  • Service type 8 is now reserved; missions are encouraged to replace the former function management service with mission-specific service types or subservice types. (PDF p. 145)
  • ST[24] file transfer adopts the CCSDS File Delivery Protocol (CCSDS 727.0-B-5) as file transaction protocol and adds downlink managers that automate the downlink of files generated on board. (PDF p. 414)
  • ST[26] parameter extraction makes parameters from other application processes' telemetry packets available to central autonomy functions such as FDIR and OBCPs. (PDF p. 462)
  • ST[27] keeps critical packets (events of mission-specified severity and negative TC acknowledgements) in a dedicated, 'bounded' on-board log, independent of ST[15]. (PDF p. 467)
  • All PUS packets are stand-alone space packets (sequence flags 0b11); TM packets carry a packet sequence count, TC packets carry a sequence count or packet name that, with the source identifier, identifies the request; the CCSDS maximum packet size is 65542 bytes. (PDF p. 487)
  • The TM packet secondary header contains the TM PUS version number (set to 2), spacecraft time reference status, message type ID (service type and subtype), message type counter, destination APID, time and an optional spare; version 0 was ESA PSS-07-101 and version 1 ECSS-E-70-41A. (PDF p. 489)
  • The packet error control field is mandatory in the TM user data field; whether checksumming is used, and whether it is the ISO 16-bit checksum or the CRC 16-bit, is declared when tailoring. (PDF p. 491)
  • The TC packet secondary header contains the TC PUS version number (2), four acknowledgement flags (bit 3 acceptance, bit 2 start, bit 1 progress, bit 0 completion), message type ID, source APID and an optional spare. (PDF p. 492)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The top-level ECSS standard for the ground segment and mission operations. It gives the rules, principles and requirements for engineering the ground segment and for preparing and carrying out operations. It also covers the customer relationships with the ground segment supplier (GSS) and with the operations supplier (OS). EGSE for spacecraft verification and the launch segment are excluded.

Clause 4 defines the domain. Operations organizations (teams of operations managers, spacecraft controllers, flight dynamics engineers and others) together with ground systems form entities. The ground segment consists of the mission operations system (monitoring and control, flight dynamics, planning, simulation, OBSW maintenance, archiving), the payload operations and data system, the ground station system and the ground communications system.

Clauses 5 and 6 are written as process chains with inputs, requirements and outputs:

  • operations engineering: requirements analysis and concept (MOCD, SSORD tailored from ECSS-E-ST-70-11, on-board services selected from ECSS-E-ST-70-41), mission operations data production (MOP, procedures, and monitoring and control databases populated with TM/TC, display and OBCP definitions), data validation against an operational simulator (System Validation Tests), team training, operational validation, configuration management, execution and disposal;
  • ground segment engineering: definition, production, AIT and verification, maintenance and disposal.

Clause 7 maps these processes onto phases A to F and their reviews (GSSRR, GSPDR, GSCDR, GSQR, ORR, FRR, IOOR, ELR, MCR). Normative Annexes A to J give the DRDs: CRD, MAR, MOCD, OEP, SSUM, OVP, MOP, OAR, operations procedures and CFISRD. Annex K discusses reuse (common M&C databases between AIT and operations), and Annex L lists the Level-3 standards ECSS-E-ST-70-01, -11, -31, -32 and -41.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Main changes from ECSS-E-70A: a process approach separating operations engineering from ground segment engineering, separate customer-supplier relationships for each, harmonization with ECSS-E-ST-10C, no assumed reference architecture, DRDs as normative annexes, and new DRDs MAR, MOP, CFISRD, OEP and SEP. (PDF p. 3)
  • Scope excludes ground systems (e.g. EGSE) and operations supporting space segment verification, covered by ECSS-E-ST-10-02, and the launch segment and its operations. (PDF p. 11)
  • A synthetic parameter is a parameter derived from telemetry and other data via an algorithm; mission operations data are the subset of mission information used to execute in-orbit operations (e.g. procedures, operations rules, monitoring and control databases). (PDF p. 14)
  • The ground segment typically comprises the mission operations system, the payload operations and data system, the ground station system and the ground communications system. (PDF p. 20)
  • The mission operations system supports mission analysis, operations preparation, simulation, planning and scheduling, monitoring and control, flight dynamics, on-board software maintenance, data archiving, user services, data product delivery, performance analysis, configuration management and system maintenance. (PDF p. 21)
  • The ground station system provides TM reception, storage and distribution, TC transmission, tracking/ranging/Doppler/meteo data acquisition, station monitoring and control, time management, network management and data distribution. (PDF p. 22)
  • Critical areas include reuse of space segment operations knowledge and data (e.g. telemetry and telecommand definitions, procedures) between space segment design, AIT and mission operations. (PDF p. 23)
  • Space segment operability requirements are compiled in the SSORD, a tailored version of ECSS-E-ST-70-11; the on-board mission operations services, their capability sets and the corresponding telecommands and telemetry are defined with the operations customer, tailoring ECSS-E-ST-70-41. (PDF p. 29)
  • Inputs to mission operations data production include the SSUM and the space segment monitoring and control database (from the operations customer) and the ground segment monitoring and control database (from the ground segment supplier). (PDF p. 33)
  • Ground system monitoring and control databases shall be populated with mission-specific data, including mission planning data, OBCPs, telemetry and telecommand definitions, display definitions, on-board software images and patches. (PDF p. 34)
  • Table 7-8 lists the key ground segment and operations documents and the reviews at which each is deliverable. (PDF p. 79)
  • Mission operations data are validated with tools representative of the space segment, mainly an operational simulator, and on a flight-representative space segment exercising all procedures, telecommands, modes and redundancies (System Validation Tests). (PDF p. 36)
  • Table 7-9 defines the ground segment and operations reviews with their purpose, timing and owner, e.g. GSSRR (phase B), GSPDR (end of phase B), GSCDR (end of phase C), GSQR (phase D), ORR (end of phase D, operations customer), ELR (end of phase E2) and MCR (end of phase F). (PDF p. 81)
  • Annex K recommends reuse of monitoring and control databases and displays between spacecraft manufacturer, check-out and operations, and commonality between EGSE and ground station space link functions (downlink reception, uplink radiation, downlink and uplink data processing). (PDF p. 124)
  • Annex L lists the level 3 standards: ECSS-E-ST-70-01 (OBCPs), -11 (space segment operability), -31 (monitoring and control data definition, Space System Model), -32 (procedure language, PLUTO) and -41 (PUS). (PDF p. 127)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A 12-page set of tree charts showing the whole ECSS document system, published by ECSS in November 2025. The first chart shows the system description ECSS-S-ST-00, the glossary ECSS-S-ST-00-01 and the five branches with their disciplines: space project management (M), product assurance (Q), engineering (E), sustainability (U) and industrialization, production and maintenance (I). The following charts list every standard per discipline for the management, industrialization, engineering (with separate E-30 mechanical and E-50 communications charts), product assurance (with a separate Q-70 materials chart) and sustainability branches. They are followed by the handbooks and technical memoranda of the PA and engineering branches, and the ECSS policy (P-00) and documentation (D-00) series.

For this wiki, two charts matter most. The E-70 'Ground systems and operations' column lists ECSS-E-ST-70C, -70-01C (on-board control procedures), -70-11C Rev.1 (space segment operability), -70-31C (monitoring and control data definition), -70-32C (test and operations procedure language), and -70-41C with its Rev.1 marked as under update. The E-50 'Communications' chart lists ECSS-E-ST-50C Rev.2, the ranging, RF and on-board bus standards, and the CCSDS adoption notices ECSS-E-AS-50-21C Rev.2 to -26C (TM coding, TM SDLP, AOS, TC coding, TC SDLP, COP-1). The older ECSS-E-ST-50-01C, -50-03C and -50-04C do not appear in that chart. Handbook ECSS-E-HB-50A appears under E-50.

The charts are useful for placing the standards covered on ECSS, E-50 communications, E-ST-70C and the standards map in their ECSS context. They are an index only and contain no technical content.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• ECSS has five branches: space project management (M-10, M-40, M-60, M-80), space product assurance (Q-10 to Q-80), space engineering (E-10 to E-80), space sustainability (U-10 space debris, U-20 planetary protection) and industrialization, production and maintenance (I-10 to I-30). They sit under ECSS-S-ST-00 (system description) and ECSS-S-ST-00-01 (glossary of terms). (PDF p. 1)
  • E-50 is 'Communications', E-70 is 'Ground systems and operations' and E-80 is 'Security'. (PDF p. 1)
  • The E-70 column lists ECSS-E-ST-70C (Ground systems and operations), ECSS-E-ST-70-01C (On-board control procedures), ECSS-E-ST-70-11C Rev.1 (Space segment operability), ECSS-E-ST-70-31C (Monitoring and control data definition), ECSS-E-ST-70-32C (Test and operations procedure language) and ECSS-E-ST-70-41C (Telemetry and telecommand packet utilization), with ECSS-E-ST-70-41C Rev.1 shown alongside a 'U' (ongoing update) marker. (PDF p. 4)
  • The engineering branch chart also lists ECSS-E-ST-80C (Security in space systems lifecycles) under E-80 and ECSS-E-ST-40C Rev.1 (Software general requirements) under E-40. (PDF p. 4)
  • The E-50 chart lists ECSS-E-ST-50C Rev.2 (Communications), ECSS-E-ST-50-02C (Ranging and Doppler tracking) and ECSS-E-ST-50-05C Rev.2 (Radio frequency and modulation), plus the on-board link and bus standards: -50-11C SpaceFibre, -50-12C Rev.1 SpaceWire, -50-13C MIL-STD-1553B, -50-14C discrete interfaces, -50-15C CAN bus, -50-16 TTE, and -50-51C/-52C/-53C SpaceWire protocols. (PDF p. 6)
  • The E-50 chart lists six CCSDS adoption notices: ECSS-E-AS-50-21C Rev.2 (CCSDS 131.0-B-5 TM synchronization and channel coding), -22C Rev.1 (132.0-B-3 TM SDLP), -23C Rev.1 (732.0-B-4 AOS SDLP), -24C Rev.1 (231.0-B-4 TC synchronization and channel coding), -25C Rev.1 (232.0-B-4 TC SDLP) and -26C (232.1-B-2 COP-1). (PDF p. 6)
  • ECSS-E-ST-50-01C, -50-03C and -50-04C (the 2008 TM/TC standards) do not appear in the November 2025 E-50 chart, whose CCSDS link-layer entries are all adoption notices. The charts give no reason for their absence. (PDF p. 6)
  • ECSS-E-HB-50A (Communications guidelines) is listed under E-50 in the engineering handbooks chart. No handbook is listed under E-70. (PDF p. 11)
  • The documentation series comprises ECSS-P-00C (standardization objectives, policies and organization), ECSS-D-00B (ECSS processes), ECSS-D-00-01C (drafting rules for standards), ECSS-D-00-02A (drafting rules for handbooks) and ECSS-D-00-11A (public review and handbook release criteria). (PDF p. 12)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Issue 4.0 (9 March 2004) of the Software User Manual for the EGSE version of SCOS-2000 that ESTEC (TOS-EMG) prepared for the Herschel/Planck instrument developers, written by Serge Valera. The EGSE and Mission Control System (EMCS) follows the PROBA approach of one system for checkout and operations, using SCOS-2000 instead of SCOS-2. It consists of the SCOS-2000 kernel with its internal MIB, the SCOE system reached through an EGSE router and gateway, the Tcl/Tk-based Test and Operations Procedure Environment (TOPE), used while PLUTO (ECSS-E-70-32) tools were not available, and a Space System Model in which each addressable system element has a 16-bit identifier, with 0x0000-0x07FF reserved for on-board application processes (APIDs).

The manual covers installation of release 2.3e P5 on SuSE Linux 7.3, configuration and start-up. For MIB engineers the key part is section 4: the minimum EGSE data set (MIN_EGSE), whose files (tcp, pcdf, pcpc, ccf, cdf, cpc, dpc, pcf, plf, vdf) a mission adapts to its own packet headers; the 'Z' prefix of its names; SPIDs 1-100 reserved for generic packets; the mergeDATA and setSCOSdata tools; and the EGSE-specific MISCconfig variables (routing mode, binary command ZBINTC, time-stamping policy, mission epoch).

Section 6 is the TOPE language reference (tcsend with verification flags and time-tagging through PUS service 11,4; fetch, subscribe, waitfor, watchdog and logging). Section 7 defines the EGSE router message header and templates 1-7, an acknowledgement policy that extends PUS service 1 with ground-station, uplink and on-board acceptance reports (subtypes 9-14), and how SCOS files incoming messages by SPID, including unknown packets. Appendices cover conventions, known bugs and migration of procedures to the Herschel/Planck CCS.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The manual details the EGSE aspects of the EGSE version of SCOS 2000 prepared by the Agency and delivered to the Herschel/Planck instrument developers. (PDF p. 7)
  • The EMCS follows the PROBA common EGSE and mission control system approach, with SCOS 2000 replacing SCOS2; it is made of the SCOS kernel with its internal MIB, the SCOE system, the test and operation procedure environment and the Space System Model. (PDF p. 9)
  • System Element identifiers range over 0x0000-0xFFFF; 0x0000-0x07FF are reserved for on-board application processes and equal the APIDs, reflecting the 11-bit CCSDS APID field. (PDF p. 10)
  • SE-ID allocation table: 0x0800 router (spacecraft identifier in MIB), EMCS clients 0x2000-0x2FFF, ground station processes 0x4000-0x4FFF, TC Front End 0x8800-0x880F, TM Front End VC0-VC7 0x8810-0x8817, EGSE gateway/router 0xF000-0xFFFF. (PDF p. 11)
  • The Oracle-based SSM repository was not yet available, so users populate mission data through the SCOS 2000 ASCII (MIB) file interfaces, extended for EGSE command and control. (PDF p. 12)
  • TOPE is a TCL/TK-based procedure environment provided because PLUTO (ECSS-E-70-32) compliant software was not yet available. (PDF p. 13)
  • The MS-Windows EGSE Router (Delphi, DCOM/ActiveX, with a TCP/IP Gateway) and TM/TC Front Ends are not used in Herschel/Planck; SRON developed a Linux-based EGSE router for Herschel. (PDF p. 14)
  • A mission adapts the MIN_EGSE data set (tcp, pcdf, pcpc, ccf, cdf, cpc, dpc, pcf, plf, vdf files) to its TM/TC packet headers; all MIN_EGSE parameter and command names start with 'Z'. (PDF p. 21)
  • SPIDs 1 to 100 are reserved for the SCOS EGSE generic setup. (PDF p. 22)
  • MISCconfig EGSE_MODE selects TC routing: 0 NCTRS only, 1 NCTRS and EGSE Router, 2 EGSE Router only (default 1); EGSE_BINCMD_NAME defaults to the binary command ZBINTC for commands not defined in the MIB. (PDF p. 23)
  • EGSE_TM_FILING_TIME_TYPE time-stamps incoming TM by EMCS time (1), ground station/SCOE time (2) or uncorrelated OBT relative to TCO_MISSION_EPOCH (3), whose default is 1958-01-01T00:00:00.000000. (PDF p. 24)
  • tcsend uses the MIB default acknowledgement flags (CCF_ACK and PCDF_VALUE where PCDF_TYPE='K') when no ack clause is given; executiontime builds an on-board schedule command (LOADTT, PUS service 11,4). (PDF p. 29)
  • The EGSE router message header: DstID (2 octets), SrcID (2), Token (4), Time (8), Msg_Type (1), Spare (1), S/C id (2, 0x66 for PROBA), then application data. (PDF p. 44)
  • Msg_Types: 1 SCOE command, 2 SCOE command verification report, 3 SCOE observation report, 4 sending TC packet request, 5 sending TC packet verification report, 6 TM packet report, 7 TM frame reports. (PDF p. 45)
  • Besides the four PUS acknowledgements, the EMCS adds GS_Ack, UL_Ack and ONB_Ack, reported as service type 1 subtypes 9 to 14 (successful/failed GS, UL and on-board acceptance). (PDF p. 46)
  • Incoming messages are filed in SCOS internal packets by SPID chosen from Msg_Type, APID, service type/subtype and the PI1/PI2 fields (per the Database Import ICD section 3.3.2.4.2). (PDF p. 57)
  • TM packets with no matching pid.dat entry are filed under EGSE_WRAPPER_PKTID_6 and can be re-distributed into proper SPID archives with PDS_DISP after the MIB is updated. (PDF p. 60)
  • Bit numbering convention: bit 0 is the first transmitted bit and the MSB of a binary value. (PDF p. 63)
  • Known bug: time parameters before 1970 display wrongly; with a 1958 epoch a raw value of 0 shows as 2094. (PDF p. 64)
  • On the H/P CCS each TOPE procedure runs as a separate process and must explicitly connect and attach to a SCOE before commanding it. (PDF p. 70)

docs.title: Promoting ESA Software as a European Product: The SCOS-2000 Example
docs.text: Document IDesa bulletin 108Date2001-11OrganisationEuropean Space Agency, ESOC (Directorate of Technical and Operational Support; Directorate of Industrial Matters and Technology Programmes)AuthorsJ-F. Kaufeler, M. Jones, H-U. KarlTypePaperStatusPublished magazine article (bulletin 108, november 2001, printed pages 72-77).Pages6

docs.title: Provenance
docs.text: Original locationhttps://www.esa.int/esapub/bulletin/bullet108/chapter8_bul108.pdfRetrieved viaInternet Archive snapshot (the original URL no longer served the file)Copied (UTC)2026-11-05T14:10:03ZSHA-2569828d719bfaf6da121d78803c5ca8261d44978858537b0e467ae27e6b5c389bfSize100.6 KBOur copyesa-bulletin-108-ch8.pdf (unchanged third-party file, not MIT; see the notice)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
An ESA Bulletin article (November 2001) by J-F. Kaufeler and M. Jones of ESOC's Ground Segment Engineering Department and H-U. Karl of the ESOC Contracts Service on the initiative to promote SCOS-2000 as a supported ESA software product, not only as licensed in-house software.

It explains why ESOC bases every mission's control system on one generic system and lists the four strategic aims of SCOS-2000: ease of configuration, functional richness, scalability and vendor independence. It gives history and numbers: work started in about 1992, the first missions (Huygens, Meteosat MTP LEOP and Teamsat) were supported in 1997, the telecommanding chain was re-engineered in 1998-2000, about 15 MEuro had been invested, and control-system costs fell by a factor of two to three. It describes the port from Solaris to Linux and the replacement of the commercial ObjectStore and Orbix by the open-source POST++ and Omniorb, with ILOGViews kept for the user interface for now.

Much of the article is about licensing: ESA's 'operational software' IPR clause, free non-exclusive licences to Member State bodies, the three licence types (run-time, development, full), and a move towards open-source-style terms under which licensees hand back kernel improvements. It compares SCOS-2000 with US commercial products, lists the support set up (user organisation, FTP documentation server, help desk), and reports early results: the first users workshop (April 2001), adoption by DLR's German Space Operations Centre, use by the Herschel/Planck payload teams for instrument checkout (checkout changes pioneered on Proba), about 30 licences, and plans for certification and a Windows port.

It documents why and how SCOS-2000 spread beyond ESOC, including into EGSE.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• ESOC has used a generic mission control system as the basis for each mission's control system for over 25 years; SCOS-2000 is its latest generic system. (PDF p. 1)
  • SCOS-2000 strategic aims: ease of configuration/customisation, functional richness, scalability and vendor independence; all four were achieved and ESOC control-system costs came down by a factor of between two and three. (PDF p. 2)
  • Work on SCOS started in about 1992; its first ESA missions, Huygens, Meteosat (MTP) LEOP and Teamsat, were supported in 1997; the telecommanding chain was re-engineered in 1998-2000; total investment was of the order of 15 MEuro. (PDF p. 2)
  • SCOS-2000 originally ran on Sun Solaris; it was modified to run under Linux, and of its three COTS products (ObjectStore, Orbix, ILOGViews) the first two were replaced by POST++ and Omniorb. (PDF p. 3)
  • SCOS-2000 was to be used for all future ESA missions, for example Rosetta, which extends up to 2013. (PDF p. 3)
  • ESOC uses three licence types: run-time licences (temporary use and trial), development licences (upgrades of operational software under ESA contract) and full licences (developments based on the software). (PDF p. 4)
  • The main competing products came from US suppliers such as Integral Systems, Storm and Braxton Technologies. (PDF p. 4)
  • Nearly 100 people from outside ESA attended the first SCOS-2000 Users Workshop in April 2001. (PDF p. 5)
  • DLR's German Space Operations Centre chose SCOS-2000 for its control centre infrastructure, and the Herschel Planck payload PIs chose it for their instrument checkout equipment; checkout support was pioneered for Proba and introduced into the evolution version. (PDF p. 5)
  • Some 30 SCOS-2000 licences were granted in a little over two years, making it the best-selling product licensed through ESOC's Contracts Service. (PDF p. 5)
  • A certification activity with the ESA Quality Department was starting, using a method customised from ISO 9126 and developed with TUV Cologne; a study showed a Windows port to be feasible. (PDF p. 6)
  • From ESOC alone, 93 software products had been licensed in 94 Member State bodies, with more than 220 licences in total. (PDF p. 6)

docs.title: Checking Whether SCOS is up to SPEC
docs.text: Document IDesa bulletin 115Date2003-08OrganisationEuropean Space Agency, Directorate of Technical and Operational Support (ESTEC and ESOC), with TÜV InterTrafficAuthorsFernando Aldea, Michael Jones, Eduardo Gomez, Hendrik SchäbeTypePaperStatusPublished magazine article (esa bulletin 115, august 2003, printed pages 58-60); running head 'Certification of SCOS-2000'.Pages3

docs.title: Provenance
docs.text: Original locationhttps://www.esa.int/esapub/bulletin/bullet115/chapter8_bul115.pdfRetrieved viaInternet Archive snapshot (the original URL no longer served the file)Copied (UTC)2026-11-05T14:10:07ZSHA-256645d5b0d24c498c1744b1c34961d3d291046dc855c8262735bcdc347ac99566aSize140.9 KBOur copyesa-bulletin-115-ch8.pdf (unchanged third-party file, not MIT; see the notice)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A three-page ESA Bulletin article (August 2003) by F. Aldea (ESTEC), M. Jones and E. Gomez (ESOC) and H. Schäbe (TÜV InterTraffic) on the independent evaluation and certification of SCOS-2000 with SPEC (Software Product Evaluation and Certification), a method developed under ESA contract and based on several international standards. SCOS-2000 was the largest product evaluated with SPEC to date.

It explains the SPEC quality model: goal properties (such as functionality) split into second-level properties (completeness, correctness, efficiency), each quantified by metrics measured with defined evaluation methods. The model covers product properties (functionality, reliability, maintainability, re-usability, operability, documentation quality) and process properties (suitability for safety, software development effectiveness, system engineering effectiveness), including space practices from ECSS-E-40 and ECSS-Q-80. A sidebar summarises SCOS-2000: a generic, distributed and scalable mission control system (down to a single-workstation 'SCOS-2000 in-a-box'), with telemetry processing, telecommanding, online database and archive, general services, the Operation Language, roles and privileges, events and actions and on-board software maintenance, configured per mission through its database and configuration files. More than 40 customer licences had been granted.

The Phase I baseline evaluation of version 2.1e found that, of 85 SPEC metrics, 10 were inapplicable, 3 were replaced and 5 of 72 missed their target, so improvement was needed before certification as Class-B (mission-critical) software. Recommendations covered documentation quality, traceability, architecture simplification and coding standards; a Phase II delta evaluation and certification were to follow, and SPEC was also being applied to RTEMS.

It is a short primary source on SCOS-2000's software quality status around 2003.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• SCOS-2000, originally operational software for ESA missions, was being promoted as an ESA product and more than 40 customer licences had been granted. (PDF p. 1)
  • Certification benchmarks the product against an agreed quality model, performed by an independent organisation (TÜV InterTraffic) using the SPEC method. (PDF p. 1)
  • SPEC goal properties are split into properties quantified by metrics; efficiency, for example, is measured by timing margins, memory margins, throughput and resource utilisation. (PDF p. 2)
  • SPEC product-related goal properties: functionality, reliability, maintainability, re-usability, operability, documentation quality; process-related: suitability for safety, software development effectiveness, system engineering effectiveness; it covers practices such as those of ECSS-E-40 and ECSS-Q-80. (PDF p. 2)
  • SCOS-2000 functions listed: TM, TC, online database, online archive, general services and utilities, Operation Language (OL), roles and privileges (USER), events and actions (EVAC) and OBSM; the typical configuration is distributed but can be scaled down to 'SCOS-2000 in-a-box'. (PDF p. 2)
  • Phase I evaluated baseline version 2.1e; Phase II is a delta evaluation and certification agreed between ESTEC, ESOC and TÜV. (PDF p. 3)
  • Of the 85 metrics defined by SPEC, 10 were inapplicable, 3 were not measured and were replaced, and 5 out of 72 failed to reach the target value. (PDF p. 3)
  • SCOS-2000 still needed improvement before it could be certified as Class-B (mission-critical) software. (PDF p. 3)
  • Phase I was preceded by a Software Criticality Analysis based on a software FMECA, performed by Critical Software (Portugal). (PDF p. 3)
  • New coding standards were to cover state-of-the-art methods such as Model Driven Architecture and the languages used to develop SCOS-2000, primarily C++ and Java. (PDF p. 3)

docs.text: Original locationhttps://ecss.nl/wp-content/uploads/2023/01/ESA-PSS-04-106_Issue1(January1988).pdfCopied (UTC)2026-11-12T17:47:51ZSHA-2562b5770a6e2adb1c4cff882f17f395e3db869198683705413a1a0bbed0288a9e0Size3.7 MBOur copyESA-PSS-04-106_Issue1-January1988-.pdf (unchanged third-party file, not MIT; see the notice)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
ESA's Packet Telemetry Standard of January 1988 is the agency's subset of the CCSDS Packet Telemetry recommendation (102.0-B-2) for spacecraft that use the ESA ground network. It is the ancestor of today's Space Packet and TM Space Data Link Protocol books (see the history page). The library copy is a scanned PDF and its text comes from OCR, so the values here were checked against the page images.

The standard defines three data structures. The Source Packet has a 6-octet header: a 3-bit version fixed at Version 2 (0b100), a type bit, a data field header flag, an 11-bit APID, segmentation flags, a 14-bit sequence count and a length field. It is followed by an optional data field header and an optional packet error control field. The Telemetry Packet carries one segment of a long Source Packet, so that a single source cannot hold the downlink. The maximum segment length (256, 512 or 1024 octets, or none) is set per virtual channel. The Transfer Frame has a 6-octet primary header with a 10-bit spacecraft ID, a 3-bit virtual channel ID (up to eight channels), frame counters and an 11-bit first header pointer. It may also carry a 4-octet secondary header that extends the VC count, and a trailer with the CLCW and a 16-bit CRC. Each frame follows the marker 0x1ACFFC1D. With Reed-Solomon coding a frame is 1115, 892 or 1784 octets long.

Later sections cover the ground extraction steps and spacecraft elapsed time in CUC format. Section 7 explains how that time is correlated with UTC through virtual channel 0 (see time correlation). The remaining sections define the two delivery services, and the appendices cover CCSDS terminology, the choice of sync marker, a CRC encoder and channel-coding performance.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The Document Change Record says Issue 1 is directly derived from the CCSDS Packet Telemetry Blue Book 102.0-B-2 (January 1987) and supersedes the previous version, TTC-A-06 Issue No. 1 (February 1986). (PDF p. 6)
  • The standard belongs to the Space Link Standards & Protocols sub-branch (PSS-04-1XX) and supersedes the PCM Telemetry Standard TTC-A-02. Spaceborne telemetry systems must comply with it whenever the ESA ground network facilities are used. (PDF p. 13)
  • It specifies three data structures: the Source Packet (the end-to-end unit), the Telemetry Packet (a segmentation unit for multiplexing long packets) and the Transfer Frame (the link unit, which supports virtual channels). Channel coding is left to the Telemetry Channel Coding Standard (reference [2]). (PDF p. 14)
  • Bit 0 is the first bit transmitted and, in a binary value, the most significant bit. An octet is an 8-bit word, and octets are numbered with the same convention. (PDF p. 17)
  • The Source Packet header is 48 bits: a 3-bit version (only Version 2, coded 100, is permitted), a type bit (0 for telemetry), a data field header flag, an 11-bit APID, 2-bit segmentation flags, a 14-bit source sequence count and a 16-bit packet length (data field octets minus 1). (PDF p. 24)
  • APID all ones identifies Idle Source Packets, which keep ground packet extraction synchronised. APID all zeros is reserved for the standard Source Packet that carries the spacecraft time sample. (PDF p. 25)
  • In a Source Packet the segmentation flags are always 11. The source sequence count runs modulo 16 384 per APID and must not be short-cycled during continuous operation, but it may restart after an interruption such as a power-off. (PDF p. 25)
  • A Source Packet is 7 to 65 542 octets long. The data field header and packet error control field are optional subdivisions of the data field, and their detailed formats are outside this standard. (PDF p. 26)
  • When a Source Packet's data field is longer than LSEGMENT it is split into Telemetry Packets with segmentation flags 01 (first), 00 (continuation) and 10 (last); 11 means unsegmented. The length field of each segment gives the length still remaining of the original data field. (PDF p. 28)
  • Worked example in the standard: a 2106-octet Source Packet with LSEGMENT = 512 becomes four Telemetry Packets carrying 512 data octets each and a last packet carrying 52 data octets. (PDF p. 51)
  • Frame lengths are fixed per physical channel. With Reed-Solomon coding the frame is 1115 octets (the CCSDS cross-support length, interleaving depth 5), 892 octets (depth 4) or 1784 octets (depth 8). Without R-S coding it is any whole number of octets from 128 to 2040. (PDF p. 34)
  • The Attached Synchronisation Marker is 1ACFFC1D (hex). A second marker, 352EF853, is proposed for cases such as forward-played tape-recorder frames embedded in the real-time stream. (PDF p. 35)
  • The 48-bit primary header holds a 2-bit version (00), a 10-bit spacecraft ID, a 3-bit virtual channel ID, an Operational Control Field flag, 8-bit master channel and virtual channel frame counts, and a 16-bit frame data field status. The status field contains the secondary header flag, synchronisation flag, packet order flag, 2-bit segment length identifier and 11-bit first header pointer. (PDF p. 36)
  • Spacecraft identifiers identify both the spacecraft and the physical link. ESA projects obtain them from the ESA Directorate of Operations (D/OPS) at ESOC, with separate identifiers for flight, development and simulated data streams. (PDF p. 37)
  • Only forward-ordered, synchronous insertion of packets is recognised, so the packet order flag must be 0 when the synchronisation flag is 0. The segment length identifier codes LSEGMENT as 256 (00), 512 (01) or 1024 (10) octets, or no segmentation (11). (PDF p. 40)
  • In the first header pointer, all ones means that no packet header starts in the frame, and all ones minus one (11111111110) marks a virtual channel in the IDLE state. (PDF p. 41)
  • The optional secondary header is 4 octets long (version 00, length field 000011) and carries 24 more bits of virtual channel frame count, mainly for frames recorded on board and played back later. If used, it must appear in every frame of the master channel. (PDF p. 43)
  • The trailer has a 32-bit Operational Control Field and a 16-bit Frame Error Control Word. When the OCF type bit is 0 the field holds the CLCW, which is mandatory with packet telecommand. The Frame Error Control Word is mandatory unless the frame is carried inside a Reed-Solomon codeblock. (PDF p. 45)
  • The frame check sequence is a CRC with generator x^16 + x^12 + x^5 + 1. The shift register is preset to all ones and the CRC covers the frame without the sync marker. The earlier TTC-A-06 issue included the marker, and existing designs based on it remain supported. (PDF p. 46)
  • Spacecraft elapsed time uses the CCSDS unsegmented time code (CUC): a P-field starting 0010, 1 to 4 coarse octets and 0 to 3 fine octets, TAI seconds and an arbitrary epoch. (PDF p. 56)
  • For time correlation, the on-board clock is sampled at the first bit of the sync marker of the virtual channel 0 frame whose VC frame count is 0 (or, optionally, every 128 down to 1 frames). The sample is sent in the APID 0 time packet, and the ground station time-tags the same marker bit in CDS-coded UTC. (PDF p. 58)
  • Two standard ESA network services are defined. Service 1, Source Packet Delivery, covers reassembly, packet accounting, time correlation and CLCW extraction for COP-1. Service 2 is Transfer Frame Delivery. (PDF p. 64)
  • Appendix A maps ESA terms to CCSDS terms: Source Packet Header = Source Packet Primary Header, Data Field Header = Secondary Header, and Telemetry Packet = the CCSDS Version 2 Telemetry Segment. ESA numbers octets from 0, unlike reference [1]. (PDF p. 71)
  • Appendix D estimates frame-loss and packet-loss probabilities for uncoded PSK, Reed-Solomon (255,223), rate-½ k = 7 convolutional coding with Viterbi decoding, and the concatenated scheme. (PDF p. 77)

ECSS-E-ST-50-04C (31 July 2008) contains an informative Annex B, 'Changes from ESA-PSS-04-107', which lists technical differences such as the renamed segmentation sublayer and packet blocking (library item ecss-e-st-50-04c31july2008, PDF p. 131). docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
ESA's Packet Telecommand Standard, Issue 2 (April 1992), is derived from the 1987 CCSDS telecommand recommendations. Issue 2 only makes editorial changes to Issue 1 of June 1990. It is the forerunner of the TC Space Data Link Protocol, COP-1 and CLTU coding specifications (see the history page). The library copy is a scanned PDF and its text comes from OCR, so the values here were checked against the page images.

The uplink is described as five layers. The physical layer defines the acquisition and idle sequences, four carrier modulation modes and the physical layer operation procedure (PLOP). The coding layer wraps each frame in a CLTU: the start sequence 0xEB90, 8-octet codeblocks (shorter ones allowed) protected by a (63,56) modified BCH code, and a tail sequence. The transfer layer defines the TC Transfer Frame and the AD, BD and BC frame types. The frame has a 5-octet header with a 10-bit spacecraft ID, a 6-bit virtual channel ID and an 8-bit sequence number, is at most 256 octets long and always ends with a CRC. The same layer defines the Unlock and Set V(R) control commands, the 32-bit CLCW, and the complete COP-1 protocol: FOP-1 and FARM-1 variables, sliding windows and state tables. The segmentation layer adds a one-octet segment header with sequence flags and a 6-bit MAP ID. The packetisation layer defines the TC packet (version 0b000, type 1).

Further sections cover systematic retransmission for deep space, optional encrypted authentication of TC segments (see link security), the three ground-station services, and the performance targets.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Issue 1 (June 1990) was directly derived from the CCSDS telecommand recommendations. Issue 2 (April 1992) marks its changes with change bars, and they are only editorial. (PDF p. 6)
  • The standard supersedes the PCM Telecommand Standard TTC-A-01. With the Radio Frequency and Modulation Standard (PSS-04-105) for the physical channel, it is mandatory whenever the standard ESA ground network is used, and the Packet Utilisation Standard covers the higher layers. (PDF p. 15)
  • The telecommand system is layered into packetisation, segmentation, transfer, coding and physical layers. Each layer reports to its peer, and the transfer layer's report, the CLCW, travels in the trailer of the telemetry Transfer Frame defined by PSS-04-106. (PDF p. 20)
  • A ground station offers the control centre three telecommand interfaces. Service 1 is the sequence-controlled service for packets without authentication. In Service 2, packets carry authentication of segments, so the control centre segments them itself. Service 3 is the expedited service for data units of 1 to 249 octets. (PDF p. 28)
  • For Service 2, the control centre inserts a 9-octet authentication tail after each segment's worth of data. In the standard's example, a packet of 300 octets becomes an 'altered' packet of 318 octets. (PDF p. 29)
  • The acquisition sequence is at least 128 bits of alternating zeros and ones, starting with a zero. At least 8 bits of idle sequence must separate successive CLTUs. The four carrier modulation modes (CMM-1 to CMM-4) are combined into a PLOP, and the standard shows ESA's PLOP-2. (PDF p. 32)
  • CLCW bit 16 ('No RF Available') and bit 17 ('No Bit Lock') report the state of the spacecraft physical layer to the ground station. (PDF p. 33)
  • A CLTU is a 16-bit start sequence EB90 (hex), one or more fixed-length TC codeblocks, and a tail sequence. The tail sequence is one codeblock of alternating zeros and ones ending in a one. (PDF p. 41)
  • Codeblocks are 8 octets (recommended), 7, 6 or 5 octets. Each holds 7 complemented parity bits of a (63,56) modified BCH code with g(x) = x^7 + x^6 + x^2 + x^0, followed by a filler bit set to 0. Shorter codeblocks are coded with leading virtual fill. (PDF p. 43)
  • The CLTU decoder has INACTIVE, SEARCH and DECODE states. It accepts a start sequence with up to one bit in error, decodes codeblocks in single-error-correction mode. A codeblock with one detected error is corrected only if its filler bit is 0, so the tail sequence (whose last bit is 1) is always rejected and the decoder returns to SEARCH. (PDF p. 48)
  • The TC Transfer Frame has a 5-octet header: 2-bit version (00), bypass flag, control command flag, 2 reserved bits, 10-bit spacecraft ID, 6-bit virtual channel ID, 2 reserved bits, 8-bit frame length (octets minus 1) and 8-bit frame sequence number. The data field is 1 to 249 octets and the 2-octet CRC is mandatory, giving frames of 8 to 256 octets. (PDF p. 59)
  • Together, the bypass and control command flags give three legal frame types: AD (0,0) for sequence-controlled data, BD (1,0) for expedited data and BC (1,1) for control commands. The combination (0,1) is illegal. (PDF p. 61)
  • The 6-bit virtual channel ID is a sub-identifier that picks the spacecraft telecommand chain (typically two chains for redundancy). ESA projects obtain both the spacecraft and the VC identifiers from ESA D/OPS at ESOC. (PDF p. 62)
  • There are two control commands. Unlock is the single octet 00000000. Set V(R) is three octets, 10000010 00000000 followed by the new V(R) value. (PDF p. 64)
  • The frame CRC uses g(x) = x^16 + x^12 + x^5 + 1 with the encoder and decoder preset to all ones, and covers the whole frame except the CRC. (PDF p. 65)
  • The 32-bit CLCW contains: control word type (0), version (00), status field (000), COP in effect (01 = COP-1), 6-bit VC ID, 2 reserved bits, the No RF Available, No Bit Lock, Lockout, Wait and Retransmit flags, a 2-bit FARM-B counter, a report type bit (set to 0) and the 8-bit report value N(R). (PDF p. 68)
  • FOP-1 has six states: Active, Retransmit without Wait, Retransmit with Wait, Initialising without BC Frame, Initialising with BC Frame, and Initial. Its variables include V(S), NN(R), the Wait and Sent queues, T1_Initial, Transmission_Limit, Timeout_Type, Suspend_State and the window width K. (PDF p. 86)
  • When the timer expires at the transmission limit, Timeout_Type 0 raises an alert and Timeout_Type 1 suspends the AD service, which can later be resumed (intended mainly for deep-space use). (PDF p. 92)
  • The FOP sliding window K must satisfy 1 <= K <= PW and K < 256. (PDF p. 93)
  • FARM-1 has the states Open, Wait and Lockout. Its sliding window width W is an even number from 2 to 254 (200 at most is recommended), split into PW = NW = W/2. A frame whose N(S) falls in the remaining lockout area causes Lockout. (PDF p. 96)
  • A TC segment has a one-octet header: 2-bit sequence flags (01 first, 00 continuation, 10 last, 11 unsegmented) and a 6-bit MAP ID. Its data field is up to 248 octets. Using bit 2 of the header as a control flag splits the 64 MAPs into 32 data and 32 control MAPs, one pair per packet assembly controller. (PDF p. 136)
  • A packet assembly controller (PAC) enters Lockout on an incorrect sequence of segments (according to the sequence flags) or an incorrect control segment format. It is unlocked or reset by the one-octet control segment 'Reset Command' 111XXXXX, where the X bits give the PAC's MAP address. (PDF p. 139)
  • The TC packet has a 6-octet header: version 1 (000), type 1, data field header flag, 11-bit APID, 2-bit sequence flags, 14-bit packet name or sequence count, and a length field (octets minus 1). Packets are 7 to 65 542 octets. (PDF p. 145)
  • The optional 16-bit packet error control field is either the frame CRC or a 16-bit checksum specified in the Packet Utilisation Standard, and its presence is implied by the APID. (PDF p. 149)
  • After checking the error control and the fixed header fields, the receiving application process reports each TC packet by telemetry as clean and conforming, clean but not conforming, or rejected as dirty. (PDF p. 150)
  • For deep space, setting the FOP-1 timer to its minimum and choosing a transmission limit makes the ground retransmit a whole frame sequence systematically, without waiting for CLCW acknowledgements. The same technique can speed up commanding during launch. (PDF p. 153)
  • Authentication appends a signature to each TC segment; the data stay in plain text because secrecy is not required. Including a count number makes each authenticated segment unique, which defeats replay of recorded commands. (PDF p. 155)
  • Three Logical Authentication Channels are provided: Principal and Auxiliary for two independent streams (for example from two control centres) and Recovery. The COP-1 control frames Unlock and Set V(R) are not authenticated. (PDF p. 156)
  • Authentication control commands use a reserved segment header: MAP 63 with the sequence flags set to unsegmented. (PDF p. 157)
  • The authentication tail is a 2-bit LAC ID, a 30-bit LAC count and an N-octet signature, within a segment of at most 249 octets. The decoder specification (reference [8]) sets N = 5, giving a 9-octet tail. (PDF p. 159)
  • The standard recommends that the uplink bit error rate be guaranteed better than 10^-5. At that rate it guarantees a frame rejection probability better than 1 in 10^5 and an undetected frame error probability better than 1 in 10^19. (PDF p. 162)
  • A typical ESA spacecraft carries two TC decoders, which produce two CLCWs. Appendix C gives two schemes for inserting them into telemetry: one selected CLCW in every frame, or the two CLCWs in alternate frames. (PDF p. 171)

Notes

This is a scanned PDF. Its text was produced by OCR (RapidOCR) and has merged words, dropped lines and badly scrambled tables (the FOP-1 and FARM-1 state tables and state-transition figures on PDF pp. 117-131 are unusable as text), so every number, field size and bit pattern in this entry was checked against rendered page images. Page numbering: printed page n is PDF page n + 14 in the body (printed page 1 is PDF p. 15). PDF p. 2 is blank, p. 14 is a blank page whose OCR is a stray character, and pp. 181-182 are blank or the back cover. Oddities: reference [2] (Part 1, Channel Service) and reference [4] (Part 3, Data Management Service) print the same number, CCSDS 203.0-B-1. Reference [3] bundles two documents and gives both the number CCSDS 202.0-B-1 (p. 7). The running heads of Appendix D (printed pp. 159-160, PDF pp. 173-174) still read 'Issue 1 (June 1990)'. Clause 11.1 calls the Unlock and Set V(R) control frames 'type BD' (p. 161), whereas Table 6.1 defines control frames as BC (p. 61). The glossary entry for AD/BD/BC says 'Command Control Flag' where section 6 says 'Control Command Flag' (p. 165). Appendix D numbers its equations E.1 to E.5 (pp. 174-177). Clause 8.2.1.1 lists the subfields as 'Version Number, Reserved Bit, Data Field Header Flag and APID' but then defines bit 3 as the Type bit (p. 145). TC packets use Version 1 (000), while the PSS-04-106 telemetry source packets use Version 2 (100). The table of contents spells the chapter 'Packetization Layer', while the body uses 'Packetisation'.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
ESA's Telecommand Decoder Specification, Issue 1. The title page dates it September 1992, but the change record, copyright line and running heads say September 1993. It is a functional design specification for the on-board telecommand front end that implements the PSS-04-107 packet telecommand standard: the TC decoder, the Authentication Unit (AU) and the Command Pulse Distribution Unit (CPDU). The library copy is a scanned PDF and its text comes from OCR, so the values here were checked against the page images.

Section 3 sets the subsystem requirements: two redundant, always-powered decoder chains, real-time CLCW monitoring, a defined cold-start state after power loss, an automated sequence-controlled service, MAP multiplexing, and authentication that is transparent to the data link layers. Sections 5 to 7 complete the coding, transfer and segmentation layers. They fix 8-octet codeblocks, explain the (63,56) code as an expurgated Hamming code with a reference decoder, start FARM-1 in Lockout at cold start, and make the spacecraft ID, VC ID, window widths and authenticated MAPs programmable.

Section 8 specifies the AU: a 40-bit signature computed with a secret 60-bit LFSR hash and a hard knapsack, fixed and programmable 2940-bit keys, three LAC registers, and control commands on MAP 63 (see link security). Section 9 defines the CPDU, which drives up to 256 command-pulse outputs from short CRC-protected TC packets for recovery when the data handling system is unavailable. Sections 10 and 11 cover the telemetry reports (including the 32-bit Frame Analysis Report) and the interfaces. The appendices give an example configuration, hexadecimal test CLTUs, and how the early Alenia Spazio and Saab Space decoders differ from this specification.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Issue 1 is a new document that complies with and completes the Packet Telecommand Standard PSS-04-107 (reference [2]). (PDF p. 4)
  • This is a functional design specification for the on-board telecommand system, and its only applicable document is PSS-04-107. Of the layers, it concerns the coding, transfer, segmentation and authentication layers. The packetisation layer applies only to the CPDU, which is included because of its critical role in emergencies. (PDF p. 15)
  • The requirements apply to free-flying ('conventional') spacecraft. Advanced Orbiting Systems such as space planes and data relay satellites are out of scope. (PDF p. 17)
  • The front end must be fully redundant, with typically two separate chains, each with a TC decoder (including the AU when used) and a CPDU. Both chains are permanently powered and ready, special wake-up procedures are not allowed, and after a power loss the subsystem enters a predefined cold-start state. (PDF p. 18)
  • ESA's worst acceptable uplink bit error rate is 10^-5. ESA favours an undetected frame error probability of 10^-14 or better, rather than the CCSDS figure of one frame in 10^9. Using the frame CRC on top of single-error-correction decoding gives better than 10^-19 at a BER of 10^-5. (PDF p. 22)
  • PSS-04-105 specifies a maximum uplink symbol rate of 4 kHz. Rates around 20 kHz were expected within a decade, so designs should support the maximum feasible symbol rate. (PDF p. 22)
  • Each TC decoder should have at least 4, and preferably up to 6, symbol-stream inputs. In the SEARCH state it locks onto whichever active input first delivers a start sequence. (PDF p. 23)
  • Mission-specific data, which must be easy to reprogram on ground, include the 10-bit spacecraft ID, the 6-bit VC ID, the FARM window widths PW and NW (2 x 8 bits), a 5-bit authenticated MAP ID pointer, the 2940-bit fixed authentication key and the 11-bit CPDU application ID. (PDF p. 24)
  • Unless ESA agrees otherwise, the TC codeblock length shall be 8 octets. (PDF p. 31)
  • The decoder abandons a CLTU if its first codeblock is rejected. It also aborts the CLTU if more than 37 codeblocks are accepted, to avoid lock-up. (PDF p. 33)
  • The (63,56) code of PSS-04-107 is an expurgated Hamming code. Its generator x^7 + x^6 + x^2 + 1 factors as (x^6 + x + 1)(x + 1), and with distance 4 it is used for single-error correction plus double-error detection. (PDF p. 34)
  • At cold start, FARM-1 enters the Lockout state with the Retransmit flag, Wait flag, FARM-B counter and V(R) all at 0. (PDF p. 41)
  • MAP 63 is reserved for controlling the Authentication Unit. Authenticated MAPs are chosen in data/control pairs by a 5-bit pointer; for example, pointer 0 selects MAPs 0 and 32. (PDF p. 44)
  • The AU generates a 40-bit signature for each TC segment. A secret 60-bit linear feedback shift register hashes the segment, its 32-bit LAC value and 24 zero bits into a 60-bit pre-signature, which then goes through the knapsack. (PDF p. 49)
  • The hard knapsack sums 60 secret 48-bit weights selected by the pre-signature bits, modulo 2^48. The 8 least significant bits are deleted, leaving the 40-bit signature. (PDF p. 54)
  • An authentication key is 2940 bits: 2880 bits of knapsack weights and 60 hash coefficients. There is a fixed key in ROM for start-up and recovery and a programmable key in RAM for normal operations. (PDF p. 54)
  • There are three LAC registers: Principal (ID 00), Auxiliary (01) and Recovery (10). The 30-bit counts start at all ones at cold start. Only the 8 least significant bits of the Recovery count are maintained in flight, in non-volatile memory, and its other 22 bits are fixed at 1. (PDF p. 56)
  • The signature field is fixed at 5 octets (N = 5), so the authentication tail is 9 octets. Clause 8.4.1 gives a maximum TC segment length of 240 octets and a minimum of 10 octets. (PDF p. 58)
  • Table 8.1 lists the authentication control commands: Dummy Segment, Select Fixed Key, Select Programmable Key, Load Fixed Key in Programmable Key Memory, Set New LAC Count Value, and Change Programmable Key Block A and B. All are sent on MAP 63 with the segment header all ones. (PDF p. 59)
  • A new programmable key is loaded with 74 'Change Programmable Key Block' commands, each carrying a 40-bit block. (PDF p. 62)
  • The CPDU lets operators reconfigure the spacecraft when there is no telemetry and only the BD service works. It is identified by its own APID. (PDF p. 73)
  • The CPDU receives whole TC packets in single segments on its own MAP interface (in practice MAP 0). Once it has accepted a packet it executes all of its instructions, because no abort is provided, and it ignores new segments in the meantime. (PDF p. 74)
  • A CPDU packet is 10 to 248 octets (an even number) and ends with the frame CRC. It must have version 000, type 1, no data field header, the programmed APID and sequence flags 11. (PDF p. 75)
  • Each CPDU instruction is two octets. The first selects one of 256 pulse outputs, and the 3 least significant bits of the second set the pulse length to D x 2^n, where D is 10 to 15 ms; the maximum, 128 D, is 1.28 to 1.92 s. (PDF p. 76)
  • The telemetry reports are the CLCW status report (the last 16 bits of the CLCW), a 16-bit CPDU status report, an 80-bit AU status report and the 32-bit Frame Analysis Report produced for every CLTU. (PDF p. 83)
  • Appendix B gives hexadecimal test sequences for test jigs: CLTUs for Unlock, Set V(R), authenticated AU commands and a CPDU packet, each with the expected CLCW, FAR and status-report values. It also recommends that implementers use ESA's Telecommand Reference software. (PDF p. 105)
  • Appendix C records that the forerunner contract specification THB/CS/2077/av, first issued in 1986, led to two TC decoder developments: one by Alenia Spazio (then Selenia Spazio) and one by Saab Space. (PDF p. 117)
  • The early specification had a fixed, non-symmetrical FARM-1 window (W = 128, PW = 120, NW = 8). This specification instead allows any mission-fixed window, and the early window can safely be treated as a symmetrical window of 16 if K is at most 8. (PDF p. 119)
  • Appendix C lists where the early decoders do not comply. For example, Alenia Spazio's decoder uses an 'Erasure mode' in the coding layer, which ESA waived. Saab Space's decoder handles FARM-1 event E10 (buffer release) incorrectly, so a set Wait flag can stall the link. (PDF p. 121)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The first Packet Utilisation Standard (PUS), ESA PSS-07-101 Issue 1 (May 1994), was prepared by ESA's Committee for Operations and EGSE Standards. It defines the application-level interface between ground and spacecraft, on top of the PSS-04-106 packet telemetry and PSS-04-107 packet telecommand standards. It is the ancestor of the ECSS PUS (see PUS-A vs PUS-C). The library copy is a scanned PDF and its text comes from OCR.

Chapter 3 lists numbered operational requirements, from telecommanding and verification to testability. Each mission is meant to treat the standard as a 'shopping list', de-select what it does not need, and record the result in a ground/space ICD. Chapter 4 fixes the packet structures. Every TC packet carries a 24-bit data field header (PUS version, checksum type, 4-bit Ack, service type and subtype) and a packet error control field. TM source packets use packet version 2 and a header with PUS version, checksum type, a spare field, type, subtype and optional CUC or CDS time. The TC sequence count may be split into a source ID and a per-source count.

Chapters 5 to 21 specify 17 service types: verification, device commanding (including CPDU packets), housekeeping and diagnostic reporting, parameter statistics, events, memory, task and function management, time management and reporting, scheduling with sub-schedules and interlocks, monitoring, large data transfer, packet transmission control, storage and retrieval, traffic management (left to Issue 2) and test. Chapter 22 summarises the requests and reports, and chapter 23 defines the parameter types (PTC/PFC). The appendices give examples, the CRC and ISO checksum algorithms, and the mission parameters.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The PUS complements the ESA packet telemetry and telecommand standards (PSS-04-106 and PSS-04-107), which cover end-to-end transport, by defining the application-level interface between ground and space for electrical integration and testing and for flight operations. (PDF p. 4)
  • The PUS sits under the Mission Data Utilisation Standards (PSS-07-10) in the PSS-07 ground segment tree. Its siblings are the Orbit & Navigation (PSS-07-102), Station M&C (PSS-07-103) and Time (PSS-07-104) Data Utilisation Standards. (PDF p. 17)
  • The standard does not define protocols between on-board application processes or the content of payload/science packets, but science packets must conform and must have a data field header. Audio and video, which are multiplexed at frame level, are out of scope. (PDF p. 17)
  • The PUS is a 'shopping list'. Missions should de-select requirements and services rather than pick them, record the result in a mission ground/space ICD, and always implement at least the minimum capability set of each service they use. (PDF p. 18)
  • The three factors that drive telemetry and telecommand demands are on-board complexity, on-board autonomy and data transmission capacity. Autonomy support is deliberately basic in this issue. (PDF p. 19)
  • The operational requirements in chapter 3 carry identifiers such as OBSCH-1. Mission-dependent values appear as named mission parameters in angle brackets (for example <TIME_CORREL_ACCUR>), often with typical values, and Appendix B lists them. (PDF p. 23)
  • A service is defined by its requests and reports, a minimum capability set and optional additional capability sets. The service provider is an on-board application process, the service user is the ground system, and reports are either responses (to a request) or indications. (PDF p. 51)
  • TC packets use packet version 0, type 1 and an 11-bit destination APID. The data field header and packet error control are mandatory, except that CPDU packets have no data field header. (PDF p. 54)
  • TC sequence flags are set to 11 (stand-alone packet) for all ESA missions. The 14-bit sequence count is split into <NUM_SOURCE_BITS> of source ID (for example, the control centre) and a sequence count kept by each source for each APID. Acknowledgement packets must include the packet sequence control field to identify the telecommand they acknowledge. (PDF p. 55)
  • The 24-bit TC data field header holds a 3-bit PUS version (0), a 1-bit checksum type (0 = ISO 16-bit checksum, 1 = CRC), a 4-bit Ack field, an 8-bit service type and an 8-bit subtype. (PDF p. 56)
  • The four Ack bits request success reports for acceptance, start of execution, progress and completion of execution. Failure reports are always generated, and reports go only to the source of the telecommand. (PDF p. 57)
  • Service types and subtypes 0 to 127 are reserved for the standard; 128 to 255 are mission-specific. (PDF p. 57)
  • TM source packets use packet version 2 (field value 4) and type 0. A data field header is mandatory except in the spacecraft time packet. APID 0 is reserved for the time packet and APID all ones for idle packets, segmentation flags are always 11, and the 14-bit count wraps without short-cycling. (PDF p. 58)
  • The TM data field header holds a 3-bit PUS version (0), a 1-bit checksum type, 4 spare bits, the service type and subtype, and an optional (mission-defined) CUC or CDS time field. The CDS format uses the CCSDS epoch of 1 January 1958. (PDF p. 59)
  • Table 4-1 numbers 17 standard services: 1 telecommand verification, 2 device-level commanding, 3 housekeeping & diagnostic data reporting, 4 parameter statistics, 5 events, 6 memory management, 7 task management, 8 function management, 9 time management, 10 time reporting, 11 onboard scheduling, 12 onboard monitoring, 13 large data transfer, 14 packet transmission control, 15 onboard storage and retrieval, 16 onboard traffic management and 17 test. (PDF p. 61)
  • Telecommand verification: subtypes 1 and 2 (acceptance success and failure) form the minimum set. Subtypes 3 to 8 report start, progress and completion of execution, each as a success/failure pair. (PDF p. 65)
  • Device command distribution covers on/off and register-load commands in TC packets, CPDU packets (no data field header, up to 256 output lines) and device commands carried directly in a TC segment for non-nominal cases. (PDF p. 67)
  • In housekeeping and diagnostic reporting, the parameter reports are subtypes 25 (housekeeping) and 26 (diagnostic). (PDF p. 80)
  • Event reporting has four subtypes: 1 normal/progress report and 2 to 4 error/anomaly reports of low, medium and high severity. Each report carries a report ID that, with the APID, defines its parameters. (PDF p. 90)
  • The time reporting service (type 10) is provided by a single application process. It emits Time Report (10,1) without a data field header, sampling the clock at the first sync-marker bit of selected virtual channel 0 frames as defined in PSS-04-106. (PDF p. 110)
  • The on-board schedule supports <NUM_SUB_SCHEDS> sub-schedules (typically five to ten) and command interlocks, so a command's release can depend on the success or failure of an earlier command in the same sub-schedule. (PDF p. 39)
  • Chapter 20 (On-board Traffic Management Service) contains only a scope statement; the specification is deferred to Issue 2 of the standard. (PDF p. 178)
  • The test service (type 17) defines only the connection test: request (17,1), with the report as subtype 2. (PDF p. 179)
  • Parameter types are a subset of ISO 8824 (ASN.1). The standard uses its own compact encodings rather than the ISO 8825 basic encoding rules because of space-link bandwidth constraints. (PDF p. 186)
  • A parameter code is a PTC (type code) plus a PFC (format code). PTC 1 is Boolean, 2 enumerated, 3 unsigned integer, 4 signed integer, 5 real, 6 bit string, 7 octet string, 8 character string, 9 absolute time, 10 relative time and 11 deduced. (PDF p. 189)
  • Appendix A specifies the CRC (A.2) and the ISO 16-bit checksum (A.3) used in the packet error control field, and gives an example of a 24-bit OBDH command in service type 2 (A.4). (PDF p. 207)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The EDDS Update Guide is a short (six-page) administrator's procedure that explains how to upgrade an existing installation of the EGOS Data Dissemination System (EDDS) from release v2.2.0 to v2.3.0. EDDS is the ESOC web-service front end through which external users retrieve telemetry, telecommand history, events and parameters from the SCOS-2000 archives.

The guide is meant to be read together with the EDDS Configuration and Installation Guide (CIG), its only applicable document. It tells the administrator to stop all EDDS components except the MariaDB database, delete the previously generated runtime distribution and the old server components (Delivery Manager, Archiver and EDDS Server) while keeping the LDAP and EDDS home directories, and merge any new configuration properties into retained configuration files with a diff tool.

The only migration step specific to this release is an update of the internal EDDS databases, driven by two tickets: missing milliseconds in historical message display logs (Edds#558) and changed privileges in the MySQL creation script (Edds#911). The step uses the EDDS Migrator component: the administrator enters the database root credentials in migrator.properties and runs migrate-db.sh, which rewrites every stored request into the new database structure. The guide recommends a database backup first and quotes an observed migration rate of about 2000 requests per minute.

For the wiki it is mainly evidence of how EDDS is deployed and versioned (MariaDB, LDAP, separate Archiver, Delivery Manager and Server processes) rather than a source on data formats.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The guide covers a single upgrade path, from EDDS v2.2.0 to EDDS v2.3.0; Issue 12.0 is described in the change log as 'Issue for EDDS v2.3.0'. (PDF p. 2)
  • Intended readers are EDDS system administrators and end users of EDDS. (PDF p. 4)
  • Before upgrading, all EDDS components except MariaDB are stopped; the old EDDS_RUNTIME_DIST directory and the DELIVERY_MGR, EDDS_ARCHIVER and EDDS_SERVER components are deleted, while the LDAP and EDDS_HOME directories are kept. (PDF p. 6)
  • Database changes for v2.3.0 are due to Edds#558 (historical message display logs missing time milliseconds) and Edds#911 (privileges in the EDDS MySQL creation script). (PDF p. 6)
  • The database migration is run with the EDDS Migrator component: set the root credentials in migrator.properties and run ./migrate-db.sh; each stored request is converted to the new structure, at an observed rate of approximately 2000 requests per minute. (PDF p. 6)
  • Glossary terms and acronyms are delegated to the separate EDDS Glossary [GLO]. (PDF p. 5)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The EDDS External User Interface Control Document (EUICD) is the formal interface specification of the EGOS Data Dissemination System. It is the document a developer needs to write a client that requests SCOS-2000 mission data from ESOC, or to parse what EDDS returns. Mission-specific Data Definition Interface Documents (DDIDs) are expected to be derived from it.

Chapters 4 to 8 describe the services (authentication, batch, stream and user management), the data types (TM, TC and event packets from the PARC, parameters from the DARC or SMON, MCS and EDDS reports, FARC files, file-system files, acknowledgements), the request-to-response mapping and every output format. These are the self-describing EDDS binary format, in which a header lists the size of each optional per-packet field, with 21 TM header fields (SSC, APID, PID, category, PI1/PI2, data stream, CUC generation and reception times, SPID, ground station, virtual channel, PUS type/subtype, time quality and more), 29 TC fields and 6 EV fields, illustrated with a GDDS-compatible hexadecimal example; XML with mission XSLT; XFDU packaging; the TDRS spreadsheet; ASCII (including a TC report modelled on the SCOS-2000 command history); length-prefixed Google Protocol Buffers; and RawSourceBinary, a bare stream of CCSDS source packets. Chapter 7 gives the request and response ID naming rules, and chapter 8 the delivery mechanisms.

Chapter 9 documents the SOAP/WSDL port types, messages and bindings, chapters 10 to 12 the e-mail, file-server and Java client API (with code examples and push notifications), and Appendices A to L the XML schema types of every request, filter, format, report, schedule and user-management element. Appendices M and N cover the TDRS-style spreadsheet and Protocol Buffers.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The EUICD defines the EDDS Web Services interface and the Stream Web Service interface; where an XML schema file exists, the schema is the primary source and the document is updated after it. (PDF p. 14)
  • Mission-specific Data Definition Interface Documents (DDIDs) are expected to be created from the EUICD. (PDF p. 14)
  • Batch responses can be zip, tar (USTAR) or tar.gz compressed, and optionally AES-encrypted at mission level; every request has acknowledgement data delivered by e-mail or as an XML document. (PDF p. 19)
  • Stream responses are read from an ActiveMQ topic or via the client API over CometD, one Google Protocol Buffers-encoded packet or parameter per message; section 4.1.3 says only DARC parameter streaming is supported (DARC 3.0.0 or later), while section 4.1.3.2 adds live TM, TC, event-log and OOL streaming through the SCOS-2000 Data Provision Services (SCOS 5.4.21 and 5.5.4 or later). (PDF p. 20)
  • TM/TC/EV 'Raw' requests return packets exactly as stored in the PARC, as hexadecimal strings wrapped in XML tags, filterable only by start/end time and (TM, EV) SPID list. (PDF p. 30)
  • Out-of-limit reports support PARC packet versions 5 (SCOS 5.4.19/5.5.2 or earlier), 6 (SCOS 5.4.20/5.5.3 or later) and 7 (with change request GAIA-SPR-694). (PDF p. 31)
  • Supported formats: Binary, EDDS Binary, XML (and XML Transform), SFDU (from the GDDS DDID), ASCII and RawSourceBinary. (PDF p. 33)
  • EDDS Binary starts with a raw header: one octet N (number of header fields) followed by N one-octet sizes; each data element is then preceded by the selected header fields. (PDF p. 35)
  • Up to 21 TM header fields are defined, including Source Sequence Counter, APID, PID and Category (derived from the APID), P1val/P2val, Data Stream, Generation and Reception Time (CCSDS CUC), SPID, Ground Station, Virtual Channel, PUS Type/Subtype, SleServiceID, Time Quality (0 GOOD, 1 INACCURATE, 2 BAD), Database Version and Domain. (PDF p. 36)
  • Each TM data element is the raw spacecraft packet in network byte order preceded by a 1-byte EDDS sequence count (wrapping after 255) and a 4-byte data length. (PDF p. 37)
  • TC header fields include PUS type/subtype, source type, APID, verification status, CUC uplink/execution/last-update/release times, sequence name, sub-schedule, command source, acknowledgement flags, verification stages, PUS source sequence count and on-board verification stages. (PDF p. 38)
  • A GDDS-compatible TM binary file is reproduced by selecting EDDS header fields 8, 10, 12, 13, 17 and 18 (SCET, packet length, ground station, virtual channel, SLE service, time quality). (PDF p. 40)
  • The ASCII TC report follows the SCOS-2000 Command History; stage columns are R (release to NCTRS/NIS), G (ground station reception), T (uplink), O (on-board reception, AD mode only), A (acceptance), SS (execution start), execution steps and CC (completion). (PDF p. 47)
  • Protocol Buffers files start with an ASCII header line ('# Key: Value; ...') giving Type and Version, followed by serialized messages each prefixed with its size as a varint. (PDF p. 47)
  • RawSourceBinary, available only for the TM Report request, is a continuous stream of CCSDS TM source packets without any additional header. (PDF p. 58)
  • Request IDs take the form [RequestType].[Subtype].[Mission].[Domain].[yyyy.DDD.hh.mm.ss.SSS] (or [RequestType].[Username].[time] for account requests), and response files append @[time].[Counter].[Extension]. (PDF p. 59)
  • The EDDS web services are WSDL-defined with SOAP bindings mapping directly onto the XML schemas, using one-way and request-response operations. (PDF p. 61)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
This is issue 7.0 (December 2014) of the EDDS External User Interface Control Document, the interface specification of the EGOS Data Dissemination System at release v1.5.0, published when ESOC's ground-segment group still belonged to the Directorate of Human Spaceflight and Operations. It defines the authentication, batch, stream and user-management services through which external users and programs obtain SCOS-2000 mission data, and the XML schemas, file formats and web-service operations involved.

The content and chapter structure match the later issues. Services and client applications come first, then data types (PARC TM, TC and event packets, DARC and SMON parameters, MCS and EDDS reports, FARC files, file-system data, acknowledgements) with the request-to-response mapping. The output formats follow: the self-describing EDDS binary with its 21 optional TM header fields and the TC and event fields, a GDDS-compatible example, XML/XSLT, XFDU, the TDRS spreadsheet, ASCII including the command-history-style TC report, and Google Protocol Buffers. The rest covers naming conventions, delivery, WSDL/SOAP port types, messages and bindings, the e-mail and file-server interfaces, the Java client API, and schema appendices A to N.

It is useful mainly as a historical baseline. In this issue packets come only from the PARC Manager interface (the SCOS-2000 Data Provision Services appear only from issue 13.0), live streaming is limited to DARC parameters with the SLES 11 DARC 2.1.1 or later, there is no RawSourceBinary format, and out-of-limit report packet versions are not yet listed. Comparing it with issues 13.0, 15.0 and 24.0 shows how the EDDS interface grew between 2014 and 2025.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Mission-specific Data Definition Interface Documents (DDIDs) are expected to be created from the EUICD, which covers only elements common to all missions. (PDF p. 13)
  • Batch responses can be zip, tar (USTAR) or tar.gz compressed and optionally AES-encrypted at mission level. (PDF p. 18)
  • Only streaming of DARC parameters is supported; it requires the SLES 11 DARC version 2.1.1 or later, which publishes samples on an ActiveMQ topic with headers such as ValueType, Value, Validity (0 Valid, 1 Invalid, 2 Unknown, 3 Expired), GenerationTime and Name. (PDF p. 19)
  • Packets are extracted only through the PARC Manager interface of the packet archive; raw requests return the PARC hexadecimal packet strings wrapped in XML. (PDF p. 27)
  • Supported formats: Binary, EDDS Binary, XML and XML Transform, SFDU (from the GDDS DDID) and ASCII. (PDF p. 30)
  • EDDS Binary files start with an EDDS Raw Header (field count N followed by N one-octet sizes), and each data element is preceded by the selected header fields. (PDF p. 32)
  • 21 optional TM header fields are defined (Table 6) and each TM data element carries a 1-byte EDDS sequence count reset after 255. (PDF p. 34)
  • A worked example shows a GDDS TM packet binary file expressed with EDDS header fields (SCET, packet length, ground station, virtual channel, SLE service, time quality). (PDF p. 37)
  • ASCII TC report stage columns follow the SCOS-2000 Command History: R (release to NCTRS/NIS), G, T, O, A, SS, execution steps and CC. (PDF p. 43)
  • Protocol Buffers binary files begin with an ASCII header line starting with '# ' and listing Type and Version. (PDF p. 44)
  • Request ID format: [RequestType].[Subtype].[Mission].[Domain].[yyyy.DDD.hh.mm.ss.SSS], with response files suffixed @[time].[Counter].[Extension]. (PDF p. 54)
  • Web services are defined in WSDL with SOAP bindings onto the XML schemas. (PDF p. 56)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Issue 13.0 (May 2017) of the EDDS External User Interface Control Document specifies the client-facing interfaces of the EGOS Data Dissemination System at release v2.2.0. It defines how external programs ask ESOC for SCOS-2000 mission data and how the results are encoded. Its structure is the same as in the neighbouring issues: services and client applications (chapter 4), data types and request-to-response mapping (5), output formats (6), request and response naming (7), delivery (8), WSDL/SOAP web services (9), e-mail and file-server interfaces (10 and 11), the Java client API (12), and the XML schema appendices A to L, plus the TDRS spreadsheet (M) and Protocol Buffers (N).

The format chapter is the technical core for telemetry engineers. It defines the self-describing EDDS binary file: a header octet giving the number of optional fields, then one size octet per field, then each packet preceded by its chosen fields. The optional fields are 21 for TM (sequence counter, APID, PID, category, SCOS-2000 PI1/PI2 and data stream, CUC generation and reception times, SPID, ground station, virtual channel, PUS type/subtype, SLE service, time quality, database version, domain), more for TC and a few for SCOS-2000 events. The chapter also gives a GDDS-compatible hexadecimal example, the XML, XFDU, TDRS spreadsheet and ASCII formats (including the command-history-style TC report with its verification-stage columns), and length-prefixed Google Protocol Buffers records for parameters and reports.

Compared with issue 7.0 (2014), this issue adds the SCOS-2000 Data Provision Services as a packet source and as the route for live packet streaming (SCOS 5.4.21/5.5.4 or later), and requires the SLES 12 DARC (3.0.0) for parameter streaming. It also documents out-of-limit report packet versions 5 to 7. Issue 15.0 later adds the RawSourceBinary format.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The EUICD describes the common elements for all missions; mission-specific Data Definition Interface Documents (DDIDs) are expected to be derived from it. (PDF p. 14)
  • Batch responses can be zip, tar (USTAR) or tar.gz compressed and optionally AES-encrypted at mission level. (PDF p. 19)
  • Parameter streaming requires the SLES 12 DARC (version 3.0.0 or later); live TM, TC, event-log and OOL packet streaming is supported only via the Data Provision Services in SCOS 5.4.21 and 5.5.4 or later. (PDF p. 20)
  • Raw packet requests return PARC data exactly as stored, as hexadecimal strings wrapped in XML tags, with only basic time and SPID filtering. (PDF p. 29)
  • Out-of-limit reports support PARC packet versions 5, 6 and 7 (version 7 with change request GAIA-SPR-694 applied). (PDF p. 30)
  • Supported formats: Binary, EDDS Binary, XML and XML Transform, SFDU (from the GDDS DDID) and ASCII; no RawSourceBinary yet. (PDF p. 32)
  • EDDS Binary raw header: one octet with the number N of header fields, then N one-octet field sizes; the selected fields precede every data element. (PDF p. 34)
  • TM data elements are the raw packet in network byte order preceded by a 1-byte EDDS sequence count (reset after 255) and a 4-byte length; 21 optional TM header fields are defined (Table 6). (PDF p. 36)
  • A GDDS-format TM binary file is reproduced by selecting EDDS header fields 8, 10, 12, 13, 17 and 18. (PDF p. 39)
  • ASCII TC report stage columns: R (release to NCTRS/NIS), G (ground reception), T (uplink), O (on-board reception), A (acceptance), SS (execution start), execution steps and CC (completion). (PDF p. 45)
  • Protocol Buffers binary files carry an ASCII '# Key: Value;' header line (Type, Version) followed by varint length-prefixed serialized messages. (PDF p. 46)
  • Request ID format: [RequestType].[Subtype].[Mission].[Domain].[yyyy.DDD.hh.mm.ss.SSS]; response files append @[time].[Counter].[Extension]. (PDF p. 57)
  • EDDS web services are described in WSDL with SOAP bindings mapping directly to the XML schemas. (PDF p. 59)
