docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Issue 24.0 (January 2025) of the EDDS External User Interface Control Document is the most recent public specification of how clients talk to the EGOS Data Dissemination System and what it returns, at release v3.6.0. It keeps everything in the 2014 to 2018 issues. The services (authentication, batch, stream, user management) and the SCOS-2000 data types are unchanged: PARC packets via the PARC Manager or Data Provision Services, DARC and SMON parameters, MCS and EDDS reports, FARC and file-system files. So are the formats: self-describing EDDS binary with optional TM/TC/EV header fields, XML/XSLT, XFDU, TDRS spreadsheet, ASCII, Protocol Buffers and RawSourceBinary, together with the naming rules, delivery options, SOAP/WSDL services, Java client API and XML schema appendices.

Close to 90 pages were added for missions run on the European Ground Systems Common Core (EGS-CC). Data can now come from the EGS-CC HBase archive (HARC) or the EGS-CC REST interface. New Egscc* request types cover parameters, parameter definitions, raw and decoded TM, TC reports, log messages, activities and out-of-limits. There are dedicated EGS-CC binary header layouts (for example a 16-field EGS-CC TM header with packet instance ID, live flag, Earth-received time, route and data partition) and Protocol Buffers messages whose times are strings of seconds since epoch with 12 decimal places. Other additions are an EDDS REST API (section 9.5, with batchRequest, getStatus, streamRequest and other operations), a section on GDDS-format requests accepted by the Request Submitter and how they map to EDDS requests, live packet streaming via Data Provision Services, a large Java code-example appendix (O) and the DevOps pipeline (P).

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Change log covers issues 1.0 (2007-04-13) to 24.0 (2025-01-10); DCRs for this issue include EDDS-1355 (pre-filtering of EGSCC requests), EDDS-1373 (align Kafka and EDDS response fields) and EDDS-1367 (activity argument data mapped to the TM parameter proto). (PDF p. 3)
  • EDDS-1271 added EGS-CC out-of-limit requests to the interface (section 6.7.3.3.16, C.100, G.88 to G.90, I.50). (PDF p. 4)
  • Live TM, TC, event-log and OOL packet streaming is supported only via the SCOS-2000 Data Provision Services (SCOS 5.4.21 and 5.5.4 or later), published on an ActiveMQ topic or forwarded over CometD. (PDF p. 23)
  • The Request Submitter also accepts GDDS-format requests, converted to EDDS requests by an XSLT (GDDS2EDDS.xsl); scheduled GDDS requests always produce 10 EDDS requests because GDDS has no end date. (PDF p. 27)
  • Packets are now extracted through the PARC Manager, the Data Provision Services, the HARC manager interface or the EGSCC REST interface; parameters come from DARC, SMON, HARC and EGSCC. (PDF p. 33)
  • New request-to-response mappings include EgsccParam to EgsccParameterResponse, EgsccPktTmRaw to PktRawResponse, EgsccPktTmReport to EgsccPktTmReportResponse and EgsccLogMessageReport to EgsccLogMessageResponse. (PDF p. 35)
  • The EGS-CC TM binary header defines 16 fields: APID, PID, CUC generation time, time quality (0 GOOD, 1 INACCURATE, 2 BAD, 255 NA), live flag, packet instance ID, Earth received time, SSC, PUS type, spacecraft ID, quality flag, virtual channel, PUS subtype, EGS-CC reception time, route and data partition. (PDF p. 42)
  • EGS-CC Protocol Buffers reports express time fields as seconds since epoch with picosecond precision, as a fixed-point string with 12 decimal places. (PDF p. 58)
  • The classic Packet TM Report proto includes spid, type, sub_type, time_quality, virtual_channel, data_unit_type, pi1, pi2, packet_length and mnemonic fields. (PDF p. 67)
  • RawSourceBinary remains a continuous stream of TM source packets without additional header, available for the TM Report request. (PDF p. 82)
  • Section 9.5 defines an EDDS REST API at /edds/EddsRestService/v1/ with POST operations such as batchRequest (returns job IDs), getStatus (returns an acknowledgement), streamRequest, reSubmit, getStatuses, getResponse and getRequest. (PDF p. 136)
  • Appendix P: the GitLab pipeline has build, publish (JFROG repository) and deploy (Kubernetes cluster) stages. (PDF p. 373)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Volume 1 (Mission Management) of the ESOC Flight Operations Plan (FOP) for ESA's INTEGRAL gamma-ray observatory, launched on a Proton on 17 October 2002 into a 72-hour highly eccentric orbit. It is the management volume of the FOP, not a procedure book, and consists of five 'books'.

Book 1 (Mission Summary) gives the orbit, mission phases, payload (SPI, IBIS, JEM-X, OMC), satellite modes, and ground segment. The ground segment is the Operational Ground Segment (Redu, Goldstone and Villafranca stations, MOC at ESOC) plus the Science Ground Segment (ISOC at ESTEC, ISDC at Versoix). Book 1 also lists the MOC elements: the INTEGRAL Monitoring and Control System (IMCS) with its timeline generation (MPS) and archive/distribution (MADDS), the FDS, PAS, OBSMS, the simulator (IOS) and ISDS. Book 2 (Management Set-Up) describes the split of tasks, the roles of the Project Scientist, the Spacecraft Operations Manager (SOM) and the operations managers, the CCB, and the Flight Control Team (5 engineers, 2 analysts for database maintenance and tools, 6 SPACONs, 1 mission planner). Book 3 (Mission Rules) gives the rules on responsibility, launch hold criteria, emergencies, redefinition of mission goals and termination.

Book 4 (Configuration Management & Change Control) is the most relevant to this wiki. It covers who may change the FOP, the procedure validation chain (procedures generated with FOPGEN against the live database, tested on the simulator), and the Operational Database (ODB), derived from the manufacturer's Satellite Database and then maintained by the FCT analysts. It also lists which TM/TC definition fields (calibration curves, aliases, out-of-limits, packet structures, TC defaults) need CCB approval. Book 5 defines shift, revolution, weekly, monthly and annual reports and anomaly reporting. See operations preparation and the MIB.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• INTEGRAL was launched by a Proton on 17 October 2002 into an orbit with 153,600 km apogee, 9,000 km perigee, 51.6° inclination and a 72 h period. Routine ground stations are Redu, Goldstone and Villafranca (backup). (PDF p. 8)
  • The Operational Ground Segment comprises the ground stations (Redu, Goldstone, Villafranca as backup, and Perth for LEOP), the MOC at ESOC and communications. The Science Ground Segment comprises ISOC at ESTEC and ISDC at Versoix. (PDF p. 10)
  • The MOC elements are the INTEGRAL Monitoring and Control System (IMCS), the Timeline Generation System (MPS, part of IMCS), the FDS, the Mission Archive & Data Distribution System (MADDS, part of IMCS), PAS, OBSMS, the INTEGRAL Overall Simulator (IOS) and the INTEGRAL Security Distribution System (ISDS). (PDF p. 11)
  • The Flight Control Team under the SOM has 5 engineers, 2 analysts (database maintenance, operations tools maintenance, mission planning support), 6 spacecraft controllers (SPACONs) and 1 mission planning engineer. (PDF p. 19)
  • Mission Rule 2.2: the countdown is stopped if MOC essential functions are not available in hot redundancy, namely the IMCS (TM reception and processing, TC generation and release), the FDS and communications (OPSLAN), or if the MOC cannot exchange TCs and data with Redu or Villafranca. (PDF p. 25)
  • Mission Rule 3.1: a spacecraft emergency covers loss of attitude, fuel problems, critical power or thermal situations, loss of on-board TM/TC functions, or loss of contact with a ground station for more than 24 hours. (PDF p. 25)
  • Only flight procedures in the approved FOP may be applied. FOP and Operational Database (ODB) changes must follow the configuration control concepts and be approved by the SOM. The MOC tracks the on-board software with the OBSMS and on-board parameters with the ODB. (PDF p. 31)
  • The MOC items under configuration control include control-room and office hardware, the IMCS, the FDS and the NCTRS, following standard ESOC rules, with all modifications approved by the SOM. (PDF p. 33)
  • Procedure validation chain: manufacturer inputs in the user manual, visual check by the SOE, an implicit parameter check because procedures are generated with FOPGEN against the actual database, optional simulator tests, and SPACON runs on the control system with the simulator. A verification matrix is kept. (PDF p. 35)
  • The ODB was derived from the Satellite Database (SDB) supplied by the satellite manufacturer before launch. The SDB is no longer maintained, and the S/C Analysts maintain the ODB and propagate approved changes to the IMCS, the FOP generation tool and the OBSMS. (PDF p. 35)
  • Instrument TM parameter fields that need CCB approval are calibration curves, aliases, out-of-limits, packet structure and new parameters. For instrument TC parameters they are default values and calibration curves. (PDF p. 39)
  • An anomaly notification is issued within one hour of an anomaly to the Project Scientist, ISOC and ISDC, followed by a full anomaly report after assessment. (PDF p. 45)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The EDDS Glossary is the common terminology and bibliography volume of the documentation set of the EGOS Data Dissemination System (EDDS), ESOC's system for disseminating archived and live mission data from SCOS-2000 to external users. Every other EDDS document (CIG, SDD, SRS, SUM, EUICD, update guide) refers to it as [GLO] instead of carrying its own lists.

It has three parts. Section 2 lists the applicable documents of the EDDS project: the ESA BSSC tailoring of the ECSS software standards for ground segments (SETG), the EDDS statement of work and project plans, the ESOC Generic Ground Systems (EGGS) configuration baselines, the EGOS document template guidelines, the ESA network security policy, BSSC Java and XML coding standards, and the early EDDS EUICD and GDDS RDM interface documents. Section 3 lists 41 reference documents, which give a useful view of EDDS's lineage: analyses of reusing TDRS, WebRM, GDDS and MUST, the SCOS-2000 TM Data Retrieval Services SRD, the TDRS ICD, the Generic Data Delivery Interface Document (GDDID), SCOS-2000 SMF service ICDs, the DARC ICD and SDD, CCSDS SLE and XFDU (CCSDS 661.0-B-1) standards. Sections 4 and 5 define about 140 acronyms (for example PARC, DARC, FARC, RDM, SPID, SCET, OBQ, OBSM) and three terms (smoke test, software predeliveries, virtual appliance).

Engineers use it to decode EDDS acronyms and to trace where EDDS sits among the ESOC ground-segment documents and standards.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The glossary is the single place where EDDS documents define applicable/reference documents, acronyms and terms; it is referenced by all other EDDS documents. (PDF p. 4)
  • The document follows the SETG standard (ESA BSSC tailoring of ECSS software engineering standards for ground segments) and sits in the SWRR document package beside the SoW, SRS, SDP, SPAP, SCMP and SVVP. (PDF p. 4)
  • Change log: first issued 2010-01-18 for the Software Requirements Review; issue 7.0 of 2017-04-10 is 'Updated for EDDS v1.8.0i1'. (PDF p. 2)
  • Among EDDS's predecessors and inputs the reference list cites the SCOS-2000 TM Data Retrieval Services SRD (S2K-MCS-SRD-0004-TOS-GIC), the TDRS External Interfaces Control Document (S2K-MCS-ICD-0017-TOS-GIC) and the Generic Data Delivery Interface Document (EGOS-MCS-GDDS-ICD-1003). (PDF p. 7)
  • CCSDS standards cited: the SLE Cross Support Reference Model (910.4-B-1) and XML Formatted Data Unit (XFDU) Structure and Construction Rules (CCSDS 661.0-B-1, Blue book, 09.2008). (PDF p. 8)
  • Acronyms defined include DARC (Data Archive), FARC (File Archive), GDDS (Generic Data Disposition System) and DDID (Data Delivery Interface Document). (PDF p. 9)
  • PARC is expanded as Packet ARChive and MUST as Mission Utility & Support Tool; OBQ, OBSM and OOL are also defined. (PDF p. 10)
  • SPID is expanded as 'SCOS- 2000 Packet ID', SCET as Spacecraft Event Time, SSC as Source Sequence Count, RDM as Raw Data Media and TDRS as Telemetry Data Retrieval Service. (PDF p. 11)
  • Only three terms are defined: smoke test, software predeliveries (mock-ups and intermediate deliveries) and virtual appliance. (PDF p. 13)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A 30-slide presentation by Nestor Peccia (ESA) at GSAW 2003 (4-6 March 2003) giving an overview of SCOS-2000, ESA's generic spacecraft control system. It opens with ESA's objectives (reusable infrastructure for any class of orbit or mission, reused for MCS, EGSE and station control), its working methodology linking studies, prototypes, products and ECSS/CCSDS standards, and its product-line licensing model (free, non-exclusive licences for European companies; 54 SCOS-2000 licences in 3 years). It characterises geostationary, low-Earth-orbit and deep-space missions and traces ESA control systems from MSSS (frame telemetry) through SCOS-I (packet telemetry) and SCOS-II to SCOS-2000.

Further slides place SCOS-2000 in the ground segment (NCTRS, ESA ground stations, SLE, flight dynamics, mission planning, a LEOP room layout and the INTEGRAL MCS as an example), list ESA and external client missions, including the Herschel/Planck central checkout system and instrument EGSE, and give the version roadmap: Classic (Solaris, ObjectStore, Orbix, up to 2.4.1), Evolution 2.1.e/2.3.e (Linux SUSE 7.3, POST, OmniOrb), 3.0 (January 2003), 3.1 and 4.0 (multi-mission, full EGSE compliance). Architecture slides cover the object-oriented component design, enabling technology and standards (CCSDS packet TM/TC, ECSS PUS, SLE), client and server processes, software layers, system interfaces and top-level components.

The functional slides are the most useful for this wiki: manual stack and autostack commanding, static and dynamic PTV, release dependencies, interlocking, the on-board queue model and multi-stage verification; the packetiser, CLCW extraction, synthetic parameters, calibration, limit and status checks and display types (AND, GRD, mimics, scrolling); and SPID-based packet filing. It ends with lessons learned and the EGOS product family.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• ESA's operational-software licence is free of charge for any ESA member state company, non-exclusive, not resaleable and for peaceful purposes only; SCOS-2000 had 54 licences in 3 years. (PDF p. 7)
  • History: MSSS 1984-1996 (centralised, frame TM/TC, FORTRAN/Assembler); SCOS-I since 1989 (packet telemetry, no generic TC chain, FORTRAN/VMS); SCOS-II 1995-1999 (distributed, C++/UNIX), superseded by SCOS-2000. (PDF p. 9)
  • SCOS-2000 interfaces NCTRS over OPSNET/ESANET to the ESA ground stations, with SLE and a planned migration to TCP/IP. (PDF p. 11)
  • A LEOP configuration has prime and backup S2K servers and NCTRS, with 15 client workstations in the Main Control Room. (PDF p. 12)
  • Client missions in development included Rosetta, Mars Express, SMART-1, Venus Express, CryoSat (first ESA mission on the evolution platform), GOCE, ADM, Herschel/Planck MCS and the Herschel/Planck Central Checkout System (Red Hat 7.2); external users included 20 European scientific institutes using Herschel/Planck instrument EGSE (SUSE 7.3). (PDF p. 14)
  • Versions: Classic (Sun, Solaris 2.6, ObjectStore, Orbix, culminating in 2.4.1); Evolution 2.1.e/2.3.e (PC, Linux SUSE 7.3 or Solaris 2.6, POST and OmniOrb); 3.0 January 2003 (lines merged, Solaris 8); 3.1 September 2003; 4.0 June 2004 (multi-mission, full EGSE compliant). (PDF p. 16)
  • Enabling standards: CCSDS packet telemetry and telecommand, the ECSS Packet Utilisation Standard and CCSDS SLE; COTS include ILOG Views, Ctree+ for the packet archive; Flex/Bison parse the OL and zlib compresses packets. (PDF p. 18)
  • Server processes include the TM packetiser, limits checker, synthetic parameter packet generator, TC multiplexer, releaser, verifier and OBQM, archive, and events and actions servers. (PDF p. 19)
  • NCTRS ground-station interfaces listed: TMP4, TCE, MKII, MPTS MKIII and STC II; FOP production tool command sequences are imported into the MIB. (PDF p. 23)
  • Commanding: manual stack (encoding, de-calibration, time-tagging, release dependencies, interlocking, static/dynamic PTV, sequences), autostack, multiplexer, releaser to NCTRS, on-board queue model and multi-stage command verifier. (PDF p. 25)
  • Monitoring: packet reconstruction from frames, CLCW extraction, quality and sequence checks, supercommutated parameter extraction, OL/compiled/hard-coded synthetic parameters, calibration, limits, expected status and status consistency checks. (PDF p. 26)
  • Displays: alphanumeric (AND) with 32 or 64 parameters, graphics (GRD) with 1-8 parameters, mimics, scrolling (SCD), telemetry query display and packet history displays. (PDF p. 27)
  • All received packets are filed centrally with C-Tree+ by type (TM, TC, event), SPID, datastream and time, with retrievals independent of real-time handling and hot switch to the backup server. (PDF p. 28)
  • EGOS product family includes NCTRS/SLE, SIMSAT, GFTS, GDDS (Generic Data Disposition System), ADAS, APES, EVA, EGSE, MPS and FDS. (PDF p. 30)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
An ESOC slide presentation from GSAW 2005 on how ESOC reuses software across mission control systems. The software infrastructure it lists is SCOS-2000 for TM processing, TC uplink and verification, archiving and displays, NCTRS as the interface to the ground station network (SLE for non-ESA stations), GDDS, TDRS and WebRM for web access by external users, and other reusable tools (the XMM file transfer system, the Envisat mission planning system, the CryoSat database editors). Reuse rests on software designed for it, on harmonised spacecraft design and on standards: CCSDS packet TM/TC, the ECSS Packet Utilisation Standard, SLE and XML.

The core idea is the 'delta' approach: MCS requirements, design, tests and maintenance are written only as differences from SCOS-2000. The talk then introduces mission families (Earth Explorer, Planetary, Observatory), where a family kernel layer on top of SCOS-2000 collects features that similar missions need but that are too specific for SCOS-2000 itself. The worked example is the Earth Explorer family. CryoSat came first as a delta against SCOS-2000, GOCE was built as a delta against CryoSat, which defined the EE kernel, and Aeolus as a delta against that kernel. Requirement counts are given at definition phase (804 in total, 592 kernel and 212 mission-specific) and in the current heritage (680 kernel, 872 in total). The slides list the features each mission contributed, for example an offline database editor and consistency checker, playback TM processing with command verification, on-board queue dump processing, a time correlator, TM data gap identification and automatic schedule execution in NIS/NCTRS. The conclusions stress early involvement of ground teams in spacecraft TM/TC design.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• ESOC's reuse rests on infrastructure components designed for reuse, harmonised spacecraft design, and standards: CCSDS packet TM/TC, the ECSS Packet Utilisation Standard, SLE and XML. (PDF p. 4)
  • The ESOC software infrastructure is listed as SCOS-2000, NCTRS (interface to the ground station network, with SLE for non-ESA stations), GDDS, and TDRS with WebRM for external users such as payload owners. (PDF p. 5)
  • The ground segment scenario shows NCTRS between ground station and MCS (SCOS-2000) on the Ops LAN, with an FTS and a Generic Data Distribution System behind firewalls on a relay LAN towards external users. (PDF p. 6)
  • In the 'delta' approach MCS requirements are written only as deltas against the software infrastructure (typically SCOS-2000), and the approach extends to design, development, testing and maintenance. (PDF p. 7)
  • ESOC mission families: Earth Explorer (low Earth orbit, short visibility), Planetary (long propagation delay, on-board autonomy) and Observatory (long visibility, proposal-based observations). (PDF p. 10)
  • CryoSat was the first mission to apply the delta approach against SCOS-2000; GOCE was defined as a delta against CryoSat, making the EE Mission Family Kernel concrete; Aeolus was defined against the EE kernel. (PDF p. 11)
  • At definition phase: CryoSat SRD 406 kernel + 35 specific (441), GOCE SRD 129 + 62 (191), Aeolus SRS 57 + 115 (172); in total 592 kernel and 212 mission-specific requirements (804). (PDF p. 13)
  • EE requirements heritage: 680 kernel requirements, 35 CryoSat-specific, 42 GOCE-specific and 115 Aeolus-specific, 872 in total. (PDF p. 14)
  • CryoSat contributions include an offline database editor and consistency check system, a command and parameter identifier extension to the command subsystem, playback TM processing with command verification, and on-board queue dump processing with automatic generation of delete commands. (PDF p. 15)
  • GOCE contributed TM data gap identification, automatic TM replay and a time correlator; Aeolus contributed weekly consolidation of playback TM and automatic schedule execution in the Network Interface System (NCTRS). (PDF p. 16)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A short ESOC slide deck from GSAW 2020 on the off-line data analytics infrastructure that sits beside the mission control systems. It sets out a generic big-data layering (raw, processing, optimised and speed layers) and maps ESOC's tools onto it. ARES (Analysis and Reporting System) provides storage and infrastructure. PyARES, the (deep) novelty detection system, the Dependency Finder and long-term data preservation (LTDP) products and collections provide data accessibility.

ARES is an off-line analysis system that evolved from ESA's MUST (Mission Utility Support tools) and is built on the EGOS User Desktop framework. It mainly stores spacecraft housekeeping data in engineering format, and also files, parameters and events, optimised for fast retrieval. The architecture slide shows ARES importing EDDS response files on its own LAN. EDDS in turn draws on the MCS archives (DARC, PARC) on the OPS-LAN. The deck motivates a multi-mission shared big-data store with Gaia's volume (around 150 million unique HKTM samples per day). It describes PyARES as a Python library for retrieval and user-defined or machine-learning processing on Spark/HBase/Protobuf. Novelty Detection and the Dependency Finder are AI tools for spotting unusual telemetry behaviour and statistical dependencies between parameters; the Dependency Finder was validated by the Mars Express flight control team. The LTDP prototype combines ARES, Elasticsearch and a REST API. Future work listed includes processing live TM streams, migrating legacy missions to Hadoop and building a curated anomaly-detection dataset.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The big-data architecture has a raw layer (full fidelity, file/folder structures), a processing layer (distributed computation), an optimised layer (structured, organised by consumer use case) and a speed layer (low latency). (PDF p. 3)
  • At ESOC, ARES provides storage/infrastructure, while PyARES, the Novelty Detection system, Dependency Finder and LTDP products and collections provide data accessibility. (PDF p. 4)
  • ARES (Analysis and Reporting System) is an off-line data analysis system that evolved from ESA's Mission Utility Support tools (MUST) and is built on the EGOS User Desktop framework (EUD). (PDF p. 5)
  • ARES mainly stores spacecraft housekeeping data in engineering format, supports generic storage of files, parameters and events, and imports EDDS response files; the diagram shows EDDS reaching the MCS archives (DARC, PARC) on the OPS-LAN. (PDF p. 5)
  • Gaia receives around 150 million unique HKTM samples per day, which is used to motivate a multi-mission shared big-data storage. (PDF p. 9)
  • PyARES is a Python library for ARES metadata and data retrieval, user-defined-function processing and machine-learning jobs (Random Forest), bringing processing to the data with PySpark over Spark, HBase and Protobuf. (PDF p. 10)
  • The Dependency Finder prototype was developed by the Artificial Intelligence & Operations Innovation Team and validated by the Mars Express Flight Control Team. (PDF p. 12)
  • The LTDP products and collections platform was prototyped with ARES (Hadoop database cluster), Elasticsearch and a RESTful API. (PDF p. 13)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A short Alcatel Space technical note for the Herschel/Planck payload module (PLM) test campaign. During those tests the warm units of the instruments were driven through a chain made of the instrument EGSE (I-EGSE), the spacecraft Central Checkout System (CCS), the PLM SCOE and a CDMU DFE (a front-end that stands in for the spacecraft Command and Data Management Unit). Because the DFE does not reproduce the full CDMU behaviour, the note records which PUS services the test set-up actually provides.

The core is a one-page table (section 3.1) that walks through service numbers 1 to 22 of the Herschel/Planck PUS tailoring. For each it states whether the DFE supplies it for telecommands and for telemetry, and which subservices or CCS functions cover it. Only services 1 (TC verification, subtypes 1-1 and 1-2), 9 (time management, subtypes 9-3, 9-4 and 9-5) and 17 (connection test) are simulated by the DFE. Everything else is either not used or 'not supplied': the DFE then acts as a mailbox and passes the packets on, and the CCS provides the function. On-board scheduling, OBCPs and event/action are replaced by CCS TCL test sequences.

Section 3.2 adds that every TM packet received by the DFE is wrapped into a PIPE message (PIPE trailer plus body) and forwarded to the CCS and to the instrument EGSEs on the CCS LAN. An engineer finds here a concrete example of how a ground test environment substitutes on-board PUS services with checkout-system functions.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The test set-up chains the instrument EGSE (I-EGSE), the CCS, the PLM SCOE / CDMU DFE and the instrument warm units; the note exists because the CDMU DFE does not completely simulate the CDMU. (PDF p. 5)
  • Service 1 (TC verification) is provided for TM with subtypes 1-1 and 1-2. (PDF p. 6)
  • Service 9 (time management) is supplied for TC with subtypes 9-3, 9-4 and 9-5; subtypes 9-6, 9-7 and 9-9 are not supplied. (PDF p. 7)
  • Service 17 (test) is available for TC and TM (17-1, 17-2) by default. (PDF p. 6)
  • 'Not Supplied' means the service is not supplied by the CDMU DFE but by the CCS, with the DFE acting as a mailbox that transfers messages. (PDF p. 6)
  • On-board operations scheduling (11), on-board control procedures (18) and event/action (19) are covered by CCS TCL test sequences, for example time-tagged TCs are generated by a dedicated CCS test sequence. (PDF p. 6)
  • Service 3 packets can be sent to the CDMU DFE to update instrument packets, but not to update the DFE's own packets. (PDF p. 6)
  • Services 4, 7, 10, 13 and 22 are marked 'Not Used'; services 20 (Information Distribution CDMS) and 21 (Science Data Transfer) are TM routed by the CCS to the I-EGSE. (PDF p. 6)
  • Any TM packet received by the CDMU DFE is put into a PIPE message (PIPE trailer plus PIPE body) and sent to the CCS and to the instrument EGSEs on the CCS LAN. (PDF p. 7)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
An Alcatel Alenia Space technical note for Herschel/Planck. It describes how the Herschel/Planck System Database (HPSDB) ingests and regenerates MIB 'bridge files' in two flavours: the S2K flavour used by the SCOS-2000-based instrument EGSE (SCOS-2000 Database Import ICD issue 5.1) and the flavour used by the spacecraft Central Checkout System (CCS). Its goal is round-trip fidelity: it lists the constraints instrument teams must respect so that files loaded into HPSDB come back out identical. Constraints in bold cannot be checked by HPSDB and remain the user's responsibility.

Chapter 4 sets out 20 general rules, G1 to G20: the object data model, HPSDB identifier instantiation (subsystem letters, positions, generic items), special numbering for S2K curves, verification stages and parameter range sets, enumerated values, the different modelling of packet commutation, defaults, TM/TC sharing of curves, the 8-bit user category flag, generic TC packet headers, XML-reserved characters, the ban on octal radix, range allocation, automatic instantiation of APIDs and descriptions, mandatory descriptions, orphan items, sorting and derived-parameter files.

Chapter 5 then works through every MIB table field by field. For each field it gives input processing, the HPSDB attribute, output processing and the constraint to respect, from VDF through the monitoring, display and commanding tables to CCS-only tables (CUR, GRP, GRPA, GRPK, SCO, TCD, TMD, LGF). It notes which tables are ignored or generated from generic data, such as PIC, TCP, PCPC and PCDF, and which are not supported, such as command sequences and parameter sets. For an engineer it shows concretely how an industrial system database mapped onto the SCOS-2000 MIB, and where the two data models disagree, for example over TM-packet-to-SPID cardinality.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• HPSDB both ingests S2K MIB files (instrument EGSE, MIB ICD 5.1, delivered by ESTEC) or CCS MIB files and generates them; the note lists the constraints on input bridge files needed to get identical output files. (PDF p. 7)
  • Constraints printed in bold cannot be filtered by HPSDB and are the user's responsibility; non-bold constraints are checked by HPSDB at bridge-file loading time. (PDF p. 7)
  • HPSDB allows an N-to-1 relation between TM packets and SPIDs, whereas the MIB ICD allows N-to-N (with only one relation valid at any time). (PDF p. 7)
  • 'S2K' in this note means the instrument EGSE version 2.3eP5, based on SCOS 2000 2.3e. (PDF p. 8)
  • At subsystem/model level an HPSDB CHAR identifier gets the subsystem letter in front ('Z' for a pseudo subsystem) and a 3-digit position appended (system pseudo position '999'); NUMBER identifiers get the subsystem number (A=00 ... Y=25, pseudo subsystem 26) in front. (PDF p. 9)
  • Generic items use subsystem letter 'G', subsystem number '07', position '000' and element number '000'; all generic items are always extracted when MIB files are produced. (PDF p. 10)
  • S2K curves referring to specific curves are coded as NUMBER(3); generic curves are coded as NUMBER(4) '1xxx', mapping to HPSDB generic curve 'G000xxx000'. (PDF p. 10)
  • S2K command verification stages are coded NUMBER(4) for specific stages and NUMBER(5) '1xxxx' for generic stages (HPSDB '07xxxx000'); parameter range sets use NUMBER(3) and '1xxx' (HPSDB 'GRxxx000'). (PDF p. 11)
  • HPSDB models packet commutation differently from SCOS: a packet or structure is a list of parameters, structures and (TC only) fixed areas with offsets, repetition counts and super-commutation attributes; it flags each TM packet as fixed (PLF only), variable (VPD only) or both. (PDF p. 12)
  • Each HPSDB item has an 8-bit category flag, one bit per user type (AIT, operations, software, flight dynamics); MIB items are loaded as 'all except FDD' and output files are filtered by user type. (PDF p. 13)
  • TC packet header types are defined generically in HPSDB; the TCP, PCPC and PCDF tables are ignored on loading, and CCF_PKTID must reference a generic HPSDB TC header. (PDF p. 14)
  • Because HPSDB uses XML, the characters > < ' " and & must never be used; short descriptions are restricted to letters, digits, blank, plus, minus and underscore. (PDF p. 14)
  • Octal radix ('O') is not allowed for unsigned integer values; only 'D' and 'H' are allowed. (PDF p. 15)
  • When an element is instantiated in a subsystem, APID, PID and UDC/MISC parameter positions are computed automatically from element-level values plus position-dependent offsets, and the last character of the short description is overwritten. (PDF p. 15)
  • Descriptions (xxx_DESCR), optional in the MIB ICD, are mandatory in HPSDB; empty ones are filled with the item identifier. Orphan items are not loaded. (PDF p. 16)
  • For PID, HPSDB keeps the TM packet definition and the SCOS packet definition in two separate tables with an n-1 relation (one TM packet references only one SCOS packet), and forces a 1-1 link between PID and VPD where the ICD allows n-1. (PDF p. 24)
  • PID_DFHSIZE defaults to 16 and must be the same for all TM source packets addressing the same SPID; PID_TIME is forced to 'Y' and only valid PID definitions (PID_VALID='Y') may be delivered. (PDF p. 25)
  • The PIC table is defined in the generic part of HPSDB and must be identical on all Herschel/Planck SCOS and CCS systems to support 'smooth transition'; it is not loaded from bridge files. (PDF p. 26)
  • CCF_HIPRI is not loaded but calculated: 'Y' if CCF_PKTID = 'GX002000', otherwise 'N'; CCF_SUBSYS is forced from the subsystem letter ('01' for A ... '26' for Z). (PDF p. 33)
  • Command sequence tables (CSF, CSS, SDF) are not supported by CCS and must not be used; HPSDB supports loading them only to interface with MOIS for operations. (PDF p. 36)
  • Parameter-set tables (PST, PSV, CPS, PVS, PSM) are likewise not supported by CCS and must not be used, although HPSDB supports loading them. (PDF p. 39)
  • Chapter 5.4 covers CCS-specific tables absent from the S2K MIB ICD 5.1: CUR (conditional calibration), GRP/GRPA/GRPK (groups), SCO (SCOE definition), TCD/TMD (TC/TM distribution) and LGF (logarithmic curves). (PDF p. 42)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Issue 03 (10 June 2002) of Alcatel Space's top-level requirements specification for all Electrical Ground Support Equipment (EGSE) used in the electrical and functional integration, environmental testing and launch operations of the Herschel and Planck satellites. It is the parent of the specifications of the individual EGSE items (CCS, TM/TC DFE, TT&C, power, CDMU and ACMS SCOEs, PLM SCOE, CDMU DFE, Herschel cryo SCOE and the EGSE interface specification), shown in a specification tree. The RF suitcase and the SVF are excluded.

After the document lists and definitions (requirements labelled GRQT-xxxx, each with an analysis, review or test check method), section 3.2 sets the functional rules: a modular EGSE, test control centralised in the Central Checkout System (CCS) with backup MMIs in all SCOEs, and commonality between instruments, between checkout and flight control, and between test levels, with both the instrument EGSEs and ESOC's flight control system based on SCOS-2000. It describes each system EGSE item: the CCS (test sequences, satellite database, pre-transmission checks, housekeeping processing, test result archive, HPSDB mirror site), the TM/TC data front end (telemetry up to 3.5 Mbps reconstructed from transfer frames, telecommands up to 4 Kbps encapsulated in CLTUs, hazardous-command filtering, CLCW evaluation, NDIU link to the MOC), the TT&C, power, 1553-bus (CDMU) and AOCS (ACMS) SCOEs, and the launch-pad equipment (COTE, spacecraft simulator).

Sections 3.3 to 3.5 give requirements common to every SCOE: archiving and logging, cold and hot start-up with self-test, local and remote modes, safety, maintainability, three 100 Mb/s Ethernet LANs, power, grounding, cable marking, transport and storage. Section 4 defines three acceptance-test levels with a verification matrix, and Annex 1 counts EGSE units per spacecraft model.

It shows where SCOS-2000-based tools sit in the Herschel/Planck checkout chain.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Scope: top-level, implementation and interface requirements for the EGSE used during the whole electrical and functional integration, environmental testing and launch operations of Herschel and Planck; the RF suitcase and SVF are not covered. (PDF p. 7)
  • Each requirement is labelled GRQT-xxxx and has a check method: Analysis, Review or Test. (PDF p. 14)
  • GRQT-0000c: the MMIs controlling test execution are centralised in the CCS, with backup MMIs in all SCOEs. (PDF p. 16)
  • Commonality areas between flight control and checkout systems include the Mission Information Base (spacecraft and instrument databases), MMIs, data archiving and distribution, on-board software management and maintenance, and the user language. (PDF p. 18)
  • Baseline: the Instrument EGSEs will be based on ESOC's SCOS-2000, and the Flight Control System provided by ESOC will be based on SCOS-2000; ILT test procedures and OBCPs should be reusable in the CCS and in operations. (PDF p. 19)
  • The CCS shall be compatible with [S2] and [S3]; telecommands are pre-transmission checked against the Satellite Database, and during SVTs commanded from the MOC a facility shall block or veto dangerous commands from ESOC. (PDF p. 28)
  • 'CCS lite' differs from the nominal CCS only in having one server instead of two. (PDF p. 28)
  • GRQT-0002b: the CCS shall support an HPSDB (Herschel/Planck System DataBase) mirror site; all archived data shall be time-correlated to 1 second (TBC). (PDF p. 30)
  • GRQT-0003 TM/TC DFE: TM acquisition up to 3.5 Mbps with packet reconstruction from transfer frames and frame-level validation; TC sending up to 4 Kbps with encapsulation into transfer frames (CLTU), hazardous TC filtering and CLCW evaluation; TM/TC exchange with the NDIU. (PDF p. 31)
  • The CDMU SCOE acts as MIL STD 1553B bus monitor and remote-terminal simulator, including injection of predefined bus errors and quick loading of mass memories. (PDF p. 36)
  • GRQT-0150: at every start-up each SCOE checks local disk free space, creates a dated directory and opens its archive and log files. (PDF p. 44)
  • GRQT-0642/0644: TCCs and CCS peripherals on the 'Main CCS LAN', SCOEs and DFE on the 'SCOE/DFE LAN', experiment EGSEs on a separate 'Instrument Station LAN', all 100 Mb/s Ethernet with TCP/IP class B addressing. (PDF p. 54)
  • GRQT-0650: an EGSE interface compatible with the ESA-provided NDIU carries TM and TC between the satellites and the MOC. (PDF p. 54)
  • GRQT-0740: EGSE equipment is designed for 230 V (+5%, -10%), 50 Hz mains power. (PDF p. 55)
  • Acceptance testing has three levels: equipment, system EGSE, and the complete H/P EGSE with the satellite. (PDF p. 66)
  • Annex 1: three CCS (two servers) and two 'CCS light' units, three TM/TC DFEs and other system SCOEs, all provided by Alenia. (PDF p. 72)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The GMV software user manual for HPSDB, the Herschel/Planck System Data Base. HPSDB is the web-based Oracle application in which industry and the instrument teams kept the spacecraft and payload monitoring and control definitions, and from which SCOS-2000 and CCS MIB 'bridge files' were generated. The manual follows a functional-description, example, cautions, probable-errors pattern for every MMI operation.

Chapter 2 covers pre-execution: the central-site and mirror-site hardware, Windows 2000 with Oracle 9i Release 2 and Oracle9iAS, installation of the RDBMS and application server, creation of the HPSDB database and deployment and removal of the application. Chapter 3 explains the data organisation. Objects pass through a working area, a reference area (only the manager can change it, by validation) and an archive area. Box objects (elements, subsystems, models and one generic box) contain item objects (TM packets, TC packets, parameters, curves and so on). Objects are classified physically as theoretical or real and logically by level. One central site holds the valid data, and mirror sites exchange XML transfer files with it.

Chapter 3 then describes the administrator, manager and user views. Topics include session, site and schema control, user management, file management, box types, reasons for change, validation, generic data and central/mirror operations. The bridge file section is the most useful to MIB users. It explains loading SCOS-2000 or CCS bridge files with configuration files (S2K_EL, S2K_SUB, S2K_TM with a naming-convention column prepended to the PID file, S2K_CUR, S2K_CVS, S2K_PRF) and generating SCOS or CCS bridge files per box. Further sections cover XML ingestion, printing, TM/TC verification data, real element on/off status and logical instantiation. Annexes give the XML schema and the verification and on/off file formats.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• HPSDB runs on Windows 2000 with Oracle 9i Release 2 (9.2.0.1.0) Standard Edition and Oracle9iAS Release 2 (9.0.3), accessed through web browsers; the central site and mirror sites have the same software environment. (PDF p. 13)
  • Objects live in three areas: the working area (modifiable by all normal users), the reference area (validated objects, changed only by the manager through validation) and the archive area (old validated data); operations are creation, checkout, deletion, validation and discard. (PDF p. 29)
  • Box objects are elements, subsystems, models or the unique generic box and contain item objects such as TM packets, TC packets, parameters and curves; objects are also classified as theoretical or real (physical instantiation) and by logical level. (PDF p. 30)
  • There is one central site holding all valid objects and several mirror sites where only real objects can be modified; sites exchange XML transfer and log files manually, with no direct synchronisation. (PDF p. 32)
  • Only SCOS-2000 and CCS bridge files can be loaded; configuration files bridge the difference between the SCOS and HPSDB data models by defining the subsystem, elements and positions for the loaded items. (PDF p. 69)
  • S2K_TM.txt is a copy of the MIB PID file with a naming-convention TM packet identifier prepended, so its fields 2 to 17 are PID fields 1 to 16 of the SCOS-2000 Database Import ICD; HPSDB reads TM packets from it instead of the PID file. (PDF p. 71)
  • S2K_CVS.txt and S2K_PRF.txt map SCOS-2000 command verification stage and parameter range set identifiers (limited to 09999) to HPSDB generic identifiers, for example verification stage 9000 to generic 079000000. (PDF p. 73)
  • Bridge file loading creates no box types or generic items and is not a SCOS bridge file validator; OL expression files must be included in the zip when derived parameters are present. (PDF p. 75)
  • Bridge files are generated per box object as SCOS or CCS file sets, with user category, version, descriptions and reason for change entered on the generation page. (PDF p. 76)
  • TM parameter and TC verification data from test campaigns can be attached manually or from files; unlike normal updates they are written directly into the reference area, and they are reset when the parameter, its curves or its packet structures change. (PDF p. 130)
  • The XML ingestion schema (Annex E) has a root element HPSDB with generic types such as TC_GN, CVS_GN, CURVE_GN, TM_GN, SCOS_TM_GN, PAR_GN, DISPLAY_GN, TC_STR_GN and TM_STR_GN. (PDF p. 145)
  • Verification files are tab-separated lines of date-time (SCOS Julian format YYYY.DDD.HH.MM.SS.mmm), type c (telecommand) or p (parameter), item name, test sequence name and issue, and site. (PDF p. 201)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The release note that accompanied one delivery of the Herschel/Planck System Data Base (HPSDB), Thales Alenia Space's industrial system database, to Astrium (ASED, Friedrichshafen). The delivery is a set of MIB files in Central Checkout System (CCS) format, filtered for AIT users, for the Herschel flight model theoretical model HERSCH_FM9. It was generated by HPSDB version 3.3.1.30 on 07/04/2008 for the Herschel IRR, and it added CDMS on-board software 3.4 and OBCP version 11.

The note follows a fixed configuration-item template: configuration item 460000, supplier, the inputs per level (generic, element, subsystem, model) with their source deliveries (HIFI 11.6, SPIRE 2.2.H1 PR, PACS 8.17, cryostat, service module, system), input changes and open NCRs, and the DBAMN database amendment requests applied. It also tabulates TM packet routing (which subsystem TM goes to which instrument EGSE, from the TMD file) and TC packet routing by APID (from the TCD file).

The output section shows the model's object tree, the theoretical subsystems at numbered positions (ACMS A105, CDMS D108, HIFI H004, cryostat K002, PACS P002, RF R101, SPIRE S002, thermal T101, power W101, EGSE Y104) with their elements. It also gives the MD5 checksum and the file-naming convention of HPSDB exports, which encodes the area, the object box type and the MIB flavour (CCS, S2K or MCS). An NCR annex records issues such as the SPIRE event naming fix and an APID curve listing the instrument APIDs. For an engineer it shows how instrument MIBs were integrated and configuration-controlled into one spacecraft database.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Delivery from Central Site HPSDB v3.3.1.30 to ASED (Friedrichshafen) of theoretical model HERSCH_FM9, file type CCS, AIT user filter, file R_TM_HERSCH_FM9_C_804071709.zip, for the Herschel IRR. (PDF p. 8)
  • Inputs are assembled by level: generic data (generic), bus profile and OBCP (element), HIFI, SPIRE, PACS and cryostat (subsystem), SVM and system data (model). (PDF p. 8)
  • Open NCRs on the instrument EGSE inputs include file formats not compatible with Windows, extra spaces in cpc.dat and a missing tpcf.dat. (PDF p. 9)
  • The TCD (TC packet routing) configuration maps APIDs to equipment: for example APIDs 0, 16, 512, 1024, 1152, 1280 and 2020 to TMTCDFE, 2017 to CDMUSCOE, 2026 to PFM_CRYO and 2042/2043/2044 to the HIFI, PACS and SPIRE EGSEs. (PDF p. 10)
  • Model HERSCH_FM9 groups theoretical subsystems at positions: A105 ACMS 3.7, D108 CDMS 3.4, H004 HIFI FM v11_6, K002 Cryostat, P002 PACS FM 8.17, R101 TTC_HER, S002 SPIRE FM 2.2.H1 PR, T101 TCS_HER, W101 EPS_H and Y104 EGSE. (PDF p. 11)
  • The delivery checksum type is MD5, and the release is identified as H-P-2-ASP-LI-1441 v 09.0 generated on 07/04/2008. (PDF p. 17)
  • HPSDB export file naming: <Area><Box><Object name><MIB type><Date>_<M>.zip, with Area R/A/W (reference, archive, working), Box TE/TS/TM/RM etc., MIB type C (CCS), S (S2K) or M (MCS), the date as YMMDDHHMN and an optional M flag for manual updates. (PDF p. 17)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A Herschel Science Centre note that completes the definition of how MIB ASCII datasets enter the Herschel Common Science System (HCSS). The HCSS used the instrument MIBs to build instrument commands and to interpret downlinked data for Quick Look Assessment and Interactive Analysis. The interface is nominally defined by two external documents: the SCOS-2000 Database Import ICD (issue 5.2, RD-1) and the Herschel/Planck Naming Convention Specification (issue 2.1, RD-2). This note clarifies their ambiguous passages and adds Herschel-specific constraints.

Section 4 settles basic file-format questions: what a line is, how many tab-separated fields a record needs, default values for empty optional fields, strict limit semantics, and the reference point and bit order of PLF_OFFBY/PLF_OFFBI. Sections 5 and 6 list the tables the HCSS needs and the ones it ignores (VDF, command sequences, parameter sets), an extra command-duration table, and rules on SPIDs, PID/PIC SID consistency, PCDF header rows, TXP ranges and description character sets. They also give the reduced field set that software release 0.2 actually interprets. Section 7 catalogues the 34 ingestion checks with their error or warning actions.

The appendices reproduce the 2002 correspondence behind the rules: HSC comments on the Alcatel naming convention, ESOC's point-by-point answers with the DCRs they raised (286, 308, 309), and a PACS/ESOC exchange on why all PUS service 1 packets then shared one SPID. For an engineer it is a rare first-hand account of how an ICD was read in practice and of the edge cases that matter when you write a MIB parser.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The MIB interface to the HCSS is defined by [RD-1] (SCOS-2000 Database Import ICD) and [RD-2] (Herschel/Planck Naming Convention), with [RD-2] taking precedence in case of conflict; this note clarifies and tailors both. (PDF p. 4)
  • The HCSS uses MIB data to define instrument-related commands and to interpret downlink data for the Quick Look Assessment (QLA) and Interactive Analysis (IA) subsystems; the raw MIB is produced by a MIB Editor outside the HCSS and delivered as ASCII files. (PDF p. 4)
  • Each line of a MIB file is one record; a table with T fields of which the last G are unused by SCOS-2000 (grey in the ICD) needs at least N = T-G fields, separated by N-1 tab characters. Line ends are LF on Unix and CR+LF on Windows. (PDF p. 9)
  • For non-mandatory fields without an explicit default, the default is 0 for integers, 0.0 for floating point and an empty string for strings. (PDF p. 10)
  • An out-of-limits condition is raised only when the value is strictly below the low limit or strictly above the high limit, for both hard and soft limits. (PDF p. 10)
  • PLF_OFFBY/PLF_OFFBI are counted from the end of the SCOS-2000 packet header, which coincides with the start of the TM source packet header when the generic SCOS-2000 packetiser is used (DCR 309); PLF_OFFBI bit 0 is the most significant bit (DCR 308). (PDF p. 10)
  • Floating-point (NUMBER) values must use the decimal point '.', not a comma. (PDF p. 10)
  • Besides the SCOS-2000 tables, HCSS ingestion requires a two-field command durations table (command short name, duration) used by the Common Uplink System (CUS). (PDF p. 12)
  • The VDF table is ignored and monitoring parameters with PCF_NATUR='C' (constants) are ignored by the HCSS final interface. (PDF p. 13)
  • The HCSS assumes a unique SPID for each packet type; Herschel packets are identified by PUS type, subtype, APID and, where appropriate, the SID. (PDF p. 13)
  • Except for pseudo commands whose names begin with 'Z', every CCF_PKTID must appear in PCDF with at least 4 rows (VERSION, TYPE, DHFLAG, APID); the note points out this contradicts the ICD statement that PCDF_TCNAME is unique. (PDF p. 13)
  • Command sequence tables (CSF, CSS, SDF, CSP) and parameter-set tables (PST, PSV, CPS, PVS) are ignored by the HCSS MIB ingestion software. (PDF p. 14)
  • Short description fields must match the regular expression [a-zA-Z0-9_]+ (no plus, minus or space), and the first character of the name plus the full description must be unique for CCF, CPC and PCF; PID_APID plus PID_DESCR must be unique. (PDF p. 14)
  • HCSS release 0.2 considers only raw parameters (PCF_NATUR='R'), supports only OCF_CODIN values 'R' and 'I', and ignores the VPD table. (PDF p. 19)
  • Section 7 lists 34 ingestion checks (7.0.1 to 7.0.34) with the action taken (error, warning or informative message), e.g. validation of input file names, uniqueness of key field combinations and field counts per line. (PDF p. 20)
  • Checks 7.0.18 to 7.0.21 require PCF_NAME, OCF_NAME, CPC_PNAME and CCF_CNAME to be unique. (PDF p. 21)
  • CPC_RADIX must be 'D', 'H' or 'O' (check 7.0.33), and PID_INTER must be null except for periodic packets with PID_TYPE=3 and PID_STYPE=25 (check 7.0.34). (PDF p. 22)
  • Requirement NMCVT-0100-C disallows I, O and Q as leading characters of mnemonics; these were reserved by the instrument control centres for HIFI, PACS and SPIRE EGSE-ILT parameters. (PDF p. 23)
  • ESOC (5 December 2002) confirmed that non-mandatory fields without default are implicitly null and that the field separator must always be present even for empty fields (DCR 286). (PDF p. 25)
  • In the PACS MIB all TC verification packets had SPID 10006, because the SCOS-2000 version of the time required all type 1 TM packets to share one SPID (the Verifier listened to a predefined SPID list). (PDF p. 28)
  • ESOC stated that Rosetta allowed any SPID and CryoSat a range of SPIDs for service 1 packets, and planned to integrate these changes into S2K R3.1. (PDF p. 29)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A 14-page interface control document prepared by Albrecht de Jonge for the HIFI instrument team and addressed to the three Herschel instrument EGSE and ICC teams (HIFI, PACS, SPIRE) and the ESA Herschel Science Centre. It defines the TCP/IP protocol of the Herschel EGSE packet router, a Java program that distributes telemetry and telecommand packets in the Packet Structure ICD format between the components of an instrument-level test set-up: a SCOS-2000 system, test-equipment interface computers, the HCSS telemetry ingester and the CDMS simulator. The same protocol was intended for HCSS ingestion of raw telemetry in later mission phases; the document is ICD #4 of the ground segment ICD list.

Every message has a 5-octet header (a 1-octet messageType and a 4-octet contentLength, most significant octet first) followed by at most 1100 octets of content (TBC). Twelve message types (USER_DATA; ADD_, DEL_, ASK_, SHOW_ and NAME_CLIENT; ADD_, DEL_, ASK_ and SHOW_BLOCK; ASK_ and SHOW_TRAFFIC) use three content structures: data-packet, client-info and route-info. Routing uses a 'packet address': the 11-bit APID for telemetry, 4096 plus the APID for telecommands, and 8192 as a reserved wildcard. Clients name themselves, subscribe to packet addresses and receive forwarded copies; block rules filter routes by source client, destination client and address, and the router reports clients, blocks and traffic counts on request. The document also gives crash-recovery rules, a network bit-rate budget, the absence of security and of error checking beyond TCP, and an example call sequence. It is a compact, real example of the packet distribution layer of a SCOS-2000-based instrument EGSE.
tags: Tools, MIB editors and related standards

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The router distributes TM and TC in the standard format of the Packet Structure ICD [AD 1] among EGSE components during instrument level tests; the same interface is to be used by the HCSS for ingesting raw telemetry later in the mission. (PDF p. 6)
  • This document is ICD #4 in the Ground Segment List of ICDs [RD 1] and covers the requirements of [AD 3] section 4.2.1. (PDF p. 6)
  • During instrument level tests the router connects a SCOS-2000 system, test equipment interface computers, the HCSS telemetry ingester and the CDMS simulator over a TCP/IP LAN; all clients open a TCP connection to the router, and forwarding is based on the packet APID plus the TM/TC distinction. (PDF p. 6)
  • The router runs on any platform supporting Java; the TCP port and the client names must be agreed for each set-up. (PDF p. 7)
  • Exceptions to [AD 3] 4.2.1: FSG-IR-4.2-21 (association of telemetry with observation context) must be met by the test equipment, and the performance requirements FSG-IR-4.2-40 and FSG-IR-4.2-50 may not be met on an overloaded platform or network. (PDF p. 7)
  • A LAN capacity of 5 Mbit/s (TBC) is assumed free for router traffic; total network bitrate is the sum of all client send and receive rates minus those of clients running on the router machine, so it pays to run the router on a major data source or sink. (PDF p. 8)
  • Recovery: after a router crash clients reconnect with the same name and repeat their forwarding requests; packets in transit or addressed to a dead client are lost; a network failure is treated as a failure of the other side. (PDF p. 8)
  • The router provides no security (access must be restricted externally) and no explicit handshake, error checking or flow control beyond TCP/IP. (PDF p. 9)
  • Message format: octet 0 messageType (1 octet), octets 1-4 contentLength (4 octets), then the content; a message is contentLength + 5 octets long, contentLength is limited to 1100 octets (TBC), and integers are stored most significant octet first. (PDF p. 9)
  • Twelve message types share three structures: type 1 USER_DATA (data-packet), types 2-6 ADD_CLIENT, DEL_CLIENT, ASK_CLIENT, SHOW_CLIENT, NAME_CLIENT (client-info) and types 7-12 ADD_BLOCK, DEL_BLOCK, ASK_BLOCK, SHOW_BLOCK, ASK_TRAFFIC, SHOW_TRAFFIC (route-info). (PDF p. 10)
  • For USER_DATA the content is a complete PS-ICD packet and contentLength = packet_length_field + 7. (PDF p. 10)
  • Packet address: for TM source packets the 11-bit APID; for TC source packets 4096 + APID (equivalent to masking out the Type and APID fields of the header); the value 8192 is reserved for special purposes. (PDF p. 10)
  • Client-info content: packetAddress (4 octets), clientAddress (4), clientPortNumber (4), messageSequenceNumber (4), then the ASCII clientName, so contentLength is at least 16 octets. (PDF p. 10)
  • Route-info content: packetAddress, sourceNameLength, destinationNameLength, messageSequenceNumber and packetCount (4 octets each) followed by the source and destination names; sourceNameLength + destinationNameLength + 20 = contentLength. (PDF p. 11)
  • The router never checks USER_DATA content; it forwards a copy to every client that has sent ADD_CLIENT for that packet address unless an ADD_BLOCK rule blocks that source-destination route. (PDF p. 11)
  • NAME_CLIENT must be the first message after connecting and the name must be unique; a client re-using the name of a disconnected client is treated as the same client for route-info messages. (PDF p. 12)
  • A block entry matches when the source name, destination name and packet address match, where a zero name length or the address 8192 acts as a wildcard; the all-wildcard combination is not allowed. (PDF p. 12)
  • Multi-message replies (SHOW_CLIENT, SHOW_BLOCK, SHOW_TRAFFIC) count messageSequenceNumber down to zero for the last message; SHOW_TRAFFIC gives packets forwarded since router start per address, source and destination. (PDF p. 13)
  • The data rate per client shall not exceed 500 kbit per second, averaged over one second (TBC). (PDF p. 13)
  • Appendix A example: client A sends TM of APID 77; client B names itself, asks for packet address 77, receives the forwarded packets and finally revokes its request. (PDF p. 14)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The Interface Requirements Document (IRD) for the Herschel Ground Segment (HGS). It numbers every interface between the HGS centres (the MOC at ESOC, the Herschel Science Centre HSC, and the HIFI, PACS and SPIRE Instrument Control Centres, both at home and at the MOC) and the HGS systems: the Herschel Common Science System (HCSS), Real-Time Analysis (RTA), on-board software maintenance (OBSM), EGSE-ILT, EGSE-IST, the Central Checkout System (CCS), the mission control system (MCS) and the MIB editor. Each interface subsection states its requirements (FGS-IR-x.y-nnn) in three groups: information flow, control flow (push, pull, notify or poll) and performance, with the source and comments in italics.

Section 3 covers the in-orbit and post-operations phases. It includes consolidated telemetry per APID and category, the telecommand history, out-of-limits information, time correlation (better than 500 ms), orbit and attitude products, planning skeleton and schedules, the spacecraft and instrument reference databases maintained by the MOC, and instrument database updates, derived-parameter definitions and procedures that flow from the ICCs via the HSC to the MOC. Section 4 covers instrument-level and system tests (ILT and IST). Here the SCOS-2000 based EGSE-ILT and the CCS stand in for the MCS, instrument databases must be in a SCOS-2000-compatible form, and the HCSS exchanges command mnemonic sequences, telemetry, test procedures and telecommand history with them.

For an engineer, the document shows the Herschel data flows end to end, and why the MIB, the TC history file and the source-packet formats had to stay identical from ILT through operations (the 'smooth transition' concept). See Herschel/Planck interface documents.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The HGS centres are the MOC, the HSC and the SPIRE, PACS and HIFI ICCs, with ICCs either at their home institutes (ICC@ICC) or at the MOC (ICC@MOC). The HGS systems include the HCSS, RTA, OBSM, EGSE-ILT, CCS with EGSE-IST, and the MCS. (PDF p. 14)
  • The IRD places no formal requirements on the CCS, because it is not applicable to the industrial contractor supplying the CCS. (PDF p. 15)
  • Design assumptions: guaranteed high-rate links (e.g. >= 256 kbps) between MOC and HSC and between HSC and ICC@ICC in routine phase, real-time commanding only from the MOC, and a non-real-time MOC-HSC interface. (PDF p. 20)
  • FGS-IR-3.1-30: the MOC delivers telemetry in a form from which the on-board source packets can be extracted. The MOC does not process science packets, which arrive as ESA standard packets, possibly with added header and trailer. Packets lost in space-ground transmission are not recovered. (PDF p. 24)
  • FGS-IR-3.1-80: consolidated telemetry is made available per category (event, TC verification, housekeeping and science telemetry per APID, plus spacecraft telemetry), and the MOC pushes it to the HSC. (PDF p. 25)
  • FGS-IR-3.1-110: any sequence of consolidated dump telemetry must be available no later than 10 minutes after its last bit reaches the MOC. The MOC is expected to need 16 hours to retrieve the dump telemetry of one operational day. (PDF p. 25)
  • FGS-IR-3.1-300 to -340: the MOC makes the telecommand history (uplink and execution status of all TCs) available for any operational period, with enough information to associate each TC with schedule commanding requests. It pushes the history at the same time as the consolidated housekeeping telemetry. (PDF p. 30)
  • FGS-IR-3.1-430: time correlation data must correlate spacecraft time with UTC to better than 500 ms at any time of the mission. (PDF p. 32)
  • FGS-IR-3.1-500: the MOC maintains the spacecraft and instrument reference databases for the HGS. The instrument database includes at least TC, TM (housekeeping, and science header only), monitoring, calibration/de-calibration and command sequence definitions. (PDF p. 35)
  • FGS-IR-3.3-40/-50: in commissioning and emergencies, the MOC delivers instrument telemetry to ICC@MOC within one minute of reception, at up to the maximum instrument on-board data rate of 300 kbps. (PDF p. 40)
  • FGS-IR-3.5-20: an ICC@ICC accesses consolidated housekeeping telemetry within 20 minutes in all phases. Consolidated science telemetry is available within 2 hours in commissioning/PV and within 32 hours in routine phase, after the MOC receives the last bit of the period. (PDF p. 46)
  • FGS-IR-4.1-70 and 4.3-50: in ILT and IST, instrument database updates are provided in the form appropriate for the SCOS-2000 based RTA system. (PDF p. 63)
  • FGS-IR-4.2-50: the EGSE-ILT to HCSS telemetry interface must carry the maximum instrument on-board rate (300 kbps) plus the maximum TEI rate (400 kbps). Telemetry must be in the HCSS within 5 seconds (FGS-IR-4.2-40). (PDF p. 65)
  • FGS-IR-4.7-40: RTA events used to trigger EGSE-ILT autonomy procedures must arrive within 0.5 s, against an expected 3-4 s end-to-end latency for triggering and executing an autonomy procedure. (PDF p. 69)
  • FGS-IR-4.10-15: instrument databases stored from the MIB editor into the HCSS must be in a format compatible with what SCOS-2000 expects. (PDF p. 71)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The Space/Ground Interface Control Document (SGICD) for ESA's Herschel and Planck spacecraft. It defines the RF and data-link interface between the two spacecraft and the ESA ground stations, and is the source document for the link budget tables. It complements the ESA PSS packet telemetry and telecommand standards with all mission-specific choices, as numbered requirements (HP-SGICD-COM-..., -STR-...).

Sections 2 to 4 cover the telecommunication system. Both links are X-band, with separate downlink and uplink frequencies for Herschel and Planck. Telemetry has four rates (Low-1 500 bps and Low-2 5 kbps on a 45884 Hz subcarrier, medium 150 kbps PCM(SP-L)/PM, high 1.5 Mbps GMSK) and concatenated Reed-Solomon (255,223, I=5) plus rate-½ convolutional coding, the 0x1ACFFC1D attached sync marker and pseudo-randomisation. Telecommands run at 125 bps and 4 kbps on a 16 kHz subcarrier. The sections also give ranging, transponder modes, antenna switching, COP-1 with AD and BD services, spacecraft and ground station parameters (Kourou, Vilspa, New Norcia), link margins and the RF suitcase compatibility test.

Sections 5 and 6 are the most useful for data engineers. They fix the TM transfer frame at 1115 octets with a secondary header (24 extra bits of VC frame count), a CLCW in every frame and a frame error control word. They assign spacecraft IDs (Herschel 0x1E6, Planck 0x1E9, avionics model 0x1EA) and the use and downlink priority of virtual channels VC0 to VC7. On the TC side they give segment MAP IDs (CPDU, active and non-active processor, CROME reinitialise, TC-only mode), packet aggregation without segmentation, two TC virtual channels for decoders A and B, and a maximum TC frame length of 256 octets. Appendices give bit numbering and field alignment conventions, acronyms, the link budget format, the bit/symbol rate definitions and the SFCG spectral emission masks.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• X-band downlink frequencies: Herschel 8468.5 MHz and Planck 8455.0 MHz (8450-8500 MHz band, Category A mission); emission bandwidths 340 kHz (low rate), 6.2 MHz (medium), 4.2 MHz (high) and 2.0 MHz (ranging). (PDF p. 11)
  • Telemetry follows the ESA Packet Telemetry Standard (PSS-04-106) without source packet segmentation. (PDF p. 12)
  • TM rates and modulation: Low-1 500 bps and Low-2 5 kbps PCM(NRZ-L)/PSK/PM on a 45884 Hz sine subcarrier, medium 150 kbps PCM(SP-L)/PM, high 1.5 Mbps GMSK (BTb = 0.25); ranging is not possible together with high-rate telemetry. (PDF p. 12)
  • Baseline TM coding is concatenated Reed-Solomon (255,223) with interleaving depth 5 and rate-½, k = 7 convolutional coding; the sync marker 1ACFFC1D is inserted before each code block and an on-board pseudo-randomiser is required. (PDF p. 13)
  • X-band uplink frequencies: Herschel 7207.8483 MHz and Planck 7196.3580 MHz, with a turnaround ratio of 749/880. (PDF p. 14)
  • Telecommands follow PSS-04-107, use PCM(NRZ-L)/PSK/PM on a 16 kHz sinusoidal subcarrier at 125 bps or 4 kbps, and the ranging tone is 698260 Hz. (PDF p. 15)
  • TC chain selection and bit-synchronisation requirements were added because of telecommand rejections observed in orbit on XMM; the rejection probability must stay below 10^-3. (PDF p. 16)
  • COP-1 shall be supported, with the AD and BD packet telecommand services in parallel. (PDF p. 18)
  • Link budget margins: nominal > 3 dB, RSS worst case > 0 dB and mean - 3 sigma > 0 dB; the required Eb/No is 2.7 dB for a frame loss probability of 10^-5 with concatenated coding (I = 5). (PDF p. 27)
  • Ground stations: Kourou 15 m and Vilspa 15 m support LEOP, while New Norcia 35 m supports all phases including routine science. (PDF p. 27)
  • The RF suitcase shall be delivered to ESOC at the latest at L-24 months and be available for at least 1 month. (PDF p. 29)
  • The only allowed TM transfer frame length is 1115 octets (8920 bits) before encoding, with a 1-octet secondary header ID, a 3-octet secondary header data field, 1099 octets of data field, a 4-octet OCF and a 2-octet FECW. (PDF p. 30)
  • Spacecraft IDs (TM and TC): Herschel FM 0x1E6 (486), Planck FM 0x1E9 (489), Avionics Model 0x1EA (490). (PDF p. 31)
  • TM virtual channels: VC0 real-time essential HK, VC1 real-time science, VC2 stored HK, VC3 stored science, VC4 real-time routine HK, VC5 and VC6 not required, VC7 idle frames. (PDF p. 31)
  • Downlink VC priority is VC0, VC4, VC2, VC1, VC3, then VC7 idle frames; partially filled frames are completed with idle packets before idle frames are sent. (PDF p. 32)
  • Every TM frame carries a CLCW in the OCF; CLCWs for the nominal decoder's VC go in frames with an even master channel frame count and those for the redundant decoder in odd ones (CLCW Standard Insertion Scheme No. 2). (PDF p. 35)
  • The first header pointer is all ones (0b11111111111) when no packet header starts in the frame, and 0b11111111110 for idle frames on VC7; the secondary header ID is 0b00000011. (PDF p. 34)
  • There is no TC packet segmentation (sequence flags 0b11); MAP IDs route to the CPDU (0), the active processor (1), the non-active processor (2), CROME reinitialise (5) and set TC-only mode (6). (PDF p. 38)
  • Packet aggregation is used to maximise uplink throughput: each packet starts at the previous start plus its Packet Length + 7 octets. (PDF p. 38)
  • TC virtual channel 0 addresses decoder A and VC 1 decoder B; the maximum TC frame length is 256 octets, so the top two bits of the 10-bit frame length field are always 0b00. (PDF p. 39)
  • Bit 0 is the first transmitted bit and the MSB (except on the IEEE 1355 link, where the LSB goes first); parameters of 16 bits or more are word aligned, and shorter parameters may not span word boundaries and are right-adjusted. (PDF p. 41)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
An evaluation report (issue 2, 12 April 2001) by L. Dubbeldam of the HIFI instrument team on the SCOS-2000 Database Editing Subsystem version 2.0, the MS Access-based MIB editor supplied by ESOC and originally written for INTEGRAL (also called the 'Integral MS Access editor'). It explains that the three FIRST (Herschel) instruments chose SCOS-2000 as the basis of their EGSE throughout integration, so they need a tool to create and maintain the MIB, and it distinguishes the MIB ASCII files, the database application, the editor forms and the data.

The report walks through the requirements of the HIFI MIB editor requirements specification (RD.3) one by one, records 30 numbered remarks, and includes replies from the editor's author (marked JH). Topics include the missing polynomial calibration (MCF) form and the rule that a numerical PCF_CURTX reference is looked up first in CAF and then in MCF; the automatic VDF version record at export; datasheet and tool-tip support; keys, cascades, validation rules, mandatory fields and default values; the PID primary key (six fields versus the ICD's five); record-count fields that SCOS-2000 does not use; CSF_NFPARS versus the task parameter file ICD; a silent conversion of (PTC,PFC)=(5,2) to (5,3); grouping of data by subsystem; import, append, export and delete tools; user-interface ergonomics; hexadecimal calibration curves; and field-length non-conformances with the import ICD (for example OCP and SPID fields).

The conclusions find version 2 much improved and a good tool. Annex A proposes report forms for numerical calibrations, command parameters, command definitions, fixed packets and variable packets, filled with example data. The document shows the state of MIB tooling at the start of the Herschel/Planck programme.
tags: Tools, MIB editors and related standards

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The three FIRST instruments decided to use SCOS-2000 as the basis of their EGSE throughout integration, so a tool to generate and maintain the MIB was required. (PDF p. 2)
  • The evaluated tool is the ESOC-supplied SCOS-2000 Database Editing Subsystem version 2.0, also called the Integral MS Access editor; its author's replies are included and marked JH. (PDF p. 2)
  • Per the editor author, when a TM parameter has category 'N' and PCF_CURTX is not null, SCOS-2000 first looks up the reference in CAF and then in MCF; MCF numbers (0 to 9999) must not coincide with CAF numbers. (PDF p. 3)
  • The VDF table is populated automatically at export time, and the local PC date had to be set to 'DD/MM/YY' for this to work. (PDF p. 4)
  • The editor keys PID on its first six fields, whereas the import ICD (section 3.3.2.4.1) defines the first five fields as unique provided field #13 contains 'Y'; INTEGRAL needed the six-field key. (PDF p. 6)
  • The INTEGRAL database is said to have more than 870,000 populated fields, and the editor code behind the forms more than 1300 pages; consistency checking was done by a separate checker application. (PDF p. 7)
  • The record-count fields of the MIB are said to be unused by SCOS-2000 ('S2K currently does not use any of them'), yet CSF_NFPARS is checked against the number of parameters in a task parameter file per the task parameter file ICD. (PDF p. 7)
  • An undocumented editor feature converted parameter code (PTC,PFC)=(5,2) into (5,3) on output; it was an INTEGRAL-specific processing to be removed. (PDF p. 7)
  • Reported non-conformances with the import ICD: OCP_RLCHK limited to six characters instead of 8, OCP low/high values of length 10 instead of 14, and SPID-type fields unable to hold 10-digit numbers. (PDF p. 10)
  • Conclusion: version 2 is greatly improved over the previous version and the SCOS-2000 database editor is a good tool to work with. (PDF p. 11)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A short user requirements document (issue 1.0, 23 August 2000) written by L. Dubbeldam for the HIFI instrument of the FIRST (later Herschel) mission, specifying an editor for the SCOS-2000 Mission Information Base. It explains that SCOS-2000 is configured by the MIB, a set of more than 30 ASCII files of mission-specific data, and that during instrument integration and test the MIB holds the instrument configuration, so a flexible and reliable editor is needed. Because the editor may be a relational database, the document also calls it 'the database'.

The requirements (numbered RQ 3.x.y) cover: data content (one table per SCOS-2000 file, holding everything needed to configure SCOS-2000); the user interface (datasheets labelled with the ICD field names, tool tips derived from the ICD descriptions, and forms that follow the MIB structure, for example PCF with OCF/OCP, CAF/CAP, TXF/TXP and MCF subforms, CPC with PRF/PRV, CCA/CCS and PAF/PAS, PID with VPD and PLF, CCF with CDF, PTV and verification, CSF with CSS, SDF and CSP, packet headers TCP/PCPC/PCDF, parameter sets and displays); data checking (unique keys, update cascades without delete cascades, validation of enumerated values, mandatory fields and ICD default values, configurable whole-database checks, record counters); grouping of data by instrument subsystem and model (QM/FM swaps) so that subsystem engineers can supply data without SCOS-2000 knowledge; and tools to import, append, export and delete sets of SCOS-2000 files.

Annex A lists 41 MIB tables grouped as operator (display), packet, packet header, parameter and parameter-set tables, each with the section and page of the SCOS-2000 database import ICD that defines it, which is a useful snapshot of the early (2000) MIB table set.
tags: Tools, MIB editors and related standards

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• SCOS-2000 is configured by the Mission Information Base (MIB), described as a set of more than 30 ASCII files containing mission-specific data; during FIRST instrument integration and test it holds the instrument configuration. (PDF p. 3)
  • RQ 3.1.2 requires one database table per SCOS-2000 file, and RQ 3.2.⅔.2.3 require datasheet columns to use the field names of the SCOS-2000 database import ICD, with tool tips derived from its descriptions. (PDF p. 3)
  • Required forms follow the MIB structure, e.g. PCF with monitoring checks (OCF, OCP), numerical (CAF, CAP), textual (TXF, TXP) and polynomial (MCF) calibration, and CCF with CDF, PTV and verification (CVP, CVE) subforms. (PDF p. 4)
  • Data checking requires enforcement of unique keys, update cascades but no delete cascades, enumerated-value validation, mandatory fields and use of the ICD default values; exported default-valued fields must not be left blank. (PDF p. 5)
  • Data must be groupable by instrument subsystem and model so that, for example, Subsys1 QM data can be replaced by Subsys1 FM data, and subsystem engineers can supply data without detailed SCOS-2000 knowledge. (PDF p. 6)
  • Tools are required to import, append, output and delete sets of SCOS-2000 files and to enter parameter-value sets in a column-per-set layout. (PDF p. 6)
  • Annex A groups the MIB tables as Operator (dpc, dpf, gpc, gpf, spc, spf), Packet (ccf, cdf, csf, csp, css, cve, cvp, cvs, pid, plf, ptv, sdf, vpd), Packet header (pcdf, pcpc, tcp), Parameter (caf, cap, cca, ccs, cpc, mcf, ocf, ocp, paf, pas, pcf, prf, prv, txf, txp) and Parameter set (cps, psm, pst, psv, pvs), with the AD-#1 section defining each. (PDF p. 8)
