docs.text:
The telecommand interface control document for HIFI, the Heterodyne Instrument for the Far Infrared on ESA's Herschel space observatory. It specifies the structure of every telecommand packet that controls the HIFI on-board software (OBS), down to the byte position, length and fixed value of each field.

Chapter 1 opens with a catalogue of all HIFI TCs, grouped by PUS service. It gives each command's name, type and subtype, function ID (FID), activity ID (AID), structure ID (SID) and total packet length. Chapter 3 gives the generic packet format. The CCSDS source packet header uses the single HIFI APID 1024, three bits of the sequence count identify the command source (ground, mission timeline, CDMS, AOCS), and the 4-octet data field header carries a 4-bit acknowledgement field, the type and subtype, and a spare octet. The packet error control field closes the packet.

Chapter 4 then details the application data of each telecommand. It covers memory management (service 6 load, dump and check of DRAM, PRAM and LCU memory), function management stop and perform activity (service 8 subtypes 2 and 4), and time management (service 9). Packet transmission control (service 14) and the connection test (service 17) follow. The bulk is service 8,4: housekeeping and autonomous checks, configuration of the FCU, HRS, WBS and LCU subsystems (FID 12), parameter scans, local oscillator vector loads and tuning, calibration, spectroscopy modes (total power, fast and slow chop, frequency switch), data simulation, goto-safe, program control (reset, boot, EEPROM, memory copy), peak-up and no-op. For an engineer it is a complete worked example of how an instrument maps its commanding onto PUS function management, and it cross-checks against the HIFI MIB command definitions.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Chapter 1 catalogues every HIFI TC with name, PUS type/subtype, FID, AID, SID and packet length (including header and CRC); memory management uses service 6 (load 6,2, dump 6,5, check 6,9). (PDF p. 10)
  • Most HIFI commanding is function management: TC(8,2) stops a function and TC(8,4) performs an activity, identified by Function ID and Activity ID (for example FID 12 configure subsystems, FID 7 scans, FID 8 local oscillator, FID 11 spectroscopy, FID 13 peak-up). (PDF p. 11)
  • Other services: HIFI_enable_time_verify is TC(9,7); packet transmission control is TC(14,1), (14,2) and (14,3); the connection test is TC(17,1). (PDF p. 14)
  • HIFI_goto_safe is TC(8,4) with FID 17, and HIFI_reset is TC(8,4) FID 16 AID 3. (PDF p. 14)
  • TC source packet header: version 0, type 1, data field header flag, APID (the HIFI OBS can only use APID 1024), sequence flags 0b11, and a 14-bit sequence count of which 3 bits identify the source and 11 bits are the counter. (PDF p. 15)
  • Command source codes in the sequence count: 0b000 ground, 0b001 mission time line, 0b010 CDMS, 0b011 AOCS; each source maintains its own 11-bit counter per APID, which wraps to 0. (PDF p. 15)
  • All commands except CPDU commands (type, subtype) = (2,3) have a data field header. (PDF p. 15)
  • Data field header: CCSDS secondary header flag 0, PUS version 0, a 4-bit ACK field (bit 3 acceptance, bit 2 start of execution, bit 1 progress, bit 0 completion), type, subtype and a spare octet; the PEC holds a checksum of all preceding fields. (PDF p. 16)
  • In memory management the 32-bit memory ID plus start address field is used as an 8-bit MID and a 24-bit start address, expressed in smallest addressable units; MIDs include 0x00 PRAM, 0x01 DRAM, 0x04 LCU and 0x11 DRAM boot mode. (PDF p. 17)
  • Time management accepts TC(9,4) enable time synchronisation, TC(9,5) time code with a 48-bit time field, and TC(9,7) enable time verification. (PDF p. 156)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A 562-page listing, apparently generated from the database, of the HIFI instrument's Mission Information Base (MIB) as of HIFI MIB issue 139, equivalent to HIFI_ASPI MIB 11.7. HIFI is the heterodyne spectrometer on ESA's Herschel. The annex to the HIFI User Manual presents the MIB tables in readable form rather than as raw SCOS-2000 ASCII files, so it is a rare complete printed example of a real instrument MIB.

Section 1.1 lists the command parameters of each HIFI subsystem (FCU, HRS, WBS, LCU, OBS) with database name, mnemonic, description, raw and engineering ranges and units. Section 1.2 gives the command-parameter de-calibration curves, textual (PAF) and numerical (CCA). Section 1.3 lists command parameter ranges. Section 1.4 lists the monitoring parameters per subsystem (ICU, FCU, HRS, WBS, LCU, OBS), with calibration, units, limits and the packet they belong to. Section 1.5 gives the textual (TXF) and numerical (CAF) calibration curves, and section 1.6 the monitoring checks (number of checks, type, low and high values, relevance-check parameter and value).

The second half defines the packets. Section 1.7 has about 187 telecommand packet definitions, each listing the bit offset, element length, element type (fixed area or editable parameter), parameter name and default value. This mirrors the TC structure in the HIFI TC ICD. Section 1.8 covers fixed telemetry packets (housekeeping, essential HK, IF power, tune and OOL reports, LCU tables) with byte and bit offsets of every parameter. Section 1.9 covers variable telemetry packets such as scan reports, with repeated groups given as position formulas. For an engineer it shows how one Herschel instrument populated the SCOS-2000 MIB tables, including its HP/HM/HD naming convention.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The annex describes HIFI MIB issue 139, equivalent to HIFI_ASPI MIB 11.7. (PDF p. 4)
  • Command parameters are listed per subsystem with database name (for example HP056191), mnemonic (HIF_ch1_mxbias0_V), description, raw and engineering minimum and maximum, and unit (for example raw 0 to 4095 for -10.000 to 10.000 mV). (PDF p. 4)
  • Command parameter conversion curves are split into PAF textual de-calibrations (for example curve 100 HRH_switch with values H and V) and CCA numerical de-calibrations. (PDF p. 31)
  • Monitoring parameters are listed per subsystem with name (HMnnn190 for ICU parameters such as HM001190 Structure_ID), mnemonic, description, raw-to-engineering calibration, unit, limits and the packet they appear in (for example ICU_housekeeping). (PDF p. 52)
  • Monitoring calibrations are split into TXF textual and CAF numerical curves, the latter given as x/y value pairs. (PDF p. 268)
  • Monitor parameter ranges list for each parameter the number of checks, check type, low and high values and an optional relevance check parameter (rlchk_mnem) with its validity value (valpar). (PDF p. 329)
  • Each telecommand packet definition lists every element by bit offset, element length, element type (A for a fixed area, E for an editable parameter), parameter name and mnemonic and default value; for example HIFI_load_DRAM_bootmode has a fixed 8-bit MID = 0x11 followed by a 24-bit OBS_mem_start. (PDF p. 355)
  • Fixed TM packet definitions give each parameter's byte offset and bit offset, for example HIFI_HK_rev_7 with HI_Prime_red at byte 1 bit 7 and Structure_ID at byte 16. (PDF p. 456)
  • Variable TM packet definitions express repeated groups as position formulas such as '46+ 2 * i' with block sizes, controlled by repetition counters such as HI_FIXREP. (PDF p. 562)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The interface control document for the Real-Time Science Interface (RTSI) of the Herschel/Planck mission control system (HPMCS). The RTSI delivers real-time telemetry source packets from the HP MOC to the instrument teams' workstations at ESOC: IW@MOC for the Planck instruments and ICC@MOC for the Herschel instruments. The RTSI runs as a single node on the HP Security Data Server (HPSDS), outside the ESOC operational network (OPSLAN) firewall. It receives packets from the HP MCS TM Packetiser and serves up to 10 PI clients. It handles only real-time telemetry from virtual channels VC-0, VC-4 and VC-1: there is no playback, no archiving, no quality checks and no time correlation.

The RTSI is simply the SCOS-2000 External Interface (EXIF) TM Packet Data Provision service over CORBA (TMP_PRO). Clients find it through the CORBA Naming Service, register filters with registerTMpackets() (lists of APIDs or SPIDs), and receive TMpacketNotifyData callbacks that carry the raw packet header and body. The document gives the CosNaming path of the service and version differences in the filter structure (APID-only before SCOS-2000 3.1; new type and subtype fields from 4.2). It also sizes the link: a worst case of 87 packets per second, or about 1.2 Mbit/s per unfiltered client. Gap detection is left to the clients, using the Space Packet sequence counter.

An appendix describes the RTSI template client (C++, omniORB): its source files, algorithm, build options inside and outside the SCOS environment, environment variables, the mission-specific ports, and example output. It belongs with the other Herschel/Planck interface documents.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The ICD covers real-time telemetry source packets passed from the HP MCS TM Packetiser to the HPSDS and on to the PI client workstations IW@MOC (Planck) and ICC@MOC (Herschel). Only real-time telemetry from VC-0, VC-4 and VC-1 is covered, and playback is not foreseen. (PDF p. 9)
  • Assumptions: point-to-point transfer using CORBA, a single RTSI node on the HPSDS outside the MOC firewall, and no time or quality checks, time correlation, replay or archiving by the RTSI. (PDF p. 11)
  • The TM Packetiser is the client of the RTSI link to the HPSDS, and the PI workstation applications are clients of the RTSI. In both cases the RTSI acts as the server. (PDF p. 11)
  • The consolidated maximum rate, taken from the HP MCS SRS [A-7], is 87 packets per second. This means 87 CORBA requests per second for each client. (PDF p. 12)
  • Transfer is CORBA over TCP/IP, and up to 10 PI client workstation connections are supported. The CORBA Naming Service runs on the RTSI workstation (HPSDS) on a configurable port. (PDF p. 15)
  • The RTSI interface is the CORBA-level interface of the SCOS-2000 TM Packet Data Provision Service, defined in EGOS-MCS-S2K-ICD-0022 [A-3] and S2K-MCS-ICD-0020 [A-4]. (PDF p. 16)
  • The RTSI does not check completeness. Clients detect gaps from the Source Sequence Counter, which increments by 1 per source packet for each on-board application (APID). (PDF p. 17)
  • Each delivered packet is a TMpacketNotifyData structure with packet attributes, the raw packet header and body byte strings, and lists of VPD parameter names and values. Clients register filters with registerTMpackets() and receive packets as CORBA callbacks. (PDF p. 19)
  • Mean source packet sizes and rates: VC0 22 bytes at under 28 per second, VC4 300 bytes at under 10 per second, VC1 800 bytes at under 49 per second. With up to 1000 bytes of overhead assumed, the worst case is 1800 x 87 x 8 = 1 252 800 bit/s (about 1.2 Mbit/s) per unfiltered client, and 12 Mbit/s for 10 clients. (PDF p. 20)
  • The CosNaming name of the EXIF TM Packet Provision service is <DOMAIN_ID>/<S2K_LOCAL_SRV_FAMILY>/"TMP_PRO_002", where 002 is the SCOS EXIF IDL version. Clients should use the constant ITMP::ServiceName from ITMP_PRO.idl. (PDF p. 21)
  • ITMP::TMpacketFilter filters on a list of SPIDs or, alternatively, APIDs. SCOS-2000 versions before 3.1 support only APID filtering. From S2K 4.2, the fields m_types, m_subTypes and m_variablePackets must also be set. The example filters LFI scientific packets on APID 0x604. (PDF p. 22)
  • The template client registers for SPID 100001000 (used for user-defined constants). It needs a C++ compiler, omniORB 4.0x and the HPMCS EXIF IDL files, and it runs on port 32000 for Herschel and 22000 for Planck. (PDF p. 23)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A conference paper from ESOC on how ESA's mission control system (MCS) infrastructure has evolved. ESOC builds its MCSs on domain-specific (not mission-specific) infrastructure: configurable, generic implementations reused across missions. The stated reasons are stable costs, shorter mission preparation, lower risk and less familiarisation effort for staff. The paper lists the design drivers this approach imposes: heterogeneous space systems, the PUS, multiple mission types, standardised interfaces, modular and layered architecture, data-driven tailoring through a TM/TC 'database' (i.e. the MIB), automation, performance, longevity, portability and scalability.

It then compares four generations: the Multi-Satellite Support System (MSSS, 1970s to late 1990s), SCOS 1 (from the early 1990s), SCOS II, renamed SCOS-2000 (in use since the early 2000s and still the basis of most ESOC control systems), and M4C (Mission Control Core based on Common Core), which offers equivalent features on the EGS-CC framework. The comparison covers the MCS's role in preparation (up to the Eclipse-based OPEN environment), planning, critical operations (display types), routine operations (from time-separated command release in MSSS to M4C activities with ground and on-board triggers, and file-based operations), and evaluation. It also covers system design: modularity, deployment (mainframe, then distributed client-server, then 'conceptually centralised' with thin clients), scalability, tailoring, extensibility, interoperability (SLE, PUS), performance, technology stacks and maintainability.

It is useful for the history of ESA control systems and for placing SCOS-2000 between MSSS and EGS-CC.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The paper names four factors behind the evolution of MCS implementations: spacecraft orbits (pass frequency and delays), space asset design (TM/TC protocols, on-board monitoring and control services, data volumes, autonomy), operations concepts, and software and IT technologies. (PDF p. 1)
  • ESA ground segments rely on domain-specific (not mission-specific) infrastructure, for strategic and programmatic reasons: shared development and maintenance costs, shorter preparation of new missions, lower risk and less familiarisation effort for staff. (PDF p. 2)
  • Control functions are tailored through a data-driven approach: TM/TC characteristics are defined in a 'database' that converts human-readable artefacts into data units for uplink and downlink. (PDF p. 3)
  • Four MCS infrastructure generations: MSSS (Multi-Satellite Support System, 1970s to late 1990s); SCOS 1 (from the early 1990s, still in some legacy missions); SCOS II, renamed SCOS-2000 (from the start of this century, the basis of most ESOC control systems); and M4C (Mission Control Core based on Common Core, equivalent features on EGS-CC). (PDF p. 3)
  • Operations preparation tools evolved from basic text editors, through stand-alone Windows tools, to OPEN, the Eclipse-based Operations Preparation Environment. (PDF p. 4)
  • MSSS could only open full-screen displays, up to three. MSSS could only authorise the release of consecutive commands at specified time intervals, whereas M4C natively executes any control action ('Activities') from ground or on-board triggers based on times, events or procedures. (PDF p. 4)
  • Both SCOS-2000 and M4C support file-based operations concepts. (PDF p. 5)
  • Deployment evolved from MSSS (two redundant mainframe instances serving all missions via hard-wired workstations), to SCOS-2000 (distributed client-server, first with 'very fat' clients, later re-engineered for remote access), to M4C ('conceptually centralised', with thin clients and options up to multi-mission virtual data centres). (PDF p. 5)
  • Ground station interfaces are standardised through CCSDS SLE. Both SCOS-2000 and M4C natively support PUS 'service level' operations. Standardisation between ground systems such as planning, flight dynamics and payload data processing is described as still lagging behind. (PDF p. 6)
  • MSSS processed TM at a few kbit/s. The SCOS-2000 based Gaia MCS sustains more than 10 Mbit/s incoming and about 1 Mbit/s of full TM processing. MSSS supported up to 20 workstations for the whole centre, while more than 50 users on one MCS are now common during LEOP. (PDF p. 6)
  • The paper concludes that the infrastructure kept up with mission demands through continuous improvement within generations and step-wise change across them. (PDF p. 7)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The interface control document for the file-based and internal interfaces of the SCOS-2000 TDRS (TM Data Retrieval Services) application. TDRS is a web-based service that lets external users retrieve archived telemetry parameter samples from a SCOS-2000 mission control system (TDRS page).

The core of the document is the retrieval request file (.req). It is an ASCII file of Field:value lines that specifies the retrieval type (FAST raw only, FAST_ENG with engineering values, or COMPLETE with validity and status), output format (MVDA, spreadsheet, column-mode spreadsheet), time format (ASD yyyy.ddd.hh.mm.ss or CCSDS ASCII A), MIB database version, optional e-mail and FTP delivery, up to 4 data streams, a single, repeated or irregular time window, and per-parameter blocks. Each parameter block gives the parameter name, optional SPID, a change-based or occurrence-based filter for supercommutated samples, every-Nth-packet sampling, validity and OOL filters, min/max thresholds and packet-by-packet or interval retrieval mode.

The ICD then specifies the outputs: the MVDA format (ASCII header plus binary Data####.dat and Time####.dat files with 8-byte Unix-epoch timestamps), the tab-separated spreadsheet files (.fst, .fen, .cmp) with raw value, validity, engineering unit and engineering value, the column-organised file (.col) with per-parameter statistics, and the user log file. The last chapters describe the internal chain: web server, PCGI CGI executables and their HTML state machine, the CORBA interface to the request manager PRQM (newRequest, getStatus, cancelRequest, getDBInfo, getParameters), and the TCP/IP protocol between PRQM and the PSRV back-end, which spawns fast or complete child processes against the SCOS-2000 kernel. Appendices give the ASCII value formats per data type and the threshold matching rules. Useful background for mission archives and MIB monitoring parameters.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Issue history runs from 1.0 (Feb 21, 2000) through 4.3 (updates for SCOS Release 3.1, March 2004), 4.4 (R_TDRS-2.1), 5.0 (TDRS Release 3.1, June 4, 2007) to 5.1 (August 22, 2008, DCR-4996). (PDF p. 3)
  • The ICD covers the retrieval request file, the MVDA fast-retrieval result files, the spreadsheet result files (complete and fast), the column-organised result file and the user log file. (PDF p. 11)
  • File types: .req retrieval request; Header.dat, Timexxxx.dat and Dataxxxx.dat MVDA files; .fst, .fen and .cmp spreadsheet files for fast, fast-with-engineering and complete retrievals; .col column-organised file. (PDF p. 15)
  • Generated file names contain retrieval ID, execution ID, user ID and an expiration day count (ddd), e.g. 0_1_SMITH_038.req. (PDF p. 16)
  • Security checks: user authentication with SSL certificates at the web interface, plus configurable maxima for parallel retrieval requests, archive requests and result-file size. (PDF p. 16)
  • Binary MVDA files are Solaris format; transfer to Linux is not supported because the MVDA format is deprecated for future TDRS installations. (PDF p. 18)
  • RetrievalType 0 = FAST (no engineering values), 1 = FAST_ENG, 2 = COMPLETE; OutputFormat 0 = MVDA, 1 = SPREADSHEET, 2 = COLUMNMODE_SPREADSHEET (default). (PDF p. 21)
  • TimeFormat 0 = ASD (yyyy.ddd.hh.mm.ss[.mmm]), 1 = CCSDS ASCII A (yyyy-mm-ddThhss.mmm), 2 = BOTH; the Dbversion (MIB database version) field is mandatory. (PDF p. 22)
  • Datastream values range 1-65535 and at most 4 data streams may be requested; time windows are SINGLE, REPEATED (overall start/stop, window length, repeat period) or IRREGULAR. (PDF p. 23)
  • Per-parameter block: ParamName (Char(8)), optional SPID (1 to 2^31-1, ignored for synthetic parameters), RetrievalFilter VALUE_AFTER/VALUE_BEFORE/VALUE_BEFORE_AFTER/ON_OCCURRENCE/NO_FILTERING; ON_OCCURRENCE uses OccurrenceStart and OccurrenceInterval for supercommutated samples. (PDF p. 24)
  • Further per-parameter options: SamplingN (every Nth packet, COMPLETE only), OnlyWhenValidityOK, OnlyWhenNotNominal (OOL state) and Min/Max threshold values (raw view for FAST, default view otherwise). (PDF p. 25)
  • In MVDA output each time sample is 8 bytes: 4-byte integer seconds since 1970 and 4-byte integer microseconds; the header DataFormat codes include S8 to S64, U8 to U64, F, D, Q, A#####, RIEEE and RMIL (MIL-STD-1750A). (PDF p. 29)
  • Spreadsheet result rows hold Time1 (ASD), Time2 (CCSDS ASCII A), Parameter, Raw, RawValidity (same texts as the SCOS-2000 telemetry desktop), EngineeringUnit (from the MCS DB) and Engineering value, tab separated. (PDF p. 32)
  • The column-organised file gives per-parameter statistics: first/last sample times, minimum and maximum (with time stamps), average and standard deviation. (PDF p. 38)
  • The PRQM CORBA interface offers newRequest, getStatus, cancelRequest, getDBInfo (available MIB databases), getParameterCount and getParameters. (PDF p. 48)
  • PRQM talks to PSRV over TCP/IP: PSRV_IF_INITREQUEST sends a PSRVretrRequest to PSRVserver, which starts a PSRVfastChild or PSRVcompleteChild; the child opens its own TCP/IP connection back to PRQM for the request's parameters. (PDF p. 55)
  • Appendix A maps SCOS-2000 internal encodings to ASCII value formats (unsigned/signed integer, boolean, logical bit string with 'b', natural, real, string, absolute time in ASD/ASCII A/ASCII B, delta time up to 365.23.59.59.999). (PDF p. 68)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Issue 5.1 (October 2001) of ESOC's SCOS-2000 Database Import ICD, the specification of the Mission Information Base (MIB) as a set of tab-separated ASCII tables that a mission's off-line database exports and the SCOS-2000 importer loads into its run-time database. This copy comes from the Herschel SPIRE archive, where it was an applicable document for the SCOS-2000-based instrument EGSE. Its change log describes it as covering SCOS-2000 R2.3 (to be implemented in R3.0) plus specific additions for EGSE systems.

Chapter 2 fixes the file conventions: one <table>.dat file per table, one file per OL synthetic parameter, tab separators, the import-time checks with their fallback values, and the import options. Chapter 3 first maps database items to tables, then summarises 46 tables and defines every field (position, name, type, length, mandatory flag or default). The tables cover monitoring (pcf, caf/cap, txf/txp, mcf, ocf/ocp, pid, pic, tpcf, plf, vpd), displays (dpf/dpc, gpf/gpc, spf/spc, ppf/ppc) and commanding: packet headers (tcp, pcpc, pcdf), commands (ccf, the EGSE-only routing table dst, cpc, cdf, ptv), sequences (csf, css, sdf, csp), verification (cvs, cve, cvp), parameter sets (pst, psv, cps, pvs, psm), de-calibrations (cca/ccs, paf/pas) and range checks (prf/prv).

Appendix A gives the PTC/PFC parameter type codes SCOS-2000 supports, mapped to the ESA PUS (PSS-07-101), with raw value formats. Appendix B draws the table relationships, and Annex 1 lists the DCRs implemented since issue 4.x. Read it alongside later issues to see how the MIB evolved: here curve identifiers are still 4-digit numbers, descriptions are 16 characters, and there are no conditional calibrations, logarithmic curves or groups.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The ICD covers only the 'generic' part of the static database relevant to SCOS-2000 functions; mission-specific extensions are possible. MIB data are exported from the off-line database (e.g. ORACLE, MS-Access) into ASCII files, transferred to the importer directory, imported, and used when applications restart. (PDF p. 9)
  • The SCOS-2000 Mission Information Base is split into a static part (the 'database') and a dynamic part (the 'history files'). The raw value differs from the encoded value except for unsigned integers; e.g. raw -1 of a 16-bit signed integer is encoded as FFFF hex. (PDF p. 10)
  • Each table is one ASCII file named after the table in lower case with extension .dat (e.g. pcf.dat); each dynamic OL synthetic parameter is a separate file named after its PCF_NAME, without extension, in a dedicated sub-directory. Fields are tab-separated and mission-specific fields are appended at the end of a record. (PDF p. 12)
  • Import-time checks truncate over-long fields with a warning, replace null mandatory fields with 0 or an empty string, drop records that break relational integrity, and reset invalid command parameter values to 0, "" or 1970.001.00.00.00; messages go to /home/sops1/Import.log. (PDF p. 13)
  • Import options are full import (default), monitoring tables only, commanding tables only, selected tables only, and 'check only'. (PDF p. 13)
  • Key fields are marked with '*' after the field position; grey rows are not used by SCOS-2000; italics mark options not yet supported; 'M' marks mandatory fields; name uniqueness is case-insensitive (A1000 and a1000 clash). (PDF p. 20)
  • Section 3.2 summarises 46 ASCII tables: vdf; 13 monitoring tables; 6 display tables; and 26 commanding tables including the new dst routing table. (PDF p. 17)
  • The VDF table is mandatory; if it holds several records the last imported one defines the database version name (VDF_NAME, Char(8)). (PDF p. 22)
  • PCF is the central monitoring table. PCF_NAME is Char(8) and may not start with 'VAR', 'GVAR' or '$' (reserved by the OL syntax); PCF_DESCR is Char(16); PCF_PID (Number(10)) links a parameter to its on-board parameter ID for PUS variable packets. (PDF p. 23)
  • PCF_PTC takes values 1 to 13; saved synthetic parameters (PCF_NATUR='S') must use PTC=13. The PCF table has 19 fields in this issue. (PDF p. 24)
  • A TM packet is identified by the PID key TYPE, STYPE, APID, PI1_VAL and PI2_VAL; several keys may map to one SPID, and PID_VALID selects among records with the same key. The APID/type/subtype-to-SPID allocation should not change once telemetry archiving starts, for the GDDS retrieval services. (PDF p. 39)
  • The optional DST table (EGSE systems only) gives, per APID, a destination ID of up to 3 dot-separated fields ('NCTRS' by default, or 'EGSE' for spacecraft and non-spacecraft commands, e.g. 'EGSE.TC.0x8800'). (PDF p. 66)
  • Command parameter calibration and range-set references (CPC_PRFREF, CPC_CCAREF, CPC_PAFREF) are Number(4) in this issue. (PDF p. 69)
  • Appendix A maps SCOS-2000 PTC/PFC pairs to the PUS; 48- and 64-bit integers (PTC ¾, PFC 15/16) are not supported. (PDF p. 105)
  • PTC=5 PFC=3 is a 32-bit MIL-STD-1750A real (normally called PTC=5, PFC=2 in ESA missions) and PTC=5 PFC=4 a 48-bit MIL-STD-1750A real; PTC=6 PFC>0 bit strings are treated as unsigned integers on the monitoring side only. (PDF p. 106)
  • PTC=11 denotes deduced parameters and PTC=13 saved synthetic parameters. (PDF p. 110)
  • Absolute times are entered as yyyy.ddd.hh.mm.ss (e.g. 2001.159.23.59.59) and relative times as ±[ddd.]hh.mm.ss[.mmm]; neither can be associated with a calibration curve. (PDF p. 112)
  • DCR-266 (EGSE) widens CCF_APID, CCF_RAPID and PID_APID from num(4) to num(5): 0 to 2047 identify on-board APIDs and 2048 to 65535 ground process IDs. DCR-241 adds a command category (CCF_TYPE='S') for which the Releaser appends no CRC. (PDF p. 120)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Draft A of version 6.7 (December 2009) of the SCOS-2000 Database Import ICD, now numbered EGOS-MCS-S2K-ICD-0001 under ESA/OPS-GIC. It specifies the MIB ASCII tables imported into the SCOS-2000 run-time database and documents SCOS-2000 releases R4.5 and R5.2. The copy was found on an INAF-OAS Redmine project server.

Compared with issue 5.1 it adds multi-domain installations, in which each domain has its own database and a General Domain holds multi-domain synthetic parameters. From R5.0, command sequence and TM display definitions are converted to XML and stored in the FARC instead of the run-time database, with a delta import. The table set grows to 51 with conditional calibration selection (cur), logarithmic calibrations (lgf) and parameter/packet groups (grp, grpa, grpk), all repatriated from the Herschel/Planck CCS. Calibration and range-set identifiers become 10-character strings, PCF descriptions grow to 24 characters, and PCF gains time-correlation and archive fields (PCF_CORR, PCF_OBTID, PCF_DARC, PCF_ENDIAN). Unix-format absolute time (PTC 9, PFC 30) and NIS/SLE throw-event command types also appear.

A new Appendix C explains how SCOS-2000 supports the PUS service by service (1 to 19): data-type restrictions, the ban on using variable packets for regular housekeeping, service 1 report-based verification, the on-board schedule model for service 11, time correlation for service 9, and services that need mission-specific code. Annex 1 lists document changes by release from R4.0 to R5.2. This draft is useful for dating when each MIB feature appeared.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Version 6.4 moved TC sequence and TM display definitions out of the POST MIB database into the FARC as XML files and added the SLE throw-event (TE) command type; 6.7 Draft A adds updates for R4.5 and R5.2.0i1. (PDF p. 5)
  • The dynamic part of the MIB is now called the 'packet archive' (it was the 'history files' in earlier issues). (PDF p. 16)
  • SCOS-2000 manages multiple 'domains', each with its own database ASCII files; the General Domain also needs a multi-domain database that only defines multi-domain synthetic parameters. (PDF p. 19)
  • Every field of a record must contain at least the separator, so null fields hold only the tab character. (PDF p. 20)
  • An off-line database consistency checker is delivered with the main SCOS-2000 release test environment from R4.0. (PDF p. 21)
  • From SCOS-2000 R5.0, sequence and display ASCII tables are converted on request into XML files imported into the FARC (not the POST run-time database), using a 'delta' approach that only updates the definitions supplied. (PDF p. 22)
  • PCF_DESCR is Char(24) (S2K-SPR-3797) and PCF_CURTX is Char(10). (PDF p. 38)
  • The PCF table has 23 fields; new fields 20-23 are PCF_CORR and PCF_OBTID (time correlation per on-board time ID), PCF_DARC (DARC integration) and PCF_ENDIAN (little-endian support). (PDF p. 50)
  • The cur table associates calibration definitions with monitoring parameters, one record per parameter/calibration couple, so a parameter can have multiple calibrations; static PTV checks may then not use its engineering value. (PDF p. 58)
  • Absolute time in Unix format, PTC=9 PFC=30 (8 octets), is listed as a SCOS-2000 extension not defined in the PUS. (PDF p. 207)
  • Appendix C lists PUS data-type exceptions: integers limited to 32 bits, (5,4) only for TC encoding, no variable bit strings (6,0), variable octet/character strings only for TC encoding, and no p-field absolute time (9,0). (PDF p. 220)
  • SCOS-2000 adds two special TC parameter types: 'Parameter ID' (encoded as the on-board PID of a named TM parameter, e.g. for TC(4,6) or TC(12,1)) and 'Command ID' (encoded as the raw bytes of a named command, e.g. for TC(19,1)). (PDF p. 220)
  • Variable TM packets cannot take part in full TM processing (validity, monitoring checks, verification, synthetic parameters), so they should not carry regular housekeeping data. (PDF p. 221)
  • For PUS service 1, the Verifier extracts the 4 bytes echoing the TC packet ID and sequence control, which must sit at the same position in all type 1 packets; progress reports can only map to progress stage 0, and failure codes are ignored. (PDF p. 222)
  • New service 3 housekeeping packets must be defined in the TM/TC database before they are enabled on board; parameter time offsets and packet generation intervals are static database values. (PDF p. 223)
  • SCOS-2000 time correlation using service 9 time reports, for free-running and synchronised clocks, is only available from R5.2; earlier it was mission-specific. (PDF p. 225)
  • DCR-2421 raises the maximum PCF_PID and PID_SPID values from 2^31-1 to 2^32-1. (PDF p. 231)
  • Functions repatriated from the Herschel & Planck Check Out System include calibration curve selection, delta limits (a change of engineering value above a threshold is out of limit) and enable/inhibit of parameters. (PDF p. 231)
  • Further repatriated changes: enable/inhibit of packets, named parameter and packet groups, calibration curve identifiers changed from NUM(4) to CHAR(10), verification stage IDs from NUM(5) to NUM(8) and range set IDs from NUM(4) to CHAR(10). (PDF p. 232)
  • The logarithmic calibration (LGF), designed for platinum thermistor temperatures, computes Y = 1 / [A0 + A1 ln(X) + A2 ln^2(X) + A3 ln^3(X) + A4 ln^4(X)]. (PDF p. 233)
  • From R5.0, mapping different TM packets to the same SPID is deprecated, because packets are now stored in a database. (PDF p. 241)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Version 6.9 (July 2010) of the SCOS-2000 Database Import ICD (EGOS-MCS-S2K-ICD-0001), the consolidated, signed issue that follows the 6.7 drafts. It is the final ICD for SCOS-2000 releases 5.3, 5.3.1 and 5.4 and merges changes made in parallel on several release lines. This copy comes from an archive.org mirror.

Its structure is the same as 6.7. Chapter 2 covers file conventions, multi-domain installations and the FARC-based handling of sequences and displays. Chapter 3 defines the 51 tables field by field: monitoring parameters, calibrations (including conditional selection and logarithmic curves), limit checks, packet identification and processing, monitoring groups, displays, TC packet headers, commands with the optional dst routing table, sequences, verification, parameter sets, de-calibrations and range checks. Appendix A lists PTC/PFC types, Appendix B shows table relationships, and Appendix C covers PUS support by service.

New in 6.9 compared with 6.7 Draft A: section 3.3.2.1.5 on System Control parameters, where the multi-domain SCTL application publishes server-family status as TM through MIB entries generated by SCTLgenerateMIB; an optional per-stage verification window, CVS_UNCERTAINTY, which overrides the default window; CVE_CVSID and CVP_CVSID aligned to Number(5); a new applicable System Control ADD; and an updated reference to NIS/NCTRS ICD Volume 2 issue 4.0.2. Annex 1 is a cumulative list of document changes from R4.0 to 6.9. Use this issue when you need the 2010-era baseline used by many ESOC missions before the 2017 version 7.0. The visible tracked-change residue shows exactly what was edited.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Version 6.9 (06/07/2010) is the final ICD for S2K53, S2K531 and S2k54, consolidating changes from s2k52, s2k53, s2k531 and s2k4.51, with updated CVE_CVSID/CVP_CVSID fields and reference documents. (PDF p. 6)
  • The change log records intermediate drafts 6.7 Draft B (20/02/2010, SCR-3774/DCR-6008) and 6.7 Draft C (24/05/2010, R5.3.1, SPR 5504 on dynamic changes to TPSD). (PDF p. 5)
  • A new applicable document AD-6 (ADD-0022, SCOS-2000 System Control ADD) is added. (PDF p. 18)
  • RD-18 is now 'ICD NIS/NCTRS Volume 2 – MCS I/F', issue 4.0.2, November 2009 (version 6.7 Draft A cited 'NCTRA-NIS/MCS ICD Volume 2', issue 3.1, July 2005). (PDF p. 20)
  • PCF has 23 fields, ending with PCF_CORR, PCF_OBTID, PCF_DARC and PCF_ENDIAN; PCF_DESCR is Char(24). (PDF p. 40)
  • New section 3.3.2.1.5: the multi-domain System Control application (SCTL) starts, stops and monitors SCOS-2000 server families and stores status changes as TM packets; the tool SCTLgenerateMIB adds default PLF, PID, TPCF, OCF, OCP, TXF/TXP, DPF and DPC entries before SCTL first runs. (PDF p. 61)
  • CVS gains an optional seventh field CVS_UNCERTAINTY (Number(5), default -1) giving a stage-specific verification window that replaces the default (S2K-SCR-3774). (PDF p. 186)
  • CVE_CVSID and CVP_CVSID are aligned to Number(5), matching CVS_ID (S2K-DCR-3909). (PDF p. 250)
  • Unix-format absolute time (PTC=9, PFC=30, 8 octets) is listed in Appendix A as a type not defined in the PUS. (PDF p. 212)
  • Appendix C (PUS support) states that SCOS-2000 can encode and decode all PUS packet types and subtypes within the data-type limits, and details special processing for services 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 17, 18 and 19. (PDF p. 227)
  • Annex 1 groups changes by release: all evolution releases, R4.0 (6.0), R4.1 (6.2/6.3), R5.0 (6.4/6.5), R4.2 (6.5), clarifications in 6.6, R5.2 (6.7) and 6.9. (PDF p. 234)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Version 7.0 (August 2017) of ESOC's SCOS-2000 Database Import ICD (EGOS-MCS-S2K-ICD-0001), the reference definition of the SCOS-2000 Mission Information Base (MIB) as tab-separated ASCII tables. This copy was published on the Solar Orbiter instrument-team site as the MIB ICD applicable to the Solar Orbiter MOC, so it is the closest available specification for reading the public Solar Orbiter MIB.

Chapter 2 sets the rules: Unix-format files with one table per <table>.dat, tab separators with every field present, synthetic parameter expression files, per-domain databases, import checks with their fallback values, and the R5 handling of sequences and displays as XML in the FARC. Chapter 3 maps database items to tables, summarises the 51 tables and defines every field with type, length, key and mandatory/default markers. It covers monitoring parameters (PCF with 23 fields), synthetic parameters, user-defined constants, dynamic configuration variables, system-control parameters, the calibrations (cur, caf/cap, txf/txp, mcf, lgf), limit checks (ocf/ocp), packet identification and decoding (pid, pic, tpcf, plf, vpd), groups and displays, and on the commanding side TC headers, commands (ccf, dst, cpc, cdf, ptv), sequences, verification, parameter sets, de-calibrations and range checks.

Appendix A lists every supported PTC/PFC pair, including Unix time (9,30), and the raw value formats. Appendix B shows the table relationships, and Appendix C describes PUS support and limitations per service. Annex 1 repeats the change history, and the new Annex 2 lists the 7.0 changes by S2K ticket. Among them: Unix file format, reserved ground-station parameter names, PIC_APID as a key, maximum TC parameter sizes, the TC(11,4) time-tag wrapper, and future CPC_ENDIAN and VPD_FIXREP=-1 extensions.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Version 7.0 Final (11/08/2017) is updated for S2K-6680, S2K-8073, S2K-8325, S2K-8137, S2K-8353, S2K-8560, S2K-8528, S2K-7551, S2K-7749, S2K-7750, S2K-6884, S2K-8572, S2K-8063, S2K-8681, S2K-8782, S2K-8226 and S2K-8778, detailed in Annex 2. (PDF p. 6)
  • RD-1 is now CG-0003 'SCOS-2000 Configuration Variables' and RD-15 is EGOS-EUD-S2K-SUM-1001 'EUD4S2K Software User Manual'. (PDF p. 19)
  • The ASCII files are in Unix format (S2K-7551); the example off-line database is now only MS ACCESS, the ORACLE reference having been removed (S2K-8137). (PDF p. 21)
  • Each record must contain every field, at least as a separator; null fields contain only the tab character. (PDF p. 22)
  • Section 3.2 summarises 51 ASCII tables, from vdf to prv, including cur, lgf, grp, grpa, grpk and the optional dst routing table. (PDF p. 30)
  • PCF_NAME (Char(8)) may not start with 'VAR', 'GVAR' or '$', and the names NNOiiii, CEBiiii, KRUiiii, MSPiiii, VL2iiii, PERiiii, REDiiii and MLGiiii (iiii = 0000-9999) are reserved for ground-station telemetry. (PDF p. 41)
  • The PCF table has 23 fields (PCF_NAME ... PCF_ENDIAN); PCF_DESCR is Char(24) and PCF_CURTX Char(10). (PDF p. 41)
  • System Control parameters: the SCTL application stores the status of monitored SCOS-2000 server families as TM packets, and SCTLgenerateMIB generates the corresponding MIB entries before SCTL first runs. (PDF p. 62)
  • The PID table has 16 fields; PID_TYPE, PID_STYPE, PID_APID, PID_PI1_VAL, PID_PI2_VAL and PID_SPID are marked as key fields, and PID_APID is Number(5). (PDF p. 84)
  • The maximum command size comes from MISC variable CMDP_MAX_BLOCK_SIZE (default 248 bytes), reduced by the header (sum of PCDF_LEN), the CRC (CMD_CRC_SIZE, default 2 bytes) and, for time-tagged commands, the TC(11,4) wrapper (CMD_LOAD_TT_NAME, default 20 bytes). (PDF p. 132)
  • Commands can be destined to the spacecraft or to other control domains such as ground equipment; throw-event commands (from R5.0) are encoded per [RD-18] for SLE and [RD-19] for NIS throw events and cannot be blocked with other entries. (PDF p. 132)
  • The CCF table has 21 fields, the last being CCF_SUBSCHED (Number(5)). (PDF p. 140)
  • CPC has 16 fields; CPC_CORR and CPC_OBTID support time-correlated encoding of time parameters, and CPC_ENDIAN (default 'B') is a future extension (S2K-7749). (PDF p. 150)
  • CVS has 7 fields; the optional CVS_UNCERTAINTY gives a stage-specific verification window that overrides the default in the TM Spacon. (PDF p. 194)
  • Absolute time PTC=9 PFC=30 (Unix format, 8 octets: 4 bytes of seconds since 1 January 1970 followed by 4 bytes of microseconds) is supported although it is not defined in the PUS. (PDF p. 221)
  • Appendix C: SCOS-2000 encodes and decodes all PUS packet types within the data-type limits, and describes service-specific processing such as service 1 report-based verification and the service 11 ground image of the on-board schedule. (PDF p. 237)
  • Annex 2 lists the 7.0 changes with the applicable SCOS releases, e.g. S2K-8073 (maximum TC parameter sizes, 5.5.3/6.0.0 or higher), S2K-8528 (PIC_APID part of the key, 4.2 or higher) and S2K-8226 (TC(11,4) encoding according to CDF, 5.5.4 and higher). (PDF p. 261)
  • S2K-6884 lists reserved parameter names, S2K-8572 and S2K-8778 forbid PCF_CORR/CPC_CORR='Y' for relative-time parameters, and S2K-7750 adds the future VPD_FIXREP value '-1'. (PDF p. 262)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The interface control document for the file-based data interface of the IFMS (Intermediate Frequency and Modem System), the ranging, Doppler and receiver equipment in ESA's ESTRACK ground stations. The interface serves data clients such as NCTRS and, for historical reasons, is called the IFMS-to-OCC (Operations Control Centre) interface. It carries radiometric and station measurement data, not TM/TC frames.

The IFMS acts as a read-only FTP server over TCP/IP. The document lists the supported FTP commands and profile (stream mode, file structure, ASCII and image types only). Clients get catalogue access through directory listings, off-line access by retrieval, and 'pseudo-on-line' access through small data-sets that cover short measurement durations. Data-sets sit under <data_set_root>/station/spacecraft/, and their file names encode station, spacecraft, year, day of year, data-set kind, DAP (data acquisition process) type, DAP start time and a sequence number. DAP types are D1/D2 (Doppler), G1/G2 (AGC), ME (meteo), RG (ranging) and OL (open loop). Gzip copies and '.raw' uncorrected ranging files are also covered.

Section 6 defines the content of each data-set. The header holds station, spacecraft, time tags, requestor (DCP or STC), why the file was opened, sample period, carrier and tone indicators and a dump of the active configuration table. The measurement records are: Doppler (NCO count, unwrapped phase and the derived one-way delta delay, with the full algorithm for coherent and non-coherent transponders), AGC (carrier level, polarisation, channel powers, lock status), meteo (humidity, pressure, temperature), ranging (delay, code number, ambiguity flag, DSP status) and binary open-loop records (a 44-byte header with magic number 0xA3C725B6 and 136 six-byte blocks of packed I/Q samples). Section 7 covers the Support-Log files and section 8 the user access rules. The annexes give the BNF syntax and example files. The copy comes from the Mars Express radio science archive.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Change history highlights: Open-Loop data-sets added in 10.2.0 (2004-03-29), a 'freqplan' configuration table added to the header in 10.3.0, IP/X.25 mentions removed and new AGC measurements added in 10.5.0, 'gmdemod' header parameters added in 10.6.0. (PDF p. 2)
  • The ICD describes the interface between the IFMS and data clients such as NCTRS; for historical reasons it is known as the IFMS-to-OCC (Operations Control Centre) interface. (PDF p. 5)
  • The interface is entirely standard FTP over TCP/IP with read-only files; the IFMS FTP server supports USER, PASS, QUIT, PORT, MODE (S only), TYPE (A and I only), STRU (F only), CWD, PWD, LIST and RETR. (PDF p. 6)
  • Pseudo-on-line delivery uses small data files of short measurement duration, set by configuration parameters (D1MaxDs, D2MaxDs, G1MaxDs, G2MaxDs, MeMaxDs, RgMaxDs); technically it is identical to off-line access. (PDF p. 8)
  • File names such as PER1_CLU3_2002_108_OP_RG_145513_0001 encode station ID, spacecraft ID, year, day of year, data-set kind, DAP type (D1, D2, G1, G2, ME, OL, RG), DAP start time hhmmss and a 4-digit sequence ID; nominal length 31 characters. (PDF p. 9)
  • Maximum DAP duration is 20 hours (72000 s); uncorrected ranging data are kept as '.raw' files in a 'raw/' subdirectory, and in this issue the IFMS software does not yet correct ranging data, so only raw files exist. (PDF p. 10)
  • Field types are B (Boolean), F (Float), I (Integer), S (String) and T (Time, 'YYYYMMDD.hhmmss.mmm'), with units in < > and accuracy in [ ]. (PDF p. 11)
  • The data-set header includes requestor_id (DCP or STC), why_opened (DAP_Started, Conf_Change, Max_Size_Reached, Tone_Lost), sample_period, carrier and tone indicators, epd_source, rg_data_corrected and the active configuration (modulator, freqplan, tracking, rcdemod, scdemod, gmdemod). (PDF p. 12)
  • Doppler records hold sample number and time, a 17.5 MHz NCO interval count, unwrapped carrier phase (turns), a spurious-carrier flag and the one-way delta delay; the ICD gives the delta-delay derivation for coherent and non-coherent transponders. (PDF p. 13)
  • Ranging records hold the round-trip delay modulo the code ambiguity, the current code number (1 to 24), ambiguity-resolution and spurious flags, estimated Doppler (KD-1) and DSP status values. (PDF p. 15)
  • Open-loop records come from the GDSP 17.5 Msps complex baseband stream; each record has a 44-byte big-endian header (magic 0xA3C725B6) and 136 blocks of 6 bytes holding 12, 6, 3 or 1 samples for 1, 2, 4 or 12-bit quantisation; a new data-set opens every minute. (PDF p. 16)
  • Six Support-Log files (D1, D2, G1, G2, ME, RG) in ~ifmsdset/support_logs/ log data-set open, close and delete events; they are intended only as a backup monitoring mechanism. (PDF p. 17)
  • External FTP users can never create, modify or delete files; data-set deletion is controlled only through the DCP and STC interfaces. (PDF p. 18)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A five-page SESP 2010 conference paper by Andy Armitage of Terma BV describing CMDVS (Commanding Monitoring Data-handling & Visualization System), a 'small' monitoring and control system that Terma developed with Satellite Services BV (SSBV) for instrument- and payload-level EGSE, with features equivalent or compatible to SCOS-2000-based central checkout systems (CCS).

The motivation section explains why SCOS-2000-based EGSE was felt to be too heavy at instrument level: complex to develop, configure and use; front ends had to be described in a separate EGSE TM/TC database; the SCOS-2000 telecommand chain was limited to 2 packets per second with checking (20 without); and maintenance on modern platforms was getting more expensive. Terma's answer was a new Qt-based system that keeps the same test language (TOPE/Tcl) and the SCOS-2000 MIB database interface, so that users and database producers need not change. At the start of 2010 all SCOS-2000 telemetry and commanding model features had been implemented.

The key idea is front-end interfacing through plugins generated from SSBV's API headers, introspected at runtime, instead of TM/TC packets, which removes the need for an EGSE database and ICDs. The paper lists improvements over SCOS-2000: variable-packet contents calibrated and limit-checked like fixed packets, variable-length parameters in TM and TC, database-driven TC headers, 64-bit PUS type codes, configurable source sequence counts and up to 64 configurable verification stages. It describes use as an intelligent SCOE (Galileo FOC SMS), subsystem simulation, reuse of the plugin approach in SCOS-2000-based CCS, and a proposal to standardise front-end API descriptions (for example CORBA IDL or WSDL). Missions named include BepiColombo, Sentinel-1 and -2, EarthCARE, Galileo FOC and SGEO.
tags: Tools, MIB editors and related standards

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• At the start of 2010 the Terma/SSBV 'small' monitoring and control system implemented all monitoring and control features of SCOS2000; it had been used at payload or instrument level on BepiColombo, Sentinel1, Sentinel2, EarthCare, Galileo FOC and SGEO. (PDF p. 1)
  • The paper states that the SCOS2000 telecommand chain is limited to 2 packets per second with checking or 20 with no checking, which is insufficient for some modern front ends. (PDF p. 1)
  • Previous monitoring and control systems are said to have cost of the order of 30 MEURO to develop; the new system kept the CCS test language and the SCOS2000 MIB database interface to preserve continuity for users and database developers. (PDF p. 2)
  • The SCOS2000 MIB database interface is described as not perfectly normalized but well known, relatively well described and well understood in industry. (PDF p. 2)
  • Front ends are interfaced through runtime-introspected Qt C++ plugins built from the SSBV API headers instead of TM/TC packets; the system was named CMDVS ('Commanding Monitoring Data-handling & Visualization System'). (PDF p. 2)
  • CMDVS makes variable-packet contents available to test sequences, calibrated and limit-checked like fixed-packet parameters, supports variable-length parameters in TM and TC, and generates TC headers entirely from the database without assuming CCSDS headers. (PDF p. 3)
  • CMDVS supports all SCOS2000 TC verification stages plus a finalisation stage, and up to 64 verification stages configurable by a mask; source sequence count strategies are configurable without touching the generic verification code. (PDF p. 3)
  • The dynamic plugin approach was reused in the SCOS2000-based CCS, where the external interface manager became a generic process with a project-specific plugin whose API is loaded automatically into test sequences. (PDF p. 5)
  • The author proposes standardising only the format in which front-end suppliers describe their APIs (for example CORBA IDL or WSDL) rather than the front-end interfaces themselves. (PDF p. 5)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A seven-page conference paper by D. Comi and R. Sala (Intecs SpA) and F. Insinga (Thales Alenia Space Italia) on the SRDB Translator, a tool that imports a SCOS-2000 MIB-format Satellite Reference Database (SRDB) into the database of ECHO, the TAS-I central checkout (EGSE) system.

The paper starts from the observation that SCOS-2000 has become the standard ESA mission control system and that SRDBs are therefore almost always based on the SCOS-2000 runtime database, while industrial checkout systems keep their own data models. It compares the two databases at the level of logical entities (monitoring parameters and calibrations, TM packets, displays, commands, verification and checks), explains why a one-to-one table mapping does not work, and classifies each item into data present in both, only in the SRDB, or only in ECHO. Two tables give concrete conversion rules: TC verification checks (stages not imported, verification window converted to milliseconds, raw-value checks discarded) and numerical calibration (10-character curve identifiers mapped to integers, radix conversion, point limits, polynomial boundaries, logarithmic curves, number of curves per parameter).

It then describes the tool: a utility of the ECHO Database Manager (MTGP) on MS SQL Server, compliant with SCOS-2000 ICD issue 6.1, with a two-step import (raw copy into staging tables, then stored procedures), merging with locally defined EGSE data and a result log. Applications are Galileo GIOVE-B, Sentinel-1 and BepiColombo (with OBC and SSMM database metrics). Limits (strict column matching across ICD issues) and future work (bidirectional transfer and an XML-based standard database exchange language) close the paper.
tags: Tools, MIB editors and related standards

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Because SCOS-2000 has become standard in ESA missions for control centres and in most cases EGSE, the Satellite Reference Database (SRDB) is almost always based on the SCOS-2000 run-time database. (PDF p. 1)
  • The input SRDB covers monitoring data, TM packets (fixed and variable), displays and reports, command packets and sequences, and commanding data (verification, de-calibration, range checks); both databases base TM/TC packet definitions on the ECSS PUS. (PDF p. 2)
  • A 1-to-1 mapping from one source table to one destination table is described as almost inapplicable; the comparison is made on logical entities. (PDF p. 2)
  • TC verification conversion: SCOS-2000 verification stages are not imported, the SCOS-2000 window (start time and duration in seconds) becomes an ECHO maximum elapsed time in milliseconds computed as (start + interval) x 1000, and checks expressed as raw values are discarded. (PDF p. 3)
  • Numerical calibration conversion: SCOS-2000 curve identifiers are Char(10) while ECHO uses Int 1..9999; hex and octal raw values are converted to decimal; ECHO point-by-point curves need 2 to 1000 points; the number of curves per parameter was extended from 4 to 99. (PDF p. 4)
  • The current SRDB Translator is compliant with SCOS-2000 ICD Issue 6.1 and runs as a utility of the ECHO Database Manager (MTGP) on MS SQL Server. (PDF p. 5)
  • The import first copies SCOS-2000 tables unchanged into staging tables, then converts them with stored procedures; a missing expected column aborts the whole import, as happened with BepiColombo databases built to an earlier ICD issue. (PDF p. 6)
  • The first version was developed for Galileo GIOVE-B, whose SCOS-2000 database was delivered as a single MS Access 2000 file; an enhanced version was made for Sentinel-1 and reused on BepiColombo. (PDF p. 6)
  • BepiColombo database metrics: OBC 3745 parameters, 521 TM packets, 399 TC packets; SSMM 1947 parameters, 1921 TM packets, 535 TC packets (about 10000 records each). (PDF p. 6)
  • The authors propose a standard satellite-database exchange interface, for example an XML-based mark-up language, to ease data exchange among EGSE systems. (PDF p. 7)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Fourteen unchanged text responses from the JPL Horizons API, packed in one zip file with a MANIFEST.txt that gives each file's exact query URL, download time (UTC), size and SHA-256. Four files hold daily heliocentric state vectors (position and velocity, ecliptic of J2000, TDB) for Solar Orbiter (target -144), Earth, Venus and Mercury from 2020-02-11 to 2030-11-19. One file holds the daily sub-observer latitude and longitude of the Sun seen from Solar Orbiter, which is the spacecraft's heliographic latitude. Nine files hold 5-minute planet-centred vectors around each Earth and Venus gravity assist. The last file is Horizons' object description for Solar Orbiter, including its flyby list.

The Solar Orbiter simulator in this wiki is built from these files. tools/build_simulator.py turns them into docs/simulator/data/ephem.json and derives perihelia, aphelia, latitude extremes, solar conjunctions and gravity-assist closest approaches.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Reference frame: ecliptic of J2000.0 (IAU76 obliquity of 84381.448 arcseconds with respect to the ICRF X-Y plane); time tags in TDB.
  • Trajectory source named by Horizons: solo_ANC_soc-orbit-stp_20200210-20301120_435_V1_00592, fitted to tracking data up to 2026-11-03.
  • Gravity assists listed by Horizons: Venus 2020-12-26, 2021-08-08, 2022-09-04, 2025-02-18, 2026-12-24, 2028-03-17, 2029-06-10, 2030-09-02; Earth 2021-11-27 at about 454 km altitude.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The interface control document between the Rosetta and Mars Express mission control systems (RMCS/MEMCS, both SCOS-2000 based and developed by Anite) and the ESOC Flight Dynamics System (FDS) on the ORATOS platforms. It lists every data flow in both directions, explains how each one travels, and records the MIB tailoring these missions used.

From the MCS to the FDS go MIB files, packetised data and tracking data files. The packetised data are TM source packets, TC history and time coefficient packets, which flight dynamics extracts from the MCS data archive with its own SCOS-2000/ORATOS Data Access (SoDA) software. The tracking data are ESA IFMS ranging, Doppler, meteo and AGC files fetched through the NIS (see NCTRS/NIS) and stored in the FARC, plus NASA/DSN ODF and media calibration files obtained via the RACSO gateway. From the FDS to the MCS go auxiliary data files for experimenters (orbit, attitude, events, comet models, FORTRAN access software), command request files (FDR for the scheduler, DOR for the manual stack), trajectory data (STDMs for ESA stations, CCSDS Orbit Data Message EPMs for the DSN), the interplanetary WIMPY and the One-Way Light Time file used by MCS time correlation.

All file exchanges except Rosetta MPTS files use the MCS File Transfer System (FTS) with the naming convention TTTT_SSSDDD_t<14 chars>_vvvvv.ROS|MEX. The document lists high-priority operational files, the manual SFTP procedure across the RACSO/OSCAR security boundary, node addresses, and complete per-mission file-type tables. Section 7.7 is valuable for MIB tailoring: ccf.dat gains a 40-character description and a CCF_SUBSCH on-board sub-schedule field, and pcf.dat gains a 24-character description and the fields PCF_WDLEN, PCF_GRPID, PCF_OFFSET and PCF_GLOBAL used to build PUS service 3 telecommands. The section also lists the utility hash files that map source-database names to SPIDs and calibration numbers.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Change record: Draft A0 (15/05/99), Draft A1 (31/03/00), Issue A0 (28/03/01) and Draft B0 (07/02/03, DCRs 173 to 207); the title page says Issue B1, 2003-03-07. (PDF p. 5)
  • The MCS converts packet definitions extracted from the Source Database into MIB files; packetised data (TM source packets, TC history packets (TBC), time coefficient history packets) are extracted from the DAS by FDS using SoDA. (PDF p. 9)
  • ESA tracking data files are stored on the IFMS at the ESA stations; the MCS obtains them via the Network Interface Subsystem (NIS) and stores them in the MCS FARC. NASA/DSN tracking files come from the FD computer RACSO. (PDF p. 10)
  • FD command request files are Flight Dynamics Requests (FDR), used by the MCS scheduler subsystem, and Direct Operations Requests (DOR), used by the TC subsystem manual stack; their format is in the CRID. (PDF p. 11)
  • STDMs for ESA tracking go from FDS to the MCS, are archived in the DAS and pass via the NIS to the station computer; EPMs (CCSDS 502) for NASA/DSN go via RACSO to JPL. (PDF p. 12)
  • FDS supplies a propagation-delay routine that uses One-Way Light Time (OWLT) files per ground station; the FD ground station ID does not correspond to the NCTRS ground station ID. (PDF p. 13)
  • All MCS-FDS file transfer except Rosetta MPTS files uses the File Transfer System (FTS); the only delivery acknowledgement is the FTS log, and FTS version numbers wrap from 99999 to 00000. (PDF p. 16)
  • The FTS is point-to-point: a file needed at two destinations (e.g. NIA and NIB) must be injected twice with different destination codes in its name. (PDF p. 17)
  • RMCS, MEMCS and FDS all run on SUN/Solaris with 100 Mbps network connections; node names include ROMCA/ROMCB, RONCTRA/RONCTRB, MEMCA/MEMCB, MENCTRA/MENCTRB and RACSO (gateway to OSCAR at JPL). (PDF p. 19)
  • FTS file naming: TTTT_SSSDDD_txxxxxxxxxxxxxx_vvvvv.yyy (type, source, destination, 'D', 14-character free text, version, ROS or MEX), all upper case; external files are encapsulated with 'tar c'. (PDF p. 21)
  • The SODA server extracts source packets and SCOS header information through the SCOS-2000 FDIF interface; ORATOS client processes pass packets to the Generic Telemetry Processor (GTP). (PDF p. 28)
  • MIB tailoring: ccf.dat CCF_DESCR is enlarged from 24 to 40 characters and a new CCF_SUBSCH field (Number(3)) identifies the on-board sub-schedule. (PDF p. 29)
  • MIB tailoring: pcf.dat PCF_DESCR is enlarged from 16 to 24 characters and PCF_WDLEN ('O' 8-bit or 'W' 16-bit), PCF_GRPID, PCF_OFFSET and PCF_GLOBAL ('G' global or 'D' detailed) are added to build service 3 telecommands; only global parameters are named in service 3 TCs. (PDF p. 30)
  • The MIB tar file includes utility files spid_hash.txt (RSDB packet name to SPID), calib_hash.txt (RSDB calibration name to calibration number), synparhash.txt (auto-generated synthetic parameter expressions) and list_of_packet_types_not_in_vpd.txt. (PDF p. 30)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Issue B5 (27 March 2003) of the Data Delivery Interface Document (DDID) shared by the Rosetta and Mars Express mission control systems (RMCS/MEMCS) at ESOC, RO-ESC-IF-5003 / MEX-ESC-IF-5003. This copy was distributed inside the Mars Express Radio Science (MRS) archive in ESA's Planetary Science Archive. The DDID is the ICD between the SCOS-2000-based mission control systems and the science communities; with the Command Request Interface Document it defines the complete PI interface. The text says this is the twelfth update and the sixth issue, re-integrating Mars Express with Rosetta.

The structure and most content match the later issue C2. It covers the Data Disposition System (DDS) requirements (FTP or web requests, 15-minute response, quotas, sampling every Nth packet, automatic forwarding), interface characteristics, access and security, and generation from the MCS Data Archive System. The data definition chapter specifies the XML on-line request, responses, acknowledgements and catalogue entries in SFDU packaging; telemetry delivered as reconstituted source packets with an 18-octet DDS packet header (SCET, length, ground station ID, VC, SLE type, time quality); command history with a DDS command header carrying CUV, CAV and CEV verification flags; auxiliary data, catalogues, error messages and RDM (CD-ROM) layouts. Appendices cover data streams and ADIDs, error handling, the MEX RDM listing, auxiliary data types, an SFDU tutorial, nomenclature conventions, MCS products (APID 1966/type 190 internal packets, time correlation, lander TC verification file, detailed agenda file) and the science network implementation.

Compared with issue C2, this issue still speaks of on-line 'quick-look' data, gives a 3-week (TBC) RDM delivery target, splits RDM days by SCOS-2000 packet generation time, has fewer ground station IDs (NASA Madrid TBD), and leaves Appendices C (accounts) and I (XML schema) to separate documents. It is useful for tracing how the ESOC data delivery interface evolved.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The DDID defines the data delivery interface between the Rosetta and Mars Express mission control systems (RMCS and MEMCS) at ESOC and their science communities, through the Data Disposition System (DDS); in this issue the on-line data are called 'quick-look' data. (PDF p. 23)
  • Section 1.4 states this is the twelfth update of the DDID and the sixth issue, and section 1.5 that it re-integrates Mars Express with the Rosetta interface requirements and design. (PDF p. 23)
  • RDMs are to be delivered within 3 weeks (TBC) of reception at the OCC, and the split by day uses the SCOS-2000 packet generation time (equivalent to the archive time). (PDF p. 29)
  • Each delivered telemetry packet carries an 18-octet DDS packet header: SCET (two 32-bit integers, seconds and microseconds since 1970), packet length, ground station ID (e.g. 0x15 Kourou, 0x17 New Norcia, 0x22 Goldstone, 0x23 Canberra, NASA Madrid TBD), virtual channel, SLE service type and time quality. (PDF p. 62)
  • For on-line data the DDS shall provide access for 3 months (TBC) after acquisition from the spacecraft. (PDF p. 34)
  • Appendix C (accounts) and Appendix I (request dialogue XML schema) are provided as separate documents (A-8 and A-7). (PDF p. 107)
  • MCS-internal telemetry packets that carry no identification of their own are identified by APID 1966 and type 190. (PDF p. 126)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The Read the Docs PDF export (release 0.1, 15 September 2023) of MIB Generator by Josef Vácha, a set of Python scripts that generate SCOS-2000 MIB ASCII tables from the C header and source files that define an instrument's TM packets and TC commands. The first chapters form a short user guide. The tool expects four C inputs: a TM .h file with packet structures and calibrations, a TM .c file with the APID array and the list of packet types with service type and subtype, a TC .h file with command structures, the TC header, decalibrations and verifications, and a common TcTm .h file. It can be installed from PyPI or GitHub and is run as the mib-gen command or the mib-gen-gui interface; a 'what to edit' chapter maps typical changes to modules.

Chapter 5 matters most to an engineer. It shows the json5 annotations written inside C comments: pack_type, spid, text_id, base_par_index and prefix (for generated parameter names), sid, vpd (fixed, count, data), cal and type for TM; service, sub, cvs, cdf, min, max, default, const_value and enum for TC. It also shows the calibration notations: mcf polynomial, lgf logarithmic, text_cal or enum textual, num_cal numerical, dec_ident decalibration and cvs_def verification stages. The remaining chapters are API reference generated from docstrings for the main, parsing, construction, generation, data, temp, utilities and gui packages. They show which tables are built (pid, pic, tpcf, pcf, plf, vpd, cur, caf/cap, txf, mcf, lgf, paf, ccf, cdf, cpc, prf, cvp, cvs, tcp, pcpc, pcdf), the type, length, uniqueness and mandatory checks driven by a table-format module, a pic de-duplication filter, an OHB Italia mnemonic check and an optional .docx summary laid out like an ICD.
tags: Tools, MIB editors and related standards

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• MIB Generator is a set of Python scripts that generate MIB databases, as used in ESA's MCS SCOS 2000, from C header (and other) files defining TM and TC packet structures; the current implementation assumes one specific formatting of the C files. (PDF p. 5)
  • Processing steps: user interaction and configuration (main, utilities), parsing of the C files (parsing), construction of Python objects for TM packets, TC commands and calibrations (construction), and generation, checking and saving of MIB tables (generation). (PDF p. 7)
  • Four C inputs are expected: a TM .h file (packet structures, entries, calibrations), a TM .c file (list of TM packet types), a TC .h file (commands, TC headers, decalibrations, verifications) and a TcTm .h file (common id structures and enums). (PDF p. 7)
  • Installation: 'pip install mib-generator' from PyPI or a clone of the GitHub repository vachaj11/MIB-Generator; prerequisites are json5, python-docx and PySide6 (GUI only). (PDF p. 9)
  • The CLI is started with mib-gen (mib-gen -p sets the input/output paths on first use, --help lists options); a simple GUI is started with mib-gen-gui. (PDF p. 11)
  • The TM .c file must hold an apidNum array mapping APID names to numbers and a tmProperties array giving each packet type its apid, serviceType and serviceSubType. (PDF p. 15)
  • Enums and #define macros are collected into one evaluation dictionary; comments of the form /{ ... }/ are parsed as json5, while ordinary // comments are ignored. (PDF p. 16)
  • Packet annotations: pack_type (matched to the .c table), base_par_index and prefix for unique parameter names (e.g. the entry 'compression' becomes LWT59202), text_id (packet name in the MIB), spid, desc and use_structure. (PDF p. 16)
  • Entry annotations: sid (identification field with const_value), type, desc, vpd ('fixed', 'count' or 'data' for variable packet definitions) and cal; nested structs are unpacked and C bit-field widths are honoured. (PDF p. 17)
  • Calibrations are declared with an mcf key (polynomial coefficients), an lgf key (logarithmic coefficients), text_cal or an annotated enum (textual) and num_cal (numerical X-Y pairs). (PDF p. 17)
  • The sample TC header comments the 4-bit version field as 1 for ECSS-E-70-41A and 2 for ECSS-E-ST-70-41C, followed by acknowledgement flags, service type, subtype and source ID. (PDF p. 18)
  • TC annotations: service and sub, cvs (verification stages; defaults apply if absent); parameter keys cdf (count/data repetition), min and max (range check), default, const_value (fixed area) and enum (decalibration). (PDF p. 19)
  • Decalibrations are enums with a dec_ident key (adding cal_ident also defines a TM textual calibration); verification stages are isolated comments with cvs_def, cvs_type, cvs_interval and default, and the sample notes that CVS_SOURCE is always R and the CVS start is 0. (PDF p. 19)
  • Tables built per TC header: tcp, pcpc and pcdf. (PDF p. 44)
  • Tables built per TC command: ccf, cpc, cdf, prf and cvp. (PDF p. 47)
  • Tables built per TM packet: pid, pic, tpcf, pcf and plf, plus cur and vpd. (PDF p. 53)
  • Calibration classes produce caf/cap (numerical), paf, lgf, mcf, txf and cvs rows; the numerical calibration syntax 'hasn't been fully decided yet'. (PDF p. 59)
  • Generation runs final checks so that the output tables adhere to the requirements on type, length, uniqueness and 'mandatoriness'. (PDF p. 69)
  • Which tables are generated is set in the data/config.json5 config file or overridden with the cfg argument of generation_hub. (PDF p. 71)
  • A .docx document listing the entries of each TM and TC packet can be generated with python-docx, in a layout that follows a standard ICD scheme. (PDF p. 72)
  • mnemon_check follows additional MIB specifications by OHB Italia, which require a unique mnemonic in the description field of some tables; tables are written as tab-separated .dat files. (PDF p. 74)
  • pic_filter reduces the packet list to one pic entry per type/subtype and warns if packets sharing a type/subtype declare their additional identification fields at different positions. (PDF p. 75)
  • Column names, types, lengths and mandatory flags of every MIB table are stored in mib_generator.data.longdata (tables_format, unique_entries, uint_pfc, time_pfc). (PDF p. 77)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The overview paper of the Astronomy & Astrophysics Solar Orbiter special issue, written after launch on 10 February 2020. It summarises the four top-level science questions, the spacecraft, the ten instruments, the mission design and the science operations approach.

Table 1 gives the mission summary: closest perihelion 0.28 au and solar-inclination milestones of 18, 24 and 33 degrees. The nominal mission starts with the Earth gravity assist in November 2021 and lasts 7 years including cruise, with a 3-year extension. The data downlink is 150 kbit/s at 1 au, stated as the requirement, with higher performance in orbit. Section 3 describes the heat shield, whose front reaches about 500 °C at perihelion, and the solar arrays, which rotate about their long axis for temperature control. Section 5 describes the sequence of Venus resonances and the resulting perihelion distances and inclinations.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Launched on 10 February 2020 at 04:03 UTC on an Atlas V 411 from Cape Canaveral (Table 1). (PDF p. 4)
  • Solar inclination milestones: 18 degrees (first reached 22 March 2025), 24 degrees (28 January 2027), 33 degrees (24 July 2029); closest perihelion 0.28 au (Table 1). (PDF p. 4)
  • Data downlink: 150 kbit/s at 1 au spacecraft-Earth distance, a requirement with higher in-orbit performance (Table 1). (PDF p. 4)
  • Nominal mission duration 7 years including cruise, the nominal mission starting with the Earth gravity assist; extended mission 3 years (Table 1). (PDF p. 4)
  • The heat shield's front reaches around 500 °C at perihelion; the solar arrays can be rotated about their longitudinal axis for temperature control (§3). (PDF p. 18)
  • Venus resonances 5:4, 4:3, 3:2, 3:2 and 3:2 progressively raise the solar inclination; the last Venus gravity assist yields 33.4 degrees (§5). (PDF p. 25)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
An NLR technical publication, a reprint of SpaceOps 2006 paper AIAA-2006-590, on how Dutch Space built and used a DOORS-based ACMS Operations Database for the Attitude Control and Measurement System of Herschel and Planck. The paper covers the missions and the industrial team: Terma wrote the application software (ASW) and the SCOS-2000-based Herschel/Planck Central Checkout System (HPCCS), and GMV built the Herschel/Planck System Data Base (HPSDB). It then describes the PUS services most relevant to the ACMS: service 3 housekeeping built on a datapool, service 5 events and service 8 function management.

The database was created in phase B. The reasons given are that the telemetry definition document had become unmaintainable, the HPSDB was immature, and using SCOS-2000 in the ACMS test equipment (SCOS-2000 as EGSE) required every TM/TC detail to be defined. The SCOS-2000 MS Access database editor was rejected because it supports only one mission and has no object-level configuration control. The DOORS module architecture deliberately mirrors the SCOS-2000 MIB tables. There are parameter modules (parameter types with PTC/PFC, units, enumerations, numerical conversions), TC modules (command characteristics, packet structures, datapool identifiers) and TM modules (packet identification criteria, packet identifiers, packet structures, alphanumeric displays), mapped onto CCF, CDF, PCF, PID, PLF, PIC, TPCF, CAF, MCF, TXF and other tables. Operational identifiers are built from HPSDB box numbers, for example AESMG002 for Herschel and AESMG003 for Planck.

Each object carries spacecraft, software and from/to version attributes. This lets per-version SCOS-2000 .dat files and HPSDB XML be generated from one source, with exports kept in CVS instead of DOORS baselines. The paper also describes generating Tcl test code and checking HPSDB-generated .dat files against the AIT ones with a 'ccsdiff' script. It ends with lessons learned, including a call for a standardised database design for operations and test data.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The ACMS Test Equipment uses the SCOS-2000 based Herschel/Planck Central Checkout System, giving commonality between tools and data in subsystem and system testing and in operations. (PDF p. 1)
  • AAS-F is prime for both satellites, AAS-I is Service Module responsible, Dutch Space (with Sener and Analyticon) is responsible for the ACMS; Terma (Denmark) develops the ASW, Saab Ericsson Space the Basic Software, Terma (Netherlands) the HPCCS and GMV (Spain) the HPSDB. (PDF p. 9)
  • Herschel/Planck TM/TC are based on the ESA PUS; the services most relevant for ACMS operations are service 3 (housekeeping, generated by the BSW from a datapool), service 5 (events from ASW and BSW) and service 8 (function management, mostly ASW). (PDF p. 10)
  • The ASW On-Board DataBase (OBDB) holds descriptions and values of over 3000 parameters; the ASW Specification exceeds 500 pages generated from DOORS. (PDF p. 10)
  • A later datapool interface let the ASW define its own 16/32/64-bit datapool entries and identifiers independently of the BSW; the ASW datapool definition is exported from the ACMS Operations Database. (PDF p. 11)
  • The HPSDB defines data at element, subsystem, model and generic levels, with theoretical and real 'boxes' and logical and physical instantiation; Dutch Space supplied ACMS input in HPSDB-compatible XML instead of using the HPSDB directly. (PDF p. 11)
  • EuroSim in the ACMS Test Equipment is commanded and monitored by the HPCCS using Remote Messages and Remote Commands (RM/RC) that have the same format as spacecraft TM/TC. (PDF p. 12)
  • The SCOS-2000 MS Access database was rejected: it supports a single mission only (not two missions plus common data), lacks object-level configuration control and cannot relate ASW TM/TC to the ASW Specification. (PDF p. 12)
  • The 'Parameter types' module stores for each type a short identification (e.g. uint16, enum8), number of bits and the PTC/PFC; parameter units are limited to four characters in SCOS-2000. (PDF p. 13)
  • The DOORS modules map onto SCOS-2000 MIB tables such as CCF, CDF, PCF, PID, PLF, PIC, TPCF, TXP, TXF, PAS, PAF, CAF, CAP, CCA, CCS, CPC and MCF (Fig. 2). (PDF p. 13)
  • Operational identifiers are constructed from HPSDB box numbers: ACMS mode parameters start with 'AESMG', and the Herschel and Planck ASW box numbers 002 and 003 give AESMG002 and AESMG003. (PDF p. 14)
  • Every object carries S/C (Herschel, Planck or Common), VersionSW, VersionFrom and VersionTo attributes, used to build version-specific SCOS-2000 and HPSDB files from the same CSV exports; formal exports are kept in CVS rather than DOORS baselines. (PDF p. 17)
  • SCOS-2000/HPCCS .dat files generated by the HPSDB are compared with those used during ACMS AIT using Dutch Space's 'ccsdiff' script. (PDF p. 18)
  • Recommendations include integrating the database with specifications, ICDs and test development, keeping identifiers independent but traceable across activities, versioning every object, using inheritance and instantiation, and standardising a database design for operations and test data. (PDF p. 18)
