docs.title: Provenance
docs.text: Original locationhttps://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19950011180/downloads/19950011180.pdfCopied (UTC)2026-11-12T17:49:09ZSHA-25699a23beaa706966258e77dde43e69ee315c8419fced0579c6960834ed4466a79Size456.2 KBOur copyntrs-19950011180-esa-pus-paper.pdf (unchanged third-party file, not MIT; see the notice)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A short ESOC conference paper that introduces the newly approved ESA Packet Utilisation Standard (PUS), ESA PSS-07-101, which ECSS-E-ST-70-41C still lists in its bibliography. It explains why the standard was needed. The ESA packet telemetry and telecommand standards (PSS-04-106 and PSS-04-107, derived from CCSDS) carry packets end to end between ground applications and on-board Application Processes identified by an APID, but they leave the internal structure and content of packets open. The ESA Committee for Operations and EGSE Standards (COES), set up in 1987 to define a monitoring and control system common to satellite checkout (EGSE) and mission control, therefore first had to define how packets are used.

The paper describes:

  • what the PUS contains: operational requirements for nominal and contingency operations, a fixed packet data field header with Service Type and Service Subtype (values 0-127 reserved for the PUS, 128-255 mission-specific, and an optional time field in telemetry), the service specifications with their service data units, and parameter encoding types;
  • the 17 standard services of that time, from Telecommand Verification (1) through Device Command Distribution, Housekeeping & Diagnostic, Statistics, Events, Memory, Task and Function Management, Time, On-Board Scheduling, On-board Monitoring, Large Data Transfer, Packet Transmission Control, Storage and Retrieval and On-Board Traffic Management to Test (17), with a paragraph on each;
  • mission tailoring: missions implement subsets of services, omit 'mission-optional' fields that belong to unused capability sets, and fix encoding lengths at mission level;
  • validation with the PUSV prototype and the PUSSAT reference satellite model (1992), and the plan for ESOC's SCOS-II to give full application-level support to PUS missions.

It is useful for the history of the PUS and for comparing the early service set, which still included Task Management, a separate Time Packet service and On-Board Traffic Management, with PUS-A and PUS-C.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• ESA's packet telemetry and telecommand standards, derived from CCSDS recommendations, cover end-to-end transfer between ground applications and on-board Application Processes but leave open the internal structure and content of packets; the PUS addresses this. (PDF p. 1)
  • An Application Process is a logical on-board entity that generates TM packets and receives TC packets, uniquely identified by an Application ID used for the end-to-end connection with the ground. (PDF p. 1)
  • The production of the PUS was the responsibility of the ESA Committee for Operations and EGSE Standards (COES), set up in 1987 to define functions common to satellite checkout (EGSE) and satellite control systems. (PDF p. 2)
  • The PUS contains operational requirements, standards for the secondary data header of TM and TC packets, a set of PUS Services (on-board service model plus full definition of the service data units), and standards for data structures and parameter encoding types. (PDF p. 2)
  • The Packet Data Field Header carries the Service Type and Service Subtype; up to 256 services and 256 subtypes per service, with 0-127 reserved for the PUS and 128-255 mission-specific. The TM and TC headers are identical except that a TM packet may carry an optional time field. (PDF p. 3)
  • The header version number allows future versions, for example packets with multiple Service Data Units as proposed by NASA/JPL for deep-space missions. (PDF p. 3)
  • 17 PUS Services were then defined: 1 Telecommand Verification, 2 Device Command Distribution, 3 Housekeeping & Diagnostic Data Reporting, 4 Statistical Data Reporting, 5 Event Reporting, 6 Memory Management, 7 Task Management, 8 Function Management, 9 Time Management, 10 Time Packet, 11 On-Board Scheduling, 12 On-board Monitoring, 13 Large Data Transfer, 14 Packet Transmission Control, 15 On-Board Storage and Retrieval, 16 On-Board Traffic Management, 17 Test. (PDF p. 3)
  • No PUS service is mandatory, but all Application Processes are expected to implement Telecommand Verification; verification can cover acceptance, start, intermediate stages and completion, selectable per command, with positive and/or negative acknowledgements. (PDF p. 4)
  • Device Command Distribution has three sub-services: distribution at TC Segment level (needing no software, e.g. to unblock or reset the Packet Assembly Controller), CPDU high-priority on/off pulses, and distribution by other Application Processes, e.g. over an internal bus. (PDF p. 4)
  • Housekeeping packets can be defined or redefined in flight, and an optional event-driven mode generates a packet only when a parameter changes by more than a threshold; a diagnostic sub-service supports high sampling rates for troubleshooting. (PDF p. 4)
  • On-Board Scheduling allows loading, deleting, reporting and controlling the release status of telecommands, time-shifting them, and interlocking a telecommand to the success or failure of an earlier one. (PDF p. 5)
  • Large Data Transfer moves a large Service Data Unit (e.g. a file or large memory load) in a sequence of smaller packets, uplink or downlink; Storage and Retrieval may use several stores, and storing all event-driven packets gives a 'lost packet recovery' capability. (PDF p. 5)
  • The Test service includes a standard Link Test ('Are you alive?') sub-service. (PDF p. 5)
  • Tailoring: missions implement only the services and sub-services they need; mission-optional fields linked to unused capability sets can be omitted; the PUS specifies only the encoding type of each field, its length being fixed at mission level. (PDF p. 6)
  • The standard was validated by the PUSV prototype on SPARC workstations with the PUSSAT reference satellite model (completed 1992) and approved by the ESA Inspector General after a review in 1993; ESOC's SCOS-II will give full application-level support to PUS missions. (PDF p. 6)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
An eight-page ESOC paper, scanned in the NASA Technical Reports Server, on how the XMM (X-ray Multi-Mirror) project chose which parts of the draft ESA Packet Utilisation Standard (PUS) to implement. The author calls this selection and tailoring of PUS services and packet structures to a mission 'missionisation'. XMM was to be the first ESA science spacecraft to use the ESA packet telemetry and telecommand standards and the first ESOC science mission on the new object-oriented, distributed flight control system infrastructure.

The paper first sets out the operations concept: real-time control from ESOC through a single ground station with up to 22 hours of contact per day, no bulk on-board storage of science or housekeeping data, and safety during non-contact periods handled by time-tagged commands, limited on-board monitoring and a history of on-board events. It then lists the selected services in three groups. On-line control covers periodic housekeeping, device commands, TC verification, non-periodic event reports, task management and science telemetry. Safety management covers time-tag commands, on-board monitoring of up to 30 parameters and storage of non-periodic packets. Operations maintenance covers memory maintenance, telemetry management, telemetry definition and test commands. For each service it gives the subtypes.

The closing figures show the TM source packet and TC packet headers of the ESA packet standards and the XMM data field headers, which are only partly legible in the scan. For an engineer it is an early, concrete example of PUS tailoring, and it shows service numbering from before the PUS was approved.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• XMM was to be the first ESA scientific spacecraft to implement the ESA packet telecommand and telemetry standards, and the first ESOC-controlled science mission to use the new object-oriented, distributed flight control system infrastructure due for deployment in 1995. (PDF p. 1)
  • The paper defines 'missionisation' as selecting services from the PUS and tailoring the related packet structures to the needs of a particular mission. (PDF p. 2)
  • XMM operations concept: real-time control from ESOC via a single ground station with up to 22 hours of contact per day; all science and housekeeping data transmitted in real time, with no bulk storage on board. (PDF p. 2)
  • Safety during non-contact periods relies on time-tagged commands, a low degree of on-board monitoring and a history of on-board events. (PDF p. 2)
  • The PUS reserves two fixed fields in the data field header for packet type and packet subtype, so that every packet is identifiable by its function and required processing. (PDF p. 3)
  • XMM numbering: periodic housekeeping is TM Type 1, device commands TC Type 2 (pulse subtype 1, register load subtype 2), TC verification TM Type 3 (subtypes 1 to 4 for acceptance and execution success or failure), non-periodic telemetry TM Type 4 (event, exception and major anomaly reports). (PDF p. 3)
  • Task management is TC Type 5 (start, stop, load task parameters, mode transition) and science telemetry is TM Type 15. (PDF p. 4)
  • Time-tag commands are TC and TM Type 7, with six subtypes from loading a command into the time-tag buffer to deleting all commands; on-board monitoring is TC and TM Type 8 and covers at most 30 parameters. (PDF p. 4)
  • Non-periodic packet storage (TC Type 11) keeps TC verification, event, exception and major anomaly reports in a cyclic buffer for retrieval after non-coverage periods. (PDF p. 5)
  • Operations maintenance uses memory maintenance (Type 6: load, dump, checksum), telemetry management (Type 9: enable or disable generation of all or specific TM packets), telemetry definition (Type 10: define new housekeeping packets for satellite systems only) and test commands (TC Type 13). (PDF p. 5)
  • Missionisation ends with expanding each packet type and subtype down to field level (purpose, length and format agreed between satellite and ground developers), documented in the XMM Packet Structure Definition (RS-PX-0032). (PDF p. 5)
  • The TM source packet header is shown as 48 bits: version number 3, type 1, data field header flag 1, application process ID 11, segmentation flags 2, source sequence count 14, followed by a 16-bit packet length. (PDF p. 7)

docs.text: Original locationhttps://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20090017706/downloads/20090017706.pdfCopied (UTC)2026-11-12T17:53:00ZSHA-25696900ed3667d4b3c1da6c24ca116bfcc67503a68158aad77502a1a30ae0c40e1Size782.1 KBOur copyntrs-20090017706-xtce-tutorial.pdf (unchanged third-party file, not MIT; see the notice)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A 90-slide NASA tutorial on XTCE 1.1, the OMG/CCSDS XML schema for describing telemetry and telecommand databases. It was written by implementers at NASA Goddard (GST Inc.) and Harris and archived on the NASA Technical Reports Server. It is a hands-on introduction for engineers who need to read or write XTCE files, and it complements the formal CCSDS books: CCSDS 660.0-B-2, the element description 660.1-G-2 and the overview 660.2-G-2. The wiki page is XTCE.

The preface gives the history: XTCE 1.0 from the OMG Space Domain Task Force in 2005, and XTCE 1.1 published by CCSDS as a Blue Book in October 2007. It also covers XML Schema and UML basics. Chapter 1 surveys SpaceSystem trees, TelemetryMetaData, CommandMetaData and NameReference path rules. Chapter 2 describes a telemetry item: the ParameterType pattern, the four DataEncodings, ValidRange, linear and polynomial calibrators, accepted type/encoding combinations, and alarms (static ranges, conditions, change-rate alarms). Chapter 3 covers SequenceContainers, entry addressing, and container inheritance with RestrictionCriteria to identify CCSDS packets by APID and length. Chapter 4 covers commanding: Arguments versus command Parameters, MetaCommand inheritance, the local CommandContainer with FixedValueEntry and ArgumentRefEntry, constraints, significance, verifiers and CommandContainerSet. Chapter 5 covers the 'forgotten' MessageSet, StreamSet, AlgorithmSet and ServiceSet. Chapter 6 discusses implementation: JAXB data binding, hard features (NameReferences, dynamic container match), native versus exchange use, and the need for agreed XTCE 'flavours', citing a NASA CCSDS mission and an ESA PUS mission exchanging most telemetry metadata. For SCOS-2000 readers, compare the MIB data model.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• XTCE 1.0 was first published in 2005 by the OMG Space Domain Task Force, active since 2000. The original submitters were ESA, Boeing Comm. Sat. and US AF SMC Det 12/VO – Lockheed Martin, joined by NASA/GSFC and Harris. CCSDS published XTCE 1.1 as a Blue Book in October 2007. (PDF p. 3)
  • XTCE is designed for bit-packed, non-self-describing streams. Its focus is the packet or minor-frame level, and CCSDS frame, Reed-Solomon and CADU handling (front-end processing) is probably outside XTCE. (PDF p. 4)
  • NameReferences are XTCE's string 'pointers'. They can be absolute or relative Unix-like paths, or path-less names resolved in the local SpaceSystem first and then up the tree. They sit outside XML parsing, so tools must implement them. (PDF p. 14)
  • There are four DataEncodings. String is UTF-8 or UTF-16. Integer is unsigned or twos complement (spelled 'Compliment' in the 1.1 schema), with calibrators. Float is IEEE or MIL-1750A, with calibrators. Binary has no calibrators. (PDF p. 19)
  • The accepted combinations include Float with IntegerDataEncoding (integer counts converted to units), Enumerated with IntegerDataEncoding (label/value pairs), and Integer/Float with BinaryDataEncoding for formats not in the XTCE list. (PDF p. 28)
  • The alarm ranges shown are WatchRange, WarningRange, CriticalRange and SevereRange around a normal range, and more severe ranges clip the lower ones. Alarms can be static ranges, conditions or change alarms (rate or delta). (PDF p. 30)
  • Entry locations in a container can be referenced from the previous entry (default), container start, container end or next entry. (PDF p. 40)
  • Container inheritance identifies packets through RestrictionCriteria on parent fields, for example APID and packet length. The example also uses SCID and VCID as session variables supplied by the system. (PDF p. 45)
  • Command Parameters are set by the system (for example a checksum), and Arguments are set by the user. Arguments are local to a MetaCommand. (PDF p. 51)
  • The MetaCommand's local CommandContainer differs from SequenceContainer. It has FixedValueEntry (for example opcodes) and ArgumentRefEntry, its RestrictionCriteria is optional, and it has no abstract attribute. (PDF p. 58)
  • MessageSet is described as deprecated. StreamSet lacks elements to fully describe the CCSDS stack from frame sync to packets, for example Reed-Solomon encoding. (PDF p. 68)
  • The hardest features to implement are NameReferences and instance references, multi-level container inheritance and include conditions, type inheritance, and dynamic container match / NextContainer. The authors knew of no implementation of the last. (PDF p. 77)
  • Full exchange needs prior agreement on an XTCE 'flavour'. A NASA CCSDS mission and an ESA PUS mission exchanged most telemetry metadata despite different packet formats. Named implementations are the GSFC JWST translator, the CNES 'Best' suite and ESA Cryosat. (PDF p. 79)

docs.text: Original locationhttps://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19950011122/downloads/19950011122.pdfCopied (UTC)2026-11-05T14:07:05ZSHA-256998298653d8f2f7aba20845054d84ae14af2e38b31f898545f7c1411f243e6b3Size732.0 KBOur copyntrs-scos2-new-generation.pdf (unchanged third-party file, not MIT; see the notice)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Conference paper by P. Kaufeler and M. Pecchioli (ESOC Mission Operations Department) and I. Shurmer (VEGA) that presents SCOSII, ESOC's third-generation generic mission control system, from the flight control team's point of view. It places SCOSII after MSSS (in service 1977) and SCOS-I (1989; Hipparcos, ERS-1, EURECA). It requires SCOSII to follow the CCSDS and ESA packet telemetry and telecommand standards and the guidelines of the ESA Committee for Operations and EGSE Standards (COES).

The paper describes a distributed client-server network of Unix workstations. Its performance goals are 2 Mbps of telemetry and 4 kbps of telecommand with up to 50 workstations, and the whole system is meant to be driven by its database. The Mission Database goes beyond earlier TM/TC characteristics databases. It holds a hierarchical model of 'System Elements' with operational modes and roles, planning data, memory images, procedures and system configuration. It is managed as Operational, Active and Draft databases under version and change control.

For monitoring, the paper introduces raw, engineering, functional and status representations of a parameter. It defines parameter validity from several factors and propagates invalidity to synthetic parameters, and it defines three classes of checks. Commanding treats procedures, command sequences and commands alike as 'Activities'. These are released through a scheduler, a manual stack or an event-driven commander after pre-execution validation, and verification supports multi-stage criteria with computed windows. The paper ends with historical replay, analysis and report generation and the release plan, naming Huygens, Artemis and Envisat as the first client missions. For this wiki it records the design ideas that came before SCOS-2000 and its MIB.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• ESOC's generic mission control system line runs from MSSS (in service 1977, still used by MARECS and ECS) to SCOS-I (1989; Hipparcos, ERS-1, EURECA) and then SCOSII. (PDF p. 1)
  • SCOSII must be compatible with CCSDS and the related ESA standards for telemetry and telecommand packets, and with the standards and guidelines of the ESA Committee for Operations and EGSE Standards (COES). (PDF p. 1)
  • Architecture: a decentralised client-server network of Unix workstations, with central servers providing system-level services such as the interface to the ground stations. (PDF p. 1)
  • Performance goals: concurrent real-time telemetry and telecommand rates of 2 Mbps and 4 kbps, display updates faster than 10 per second, and retrieval in 5 s (data a few weeks old) to 30 s (data several years old) with up to 50 workstations in use. (PDF p. 2)
  • The system can be descoped to a mini-system on a single SUN workstation and, thanks to portability, even on a PC. (PDF p. 2)
  • The mission is modelled as a whole-part hierarchy of 'System Elements' (mission down to devices hosting measurements and command items) with associated 'Operational Modes' and 'Roles'; modelling is initially limited to data routing, power control and redundancy. (PDF p. 3)
  • The SCOSII Operations Language provides mini-languages for procedural knowledge, events and actions, and selection strategies. (PDF p. 3)
  • Three database types: Operational (any number of versions), Active (the Operational database currently supporting real-time operations) and a single Draft database used to build a new Operational one. (PDF p. 4)
  • Source databases from spacecraft or payload manufacturers (typically several thousand telemetry parameters) are imported in electronic form, e.g. ORACLE or ASCII, with consistency checking that the user can switch off during preparation. (PDF p. 4)
  • Parameter representations: Raw (uncalibrated), Engineering (calibrated), Functional (e.g. derivative, integral, mean, max) and Status (state of the applicable checking). (PDF p. 5)
  • Parameter validity depends on power, data unit quality, data routing, age, stability (transients after commanding) and user-defined status; invalidity propagates, e.g. to synthetic parameters using an invalid parameter. (PDF p. 5)
  • Checking categories: Operational Status Checks, Operational Constraints Checks (never to be violated or disabled) and Behaviour Checks based on predicted on-board status. (PDF p. 5)
  • An 'Activity' is a Procedure, a Command Sequence or a Command, all treated in the same way; execution facilities are the Scheduler (with Sub-Schedules), the Manual Stack and the Event Driven Commander (EDCRs). (PDF p. 6)
  • Pre-Execution Validation (PEV) checks have three components: feasibility, safety and dynamic (e.g. time window and interlock) checks. (PDF p. 6)
  • Command verification supports multi-stage criteria (e.g. reception on-board, reception by application, execution stages); SCOSII computes a verification window per stage from expected execution times and user margins. (PDF p. 6)
  • History is viewed in 'Replay as Live' mode (interactive technical analysis) or 'Video Replay' mode (same data and workstation layout as at reception). (PDF p. 7)
  • Release 1 preliminary delivery expected November 1994; Release 2 (1995-6) and Release 3 (1996-7) add modelling, mission planning and data distribution; first client missions HUYGENS, ARTEMIS and ENVISAT, to be launched in 1997-1998. (PDF p. 7)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Conference paper by A. Baldi (ESOC Flight Control Systems Department), D. Elgaard and S. Lynenskjold (Computer Resources International) and M. Pecchioli (ESOC Mission Operations Department) on the Operations Language (OL) of SCOSII, the generic mission control system then in development at ESOC. It explains why a dedicated language was needed. In MSSS, operations engineers specified derived-value algorithms on paper and software engineers coded them. In SCOS-I the algorithms were written in extended FORTRAN and linked into the control system, so errors showed up only as run-time crashes. Checkout languages (ETOL, ELISA) and ESOC studies (Expert Operator's Associate, Meteosat Workstation, User Language Study) shaped the requirements.

The paper sorts mission knowledge into four kinds. Declarative knowledge, such as calibration curves, is entered through forms. Expressive knowledge (derived parameters, command validation conditions) and procedural knowledge (operations procedures) are written in the OL. Special knowledge needs new software. The OL sits in a three-layer model of interaction, logical and physical layers, joined by an explicit object-oriented data model that acts as a 'contract'. Parameters, limits, values and system elements such as heaters are objects with attributes and services. Default attributes let P112 stand for its engineering value, and values computed from invalid inputs are themselves invalid.

The language is strongly typed and interpreted. A script has a declaration part and an executable part with the usual imperative constructs, and the paper includes a worked derived-parameter example. It was implemented in C++ with lex and yacc, and parse trees are built at database preparation time. The status section covers the release plan, the FOPGEN procedure editor and the related COES standardisation. Readers of synthetic parameters will recognise the name OL; whether SCOS-2000's OL derives from this design is not stated here.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• SCOSII is a generic system configured through databases holding the mission-specific knowledge; the OL lets operations engineers edit, test, validate and install scripts (e.g. derived-parameter expressions and flight procedures) without software support engineers. (PDF p. 1)
  • In MSSS derived-value algorithms were coded by software engineers from paper specifications; in SCOS-I they were written in FORTRAN with a few extra constructs, compiled and linked with the control system, so errors surfaced only as run-time crashes and neither system offered version or configuration control. (PDF p. 2)
  • ESA checkout languages cited as precedents: ETOL (ESA Test Operations Language, ref. [10]) and ELISA (Extended Language for Instrument and Spacecraft AIV, ref. [9]). (PDF p. 2)
  • First SCOSII client missions: Huygens (97), Artemis (97) and Envisat (98). (PDF p. 2)
  • Mission knowledge categories: declarative (forms-based, e.g. calibration curves), expressive (OL, e.g. derived parameters, command validation conditions), procedural (OL, e.g. operation and report procedures) and special (requires software expansion). (PDF p. 3)
  • Layered model: interaction layer (user interface), logical layer (centred on the OL) and physical layer (generic control-system services); the object-oriented data model is the contract between logical and physical layers and cannot be changed through the OL. (PDF p. 3)
  • The OL is interpreted and strongly typed; the data model is part of the type system, so wrong access to physical-layer objects is detected at preparation time; all OL definitions are part of the database configuration under version control. (PDF p. 4)
  • Worked example: derived parameter P117 is set to the upper limit of P112 when P112 is above limits, otherwise to P112's engineering value. (PDF p. 4)
  • Default attributes: the expression 'P112' evaluates as 'P112.eng.value'; a Parameter offers a 'delta' service for historical samples; a Value carries a validity. (PDF p. 5)
  • Statements offered: assignment, wait, function invocation, goto-label, if-then-else, select-case, while-do, repeat-until, for-in-list-do and for-to-step-next, with numeric, boolean, string, time, list, set, matrix, vector and map expressions. (PDF p. 5)
  • Implementation: specified with OMT, programmed in C++, scanner and parser generated with lex and yacc; the parse tree is built at preparation time and used directly by the interpreter. (PDF p. 5)
  • A Value computed from non-valid Values is itself non-valid, which propagates invalidity through expression evaluation. (PDF p. 6)
  • No language constructs for parallelism or synchronisation: conditions such as interlocks between procedure executions are handled by the physical layer. (PDF p. 7)
  • FOPGEN, a WYSIWYG tool for operational documentation, was to generate operation procedures in the SCOSII OL. (PDF p. 7)
  • Conclusion: the language is deliberately 'kept simple and stupid', leaving intelligent behaviour to physical-layer objects; porting scripts between missions can be hard because each mission may have its own data model. (PDF p. 8)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The Object Management Group specification document for XTCE version 1.3, the XML information model and exchange format for spacecraft telemetry and telecommand databases. It is short (31 pages), because the normative content is the W3C XML schema 'SpaceSystem.xsd', which is published separately and only referenced from Annex A (schema revision 20250214). The prose is an architectural overview. It is a newer version than the XTCE 1.2 carried by CCSDS 660.0-B-2, and the CCSDS Green Books 660.1-G-2 and 660.2-G-2 explain it in more depth. The wiki page is XTCE.

The foreword and introduction give the motivation: spacecraft makers and operators each define TM/TC data in their own formats, which forces repeated translation and revalidation. XTCE also deliberately avoids packet or TDM vocabulary. Clauses 1-5 give the scope (structure of CCSDS packets and TDM frames, encodings, command definitions, but not distribution protocols, RF, displays or flight software), conformance (a compliant database validates against the schema), normative W3C references and terms. Clause 6 walks through the model. It covers the SpaceSystem hierarchy and its naming rules, TelemetryMetaData (ParameterTypeSet with the four DataEncodings, ParameterSet, ContainerSet with BaseContainer and RestrictionCriteria, MessageSet, StreamSet, AlgorithmSet), CommandMetaData (ArgumentTypeSet, MetaCommandSet with constraints, significance, alarm suspension, interlocks, eight verifier stages and parameters to set), ServiceSet, and the common MatchCriteria, Polynomial and Unit types. Annex B lists the schema style rules, and Annex C is a bibliography that includes the SCOS-2000 Database Import ICD 5.0 and the ESA PUS. This makes it a direct link to the MIB world: compare the MIB data model.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Contributors named in the foreword are Lockheed Martin, ESA, Boeing, NASA GSFC, USAF SMC, L-3 Harris, Peraton, Raytheon, SciSys, Kratos S1, CSC and GST. (PDF p. 7)
  • The normative part is a single XML schema compliant with the W3C recommendation of 2 May 2001. All elements belong to one root object, the SpaceSystem. (PDF p. 8)
  • XTCE deliberately avoids TDM and packet nomenclature ('minor frame', 'major frame', 'packet' appear only in examples). It does not itself use CCSDS or IRIG-106 formats, but it can build container libraries for systems that implement them. (PDF p. 8)
  • Out of scope are data distribution, command and data protocols, RF and analog streams, data grouping, visualisation, scheduling, orbital properties, displays and flight software. XTCE is a metadata specification, not a specification for transferring live or historical TM/TC data. (PDF p. 11)
  • A compliant database is an XML file that complies with the schema. Fully compliant software interprets and/or generates any compliant database. (PDF p. 11)
  • Names may contain digits, a-z letters, underscores, hyphens or backslashes and are case sensitive. '/' separates SpaceSystems, '.' selects aggregate members, '[ ]' index arrays, and ':' is reserved for alias namespaces. (PDF p. 15)
  • IntegerDataEncoding supports unsigned, signMagnitude, twosCompliment, onesCompliment, BCD and packedBCD. FloatDataEncoding supports IEEE754_1985 and MILSTD_1750A. String encodings are UTF-8 or UTF-16 with fixed, terminated or leading-size length. All four DataEncodings can carry CRC or parity checks. (PDF p. 17)
  • A DataEncoding describes how a Parameter is transmitted, not how it is stored. The ParameterType size attributes are only precision hints, and ground systems may use larger native formats. (PDF p. 18)
  • SequenceContainer inheritance through BaseContainer and RestrictionCriteria (a MatchCriteria) both minimises description effort and identifies containers, for example minorFrame 20. Inheritance may be arbitrarily deep. (PDF p. 19)
  • The StreamSet offers three stream types: FixedFrameStream, VariableFrameStream and a custom stream processed by named custom algorithms. (PDF p. 20)
  • Parameters are scoped per SpaceSystem, so telemetry-side definitions can be reused on the command side and vice versa. (PDF p. 22)
  • Significance levels are none, watch, warning, distress, critical and severe. The verifier stages are TransferredToRange, TransferredFromRange, Received, Accepted, Queued, Execution, Complete and Failed. 'Complete' verifiers add to the base MetaCommand's list, while the others override it. (PDF p. 25)
  • The normative schema is published at https://www.omg.org/spec/XTCE/20250214/SpaceSystem.xsd. The URL encodes the year, month and revision of the schema at adoption. (PDF p. 27)
  • Schema style rules: types end in 'Type', attributes are camelCase starting lowercase, unit hints go in names (for example dataRateInBPS), collections go in 'List' (ordered) or 'Set' (unordered), and non-schema validity checks are given as appinfo annotations. (PDF p. 29)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A five-page ESOC paper presenting OPEN (the 'OPEN Preparation Environment'), ESA's software framework for preparing the tailoring data of systems built on the European Ground Systems Common Core (EGS-CC). It is the third in a series by the same authors, after their SESP 2017 and SpaceOps 2018 papers, and focuses on the community and licensing model rather than on functions.

OPEN has two layers. The OPEN layer provides generic data-management services (access control, version control, reporting, consistency checking, scripting, compare and merge, and model visualisation) on the Eclipse Rich Client Platform and the Eclipse Modeling Framework, and knows nothing of EGS-CC except the Configuration Item concept. The OPEN-CC layer adds EGS-CC-aware functions on top of the EGS-CC Conceptual Data Model (CDM). Products built on it are OPEN-M (mission operations preparation for ESOC flight control teams, part of MICONYS-CC), OPEN-S (ground station M&C preparation for GSMC-CC), OPEN-D (EGS-CC system configuration data) and ESTEC's Mission Model Editor (MME) for AIT engineers.

For MIB readers, the key point is that OPEN-M includes a converter from the SCOS-2000 MIB (ICD 6.9) to the EGS-CC CDM. The paper calls the EGS-CC model semantically richer, and the converter was being validated with data from BepiColombo, ExoMars TGO, Gaia, JUICE and the Sentinels. The paper also explains the ESA Community License with weak copyleft, which allows proprietary extensions, the restriction of redistribution to ESA Member States, the start of development in 2017 with several contractors, and the plan to be fit for operational use by 2020.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• OPEN was already used at ESTEC and ESOC on three ESA projects and is the backbone of the MME (AIT engineers), OPEN-M (ESOC flight control teams on EGS-CC based mission control systems) and OPEN-S (ESOC ground station operators). (PDF p. 1)
  • Generic OPEN services include access control, version control, reporting, consistency checking, scripting, data compare and merging, plus editors and browsers tailored to the EGS-CC monitoring and control models. (PDF p. 1)
  • The OPEN layer is built on the Eclipse Rich Client Platform and Eclipse Modeling Framework, has no dependency on OPEN-CC or EGS-CC and, apart from the Configuration Item concept, is agnostic to EGS-CC concepts. (PDF p. 2)
  • OPEN's source code does not include the EGS-CC Conceptual Data Model; the CDM is defined by the EGS-CC LDM library supplied with the EGS-CC binaries, and any EMF-compatible model or CDM extension can be loaded. (PDF p. 2)
  • OPEN's non-graphical model visualisation fully replaces the HTML EGS-CC Reference Manual for Data Model. (PDF p. 3)
  • OPEN-M is the preparation environment product of MICONYS-CC; OPEN-S prepares the GSMC-CC adaptation layer to ground station subsystems; OPEN-D manages EGS-CC system configuration data. (PDF p. 3)
  • OPEN-M includes a converter from SCOS-2000 MIB 6.9 to the EGS-CC Conceptual Data Model, validated with BepiColombo, ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter, Gaia, JUICE and Sentinel data. (PDF p. 3)
  • OPEN and OPEN-M are licensed under the ESA Community License with Weak Copyleft; extensions may be proprietary, and redistribution outside ESA Member States requires authorisation by ESA's Technology Transfer Board. (PDF p. 4)
  • Implementation of OPEN, OPEN-M and OPEN-S started in 2017 with more than six companies under ESA lead; JUICE and Sentinel flight control engineers were the first OPEN-M users, and OPEN-M was to be fit for operational use by 2020. (PDF p. 4)
  • Next extensions foreseen: User Defined Display editors, management of constellations and management of the EGS-CC System Configuration. (PDF p. 5)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
An ESA Earth Observation (EO) technical note that states, as numbered requirements (R-001 to R-720), what the payload data ground segment needs from a satellite's on-board data architecture. The aim is efficient, standardised payload data processing, simulation and algorithm development. It is explicitly not about TT&C/S-band links: housekeeping TM and telecommands remain under separate rules and may follow PUS. It also covers missions that use CFDP as well as the Space Packet Protocol for payload downlink, a new departure for EO, where downlink happens over multiple short passes through commercially procured ground stations.

The main rules follow from APID-based routing. Payload data falls into observation, internal calibration, external calibration and instrument ancillary categories. Every stream needing distinct ground processing gets its own APID, and routing from instrument to Level-1 processor relies solely on the APID (or, for CFDP, on the file name). Platform and instrument ancillary data go in dedicated packets, and navigation goes in a NAVATT packet carrying Earth-fixed PVT, inertial quaternions and time-correlation data. All payload packets carry a common CCSDS-compliant secondary header with a PUS-C time field. The PUS-C header format is allowed, but the service type and subtype must not discriminate data types. Packets must be self-contained, with no sub-commutation, no SID usage and no padding.

Further rules cover link-layer aspects (no AOS insertion zone, VC packet service, payload VCs separate from TT&C, one physical channel per packet store), file operations (segregated files named per the RAW/L0 specification, configurable destination and priority, repeat and complete re-download, open-loop CFDP Class 1 sizing), time- and position-based scheduling, and complete-sequence downlink. The note gives a mission-level rationale for APID allocation that contrasts with PUS-style SID multiplexing.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The note gives inputs for an on-board data architecture that enables standardised payload CCSDS data analysis, generation, simulation, algorithm development and ground processing. It does not apply to TT&C/S-band data links. (PDF p. 7)
  • End-to-end routing from on-board source to ground sink uses the Primary Space Packet Header or the CFDP file type identified by file name. Unmodified commercial CCSDS ground equipment (demodulators and FEPs) is assumed, and open-loop payload downlink is preferred. (PDF p. 7)
  • R-001: payload data is categorised as Observation, Internal Calibration, External Calibration and Instrument Ancillary. Instrument HKTM and platform ancillary data are excluded. (PDF p. 12)
  • R-010/R-020: the APID is the logical stream identifier, and routing to ground processes is based exclusively on it. Each packet type requiring distinct processing gets a dedicated APID (e.g. separate APIDs per calibration type, observation mode and test mode), unique on the satellite even across RF channels, VCs or files. (PDF p. 12)
  • R-050: ancillary packets from different on-board sources use different APIDs, e.g. platform versus instrument ancillary, navigation versus thermal. A single aggregated NAVATT packet built from the data pool uses one APID. (PDF p. 13)
  • R-110 to R-130: all payload packets carry a common secondary header compliant with CCSDS 133.0-B-2 §4.1.4.2, with a time stamp formatted per PUS-C (PTC 9 or PTC 10). The PUS-C secondary header is permitted but not mandated, and its service type and subtype are not used to discriminate data types. (PDF p. 13)
  • R-140 to R-160: each payload packet must be decodable on its own (no round-robin or slice-based sub-commutation), PUS Structure IDs (SIDs) must be avoided for payload data, and no padding is allowed. (PDF p. 14)
  • R-200 to R-260: PVT goes in the platform NAVATT packet in an Earth-fixed frame consistent with GNSS (default 1 Hz), attitude quaternions in an inertial frame consistent with the AOCS, and time-correlation parameters (e.g. OBT latched at the GNSS PPS) in NAVATT as well. (PDF p. 15)
  • R-300/R-320: platform ancillary packets are always generated and available for downlink whatever the instrument state, and the allocation of any payload data type to any packet store must be configurable from ground. (PDF p. 16)
  • R-400 to R-450: the AOS insertion zone is avoided, recorded payload packets go through the VC Packet Service, payload data and platform ancillary data use VCs separate from TT&C, and each packet store is downlinked over a single physical channel. (PDF p. 17)
  • R-510 to R-565: payload files carry unique names that identify type and instance for routing without inspecting content. Downlink destination (CFDP destination ID) and priority are configurable, and files can be downlinked more than once or fully re-downloaded after an interrupted pass. (PDF p. 17)
  • R-590/R-595: with unreliable links and CFDP Class 1, the file size is chosen small enough to minimise unrecovered data. The system should meet performance with an open-loop CFDP Class-1 approach (goal). (PDF p. 19)
  • R-600 to R-720: operations can be planned with time-tagged and position-tagged on-board schedules. Downlinks use only complete Space Packet sequences (via the segmentation flag), and downlink control is autonomous, with configurable margins around ground-station visibility. (PDF p. 19)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
An ESOC paper on adopting the European Ground Systems Common Core (EGS-CC) as the basis for ESA's next generation of mission control and ground station monitoring and control systems (ancillary systems and the move to EGS-CC). It is the earlier, more conceptual companion of the 2019 SESP paper in library item airdrive-b8b986f.

The paper explains why ESOC is moving on from SCOS-2000: the current generation faces obsolescence and was designed around one kind of controlled system, PUS spacecraft. EGS-CC offers a kernel with no assumptions about the controlled system. The objectives include supporting heterogeneous and 'system of systems' controlled systems, off-the-shelf black-box reuse, and simpler model-based operations. The paper lists the disruptive changes this brings. Terminology changes, and there is a new engineering culture with prescribed SDE processes. The technology stack drops C++, CORBA and SQL. Users must learn the EGS-CC Conceptual Data Model instead of the familiar 'SCOS-2000 MIB ICD'. Operations move to model-based control of elements with parameters, events and activities.

The infrastructure decomposition (development environment, preparation environment, Linux/Windows platform baseline, EGS-CC, extension and adapter components, ancillary applications) is followed by the design drivers for mission control and ground station M&C systems. The products are MICONYS-CC, GSMC-CC and the OPEN preparation environment. The functional extensions planned for mission control fall into two groups. Operations services cover file-based operations (transfer, file store and file utilisation services), on-board software management built on PUS service 6, and automated schedule execution alongside service 11. M&C adaptation covers file-based reception of TM frames, a CFDP wrapper, CSTS monitoring data (the successor of SLE), the CORBA ground station M&C ICD and ground system M&C adapters. The paper closes with the programmatics of the EGOS-CC Project.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The EGS-CC kernel was designed without implementation or interface assumptions about the controlled system; at ESOC, SCOS-2000 is the basis of mission control systems and more recently also ground station network operations. (PDF p. 1)
  • SCOS-2000 was designed for spacecraft exchanging TM/TC with the M&C system on the basis of the ECSS Packet Utilisation Standard; EGS-CC adds an abstraction layer to operate any type of system, including ground segment systems. (PDF p. 2)
  • The current infrastructure specification contains thousands of user and software requirements, so a top-down hierarchical functional model and a 'functional gap analysis' of EGS-CC were used instead of a flat specification. (PDF p. 3)
  • The EGS-CC technology stack drops technologies used in current ground data systems (no C++, no CORBA, no SQL). (PDF p. 4)
  • Teams familiar with the 'SCOS-2000 MIB ICD' must learn the EGS-CC Conceptual Data Model (CDM), which defines similar data types with a largely different approach and data semantics. (PDF p. 4)
  • EGS-CC uses 'model based operations': the controlled system is a hierarchy of elements with M&C aspects (state parameters, events, control activities); this is standard practice for ESA ground station network operations but a significant change for spacecraft operations. (PDF p. 4)
  • The platform baseline supports two Linux distributions for the back-end and Windows for the front-end. (PDF p. 5)
  • EGOS (European Ground Operation System) is ESOC's brand name; the EGS-CC based products are MICONYS-CC (mission control system infrastructure) and GSMC-CC (ground station M&C), each with the OPEN preparation environment. (PDF p. 7)
  • File based operations will offer file transfer management, file store management (including a ground image of the on-board file store) and file utilisation services (e.g. executing loaded TC files). (PDF p. 9)
  • On-board software management assumes on-board memories are managed through PUS Service 6; automated schedule execution complements the basic time-tagging in EGS-CC for Mission Planning schedules (PUS Service 11 or MCS). (PDF p. 9)
  • The EGS-CC Reference Implementation provides components to interface a PUS-based spacecraft via SLE and some SCOE adapters; ESA adds file-based TM frame reception (for EO missions with short passes, and AIT replay) with manifest metadata. (PDF p. 9)
  • File exchange with the spacecraft will be based on CCSDS CFDP; CSTS, described as the new generation of SLE, also provides monitoring data from ground station equipment; ESA ground station equipment is controlled through the CORBA M&C ICD. (PDF p. 10)
  • EGOS-CC Phase B is complete; development of the EGS-CC extensions (EGOS-CC Components) is planned to start in Q2 2017. (PDF p. 10)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Final presentation of an ESA study, PUSCGen, that built tools for deploying PUS-C (ECSS-E-ST-70-41C) in projects. The motivation is the size of the PUS-C document: the study wanted to check its internal consistency by generating its content systematically from the PUS foundation model (clause 5 of the standard), and to make tailoring easier.

Part I: the foundation model is captured in Object Role Modelling (ORM) with the NORMA tool. The specification of clauses 6 and 8 is treated as a population of that model. The review produced 21 change requests to PUS-C (7 major, 7 minor and 7 editorial) and a relational database generated from the ORM model. One limitation is that the 'system objects' accessed by subservices are modelled only generically.

Part II: the toolset has three applications. A Population Tool defines and tailors service, subservice, capability, message, instruction and notification types. DOC-GEN regenerates ECSS-E-ST-70-41C-style chapters 6 and 8 and annexes C and D, and a full population can reproduce the standard closely. ASN1-GEN produces ASN.1/ACN definitions of the TC/TM, which ESA's ASN1SCC compiler turns into data structures, C encoders and decoders, Python bindings and ICDs.

Part III: SDL and MSC models of services 1, 6, 9, 12 and a generic service template show that most services are nearly stateless, and that some service 1 notifications are not properly defined.

Part IV: deployments. Proba-3 added a housekeeping-compression subservice to service 3 and a mission-specific reaction-wheel service 8. A CoreSight tracing R&D project used services 1, 6 and custom 192. An MSP430 TASTE CubeSat demo used services 1, 2, 3 and custom 222. A Spacebel initiative aims to link the ASN.1 output to its SRDB tooling, whose SRDB components can be integrated in SCOS2000, for example.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Given the size of the PUS-C document, the project targeted internal consistency (content produced systematically from the foundation model) and usability (a toolset easing tailoring of the PUS). (PDF p. 3)
  • Objectives: verify and validate the PUS foundation model (clause 5), extend it to cover the functional specification (clause 6), build a PUS foundation database with an ORM tool, generate the full or tailored standard and ASN.1 code, and verify system requirements with SDL and MSC. (PDF p. 4)
  • The foundation model is expressed in Object Role Modelling (ORM) using the NORMA tool; the PUS specification (clauses 6 and 8) is a population of this model. (PDF p. 7)
  • Subservice 'system objects' (e.g. Function, Memory) are modelled only generically; specific modelling was performed in the scope of ATOP. (PDF p. 10)
  • The modelling produced 21 change requests against PUS-C: 7 major (functional problem), 7 minor (internal consistency or not covered by the foundation) and 7 editorial. (PDF p. 11)
  • The toolset has three applications: a Population Tool (definition and tailoring), DOC-GEN (ECSS-E-ST-70-41C compatible document generation) and ASN1-GEN (tailoring and ASN.1/ACN generation). (PDF p. 12)
  • A population of the entire PUS-C was created, from which chapters 6 and 8 and annexes C and D of ECSS-E-ST-70-41C can be regenerated with good fidelity; discrepancies found were reported to ESA. (PDF p. 16)
  • Mission tailoring selects service, subservice and capability types and defines the abstract types, subject to dependency and exclusion constraints between capabilities; abstract types and arguments are tailored by editing ASN.1/ACN. (PDF p. 18)
  • ASN.1/ACN generation needs 'implicit knowledge' definitions such as the CCSDS packet encapsulation of ECSS-E-ST-70-41C chapter 7; ESA's ASN1SCC compiler then generates data structures, C encoders/decoders with optional Python bindings, and ICDs. (PDF p. 19)
  • Almost all PUS-C services follow a simple, practically stateless template; services 1, 6, 9, 12 and a generic service template were modelled in SDL. (PDF p. 22)
  • MSC modelling found issues in the SDL models; the generation of certain Service 1 notifications is not properly defined in the standard. (PDF p. 28)
  • Proba-3 use case: service 3 extended with a housekeeping compression subservice (Pocket), and a mission-specific reaction wheels management service (S8 in Proba-3) with commanding, FDIR, rate sensor and direct commanding subservices. (PDF p. 30)
  • CoreSight R&D project (not flight software) used PUS-C services 1, 6 and custom 192; two engineers built most of the population after a 2-hour training, and ESA's ASN1SCC v4 and DMT produced the ICD, C TC/TM transcoders and Python bindings. (PDF p. 33)
  • The MSP430 TASTE demo uses services 1, 2, 3 and custom 222 with bare-bone encapsulation instead of CCSDS; the first iteration from concept to ASN.1/ACN took about 5 hours. (PDF p. 37)
  • Generated requirement sample: subservice requirements with message type 'TC[222,1] switch mode' and a failed start of execution notification on rejection. (PDF p. 38)
  • A Spacebel initiative links the ASN.1/ACN output to its SRDB tooling (for integration in SCOS2000, for example), so that on-board software and SRDB are consistent by construction; the method also applies to older PUS versions. (PDF p. 39)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The interface requirements specification for the Herschel and Planck system-level EGSE (Electrical Ground Support Equipment). It covers how the Central Checkout System (CCS) talks to every SCOE (Specific Check-Out Equipment), the TM/TC and CDMU front ends (DFE) and the instrument EGSEs (Instrument Stations, IS). It also covers the electrical interfaces between the EGSE, the units under test (SVM, PLM, spacecraft) and other EGSE items. Section 3 shows the Planck and Herschel EGSE architectures (CCS, packet router, SCOE/DFE LAN, IS LAN, NDIU links to ESOC) and the PLM, spacecraft and launch configurations.

Section 4 is the core: the PIPE protocol (Packet Interface Protocol for EGSE) over TCP/IP on 100 Mb/s Ethernet. Each message is a 10-byte PIPE header (message ID, VCID, remaining length, request ID, synchronisation word 0xFADE) followed by an unchanged Herschel/Planck source packet. Message IDs separate spacecraft TCs (0x80), SCOE remote commands (RC, 0x44, PUS-style packets of type (8,4)), telemetry (0x20), SCOE remote monitoring (RM, 0x10: periodic (3,25) housekeeping and (5,x) events), alive packets (0x11), acknowledgements, TC echo (0xA0) and TC report (0x57). The document defines the RC and RM packet headers and the CCS client / SCOE server connection rules. It also defines the TC hand-shake with 5-second acknowledgement time-outs and AD/BD-mode TC reports derived from the CLCW. Finally, it gives the APID and host table for every EGSE item, NTP time synchronisation, data rates, and how RC and RM definitions enter the HPSDB (the Herschel/Planck MIB) with naming conventions.

Sections 5 and 6 give the electrical harness interfaces and the verification matrix. This is one of the clearest public descriptions of how a SCOS-2000-era checkout system wrapped CCSDS/PUS packets for ground equipment.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The document has two parts. §4 covers the communication protocol between the CCS and all EGSE items. Remote Commanding/Remote Monitoring (RC/RM) of SCOEs and front ends is distinct from satellite TC and TM. §5 covers the electrical interfaces between EGSE and the units under test and between EGSE items. (PDF p. 9)
  • The CCS alone sends telecommands and commands the SCOEs, and it archives all low-rate telemetry, telecommand data and other CCS/SCOE traffic. (PDF p. 23)
  • PIPE embeds TM/TC packets unchanged behind an information header. For Herschel/Planck the maximum complete TC (and RC) packet is 248 bytes and the maximum TM (and RM) packet is 1024 bytes, per the PS-ICD [S4]. (PDF p. 24)
  • IFRQT-0010: EGSE communication uses 100 Mb/s Ethernet with TCP/IP and class B addressing. CCS-SCOE traffic uses the SCOE/DFE LAN and CCS-instrument station traffic uses the IS LAN. (PDF p. 25)
  • The CCS is the client and each SCOE/DFE/IS a server that accepts connections automatically. The CCS expects at least one message from each server every 60 seconds (no keep-alive in the other direction), and it drops the connection on header length or synchronisation errors, 5-second read/write time-outs or 60 s of silence. (PDF p. 27)
  • The bit numbering is CCSDS style (bit 0 is the first transmitted bit and the MSB), and the byte order is big-endian. (PDF p. 28)
  • The PIPE header is 10 bytes: Message ID (1), VCID (1, TM only), Remaining length (2, body length + 6), Request ID (4, echoed in ACKTC/ACKRC and TC Report) and Synchronisation Word (2, always 0xFADE). (PDF p. 29)
  • RM packets are TM source packets with a 10-byte data field header (PUS version 0, type, subtype, spare, 6-byte CUC time with 4 bytes coarse and 2 bytes fine, TAI epoch 1958-01-01). The packet error control field is not used. (PDF p. 32)
  • RC packets are TC packets of type 8, subtype 4, with the acknowledge field set to 0b0001. The application data is Function ID (1 byte), Activity ID (1 byte), SID (2 bytes) and optional parameters, and the source part of the sequence count is 0b000. (PDF p. 35)
  • Message IDs: 0x80 TC, 0x44 RC (8,4), 0x20 TM acquisition and distribution, 0x10 RM periodic (3,25) or asynchronous (5,1), 0x11 alive, 0x50/0x51 ACKRC (1,1)/(1,2), 0x55/0x56 ACKTC (1,1)/(1,2), 0xA0 TC Echo, and 0x57 TC Report (5,1) success or (5,4) transmission failure. (PDF p. 37)
  • TC hand-shake (IFRQT-0161): the DFE checks and queues each TC and returns ACKTC, encodes it into a CLTU, decodes the CLTU back into a TC Echo, and always sends one TC Report as final confirmation. In AD mode the report follows the CLCW check; in BD mode it follows DFE acceptance. The CCS waits up to 5 s for each ACK before sending the next TC. (PDF p. 39)
  • The CCS routes incoming packets to their destinations by SPID (APID + type + subtype + SID), using a distribution table defined in the HPSDB. (PDF p. 50)
  • Periodic RM packets are sent at 1 packet/s for the POWER and PLM SCOEs and 1 packet/10 s for all other items. Every SCOE reports common parameters: local/remote mode, software activity, on-line/off-line status, self-test status and SCOE set (AVM, Herschel, Planck). (PDF p. 52)
  • EGSE APIDs: CCS 2016 (0x7E0), CDMU SCOE 2017, ACMS SCOE 2018, TT&C SCOE 2019, TM/TC DFE 2020, CDMU DFE 2028, 1553 bus monitor 2029, and instrument EGSEs HFI 2040, LFI 2041, HIFI 2042, PACS 2043, SPIRE 2044 (0x7FC). (PDF p. 78)
  • SCOE subcontractors supply all RM and RC parameter definitions for the HPSDB in a prescribed format, with mnemonics such as YC/YP (commands and parameters) and YM (monitoring), and PTC/PFC types. (PDF p. 79)
  • EGSE items synchronise time with NTP, using the CCS as server. Two TM/TC DFE interfaces connect to the ESA NDIU for TM frames and TC CLTUs to the MOC. The TM link from DFE to CCS carries up to 150 kbps and the TC link up to 4 kbps. (PDF p. 82)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Issue 1.8 (18 January 2006) of the external interface control document of the Herschel/Planck Central Checkout System (CCS), the SCOS-2000-based EGSE that Terma B.V. built for satellite-level testing. The document is short because it delegates most of its content: the CCS interfaces to the SCOE/DFE LAN, the instrument station LAN and the World Wide Web station are defined in the EGSE Interface Requirement Specification H-P-1-ASPI-IS-0121 (the PIPE protocol), and the database interface follows the SCOS-2000 Database Import ICD issue 5.1. What this ICD adds is the format of the HPSDB 'update files' that the CCS writes (tab-separated records of validated telecommands and parameters with the test sequence name and issue and the host), and, above all, the Herschel/Planck exceptions and additions to the MIB ICD for the 'bridge files' exported by the Herschel/Planck System Database (HPSDB).

Those changes make it a valuable record of MIB tailoring for an EGSE. They cover danger actions that start a test sequence named danger_<parname>; a 'D' delta out-of-limit check type in OCP; a new CUR table for calibration selection driven by an integer applicability parameter; parameter and packet groups (GRP, GRPA, GRPK); reserved 'YZ' names for EGSE system parameters and reserved SPIDs 100 to 999; equipment and routing tables (SCO, TCD, TMD) that send TC APIDs and TM SPIDs to particular SCOEs or EGSEs; the move of the extrapolation flag from PCF_INTER to a new CAF_INTER; character identifiers for calibration curves and range sets and 10-digit CVS IDs (ECP #1); a logarithmic calibration table LGF (ECP #3); and default sub-schedule ID fields in CCF and CSF (ECP #9-#12). Relationship diagrams and a table of all affected .dat files close the document.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Scope: the interface is fully defined in [AD-002] (SCOS-2000 Database Import ICD, S2K-MCS-ICD-0001-TOS-GCI issue 5.1), with the explicit exceptions and additions described in this document. (PDF p. 7)
  • External interfaces of the CCS: SCOE/DFE LAN, Instrument Station LAN and WWW station (all defined in [AD-001]), and the Herschel-Planck database files (HPSDB update files and bridge files). (PDF p. 8)
  • The CCS implements the PIPE protocol (defined in [AD-001]) towards the SCOEs and the TM/TC DFE, including DFE TM-Dump telemetry, and towards the instrument EGSEs. (PDF p. 8)
  • HPSDB update files are tab-separated ASCII lines <datetime> <type> <name> <tseq name> <tseq issue> <host>, with datetime in the SCOS standard format YYYY.DDD.HH.MM.SS.mmm and type c (telecommand) or p (parameter); the MIB database issue is given by vdf.dat. (PDF p. 9)
  • A danger action always starts a test sequence; the sequence started when a parameter exceeds its danger limits is named 'danger_<parname>' (case sensitive), e.g. danger_PAR_A. (PDF p. 9)
  • OCP_TYPE gains the value 'D' (Delta OOL), with the delta value stored in OCP_LVALU, alongside 'S' soft, 'H' hard, 'C' status consistency and 'E' event generation only. (PDF p. 10)
  • PCF_INTER is ignored in the HPCCS implementation of SCOS-2000; the extrapolation flag ('P' extrapolate, 'F' invalid, default 'F') is carried instead by the new field CAF_INTER (issue 1.4 change). (PDF p. 11)
  • New table CUR (CUR_PNAME, CUR_POS, CUR_RLCHK, CUR_VALPAR, CUR_SELECT) selects a calibration when the raw value of an integer applicability parameter equals CUR_VALPAR; expressions are evaluated in CUR_POS order and only the first true one is activated; PCF_CURTX must then be null. (PDF p. 12)
  • Grouping tables: GRP (GRP_NAME, GRP_DESCR, GRP_GTYPE 'PA' parameter group or 'PK' packet group), GRPA (group name, PCF parameter name) and GRPK (group name, PID SPID). (PDF p. 13)
  • Parameter names whose first two characters are 'YZ' are reserved: 'Y' identifies the EGSE subsystem and 'Z' identifies system parameters; names may not start with VAR, GVAR or $ because of the OL syntax. (PDF p. 14)
  • PID_SPID allowed values are 0 to 99 and 1000 to 4294967295; values 100 through 999 are reserved for internal EGSE usage. (PDF p. 14)
  • New table SCO defines each equipment (SCO_NAME, SCO_HOST, SCO_PORT); TCD routes TC packets by APID and TMD routes TM packets by SPID to equipment named in SCO. (PDF p. 14)
  • ECP #1 changes calibration curve IDs from NUM(4) to CHAR(10), range set IDs from NUM(4) to CHAR(10) and CVS IDs from NUM(5) to NUM(10); ECP #3 adds a logarithmic calibration curve. (PDF p. 15)
  • Logarithmic calibration table LGF (LGF_IDENT, LGF_DESCR, LGF_POL1..LGF_POL5) computes Y(X) = 1 / (POL1 + POL2 ln X + POL3 (ln X)^2 + POL4 (ln X)^3 + POL5 (ln X)^4). (PDF p. 19)
  • CVS_ID becomes Number(10) in the range 0 to 2147483647, and CVP_CVSID/CVE_CVSID are widened accordingly. (PDF p. 19)
  • ECP #9-#12 add CCF_SUBSCHEDID and CSF_SUBSCHEDID (Number(5)): the default on-board sub-schedule for execution-time-tagged loading, range 1 to 65535 but restricted for Herschel Planck by the PSICD. (PDF p. 19)
  • Table 9.13-1 lists the affected MIB files: CAF, CAP, CCA, CCS, CPC, CSP, CVE, CVP, CVS, OCP, PAF, PAS, PCF, PID, PRF, PRV modified; CUR, GRP, GRPA, GRPK, LGF, SCO, TCD, TMD new; all other [AD-002] tables unchanged. (PDF p. 22)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Appendix I of the Data Delivery Interface Document (DDID) shared by the Rosetta, Mars Express and Venus Express Mission Control System (RMCS), issue C3 of 21 August 2007, published by ESOC. The main DDID is the ICD that governs delivery of mission data from the control centre to the Principal Investigators; this appendix defines the XML schema for the file-based request mechanism of the data delivery system, which is based on ESOC's Generic Data Disposition System (GDDS). Its stated scope is the format of on-line data requests, acknowledgements and catalogue entries, and it notes that XML might one day replace SFDU for the data themselves.

The appendix reproduces six XSD files, each with a description, include list, table of types and full definition. GDDSCommon.xsd holds the basic types: a non-empty string, a date-time or duration time choice, delivery methods (RDM raw data media, FTP, Online with hex-binary inline response), compression (NONE or ZIP), user, format (including an SFDU-required flag), data and request information. GDDSMission.xsd holds the mission-specific keyword types: request keywords (sample rate, maximum volume, time type, application, event type, severity, workstation, message filter), filter keywords (source and SCOS-2000 packet generation time, PUS type and subtype, P1/P2 identification values, name, creation, uplink, execution and event times, MIB release and issue, validity, volume) and catalogue keywords, plus event types (LOG, MIB, SOFTWARE, SYSTEM) and severities. MissionDataDef.xsd lists the high-level data types TLM, CMH, EVT and AUX and the format option RMCS_SPECIAL. GDDSCatalogue.xsd, GDDSRequest.xsd (a recursive filter-expression tree with leaf comparisons and AND, OR and NOT nodes) and GDDSAcknowledgement.xsd define the catalogue, request and acknowledgement documents.

It is the concrete schema behind the GDDS 'recursive query language defined in XML' and the predecessor of the EDDS request formats.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The appendix defines the XML schema for the data delivery interfaces, covering on-line data requests, acknowledgements and catalogue entries, for use by external users. (PDF p. 9)
  • It was introduced together with a file-based request mechanism based on XML; the change forecast notes that XML may replace SFDU 'in the distant future'. (PDF p. 9)
  • Delivery methods are RDM, FTP and Online; Online delivery returns the data inline as xsd:hexBinary with a displayAsHex flag, and compression is NONE or ZIP. (PDF p. 11)
  • Filter keywords include SourcePktsGenTime, S2KPktsGenTime, Type, SubType, P1Val and P2Val, Name, CreationTime, UplinkTime, ExecutionTime, EventTime, Release, Issue and Validity. (PDF p. 15)
  • Event types for filtering are LOG, MIB, SOFTWARE and SYSTEM, and severities are INFORMATION, WARNING, ERROR and FATAL ERROR. (PDF p. 16)
  • High-level data types are TLM, CMH, EVT and AUX, with the mission-specific format option RMCS_SPECIAL. (PDF p. 17)
  • Requests are an onlineRequest with general request information and one or more data items, each with a data type, data source, catalogue-request flag, keywords, optional onEvent trigger and a recursive filter expression. (PDF p. 23)
  • Filter expressions are trees of leaf nodes (OP_GT, OP_LT, OP_EQ, OP_GTE, OP_LTE on a keyword value pair), unary nodes (OP_NOT) and binary nodes (OP_AND, OP_OR). (PDF p. 22)
  • Acknowledgements report the actual start time, operating hardware and software, DDS version, error message and, per item, the actual volume. (PDF p. 25)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The Data Delivery Interface Document (DDID) shared by the Rosetta, Mars Express and Venus Express mission control systems at ESOC (RO-ESC-IF-5003 / MEX-ESC-IF-5003 / VEX-ESC-IF-5003, issue C2, 21 February 2006). It is the ICD between these SCOS-2000-based control systems and the science communities, and covers three kinds of data: on-line data requests from the Principal Investigators to the Data Disposition System (DDS), the on-line data sent back, and off-line full data sets on Raw Data Media (RDM, CD-ROM for Mars and Venus Express). Together with the Command Request Interface Document it defines the complete interface to the PIs.

The early chapters list the DDS requirements (FTP or web requests, delivery within 15 minutes, 3 months on-line for Mars Express, quotas, at least 1000 Mbytes per day, sampling every Nth packet, automatic forwarding), the interface characteristics, access, security and error handling. Chapter 7 defines each data item: the XML on-line request (OnlineRequestType, delivery, format and filter keywords), responses, acknowledgements and catalogue entries packaged as CCSDS SFDUs; telemetry data delivered as reconstituted source packets, each preceded by an 18-octet DDS packet header (SCET in seconds and microseconds since 1970, packet length, ground station ID, virtual channel, SLE service type, time quality); command history as raw TC packets with a 30-octet header (uplink and execution times and the CUV, CAV and CEV verification stages per virtual channel) or as printouts; auxiliary data, catalogues, error messages and the RDM SFDU and file views.

Twelve appendices cover data streams and ADIDs (including Super APIDs), error handling, accounts, the MEX RDM listing, auxiliary file types, an SFDU tutorial, bit and octet numbering, flight-dynamics and planning products, the XML schema, MCS-generated packets (APID 1966, type 190), the time-correlation procedure and packet, the lander TC verification and detailed agenda files, and the science network implementation.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The DDID defines the data delivery interface between the Rosetta, Mars Express and Venus Express mission control systems at ESOC and their science communities; the component supporting that interface is the Data Disposition System (DDS). (PDF p. 25)
  • DDS requirements include FTP or web delivery on request, start of delivery within 15 minutes, 3 months of on-line data availability, up to 12 queued requests per user, at least 1000 Mbytes per day in total and a per-user quota. (PDF p. 29)
  • RDM delivery to PIs is planned for Mars Express and Venus Express but not for Rosetta; the MEX RDM is a CD-ROM holding by default one day of data, split by on-board packet generation time. (PDF p. 30)
  • Data packaging follows the CCSDS Standard Formatted Data Unit (SFDU) recommendation, applied simply enough that PIs can treat the extra header fields as spare bytes. (PDF p. 32)
  • On-line responses are extracted from the MCS Data Archive System (DAS); VC0 telemetry is normally available within seconds of ground-station reception, and auxiliary files or periodic TM/TC sets can be sent automatically to registered PIs. (PDF p. 38)
  • Each delivered telemetry packet is preceded by an 18-octet DDS packet header: SCET (8 octets), packet length (4), ground station ID (2), virtual channel ID (2), SLE service type (1) and time quality (1: 0 good, 1 inaccurate, 2 bad). (PDF p. 64)
  • SCET is the calibrated generation time of the first bit of the packet, coded as two 32-bit integers (seconds since 1 January 1970 and microseconds); time correlation packets (APID 1966, type 190, subtype 40) carry ground station ID 0. (PDF p. 65)
  • Raw TM is returned in chronological order of either the source packet generation time (OBT converted to UTC) or the SCOS-2000 packet generation time (reception by the MCS); the SPID is described as an ID internal to the MCS. (PDF p. 66)
  • Command history raw packets carry a 30-octet DDS command header with uplink time, execution time and verification flags for the uplink (CUV, CLCW-based), acceptance (CAV) and execution (CEV) stages per virtual channel. (PDF p. 68)
  • Telemetry ADIDs are derived from the APID: the 7-bit process ID as two hex digits plus the packet category as one hex digit, e.g. process ID 51 and category 4 give EROST334; Super APIDs are negative values standing for a predefined list of APIDs. (PDF p. 107)
  • MCS-internal packets use APID 1966 and type 190 (for example bad transfer frames subtype 20, good frames 21, bad packets 30, time correlation coefficients 40), stored with a SCOS-2000 TM header but no source packet header. (PDF p. 134)
  • Time correlation: the packetiser corrects the ERT of each VC0 'zeroth' frame for ground delay, one-way light time and on-board delay, creates time telemetry packets (type 190, subtype 0, APID 0), and the FCT computes a least-squares fit whose gradient should be nominally 1. (PDF p. 136)
  • The time correlation coefficient packet data field is 240 bits: gradient, offset and standard deviation as 64-bit IEEE doubles and a 48-bit CCSDS CUC generation time, big-endian. (PDF p. 137)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A seven-page quick-start from the Herschel PACS instrument team (reference PICC-ME-MN-001, V 2.0, 20 April 2004) for running the SCOS-2000-based instrument EGSE used during PACS instrument level tests (ILT). Version 2.0 updates the October 2003 original for SCOS 2000 V2.3e Patch 3.

It gives the start-up order of the EGSE software. First the operator starts the EGSE router and EGSE gateway together, then a single TeiGateway instance. Next comes the SCOS 2000 task launcher (s2.start, which must be run from a csh rather than a tcsh terminal). There the 'EGSEsrv' button selects all server applications and the 'Client' button the standard client applications used during PACS ILT. The operator then logs in through the 'Users' button of the desktop top bar. The Test and Operations Procedure Environment (TOPE) has its own launcher (exif.start), with the external-interface tasks EXIF_TMM, EXIF_TM1, EXIF_CHM, EXIF_CH1 and TOPE1.

A short table maps launcher names to SCOS-2000 applications: MON (telemetry desktop with alphanumeric, strip-chart, scrolling and mimic displays), VPD (variable packet display), MSTK (manual command stack), TCHIST (telecommand history), OOL (out-of-limits display) and EVLOG (message display). The guide also explains that starting a second TOPE procedure suspends the running one. To run procedures in parallel, the operator opens another TOPE window with its own EXIF_CHx task. The 'Useful Documents' list names the TOS-GCI user manual of each SCOS-2000 operator application, so the guide also serves as an index of the 2.3e manual set used on Herschel/Planck.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Acronyms defined: EXIF (SCOS External Interface services), ILT (Instrument Level Test), TCL (Tool Command Language) and TOPE (Test and Operations Procedure Environment). (PDF p. 3)
  • SCOS 2000 and TOPE are not started at login; both are started manually. (PDF p. 3)
  • The EGSErouter and EGSEgateway are started together with one command and log to two pop-up terminal windows; only one TeiGateway instance is allowed. (PDF p. 4)
  • The SCOS 2000 task launcher must be started from a plain csh login terminal, not tcsh; the 'EGSEsrv' button selects all SCOS 2000 server applications, and start-up takes a few minutes. (PDF p. 4)
  • The SCOS 2000 desktop has a top bar with the workstation settings and a bottom bar showing the three most recent log messages; the alarm tone can be switched off from the top bar. (PDF p. 5)
  • The 'Client' button of the task launcher starts the standard SCOS 2000 client applications used during PACS ILT. (PDF p. 6)
  • TOPE is started from its own launcher with the tasks EXIF_TMM, EXIF_TM1, EXIF_CHM, EXIF_CH1 and TOPE1. (PDF p. 6)
  • Application names: MON telemetry desktop, VPD variable TM packet display, MSTK manual command stack, TCHIST telecommand history, OOL out-of-limit display, EVLOG message display; the digit after the name gives the screen. (PDF p. 7)
  • A TOPE procedure started while another is running suspends the active one until it ends; parallel procedures need another TOPE window and another EXIF_CHx task. (PDF p. 7)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Minutes (reference TOS-OF/2000/318/SJD/HS, dated 20 April 2000) of the meeting at ESOC between ESA and the FIRST and Planck instrument principal-investigator (PI) groups. The subject was adopting SCOS-2000 for instrument EGSE and real-time assessment (RTA). ESOC was represented by J F Kaufeler, J Dodsworth and N Peccia, and ESTEC by B E Melton, J Riedinger and P Estaria. The other participants came from TESRE/CNR, OAT, MPE, RAL, LAL, LABEN, IAS, SRON and KUL.

The minutes follow the agenda. C Mazza (Head of TOS-G) stated that ESA/TOS would support SCOS 2000 for both flight operations and EGSE development. P Estaria confirmed SCOS 2000 as the baseline for MOC operations. ESOC reported that the Solaris COTS set would also be available on Linux and that ObjectStore would probably be replaced. B Melton's PROBA account covers several points. SCOS 2 was the basis of the system, and its ORACLE database was extended to the SCOE equipment. A Delphi-based router carries a TM processor that extracts virtual channels or packets from transfer frames. The TC COP protocol runs in the router through a COTS product. Messages to and from the SCOEs are routed by APID, using APIDs outside the spacecraft range. Test procedures were written in Tcl/Tk.

The minutes go on to record licence and service terms (help desk included in a 35 KEURO/year/user service price), the handling of the PIs' Delta URD (ESOC keeps one product line; changes are funded as ESA infrastructure or by the customer) and the PIs' need for a core option by May 2001 for DPU testing. All PI groups unanimously stated their intention to use SCOS 2000 as the basis for EGSE and RTA. Companions: the agenda, the slides and the licence note; see SCOS-2000 as EGSE.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• C Mazza: SCOS 2000 is a stable, mature, reliable product, and ESA/TOS will support it for both flight operations and EGSE development. (PDF p. 1)
  • The baseline for MOC operations is SCOS 2000; ESOC was to ask for a comment in the ITT that SCOS 2000 is the baseline for the core of the Flight Control System. (PDF p. 1)
  • ESOC confirmed that the COTS set available for Solaris would be available on Linux (Windows NT under investigation) and that ObjectStore would probably be replaced by a cheaper object database. (PDF p. 2)
  • PROBA EGSE: SCOS 2 was the basis; its ORACLE database was extended to the SCOE equipment, addressed like a spacecraft subsystem; the router is Delphi based. (PDF p. 2)
  • The PROBA TM processor takes transfer frames and extracts virtual channels or packets for onward routing; TM throughput depends on packet size, number of VCs and DMA characteristics. (PDF p. 2)
  • The TC COP protocol is built into the PROBA router using a COTS product from De Lande Long; this is probably not needed for an instrument SCOE. (PDF p. 2)
  • The test procedure environment (TPE) accesses the ORACLE database directly at compilation time; messages to SCOEs are routed by APID, using APIDs outside the spacecraft range. (PDF p. 2)
  • A common project database is to be provided by the Prime; ESOC's options were ORACLE, MS Access or custom solutions, and the MS-Access-based Integral database tool is compatible with SCOS 2000. (PDF p. 2)
  • A first-level help desk is included in the service option price of 35 KEURO/year/user. (PDF p. 3)
  • ESOC keeps one SCOS 2000 product line; changes are either infrastructure enhancements (ESA funded) or project-specific (customer funded), possibly delivered as add-ons. (PDF p. 3)
  • The PIs need a core option by May 2001 to support DPU testing; the three FIRST instruments agreed a common EGSE development with requirements frozen about June 2000. (PDF p. 3)
  • The interface with FINDAS will use DDS in the mission; the ESOC infrastructure would be ready between the end of 2001 and mid 2002. (PDF p. 4)
  • Conclusion: all PI groups unanimously stated their intention to use SCOS 2000 as a basis for EGSE and RTA, to be reflected in the ITT documentation (IID). (PDF p. 4)
