docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Complete slide set from the SCOS-2000 meeting with the FIRST/Planck instrument PI groups at ESOC on 18-19 April 2000, compiled into one PDF. Slides 1-37 are the ESOC TOS-GC presentation, led by J-F. Kaufeler (H/TOS-GC). They summarise who used SCOS-2000: SOHO (telemetry only, 1995), Huygens, TeamSat and MTP (1997), and at the time Integral, MSG, Rosetta, ERS and PROBA, with Smart-1, Envisat, XMM, Mars Express, FIRST/Planck, CryoSat and GOCE to follow. They explain the change of name from SCOS-2 (up to R1.4) to SCOS-2000 (from R2.0, 1999): a new telemetry chain, an ILOG-based MMI, ObjectStore and CORBA. They also give the release plan through R3.0 (PC and Linux, ObjectStore replaced, mid 2001) and R4.0 (1Q 2002).

The EGSE part draws the parallel between SCOEs, router and SCOS-2000 EGSE on one side and ground station, NCTRS and SCOS-2000 MCS on the other. It reuses PROBA elements: the EGSE router (1 Mbps TM and 4 kbps TC on a Windows NT PC), the SCOS TCP/IP gateway, a TM/TC front end that extracts CCSDS packets and needs a COTS TC encoder for the ground-space protocol and COP-1, a Tcl/Tk test procedure environment, and ORACLE or MS-Access database editors.

The remaining TOS slides set out the offer. The software is free under licence, while the PIs buy hardware and COTS (ILOG Views, Ctree+, Orbix, ObjectStore, STL); indicative prices are given for support and a 35 Keur/year/user service. Slides 38-44 are P. Estaria's 'SCOS - 2000 EVALUATION' (PT - 07671) with the FIRST/Planck project position. The last two pages are the TOS licence, support and service note. See SCOS-2000 as EGSE.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• SCOS-2000 utilisation: past 1995 SOHO (TLM only) and 1997 Huygens, TeamSat, MTP (Eumetsat); present Integral and MSG (successful SVTs), Rosetta, ERS, migration from SCOS-1 and PROBA (MCS + EGSE). (PDF p. 6)
  • Planned users: Smart-1, Envisat and XMM (migrations from SCOS-1), Mars-Express, First/Planck MOC and the Earth Core Explorers (Cryosat, GOCE); First/Planck EGSE and PIs marked '??'. (PDF p. 7)
  • Naming: SCOS-2 until 1998 (up to release R1.4) and SCOS-2000 from 1999 (from R2.0), an evolution with a new TLC chain, architectural consolidation, an MMI fully based on ILOG, systematic use of Object-Store and CORBA-based distribution and external interfaces. (PDF p. 8)
  • Release status: R2.0 Sep. 1999 (Integral SVTs), R2.1 Mar. 2000 (MSG SVTs), R2.2 Sep. 2000 (end of nominal project). (PDF p. 9)
  • Evolution: Release 3.0 (mid 2001) ports SCOS-2000 to PC with an OS shell, replaces Object Store and ports first to Linux; Release 4.0 (1Q 2002) allows multiple SCOS-2000 versions on one machine to support constellation missions. (PDF p. 10)
  • Commonality: SCOEs connect through the ROUTER to a SCOS-2000 EGSE, just as a ground station connects through NCTRS to a SCOS-2000 MCS. (PDF p. 13)
  • PROBA checkout facility elements: EMCS, a router (TM reception, TC transmission, SCOS gateway), a Tcl/Tk procedure automation tool used for AIV and operations, and ORACLE-based database editors. (PDF p. 14)
  • Router performance on a Windows NT PC: 1 Mbps TM input and recording via a DMA parallel card, 4 kbps TC via an RS422 card, CPU load below 15 %, and about 2 % CPU per distributed virtual channel. (PDF p. 18)
  • The TM/TC front end extracts and distributes CCSDS telemetry packets from a digital stream and turns command-packet requests into a CCSDS data stream; with the ground-space protocol the TC part needs a COTS 'TC ENCODER SHELL' (about 10 Keur). (PDF p. 20)
  • SCOS-2000 COTS: ILOG Views, Ctree+, Orbix, ObjectStore and the STL library; run-time licences cost 2200 EUR per client plus 300 EUR per client per year. (PDF p. 31)
  • The TC transmission software shell (10 Keur per PC) is required only if the CCSDS COP1 protocol is used. (PDF p. 32)
  • Indicative service prices: SCOS-2000 installation 10 Keur per site, a developer course 4 Keur, consultancy 14 Keur per man-month per user, and the maintenance service 35 Keur per year per user (including membership of the SCOS-2000 Board). (PDF p. 36)
  • Evaluation history: SCOS-2000 version 0.2 was evaluated on 3-5 November 1999 by the RTA CWG; PACS captured extra requirements in a Delta URD (04/04/00), not yet consolidated. (PDF p. 39)
  • Project position: EGSEs are provided by industry (ESA/IPC(89)126); selecting SCOS-2000 as instrument EGSE kernel is entirely a PI decision, and the project provides no technical support, hardware, software or funding. (PDF p. 41)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
One-page agenda for the SCOS 2000 meeting held in ESOC room H1 from 14:00 on 18 April to 16:30 on 19 April 2000. At the meeting ESA presented SCOS-2000 and the EGSE elements around it to the FIRST and Planck instrument teams, who were deciding whether to build their instrument EGSE on it.

The agenda has eleven items. C. Mazza opens and P. Estaria gives the introduction. J-F. Kaufeler then presents the SCOS 2000 status and the EGSE and supporting elements: router, test procedure environment (TPE), Tcl/Tk, WINFOPS/MOIS and database tools. He also covers the options for SCOS 2000 systems, the licence agreement and COTS, and service and support. Item 8 is the SCOS 2000 Delta URD: PACS presents the instrument teams' additional requirements and ESOC comments on them. The meeting closes with practical arrangements, a summary and conclusions by P. Estaria and J. Dodsworth, and any other business.

The agenda is the key to the companion material from the same meeting. The minutes use its numbering, and the slides follow its order. Together they record the PI groups' decision to base their EGSE and real-time assessment on SCOS-2000, discussed in SCOS-2000 as EGSE and Herschel and Planck.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Venue and time: ESOC Room H1, starting 14:00 on April 18th and ending 16:30 on April 19th 2000. (PDF p. 1)
  • Item 4 (EGSE and Supporting Elements) covers the Router, TPE, Tcl/TK, WINFOPS/MOIS and database tools. (PDF p. 1)
  • Items 3 to 7 and 9 are all presented by J-F. Kaufeler. (PDF p. 1)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
This 2025 issue of the EDDS Software Design Document describes the architecture of the EGOS Data Dissemination System at release v3.6.1. It keeps the full 2018 design (library item sdd). Users without access to the SCOS-2000 monitoring and control facilities submit batch, stream and management requests through the MMI, the web portal or SOAP web services. Requests travel over ActiveMQ to an Archiver that stores them in a database and to an EDDS Server that runs chain-of-responsibility pipelines (data manager, filter, formatter, encryption, compression) against the PARC, SCOS-2000 Data Provision Services, DARC, SMON, FARC and file-system providers. A Delivery Manager returns the results, and Secure File Transfer crosses the ESOC firewall.

What is new is support for missions run by the European Ground Systems Common Core (EGS-CC). Two new data providers fetch EGS-CC historical data (TM, TC, parameters, messages, events): the HARC provider uses the EGS-CC 'ARC standalone' Java library against the EGS-CC HBase archive, and the EGSCC REST provider uses REST end points, with data delivered over HTTP or Kafka and a STOMP client. Sections 7 and 8 give the architecture and batch-request scenarios for both. Section 10 documents the GitLab DevOps pipeline that builds Docker images and deploys EDDS to a Kubernetes cluster with Helm.

Three appendices matter for data users. Appendix B outlines the ARC standalone API. Appendix C compares the fields of an EGS-CC TM packet report with the SCOS-2000 one: EGS-CC lacks SPID, PI1/PI2, packet length, mnemonic and ground-station fields, and the SPID is mapped to the EGS-CC packet ID. Appendix D maps EGS-CC dataspaces and data partitions onto EDDS domains and data partitions.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Change log runs from issue 1.0 (2007-04-13, post-PDR) to 25.0 (2025-03-07) for EDDS v3.6.1i1; issues 16.0 to 24.0 cover EDDS v2.4.0 to v3.6.0. (PDF p. 3)
  • Data services remain split into batch services (finite stored data set, optionally scheduled or recurring) and stream services (continuous live data). (PDF p. 15)
  • Packet streaming of live TM, TC, events and out-of-limits data is only supported through the SCOS-2000 Data Provision Services; clients pull the stream from the ActiveMQ bus to a CometD stream via the client API. (PDF p. 67)
  • The HARC data provider retrieves EGS-CC historical data (TM, TC, parameters, messages, events) from the EGS-CC HBase archive through the ARC standalone Java API, distributed through the ESOC Nexus; batch only. (PDF p. 68)
  • The EGSCC REST data provider retrieves EGS-CC data through the EGS-CC REST API acting as a STOMP client. (PDF p. 69)
  • Unlike SCOS-2000, EGS-CC saves all processed data in its archive; the ARC standalone singleton inside the EDDS Server fetches batch data from the HBase archive using configuration files supplied by the EGS-CC team. (PDF p. 148)
  • In the REST architecture EGS-CC delivers data to EDDS through HTTP or Kafka, and the JSON data are transformed into EDDS intermediate objects before filtering and formatting. (PDF p. 152)
  • The GitLab CI pipeline has three stages (package_source, build_publish_image, Helm_deploy); Docker images are built per EDDS component and deployed to a Kubernetes cluster. (PDF p. 155)
  • ARC standalone interfaces: IOpaqueDataRepository queries TM/TC data and IProcessedDataRepository queries parameter data from the HBase archive. (PDF p. 158)
  • EGS-CC TM report fields (proto format) include Apid, Packet_id, Generation_time, Earth_received_time, Source_sequence_counter, Pus_type, Pus_sub_type, Spacecraft_id, Virtual_channel_id, Route, Body and Datapartition; the SPID is mapped to the Packet ID. (PDF p. 160)
  • Fields of the SCOS-2000 TM report that are not applicable to EGS-CC include Spid, Pi1, Pi2, Packet_length, Mnemonic, Domain, Ground_station, Sle_service_id and Database_version, with possible impact on ARES. (PDF p. 160)
  • Each EGS-CC mission has one static dataspace, mapped to an EDDS domain, and many dynamic data partitions (sessions such as Live and Playback), mapped to EDDS data partitions. (PDF p. 161)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The EDDS Software Design Document gives the top-level architectural design of the EGOS Data Dissemination System at release v2.3.0. EDDS gives users without access to the SCOS-2000 monitoring and control facilities controlled access to mission data: telemetry, telecommand history, events, parameters, files and reports. Detailed design is left to the JavaDoc.

Section 4 sets out the three service families: management services (accounts, roles, quotas), data services, split into batch requests that return a finite data set and stream requests that deliver live data, and notification services. It also describes the client applications (web portal, standalone and web MMI, and user programs calling the SOAP web services defined in the EUICD) and the network context: the Web Server sits in the RELAY LAN or Office LAN, the EDDS Server and data providers in the OPS LAN. EDDS reads packets from the PARC, parameters from the DARC and SMON, files from the FARC, and uses SCOS-2000 to produce MCS reports.

Section 6 describes the architecture. SOAP requests enter at the Web Server, pass over an ActiveMQ message bus and are stored by the Archiver in a relational database. The EDDS Server dispatches them to data providers through Camel routes, and the Delivery Manager returns results by e-mail, FTP or SFTP, with Secure File Transfer (SFT) carrying files across the ESOC firewall. Each provider is a chain-of-responsibility pipeline of data manager, filter, formatter, encryption and compression. The PARC provider explains how EDDS adds APID, type and subtype filtering on top of the SPID-only PARC CORBA interface by loading the SCOS-2000 packet definitions. It also covers the newer SCOS-2000 Data Provision Services, which deliver packets already decoded.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The SDD covers only the top-level architecture; detailed design is in the JavaDoc generated from the source code (section 7.2). (PDF p. 7)
  • EDDS provides mission data to users without MCS access but provides no analysis tools; data include telemetry, science and non-science data, telecommand history and auxiliary data such as flight dynamics data. (PDF p. 14)
  • Data services are either batch (a request lists data types with filters per type and returns a finite data set via the chosen delivery method, optionally scheduled or recurring) or stream (continuous data actively pulled by the client). (PDF p. 14)
  • Users reach EDDS through the web portal, the standalone or web MMI, or their own programs using the SOAP web-services interface described in the EUICD. (PDF p. 15)
  • Internal clients use the OPS LAN or Office LAN; external clients reach the EDDS Web Server in the RELAY LAN; the Web Server includes a Delivery Manager for e-mail, FTP and SFTP delivery. (PDF p. 16)
  • EDDS uses the PARC for TM, TC and event packets, the DARC and SMON for telemetry parameters, the FARC for mission files and SCOS-2000 for MCS reports. (PDF p. 18)
  • The Request Submitter polls a directory for request files in EDDS or GDDS format; GDDS-format requests are validated against the GDDS schema and converted to EDDS format by XSLT. (PDF p. 18)
  • SOAP requests are passed over a message bus and stored in a relational database by the EDDS Archiver, which also schedules recurring batch requests; the EDDS Server executes requests against FARC, DARC, SMON, Data Provision Services and PARC. (PDF p. 22)
  • To meet ESOC network security rules, all connections are initiated from the OPS LAN; the EDDS Server reaches the ActiveMQ broker by JMS on default port 61616 and responses return to the RELAY LAN via the SFT daemon. (PDF p. 28)
  • The PARC CORBA interface allows queries by SPID only, with no type/subtype filtering; EDDS adds APID, TYPE and SUBTYPE filters by loading the SCOS-2000 packet definition table and mapping APIDs to SPIDs. (PDF p. 64)
  • The SCOS-2000 Data Provision Services deliver archive data already decoded and can supply TM parameter information; packet streaming (live TM, TC, events and out-of-limits) is only supported through Data Provision Services. (PDF p. 65)
  • COTS used include Apache Camel 2.14.1 as routing engine, Spring Framework 4.1.3, MyBatis and the XFDU library 1.1 for XML Formatted Data Units. (PDF p. 21)
  • The EDDS database is accessed through MyBatis with a one-to-one mapping between tables and Java models, behind a 'DaoAccess' façade. (PDF p. 133)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The communications interface control document for the Data Processing Unit (DPU) of the Solar Wind Analyser (SWA) on ESA's Solar Orbiter. It is the definitive description of every telecommand the SWA DPU flight software accepts and every telemetry packet it produces, at bit level, and is the companion to the SWA instrument database (IDB/MIB).

The first chapters describe SWA's four sensors: two Electron Analyser Systems (EAS1, EAS2), the Proton Alpha Sensor (PAS) and the Heavy Ion Sensor (HIS), all connected to the DPU over 10 Mb/s SpaceWire. They also cover the DPU hardware and the software layers: a PROM boot software, an application layer (PCMSW for TC handling, modes, FDIR and time, and SDPSW for moment calculation and compression), a PUS services library, ExOS and drivers on VxWorks and a LEON2 CPU. Chapter 5 shows the common packet headers and the APID scheme (process IDs 95 to 99 combined with packet categories) and maps each TM type to its PID, packet category and SIDs.

Chapter 6 specifies the telecommands by handling component, each with description, allowed DPU states, word-by-word TC format and acceptance (TARF) and execution (TECF) error codes. These are the PUS manager (services 3, 5, 6, 9, 17, 20 and private service 200 monitoring and event handling), the DPU manager, the sensor manager, the EAS1/EAS2 managers (private services 201/202), the PAS manager (203) and the HIS manager, including HIS internal commands (204). Chapters 7 to 10 define the cyclic HK and diagnostic TM(3,25)/(3,26) parameters, the asynchronous reports, the service 20 inter-instrument contribution and the TM(21,x) science packets of each sensor. Chapters 11 to 16 cover internal sensor protocols, macros, the event catalogue, TARF/TECF codes and configuration parameters. For MIB readers it explains what the SWA packets and parameters mean.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• SWA consists of two Electron Analyser Systems (EAS1, EAS2), a Proton Alpha Sensor (PAS) and a Heavy Ion Sensor (HIS), all connected to the DPU through 10 Mb/s SpaceWire links. (PDF p. 23)
  • The DPU hardware has a rigid-flex backplane with six SpaceWire splitters, two Data Processing Modules (each a CSP board plus a CPU board) and two Power Conditioning and Distribution Modules. (PDF p. 24)
  • The DPU software buffers 5 minutes of EAS1, EAS2 and PAS high time resolution data for transmission when an event trigger is received, and uses PUS service 20 to exchange event conditions and data with other Solar Orbiter instruments. (PDF p. 25)
  • Software layers: application software (PCMSW and SDPSW), a PUS and mission services library, and machine services (VxWorks RTOS, ExOS and BSP) running on a LEON2 CPU. (PDF p. 26)
  • The boot software is a self-standing image resident and executed in PROM that cannot be patched; it checks RAM, MRAM and EDAC and loads the application from MRAM to RAM. (PDF p. 29)
  • The CCSDS packet transfer protocol over SpaceWire is defined in the spacecraft SpaceWire Application Protocol Specification (RD[4]), and TC/TM packet formats in the Solar Orbiter TM-TC and Packet Structure ICD (RD[3]). (PDF p. 32)
  • APID characterisation (Table 1) uses process IDs 95 to 99 with packet categories: for example PID 95 PKC 5 for S20 HK and PKC 12 for low-latency TM(21,x); PID 96 PKC 4 normal HK TM(3,25), PKC 8 diagnostic TM(3,26), PKC 12 normal science; PID 97 PKC 12 optional burst/trigger; PID 98 PKC 4 ground monitoring HK and PKC 12 core burst; PID 99 PKC 1 verification, PKC 4 HK for OBC action, PKC 7 events, PKC 9 dumps and private reports. (PDF p. 33)
  • Private report packets include TM(200,249) monitoring configuration, TM(200,250) configuration parameters, TM(200,251) macro contents, TM(200,252) boot report, TM(200,253) error/log, and TM(201,200), TM(202,200) and TM(203,200) for EAS1, EAS2 and PAS parameter reports. (PDF p. 34)
  • PUS manager TCs include TC(3,5)/(3,6) enable/disable HK, TC(3,129) modify HK rate, TC(5,5)/(5,6), TC(6,2), (6,5), (6,9) and (6,129) abort dump, TC(9,129) accept time update, TC(17,1), and private TC(200,170-176) for monitoring and error/event handler control. (PDF p. 35)
  • EAS1 and EAS2 are commanded with private service types 201 and 202 (for example subtype 129 enter IDLE mode, 131/132 switch on/off, 134 enter RUN mode). (PDF p. 105)
  • HIS power is commanded by the DPU with TC(200,153) switch on and TC(200,154) switch off (low-level, no macro), and TC(200,155) starts a HIS macro. (PDF p. 188)
  • HIS internal telecommands use service type 204, for example TC(204,128) SWA_TC_HIS_MRAM_WR and TC(204,129) SWA_TC_HIS_MEM_COPY. (PDF p. 191)
  • TC formats are given word by word: the SWA DPU TCs carry PID 95 in the APID, PUS version number 1, the Ack flags, service type and subtype and a source ID, followed by application data and the PEC. (PDF p. 189)
  • Each TC lists its allowed DPU states and its TARF (acceptance failure) and TECF (execution failure) error codes, for example DpuNotPlausibleTcError 0xA7FF. (PDF p. 188)
  • Chapter 13 catalogues the DPU events with event ID, code, severity level and auxiliary data words, for example TcAcqError 0xA9ED when a TC cannot be de-queued from ExOS. (PDF p. 368)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
An 80-slide ESOC training presentation, 'EDDS / DDID – Presentation & Demo', first given on 28 September 2017 by Daniel Werner (Mission Data Systems Manager for BepiColombo) and Rui Santos (Technical Officer for EDDS), and updated by Paula Margarido for Solar Orbiter in January 2019. It introduces external users (instrument teams and the Science Ground Segment) to the Solar Orbiter Data Delivery Interface Control Document (DDID) and to the EGOS Data Dissemination System (EDDS).

The DDID part gives the document status (issue 1.0 of 2013, issue 1.2 expected in mid 2019), its relation to the generic EDDS External User ICD (issue 15.0, February 2018), how change records and attached XML schema files are provided, and the relevant chapters. The EDDS part explains its purpose (controlled access to mission data for users without MCS access), the archives it reads (PARC, DARC, FARC and file system), what it is not (a data warehouse or analysis tool), client baselines, the web, Java Web Start and standalone clients, security (LDAP users, roles, data access and quota sets, HTTPS, SFTP, AES encryption), batch and stream services and delivery options, and the architecture (EUD-based client, Tomcat web server, EDDS server, delivery manager).

A long section walks through the client user interface with example requests, then lists every batch request type (PARC TM/TC/event raw, report, gap and statistics requests, out-of-limits reports, DARC parameter requests, FARC and file-system requests) and the response formats (ProtoBuf binary, EDDS Raw, GDDS Binary, XML, XSLT transform, ASCII), together with the SCOS-2000 packet header concept. It ends with good practice (compression, file-split naming), recommendations (packet reports with raw data, ProtoBuf), and a questionnaire on network and SFTP/GFTS set-up.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The Solar Orbiter DDID complements the generic EDDS External User ICD (EGOS-GEN-EDDS-ICD-1001, issue 15.0 of 2018/02/16); at the time, DDID issue 1.0 (2013/09/10) was current and issue 1.2 was expected in mid 2019, issue 1.1 having been internal only. (PDF p. 5)
  • XML schema files are attached to the DDID PDF as a ZIP file with a dummy '.removeThisExtension' suffix to by-pass PDF reader security. (PDF p. 7)
  • EDDS provides controlled access to mission data for users without access to the MCS, by retrieving data from PARC (packets), DARC (parameters), FARC (files) and the file system; it keeps backward-compatible interfaces of its predecessors GDDS and TDRS. (PDF p. 10)
  • EDDS is not a data warehouse (response files are stored only for a limited time) and not a post-processing or analysis tool. (PDF p. 11)
  • EDDS users are authenticated against an LDAP server; access is based on user roles, data access sets, operation data sets and quota sets; HTTPS and SFTP are used and AES encryption of data is supported. (PDF p. 15)
  • EDDS components: an EUD-based client, an Apache Tomcat web server (HTTPS/SOAP portal and authentication), the EDDS server (authorisation, quota, retrieval, filtering, formatting, compression, encryption) and a delivery manager. (PDF p. 19)
  • 'Packet TM' returns raw source packets without extra headers, while 'Packet TM Raw PARC data' returns the full SCOS-2000 packet with common and TM headers; 'Packet TC Report' is the TC history. (PDF p. 46)
  • The out-of-limits record report shows only raw values, not engineering values. (PDF p. 49)
  • Response formats are Binary (Google ProtoBuf or physical files), EDDS Raw (ASCII hex string), GDDS Binary, XML (with XSLT transform) and ASCII; ProtoBuf is described as the best-performing format, and framed messages are length-prefixed. (PDF p. 60)
  • Recommendations: use 'Pkt Reports' including raw data, and the Binary (ProtoBuf) response format whenever possible; request zip or tar.gz compression. (PDF p. 72)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The Solar Orbiter TM-TC and Packet Structure Interface Control Document (SOL.S.ASTR.TN.00079, issue 7), written by Airbus Defence and Space for ESA and generated from its DOORS requirements database. It is the baseline definition of the structure and syntax of all application-level TM/TC traffic between the on-board computer, the solid-state mass memory, the ten payload instruments and the star trackers, based on PUS-A (ECSS-E-70-41A).

Chapters 3 and 4 define the packet and frame layers as used on the spacecraft: the TC source packet (7-bit process ID plus category 12, at most 242 octets of data field, PUS version 1 header, CRC), TC segments (MAP ID 0 for CPDU high-priority commands and 1 for normal commands, packet aggregation without segmentation), the TC transfer frame (spacecraft ID 0x28A = 650, VC 1 and 2 for the two decoders, a maximum frame length of 256 octets, AD/BD/BC frame types); the TM source packet (up to 4112 octets, 10-octet data field header with CUC 4+2 time) and the TM transfer frame (1115 octets, VC usage and priority, CLCW in every frame, a 3-octet secondary header extending the VC frame count).

Chapter 5, the bulk of the document, lists every service and subservice tailored for Solar Orbiter (standard services 1 to 22 and private services such as 130 TM extraction, 133 file management, 134 TC sequencer, 139 parameter management and 142 functional monitoring), with packet layouts and parameter definitions, and which unit must implement each. Annexes define bit numbering, field alignment, the time and idle packets, the CRC algorithm with test vectors, the APID/category/process ID allocation, source and destination IDs, failure and event IDs and service 3 SIDs. It is the primary reference for decoding real Solar Orbiter packets against the MIB.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The ICD is the baseline definition of all application-level TM/TC data structures on board Solar Orbiter (OBC, SSMM, 10 payload instruments, star tracker), based on ECSS-E-70-41A; non-standard use of standardised PUS services is forbidden and user-specific packets must be private services. (PDF p. 11)
  • TC APID = 7-bit Process ID plus 4-bit Packet Category fixed to decimal 12; sequence flags are always 11 (stand-alone); the sequence count is kept per APID and Source ID and is not checked on board. (PDF p. 15)
  • The maximum TC packet data field is 242 octets: 4 octets data field header, 236 octets application data and 2 octets packet error control. (PDF p. 16)
  • In the TC data field header the PUS version is 1; only the acceptance (bit 3) and completion (bit 0) acknowledgement flags are used, with start and progress set to zero. (PDF p. 17)
  • TC segments are never segmented (sequence flags 11); MAP ID 0 is for CPDU commands TC(2,3) and MAP ID 1 for normal commands, and several packets may be aggregated in one segment. (PDF p. 18)
  • The CCSDS spacecraft ID is 0x28A (650) for TM and TC; TC virtual channels 1 and 2 address the two on-board decoders, and the maximum TC frame length is 256 octets. (PDF p. 21)
  • The maximum TM source packet is 4112 octets; packets longer than the 1099-octet frame data field are spread over frames. APID 0 is reserved for the time packet and all ones for idle packets. (PDF p. 23)
  • The TM source sequence count is maintained per APID and Destination ID, and the TM data field is at most 4106 octets (10 octets header plus 4096 source data); packet time uses CUC with 4 coarse and 2 fine octets. (PDF p. 25)
  • The only allowed TM frame length is 1115 octets; every frame carries a CLCW in the OCF and a secondary header with a 3-octet extension of the VC frame count (secondary header ID 0b00000011). (PDF p. 27)
  • Downlink priority is VC4 real-time high priority, VC5 critical event log, VC0 real time, VC1 OBC mass memory playback, VC2 and VC3 SSMM playback, and VC7 idle frames; only VC2 and VC3 may contain compressed packets. (PDF p. 28)
  • The standard spacecraft time packet has APID 0, no data field header, 8 octets of data (C=7) with P-field 0b00101110 (4+2 CUC), and its time refers to the leading edge of the ASM of VC0 frame count 0. (PDF p. 265)
  • The packet error control CRC uses G(x) = x^16 + x^12 + x^5 + 1 with the register initialised to all ones; test vectors include 00 00 -> 1D0F and AB CD EF 01 -> 04A2. (PDF p. 268)
  • Packet categories: 0 time, 1 TC verification, 2 high-priority TM, 3 tables, 4 routine HK, 5 functional cyclic, 6 functional non-cyclic, 7 events, 8 diagnostic, 9 dump, 10 file transfer, 11 context, 12 science or TC, 15 idle. (PDF p. 272)
  • Process IDs: 10 to 16 OBC CSW applications (DMS, AOCS, payload, platform, system control, OBCP, thermal), 30 to 32 SSMM, 40/41 star trackers, 49 payload broadcast, 50 to 104 instruments (for example SWA 95 to 99), 112 to 127 EGSE. (PDF p. 273)
  • Ground source IDs are 110 mission timeline, 111 TC sequences, 112 recovery actions, 113 backup mission timeline and 120 direct commands; on-board sources are 15 OBCP, 14 system control and 11 AOCS. (PDF p. 275)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The Solar Orbiter E-FECS ICD (SOL-SGS-ICD-0006, issue 3.0, 5 October 2021, prepared by Christopher Watson at the Science Operations Centre, ESAC) defines the mission-planning interface through which the SOC tells the instrument teams the global planning constraints before they prepare their Instrument Operations Requests (IORs) in short-term planning. The E-FECS (Enhanced Flight Events and Communications Skeleton, also called the planning skeleton) is an XML file produced by the SOC after long-term planning (LTP), based on the MOC's FECS and the flight-dynamics PTEL, to which the SOC adds science-planning windows.

Chapter 2 describes every event type and what it implies for instrument planning. Time stamps use the CCSDS ASCII time code B day-of-year format (YYYY-DDDThhssZ, no sub-seconds, mandatory Z), and the document notes that the legacy planning systems ignore leap seconds. MOC-originated events include thruster firings (TCM, WOL), NAV windows, HGA/MGA/solar-array movements, VSTP pointing update markers, calibration events, rolls, remote-sensing windows (RSWs), solar conjunctions, pass and dump events, PTR windows, power, STP/LTP boundaries, maintenance windows, Sun-distance and thermal-control events, and ENG_WIN windows during which instrument TM/TC routing over the SSMM/SpaceWire network is suspended. SOC-added events include attitude disturbances, a pointing-type enumeration, slews, EMC noisy/quiet windows, in-situ burst coordination, RS-extended windows, TAC windows (re-routing of an instrument's science APIDs to a small turn-around-calibration store), heat-shield door operations, backup-plan split points and PSP events.

Chapter 3 covers delivery by GFTS at T-20 weeks for each six-month period and the file naming EFECS_M<nn>_V<vv>.xml (B instead of V for backup plans); chapter 4 points to the XML schema; chapter 5 lists open and resolved issues, including packet-store resizing and EMC from power variability.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The E-FECS is the mission-planning interface by which the SOC gives the instrument teams the global planning constraints before they plan IORs at STP; it is also called the Planning Skeleton and is used only in Cruise Phase, NMP and EMP. (PDF p. 8)
  • MOC provides the FECS (from MOC-FCT, specified in the PLID Annex B) and the PTEL (from MOC-FD); the SOC produces the E-FECS after LTP, mainly by adding windows to the MOC inputs. (PDF p. 9)
  • All E-FECS event times use the CCSDS ASCII time code B day-of-year form YYYY-DDDThhssZ, with sub-seconds excluded and the Z suffix mandatory; short windows carry an integer duration in seconds. (PDF p. 13)
  • The legacy planning systems at MOC and SOC do not recognise leap seconds, so a window containing a leap second may last one second longer than indicated. (PDF p. 14)
  • During ENG_WIN windows all TM and TC routing from and to an instrument is suspended or not guaranteed because of SSMM/SpaceWire routing maintenance, so no planned instrument TCs may be submitted. (PDF p. 28)
  • Low-latency data written to SpaceWire before the start of a PASS event will be downlinked in that pass (excluding special cases such as post-conjunction catch-up). (PDF p. 22)
  • TAC windows re-route all of an instrument's science APIDs (other than low-latency data) to a small shared turn-around-calibration store; the downlink always serves HK and low-latency data first. (PDF p. 40)
  • E-FECSs are delivered by GFTS about T-20 weeks before each roughly six-month planning period and are named EFECS_M[mtp-cycle-number]_V[version].xml, with B instead of V for backup plans. (PDF p. 45)
  • Resizing SSMM packet stores loses data unless the stores are empty and needs a brief window without SSMM memory operations; how to represent resizing opportunities in the E-FECS is still open. (PDF p. 48)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A technical note from the Solar Orbiter Science Ground Segment at ESAC (SOL-SGS-TN-0007, issue 2.0, 7 October 2016, prepared by Luis Sanchez) recording the agreements reached by the instrument teams in the Science Operations Working Group on exchanging real-time information on board, so that instruments can react autonomously to solar events and synchronise observations (for example coordinated burst-mode triggering).

The mechanism uses two PUS services. Instruments never talk to each other directly: each participating instrument sends an inter-instrument communication (IIC) housekeeping packet TM(3,25), with its own PID, category CAT 5 and a SID, to the on-board computer, which extracts the parameters into its data pool. Up to 8 times per second the OBC assembles a TC(20,128) packet (service 20, on-board parameter management, mission-specific subtype 128) carrying 36 octets of platform data and up to 200 octets of instrument data, and distributes it to the instruments, with distribution enabled, disabled and timed per instrument by TC(20,1) and TC(20,2). The same TC(20,128) also acts as an OBC heartbeat that lets instruments go safe if the spacecraft enters Survival Mode.

The note gives the agreed generation and distribution cadences, a common 4-byte heartbeat copied from the OBT coarse time, spare-allocation rules, and the platform parameters offered (thruster-firing and solar-array flags, AOCS mode and convergence, roll rate and angle, reaction-wheel speeds and validities). It then specifies byte by byte the IIC TM(3,25) data field of EPD, EUI, MAG, METIS, PHI, RPW, SOLOHI, STIX, SWA and SPICE, the allocation summary, and the complete 236-byte TC(20,128) data field. It is a worked example of a mission-specific PUS service extension and of parameter definitions that end up in the MIB.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Instruments communicate only with the OBC: each sends Service 3 TM(3,25) packets to the OBC, and the OBC returns Service 20 TC(20,128) packets carrying parameter data from all participating instruments; TC(20,128) also serves as an OBC heartbeat for autonomous safing if the spacecraft enters Survival Mode. (PDF p. 6)
  • The nominal maximum delay from TM(3,25) generation to parameter extraction into the OBC datapool is 250 ms. (PDF p. 6)
  • MOC requests that IIC TM(3,25) packets use CAT 5, and the IIC packets need a PID different from other TM(3,25) packets because they are not downlinked; PID+CAT+SID identifies the packet to the OBC, and the SID is not put into the datapool. Bit 0 is the MSB in all packet tables. (PDF p. 6)
  • The OBC assembles TC(20,128) up to 8 times per second (8 Hz), with 36 octets of platform data and up to 200 octets of instrument data; TC(20,1) and TC(20,2) enable or disable distribution per instrument, with a period from 1 CSW cycle (125 ms) to 65535 cycles, and 0 meaning one-shot. (PDF p. 7)
  • The total nominal maximum delay for data distribution between instruments is 500 ms (250 ms to extraction plus 250 ms to distribution). (PDF p. 7)
  • Agreed TM(3,25) generation cadences: MAG 8 Hz, SWA 0.25 Hz, EPD, RPW, EUI, METIS, PHI, SOLOHI and STIX 1 Hz; SPICE does not participate. All instruments receive TC(20,128) at 1 Hz except SWA at 8 Hz. (PDF p. 8)
  • Each instrument puts at the start of its IIC TM(3,25) data a 4-byte heartbeat copied from the OBT coarse time field (1 s resolution), so stale data can be identified. (PDF p. 9)
  • IIC packet identifiers: EPD PID 100/SID 100 (30 bytes), EUI PID 57/SID 10, MAG PID 65/SID 20, METIS PID 69/SID 20, PHI PID 74/SID 6, RPW PID 81/SID 6, SOLOHI PID 84/SID 5, STIX PID 94/SID 4, SWA PID 95/SID 255 and SPICE PID 88/SID 7, all CAT 5. (PDF p. 12)
  • The TC(20,128) data field totals 236 bytes: spacecraft 1-36, EPD 37-66, EUI 67-89, MAG 90-109, METIS 110-129, PHI 130-143, RPW 144-176, SOLOHI 177-190, STIX 191-206, SWA 207-222 and SPICE 223-236 (all SPICE bytes spare). (PDF p. 25)
  • Platform data offered in TC(20,128) include a thruster-firing-expected flag, a solar-array steering flag, the current AOCS mode (enumerated SASM, WSM, NCM and OCM sub-modes), an AOCS convergence flag, roll rate and roll angle, and the four reaction-wheel speeds with validity flags. (PDF p. 10)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
ESA's definition study report for Solar Orbiter, written before mission adoption, when launch was planned for January 2017. Chapters 2 to 4 set out the science questions, the measurement requirements and the ten-instrument payload. Chapter 5 covers the baseline trajectory with Venus resonances, the spacecraft design, configuration, system budgets, technical challenges and the radiation environment. Chapter 7 describes the ground segment and science operations, and chapter 8 the management.

For the OPEN-SPACE-INFO simulator the report is the source of the engineering anchors. The solar array is sized to deliver 974 W at a worst-case aphelion of 1.47 au, against a 919 W hibernation demand at 630 W/m2. The payload receives 180 W at a regulated 28 V. The downlink requirement is 150 kbit/s at 1 au to the 35 m Malargüe antenna, with daily 9-hour passes in the nominal phase. The solid-state mass memory stores up to 549 Gbit. Four reaction wheels are off-loaded with 10 N thrusters, and the solar arrays tilt about their long axis to limit cell temperature at perihelion, where the flux reaches about 13 times its 1 au value. Remote sensing is planned in three 10-day windows per orbit, centred on perihelion and on the latitude extremes.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Mission summary: three-axis stabilised platform, heat shield, two adjustable two-sided solar arrays; 150 kbit/s downlink at 1 au spacecraft-Earth distance; Malargüe 35 m antenna, 4 to 8 hours per day effective. (PDF p. 5)
  • The solid-state mass memory stores up to 549 Gbit (823 Gbit with the redundant bank); four reaction wheels are complemented by 10 N thrusters used for safe mode, wheel off-loading and manoeuvres (§5.3.6). (PDF p. 83)
  • The solar array, based on the BepiColombo MPO design, supplies 974 W at the worst-case aphelion of 1.47 au; the PCDU uses a maximum power point tracker and a regulated 28 V main bus; a lithium-ion battery (§5.3.6). (PDF p. 83)
  • The solar-radiation-pressure torque profile, influenced by the solar-array tilt direction, determines the frequency of wheel off-loading (§5.4.1). (PDF p. 84)
  • The HGA may need to be stowed in the shadow of the heat shield during close perihelion passages (§5.4.1). (PDF p. 85)
  • Power budget: the sizing case is hibernation at 1.468 au, 919 W at 630 W/m2; 180 W at a regulated 28 V go to the payload in the science phase (§5.5.2). (PDF p. 92)
  • Link and storage budgets: 150 kbit/s at 1 au via the HGA to Malargüe; in-situ instruments produce data continuously, remote-sensing instruments during three 10-day windows per orbit (§5.5.3-5.5.4). (PDF p. 93)
  • Solar flux reaches up to 12.7 Earth solar constants at perihelion; the solar array is tilted about its longitudinal axis to keep cell temperature manageable (§5.6). (PDF p. 94)
  • For thermal reasons the HTHGA may have to be folded several times during the mission; maximum flux 17424 W/m2 at 0.28 au, minimum 784 W/m2 at 1.32 au (§5.6, §5.7). (PDF p. 95)
  • Ground stations: ESA deep-space antennas at New Norcia, Cebreros and Malargüe; in the nominal phase Malargüe takes daily 9-hour passes, 8 hours of which are for science telemetry (§7.1.1). (PDF p. 101)
  • An encounter typically consists of a 10-day window centred on perihelion and two 10-day windows centred on the highest latitudes (§7.2.3). (PDF p. 103)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The Solar Orbiter Data Delivery Interface Control Document (DDID), SOL-ESC-IF-05011 issue 1 revision 2 (26 June 2019), prepared at ESOC by L. Michienzi and P. Margarido and approved by the Solar Orbiter operations, ground segment and science managers. It is the mission-specific complement to the generic EDDS External User ICD and describes how the Science Ground Segment (SGS) and Principal Investigators obtain Solar Orbiter data from the MOC's Data Dissemination System (DDS), which is based on the ESOC EGOS Data Dissemination System (EDDS).

The document covers the data exchange concept (HTTPS web interface, EDDS client, XML batch and stream requests, SFTP delivery, scheduled requests and file subscriptions), operational assumptions, quotas and access restrictions by APID, SPID, parameter, file and time range, server set-up (cold-redundant prime and backup), security, backup and availability (at least 95% over a month), and the mapping of each data type onto the MCS long-term archive (PARC for packets and reports, DARC for parameters, FARC for files).

Its most technical part, chapter 7, documents the SCOS-2000 packet (TDEV) format as delivered: the common header fields (filing and creation times, simulation flag, ground station IDs, packet type, structure version 5, time-stamp policy and time quality, stream IDs mapped to virtual channels, filing key = SPID, mission ID 650, MIB release and issue), the TM header (TPSD, RouteID data unit type and qualifier, APID, SSC, PUS type and subtype), the TC header (uplink, execution and last-update times, PTV flag) and the handling of missing frames. Chapter 8 lists the data products, including the MCS-internal packets on APID 1966 and the time-correlation packets, command history, auxiliary file types, and service-13 TM files with their metadata event packets. Chapter 10 specifies RAPID files, the nominal OGS-to-SGS packet transfer via GFTS, with their naming and record format.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The Solar Orbiter DDID is a mission-specific complement to the generic EDDS External User ICD [A-1]; the two are meant to be read together, and the DDID only gives Solar Orbiter specifics. (PDF p. 7)
  • The primary distribution mechanism is the EDDS (HTTPS web interface, EDDS client, XML batch or stream requests, SFTP delivery); the nominal OGS-to-SGS distribution uses GFTS to forward RAPID binary files containing all packets processed and archived by the MCS. (PDF p. 11)
  • DDS responses come from the MCS long-term archive: packets, events and TC data from PARC, auxiliary and TM files from FARC, and TM parameters from DARC; spacecraft TM is normally available within seconds of ground-station reception. (PDF p. 16)
  • All DDS data are big-endian; times are 4 bytes of seconds since 1 January 1970 (not counting leap seconds) followed by 4 bytes of microseconds. (PDF p. 18)
  • Each SCOS-2000 (TDEV) packet has a common header followed by a TM, TC or event specific header; for TM the packet data is the full un-stripped source packet starting with the CCSDS primary header version number. (PDF p. 19)
  • The MCS stores an extra TC packet per command with SPID 200 holding the static MIB PTV/CEV details; external users should ignore it. TC packets use SPIDs 100 and 200. (PDF p. 19)
  • Common header: packet type 1 TM, 2 TC, 3 Event; structure version 5 for Solar Orbiter; ground station IDs include 21 Kourou, 22 Perth, 23 New Norcia, 24 Cebreros, 25 Malargüe and 30 Maspalomas. (PDF p. 20)
  • Time-stamp policy values are 0 creation time, 1 frame transmission time (ERT minus propagation delay) and 2 correlated SCET, with time quality 0 good, 1 inaccurate, 2 bad; stream IDs 1000-1003 map to online VC0-VC3 (real-time, playback, science, file transfer). (PDF p. 21)
  • The filing key is the SCOS-2000 SPID that maps to the MIB packet definition; the mission ID is 650, and the DB Rel and DB Iss fields record the MIB VDF_RELEASE and VDF_ISSUE used when the packet was archived. (PDF p. 21)
  • The TM header's RouteID low byte gives the data unit type (0 transfer frame, 1 source packet, 2 internal MCS packet) and a qualifier (for example 1 bad, 2 idle, 4 service 9 time packet). (PDF p. 23)
  • The TC command details data are produced by overlaying a C++ class on memory of a 32-bit platform, so fields are 32-bit aligned with padding. (PDF p. 25)
  • MCS-internal packets use APID 1966 (SPIDs 66810-66999) and should be filtered out, except the time-correlation packets: report SPID 66840 (TM 164,1), time couple 66841 (164,2) and coefficients 66842 (164,3). Spacecraft time packets have APID 0. (PDF p. 26)
  • Service-13 TM files are stored in FARC as 'DLPP Files' named <PS_ID>_<file_reconstruction_timestamp>, with metadata in event packets of SPID 4000. (PDF p. 31)
  • RAPID files are named PARC_<Type>_<FirstPacketTime>__<LastPacketTime>, close every 50 seconds, and contain length-prefixed records with an action type (0 insert, 1 update, 2 delete) and a sync marker 0x1ACFFC1D before each SCOS-2000 packet. (PDF p. 35)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A chapter of ESA SP-1291, 'Mars Express: The Scientific Investigations' (June 2009), by J. Zender (ESTEC), F. Delhaise (ESOC), C. Arviset (ESAC) and some thirty co-authors from ESA and the instrument teams. It traces Mars Express data from the spacecraft through the ground segment and the instrument teams to the Planetary Science Archive (PSA).

The ground-segment sections are the most relevant to this wiki. They define the processing levels (level 0 raw telemetry, level 1 cleaned, merged and time-ordered packets, level 1a separated by instrument, up to level 3) and their CODMAC and PDS equivalents. They describe the ESOC Operations Control Centre shared by Rosetta, Mars Express and Venus Express: the SCOS-2000-based Mission Control System (real-time housekeeping processing, command verification, out-of-limit checks, calibration, UTC time stamping with an accuracy below 2 ms, command history), the Data Distribution System (DDS) built on the Generic Data Disposition System (GDDS), the Mission Planning System and the Flight Operations Procedure system. They explain how NCTRS receives Earth-reception-time-stamped telemetry from the ground stations and forwards telecommands, and how the DDS handles XML requests (standing orders, web or FTP), retrieves data from the SCOS-2000 packet and file archives over CORBA, and delivers by web, FTP or CD-ROM, with SFDU-based formats and a ten-year archive of level 1 data.

The later sections cover the PDS standard (ODL keyword=value labels, data dictionary, catalogue files, EAICDs), the archive process and peer review, the PSA user interfaces, and the datasets of each instrument (ASPERA-3, HRSC, MaRS, OMEGA, PFS, SPICAM, MARSIS) and SPICE kernels.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Processing levels in the Mars Express archive plan: level 0 raw telemetry as received at the ground station; level 1 cleaned, merged, time-ordered data in packet format; level 1a separated by instrument; level 1b sorted by data type and mode; level 2 calibrated; level 3 higher-level products. (PDF p. 5)
  • Rosetta, Mars Express and Venus Express share nearly identical data management systems at the ESOC Operations Control Centre, to reduce cost, risk and development time. (PDF p. 5)
  • The SCOS-2000-based MCS processes housekeeping data in real time (command verification, out-of-limit detection, calibration) and time-stamps telemetry by converting on-board time to UTC with an accuracy below 2 ms. (PDF p. 5)
  • The DDS is based on the Generic Data Disposition System (GDDS) and also produces raw data media for permanent archiving; the MCS itself has no remote access, so external users reach mission data only via the DDS. (PDF p. 6)
  • NCTRS is the ground-station interface of the MCS: it receives telemetry already time-stamped with Earth Reception Time, forwards telecommands to the stations, and stores tracking data (antenna angles, range, Doppler). (PDF p. 6)
  • Mission products include payload science data, all platform and payload housekeeping and auxiliary data (TC history, station visibility, orbit, attitude); a common SFDU-based interchange standard is used, and all level 1 data are archived for ten years after the end of the mission. (PDF p. 7)
  • The SCOS-2000 mission archive has a packet archive (historical TM, TC and derived data) and a file archive (flight dynamics and planning data); GDDS requests come as standing orders, via the web interface or as FTP request files, expressed in a recursive XML query language. (PDF p. 7)
  • The DDS server initiates archive retrievals on the MCS via a CORBA-based interface and delivers data online, by FTP or on CD-ROM; online retrieval embeds the data as a byte stream in the XML response and is meant only for previews. (PDF p. 8)
  • The PDS standard was chosen early for Rosetta, Mars Express and SMART-1; it uses the Object Description Language (keyword = value labels) with keywords defined in the Planetary Science Data Dictionary. (PDF p. 9)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A SpaceOps 2025 paper from the ESTRACK Scheduling Office (ESO) at ESOC on cross support: booking ground station passes from other networks for ESA missions, and selling ESTRACK deep-space capacity to other agencies and commercial users. ESTRACK interfaces with 6 providers and serves 5 external partners, using CCSDS Service Management (SM) formats wherever possible. These are the Simple Schedule Format (SSF) and the then-draft Service Management Utilization Request Formats (SMURF).

The paper describes the internal tools. The ESTRACK Planning System (EPS) solves the users' standing orders into a baseline booking, covering 4 weeks for low Earth orbit and up to 12 months for deep space. The ESTRACK Management System web Portal (EMSP) handles change requests as a state machine, as user or provider, through the web or system to system over REST and files. External formats are mapped onto a stable core by XSL transforms ('XSL shielding'), so that each bilateral interface can change independently.

It identifies the minimal common data set of every cross-support interface (spacecraft, ground station, beginning and end of track, service definition, service parameters, user and provider IDs). It contrasts 'replace all' bulk requests with SMURF add/modify/delete requests. It explains why ESTRACK closes the loop with the provider's SSF support list rather than per-request confirmation (SPDF), and why named service bundles such as 'TTC' worked better than layered CCSDS functional services. The lessons learned favour minimal exchanged information, files as well as REST, and XML with XSD validation. The way forward and conclusion discuss standing orders, flexible requests and other CCSDS SM topics (SMAC, SACP, SMASH), against the risk of proprietary commercial APIs. It is a practical companion to SLE service management.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The latest ESTRACK Deep Space Terminal loading forecast shows ESTRACK deep-space capacity being exhausted, so access to external resources is needed at peak periods. (PDF p. 1)
  • In two decades the number of ESA flying spacecraft tripled while ESTRACK capacity stayed stable. ESTRACK now interfaces with 6 providers and serves 5 external partners, and uses CCSDS Service Management [1] for its interfaces whenever possible. (PDF p. 2)
  • The EPS solver turns mission agreements and standing orders into a baseline booking covering typically 4 weeks for the LEO network and up to 12 months for deep-space assets. Change requests are checked for validity, conflict, technical feasibility and, for external providers, availability. (PDF p. 2)
  • The SSF data format [2] proved a good way to 'close the loop' in all circumstances, such as provider-initiated changes, pending negotiations and disputed cancellations. Immediate confirmation alone does not cover every case. (PDF p. 3)
  • EMSP supports both REST and file-based exchange, and treats manual and machine-generated requests identically. Gaia's MPS used standing orders to specify tracking time for every day of its 10-year mission (daily downlink needs of 6 to 24 hours). (PDF p. 4)
  • All exchanges are XML files. XSL transforms ('User-Provider translators') map each third party's format onto a stable core, so that each point-to-point interface is independent and transforms can be edited without stopping the application. (PDF p. 5)
  • Every cross-support interface contains five items: user (spacecraft codename), resource (site or terminal), beginning of track, end of track, and service definition. Service parameters, user ID and provider ID complete the minimal set. With it, ESTRACK interfaces with 6 agencies and 5 commercial entities. (PDF p. 6)
  • Since 2017 ESTRACK has used the published SSF and the draft SMURF (White Book 0.06) for all new interfaces. SMURF's add/modify/delete requests allow per-request change tracking, at the cost of more complexity in the booking system than legacy 'replace all' requests. (PDF p. 6)
  • ESTRACK network operations are fully automated: each service type maps to a scheduling template. A published catalogue of 'user scheduled events' (e.g. start/stop uplink or recording at absolute times) has become a de facto standard for ESTRACK users and providers. (PDF p. 7)
  • File-based interfaces proved more robust than REST alone, because cybersecurity changes can block ports with little notice. The CCSDS layered functional service list (online telemetry, uplink, ranging, DDOR...) was awkward in practice, and bundled service names such as 'TTC' worked better. (PDF p. 7)
  • Individual request confirmation (CCSDS SPDF) was rated essential during EPS design but never used. ESTRACK relies on the passes listed in the SSF reply, and only one provider supports SPDF. (PDF p. 8)
  • SMURF proposes flexible requests (earliest start, latest end, minimum and maximum track duration), but no implementation supports them yet. (PDF p. 9)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A SpaceOps 2023 paper from RHEA Group on how operations-preparation tooling can ease a mission's move from SCOS-2000 to EGS-CC. It starts from the observation that migrating control systems means retesting, a learning curve and loss of knowledge. It introduces RHEA's component-based ASTRAL ground segment offering (Prepare, Plan, Schedule, Automate, Control, Orbit, etc.), in which ASTRAL-Control runs on either SCOS-2000 or EGS-CC and ASTRAL-Prepare is the successor of RHEA's MOIS.

The technical core covers three parts. First, the ASTRAL-Prepare plug-in data model (data types, common and specific properties, consistency checks, product generation and publication). Second, the Mission Model Editor (MME), now part of EGS-CC, which presents the EGS-CC Technical Data Model (TDM) as a tree of packets, parameters and procedures with one M&C element per configuration item. MME extends ESA's OPEN framework and so inherits its SCOS-2000 MIB importer. Third, the Procedure Model Editor (PME), built on an Extensible Procedure Model (XPM) of steps, statements and branching. The XPM is exposed through an Xtext DSL (PDSL), with Groovy expressions and a Sirius flowchart view, and can be exported to EGS-CC activity lists, SCOS-2000 MIB command sequences or other operations languages, or executed directly. Client-server data and automation servers use EGS-CC (and possibly SCOS-2000) adapters, and ASTRAL-Schedule can run legacy MOIS Writer and PME procedures in the same plan.

The transition scenarios are: convert Writer procedures to PDSL, phase PME in alongside Writer on SCOS-2000, then convert the MIB to the TDM with the MME's MIB importer and check the whole procedure set in an SVN-backed sandbox. See operations preparation.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• EGS-CC consists of a core and a reference implementation, and one concrete system is the EGSE Reference Facility (ERF), maintained by ESTEC. The paper states that EGS-CC is replacing the legacy SCOS-2000 mission control system. (PDF p. 1)
  • For ESA mission operations, EGOS-CC tailors EGS-CC by integrating existing ESOC tools. Operators may have legacy procedures and spacecraft databases based on the SCOS-MIB that they want to reuse with EGS-CC. (PDF p. 1)
  • ASTRAL-Prepare is the latest evolution of RHEA's MOIS, which has supported over 100 spacecraft. ASTRAL-Control has been deployed with ESA's Community Source SCOS-2000 and also supports EGS-CC. (PDF p. 2)
  • Data types already implemented in ASTRAL-Prepare include OBCPs, mission planning rules, PLUTO scripts, Writer procedures and Word documents, and Synthetic-S2K scripts. (PDF p. 4)
  • The MME is an editor for EGS-CC Technical Data Model (TDM) data. It enforces one M&C element per configuration item file so that sub-trees can be maintained independently. It extends ESA's OPEN framework and thereby benefits from its SCOS-2000 MIB importer. (PDF p. 4)
  • PME procedures can generate EGS-CC activity lists and SCOS-MIB sequences (linear command sequences without logic), and executable artefacts such as OBCPs in OL, Tcl/TOPE automation and SPELL. (PDF p. 5)
  • The minimal XPM has Procedure, Steps (with optional precondition and confirmation) and Statements for branching (SelectCase, ForEach, For, While, If), control (synchronise, set variable, prompt, log) and execution (execute activity/TC, check state, wait for state or event, expect packet, set monitoring). (PDF p. 6)
  • PDSL is an Xtext grammar over an EMF model. Boolean and arithmetic expressions are delegated to Groovy (Python also possible), and procedures can be debugged step by step in the editor. The PME currently supports two DSLs: one for AIT test procedures and one for ESOC flight control procedures. (PDF p. 7)
  • For SCOS-2000 automation with PME, no SCOS-2000 adapter is needed in the procedure data server: the MME handles MIB import and the SCOS-2000 automation server needs no MIB access. (PDF p. 9)
  • The Scheduler has been used at ESOC for many years to run Writer procedures with SCOS-2000 via the Writer Automation Server, and now also controls PME procedures, so both can run in one plan. (PDF p. 10)
  • The SCOS-2000 baseline procedure format is stored in a per-procedure database, edited in the forms-based Writer (using MS Excel for visualisation) and a flowchart editor. Some ESOC missions automate routine pass operations with Writer procedures and the MOIS Scheduler, and an event monitor starts contingency recovery procedures on known events. (PDF p. 12)
  • When moving to EGS-CC, the SCOS MIB is replaced by the EGS-CC TDM. MIB data is converted with the MME's MIB importer, import problems are flagged in the MME, and PME procedures need no conversion. (PDF p. 13)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A DLR/GSOC conference paper on V3C ('Verlegefähiges' Compact Control Center). V3C is a complete mission operations system for small, single-purpose LEO Earth-observation satellites that runs on a single COTS laptop and can be set up away from a control centre, for 'Responsive Space' use cases such as disaster response, security, science and education. It is demonstrated with DLR's BIROS satellite.

The monitoring and control system is built from GSOC multi-mission tools. GECCOS is GSOC's branch of ESA's SCOS-2000 and serves as both real-time MCS and offline TM processor. Satmon provides displays, ProToS handles procedures and automation, and an XML2SSF Merger turns flight procedure templates into GECCOS Saved Stack Files. The MIB is the central source of TM/TC definitions for all these tools. GECCOS speaks the bespoke NCTRS protocol. An SLE Switch Board (SSB) bridges NCTRS to standard SLE for ground stations, and is to be moved inside V3C for the remote demonstration. The paper also describes the mission planning tools (SPOT for swath preview and ordering, Pinta/Plato for timelines). It analyses orbit-determination errors when solar-flux and Earth-rotation auxiliary data cannot be updated offline: about 60 km maximum error after three days at 500 km from missing solar flux, and 7.6 km per missed leap second.

Deployment is fully 'infrastructure as code'. Packer, Vagrant and Ansible build six VMs (SLES 11/15 and Windows Server 2019 hosting GECCOS, GECCOS offline, Satmon, flight dynamics and an Ansible control node) on a Dell laptop, with GitLab CI/CD environments for operations and simulation. The first demonstration replaced the regular BIROS system at GSOC. It used NCTRS, NTP and synchronisation products (TC history, on-board queue model, TM check results) so that the regular system could take over at any time. The paper ends with the COVID-19 constraints and an outlook.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• V3C design drivers: movable between places of operation, independent of facilities and permanent Internet access, standards-compliant external interfaces, quick roll-out of copies, operated by one operator, and able to demonstrate BIROS optical imaging. (PDF p. 3)
  • The ground segment assumes a standardised antenna interface such as CCSDS SLE so that it can be plugged into any ground station network implementing the standard; BIROS is in a 510 km sun-synchronous orbit with a mass of about 130 kg. (PDF p. 3)
  • For the first demonstration the bespoke NCTRS protocol is used for ground station connectivity; it is to be replaced by SLE by integrating the SSB component into V3C. (PDF p. 5)
  • The MCS consists of GECCOS (real-time M&C and offline TM processing), Satmon (displays), ProToS (procedures and automation), the XML2SSF Merger and the Mission Information Base as common source of TM and TC definitions. (PDF p. 5)
  • GECCOS is GSOC's M&C software branched off ESA's SCOS-2000; it uses the bespoke NCTRS interface or ingests TM from files, and the SLE Switch Board translates NCTRS to the standard SLE protocol. (PDF p. 6)
  • Saved Stack Files (SSF) are the native GECCOS format and cannot express branching procedures in an automated way; the ProToS execution engine connects directly to GECCOS to supervise branching procedures. (PDF p. 8)
  • The MIB is used by all MCS tools as the central source for TM and TC definitions; the XML2SSF Merger fills flight procedure XML templates with parameter values from operators, the mission planning timeline or flight dynamics. (PDF p. 8)
  • Missing leap seconds cause coordinate-transformation errors; at 500 km orbit height the position error is 7.6 km per leap second. (PDF p. 13)
  • Missing solar flux auxiliary data have the largest impact, accumulating to 60 km in three days at 500 km in a maximum error estimation; laptop clocks need NTP or GNSS/DCF77 synchronisation to at least 1 s. (PDF p. 13)
  • Hardware: a COTS laptop (128 GiB RAM, 8-core CPU, 4 TB SSD) running Ubuntu and VirtualBox; all components run in VMs, without redundancy. (PDF p. 14)
  • VM layout: ctl01 (SLES 15, Ansible control node), dpc01 (Windows Server 2019, Satmon client, ProToS, Pinta/Plato, SPOT), mcs01 (SLES 11, GECCOS server, XML2SSF Merger, SSB), dps01 (SLES 15, Satmon server, RGB processor), olp01 (SLES 11, GECCOS offline), fds01 (SLES 15, FD services). (PDF p. 15)
  • During the first campaign BIROS was commanded with real-time and time-tagged telecommands, including blind acquisitions; sync products to the regular BIROS system comprise sent-TC lists and acknowledgements, the on-board queue model and TM check results. (PDF p. 17)
  • The project officially started in October 2020 (preliminary work from April 2020) and was developed largely from home because of the pandemic. (PDF p. 18)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A short SpaceOps 2025 paper on SPOT Cruise and SPOT JUICE, web tools that Starion's service team at ESAC built under ESA's EFC2 frame contract. The tools let instrument teams create and deliver payload command requests to ESOC. At ESOC, payload requests are part of the Command Request File (CRF) concept: XML files that carry 'occurrences' such as telecommands, sequences, automation procedures and events for the mission planning and control systems. The tools produce Payload Operations Requests (POR) and Payload Direct Operations Requests (PDOR), subtypes of CRF. They check the requests against the mission's operational database, the MIB (which this paper expands as 'Mission Information Database'), and against the ESOC operations-planning ICDs.

Before this framework, each team built its own CRFs, and mismatches with the MIB or the ICDs caused many iterations with the ESOC flight control team. The BepiColombo tool (launch October 2018, a 7.2-year cruise with 9 flybys) supported the near-Earth commissioning phase, six-monthly instrument check-outs and flyby science, with more than about 1500 PORs generated. Its features include COSMOS LDAP access control, a POR/PDOR editor, MIB compatibility checks, handling of MIB updates and conflict resolution, flight dynamics and science events, product generation and direct submission to the MOC with delivery and acknowledgement monitoring, 3D flyby visualisation, timeline and resource simulation, and a MOIS-compatible procedure builder. The JUICE version (adapted in 2021) keeps the editor and delivery functions and had produced more than about 700 requests by the 2024 lunar-Earth gravity assist. The paper also mentions interest from HERA and ARIEL. It is useful context for how commanding definitions in the MIB and sequences are used outside the control centre.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• At ESOC, payload requests are part of the Command Request File (CRF) concept, which encapsulates telecommands, sequences, automation procedures and mission-critical events, collectively called occurrences. (PDF p. 1)
  • POR (Payload Operations Request) and PDOR (Payload Direct Operations Request) are subtypes of CRF; the tool's requests follow the CRF XML format and the applicable MIB of the ESOC ground data systems. (PDF p. 3)
  • Decentralised CRF creation in earlier missions caused extensive interaction with the ESOC Flight Control Team because of incompatibilities with the MIB and the ICDs of ESOC systems. (PDF p. 1)
  • BepiColombo (launched October 2018 with JAXA) has a 7.2-year cruise with 9 planetary flybys: 1 Earth, 2 Venus and 6 Mercury. (PDF p. 2)
  • SPOT Cruise produces CRFs compatible with the ESOC Mission Planning System, Mission Control System and the applicable MIB; more than about 1500 BepiColombo payload operation requests have been generated since launch. (PDF p. 4)
  • SPOT Cruise features include COSMOS LDAP access control, MIB compatibility checks, MIB update handling and conflict resolution, direct submission to the MOC with delivery and acknowledgement monitoring, and a MOIS-compatible procedure builder. (PDF p. 4)
  • The JUICE version (SPOT JUICE) was adapted in 2021 without 3D flyby visualisation, procedure builder or simulation; more than about 700 JUICE payload operation requests were generated, including for the August 2024 LEGA. (PDF p. 5)
  • The framework's key functions are CRF editing, management of MIB updates, MIB compatibility validation, ICD compliance verification, and CRF generation and delivery. (PDF p. 6)

docs.title: Provenance
docs.text: Original locationhttps://publications.spaceops.org/2025/download_by_id.php?id=0309Copied (UTC)2026-11-05T14:07:07ZSHA-256ebde588f5060888d5101be8339acbdb5124944d0ba3527b5b69cee033e79cb26Size836.6 KBOur copyspaceops2025-0309-mpd-edds.pdf (unchanged third-party file, not MIT; see the notice)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A SpaceOps 2025 paper by ESA/ESOC, CGI and NASA JPL presenting the CCSDS Mission Product Distribution (MPD) services. MPD is a draft CCSDS Mission Operations (MO) standard from the Spacecraft Monitoring and Control working group for querying, retrieving and subscribing to mission data products across agencies. It is specified with the MO Message Abstraction Layer (MAL), and consumer and provider interfaces can be auto-generated for Java, C, C++ and Go.

The information model separates ProductType (with attribute definitions) from Product instances (creation and content dates, source, attributes, body). StandingOrder captures a subscription, with ProductFilter, TimeWindow and AttributeFilter (value range, value set, string pattern) for selection. There are three services. Product Retrieval offers listProducts, getProducts and deliverProductFiles. Order Management offers list, submit and cancel for standing orders. Product Order Delivery offers notifyProductDelivery and deliverProducts. Use cases cover on-demand retrieval, scripted pulling, subscriptions, and delivery by service message or file transfer to a URI.

For this wiki the main interest is section 3.1, which maps ESA's EDDS onto MPD (see EDDS request and data formats). The EDDS interface is a SOAP/WSDL service with XML schema plus a REST service. Its batch and stream requests correspond to standing orders, getResponse to delivery notifications, getJobs and getStatus to listStandingOrders, and getCatalogue to listProducts. The paper notes that EDDS lacks advanced metadata filtering and live delivery notifications, and that EDDS product types such as PktTm, PktTc and PktEv are specific to the SCOS and EGS-CC data models. NASA AMMOS DataDrive is mapped in the same way. An ESA/JPL prototype built during 2024 on ESA's Java MO stack validated the draft and found naming, nullability and field-type issues. The paper closes with future applications and enhancements.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• MPD is being standardised by the CCSDS Spacecraft Monitoring and Control (SM&C) Working Group on top of the CCSDS Mission Operations (MO) framework, whose core is the Message Abstraction Layer (MAL); machine-readable service specifications are published in the SANA registry. (PDF p. 2)
  • MPD defines three services: Product Retrieval, Order Management and Product Order Delivery; use of MO MAL is the default but not mandatory. (PDF p. 3)
  • Information model: ProductType (name, description, AttributeDef list), Product (type, creationDate, contentDate, source, attributes, file metadata, body) and StandingOrder (filter, delivery method, validity window, target). (PDF p. 4)
  • Filtering uses ProductFilter (type, domain, sources, attribute filters), TimeWindow and AttributeFilter variants ValueRange, ValueSet and StringPattern. (PDF p. 5)
  • Product Retrieval operations: listProducts, getProducts (progress interaction) and deliverProductFiles (transfer to a URI with per-file status); Order Management: listStandingOrders, submitStandingOrder, cancelStandingOrder. (PDF p. 5)
  • Product Order Delivery publishes notifyProductDelivery for file-transfer deliveries and deliverProducts for full product instances via publish-subscribe. (PDF p. 6)
  • The EDDS interface is a SOAP-based WSDL service with XML schema (data requests, job submission and tracking, catalogue queries, user account management); EDDS also offers a REST-based service. (PDF p. 6)
  • EDDS-to-MPD mapping: batchRequest()/streamRequest() to submitStandingOrder(); getResponse() to notifyProductDelivery()/deliverProducts(); getJobs()/getStatus() to listStandingOrders(); getCatalogue() to listProducts() + ProductFilter; FileServerDelivery/ServerDelivery to FILETRANSFER/SERVICE_COMPLETE. (PDF p. 6)
  • EDDS has no advanced filtering and metadata search, does not typically forward live delivery notifications (job status is polled) and uses login credentials yielding authorisation tokens; EDDS product types PktEv, PktTc and PktTm are specific to SCOS and EGS-CC data models. (PDF p. 7)
  • ESA and NASA/JPL each built an independent MPD provider prototype during 2024 (completing in 2025) against a shared Java MO test harness with file:// transfers only, a mandatory step before Blue Book publication. (PDF p. 8)
  • Prototyping found structural naming inconsistencies, misapplied nullable attributes and inappropriate field types, which were fixed in the data model. (PDF p. 9)
  • MPD was expected to be published as a CCSDS Blue Book in Q3–Q4 2025, with a Prototype Report (Yellow Book) in preparation. (PDF p. 11)

docs.title: Provenance
docs.text: Original locationhttps://publications.spaceops.org/2025/download_by_id.php?id=0477Copied (UTC)2026-11-05T14:12:29ZSHA-25623e8db0102441cfc6fa8d3bd6059f76c4424642f7d07b462163561c06f408376Size378.7 KBOur copyspaceops2025-egs-cc.pdf (unchanged third-party file, not MIT; see the notice)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A short ESOC status paper (SpaceOps 2025) on replacing SCOS-2000 and the rest of the MICONYS suite with an MCS based on the European Ground Systems Common Core (EGS-CC), called MCS-CC (ancillary systems and the move to EGS-CC). The authors give the timeline: EGS-CC is first expected to enter operations in 2026, the migration of more than 40 ESOC missions will take at least seven years, and SCOS-2000 therefore reaches end of life no earlier than 2033. In April 2024 ESOC reconfirmed that the next MCS will be EGS-CC based. Swarm (three satellites, launched 2013) was chosen as the pilot migration of a flying mission, followed by Ariel (first SVTs in 2027, launch in 2029) as the first mission to launch on EGS-CC, and later a fully TDM-native ground segment.

The most useful part for MIB readers is the tailoring-data migration path. Category 1 missions, such as Swarm, keep their SCOS-2000 MIB and the existing tools (MOIS, ProToS, MATIS, DABYS, FOPPER). OPEN-M sits in between, and an S2K-MIB-to-EGS-CC-TDM converter imports the data into the MCS. Category 2 missions (Ariel expected) migrate all tailoring data to OPEN-M with converters and drop the MIB-based tools. Category 3 missions receive data from industry directly in the EGS-CC Tailoring Data Model. The paper also discusses the challenges: a new archive that must hold frames, packets, parameters, events, logs, alarm states and activities efficiently, an extensive test campaign, and user-interface issues in a large community. Recent Swarm-driven work covers pre-release checks in the commanding chain, playback TM, a user interface for SLE links, historical retrieval, a refurbished time correlation and on-board queue modelling. The next features are file-based operations, on-board software maintenance, security and PUS-C, with an operational solution targeted for 2027.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• SCOS-2000 and complementary systems form the MICONYS (MIssion CONtrol sYStem) suite at ESOC; in April 2024 ESOC re-confirmed that the next generation MCS will be based on EGS-CC. (PDF p. 1)
  • The transition is predicted to take at least 7 years from EGS-CC first entering operations in 2026, putting the SCOS end of life no earlier than 2033; more than 40 missions at ESOC are involved. (PDF p. 2)
  • Expected benefits include a common data model for TM/TC artefacts across pre- and post-launch phases, a common code base for ESOC missions, a common solution for MCS and ground station M&C, native automation and installation-free web access. (PDF p. 3)
  • Swarm (three satellites launched in 2013 to study Earth's magnetic field) is the pilot mission, allowing a risk-free transition while the S2K system remains available. (PDF p. 4)
  • Adoption phases: design and development (largely completed), testing and validation (migrate Swarm, prepare Ariel with first SVTs in 2027 and launch in 2029, then a TDM-native ground segment) and operational roll-out, expected to complete in the early 2030s. (PDF p. 4)
  • Category 1 missions natively use an S2K MIB (e.g. Swarm) with S2K tools such as MOIS, ProToS, MATIS, DABYS and FOPPER; OPEN-M is the intermediate and an S2K MIB to EGS-CC TDM converter imports the tailoring data into the MCS. (PDF p. 5)
  • Category 2 missions (Ariel expected, to be confirmed) migrate all tailoring data to OPEN-M using converters for the S2K MIB, MOIS and ProToS procedures and the FOPPER database; Category 3 missions receive tailoring data directly in EGS-CC TDM format from industry. (PDF p. 5)
  • The EGS-CC archive must store telemetry frames, packets, parameters, events, log messages, alarm states and control activities while balancing storage speed and volume against retrieval performance. (PDF p. 6)
  • Recent Swarm-driven enhancements: commanding chain pre-release checks, playback TM processing, a UI for SLE links, historical data retrieval, refurbished time correlation and on-board queue modelling, delivered partly in EGS-CC and partly in the MCS-CC layer. (PDF p. 6)
  • Next features: file based operations, on-board software maintenance, security and PUS-C including support for the Generic Operational Interface Requirements; validation through most of 2026 towards a fully operational solution in 2027. (PDF p. 6)
