docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Seven slides presented by P. Estaria for the ESA FIRST/Planck project at the SCOS-2000 meeting at ESOC on 18-19 April 2000 (reference PT - 07671). They give the project's formal position on whether the instrument teams should use SCOS-2000.

The history slide gives the background. The RTA CWG evaluated SCOS-2000 version 0.2 on 3-5 November 1999 as a possible framework for a common real-time assessment (RTA) system for the FIRST and Planck instruments. Since then the instrument groups had widened the scope to using SCOS-2000 as an EGSE kernel. PACS had gathered the extra requirements, covering missing RTA functions and expected EGSE features, in a 'consolidated' Delta URD of 4 April 2000. The slide warns that this URD could not yet be considered consolidated. ESOC had provided a draft software licence agreement, a service and support proposal and a description of the PROBA EGSE elements. The aim of the meeting was to give the PI groups everything they needed to decide.

The project position follows ESA science directorate policy. EGSEs are provided by industry under the spacecraft contract (ESA/IPC(89)126), the Agency delivers as little as possible to industry, the ground segment is part of the overall system trade-off, and commonality between flight control and checkout systems is to be pursued (also a goal for Rosetta and MEX). The choice of SCOS-2000 is entirely a PI decision. The project can supply no technical support, hardware, software or funding for direct or indirect costs, and accepts no responsibility for problems. Its coordination role ended with the termination of the RTA CWG. See SCOS-2000 as EGSE and Herschel and Planck.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• SCOS-2000 (version 0.2) was evaluated on 3-5 November 1999 by the RTA CWG as a possible 'framework' for a common RTA system for the FIRST and Planck instruments. (PDF p. 2)
  • The instrument groups then considered an expanded scope for SCOS-2000: its use as an EGSE kernel. (PDF p. 2)
  • PACS captured the additional requirements in a 'consolidated' Delta URD (04/04/00), which the slide notes cannot yet be considered consolidated. (PDF p. 2)
  • ESOC provided a draft SCOS-2000 software licence agreement proposal, a service and support proposal, and a description of existing EGSE elements from PROBA. (PDF p. 3)
  • ESA (D/SCI) policy: EGSEs are provided by industry as part of the spacecraft procurement contract (ESA/IPC(89)126), with a minimum of Agency deliverables to industry. (PDF p. 4)
  • Commonality and compatibility between the Flight Control System and the Check Out System is to be pursued within project constraints, also a goal for Rosetta and MEX. (PDF p. 4)
  • Selecting SCOS-2000 as instrument EGSE kernel or for any other function is entirely a PI decision; the project can provide no technical support, hardware, software or financing. (PDF p. 5)
  • Costs not covered include direct costs (hardware, licences, Delta URD developments, installation, maintenance, training) and indirect costs via an increase of the MOC CaC. (PDF p. 6)
  • The project's coordination of the SCOS-2000 evaluation ended with the termination of the RTA CWG. (PDF p. 6)
  • The benefits of commonality and compatibility are expected to be substantial but have not been quantified. (PDF p. 7)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Issue 1.0 (19 February 2007) of a RAL technical note by Asier Abreu Aramburu for the Herschel SPIRE instrument. It is a step-by-step procedure for building and maintaining the Versant databases used with the Herschel Common Science System (HCSS) in the SPIRE test environments (ILT, AVM, IST, HSC). It also explains how the uplink definitions are kept under configuration control.

Section 2 starts with the prerequisites: Versant ODBMS 7.0.1.1, Java 1.5 and SPIRE build #478 or later. It then gives each database creation step with its expected console output. The database is allocated, public access is granted, telemetry source packets are indexed by time, and mission configuration config1 is created. Next the MIB is ingested with ingestmib, which reads the MIB files from the directory in the hcss.mib.datadir property and runs semantic checks. Serious problems abort the ingestion; minor ones are only written to mibchecker.log. The remaining steps load calibration tables and Common Uplink System (CUS) definitions, set the initial observation identifier (OBSID) in hexadecimal, and bind MIB and CUS definitions into an instrument model with cus -createinsmodel. Further procedures cover adding a configuration to an existing database, deletion, and backup and restore with vbackup.

Section 3 covers configuration control. CUS definitions, TestControl scripts and CCS templates are kept per campaign in the ESA CVS repository and tagged LABEL_CONFIGN (for example AVM_TEST_CONFIG6). Once ingested, the database versions them automatically, so CVS version 1.2 becomes 1.2.1. The note also documents the TestSetup.txt calibration table. Its keys (configuration, env, test_type, instrument, condition, dbg_level) let the same definitions run in every environment. See MIB tooling and Herschel/Planck ground segment.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Applicable to all SPIRE test environments (ILT, AVM, IST, HSC); the test setup is the system that operates the instrument in real or semi-real time, monitors it and archives its telemetry. (PDF p. 4)
  • Required software: Versant ODBMS v7.0.1.1 or higher, Java Run Time Environment v1.5.0 or higher, and a SPIRE build #478 or higher containing the corresponding HCSS release. (PDF p. 5)
  • HCSS key parameters for database creation are kept in the user.props file under the user's .hcss directory. (PDF p. 5)
  • Database creation sequence: db_admin -i (allocate), dbuser -add -P (public access), a btree index on herschel.versant.ccm.TmSourcePacketImpl _time, and missetup -addconfig config1. (PDF p. 6)
  • A new database starts with configuration config1; later changes to definitions or calibration tables need a new configuration to take effect. (PDF p. 7)
  • MIB ingestion reads the MIB from the directory named by property hcss.mib.datadir; other settings include hcss.mib.instrument=SPIRE, hcss.mib.cus_file=cus.script and a TC command list under the MIB's auxil/tcmds. (PDF p. 8)
  • ingestmib MIB_LABEL runs semantic checks: serious problems raise ValidationProblemsFoundMibException and stop the ingestion; non-serious problems are logged in mibchecker.log and the MIB is still ingested (example label SPIRE_MIB_2.2.G1). (PDF p. 9)
  • Calibration tables are loaded with UploadCaltables.csh, and CUS definitions (building blocks, procedures and modes in one CUS_Definitions.file) through cusgui or IngestCUSDefinitions.csh. (PDF p. 10)
  • The initial OBSID is set in hexadecimal without the '0x' prefix, e.g. 0x30012001 is given as 30012001. (PDF p. 11)
  • 'cus -createinsmodel config1' associates the MIB and CUS definitions in an instrument model for the configuration; missetup -listmodels lists the models (e.g. SPIRE PFM5). (PDF p. 11)
  • Configuration control exists so that it is later known which version of which script produced a given set of SPIRE telemetry. (PDF p. 15)
  • Tags follow TAG NAME = LABEL_CONFIGN, e.g. AVM_TEST_CONFIG6. (PDF p. 18)
  • Every definition or calibration table ingested into the database gets an extra automatic version number: a CVS version 1.2 becomes 1.2.1; during a test, changes are tracked only through database versions. (PDF p. 18)
  • A new mission configuration is a snapshot that freezes the ingested script and calibration table versions. (PDF p. 19)
  • TestSetup.txt keys: configuration, env (moc, ilt, hsc, ist, par per ICD FIRST-FSC-DOC-0200), test_type (ft or pr), instrument (prime or redundant), condition (warm above 100 K, cool, cold below 10 K) and dbg_level (0 or 1). (PDF p. 20)

docs.title: Provenance
docs.text: Original locationhttps://archives.esac.esa.int/hsa/legacy/ADP/SPIRE/SPIRE_docs/SPIRE_Internal_Documents/001155_NOT_Naming_Convention/NOT001155%20SPIRE%20MIB%20Naming%20Convention_1-2.pdfCopied (UTC)2026-11-05T14:09:59ZSHA-256231295c605ac8feed4ab7c8eb48dbb6283a5ddd217cb54f3377eadeea291031dSize26.3 KBOur copyspire-mib-naming-convention-1.2.pdf (unchanged third-party file, not MIT; see the notice)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A five-page SPIRE technical note that turns the Herschel/Planck system-level naming convention (H-P-1-ASPI-SP-0141, AD01) into concrete identifier patterns for the SPIRE instrument's MIB, the set of SCOS-2000 ASCII tables defined by the SCOS2000 Database Import ICD (issue 5.0, RD01). SPIRE delivered its MIB to the Herschel/Planck system database, so every key field had to follow a shared scheme.

Section 2 gives one pattern per MIB key field: command names (CCF_CNAME, SCiiippp), command parameters (CPC_PNAME, SPiiippp), monitoring parameters (PCF_NAME, SMiiippp), monitoring packets (PID_SPID, tttnnnnppp), numerical, textual and polynomial calibration identifiers (tttnnnrrr) and the alphanumeric, graphic and scrolling display identifiers (SA, SG, SL prefixes). Each pattern also cites the matching AD01 convention number. Section 3 defines the building blocks: system-element type numbers (OBS 480, DPU 490, DCU 500, MCU 510, SCU 520, EGSE 528, TFCS 529) with their subsystem letters, position identifiers per instrument model (AVM, QM, FM, FS), real-element numbers per configuration, fallback numeric 'alternative IDs' for calibration curves in case SCOS-2000 could not handle 8-character names, and one-letter parameter-unit codes such as K for temperature and V for voltage.

An engineer can use it as a decoder ring for SPIRE mnemonics in Herschel databases, and as a compact real example of how an instrument team tailored generic MIB naming to its own hardware tree. It also covers ground-only EGSE and test-facility (TFCS) parameters.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The note applies the Herschel/Planck System Database (HPSDB) naming convention (AD01) to the SPIRE MIB, which is delivered conforming to the SCOS2000 Database Import ICD (RD01). (PDF p. 1)
  • The SPIRE MIB must also define parameters from the SPIRE EGSE and other test equipment such as the TFCS; these follow the same naming format as instrument parameters. (PDF p. 1)
  • Command names (CCF_CNAME, also used in CDF_CNAME and PTV_CNAME) follow the pattern SCiiippp; command parameters (CPC_PNAME, CDF_PNAME) follow SPiiippp; monitoring parameters (PCF_NAME, OCF_NAME, OCP_NAME, PLF_NAME, PTV_PARNAM) follow SMiiippp. (PDF p. 1)
  • Monitoring packets (PID_SPID, TPCF_SPID, PLF_SPID) use the numeric pattern tttnnnnppp; command and monitoring calibrations (CCA, PAF, CAF, TXF, MCF numbers) use tttnnnrrr, with an alternative identifier sss. (PDF p. 1)
  • Display identifiers use SAiiippp for alphanumeric displays (DPF_NUMBE), SGiiippp for graphical displays (GPF_NUMBE) and SLiiippp for scrolling displays (SPF_NUMBE). (PDF p. 2)
  • In the patterns, iii is the theoretical parameter identifier (first character = subsystem ID, third character = parameter unit ID), nnn/nnnn are running numbers, ttt is the system element number, rrr the real element number, ppp the position identifier and sss the alternative identifier. (PDF p. 2)
  • SPIRE system element type numbers are OBS 480, DPU 490 and DCU 500, with subsystem letters such as T (Telemetry), D (Data), B (Bias), L (LIA), P (Photometer) and S (Spectrometer). (PDF p. 2)
  • Further system element numbers are MCU 510, SCU 520, EGSE 528 and TFCS 529; EGSE subsystems include the CDMS and DRCU simulators, and TFCS subsystems include the black body, cryostat, FTS and laser. (PDF p. 3)
  • Position identifiers are the unique System Element numbers per instrument model (AVM, QM, FM, FS); the DPU has distinct prime (4901) and redundant (4912) identifiers. (PDF p. 3)
  • Real element numbers for the first configuration are 100 (AVM), 300 (QM), 500 (FM) and 700 (FS) for most elements, incremented by 1 for each new configuration; the DPU uses 1001/2002, 3001/4002, 5001/6002 and 7001/8002. (PDF p. 4)
  • Alternative numeric IDs for calibration curves (used if SCOS2000 cannot handle 8-character field names) are allocated in blocks of 50: OBS 500-549, DPU 550-599, DCU 600-649, MCU 650-699, SCU 700-749. (PDF p. 4)
  • Parameter unit IDs are single letters, e.g. A current, F status flag, H frequency, K temperature, M mode, N count, T time, V voltage and W power. (PDF p. 4)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Two-page note from ESOC's TOS directorate, initialled JFK and marked draft-1 (19 April 2000). It tells FIRST/Planck instrument groups how to apply for ESA software and what support they could buy. The minutes of the same meeting record J-F. Kaufeler's action to provide such a licence-application template.

The note lists the software TOS could offer for payload EGSEs. First is SCOS-2000 itself. Next is the PROBA EGSE system: a router with SCOS gateway and TM and TC modules, a Tcl/Tk automation tool with SCOS interfaces, and an ORACLE database for SCOE and spacecraft data. The list ends with the MS-Access-based Integral database and the MS-Access-based Winfops/Mois procedure preparation system. Under ESA's convention for operational software, any body of an ESA member state could apply for a free licence. A request names the organisation, the software items, the licence type (documentation only, a time-limited trial, run-time, or source code) and the purpose of use. The licence is non-exclusive and ESA keeps ownership. The requester learns which COTS products are needed and whether an ESOC contract gives preferential terms.

The second page separates chargeable support from service. Support covers installation, teaching, design courses and consultancy. Service is a maintenance phase for software the customer has not modified, with a help desk, SPR fixes, CRQ planning, systematic updates and membership of the user group. The customer buys hardware and COTS licences. Contracts could be Fixed Unit Time (FUP) or Firm Fixed Price (FFP), and the cost figures in the 18 April presentation were declared indicative. The note is a primary source on how SCOS-2000 was distributed outside ESOC (SCOS-2000 as EGSE).

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Software items proposed by TOS for payload EGSEs: SCOS-2000; the PROBA EGSE system (Router with SCOS gateway and TM & TC modules, a TCL/TK-based Automation Tool, and an ORACLE database for SCOE and spacecraft data); the MS-Access-based Integral DB; and the MS-Access-based Winfops/Mois procedure preparation system. (PDF p. 1)
  • Per ESA convention for operational software, any ESA member state body may apply for a licence to any of these items free of charge. (PDF p. 1)
  • A request identifies the organisation, the software items, the licence type (documentation only, trial version of limited duration, run-time version, or source code) and the purpose of use. (PDF p. 1)
  • The licence is non-exclusive and ESA retains ownership; the software cannot be sold to a third party. (PDF p. 1)
  • Where underlying COTS are needed, the requester receives their product identification and vendor and, if applicable, a reference to an ESOC contract allowing deployment at preferential conditions. (PDF p. 1)
  • The customer procures the necessary hardware and COTS licences. (PDF p. 2)
  • Support (initial phase): installation, installation with teaching, a course on the software design and use, or consultancy on specific requirements. (PDF p. 2)
  • Service (maintenance, software untouched by the customer): help desk, Software Problem Reports fixed in later releases, discussion and planning of Change ReQuests, systematic updates, and membership of the software user group. (PDF p. 2)
  • Contracts may be Fixed Unit Time (FUP, e.g. labour) or Firm Fixed Price (FFP); cost figures shown in the presentation on 18.04.2000 are indicative. (PDF p. 2)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
This Software Release Note (SRN) accompanies delivery EDDS-R2.3.0i1 of the EGOS Data Dissemination System, ESOC's service for giving external users access to telemetry, telecommand and event packets, parameters and reports from the SCOS-2000 mission control system and its archives.

It records what was delivered and what it depends on. Section 2.2 lists the systems the release was verified against: SCOS 6.0.1 with its integrated packet archive (PARC), the DARC data archive 3.0.0, the FARC file archive 3.1.0, the EGOS User Desktop (EUD) 3.1.8 on which the EDDS MMI is built, and the ESOC SLES 12 platform baseline. Section 2.3 describes a known limitation in the file-system view when thousands of files are handled at once (ticket EDDS-938). Section 2.4 tabulates 43 problem reports and change requests fixed in v2.3.0; several concern packet decoding, for example command-parameter decoding for SCOS-2000 6.2.0 and later, TM header decoding for non-standard headers, a request for pure spacecraft packets, and a packet TM stream client.

Sections 2.5 and 2.6 give the inventory of the three delivery CDs and the issue of every EDDS document in the baseline (CIG, glossary, EUICD, SDD, SRS, SUM, upgrade guide and five technical notes). Section 2.9 lists requirements de-scoped in earlier releases, for example duplicate-packet filtering by APID with SSC, SCET or OBT, calibration choices, RDM media production, and several SMF-based report filters. Use it to date a given EDDS document set and to see which SCOS-2000 and archive versions it matches.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The release described is EDDS v2.3.0 (delivery EDDS-R2.3.0i1), organised on three CDs (documentation, COTS and source code). (PDF p. 5)
  • EDDS interfaces with the DARC, FARC and PARC systems, and its MMI is based on the EGOS EUD software. (PDF p. 7)
  • Verified against SCOS 6.0.1 (PARC integrated with 6.0), DARC 3.0.0, FARC 3.1.0, EUD 3.1.8 and SLES 12 platform baseline SLES12-064-ESOCL01-I1R0; EDDS needs the DARC-dataprovision-3.0.0.jar library even with older DARC versions. (PDF p. 7)
  • Known limitation EDDS-938: processing a large number of files together (for example erasing thousands) causes a file-system error attributed to LDAP connections that Tomcat fails to handle. (PDF p. 7)
  • Fixes in v2.3.0 include EDDS-970 'Decode of command parameters fail for S2K 6.2.0+', EDDS-979 'Incorrect decoding of TM header when it's not the vanilla one' and EDDS-934 'EDDS Packet TM stream client'. (PDF p. 7)
  • Further changes include EDDS-958 'Request to provide pure spacecraft packet', EDDS-966 on BIT parameters in Protobuf response files and EDDS-935 on request status when an SPID is not in pid.dat. (PDF p. 8)
  • The baseline document set at this release: CIG i14r0, Glossary i7r0, EUICD i15r0, SDD i13r0, SRN i14r0, SRS i18r0, SUM i14r0, EDDS Upgrade Guide i12r0, plus FAT report, SVTD and technical notes TN-1001 to TN-1006. (PDF p. 9)
  • De-scoped requirement EDDS-SR-07690 would have let a mission choose the duplicate-packet key (APID and SSC, APID and SCET, or APID and OBT). (PDF p. 10)
  • De-scoped requirements on calibration (EDDS-SR-00720, -05550) note that data retrieved from the DARC are processed as received, with no calibration required or possible. (PDF p. 10)
  • RDM (Raw Data Media) delivery requirements for TM, TC and EV packets, MCS reports, archived files and TM parameters were de-scoped. (PDF p. 11)

docs.title: Provenance
docs.text: Original locationhttps://solarorbiter.irap.omp.eu/documents/EDDS/docs/EGOS-GEN-EDDS-SRS.pdfCopied (UTC)2026-11-05T14:02:35ZSHA-2563a7b3cf9e072eb0e48e31083de9d058c494066e9646d46e37053ddd3946d8717Size2.0 MBOur copySRS.pdf (unchanged third-party file, not MIT; see the notice)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The EDDS Software Requirements Specification defines what the EGOS Data Dissemination System must do, at the level of release 2.3.0. It is the richest source in the EDDS set on why EDDS exists and what data it serves.

Section 4 gives the background. EDDS replaces and merges three ESOC ground-segment subsystems that gave users outside the control room access to SCOS-2000 data: the Telemetry Data Retrieval System (TDRS), Web Remote Monitoring (WebRM) and the Generic Data Disposition System (GDDS). It also takes ideas from the MUST parameter-analysis prototype. Section 4 then defines the data types (TM, TC and event packets with statistics; TM parameters from the DARC parameter archive or generated on the fly by SMON; MCS and EDDS reports; FARC archived files; acknowledgements), the delivery mechanisms (file server over SFTP, EDDS server download, stream in timely or complete mode, e-mail) and the formats (binary with a configurable EDDS header, XFDU, XML with mission XSLT, TDRS-style spreadsheet, ASCII, GDDS binary). A further subsection explains the ESOC network security domains (OPS, Office, Relay, PISA LANs, public Internet).

Section 5 holds about 400 numbered requirements (EDDS-SR-xxxxx), each with need, priority, stability, verification method and source. Many trace back to the TDRS SRD, the GDDS SRD or the WebRM baseline. They specify, for example, the TM packet filters (type, subtype, APID, PI1/PI2, virtual channel, SPID, SSC, spacecraft ID, on-board or reception time), the content of EDDS TM and TC binary packet headers, duplicate-packet handling, CCSDS ASCII time codes in spreadsheet output, quotas, roles, scheduling, security and MMI.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Parameter data: ESA mission control systems generate parameters on the fly from packets, so a dedicated parameter archive (DARC) was developed to meet EDDS performance criteria, alongside the new packet archive (PARC). (PDF p. 13)
  • EDDS requirements are based on three existing subsystems, TDRS (parameter extraction from SCOS-2000 history files into MVDA or spreadsheet files), WebRM (remote monitoring over CORBA external interfaces) and GDDS (web and FTP front end to MCS archive data), plus the MUST analysis prototype. (PDF p. 13)
  • EDDS is multi-mission: user accounts and privileges group users by mission and domain, behind a single authentication entry point. (PDF p. 14)
  • Data-type/format matrix: TM and TC packets in EDDS binary, XFDU, GDDS_BINARY and SFDU; reports in XML/ASCII; parameters additionally in TDRS spreadsheet format; formats marked * support splitting responses into chunks and suspend/resume. (PDF p. 15)
  • Packets are delivered as processed by the MCS in network byte order; parameters come either from the DARC (fast, configurable subset) or from SMON, generated on the fly from the packet archive (slower but all parameters). (PDF p. 16)
  • MCS reports follow SCOS-2000 release 5 reports: TM packet, TM gap, TM parameter, TC packet, OBEV, OOL, OBQ, event record, command record and OBSM reports, provided in XML with mission XSLT for final formatting. (PDF p. 16)
  • Stream delivery supports offline (archived) and online data; online mode is either 'timely' (drops data to meet latency) or 'complete' (delivers everything, possibly late). (PDF p. 17)
  • Binary format means data as received from the MCS in network endian order with a configurable EDDS header prepended to each packet; the spreadsheet format follows the TDRS External ICD. (PDF p. 19)
  • Requirement terms: Need (E, D1, D2, D3), Priority 1-3, Stability S/N and Type codes; a 'domain' is an instance of an MCS or data archive. (PDF p. 12)
  • EDDS-SR-00320 lists TM packet filters: type, subtype, APID (including PID and PCAT), P1, P2, virtual channel, domain, on-board or reception time, quality flag, database version, ground station ID, SPID, SSC and spacecraft ID. (PDF p. 36)
  • EDDS-SR-00780 lets each mission choose the EDDS TM packet header fields (SSC, APID, P1, P2, virtual channel, OBT, reception time, validity, SPID, PID, ground station, data unit type, type, subtype, time quality, mnemonic). (PDF p. 39)
  • Duplicate packets can be defined per mission as APID+SSC, APID+SCET or APID+OBT. (PDF p. 40)
  • Spreadsheet output offers CCSDS ASCII time code A and B formats (EDDS-SR-00650). (PDF p. 62)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Issue 22.0 (2025) of the EDDS Software User Manual covers the client of the EGOS Data Dissemination System at release v3.6.0. It keeps the structure and most of the text of the 2018 issue (library item sum): client installation and requirements, the mission web page, the Java client API, user-access set-up with data access sets, operation data sets, quota sets, roles and groups, a reference tour of every client view, and appendices with the date/time, duration and CRON formats and every request form.

The main additions concern missions controlled by the European Ground Systems Common Core (EGS-CC). Two new batch request families sit beside the classic FARC, DARC, PARC, SMON, file-system and SCOS-2000 Data Provision Service requests. HARC requests read the EGS-CC HBase archive and return parameters, parameter definitions, raw TM, TM and TC reports, log messages and activity reports. EGSCC REST requests read through the EGS-CC REST interface and add out-of-limit reports. The DCRs record further changes: pre-filtering of EGS-CC requests, alignment of Kafka and EDDS response fields, EGS-CC OOL requests, quotas that also restrict TC requests, and filtering of request views by mission or user.

Two new reference sections help in reading EDDS outputs. Section 5.4 lists every request status (from SUBMITTED, QUEUED and ACTIVE to DELIVERED, DELIVERED_PARTIAL_RESULTS, SERVER_COMPLETED and the ERROR_* states), and section 5.5 lists the response compression options (TAR, TARGZ, ZIP). Section 6.5 describes the GitLab DevOps pipeline used to build and deploy EDDS.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Issue 22.0 is 'Issue for EDDS v.3.6.0i1'; issues 15.0 to 21.0 covered EDDS v2.4.0 to v3.5.0 (2020 to 2024). (PDF p. 3)
  • DCRs record changes including EDDS-1355 (pre-filtering of EGSCC requests), EDDS-1373 (align Kafka and EDDS response fields), EDDS-1271 (EGSCC OOL requests) and EDDS-1376 (quotas restricting TC requests). (PDF p. 4)
  • Batch requests now go to the FARC, DARC, PARC and HARC archives plus EDDS reports; PARC data come via the PARC Manager, Data Provision Services or SMON, and HARC data via HBase. (PDF p. 17)
  • HARC requests (EGS-CC HBase archive) include Egscc parameter, Egscc parameter definition, Packet TM Raw EGSCC Data, Egscc TM Report, Egscc Packet TC Report, Egscc Packet TM, Egscc Log Message Report and Egscc Activity Report (activities with raw and engineering values). (PDF p. 17)
  • EGSCC (REST) requests add an Egscc Out of Limit Report returning out-of-limit data with path, state, alarm state and value. (PDF p. 17)
  • Packet TM Report's RAWSOURCEBINARY output is a binary file of the uninterrupted flow of RawBodyData; the TM Gap Report requires SCOS 5.4.18+ or 5.5.2+. (PDF p. 18)
  • SCOS-2000 Data Provision Services (SCOS v5.4.21+ and 5.5.4+) deliver PARC packet data over CORBA without EDDS having to decode it. (PDF p. 19)
  • PARC stream request forms can still only be saved, not submitted, because streaming from the PARC is not available in this release. (PDF p. 19)
  • Request statuses include SUBMITTED, QUEUED, ACTIVE, DELIVERED, DELIVERED_PARTIAL_RESULTS, COMPLETED_NO_RESULTS, SERVER_COMPLETED, CANCELED, SUSPENDED and DELIVERED_RESP_DELETED, plus error states such as ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED and ERROR_LIMIT_EXCEEDED. (PDF p. 20)
  • Further error states are ERROR_INVALID_REQUEST, ERROR_UNKNOWN, ERROR_DELIVERY and ERROR_LOCALLY_DELIVERED; response compression options are TAR, TARGZ and ZIP. (PDF p. 21)
  • The EDDS DevOps pipeline has three manually triggered stages, package_source, build_publish_image (publishing to the JFROG repository) and helm_deploy. (PDF p. 73)
  • Client requirements are unchanged from 2018 in the text: Windows 7 or SLES 12, Java 1.8.0_72, Tomcat port 8080 typical. (PDF p. 13)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The EDDS Software User Manual explains how end users and mission administrators use the EGOS Data Dissemination System client, release v2.3.0. The client is an Eclipse-RCP application based on the EGOS User Desktop, available standalone or as a web application. It gives access to data from the SCOS-2000 archives and related ESOC systems (archives).

Section 4 covers client requirements (Java 8, Windows 7 or SLES 12, Tomcat port 8080), the mission EDDS web page and the Java client API that wraps the EDDS WSDL. Section 5 is a quick start. Administrators build access rights from data access sets, operation data sets, quota sets (which can restrict SPIDs, APIDs and parameter names), roles and groups. The section then catalogues every request type. Batch requests cover FARC files, catalogues and subscriptions; DARC parameters, definitions, previews and statistics; PARC TM, TC and event packets (EDDS-header binary, raw PARC XML, reports, statistics, TM gap reports, OOL records); SMON on-the-fly parameters; file-system catalogues; and SCOS-2000 Data Provision Service requests, which return already-decoded packets. Stream requests cover DARC parameters, with PARC streams defined but not yet submittable.

Section 6 walks through the client views: login, user management, request summary, request forms, live stream viewer, parameter and quota views, file view and message displays. It also covers the web application, Request Submitter and Performance Processor. Appendix A defines the date/time, day-of-year, ISO duration and CRON formats used in forms, and Appendices B and C show every batch and stream request form. For a wiki reader it is the practical companion to the EUICD's formal request and response formats.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The standalone EDDS client is based on EUD and Eclipse RCP, downloaded from the mission's EDDS web page; it needs Java 1.8.0_72 on Windows 7 or SLES 12 and talks to the web server, typically on Tomcat port 8080. (PDF p. 11)
  • The EDDS Client APIs are a Java library implementing the EDDS WSDL interfaces behind a façade usable by any client application. (PDF p. 12)
  • User access is configured per mission through Data Access Sets, optional Operation Data Sets and Quota Sets (which can restrict SPIDs, APIDs and parameter names), assigned to roles and then to users or groups. (PDF p. 14)
  • Batch requests go to three archives (FARC, DARC, PARC) plus EDDS reports; PARC data can be obtained via the PARC Manager, the Data Provision Services or SMON. (PDF p. 15)
  • DARC requests: Parameter (timestamps and values), Parameter Definition (description, type, unit), Parameter Preview and Parameter Statistics (min, max, average, standard deviation, valid/invalid sample counts). (PDF p. 15)
  • Packet TM returns raw packets with headers as set in the EDDS header configuration; Packet TM Raw PARC data returns packets exactly as stored in the PARC, one XML element per packet; Packet TM Report gives header fields (SPID, APID, type, subtype, data stream, times) plus raw data. (PDF p. 15)
  • The RAWSOURCEBINARY output format of the Packet TM Report is a binary file holding the uninterrupted flow of the RawBodyData content; the TM Gap Report requires SCOS 5.4.18 or later, or 5.5.2 or later. (PDF p. 15)
  • The OOL Record Report returns records with timestamps, record types, parameter states, values and limits, showing raw values only, not engineering values. (PDF p. 16)
  • Data Provision Services in SCOS (v5.4.21 and later, 5.5.4 and later) let EDDS retrieve packet data from the PARC over CORBA without having to decode it; the Packet TM Report can then include parameter information. (PDF p. 16)
  • Stream requests are supported for DARC parameters; PARC stream forms (TC, TM, SCOS event log, out of limits) can be saved but not yet submitted in this release. (PDF p. 17)
  • Form time formats: dateTime 'YYYY-MM-DDThhss[.xxxxxxZ]' and day-of-year 'YYYY-DDDThhss[.xxxxxxZ]'; durations use the 'PnYnMnDTnHnMnS' form. (PDF p. 69)

docs.text: Original locationhttps://archives.esac.esa.int/hsa/legacy/ADP/SPIRE/SPIRE_docs/SPIRE_Internal_Documents/000900_ICS_ICD_TC_History/TC_History_ICD.pdfCopied (UTC)2026-11-12T17:48:33ZSHA-25653cedc8ac4b01e7e20c2a2389489931ac684f6d2013d81a4befe0aaa2e69272eSize175.4 KBOur copyTC_History_ICD.pdf (unchanged third-party file, not MIT; see the notice)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The interface control document for the TC History File (THF). The THF is the file through which the commanding history of a test or operational period reaches the Herschel Common Science System (HCSS). It is ICD#5 in the Herschel ground segment list of ICDs and applies to every mission phase. The file comes from the SCOS-2000 based EGSE in instrument-level tests (ILT), from the Central Checkout System (CCS) in integrated system tests (IST), and from the MOC in operations. The ICD fixes only the file format. Generation in ILT is covered by ICD#8, and ingestion into the HCSS by the TC History technical note.

It quotes the ground segment IRD requirements behind the interface. The MOC must make the TC history of any period available, including uplink and execution status. The HSC uses it to flag observations not commanded as scheduled, and the ICCs use it to verify instrument commanding, with the HCSS pulling the data. It also covers the file naming convention (THF_yymmdd_cccc.DAT), security, backup and the expected volume (about one file per day).

The core is the data definition. The THF is ASCII, with fixed-length, blank-padded fields and no delimiters. A 93-character header record is followed, for each released command, by a 'C' command record (187 characters), a 'B' bit-pattern record (512 hex digits, i.e. a 256-octet TC) and zero or more 'P' parameter records (153 characters). The command record carries the SCOS-2000 command history attributes: release and execution times, static/dynamic PTV and CEV check states, group/block flags, interlock type and stage, source type, and a 17-character verification-status string with one status letter per stage. That string maps directly onto SCOS-2000 command verification.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The THF format is expected by the HCSS in all mission phases (ILT, IST and Ops). The document is ICD#5 of the ground segment list of ICDs [RD5]. (PDF p. 7)
  • Requirement IR-3.1-300: the MOC makes TC history (uplink and execution status of all TCs) available to the HSC for any operational period. The HSC uses it to flag observations not commanded as scheduled, and ICCs use it for command verification. Under IR-3.1.330 the HSC pulls the data from the MOC. (PDF p. 10)
  • In ILT the THF is delivered from SCOS-2000, and in IST from the CCS. The data source in operations is the MOC, with retrieval covered by the DDID. (PDF p. 10)
  • The THF is read mainly by the HCSS TCHistoryIngestor. A failed transfer is detected at ingestion, which aborts the processing (possibly rolling back database transactions) and requests the file again. (PDF p. 12)
  • The file naming convention is THF_yymmdd_cccc.DAT: yy, mm and dd give the start date of the data, and cccc is a cyclic counter for files generated on the same day. (PDF p. 12)
  • Each THF covers a configurable time window. Because a THF might cover the whole mission, the window is written HHHHH:MM:SS (TBC) rather than HH:MM:SS. About one THF per day is expected. (PDF p. 14)
  • The THF is ASCII. Each record is fixed-format, fixed-length and newline-terminated, with no field delimiters, and every field is left-justified and blank-padded. (PDF p. 15)
  • The header record is 93 characters: file name (40), first and last TC release times (21 each, YYYY.DDD.HH.MM.SS.SSS) and time window (11). (PDF p. 15)
  • The command data record ('C', 187 characters) holds the HCSS TCID (unsigned 32-bit integer), name (11), description (25), parent sequence (9), release time, and the predicted execution time (uplink time plus propagation delay for immediate commands, or the time-tag). It also holds the static PTV, dynamic PTV and CEV check states, the group and block flags, and the interlock status (type L/G/S and stage). (PDF p. 16)
  • The verification status field is 19 characters with up to 17 stages: release from SCOS-2000, ground station reception, uplink, on-board reception, on-board application acceptance, start of execution, execution steps 0-9 and completion. Each stage is one status letter: F, S, P, I, T, U, X or blank. (PDF p. 17)
  • The bit pattern record ('B', 513 characters) carries a hex encoding of a 256-octet TC bit pattern. It does not apply to ILT. (PDF p. 18)
  • The parameter data record ('P', 153 characters) gives the parameter name (11), description (currently blank), raw/engineering representation, radix (Dec/Hex/Oct, for unsigned raw values only) and value (88). (PDF p. 18)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Issue 0.2 (18 March 2003) of a technical note by M.J. Graham on the design of the TC history ingestion process in the Herschel Common Science System (HCSS). It covers the instrument level test (ILT) phase, HCSS version 0.1.x. The process fetches telecommand history from SCOS-2000, converts it for the HCSS archive and links each record to the telecommand that the HCSS generated.

The note traces the process to requirement HCSS-UR-3.1-1111 and use case UCF-759 and lists its assumptions. SCOS-2000 produces an ASCII TC history file (THF). Commands from HCSS schedules carry a 32-bit TCID, while manual commands have a null TCID. OBSID and BBID setting commands identify observations and building blocks. TC history times are UT, schedule times TAI, and ILT schedules use only relative times. Event-driven TCs generated on board are out of scope.

There are two components, joined by TCP/IP. A THF server asks SCOS-2000 for a time window, receives the THF file name, reads the file from the directory SCOS-2000 writes to, and passes it on. A TC history ingestor checks the file and creates a TcHistory object per TC. It links each object to its TC by TCID, updates the success flags of observations and block executions, and reports missing TCs and missing history records. The link to SCOS-2000 uses TCP/IP, with a CORBA interface planned.

Section 3 describes the nl.esa.herschel.tchingest package and its FileIngestion API, shared with OOL ingestion. Section 4 records design decisions. Manual TCs are stored without associations (SCR-0119), orphan histories are kept and logged as errors (SPR-0118), and the database is committed once per THF, typically one per day. The operator view is in the TC history and OOL user manual. See Herschel/Planck ground segment and archives.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• This issue covers the ILT mission phase (HCSS 0.1.x), which requests data from SCOS-2000 over a TCP/IP interface; later versions were to use a CORBA interface. (PDF p. 4)
  • The process retrieves TC history from SCOS-2000, converts it for storage in the HCSS archive and associates each TC history record with its TC. (PDF p. 5)
  • Requirements: HCSS-UR-3.1-1111 (associate TC history with the commanding requests in the Observations Schedule) and UCF-759 (verify TC history against observation executions and flag failed, missing and additional commands). (PDF p. 5)
  • Assumptions: the TC history file (THF) is an ASCII file produced by SCOS-2000; HCSS schedule commands are tagged with a 32-bit TCID while manual commands have a null or default TCID; OBSID and BBID commands relate history to observations. (PDF p. 5)
  • TC history times are UT while schedule times are TAI, and ILT schedules use only relative times, so time conversion is needed; on-board generated event-driven TC packets are out of scope; the THF holds values only for editable command parameters. (PDF p. 5)
  • Two components communicate via TCP/IP: a THF server, which requests a time period from SCOS-2000, receives the THF name and retrieves the file, and a TC history ingestor, which validates it, creates TCHistory objects and associates them by TCID. (PDF p. 6)
  • The ingestor checks that the first line of the THF matches the TC History File ICD and that the file covers the requested time window; it runs continuously and requests a new THF after a configured wait. (PDF p. 6)
  • Package nl.esa.herschel.tchingest has subpackages api, bin, doc, server, test and util; the FileIngestion interface (getFile, checkFile, processFile, initStore, commitData) is shared by TC history and OOL ingestion. (PDF p. 7)
  • SCOS-2000 places the requested THF in a preconfigured directory, so THFServer must run on the SCOS-2000 host or have access to that directory (e.g. networked disks). (PDF p. 9)
  • For manual TCs (TCID = 0) the ingestor assigns the Observation and Building Block whose time period contains the record's time stamp. (PDF p. 10)
  • TC history records for manual commands are made persistent without associations (SCR-0119); a TcHistory with a non-zero TCID whose TC is missing is persisted and an error is logged (SPR-0118). (PDF p. 10)
  • If all TCs of a Building Block succeed its uplinked status is set to successful; if all TCs of an Observation succeed its executed status is set to successful. (PDF p. 11)
  • A database commit is done only at the end of processing a THF; typically one THF per day is expected, containing a day's TC history. (PDF p. 11)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Issue 2.3 (13 November 2008) of the software user manual, by M.J. Graham and S. Guest, for the processes that ingest telecommand history and out-of-limits (OOL) data from SCOS-2000 into the Herschel Common Science System (HCSS) database. The change record runs from the first combined version (October 2003) through IST support and a command-line retrieval mode (2004) and timeout and delete properties (2007) to support for OOL files in Data Disposition System (DDS) format (2008).

Each data type uses three components. A file retriever asks SCOS-2000 for a Telecommand History File (THF) or an Out-of-Limits file (ORF). A file server delivers the files over TCP/IP in ILT client-server mode. An ingestor validates each file, skips objects already in the database, stores the rest and links them to TCs, observations and building blocks. It also flags gaps in the TC IDs. In IST mode the user copies files from the SCOS machine and names them on the command line. The OOL ingestor treats files ending in .OOL or .TLM as DDS format.

Section 3 is a tutorial covering every hcss.tchool.* configuration property and its default: THF and ORF server ports 3187 and 3188, SCOS-2000 port 2209, a 60 000 ms retry wait with at most 5 attempts, a 1000 ms time tolerance, the SCOS output directory and the time zone. It also covers the commands thfserver, orfserver, tchoolretrieve, tchingest and oolingest. Appendix A gives the diagnosis and recovery for each exception: configuration, connection, database store and THF record-length errors. Appendix B lists warnings such as TCs missing from the database, time mismatches and TCs without history. The design is in the TC history ingestion note. See monitoring checks, GDDS and DDIDs and Herschel/Planck ground segment.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• This issue is applicable to HCSS release 0.2, described as the first HCSS release to support the integrated system testing (IST) phase while continuing to support instrument level tests (ILT). (PDF p. 4)
  • Components per data type: a file retriever that extracts a Telecommand History file (THF) or Out-of-Limits file (ORF) from SCOS-2000, a file server that supplies files over TCP/IP at periodic intervals (ILT), and an ingestor that works on files directly (IST) or via the server (ILT). (PDF p. 6)
  • The OOL ingestor also accepts DDS-format files as retrieved from the MOC in the routine phase. (PDF p. 6)
  • If the SCOS-2000 connection is lost, the file server waits a set time and retries a set number of times before aborting. (PDF p. 6)
  • Ingestion validates the file and its time window, skips objects already in the database, makes new objects persistent even if linking later fails, links them where possible and commits. (PDF p. 7)
  • The TC history ingestor checks the THF's first line, links each TCHistory object to its TC (none for manual commands), updates the success flags of Observations and Block Executions, and detects missing history from gaps in the TC IDs; OOLPacket objects are linked to the building block closest in time. (PDF p. 7)
  • Default file-server settings: servers 127.0.0.1, THF server port 3187, ORF server port 3188, attemptwaittime 60000 ms, maxattempts 5, fileperiod 60000 ms. (PDF p. 8)
  • Default SCOS-2000 settings: s2kserver 127.0.0.1, s2kport 2209, s2kdirectory /spired/HPR, s2ktimezone UTC, delete true, timeout 2000 ms. (PDF p. 9)
  • Default date format yyyy/MM/dd-HHss; the alternative yyyy.DDD.HH.mm.ss matches the time format used in THF and ORF files. (PDF p. 9)
  • Two times are deemed equal if they differ by less than hcss.tchool.timetolerance, default 1000 ms. (PDF p. 10)
  • Commands: thfserver and orfserver (ILT, on or with visibility of the SCOS-2000 machine); tchoolretrieve [TC | OL], which opens a GUI if no type is given (IST); tchingest and oolingest [file1] [file2] ..., which use client-server mode if no files are given. (PDF p. 10)
  • oolingest treats a file whose name ends in '.OOL' or '.TLM' as DDS format and any other file as SCOS format. (PDF p. 11)
  • Exception A.18: the TCH and OOL persistent classes are not initialised by initv and must be defined in the Versant schema with com.versant.DefineClass. (PDF p. 14)
  • THF format errors (missing header record, wrong header time format, Command Data, Bit Pattern or Parameter Data Record of incorrect length) abort the ingestion attempt until the next scheduled retrieval. (PDF p. 15)
  • Warning B.3: a first or last TC time stamp outside the requested THF time by more than the tolerance may indicate a time mismatch between SCOS-2000 and the ingestion process. (PDF p. 16)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A two-page commercial data sheet from Terma for three related spacecraft control and checkout products: SCS5 (multi-user operations version, used for all mission phases from operations preparation and launch to routine operations), CCS5 (multi-user checkout version, used within an EGSE for spacecraft assembly, integration and test) and TSC (a lightweight single-user version, for example for instrument or payload testing).

The sheet lists the functional scope: telemetry reception and frame processing (virtual channel filtering, gap detection, authentication, decryption), parameter monitoring and alphanumeric, graphic and synoptic displays, commanding with a manual stack, CLTU generation and COP-1 flow control, command verification history, archiving and retrieval, session management, reporting and hot redundancy. Automation uses the TOPE procedure language, which includes Tcl/Tk 8.6.

Of direct interest to MIB readers, the TM/TC database is described as the SCOS-2000 MIB ICD 6.9 'extended' (for example unlimited field lengths, multiple databases, deduced parameters in TM and TC, big- and little-endian parameters, VPD_CHOICE and dynamic housekeeping definitions); the command sequence tables are not supported. The archive is an open format of raw binary segmented files indexed in MySQL or PostgreSQL. Supported standards include ECSS-E-ST-50-01C/03C/04C, ESA PSS-04-106/107/151, several CCSDS Blue Books and PUS ECSS-E-70-41A; protocol drivers cover EDEN, C&C, ZDS Cortex, ESA NIS and SLE RAF and F-CLTU. It also describes a Qt-based user interface, an SVF mode, TM simulation and TC modelling, and the Windows and Linux platforms.

It is useful as evidence of how commercial EGSE products reuse the SCOS-2000 MIB as their database format.
tags: Tools, MIB editors and related standards

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• SCS5 and CCS5 are multi-user products and TSC is the much lighter single-user version; CCS5 is used in EGSE for spacecraft assembly and integration testing, SCS5 for all phases of spacecraft operations. (PDF p. 1)
  • Commanding features include a manual stack, CLTU generation, COP-1 handling and flow control, and command verification history; TM processing includes VC filtering, gap detection, authentication and decryption. (PDF p. 1)
  • The TM/TC database is the SCOS2000 MIB ICD 6.9 'extended', for example with unlimited field lengths, deduced parameters in TM and TC, big- and little-endian parameters, VPD_CHOICE and dynamic HK definition. (PDF p. 1)
  • TC sequence tables of the MIB are not supported; TOPE or command stack files are to be used instead. An online MIB table browser exists and all tables are accessible from TOPE. (PDF p. 2)
  • Automation uses the TOPE language, which includes Tcl/Tk 8.6 and extension packages such as [incr Tcl]. (PDF p. 2)
  • Archive format: raw binary segmented files with header and content, with an index stored in an RDBMS (MySQL or PostgreSQL). (PDF p. 2)
  • Listed PUS support is ECSS-E-70-41A; frame/packet coding standards listed are ECSS-E-ST-50-01C, 03C, 04C, ESA PSS-04-106, 107, 151 and CCSDS 102.0-B-5, 201.0-B-3, 202.0-B-3, 202.1-B-2 and 301.0-B-3. (PDF p. 2)
  • Main protocols: EDEN and C&C for checkout/EGSE, ZDS Cortex and ESA NIS for ground stations, and SLE (RAF and F-CLTU) with the uNIS option. (PDF p. 2)
  • Software platform is C++ on Qt 5.7 (commercial); runs on Windows (tested on Windows 7) and Linux (tested on RHEL7, installed as RPM). (PDF p. 2)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A 56-slide public product presentation by Terma, dated 13 March 2024, on CCS5 (multi-user checkout and operations system) and TSC (single-user version for instruments, payloads and SCOE AIT), part of the Terma Ground Segment Suite (TGSS).

It explains the motivation: legacy European systems such as SCOS-2000, OC and CGS were judged hard and costly to maintain, so Terma wrote a completely new implementation that stays compatible with the SCOS-2000 MIB data model (ICD 6.9 to 7.2) and with SCOS-2000 TOPE scripting, so that users need little retraining. Slides list the supported standards (PUS-A and PUS-C, CCSDS packets and CFDP, TM frames, TC CLTU and COP-1, CCSDS 355.0/355.1 SDLS and ESA PSS-04-151 authentication, CubeSat Space Protocol), the MIB extensions (unlimited field lengths, variable packets, deduced parameters in TM and TC, configurable length indicators, endianness, several synthetic-parameter languages), and the EGSE packet-level plugins (EDEN, C&C, serial, CAN, ZMQ, NATS) and MCS frame-level drivers (NIS with optional SLE, Cortex, NDIU LITE, KSAT LITE).

Further slides cover performance figures, Qt/QML displays and mimics, TOPE (Tcl/Tk) automation and debugger, the archive (RDBMS index plus segmented raw binary files with nanosecond time stamps), history browsers and retrieval tools, merging MIBs from several suppliers, SVF mode, TM simulation from the MIB, TC modelling, AutoPilot and fleet views, constellation and Kubernetes cloud deployment, related tools (TRACK, PLAN, STAT), instrument and payload EGSE use cases, user roles, quality process and licensing.

It shows how the SCOS-2000 MIB has become a de facto exchange format beyond ESOC's own software.
tags: Tools, MIB editors and related standards

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Terma decided on a fully new implementation of compatible products using the SCOS2000 MIB data model, because legacy European systems (e.g. SCOS2000, OC, CGS) were becoming difficult and uneconomic to maintain; TSC is single user (instruments, payloads, SCOE AIT) and CCS5 multi-user (satellite-level AIT and operations). (PDF p. 3)
  • The TM/TC features follow and enhance those of the SCOS2000 MIB (ICD 6.9 to 7.2) and support ECSS PUS-A and PUS-C, while PUS is not mandatory. (PDF p. 7)
  • MIB enhancements include unlimited field lengths, global variable packets and parameters, deduced parameters in TM and TC, configurable length indicators for variable-length parameters, endianness support, automatic TC header time stamps and several synthetic-parameter languages. (PDF p. 7)
  • EGSE packet-level plugins (EDEN, C&C, serial, CAN, ZMQ, NATS) cannot be mixed in one program, while MCS frame-level protocols (NIS with optional SLE, Cortex, NDIU LITE, KSAT LITE) can be combined in any combination. (PDF p. 8)
  • Quoted maximum performance: about 150,000 TM parameter updates/s, about 1500 TM packets/s, about 5 Mbit/s monitored housekeeping and 80 Mbit/s unmonitored data, and about 500 TC/s (TSC) or 100 TC/s (CCS) with verification. (PDF p. 12)
  • TOPE (Test & Operations Procedure Executive) is Tcl/Tk based, with syntax and basic commands derived from SCOS2000 TOPE; it adds session control, TM packet simulation, TC modelling, COP-1 control and frame-level coding and decoding. (PDF p. 31)
  • Archive indexes are stored in an RDBMS (MySQL, MariaDB or PostgreSQL; TSC uses SQLite), TM parameters are stored on change, raw data is kept in segmented binary files with nanosecond time stamps, and every TC verification stage is recorded. (PDF p. 35)
  • MIBs from different suppliers (platform, payloads, instruments, EGSE) can be merged, dropped and loaded without restart, with online viewing, search, filter and patch features. (PDF p. 40)
  • TM packets can be simulated from the MIB definition by inverting TM processing, for example to simulate a platform or act as a SCOE controller. (PDF p. 42)
  • Built-in security support covers CCSDS 355.0-B-1 and 355.1-B-1 extended procedures (CMAC, HMAC, GMAC, CBC-MAC; ECB, GCM, CCM) and ESA PSS-04-151 hard-knapsack authentication with a 'Sentinel1' CMAC enhancement. (PDF p. 44)
  • AutoPilot uses NATS publish/subscribe messages carrying JSON or CBOR, supports constellations of up to 9999 spacecraft and is also accessible from Python. (PDF p. 25)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Version 1.0 (cover date 31 October 2018) of the ESA/ESOC technical note, prepared by the SCOS-2000 GIMUS team, that explains time correlation (TCO) in SCOS-2000. Time correlation relates the on-board time (OBT) of a spacecraft clock to ground UTC. The Packetiser needs it to time-stamp packets and the Releaser to encode time-tagged telecommands.

The mechanism works as follows. The spacecraft latches its clock when it transmits a frame whose counter is a multiple of N (a power of 2 up to 256) and reports the value in a later time packet. SCOS-2000 takes the earth reception time (ERT) of that frame and subtracts the ground, propagation and on-board radiation delays to get the frame transmission time. Adding the latching delay gives the OBT latching time, and the result is an OBT/UTC time couple. The couple is accepted only if the time packet arrives within a plausibility window. Coefficients come from a least-squares fit for a free-running clock, or from a single-couple difference (gradient 1) for a clock synchronised to e.g. GPS, and are expressed relative to the last couple used. The deviation of each new couple classifies the coefficients as accurate, valid or invalid and drives automatic recalculation and reset. A separate check confirms synchronisation against the expected TAI/UTC offset.

The note gives the byte layouts of the ground-generated Time Couple and Time Correlation (coefficient) packets, the SPIDs used for testing, and definitions of every time and delay involved (FTT, OLT, frame radiation and reception times, OWLT, ground delay). It then describes the TCO engine in the packetiser, the client library with its CUC and CDS time formats, and the CORBA TCO server with its MISC configuration variables. See also downlink.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Time correlation relates the OBT of an event to its time as seen by SCOS-2000; it is mainly needed by the Packetiser for time-stamping packets and by the Releaser for encoding time-tagged commands. (PDF p. 10)
  • The TCO server stores the gradient and offset (a1, a0) of a linear OBT-to-UTC function in Coefficient Packets; a1 = 1 for a synchronised (e.g. GPS) clock, otherwise a least-squares fit over a set of time couples is used. (PDF p. 10)
  • Correlation status from the deviation and two configurable limits (accuracy <= validity): ACCURATE and VALID, INACCURATE and VALID, or INACCURATE and INVALID. (PDF p. 11)
  • Testing without real TCO data: packets are injected through the TM-TC Test Tool; the packet chain is Time Report (SPID 1000005), Time Couple (SPID 1000098) and Time Coefficients (SPID 1000099). (PDF p. 11)
  • On-board sampling is triggered by transmission of a frame whose frame counter is a multiple of N, N a power of 2 between 1 and 256; the latched OBT is downlinked in a later frame's time packet. (PDF p. 13)
  • FTT = ERT - ground delay - propagation delay - on-board processing delay; the OBT latching time is FTT + on-board latching delay, and with the reported OBT it forms a time couple. (PDF p. 13)
  • A time packet creates a time couple only if it arrives within a configured interval after the triggering frame (plausibility check); otherwise it is ignored. (PDF p. 14)
  • In automatic mode coefficients are recalculated whenever the deviation exceeds half the accuracy limit; invalid couples are first discarded as rogues, and after a configurable number a new correlation is started. (PDF p. 15)
  • Algorithms: 'free running clock' (least squares, UTC(OBT) = UTC_N + Gradient * (OBT - OBT_N) + Offset) and 'synchronised on board clock' (difference of the last time couple); the conversion is relative to the last couple used, for higher time resolution. (PDF p. 16)
  • The Packetiser supports three time-stamping options: archive filing time, frame transmission time (ERT minus delays), or on-board generation time from the OBT in the packet data field. (PDF p. 17)
  • Time Couple Packet: OBT (64 bits, TDSsunTime), OLT, FTT and ERT (96 bits each: seconds, microseconds, picoseconds), light time delay, on-board frame radiation delay, OBT latching delay and ground station delay (doubles), ground station ID (32 bits) and deviation. (PDF p. 21)
  • Time Correlation Packet: version (1), algorithm (1 = DIFFERENCE, 2 = LEAST SQUARE), synchronisation-check flag, validity, accuracy and synchronisation status bytes, spare, then gradient, offset (now obsolete), OBT_N, UTC_N and display offset as IEEE 64-bit doubles. (PDF p. 23)
  • Frame Radiation and Frame Reception Time are defined at the leading edge of the first bit of the Attached Sync Marker; for SLE service providers ERT equals the Frame Reception Time and the ground delay is 0. (PDF p. 26)
  • Example frame rule: real-time VC0 data with VCFC % 32 = 0. (PDF p. 31)
  • Plausibility check: FTTreport - FarLimit <= FTTobt <= FTTreport - CloseLimit, with MISC variables TCO_FAR_FTT_PLAUSIBILITY_LIMIT and TCO_CLOSE_FTT_PLAUSIBILITY_LIMIT. (PDF p. 32)
  • Auto-reset: after TCO_AUTORESET_INVALID_DEVIATIONS consecutive deviations beyond the validity interval, the time-couple buffer is emptied and recalculation waits for two new time couples. (PDF p. 33)
  • Time formats: TCOtimeFormatCUC is parameterised by the PFC from which the CUC variants are derived; TCOtimeFormatCDS handles CDS; missions may subclass TCOtimeFormat for other formats. (PDF p. 38)
  • The TCO server is a resident process with a CORBA interface and one TCOserverImpl per on-board clock; it produces and stores time-couple and coefficient packets and converts historical times using archived coefficients. (PDF p. 39)
  • To avoid ambiguity after OBT resets, creating a new coefficient packet deletes archived coefficient packets for OBTs within the validity period of the last generated coefficients. (PDF p. 41)
  • MISC variables are duplicated per on-board clock using the suffix '_n' for the nth OBT. (PDF p. 42)
  • Synchronisation check: the expected TAI/UTC difference (TCO_TAI_UTC_DIFFERENCE) minus the current correction must be within the accuracy interval (TCO_ACCURACY_INTERVAL). (PDF p. 43)

docs.text:
The ESOC TOS-GC presentation 'FIRST/PLANCK – SCOS-2000' given to the FIRST and Planck instrument PI groups at ESOC on 18-19 April 2000, as filed in the SPIRE archive with the speakers' other material appended. It is the main technical record of what ESA offered the instrument teams for their EGSE. J-F. Kaufeler (H/TOS-GC) reviewed the state of SCOS-2000. It had been used for SOHO telemetry since 1995 and for Huygens, TeamSat and MTP since 1997, and at the time served Integral, MSG, Rosetta, ERS and PROBA. The rename from SCOS-2 to SCOS-2000 at R2.0 (1999) brought a new telemetry chain, an ILOG MMI, ObjectStore and CORBA. Releases ran from R2.0 (September 1999) to R4.0 (1Q 2002), with the port to PC and Linux in R3.0.

The EGSE section draws on PROBA. One kernel serves checkout (SCOEs, router, SCOS-2000 EGSE) and operations (ground station, NCTRS, SCOS-2000 MCS). The router handled 1 Mbps TM and 4 kbps TC on a Windows NT PC. A TM/TC front end extracts CCSDS packets and needs a COTS encoder shell when the COP-1 protocol is used, and a Tcl/Tk test procedure environment drives procedures through parameter and command interface servers.

The commercial slides cover licences (software free, COTS and hardware bought by the user), hardware and COTS costs, installation, training and consultancy prices, and a maintenance service at 35 Keur per year per user. P. Estaria's project-position slides (PT - 07671) follow. They state that choosing SCOS-2000 was a PI decision and that the project could not fund it. The TOS licence and service note (draft-1) closes the set. See SCOS-2000 as EGSE and Herschel and Planck.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• SCOS-2000 utilisation: past 1995 SOHO (TLM only) and 1997 Huygens, TeamSat, MTP (Eumetsat); present Integral and MSG (successful SVTs), Rosetta, ERS, migration from SCOS-1 and PROBA (MCS + EGSE). (PDF p. 6)
  • Planned users: Smart-1, Envisat and XMM (migrations from SCOS-1), Mars-Express, First/Planck MOC and the Earth Core Explorers (Cryosat, GOCE); First/Planck EGSE and PIs marked '??'. (PDF p. 7)
  • Naming: SCOS-2 until 1998 (up to release R1.4) and SCOS-2000 from 1999 (from R2.0), an evolution with a new TLC chain, architectural consolidation, an MMI fully based on ILOG, systematic use of Object-Store and CORBA-based distribution and external interfaces. (PDF p. 8)
  • Release status: R2.0 Sep. 1999 (Integral SVTs), R2.1 Mar. 2000 (MSG SVTs), R2.2 Sep. 2000 (end of nominal project). (PDF p. 9)
  • Evolution: Release 3.0 (mid 2001) ports SCOS-2000 to PC with an OS shell, replaces Object Store and ports first to Linux; Release 4.0 (1Q 2002) allows multiple SCOS-2000 versions on one machine to support constellation missions. (PDF p. 10)
  • Commonality: SCOEs connect through the ROUTER to a SCOS-2000 EGSE, just as a ground station connects through NCTRS to a SCOS-2000 MCS. (PDF p. 13)
  • PROBA checkout facility elements: EMCS, a router (TM reception, TC transmission, SCOS gateway), a Tcl/Tk procedure automation tool used for AIV and operations, and ORACLE-based database editors. (PDF p. 14)
  • Router performance on a Windows NT PC: 1 Mbps TM input and recording via a DMA parallel card, 4 kbps TC via an RS422 card, CPU load below 15 %, and about 2 % CPU per distributed virtual channel. (PDF p. 18)
  • The TM/TC front end extracts and distributes CCSDS telemetry packets from a digital stream and turns command-packet requests into a CCSDS data stream; with the ground-space protocol the TC part needs a COTS 'TC ENCODER SHELL' (about 10 Keur). (PDF p. 20)
  • SCOS-2000 COTS: ILOG Views, Ctree+, Orbix, ObjectStore and the STL library; run-time licences cost 2200 EUR per client plus 300 EUR per client per year. (PDF p. 31)
  • The TC transmission software shell (10 Keur per PC) is required only if the CCSDS COP1 protocol is used. (PDF p. 32)
  • Indicative service prices: SCOS-2000 installation 10 Keur per site, a developer course 4 Keur, consultancy 14 Keur per man-month per user, and the maintenance service 35 Keur per year per user (including membership of the SCOS-2000 Board). (PDF p. 36)
  • Evaluation history: SCOS-2000 version 0.2 was evaluated on 3-5 November 1999 by the RTA CWG; PACS captured extra requirements in a Delta URD (04/04/00), not yet consolidated. (PDF p. 39)
  • Project position: EGSEs are provided by industry (ESA/IPC(89)126); selecting SCOS-2000 as instrument EGSE kernel is entirely a PI decision, and the project provides no technical support, hardware, software or funding. (PDF p. 41)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A 25-slide status presentation on the PUS-C revision of the ECSS Packet Utilization Standard (ECSS-E-ST-70-41C), given by ESA's working-group convenor Serge Valera, with co-authors from Spacebel and Thales Alenia Space, at the SAVOIR On-board Mass Memory Day on 13 February 2014. It explains why PUS-A was upgraded: 190 change requests, removing PUS-A deficiencies, meeting future mission needs, consistency with newer ECSS and CCSDS standards, ECSS drafting rules with named requirements, and backward compatibility where possible. It lists the working-group members from ESA, Astrium, CNES, DLR, EUMETSAT, Spacebel and TAS.

The slides present the new document structure of about 630 pages: the PUS foundation model, the service type system specification and the service type interface specification, plus Annexes A-D. They explain the foundation model's generic type and generic deployment abstraction levels, and how the standard service type model, the mission-specific service type model and the space-system service model relate. A table lists the standard service types (ST 1-23), with ST 20-23 new and ST 13 and ST 24 'TBC'.

The mass-memory-related topics are:

  • the open options for transferring large data and large packets (keep PUS-A service 13, add a new service 24, or leave segmentation to the lower layers);
  • the three subservices of the reworked ST[06] memory management (raw, structured and common);
  • the new ST[23] file management service and its file-handling and file-copy subservices, which is independent of any file delivery protocol such as CFDP, and how ST18, ST21, ST6 and ST20 interact with files.

Backup slides illustrate request/instruction and report/notification slots, using a [11,4] schedule insertion as the example.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• The PUS-A to PUS-C upgrade processed 190 change requests, aiming to remove PUS-A deficiencies, meet future mission needs, align with new ECSS/CCSDS standards, apply ECSS drafting rules (named requirements) and keep backward compatibility when possible. (PDF p. 2)
  • The working group included ESA (S. Valera convenor, M. de Lande Long book captain), Astrium, CNES, DLR, EUMETSAT, Spacebel and TAS. (PDF p. 3)
  • The PUS-C draft is about 630 pages: foundation model about 30 pages, service type system specification about 320 pages, service type interface specification about 180 pages; Annexes cover CPDU (normative), IEEE/MILBUS real formats, CRC and ISO checksum, and a summary of requests and reports. (PDF p. 4)
  • The foundation model has a generic type abstraction level (service, subservice and message types; request, instruction, report and notification types; transactions) and a generic deployment abstraction level (the space-system service model obtained by instantiation). (PDF p. 8)
  • The service type interface requirements specify how requests travel in CCSDS SPP and PUS telecommand packets, and how reports travel in CCSDS SPP and PUS telemetry packets. (PDF p. 11)
  • Standard service types in the Feb 2014 draft: ST 1-6, 8, 9, 11, 12, 14, 15, 17, 18, 19, plus new ST 20 parameter management, 21 request sequencing, 22 position-based scheduling and 23 file management; ST 13 large data transfer and ST 24 large packet transfer were TBC. (PDF p. 12)
  • Large transfers raise two issues: packets up to 65 KB (CCSDS packets) and memory areas larger than 65 KB. One option is to keep PUS at the application layer, require support for any CCSDS packet up to 65 KB, and leave segmentation to ECSS-E-50/CCSDS data-link mechanisms. (PDF p. 15)
  • ST[06] is split into raw data memory, structured data memory (memory objects such as files and tables) and common memory management subservices, supporting 'flat' and 'structured' file systems. (PDF p. 17)
  • ST[23] has file handling and file copy subservices, and the standard does not impose a file delivery protocol such as CFDP. (PDF p. 19)
  • ST18 can load an OBCP by reference and ST21 a request sequence by reference; ST6 base-plus-offset addressing is extended to files; ST20 allows dynamic creation of parameters. (PDF p. 21)
  • Example: an on/off device command instruction is inserted into a time-based schedule by a request carried in a [11,4] TC packet. (PDF p. 23)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A 35-slide talk by Serge Valera (ESA ESTEC/TEC-SWM, convenor of the PUS-C working group) at ADCSS-2015, reporting the status of ECSS-E-ST-70-41C (PUS-C) shortly before its final draft. The timeline runs from 190 change requests in 01/2011, through over 600 discrepancy reports from the four-month public review of draft DIR1 in 12/2014, to delivery of the final draft to ECSS planned for 12/2015.

The slides set out:

  • the document structure: foundation model, service type system requirements, space/ground interface and service type interface requirements, Annexes A-D, with about 150 generic, 2300 system, 750 interface and 500 tailoring requirements;
  • what differs from PUS-A;
  • the standardized service types ST 1-23, with per-service highlights. ST2 gains register acquisition and low-level commands; ST3 gains functional reporting configuration; ST6 has four subservices; ST11 is re-assessed into ST11, ST21 and ST22; ST13 becomes a simplified large packet transfer for packets up to 65 KB without retransmission; ST20 defines parameters by memory address plus PTC/PFC; ST23 has file handling and remote file copy, e.g. over CFDP;
  • the public review statistics per service, and the main review outcomes.

The second half explains why PUS-C is built on a formal PUS Foundation Model. It uses fact-based modelling (ORM/NORMA) to remove ambiguity and ease tailoring, with an example rule: standard service type IDs are 1-127 and mission-specific IDs 128-255. It also shows ASN.1/ACN code generation (ASN1SCC, TASTE, PROBA-3 ASPIICS), an ESA TRP invitation to tender for PUS-C tooling, and the PUS-FDB prototype database that generated parts of clauses 6 and 8 and Annex D.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Timeline: 01/2011 190 change requests; 12/2014 620 discrepancy reports from the 4-month public review of ECSS-E-ST-70-41C DIR1; 12/2015 final draft delivery to ECSS. (PDF p. 2)
  • Approximate requirement counts: clause 5 (generic) 150, clause 6 (system) 2300, clauses 7 and 8 (interface) 750, tailoring 500. (PDF p. 3)
  • PUS-C standardized service types: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23. (PDF p. 5)
  • ST2 device access adds register contents acquisition, CPDU commands distributed by on-board software, and physical/logical low-level commands. (PDF p. 6)
  • ST3 adds a 'functional parameter reporting configuration' subservice to operate on sets of HK or diagnostic packets with fewer requests. (PDF p. 7)
  • ST6 defines four subservices: raw data memory management, structured data memory management, common memory management and memory configuration (e.g. scrubbing, write protection). (PDF p. 8)
  • PUS-A time-based scheduling was re-assessed into three service types: ST11 time-based scheduling (with sub-schedules and groups), ST21 telecommand sequencing and ST22 orbit/position-based scheduling. (PDF p. 9)
  • ST13 large packet transfer simplifies PUS-A large data transfer to uploading and downloading CCSDS packets of at most 65 KB, with no retransmission. (PDF p. 10)
  • In ST20 a parameter is defined by its mapped on-board memory address, its PTC and its PFC. (PDF p. 11)
  • ST23 supports flat and structured (directory) file systems, with a file handling subservice and a remote file copy subservice that interfaces to a file transfer layer such as CCSDS CFDP. (PDF p. 14)
  • Public review totals: 464 reports by agencies, 156 by industry and 44 by the WG (664), of which 72 major, 413 minor and 179 editorial; 623 disposed and 41 open in October 2015. The foundation model (72) and ST12 (58) drew the most. (PDF p. 15)
  • Review outcomes included CRC as an alternative to the ISO checksum, checksums longer than 16 bits, state machines and sequence diagrams, and a complete remodelling of real-time forwarding control. PUS-C mainly addresses on-board capabilities and assumes generic ground segments implement all standardized capabilities. (PDF p. 17)
  • PUS-C was drafted with fact-based modelling (ORM) to remove PUS-A ambiguities, ensure consistency, ease tailoring and enable automatic generation of software and documentation. (PDF p. 20)
  • Service type identifiers are unsigned integers 1-255: standard service types use 1-127 and mission-specific service types 128-255. (PDF p. 22)
  • ESA uses ASN.1/ACN with the ASN1SCC compiler to generate PUS packet encoders and decoders, e.g. for the PROBA-3 ASPIICS payload and the TASTE toolkit. (PDF p. 26)
  • ESA ITT 15.132.06 (TRP, open competition, publication foreseen December 2015) covers deploying PUS-C in projects with an automatic generation toolset. (PDF p. 28)
  • The PUS-FDB prototype (conceptual model from clause 5, transformed by NORMA into a relational Oracle SQL model) was used to generate the message-type sub-clauses of clauses 6 and 8 and Annex D. (PDF p. 32)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A chapter from ESA SP-1295 that follows Venus Express data from the ground station to the scientific archive. It defines processing levels 0 to 3: Level-1 is cleaned, merged, time-ordered frame data from NCTRS, and Level-1a is Level-1 separated per instrument for the DDS. It then describes the ESOC data processing systems, a delta development of the joint Rosetta and Mars Express systems. The Venus Express Mission Control System (VMCS), based on SCOS-2000, handles TM/TC, command verification, out-of-limit detection, calibration and a full command history, and converts on-board time to UTC to better than 2 ms (time correlation). Other parts are the Mission Planning System, the offline FOP system that imports procedures and sequences into the operational database, and NCTRS, which receives ERT-stamped telemetry from the ground stations, forwards telecommands and collects tracking data.

The core of the chapter for this wiki is raw-data dissemination. The VDDS, based on the GDDS, takes XML requests (standing orders, web interface or FTP request files) in a recursive query language. It retrieves from the SCOS-2000 packet archive and file archive (archives) through a CORBA interface and delivers results over the web, by FTP or on DVD. The VDDS also produces DVDs in the CCSDS Standard Formatted Data Unit format. TDRS (TDRS) extracts parameters from fixed-length packets in the history archive, with optional calibration and validity/OOL evaluation, and delivers spreadsheets. The second half covers the science side: PDS standard concepts (ODL keyword = value labels, catalogue files, VOLDESC.CAT), the archive process (Archive Plan, EAICD, DAWG, a validation tool, three-month data-collection and six-month preparation phases, peer review), conversion of auxiliary data to NAIF SPICE kernels by Perl scripts polling the DDS, Level-1b quicklook with QBTool, and the Planetary Science Archive online services.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Each instrument team retrieves spacecraft, ancillary and instrument data from the Data Distribution System (DDS) at ESOC; ESOC removes errors arising in the space-to-ground transmission. (PDF p. 1)
  • Processing levels: Level-0 raw TM; Level-1 cleaned, merged, time-ordered frame data created by NCTRS; Level-1a separated by instrument as requested by the DDS; Level-1b sorted by data type and mode (uncalibrated); Level-2 calibrated; Level-3 higher-level products. (PDF p. 2)
  • The Venus Express control concept was inherited from Rosetta and Mars Express, with a single control centre and the ESA deep space antennas at New Norcia and Cebreros; the VEX data systems are a delta development of the shared Rosetta/Mars Express systems. (PDF p. 3)
  • The VMCS, based on SCOS-2000, performs command verification and out-of-limit detection, timestamps TM by converting on-board time to UTC with better than 2 ms accuracy, and also manages the operational database and on-board software maintenance. (PDF p. 3)
  • The Venus Express Data Disposition System (VDDS) is based on the GDDS and produces daily Raw Data Media and instrument DVDs sent to VSOC. (PDF p. 3)
  • The MCS receives TM via NCTRS after the ground station has time-stamped it with Earth Reception Time; NCTRS also stores tracking data (antenna angles, range, Doppler) for FDS via FTS and for PIs via the DDS, and forwards files such as station schedules to the station. (PDF p. 4)
  • DVDs are formatted using the CCSDS Standard Formatted Data Unit concept; the OCC archives all Level-1 data for 10 years after end of mission; external access is only via the VDDS and TDRS. (PDF p. 4)
  • The SCOS-2000 mission archive has a packet archive (historical TM, TC and derived data) and a file archive (flight dynamics and planning data); DDS requests come as standing orders, via the web or as FTP request files in a recursive XML query language, and are served through a CORBA interface to the VMCS. (PDF p. 5)
  • DDS online retrieval is for previewing small amounts of data, embedded as a byte stream in the XML response; full deliveries go via FTP, http or DVD. (PDF p. 6)
  • TDRS is a SCOS-2000 external interface retrieving parameters from the History File Archive, with optional calibration, validity and out-of-limit evaluation; it supports only fixed-length packets. (PDF p. 6)
  • PDS labels use the Object Description Language with keyword = value pairs defined in the Planetary Science Data Dictionary; datasets need catalogue files under CATALOG and a top-level VOLDESC.CAT. (PDF p. 7)
  • The Auxiliary Data Conversion System (Perl scripts) polls the ESOC DDS several times a day for orbit, attitude and time-correlation data and converts them into SPICE SPK, CK and SCLK kernels and ORBNUM files. (PDF p. 11)
  • The first scientific data from Venus Express were distributed in May 2007. (PDF p. 12)
