docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The Yamcs Server Manual, release 5.14.1-SNAPSHOT (240 pages), published by Space Applications Services, documents Yamcs, a monitoring and control server written in Java (with RocksDB storage) for spacecraft, payloads, instruments and test equipment. It explains the monitoring and control model: XTCE-style telemetered, derived, local and constant parameters plus system parameters, limits and alarms, command transmission constraints, significance levels and user-defined verification stages. It then covers the server architecture (instances, data links, streams, processors, services, plugins, stream and parameter archives, buckets) and time handling (milliseconds since 1970 TAI including leap seconds; mission, reception, generation and earth reception times).

For a TM/TC engineer the central chapters are the Mission Database and Data Links. The first covers data types and encodings, containers with inheritance, algorithms in JavaScript, Python or Java, command definitions, and the XTCE and Excel spreadsheet loaders, with an explicit list of unsupported XTCE features. The second covers packet input streams, packet preprocessors (generic, ISS, cFS, CSP and a PUS preprocessor for ECSS-E-ST-70-41C with CUC time decoding), command postprocessors (including wrapping of time-tagged commands into PUS TC[11,4]) and CCSDS frame processing. Frame processing handles TM, AOS and USLP downlink and TC uplink with CLTU encoding (BCH or LDPC), Reed-Solomon decoding, COP-1 and SDLS authenticated encryption. Later chapters describe processors and the command processing chain step by step, command queues and transmission constraints, activities and the timeline, services (parameter archive, time correlation, CFDP classes 1 and 2, replication), security and authentication modules, the web interface, the yamcsadmin and yamcsd programs, plugins and the internal SQL language. Because it names the CCSDS Blue Book behind each feature, the manual is a practical cross-reference between the standards and a working implementation.

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
• Yamcs is implemented entirely in Java and uses RocksDB as its storage engine; the preferred platform is Linux x64, and functionality is exposed through an embedded web server and an HTTP-based API. (PDF p. 14)
  • Following XTCE, Yamcs distinguishes telemetered, derived, local and constant parameters, and adds system parameters and command/command history parameters for use in verifiers; XTCE's predefined execution stages are not enforced and users may define any number of stages, each with a verifier. (PDF p. 15)
  • Data links carry three kinds of data: telemetry packets, telecommands and (from the ISS ground segment heritage) processed parameters; built-in links exist for UDP and TCP, and SLE links are provided by a plugin. (PDF p. 16)
  • All CCSDS frame processing is done in data links: a frame link demultiplexes frames into sub-links for realtime and dump data, each applying a packet preprocessor before the streams. (PDF p. 17)
  • Yamcs time is a signed 8-byte count of milliseconds since 1970-01-01 00:00:00 TAI including leap seconds, using the IERS UTC-TAI.history leap-second table; a high-resolution Instant adds picoseconds. (PDF p. 19)
  • Generation time is set by the preprocessor from the packet (or local time with useLocalGenerationTime); free-running on-board clocks are converted with the Time Correlation Service. (PDF p. 20)
  • The XTCE loader is deliberately tolerant and backward compatible with XTCE 1.0 and 1.1; unsupported concepts include Stream, Message, ParameterSegmentRefEntry, ContainerSegmentRefEntry, DiscreteLookupList, ErrorDetectCorrectType, ContextSignificanceList, ParameterToSetList, ParameterToSuspendAlarmsOnSet and RestrictionCriteria/NextContainer. (PDF p. 44)
  • For command arguments Yamcs allows sizeInBitsOfSizeTag = 0 (no size tag) for compatibility with systems such as SCOS-2k, although XTCE requires a size tag greater than 0; float encodings IEEE754_1985, MILSTD_1750A and STRING are supported. (PDF p. 44)
  • If several CompleteVerifiers are declared, the first one to succeed completes the command, whereas XTCE requires all to succeed; command arrays and ArgumentRefEntry IncludeCondition/RepeatEntry are not supported. (PDF p. 45)
  • The spreadsheet loader only accepts Excel 97-2003 (.xls) files; .xlsx is not supported. (PDF p. 45)
  • Spreadsheet sheets recognised: General (required), ChangeLog, DataTypes, Parameters, DerivedParameters, LocalParameters, Containers, Algorithms, Alarms, Commands, CommandOptions, CommandVerification and Calibration; sheet-name prefixes such as SYSTEM1|SYSTEM2|Containers describe sub-systems. (PDF p. 46)
  • Archived packets use (generation time, sequence count) as primary key, so a packet with an existing pair is discarded as a duplicate; Yamcs originated in the ISS world where packets carry reliable GPS-synchronised timestamps. (PDF p. 80)
  • Three time synchronisation strategies are described: no synchronisation (local time), on-board resync at reset (as in cFS) and a ground-maintained correlation, the method specified by the ESA PUS standard. (PDF p. 80)
  • The CUC time decoder follows CCSDS 301.0-B-4 chapter 3.2; time decoders return relative milliseconds that are converted with an epoch, or treated as raw counts for the Time Correlation Service when no epoch is given. (PDF p. 81)
  • The PUS packet preprocessor verifies and identifies ECSS PUS packets according to ECSS-E-ST-70-41C and uses the first 4 bytes of the CCSDS primary header as the archive sequence count. (PDF p. 84)
  • The PUS command postprocessor can embed a command issued with the pus11ScheduleAt option into a TC[11,4] request (optional sub-schedule and group IDs; implicit CUC P-field 0x2e by default) and fills in length, sequence count and CRC of embedded TC packets. (PDF p. 89)
  • The SCOS-2000 MIB loader (yamcs-scos2k) annotates command parameters with (PTC, PFC) = (12, 1) as embedded TC packets; error detection options are 16-SUM (Columbus/ISS), CRC-16-CCIIT, ISO-16 and NONE. (PDF p. 90)
  • CCSDS frame processing supports parts of CCSDS 132.0 (TM SDLP), 732.0 (AOS), 232.0 (TC SDLP), 732.1 (USLP), 231.0 and 131.0 (synchronisation and channel coding), 232.1 (COP-1), 133.0 (Space Packet), 133.1 (Encapsulation) and 355.0 (SDLS). (PDF p. 99)
  • Downlink frame types are AOS, TM and USLP, received by the built-in UdpTmFrameLink or SLE; the MAP service is supported only for TC frames, not USLP. (PDF p. 100)
  • Frames with a version number other than 0 (TM), 1 (AOS) or 12 (USLP), a wrong spacecraft ID, length or CRC are discarded; AOS spacecraft IDs may use 10 bits via the signalling-field SCID extension. (PDF p. 101)
  • Reed-Solomon is the only raw-frame codec: errorCorrectionCapability 8 or 16 selects RS(255,239) or RS(255,223), with interleaving depth default 5. (PDF p. 103)
  • In a PACKET virtual channel the first 3 bits distinguish CCSDS space packets (000) from encapsulation packets (111); idle space packets (APID 0x7FF) and idle encapsulation packets (first byte 0x1C) are discarded, and TM idle frames use first header pointer 0x7FE. (PDF p. 103)
  • Uplink packs TC packets into TC transfer frames and optionally CLTUs (BCH, LDPC64, LDPC256 or CUSTOM); Yamcs does not segment TC packets, so maxFrameLength limits the TC packet size. (PDF p. 104)
  • Since Yamcs 5.5.4 CLTU randomisation follows issue 4 of CCSDS 231.0: before encoding for BCH, after encoding for LDPC (versions up to 5.5.3 always randomised before encoding, as in issue 3). (PDF p. 105)
  • COP-1 options: cop1T1 retransmission timeout (default 3 s), cop1TxLimit, slidingWindowWidth (FOP_SLIDING_WINDOW_WIDTH K, default 10) and bdAbsolutePriority; without COP-1 a TC queue of default 10 commands is used. (PDF p. 106)
  • If initialClcwWait is positive, Yamcs waits that many seconds at link start-up for a CLCW and sets its ground counter vS to the on-board nR; otherwise synchronisation must be initiated manually. (PDF p. 107)
  • Commands with the cop1Bypass attribute are sent in BD frames, bypassing COP-1; BC frames are generated only by the COP-1 state machine; unsynchronised commands wait in a queue or are rejected with a NACK on the Sent acknowledgment. (PDF p. 108)
  • Built-in SDLS security association AES-256-GCM-128: authenticated encryption, GVCID context, 12-octet IV, 4-octet sequence number, no padding, 16-octet MAC, 256-bit key shared for authentication and encryption. (PDF p. 108)
  • The Time Correlation Service fits ob_time = m * obt + c from (obt, ert) samples, using ob_time = ert - (tof + onboardDelay). (PDF p. 169)
  • The CFDP service implements CCSDS 727.0-B-5 class 1 (unacknowledged) and class 2 (acknowledged) transfers between the spacecraft and Yamcs buckets; classes 3 and 4 are not supported. (PDF p. 175)
  • CFDP limitations: Keep Alive and Prompt PDUs are not used, filestore requests are not supported, only proxy put and directory listing user operations are supported, and remote suspend/resume is not supported. (PDF p. 176)

docs.title: The MIB: Mission Information Base
docs.text:
The Mission Information Base (MIB) is the body of data that tells ESA's mission control system SCOS-2000 everything it must know about one spacecraft: every telemetry parameter and how to extract, calibrate and limit-check it, every telemetry packet and how to recognise it, every telecommand and how to encode, check and verify it, and the command sequences and displays built on top of them. The MIB is delivered to SCOS-2000 as a set of tab-separated ASCII files, one file per table, whose layout is fixed by the SCOS-2000 Database Import ICD (EGOS-MCS-S2K-ICD-0001). SCOS-2000 then imports these files into its own run-time database.1

This page explains what the MIB contains and how the interface works. It then maps all 53 tables of the ICD and takes a tour of a real, publicly posted MIB: the one used to operate Solar Orbiter. Related pages go deeper:

  • MIB data model: how the tables reference each other (keys and join paths).
  • MIB parameter types: the PTC/PFC codes that define every value's encoding.
  • History of the Database Import ICD: how the tables evolved from issue 3.2 (1999) to 7.2 (2019).
  • Topic pages on monitoring, calibration, monitoring checks, commanding, command verification, sequences and parameter sets, displays, synthetic parameters, mission tailoring and tooling.
  • One generated reference page per table under MIB tables, and the interactive MIB explorer for browsing the Solar Orbiter data.

docs.title: Static database and dynamic archive
docs.text: The ICD divides the SCOS-2000 Mission Information Base into two parts. The static part, usually just called "the database", holds the definitions described on this page. The dynamic part is the packet archive, which holds the telemetry and telecommand history that SCOS-2000 records during operations.2 The Database Import ICD only concerns the static part. The other sources in this library also use "MIB" for the static database, for example the HIFI team's description of the MIB as a set of ASCII files,22 and that is how this wiki uses the word. Issue 5.1 of the ICD (2001) still called the dynamic part the "history files"; issue 6.7 replaced that term with "packet archive".34

docs.title: The scope of the ICD: generic tables only
docs.text:
The ICD describes how a "client mission" must present its data so that the SCOS-2000 importer can read it. It covers only the "generic" portion of the static database, meaning the data that standard SCOS-2000 functions need. The abstract states explicitly that mission-specific extensions are possible.5 Two mechanisms support this:

  • Extra fields. A mission may add its own fields to any table, but only at the end of each record. The length of these extra fields is limited only by the maximum string size of the computer that runs the importer.6
  • Extra tables and files. A mission may deliver further files for its own applications. For some tables that SCOS-2000 itself does not use, the ICD prints a complete suggested structure, so that mission-specific implementations stay harmonised. These "grey" tables are not imported.8

The Solar Orbiter MIB uses both mechanisms (see the tour below). Mission tailoring in general is covered in Mission tailoring of the MIB.

docs.title: Raw, engineering and encoded values
docs.text:
Three words describe a parameter's value throughout the ICD, and the distinction matters for every table:2

Term Meaning in the ICD Raw value For a monitoring parameter, the value before calibration. For a command or sequence parameter, the value after de-calibration. For a synthetic parameter, the output of its OL or hard-coded routine. Engineering value The calibrated value, for example a temperature in °C. Encoded value The actual bits carried in the TM or TC packet. SCOS-2000 encodes and decodes it automatically according to the parameter type, and never displays it.

The raw value and the encoded value are identical only for unsigned integers. The ICD's own example: a 16-bit signed integer with raw value −1 has the encoded value 0xFFFF.2 The encoding rules for each type are on MIB parameter types.

docs.title: Names and identifiers
docs.text: When an item's unique ID is an alphanumeric string (typically up to 8 characters, such as a parameter name), the ICD calls it a name. When the ID is a number (such as a command verification stage), it calls it an identifier.2 Names must be unique regardless of letter case: A1000 and a1000 may not coexist, and the importer does not warn if they do. Spaces inside names are discouraged.7 Some names are reserved. Monitoring parameter names may not start with VAR, GVAR or $, because the Operations Language uses those prefixes to identify other kinds of objects. The prefixes NNO, CEB, KRU, MSP, VL2, PER, RED and MLG followed by four digits are reserved for ground-station telemetry.9

docs.title: From the off-line database to the run-time system
docs.text:
The ICD describes a four-step activation process:1

  1. The mission's MIB is converted or exported from its off-line database system into ASCII files that follow the ICD.
  2. The ASCII files are copied to a directory that the SCOS-2000 importer can read.
  3. The importer converts them into the SCOS-2000 run-time database format and location.
  4. Each application that needs the data uses it after its next restart.
flowchart LR
  subgraph offline["Off-line (mission side)"]
    SRC["Spacecraft / instrument database<br/>(e.g. SRDB, HPSDB, MS Access editor)"]
    EXP["Export to ASCII tables<br/>pcf.dat, pid.dat, ccf.dat, ...<br/>+ synthetic parameter files"]
    SRC --> EXP
  end
  subgraph scos["SCOS-2000 (per domain)"]
    DIR["Import directory<br/>(configurable per domain)"]
    IMP["Database importer<br/>format, length, mandatory-field<br/>and relational-integrity checks"]
    RT["Run-time database"]
    XML["Sequence and display definitions<br/>converted to XML (from R5.0)"]
    FARC["FARC (file archive)"]
    APPS["Applications: TM processing,<br/>command sources, TM desktop"]
    DIR --> IMP --> RT --> APPS
    DIR --> XML --> FARC --> APPS
  end
  EXP --> DIR

The diagram combines §1.1 and §2.5 of the ICD.111 The ICD sets no rules on how the off-line database is built or maintained. It mentions MS Access as a typical off-line system. Issue 5.1 also named ORACLE, and issue 7.0 removed that reference (change S2K-8137).101213

docs.title: Where missions get their MIB
docs.text:
In practice, the MIB is generated from a larger engineering database that the spacecraft prime contractor or instrument team maintains. The sources in this wiki's library describe several such set-ups:

  • The ICD's own view. Appendix C notes that new housekeeping packets are best defined in the TM/TC database first, with the matching PUS service 3 commands then generated from that definition. ESA missions typically do this in a mission-specific "TM/TC database manager", not in the run-time SCOS-2000 kernel.67 The library sources do not name or describe a specific ESA database-manager product (such as a "DBM").
  • Satellite Reference Database (SRDB). A paper by Intecs and Thales Alenia Space Italia (the PDF carries no date; the newest document it cites is ICD issue 6.1 of 2006)17 notes that SCOS-2000 had become standard in ESA missions, so the SRDB holding all spacecraft data definitions was "almost always" based on the SCOS-2000 run-time database. Their SRDB Translator imports a SCOS-2000-compliant SRDB into the ECHO checkout system. It was first developed for Galileo GIOVE-B, whose SRDB was delivered as a single MS Access 2000 file, and was reused for Sentinel-1 and BepiColombo.1415 The paper also documents mismatches between data models. Two examples: SCOS-2000 numerical calibration curve IDs are Char(10), while ECHO uses integers from 1 to 9999. SCOS-2000 handles logarithmic curves, which ECHO originally did not.16
  • Solar Orbiter. The spacecraft TM/TC ICD states that on-board parameter IDs are defined in the SRDB and are frozen for a given central software (CSW) release.18
  • Herschel/Planck. The Herschel/Planck System Data Base (HPSDB), developed by GMV, kept data consistent between engineering, on-board software, AIT and flight operations.19 An Alcatel Alenia Space technical note describes how HPSDB ingested instrument MIBs written to ICD issue 5.1, and generated SCOS-2000 or Central Checkout System MIB files from its own object model. It lists the constraints that make a round trip loss-free. For example, the output files are sorted by the ICD primary keys, orphan items are not loaded, and every description field must be filled in.2021
  • Instrument teams. For the Herschel (then "FIRST") instruments, which used SCOS-2000 as EGSE, the HIFI team specified a MIB editor. It required one table per SCOS-2000 file and column names exactly as in the ICD, and it described the MIB as "more than 30 ASCII files".22 Their evaluation of ESOC's MS Access-based editor (the "Integral MS Access editor", version 2.0) shows typical problems. In the version they assessed, a polynomial curve could not be referenced from PCF_CURTX, and the VDF table was filled in automatically at export.23

Tools and open-source libraries that read and write MIBs are collected in MIB tooling. The relationship between the MIB and the CCSDS XTCE exchange format and the ECSS monitoring and control data definition standard is discussed on those pages.

Configuration identification in ECSS-E-ST-70-31C

ECSS-E-ST-70-31C requires that any electronic database used to transfer monitoring and control data is under configuration management. The database must carry an identifier, a version number, a generation date, a supplier ID and a list of its files with checksums.24 In the MIB, the vdf table plays a comparable role for identification (see below), although the ICD defines no checksums.

docs.title: Location and naming
docs.text:
Each ASCII file holds exactly one table, which is why the ICD uses "ASCII file" and "ASCII table" interchangeably.2 The rules for files are:25

  • Each file is named after its table in lower case with the extension .dat, for example pcf.dat. The operating system is case sensitive, so the lower-case rule is binding, even though the ICD text writes table names in either case.2
  • SCOS-2000 can control several domains (separately managed entities). Each domain has its own set of ASCII files in a configurable directory, with sub-directories for the synthetic parameter files.
  • The General Domain also needs the files of every domain, plus its own small "multi-domain database". That database contains only multi-domain synthetic parameters.
  • Each dynamic synthetic parameter is defined in its own file. The file is named exactly after the parameter (PCF_NAME), without an extension, and contains the Operations Language (OL) expression.25 For dynamic OL parameters, the importer reads these files from the directory given by the MISCconfig variable IMPT_EXPR_DIR. SPEL-based parameters come from IMPT_SPEL_DIR.26 See Synthetic parameters and the OL language.

Issue 5.1 gave the typical locations as /home/sops1/data/ASCII and /home/sops1/data/ASCII/SYNTHETIC. The multi-domain rules first appear in the later issues.27

docs.title: Record structure
docs.text:
The record syntax is deliberately simple:106

Rule Detail Line format Unix text files. One line per record. End of file is EOF. (The "Unix format" statement was added in issue 7.0, change S2K-7551.13) Field separator One TAB character. A mission may use a different separator, but the importer must then be reconfigured. Empty fields Every field must be present. A null field consists of its separator only, so two TABs in a row mean an empty field. Field order Fixed. It is the order of the "Fi. Nr" column in the ICD. Mission fields go after the last ICD field. Field length The lengths in the ICD are maxima. Shorter values are allowed. A longer value is truncated with a warning. Sorting Some tables have no position field, so their records must arrive sorted. The ICD says so for each table where this applies, for example "The VPD is expected to be sorted in VPD_TPSD and VPD_POS order".28

docs.title: Field types and value syntax
docs.text:
Each field is declared either Number(n) or Char(n), where n is the maximum number of digits or characters.78

  • Number fields take integers only (signed or unsigned). In issues 6.7 Draft A, 6.9 and 7.0, integers may be written in decimal, hexadecimal or octal using the C++ convention. 0x12F4 is hexadecimal, 0767 is octal and 767 is decimal. Floating-point values must be written in decimal. Issue 5.1 still required decimal for everything unless a field said otherwise.83029
  • Char fields take alphanumeric ASCII characters (A–Z, 0–9) plus underscore, plus, minus, dot and dash. Other characters "shall be avoided".7
  • Some fields have no declared length. Their length depends on another limit. This is the case for command parameter values, whose size is bounded by the maximum allowed command size.7
  • A parameter value must use the syntax of its parameter type. Absolute times, for example, are written yyyy.ddd.hh.mm.ss (see parameter types).7

docs.title: Mandatory fields, defaults and presentation conventions
docs.text:
The last column of every ICD table, "Ma/Def", is either M (mandatory: the field may not be null) or an import default, which the importer uses when an optional field is left null. An optional null field without a default is imported as null. All key fields are mandatory. The ICD stresses that an import default is not the same as a default proposed by an off-line database editor.8

Fields whose position number carries an asterisk (1*) are table keys. The table may contain only one record for each combination of key values. The ICD's example: plf is keyed on PLF_NAME and PLF_SPID, so one parameter can appear only once in a given packet.7 The data model page lists the keys of every table.

The printed ICD also uses typography as a signal:78

  • a grey row marks a field that SCOS-2000 never uses. Such fields usually exist for the off-line consistency checker or for historical reasons;
  • italics mark options or fields that SCOS-2000 does not support yet;
  • a whole grey table is not imported at all. It is printed as a suggested structure for mission-specific applications.

docs.title: A real record, field by field
docs.text:
The first record of pid.dat in the Solar Orbiter MIB released on 2025-09-16, with each TAB shown as →:31

0→0→1→0→0→1000002→Bad complete transfer frame→→-1→0→N→→Y→1→N→

Read against the 16 fields of the ICD's pid table, this is: PID_TYPE=0, PID_STYPE=0, PID_APID=1, PID_PI1_VAL=0, PID_PI2_VAL=0, PID_SPID=1000002, PID_DESCR="Bad complete transfer frame", PID_UNIT empty, PID_TPSD=−1 (not a variable packet), PID_DFHSIZE=0, PID_TIME=N, PID_INTER empty, PID_VALID=Y, PID_CHECK=1, PID_EVENT=N, PID_EVID empty. The record ends with a TAB followed by the newline. TYPE=STYPE=0 is the ICD's convention for a packet that is identified by APID alone.32 Two other ground-frame packets (SPIDs 1000003 and 1000006) use the same lookup key and are also flagged valid, which the ICD resolves at import by keeping only the last valid record (see data model).3133 All .dat files of this release use LF line ends only and contain nothing but printable ASCII and TABs.31 The SWA instrument database is different: all 20,552 lines of its .dat files end in CR LF (DOS line ends), although issue 7.0 states that the files are in Unix format.4510

Commands used to inspect the raw files 
# field counts per line, for each table file
for f in *.dat; do printf "%s " $f; awk -F'\t' '{print NF}' "$f" | sort | uniq -c; done
# any byte outside TAB, LF and printable ASCII?
LC_ALL=C grep -c -P '[\x00-\x08\x0b-\x1f\x7f-\xff]' pcf.dat   # -> 0
LC_ALL=C grep -c $'\r' pcf.dat                          # -> 0

docs.title: What the importer checks
docs.text:
The importer is designed to catch only "the most dangerous inconsistencies", not every possible one. Ensuring consistency is the job of the off-line database system. From R4.0 an off-line consistency checker is delivered with the SCOS-2000 test environment.34 The checks and their effects are:35

Check Effect when it fails Field characteristics (type, length) against the ICD Warning (if the warning flag is set when the import is launched). A field that is too long is truncated. Mandatory field (M) left null Warning. The value is set to 0 for numbers and to an empty string for strings. Relational integrity (for example, a reference to a parameter that does not exist) The record is not imported, with a warning. Syntax of command and sequence parameter values against their type Warning. The value is replaced by 0 (integers, reals, delta times), an empty string, or 1970.001.00.00.00 (absolute times).

All importer messages go to an ASCII log file that is overwritten at each import. The ICD gives the path /home/sops1/Import.log.35 The vdf table is explicitly declared mandatory: vdf.dat must exist in the import directory with at least one record.36

docs.title: Import options
docs.text:
Issue 7.0 lists two options:37

  • Full database import (default). This builds a completely new internal database. It can target one domain via a command-line domain identifier. From a specific domain only that domain's database can be imported. From the General Domain any domain, including the multi-domain database, can be imported. The importer cross-checks the domain identifier in vdf against this option.36
  • Check only. This changes nothing and only reports the results of the structure and field-length checks.

Issue 5.1 also offered "Monitoring tables only", "Commanding tables only" and "Selected tables only".38 The 7.0 change log records their removal from §2.5, because the evolution line of SCOS-2000 did not support them.4

docs.title: Sequences and displays live in the FARC (from R5.0)
docs.text:
From SCOS-2000 release 5.0, command sequence and TM display definitions are no longer loaded into the run-time ("POST") database. On user request, the importer converts the relevant ASCII tables into XML files and stores them in the FARC (File Archive79; see Mission archives). Command sources and the TM desktop then load the definitions from there.11 This has two consequences:11

  1. Sequences and displays can be updated without importing a new version of the whole TM/TC database.
  2. The conversion is a delta import. Only the definitions present in the delivered files are updated, and existing definitions in the FARC are kept. Displays created in the TM desktop editor survive a re-import as well.39

The ASCII tables affected are csf, css, sdf and csp for sequences, and dpf/dpc, gpf/gpc and spf/spc for displays.1139 The XML formats are specified in two separate ICDs: ICD-0051 for TC sequences and ICD-5001 for TM displays and printouts.40

docs.title: The database version: vdf
docs.text:
vdf names the database version. If it holds several records, the last one imported sets the internal name and description. The version name is shown on displays and used to make sure, for example, that a saved command stack is loaded against the same database version that created it.36

# Field Type Meaning Default 1 VDF_NAME Char(8) Name of the database version M 2 VDF_COMMENT Char(32) Free comment — 3 VDF_DOMAINID Number(5) Domain identifier (0 to 2^16−1). If null, the local domain is assumed. — 4 VDF_RELEASE Number(5) Database release (0 to 2^16−1) 0 5 VDF_ISSUE Number(5) Database issue (0 to 2^16−1) 0

Fields 3 to 5 appeared with SCOS-2000 R4.0 (ICD 6.0). Issue 5.1 has only VDF_NAME and VDF_COMMENT.364142

The real data shows two quite different styles:

  • Solar Orbiter delivers one record per release. The 2025-09-16 MIB has VDF_NAME=25925PFM, VDF_COMMENT=20250916-CSW3.1.2_MAS7.33, domain 0, release 25925, issue 733. The 2020-04-16 MIB has 10720PFM, 20200416-CSW3.0.3p1_MAS6.51, 0, 10720, 651.3143
  • The SWA instrument database uses vdf as a release history with 70 records, from SWA_00.2 ("Received from MSSL") to SWA_6.3.4 ("Released on 29/11/2021"). By the ICD rule only the last record counts. 67 of the 70 names are longer than Char(8), the longest having 14 characters, so the SCOS-2000 importer would truncate them with a warning.4535

Inference

In the Solar Orbiter VDF, the number at the start of VDF_NAME (25925, 10720) repeats VDF_RELEASE, and the suffix of the comment repeats VDF_ISSUE (MAS 7.33 → 733). "CSW" matches the Solar Orbiter abbreviation for Central Software.46 What "MAS" stands for is not stated in the available sources.

SQL used 
-- solo-2025-09-16.sqlite, solo-2020-04-16.sqlite (column VDF_DOMAINID is named VDF_DOMAIN there)
SELECT * FROM vdf;
-- swa-idb.sqlite
SELECT rowid, * FROM vdf ORDER BY rowid DESC LIMIT 3;
SELECT count(*), sum(length(VDF_NAME) > 8), max(length(VDF_NAME)) FROM vdf;   -- 70 | 67 | 14

The 26 commanding tables split into 3 for packet headers, 5 for commands, 4 for sequences, 3 for verification, 5 for parameter sets and 6 for calibration and range checks of command parameters.49 The summary list in §3.2 names only 51 of them: the printout tables ppf and ppc appear only in their own sections of §3.3.2.7.4752 Each table name below links to its generated reference page. The "ICD §" column gives the 7.0 section, and "PDF p." gives the page in the 7.0 PDF where the table starts.

docs.title: Tables that are not ordinary imports
docs.text:
Several tables are read directly by applications or are not used at all, so a missing or "wrong" record in them behaves differently:

Table(s) Status according to ICD 7.0 pic Loaded directly by the TM packetiser, not imported into the run-time database50 gpf, gpc Not imported. Read directly by SCOS-2000 applications.51 ppf, ppc Need not be imported. They can serve as initialisation files read directly by the application. The ICD notes that printouts could at that time only be defined with the SCOS-2000 editor.52 cps Not used by SCOS-2000. Parameter set membership comes from the other parameter set tables.53 dpf…spc, csf…csp Converted to XML in the FARC from R5.0 (above)11

docs.title: How the families fit together
docs.text:
The diagram below shows the main dependencies between families. The full keys and references are on the data model page.

flowchart TB
  subgraph TM["Monitoring"]
    PID["pid / pic / tpcf<br/>packet identification"] --> PLF["plf (fixed) / vpd (variable)<br/>parameter location"]
    PLF --> PCF["pcf<br/>parameters"]
    PCF --> CAL["cur, caf/cap, txf/txp,<br/>mcf, lgf<br/>calibrations"]
    PCF --> OOL["ocf / ocp<br/>monitoring checks"]
    GRP["grp / grpa / grpk<br/>groups"] --> PCF
    GRP --> PID
  end
  subgraph DISP["Displays"]
    D["dpf/dpc, gpf/gpc,<br/>spf/spc, ppf/ppc"]
  end
  subgraph TC["Commanding"]
    TCP["tcp / pcpc / pcdf<br/>packet headers"]
    CCF["ccf / dst<br/>commands"] --> TCP
    CCF --> CDF["cdf<br/>command layout"] --> CPC["cpc<br/>command parameters"]
    CPC --> TCAL["cca/ccs, paf/pas<br/>(de-)calibration"]
    CPC --> RNG["prf / prv<br/>range checks"]
    CCF --> PTV["ptv<br/>pre-transmission validation"]
    CCF --> VER["cvp → cvs → cve<br/>verification"]
    SEQ["csf / css / sdf / csp<br/>sequences"] --> CCF
    PS["pst / psv / cps / pvs / psm<br/>parameter sets"] --> CCF
    PS --> SEQ
  end
  D --> PCF
  PTV --> PCF
  VER --> PCF
  CDF -.->|"dynamic default (CDF_TMID)"| PCF

The relationships follow the summaries in §3.3.2 and §3.3.3 of the ICD.4854 Commands depend on monitoring in three places: pre-transmission validation (ptv), verification expressions (cve) and dynamic defaults (cdf). In all three, the monitoring parameter must be one that the TM model actually processes: a parameter with a plf entry, or a synthetic parameter.55

docs.title: Special kinds of monitoring parameter
docs.text:
Not every row in pcf is a parameter extracted from spacecraft telemetry. The field PCF_NATUR gives the parameter's nature:56

PCF_NATUR Nature Where the value comes from R Raw telemetry parameter (also a "dynamic" user-defined constant) Extracted from TM packets using plf or vpd D Dynamic OL synthetic parameter Evaluated from an OL expression file P SPEL-based dynamic synthetic parameter Evaluated from a SPEL file. Only in the EGSE delivery of SCOS-2000.26 H Hard-coded synthetic parameter C++ code linked into SCOS-2000 S Saved synthetic parameter Computed centrally by the SPPG and stored in "synthetic packets" C Constant ("static" user-defined constant) PCF_PARVAL

The MIB also describes packets that SCOS-2000 generates itself, because they are processed like spacecraft telemetry and so need pid, tpcf and plf entries:57

  • the constants TM packet carrying the dynamic user-defined constants, which operators set through TM SPACON;58
  • the MISC packet, in which the MISC server publishes selected dynamic configuration variables as pseudo-telemetry. These must be typed as 32-bit signed integers (PTC 4, PFC 14), double reals (5/2) or character strings (8/n);59
  • synthetic packets, which hold the saved synthetic parameters. Each one occupies a 13-byte slot in its packet;60
  • system control packets of the SCTL application. A tool, SCTLgenerateMIB, appends default entries for them to the MIB ASCII files.61

The Solar Orbiter MIB defines exactly such packets on APID 1966, with mission-specific type numbers between 160 and 166 and 251. Examples are SPID 66830 "Dynamic UDCs" (160/3), 66832 "MISC_PACKET" (160/5), 66838 "Saved Synthetics" (251/2) and 66840 "Time Correlation Report" (164/1). It also defines packets with APIDs from 2048 to 2065, named "LMS_CEB", "LMS_MLG" and "LMS_NNO". That APID range is the one the ICD reserves for packets not generated by the spacecraft.3162 In packet 66838, the two saved synthetic parameters NTTSS030 and NTTSS031 sit at byte offsets 0 and 13, which matches the 13-byte slot rule.3160

SQL used 
SELECT PID_TYPE, PID_STYPE, PID_APID, PID_SPID, PID_DESCR FROM pid
 WHERE CAST(PID_APID AS int) > 2047 OR PID_APID = '1966' OR CAST(PID_SPID AS int) >= 1000000
 ORDER BY CAST(PID_SPID AS int);
SELECT PLF_NAME, PLF_SPID, PLF_OFFBY FROM plf WHERE PLF_SPID = '66838';

docs.title: SCOS-2000 and the PUS services
docs.text:
Appendix C of the ICD (added in issue 6.7, change S2K-DCR-5303) states how far SCOS-2000 supports the Packet Utilization Standard, and therefore what a MIB can describe.63 In general, SCOS-2000 can decode and encode every PUS packet type and subtype, within the limits on data types and structures described on MIB parameter types. However, it adds special processing for only a few services:64

PUS service Specific SCOS-2000 support and notable limitations (ICD 7.0 Appendix C) 1 Verification The verifier matches reports to commands through the 4 echoed header bytes, which must be at the same position in every type-1 packet. The subtype-to-stage mapping is mission-wide. Progress reports map only to progress step 0. Failure codes are ignored.65 2 Device access No specific processing. Commands can be blocked at TC segment level, but not aggregated inside one packet.66 3 Housekeeping No specific processing. Every packet must already be in the MIB before it is enabled on board. Sample time offsets and generation intervals are static in the MIB.67 4, 12 All reports are variable packets, so the variable-packet limitations apply (see below).68 5 Event reporting Any TM packet can raise a SCOS-2000 event with a severity and message (PID_EVENT, PID_EVID).68 6 Memory management Handled by the OBSM subsystem. The packet structures are mission-specific.69 9 Time management Time reports feed time correlation (generic from R5.2).70 11 Time-based scheduling Automatic wrapping in TC(11,4), a ground model of the on-board schedule and delayed verification. The packet structure follows Rosetta. Absolute time tags only.71 13 Large data transfer Not supported generically. Needs a mission-specific implementation.72 15 On-board storage No modelling of on-board stores. Packets wrapped in (15,8) are not unwrapped.72 19 Event-action Easier to define with "Command ID" parameters, but the embedded TC uses fixed header values.73

The variable-packet limitation applies throughout. Values extracted from variable packets (vpd) do not take part in full TM processing: validity, monitoring checks, validation/verification and synthetic parameters. The reason is that their identity and time reference become known only when the packet is opened. The ICD therefore advises against using variable packets for regular housekeeping.74 Solar Orbiter's use of PUS is described in How Solar Orbiter uses PUS.

docs.title: A tour of the Solar Orbiter MIB
docs.text:
Releases of the operational Solar Orbiter MIB are publicly posted on the solarorbiter.irap.omp.eu document server. This wiki holds two releases and the SWA instrument database. Their library pages give the original URLs and the time each was copied.314345

The full story of the Solar Orbiter MIB is on The Solar Orbiter MIB and Solar Orbiter SWA instrument database. Every parameter, packet, command and sequence can be browsed in the MIB explorer.

Some observations from these numbers:

  • Scale. The 2025 release defines 126,745 monitoring parameters and 11,150 TM packet types on 293 distinct APIDs, located by 400,792 plf records. It also defines 5,454 telecommands and 3,404 command sequences.31
  • Fixed and variable packets. 9,056 of the 11,150 packets have a fixed layout in plf, and 2,063 have a variable layout in vpd (a TPSD other than −1). No packet has both, and 31 have neither.31
  • Growth. Between April 2020 and September 2025, the number of parameters grew by 24,641 (24,801 names added, 160 removed), packets by 2,123 (2,135 SPIDs added, 12 removed) and commands by 216 (239 added, 23 removed). The number of sequences grew by 703 (790 added, 87 removed) and the number of sequence elements (css) by 53%.3143
  • Unused features. Solar Orbiter defines no logarithmic calibrations, no parameter sets and no graphic displays. The 2025 release declares one parameter group (GRPPAR, "Example for Parameters") but gives it no members (grpa is empty). The only populated group is the packet group GRPHK with 4 packets. Only five static pre-transmission checks exist, all added after 2020.3143
  • Parameter natures. In 2025, 125,161 parameters are raw telemetry (R), 1,582 are dynamic OL synthetics (D) and 2 are saved synthetics (S). The release ships 1,582 synthetic parameter files, one per D parameter.31

docs.text:
Counting the TAB-separated fields per line shows how closely each delivery follows the ICD issues (see ICD history):314544

Table ICD 5.1 ICD 7.0 SolO 2025 SolO 2020 SWA IDB STIX IDB pcf 19 23 23 23 19 19 cpc 13 16 15 15 13 13 cvs 6 7 7 7 6 6 ccf 20 21 21 21 21 21

The ICD explicitly allows pcf records with 19 to 23 fields, for backward compatibility.75 The Solar Orbiter cpc file stops at CPC_OBTID (field 15), which is the layout of issues 6.7 and 6.9. It omits CPC_ENDIAN, which issue 7.0 adds as a future extension.76 The SWA files mix generations: pcf, cpc, cvs, caf (7 fields) and pic (6) have the issue 5.1 lengths, while vdf (5), ccf (21) and dpc (7) have the lengths introduced with issue 6.0.4541 The STIX instrument database v2.26.38 shows the same pattern (caf 7, pic 6, vdf 5 fields; see the STIX page).44

docs.title: Mission-specific files
docs.text:
Besides the ICD tables, the 2025 release contains files that the ICD does not define:31

File Records Columns First values seen ASW_sw_para.dat 105,222 3 a MIB name (77,565 match pcf, 3,676 cpc, 2,221 ccf) and a long software symbol name (e.g. SSEA_SEGMENTS_END_TIME_C) pcf_glob_det.dat 56,631 3 two parameter names (all present in pcf) and a number dup.dat 69 2 an SPID and an APID (all present in pid) s13a.dat, s13p.dat, s13t.dat 7, 11, 12 6–7 labels such as PLAIN, OBCP, TCFA "OMM TC Files (A)"

Inference

From the column contents, ASW_sw_para appears to map MIB names to on-board software symbol names, and the s13* files appear to configure large-packet or file transfer categories. These purposes are not documented in the ICD. They are deduced from the data and discussed further on The Solar Orbiter MIB.

docs.title: Where the real data departs from the ICD
docs.text:
Real MIBs are not always fully within the ICD limits. Two examples from the 2025 release:

  • CCF_DESCR is Char(24) in the ICD,77 yet 2,876 Solar Orbiter commands have longer descriptions, up to 40 characters.31 A standard SCOS-2000 importer would truncate them with a warning, which for a display-only text has no further effect.35 How Solar Orbiter's own ground tools handle the longer field is not stated in the available sources (see tailoring).
  • The header layout NOM_TC uses a pcdf element type O for its "Source ID" field, linked to a header parameter DFH_SRC. ICD 7.0 lists only the types F, A, T, S, K and P.7831 In the 2020 release the same field was still a fixed area (F, value 0), and DFH_SRC did not exist in pcpc.43 See the data model page.

Referential integrity is otherwise very good. All 400,792 plf records point to an existing packet, and all but one point to an existing parameter. The exception is NYM0796V in SPID 66028.31

SQL used 
-- row counts (repeat for each table and database)
SELECT count(*) FROM pcf;
-- parameter natures
SELECT PCF_NATUR, count(*) FROM pcf GROUP BY 1;                 -- R 125161 | D 1582 | S 2
SELECT count(*), sum(NAME IN (SELECT PCF_NAME FROM pcf WHERE PCF_NATUR='D')) FROM synthetic;
-- APIDs, fixed vs variable packets
SELECT count(DISTINCT PID_APID) FROM pid;                        -- 293
SELECT sum(PID_TPSD <> '-1' AND PID_TPSD <> ''), count(*) FROM pid;   -- 2063 | 11150
SELECT count(DISTINCT PLF_SPID) FROM plf;                        -- 9056
-- integrity of plf
SELECT count(*), sum(PLF_SPID IN (SELECT PID_SPID FROM pid)),
       sum(PLF_NAME IN (SELECT PCF_NAME FROM pcf)) FROM plf;    -- 400792 | 400792 | 400791
SELECT * FROM plf WHERE PLF_NAME NOT IN (SELECT PCF_NAME FROM pcf);
-- over-long command descriptions
SELECT sum(length(CCF_DESCR) > 24), max(length(CCF_DESCR)) FROM ccf;   -- 2876 | 40
SELECT PCDF_TYPE, count(*) FROM pcdf GROUP BY 1;        -- run on both releases
SELECT * FROM grp; SELECT * FROM grpk;
-- growth: names added and removed between releases
ATTACH 'solo-2020-04-16.sqlite' AS o;
SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM pcf WHERE PCF_NAME NOT IN (SELECT PCF_NAME FROM o.pcf)),
       (SELECT count(*) FROM o.pcf WHERE PCF_NAME NOT IN (SELECT PCF_NAME FROM main.pcf));
                                                                -- 24801 | 160 (same for pid, ccf, csf)
-- mission-specific files
SELECT count(*), sum(COL1 IN (SELECT PID_SPID FROM pid)), sum(COL2 IN (SELECT PID_APID FROM pid)) FROM dup;
SELECT count(*), sum(COL1 IN (SELECT PCF_NAME FROM pcf)), sum(COL2 IN (SELECT PCF_NAME FROM pcf)) FROM pcf_glob_det;
SELECT count(*), sum(COL1 IN (SELECT PCF_NAME FROM pcf)), sum(COL1 IN (SELECT CPC_NAME FROM cpc)),
       sum(COL1 IN (SELECT CCF_CNAME FROM ccf)) FROM asw_sw_para;

docs.title: Calibration in the MIB
docs.text:
A telemetry parameter arrives as bits. SCOS-2000 first decodes them according to the parameter type into a raw value, then applies a calibration to obtain the engineering value, the number or text an operator reads. The ICD distinguishes three forms. The encoded value is the actual bits in the packet. The raw value is the value before calibration (for telemetry) or after de-calibration (for commands). The engineering value is the calibrated value. Raw and encoded values coincide only for unsigned integers. For a synthetic parameter, the raw value is whatever its OL or hard-coded routine returns.1 In the MIB, calibrations are separate, named objects that many parameters can share. This page covers the four monitoring calibration types, the conditional selection mechanism (CUR) and the command-side (de-)calibrations. Where each table sits in the overall model is shown on MIB data model. How calibrated values feed limit checks is on Monitoring checks.

Any monitoring parameter can be calibrated: raw telemetry, user defined constants and synthetic parameters alike. The only condition is that its raw representation is numerical. Strings and times cannot be calibrated.2 All Solar Orbiter numbers below come from this wiki's SQL queries on release MIB__20250916M25925PFMS001_SOL.32

docs.title: The calibration tables at a glance
docs.text:
Kind Definition table Values table Engineering value Solar Orbiter definitions Parameters using it directly Numerical (piecewise linear) CAF CAP linear interpolation between (raw, eng) points 679 (7,830 points) 3,433 Textual (aliases) TXF TXP text for each raw range 1,003 (35,032 ranges) 26,533 Polynomial MCF (in MCF) \(A_0 + A_1X + \dots + A_4X^4\) 229 970 Logarithmic LGF (in LGF) \(1/(A_0 + A_1\ln X + \dots + A_4\ln^4 X)\) 0 0 Conditional selection CUR chooses one of the above at run time 1,974 rows 907 parameters Command numerical CCA CCS engineering ↔ raw, both directions 99 (1,226 points) 327 command parameters Command textual PAF PAS text ↔ raw, both directions 624 (11,834 aliases) 1,624 command parameters

Table structure from the ICD;34 Solar Orbiter counts from the 2025 release.32

flowchart TD
    A["Raw value of parameter P<br/>(decoded from PTC/PFC)"] --> B{"PCF_CURTX set?"}
    B -- yes --> D["Single calibration<br/>named in PCF_CURTX"]
    B -- no --> C{"CUR rows for P?"}

    C -- yes --> E["Evaluate CUR rows in CUR_POS order:<br/>first row with CUR_RLCHK = CUR_VALPAR wins"]
    E --> D
    D --> F{"Kind of calibration"}
    F -- "CAF/CAP" --> G["Piecewise linear interpolation<br/>outside range: extrapolate (P) or invalid (F)"]
    F -- "TXF/TXP" --> H["Text of matching range<br/>no match: invalid (stars)"]
    F -- MCF --> I["Polynomial, degree 4 or less"]

Selection logic from the PCF and CUR field definitions.697

docs.title: How a parameter selects its calibration
docs.text:
Two PCF fields link a parameter to its calibration. PCF_CATEG says which family is allowed: N (numerical, polynomial or logarithmic), S (status, textual calibration only) or T (text, no calibration).5 PCF_CURTX names the calibration when there is exactly one. It must match a TXF_NUMBR when PCF_CATEG = S, and a CAF_NUMBR, MCF_IDENT or LGF_IDENT when PCF_CATEG = N. It is mandatory for status parameters. It must stay empty for text parameters, strings (PTC 7, 8), times (PTC 9, 10), and for any parameter calibrated through the CUR table.6 Because CAF, MCF and LGF names share the single PCF_CURTX field, the ICD requires that polynomial and logarithmic identifiers never collide with other non-textual calibration names. It suggests a naming convention or reserved ranges to ensure this.1415 The SPIRE instrument team's MIB naming convention, for example, uses one pattern, tttnnnrrr (system element number, running number, real element number), for numerical, textual and polynomial calibrations as well as for the command-side curves.26

In Solar Orbiter, every non-empty PCF_CURTX resolves to an existing definition: 26,533 textual, 3,433 numerical and 970 polynomial references. No parameter that appears in CUR also has PCF_CURTX set, as the ICD requires.32 Most Solar Orbiter telemetry calibration names end in TM: 649 of 679 CAF curves, 931 of 1,003 alias sets and all 229 polynomials. Most command calibration names end in TC: 97 of 99 CCA curves and 547 of 624 PAF sets. This is a convention visible in the data, not an ICD rule, and it has exceptions, such as the telemetry curve CDST0007TC below.32

docs.title: Numerical calibrations: CAF and CAP
docs.text:
A numerical calibration, also called a calibration curve, is a list of (raw, engineering) points. The CAF holds one record per curve and the CAP one record per point.1011

Table # Field Type M / default Meaning CAF 1* CAF_NUMBR Char(10) M curve name CAF 2 CAF_DESCR Char(32) description CAF 3 CAF_ENGFMT Char(1) M engineering format of the CAP values: I signed integer, U unsigned integer, R real CAF 4 CAF_RAWFMT Char(1) M raw format of CAP_XVALS: I, U or R; must be compatible with the parameter type CAF 5 CAF_RADIX Char(1) radix of unsigned raw values: D decimal, H hexadecimal, O octal CAF 6 CAF_UNIT Char(4) engineering unit, for consistency checks against PCF_UNIT CAF 7 CAF_NCURVE Number(3) number of CAP points CAF 8 CAF_INTER Char(1) F outside the curve: P extrapolate linearly from the first two or last two points, F return an invalid value CAP 1* CAP_NUMBR Char(10) M curve name CAP 2* CAP_XVALS Char(14) M raw value, in CAF_RAWFMT; unsigned values in CAF_RADIX CAP 3 CAP_YVALS Char(14) M engineering value, in CAF_ENGFMT, always decimal

Field definitions from ICD §3.3.2.2.2–3.3.2.2.3.1011

Between two points SCOS-2000 interpolates linearly. Issue 6.9 of the ICD states this in its description of CAF_INTER: a value between two points of the curve is interpolated from the points on either side. Issue 7.0 describes only the behaviour outside the curve, by linear extrapolation from the end points.2810 For a raw value \(x\) with \(x_i \le x \le x_{i+1}\):

\[y = y_i + (x - x_i)\,\frac{y_{i+1} - y_i}{x_{i+1} - x_i}\]

Outside the range of CAP_XVALS, CAF_INTER decides. With P, the end segment is extended. With F, the default, the engineering value is invalid.10 The flag belongs to the curve, not to the parameter. SCOS-2000 ignores PCF_INTER, so all parameters sharing a curve extrapolate the same way. If two parameters need different behaviour, the curve must be duplicated.107 The change log of ICD issue 6.9 records that CAF_INTER had existed in SCOS-2000 since release R4 but had never been documented (S2K-SPR-4911).27 The ECSS-E-ST-70-31C data model describes the same "linear interpolation" interpretation function, with an extrapolation attribute whose values are "extrapolate" and "invalid". It adds that every interpretation function must give a unique engineering value for each raw value.30 When calibration fails, the engineering value carries a validity reason. The SCOS-2000 EGSE test language, for instance, defines a VAL_CALIBRATION ("Calibration failed") validity bit.31

The two value fields are 14-character strings. That caps the precision of the curve: Solar Orbiter's longest CAP_YVALS strings, such as 80.59995922672, use all 14 characters.1133

Solar Orbiter usage. The 679 curves come in three format combinations: 612 map unsigned decimal raw values to reals (U/R/D), 66 map signed raw values to reals (I/R) and one maps real raw values to reals (R/R). No curve sets CAF_INTER, so every Solar Orbiter numerical calibration returns an invalid value outside its points. CAF_NCURVE matches the actual CAP count for every curve. 442 curves have only 2 points, a straight line, and 105 have 7. The largest have 229 points (CITP1054TM "Temp_NTC_MOU(PFM)") and 1,024 points (CDST0007TM "Rng_Mod_Index_Sel"). The second one stores CAF_NCURVE = 1024, a four-digit value in a field the ICD declares as Number(3).10 76 curves are not referenced by any PCF or CUR record, CDST0007TM among them. The most common units are A (363 curves), V (73) and degC (46).33

docs.title: Worked example: NMUD1113
docs.text:
NMUD1113 ("IMU11 SIA temperature", 12-bit unsigned, unit degC, 3 decimals) uses the 11-point curve CMUT0013TM "FOG 200E temperature" (U/R/D). The points are real MIB data:34

Raw 430 707 984 1261 1538 1815 2092 2369 2646 2923 3200 degC 80.600 61.577 48.640 38.380 29.475 21.219 13.110 4.649 −4.883 −17.041 −38.255

(Engineering values rounded to three decimals here; the MIB stores up to 14 characters.) The curve falls as the raw count rises. Take an illustrative raw value of 1000, encoded as 0x3E8 in the 12-bit field at octet 69, bit 4 of the packet (monitoring page). It lies between 984 and 1261, so

\[y = 48.63986 + (1000 - 984)\,\frac{38.37965 - 48.63986}{1261 - 984} = 48.63986 - 0.59265 = 48.047\ \text{degC}.\]

This value sits just above the 48 degC soft high limit of this parameter's checks, as the monitoring checks page shows. An illustrative raw value of 400 lies below the first point. Since CAF_INTER is empty (default F), the engineering value would be invalid. The arithmetic follows the ICD rule;10 the raw values are illustrative, not taken from downlinked telemetry.

docs.title: Two-point curves and signed or real raw values
docs.text:
A two-point curve is a linear scale factor with an offset. CAHP0002TM "Motor current" maps raw 0 to 0 mA and raw 4095 to 999.75586 mA. Twelve current parameters of the APMHA/APMHB units use it, for example NAHD0074 "APMHA_Hold_El_current" (12-bit unsigned). A raw value of 2048 therefore reads 2048 × 999.75586 / 4095 = 500.000 mA (real curve, illustrative raw value).33

Signed raw formats (CAF_RAWFMT = I) work the same way on two's-complement values. CAHP0000TM "Coarse position" maps −2048 → −180 and 2047 → 179.91211 deg, and CAHP0009TM "Position" maps −1048576 → −180 and 1048575 → 179.99983 deg. The single real-raw curve, CCFX0001TM "LCL and HTR summed current", maps 0 → −0.1244 A and 409500 → 111.91 A.33

docs.title: Textual calibrations: TXF and TXP
docs.text:
A textual calibration, or alias set, turns raw values into words: 0 → OFF, 1 → ON. The TXF holds one record per alias set and the TXP one record per (range, text) pair.1213

Table # Field Type M / default Meaning TXF 1* TXF_NUMBR Char(10) M alias set name TXF 2 TXF_DESCR Char(32) description TXF 3 TXF_RAWFMT Char(1) M raw format: I, U or R; must be compatible with the parameter type TXF 4 TXF_NALIAS Number(3) number of TXP records TXP 1* TXP_NUMBR Char(10) M alias set name TXP 2* TXP_FROM Char(14) M lower raw value of the range, in decimal TXP 3 TXP_TO Char(14) M upper raw value of the range, in decimal TXP 4 TXP_ALTXT Char(14) M text shown for any raw value in TXP_FROM…TXP_TO

Field definitions from ICD §3.3.2.2.4–3.3.2.2.5.1213 A raw value that falls in no range yields an invalid engineering value shown as stars (****).7 The Herschel ground segment added two constraints: TXP_FROM must not exceed TXP_TO, and ranges in a set must not overlap.24 The Herschel/Planck database tooling also aligned text field lengths with the command-side PAF table.25

Solar Orbiter usage. 994 of the 1,003 alias sets use unsigned raw values and 9 use signed ones; 29 TXP rows start at a negative value. Only 31 of the 35,032 TXP rows cover a real range (TXP_FROM ≠ TXP_TO). The others map single values. The longest texts use all 14 characters. Two sets disagree with their own count: CYCT0002TM declares 2 aliases but has 3, and CYNT0002TM declares 2 but has 1.35

Typical sets:35

  • CCDT0065TM "SCV OFF/ON type": 0 NOT_APPLICABLE, 1 OFF, 2 ON. It calibrates the status parameters that serve as validity parameters for thousands of others (monitoring page).
  • CCDT0011TX: 0 VALID, 1 UNCHECKED, 2 INVALID, 4 BELOW_LOW, 5 ABOVE_HIGH, 6 OUT_OF_LIMIT. It decodes the checking statuses in the on-board monitoring reports (monitoring checks).
  • CDMTX000TM "DEU last received 1553 command", with 1,192 entries. It is one of the few sets with real ranges, for example 134217793…134256128 → MOTOR 1 CLOSE.

A 19,803-entry alias set: on-board parameter IDs

PARAMIDTM "Parameter ID" has 19,803 TXP rows. Each maps an on-board parameter ID to the SCOS-2000 name of the parameter whose PCF_PID has that value, for example 167776256 (0x0A001000) → NCDT00B0 "OBCHP_No_Of_TC_Acc_Succs". A join confirms that all 19,803 rows agree with the PCF. The set includes 0 → DUMMYVAL, a PCF entry described as "ALWAYS_VALID". 1,627 parameters name it in PCF_CURTX. One of them is NCD0C095 "OBCHP_Monitored Par ID" in the on-board monitoring reports, so the report shows a parameter name instead of a 32-bit number.35 Note that TXF_NALIAS is declared Number(3),12 yet this set, and three others with more than 999 entries (CCDT0004TX "Event ID list" 1,419, CDMTX000TM 1,192, CCDT0384TM 1,173), store four- and five-digit counts.35

docs.title: Polynomial calibrations: MCF
docs.text:
A polynomial calibration needs no table of points. SCOS-2000 computes14

\[Y = A_0 + A_1 X + A_2 X^2 + A_3 X^3 + A_4 X^4\] # Field Type M / default Meaning 1* MCF_IDENT Char(10) M name; must not collide with CAF or LGF names 2 MCF_DESCR Char(32) description 3 MCF_POL1 Char(14) M \(A_0\), real 4 MCF_POL2 Char(14) 0 \(A_1\) 5 MCF_POL3 Char(14) 0 \(A_2\) 6 MCF_POL4 Char(14) 0 \(A_3\) 7 MCF_POL5 Char(14) 0 \(A_4\)

Field definitions from ICD §3.3.2.2.6.14

Solar Orbiter usage. Of the 229 polynomials, only 3 have a non-zero \(A_2\) and only 1 reaches the fourth order. The rest are linear.36 The simplest is CCAX0001TM "K to C": \(Y = -273.15 + X\), used by real-valued parameters such as NCAP044A "FSSXPA_limFiltTemp". Many instrument curves are pure scale factors, such as CIAP0007TM "E33VD" with \(A_1 = 0.001612\).36

Worked example. CIAP0081TM "DPU_TMP" uses all five coefficients (real MIB values): \(A_0 = 180.65\), \(A_1 = -0.4018\), \(A_2 = 0.0003508\), \(A_3 = -0.0000001434\), \(A_4 = 0.000000000021\). It calibrates 16-bit unsigned instrument thermistor channels, for example NIA00836 "PCDM_HK_IMON_THERM_A" and NCL3Z019 "S130 Ex SWA Thermistor A".36 For an illustrative raw value \(X = 1000\):

\[Y = 180.65 - 401.8 + 350.8 - 143.4 + 21.0 = 7.25\]

MCF_POL5 is written as 0.000000000021, exactly 14 characters. The Char(14) field limits how small a coefficient can be written without exponent notation.1436 Other Solar Orbiter values do use exponent notation, for example 8.06E-4.36

docs.title: Logarithmic calibrations: LGF
docs.text:
The logarithmic calibration is the inverse of a polynomial in \(\ln X\):15

\[Y = \frac{1}{A_0 + A_1 \ln X + A_2 \ln^2 X + A_3 \ln^3 X + A_4 \ln^4 X}\]

The LGF has the same layout as the MCF: LGF_IDENT Char(10) key, LGF_DESCR Char(32), and LGF_POL1…LGF_POL5 Char(14) for \(A_0\)…\(A_4\), with \(A_0\) mandatory and the others defaulting to 0.15

Inference

Expressing \(1/Y\) as a polynomial in \(\ln X\) resembles a generalised Steinhart–Hart thermistor equation, where the inverse temperature is a polynomial in the logarithm of the resistance. That may be what the table was designed for. The ICD does not say so.

Solar Orbiter defines no logarithmic calibration: the LGF table is empty.32

docs.title: Conditional selection: CUR
docs.text:
Some parameters need different calibrations at different times. A sensor read by either of two electronics units, or by an engineering model and a flight model, has a different curve for each. The CUR attaches several calibrations to one parameter, each guarded by an applicability condition.9

# Field Type M Meaning 1* CUR_PNAME Char(8) M calibrated parameter (PCF_NAME) 2* CUR_POS Number(2) M evaluation order, lowest first 3 CUR_RLCHK Char(8) M applicability parameter 4 CUR_VALPAR Number(5) M raw value of CUR_RLCHK that activates this calibration 5 CUR_SELECT Char(10) M calibration to apply: a TXF_NUMBR for status parameters, otherwise a CAF_NUMBR, MCF_IDENT or LGF_IDENT

Field definitions from ICD §3.3.2.2.1.9

The rules:9

  • Rows are evaluated in CUR_POS order, and only the first row whose condition CUR_RLCHK = CUR_VALPAR holds is used.
  • Applicability parameters must be integer-valued (raw) and processed by the telemetry model, the same restriction as for validity parameters.
  • All calibrations attached to one parameter must give the same engineering format: ASCII for textual, real for polynomial, logarithmic and real-valued numerical curves, integer or unsigned integer for the corresponding numerical curves.
  • Static PTV definitions may not use the engineering value of a conditionally calibrated parameter. The Variable Packets Display and the Packet History display show its raw value instead of the calibrated one.

The ECSS-E-ST-70-31C data model has the same construct in neutral form: a parameter carries an ordered list of interpretation functions, each with a selection condition, and the first one whose condition is true is applied.30

flowchart LR
    S["Sample of P<br/>(raw value x)"] --> P1{"CUR_POS 1:<br/>RLCHK₁ valid and = VALPAR₁?"}
    P1 -- yes --> C1["apply CUR_SELECT₁"]
    P1 -- no --> P2{"CUR_POS 2:<br/>RLCHK₂ = VALPAR₂?"}
    P2 -- yes --> C2["apply CUR_SELECT₂"]
    P2 -- no --> PN{"... last row"}
    PN -- no --> X["no applicable calibration"]

Inference

The ICD does not say what the engineering value is when no CUR row applies. The final box in the diagram reflects this gap and is not a documented SCOS-2000 behaviour. The SCOS-2000 EGSE language lists a validity bit VAL_UNKNOWN_CRITERIA ("Unknown applicability criteria"),31 which suggests the value is flagged invalid, but no source states this for CUR.

Solar Orbiter usage. The CUR has 1,974 rows for 907 parameters, using 52 distinct applicability parameters and 382 distinct calibrations: 1,944 rows point to CAF curves and 30 to alias sets. 865 parameters have exactly two alternatives, 26 have four, 4 have seven, 8 have eight and 4 have twelve.37

docs.title: Example: engineering model or flight model?
docs.text:
The dominant selector, used in 1,718 of the 1,974 rows, is NPWZ0000 "PCDU_MODEL". It is a dynamic user defined constant: an R-nature parameter in the internal "Dynamic UDCs" packet (SPID 66830), set from the ground rather than downlinked.37 Its alias set AYMODELE maps 10 → EM and 11 → FM, among other values. For 859 parameters, the CUR holds one row selecting an EM curve when NPWZ0000 = 10 and one selecting an FM curve when it equals 11.37

NCAB0EP0 "CPS A TLV LCL Cur" (unit A, 3 decimals) is one of them (real MIB data):37

CUR_POS Condition CUR_SELECT Curve points (raw → A) 1 NPWZ0000 = 10 (EM) CPWP3005TM 0 → −0.1127; 4095 → 1.141 2 NPWZ0000 = 11 (FM) CPWP8005TM 0 → 0; 432 → 0; 457 → 0.0201; 517 → 0.05; 638 → 0.1001; 2879 → 1.002; 4095 → 1.4909

With an illustrative raw value of 500, the EM curve gives −0.1127 + 500 × 1.2537 / 4095 = 0.040 A. The FM curve interpolates between 457 and 517 and gives 0.0201 + 43 × 0.0299 / 60 = 0.042 A. At this raw value the two curves differ by about 1 mA. The FM curve is also flat at 0 A up to raw 432, a dead band that the EM straight line does not have.

A second, subtler use: the MAG instrument's mode parameters NIM01028 "MAG Previous Mode ID" and NIM01029 "MAG Current Mode ID" choose their alias set from the instrument software version, NIMD6605 or NIMD6609 "Sw Version Number" equal to 310, 320 or 420. A last row keys on an event ID. The text attached to a mode number therefore follows the instrument software version.37

docs.title: Calibration and the rest of the MIB
docs.text:
Calibrations reach far beyond displays:

  • Limit checks. OCF_INTER = C makes the OCP limits engineering values. This is allowed only for calibrated parameters, and OCF_CODIN must match the calibrated format: R for real curves and polynomials, I for integer curves, A for alias sets.16 See monitoring checks.
  • Displays. The format code N (normal) shows the engineering value: in alphanumeric displays (DPC_FORM) for parameters with one or more calibrations, in the Variable Packets Display (VPD_FORM) only for parameters with a single calibration in PCF_CURTX.17 See display definitions.
  • Command verification and validation. PTV and CVE checks can compare raw or engineering values (PTV_INTER, CVE_INTER), with the restriction above on conditionally calibrated parameters.189 See command verification.
  • Synthetic parameters. A calibrated synthetic parameter treats its computed value as raw. PCF_SPTYPE lets the off-line checker catch synthetic parameters that already return engineering values but are wrongly given a calibration.8 See synthetic parameters.
  • Retrieval. A complete TDRS result file lists, for each sample, the raw value, its validity, the engineering unit, the engineering value and its validity. The engineering column stays empty for a parameter without calibration.29

docs.title: Command-side (de-)calibration: CCA/CCS and PAF/PAS
docs.text:
Commands need the opposite conversion. An operator types an engineering value ("0.25 degree per second", "Standby") and SCOS-2000 must encode a raw number. The command-side tables are used in both directions: engineering to raw for encoding and display, raw to engineering for display. They serve both command and sequence parameters, again only for numerical raw representations.19 The ICD adds a warning that follows from the bidirectional use: a command calibration must be one-to-one, or the raw value for a given engineering value would be ambiguous.19

Table # Field Type M / default Meaning CCA 1* CCA_NUMBR Char(10) M curve name CCA 2 CCA_DESCR Char(24) description CCA 3 CCA_ENGFMT Char(1) R engineering format I, U, R CCA 4 CCA_RAWFMT Char(1) U raw format I, U, R CCA 5 CCA_RADIX Char(1) D radix of unsigned raw values; may differ from the parameter's display radix CCA 6 CCA_UNIT Char(4) unit, checked against CPC_UNIT/CSP_UNIT CCA 7 CCA_NCURVE Number(3) number of CCS records CCS 1* CCS_NUMBR Char(10) M curve name CCS 2 CCS_XVALS Char M engineering value, decimal CCS 3* CCS_YVALS Char M raw value, in CCA_RADIX if unsigned PAF 1* PAF_NUMBR Char(10) M alias set name PAF 2 PAF_DESCR Char(24) description PAF 3 PAF_RAWFMT Char(1) U raw format I, U, R PAF 4 PAF_NALIAS Number(3) number of PAS records PAS 1* PAS_NUMBR Char(10) M alias set name PAS 2 PAS_ALTXT Char M text (engineering) value PAS 3* PAS_ALVAL Char M raw value, decimal

Field definitions from ICD §3.3.3.6.2021 Note the reversal compared with CAP: in CCS the X column holds the engineering value and the key is the raw Y column, as the ICD itself remarks.20 The value fields of CCS and PAS have no fixed length. Their maximum depends on the maximum command size.2021

A command parameter (CPC) chooses its conversion with CPC_CATEG. The values are C numerical (then CPC_CCAREF names a CCA), T textual (then CPC_PAFREF names a PAF), B both (not supported), A command ID, P parameter ID, and N or empty for none. CPC_INTER = E says that the default value CPC_DEFVAL is written in engineering form, which needs a calibration. CPC_DISPFMT gives the engineering format used for input and display.23 Parameters of type deduced take their calibration from the associated telemetry parameter.23 Range checks (PRF/PRV) can likewise be stated in raw or engineering form.22 The commanding page covers the CPC in full.

Solar Orbiter usage. Of the 7,155 command parameters, 327 use a numerical (de-)calibration and 1,624 a textual one. 152 are parameter IDs, 2 are command IDs and 5,050 have none. 316 parameters give their default in engineering form (5 numerical, 311 textual). The 99 CCA curves are mostly real-to-unsigned (80) or real-to-signed (17), and 80 of them have just two points. The 624 PAF sets use unsigned raw values in all but 2 cases.38 Command and telemetry calibrations live in separate tables, but names can coincide: 8 CCA names also exist in the CAF and 86 PAF names also exist in the TXF.38

docs.title: Worked example: a signed rate command
docs.text:
CAHP0000TC "Periodic TC angular rate" (engineering real, raw signed, unit dg/s) has two CCS points: −0.5 → −1024 and 0.49951 → 1023. It is used by RAHD0000 "Go To Elevation Rate" (PTC 4, PFC 7: an 11-bit signed integer, range −1024…1023) in command ZAHG0000 "H-APME_A Go To Az-El", a TC(2,128) to APID 172. These are real MIB data.39 For an illustrative engineering value of 0.25 dg/s:

\[\text{raw} = -1024 + (0.25 + 0.5)\,\frac{1023 + 1024}{0.49951 + 0.5} = 512.003 \approx 512\]

The 11-bit two's-complement encoding of 512 is 0b01000000000 (0x200). For −0.25 dg/s the raw value is −511.999 ≈ −512, encoded as 2048 − 512 = 1536 (0x600). How SCOS-2000 rounds a non-integer de-calibrated value is not stated in the available sources. The end points span the full 11-bit range, so one raw step is 0.99951 / 2047 ≈ 0.000488 dg/s, which equals 0.5/1024.

docs.title: Worked example: a textual default
docs.text: PIC00020 "Mode" (16-bit unsigned, CPC_CATEG = T, CPC_PAFREF = CICT0005TC, CPC_INTER = E, CPC_DEFVAL = Standby) appears in ZIC00010 "MODE_SET" and ZIC00410 "MODE_CONFIGURE". The alias set maps Standby → 0, Engineering → 1, Operate → 2, Boot_Maintenance → 4 and SAFE → 255. Unless the operator changes it, the command is encoded with raw value 0 (real MIB data).39 Each text appears once in the set, as the one-to-one rule for command calibrations requires.19

docs.title: Same quantity, both directions: range modulation index
docs.text:
Solar Orbiter shows how the two sides can be kept consistent. Command ZDSG0019 "DST A Set ST Rng mod idx" carries RDSD0015 "X-Band Rng Mod Idx_A_STD" (10-bit unsigned) with default 0.35 in engineering form. Its CCA CDST0007TC "Rng_Mod_Index_Sel_STD" maps 0.2 → 0 and 6.48 → 1023. A CAF curve with the same name and the inverse points (raw 0 → 0.2, raw 1023 → 6.48) calibrates the telemetry parameter NCFT29H0 "DST TX RNG Mod Idx". The CUR selects it when NCFT29K0 "DST TX Ranging Select" equals 1 (STDESA), and selects CDST0010TC when it equals 0 (PN). Neither curve declares a unit (real MIB data).39

The default 0.35 de-calibrates to (0.35 − 0.2) × 1023 / 6.28 = 24.43. If the command is encoded with raw 24, the telemetry echo reads back 0.2 + 24 × 6.28 / 1023 = 0.347. The difference of about 0.003 comes from quantisation: one raw step is 6.28 / 1023 ≈ 0.006 (worked from the real curves; the rounding to 24 is an assumption, see the note above).

SQL used

Run against solo-2025-09-16.sqlite. All columns are text, hence the casts.

-- which family each PCF_CURTX points to
SELECT count(*) FROM pcf c JOIN caf a ON a.CAF_NUMBR = c.PCF_CURTX;   -- 3,433
SELECT count(*) FROM pcf c JOIN mcf a ON a.MCF_IDENT = c.PCF_CURTX;   -- 970
SELECT count(*) FROM pcf c JOIN txf a ON a.TXF_NUMBR = c.PCF_CURTX;   -- 26,533
SELECT count(*) FROM pcf WHERE PCF_CURTX <> '' AND PCF_CURTX NOT IN
  (SELECT CAF_NUMBR FROM caf UNION SELECT MCF_IDENT FROM mcf
   UNION SELECT TXF_NUMBR FROM txf UNION SELECT LGF_IDENT FROM lgf);  -- 0

-- numerical curves
SELECT CAF_ENGFMT, CAF_RAWFMT, CAF_RADIX, CAF_INTER, count(*) FROM caf GROUP BY 1,2,3,4;
SELECT count(*) FROM caf a WHERE CAST(CAF_NCURVE AS int) <>
  (SELECT count(*) FROM cap WHERE CAP_NUMBR = a.CAF_NUMBR);            -- 0
SELECT * FROM cap WHERE CAP_NUMBR = 'CMUT0013TM' ORDER BY CAST(CAP_XVALS AS int);

-- textual calibrations
SELECT count(*) FROM txp WHERE TXP_FROM <> TXP_TO;                     -- 31
SELECT count(*) FROM txp t JOIN pcf c ON c.PCF_NAME = t.TXP_ALTXT
   AND c.PCF_PID = t.TXP_FROM WHERE t.TXP_NUMBR = 'PARAMIDTM';         -- 19,803

-- conditional selection
SELECT count(DISTINCT CUR_PNAME), count(DISTINCT CUR_RLCHK), count(DISTINCT CUR_SELECT) FROM cur;
SELECT CUR_RLCHK, CUR_VALPAR, count(*) FROM cur GROUP BY 1,2 ORDER BY 3 DESC;
SELECT * FROM cur WHERE CUR_PNAME IN ('NCAB0EP0', 'NCFT29H0', 'NIM01029') ORDER BY 1, CAST(CUR_POS AS int);

-- command side
SELECT CPC_CATEG, CPC_INTER, count(*) FROM cpc GROUP BY 1,2;
SELECT * FROM ccs WHERE CCS_NUMBR IN ('CAHP0000TC', 'CDST0007TC');
SELECT * FROM pas WHERE PAS_NUMBR = 'CICT0005TC';
SELECT count(*) FROM cca WHERE CCA_NUMBR IN (SELECT CAF_NUMBR FROM caf);  -- 8
SELECT count(*) FROM paf WHERE PAF_NUMBR IN (SELECT TXF_NUMBR FROM txf);  -- 86
