docs.title: Other missions and SCOS-2000 users
docs.text:
Most of what this wiki knows about SCOS-2000 and the MIB comes from three mission documentation sets: Solar Orbiter, Herschel and Planck and Rosetta, Mars Express and Venus Express. Many more missions appear in the library sources, usually in passing: in ESA's own lists of SCOS-2000 users, in conference papers on the mission-family approach, in papers on test tools and database converters, and in recent papers on payload commanding and on the transition to EGS-CC. This page collects those statements, mission by mission, and says where each one comes from. It does not add facts from memory: when a source is silent about something (launch dates, current status, the content of a mission's database), the page says so.

How to read this page

Mission lists from 2000 and 2003 describe plans at the time ("development ongoing", "in evaluation"); they are historical statements, not confirmations of what was finally built. No database (MIB) of any mission on this page is in the library; only the Solar Orbiter MIB is publicly available as data, and the queries quoted below run on it.

docs.title: Before SCOS-2000: four generations of control systems
docs.text:
ESOC decided in 1974 to develop a reusable mission control infrastructure. The first generation, the Multi Mission Support System (MSSS; "Multi-Satellite Support System" in the 2007 ESA Bulletin), entered service in 1977 and, when the SCOS-II paper was written, was still used by the MARECS and ECS missions; the second, SCOS-I, followed in 1989 and supported Hipparcos, ERS-1 and EURECA.125 The third, SCOS-II, was a distributed client-server system on Unix workstations; its first client missions were to be Huygens (1997), Artemis (1997) and Envisat (1998).12 SCOS-2000 then replaced SCOS-II.

timeline
  title ESOC mission control infrastructure (as stated by the sources)
  1977 : MSSS enters service (MARECS, ECS)
  1989 : SCOS-I (Hipparcos, ERS-1, EURECA) - packet telemetry, no generic TC chain
  1995-1999 : SCOS-II - distributed, C++/UNIX, generic TC chain
  1997 : First SCOS(-2) missions - Huygens, Meteosat MTP LEOP, Teamsat
  1999 : SCOS-2000 R2.0 (INTEGRAL SVTs)
  2000 : R2.1 (MSG SVTs) : R2.2 planned for September
  2003 : R3.0 (classic and evolution lines merged) : R3.1 planned for September
  2004 : R4.0 planned - multi-mission, full EGSE compliance

The sources do not agree on every date. Peccia's 2003 slides give MSSS as 1984-1996, SCOS-I "since 1989" (packet telemetry, no generic telecommand chain) and SCOS-II as 1995-1999, "superceded by SCOS-2000"; the ESA Bulletin of 2001 says work on SCOS started around 1992 and supported its first missions - Huygens, the Meteosat (MTP) LEOP and Teamsat - in 1997, and the 2000 presentation names the product SCOS-2 up to release R1.4 (until 1998) and SCOS-2000 from release R2.0 (1999).3910 The release dates in the timeline come from the 2000 presentation of April 2000 (R2.0 September 1999 for the INTEGRAL system validation tests, R2.1 March 2000 for MSG, R2.2 planned for September 2000) and from the slides of March 2003 (R3.0 January 2003, R3.1 planned for September 2003, R4.0 planned for June 2004).114 The release history as a whole, including the later issues of the Database Import ICD that name R2.2 and R4.0, is on SCOS-2000; the parallel history of ESA's packet standards is on From ESA PSS to CCSDS and ECSS.

docs.title: Who used SCOS-2000: ESA's own lists
docs.text:
Two ESA presentations list the client missions. The table merges them; "2000" is the presentation to the FIRST/Planck instrument teams of 18 April 2000, "2003" Peccia's GSAW slides of March 2003.1256

Mission 2000 list 2003 list Notes from the sources SOHO past: 1995 (telemetry only) existing (NASA Goddard) Huygens, Teamsat, MTP (EUMETSAT) past: 1997 existing Huygens interfaced via the NASA system at JPL INTEGRAL present: successful SVTs existing see below MSG present: successful SVTs existing (LEOP system) Meteosat Second Generation ERS present: first delivery end 1999, migration from SCOS-1 - PROBA present: MCS + EGSE existing see below Rosetta present: AD phase development (10-year mission) Rosetta, MEX, VEX SMART-1 future development experimental propulsion Envisat future: migration from SCOS-1 - XMM future: MOC + SOC, migration from SCOS-1 - Mars Express future development Rosetta, MEX, VEX Venus Express - development Rosetta, MEX, VEX FIRST/Planck (Herschel/Planck) future: MOC; EGSE + PIs "??" MCS; CCS (EGSE); instrument EGSE (external users) Herschel and Planck Earth Core Explorers CryoSat, GOCE future development see below ADM (Aeolus) - development Vega launcher EGSE - in evaluation Galileo MCS (34 satellites) - in evaluation

External users listed in 2003 were Canada (Radarsat 2, telecommunication satellites under evaluation), DLR-GSOC (GRACE, BIRD), Eutelsat (a new MCS called NEO), the Italian Space Agency (Cosmos Skynet), the Italian aeronautical research centre (an unmanned space vehicle), 20 European scientific institutes (including the Herschel/Planck instrument EGSE on SUSE 7.3) and Japanese telecommunication satellites under evaluation.6 The same slides count "54 Licenses in 3 years" and explain the licensing model: ESA keeps ownership and grants non-exclusive, free-of-charge licences to companies of ESA member states, for peaceful use, with improvements preferably returned to ESA.7

docs.title: INTEGRAL
docs.text:
INTEGRAL is the first mission the sources tie to a specific SCOS-2000 release: R2.0 of September 1999 was the release for the INTEGRAL system validation tests.11 Peccia's slide of an SCOS-2000-based MCS in its ground-segment context uses INTEGRAL as the example: an INTEGRAL monitoring and control system (IMCS) fed by an operations database (ODB) built from the satellite database import, an INTEGRAL overall simulator, a mission planning system, the flight dynamics system, an off-line evaluation system and long history file, and an INTEGRAL Security Distribution System delivering data and CD-ROMs to the INTEGRAL Science Operations Centre (ISOC) and the INTEGRAL Science Data Centre (ISDC).8

INTEGRAL also left two tools behind. Its MS Access database editor, "compatible with SCOS 2000", was offered to the FIRST/Planck teams in 2000 as a database option.1413 The HIFI team evaluated it in April 2001 as the SCOS-2000 Database Editing Subsystem, version 2.0, "also referred to as the Integral MS Access editor"; the developer's answers in that report explain INTEGRAL's choices, for example keys on the first six fields because of the structure of the incoming satellite database, commands with more than 200 parameters, and consistency checking planned in a separate application.17 On the science side, the ISDC in Geneva reused software it had developed for INTEGRAL to build the Planck LFI telemetry handler and quick-look displays.18 MIB tooling covers database editors in general; INTEGRAL's flight procedures and configuration control are on operations preparation.

docs.title: XMM-Newton, Envisat and ERS: migrations from SCOS-1
docs.text: The 2000 presentation lists Envisat and XMM (MOC and SOC) as future migrations from SCOS-1, and ERS as a migration with a first delivery at the end of 1999.12 The 2005 GSAW slides cite software that started as mission developments and was reused widely: the File Transfer System from XMM and the Mission Planning System from Envisat (and database editors from CryoSat).19 XMM also shaped the Herschel/Planck requirements: the annex on the satellite users manual of the Herschel/Planck OIRD "is derived directly from the example of the XMM mission".23 The SCOS-II paper also names Envisat as a 1998 client of that earlier system.2

docs.title: PROBA
docs.text: PROBA, a technology satellite with a 32-bit processor, an Earth-observation imager and experiments in on-board autonomy and planning, used a 2-m antenna at Redu independent of the ESA network.15 Its common EGSE and mission control system was built on SCOS 2 with an ORACLE database extended to the SCOE equipment, a router written in Delphi, LabVIEW applications and a Tcl/Tk procedure language; the router and Tcl/Tk tool were then offered to the FIRST/Planck teams.1513 The EGSE & Mission Control System (EMCS) delivered to the Herschel/Planck instrument teams states that it is "based on the PROBA approach, but uses SCOS 2000 in place of SCOS 2", and that the MS-Windows EGSE router developed by ESTEC for PROBA was not used on Herschel/Planck.16 See SCOS-2000 as EGSE.

docs.title: SMART-1
docs.text: SMART-1 appears in both client lists (an experimental propulsion mission due for launch in 2003 in the 2003 list) and, with Rosetta and Mars Express, among the planetary missions for which ESA decided early to archive data in NASA's Planetary Data System (PDS) format.12524

docs.title: The Earth Explorer family: CryoSat, GOCE, Aeolus and Swarm
docs.text:
The Earth Explorer missions form ESOC's Earth observation family: low orbits (250-800 km), often polar, with about 15 short passes of about 10 minutes a day over a single station, and very similar operational concepts despite different platforms.26 Their on-board time management illustrates the differences: CryoSat synchronises its time via the French DORIS payload and ground beacons, GOCE uses an on-board counter kept in step by the ground, and Aeolus has a GPS receiver in addition to its counter.26 The 2007 article records that CryoSat, the first Earth Explorer Opportunity mission, was lost in a launch failure in October 2005, that GOCE was foreseen for launch at the end of 2007 and Aeolus in 2008, and lists CryoSat-2, Swarm, EarthCARE and the GMES Sentinels as future members.26

For this family ESOC used a three-layer delta approach, inserting an Earth Explorer Mission Kernel between SCOS-2000 and each mission.27 CryoSat was the first mission specified as a delta against SCOS-2000, GOCE as a delta against CryoSat (which defined the kernel in practice), and Aeolus as a delta against the kernel.20

Requirements at definition phase Kernel Mission-specific Total CryoSat SRD 406 35 441 GOCE SRD 129 62 191 Aeolus SRS 57 115 172 Total 592 212 804

The table reproduces the counts on the GSAW 2005 slide.21 The same slides list what each mission contributed to the kernel: CryoSat brought an off-line database editor and consistency checker, command and parameter identifier extensions, playback telemetry processing with command verification, a mission planning system, the file transfer system, handling of bad time quality per virtual channel, configurable on-board software maintenance, on-board queue dump processing, XML-based ground interface files and the prime/backup real-time plus off-line archive server architecture; GOCE added planning enhancements, telemetry gap identification, task parameter files with microsecond times, automatic telemetry replay and a time correlator; Aeolus added weekly playback consolidation, OBSM enhancements, orbital coordinates and automatic NIS schedule execution.22

CryoSat also changed SCOS-2000 itself. In 2002 ESOC reported that CryoSat had implemented a range of SPIDs for service 1 report packets (Rosetta had allowed any SPID), to be integrated in R3.1.29 The MIB ICD records a "Cryosat special command/sequence parameter types repatriation" in ICD version 6.0: command or sequence parameters of type Command ID (encoded automatically as the raw data of another command), of type Parameter ID (encoded as a telemetry parameter's on-board identifier) and a default sub-schedule ID for time-tagged commands in the ccf and csf tables; ICD 6.1 also integrated a sustaining DCR labelled CRY-OG-655 (DCR 3398) that updated the descriptions of PID_PI1_VAL and PID_PI2_VAL - the "CRY" prefix suggests CryoSat, but the annex does not say so.3031

The three CryoSat features are used by Solar Orbiter today. In the September 2025 release, 2 command parameters have CPC_CATEG = A (Command ID: "Complete TC packet" and "TC to send upon event"), used for example by ZCD00B04 "Insert Telecommands in Command Schedule", TC(11,4), and by event-action definitions such as ZCS01301, TC(19,1); 152 parameters have CPC_CATEG = P (Parameter ID); and 5 304 of 5 454 commands and all 3 404 sequences give a sub-schedule ID.343233

SQL used (CryoSat-heritage features in the Solar Orbiter MIB) 
-- solo-2025-09-16.sqlite
SELECT CPC_CATEG, count(*) FROM cpc GROUP BY 1;            -- A 2, P 152, C 327, T 1624, N 4991, '' 59
SELECT CPC_NAME, CPC_DESCR FROM cpc WHERE CPC_CATEG = 'A';  -- PCD0B044, PCD13013
SELECT c.CDF_CNAME, f.CCF_DESCR, f.CCF_TYPE, f.CCF_STYPE FROM cdf c JOIN ccf f ON f.CCF_CNAME = c.CDF_CNAME
 WHERE c.CDF_PNAME IN (SELECT CPC_NAME FROM cpc WHERE CPC_CATEG = 'A');
SELECT count(*), count(nullif(CCF_SUBSCHEDID, '')) FROM ccf;  -- 5454 | 5304
SELECT count(*), count(nullif(CSF_SUBSCHEDID, '')) FROM csf;  -- 3404 | 3404

Swarm, a constellation of three Earth magnetic field satellites launched in 2013, is the first mission ESOC is migrating to an EGS-CC-based MCS (see the last section).59

docs.title: Galileo
docs.text: Peccia's 2003 list has a Galileo MCS for 34 satellites "in evaluation".5 Two later papers show Galileo using SCOS-2000-format databases in testing. Thales Alenia Space Italia and Intecs wrote the first version of their SRDB Translator for the Galileo GIOVE-B project, whose satellite reference database was a mission-tailored SCOS-2000 database delivered as a single MS Access 2000 file and validated with TAS-I's own ECHO checkout system.36 Terma's CMDVS monitoring and control system, compatible with the SCOS-2000 database and test language, was used at payload or instrument level on Galileo FOC, and a Galileo FOC thermal monitoring SCOE ran it on a small low-power PC.3942

docs.title: Sentinel-1, Sentinel-2, EarthCARE and SGEO
docs.text:
The Comi paper explains why converters exist at all: SCOS-2000 had become a standard for ESA mission control centres and in most cases for EGSE, so satellite reference databases were "almost always" based on the SCOS-2000 run-time database.35 For Sentinel-1, where TAS-I validated at satellite level and a SCOS-2000 database was an imposed requirement, an enhanced SRDB Translator let the AIV team keep using ECHO.3637 Terma reports CMDVS at payload or instrument level on Sentinel-1, Sentinel-2, EarthCARE and SGEO (and BepiColombo and Galileo FOC).39 A small trace of Sentinel-2 reached Solar Orbiter: issue 2 of the Solar Orbiter packet structure ICD updated its APID table "based on SW donor being Sentinel 2".43

Terma's paper also gives numbers that matter for anyone building on SCOS-2000 as EGSE: the SCOS-2000 telecommand chain handled 2 packets per second with checking or 20 without; CMDVS supports all SCOS-2000 verification stages plus a finalisation stage, with up to 64 stages configurable by mask; and the MIB interface was described as "not perfectly normalized" but well known and understood.4041

docs.title: BepiColombo
docs.text:
In 2007 ESOC expected BepiColombo (then due for launch to Mercury in 2013) and Solar Orbiter (2015) to join the interplanetary family of Rosetta, Mars Express and Venus Express.28 A 2025 paper gives the launch as October 2018, in cooperation with JAXA, followed by a 7.2-year cruise with nine planetary flybys.50 The documents in this library show how closely BepiColombo and Solar Orbiter are tied on the ground:

  • the Solar Orbiter Data Delivery ICD was tidied up and aligned "with the BepiColombo DDID" in its issue 1 revision 2, refers time correlation to a BepiColombo technical note, lists a "(Solar Orbiter/BepiColombo) Packetiser ICD" and the "BepiColombo and Solar-Orbiter MCS SRS" among its documents, and says that the two missions share the EDDS backup server;454647
  • the Solar Orbiter packet structure ICD, in the definition of the telecommand acknowledgement flags, still reads "The bit settings defined for BepiColombo are as follows";44
  • TAS-I used the Sentinel-1 version of its SRDB Translator on BepiColombo to import SCOS-2000 databases for on-board computer and mass-memory tests; those databases followed an earlier ICD issue and needed added columns before import. The paper's metrics for the two databases are:38
BepiColombo database OBC SSMM Approximate number of records 10 000 10 000 Parameters 3 745 1 947 TM packets 521 1 921 TM samples 2 944 2 540 TC packets 399 535 TC samples 427 1 445

Inference

The leftover BepiColombo sentence in the Solar Orbiter ICD and the shared packetiser ICD suggest that the Solar Orbiter TM/TC definitions were derived from BepiColombo's. The sources state the shared documents, not the derivation.

During the cruise, BepiColombo instrument teams send their commanding requests to the MOC as Command Request Files (CRFs): Payload Operations Requests (PORs) and Payload Direct Operations Requests (PDORs). Since launch more than about 1 500 of them were produced with SPOT Cruise, a web tool built at ESAC that checks each request against the applicable MIB, handles MIB updates and conflicts, and delivers the CRF to ESOC's mission planning and control systems.5051 The paper expands MIB as "Mission Information Database" and explains the motivation: before this centralised framework, users' own CRF tools often clashed with the MIB and the ESOC ICDs, causing long exchanges with the flight control team.49 When ESOC started developing its EGS-CC based systems, the BepiColombo simulator was the mission simulator used for parallel test sessions.55

docs.title: JUICE
docs.text: JUICE, launched in April 2023 and due at Jupiter in 2031, adapted the BepiColombo CRF editor in 2021 as SPOT JUICE, without the 3D flyby visualisation, procedure builder and simulation functions; it supported payload ground testing, near-Earth commissioning, six-monthly check-outs and the Lunar-Earth gravity assist of August 2024, with more than about 700 requests.52 Hera and Ariel have shown interest in the framework.53 In 2019 the JUICE MCS (J-MCS) was "the first target mission control system to be developed based on EGOS-CC", with a pilot to demonstrate maturity before a commitment due in September 2019.54 Whether that commitment was confirmed for JUICE is not stated in the available sources; the 2025 SpaceOps paper names Swarm and Ariel as the first EGS-CC missions.59

docs.title: Solar Orbiter
docs.text: Solar Orbiter has its own pages: Solar Orbiter, the Solar Orbiter MIB, its use of PUS and the SWA instrument database.

docs.title: The EGS-CC era
docs.text:
For decades ESOC has monitored and controlled satellites with SCOS-2000 and complementary products forming the MICONYS (MIssion CONtrol sYStem) suite; the 2025 SpaceOps paper states that "the signs of obsolescence of SCOS-2000 based solutions can no longer be ignored".56 In April 2024 ESOC re-confirmed that the next-generation MCS will be based on the European Ground Systems Common Core (EGS-CC); the transition is predicted to take at least 7 years from the first operational use of EGS-CC (in 2026), which puts the end of life of SCOS no earlier than 2033, driven by the number of missions involved (above 40).5758 Swarm was chosen as the pilot for migrating a flying mission at no risk, with SCOS-2000 still available in parallel; Ariel (first SVTs in 2027, launch in 2029) is to be the first mission prepared for launch on the new system.59

The migration of tailoring data is planned in three categories:60

Category Tailoring data Tools 1 (e.g. Swarm) Native SCOS-2000 MIB, converted on import into the EGS-CC tailoring data model (TDM) S2K generation tools MOIS, ProToS, MATIS, DABYS, FOPPER; OPEN-M as intermediate; may stay in category 1 2 (Ariel expected, to be confirmed) Originally an S2K MIB, fully migrated to EGS-CC formats with converters OPEN-M replaces MOIS, MATIS preparation, ProToS, FOPPER, DABYS and other MIB tools 3 (new missions) Delivered by industry directly in EGS-CC TDM format everything in OPEN-M, also for AIV

Current work for Swarm covers commanding-chain enhancements (pre-release checks), playback telemetry, SLE link handling, historical data retrieval, a refurbished time correlation and on-board queue modelling; file-based operations, on-board software maintenance, security and PUS-C use cases (with the Generic Operational Interface Requirements) come next, with a fully operational solution expected in 2027.61 The ancillary products and the EGS-CC context are described on Ancillary systems, MICONYS and the move to EGS-CC, and the OPEN preparation environment on operations preparation; how a MIB maps to other data models is discussed on XTCE and ECSS-E-ST-70-31C.

docs.title: Mission identifiers in SCOS-2000 headers
docs.text: The SCOS-2000 packet header that ESOC archives and delivers to users carries a spacecraft ID and an MCS mission ID; for Solar Orbiter both are 650, and the DDID adds that the mission ID should not be used by external users.48 The values used by other missions (for example BepiColombo or JUICE) are not stated in the available sources; this wiki has no library document that lists them.

docs.title: Rosetta, Mars Express and Venus Express
docs.text:
Rosetta (launched March 2004 towards comet Churyumov-Gerasimenko), Mars Express (launched June 2003) and Venus Express (launched November 2005) form ESOC's interplanetary mission family: missions on Earth-escape trajectories that share a common spacecraft platform, and therefore the same processors and major software functions, similar sensors, actuators and mass-memory interfaces, reused payloads, similar autonomy and identical operator interaction with the mission control system.1 The three ground segments were built as one: Rosetta and Mars Express share near-identical data management systems and on-board software, most data-system components were developed jointly, and Venus Express was a delta development of the existing system.116 One set of interface documents serves all three missions - the Data Delivery Interface Document carries three document numbers, RO-ESC-IF-5003, MEX-ESC-IF-5003 and VEX-ESC-IF-5003.16

This page describes that family's data systems as the public documents show them: the SCOS-2000 based Mission Control System (RMCS, MEMCS, VMCS), the GDDS-based Data Disposition System that delivered data to the principal investigators (PIs), the formats of everything that crossed that interface, the interface to flight dynamics (including the mission's MIB extensions), the interface to the ground station IF and modem system, and the lessons that went back into SCOS-2000 and on to Solar Orbiter.

Sources on this page

The library holds the DDID issue C2 (21/02/2006, copied 2026-11-05 14:12:01 UTC from the NASA PDS Small Bodies Node), its XML-schema Appendix I issue C3 (21/08/2007, copied 14:12:03 UTC), the older Rosetta/Mars Express issue B5 (2003/03/27, copied 14:12:08 UTC from ESA's Planetary Science Archive), the MCS-FDS ICD RO-ESC-ID-5003 issue B1 (2003-03-07), the IFMS-OCC ICD issue 11.4.0 (2006-08-09) and the Mars Express (ESA SP-1291) and Venus Express (ESA SP-1295) data-handling chapters. Original URLs, copy times and checksums are on each library page and on Sources and copies.

docs.title: One family, one system: the delta approach
docs.text:
ESOC's "mission family" concept groups missions with a high degree of commonality in platform or operational profile; at the time of the 2007 ESA Bulletin article the families in use were interplanetary, Earth observation, observatory and navigation.1 Interplanetary missions need things that Earth-orbiting missions do not: long signal delays must be taken into account in telecommand verification and telemetry time-stamping, special commanding protocols such as file transfer handle the delayed space-ground interaction, and the MCS must cope with two or more parallel data streams - one real-time and one or more carrying the telemetry recorded during long non-coverage periods.1 The GSAW 2005 view of the same idea summarises the planetary family as "long propagation delay, on-board autonomy".4

flowchart TB
  subgraph L3["Mission-specific layer"]
    R["Rosetta MCS (RMCS)"]
    M["Mars Express MCS (MEMCS)"]
    V["Venus Express MCS (VMCS)"]
  end
  K["Interplanetary family kernel<br/>(introduced later; Rosetta migrated in months,<br/>Mars Express in weeks)"]
  S["SCOS-2000 infrastructure<br/>(e.g. release 3.1 for VEX at launch)"]
  R --> K
  M --> K
  V --> K
  K --> S

For the interplanetary MCS a two-layer delta approach was used: effectively one system that could serve each of the three missions by reconfiguration, so that the effort for one mission covered all three.2 For the family's operational simulators, the article adds, the teething problems of immature or late on-board software and early spacecraft documentation were mainly borne by the first mission of the family, Rosetta.2 When Venus Express was preparing for launch its MCS used the then most recent SCOS-2000 (version 3.1) while the flying Rosetta and Mars Express stayed on the previous version; after Venus Express validation, migrating Rosetta to the new interplanetary kernel took a few months and Mars Express only a few weeks.3

Inference

The article calls the original interplanetary MCS approach "two-layer" (one reconfigurable system above SCOS-2000) and later speaks of a "new interplanetary kernel". Drawing that kernel as a separate layer between the missions and SCOS-2000, as in the diagram above, is this wiki's reading of those two statements.

docs.title: The ground segment
docs.text:
The Mars Express and Venus Express chapters describe the same Operations Control Centre (OCC) architecture:611

  • the Mission Control System (MCS; VMCS for Venus Express), based on SCOS-2000, which exchanges telemetry and telecommands with the ground stations, processes housekeeping in real time (command verification, out-of-limits checks), converts on-board time to UTC with an accuracy better than 2 ms, calibrates parameters, pre-transmission-validates and sends commands, keeps a complete command history and manages the operational database and the on-board software;
  • the Data Disposition (or Distribution) System (DDS; VDDS for Venus Express), based on the Generic Data Disposition System (GDDS), for remote near-real-time and off-line access by the scientific community and for the regular production of raw data media;
  • the mission-specific Mission Planning System (MPS), producing machine-readable schedules for the spacecraft and the ground stations;
  • the off-line Flight Operations Procedure (FOP) system, whose procedures and command sequences are imported into the operational database;
  • for Venus Express, the Telemetry Data Retrieval System (TDRS), giving authorised users intranet and internet access to telemetry parameter values.11

Telemetry reaches the MCS through the Network Controller and Telemetry Receiver System (NCTRS), after the station has time-stamped it with the Earth Reception Time (ERT); NCTRS also forwards telecommands, stores tracking data (antenna angles, range, Doppler) for the Flight Dynamics System via the File Transfer System and for the PIs via the DDS, and sends station files such as antenna pointing data.712

flowchart LR
  GS["ESA deep-space stations<br/>(New Norcia, Cebreros)<br/>and NASA DSN"] -- "TM frames + ERT" --> NC["NCTRS / NIS"]
  NC -- "TC" --> GS
  NC <--> MCS["MCS on SCOS-2000<br/>(RMCS / MEMCS / VMCS)"]
  MCS --> DAS[("Data Archive System:<br/>packet archive (TM, TC, derived)<br/>+ file archive (FD, planning)")]
  FDS["Flight Dynamics (ORATOS)"] -- "aux files, OWLT, FDR/DOR" --> MCS
  NC -- "tracking files (IFMS)" --> MCS
  MPS["Mission Planning System"] --> MCS
  FOP["FOP system"] --> MCS
  DAS -- "CORBA retrievals" --> DDS["DDS (GDDS)<br/>front-end LAN"]
  DAS --> TDRS["TDRS (VEX)<br/>parameter retrieval"]
  DDS -- "Web / FTP<br/>XML requests" --> PI["PI teams"]
  DDS -- "CD-ROM (MEX) / DVD (VEX)" --> PI
  PI -- "PDS datasets" --> PSA[("Planetary Science Archive")]

The diagram combines the OCC component lists, the GDDS description and the MCS-FDS interface.691470 Data levels used in the archive plans are: Level 0 raw telemetry at the station, Level 1 cleaned, merged and time-ordered packets, Level 1a separated by instrument (what the DDS delivers), Level 1b sorted by data type and mode by the instrument team, Level 2 calibrated and Level 3 higher-level products; datasets follow NASA's Planetary Data System (PDS) standard before ingestion into ESA's Planetary Science Archive (PSA).1015 The OCC archives all Level 1 data for ten years after the end of the mission.813

docs.title: How the GDDS works
docs.text: The DDS lets PIs and other external users request data extracted from the mission archives maintained by the SCOS-2000 kernel. That archive has two parts: a packet archive with historical telemetry, telecommand and derived data, and a file archive with flight dynamics and planning data; a SCOS-2000 file generation process can also create file-based summaries such as command history reports.914 Requests arrive in three ways - scheduled "standing orders", the web interface, or request files sent by FTP - and are expressed in a recursive XML query language, used internally and exposed on the FTP interface, which allows filters to be combined.9 A central DDS server keeps a request list, initiates (often several) low-level archive retrievals from the MCS over a CORBA interface and collates the results into a single delivery per request; it also keeps the database of authorised users and their delivery addresses.914 Delivery is on line through the web interface (for previewing small amounts, embedded as a byte stream in the XML response), by FTP, or on physical media.914 The general GDDS concept and its successor EDDS are described on GDDS and mission DDIDs and EDDS.

docs.title: Purpose and history
docs.text:
The DDID defines the data delivery interface between the RMCS, MEMCS and VMCS and their science communities: requests for on-line data sent by PIs, the on-line data sent back, and the off-line full data sets on Raw Data Media (RDMs). Together with the Command Request Interface Document (CRID, RO-ESC-IF-0004) it defines the complete interface between the MCS and the science communities, and it is "broadly based on the Cluster DDID".1824 Its applicable documents include CCSDS 620.0-B-2.1 (SFDU structure and construction rules), ESA PSS-04-106 (packet telemetry) and the Rosetta/MEX and VEX generic TM/TC ICDs; the reference documents include CCSDS 301.0-B-2 for time codes.19

Issue Date Notable content Draft A0-A4 30/04/99 - 10/03/00 Initial Rosetta drafts; A4 adds telemetry delivery by APID B0 31/05/01 Updates after the Draft A4 review B1-B3 21/06/01 - 2002 Becomes a common Rosetta/Mars Express document; Rosetta PIs added; DDID review of January 2002 B5 2003/03/27 The Rosetta/Mars Express issue in the library B6 31/08/2003 MEX science network, Madrid station ID, new file types, removal of the "quick-look" concept C0 12/07/2004 RDM naming, super-APIDs, asteroids Lutetia and Steins, updates for Venus Express C1 01/07/2005 VMCS added throughout; separate VEX tables C2 21/02/2006 Fixes a document corruption (characters replaced by quotation marks)

The table summarises the change records of issues B5 and C2.1763 The XML schema appendix (Appendix I) was introduced with issue B1 in July 2001 together with the file-based XML request mechanism; issue C3 (August 2007) added event keywords, and the appendix notes that XML might replace SFDU "in the distant future".6566

docs.title: What the DDS must do
docs.text:
The on-line requirements, taken from the RMCS/MEMCS User Requirements Document, are:20

Requirement Value Delivery mechanism File transfer or Web interface, always in response to a user request (client-server, DDS is the server) Request content One request command per request file: a subset of packets of one data source (APID), one auxiliary file, a set of auxiliary files of one type over a time range, or a catalogue Response content Acknowledgement, catalogue entry and the data in the same transfer; an error message in the acknowledgement on failure Latency Start of data within 15 minutes of the request (subject to volume and load) On-line retention 3 months for Mars Express; the entire mission for Rosetta Queue Up to 12 requested files per user at a time Capacity At least 1000 MB per day in total, split into configurable per-user quotas agreed with the Project Scientist; a file that would exceed the day's quota is not delivered Sub-sampling Every N-th packet on request (SampleRate) Automatic delivery New versions of selected auxiliary files, and periodic TM/TC files, sent to registered PIs

The retention figures come from §5.4 rather than from the requirement list, which states 3 months.26 Off-line delivery was planned for Mars Express and Venus Express but not for Rosetta: an RDM (CD-ROM for Mars Express) holds an integer number of days of data split on the on-board generation time (default one day per CD-ROM for MEX), up to four RDMs per period, with only the auxiliary data of the same period and all format descriptions on every medium so that each RDM is self-describing; RDMs are produced inside ESOC by an automatic scheduler and delivered within one month (nominally three weeks for MEDDS).2131 Mars Express PIs received CD-ROMs weekly, and Venus Express data went on DVDs, one copy to the VSOC and one kept at the VMOC.813

docs.title: The interface itself
docs.text:
Requests are made through the mission's web interface or by FTP with an ASCII XML request file, and responses come back by FTP or through the web interface; the PI side needs a web browser, FTP and an RDM reader, and the DDS hardware was a Sun/Solaris 8 server with 1 GB of memory.23 To avoid partial transfers, FTP transfers in both directions use a two-step put-and-rename with a temporary file name; a PI who receives neither data nor an error message within 2 hours resubmits.25 The DDS hosts sit on ESOC's front-end LAN, separated from the operational LAN that hosts the rest of the MCS by a bridge; access is restricted to an authorised user list controlled by the Project Scientist, each user's data go to a pre-specified node, auxiliary data are open to all authorised users and experiment data only to their own team.27 No integrity checks beyond the transport protocol are foreseen, and outages of several days over the public internet are possible.2728

sequenceDiagram
  participant PI as PI host
  participant DDS as DDS server (GDDS)
  participant DAS as MCS Data Archive System
  PI->>DDS: FTP put request.TMP, then rename to request.XML
  DDS->>DDS: check request, authorised user, daily quota and queue (max 12)
  DDS->>DAS: one or more CORBA retrievals (per data stream / history file)
  DAS-->>DDS: packets or files
  DDS->>DDS: collate; optional SFDU packaging; optional ZIP
  DDS->>PI: FTP put (temporary name, then rename) to the user's node
  Note over PI,DDS: response = acknowledgement + catalogue entry + data, or an error message

The sequence is assembled from the DDID's interface, failure-protection and generation sections and the GDDS descriptions.2325299

docs.title: Data items crossing the interface
docs.text:
Data item DDID section Direction On-line data request 7.1 to the DDS On-line response, acknowledgement, catalogue entry, on-line data 7.2-7.5 from the DDS Telemetry data 7.6 from the DDS Command history data (raw packets, printouts) 7.7 from the DDS Auxiliary data, catalogue data 7.8-7.9 from the DDS Error message 7.10 from the DDS Off-line data delivery, RDM (SFDU view and file view) 7.11-7.13 from the DDS

The list is the DDID's §6.3 table.30 A PI can request four kinds of data: telemetry, telecommand, auxiliary and catalogue data.38

docs.title: The XML request
docs.text:
A request (onlineRequest) contains one general block and one or more item blocks. The general block (RequestInfoType) has a free comment, user information, a delivery block with exactly one of RDM, FTP or Online, format options (compression NONE or ZIP, SFDUrequired, an optional mission format) and an optional earliest start time.3267 Each item (DataItemType) gives a data type, a data source mnemonic (typically an APID, a "super-APID" or an auxiliary file type), a catalogue flag, optional keywords and an optional filter tree.33 Keywords include SampleRate (every N-th packet, applied per history file - VC0 and VC1, real time and playback - before merging) and VolumeSize (a byte limit that stops the delivery at whichever of end time or volume comes first; the C3 schema names this request keyword MaxVolumeSize).3467 Filters are trees of unary (OP_NOT), binary (OP_AND, OP_OR) and leaf nodes; leaves compare a filterable keyword with OP_GT, OP_LT, OP_EQ, OP_GTE or OP_LTE.35 The schema names the binary node element bin, whereas the DDID table calls it "Binary".6835

Filterable keywords are SourcePktsGenTime (on-board time converted to UTC), S2KPktsGenTime (the time the MCS archived the packet), Type, SubType, P1Val, P2Val (packet SID values; omitted means wildcard), ExecutionTime and UplinkTime for command history, and Name, TimeSpan, Release and Issue for auxiliary files.36 The C3 schema also contains CreationTime, EventTime and Validity filter keywords, the data type EVT and event request keywords (Application, EventType, Severity, Workstation, MessageFilter); its change record says that this issue added the event keywords.6765

Illustrative request (constructed for this page)

The element names below are those of the C3 schema; the values are made up. The request asks for every 10th housekeeping packet of APID 1966, type 190, generated between two UTC times, delivered by FTP without SFDU packaging.

<onlineRequest xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
               xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation="GDDSRequest.xsd" userRequestId="wiki-example-1">
  <general>
    <comment>illustrative request</comment>
    <userInfo><username>PI_ACCOUNT</username><FTPpassword>********</FTPpassword></userInfo>
    <destInfo><FTP><filename>tco_packets</filename><directory></directory></FTP></destInfo>
    <formatInfo><compression>NONE</compression><SFDUrequired>false</SFDUrequired></formatInfo>
    <dataInfo/>
  </general>
  <item>
    <dataType>TLM</dataType>
    <dataSource>1966</dataSource>
    <catalogueRequest>false</catalogueRequest>
    <keyword><SampleRate>10</SampleRate></keyword>
    <filter>
      <bin operation="OP_AND">
        <lhs><leaf operation="OP_GTE"><valuePair><SourcePktsGenTime><a_dateTime>2005-01-01T00:00:00Z</a_dateTime></SourcePktsGenTime></valuePair></leaf></lhs>
        <rhs><leaf operation="OP_LT"><valuePair><SourcePktsGenTime><a_dateTime>2005-01-02T00:00:00Z</a_dateTime></SourcePktsGenTime></valuePair></leaf></rhs>
      </bin>
    </filter>
  </item>
</onlineRequest>

The DDID explains a subtlety of command history requests: SCOS-2000 associates seven times with a telecommand (specified release, uplink and execution times; actual uplink and execution times updated by verification; and the packet filing and creation times, which are the primary and secondary keys of the TC history file). The DDS can only retrieve by the two keys, so the times in a returned header may differ slightly from those in the request; requesting by specified execution time is recommended.37

docs.title: Telemetry data and the DDS packet header
docs.text:
Requested telemetry arrives as a time-ordered set of complete, unsegmented packets, each preceded by an 18-octet DDS packet header; the MCS has already reassembled packets from transfer frames, and the packet contents are unprocessed.39 The header is bit- and byte-packed rather than written in PVL for compactness.40

The packet itself complies with ESA PSS-04-106 and is specialised by the mission's generic TM/TC ICDs, which are not in the library.41 The SCET (Spacecraft Event Time) is the calibrated time of generation of the first bit of the packet, held as two 32-bit integers in the Sun/Solaris format.3940 The header field values are:40

Field Values defined in issue C2 Ground station ID 0x0D ESA Villafranca 2, 0x15 ESA Kourou, 0x16 NDIULite (SVTs), 0x17 ESA New Norcia, 0x18 ESA Cebreros, 0x22/0x67 NASA Goldstone (old/new), 0x23/0x70 NASA Canberra (old/new), 0x24/0x6C NASA Madrid (old/new), 0x7F ESA/ESOC test station, 0x82 NDIU classic (SVTs); the DSN ID change-over took place in November/December 2003 SLE service 0-3 real-time SLC, MC, VC and bad frames; 4-7 the same with real-time flow control; 8-11 the same off-line Time quality 0 good, 1 inaccurate, 2 bad (see time correlation below)

The SLE code names the service channel through which the frames arrived; the DDID lists only the abbreviations SLC, MC and VC plus bad frames. This wiki reads MC and VC as the master-channel and virtual-channel SLE return services (the DDID does not expand them); the expansion of SLC is not stated in the available sources.

The same numbers in 2019

The ESA station IDs in this header are the decimal numbers that the Solar Orbiter DDID of 2019 lists for the ground station field of the SCOS-2000 packet header: 0x15 = 21 Kourou, 0x17 = 23 New Norcia, 0x18 = 24 Cebreros; Solar Orbiter adds 22 Perth, 25 Malargüe and 30 Maspalomas. The time quality values 0 good, 1 inaccurate, 2 bad are also identical.4098

Packets in one delivery file are in chronological order of either the source packet generation time or the S2K packet generation time, depending on the time keyword used. The DDID's example: with SPIDs 1200-1202 defined on APID 10 and SPID 1203 on APID 23, a request for APID 10 returns the APID 10 packets of all three SPIDs interleaved by time. The SPID is "an ID number internal to the Mission Control System".41 SPIDs are defined in the MIB's pid table.

docs.title: Command history and verification flags
docs.text:
Command history comes either as raw TC packets or as printouts in full or brief mode.43 Each raw packet is preceded by a DDS command packet header:44

The command uplink stage (CUV) is the CLCW-based verification that the frame reached the spacecraft (COP-1); CAV and CEV are the acceptance and execution stages verified separately on real-time (VC0) and playback (VC1) telemetry.44 Each flag word is 16 bits with exactly one bit set, numbered from the least significant bit; a word of zeros means the stage was not applicable.45

stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> IDLE
  IDLE --> PENDING: stage window opens
  PENDING --> PASSED: success in TM
  PENDING --> FAILED: failure in TM
  PENDING --> UNKNOWN: window closes, no TM
  UNKNOWN --> UNVERIFIED: consolidated by controllers
  PENDING --> TIMED_OUT: CUV only, no response
  PENDING --> ASSUMED: CUV only, later CAV/CEV passed
  TIMED_OUT --> ASSUMED: CUV only, later CAV/CEV passed
  PASSED --> [*]
  FAILED --> [*]
  UNVERIFIED --> [*]

Inference

The DDID defines the statuses and says that only PASSED, FAILED and UNVERIFIED are final; the transitions in the diagram are this wiki's reading of those definitions. The stage model itself is the SCOS-2000 one described on Command verification in the MIB.

Two inconsistencies in issue C2 are worth knowing: the text calls the header 30 octets long and says the data record starts at octet 30, but the table continues with the command and parent-sequence names at octets 30-45 (46 octets in total); and the issue B5 text has the same 30-octet statement.4464 The data record is the encoded telecommand packet as sent to the spacecraft in a transfer frame.45

docs.title: Data sources and ADIDs
docs.text: Every delivered stream has a data source and a data type - CAT catalogue, AUX auxiliary, TLM telemetry, CMH command history - and a registered data description identified by an ADID.46 Per mission, ADIDs start with EROS, EMEX or EVEX: D001-D008 describe the RDM directory listing, cumulative index, off-line and on-line catalogue formats, acknowledgement, volume production information and master or partial catalogue; Txxx describes telemetry for one APID or one super-APID (all telemetry of one instrument); C001-C003 describe command history packets and full or brief printouts.46 Rosetta's super-APIDs -1 to -20 cover the instruments (LCC, RPC, OSIRIS, ALICE, MIRO, ROSINA, COSIMA, CONSERT, VIRTIS, GIADA) and service-specific streams for the RSOC and RPC (acknowledgement service 1, housekeeping service 3, events service 5, dumps service 6, science service 12) - several of these ADIDs are printed with the prefix ESOS (for example ESOSTLCC) instead of EROS; auxiliary sources include attitude (ATNR, ATPR), comet characteristics, environment and kinematics, Doppler files for flight dynamics and the radio-science AGC files AGC1/AGC2 from the IFMS.46 Mars Express has super-APIDs such as EMEXTHRS (HRSC), EMEXTPFS (PFS) and EMEXTASP (ASPERA-3).47

docs.title: SFDU packaging
docs.text:
The DDS packages deliveries as CCSDS Standard Formatted Data Units (SFDUs), chosen because the data come in many packet and file sizes and each RDM must be understandable without external documentation; on-line users who do not want SFDUs can treat the extra header bytes as spare or switch packaging off.22 The building block is the Label-Value-Object (LVO): a fixed 20-octet label followed by a value field.48

Class IDs fall into structure classes (Z exchange data unit, F description data unit, U application data unit), service classes (R replacement, C data administration) and data classes (I application data, S supplementary, D and E data description, K catalogue attributes, V volume production).48 CCSDS ADIDs start with CCSD, for example CCSD0001 (value contains LVOs), CCSD0003/CCSD0004 (PVL statements), CCSD0005 (a description data unit) and CCSD0009 (an application data unit).49 All products are packed in an Exchange Data Unit (EDU); a telemetry delivery is a CCSD Z 0001 EDU holding a V LVO with the request and response status, a K LVO with the catalogue entry and an I LVO whose value is the sequence of DDS headers and packets.5042 The DDID's delimitation paragraph mentions an ID "A" with an eight-octet decimal length, while the list of IDs gives "B" (binary length) and "F"; the C2 text is inconsistent here.48

docs.title: MCS products: internal packets, time correlation and command files
Packets created or relabelled by the MCS
docs.text: Appendix K lists the packets that originate in the MCS. Externally generated data that the MCS cannot place elsewhere get APID 1966 and type 190: bad telemetry packets (subtype 30), packets undefined in the database (38), and good, bad and idle transfer frames (21, 20, 29); idle and time packets keep their externally defined APID with type 190 (subtype 0 for idle packets).51 Packets generated inside the MCS have no source packet header, only the SCOS-2000 TM packet header and a data field: the time correlation coefficient packet (1966/190/40) and the telemetry constants packet (1966/190/0), which carries operator-set parameters from the TM Spacon process.5156

docs.title: Time correlation
docs.text:
The procedure follows ESA PSS-04-106: on board, the elapsed-time clock is sampled at the leading edge of the first bit of the attached sync marker of the VC0 frame with frame count 0 (or every 128, 64, ..., 1 frames) and sent in the spacecraft time source packet before the counter has advanced 255 frames; on ground the reception of the same bit is time-tagged in UTC.52 Rosetta, MEX and VEX could select one in every 256, 128, 64, 32 or 16 VC0 frames.52 At ESOC the packetiser takes the station's ERT of each "zeroth" VC0 frame and removes three delays - station internal (a fixed part per station plus a bit-rate part), the propagation delay from the Flight Dynamics one-way light time (OWLT) file, and the on-board frame processing (fixed plus bit-rate part) - to get the UTC at which the time packet was generated, and then emits a "time telemetry" packet (type 190, subtype 0, APID 0) pairing that UTC with the spacecraft time.53

flowchart LR
  F["VC0 frame, count 0<br/>ERT from station clock"] --> C1["- ground station delay<br/>(fixed + bit-rate part)"]
  C1 --> C2["- propagation delay<br/>(FD OWLT file)"]
  C2 --> C3["- on-board delay<br/>(fixed + bit-rate part)"]
  C3 --> U["UTC of time-packet generation"]
  P["next spacecraft time packet<br/>(OBT sample)"] --> T
  U --> T["time telemetry packet<br/>type 190 / subtype 0 / APID 0"]
  T --> A[("archive")]
  A -- "FCT selects a time range" --> L["least-squares fit"]
  L -- "accepted, with validity start" --> K["TCO coefficient packet<br/>APID 1966 / 190 / 40"]

The Flight Control Team triggers the fit manually over a chosen time range, accepts or rejects the result and gives a validity start time; a correlation stays valid until the next one, and packets stored on board are time-stamped with the correlation valid for their OBT, not the current one. The gradient should be nominally 1; one "substantially different from 1 should be treated with caution".53 The coefficient packet is not a spacecraft packet; its big-endian data field is 240 bits:54

For this packet the SCET in the DDS header is the time from which the correlation is valid.54 The time quality of every other packet follows from the top bit of its OBT (set = invalid OBT): 0 good uses the correlation; 1 inaccurate means an invalid OBT on VC0, time-stamped with the frame ERT minus the delays; 2 bad is the same on VC1. Plausibility checks then compare a VC0 time stamp with the frame-derived UTC (at most a configurable, usually 2 s, ahead and 15 s behind) and a VC1 time stamp only for the "ahead" case; with autocorrection enabled, failures become bad with the frame time, otherwise a warning is logged.55 The current SCOS-2000 mechanism is described on Time correlation in SCOS-2000.

docs.title: Lander telecommand verification file (LTVF) and a decoded example
docs.text:
The LTVF is a human-readable text file of the bit patterns of the commands on a manual stack, created on request for Lander operations; it lists for each command the stack row, mnemonic, description, source sequence count (SSC), PUS version, packet error control, packet header and data field.57 Its example contains 18 real encoded commands. Row 9, ZSV00007 "Set Period of HK packet 1 generation", reads:58

Header : 1F 9C C0 01 00 09 19 03 1B 00      CRC: 3CBB
Data   : 00 01 00 50
Bytes Field Value Meaning 1F 9C Packet ID 0b000 1 1 11110011100 TC packet with data field header, APID 1948 C0 01 Sequence control flags 0b11, count 1 stand-alone packet, SSC 1 (the LTVF "SSC" column shows 0001) 00 09 Packet length 9 data field of 10 octets = 4 header + 4 application data + 2 CRC 19 Data field header byte 0 0b0 001 1001 PUS version 1; acknowledge acceptance and completion 03 1B Service type / subtype 3 / 27 housekeeping service, subtype 27 00 Source ID 0 00 01 00 50 Application data not decoded in the source 3C BB Packet error control 0x3CBB CRC over the 14 preceding octets

The PUS-A primary and data field header layouts are those of ECSS-E-70-41A §5.3.2-5.3.3; with the CRC-16 of its Annex A.1 (generator x^16 + x^12 + x^5 + 1, register preset to all ones) the 14 octets give 0x3CBB, exactly the value in the file. The same check reproduces the CRCs of rows 1, 4, 6 and 10.858858

Inference

PUS-A defines service 3 subtypes 1 to 26 only, so subtype 27 is a Rosetta-specific command, presumably the one named in the row description; its definition (the Rosetta/MEX generic TM/TC ICD) is not in the library.87 The LTVF "PUS" column shows 00 for every row while the encoded headers carry PUS version 1; the meaning of that column is not stated in the available sources. Row 4 (ZRP230D4, "MACRO: Execute Macro") uses service 230, which lies in the mission-specific range 128-255 of PUS-A.86

How the CRC check was done

A 20-line Python function computing the PUS-A CRC (initial value 0xFFFF, polynomial 0x1021, MSB first, no final XOR) was run with python3 -I on the hexadecimal strings of rows 1, 4, 6, 9 and 10 of the LTVF example; all five results equal the printed CRCs (D764, 1043, EAEC, 3CBB, 4AA0).

docs.title: Detailed Agenda Files (DAF)
docs.text:
DAFs are text files that import telecommands into the RMCS/MEMCS/VMCS command sources (pass stack, mission timeline (MTL) stack, manual stack), normally written by the Mission Planning and Scheduling applications; MTL DAFs are also delivered to users through the DDS for traceability of their requests.59 They extend the SCOS-2000 Stack Import Interface (S2K-MCS-ICD-0002) and assume that the command definitions in the run-time database come from the same version of the mission database as the DAF; a version mismatch raises a warning.5960 Pass DAFs contain category (a) commands with absolute or ASAP release times; MTL DAFs carry service 11 time-tagged commands or deletions. The categories are (a) absolute release times, (b) absolute execution times with ASAP release, © release times relative to the first command, and (d) a mixture.60

Final DAFs follow the file transfer system naming ffff_sordes_txxxxxxxxxxxxxx_vvvvv.ROS, with MDAF or PDAF as type, SCH (Rosetta scheduler) as source, RMA (RMCS prime) as destination, D for data, a 14-character field holding __YYMMDDhhmmss and a five-digit version.61 A file is a sequence of |-separated records: a base header (category, source, database version, start time, pass), then per command a header record (type, identifier, dispatch and release conditions, group, block and interlock conditions, verification stage, static and dynamic PTV states, parameter count, time-tagging, planning state, execution time, parent sequence, destination subsystem, source, earliest and latest release, insert/delete state, external ID) followed by one record per editable parameter (CDF_ELTYPE = E) in the order of CDF_BIT.62 These fields map onto the commanding tables and sequences of the MIB.

docs.title: The MCS-FDS interface and the mission's MIB extensions
docs.text:
The Flight Dynamics System - Mission Control System ICD (RO-ESC-ID-5003, issue B1, 2003-03-07, prepared by Anite Systems for Rosetta and Mars Express) specifies everything exchanged between the MCS and ESOC flight dynamics.69 From the MCS, flight dynamics receives the MIB files extracted from the source database, packetised data (TM source packets, TC history packets and time coefficient history packets) retrieved from the DAS by the SCOS-2000/ORATOS Data Access software (SoDA) through the SCOS-2000 FDIF interface, tracking data files, and payload auxiliary data (scenario parameter lists from the RSOC).7071 ESA tracking files (ranging, Doppler 1 and 2, meteorological data, antenna angles, received signal strength) are stored on the IFMS at each station; the MCS "via the Network Interface Subsystem (NIS)" fetches them and stores them in the MCS FARC, while NASA/DSN tracking data come from the flight dynamics computer RACSO.70 In the other direction flight dynamics sends orbit, attitude, event and cometary files (archived in the DAS for the PIs), Flight Dynamics Requests and Direct Operations Requests (command request files defined in the CRID), trajectory data for ESA stations (STDMs, sent on through NIS) and for the DSN (EPMs, via RACSO to JPL), the OWLT file and the "interplanetary WIMPY" with ground station information.70 Mission archives and NCTRS and NIS describe the FARC and NIS in general.

All files use the FTS naming TTTT_SSSDDD_txxxxxxxxxxxxxx_vvvvv.yyy (document type, source, destination, D, 14 free characters, version 00000-99999 with wrap-around, mission ROS or MEX, all upper case); external files are wrapped with tar inside an FTS file.72 The file tables list 40 file types for Rosetta and 33 for Mars Express, for example D1FD/D2FD Doppler, RGFD ranging, MTFD meteo and AAF_ antenna angles from the NIS nodes, ODF_ DSN tracking, OWLT, STDM, EVTR/EVTM event files, the planning files FECS, FTL_, PTR_ and SECS for Mars Express, and MIB_ - the MCS database files, sent from the MCS to flight dynamics (for Mars Express also to the MPX and POS nodes).7374

docs.title: The MIB as delivered to flight dynamics
docs.text:
The MIB files are generated from the source database and tarred into one file. They follow the SCOS-2000 MIB ICD with mission-specific extensions:75

Table Extension Definition ccf.dat CCF_DESCR widened Char(40) instead of 24 characters ccf.dat CCF_SUBSCH (field 20) Number(3), the on-board sub-schedule of the command pcf.dat PCF_DESCR widened Char(24) instead of 16 characters pcf.dat PCF_WDLEN (field 20) O = 8-bit or W = 16-bit boundary in the service 3 command pcf.dat PCF_GRPID (21), PCF_OFFSET (22) group ID and offset of the corresponding on-board parameter pcf.dat PCF_GLOBAL (23) G global or D detailed; only global parameters are named in service 3 telecommands

Utility files travel with the tables: spid_hash.txt (source database packet name to SPID), calib_hash.txt (calibration name to calibration number), synparhash.txt (expressions of automatically generated synthetic parameters) and a list of packet types not converted into the vpd table.75 The DAF section names the mission database "RSDB" and the run-time database "RTDB", and the DAF reference list gives Database Import ICD issue 4.2 as the baseline of the time.6059

Inference: the same extensions in the Solar Orbiter MIB

Solar Orbiter's MCS shares its packetiser ICD and its MCS software requirements with BepiColombo (see Other missions).97 Its September 2025 MIB shows traits that match the Rosetta/MEX extensions: 2 876 of its 5 454 command descriptions are longer than the 24 characters of CCF_DESCR in ICD 7.0, the longest being exactly 40; parameter descriptions are at most 24 characters, the width that ICD 7.0 adopted after ICD 5.1's 16; all but 150 commands carry CCF_SUBSCHEDID, the sub-schedule field that ICD 6.0 standardised; and a non-ICD table pcf_glob_det links 8 704 "global" parameters to 56 631 "detailed" ones, with a third column whose values (0, 3, 4, 5, ...) look like bit offsets, the global/detailed split that PCF_GLOBAL expressed for Rosetta.9993949596 The lineage is this wiki's reading; no source states that Solar Orbiter inherited these conventions from Rosetta. The table is described on Mission tailoring.

SQL used (Rosetta-style traits in the Solar Orbiter MIB) 
-- solo-2025-09-16.sqlite
SELECT count(*), sum(length(CCF_DESCR) > 24), max(length(CCF_DESCR)) FROM ccf;  -- 5454 | 2876 | 40
SELECT max(length(PCF_DESCR)) FROM pcf;                                         -- 24
SELECT count(*), count(nullif(CCF_SUBSCHEDID, '')) FROM ccf;                     -- 5454 | 5304
SELECT count(DISTINCT COL1), count(DISTINCT COL2) FROM pcf_glob_det;            -- 8704 | 56631
SELECT g.COL1, g.COL2, g.COL3, d.PCF_DESCR FROM pcf_glob_det g
  JOIN pcf d ON d.PCF_NAME = g.COL2 WHERE g.COL1 = 'NAH0Z000';                  -- offsets 0, 3, 4, 5, ...

docs.title: The IFMS-OCC interface: tracking and radio-science data
docs.text:
The IF and Modem System (IFMS) in the ESTRACK stations produces the Doppler, ranging, gain and meteorological data (the measurements themselves are described on RF and ranging) that flight dynamics receives and that the DDS offers to radio-science users as AGC1/AGC2 files.7046 Its IFMS-OCC interface ICD (MakaluMedia, issue 11.4.0, 2006-08-09) describes the interface between the IFMS and data clients such as NCTRS; the library copy was taken from a Mars Express radio-science data set in ESA's Planetary Science Archive.76 The interface is pure FTP over TCP/IP: the IFMS is a read-only file server (stream mode, file structure, ASCII or image type), catalogue access is a directory listing, and "pseudo-on-line" access means fetching small data-set files that cover a short measurement duration.7778

Data sets live under <root>/station/spacecraft/ and are named like PER1_CLU3_2002_108_OP_RG_145513_0001: station (4 characters), spacecraft (4), year, day of year, data-set kind (e.g. OP, TS, CL), DAP type, DAP start time hhmmss and a sequence ID that grows when a data set is closed and reopened (up to 7200 for a 20-hour DAP, coded on five digits beyond 9999); uncorrected ranging data get a .raw extension and compressed copies .gz.79 The ICD's own example states the DAP start as 1999-04-18 14:55:13 although the file name carries 2002, day 108 and 145513.79

DAP type Content of each sample (besides sample number and time) D1, D2 Doppler 17.5 MHz NCO clock count, unwrapped carrier phase (turns), spurious-carrier flag, accumulated one-way delta delay (s) G1, G2 gain (AGC) carrier level (dBm), polarisation angle, incoherent AGC gain, channel A/B input power, carrier lock status ME meteo humidity (%), pressure (hPa), temperature (°C) RG ranging round-trip delay modulo ambiguity, code number 1-24, ambiguity-resolved flag, spurious flags, Doppler estimate, DSP lock and quality figures OL open loop binary records of complex RHC and LHC baseband samples

Every data set starts with a header (station, spacecraft, kind, DAP type, reference time tag, first and last sample times, requestor DCP or STC, reason for opening such as DAP_Started or Max_Size_Reached, number of samples, sample period, oscillator and carrier indicators, ranging correction flag, sequence ID and the active configuration tables).80 The Doppler section gives the algorithm that turns phase counts into delta delay, with different formulas for coherent and non-coherent transponders.8182

Open-loop data sets are binary: records of a 44-byte header (magic number 0xA3C725B6, length, message word, sample time and offset, filter centre frequency, gain and offsets) followed by 136 blocks of 6 bytes; depending on quantisation (1, 2, 4 or 12 bits) a block holds 12, 6, 3 or 1 complex samples of both polarisations, packed from the most significant bit.83

The ICD is not fully consistent here either: the record layout comments the message word as type "3, 4, 5 or 6 dep on quantization", while the encoding table fixes bits 2-0 to message type 7 and puts the quantisation in bits 5-3, and it describes a sp_frameid word that the record layout does not contain.83 Support-log files record data-set open, close and delete events as a backup monitoring aid.84

docs.title: What the family gave back to SCOS-2000
docs.text:
The SCOS-2000 documents record several capabilities that started as Rosetta mission specifics:

  • Service 1 SPIDs. In 2002 SCOS-2000 gave all TM(1,x) packets the same SPID because the verifier listened to a fixed SPID list; Rosetta modified it to accept any SPID for service 1 packets, and integration of the Rosetta (and Cryosat) changes was planned for R3.1.89 See Herschel and Planck.
  • Service 11 ground model. The on-board queue model in SCOS-2000 assumes the structure of the Rosetta spacecraft's service 11 packets as its reference implementation; missions with a different structure need modifications.90
  • Service 13 uplink. SCOS-2000 has no generic support for large data transfer, but a mission-specific uplink implementation exists from Rosetta, based on SCOS-2000-R3.1.91 See ST[13] Large packet transfer.
  • Reference documents. The MIB ICD issue 7.0 still lists the Rosetta Space/Ground ICD (RO-ESC-IF-5002, 1998) among its reference documents.92

Already in 2003, ESOC listed the Rosetta, Mars Express and Venus Express MCSs among the SCOS-2000 client missions under development.5 Their data-delivery ideas - XML requests, catalogues, the SCOS-2000 packet header in deliveries, time quality - live on in EDDS and the Solar Orbiter DDID.

docs.title: Solar Orbiter
docs.text:
Solar Orbiter is the ESA mission whose ground data systems are documented best in the public record that this wiki draws on. Its Mission Operations Centre (MOC) is ESOC and its Science Operations Centre (SOC) is ESAC.1 A set of interface documents, a training presentation and more than a hundred releases of the operational Mission Information Base were posted on the document server of the SWA/PAS team at IRAP (solarorbiter.irap.omp.eu), from where this wiki copied them.6769 Together they describe the whole chain: how on-board applications format telemetry (TM) and telecommand (TC) packets, how the packets travel in frames, how the SCOS-2000-based Mission Control System (MCS) archives them, how external users get them through the EDDS, and how the science planning interface constrains instrument commanding.

This page is the entry point. The data-driven pages are:

  • The Solar Orbiter MIB - row counts, subsystems, APIDs, calibrations, synthetic parameters, commands and the 2020-to-2025 evolution of the real database.
  • How Solar Orbiter uses PUS - every standard and private service found in the MIB, mapped to the PUS pages.
  • Solar Orbiter SWA instrument database - the two copied SWA instrument database versions (6.3.4 and 6.5.0), their release notes and how they relate to the spacecraft MIB.
  • Solar Orbiter STIX instrument database - the same analysis for the STIX instrument database 2.26.38.
  • Solar Orbiter instrument interfaces: SWA DPU ICD and EID-A - what ESA required of every instrument in 2007 and how one instrument, SWA, defined its packets and services.
  • The Solar Orbiter simulator, which flies the spacecraft along its JPL Horizons trajectory and generates, decodes and checks real MIB housekeeping packets and telecommands.
  • The MIB explorer, where every parameter, packet, command and sequence of the September 2025 release can be browsed, with separate views of the SWA 6.5.0 and STIX instrument databases.
