docs.title: How it all fits together
docs.text:
A temperature sensor on a spacecraft produces a number. Before an engineer in Darmstadt or a scientist at a university sees that number as "25 °C, in limits", it passes through a chain of standards and systems. On-board software packs it into a report defined by the ECSS Packet Utilization Standard (PUS). The report travels inside a CCSDS Space Packet. Packets are multiplexed into transfer frames, and the frames are protected by channel coding for the radio link. A ground station recovers the frames and hands them over the ground network using Space Link Extension (SLE) services. The SCOS-2000 mission control system then decodes every bit, using a database that describes every packet, parameter and command: the Mission Information Base (MIB). Finally the data are archived and disseminated to users through EDDS. Telecommands make the reverse trip, with a retransmission protocol (COP-1) and a verification loop that closes in the telemetry.113335773

This page explains the whole chain once, at the level an engineer new to ESA mission operations needs, and links every step to the page that explains it in full. Two real examples from the public Solar Orbiter MIB run through it: a solar-array drive temperature on the way down and a connection-test command on the way up.

How to read this wiki

Every factual statement carries a footnote with the document, clause and PDF page. Each footnote links to a library page that records where the copy came from and when it was taken (sources and copies). Text marked Inference is this wiki's own reasoning. The glossary expands every acronym, and the MIB explorer lets you browse, one entry per parameter, packet and command, every MIB-format database this wiki holds as data: the Solar Orbiter spacecraft MIB of September 2025 (126,745 parameters) and April 2020 (102,104), and the instrument databases of SWA (2,885 parameters) and STIX (681).88959697 Where the standards came from is told on the history page.

docs.title: The layers at a glance
docs.text:
Step What happens Data unit Defined by Explained in 1 Application processes sample parameters and run standard services PUS request or report (a "message") ECSS-E-ST-70-41C (PUS-C, 2016); ECSS-E-70-41A (PUS-A, 2003) PUS, PUS-A vs PUS-C 2 The message is wrapped in a packet with an APID and a sequence count Space Packet, 7 to 65,542 octets CCSDS 133.0-B-2 Space Packet, PUS packets 3 Packets from many sources share one link through virtual channels TM, TC, AOS or USLP Transfer Frame CCSDS 132.0, 232.0, 732.0, 732.1; COP-1 in 232.1; optional security in 355.0 TM SDLP, TC SDLP, AOS, USLP, COP-1, identifiers, SDLS 4 Frames are delimited, randomised and error-protected ASM plus codeblocks (TM); CLTU (TC) CCSDS 131.0-B-5 (and -B-6), 231.0-B-4 TM coding, CLTU 4a The coded symbols modulate a radio carrier, which also carries ranging and Doppler Channel symbols on the RF link CCSDS 401.0-B; ECSS-E-ST-50-05C, ECSS-E-ST-50-02C RF and ranging 5 The ground station receives and annotates the data and the network extends the link to the user SLE transfer-service operations over TCP/IP CCSDS 910.3-G-3, 910.4-B-2, 911.x, 912.x, 913.1; service management 902.x SLE, service management, NCTRS and NIS 6 The control system identifies packets, extracts, calibrates and checks parameters, and builds commands SCOS-2000 packet (SPID), parameter sample SCOS-2000 Database Import ICD (the MIB) SCOS-2000, MIB 7 Packets, parameters and files are archived and served to users Archive records; EDDS responses EDDS interface documents; mission DDID Archives, EDDS

Sources for the rows: the PUS scope and space-to-ground interface clauses; the Space Packet size rules; the CCSDS data link and physical layer overview; the RF standards' scopes; the SLE concept; the ICD scope; the EDDS design.16233986100101335775

The CCSDS overview places these protocols in a five-layer model (physical, data link, network, transport, application). The data link layer has two sublayers: the Data Link Protocol Sublayer, which moves higher-layer data in Transfer Frames, and the Synchronization and Channel Coding Sublayer, which delimits, synchronises and protects those frames on the link. Below it, CCSDS has one omnibus physical-layer standard, Radio Frequency and Modulation Systems (CCSDS 401.0), for links between spacecraft and ground stations; short-range links between spacecraft, landers and relays use the separate Proximity-1 protocol family.9899 The Space Packet Protocol sits above the data link layer. The PUS is an application-layer protocol on top of it; the ECSS communications handbook of 2008 notes that ESA and ECSS developed it independently and that CCSDS has not adopted it.2311

docs.title: 1. On board: parameters, application processes and services
docs.text:
An on-board application process is the unit that sends and receives packets: its APID names the source of each telemetry packet and the destination of each telecommand packet.17 It can be software, firmware or hardware, a spacecraft can have one or many, and the PUS does not prescribe how they map onto subsystems and computers.13 Application processes host subservice providers and subservice users; usually the providers are on board and the users on the ground, but the standard does not require this. A message that a user sends to a provider is a request; a message that a provider sends back is a report. The PUS distinguishes three kinds of report: verification reports (routing, acceptance, start, progress and completion of a request), data reports (on request or autonomous, for example periodic housekeeping) and event reports.13

The PUS is a menu. It defines a set of service types, every one optional, and each mission selects which services each application process implements and at what capability level. The result is documented in a mission "Space-to-Ground Interface Control Document".12 ECSS-E-ST-70-41C defines 20 standard service types; identifiers 7, 10 and 16 are reserved because earlier versions used them.14

ID Service type ID Service type 1 request verification 13 large packet transfer 2 device access 14 real-time forwarding control 3 housekeeping 15 on-board storage and retrieval 4 parameter statistics reporting 17 test 5 event reporting 18 on-board control procedure 6 memory management 19 event-action 8 function management 20 parameter management 9 time management 21 request sequencing 11 time-based scheduling 22 position-based scheduling 12 on-board monitoring 23 file management

Names as printed in ECSS-E-ST-70-41C Table 4-1.14 The 2003 issue, PUS-A, had 16 services; ST[20] to ST[23] are new in issue C.1514 The full message list is in the message type catalogue. The PUS is one of five "level 3" standards under ECSS-E-ST-70C, Ground systems and operations; the others cover on-board control procedures (OBCPs, ECSS-E-ST-70-01), space segment operability (-70-11), monitoring and control data (-70-31) and the PLUTO procedure language (-70-32).103 See ECSS-E-ST-70C, OBCPs and PLUTO.

A parameter is the smallest unit of monitoring: a temperature, a voltage, a status bit. The PUS housekeeping service collects sampled parameters into reports. Each report structure has an identifier, a collection interval and an ordered list of parameters, some of them super-commutated (sampled several times per report).93 The ground must know the layout of every report it can receive. The SCOS-2000 ICD states this plainly: a new housekeeping packet defined on board through service 3 is not processed until its definition has also been added to the TM/TC database, and ESA missions usually create the definition in the database first and generate the service 3 commands from it.66 That is the first reason the MIB exists.

docs.title: 2. Packets: a PUS message inside a CCSDS Space Packet
docs.text:
When messages travel between ground and space, the PUS puts them in CCSDS Space Packets.13 A telecommand packet carries a request from a ground application process to an on-board one; a telemetry packet carries a report the other way.16 A Space Packet is a 6-octet primary header followed by a data field of 1 to 65,536 octets, so a packet is 7 to 65,542 octets long.23

The fields, as the PUS uses them:2417

Field Bits Values Meaning Packet Version Number 3 0b000 Identifies a Space Packet (a "version 1 CCSDS packet") Packet Type 1 0 TM, 1 TC Direction of the packet Secondary Header Flag 1 0 or 1 Every PUS TM packet has a secondary header except spacecraft time packets; every PUS TC packet has one except CPDU command packets Application Process Identifier 11 0 to 2047 Source of a TM packet, destination of a TC packet; all ones is reserved for idle packets Sequence Flags 2 0b11 The PUS uses only stand-alone packets Packet Sequence Count or Packet Name 14 0 to 16,383 TM: incremented for each released packet, wrapping from \(2^{14}-1\) to 0; TC: a count or a name that, with the source ID, identifies the command Packet Data Length 16 0 to 65,535 Number of octets in the data field minus one

Inside the data field, the PUS adds its own secondary header. The service type and message subtype in it name the message, for example TM[3,25] for a housekeeping parameter report or TC[17,1] for an are-you-alive connection test,84 and the structure of the rest of the packet follows from that pair.1921 In PUS-C the headers look like this:1820

The packet ends with a 16-bit packet error control field. It is mandatory for telecommands and a mission option for telemetry, and the mission chooses between an ISO 16-bit checksum and a 16-bit CRC.1921

Solar Orbiter speaks PUS-A

A mission applies the PUS issue its interface documents name. The Solar Orbiter TM/TC ICD sets the PUS version field to 1 (ECSS-E-70-41A) in both directions. Its TM data field header is 10 octets, its largest TM source packet is 4,112 octets, and its 11-bit APID is split into a 7-bit process ID and a 4-bit packet category.8185 PUS-A's TC header is 1 + 3 + 4 + 8 + 8 bits plus an optional source ID whose size the mission chooses.22 See PUS-A vs PUS-C and how Solar Orbiter uses PUS.

The Space Packet Protocol itself does not route. Every node that handles a packet looks at the APID and forwards it along a path that management has set up; the APID-to-path rules are agreed per mission and are not part of the protocol.7 CCSDS also defines an Encapsulation Packet for carrying other protocols' data units over the same links.4

docs.title: 3. Frames: many packet streams share one link
docs.text:
A spacecraft has one downlink but many packet sources and data types with different needs: real-time housekeeping, recorded science, event logs. The data link protocols solve this with virtual channels. A physical channel (the bit stream in one direction) is split into several logical channels; every transfer frame belongs to exactly one of them. All frames with the same transfer frame version number and spacecraft ID form a master channel.4 Most missions use the TC Space Data Link Protocol forward and the TM Space Data Link Protocol in return, and only one data link protocol may be used on a given physical channel.8

Identifier TM SDLP TC SDLP AOS SDLP USLP Transfer Frame Version Number Version 1 (encoded 0b00) Version 1 (encoded 0b00) Version 2 Version 4 Spacecraft ID 0 to 1023 0 to 1023 0 to 255 0 to 65,535 Virtual Channel ID 0 to 7 0 to 63 0 to 63 0 to 63 MAP ID none 0 to 63 none 0 to 15

After CCSDS 130.0-G-4 Table 3-1. The values are registered in the Space Assigned Numbers Authority (SANA). TM and TC frames share version 1 and are told apart by the ASM or start sequence that precedes them. AOS issue 5 (CCSDS 732.0-B-5, October 2025) widens the AOS spacecraft ID to 10 bits; missions on issue 4 or earlier keep the 8-bit field.589104 Every identifier field, its reserved values and how SANA assigns spacecraft IDs are on space link identifiers. TM, TC, AOS and USLP frames can also carry the optional Space Data Link Security protocol for authentication and encryption; see security in CCSDS space links.3

docs.title: Telemetry frames
docs.text:
TM frames have a fixed length on a physical channel during a mission phase, which makes synchronisation on a weak, noisy signal simple and robust.9 A TM frame is a 6-octet primary header, an optional secondary header of up to 64 octets, a data field, an optional 4-octet Operational Control Field (OCF) and an optional 2-octet Frame Error Control Field (FECF).25

Packets are packed end to end into the data fields of the frames of their virtual channel; a long packet can span frames, and the First Header Pointer tells the receiver where the first new packet starts.26 Neither the TM nor the AOS data link protocol retransmits lost frames: if complete delivery matters, a higher layer must provide it.4

docs.title: Telecommand frames and COP-1
docs.text:
TC frames have a variable length, given in the header, so that short commands go out with little delay.9 A TC frame is a 5-octet header, a data field of up to 1,019 or 1,017 octets and an optional 2-octet FECF, to a maximum of 1,024 octets (5 + 1,017 + 2 = 1,024 when the FECF is present). The ECSS adoption notice makes the FECF mandatory and keeps only the 1,017-octet figure.2728

The Communications Operation Procedure-1 gives the forward link reliable, in-order delivery. It is a "go-back-n" retransmission scheme: the sending end runs FOP-1, the spacecraft runs FARM-1, and FARM-1 accepts Type-A frames only in strict sequence. FARM-1 reports its state in the Communications Link Control Word (CLCW), which travels back in the 4-octet OCF of the telemetry frames; FOP-1 retransmits on a "Retransmit" flag in the CLCW or on a timeout. Type-B frames bypass the sequence check and are used for control commands and recovery.2910925 The COP-1 page has the state machines.

Solar Orbiter's link configuration

Spacecraft ID 0x28A (650) on both links. TM frames are always 1,115 octets (8,920 bits) with a 1,099-octet data field; TM source packets longer than that are split across frames. Virtual channels carry, from highest to lowest downlink priority, real-time high-priority TM (VC4), real-time TM (VC0), the critical event log (VC5), playback from the on-board computer's mass memory (VC1) and from the solid-state mass memory (VC2, then VC3), and idle frames (VC7); the ICD lists VC5 second but sends it only when neither VC4 nor VC0 has data. TC frames are at most 256 octets on one of two virtual channels, one per on-board TC decoder.858687

docs.title: 4. Channel coding: getting bits through the noise
docs.text:
The Synchronization and Channel Coding Sublayer adds three functions to a stream of frames: delimiting and synchronising them, error-correcting coding, and bit-transition generation (pseudo-randomisation).6

Function Telemetry (CCSDS 131.0-B-5) Telecommand (CCSDS 231.0-B-4) Error correction / validation Convolutional + FECF; Reed-Solomon; concatenated; turbo + FECF; LDPC; plus SCCC and DVB-S2 for high rates BCH; BCH + FECF; CCSDS 231.0-B-4 also specifies LDPC codes Pseudo-randomisation Cyclic pseudo-noise sequence (optional in 131.0-B-5; mandatory from 131.0-B-6, April 2026) Cyclic pseudo-noise sequence; with BCH required unless the designer verifies operation without it, always applied with LDPC Frame synchronisation 32-bit (or longer) Attached Sync Marker 16-bit Start Sequence (BCH); 64-bit Start Sequence with LDPC

After CCSDS 130.0-G-4 Table 3-3, CCSDS 131.0-B-6 and CCSDS 231.0-B-4.61053290106

On the downlink every frame (or codeblock) is preceded by an Attached Sync Marker; for uncoded, convolutional, Reed-Solomon and rate-⅞ LDPC data it is the 32-bit pattern 0x1ACFFC1D.30 On the uplink the unit of transmission is the Communications Link Transmission Unit (CLTU): a start sequence, the frame encoded as a series of codewords, and, for BCH coding, a tail sequence. A BCH codeword carries 56 information bits, 7 parity bits and a filler bit set to zero.3132

The 64-bit LDPC start sequence is 0x034776C7272895B0, and the (512, 256) LDPC code uses no tail sequence at all because a conventional LDPC decoder reliably fails when it runs past the end of the CLTU.32 The details are on the TM coding and CLTU pages.

The coded symbols finally modulate a radio carrier. CCSDS 401.0 and ECSS-E-ST-50-05C define the frequency bands, spectral limits and permitted modulations, and ECSS-E-ST-50-02C the ranging and Doppler tracking that share the same link.10010110298 The Solar Orbiter MIB shows the choices as data: the deep-space transponder housekeeping report ("PLF DST HK", SPID 33793) reports a telemetry modulation scheme of GMSK or SPL and a telecommand bit rate between 7.8125 and 4000 bit/s.107 See radio frequency, modulation and ranging.

docs.title: 5. The ground station and the ground network
docs.text: ESA's ground stations form the ESTRACK network.5376 At ESOC the operational LAN (OPSLAN) is the centre of the IP-OPSNET network that connects to the ESTRACK ground stations; it is a restricted network, and data for outside users must be relayed through separate RELAY LANs.76 In SLE terms, the SLE System at the ground end of the space link demodulates the signal, terminates the space link protocols and adds annotation: the time of reception, the receiving location, and the quality and sequence status of each data unit.3537 The station's Intermediate Frequency and Modem System (IFMS) also measures Doppler, ranging, signal gain (AGC) and meteorological data and offers them as files over FTP.5354 For Rosetta and Mars Express the mission control system fetched these files through its Network Interface Subsystem, stored them in the file archive and passed them to flight dynamics.55

docs.title: Space Link Extension
docs.text:
SLE standardises how space link data units travel on the ground, so that the ground assets of different organisations can work together without ad hoc gateways built for each new mission and one agency's station can serve another agency's spacecraft.34 It "extends" the space link in three ways: over distance (processing can happen far from the antenna), in information (annotation) and in time (data can be stored and delivered later).36 SLE has transfer services, which move the data, and management services, which schedule them.33 How a mission books station time through service agreements and service packages is on SLE service management.

Direction Service What the user receives or sends Return Return All Frames (RAF) All frames from one space link symbol stream Return Return Channel Frames (RCF) One master channel or selected virtual channels Return Return Operational Control Field (ROCF) The OCFs (CLCWs) of a master or virtual channel Return Return Frame Secondary Header (RFSH) Frame secondary headers Return Return Space Packet (RSP) Packets with selected APIDs from one virtual channel Forward Forward Space Packet (FSP) Packets for uplink, without coordinating with other users Forward Forward TC Virtual Channel Access (FTCVCA) Complete virtual channels for uplink Forward Forward TC Frame (FTCF) TC frames to be turned into CLTUs Forward Forward CLTU (FCLTU) Ready-made CLTUs for radiation

After CCSDS 910.3-G-3 §4.2.1 and §4.3.1.3839 The ROCF service matters on the forward side as well: the CLCW it delivers tells the CLTU service provider whether the physical link is available and tells the provider of the VC and packet services whether TC frames must be retransmitted under COP-1.39 Over terrestrial networks, SLE runs on TCP/IP with ASN.1 encoding using the Internet SLE Protocol (ISP1).40 The library holds the 2023 issues of the RAF, RCF and ROCF and FCLTU specifications, the historical Forward Space Packet book with its API, the ISP1 and API books, and the cross support reference model and service management documents; the standards landscape lists their issues.

docs.title: NCTRS and NIS: the control centre's door
docs.text:
At ESOC, SCOS-2000 does not talk to stations directly. The NCTRS sits between the mission control system and the ground station network and uses SLE for non-ESA stations.49 The sources expand the acronym in several ways, among them "Network Control and TM/TC Router System" and "Network Controller and Telemetry Receiver System".4951 For Mars Express it received telemetry already checked and time-stamped with the Earth reception time by the station equipment, passed it to the mission control system, collected the telecommands from the control system and forwarded them to the right station, and also handled tracking data and station files.51 In the SCOS-2000 R5 era the SLE service user role belongs to the NIS, while the station's TMTCS is the SLE service provider.72 The acronym appears as "Network Interface System" in an ESOC presentation and as "Network Interface Subsystem" in the Rosetta and Mars Express flight dynamics ICD.9155 SCOS-2000 can send two kinds of "throw event" directives: SLE throw events go to the station equipment, NIS throw events are executed by the NIS itself.7270

The Solar Orbiter MIB shows this interface as data. It defines six NIS throw-event commands (open and close the TC link, the TM link and the session) on a header called NOS2KHDR, and two COP-1 control frames, UNLOCK ("FARM UNLOCK directive") and SETVR ("SETV( R ) Directive"), as command type F, which the ICD defines as BC control frames. Three more directives (RESET "PAC RESET directive", REIN_TTR and TC_ONLY) have type R, a control segment.7088

Inference

The sources place the SLE service user (NIS) on the control-centre side and the FCLTU provider at the station, and the MIB defines FARM control frames as commands. Together this implies that TC frames, COP-1's FOP-1 and CLTU generation run on the ground side before the FCLTU interface. Which ESOC component hosts FOP-1 is not stated in the available sources.

docs.title: 6. The control centre: SCOS-2000 and the MIB
docs.text: SCOS-2000 is ESA's mission control system kernel, a distributed client-server system built on the CCSDS packet standards, the PUS and SLE.43 Its servers include the packetiser, the limit checker, the synthetic-parameter generator, the command multiplexer, releaser, verifier and on-board queue model, the archive and the event servers.44 The packetiser rebuilds packets from frames, extracts the CLCW and checks quality and sequence continuity; the command side offers manual and automatic stacks, pre-transmission validation and multi-stage verification.4645

docs.title: What the MIB is
docs.text: The SCOS-2000 Mission Information Base has a static part, the "database", and a dynamic part, the packet archive.58 The static part reaches SCOS-2000 as a set of tab-separated ASCII tables, one file per table named after it (pcf.dat, pid.dat, ...), exported from the mission's off-line database and imported into the run-time system.5759 The Database Import ICD (EGOS-MCS-S2K-ICD-0001) defines those tables. It distinguishes three representations of a value: the encoded bits in the packet, the raw value after type decoding, and the engineering value after calibration; for a 16-bit signed integer, raw −1 is encoded as 0xFFFF.58 The data model page shows how the tables relate. Independently of any tool, ECSS-E-ST-70-31C specifies what monitoring and control data a supplier delivers, and ECSS-E-ST-70-32C the language of the procedures that use it.103 How missions build and maintain such databases and procedures is on operations preparation, with the ECSS-E-ST-70-31C and PLUTO pages for the standards.

docs.title: How a telemetry packet is decoded
docs.text:
flowchart TB
  A["Incoming TM source packet"] --> B["Read APID, service type, subtype<br/>(positions set by configuration)"]
  B --> C{"PIC: extra identification<br/>fields for this type/subtype?"}
  C -->|yes| D["Read PI1 / PI2 at the offsets<br/>and widths given in PIC"]
  C -->|no| E["Key = APID, type, subtype, 0, 0"]
  D --> F["PID: key to SPID (and TPSD)"]
  E --> F
  F --> G["PLF: each parameter's byte and bit<br/>offset in this SPID (fixed packets)"]
  F --> H["VPD: variable packet layout (TPSD)"]
  G --> I["PCF: PTC/PFC decode the raw value;<br/>validity parameter, calibration, checks"]
  H --> I
  I --> J["CAF/CAP, TXF/TXP, MCF, LGF:<br/>raw to engineering"]
  J --> K["OCF/OCP: limit and status checks"]
  K --> L["Displays, archive, out-of-limit events"]

The packet identification and extraction logic of ICD 7.0 §3.3.2.4 and §3.3.2.5.606263

The key that identifies a packet is the combination of type, subtype, APID and up to two extra identification values (PI1, PI2); it maps to a SCOS-2000 Packet ID (SPID). Packets without a PUS header are identified by APID alone. Spacecraft APIDs are 0 to 2047; values 2048 to 65,535 are for packets generated by SCOS-2000 applications or by other control domains such as test equipment.6061 The parameter type codes PTC and PFC then tell the decoder how to read each field: PTC 3 is an unsigned integer and PFC 12 makes it 16 bits wide.64

docs.title: Follow one temperature (real definitions, illustrative raw value)
docs.text:
Parameter NCFT55Y0, "SADE A PY SADM temp", is a Solar Orbiter temperature in degC that the MIB places in the solar-array drive equipment: it travels in the packet "PLF SADE HK" and uses the curve "SADA Temp TM:SA6,7,8". The library does not expand the abbreviations SADE, SADM and SADA. All definitions below come from the 2025-09-16 MIB.88

Step MIB table Value in the Solar Orbiter MIB What SCOS-2000 does with it Recognise the packet pic Type 3, subtype 25: PI1 at octet 16, 8 bits Reads PI1 right after the 6-octet primary header and the 10-octet data field header; in this packet that octet is parameter NCD030A1, "OBCHP_HK SID" Name the packet pid, tpcf (3, 25, APID 212, PI1 89) → SPID 33513, "PLF SADE HK", mnemonic YCF1Z089, TPCF_SIZE 273 octets (documentation only)92 Files and distributes the packet under SPID 33513 Find the parameter plf Octet 50, bit 0 in SPID 33513 (also in SPIDs 33521 and 33582) Extracts the bits Decode pcf PTC 3, PFC 12 (16-bit unsigned), raw nature R, on-board ID 219357222 Builds the raw value Check validity pcf PCF_VALID = NCSD3KG3 "SADE A SCV Status.scvTm", PCF_VALPAR = 2 Marks the sample valid only while that status reads raw 2, which textual calibration CCDT0065TM names ON Calibrate caf, cap Curve CSDP0006TM, "SADA Temp TM:SA6,7,8", 146 points, unsigned raw, real engineering, unit degC Converts raw to °C Check limits ocf No monitoring check is defined for this parameter None

Two calibration points show the shape of the curve: raw 8192 is 25 °C and raw 12235 is 0 °C, and the curve spans raw 1602 (90 °C) to 16119 (−55 °C). An illustrative raw value of 8192 at octet 50 is therefore displayed as 25 °C.88 The calibration's extrapolation flag is empty, and the ICD default F returns an invalid engineering value outside the curve's range.65

Inference

The curve falls as the raw count rises, as a thermistor's would. ICD issue 7.0 does not say how SCOS-2000 computes values between two points. Issue 6.9 describes interpolation from the points on either side, and ECSS-E-ST-70-31C defines a linear-interpolation interpretation function, so linear interpolation is the natural reading.108109

SQL used 
-- solo-2025-09-16.sqlite (MIB__20250916M25925PFMS001_SOL)
SELECT * FROM pic WHERE PIC_TYPE='3' AND PIC_STYPE='25';          -- PI1 offset 16, width 8
SELECT * FROM pid WHERE PID_SPID='33513';                          -- 3,25,212,89 -> 33513
SELECT * FROM tpcf WHERE TPCF_SPID='33513';                        -- YCF1Z089, 273
SELECT PLF_SPID, PLF_OFFBY, PLF_OFFBI FROM plf WHERE PLF_NAME='NCFT55Y0';
SELECT * FROM pcf WHERE PCF_NAME IN ('NCFT55Y0','NCSD3KG3');
SELECT * FROM txp WHERE TXP_NUMBR='CCDT0065TM';                    -- 0 NOT_APPLICABLE, 1 OFF, 2 ON
SELECT * FROM caf WHERE CAF_NUMBR='CSDP0006TM';
SELECT CAP_XVALS, CAP_YVALS FROM cap WHERE CAP_NUMBR='CSDP0006TM';
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ocf WHERE OCF_NAME='NCFT55Y0';                 -- 0

The downlink walk-through and the telemetry worked example decode complete packets byte by byte.

docs.title: How a telecommand is built
docs.text:
On the command side the central table is ccf, one row per command. Its parameters are defined in cpc and placed in the application data by cdf; pre-transmission checks live in ptv; verification stages in cvs, linked to commands through cvp; and each command names a packet-header template in tcp, whose fields are laid out by pcdf.67 The header fields take their values from the command definition (APID, type, subtype, acknowledgement flags) or are filled in by the command subsystem (length, sequence count).68 The default maximum command size is 248 octets, and the total CLTU size is limited to a mission-specific value.69

Solar Orbiter's standard header template NOM_TC ("NOM_DH_TC_Packet_Header"), used by 5,318 of the 5,454 commands in the ccf table, lays out the PUS-A packet header like this:8822

The 32 bits after the primary header are the 4-octet TC data field header that the Solar Orbiter TM/TC ICD specifies.82 The 8-bit Source ID element uses PCDF_TYPE O. The Database Import ICD issues in the library (5.1, 6.7 Draft A, 6.9 and 7.0) list only the types F, A, T, S, K and P, so how SCOS-2000 fills this field for Solar Orbiter is not stated in the available sources.6883

docs.title: Follow one command (real definitions)
docs.text:
Command ZCD01101, "Perform Connection Test", is the PUS test service request TC(17,1) to APID 172, with no parameters, header NOM_TC and acknowledgement flags 9 (0b1001).88 In PUS-A's numbering, bit 3 of the Ack field requests an acceptance report and bit 0 a completion report, so 9 asks for both.22 The MIB links the command to two verification stages: 14001, type A (acceptance), and 14007, type C (completion), both based on TM reports (source R) and both opening 0 s after release with a 20 s interval.8871 Report-based stages are closed by the PUS verification reports, whose packets are implicitly known from their type and subtype.71 The MIB defines matching packets: "Telecommand Acceptance Report - Success" TM(1,1) and "Telecommand Execution Completed Report - Success" TM(1,7) on APID 161, and "Connection Test Response Report" TM(17,2) on APID 167.88

sequenceDiagram
  autonumber
  participant OP as Operator
  participant S2K as SCOS-2000 (stack, releaser, verifier)
  participant NCT as NCTRS / NIS
  participant GS as Ground station
  participant SC as Spacecraft (FARM-1, APID 172)
  OP->>S2K: Load ZCD01101 on the manual stack
  S2K->>S2K: Encode with NOM_TC header, Ack = 9, add CRC
  S2K->>NCT: Release TC packet
  NCT->>GS: TC frame in a CLTU (FCLTU)
  GS->>SC: Radiate CLTU
  SC-->>GS: CLCW in the OCF of the TM frames
  SC-->>S2K: TM(1,1) acceptance success (APID 161)
  S2K->>S2K: Close stage 14001 (A)
  SC-->>S2K: TM(17,2) connection test report (APID 167)
  SC-->>S2K: TM(1,7) completion success (APID 161)
  S2K->>S2K: Close stage 14007 (C)

Sequence after the SCOS-2000 commanding functions, the ICD verification stages and the COP-1 concept; command, stages and report packets from the MIB.45712988

Inference

The MIB does not say which report APIDs answer a command sent to APID 172; this wiki matched them. With Solar Orbiter's split of the APID into a 7-bit process ID and a 4-bit packet category, APIDs 172, 161 and 167 all belong to process 10 (categories 12, 1 and 7), which is why the diagram shows the reports coming from 161 and 167.81

SQL used 

-- solo-2025-09-16.sqlite (MIB__20250916M25925PFMS001_SOL)
SELECT * FROM ccf WHERE CCF_CNAME='ZCD01101';
SELECT * FROM pcdf WHERE PCDF_TCNAME='NOM_TC';
SELECT CCF_PKTID, COUNT(*) FROM ccf GROUP BY CCF_PKTID;     -- NOM_TC 5318 of 5454
SELECT * FROM cvp WHERE CVP_TASK='ZCD01101';                -- stages 14001, 14007
SELECT s.* FROM cvs s JOIN cvp p ON p.CVP_CVSID=s.CVS_ID WHERE p.CVP_TASK='ZCD01101';
SELECT PID_TYPE, PID_STYPE, PID_APID, PID_SPID, PID_DESCR FROM pid
  WHERE (PID_TYPE='1' AND PID_STYPE IN ('1','7') AND PID_APID='161')
     OR (PID_TYPE='17' AND PID_STYPE='2' AND PID_APID='167');
SELECT CCF_CNAME, CCF_DESCR, CCF_CTYPE, CCF_PKTID FROM ccf
  WHERE CCF_CTYPE IN ('F','R','N');                       -- COP-1 and NIS directives
The cvp and cvs columns carry their ICD names (CVP_TASK, CVP_TYPE, CVP_CVSID; CVS_ID, CVS_TYPE, CVS_SOURCE, CVS_START, CVS_INTERVAL, CVS_SPID, CVS_UNCERTAINTY) in the current build of the database.

The uplink walk-through and the telecommand worked example build a complete command down to the CLTU.

docs.title: Time: from on-board clock to UTC
docs.text: A PUS telemetry packet carries its on-board time tag in the time field of its secondary header, and the ground must translate that into UTC.18 SCOS-2000 does this by time correlation. The spacecraft latches its clock when it transmits a frame whose frame count is a multiple of N (a power of 2 between 1 and 256) and reports the latched time in a later time packet. The ground knows the Earth reception time of the triggering frame from the NIS header and subtracts the ground, propagation and on-board delays. Each pair of on-board time and UTC is a "time couple"; a least-squares fit over many couples gives a gradient and an offset, or for a clock synchronised to an external source such as GPS only the offset is computed.56 For Mars Express the conversion was accurate to better than 2 ms.50 See time correlation and CCSDS time codes.

docs.title: 7. Archives and dissemination
docs.text:
SCOS-2000 files every packet it receives, indexed by type, SPID, data stream and time, and serves retrievals independently of real-time processing.47 In the EGOS ground system the archives are separate components: the packet archive (PARC) holds telemetry, telecommand and event packets, the parameter archive (DARC) holds parameter values, and the file archive (FARC) holds mission files.7580 A dedicated parameter archive was built because generating parameter values on the fly from packets could not meet the dissemination system's performance targets.78

For Mars Express, the MCS sat on the operational LAN, only ESOC operations staff could reach it, and external users reached mission data through the DDS.52 The EGOS Data Dissemination System (EDDS) gives users who have no access to the MCS monitoring and control facilities controlled access to telemetry packets and parameters, telecommand history, events and auxiliary files through batch requests (a finite data set, possibly scheduled) and stream requests (a continuous feed), plus management and notification services.737479 Its requirements were based on three earlier ground-segment subsystems and a fourth prototype:77

Predecessor Role TDRS (Telemetry Data Retrieval System) Extracted parameter values from the SCOS-2000 archive into MVDA or spreadsheet files, via web browser and e-mail WebRM (Web Remote Monitoring) Remote monitoring with SCOS-2000-style displays GDDS (Generic Data Disposition System) Web and FTP front ends for packets, files and catalogues from the MCS archive MUST (Mission Utility & Support Tools) Prototype parameter archive with analysis clients

After the EDDS Software Requirements Specification §4.2.77

The older generation is visible in the Mars Express documents: its Data Distribution System was based on the GDDS, took XML requests, used SFDU-based data interchange and also mailed weekly CD-ROMs to the principal investigators.52 Solar Orbiter uses the EDDS as its primary distribution mechanism and, as its nominal route to the Science Ground Segment, RAPID binary files that contain every packet the MCS receives, forwarded by the GFTS file transfer software.79 Each mission documents its delivery products in a Data Delivery Interface Document (DDID): see GDDS and DDIDs and EDDS formats.

docs.title: Why so many standards?
docs.text: The chain is layered so that each part can change on its own. ESA's control systems show the history. MSSS processed frame telemetry and telecommand; the SCOS-II paper says it entered service in 1977, while a 2003 ESA presentation gives 1984 to 1996. SCOS-I (from 1989) moved to packet telemetry; SCOS-II and then SCOS-2000 added a generic telecommand chain on a distributed architecture.11042 The standards evolved alongside: ESA's own PSS documents adapted CCSDS recommendations with European options and have all been withdrawn in favour of ECSS standards or CCSDS books; the history page traces the packet standards of 1988 to 1994 into today's documents.111 ESOC's reuse strategy rests on the same standards: CCSDS packet TM/TC, the ECSS PUS, SLE and XML.48 ESOC presents the payoff as cost and risk reduction, because a new mission develops and validates only a small amount of new software.94 CCSDS presents it as cross support: ground station owners can offer standard services to any operator whose spacecraft uses the CCSDS space link protocols.34 The standards landscape explains who publishes each document, how the issues relate and which ones this wiki holds.

docs.title: Downlink: from on-board parameter to operator display
docs.text:
A temperature measured on board a spacecraft passes through about a dozen transformations before an operator sees it as a number with a unit and a colour on a screen. The on-board software samples it and places it in a PUS housekeeping report. The report travels in a Space Packet, the packet is cut into fixed-length TM transfer frames, and the frames are protected by channel coding and modulated onto a radio carrier. On the ground the station recovers the frames and forwards them over Space Link Extension (SLE) services. At ESOC, NCTRS hands them to the SCOS-2000 mission control system, which rebuilds the packets, identifies them with the MIB, extracts and calibrates the parameter, checks its limits, archives it, displays it, and makes it available to external users through EDDS. This page walks through each stage in transmission order. It says what each layer adds and why, and it links to the page that covers that layer in full. Real values from the public Solar Orbiter documentation and MIB are used throughout. The return path for commands is described on Uplink, and the overall picture is on How it all fits together.

At a glance

Stage Data unit Governing document Detailed page Sampling, reporting on-board parameter, TM[3,25] / TM[5,x] report ECSS-E-ST-70-41C (PUS-C); Solar Orbiter uses ECSS-E-70-41A (PUS-A)111723 ST[03], ST[05] Packetisation Space Packet (6-octet primary header + PUS TM secondary header) CCSDS 133.0-B-227 Space Packet, PUS packets Framing TM Transfer Frame (fixed length, 6-octet header, optional OCF and FECF) CCSDS 132.0-B-332 TM SDLP, AOS Coding, sync codeblock or codeword plus ASM = CADU CCSDS 131.0-B-545 TM coding Ground transfer RAF / RCF / ROCF SLE-SDU (annotated frame) CCSDS 911.1, 911.2, 911.5515960 SLE return services Control centre entry transfer frame with a NIS header (reception time) ESOC infrastructure6267 NCTRS and NIS Processing SCOS-2000 TM packet (SPID), parameter sample SCOS-2000 Database Import ICD 7.080 MIB monitoring Dissemination EDDS batch or stream response EDDS ICDs, Solar Orbiter DDID68 EDDS
