docs.title: Before packets
docs.text:
ESA's space link standards were the PSS-04 branch, "Space Data Communications". It had two sub-branches: space link standards and protocols (PSS-04-1XX) and spacecraft data interfaces and protocols (PSS-04-2XX). Their stated purpose was to keep spacecraft TT&C subsystems compatible with ESOC's tracking and data network and ESTEC's satellite check-out facilities.2 The packet standards replaced older pulse code modulation (PCM) standards: PSS-04-106 superseded the PCM Telemetry Standard TTC-A-02, and PSS-04-107 the PCM Telecommand Standard TTC-A-01.529

Kaufeler's paper on the PUS, which cites the May 1994 issue of PSS-07-101, describes the world they replaced. Telemetry parameters were digitised analogue read-outs and register states sampled at fixed positions in a telemetry format; control used fixed-length telecommand frames carrying simple register loads or switch commands; and the link guaranteed neither reliable nor complete delivery. As more functions moved into on-board software during the 1980s, that hardware-oriented interface became a constraint, and CCSDS recommended packets as the remedy.74

Both packet standards call themselves a "derived subset" of the CCSDS recommendations. They warn that other agencies were only starting their own CCSDS-based standards, so cross-support had to be negotiated case by case.2449 ESA's choices were therefore narrower than CCSDS's: one packet version, one frame version, one secondary header format and forward packet order only.9161817

docs.title: PSS-04-106: the Packet Telemetry Standard (1988)
docs.text: PSS-04-106 defined three data structures: the Source Packet that an on-board application process hands over, the Telemetry Packet used to segment long source packets, and the Transfer Frame that carries them in fixed-length frames over virtual channels.57 Its bit numbering is the one CCSDS books still use: bit 0 is the first bit transmitted and is the most significant bit of a value.6107

docs.title: Source packets and segmentation
docs.text:
A source packet had a 48-bit header and a data field of 1 to 65 536 octets, so a packet was 7 to 65 542 octets long, exactly the limits of today's Space Packet.11108

Field Bits Values Meaning in 1988 Version Number 3 0b100 "Version 2"; the only version the standard permits Type 1 0 Telemetry; 1 would be telecommand. The opening sentence of §4.2.1.1 calls this bit "Reserved Bit", while Figure 4.1 and item (b) call it Type; §8.2.1.1 of PSS-04-107 repeats the same wording Data Field Header Flag 1 0 or 1 Presence of an optional data field header (the CCSDS "secondary header"), whose format the standard leaves open Application Process ID 11 all ones; all zeros Identifies the instrument or subsystem and the process in it; all ones is the idle packet, all zeros the spacecraft time packet; IDs are assigned by the mission control authority Segmentation Flags 2 11 in a source packet 01 first, 00 continuation, 10 last, 11 unsegmented Source Sequence Count 14 modulo count Per APID; must not be short-cycled, but may restart after a power cycle; not required for idle packets Packet Length 16 C Number of data-field octets minus one

Sources: §4.2, Figure 4.1 and §4.3.1.1.910111244

The Telemetry Packet was the segment. To stop long source packets from capturing the downlink, any source packet whose data field exceeded a per-virtual-channel limit LSEGMENT was cut into telemetry packets carrying the same header, with the segmentation flags marking first, continuation and last segments. LSEGMENT could be 256, 512 or 1024 octets, or 65 536 for no segmentation, and was signalled in every frame by the 2-bit Segment Length Identifier. In segments the length field did not give the segment's own length but the part of the original data field still to come.81217 The standard's own example cuts a 2106-octet source packet (2100 octets of data) with LSEGMENT = 512 into four 518-octet segments and a 58-octet last segment, with length fields 2099, 2099, 1587, 1075, 563 and 51 across the original and its five pieces.13 Appendix A explains that ESA renamed CCSDS terms: the CCSDS "Version 2 Telemetry Segment" became the ESA "Telemetry Packet", the CCSDS "secondary header" the "data field header", and octets were numbered from 0 rather than from 1.25

docs.title: The transfer frame
docs.text:
The 48-bit frame primary header of 1988 is field for field the header of CCSDS 132.0-B-3 of 2021: version 2 bits, spacecraft ID 10, virtual channel ID 3, operational control field flag 1, master channel frame count 8, virtual channel frame count 8, and a 16-bit data field status with secondary header flag, synchronisation flag, packet order flag, segment length identifier and first header pointer.16114

Element PSS-04-106 (1988) CCSDS 132.0-B-3 (2021) and ECSS Header fields Frame identification, counts, data field status as above Same sizes and order; "frame identification" is no longer a named group, and version plus spacecraft ID form the Master Channel Identifier Spacecraft ID From ESA's Directorate of Operations at ESOC; separate IDs per physical link, for development vehicles and simulators Assigned by SANA, static through all mission phases Segment Length ID Selects LSEGMENT Must be 11 when the synchronisation flag is 0; kept only because earlier versions used it for source packet segments, which are no longer defined First header pointer All ones when no header starts; all ones minus one for an idle virtual channel; all ones for asynchronous data Same two reserved values, but all ones minus one now marks an "only idle data" frame rather than an idle virtual channel; undefined when the synchronisation flag is 1 Frame length 892, 1115 or 1784 octets with Reed-Solomon (interleaving 4, 5 or 8); 128 to 2040 octets without; fixed for the whole mission Up to 2048 octets, constant per mission phase rather than per mission Secondary header One format: 4 octets, a 24-bit extension of the virtual channel frame count 2 to 64 octets Trailer Optional 32-bit operational control field (type 1 = CLCW, type 2 reserved); 16-bit CRC mandatory without Reed-Solomon Type-2 reports are project-specific when bit 1 is 0; with bit 1 set they were still "reserved" in ECSS-E-ST-50-03C (2008) but carry an SDLS frame security report in 132.0-B-3; the CRC polynomial is unchanged

Sources: PSS-04-106 §5.2 to §5.7; CCSDS 132.0-B-3 §4.1; ECSS-E-ST-50-03C Annex B.16141718192011411511611911311711892

The 32-bit attached synchronisation marker 0x1ACFFC1D and the second marker 0x352EF853 for frames played back from a tape recorder inside another stream are both in PSS-04-106, and both survive with the same purpose in CCSDS 131.0-B-5.15120 The frame error control word used the CCITT polynomial \(x^{16}+x^{12}+x^{5}+1\) with an all-ones preset; a footnote records that the previous ESA issue, TTC-A-06, had included the synchronisation marker in the checked data, which was no longer permitted, although old designs would still be supported.20

docs.title: Time, ground processing and services
docs.text:
Spacecraft elapsed time was a free-running counter in the CCSDS unsegmented time code (CUC): a P-field 0b0010xxyy with 1 to 4 octets of coarse time and 0 to 3 octets of fine time, in TAI seconds from an arbitrary epoch. Time correlation sampled the clock at the first bit of the synchronisation marker of the virtual channel 0 frame whose virtual channel count was 0 (or every 2n frames, n = 0 to 8, coded in the first octet of the packet), and sent the sample in a source packet with APID 0 and no data field header. The ground time-tagged the same marker in UTC and derived the correlation.22 (The printed P-field table repeats the value 00100111 where 00100110 would complete the pattern, a misprint visible on the page image.)22 This scheme was later transcribed into Annex C of ECSS-E-70-41A; see ST[09] Time management.97

The ground was expected to acquire frames, demultiplex virtual channels, extract telemetry packets and rebuild source packets, delivering incomplete ones with their gaps flagged.21 ESA offered two network services: Service 1, source packet delivery per virtual channel with time correlation and CLCW servicing; and Service 2, transfer frame delivery, for frames whose contents were not standard forward-ordered telemetry packets or standard playback frames. A per-virtual-channel form of Service 2 was also what the network itself used to extract asynchronously inserted playback frames.23 How a ground station hands packets and frames to a control centre today is described under SLE.

docs.title: PSS-04-107: the Packet Telecommand Standard (1990, 1992)
docs.text:
PSS-04-107 described the uplink as five layers, each with its own data unit.30

Layer (PSS-04-107) Data unit Main job Today Packetisation TC Packet End-to-end transport to an on-board application process Space Packet, PUS Segmentation (with optional authentication sublayer) TC Segment Segmenting packets into frames, multiplexing up to 64 MAPs MAP and segment header of CCSDS 232.0; authentication left out (see the inference note further down) Transfer (COP-1, frame header and frame error control sublayers) TC Transfer Frame and CLCW Error-free, in-sequence delivery by retransmission TC SDLP and COP-1 Coding CLTU Synchronisation and error correction CCSDS 231.0 Physical CLTU symbols on the carrier Activating and deactivating the RF link; most of it in ESA's RF and modulation standard PSS-04-105 RF and ranging

Sources: PSS-04-107 §1.2, §3.2 and Figure 3.1; the "today" column follows the ECSS-E-ST-50-04C annex of changes.293093

docs.title: Physical and coding layers
docs.text:
The physical layer was a sequence of four carrier modulation modes (CMM-1 unmodulated carrier, CMM-2 acquisition sequence of at least 128 bits, CMM-3 one CLTU, CMM-4 idle sequence of at least 8 bits between CLTUs), applied in the order of ESA's PLOP-2. Two CLCW bits, "No RF Available" (bit 16) and "No Bit Lock" (bit 17), reported the physical link back to the ground.32

The CLTU (Command Link Transmission Unit) began with the 16-bit start sequence 0xEB90, followed by codeblocks and a tail sequence one codeblock long, made of alternating zeros and ones and ending with a one.33 Each codeblock carried 4, 5, 6 or 7 information octets (the 8-octet codeblock, with 7 information octets, was recommended) plus one octet holding seven complemented parity bits of a (63,56) modified BCH code with generator \(g(x)=x^7+x^6+x^2+1\) and a filler bit of 0. Shortened codeblocks were encoded as if preceded by zero "virtual fill".3334 Decoding corrected single errors, and the filler bit let the decoder reliably reject the tail sequence.35 CCSDS 231.0-B-4 keeps the start sequence, the code and the complemented parity, but defines only the 8-octet codeword, a different tail pattern (0xC5C5C5C5C5C5C579) and LDPC options; ECSS-E-ST-50-04C lists the dropped 56-, 48- and 40-bit codeblocks, the changed tail and the added randomisation among its changes from PSS-04-107.12712893

docs.title: The transfer frame and COP-1
docs.text:
The TC frame of 1992 had a 5-octet header, 1 to 249 octets of data and a mandatory 2-octet CRC, for 8 to 256 octets in all. The bypass and control command flags gave the three legal frame types still used today: AD (sequence-controlled data), BD (expedited data) and BC (control commands); the fourth combination was illegal.3638 Two control commands configured the receiver: UNLOCK (one octet 0x00) and SET V(R) (0x82 0x00 plus the new value).37

Field PSS-04-107 (1992) CCSDS 232.0-B-4 (2021) Octets 1–2 Version 2, bypass 1, control command 1, Reserved Field A 2, spacecraft ID 10 Same; Reserved Field A renamed Reserved Spare Octet 3 Virtual channel ID 6, Reserved Field B 2 Virtual channel ID 6, then the two most significant bits of the frame length Frame length 8 bits (bits 24–31 of the header), frame at most 256 octets 10 bits (bits 22–31), frame at most 1024 octets Frame error control Mandatory Optional, but if used present in every frame of the channel Flag combination 0/1 Illegal Reserved for future application Segment header Every virtual channel carries TC segments Optional; frames may carry several packets ("blocking")

Sources: PSS-04-107 §6.2.2; CCSDS 232.0-B-4 §4.1; ECSS-E-ST-50-04C Annex B, whose Table B-1 records that Reserved Field B became part of the frame length.3612212393

Real bytes from 1993: an UNLOCK frame from the PSS-04-151 test sequences

Appendix B of PSS-04-151 gives encoded test CLTUs for decoder test jigs, for a mission with spacecraft ID 0x123 and virtual channel ID 0x12. Its first CLTU, a BC frame carrying UNLOCK, is printed as 55 EB 90 / 31 23 48 07 00 00 EC 0E / 95 55 55 55 55 55 55 70 / 55 55 55 55 55 55 55 55 (bytes read from the page image).61 Read with the PSS-04-107 layout: after a leading 55, 0xEB90 is the start sequence; the first codeblock carries the frame header 31 23 48 07 00, the control command 00 and the first CRC octet EC, then the parity octet 0E; the second codeblock carries the second CRC octet 95 and six fill octets 55, then its parity octet 70; the last eight 55 octets are the tail sequence. The expected frame analysis report lists two codeblocks, no corrections, an accepted BC frame, input 0 and last MAP 63.613337

Inference

This wiki recomputed the check fields of that test CLTU: the CRC with the PSS polynomial and all-ones preset over 31 23 48 07 00 00 gives 0xEC95, and the (63,56) BCH parity octets of the two codeblocks come out as 0x0E and 0x70, matching the printed bytes. The recomputation is this wiki's, not part of the source.

COP-1 at the sending end (FOP-1) had six states: Active, Retransmit without Wait, Retransmit with Wait, Initialising without BC Frame, Initialising with BC Frame, and Initial. The receiving FARM-1 had three: Open, Wait and Lockout.4041 The FARM sliding window W was an even number from 2 to 254, fixed for the whole mission unless otherwise specified, with 200 the largest recommended value, and split into equal positive and negative halves (PW = NW = W/2).41 PSS-04-107 also described systematic retransmission for deep space, setting the FOP-1 timer to its minimum so that a sequence is repeated a fixed number of times without waiting for acknowledgement.46 ECSS-E-ST-50-04C later called this older procedure COP-1A and its own version COP-1B; the differences affect only the sending end.93 The CCSDS 232.1 issue of 2010 added a systematic retransmission option.125

The 1992 CLCW has the field sizes of today's CLCW. The differences are names and two values: CCSDS now calls it the Communications (not Command) Link Control Word, bit 23 "Report Type" became a reserved spare, and the status field may be used by the mission instead of being fixed at zero.3912493

docs.title: Segments, MAPs and packets
docs.text:
Every TC frame carried a segment: a one-octet header and up to 248 data octets (fewer when an authentication trailer was appended). The 6-bit MAP identifier gave up to 64 Multiplexer Access Points per virtual channel; PSS-04-107 could split them into 32 data MAPs and 32 control MAPs by bit 2, pairing one of each per Packet Assembly Controller (PAC). A one-octet control segment 111xxxxx reset a PAC that had entered lockout.4243

The TC packet of 1992 already used version 0b000 (Version 1), the value every Space Packet uses today, while the telemetry packet of 1988 used 0b100.449109 Its sequence flags marked components of a higher-layer data structure rather than segments, and its optional 16-bit packet error control field could be the frame CRC or a 16-bit checksum to be defined in the PUS.44 The receiving application was to check the error field, then version, type, APID and length, and report "clean and conforming", "clean but not conforming" or "rejected, dirty" by telemetry; compare the acceptance reports of ST[01].45

docs.title: Network services and authentication
docs.text:
ESA ground stations offered three telecommand interfaces to the control centre: Service 1, sequence-controlled delivery of packets that the station segments; Service 2, the same for packets pre-segmented and signed by the control centre; and Service 3, expedited delivery of ready-made segments of 1 to 249 octets.31 Section 10 specified optional encrypted authentication of TC segments: a plain-text segment with an appended signature, computed from a secret key, the data and a count, so that recorded commands could not be replayed. The authentication tail held a 2-bit logical authentication channel (LAC) identifier, a 30-bit LAC count and an N-octet signature; three LACs were foreseen (principal, auxiliary, recovery). COP-1 control frames were not authenticated.47 PSS-04-107 already notes that the decoder specification uses a 5-octet signature, making a 9-octet tail, and PSS-04-151 fixed the LAC identifiers: 00 principal, 01 auxiliary, 10 recovery.4756

The standard recommended that the uplink bit error rate be guaranteed better than 10-5; at that rate it guaranteed a frame rejection probability better than 1 in 105 and an undetected error probability better than 1 in 1019.48 ECSS-E-ST-50-04C later left authentication outside its scope and dropped the segment trailer.93 How a control centre hands packets, frames or CLTUs to a station today is described under SLE, in particular the Forward Space Packet and Forward CLTU services, and link-layer authentication under security in CCSDS space links.

docs.title: PSS-04-151: the Telecommand Decoder Specification (1992, 1993)
docs.text:
PSS-04-151 is a functional design specification of the on-board end of PSS-04-107: coding, transfer, segmentation and authentication layers, plus the Command Pulse Distribution Unit (CPDU).51 Its cover says September 1992, but the change record, page headers and copyright line say September 1993; PSS-07-101 and ECSS-E-70-41A cite it as September 1993.506698

Requirements. The decoder was to be redundant (typically two chains), always ready without "wake-up" procedures, return to a defined "cold start" state after power loss, accept at least 4 (preferably 6) symbol stream inputs, and hold re-programmable "mission-specific data": spacecraft ID (10 bits), VC ID (6 bits), FARM window widths PW and NW (8 bits each), an authenticated-MAP pointer (5 bits), the 2940-bit fixed authentication key and the CPDU application ID (11 bits).5254 It notes the 4 kHz maximum uplink symbol rate of the RF standard, with about 20 kHz expected within the next decade, and the undetected-error target that ESA preferred (10-14) over CCSDS's (10-9).53

Authentication unit. The signature was 40 bits. A secret 60-bit linear feedback shift register hashed the segment, the 32-bit LAC value and 24 bits of virtual fill into a 60-bit pre-signature; a "hard knapsack" of sixty secret 48-bit weights turned it into a 48-bit sum, of which 40 bits were kept. The full key was therefore 2940 bits, held twice: a fixed key in ROM for start-up and recovery and a programmable key in RAM for normal use.5556

CPDU. The CPDU let the ground reconfigure the spacecraft when only the expedited service worked. It took one complete packet per segment (normally on MAP 0), checked an even length, a 16-bit CRC, the version (000), type (1), data field header flag (0), its own APID and sequence flags (11), then executed 2-octet instructions: one of 256 pulse outputs and a pulse length of 2k × D, where D was 10 to 15 ms and k the 3-bit code. A packet held 1 to 120 instructions (10 to 248 octets).5758

Telemetry reports. The decoder produced a 16-bit CLCW status report (the second half of the CLCW), a 16-bit CPDU status report, an 80-bit authentication unit status report and a 32-bit Frame Analysis Report for every CLTU.5960

Early implementations. Appendix C is a rare first-hand record. The decoder's forerunner was an ESA contract specification, THB/CS/2077/av, first issued in 1986 when two identical contracts were placed with Selenia Spazio (later Alenia Spazio) and Saab Space, and last updated in May 1988. It had a fixed, asymmetric FARM window (W = 128, PW = 120, NW = 8), no in-flight programmable hash coefficients and no minimum authenticated segment length. The appendix also says that issue 1 of PSS-04-107 was only published at the beginning of 1991, although its change record dates it June 1990. It then lists the remaining non-compliances of both companies' chips: ESA waived Alenia Spazio's coding-layer and telemetry-report deviations, while Alenia's authentication chip still awaited the upgrades; Saab Space's chip lacked the upgrades and the company intended to redesign it.626327 Appendix B adds that ESA's telecommand reference software, recommended for building decoder test equipment, lacked FOP-1's Suspend and Resume states, which it says CCSDS had defined very late for deep-space needs, as well as the authentication software.61

Afterwards. ECSS never replaced PSS-04-151; the 2008 ECSS handbook notes that it contained important information and that ECSS was considering a decoder handbook.91 Its CPDU chapter was transcribed into Annex D of ECSS-E-70-41A, and the CPDU packet survives in ECSS-E-ST-70-41C as the one telecommand without a secondary header.98103 See ST[02] Device access.

docs.title: PSS-07-101: the first Packet Utilisation Standard (1994)
Origins
docs.text: According to Kaufeler, ESA set up the Committee for Operations and EGSE Standards (COES) in 1987 to define what a satellite check-out system (EGSE) and a satellite control system have in common, so that one system could serve pre-launch tests and operations. Packets made many implementations of the same control function possible, so COES's first task became a standard for how packets are used. A prototype called PUSV, with a reference satellite model PUSSAT, validated it in 1992; after an Agency-level review in 1993 the Inspector General approved it.7577 PSS-07-101 sits in the PSS-07 "Ground Segment Infrastructure" branch, under the Mission Data Utilisation Standards (PSS-07-10) next to orbit and navigation, station monitoring and control, and time data utilisation standards (PSS-07-102 to -104).68

docs.title: What it defined
docs.text:
The standard is a set of operational requirements (chapter 3), service specifications (chapters 4 to 21, summarised in chapter 22) and parameter types (chapter 23).67 It was meant as a "shopping list": missions de-select what they do not need, document the result in a mission ground/space ICD, and implement each chosen service at least at its minimum capability set.69 It did not standardise science data content, but required science packets to carry the data field header.69

Around these headers PSS-07-101 fixed the primary header values for ESA missions: telecommand packets version 0 (value 0), sequence flags 11, and a sequence count split into a mission-sized source ID and a per-source count; telemetry packets "Version 2 (value = 4)", segmentation flags 11, a never-short-cycled count per APID, APID 0 for the time packet and all ones for idle packets. The data field header was mandatory except in CPDU commands and the time packet, and the packet error control was mandatory in telecommands.7071

Type PSS-07-101 (1994) ECSS-E-70-41A (2003) ECSS-E-ST-70-41C (2016) Rev.1 DIR1 (2024 draft) 1 Telecommand verification Telecommand verification Request verification Request verification 2 Device-level commanding Device command distribution Device access Device access 3 Housekeeping and diagnostic data reporting same Housekeeping Housekeeping 4 Parameter statistics reporting same same same 5 Event reporting same same same 6 Memory management same same same 7 Task management Not used Reserved Reserved 8 Function management Function management Function management Reserved 9 Time management Time management Time management Time management 10 Time reporting Not used Reserved Reserved 11 Onboard scheduling On-board operations scheduling Time-based scheduling same 12 Onboard monitoring same same same 13 Large data transfer same Large packet transfer same 14 Packet transmission control Packet forwarding control Real-time forwarding control same 15 Onboard storage and retrieval same same same 16 Onboard traffic management Not used Reserved Reserved 17 Test Test Test Test 18–27 — 18 on-board operations procedure, 19 event-action adds 20 parameter management, 21 request sequencing, 22 position-based scheduling, 23 file management adds 24 file transfer, 25 file data storage, 26 parameter extraction, 27 critical packet log management

Sources: PSS-07-101 Table 4-1 (page image checked), ECSS-E-70-41A Table 2, ECSS-E-ST-70-41C Table 4-1 and the Rev.1 DIR1 Table 4.2-1.7296100105 The per-service pages start at ST[01]; the message type catalogue lists today's subtypes.

Chapter 23 introduced the parameter type code (PTC) and parameter format code (PFC): Boolean (PTC 1), enumerated (2), unsigned and signed integers (3, 4), IEEE 754 reals (5), bit, octet and character strings (6 to 8), absolute and relative time (9, 10) and deduced (11), described as a subset of ASN.1 types with a simpler tabular notation.73 The SCOS-2000 Database Import ICD still points to PSS-07-101 for this nomenclature, so the PTC and PFC columns of the MIB descend from this chapter; see also PUS parameter types.131130

docs.title: The mid-1990s papers: the PUS and XMM
docs.text:
Kaufeler's paper summarises the standard for an outside audience: 17 services, 256 service types and 256 subtypes with 0 to 127 reserved, a data field header identical for TM and TC except for the optional time, and tailoring through capability sets, mission-optional fields and mission-chosen encoding lengths. It notes a NASA/JPL proposal for packets with several service data units as a reason for future PUS versions, and says that ESOC's SCOS-II would give full application-level support to PUS missions.7677

Nye's paper on XMM shows "missionisation" of the still unapproved PUS. XMM was due for launch at the end of 1999, with up to 22 hours of contact a day and no bulk on-board storage. According to the paper it was to be the first ESA science spacecraft using the ESA packet standards and the first ESOC science mission on the new flight control infrastructure due in 1995.78 It grouped its packet types into on-line control, safety management and operations maintenance:79

XMM packet type Use Subtypes named TM 1 Periodic housekeeping — TC 2 Device commands 1 pulse, 2 register load TM 3 Telecommand verification 1 and 2 acceptance success and failure, 3 and 4 execution success and failure TM 4 Non-periodic telemetry 1 event, 2 exception, 3 major anomaly report TC 5 Task management 1 start, 2 stop, 3 load task parameters, 4 mode transition TC/TM 6 Memory maintenance 1 load, 2 dump, 3 checksum TC/TM 7 Time-tag commands 1 load to 6 delete all TC/TM 8 On-board monitoring of up to 30 parameters 1 to 7 TC/TM 9 Telemetry management 1 report status, 2 to 5 enable or disable all or specific packets TC/TM 10 Telemetry definition 1 report, 2 define, 3 delete housekeeping packets TC 11 Non-periodic packet storage 1 report, 2 enable, 3 disable TC 13 Test (link alive) — TM 15 Science telemetry —

Inference

XMM's type numbers do not follow PSS-07-101 Table 4-1 (for example verification is 3 at XMM but 1 in the PUS, housekeeping 1 at XMM but 3 in the PUS). The XMM paper calls them "packet types" of the mission's packet structure definition, so they look like a mission numbering built on the PUS header rather than the PUS service numbers; the paper does not say so. The two papers carry consecutive NASA report numbers (N95-17595, N95-17596) and consecutive printed page ranges (1229–1234 and 1235–1242).74777879 The two SCOS-II papers in the library carry report numbers from the same series (N95-17533 for the OL paper, printed pages 689–696; N95-17537 for the SCOS-II paper, printed pages 719–725), and the SCOS-II paper cites the OL paper as "SpaceOps 94".838081 All four therefore probably come from the same SpaceOps 94 proceedings volume, but the PUS and XMM copies do not name their venue.

docs.title: How the version fields moved
docs.text:
Field 1988–1994 (PSS) 2003 (ECSS, CCSDS) Today TM packet version 0b100, "Version 2" (PSS-04-106; PSS-07-101 "value = 4") Value 0 (ECSS-E-70-41A) 0b000, Version 1 CCSDS packet (133.0-B-2; PUS-C) TC packet version 0b000, "Version 1" (PSS-04-107) or "Version 0 (value 0)" (PSS-07-101) Value 0 0b000 TM frame and TC frame version 0b00 0b00 0b00; TM and TC frames are told apart by the ASM or the start sequence PUS version 0, in 3 bits 1, in 3 bits 2, in 4 bits (ECSS-E-ST-70-41C)

Sources: the packet and header clauses of each document.97144709495109101102103114 The Herschel/Planck packet ICD of 2008 shows the switch in practice: its telemetry version must be 000, "consistent with" CCSDS 102.0-B-4 (November 1995) and superseding PSS-04-106, while its PUS version is still 0.132

Inference

The sources show that ESA telemetry packets moved from version 100 to 000 between the PSS-07-101 of May 1994 and ECSS-E-70-41A of 2003 (which points to CCSDS 102.0-B-5 for its telemetry packet), and the Herschel/Planck ICD ties 000 to CCSDS 102.0-B-4 of 1995. They do not state when or why CCSDS stopped using the "Version 2" segmented telemetry packet. CCSDS 132.0-B-3 only records that source packet segments are no longer defined and fixes the segment length identifier at 11, PSS-04-106's code for "no segmentation".1161795

The header also changed shape. PSS-07-101 put the telecommand source ID inside the primary header's sequence count and a checksum-type bit in the data field header; ECSS-E-70-41A moved the source ID into the data field header, made the first bit of the telecommand header a CCSDS secondary header flag set to 0 (a spare bit, formerly that flag, in telemetry), fixed the error-control type per application process as a mission constant, and added an optional packet sub-counter and destination ID to telemetry; ECSS-E-ST-70-41C widened the PUS version to 4 bits, fixed the source ID at 16 bits and made a 16-bit message type counter and a 16-bit destination ID fixed fields of the telemetry header.709495102103 The bit-level details are on PUS packet structures and PUS-A vs PUS-C.

docs.title: From PSS to today's books
docs.text:
PSS-era element Where it lives today Main changes recorded by the sources Source packet (PSS-04-106 §4.2) and TC packet (PSS-04-107 §8) CCSDS 133.0-B-2 Space Packet One version 000 for both directions; segmentation by telemetry packets gone; sequence flags kept with the same codes; APID all ones still idle; APID 0, which PSS-04-106 reserved for the time packet, is not reserved in 133.0-B-2 (only the idle APID is) Telemetry transfer frame (PSS-04-106 §5) CCSDS 132.0-B-3; ECSS-E-ST-50-03C Same header; master channels distinct from physical channels; longer secondary headers; frame up to 2048 octets Synchronisation markers and Reed-Solomon framing CCSDS 131.0-B-5 Same 0x1ACFFC1D and embedded marker 0x352EF853; more codes CLTU and TC codeblock (PSS-04-107 §5) CCSDS 231.0-B-4 64-bit codewords only; new tail sequence; randomisation; LDPC TC transfer frame (PSS-04-107 §6.2) CCSDS 232.0-B-4; ECSS-E-ST-50-04C 10-bit frame length (1024 octets); optional CRC; optional segment header; packet blocking COP-1 and CLCW (PSS-04-107 §6.3 and §6.2.3) CCSDS 232.1-B-2 and 232.0 §4.2 COP-1A → COP-1B (sending end only); "Communications"; status field for mission use TC segment and MAP (PSS-04-107 §7) Segment header of CCSDS 232.0 Optional instead of universal; segment trailer removed Segment authentication (PSS-04-107 §10, PSS-04-151 §8) No direct successor in the TC books ECSS-E-ST-50-04C places authentication out of scope Telecommand decoder and CPDU (PSS-04-151) No ECSS standard; CPDU in ECSS-E-70-41A Annex D and ECSS-E-ST-70-41C clause 9 Decoder handbook only considered (2008) Spacecraft time packet and correlation (PSS-04-106 §7) ECSS-E-70-41A Annex C; ST[09]; time codes Transcribed into the PUS of 2003 Packet Utilisation Standard (PSS-07-101) ECSS-E-70-41A → ECSS-E-ST-70-41C → Rev.1 DIR1 PUS versions 1 and 2; some service types retired, others renamed or added

Sources: the ECSS annexes of changes from PSS-04-106 and PSS-04-107, the CCSDS clauses cited above, the ECSS handbook and the PUS annexes and service tables.1092931101111141201271281221249197981039996100

Inference

The closest modern counterpart of PSS-04-107's segment authentication is CCSDS Space Data Link Security, which authenticates at the data link layer.129 No source in the library links the two. Similarly, PSS-07-101 lists a "Packet Data Description Standard" (PSS-07-201) and "Space Segment Operability Requirements" (PSS-07-501) as "to be issued";66 their subjects match what ECSS later covered in ECSS-E-ST-70-31C and ECSS-E-ST-70-11C, but the sources do not say that one grew out of the other.

The ECSS handbook of 2008 sums up the policy shift. ESA had not adopted CCSDS books directly but republished modified versions as PSS documents; ECSS first continued that practice for the core TM/TC standards, then began to phase it out in favour of adoption notices. It also notes that the PUS was developed by ESA and ECSS independently of CCSDS, and that ECSS combined in one standard the telecommand protocols that CCSDS splits into three books.8990 How the adoption notices work is on ECSS-E-ST-50 communications.

docs.title: The parallel lineage: ESOC's control systems
docs.text:
The standards and ESOC's mission control systems (MCS) evolved together. In 1974 ESOC decided to build reusable MCS infrastructure; the first generation, MSSS, entered service in 1977, and SCOS-I followed in 1989 for Hipparcos, ERS-1 and EURECA.80 The SCOS-II paper required the new system to be compatible with the CCSDS and ESA packet standards and with COES's standards and guidelines. Its Release 1, with a preliminary delivery expected in November 1994, added a commanding function that SCOS-I lacked; Huygens, Artemis and Envisat were the planned first clients.8081 The companion paper on the SCOS-II Operations Language recalls that MSSS derived parameters were specified on paper and coded by software engineers, and SCOS-I ones were written in FORTRAN by operations engineers.82 ESA's Bulletin later dated the start of work on SCOS to about 1992 and its first missions (Huygens, Meteosat MTP LEOP, Teamsat) to 1997.84

Generation Period stated by the sources What the sources say about TM/TC MSSS from 1977; in use until the end of the 1990s Supported only TM rates of a few kbit/s and up to 20 user workstations for all missions SCOS-I from 1989 (beginning of the 1990s in 2019) No commanding function SCOS-II, renamed SCOS-2000 first missions 1997; operational "since the beginning of this century" Built for the packet standards and COES; native support of PUS service-level operations M4C on EGS-CC being developed in 2019 Equivalent functions to SCOS-2000; native PUS support

Sources: the SCOS-II paper, Bulletin 108 and the ICALEPCS 2019 paper.808184858687 In 2019 ESOC credited the PUS with a "good level of standardisation" of on-board services that made common ground solutions possible, and its reference for the PUS was still ECSS-E-70-41A.8588 The Gaia control system, built on SCOS-2000, can sustain more than 10 Mbit/s of incoming data, several orders of magnitude beyond MSSS.87 The full story of these systems is on SCOS-2000 and ancillary systems and EGS-CC; the database line from the 1990s to the MIB is on the history of the Database Import ICD.

docs.title: What survives
docs.text:
Reading the PSS standards explains several details of today's books:

  • The Space Packet's 7 to 65 542-octet range, the meaning of the sequence flags and the idle APID of all ones are unchanged since 1988.1112108111110
  • The TM frame header and the reserved first header pointer values are unchanged; the segment length identifier is a fossil of telemetry packet segmentation.1617116119
  • The TC frame's two spare bits after the VC ID became frame-length bits, which is why a TC frame can be 1024 octets today but only 256 in PSS-04-107.93122
  • The CLCW, the AD/BD/BC frame types, UNLOCK and SET V(R) are recognisably those of 1992.393637124123
  • PUS service numbers 1 to 6, 8, 9, 11 to 15 and 17, the 8-bit type and subtype, the 0 to 127 standard range and the PTC/PFC codes come from PSS-07-101.727073100
  • The CPDU packet still has no secondary header, as in PSS-04-151, whose CPDU required the data field header flag to be 0.57103

docs.title: The standards landscape
docs.text:
The chain described in How it all fits together is specified by documents from several publishers. The space agencies' CCSDS writes the space link and ground cross-support protocols. ECSS writes the European engineering standards, adopts CCSDS books into its own system and owns the Packet Utilization Standard. ISO publishes many CCSDS Recommended Standards as ISO standards. ESA and ESOC write the interface documents of their own ground software, such as the SCOS-2000 Database Import ICD that defines the MIB, and every mission adds its own interface control documents on top.1649

Each family has its own numbering, its own way of issuing revisions and its own idea of what is binding. This matters in practice because a document names the editions it was written against, and those editions stay in force for whoever applies it. The Solar Orbiter packet ICD applies the PUS of 2003; the SCOS-2000 ICD issue of 2017 still points at the ESA PUS of 1994 and at the CCSDS time code issue of 1990.1211 This page explains how to read each family's document numbers, how the families depend on each other, and which edition of every document this wiki holds.

docs.title: Book colours
docs.text:
CCSDS publishes in coloured "books". The colour is also a letter inside the document number.

Colour Letter Category Wording on the cover or in citations Example in this wiki Blue B Recommended Standard: prescriptive interfaces, protocols and encodings "Recommendation for Space Data System Standards" CCSDS 133.0-B-2 Space Packet Protocol Magenta M Recommended Practice: consensus "best" or "state of the art" ways to apply standards "Recommendation for Space Data System Practices" CCSDS 914.0-M-2 SLE API core; CCSDS 320.0-M-7, which was a Blue Book until issue 6 Green G Informational Report: overviews, rationale, performance data, tutorials "Report Concerning Space Data System Standards" CCSDS 130.0-G-4 overview of the protocols Orange not shown in the sources Experimental Specification: research results, not a standard not in the library none Yellow Y CCSDS Record: charters and procedures "CCSDS Record" CCSDS A02.1-Y-4 Organization and Processes, cited in the forewords Silver -S suffix Historical: superseded or obsolete documents "(Historical)"; the cover of a historical copy says it is "no longer current" SCPS-NP 713.0-B-1-S; Forward Space Packet 912.3-B-3-S (September 2022); held as historical copies: 910.4-B-2, 912.3-B-3, 135.0-B-4 Red R Draft Recommendation, circulated before approval "Draft Recommendation" CCSDS 910.11-R-1 (SLE service management, 2006) and 727.0-R-5 (CFDP, 2001), both cited as drafts; the library's 902.4-B-1 is a "proposed draft" whose cover is already laid out as a Blue Book dated September 2026

Sources: the ECSS communications handbook §3.1.2, the reference lists of CCSDS 130.0-G-4 and 910.3-G-3, the normative references of ECSS-E-70-41A and the covers and document control pages of the books themselves.122275926121120123

A book can change colour between issues: the spacecraft identifier procedures were Blue Books 320.0-B-1 to -B-6 (1993 to 2013) and became the Recommended Practice 320.0-M-7 in November 2017, which also introduced the frequency band as a qualifier of the identifier and moved the request form to the SANA web site.121 A book can also change number: the XTCE Green Book 660.2-G-2 (February 2021) lists as its own first issue a 660.0-G-1 of July 2006.122

A Green Book usually accompanies a Blue Book: the specification of a protocol is in the Blue Book and its rationale in the Green Book.19 In this library, CCSDS 130.1-G-3 and 230.1-G-3 summarise the concept and rationale of TM and TC synchronization and channel coding, 130.2-G-3 does the same for the TM, TC and AOS data link protocols, 660.1-G-2 describes the XTCE elements, and 910.3-G-3 describes the SLE services.22109248 The Green Books added to the library in November 2026 follow the same pattern: 350.5-G-2 is the summary of concept and rationale of the Space Data Link Security protocol, 130.3-G-1 an informational report on the Space Packet Protocols, 350.0-G-3 a report on the application of security to CCSDS protocols, 660.2-G-2 an informational report on XTCE and 902.0-G-1 the concept of extensible cross support service management.128

docs.title: Anatomy of a document number
docs.text:
CCSDS 232.0-B-4 Cor. 1
      │     │ │  └── Technical Corrigendum 1 (October 2023), incorporated in the copy
      │     │ └───── Issue 4 (October 2021)
      │     └─────── B = Blue Book, a Recommended Standard
      └───────────── 232.0 = the book's number (here TC Space Data Link Protocol)

The ECSS handbook spells out the rule: a Blue Book number contains the letter B, a Green Book number the letter G, and the last number is the issue.12 The book numbers cluster by subject, as the reference lists and the books held show:2223128

Number range Subjects in the library and in the CCSDS 130.0-G-4 references 120–135 Data compression (120.0-G, 121.0 to 123.0), overview reports (130.x, including the Space Packet Protocols report 130.3-G), TM coding including SCCC and DVB-S2 (131.x), TM SDLP (132.0), packets (133.x), space link identifiers (135.0, historical) 210–211, 230–232 Proximity-1 (210.0-G, 211.x); TC coding (230.1, 231.0); TC SDLP (232.0); COP-1 (232.1) 301–355 Time codes (301.0); spacecraft ID assignment (320.0-M); security (350.0-G and 350.5-G reports, 351.0-M, cryptographic algorithms 352.0, SDLS 355.0 and its extended procedures 355.1) 401 RF and modulation 524, 660 Mission operations services (524.1); XTCE (660.0-B, 660.1-G, 660.2-G) 700–735 USLP overview (700.1-G); IP over CCSDS (702.1); SCPS (713–717); CFDP (720.1, 727.0); AOS (732.0) and USLP (732.1); DTN, LTP and BP (734.x); AMS (735.1) 901–922 Cross support: architecture (901.1-M), service management (902.0-G concept, 902.4-B service package data formats), SLE concept and reference model (910.3-G, 910.4-B), return services (911.x), forward services (912.x, including the historical Forward Space Packet 912.3), ISP1 (913.1), APIs (914.0-M core, 915.1-M return all frames, 916.3-M forward space packet), Cross Support Transfer Services (922.1, monitored data)

Inference

CCSDS does not publish this range table in the available sources; it is this wiki's grouping of the numbers that appear in the reference lists and on the books held. The retired Space Link Identifiers Blue Book, whose registries SANA replaced, is named in CCSDS 130.0-G-4 without its number; the library's historical copy shows that it is 135.0 (issue 4, October 2009).23120 The second part after the dot (133.0, 133.1) separates sibling books on the same subject, for example the Space Packet and Encapsulation Packet protocols.

docs.title: Issues, editorial changes and corrigenda
docs.text:
Every CCSDS book in this library opens with a Document Control table that lists each issue and its status ("Original issue, superseded", "Current issue"), followed by two kinds of later amendment:2932

  • An Editorial Change (EC) corrects presentation without touching the technical content. CCSDS 133.0-B-2 has two: EC 1 (October 2020) adds a missing arrowhead to figure 2-1 and makes clear that a link uses either the Encapsulation Packet or the Space Packet protocol; EC 2 (September 2024) removes duplicated table-of-contents entries and changes the page size to A4.29 The same A4 change appears in several other editorial changes of 2024, for example those of 231.0-B-4, 727.0-B-5 and 232.0-B-4.313432
  • A Technical Corrigendum (Cor.) changes technical text within an issue. CCSDS 232.0-B-4 Cor. 1 (October 2023) expands the discussion of the order of processing between the TC data link protocol, COP-1 and SDLS. CCSDS 232.1-B-2 Cor. 1 (April 2019) adds support for USLP and clarifies the FARM-1 window widths. CCSDS 914.0-M-2 Cor. 1 (August 2016) moves the hash algorithm reference to CCSDS 913.1-B.323337 The cover of 232.0-B-4 then states that the "current issue includes all updates through Technical Corrigendum 1".27 The cover of CCSDS 320.0-M-7 carries the same kind of note for its Cor. 1 (July 2019), which adds USLP frames and redefines the frequency bins with ITU frequency ranges; CCSDS 231.0-B-4 Cor. 1 (July 2026) revises the CLTU tail sequence of 5.2.4.2 and adds a note and probability details to it.121124
  • Not every amendment called editorial is purely presentational: the Editorial Change 1 of CCSDS 732.0-B-5 (October 2025) corrects a note and the issue year but also, in the words of its document control, "upgrades section 4.1.2.6 to Reed-Solomon (15,11) code".126 The first amendment of CCSDS 131.0-B-6 (May 2026) is called an "Editorial Correction" and fixes numbering in the table of contents, a table and four figures.125

Each new issue lists its substantive changes. CCSDS 131.0-B-5 (September 2023) revises the pseudo-randomiser to avoid spectral spikes on high-rate links; CCSDS 133.0-B-2 (June 2020) removes network-type terminology from the Space Packet Protocol; CCSDS 133.1-B-3 renames the "Encapsulation Service" to the "Encapsulation Packet Protocol" and drops the Space Packet from its formats; CCSDS 732.1-B-3 (June 2024) adds VC Packet and VC Access services to USLP and allows more than one frame per CLTU; the 2023 SLE issues add support for USLP frames.2829303536 For two books the library also holds a newer issue: CCSDS 732.0-B-5 (October 2025) extends the AOS Spacecraft Identifier to 10 bits and the M_PDU First Header Pointer to 16 bits for frames of up to 65 536 octets, and CCSDS 131.0-B-6 (April 2026) adds an interleaver for turbo codewords, allows slicing for all block codes and makes the pseudo-randomizer mandatory.126125 The TM coding and AOS pages describe what changed.

docs.title: File names on ccsds.org
docs.text:
Most of the library's CCSDS copies come from ccsds.org/Pubs/; four recent ones (131.0-B-6, 732.0-B-5, 231.0-B-4 with Cor. 1 and the 902.4-B-1 draft) were served from an upload directory of the same site. In both places each file name compresses the number, the colour, the issue and the later amendments:108128

File name Document control in the copy Reading 130x0g4e1.pdf 130.0-G-4, EC 1 (February 2024) 130.0, Green, issue 4, EC 1 133x0b2e2.pdf 133.0-B-2, EC 1 and EC 2 133.0, Blue, issue 2, EC 2 232x0b4e1c1.pdf 232.0-B-4, Cor. 1 (October 2023), EC 1 (October 2024) 232.0, Blue, issue 4, EC 1, Cor. 1 232x1b2e2c1.pdf 232.1-B-2, EC 1, EC 2, Cor. 1 (April 2019) 232.1, Blue, issue 2, EC 2, Cor. 1 914x0m2c1.pdf 914.0-M-2, Cor. 1 (August 2016) 914.0, Magenta, issue 2, Cor. 1 910x3g3.pdf 910.3-G-3, no amendments 910.3, Green, issue 3 401x0b32.pdf 401.0-B-32 401.0, Blue, issue 32 (the issue number may have two digits) 320x0m7c1.pdf 320.0-M-7, Cor. 1 (July 2019) 320.0, Magenta, issue 7, Cor. 1 231x0b4e1c1.pdf 231.0-B-4, EC 1 (October 2024), Cor. 1 (July 2026) 231.0, Blue, issue 4, EC 1, Cor. 1 131x0b6ec1.pdf 131.0-B-6, Editorial Correction 1 (May 2026) 131.0, Blue, issue 6, ec1 instead of e1 732x0b5ec1.pdf 732.0-B-5, EC 1 (October 2025) 732.0, Blue, issue 5, ec1 910x4b2e1s.pdf 910.4-B-2, EC 1 (July 2007); cover "CCSDS Historical Document" 910.4, Blue, issue 2, EC 1, historical 912x3b3s.pdf, 135x0b4s.pdf 912.3-B-3 and 135.0-B-4; historical covers historical, no amendments

Inference

CCSDS does not explain its file naming in the available sources. The reading in the last column is this wiki's, and it matches the document control table of every copy listed in the version matrix: x replaces the dot, the colour letter and issue follow, then e<n> for the latest editorial change and c<n> for the latest corrigendum, and a final s marks a historical (silver) copy. The two copies of 2025 and 2026 issues were served from a different directory of the CCSDS site and write the editorial amendment as ec1; whether that is a new convention is not stated in the available sources.

docs.title: Review cycle, status and binding force
docs.text: The Blue Books carry a standard statement of intent, quoted here from the Space Packet Protocol. Participation in CCSDS is voluntary and its recommendations bind no agency. An agency that endorses one agrees to keep its own related standards in accord with it and to tell the other members about them. Each Recommended Standard is reviewed within five years of issue to decide whether it stays, changes or is retired; a new issue does not make existing implementations non-compliant, although members are encouraged to plan new work against the newer issue.16 Books are approved by the CCSDS Management Council under the procedures of CCSDS A02.1-Y-4.1720 Retired books keep their number with an -S suffix, for example the historical SLE Forward Space Packet book 912.3-B-3-S of September 2022.222

docs.title: ECSS: standards, adoption notices, handbooks and drafts
docs.text:
The ECSS page describes the ECSS system in full; this section covers what is needed to read the version matrix.

Element Meaning Example ECSS-E- Space engineering branch (the others are M management, Q product assurance, U sustainability, I industrialization, production and maintenance, and S for the system documents) ECSS-E-ST-70-41C -50, -70 Discipline within the branch: E-50 communications, E-70 ground systems and operations ECSS-E-ST-50-04C, ECSS-E-ST-70-01C -ST- Standard (normative, numbered requirements) ECSS-E-ST-50C Rev.2 -AS- Adoption notice: applies another body's standard (in E-50 a CCSDS book) "with the following modifications" ECSS-E-AS-50-25C Rev.1 -HB- Handbook: informative, not part of the standards, which prevail in any conflict ECSS-E-HB-50A -TM- Technical memorandum, listed with the handbooks and "made available" rather than published ECSS-E-TM-10-20A (not in the library) Letter after the number Issue letter. For the standards in the library first issued before 2008 the sequence is A, then C, and issue B was "never issued"; those first issued later start directly at C: ECSS-E-ST-70-01C of 2010 (A and B "never issued") and the adoption notices of 2021, whose change logs call issue C the "First issue" ECSS-E-70-41A, ECSS-E-ST-70-41C, ECSS-E-ST-70-01C, ECSS-E-AS-50-26C Rev.1, Rev.2 Revision of an issue ECSS-E-ST-50C Rev.2, ECSS-E-AS-50-21C Rev.2 DIR1 Draft distributed for public review ECSS-E-ST-70-41C Rev.1 DIR1

Sources: the change logs, scopes and title pages of the documents listed, and the ECSS Trees.421355414154846491436452129134

docs.title: Adoption notices in practice
docs.text:
An adoption notice is a short document that lists, clause by clause, what ECSS changes in a CCSDS book; everything else applies unchanged.47 ECSS-E-AS-50-25C Rev.1 (13 January 2023) adopts CCSDS 232.0-B-4 and, among other changes, makes the TC frame's Frame Error Control Field mandatory instead of optional and keeps only the 1,017-octet maximum for the frame data field.48 ECSS-E-AS-50-26C (1 March 2021) adopts COP-1 (CCSDS 232.1-B-2) and adds an "FDU aborted indication" that FARM-1 sets when it accepts a Type-BD frame but has no buffer for it.51 It notes that the CCSDS corrigendum published in the meantime does not affect the adoption.49 The other four notices are summarised on the ECSS-E-ST-50C page: for example ECSS-E-AS-50-24C Rev.1 allows only one TC frame per CLTU and always decodes BCH in single-error-correction mode, and ECSS-E-AS-50-23C Rev.1 forbids the AOS Replay Flag value '1'.146147 Six notices together replace the three 2008 ECSS link standards:4350

Superseded ECSS standard (31 July 2008) Adoption notice CCSDS book adopted (per ECSS-E-ST-50C Rev.1, 2021) Latest revision in the library and the issue it adopts Wiki page ECSS-E-ST-50-01C TM synchronization and channel coding ECSS-E-AS-50-21 131.0-B-3 (Sept. 2017) -21C Rev.2 (5 Dec. 2024): 131.0-B-5 (Sept. 2023) TM coding ECSS-E-ST-50-03C TM transfer frame protocol ECSS-E-AS-50-22 132.0-B-2 (Sept. 2015) -22C Rev.1 (13 Jan. 2023): 132.0-B-3 (Oct. 2021) TM SDLP (ECSS-E-ST-50-03 covered only the TM frame) ECSS-E-AS-50-23 732.0-B-3 (Aug. 2016 per ECSS; Sept. 2015 per the CCSDS document control, see AOS) -23C Rev.1 (13 Jan. 2023): 732.0-B-4 (Oct. 2021) AOS ECSS-E-ST-50-04C clauses 8 and 9 ECSS-E-AS-50-24 231.0-B-3 (Sept. 2017) -24C Rev.1 (13 Jan. 2023): 231.0-B-4 (July 2021) CLTU ECSS-E-ST-50-04C clauses 5 and 6 ECSS-E-AS-50-25 232.0-B-3 (Sept. 2015) -25C Rev.1 (13 Jan. 2023): 232.0-B-4 (Oct. 2021) TC SDLP ECSS-E-ST-50-04C clause 7 ECSS-E-AS-50-26 232.1-B-2 (Sept. 2010) -26C (1 March 2021): 232.1-B-2 (Sept. 2010) COP-1

Fourth column: the scope clause of each notice.145

The adoption notices themselves warn that the CCSDS book that applies is the one named in the latest version of each notice.47 ECSS-E-ST-50C Rev.2 (5 December 2024) took the logical step of no longer naming any CCSDS issue in its own table, so that it need not be revised each time CCSDS updates a book; only the notices are.135 Two adopted issues have meanwhile been superseded by CCSDS: the library holds 131.0-B-6 (April 2026) and 732.0-B-5 (October 2025), and whether ECSS has revised -21 or -23 to follow them is not stated in the available sources.125126 The pattern goes back further: before ECSS, ESA republished CCSDS books in its PSS series with European options, and ECSS-E-ST-50-03C and -04C still carry annexes of differences from ESA PSS-04-106 (the Packet Telemetry Standard of January 1988) and ESA PSS-04-107 (the Packet Telecommand Standard, issue 2, April 1992).345148

docs.title: ISO adoption of CCSDS books
docs.text: CCSDS describes its own process as producing recommendations that are "subsequently adopted by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) for use by any space organization".6 The ECSS handbook adds that many CCSDS Recommended Standards are published as ISO standards.1 This wiki's library holds the CCSDS editions only. The ISO numbers that correspond to the books on this page, and which CCSDS issue each ISO edition reproduces, are not stated in the available sources. The traffic also runs the other way into ECSS: the ECSS Trees list adoption notices of ISO and IEC standards outside the E-50 discipline, such as ECSS-E-AS-11C (ISO 16290, technology readiness levels), ECSS-U-AS-10C Rev.2 (ISO 24113, space debris mitigation) and ECSS-Q-ST-40-12C (fault tree analysis, an adoption of IEC 61025).130133132

docs.title: The withdrawn ESA PSS series
docs.text:
ESA's PSS documents adapted CCSDS books to European missions by including or excluding options, and all of them have been withdrawn in favour of ECSS standards or CCSDS books.3 The four packet standards are now in the library as scans (their text is OCR and is not quoted here); they also survive in the reference lists of later documents:

PSS document Title and issue Prepared by Cited by ESA PSS-04-106 Packet Telemetry Standard, issue 1, January 1988; derived from CCSDS 102.0-B-2 (January 1987), superseding an ESA document TTC-A-06 of February 1986 Standards Approval Board (STAB) for Space Data Communications TDRS ICD; ECSS-E-ST-50-03C Annex B; PSS-04-1071147445117 ESA PSS-04-107 Packet Telecommand Standard, issue 2, April 1992 (issue 1 of June 1990, derived from the CCSDS Telecommand recommendations; issue 2 only editorial) STAB Herschel/Planck operations interface requirements; SCOS-2000 Database Import ICD 5.1 to 7.0 (printed "PSS-074-107"); ECSS-E-ST-50-04C Annex B11611111118148 ESA PSS-04-151 Telecommand Decoder Specification, issue 1, September 1992 STAB PSS-04-107 (as "to be issued in 1991/92"); ECSS-E-HB-50A, which notes that ECSS has no equivalent; the bibliography of ECSS-E-ST-70-41C, which dates it "September 1993"113117150119 ESA PSS-07-101 Packet Utilisation Standard, issue 1, May 1994 Committee for Operations and EGSE Standards (COES) PSS-04-107 (as "to be issued in 1991/92"); SCOS-2000 Database Import ICD 5.1 to 7.0; ECSS-E-ST-70-41C, which calls it PUS version 0 and lists it in its bibliography1131171111857119 ESA PSS-05 ESA Software Engineering Standard, issue 2, February 1991 (not in the library) not stated TDRS ICD74

The PSS reference lists name further members of the series that the library does not hold: the Telemetry Channel Coding Standard PSS-04-103, the Radio Frequency and Modulation Standard PSS-04-105 and the Time Code Formats and Procedures Standard PSS-04-202.115117 The copy of PSS-04-106, although its cover and change record say January 1988, lists PSS-04-103 and PSS-04-105 as issue 1 of 1989; whether it is a later reprint is not stated in the available sources.115114 How the PSS standards defined the packets and frames, and how they map onto today's books, is on the history page.

docs.title: ESOC infrastructure documents
docs.text:
ESOC's ground software is documented under structured references. The covers give the reference, the issue or version and the date, and usually the responsible ESOC unit.

Reference pattern Examples in the library Unit on the cover S2K-MCS-<type>-<nnnn>-TOS-<unit> S2K-MCS-ICD-0001-TOS-GCI, Database Import ICD issue 5.1, 26 October 2001; S2K-MCS-SRD-0004-TOS-GIC (TDRS requirements) and S2K-MCS-GLO-0001-TOS-GIC (glossary), cited ESA/TOS-GCI6974 EGOS-MCS-S2K-<type>-<nnnn> EGOS-MCS-S2K-ICD-0001 (Database Import ICD 6.7 Draft A, 6.9, 7.0); EGOS-MCS-S2K-ICD-0017 (TDRS external interfaces); EGOS-MCS-S2K-TN-1030 (time correlation); EGOS-MCS-S2K-ICD-1005 (RAPID ICD, cited) ESA/OPS-GIC; ESA/OPS-GDI on the 2018 note72737592 EGOS-GEN-EDDS-<type>-<nnnn> SDD-1001, SRS-1001, SUM-1001, ICD-1001 (the EUICD), CIG-1001, EUG-1001, GLO-0001 OPS-GI (Directorate of Operations and Infrastructure); HSO-GI (Directorate of Human Spaceflight and Operations) on the covers of EUICD 7.0 (December 2014) and glossary 7.0 (April 2017)76828389 EGOS-MDW-EDDS-<type>-<nnnn> Alternative references to EDDS documents: the issue 1 SDD of 2007 and the EUICD in the SRS 18.0 reference lists, the SRS in the Solar Orbiter DDID cited only7992 EGOS-NIS-<item>-ICD-<nnnn> EGOS-NIS-NCTR-ICD-0002, NIS/NCTRS volume 2 MCS interface, issue 4.0.2 (November 2009); EGOS-NIS-NIS-ICD-0003, NIS throw events, issue 1.3 (November 2007) cited only11 TYPE-NUMBER short form Inside SCOS-2000 documents: SRD-0003 (Monitoring SRD), ADD-0007 (Operations Language ADD), SUM-0018 (MIB Applications SUM), CG-0003 (configuration variables), GLO-0001 (glossary), CIDL-0001 (document control list) —10

The document types are the usual software life-cycle set: ICD (interface control document), SRD (software requirements document) and SRS (software requirements specification), ADD (architectural design document) and SDD (software design document), SUM (software user manual), CIG (configuration and installation guide), EUG (update guide), TN (technical note), GLO (glossary) and SRN (software release note).10747678868890 The applicable issue of each SCOS-2000 document for a given software release is fixed by the SCOS-2000 document control list.10

Inference

The middle segments of the references (MCS, GEN, MDW, NIS, S2K, EDDS) look like a domain and a product code, and the unit codes track ESOC's organisation at the time of issue: TOS appears in 2001, when the SCOS-2000 team's department belonged to the ESA Directorate of Technical and Operational Support, and OPS and HSO appear later.99 The sources do not define the segments. The same EDDS documents are cited under both EGOS-MDW-EDDS-... and EGOS-GEN-EDDS-... references, and the Solar Orbiter DDID also names the EUICD as MDS-MCS-SW-ICD-1001-OPS-GD.9279

docs.title: Mission documents and MIB deliveries
PUS-A, PUS-C and the 2024 Rev.1 draft
docs.text:
The Packet Utilization Standard has three generations, and the version field in every PUS packet header says which one a packet follows: 0 for ESA PSS-07-101, 1 for ECSS-E-70-41A, 2 for ECSS-E-ST-70-41C.5758

One consequence is visible in the Space Packet itself. PUS-A, written against CCSDS 102.0-B-5, reserves APID 0 for the time packet and all ones for idle packets; Solar Orbiter's ICD repeats both reservations. CCSDS 133.0-B-2 notes that the only reserved APID value is now the one for idle packets.611418 A mission's ICD, not the latest Blue Book, defines what its packets mean.

Reading a mission document

Start from its applicable-documents list. It names the editions the design was frozen against; read those editions, then use the later ones in this wiki to understand where the mission sits relative to current practice. The library pages give the publisher URL and copy time of every edition held here.

docs.title: Uplink: from operator command to on-board execution
docs.text:
A telecommand starts as a line in the MIB: a name, a packet header template, a list of parameters with their calibrations and allowed ranges, and the checks that will tell the ground whether it worked. An operator loads it onto a SCOS-2000 command stack, edits its parameters, and releases it. SCOS-2000 checks it (pre-transmission validation), encodes it as a PUS telecommand packet, and puts it into a TC transfer frame. The frame is protected by COP-1 retransmission and encoded as a CLTU. The SLE FCLTU service then radiates it at the ground station within its scheduled time window. On board, the decoder checks the frame, the FARM accepts it in sequence, and the destination application executes the request and reports back with PUS ST[01] verification reports. The ground matches these, and selected telemetry parameters, against the verification stages defined in the MIB. This page follows the command through every stage, links each one to its detailed page, and uses real Solar Orbiter definitions. The telemetry direction is described on Downlink.

At a glance

Stage Data unit Governing document Detailed page Definition command (CCF), parameters (CPC/CDF), header (TCP/PCDF) SCOS-2000 Database Import ICD 7.01 Commanding in the MIB Sequencing sequence (CSF/CSS/SDF/CSP) same13 Command sequences Release stack entry, PTV, interlock same; ESA SCOS-2000 presentation, GSAW 20031226 SCOS-2000 Packet PUS TC packet: primary header, TC secondary header, application data, CRC ECSS-E-ST-70-41C / ECSS-E-70-41A, CCSDS 133.0-B-23647 PUS packets Frame TC transfer frame (5-octet header, segment header, FECF) CCSDS 232.0-B-460 TC SDLP Reliability AD/BD/BC frames, CLCW CCSDS 232.1-B-270 COP-1 Coding CLTU (start sequence, BCH codewords, tail sequence) CCSDS 231.0-B-479 CLTU Radiation PLOP-1/PLOP-2, FCLTU CCSDS 231.0-B-4, CCSDS 912.1-B-58690 FCLTU Verification TM[1,x] reports, CVS/CVE/CVP stages ECSS-E-ST-70-41C ST[01]; ICD 7.04218 ST[01], command verification

    S --> V["Release: static and dynamic PTV, interlocks"]
