docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A["TM transfer frames<br/>1115 octets, SCID 650"] -->|"first header pointer,<br/>packet length"| B["TM source packet<br/>37 octets"]
    B --> C["TM packetiser:<br/>APID, type, subtype<br/>+ PIC: PI1 = SID"]
    C -->|"PID lookup"| D["SCOS-2000 TM packet<br/>filing key SPID 59208"]
    D --> E["Parameter extraction<br/>PLF offsets + PCF PTC/PFC"]
    E --> F["Calibration<br/>TXF/TXP, CAF/CAP, MCF"]
    F --> G["Monitoring checks<br/>OCF/OCP"]
    G --> H["Displays, archive,<br/>EDDS delivery"]

The order of the steps follows the ICD's description of the telemetry packetiser and of parameter extraction from fixed packets.3236 The frame-level steps are specified by the Solar Orbiter ICD and by CCSDS 132.0-B-3.1026

docs.title: Step 0: from frames to packets
docs.text:
Solar Orbiter telemetry transfer frames have one allowed length of 1115 octets (8920 bits) before encoding, carry the CCSDS spacecraft identifier 650 (0x28A), always have a frame secondary header, always carry a Command Link Control Word in the operational control field and always end with a frame error control word.10 The frame data field has a constant size of 1099 octets and TM source packets may be up to 4112 octets long, so a long packet is split across frames.5 Data sources are mapped onto virtual channels: real-time TM uses VC0, playback from the on-board computer mass memory VC1, playback from the solid state mass memory VC2 and VC3, high-priority real-time TM VC4, the critical event log VC5 and idle frames VC7; VC6 is marked "not required".11

The receiver locates the first packet of a frame with the 11-bit first header pointer and finds each following packet from the packet length field of the one before.1026 The first header pointer is all ones (0b11111111111) when no packet starts in the frame, and 0b11111111110 for Solar Orbiter idle frames on VC7.10 Our 37-octet packet is short enough to sit inside one frame data field, but it may also straddle two frames. The details are on TM Space Data Link Protocol.

docs.title: Step 1: the Space Packet primary header
docs.text:
Every Solar Orbiter TM source packet starts with the 6-octet CCSDS Space Packet primary header, which ECSS-E-70-41A (PUS-A) reuses unchanged.2420

Field Bits Solar Orbiter rule This packet Version number 0-2 0b000 for all TM; the ground rejects any other value with an alarm 0b000 Packet type 3 0 for telemetry 0 Data field header flag 4 1 for every TM packet except the standard spacecraft time packet 1 APID 5-15 7-bit Process ID followed by 4-bit packet category; APID 0 is the time packet, all ones the idle packet 1092 = PID 68, category 4 Grouping flags 16-17 11 stand-alone; 01/00/10 mark a group of self-contained packets answering one request 0b11 Source sequence count 18-31 separate counter per APID and destination ID, +1 per packet, wraps from \(2^{14}-1\) to 0 and must never "short-cycle" illustrative: 1234 Packet length 32-47 octets in the packet data field minus one; at most 4106 octets (10-octet header + 4096 source data) 30

Rules from the Solar Orbiter ICD §4.2.1;678 field positions from CCSDS 133.0-B-2 §4.1.3.24 Solar Orbiter numbers bits from 0 at the most significant, first transmitted bit and transmits the most significant byte first, the same convention as CCSDS.1625

The packet length is fixed by the definition: the TPCF gives 37 octets, and the last PLF entry ends at octet 36 (see step 4), so the field must read 37 − 6 − 1 = 30.61 The MIB sets PID_CHECK to 0 for this packet, which tells the packetiser not to verify a packet error control field.5933 Only 6 of the 11,150 PID rows set it to 1: three describe complete transfer frames (APID 1) and three sit on APID 1966, which the Solar Orbiter data delivery ICD uses for packets generated by the control system, such as time correlation packets.5830 None is a spacecraft source packet. The Solar Orbiter TM source packet drawing (figure 4.2-1) ends with the source data and has no packet error control field; the ICD defines that field and its CRC for telecommand packets only.612

docs.title: Step 2: the PUS data field header (PUS-A, version 1)
docs.text:
Solar Orbiter does not use PUS-C. Its packet ICD applies ECSS-E-70-41A of 30 January 2003 (PUS-A) as applicable document AD1 and states that the on-board application-layer data structures follow that standard.34 The TM data field header carries PUS version number 1, the value PUS-A prescribes; PUS-C later records that version 1 "corresponds to the ECSS-E-70-41A".92123 The time field uses the CCSDS unsegmented time code (CUC) with 4 octets of coarse time and 2 octets of fine time, and the whole header is 10 octets long.98

Field Bits Values Meaning Spare 1 0 PUS-A keeps this bit at zero for symmetry with the TC header; it used to be a CCSDS secondary header flag. PUS version number 3 0b001 Version 1 (ECSS-E-70-41A). Version 0 was the older ESA PUS. Spare 4 0b0000 Completes the octet; Solar Orbiter requires all spares to be zero. Service type 8 3 Housekeeping and diagnostic data reporting. Service subtype 8 25 Housekeeping parameter report. Destination ID 8 0x00 Solar Orbiter uses the optional destination field. Packets of categories 2, 3, 4, 8 and 9 always carry 0 (ground). Time 48 CUC, 4 + 2 octets The time at which generation of the packet started.

Field definitions from PUS-A §5.4.3,21 Solar Orbiter values from SOL.S.ASTR.TN.00079 §4.2.2.1 and Annex 8 §13.3.919 PUS-A also defines an optional packet sub-counter; Solar Orbiter does not include it: figure 4.2-2 of the ICD has no such field.9

Checked against the drawing

Figure 4.2-2 of the Solar Orbiter ICD, which draws this header, is a picture and is not part of the extracted text. Read directly in the PDF (page 26), it lists exactly the fields and sizes above, in this order: spare (1 bit), PUS version = 1 (3 bits), spare = 0 (4 bits), service type (8 bits), service subtype (8 bits), destination ID (8 bits) and S/C time (48 bits, CUC), and the ICD notes that this uses optional fields of PUS-A.9 The MIB agrees on the total: the PIC places the SID at octet 16 = 6 + 10, and every spacecraft TM packet in the PID table has PID_DFHSIZE = 16, except the time report TM(9,2) on APID 0, which has no data field header and PID_DFHSIZE = 6.6058

Solar Orbiter (PUS-A, version 1)PUS-C (version 2), for comparison Octet Content 6 spare (1) + version 001 (3) + spare (4) 7 service type 8 service subtype 9 destination ID (8 bits) 10-15 time, CUC 4 + 2 octets

Sources: PUS-A §5.4.3 and the Solar Orbiter ICD.219

Bits Content 4 TM packet PUS version number, set to 2 4 spacecraft time reference status 8 + 8 message type: service type ID, message subtype ID 16 message type counter 16 destination ID variable time (PFC declared by the mission) optional spare

A PUS-C header with the same 6-octet time would be 13 octets long, three more than Solar Orbiter's.23 The differences between issues are summarised on PUS-A vs PUS-C and PUS packet structures.

docs.title: The time field
docs.text:
The 6-octet time is a CUC T-field: an unsegmented binary count of seconds followed by a binary fraction of a second.27 In the packet header the P-field is implicit. The standard spacecraft time packet TM(9,2), which has no data field header, carries the same 4 + 2 format together with an explicit P-field 0b00101110.15 Read with CCSDS 301.0-B-4, that P-field means: no extension (bit 0 = 0), agency-defined epoch (bits 1-3 = 010, a level 2 time code), 4 octets of coarse time (bits 4-5 = 11, i.e. 3 + 1) and 2 octets of fine time (bits 6-7 = 10).27 The Solar Orbiter ICD gives 00:00 on 1 January 2000 as the spacecraft zero time reference, and also says that the on-board time starts at 0 at computer power-up and is then set by TC(9,128) relative to an arbitrary zero point.14 With 2 octets of binary fraction, the fine time resolution is \(2^{-16}\) s, about 15.26 µs.27

The MIB describes the same format. In the time report (SPID 9999, APID 0, PID_DFHSIZE = 6) the PLF places the S-field NCD09021 at octet 6, the P-field NCD09022 at octet 7 and the on-board time NCD09023 at octet 8, and NCD09023 has PTC 9 / PFC 17.54 ICD Appendix A defines PTC 9 / PFC 17 as an absolute time in CUC format with 4 octets of coarse and 2 octets of fine time, 6 octets in all.53

Inference

The Solar Orbiter ICD calls the packet time format "CUC 9/17".9 It does not explain the label; it is presumably the same SCOS-2000 PTC/PFC pair 9/17.

The ICD adds that the structure of the time field "allows the identification of non-synchronised time", but does not explain how; the phrase occurs nowhere else in its text.9 The ground converts on-board time to UTC by time correlation, using the time packets on VC0.14

docs.title: Step 3: how SCOS-2000 identifies the packet
docs.text:
The SCOS-2000 telemetry packetiser cannot interpret a packet from its APID alone. It reads the APID from the primary header and the type and subtype from configured positions. If the PIC asks for it, it then extracts up to two more identification fields (PI1, PI2) from the data field. With the full key it looks up the PID, which gives the processing keys: the SPID for fixed packets and the TPSD for variable ones.32

flowchart TD
    A["Received packet:<br/>APID 1092, type 3, subtype 25"] --> B{"PIC row for<br/>3 / 25 / APID 1092?"}
    B -- no --> C{"PIC row for<br/>3 / 25 (any APID)?"}
    B -- yes --> E
    C -- "yes: PI1 at octet 16,<br/>8 bits; PI2 unused" --> E["Extract PI1 = 108"]
    C -- no --> F["Search PID with PI1 = PI2 = 0"]
    E --> G["PID lookup:<br/>3, 25, 1092, 108, 0"]
    G --> H["SPID 59208, TPSD -1<br/>(fixed packet, PLF)"]

The precedence rules come from the ICD's PIC description.34 The Solar Orbiter MIB has one PIC row for type 3 / subtype 25, with no APID, so it applies to every APID:60

PIC_TYPE PIC_STYPE PIC_PI1_OFF PIC_PI1_WID PIC_PI2_OFF PIC_PI2_WID PIC_APID 3 25 16 8 -1 0 (empty: all APIDs)

PIC_PI1_OFF counts octets from the start of the TM source packet, which SCOS-2000 files complete in the body of its own packet; PIC_PI1_WID is in bits. An offset of -1 means "no second identification field".34 Octet 16 is the first octet of the source data, which the Solar Orbiter ICD defines as the 1-octet SID of a TM(3,25).13 PUS-A also says the ground identifies a housekeeping report by its SID together with the APID and the packet nature.22

The PID row that matches the key is:59

Field Value Meaning (ICD §3.3.2.4.1) PID_TYPE, PID_STYPE 3, 25 PUS type and subtype; 0 would mean "no data field header" PID_APID 1092 APID; 0-2047 for spacecraft packets PID_PI1_VAL, PID_PI2_VAL 108, 0 values of the extra identification fields PID_SPID 59208 SCOS-2000 packet ID: names the fixed structure in the PLF and is the archive filing key PID_DESCR TM(3,25) - HK SID 108 - HVU - LED free text, also used for event messages PID_UNIT (empty) on-board subsystem, reserved for future filtering PID_TPSD -1 not a variable (VPD) packet PID_DFHSIZE 16 start offset for variable-packet processing; irrelevant for a fixed packet PID_TIME Y the packet carries a time field PID_INTER (empty) no generation period declared; the ICD's "expired" timeout is computed from this field, which it says to leave empty for non-periodic packets PID_VALID Y this key combination is the valid one PID_CHECK 0 do not check a packet error control field PID_EVENT, PID_EVID N, (empty) do not raise a SCOS-2000 event on reception

Field meanings from the ICD;33 the expiry rule from the PCF remark.41 The matching TPCF row gives the mnemonic YIT59208 shown on displays and a size of 37 octets.59 The ICD recommends that TPCF_SIZE include the SCOS-2000 packet header when the field is used to size history files, but the field is informative only and is not imported.35

Inference

TPCF_SIZE = 37 equals the length of the bare source packet. Solar Orbiter's MIB therefore appears to fill this field with source packet sizes, without the SCOS-2000 header. The same holds for the other packets inspected on this page.

docs.title: The SCOS-2000 packet around it
docs.text: Once identified, the source packet is filed and distributed as a SCOS-2000 packet. The Solar Orbiter data delivery ICD describes that wrapper as a common header followed by a TM-specific header, and then the full, un-stripped source packet.28 For Solar Orbiter the common header carries spacecraft ID 650, packet structure version 5, a stream ID that maps to the virtual channel (for example 1000 for VC0 real-time non-science data), and the SPID as "filing key". It also stores the MIB release number (VDF_RELEASE) used when the packet was archived.29 The TM header repeats the TPSD, the APID, the source sequence count and the type and subtype.31 Adding up the field lengths listed in the DDID gives 60 octets for the common header and 16 for the TM header, 76 in total, so our packet is stored as 76 + 37 = 113 octets. The ICD quotes the same 76 octets for SCOS-2000 packet header version 4.35

docs.title: Step 4: the PLF layout
docs.text:
For fixed packets the PLF lists every parameter occurrence. PLF_OFFBY is the octet offset from the start of the source packet (the end of the SCOS-2000 header) and PLF_OFFBI the bit within that octet, with bit 0 the leftmost. The length is not in the PLF: it follows from the parameter's PTC/PFC pair in the PCF.3739 The eleven entries of SPID 59208 are:61

Octets PLF_OFFBY / OFFBI Parameter Description PTC / PFC → width Calibration (PCF_CURTX) Unit 16 16 / 0 NIT83001 HK_SID 2 / 8 → 8-bit enumerated textual CITT1120TM 17-18 17 / 0 NIT0E070 SCREEN_Param 3 / 12 → 16-bit unsigned none 19-20 19 / 0 NIT0E071 MCP_Param 3 / 12 → 16-bit unsigned none 21-22 21 / 0 NIT0E072 SAFE_Param 2 / 16 → 16-bit enumerated textual CITT1072TM 23-24 23 / 0 NIT0E0B6 HVU_mcp_V 3 / 12 → 16-bit unsigned numerical CITP1058TM V 25-26 25 / 0 NIT0E0BF HVU_mcp_i 3 / 12 → 16-bit unsigned numerical CITP1088TM uA 27-28 27 / 0 NIT0E0B5 HVU_temp 3 / 12 → 16-bit unsigned numerical CITP1074TM degC 29-30 29 / 0 NIT0E0B7 HVU_scr_V 3 / 12 → 16-bit unsigned numerical CITP1089TM V 31-32 31 / 0 NIT0E090 LED_curr_set 3 / 12 → 16-bit unsigned polynomial CIT01081TM 33-34 33 / 0 NIT0E0AN led_cal_nom 3 / 12 → 16-bit unsigned polynomial CIT01081TM 35-36 35 / 0 NIT0E0BN led_cal_red 3 / 12 → 16-bit unsigned polynomial CIT01081TM

Positions and types from the MIB;6162 widths from ICD Appendix A, where PTC 2 is an unsigned enumerated value of PFC bits and PTC 3 / PFC 12 an unsigned 16-bit integer.52 Every entry has PLF_NBOCC = 1 (no super-commutation), PLF_LGOCC = 0, PLF_TIME = 0 (every sample takes the packet time stamp) and PLF_TDOCC = 1.6137 The packet has no gaps: octets 16 to 36 are fully covered. PTC/PFC codes are explained on MIB parameter types and PUS parameter types.

Layout from the MIB PLF and PCF tables.6162 The data field as a whole is 10 + 21 = 31 octets, which matches the packet length field value 30 from step 1.

Inference

Three of the four numerical curves (CITP1058TM, CITP1088TM, CITP1089TM) span raw values 0 to 4095 (CAP_XVALS), the temperature curve CITP1074TM stays inside 1130 to 2689, and the Solar Orbiter ICD requires parameters of 8 bits or more to be right-aligned in their octets.6317 This suggests that the values are 12-bit converter counts right-aligned in 16-bit slots, with the top four bits normally zero. The MIB itself declares 16-bit fields, so SCOS-2000 extracts and calibrates all 16 bits.

docs.title: For contrast: a bit-packed packet
docs.text:
Not every packet is this tidy. In the PHI instrument's report PHI_monitoredHousekeeping (SPID 53001, APID 1156, SID 1) several parameters share an octet and PLF_OFFBI does real work.65 Octets 17 and 18 hold seven status fields, and a 16-bit parameter overlaps all of them:

The parameter NIPGH102 (PHI_MONHK_status, PTC 3 / PFC 12) starts at octet 17 bit 0 and spans the same 16 bits, so SCOS-2000 extracts the whole status word as well as its fields.65 The ICD explicitly allows such overlapping PLF entries and gaps.37

docs.title: Step 5: five parameters in depth
docs.text:
All eleven parameters are raw telemetry parameters (PCF_NATUR = R) with no validity parameter (PCF_VALID empty), no on-board parameter ID (PCF_PID empty), no status consistency checking (PCF_USCON = N) and PCF_SUBSYS = 110.62 Without a validity parameter no validity condition is evaluated for these samples.40 The ICD declares the parameters of a periodic packet "expired" when no new packet arrives within PID_INTER plus a global margin; with PID_INTER empty, this packet declares no period for that check.4133

Inference

The ICD does not say explicitly how SCOS-2000 treats a periodic report whose PID_INTER is empty. Since it prescribes an empty field for non-periodic packets, SPID 59208 is presumably handled like a non-periodic packet, with no expiry timeout.

PCF_INTER = F is present but ignored: SCOS-2000 takes the extrapolation rule from the calibration curve.43 The CUR table has no rows for these parameters, so each one has at most the single calibration named in PCF_CURTX.6345

docs.title: 5.1 NIT83001 HK_SID: a textual calibration
docs.text:
PCF field Value Meaning PCF_PTC / PCF_PFC 2 / 8 8-bit enumerated value PCF_CATEG S status parameter: needs a textual calibration PCF_CURTX CITT1120TM name of the TXF entry

The TXF row CITT1120TM ("HK SID") has raw format U and 18 aliases in the TXP. Each alias maps a single raw value (TXP_FROM = TXP_TO) to a text: 1 → SID_1_BOOT, 20 → IIC_SID_20, 101 to 110 → HK_SID_101 to HK_SID_110, 112 → TASKs_Status, 113 to 116 → HK_SPARE_1 to HK_SPARE_4 and 120 → IIC_COPY.63 A raw value with no alias gives the invalid engineering value ****.43 Category S must be used only with a textual calibration and makes PCF_CURTX mandatory.42 Textual calibrations are described on Calibration in the MIB.48

In this packet the SID can only ever be 108, because the packetiser used it to choose SPID 59208. The textual calibration is still useful: the same parameter NIT83001 is the SID field of 18 METIS packets in the PLF (SPIDs 59201 to 59221 and 59290), so one alias set serves them all.61

docs.title: 5.2 NIT0E072 SAFE_Param: a 16-bit status word with two states
docs.text: NIT0E072 is a 16-bit enumerated parameter (PTC 2 / PFC 16), category S, calibrated by CITT1072TM "HV_SAFE STATUS", which has exactly two aliases: raw 0 → HV_ENABLED, raw 1 → HV_DISABLED.63 Any other raw value would show ****.43 No status check (OCP) is attached.64

docs.title: 5.3 NIT0E0B6 HVU_mcp_V: a two-point numerical curve
docs.text:
PCF field Value CAF field Value PCF_PTC / PFC 3 / 12 CAF_NUMBR CITP1058TM ("hvu_mcp_v") PCF_CATEG N CAF_ENGFMT / RAWFMT / RADIX R / U / D PCF_CURTX CITP1058TM CAF_UNIT V PCF_UNIT V CAF_NCURVE 2 PCF_DECIM 2 CAF_INTER (empty → default F) PCF_DARC 1

Values from the PCF and CAF;6263 field meanings from the ICD.434446 The CAP holds two points, (0, −330.4) and (4095, 1084.372).63 ICD 7.0 defines a numerical curve as a list of raw/engineering point pairs and uses CAF_INTER only for raw values outside the range; it does not spell out the rule inside the range.4647 The earlier ICD issue 6.9 describes it: a value between two points is interpolated linearly from the points on either side.57 The ECSS ground-segment data standard ECSS-E-ST-70-31C defines this kind of interpretation function the same way.56 Read that way, two points make the curve a straight line:

\[V = -330.4 + x \cdot \frac{1084.372 - (-330.4)}{4095} \approx -330.4 + 0.345488\,x \quad \text{[V]}\]

Engineering values are real numbers (CAF_ENGFMT = R) shown with 2 decimals (PCF_DECIM). CAF_INTER is empty, and its import default F makes a raw value outside 0-4095 return an invalid engineering value instead of an extrapolated one.46 PCF_DARC = 1 asks the parameter archive (DARC) to add the parameter to its recording list. The field is read by DARC only and not imported by SCOS-2000.44 See Mission archives.

NIT0E0BF HVU_mcp_i and NIT0E0B7 HVU_scr_V use the same pattern with their own two-point curves: CITP1088TM from (0, −61.3) to (4095, 121.77) µA, and CITP1089TM from (0, −2220.18) to (4095, 7585.263) V.63

docs.title: 5.4 NIT0E0B5 HVU_temp: a 175-point curve with limits
docs.text:
The temperature uses CITP1074TM "HVU_Temp" (engineering format R, raw U, decimal, unit degC, 175 points, CAF_INTER empty).63 Its raw points run from 1130 (−56.75671214 °C) to 2689 (67.29716203 °C), in steps of 9 raw counts except for the first and last intervals.63 A selection of points:

CAP_XVALS (raw) 1130 1512 1647 1917 2034 2043 2502 2610 2689 CAP_YVALS (°C) −56.7567 −30.1346 −20.2692 0.2396 9.7533 10.4941 50.0829 59.9437 67.2972

Points from the CAP table, rounded to 4 decimals here.63 The curve is not a straight line: the slope grows from about 0.067 °C per count at the cold end to about 0.094 °C per count at the warm end (computed from the CAP points by this wiki). Because CAF_INTER defaults to F, any raw value below 1130 or above 2689 has an invalid engineering value.46

This is the only parameter of the packet with monitoring checks:64

Table Field Value Meaning OCF OCF_NBCHCK 2 two consecutive violating valid samples are needed to declare the parameter out of limits OCF OCF_NBOOL 2 two OCP records follow OCF OCF_INTER C limits are in calibrated (engineering) values OCF OCF_CODIN R limits are real numbers OCP pos. 1 OCP_TYPE, LVALU, HVALU S, −20, 50 soft limits, no applicability condition OCP pos. 2 OCP_TYPE, LVALU, HVALU H, −30, 60 hard limits, no applicability condition

Values from the MIB;64 meanings from the ICD.5051 Limit checks always come in low/high pairs, soft and hard pairs must follow each other in the order soft then hard, a value exactly equal to a limit is not out of limits, and a parameter violating both is displayed at the higher criticality.51 Mapped back through the curve (by this wiki's interpolation), the soft band −20 °C to 50 °C corresponds to raw values of about 1651 to 2501 and the hard band −30 °C to 60 °C to about 1514 to 2611. More on checks: Monitoring checks.

docs.title: 5.5 NIT0E090 LED_curr_set: a polynomial
docs.text:
NIT0E090 is calibrated by the MCF polynomial CIT01081TM "ILED", with coefficients A0 = 0, A1 = 6.6E-5 and A2 = A3 = A4 = 0.63 SCOS-2000 evaluates \(Y = A_0 + A_1 X + A_2 X^2 + A_3 X^3 + A_4 X^4\),49 here simply

\[Y = 6.6 \times 10^{-5} \cdot X\]

A full-scale 12-bit count of 4095 gives 0.27027. PCF_UNIT is empty and the MCF table has no unit field, so the display shows a bare number with 2 decimals.6249 led_cal_nom and led_cal_red share the same polynomial.61 A polynomial needs no point table and no extrapolation flag: it is defined for every raw value.49

The two remaining parameters, SCREEN_Param and MCP_Param, have no calibration. The ICD says that the unit of an uncalibrated parameter would be shown next to the raw value, but both units are empty here.38

docs.title: Step 6: decode an illustrative byte string
docs.text:
The 37 octets below were constructed by this wiki to match the definition above. The sequence count (1234), the time (coarse 0x2F5E1000, fine 0x8000) and every parameter value are invented.

offset  00 01 02 03 04 05 06 07 08 09 0A 0B 0C 0D 0E 0F
0x00    0C 44 C4 D2 00 1E 10 03 19 00 2F 5E 10 00 80 00
0x10    6C 00 00 00 00 00 01 03 BC 05 5B 07 F8 03 9F 0B
0x20    B8 00 00 00 00
Octets Bytes Field Raw Decoded / engineering 0-1 0C 44 version, type, DFH flag, APID 0b000, 0, 1, 1092 TM packet with data field header from APID 1092 (PID 68, category 4) 2-3 C4 D2 grouping flags, sequence count 0b11, 1234 stand-alone packet, count 1234 (illustrative) 4-5 00 1E packet length 30 31-octet data field, 37-octet packet 6 10 spare, PUS version, spare 0, 1, 0 PUS-A version 1 7-8 03 19 type, subtype 3, 25 housekeeping parameter report 9 00 destination ID 0 ground 10-13 2F 5E 10 00 coarse time 794 693 632 seconds of on-board time (illustrative) 14-15 80 00 fine time 32 768 + 0.5 s 16 6C NIT83001 HK_SID 108 HK_SID_108 → PI1 = 108 → SPID 59208 17-18 00 00 NIT0E070 SCREEN_Param 0 0 (no calibration) 19-20 00 00 NIT0E071 MCP_Param 0 0 (no calibration) 21-22 00 01 NIT0E072 SAFE_Param 1 HV_DISABLED 23-24 03 BC NIT0E0B6 HVU_mcp_V 956 −330.4 + 956 × 0.345488 = −0.11 V 25-26 05 5B NIT0E0BF HVU_mcp_i 1371 −61.3 + 1371 × 0.044706 = −0.01 uA 27-28 07 F8 NIT0E0B5 HVU_temp 2040 between (2034, 9.7533) and (2043, 10.4941): 9.7533 + 6 × 0.082314 = 10.25 degC, within soft limits 29-30 03 9F NIT0E0B7 HVU_scr_V 927 −2220.18 + 927 × 2.394492 = −0.49 V 31-32 0B B8 NIT0E090 LED_curr_set 3000 6.6E-5 × 3000 = 0.20 33-34 00 00 NIT0E0AN led_cal_nom 0 0.00 35-36 00 00 NIT0E0BN led_cal_red 0 0.00

Header rules from the Solar Orbiter ICD and PUS-A;6921 parameter definitions and calibration data from the MIB;61626364 arithmetic by this wiki, rounded to PCF_DECIM = 2 decimals. The raw values were picked so that the high-voltage readings sit near zero, consistent with the illustrative HV_DISABLED state; this is a narrative choice, not spacecraft behaviour.

A few "what if" cases show the checks at work:

  • HVU_temp raw 2560 (0A 00) calibrates to about 55.3 °C. That is above the soft high limit (50) but below the hard high limit (60). After two consecutive such samples (OCF_NBCHCK = 2) the parameter is reported soft out of limits.6450
  • HVU_temp raw 1000 lies below the first calibration point (1130). With CAF_INTER = F the engineering value is invalid.46 Limit checks work on valid values only, so this sample is not limit-checked at all.51
  • SAFE_Param raw 2 has no alias in CITT1072TM, so the display shows ****.43
  • SID 107 instead of 108 (octet 16 = 6B) would make the PID lookup return SPID 59207 ("HK SID107 - PMP Polarization"), and an entirely different PLF layout would apply.59

The same decoding, written as a short Python sketch (illustrative code, not part of SCOS-2000):

import struct
pkt = bytes.fromhex("0C44C4D2001E100319002F5E100080006C0000000000"
                    "0103BC055B07F8039F0BB800000000")
w0, w1, plen = struct.unpack(">HHH", pkt[:6])
apid, ssc = w0 & 0x7FF, w1 & 0x3FFF            # 1092, 1234
svc, sub, sid = pkt[7], pkt[8], pkt[16]         # 3, 25, 108
coarse, fine = struct.unpack(">IH", pkt[10:16])
obt = coarse + fine / 65536                     # on-board seconds
raw = lambda off: struct.unpack(">H", pkt[off:off + 2])[0]
hvu_mcp_v = -330.4 + raw(23) * (1084.372 + 330.4) / 4095   # CITP1058TM
led_curr = 6.6e-5 * raw(31)                                  # CIT01081TM

docs.title: Step 7: what happens after decoding
docs.text: SCOS-2000 has no special processing for service 3 packets: each one must be defined in the database before the spacecraft starts sending it. The time stamp of each parameter sample is the packet time plus the static offset in the database (PLF_TIME, 0 here). The collection interval is also static and does not follow service 3 commands that change it on board.55 With the packet time stamped, each sample is calibrated, checked and archived, and is then available to displays, to the parameter archive and to external users through EDDS. The archived SCOS-2000 packet carries a time-stamp policy flag: for spacecraft TM it can be the correlated spacecraft event time, with a quality flag.29 The Downlink page follows that chain further.

docs.title: Related pages
docs.text:
• The command that switches this report on, byte by byte: Worked example: building a real Solar Orbiter telecommand.
  • The layers used here: TM SDLP, Space Packet, PUS packet structures, ST[03] housekeeping, time codes and the identifiers (SCID, VCID, APID) on space link identifiers.
  • The MIB tables: monitoring, calibration, monitoring checks and the tool-independent model of ECSS-E-ST-70-31C.
  • Where the source packet, frame and time packet conventions came from: From ESA PSS to CCSDS and ECSS.
  • Other Solar Orbiter databases decoded the same way: the STIX and SWA instrument databases, specified through the instrument interface documents.
SQL used

Run against solo-2025-09-16.sqlite (release MIB__20250916M25925PFMS001_SOL) and, for the comparison, solo-2020-04-16.sqlite. All columns are stored as text.

SELECT * FROM vdf;
-- candidate HK packets: parameter count and calibration kinds per SPID
WITH x AS (SELECT p.PID_SPID spid, p.PID_APID apid, t.TPCF_SIZE sz, c.PCF_NAME pn, c.PCF_CURTX cx
             FROM pid p JOIN tpcf t ON t.TPCF_SPID = p.PID_SPID
             JOIN plf l ON l.PLF_SPID = p.PID_SPID JOIN pcf c ON c.PCF_NAME = l.PLF_NAME
            WHERE p.PID_TYPE = '3' AND p.PID_STYPE = '25')
SELECT spid, apid, sz, count(*) n,
       sum(cx IN (SELECT CAF_NUMBR FROM caf)) ncaf, sum(cx IN (SELECT TXF_NUMBR FROM txf)) ntxf,
       sum(cx IN (SELECT MCF_IDENT FROM mcf)) nmcf, sum(pn IN (SELECT OCF_NAME FROM ocf)) nlim
  FROM x GROUP BY spid HAVING n BETWEEN 5 AND 45 AND ncaf >= 1 ORDER BY n;
-- adding "AND ntxf >= 1 AND nmcf >= 1 AND nlim >= 1" leaves SPIDs 59208 (11) and 54101 (44)
SELECT count(*), count(DISTINCT PID_APID) FROM pid WHERE PID_TYPE = '3' AND PID_STYPE = '25';
-- identification
SELECT * FROM pic WHERE PIC_TYPE = '3';
SELECT * FROM pid WHERE PID_SPID = '59208';
SELECT * FROM tpcf WHERE TPCF_SPID = '59208';
SELECT PID_PI1_VAL, PID_SPID, PID_DESCR FROM pid WHERE PID_APID = '1092';
SELECT PID_DFHSIZE, PID_TIME, count(*) FROM pid GROUP BY 1, 2;
SELECT PID_CHECK, count(*) FROM pid GROUP BY 1;
-- time report: OBT parameter type
SELECT l.PLF_NAME, l.PLF_OFFBY, c.PCF_DESCR, c.PCF_PTC, c.PCF_PFC
  FROM plf l JOIN pcf c ON c.PCF_NAME = l.PLF_NAME WHERE l.PLF_SPID = '9999';
-- layout, parameters, calibrations, checks
SELECT l.*, c.* FROM plf l JOIN pcf c ON c.PCF_NAME = l.PLF_NAME
 WHERE l.PLF_SPID = '59208' ORDER BY cast(l.PLF_OFFBY AS int), cast(l.PLF_OFFBI AS int);
SELECT * FROM txf WHERE TXF_NUMBR IN ('CITT1120TM', 'CITT1072TM');
SELECT * FROM txp WHERE TXP_NUMBR IN ('CITT1120TM', 'CITT1072TM');
SELECT * FROM caf WHERE CAF_NUMBR LIKE 'CITP10%';
SELECT * FROM cap WHERE CAP_NUMBR IN ('CITP1058TM', 'CITP1074TM', 'CITP1088TM', 'CITP1089TM')
 ORDER BY CAP_NUMBR, cast(CAP_XVALS AS int);
SELECT * FROM mcf WHERE MCF_IDENT = 'CIT01081TM';
SELECT * FROM cur WHERE CUR_PNAME IN (SELECT PLF_NAME FROM plf WHERE PLF_SPID = '59208');  -- no rows
SELECT * FROM ocf WHERE OCF_NAME = 'NIT0E0B5';
SELECT * FROM ocp WHERE OCP_NAME = 'NIT0E0B5';
-- bit-packed contrast
SELECT l.PLF_NAME, l.PLF_OFFBY, l.PLF_OFFBI, c.PCF_PTC, c.PCF_PFC, c.PCF_DESCR
  FROM plf l JOIN pcf c ON c.PCF_NAME = l.PLF_NAME WHERE l.PLF_SPID = '53001';

docs.title: Reference catalogue
docs.text:
This catalogue merges the reference lists of all 200 library sources: 1506 distinct documents, cited 2920 times in total. 84 of them are in our library; the rest are cited but not publicly available as far as we know (for example ESA-internal SUMs, ADDs and ICDs). Entries are merged by normalised document identifier, or by title when there is no identifier, so variant spellings may still appear separately.

Looking for an internal document?

Many SCOS-2000 documents are distributed only with the software (MICONYS, under the ESA Software Community License). The catalogue tells you their exact identifiers and which public documents cite them.

docs.title: SCOS-2000: ESA's mission control system
docs.text:
SCOS-2000 (often shortened to S2K) is the generic mission control system (MCS) developed by ESA's European Space Operations Centre (ESOC) in Darmstadt. It receives, processes, displays and archives spacecraft telemetry, and it prepares, releases and verifies telecommands. For more than two decades it has been the kernel on which ESOC builds the dedicated control system of each mission,1681 and it has also served as the core of instrument and spacecraft checkout systems.1356 A mission does not program SCOS-2000. It configures it, mainly with a database that describes its telemetry, telecommands and displays: the Mission Information Base (MIB).171

This page tells the history of SCOS-2000 and puts it in context: its ancestors, its releases, the missions and organisations that used it, its licensing and user community, its independent quality certification, the "mission family" strategy that made it cheaper, ESOC's own comparison of its four control-system generations, and the planned replacement by the European Ground Systems Common Core (EGS-CC). The companion pages explain the internals:

  • SCOS-2000 architecture: servers, client applications, the telemetry and telecommand chains, archives, events, external interfaces and configuration.
  • SCOS-2000 as EGSE and central checkout: the EGSE variant, the TOPE test language and the Herschel/Planck checkout systems.
  • Operations preparation: the databases, procedures and tools that prepare a SCOS-2000 mission, with the INTEGRAL and CHEOPS practice.
  • Ancillary systems, MICONYS and the move to EGS-CC, and the pages on EDDS, TDRS, archives, NCTRS and NIS and time correlation.

The packet standards that SCOS-2000 implements have their own history, from the ESA PSS standards to CCSDS and ECSS; it is told on From ESA PSS to CCSDS and ECSS.

docs.title: At a glance
docs.text: Aspect Summary Source Owner and developer ESA/ESOC, with European industry as contractors. ESA holds the intellectual property rights as "operational software". <sup>52</sup><sup>14</sup> Lineage MSSS (1970s), SCOS-I (1989), SCOS-II (mid-1990s), renamed SCOS-2000 from release R2.0 in 1999 <sup>25</sup><sup>42</sup> First operational missions Huygens, the Meteosat (MTP) LEOP and Teamsat, in 1997. SOHO used it for telemetry only from 1995. <sup>53</sup><sup>41</sup> Architecture Distributed client-server system on networked workstations. It scales down to a single-workstation "SCOS-2000 in-a-box". <sup>1</sup><sup>22</sup> Technology C++ with the STL on Unix. Solaris first, then Linux. COTS libraries for GUI, archive and middleware (ILOG Views, C-Tree+, ObjectStore or POST++, Orbix or omniORB). By 2014 the Java/Eclipse-based EGOS User Desktop (EUD) was used as a replacement GUI for SCOS-2000. <sup>21</sup><sup>128</sup> Standards CCSDS packet telemetry and telecommand, the ECSS Packet Utilisation Standard (PUS) and the CCSDS Space Link Extension (SLE) <sup>21</sup><sup>71</sup> Configuration ASCII database tables (the MIB) defined by the Database Import ICD, plus system configuration files <sup>1</sup><sup>71</sup> Performance (2019) The SCOS-2000-based Gaia MCS sustains more than 10 Mbps of incoming data and about 1 Mbps of full TM processing; more than 50 users on one MCS is common in a LEOP <sup>105</sup> Licence Free of charge and non-exclusive for bodies in ESA member states, for peaceful purposes <sup>52</sup><sup>14</sup> Successor EGS-CC, which ESOC reconfirmed in April 2024 as the basis of its next MCS; ESOC's EGS-CC-based mission control core is called M4C. SCOS end of life is predicted no earlier than 2033. <sup>82</sup><sup>83</sup><sup>102</sup>

docs.title: What a mission control system does
docs.text:
ESA's Bulletin describes the MCS as the software that lets the operators on the ground interact with a satellite. It receives, interprets, analyses and archives the telemetry, and it generates, verifies and uplinks the commands that control the satellite's operations. Through it the Flight Control Team assesses the health of the satellite and commands it to meet the mission goals. The MCS is critical, so it goes through comprehensive verification and validation, and so does the operational data that configures it, such as the database of the spacecraft's telemetry and command data. An MCS usually also supports mission planning, data analysis and distribution, database management and on-board software management.7

In 2003 ESA listed the functions that SCOS-2000 covers: telemetry processing, telecommanding, an online database, an online archive, general services and utilities, an operations language (OL), roles and privileges, events and actions, and on-board software maintenance (OBSM).1 A mission configures these functions to its own needs through the database (telemetry, telecommand and display characteristics) and through the system configuration files.1 The architecture page describes how these functions are split into server processes and client applications.

flowchart LR

  GS -->|"TM, TC, admin messages<br/>(via NCTRS)"| S2K["SCOS-2000<br/>servers"]
  S2K --> CL["SCOS-2000 clients<br/>(control room workstations)"]

The diagram condenses the ESOC system overview presented at GSAW 2003: ground stations connect through NCTRS (named "Network Controller & TM Router System" on the INTEGRAL slide) to the SCOS-2000 server, which serves the client workstations and exchanges data with flight dynamics, mission planning and simulators.17

docs.title: Lineage: from MSSS to SCOS-2000
docs.text:
ESOC has built its mission control systems on reusable infrastructure since the 1970s. Its stated objective is reusable infrastructure for any class of orbit and mission, with the same system reused wherever possible for the MCS, the EGSE and station control.12 In 1974 ESOC decided to develop a reusable MCS infrastructure for the missions it operated. This started a product line whose first member, the Multi Mission Support System (MSSS), entered service in 1977.25 The Bulletin article of 2007 calls MSSS the "Multi-Satellite Support System", developed in the 1970s and used for over 20 years. It dates the first generation of the Spacecraft Control and Operations System (SCOS) to the mid-1980s and its replacement by SCOS-2000 to the late 1990s.5 In 2019 ESOC counted "more than 40 years" of this infrastructure-based approach and four generations: MSSS, SCOS 1, SCOS II (renamed SCOS-2000) and the EGS-CC-based M4C, compared in Four generations compared below.102

Generation Period Architecture Telemetry Telecommand Technology Missions named in the sources MSSS entered service 1977 Centralised processing; monolithic applications serving many spacecraft of different types Frame-based TM/TC processing Frame-based FORTRAN, assembler MARECS, ECS (still in use in 1994) SCOS-I since 1989 Centralised, derived from MSSS, but one spacecraft per system Packet telemetry No generic TC chain FORTRAN on VMS Hipparcos, ERS-1, EURECA SCOS-II 1995–1999 Distributed client-server on Unix workstations Packet telemetry Generic TC chain C++ on Unix Huygens, Artemis, Envisat (planned first clients) SCOS-2000 from 1999 (R2.0) Distributed client-server, CORBA-based distribution Packet telemetry Re-engineered TC chain C++ on Solaris, then Linux see Missions

The architecture, TM/TC and technology columns of the first three rows follow the GSAW 2003 history slide.15 The MSSS and SCOS-I missions come from the SCOS-II paper,25 the SCOS-II client missions from the same paper,32 and the SCOS-2000 row from the ESOC presentation of April 2000 and Bulletin 108.425354

Dates differ between sources

The GSAW 2003 slide gives "MSSS - 1984-1996", while the SCOS-II paper says MSSS entered service in 1977 and Bulletin 130 says it was developed in the 1970s.15255 The 1984–1996 range may describe a later MSSS period, but the sources do not explain the difference. This wiki uses 1977 as the entry into service. ESOC's ICALEPCS paper of 2019 gives coarser periods: MSSS in operational use from the 1970s to the end of the 1990s, SCOS 1 from the beginning of the 1990s (the SCOS-II paper dates SCOS-I to 1989) and still in use in "some legacy missions" in 2019, and SCOS II, later renamed SCOS-2000, from the beginning of the 2000s, later than the first operational missions of 1997 named by Bulletin 108.1022553 The expansion of MSSS also varies: "Multi Mission Support System" in the SCOS-II paper, "Multi-Spacecraft Support System" in the OL paper, and "Multi-Satellite Support System" in Bulletins 108 and 130 and in the 2019 paper.2534525108

docs.title: SCOS-II: the new generation (1994)
docs.text:
The SCOS-II paper, written by ESOC's Mission Operations Department, explains why ESOC replaced SCOS-I. Its reference list, and that of the OL paper below, place both papers in the SpaceOps 94 proceedings.3240 The concepts of MSSS and SCOS-I came from the mission control needs of the 1970s, when spacecraft were hard-wired. Spacecraft such as EURECA and ERS-1 carried much more on-board software and autonomy, and the old systems reached their limits.25 The new system had to reduce mission adaptation and maintenance costs, make mission preparation, execution and evaluation more efficient, increase operational quality and reliability, last at least 10 years, and serve missions of any type, size and complexity.25 It also had to be compatible with the CCSDS and ESA packet standards and with the guidelines of ESA's Committee for Operations and EGSE Standards (COES).25

The design choices made for SCOS-II still shape SCOS-2000:

  • Client-server distribution. A network of Unix workstations, with a dedicated workstation for each operational user and central servers for system-level services such as the ground station interface. One SCOS-II instance controls several satellites of the same family rather than several unrelated missions.26
  • Scalability and roles. The same system can be the prime MCS, a "mini-backup" at a TT&C station, or (because it follows COES) a checkout system. For a simple mission it can be descoped to a single Sun workstation or even a PC.27
  • Database-driven configuration. Not only TM/TC processing but display layouts, default behaviours and user privilege sets come from the mission database.27
  • Ambitious performance goals. Concurrent real-time rates of 2 Mbps telemetry and 4 kbps telecommand, display updates faster than 10 per second, retrievals within 5 s for data a few weeks old and 30 s for data several years old, with up to 50 workstations in use.27
  • Parameter validity. Each parameter's validity combines power status, the quality of the data unit that carried it, the data route, the age of the value, stability after commanding, and user-defined criteria. Invalidity propagates, for example to synthetic parameters that use an invalid input.29
  • Three kinds of checks. Operational status checks, operational constraint checks (rules that must never be violated) and behaviour checks against the predicted on-board state.29
  • Uniform "activities". A procedure, a command sequence and a single command are all activities with pre-requisites, execution monitoring and verification. Pre-execution validation combines feasibility, safety and dynamic checks. Activities are released by a scheduler, a manual stack or an event-driven commander.30
  • Online history. Replay "as live" or as "video replay", data access strategies, data analysis and report generation were to become part of the MCS itself.31

SCOS-II also planned a mission model of "system elements" with operational modes and roles, a library of reusable elements and a prediction function.28 Release 1 was due as a preliminary delivery in November 1994, with releases 2 (1995–6) and 3 (1996–7) adding modelling, mission planning and data distribution. The first client missions were to be Huygens, Artemis and Envisat, launched in 1997–1998.32

Inference

Several SCOS-II ambitions, such as the system-element mission model and the event-driven commander, do not appear as such in SCOS-2000's database interface (the MIB tables describe parameters, packets, commands and displays, not a model of system elements). The idea of operating through a model of the space system returns with the Monitoring and Control Model of EGS-CC.88 This reading is the wiki's own; the sources do not draw the connection.

docs.title: The SCOS-II Operations Language (OL)
docs.text:
A companion SpaceOps 94 paper by ESOC and Computer Resources International (CRI) introduced the SCOS-II Operations Language (OL).33 Its motivation was the slow turnaround of derived parameters in earlier systems. In MSSS an operations engineer wrote an algorithm on paper and a software engineer coded it. In SCOS-I the engineer wrote FORTRAN with a few extra constructs, which was compiled and linked into the control system, so an error only showed up as a run-time crash. Neither system supported version and configuration control of these algorithms.34 The OL let operations engineers edit, test, validate and install expressions and procedures themselves, without software support engineers.33

The paper divides mission knowledge into four kinds: declarative (for example calibration curves, entered through forms), expressive (derived parameters, command validation conditions, written in the OL), procedural (operations procedures, also in the OL) and special knowledge that still needs software extensions.35 The implementation has three layers: an interaction layer (the user interface), a logical layer centred on the OL, and a physical layer with the control system's services. An explicit object-oriented data model is the "contract" between the logical and physical layers.3536

Property SCOS-II OL design Source Typing Strongly typed, so wrong use of data-model objects is caught at preparation time 36 Execution Interpreted; the parse tree is built when the database is configured and reused at run time 3638 Unit An OL script: a declaration part (local variables, functions) and an executable part (statements) 36 Objects Parameters with name, description, limit, raw and engineering values; a default attribute, so P112 means the engineering value 37 Validity Every value carries a validity status; a value computed from invalid inputs is itself invalid 38 Constructs Assignment, wait, function call, goto, if-then-else, select-case, while, repeat-until, two kinds of for loop; numeric, boolean, string, time, list, set, vector, matrix and map expressions; mathematical, statistical, bit-manipulation and time functions 37 Concurrency No language constructs for parallelism; the physical layer handles interlocks between procedure executions 39 Implementation Designed with OMT, written in C++, scanner and parser generated with lex and yacc 37

The paper's example derives parameter P117 from P112: if the limit status of P112 is above limits, P117 takes the upper limit value, otherwise it takes the engineering value of P112 ("if (P112.limit == ABOVE_LIMITS) then P117 := P112.limit.upper; else P117 := P112; endif;").37 The authors called the language deliberately "kept simple and stupid", with the intelligence in the physical-layer objects. They noted that OL scripts are hard to port between missions whose data models differ.40 SCOS-2000 kept the OL for synthetic parameters: the MIB delivers one OL expression file per dynamic synthetic parameter, and the Solar Orbiter MIB of September 2025 contains 1,582 of them (see the architecture page and synthetic parameters and the OL language).6496

docs.title: From SCOS-2 to SCOS-2000
docs.text: An ESOC presentation of April 2000 explains the name. The system was called "SCOS-2" up to release R1.4 (until 1998) and "SCOS-2000" from release R2.0 (from 1999). SCOS-2000 is an evolution of SCOS-2 based on operational experience. Its differences are a new telecommand chain, architectural consolidation, a user interface fully based on ILOG, systematic use of the ObjectStore object database, and CORBA for better distribution and for new external interfaces.42 ESA's Bulletin of November 2001 gives the same history from another angle. Work on SCOS started in about 1992, the first ESA missions were supported in 1997, and the telecommanding chain was re-engineered in 1998–2000. The total investment, including ESA's internal effort, was about 15 MEuro.53

The plans changed over time. In April 2000, ESOC planned R3.0 for mid-2001 (port to PC and Linux, an operating-system shell, replacement of ObjectStore) and R4.0 for early 2002 (several SCOS-2000 versions on one machine, constellation support, higher-level monitoring functions).44 The GSAW 2003 status shows R3.0 delivered in January 2003 and R4.0 planned for June 2004.20

Release 5 and later

The available sources do not give the release date of R5.0, and no ESOC document in the library describes R5 as a whole. What the Database Import ICD shows is that R5.0 stored telemetry packets "in a database" (so there was no longer any gain in letting several packets share one SPID), moved command sequences and displays out of the run-time database into the FARC, and added SLE and NIS throw-event commands.6061 The year of R6.0 is also not stated in the available sources; the earliest dated mention found is the EDDS release note of February 2018, which lists SCOS 6.0.1 as a tested dependency.66

docs.title: ESA missions
docs.text:
The sources list SCOS-2000 users at several points in time.

Snapshot Missions Source April 2000, past SOHO (1995, telemetry only); Huygens, Teamsat and MTP (Eumetsat) in 1997 41 April 2000, present INTEGRAL and MSG (successful SVTs), Rosetta ("AD phase"), ERS (first delivery end of 1999, migration from SCOS-I), PROBA (MCS and EGSE) 41 April 2000, future SMART-1, Envisat and XMM (migrations from SCOS-I), Mars Express, FIRST/Planck MOC, CryoSat, GOCE 41 March 2003, done SOHO (NASA Goddard), Teamsat, MTP, Huygens (via the NASA system at JPL), PROBA, MSG LEOP, INTEGRAL 19 March 2003, in development Rosetta, Mars Express, SMART-1, Venus Express, CryoSat, GOCE, ADM, Herschel/Planck MCS and central checkout (EGSE), Vega launcher EGSE and Galileo MCS (both under evaluation) 19 May 2007, mission families Interplanetary: Rosetta, Mars Express, Venus Express, then BepiColombo and Solar Orbiter. Earth observation: CryoSat, GOCE, Aeolus, then CryoSat-2, Swarm, EarthCARE and Sentinels. 8 2019 SCOS-2000 is the basis of "the vast majority" of ESOC control systems, for operational missions and for those to be launched next; the Gaia MCS is the paper's performance example 102105 2025 More than 40 missions at ESOC; Swarm chosen as the pilot for migration to EGS-CC 8284 2025, outside ESOC CHEOPS, an ESA mission operated by its consortium, with an MCS on SCOS-2000 5.4.2 at INTA's Torrejón centre (CEIT) in Spain 117120

GSAW 2003 shows how a SCOS-2000-based MCS fits in a ground segment, using INTEGRAL as the example: the MCS imports the satellite database, connects to the stations through NCTRS, exchanges data with flight dynamics, mission planning and the simulator, and feeds an operations archive and the science centres.17 A launch and early orbit phase (LEOP) configuration of that time had a prime and a backup SCOS-2000 server and a prime and a backup NCTRS, with SCOS-2000 client workstations spread over the Main Control Room (15), the Project Control Room (6), the Dedicated Control Room (6), the Software Support Room (4), the Simulation Room (2) and the PI Support Area (2).18

A current example is Solar Orbiter, whose MIB is public. The release of 16 September 2025 defines 126,745 monitoring parameters, 11,150 telemetry packet definitions on 293 APIDs, 5,454 commands and 3,404 command sequences. Five and a half years earlier, the release of 16 April 2020 had 102,104 parameters, 9,027 packet definitions, 5,238 commands and 2,701 sequences.9697
