docs.title: SCOS-2000 architecture
docs.text:
SCOS-2000 is described by ESA as a mission control system kernel: a set of object-oriented components that system developers can reuse, and a set of generic executables that a mission can use as they are when their functions match its needs. The same kernel is meant for spacecraft control and for checkout systems, can be extended with mission-specific functions, and is distributed, scalable, configurable and open.1 This page explains how that kernel is organised and how data flows through it. It starts with the overall structure, then follows telemetry from the ground station to the operator's display and telecommands from the operator to the spacecraft, and ends with archives, events, external interfaces, configuration and multi-domain operation.

The descriptions come mostly from ESA presentations and interface documents of 2000–2018. SCOS-2000 changed considerably between releases (see releases), so each statement is dated by its source. The mission database that configures all of this is described in the MIB and its topic pages.

docs.title: Clients and servers
docs.text:
SCOS-2000 inherits the client-server design of SCOS-II: each operator works on a workstation with local processing and local caches, while central servers coordinate the system and host the interfaces to the ground stations.163 The GSAW 2003 presentation lists the processes on each side:3

Side Processes Domain Server (prime and backup) Packetiser TM Behaviour (limits) checker TM Synthetic parameter packet generator TM Multiplexer, Releaser, Verifier, On-Board Queue Model (OBQM) TC Archive TM, TC, events Events & Actions servers Events Configuration server (MISCdynamic) System Client (MMI applications) Desktop (with alarm display) System Monitoring display container, out-of-limits (OOL) display TM Event logger Events Manual and automatic stacks, TC history TC Caches TM, TC, events Configuration client (TM and TC "SPACON") System

A typical configuration is a network of workstations, but the system can be scaled down to a "SCOS-2000 in-a-box" on a single workstation for simpler missions.13 ESOC's LEOP configuration of 2003 had prime and backup SCOS-2000 servers, prime and backup NCTRS, and 35 client workstations spread over six rooms (15 + 6 + 6 + 4 + 2 + 2).11

docs.title: Functional subsystems and layers
docs.text:
ESA groups the functions of SCOS-2000 into subsystems with short names: telemetry processing (TM), telecommanding (TC), the online database (DB), the online archive (ARCH), general services and utilities, the Operations Language (OL), roles and privileges (USER), events and actions (EVAC), and on-board software maintenance (OBSM).13 The GSAW 2003 slides arrange the software in layers, from persistent storage and database access at the bottom, through the telemetry, command and user models, to the applications on top:4

flowchart TB
  subgraph APP["Applications"]
    direction LR
    TMD["Telemetry displays"] --- CMDG["Commanding"] --- PROC["Procedure execution"] --- OBSMA["OBSM"] --- MMI["MMI, roles & privileges, utilities"]
  end
  subgraph MOD["Models and services"]
    direction LR
    TMM["Telemetry model"] --- OL["Operations Language"] --- CM["Command model"] --- UM["User model"] --- ARCH["Archiving"] --- EVA["Event & action handling"]
  end
  subgraph BASE["Infrastructure"]
    direction LR
    GSI["Ground station & external interfaces"] --- MIBA["MIB applications (database access)"] --- PS["Persistent storage"]
  end
  APP --> MOD --> BASE

The diagram is this wiki's condensed reading of the "SCOS-2000 Software Layers" slide.4

docs.title: Enabling technology
docs.text:
Area Technology (2003) Design Object-oriented analysis and design, UML with Rational Rose Languages C++ with the STL on Unix GUI library ILOG Views Packet archive C-Tree+ Object database ObjectStore (classic line); POST++ (evolution line) CORBA Iona Orbix, CORBA 2.1 (classic); omniORB, CORBA 2.3 (evolution) Public-domain tools Flex and Bison (OL parsing), Tcl/Tk (old task launcher), a2ps (printouts), zlib (packet compression) Space standards CCSDS packet TM/TC, ECSS PUS, SLE for ground station interoperability

All rows come from the "Enabling Technology" slide of GSAW 2003.2 The ESOC presentation of April 2000 adds that the new CORBA-based external interfaces were one of the main differences between SCOS-2 and SCOS-2000.14

docs.title: Context and interfaces
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  NCTRS["NCTRS<br/>(ground stations)"] -->|"TM frames, report packets,<br/>admin messages"| S2K
  S2K -->|"TC requests"| NCTRS
  DBM["Spacecraft database manager"] -->|"ASCII database (MIB)"| S2K
  FOP["Procedure production tool"] -->|"TC sequences"| S2K
  SDE["On-board software SDE"] -->|"memory images,<br/>symbol tables"| S2K
  S2K -->|"dump images"| SDE
  FDS["Flight dynamics (ORATOS)"] <-->|"TM packets,<br/>task parameter files"| S2K
  MPS["Mission planning"] -->|"command schedules"| S2K
  EXT["External client systems<br/>(e.g. TDRS)"] <-->|"packets, parameters,<br/>commands, events"| S2K
  S2K(["SCOS-2000"]) --> U["Users: displays,<br/>printouts"]

The diagram follows the "System Overview" and "System interfaces" slides. The ground station interface is NCTRS, with protocols for the station equipment of that time. The spacecraft database arrives as ASCII files produced with a database editing tool. Flight dynamics receives real-time and retrieved TM packets and sends task parameter files. Other systems connect through APIs for packets, parameters, commands and events.5

docs.title: Operator applications
docs.text:
Operators start SCOS-2000 from a task launcher. In the Herschel PACS instrument test set-up of 2004, the command s2.start opened the launcher; one button selected all server applications and another the standard client applications. The desktop then showed a top bar with the workstation settings, user login and alarm-tone control, and a footer with the three most recent log messages.2223 The client applications and their launcher names were:25

Launcher name Application Purpose MON Telemetry desktop Alphanumeric, strip chart, scrolling and mimic TM displays VPD Variable packet display Contents of variable TM packets MSTK Manual stack Manual telecommand release TCHIST Telecommand history Status of every released command and its verification stages OOL Out-of-limits display Parameters currently out of limits EVLOG Event logger (message display) Scrolling display of SCOS-2000 log messages

The 2003 slides list the display types in more detail.9

Display Description Alphanumeric display (AND) 32 or 64 parameters Graphic display (GRD) 1 to 8 parameters against time, strip chart emulation, or parameter against parameter Mimic displays Schematic displays, with an editor Scrolling display (SCD) Parameter values scrolling with time Telemetry Query Display (TQD) Query of one parameter, with an OL editor and a panel showing each validity condition Out-of-limits displays Current limit violations Packet displays Variable Packet Display, Telemetry Packet History Display, On-Board Event History Display Command displays Command History Display, Command Query Display, On-Board Queue Display (OBQD) TM and TC SPACON Online control of processing: filing on/off, reset of status consistency checks, limit values, calibration points, OL expressions

The display types and SPACON functions come from the monitoring and commanding slides of GSAW 2003.897 The TQD validity panel is described in the EMCS user manual and its OL editor in the ICD.2755 The MIB defines AND, GRD, SCD and printout layouts; see display definitions in the MIB.

Each application has its own user manual. The 2004 guide lists manuals for the external interface and TOPE, the desktop, the event logger, the telemetry desktop, the OOL display, the variable packet display, the manual stack and the command history.26 The Database Import ICD references further manuals and design documents, among them the monitoring, commanding and system-level software requirements documents, the OL design document, the Synthetic Parameters user manual, the Events & Actions user manual, the MIB Applications user manual, and interface documents for stack import, task parameter files and telemetry parameter injection.44

docs.title: The telemetry chain
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  F["TM transfer frames<br/>from NCTRS"] --> PK["Packetiser<br/>frame checks, packet<br/>reconstruction, CLCW"]
  PK -->|"CLCW"| TC["TC chain<br/>(COP-1)"]
  PK --> ID["Identification<br/>APID, type, subtype,<br/>PI1/PI2 -> SPID"]
  ID --> AR[("Packet archive<br/>filed by SPID, stream, time")]
  ID --> DS["Distribution to<br/>client caches"]
  DS --> TMM["Telemetry model<br/>extraction (plf/vpd), validity,<br/>calibration, synthetics"]
  TMM --> BC["Behaviour checks<br/>limits, status, delta,<br/>status consistency"]
  BC --> DISP["Displays, OOL,<br/>events"]
  AR -.->|"retrieval"| DS

The steps are those of the "Monitoring functions" and "Top level components" slides of GSAW 2003.86 The sections below follow the chain.

docs.title: Packetiser
docs.text:
The telemetry packetiser receives telemetry transfer frames, report packets and administrative messages. It reconstructs packets from frames, extracts the Command Link Control Word (CLCW) for the commanding chain, and applies quality, continuity and sequence checks.86 The Database Import ICD added the Packetiser in issue 5.0 for release R2.2e.43 To recognise a packet, the packetiser reads the APID from its fixed place in the header, and the PUS type and subtype from a position set in the configuration (the same position for all packets of a spacecraft). For some type and subtype combinations it also reads up to two additional identification fields from the application data, as specified in the pic table. It then looks up the pid table to find the processing keys: the SCOS-2000 Packet ID (SPID) for fixed packets and the Telemetry Packet Structure Definition (TPSD) for variable packets.59 Packets without a data field header are identified by APID alone.60

The ICD turns two on-board design choices into explicit constraints: the type and subtype must sit at the same place in every TM packet, and every packet with the same type and subtype must carry its additional identification fields at the same place.59 From R5.0 each distinct TM packet must have its own SPID, because packets are stored in a database and sharing SPIDs caused retrieval and display problems.6049 The packetiser can check the packet error control field (when PID_CHECK is 1) and can generate an event when a packet arrives (when PID_EVENT is I, W or A).61

Time stamping. Every frame and packet that is filed or distributed gets a time stamp, which is the prime filing key of the history files. The packetiser supports three options: the time of filing in the archive (useful when replaying old frames during tests), the Frame Transmission Time derived from the Earth Reception Time minus ground, propagation and on-board delays, or the on-board time in the packet converted to UTC through the time correlation library.37 The time correlation function itself (time couples, least-squares or synchronised-clock coefficients, accuracy and validity status) is described on Time correlation in SCOS-2000.36

docs.title: The telemetry model: extraction, validity and calibration
docs.text:
Parameter extraction follows the plf definitions for fixed packets (including super-commutated parameters) and the vpd definitions for variable packets.859 Variable packets have a limitation: the values extracted from them cannot take part in the full TM processing (validity, monitoring checks, verification, synthetic parameters), because their parameter identities and time references are only known once each packet is opened. The ICD therefore advises against using variable packets for regular housekeeping.68

Every value carries a validity. The TOPE interface of the EGSE version exposes the validity as a bit set, and its list shows the causes that SCOS-2000 tracks: state validity false, system element not powered, transport route off, a telecommand scheduled for the parameter (transient), transport errors, an expired value (packet not arrived), unknown state, calibration failure, a time before the mission epoch, a packet not configured in the cache, an uninitialised value, retrieval errors, database errors, unknown fields or types, overflow, division by zero, and OL parse errors.27 These causes extend the validity factors already planned for SCOS-II: power, data unit quality, data routing, age, stability after commanding and user-defined status.18

The raw value of a parameter is its value before calibration. It is not the same as the encoded bits, except for unsigned integers: a raw value of -1 in a 16-bit signed integer parameter is encoded as 0xFFFF.45 Calibration turns raw values into engineering values. See calibration in the MIB and MIB parameter types.

docs.title: Behaviour checking
docs.text:
The behaviour checker applies the monitoring checks defined in the ocf and ocp tables. The ICD defines limit checks and status checks (each with soft or hard severity), delta checks on the change since the last valid value, and status consistency checks against a reference value that SCOS-2000 maintains from the predicted or detected effect of commands. A fifth type, E, does not raise an out-of-limits state at all: it generates a SCOS-2000 event whose full ID is BEHV:: followed by the parameter name, which can then trigger actions.58 Each check has an applicability condition (a parameter equal to a value), except status consistency checks, whose applicability is always true. The checks of a parameter are evaluated in order and the search stops at the first applicable check or soft/hard pair, unless the global variable BEHV_STOP_FIRST_SET says otherwise.58 Details are on monitoring checks.

The Solar Orbiter MIB of September 2025 uses four of the five OCP_TYPE codes: 4,153 H, 3,096 S, 105 delta (D) and 15 status consistency (C) check records, and no event-only (E) checks.75 SCOS-II had planned "behaviour checks" against a predicted on-board state.18

SQL used 
-- solo-2025-09-16.sqlite
SELECT OCP_TYPE, count(*) FROM ocp GROUP BY 1;
-- C|15   D|105   H|4153   S|3096
SELECT PID_EVENT, count(*) FROM pid GROUP BY 1;
-- (blank)|1162   A|6360   I|1374   N|1095   W|1159
SELECT PID_CHECK, count(*) FROM pid GROUP BY 1;
-- 0|11144   1|6
SELECT PID_EVENT, PID_TYPE, PID_STYPE, count(*) FROM pid
 WHERE PID_EVENT IN ('A','I','W') GROUP BY 1, 2, 3;
-- A|1|2|274   A|1|8|1477   A|5|3|2911   A|5|4|1698   I|5|1|1374   W|5|2|1159
SELECT PID_TYPE, PID_STYPE, PID_APID, PID_DESCR FROM pid WHERE PID_CHECK = '1';
-- 0|0|1|Bad/Idle/Good complete transfer frame (3 rows)
-- 166|1..3|1966|MATIS BASIC HKTM OK, MATIS RX LOCK EXPECTED, MATIS SSMM FTS COMMANDING

The same MIB flags 8,893 of its 11,150 packet definitions to raise an event on reception: 6,360 with severity Alarm, 1,374 Info and 1,159 Warning (the other 2,257 have N or the default, which is N). The severities follow the PUS report types: all 1,374 Info events are (5,1) reports and all 1,159 Warning events are (5,2) reports, while the Alarm events are (5,3) and (5,4) event reports (2,911 and 1,698) and (1,8) and (1,2) failure reports (1,477 and 274). See ST[05] event reporting and ST[01] request verification. Only 6 packet definitions ask the packetiser to check the packet error control field: the three transfer-frame entries on APID 1 and three type 166 packets on APID 1966 described as MATIS reports, so no spacecraft source packet definition has PID_CHECK = 1.7561

Inference

Two readings here are the wiki's own. First, the status consistency check, whose reference value follows the commands sent, can be seen as a simple form of the SCOS-II behaviour checks against a predicted on-board state; neither source draws the link. Second, since no spacecraft packet definition in the Solar Orbiter MIB sets PID_CHECK, packet error control is probably checked elsewhere in the ground chain or not at all at packet level. The MIB does not say which.

docs.title: Synthetic parameters and the OL
docs.text:
Synthetic parameters are monitoring parameters whose value SCOS-2000 calculates (the ICD notes that older systems called them derived parameters). Once calculated they behave like telemetry: they can be displayed, calibrated, limit-checked and used in other synthetic parameters. Their validity follows from the validity of their inputs and can be restricted further with an explicit validity condition.5254 The field PCF_NATUR of the pcf table selects the kind:525355

PCF_NATUR Kind How it is calculated Stored? D Dynamic OL synthetic OL expression in a file named after the parameter, evaluated locally when an application needs it, every time a contributing value or validity changes; recalculated in retrieval No P SPEL synthetic Like D, written in the Synthetic Parameter Expression Language; only in the EGSE delivery of SCOS-2000 No H Hard-coded synthetic C++ code, written directly or produced by the OL compiler, linked into a library; cheaper to run but not visible or editable online No S Saved synthetic Calculated centrally by the Synthetic Parameters Packet Generator (SPPG) from a linked D or H parameter, stored in synthetic packets Yes C Static user-defined constant Constant from PCF_PARVAL, changeable with the OL editor of the TQD – R Raw telemetry (and dynamic user-defined constants) Extracted from a packet; dynamic constants come from an internal "constants" packet set through TM SPACON or the parameter injection interface –

SCOS-2000 evaluates synthetic parameters in cascade: a new sample of parameter A triggers A, then any B that uses A, then any C that uses B. Up to R3.1 this forbade circular dependencies. Later releases calculate each parameter only once per update cycle.54 The ICD warns that synthetic parameters that use super-commutated inputs are evaluated once per sample and can be very demanding.53

Saved synthetic parameters exist because dynamic ones are recalculated on each workstation and again in retrieval. A saved value is calculated once, centrally, and stored with its validity, so every display shows the same value when moving backwards or forwards in history, even after the definition changes. The cost is that a synthetic packet is only generated when its triggering TM packet arrives, so not every intermediate value is kept. Each saved parameter occupies a 13-octet slot in its synthetic packet.53

docs.title: Example: saved synthetics in the Solar Orbiter MIB
docs.text:
The Solar Orbiter MIB of September 2025 has 1,582 dynamic OL synthetic parameters (each with its OL file), 2 saved synthetic parameters, and no hard-coded, SPEL or constant parameters.75 The two saved parameters, NTTSS030 and NTTSS031, hold the time of the last carrier lock of the two transponders labelled DST-1 and DST-2. Each is linked through PCF_RELATED to a dynamic OL parameter (NTTSX030, NTTSX031). Both are stored in the synthetic packet SPID 66838, defined in pid as type 251, subtype 2 on APID 1966 with the description "Saved Synthetics", and in tpcf as SAVED_SYNTH. Their plf entries sit at byte offsets 0 and 13: exactly one 13-octet slot each, as the ICD requires.7553

The OL file of NTTSX030 (real MIB data, comments omitted) updates a global variable with the time of the receiver lock parameter only when that parameter's raw value is 1 (locked), and otherwise returns the previous saved value through a "static reference" to $NTTSS030:

if (NDSD0021.raw == 1) then
GVAR_DST_1_LastCarrierLockTime := NDSD0021.time;
endif;
$NTTSS030;

The if (...) then ... endif; form and the := assignment are the same as in the SCOS-II OL example of 1994 described on the overview page, and the ICD documents the .raw and .eng parameter views of the SCOS-2000 OL.752155 The full OL syntax is documented in the SCOS-2000 Synthetic Parameters user manual, which is not in this wiki's library.5244 See synthetic parameters and the OL language.

SQL used 
-- solo-2025-09-16.sqlite
SELECT PCF_NATUR, count(*) FROM pcf GROUP BY 1;     -- D|1582  R|125161  S|2
SELECT count(*) FROM synthetic;                       -- 1582
SELECT PCF_NAME, PCF_DESCR, PCF_RELATED FROM pcf WHERE PCF_NATUR = 'S';
-- NTTSS030|Last C_Lock DST-1|NTTSX030   NTTSS031|Last C_Lock DST-2|NTTSX031
SELECT PLF_NAME, PLF_SPID, PLF_OFFBY, PLF_OFFBI FROM plf WHERE PLF_NAME IN ('NTTSS030','NTTSS031');
-- NTTSS030|66838|0|0   NTTSS031|66838|13|0
SELECT PID_TYPE, PID_STYPE, PID_APID, PID_SPID, PID_DESCR FROM pid WHERE PID_SPID = '66838';
-- 251|2|1966|66838|Saved Synthetics
SELECT * FROM tpcf WHERE TPCF_SPID = '66838';         -- 66838|SAVED_SYNTH|26
SELECT SOURCE FROM synthetic WHERE NAME = 'NTTSX030';

docs.title: Internally generated packets
docs.text:
Several SCOS-2000 functions publish their state as internal TM packets, so that the normal monitoring displays, checks and archives can handle it. The ICD names the SPPG synthetic packets, the "constants" packet of dynamic user-defined constants, the "MISC" packet with selected dynamic configuration variables, and the system control packets of the multi-domain SCTL application. It recommends giving each of them a pid entry with a type, subtype and APID combination that no other source uses.60555657 In the Solar Orbiter MIB the saved synthetic packet uses type 251 on APID 1966 (see above). The same MIB also has pid entries for bad, idle and good complete transfer frames (SPIDs 1000002, 1000003 and 1000006, APID 1, type and subtype 0), which the ICD does not list among the internal packets.75

Inference

The transfer-frame entries probably let the archive and the packet history displays handle the frames that the packetiser files (GSAW 2003 lists TM transfer frames among its inputs, and TN-1030 says that frames as well as packets are time-stamped for filing).637 The MIB does not document their purpose.

SQL used 
-- solo-2025-09-16.sqlite
SELECT PID_TYPE, PID_STYPE, PID_APID, PID_SPID, PID_DESCR FROM pid
 WHERE CAST(PID_SPID AS int) >= 1000000 ORDER BY CAST(PID_SPID AS int);
-- 0|0|1|1000002|Bad complete transfer frame
-- 0|0|1|1000003|Idle complete transfer frame
-- 0|0|1|1000006|Good complete transfer frame

docs.title: The telecommand chain
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  subgraph SRC["Command sources"]
    MS["Manual stacks"]
    AS["Autostack"]
    EXT["External sources<br/>(TOPE/EXIF, command injection,<br/>stack import, task parameter files)"]
  end
  SRC --> MUX["Multiplexer"]
  MUX --> PTV["Pre-transmission validation<br/>static and dynamic PTV"]
  PTV --> REL["Releaser<br/>encoding, CRC, time-tag wrapping,<br/>interlocks"]
  REL -->|"TC packets"| NCTRS["NCTRS / ground station"]
  NCTRS -->|"UV acknowledgements"| VER["Verifier<br/>multi-stage verification"]
  TMR["TM: service 1 reports<br/>and parameters"] --> VER
  REL --> OBQM["On-Board Queue Model<br/>(service 11)"]
  VER --> HIST["Command history"]

The structure follows the GSAW 2003 "Commanding functions" slide.7

docs.title: Command sources
docs.text: The manual stack is the operator's main tool. In 2003 it could load commands and sequences with parameters, de-calibrate parameter values, time-tag commands for on-board execution, and set release dependencies by grouping, blocking, delta release times and interlocking. It had a master manual mode and a wait mode, applied static and dynamic pre-transmission validation (PTV), and could save and load commands, sequences, stack files and task parameter files (TPFs). Sequences accept formal parameters and absolute start or execution times. The autostack offers a restricted subset with no editing, driven by release or execution times.7 A multiplexer lets several sources command in parallel.7 Command sequences and their parameters are defined in the MIB (see command sequences and parameter sets); from R5.0 they are converted to XML and loaded from the file archive.48

docs.title: Release
docs.text:
The releaser is the interface to the external command destination, NCTRS.7 It builds the packet from the header definition and parameters in the MIB (see commanding in the MIB) and automatically appends the 16-bit CRC unless the command type says otherwise.65 Commands with an execution time-tag are automatically wrapped in service (11,4) commands.73 The maximum command size is set by a configuration variable, with a default of 248 octets that must leave room for the header, the CRC and the time-tag wrapper.63 Interlocks hold further commands until a given verification stage of a previous command is reached.6530

The command type CCF_CTYPE marks commands that are not ordinary packets. R is a control segment (a "reset map" command) and F a control frame (a BC frame: Unlock or Set V(R)); for both, the MIB defines the frame data field rather than a packet header. S is a packet without a packet error control field, typically for EGSE equipment. From R5.0, T is an SLE throw event, sent to the SLE service provider at the ground station, and N is a NIS throw event, executed by the NIS and not forwarded to the station.6564

The Solar Orbiter MIB uses three of these types. Its control frames are UNLOCK and SETVR, its control segments are RESET, REIN_TTR and TC_ONLY, and six NIS throw events open and close the session and the TM and TC links (for example EGENRTCO, "GENERIC OPEN TC LINK"). The throw events use a dedicated packet header named NOS2KHDR, described as "NIS Throw Events".75 See COP-1 for the Unlock and Set V(R) directives and NCTRS, NIS and the ground station interface for throw events.

SQL used 
-- solo-2025-09-16.sqlite
SELECT CCF_CNAME, CCF_DESCR, CCF_CTYPE, CCF_PKTID FROM ccf WHERE CCF_CTYPE <> '';
-- EGENRTCC|GENERIC CLOSE TC LINK|N|NOS2KHDR   EGENRTCO|GENERIC OPEN TC LINK|N|NOS2KHDR
-- EGENRTMC|GENERIC CLOSE TM LINK|N|NOS2KHDR   EGENRTMO|GENERIC OPEN TM LINK|N|NOS2KHDR
-- ESESIONC|CLOSE SESSION|N|NOS2KHDR          ESESIONO|OPEN SESSION|N|NOS2KHDR
-- REIN_TTR|Reinit TTR|R|NO_HDR  RESET|PAC RESET directive|R|NO_HDR  TC_ONLY|CPDU TC_Only|R|NO_HDR
-- SETVR|SETV( R ) Directive|F|NO_HDR  UNLOCK|FARM UNLOCK directive|F|NO_HDR
SELECT * FROM tcp;   -- HPC1_TC, NO_HDR, NOM_TC, NOS2KHDR (NIS Throw Events)

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
The verifier performs multi-stage verification of each released command and disables status consistency checks on the telemetry parameters that the command affects.7 SCOS-2000 supports two kinds of verification stage. Report-based stages wait for PUS service 1 reports. Parameter-based stages check monitoring parameter values against criteria within a time window.66 For service 1, the verifier extracts the 4 octets that echo the command's packet ID and sequence control from each report, to identify the command instance. The echo must be at the same place in all type 1 reports. The subtype alone decides success or failure; the failure code is ignored. Progress reports can only feed progress stage 0.7067 See ST[01] request verification and command verification in the MIB.

The full list of stages appears in the EGSE user manual, which gives the order that the TOPE language reports for each stage:28

Order Stage Meaning 0 PTV_DYNAMIC Dynamic pre-transmission validation 1 PTV_STATIC Static pre-transmission validation 2 MCS_RELEASE Release by the MCS 3 UV_GS_RECEIVE Received by the ground station (or EGSE TC front end) 4 UV_GS_UPLINK Uplinked 5 UV_ONB_ACCEPT Accepted on board (reported by the ground station or TC front end when the spacecraft confirms reception of an AD-mode command) 6 EV_APP_ACCEPT Accepted by the application process 7 EV_START_EXEC Start of execution 8–17 EV_PROGRESS_0 to EV_PROGRESS_9 Progress steps 0 to 9 18 EV_END_EXEC Completion of execution

Each stage has a status. The values listed are IDLE, PENDING, PASSED, FAILED, UNVERIFIED, UNKNOWN, TIMEOUT, SUPERSEDED, UNCERTAIN_FAILED, UNCERTAIN_PASSED, AFFECTED, SCC and NOT_APPLICABLE.28 The stages prefixed "UV" are reported by the ground side (the ground station through NCTRS, or the EGSE TC front end). Those prefixed "EV" concern execution by the application process, reported through service 1 or derived from telemetry conditions.29

In the Solar Orbiter MIB, the 206 verification stages are all acceptance or completion stages: 16 report-based acceptance stages, 23 report-based completion stages and 167 parameter-based completion stages. There are no start or progress stages.75

SQL used 
-- solo-2025-09-16.sqlite; cvs uses generic column names: COL2 = CVS_TYPE, COL3 = CVS_SOURCE
SELECT COL2, COL3, count(*) FROM cvs GROUP BY 1, 2;
-- A|R|16   C|R|23   C|V|167

docs.title: The on-board queue model
docs.text: The On-Board Queue Model (OBQM) keeps a ground image of the on-board schedule of time-tagged commands, displayed in the On-Board Queue Display.7 The ICD lists what SCOS-2000 does for ST[11] time-based scheduling: it wraps execution time-tagged commands in (11,4) commands, models the effect of service 11 commands on the ground image, reconstructs the image from spacecraft reports (from R5.2), supports delayed verification of time-tagged commands with live and playback telemetry, and generates service 11 commands from selections in the ground image. The limits are that the command structures follow the Rosetta reference implementation, each (11,4) command carries one TC packet, only absolute time tags are supported, and interlocks and the time-shift command are not modelled.73

docs.title: Archives
docs.text:
SCOS-2000 files every received packet centrally. In 2003 the archive used C-Tree+ with non-circular filing (files grow continuously and are split for long-term archiving), fixed or variable length records, and filing by type (TM, TC, event), SPID, data stream (a logical grouping such as real-time or playback) and time. Retrievals run independently from real-time processing. Packets are distributed to client caches over TCP/IP. Administrators can switch filing on and off globally with the PDSadmin tool, switch hot to the backup server, and use an administration tool to delete, dump, export, print or re-send packets and to split the archive.10 In the EGSE delivery of 2004, each SPID archive was an index file and a data file in the hfiles directory. Each record had a header used for retrieval and a body with the received data.31

Retrieval can start at any time, select a data stream, and merge up to 4 streams on one display. Synthetic parameters are recalculated for retrieved data.8 The ICD calls this dynamic part of the Mission Information Base the packet archive, in contrast with the static database.45 Release 5 changed both parts. From R5.0 packets are stored in a database, and sequence and display definitions are converted to XML and kept in the File Archive (FARC) instead of the run-time database.4948

Later ESOC systems added further archives around SCOS-2000: the Packet ARChive (PARC) and the Data Archive (DARC) for parameters, with the PCF_DARC field of the MIB selecting the parameters to archive.4251 They are described on mission archives: PARC, DARC and FARC.

docs.title: Events and actions
docs.text:
SCOS-2000 events are messages with a severity, stored in the archive (so they can be retrieved) and notified live to operators, with severities configurable by role.72 They come from several places:

  • the packetiser, when a packet flagged with PID_EVENT arrives; the event text comes from the packet description and the event ID has the form TPKT_OBE:: plus a number between 1 and 9999;62
  • the behaviour checker, for checks of type E, with the ID BEHV:: plus the parameter name;58
  • SCOS-2000 applications themselves, whose event numbers start at 10000.62

The Events & Actions servers react to events with configured actions. The ICD gives the examples of sending an e-mail, setting a configuration variable and running a script.583 The event logger shows the event stream to operators.25 SCOS-II had already planned an "Events & Actions" facility, in which user-defined events identified in the incoming data are logged and trigger actions such as recovery or diagnosis, and "event-driven commanding routines" that react automatically to on-board anomalies.2019

docs.title: EXIF and TOPE
docs.text:
The SCOS External Interface services (EXIF) are an extension module of SCOS-2000 with a CORBA interface. External applications use it to acquire telemetry, send commands, raise events or alarms, and retrieve historical data. Some EXIF services inject events, parameters or commands into SCOS-2000. Others deliver telemetry parameters, TM packets, events or command history to the requesting application. EXIF is made of several CORBA servers, found through the CORBA naming service.38 In the PACS set-up of 2004, the EXIF tasks EXIF_TMM, EXIF_TM1, EXIF_CHM and EXIF_CH1 were started from a separate launcher (exif.start) together with the TOPE test language. Each additional TOPE client needed its own EXIF_CHx task.2433

The Test and Operations Procedure Environment (TOPE) is a Tcl extension that uses EXIF to send commands, fetch and subscribe to parameters, and follow command verification. It is described in detail on SCOS-2000 as EGSE.3238

docs.title: Other interfaces
docs.text:
Interface Purpose Source NCTRS TM frames and packets in, TC packets out, administrative messages, throw events 564 Flight Dynamics Interface (FDIF) Live packets to registered clients; used by Planck LFI to feed its Level 1 pipeline 539 Task Parameter File (TPF) Command requests from flight dynamics and other systems 544 Stack Import Command stacks prepared outside SCOS-2000 44 Command Injection Service Commands from external applications 35 Telemetry Parameter Injection Values for dynamic user-defined constants 5544 Data retrieval services (e.g. TDRS) Packets and parameters for external client systems 5

The Planck LFI instrument team shows how these interfaces were used in practice. Its real-time assessment system used SCOS-2000 to receive telemetry, keep a local database of raw packets, check for missing, damaged or duplicated packets, display housekeeping values in engineering units, send telecommands, and raise out-of-limits alarms. A task built on the Flight Dynamics Interface let the team's telemetry handler register as a SCOS-2000 client, choose the packets to receive, and be notified of each live packet. For its own tests, the team modified the SCOS-2000 Telemetry Receiver (TMR), part of the SCOS-2000 simulators, to replay simulated housekeeping and science telemetry.39 See EDDS and TDRS for ESOC's data dissemination systems.

docs.title: MISCconfig and configuration variables
docs.text:
Most SCOS-2000 behaviour is set by configuration variables in the MISCconfig file, documented in the SCOS-2000 Configuration Variables guide.44 Examples in the MIB ICD include the position of type and subtype in TM packets, the directory of the OL expression files (IMPT_EXPR_DIR), the default on-board clock (TCO_DEFAULT_OBT_ID), the maximum command size, and the name of the time-tag wrapper command.59525063 The EGSE user manual of 2004 lists the EGSE-specific variables: the routing mode, gateway hosts and ports, the SPIDs for system packets, time-stamping and checksum options, and the mission epoch.34 See SCOS-2000 as EGSE.

Some variables can change at run time. The MISC server keeps their state, distributes changes to its clients, and publishes selected variables in the internal "MISC" TM packet. Each published variable needs pcf and plf entries, as a 32-bit signed integer, a double precision real or a character string. Only numeric variables can be fully processed by the monitoring applications. Their positions in the packet must stay the same across database versions, so that older MISC packets in the archive can still be read.56

docs.title: MIB import
docs.text: The static database enters SCOS-2000 through the importer, which reads the ASCII tables (one .dat file per table, tab-separated) and the synthetic parameter files and builds the run-time database. The importer checks field formats and lengths, mandatory fields, relational integrity and parameter value syntax, and logs its messages to a file that is overwritten at each import. It can import a whole database or only check it.47 Its full description is on the MIB.

docs.title: Domains and multi-mission operation
docs.text:
SCOS-2000 is a single system that can manage and control several entities called domains. Each domain has its own directory of MIB files and synthetic parameter files. A special General Domain needs the files of all domains plus its own multi-domain database, which only defines multi-domain synthetic parameters. An import started from the General Domain can import the database of any domain; an import started from a specific domain only imports that domain.46 The multi-domain System Control application (SCTL) starts, stops and monitors the SCOS-2000 server families, and records their status in TM packets that the normal displays can show.57

Multi-mission support grew over time. SCOS-II was designed to control several satellites of one family, not several missions.16 In April 2000 ESOC planned R4.0 to allow several SCOS-2000 versions on one machine and to support constellations.15 In 2003 R4.0 was announced as multi-mission (constellations and formation flying; LEO, GEO and deep space).12

docs.title: Performance and limitations
docs.text:
Figure Value Source SCOS-II design goals 2 Mbps TM and 4 kbps TC concurrently, more than 10 display updates per second, up to 50 workstations 17 SCOS-2000 telecommand chain (2010, Terma) About 2 packets per second with checking, 20 without 40

The ICD documents several functional limits besides those already mentioned. The deduced data structure of PUS is not supported, only deduced parameter fields. Variable packets cannot feed the full TM processing. The generation interval of periodic housekeeping packets is static in the database, and the time stamp of each sample in a housekeeping packet is the packet time plus a fixed offset from the database. Commands can be blocked into one TC segment, but not aggregated into one TC packet. There is no specific processing of services 2, 3, 4, 5, 8, 12, 14 and 15 (for service 15, packets downlinked inside (15,8) reports are not extracted), and services 6 and 13 need mission-specific implementations.697174 Terma, an industrial user, added that recent ESOC developments tended to increase the size and complexity of SCOS-2000, and that some key parts of the code base had been approached in a "short term way" and needed refactoring.4041

docs.title: Mission archives: PARC, DARC and FARC
docs.text:
Everything a SCOS-2000 mission control system receives, sends or produces ends up in one of three archives of ESA's ground operation software (EGOS):

  • the PARC, the packet archive, holding SCOS-2000 telemetry, telecommand and event packets;
  • the DARC, the parameter archive, holding decoded telemetry parameter samples;
  • the FARC, the file archive, holding mission files: flight dynamics and planning products, MIB releases, files reconstructed from the downlink, and SCOS-2000's own sequence and display definitions.

For Solar Orbiter all three run on the mission control system's long-term archive (LTA) server on the operational LAN, and the data dissemination system (EDDS) answers every external request from them.3836 This page collects what the public documents say about the three archives. Their own interface and design documents are not public, so much of the picture comes from their clients (EDDS, the time correlation server, the MIB import) and from the Solar Orbiter Data Delivery ICD; where the sources are silent, the page says so.

docs.title: Names
docs.text:
Acronym Expansion as printed Source PARC Packet ARChive EDDS glossary1 PARC Packet Archive EDDS SDD3 DARC Data Archive EDDS glossary1 DARC Parameter Archive Solar Orbiter DDID; Database Import ICD 7.0 ("Parameter Archive (DARC) system")3357 DARC "a dedicated parameter archive"; the SDD calls its content the "Telemetry Parameter Archive" EDDS SRS; EDDS SDD2213 FARC File Archive EDDS glossary; Solar Orbiter DDID133 LTA Long Term Archive Solar Orbiter DDID33 RAPID Raw Archive Packet Interceptor Dumper Solar Orbiter DDID33 PDS Packet Distribution System EDDS glossary1 CPD Client Packet Distributor EDDS SDD3

The two expansions of DARC describe the same component; its content is parameters.

docs.title: Where the archives sit
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph OPS[Operational LAN]
        PKT[SCOS-2000 packetiser,<br/>releaser, event system] --> PARC[(PARC<br/>TM / TC / EV packets)]
        PARC --> DARC[(DARC<br/>parameter samples)]
        FILES[Flight dynamics, planning,<br/>NIS tracking files,<br/>MIB import, service 13 files] --> FARC[(FARC<br/>mission files)]
        TCO[TCO server] --> PARC
        PARC --> RAPID[RAPID files<br/>every 50 s]
    end
    subgraph RELAY[Relay LAN]
        EDDS[EDDS server and<br/>data providers]
    end
    PARC -- "PARC Manager / Data Provision Services (CORBA)" --> EDDS
    DARC -- "DARC Java API, ActiveMQ" --> EDDS
    FARC -- "FARC Java API, topic notifications" --> EDDS
    RAPID -- "GFTS across firewalls" --> SGS[Science ground segment]
    EDDS --> USERS[External users]

The flows are assembled from the Solar Orbiter DDID (sources of each data type, RAPID, the Generic File Transfer System GFTS), the EDDS SDD (data provider interfaces) and the import ICD (MIB content in the FARC).38486858

Inference

The arrow from PARC to DARC is this wiki's reading: SCOS-2000 decommutes parameters from packets, and the DARC returns, for each sample, the SPID and generation time of the packet it came from, which suggests that it is populated from processed packets. How samples actually reach the DARC is not stated in the available sources.21

EDDS supports several deployment scenarios: data providers in the operational LAN, replicated in the relay LAN, split between the two, or replicated in the office LAN; when they are outside the operational LAN, the only interaction with it is their synchronisation by the Secure File Transfer daemon.7 The EDDS SRS recommends, for security and performance, replicating the long-term archives to the EDDS LAN.25 For Solar Orbiter, the redundancy of the back end (the data providers on the MCS) is that of the MCS itself, the DDS being reconfigured to the backup source if needed.37

docs.title: History: from history files to three archives
docs.text:
History files. In the SCOS-2000 of the early 2000s the MIB was described as a static part, the "database", and a dynamic part, the "history files".53 Up to S2K-R5 the SPID of a telemetry packet also decided which history file the packet was archived in.55 Issue 5.1 therefore asks that the mapping between packet identification fields and SPIDs not change once archiving has started, and that PID entries whose SPIDs are present in the history files not be deleted, so that retrieval services "such as the Generic Data Distribution System" keep working.54 The Rosetta/Mars Express/Venus Express DDID speaks of the MCS Data Archive System (DAS), "not to be confused with the long term data archive", from which the DDS and Flight Dynamics' SCOS-2000/ORATOS Data Access (SoDA) software retrieved packets; TC packets were retrieved by the primary key of the TC history file (packet filing time) or its secondary key (specified execution time).646566 The SCOS-2000 TM retrieval service TDRS likewise extracted parameter values from fixed-length packets in "the SCOS-2000 history file archive".22

Renaming. Among the clarifications of ICD issue 6.7, one asks that remaining mentions of "History files" be replaced by "packet archive".63

FARC. From SCOS-2000 release 5.0, command sequence and display definitions are converted to XML and imported into the FARC instead of the run-time database (ICD issue 6.4, 2007).5862 Aeolus contributed to the Earth Explorer kernel the management of on-board software configurations through sequences stored in a "Central File Archive".69

DARC. The DARC was developed because, in the words of the EDDS SRS, mission control systems "generate parameter data on the fly", which could not meet EDDS performance; a design document for it existed by January 2009 (issue 1.0). The same SRS section adds that a "new packet archive low level component" (PARC) had been finalised within EGOS.2223 The MIB gained the field PCF_DARC for it with ICD issue 6.7 (S2K-DCR-5146, and SPR-5711 adding PCF_DARC and PCF_ENDIAN "for DARC integration"), applicable from SCOS-2000 R5.2.63 The DARC ICD and design document reached issue 2.0 in June 2014.2 EDDS later had to distinguish DARC versions up to 2.2.2 (millisecond time stamps, engineering values only) from 2.3.0 and later (microseconds, raw values, parent packet information).2621

timeline
    title Archive milestones in the public documents
    2001 : ICD 5.1 - MIB = database + history files
    2003 : Rosetta/MEX FDS-MCS ICD - Flight Dynamics extracts packets from the MCS DAS
    2006 : RO/MEX/VEX DDID issue C2 - the DDS reads the MCS DAS
    2007 : ICD 6.4 - sequences and displays as XML in the FARC (S2K R5.0) : TN on web services and PARC enhancements for EDDS
    2009 : DARC SDD issue 1.0 : ICD 6.7 - PCF_DARC for DARC integration (R5.2)
    2014 : DARC ICD and SDD issue 2.0
    2017 : ICD 7.0 FINAL
    2018 : EDDS SDD 15.0 - PARC Manager, Data Provision Services, DARC and FARC data providers
    2019 : Solar Orbiter DDID - PARC, DARC and FARC on the MCS LTA, RAPID to the SGS

Sources: the cited ICD issues and the reference lists of the EDDS SRS and glossary.5366646222363431

docs.title: What it holds
docs.text:
The PARC stores SCOS-2000 packets, also called TDEV packets: a common header, a header specific to telemetry (TM), telecommand (TC) or event (EV) packets, and the packet data.39

  • For spacecraft TM the packet data are the complete source packet from its primary header onwards. Some packets instead contain a whole transfer frame (for example frames filed while a science packet is incomplete) or MCS-internal data on separate data streams.4044
  • For TC the packet data are not the telecommand alone but everything the TC History needs: static information from the MIB, release conditions, verification status and finally the packet sent. SCOS-2000 also files, with SPID 200, a separate packet with the static PTV/CEV details of each command; released commands use SPID 100. Because the MIB on the MCS may change, storing the static information with each command is the only way to interpret old commands correctly.404342
  • For EV the packet data are MCS event messages, for example the metadata of TM files reconstructed from the downlink.40
  • MCS-internal packets on APID 1966: file transfer model metadata, good, bad and idle mini transfer frames, bad telemetry packets, missing packet detection, packets with no assigned SPID, dynamic user-defined constants, TC Spacon and MISC configuration packets, time correlation report, couple and coefficient packets, and releaser packets including ground station responses.45
  • The time correlation server files its couples and coefficients here, deletes couple packets in the PARC on request, and finds the earliest valid coefficients by querying it.70

Telemetry and event packets are written once; the same packet can be stored twice (for example after a re-call to fill a gap), differing only in some header fields such as the reception time. TC packets, in contrast, are updated in place each time their verification status changes; their release time is a unique key.49

docs.title: Keys and header
docs.text:
The common header carries the two keys. The filing time is part of the primary key and is the EDDS "generation time": for spacecraft TM, the time stamp chosen by the time-stamping policy (normally the correlated on-board generation time), for TC the release time. The creation time is a secondary key, the EDDS "storage" or "reception" time: for TM roughly when the packet was received and stored, for TC its (estimated) execution time.41 The Filing Key is the SPID.42

The field list is the Solar Orbiter DDID's simplified version of the SCOS-2000 Packet Management ADD; for Solar Orbiter the S/C ID and mission ID are 650, context and domain 0, and the header version 5.41 A TM packet adds a 16-octet header (validity, TPSD, route ID with data unit type and qualifier, APID, source sequence count, PUS type and subtype).42 The full field semantics are on EDDS request and data formats.

Inference: header sizes

The fields above add up to 60 octets and the TM header to 16, i.e. 76 octets, which is the SCOS-2000 TM packet header length that the import ICD gives for header version 4 (64 octets for versions 0 to 3).414256 Solar Orbiter's version 5 therefore appears to keep the version 4 size; no source states it.

The DB release and DB issue fields record the MIB version used when the packet was archived, from VDF_RELEASE and VDF_ISSUE of the vdf table.41 In the public releases these are 10720/651 (MIB of 2020-04-16, comment "20200416-CSW3.0.3p1_MAS6.51") and 25925/733 (2025-09-16, "20250916-CSW3.1.2_MAS7.33").7677 The Stream ID separates data streams: for Solar Orbiter 1000 to 1003 are VC 0 real-time non-science, VC 1 playback non-science, VC 2 science and VC 3 file transfer online, 2000 to 2003 the offline equivalents, stream 1 for TC, 1000 and 1001 for events, and 65535 for internal packets such as superseded time correlation coefficients.41

TPCF_SIZE and the archive

The import ICD keeps a field TPCF_SIZE in tpcf solely for mission tools that generate "History Files configuration files", recommending the full SCOS-2000 packet size (header plus source packet) for fixed packets and 0 for variable ones.56 Solar Orbiter fills it with source packet sizes, for example 14 octets for the time report.76

docs.title: Access paths
docs.text:
EDDS reaches the PARC in two ways:10142719

Path Interface Capabilities and limits PARC Manager CORBA (method viewSelectMode of the view operation interface); registered in the CORBA name server, hard-coded as "PAMASviews" up to SCOS 5.4 Batch only. Queries by SPID only, not APID, and no filtering by type or subtype; EDDS maps APID, type, subtype and PI1/PI2 to SPIDs using the mission's pid.dat and filters the rest itself. Supports the "PARC raw" request types and the TM gap report Data Provision Services CORBA HFC.StreamingService: retrieveRange for history (markers, a batch per call, 60 s processing limit), subscribe for live data; Command, Packet, Event and Out of Limits provision services Data already decoded, decoupling EDDS from packet details; parameter information for TM; the only path for streaming

Batch retrieval selects by the PARC primary and secondary keys and the data stream, retrieves in fixed-size arrays, then filters, formats, compresses and encrypts.14 The EDDS user manual lists SMON, the SCOS-2000 monitoring service, as a third route to PARC data; SMON requests return parameter values with out-of-limit information rather than packets.19 The TM gap report needs SCOS 5.4.18 or 5.5.2 or later.19 The "new PARC API" introduced dataspaces: a request may name the dataspace to read, the first in the list being the PARC's current one.92027

Inference

A dataspace looks like a separate partition of the archive (for example for tests, simulations or reprocessing) within one mission and domain. A later issue of the EDDS SDD has an appendix "Dataspace and Datapartition in EGS-CC", requiring every EDDS request to EGS-CC to name a dataspace and a datapartition, so the concept carried over to EGS-CC. None of the available sources defines a PARC dataspace.92415

docs.title: RAPID: mirroring the packet archive
docs.text:
RAPID files are binary files of SCOS-2000 packets produced by the MCS packet archive process. They were designed for mirroring packet archives across a firewall (Solar Orbiter also uses them to keep the prime and backup MCS in step), and they are the nominal way the Solar Orbiter science ground segment (SGS) receives all packet data.4850

  • Three files are open at any time, for TM (including time packets and coefficient packets), TC and EV. Each is closed after a configurable time (50 s for Solar Orbiter) and then pushed by the Generic File Transfer System (GFTS)33 across the operational LAN and corporate firewalls, up to 5 transfers in parallel to clear a backlog, so files may arrive out of order; two weeks of RAPID files are kept for recovery.485035
  • Packets appear in the order the MCS received them, so re-dumped or re-called data arrive out of generation order, and updated TC packets reappear in full.48
  • Names are PARC_<Type>_<FirstPacketTime>__<LastPacketTime>, with times in YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS.mmmmmm: reception time for TM, last update time for TC, MCS creation time for EV; for example PARC_TM_2019-04-04T12:30:00.000000__2019-04-04T12:32:50.000000.51
  • A C++ library for reading RAPID files can be delivered to the SGS.51

A RAPID file is a sequence of records, each preceded by a 32-bit length. A record has a fixed part and a variable part:52

Field Octets Meaning ID 8 Version of the record structure, value 1 ST, ET 8 + 8 Time range of packets to delete; present but not used AT 8 Action time: MCS time of the insert or update in the original archive, 64-bit microseconds since 1970 DS 8 Size of the PACKET field TYPE 4 0 insert (any packet), 1 update (a TC packet to overwrite), 2 delete (should not occur; ignore) SM 4 Sync marker 0x1ACFFC1D NS 4 Not used FS 4 Size of FIL, 0 for Solar Orbiter FIL 0 Filter information for deletions, absent PACKET DS The SCOS-2000 packet with its headers

Inference

The sync marker 0x1ACFFC1D is the same 32-bit pattern as the CCSDS attached sync marker of telemetry frames, presumably chosen to make record boundaries easy to verify.5271 The reuse is not commented on in the source.

Which ICD defines RAPID?

The Solar Orbiter DDID references a "RAPID ICD", EGOS-MCS-S2K-ICD-1005; the EDDS glossary lists the same number as the "System management SCOS-2000 - SFM service ICD", issue 5 of 2008.322 One of the two references is wrong, or the number was reused; neither document is public.

docs.title: What it holds
docs.text:
The DARC stores telemetry parameter samples. EDDS documents several properties:

  • Engineering values. Up to DARC 2.2.2 only engineering values are kept, so the TDRS-compatible spreadsheet output cannot show raw values; from 2.3.0 the raw value and its type, the parent packet (the SPID for SCOS-2000) and the parent packet's generation time are also returned, and time stamps have microsecond rather than millisecond resolution.172126
  • No limit status, no statistics. The DARC does not provide the out-of-limit status of samples, and it does not compute statistics: EDDS reads all the data to compute them.17
  • Recording list. Not every parameter is archived. The MIB field PCF_DARC adds a parameter to the recording list (1) or leaves the DARC configuration unchanged (0, the default); it is not imported by SCOS-2000, only read by the DARC.57
  • Consolidation and dataspaces. The DARC has a "last consolidation time" per dataspace, which EDDS shows and lets users take as the end of a parameter request.92420
  • Live stream. Live parameter samples are published on an ActiveMQ topic (an example name in the CIG is esa.egos.darc.realtimeParams); EDDS re-encodes them in Google Protocol Buffers.1326

In the Solar Orbiter MIB, 49,330 of 126,745 monitoring parameters (39 %) have PCF_DARC = 1; in the 2020 release, 43,456 of 102,104 (43 %).7677 All other parameters leave the field empty.

Inference

With 0 meaning "no change", an empty PCF_DARC presumably leaves those parameters out of the recording list unless the DARC is configured otherwise; their values remain available from the packets in the PARC. The ICD does not say what the DARC does with parameters never flagged.57

docs.title: Access
docs.text: EDDS uses the DARC Java API (IDataRetrieval, with getParamSamples and getStaticParameterList) for five request types: parameters, statistics, definitions, preview and report. When all parameters are requested with no quota restriction and no TDRS formatting, EDDS retrieves everything in one DARC sample request; otherwise it requests each parameter and merges.18 The CIG configures it with a database host, schema, user, dataspace and the edds.darc.post.2.3.0 switch.26 SCOS-2000's own monitoring service SMON is an alternative parameter source that also returns out-of-limit information.19

docs.title: What it holds
docs.text:
Content Source Auxiliary files from flight dynamics, mission planning and ground station scheduling For Solar Orbiter: MIB, attitude (ATT, AttitudePTEL), events (EVT), orbit (Orbit, short and long term), one-way light time (OWLT), station visibility and link budget (VISTA), HGA blockage (HGAB), short-term solar aspect (SolarAspectST), CRF files (CRFG), user events (UEVT), station scheduling events (EVFM)46 TM files downlinked with the Solar Orbiter service 13 protocol Stored under the data directory as file type "DLPP Files", named <PS_ID>_<file_reconstruction_timestamp>, e.g. 13_2014.336.13.54.07.057; plain concatenations of TM packets, not split into the PARC in the baseline47 Tracking data from the ground stations For Rosetta and Mars Express, the MCS obtained the ESA IFMS files through the NIS and stored them in the FARC, along with NASA/DSN tracking files67 Command sequence and display definitions (XML) Since SCOS-2000 R5.058

The EDDS view of the FARC is a catalogue (file type, creation time, release and issue per file), files retrieved by name, type or time, and subscriptions.19 A domain value of −1 denotes the FARC's "No Domain".9 With the "Consolidated FARC" version 2.0i5, EDDS must also be configured with the zone of the FARC server.28 The client interface is the FARC Client Services API (EGOS-GEN-FARC-ICD-1001, issue 4.5 of 2012), not public; EDDS isolates itself from FARC versions behind an interface jar.2911

docs.title: Subscriptions
docs.text: When a file changes, the FARC server posts a message on a message bus topic; EDDS matches it against its subscription table and either delivers the new version by a file request or sends an e-mail, and drops subscriptions to deleted files.12 Solar Orbiter users can subscribe to any auxiliary file received by the file archive, whether it comes from an external or an internal source.34 Streaming makes no sense for files and is not supported.12

docs.title: MIB content in the FARC
docs.text:
The FARC holds MIB-derived content in two senses.

  1. Run-time definitions. From SCOS-2000 R5.0, sequence (csf, css, sdf, csp) and display (dpf, gpf, spf and related) definitions in the ASCII MIB are converted on request into XML files and imported into the FARC, not into the POST run-time database; command sources and the TM desktop load them from there. Sequences and displays are thus imported independently of a new TM/TC database, and incrementally: only the definitions in the imported files change, the others stay available.585960 The XML formats are in the TC Sequences definitions ICD (ICD-0051) and the TM Displays and Printout definitions ICD (ICD-5001), both not public.61 See Command sequences and Display definitions.
  2. MIB releases as files. Solar Orbiter's FARC holds the mission database file as auxiliary file type MIB, available through EDDS; Rosetta and Mars Express distributed it as file type MIB_, tarred, to Flight Dynamics.4668 The public MIB releases on this wiki (2020, 2025) are such files.

docs.title: Beyond the MCS archives
docs.text: A 2020 ESOC presentation describes ARES (Analysis and Reporting System), an off-line analysis system evolved from MUST and built on the EGOS User Desktop, mainly for housekeeping data in engineering format. Its server reads EDDS response files fed from the DARC and PARC on the operational LAN; a multi-mission shared store aims at keeping all data rather than a subset (Gaia alone receives around 150 million unique housekeeping samples a day), ARES itself being described as a Hadoop database cluster, and the PyARES library brings Spark-based processing to the data.72737475

docs.title: What is not public
docs.text:
Document Reference Mentioned in DARC ICD EGOS-GEN-DARC-ICD-1001, issue 2.0, 2014-06-06 EDDS glossary and SDD25 DARC Software Design Document EGOS-GEN-DARC-SDD-1001, issue 1.0 (2009) and 2.0 (2014) EDDS SRS and glossary232 Analysis of Web Services and PARC Enhancements to support EDDS EGOS-MDW-EDDS-TN-1002 (also printed EGOS-MDW-TN-1002), 2007-04-13 EDDS glossary and SDD25 FARC Client Services API EGOS-GEN-FARC-ICD-1001, issue 4 revision 5, 2012-10-31 EDDS CIG29 SCOS-2000 Packet Management ADD (SCOS-2000 packet structure) EGOS-MDS-S2K-ADD-0024 Solar Orbiter DDID32 RAPID ICD EGOS-MCS-S2K-ICD-1005 Solar Orbiter DDID32 TC sequences and TM displays XML ICDs ICD-0051, ICD-5001 ICD 7.061 Data Disposition System SRD (GDDS) EGOS-MCS-GDDS-SRD-5720 EDDS glossary2

Questions the public sources leave open: the storage technology of the PARC and the FARC (the CIG names only a DARC "database" with host and schema), retention and consolidation policies, how the DARC is fed, what a dataspace is exactly, and how PARC dataspaces relate to DARC ones.26 HARC, a further source named next to the PARC and DARC in the current EDDS documents, is not an SCOS-2000 archive: the EDDS SDD describes its HARC data provider as retrieving data from the EGOS-CC HBase archive.3016
