docs.title: EDDS: EGOS Data Dissemination System
docs.text:
The EGOS Data Dissemination System (EDDS) is the component of ESA's ground operations software (EGOS) that gives controlled access to mission data to people who have no access to the monitoring and control facilities of a SCOS-2000 mission control system (MCS).1 A principal investigator who wants every raw packet of an instrument, an industrial team that needs a month of housekeeping parameters, or a science operations centre that subscribes to new orbit files all use the EDDS. The EDDS itself does not analyse data. It retrieves data from the mission archives, filters and formats it, and delivers it as files or as a live stream.2

The EDDS replaced three older SCOS-2000 add-ons: the Telemetry Data Retrieval System (TDRS), Web Remote Monitoring (WebRM) and the Generic Data Disposition System (GDDS). Its requirements also took ideas from the MUST parameter-analysis prototype.3 This page describes the system: history, services, architecture, processing chain, security model and the public document set. The companion page EDDS request and data formats gives the XML request structures and the binary layouts byte by byte.

Name variants

All EDDS documents in the library expand EDDS as "EGOS Data Dissemination System".4 A 2025 SpaceOps paper by ESOC and JPL authors expands it as "EGOS Data Disposition System" instead, which echoes the older GDDS name.5 This wiki uses the expansion printed in the EDDS documents themselves.

docs.title: At a glance
docs.text: Aspect Summary Purpose Controlled access to science and non-science MCS data for users outside the MCS<sup>2</sup> Users Principal investigators, industry and other ESA sites, analysis and engineering staff, science operations centres<sup>6</sup> Data sources Packet archive (PARC), parameter archive (DARC), on-the-fly parameters (SMON), file archive (FARC), a served file-system directory, SCOS-2000 Data Provision Services, and in recent releases the EGS-CC HBase archive and EGS-CC REST services<sup>7</sup><sup>8</sup> Services Authentication, batch, stream and user management, plus asynchronous notifications<sup>9</sup><sup>10</sup> Interfaces SOAP web services described in WSDL, a REST/JSON API, e-mail acknowledgements, push delivery to a client (S)FTP server<sup>11</sup><sup>12</sup> Formats EDDS binary ("EDDS raw"), GDDS binary, SFDU, Google Protocol Buffers binary, XML (with XSLT transforms), ASCII, TDRS spreadsheet, XFDU packaging, RawSourceBinary<sup>13</sup> Main technologies Apache Tomcat, JAX-WS, ActiveMQ, Camel, MariaDB, OpenLDAP, Quartz, CometD, Eclipse RCP/RAP, XFDU library<sup>14</sup> Latest version in the library EDDS v3.6.1 (SDD and CIG issue 25.0, 2025-03-07)<sup>15</sup>

docs.title: Where the EDDS sits
docs.text:
The EDDS lives between the operational LAN, which holds the MCS and its archives, and the users outside. The figure is this wiki's simplified summary of the SDD system-context and deployment figures.1617

flowchart LR
  subgraph OPS["OPS LAN (ESA restricted network)"]
    MCS["SCOS-2000 MCS"] --> PARC[(PARC<br/>packets)]
    MCS --> DARC[(DARC<br/>parameters)]
    MCS --> FARC[(FARC<br/>files)]
    SRV["EDDS Server<br/>+ data providers"]
    ARCH["EDDS Archiver<br/>+ MariaDB"]
    LDM["LDAP master"]
    PARC --> SRV
    DARC --> SRV
    FARC --> SRV
  end
  subgraph RELAY["RELAY LAN (ESA external service network)"]
    WEB["EDDS Web Server<br/>(SOAP / REST / CometD)"]
    MQ{{"ActiveMQ broker"}}
    DM["Delivery Manager<br/>+ FTP server"]
    LDS["LDAP slave"]
  end
  subgraph USERS["Users (Internet, ESA networks)"]
    MMI["EDDS MMI<br/>standalone or web"]
    API["User client<br/>(Java API, SOAP, REST)"]
    FS["User SFTP server"]
  end
  SRV <-->|"JMS, opened from OPS LAN"| MQ
  ARCH <--> MQ
  WEB <--> MQ
  SRV -->|"response files via SFT"| DM
  LDM -->|"replication"| LDS
  WEB --- LDS
  MMI <-->|"HTTPS"| WEB
  API <-->|"HTTPS"| WEB
  DM -->|"SFTP push"| FS

Mission data never leaves the OPS LAN through an inbound connection. The EDDS Server connects out to the message broker, and response files cross the firewall through the Secure File Transfer (SFT) daemon.18 The same deployment can be mirrored for internal users on the Office LAN.16

docs.title: The four systems the EDDS replaced
docs.text:
The SRS traces the EDDS to three SCOS-2000 ground-segment subsystems and one prototype.3

Predecessor What it did What the EDDS kept TDRS (Telemetry Data Retrieval System) Extracted TM parameter values from the SCOS-2000 history-file archive and returned them as MVDA or spreadsheet files. Only fixed-length TM packets were handled. Web browser and e-mail interface, with user interface and retrieval separated for security and performance.3 Parameter retrieval, the TDRS spreadsheet format (via XSLT or a native formatter)1920122 WebRM (Web Remote Monitoring) Remote monitoring without physical MCS access. CORBA-based injection and provision servers, plus a Java client with SCOS-2000 look-and-feel displays.3 Stream services, the display client concept21 GDDS (Generic Data Disposition System) Web and FTP front ends that multiplex requests from many users. CORBA/FTP interface to the MCS archive for continuous data (packets), files and catalogues.3 GDDS FTP-service requests (via the Request Submitter and an XSLT) and the GDDS binary response format19 MUST (Mission Utility & Support Tool) Server/client prototype that builds its own parameter archive from scheduled MCS packet requests, with analysis clients.3 Batch retrieval of parameter definitions and batch or stream retrieval of parameter data for MUST-like clients22

The ESOC infrastructure slide of a 2005 Ground System Architectures Workshop talk shows the pre-EDDS picture. It lists SCOS-2000, NCTRS and GDDS, and describes "TDRS and WebRM" as the web interfaces that give external users such as payload owners live telemetry, command verification, telemetry retrieval and statistics.23

docs.title: Timeline
docs.text:
The dates come from the change logs and reference lists of the EDDS documents.24152526

timeline
    title EDDS milestones (from the document change logs)
    2005 : EDDS Concepts technical note, Draft C (26 Sep)
    2006 : Analysis of TDRS, WebRM, GDDS and MUST for reuse (22 Feb)
    2007 : SDD and EUICD issue 1.0 after the PDR (13 Apr)
    2010 : Glossary for the software requirements review (18 Jan) : CIG first issue (28 May) : Provisional acceptance delivery (11 Oct)
    2011 : Final acceptance delivery (29 Mar) : EDDS v1.1.0 (Sep)
    2014 : EDDS v1.5.0 (17 Dec)
    2016 : EDDS v2.0.0 (4 Jul)
    2018 : EDDS v2.3.0 (16 Feb)
    2020 : EDDS v2.4.0 (11 Feb) : EDDS v3.0.0 (30 Sep)
    2025 : EDDS v3.6.0 (10 Jan) : EDDS v3.6.1 (7 Mar)

Two of the SRS reference documents give the design lineage. One is the 2003 "SCOS-2000 TM Data Retrieval Services SRD" (the TDRS requirements). The other is "TDRS External Interfaces Control Document" issue 4.3 of 2004.24 SRS issue 18.0 has 551 numbered requirements (551 distinct EDDS-SR-nnnnn identifiers, each with a "Need:" line). Their "Source:" fields cite [RD-3] (listed as the TDRS SRD) in 29 requirements, [RD-4] (listed as the GDDS requirements document) in 25, [RD-5] (listed as the WebRM baseline) in 24 and [RD-6] (listed as the MUST Repository ICD) in 30; a few requirements cite several. Most of the others name a review (SWRR, SWRR2) or a product-backlog item, and 138 give no source at all. This wiki counted these fields in the extracted text, including sources that wrap onto a second line.27

Inference: the reference labels may be shifted

The identifiers quoted after the labels do not always fit the listed documents. Every [RD-4] citation carries an SR-TMDR-nnnnnn identifier, and every [RD-6] citation carries R-WEB-nnnn identifiers, although [RD-6] is listed as a MUST document.27 The SRS is known to mis-number other references (it cites the SLE reference model as [RD-15], which is listed as [RD-13]).21 Which predecessor document each requirement really came from is therefore uncertain.

The project followed an agile method. The SDD says requirements and solutions evolve through cross-functional teams, and that the detailed design lives in the JavaDoc rather than in the document.28

docs.title: Purpose and users
docs.text:
The SRS names two user groups: those who need remote monitoring, and those who analyse spacecraft data. Remote monitoring is served by stream services. Analysis is served by file-based delivery of archived data, reports and statistics.2 Binary packet deliveries are often used by principal investigators to populate their own local archives. The SRS models this explicitly as the use case "Populate Local Archive".29

The system is deliberately not an analysis tool. The SRS says the EDDS provides MCS data in a format that facilitates analysis and aims to support many formats that can be added or retired.2 An ESOC presentation for Solar Orbiter users puts it more bluntly. The EDDS is not a data warehouse, since response files are stored only for a limited time. It is not a post-processing tool either, because its display and analysis features are very limited.30

Two more design goals shape the architecture:

  • Multi-mission and multi-domain. One authentication entry point serves autonomous mission domains, and every request names its mission and domain.2 A domain is an instance of an MCS or data archive, independent of all others. A mission groups domains, and contexts such as live operations, testing or training.31
  • Generic archive access. The EDDS should be able to front any data archive, not only the MCS, through a generic extension layer.232 Recent releases use this layer for EGS-CC data providers.7

docs.title: Data types
docs.text:
The EUICD organises everything the EDDS can deliver into six data-type families. The table shows which delivery mechanisms each family supports in issue 24.0.33

Family Data types File server EDDS server Stream E-mail Packet TM, TC and EV in "EDDS raw" and "PARC raw" forms, packet statistics ✓ ✓ ✓ (not statistics) – Parameter TM parameter samples, statistics, preview, definition ✓ ✓ ✓ (samples only) – Report MCS reports, EDDS reports ✓ ✓ – – Archived files File, catalogue ✓ ✓ – – File system File catalogue, folder catalogue, file ✓ ✓ – – Acknowledgement Request status records ✓ ✓ – ✓
  • Packets are telemetry (TM), telecommand (TC) and MCS event (EV) packets as stored by the MCS, in network byte order. The "raw" variants return the archived packet as a hexadecimal string wrapped in XML. They can only be filtered by start time, end time and (for TM and EV) a list of SPIDs.34 An EV packet is an MCS event: the EUICD and SUM call it the "SCOS Event Log". The SRS lists on-board event (OBEV) reports as a separate report type, so an EV packet is not a spacecraft PUS event report.35
  • Parameters come either from the dedicated parameter archive DARC, or are generated on the fly by SMON from archived packets. The DARC is fast but holds only the subset of parameters a mission chooses to archive. The SMON path is slower but can reach every parameter.36 Parameter definitions (name, description, subsystem, unit) are derived from the spacecraft database, the MIB.3637 The EUICD warns that samples are not guaranteed to be time-ordered. A resumed request may also contain duplicates, unless the split size is set to 0 so that the whole request restarts.37
  • Reports: the MCS reports are the TM packet report, TM packet gap report, TC packet report, out-of-limits (OOL) data report and event record report. The EDDS reports are the system log and the EDDS usage report. Status and request-summary reports are listed but not supported in issue 24.0.38 For OOL reports the EDDS understands PARC OOL packet versions 5, 6 and 7, which correspond to different SCOS-2000 releases.38
  • Archived files are FARC contents: flight dynamics, mission planning and TT&C station files, plus catalogues. Where the FARC supports it, a user can subscribe so that a changed file is fetched automatically.39 The SRS adds that the mission database itself should be retrievable from the FARC, since TM, TC or EV data are of little use without it.40
  • Acknowledgements are status records generated by the EDDS. They are produced when a request is received, and when it completes or fails.4142

docs.title: Services
docs.text: The EUICD exposes four services to clients: authentication, batch, stream and user management.9 The SDD groups the same functions as data services (batch and stream), management services and notification services.10

docs.title: Batch service
docs.text:
A batch request is an XML document that lists data types and a filter per type, and names a delivery method. The EDDS retrieves the data, builds the data set, delivers it, and then considers the request complete. A batch request can carry a schedule, for one-shot, cyclic or standing execution.4322 The response is a binary or ASCII file, optionally compressed or encrypted, or an XML file shown in the client. Compression is applied by default. The supported archive forms are zip, tar (USTAR, uncompressed) and tar.gz. AES encryption can be enabled or disabled per mission.43

Users can edit a request in the client's forms, save it on the server, reload and re-edit it, or write the XML by hand and upload it. Uploaded requests are validated against the XML schema, and then checked for privilege and for mission-specific semantics (for example, the end date must be after the start date).44 Request queues are per mission, persistent on disk, and dispatched with a priority algorithm.44

docs.title: Stream service
docs.text:
A stream request opens a continuous flow of data that ends only when the stream is closed by the client, an administrator or the MCS.45 The SRS bases the stream concept on the offline and online modes of the SLE return services. "Offline" means previously archived data; "online" means data routed as it arrives. Online delivery has two modes. Timely mode drops data to meet a delivery deadline; complete mode delivers everything, possibly with a long delay.2146

In issue 24.0 of the EUICD the stream data are published on ActiveMQ topics. Clients read them either directly from the topic, or through the client API over CometD/Bayeux after calling startStreamData(RequestID).46

Stream Source Topic Bayeux channel Body format Parameters DARC (v3.0.0 or later, SLES 12) parameter stream topic PARAM_STREAM Protocol Buffers parameter record Packet TM Data Provision Services (SCOS 5.4.21 / 5.5.4 or later) esa.egos.edds.packet.stream.tm PKT_TM_STREAM As the binary Packet TM Report Packet TC Data Provision Services esa.egos.edds.packet.stream.tc PKT_TC_STREAM As the binary Packet TC Report Packet EV Data Provision Services esa.egos.edds.packet.stream.ev PKT_EV_STREAM As the binary Event Record Report Out of limits Data Provision Services esa.egos.edds.packet.stream.ool PKT_OOL_STREAM As the binary OOL Record Report

The topics and channels are from EUICD §4.1.3 and §12.1.8.6.4647 For DARC streaming, the EDDS subscribes to a DARC-owned topic with a JMS selector built from the request filter. Each DARC message carries header fields: ValueType, Value, Validity (0 valid, 1 invalid, 2 unknown, 3 expired), SystemElement, Source, State, GenericData, GenerationTime (Unix time) and Name. The EDDS re-encodes them as Protocol Buffers records tagged with RequestId and MISSION_NAME.48

Inference

The sources disagree about packet streaming. EUICD 24.0 §4.1.3 says only DARC parameter streaming is supported, yet §4.1.3.2 to §4.1.3.6 describe live TM, TC, EV and OOL streaming through the Data Provision Services.46 SUM 22.0 says PARC stream forms can be saved but not submitted.49 Both the EUICD (§4.1.3.2) and the SDD (§6.2.9.8.2) state that live packet streaming works only through the Data Provision Services, not the PARC Manager.4678 This wiki reads the "only DARC" sentence and the SUM note as left over from releases without that back end. Which missions use packet streaming is not stated in the available sources.

A lightweight EDDS Stream Client attaches to an ACTIVE stream request and dumps the data to files at a fixed interval. SDD §6.2.5 lists TM, TC, OOL, event and parameter streams, and XML, Protocol Buffers, GDDS (TM and TC only) and "RawBody" binary outputs, and the EUICD defines recording file names for all five stream types.5051 Other passages still describe it as TM-only: SDD §4.5.5 and §6.1.7.5, and CIG §3.6.6, which allows only the Packet TM stream type.5253

docs.title: User management and the access model
docs.text:
The SRS describes the problem this model solves: user-account administration used to cost ESA support staff a lot of effort.55 The EDDS therefore has a single authentication entry point and a layered model:

  • Accounts belong to users. After logging in, a user picks a mission and a role for the session.5556
  • A role bundles privileges. They cover which operations may be performed, which data types may be accessed, which services may be used, which quotas apply, and the request priority.55
  • The generic roles are System Administrator ("super user"), Mission Administrator, Manager (administers a group of users under one role, for example a PI institute) and Investigator (data access only).55

In the implemented system, the SUM shows roles assembled from three kinds of reusable sets, plus groups.5758

Object What it controls Data Access Set Data sources and request types a role may issue. A role without one cannot issue batch requests. Operation Data Set User-management operations the role may perform (for example create but not delete quota sets) Quota Set Limits: requests per period, ongoing requests (ACTIVE or QUEUED), data volume per period, disk space, and SPID, APID, parameter-name, TC-name, FARC file name/type and file-system folder restrictions, data time range and maximum time-filter duration Role Name, contact details, the sets above, a priority, enabled flag Group Binds users to roles. Disabling a group locks all its users out.

Quota periods are given as cron expressions. With several quota sets on one role, the smallest numerical limit applies, but the SPID, APID, parameter-name and file restrictions are combined as a union. APID restrictions are converted to SPID lists before checking.58 EDDS and Mission Administrators act as super users and need no sets.58

User records live in LDAP. The EDDS can also authenticate users against a separate "central LDAP", so that removing someone centrally also locks them out of the EDDS.59 The Solar Orbiter DDS uses the quota mechanism to limit each external user to certain APIDs, SPIDs, parameter names, file names or types, data volumes and relative time ranges. The DDID gives "the last 12 months" as an example.60

docs.title: Web-service operations
docs.text:
The EDDS port type in the WSDL is shared by batch and stream services. Every operation runs in a session. Most operations can raise requestFault, authorizationFault or sessionFault. The exceptions are logIn, which raises authenticationFault or passwordExpiredFault, checkUserPassword (authenticationFault, sessionFault), and the one-way logOut and hasSessionExpired, which declare no fault.61 The operations, grouped by purpose:

Group Operations Session logIn, logOut, hasSessionExpired, checkUserPassword Batch and stream submission batchRequest, streamRequest, reSubmit, startStreamData, stopStreamData Monitoring and control getStatus, getStatuses, getJobs, getJobsWithStatus, getJobsWithStatusAndLimit, cancel, suspend, resume, deleteData, deleteRequest, getHistoricalLog, stopHistoricalLogRetrieval Retrieval of results and templates getResponse, getRequest, getStreamRequest Catalogues and metadata getParamDefinitions, getCatalogue, getFarcCatalogue (deprecated), getDataspaces, getAlias, getLastConsolidation, getAllowedRequestTypes, getTransformations User management accountRequest, getUsers, getMissions, getMissionsAndDomains, getRoles, getUserAccountDetails, getMissionDetails, getUserQuota, getQuotaDetails, hasPermissionToSeeAllUsers

The table follows EUICD §9.2.1.1.61 Issue 24.0 adds a REST API at .../edds/EddsRestService/v1/ that mirrors these operations with JSON bodies. The REST API adds a JSON Web Token (JWT, RFC 7519) authentication layer on top of the older session mechanism, which the EUICD itself calls insecure.12 The Java client API (edds-ws-client, version 3.6.0 in issue 24.0) wraps the services, and a NotificationManager delivers asynchronous push notifications over CometD.4762

A 2025 SpaceOps paper maps these operations onto the new CCSDS Mission Product Distribution (MPD) services. batchRequest/streamRequest map to standing orders, getResponse to product delivery, getCatalogue to product listing, and the file-server and server deliveries to MPD delivery methods.63

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
The SDD's component summary, simplified:64

Component Role EDDS MMI (standalone Eclipse RCP application, or web application on Eclipse RAP) Builds batch, stream and user-management requests, shows status, downloads responses, administers users. No XML knowledge needed.65 EDDS Client API Java façade over the SOAP and REST services, used by the MMI and by third-party tools such as MUST and ARES6462 EDDS Web Server JAX-WS web application in Tomcat. It authenticates users, validates requests, checks privileges and serves notifications. It normally runs on the RELAY LAN.66 EDDS Archiver Stores incoming requests in MariaDB, schedules them with Quartz, creates and updates the single acknowledgement per request, archives log messages67 EDDS Server One instance per mission. It authorises requests, checks quotas, queues by priority, routes each request to a data provider, and produces response files.68 Data providers PARC Manager and Data Provision Services (packets), DARC and SMON (parameters), FARC (files), file system, EDDS reports, HARC (EGS-CC HBase archive), EGS-CC REST764 Delivery Manager Polls for finished response files and delivers them (local FTP area or push to user (S)FTP). It also sends e-mail and deletes expired responses.69 Secure File Transfer (SFT) Separate ESOC product that moves files between two LANs through a firewall over TCP/IP. GFTS can play the same role.70 Request Submitter Polls a directory for EDDS or GDDS request files and submits them; GDDS requests are first converted by XSLT71 Stream Client Saves the data of an active stream request to files at intervals50

The services are defined as WSDL files plus XSD schemas. JAX-WS wsimport generates the client stubs, server skeletons and bean classes from them. These are the baseline of the client API, web server, server and data providers.72

docs.title: The message bus
docs.text:
All components talk through an ActiveMQ JMS broker. The SDD explains the two JMS primitives the design relies on. A message on a queue goes to exactly one listener, which allows load balancing. A message on a topic goes to every listener, which suits status broadcasts. Persistent queues and topics keep messages until a consumer returns.73 The choice explains several operating rules:

  • Run only one Archiver. Log messages arrive on topics, so two Archivers would store every log twice.74
  • Several EDDS Servers per mission are possible, because batch requests sit on a queue. But on start-up a server re-processes any request left ACTIVE in the database, so two servers could fight over the same request.74
  • Cancel and suspend messages are sent on topics. Nobody knows which server is processing a given request, so every server must see the message.75

Typical destinations include esa.egos.edds.request.batch.unprocessed (web server to Archiver), esa.egos.edds.request.batch.tobeprocessed (Archiver to Server), esa.egos.edds.update.ack (acknowledgement updates, applied only by the Archiver) and esa.egos.edds.email.queue (outgoing mail).6775

docs.title: Deployment and network security
docs.text:
The SRS lists the ESOC networks the EDDS must serve.76

Security domain ESOC networks Served by EDDS ESA Restricted Networks OPS LAN Yes ESA Internal Service Networks OFFICE LAN, PRE-OPSLAN, SIMLAN OFFICE LAN and PRE-OPSLAN only ESA External Service Networks RELAY LAN, CITI DMZ, PISA LAN, ACCESS LAN All except ACCESS LAN Non-ESA Networks Public Internet Yes

ESOC's security rules allow no inbound connections into the OPS LAN, no permanent connections between the OPS LAN and an outside LAN, and only connections initiated from inside.18 The EDDS satisfies them as follows:

  • The EDDS Server on the OPS LAN opens its JMS connection to the broker on the RELAY LAN. The connection is not permanent and is re-established when lost.1877
  • Response files go back to the RELAY LAN through SFT. Several SFT instances can be used, for example to separate stream and batch traffic.70
  • The LDAP master sits inside and pushes changes to the LDAP slave outside. It uses slurpd in "one shot" mode, so the replication connection is not permanent either.18

The SDD describes four deployment scenarios.17

Scenario Where the data providers are Pros Cons 1. Base OPS LAN; Web Server and file server on RELAY LAN Simplest; easy access to OPS LAN components Heavy file traffic through the OPS LAN firewall 2. Replicated outside Copies on the RELAY LAN, synchronised by SFT Little firewall traffic Some services impossible; data replicated into a less secure LAN 3. Split Some inside, some outside; two EDDS Server instances All services, better performance Complex configuration; replication 4. Office LAN replica Copies on the Office LAN; separate web and EDDS servers for internal and external users Performance for internal users; data replicated once Complex; data in a less secure internal LAN

For scalability, one Web Server and one Archiver are shared by all missions. There is one EDDS Server per mission, one set of data-provider drivers per mission and domain, one Delivery Manager, optional Stream Clients, and at least two SFT instances (one per firewall side) per mission and domain.74

docs.title: Data providers
docs.text:
The EDDS Server reaches every archive through a data-provider driver with the same handler chain: data retrieval, then filter, formatter, optional compression and optional encryption.64 The list has grown over time. SDD issue 15.0 (EDDS v2.3.0, 2018) describes PARC and Data Provision, FARC, file-system, DARC and SMON providers only. The HARC and EGS-CC REST providers first appear in the library's issue 25.0 (2025).12386

Provider Archive and interface Batch Stream Notes PARC Manager Packet archive via CORBA ✓ – Queries only by SPID. The EDDS adds APID, type and subtype filtering by mapping APIDs to SPIDs with the MIB pid.dat.7879 Data Provision Services Packet archive via a SCOS-2000 CORBA service that returns decoded data ✓ ✓ Only path for live packet streams; can also return parameter information for TM78 DARC Parameter archive via Java API ✓ ✓ Stream via a Camel route from the DARC broker80 SMON On-the-fly parameters from packets via CORBA ✓ – The EDDS starts or restarts its own SMON instance via the SCOS-2000 task interface. Only one SMON request may be active at a time.8182 FARC File archive via Java API, behind a versioned interface JAR ✓ – Catalogues and subscriptions; FARC changes arrive as JMS notifications83 File system Indexed directory on the EDDS Server ✓ – File and folder catalogues, file retrieval packaged as TAR, subscriptions8485 HARC EGS-CC HBase archive via the ARC Standalone Java API ✓ – EGS-CC TM, TC, parameters, messages and events; the SUM also lists activity reports868 EGS-CC REST EGS-CC REST endpoints as a STOMP client, with data returned over HTTP or Kafka ✓ – A session token is requested for every EDDS request8788

The MIB inside the EDDS

The EDDS needs a copy of some MIB files for every domain it serves. It uses pid.dat to convert SPIDs to APIDs and back, and tpcf.dat for packet descriptions. For the TC reports it also needs the command subsystem and command host files and MISCbase.ids, plus two hand-written mappings: command source types (CMDsourceTypeMapping.properties) and command request status types (CMD_ttRqstObqStatusMapping.properties). With the Data Provision Services it additionally needs MISCcontext_SHARED.sta to map domain and data stream names. The CIG warns that stale copies break filters such as an APID search.89 An SRN issue 14.0 fix concerns a "request incorrect status when SPID not in pid.dat".90 For scale, the September 2025 Solar Orbiter MIB has 11,150 packet definitions spread over 293 APIDs. One APID can stand for hundreds of SPIDs: APID 263 alone has 699, and 64 APIDs have 24 or more.91

SQL used

Run against solo-2025-09-16.sqlite (all columns are stored as text).

-- packet definitions, distinct APIDs and the SPID range
SELECT count(*), count(DISTINCT PID_APID),
       min(CAST(PID_SPID AS int)), max(CAST(PID_SPID AS int))
FROM pid;
-- result: 11150 | 293 | 101 | 1000006
-- SPIDs per APID
SELECT PID_APID, count(*) c FROM pid GROUP BY PID_APID ORDER BY c DESC LIMIT 1;
-- result: 263 | 699
SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT PID_APID FROM pid GROUP BY PID_APID HAVING count(*) >= 24);
-- result: 64

docs.title: How a batch request flows
docs.text:
The SDD scenario for an archived-packet request delivered by the Delivery Manager:77

sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User / EDDS MMI
    participant W as Web Server
    participant Q as ActiveMQ
    participant A as Archiver + DB
    participant S as EDDS Server
    participant P as PARC provider
    participant D as Delivery Manager
    U->>W: logIn(user, password)
    W->>W: check against LDAP slave, open session
    W-->>U: sessionId
    U->>W: batchRequest(RequestMessagePart)
    W->>W: authenticate, validate, check privileges
    W->>Q: request ... .batch.unprocessed
    Q->>A: deliver
    A->>A: schedule (Quartz), assign job IDs, store, create acknowledgement
    A-->>U: job ID list (via Web Server)
    A->>Q: request ... .batch.tobeprocessed (delayed if scheduled)
    Q->>S: deliver (connection opened from OPS LAN)
    S->>S: authorise, check quota, queue by priority
    S->>P: execute (retrieve, filter, format, compress, encrypt)
    P-->>S: response file(s), progress updates
    S->>D: response file via SFT to the Delivery Manager inbox
    D->>D: deliver (local FTP or push to user SFTP), e-mail if requested
    D->>Q: acknowledgement updates
    Q->>A: update acknowledgement (single writer)

The steps inside the EDDS Server follow a chain of responsibility.68

  1. Authorisation: the user's role must allow the request. The acknowledgement is updated.
  2. Quota check: if a generic quota check fails, the request is not executed and the acknowledgement explains why.
  3. Execution: requests are queued by role priority, with a configurable number running in parallel. A BatchRequestHandlerFactory combines retrieval, filtering and formatting handlers for the specific archive. Results are transformed by XSLT if requested, then encrypted and compressed.6877

On a provider error the server can retry at configured intervals. The request stays ACTIVE, and the acknowledgement records the retries and the reason.77 Persistent messages mean that requests survive a server crash. On start-up the server also recovers SUBMITTED requests whose execution time is in the past.68 Suspending a request marks the last sample of the last finished file in the acknowledgement. Resuming restarts from there, with a possible small overlap; the overlap is larger for raw and OOL requests, because the PARC returns undecoded packets in batches.75

docs.title: Request states
docs.text:
The EUICD state enumeration and the SUM's status table give the life cycle. ACTIVE appears in the SUM and SDD, and in the EUICD's own streaming text, but not in the EUICD enumeration (Appendix D.44).929346 The SDD also spells the deleted state DELIVERY_RESP_DELETED once, where the EUICD and SUM write DELIVERED_RESP_DELETED.95

Inference

No source draws the state machine. The transitions below are this wiki's reading of the state descriptions in the SUM and EUICD and of the processing steps in the SDD.93687595

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> SUBMITTED: stored by Archiver
    SUBMITTED --> CANCELED: cancel before start
    SUBMITTED --> QUEUED: taken for execution
    SUBMITTED --> ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED
    SUBMITTED --> ERROR_INVALID_REQUEST
    SUBMITTED --> ERROR_LIMIT_EXCEEDED: quota
    QUEUED --> ACTIVE
    QUEUED --> CANCELED
    ACTIVE --> SUSPENDED: suspend
    SUSPENDED --> ACTIVE: resume
    ACTIVE --> CANCELED
    ACTIVE --> ERROR_SERVER_NOT_AVAILABLE: provider missing
    ACTIVE --> COMPLETED_NO_RESULTS
    ACTIVE --> SERVER_COMPLETED: files to Delivery Manager
    SERVER_COMPLETED --> DELIVERED
    SERVER_COMPLETED --> DELIVERED_PARTIAL_RESULTS
    SERVER_COMPLETED --> ERROR_LOCALLY_DELIVERED: push failed, file kept on EDDS FTP
    SERVER_COMPLETED --> ERROR_DELIVERY
    DELIVERED --> DELIVERED_RESP_DELETED: response deleted
    ACTIVE --> ERROR_UNKNOWN

docs.title: Delivery mechanisms
docs.text:
Mechanism How it works Protocol EDDS Server (default) The response stays on the EDDS FTP area. It is downloaded with the client (getResponse) or by SFTP with the EDDS account. HTTPS, SFTP File Server (push) The Delivery Manager uploads with PUT to the user's server, with configurable retries. FTP is used if no SFTP credentials are given. Unless "keep file after delivery" is set, the copy on the EDDS is deleted after success. SFTP or FTP E-mail Acknowledgements only. The EDDS sends mail but never reads it. SMTP/SMTPs Stream Client application connected to the web server HTTPS (CometD)

The table combines the SRS, SDD and EUICD.9495969754 Files of a split response are delivered one by one as soon as each is ready. FTP account details are stored encrypted in the database. Expired responses are deleted by scheduled JMS messages, after a retention period set by the mission administrator.6995 Failed deliveries go to a "failed" directory and must be moved back by hand to retry.95

The SRS still lists RDM (raw data media) and "display" as delivery mechanisms inherited from the GDDS and WebRM.98 The EUICD issue 24.0 delivery chapter describes only file server, EDDS server and stream.96

docs.title: Performance targets
docs.text:
SRS Appendix D sets throughput targets per data type and delivery path.99

Data type Client File server / EDDS server RDM Display Stream, online Stream, offline TM, TC or EV packets – 500 packets/s TBD as stream 20 kbit/s (*1) or 300 kbit/s (*2) 20 kbit/s (*1) or 300 kbit/s (*2) Packet statistics 500 packets/s 500 packets/s – – – – TM parameters – 10,000 samples/s TBD as stream 500 samples/s 10,000 samples/s Parameter statistics and definitions 10,000 samples/s 10,000 samples/s – – – –

The markers *1 and *2 are not explained in the SRS: its legend only defines kps (kbit/s), sps and pps. Reports, files, catalogues and acknowledgements are "TBD".99 The Solar Orbiter DDID adds an availability requirement of at least 95 % over a month, including maintenance downtimes.100

docs.title: The Solar Orbiter DDS in brief
docs.text:
Solar Orbiter's "DDS" is an EDDS installation at ESOC, described in the mission's Data Delivery Interface Control Document (DDID) SOL-ESC-IF-05011.101 Its main features:

  • Prime and backup servers on the RELAY LAN, the backup in cold redundancy. A switch-over means users re-point their client. Scheduled requests must be resubmitted, and temporarily stored responses must be requested again.102100
  • Data come from the MCS long-term archive (LTA): packets from its PARC, parameters from its DARC and files from its FARC. TM is retrievable "within seconds" of reception at the station.103
  • File-server push over SFTP is the nominal delivery. Users whitelist the DDS addresses and can use an ESA-provided SSH public key instead of a password. Server-side storage is not a baseline option.104102
  • The nominal route to the Science Ground Segment is not the EDDS but RAPID files forwarded by GFTS, described on the formats page.104

The DDID publishes the server host names and IP addresses for firewall configuration. This wiki does not repeat them. The full Solar Orbiter specifics, including SCOS-2000 packet headers, internal packets and RAPID records, are on the formats page.

Other ESOC tools consume EDDS output too. The ARES analysis system, the successor of MUST, imports EDDS response files fed from the MCS DARC and PARC.105

docs.title: The document set
docs.text:
The library holds 14 EDDS documents copied from the Solar Orbiter EDDS document area at IRAP on 2026-11-05. Each library page gives the exact URL, copy time and checksum. Several file names do not match the version printed inside.

Library page Document File name at source Printed version and date EDDS release Copied (UTC) srs Software Requirements Specification, EGOS-GEN-EDDS-SRS-1001 EGOS-GEN-EDDS-SRS.pdf 18.0, 2018-02-16 2.3.0 2026-11-05 14:02:35 sdd Software Design Document, EGOS-GEN-EDDS-SDD-1001 EGOS-GEN-EDDS-SDD.pdf 15.0, 2018-02-16 2.3.0 2026-11-05 14:00:17 sdd-v24 Software Design Document EGOS-GEN-EDDS-SDD.v24.pdf 25.0, 2025-03-07 3.6.1 2026-11-05 14:01:34 euicd-unversioned External User ICD, EGOS-GEN-EDDS-ICD-1001 EGOS-GEN-EDDS-EUICD.pdf 7.0, 2014-12-17 1.5.0 2026-11-05 14:19:57 euicd-v13 External User ICD EGOS-GEN-EDDS-EUICD v13.pdf 13.0, 2017-05-05 2.2.0 2026-11-05 13:56:04 euicd-i15r0 External User ICD EGOS-GEN-EDDS-ICD-1001_EUICD_i15r0_2.pdf 15.0, 2018-02-16 2.3.0 2026-11-05 13:57:31 euicd-v25 External User ICD EGOS-GEN-EDDS-EUICD.v25.pdf 24.0, 2025-01-10 3.6.0 2026-11-05 13:59:26 sum Software User Manual, EGOS-GEN-EDDS-SUM-1001 EGOS-GEN-EDDS-SUM.pdf 14.0, 2018-02-16 2.3.0 2026-11-05 14:05:49 sum-v22 Software User Manual EGOS-GEN-EDDS-SUM.v22.pdf 22.0, 2025-01-10 3.6.0 2026-11-05 14:07:57 cig-i14r0 Configuration and Installation Guide, EGOS-GEN-EDDS-CIG-1001 EGOS-GEN-EDDS-CIG-1001-i14r0_2.pdf 14.0, 2018-02-16 2.3.0 2026-11-05 14:09:15 cig-v24 Configuration and Installation Guide EGOS-GEN-EDDS-CIG.v24.pdf 25.0, 2025-03-07 3.6.1 2026-11-05 14:10:02 eug EDDS Update Guide, EGOS-GEN-EDDS-EUG-1001 EGOS-GEN-EDDS-EUG.pdf 12.0, 2018-02-16 2.2.0 to 2.3.0 2026-11-05 14:10:09 srn Software Release Note EGOS-GEN-EDDS-SRN.pdf 14.0, 2018-02-16 2.3.0 2026-11-05 14:10:20 glo EDDS Glossary, EGOS-GEN-EDDS-GLO-0001 EGOS-GEN-EDDS-GLO.pdf 7.0, 2017-04-10 see below 2026-11-05 14:03:37

The versions, dates and releases come from each title page and change log.106107151081091101111121131142611511625

What each document is for:

  • The SRS gives the general description (predecessors, data types, logical model, use cases) and about a hundred pages of numbered EDDS-SR-nnnnn requirements with need, priority, stability and verification method.117
  • The SDD covers the top-level architecture and the component and sub-component design. Issue 25.0 adds chapters on EGS-CC integration (HARC and REST) and DevOps (GitLab pipeline, Docker images, Helm deployment).87118
  • The EUICD is the user-facing contract: services, data types, formats, naming, delivery, the WSDL operations and the full XML schemas as appendices. It states that the XSD files take precedence over the document, and that missions write their own DDIDs on top of it.119
  • The SUM explains the client application step by step, including the status table and user-management screens.57
  • The CIG covers building and deploying every component, firewall and SSL configuration, the MIB files the server needs, and the XML files that describe header layouts.89120
  • The EUG gives upgrade steps, here the database migration tool for v2.2.0 to v2.3.0.115
  • The SRN for v2.3.0 lists tested dependencies (SCOS 6.0.1, DARC 3.0.0, FARC 3.1.0, EUD 3.1.8, SLES 12), known limitations and the delivered fixes.121
  • The GLO holds references, acronyms and terms used across the set.25

Inference: version mismatches to keep in mind

  • EGOS-GEN-EDDS-EUICD.v25.pdf is EUICD issue 24.0, and SDD.v24 and CIG.v24 are issue 25.0.1111526
  • Inside issue 25.0 of the SDD and CIG, the body page footers still read 24.0 (2025-01-10). The SDD's front matter even shows "24.0.0 2023-11-01", and the CIG's first front-matter footer reads "ISSUE: 25.0 2024-03-08".124125
  • The SRN title page says 2018-02-16, but its change log dates issue 14.0 2017-02-16.116
  • The EUICD 15.0 change log dates the issue 2018-01-15, while the title page says 2018-02-16.110
  • Glossary issue 7.0 (April 2017) says "Updated for EDDS v1.8.0i1", although the other documents had reached v2.2.0 by May 2017.25

This wiki always cites the version printed on the title page and names the slug, so a reader can open the right file.
