docs.title: SCOS-2000 as EGSE and central checkout
docs.text:
Before a spacecraft flies, it is tested on the ground. Its units, instruments and finally the complete satellite are connected to electrical ground support equipment (EGSE): the electrical and electronic equipment that supports assembly, integration, functional and environmental testing, ground station compatibility tests and launch operations.1 The heart of a system-level EGSE is the Central Checkout System (CCS), from which tests are prepared, run and archived. Around it sit Specific Check Out Equipment (SCOE) units, each dedicated to one subsystem or interface.122

ESA designed SCOS-2000 to serve both mission control and checkout. Its stated objective is to reuse the same system for the MCS, the EGSE and station control wherever possible.16 This page describes how that worked in practice: the PROBA heritage, the "EGSE and Mission Control System" (EMCS) that ESA delivered to the Herschel/Planck instrument teams, the TOPE test language, the Herschel/Planck instrument and central checkout systems, commercial products that keep SCOS-2000 compatibility, translators between databases, and the migration of TOPE procedures to EGS-CC. The internals of the kernel are on SCOS-2000 architecture; the Herschel/Planck interface documents behind the test systems (router, PIPE, CCS external interfaces) are read field by field on Herschel/Planck interface documents.

docs.title: Why one system for test and operations
docs.text:
Several ESA policies pushed checkout and operations towards common tools. In April 2000 the FIRST/Planck (later Herschel/Planck) project summarised ESA's science directorate policy: EGSE is procured by industry as part of the spacecraft contract, the agency delivers as little as possible to industry, and commonality between the flight control system and the checkout system is to be pursued within the project's constraints. The same goal applied to Rosetta and Mars Express.29 The Herschel/Planck EGSE specification lists the expected benefits: less duplicated effort, lower risk and cost, and more synergy between AIV and flight operations. It names the areas where commonality is pursued: the Mission Information Base, user interfaces, data archiving and distribution, on-board software management and maintenance, and the user language for test procedures and in-orbit operations.7

ESA's Bulletin of 2007 confirms the result: common tools for spacecraft checkout and for operations preparation gave a seamless transition from manufacture to operations, which Herschel and Planck exploited.17 The modifications that made SCOS-2000 usable for spacecraft and instrument checkout were pioneered for the PROBA technology satellite and then merged into the evolution version of SCOS-2000.18

flowchart LR
  subgraph AIT["Assembly, integration and test"]
    SCOE["SCOEs"] <--> R["EGSE router"] <--> E["SCOS-2000 EGSE"]
  end
  subgraph OPS["Operations"]
    GS["Ground station"] <--> N["NCTRS"] <--> M["SCOS-2000 MCS"]
  end
  MIB[("Same MIB")] --- E
  MIB --- M

The diagram follows the "Commonality" slide of ESOC's April 2000 presentation: the same kernel talks to SCOEs through a router during tests and to ground stations through NCTRS in operations.19 The shared MIB is not on that slide; it is added from the Herschel/Planck EGSE specification, which names the Mission Information Base as the first area of commonality.7

docs.title: The PROBA heritage
docs.text:
PROBA (Project for On-Board Autonomy) was a small technology satellite with a 32-bit processor, an Earth-observation imager and a test bed for automatic operations, including on-board mission planning. Its ground station was a 2 m antenna at Redu, independent of the ESA network.30 For PROBA, ESA built a common EGSE and mission control system on SCOS-2 (release R1.4), and planned to move it to SCOS-2000 R2.2 by the end of 2000.3423 In April 2000 ESOC offered the reusable PROBA elements plus two additional database and procedure tools:202425

Element Description SCOS-2000 The kernel EGSE router TM reception, TC transmission and the SCOS gateway Procedure automation tool Based on the free Tcl/Tk language; used for complex procedures in AIV and in PROBA operations Database editors Based on ORACLE, used for both spacecraft and SCOE data (the SCOE equipment was addressed like a spacecraft subsystem) Integral database editor (additional) Based on MS-Access, used for INTEGRAL Winfops/MOIS (additional) Based on MS-Access, for procedure preparation and simple (tabular) automation

The meeting minutes add that messages to the SCOEs were routed by APID, using APIDs outside the spacecraft range, and that the PROBA procedure environment read the ORACLE database directly at compile time.30 On a Windows NT PC, the router sustained 1 Mbps of telemetry (input through a DMA parallel card) and 4 kbps of telecommands (through an RS-422 card) at less than 15 % CPU load. Distributing the data cost about 2 % CPU per virtual channel.21 Full ground-space commanding needed a commercial product, the "TC Encoder Shell" from De Lande Long, priced at about 10 kEUR per PC and needed only when the CCSDS COP-1 protocol was used.2226

docs.title: The EMCS: EGSE and Mission Control System
docs.text:
The document "EGSE based on SCOS 2000: the EGSE & Mission Control System", a software user manual written at ESTEC, describes the EGSE version of SCOS-2000 that ESA delivered to the Herschel/Planck instrument developers. Issue 4.0 of March 2004 covers the "SCOS EGSE Release 2.3e P5", installed on Linux SuSE 7.3. The manual complements the generic SCOS-2000 documentation with installation and configuration procedures, the TOPE language reference and the EGSE message formats.3332 Earlier issues followed SCOS-2000 R2.1.1 (2001) and R2.3e with ESOC patches (2003). Issue 3.0 introduced a new language grammar to ease the transfer of procedures to the Herschel/Planck CCS.32

The EMCS has four parts:34

flowchart TB
  TOPE["Test and Operation Procedure Environment (TOPE)"] -->|"parameters, commands, events"| K
  K["EMCS kernel<br/>SCOS-2000 + internal MIB"]
  SSM[("Space System Model")] --- K
  K -->|"TM & TC"| FE["TM/TC front end SCOE"]
  K -->|"stimulation & measurement"| SCOE["System and instrument SCOEs"]
  FE -->|"TM & TC"| UUT["Unit under test / spacecraft"]
  SCOE --> UUT
  K --> DIST["TM distribution to users"]

docs.title: The Space System Model and system element identifiers
docs.text:
The Space System Model (SSM) is an information system holding the mission information that the EMCS and its users need. The concept comes from ECSS-E-00 and was to be specified in ECSS-E-70-31 (see ECSS-E-ST-70-31C).35 The space system is a hierarchy of system elements (SE): the spacecraft with its data handling system, on-board software and application processes, and the ground segment with the EMCS, SCOS and the SCOEs. Elements that take part in monitoring and control get a 16-bit SE identifier. For on-board application processes, the SE identifier is the APID; the 11-bit APID field of CCSDS packets reserves 0x0000 to 0x07FF for them.35 The SSM allocates the other identifiers:37

SE identifier Type Use 0x0000–0x07FF APID Spacecraft application processes 0x0800 Router Reserved (spacecraft identifier in the MIB) 0x1000–0x1FFF – SCOS-2 tasks 0x2000–0x2FFF – EMCS clients (for example TOPE) 0x4000–0x4FFF – Ground station application processes 0x8000–0x87FF APID Alternative routing of spacecraft application processes via "EGSE_8000" 0x8000–0x8FFF – SCOE application processes 0x8800 Router Alternative routing of spacecraft application processes via the TC front end 0x8801 APID TC front end controller 0x8810–0x8817 APID TM front end, virtual channels 0 to 7 0x8818 APID TM front end controller 0xF000–0xFFFF – EGSE gateway and router tasks

Decimal values in the source

The manual prints the decimal equivalent of 0x1000 as 4099 and the SCOE range 0x8000–0x8FFF as 34816–36863. The hexadecimal values above are given as printed; 0x1000 is 4096 and 0x8000 is 32768 in decimal (the manual's own Appendix B uses 0x8000 = 32768 as its example). The printed decimal range 34816–36863 corresponds to 0x8800–0x8FFF instead, so either the hexadecimal start or the decimal start of the SCOE range is a misprint; the sources do not say which.3767

The SE type tells the kernel what it can do with an element. Elements of type APID process requests, so activities (telecommands, procedures, stimuli) can be attached to them. Elements of type Router only carry requests and reports onward. SCOS-2000 was changed to control any element that processes requests, whether it is on board or on the ground.36 An Oracle-based SSM repository was under development but not yet available in 2004, so users populated the mission data through the SCOS-2000 ASCII files, extended for EGSE needs.37

docs.title: The EMCS kernel and the SCOE
docs.text:
The kernel is SCOS-2000 with three additions: it can route commands to the spacecraft through the ground station or through a SCOE, it can monitor and control ground processes such as SCOE applications, and it can send commands and process telemetry that are not predefined in the database.38 It connects to the SCOEs over TCP/IP.40

For PROBA, ESTEC built the EGSE router, a generic facility on Windows for integrating and remotely controlling SCOE equipment. The router provides location transparency, client management with several clients per connection, data transparency, and message delivery either by asynchronous call-back or by synchronous polling. It was written in Delphi as an ActiveX server using Microsoft DCOM, usable from any ActiveX language (Delphi, C++, LabView, Java). Systems without DCOM, such as SCOS-2000, connect through a TCP/IP gateway.41 The Windows TM front end extracts, archives and distributes CCSDS telemetry packets from a bit stream, either from an on-board data handling interface simulator or from baseband equipment. The TC front end turns command requests into a CCSDS stream, using the commercial TC Encoder Shell for the full ground-space protocol.42 For Herschel/Planck the Windows router and front ends were not used. SRON developed a Linux router for Herschel, compatible with the ESTEC set-up on the SCOS side but not on the SCOE side.40 A packet router ICD written at SRON in 2001 is summarised below; that it specifies this Linux router is this wiki's reading, since the ICD names Java but no operating system.117

docs.title: EGSE message format
docs.text:
Messages between ground applications on the EGSE router share one header, defined in the EGSE Gateway ICD:56

Field Size Meaning DstID 2 octets Unique identifier of the destination ground application SrcID 2 octets Unique identifier of the sending application Token 4 octets Unique message identifier, used in reports about the processing of the message Time 8 octets SunOS time format: 4 octets of seconds since 1970-01-01T00:00:00 and 4 octets of remaining microseconds Msg_Type 1 octet Template number that defines the application data layout Spare 1 octet 0 S/C id 2 octets Spacecraft identifier; 0x66 for PROBA Application data any Layout given by the template

The field sizes and meanings come from §7.1 of the EMCS manual.56 The message types are:56

Msg_Type Template Direction (from the manual's descriptions) 1 SCOE command SCOS-2000 to a SCOE 2 SCOE command verification report SCOE to SCOS-2000 3 SCOE observation report SCOE to SCOS-2000 4 Sending TC packet request SCOS-2000 to the TC front end 5 Sending TC packet verification report TC front end to SCOS-2000 6 TM packet report TM front end to SCOS-2000 7 TM frame reports (application data not defined in the manual)

Template 1 (SCOE command) keeps the PUS application data but replaces the CCSDS and PUS headers by the EGSE header. The parameter structure follows the PUS service type and subtype and is defined in the MIB.58

Template 2 (SCOE command verification report) carries service type 1 with a subtype from 1 to 8, the 4-octet token of the SCOE command, a step number (for subtypes 5 and 6 only; its size is not printed), a 1-octet code and parameters. Footnotes in the manual say that neither step-level progress reporting nor the code was supported by the EMCS server in 2004. The subtypes are 1 successful acceptance, 2 failed acceptance, 3 successful start, 4 failed start, 5 successful progress, 6 failed progress, 7 successful completion and 8 failed completion, mirroring ST[01].59

Template 3 (SCOE observation report) lets an EGSE application send any feedback to SCOS, in a structure modelled on a PUS telemetry packet: service type, subtype and a parameter structure like PUS source data. It is sent with the router's "smData" service.60

Template 4 (sending TC packet) asks the TC front end to uplink a complete CCSDS/PUS TC packet:61

In BD mode, the UL_Ack report says whether the packet was completely sent to the spacecraft. In AD mode, it says whether the packet was confirmed by the COP-1 protocol through the CLCW. In 2004 the mapping from service type and subtype to MAPID was hard-coded in the SCOS-to-SCOE interface, as it had been for PROBA.61 See TC Space Data Link Protocol and COP-1 for AD and BD frames, MAP IDs and the CLCW.

Template 5 (sending TC packet verification report) returns service type 1 with subtypes 9 to 14: 9 successful GS, 10 failed GS, 11 successful UL, 12 failed UL, 13 successful on-board acceptance, 14 failed on-board acceptance. It also carries the 4-octet EGSE command token, a code and parameters. SCOS-2000 injects these reports as telemetry packets.62

Template 6 (TM packet report) wraps a full CCSDS/PUS telemetry packet received by the TM front end. Service 1 reports inside it are injected with a packet ID known to the SCOS-2000 verifier.63

SPID values for injected verification reports

The manual gives the packet IDs used to inject Template 5 and service 1 reports as 10005 and 10006 in §7.7 and §7.8, but lists the defaults of the corresponding configuration variables (EGSE_VER_TC_GS_PKTID, EGSE_VER_TC_REP_PKTID) as 23 and 24 in §4.2.626345 The sources do not explain the difference; the values are configurable in any case.

docs.title: The acknowledgement policy
docs.text:
PUS defines four acknowledgements that a command can request from the on-board application process: acceptance, start, progress and completion. The EMCS extends this so that a command can be followed through the EMCS kernel, NCTRS and the SCOEs as well. Any element that processes requests, on board or on the ground, may report with the four PUS acknowledgements (Template 2 for SCOE commands, Template 6 for TC packets). Three further acknowledgement requests, with six reports (service 1 subtypes 9 to 14), follow the ground front ends:57

Acknowledgement Issued by When GS_Ack Ground station or SCOE TC front end The telecommand is received UL_Ack Ground station or SCOE TC front end A BD-mode telecommand has been sent to the spacecraft ONB_Ack Ground station or SCOE TC front end The spacecraft confirms reception of an AD-mode telecommand 
sequenceDiagram
  participant T as TOPE procedure
  participant E as EMCS kernel (SCOS-2000)
  participant F as TC front end / ground station
  participant S as On-board application
  T->>E: tcsend
  E-->>T: ECH ack/nack (always)
  E-->>T: Static and dynamic PTV ack/nack (per MIB and TC SPACON)
  E->>F: Template 4 (TC packet)
  F-->>E: GS ack/nack (always)
  F->>S: Uplink
  F-->>E: UL ack/nack (always)
  F-->>E: ONB ack/nack (AD mode only)
  S-->>E: Acceptance, start, progress, completion (service 1, if requested and supported)
  E-->>T: Completed notification (after completion or any failure)

The sequence follows the table of conditional reporting in §7.2. The External Command Handler (ECH) always confirms receipt, the PTV reports depend on the MIB and the TC SPACON settings, the ground reports are always delivered, and the on-board reports depend on the application process. The manual warns that the order of the reports cannot be guaranteed. SCOS-2000 can also verify execution through telemetry conditions (the CEV, confirmation of execution verification) instead of, or in addition to, service 1 reports.57

docs.title: Internal archives and packet identification
docs.text:
The SCOS EGSE stores every received message (Templates 2, 3, 5 and 6) as an internal SCOS packet with a SPID. SPIDs 0 to 100 are reserved for kernel needs (§4.1.1 says 1 to 100) and can be reallocated through the configuration and the minimum EGSE data set.6443 The SPID is chosen from the template number, the APID, the service type and subtype, and the PI1 and PI2 identification fields, as for spacecraft packets.64 Specific processing then applies:65

  • Time stamping depends on EGSE_TM_FILING_TIME_TYPE: 1 uses the reception time on the SCOS machine, 2 uses the time field of the router header, and 3 converts the on-board time in the packet through time correlation, with a sanity check. A packet whose on-board time differs from the current time by more than EGSE_TM_OBT_THRESHOLD gets the current time instead, a warning, and the type "PR" rather than "PG" in the packet history.
  • Checksum verification: packets that fail can be discarded, or archived in a dedicated data stream and flagged invalid together with all their parameters.
  • Request verification: Template 2, Template 5 and service 1 reports go to the SCOS-2000 verifier and are stored under system SPIDs.
  • Unknown messages: an observation report or TM packet without a matching pid entry is "rejected" and filed under a wrapper SPID. After the MIB is updated and re-imported, the PDS_DISP task copies the stored messages into their proper SPID archives.66

docs.title: Configuration: MISC variables and system SPIDs
docs.text:
The EGSE-specific variables in the MISCconfig file include:45

Variable Default Meaning EGSE_MODE 1 0: the TC releaser connects only to NCTRS; 1: to NCTRS and the EGSE router; 2: only to the EGSE router NCTRS_EGSE_TC_SERVER, ..._PORT localhost, 2222 Host and port of the SCOS gateway that connects to the router EGSE_EGW_SERVER, ..._PORT localhost, 9876 Host and port of the router's EGSE gateway EGSE_BINCMD_NAME ZBINTC "Binary command" for uploading commands not defined in the MIB; to be removed from the MIB where not authorised EGSE_VER_SCOE_PKTID 22 SPID of SCOE command verification reports EGSE_SEND_CHKSUM_ERROR_PKT 1 Archive (1) or drop (0) TM packets that fail the checksum EGSE_STREAM_ID_FOR_CRC_ERROR 65534 Data stream for packets that fail the checksum EGSE_TM_FILING_TIME_TYPE 1 Time stamping: 1 EMCS time, 2 ground station or SCOE time, 3 on-board time EGSE_TM_OBT_THRESHOLD 60 Sanity threshold for on-board times EGSE_DUPLICATE_GS_UL 1 Simulate an on-board acknowledgement for each UL report received in BD mode EGSE_WRAPPER_PKTID_3, _6 20, 21 SPIDs for unknown observation reports and unknown TM packets IMPT_DST_FILE dst.dat File with the routing configuration of system elements OOL_PACKET_APID 3000 SPID for out-of-limits event packets TCO_MISSION_EPOCH 1958-01-01T00:00:00.000000 Mission epoch (the manual says the default is 1970)

docs.title: The minimum EGSE data set
docs.text: The EGSE needs some generic MIB definitions to work. They are delivered as MIN_EGSE_v2, and every name in it starts with the letter "Z" so that it is easy to recognise.43 A mission adapts the TC packet header (tcp, pcdf, pcpc), the time-tag wrapper command ZLOADTT and the binary command ZBINTC (ccf, cdf, cpc), the definitions that decode rejected and service 1 packets (dpc, pcf, plf), and the version entry (vdf).43 Two scripts manage databases: mergeDATA merges several data sets (for example MIN_EGSE and one instrument) into a new set, and setSCOSdata points SCOS-2000 at a given MIB, links its TOPE procedures, installs its archive and cache configuration, and runs the import.44 See the MIB for the tables and MIB tooling for editors.

docs.title: Command routing in the MIB: the dst table
docs.text:
The MIB table dst routes commands by APID. The ICD says it is optional and only used by SCOS-2000-based EGSE systems. Each route is a string of up to three dot-separated fields: the destination system (NCTRS, the default, or EGSE), the request type (SCOE for non-spacecraft commands, TC for spacecraft commands) and, for spacecraft commands not sent through NCTRS, the address of the ground equipment that sends them. The ICD's example EGSE.TC.0x8800 sends spacecraft commands through the SCOE and the TC front end 0x8800.112 This matches the system element 0x8800 of the EMCS manual.37

The Solar Orbiter MIB of September 2025 still contains exactly one dst record, as did the release of April 2020: APID 1372 is routed to EGSE.TC.0x8800. All 91 commands on APID 1372 have names starting with ZIC, and 7 of their descriptions mention the SPICE instrument; for example ZIC00085 is described as opening the door of the SPICE optics unit.113114

Inference

The dst record is probably a leftover of instrument-level testing on a SCOS-2000-based EGSE, carried into the flight MIB because the instrument database was merged into the spacecraft database. In the mission control system, which sends commands through NCTRS, it has no evident use. Neither the MIB nor the sources say why it is there.

SQL used 
-- solo-2025-09-16.sqlite
SELECT * FROM dst;                                     -- 1372|EGSE.TC.0x8800
SELECT count(*) FROM ccf WHERE CCF_APID = '1372';      -- 91
SELECT count(*) FROM ccf WHERE CCF_APID = '1372' AND CCF_CNAME LIKE 'ZIC%';   -- 91
SELECT count(*) FROM ccf WHERE CCF_APID = '1372'
   AND (CCF_DESCR LIKE '%SPICE%' OR CCF_DESCR2 LIKE '%SPICE%');            -- 7
SELECT CCF_CNAME, CCF_DESCR, CCF_DESCR2 FROM ccf WHERE CCF_CNAME = 'ZIC00085';
-- ZIC00085|SDM_OPEN_DOOR|Open the door to the SPICE Optics Unit
-- solo-2020-04-16.sqlite
SELECT * FROM dst;                                     -- 1372|EGSE.TC.0x8800

docs.title: TOPE: the Test and Operations Procedure Environment
docs.text:
ECSS-E-70-32 specifies a common procedure language for test and operations, PLUTO (Procedure Language for Users in Test and Operations; see ECSS-E-ST-70-32C). When PLUTO tools were not yet available, ESA delivered to the Herschel/Planck instrument teams a procedure environment based on Tcl/Tk, called TOPE (Test and Operations Procedure Environment). TOPE starts commands to the spacecraft or the SCOEs through the EMCS kernel, follows their execution through the reports that SCOS returns, and monitors the space system through telemetry and ground parameters.39 Procedures may use any low-level Tcl/Tk function. The constructs defined since issue 3.0 of the manual are not compatible with the earlier TOPE language.46 Later sources expand the acronym differently: GMV writes "Test procedure, preparation and execution" and Terma "Test & Operations Procedure Executive".10592

TOPE talks to SCOS-2000 through the EXIF CORBA services (see architecture). A 2019 GMV paper classifies TOPE's EGSE commands by their interaction pattern:105

Pattern Commands Mechanism Synchronous fetch, syslog, the database patch commands Direct CORBA calls on EXIF Asynchronous subscribe for TM packets and parameters Registration is synchronous; updates arrive later as Tcl variable updates Synchronous with asynchronous progress tcsend, callasync A call followed by progress notifications Local waiting, logging, data access, conversions No interaction with the EGSE

docs.title: Sending commands: tcsend
docs.text:
tcsend <CommandName> <Arguments> <Parameters> sends a command to the unit under test or to a SCOE. All arguments are optional:4748

Argument Meaning via <string> Routing: server (EGSE or NCTRS), encoding style (TC or SCOE), destination 0x0000–0xFFFF; default from the dst table mapid <n>, vcid <n> MAP ID and virtual channel for TC-style commands (defaults from the configuration or CCF_MAPID) checks {...} Static PTV, dynamic PTV and CEV checks on or off (ALL by default, or NONE) ack {...} Acknowledgements to request: ACCEPT, START, PROGRESS, COMPLETE, ALL or NONE; default from CCF_ACK and the header definition referby <Varname> Tcl variable updated with each acknowledgement report userrequestid <id> End-user identifier of the request releasetime <time> Absolute release time YYYY.DDD.HH.MM.SS.UUUUUU; otherwise as soon as possible executiontime <time> Builds an on-board schedule command (service 11,4) to execute at that time ilocktype, ilockstage Interlock type (NONE, LOCAL, GLOBAL, SUBSYS_LOCAL, SUBSYS_GLOBAL) and the stage that releases it nowait Do not wait automatically for stage UV_GS_RECEIVE

Each parameter is a list {name value [format] [RAW|ENG|DEFAULT]}. The default format is a string that SCOS converts to the parameter's type. The explicit formats are long (32-bit signed), unsigned long, IEEE single-precision float, boolean, string, binary string, time, short, unsigned short, char and octet. Binary parameters can be given as characters or as a hex string.48 tcsend returns a unique request ID, or throws a Tcl exception on failure.48 Absolute times use YYYY.DDD.HH.MM.SS.mmmmmm, relative times [+|-]HH.MM.SS.mmmmmm with abbreviations allowed.49

The report variable is read with access functions: getrequestid, getstage, getstatus, getstagehistory, getcompleted, getupdatetime, getuserrequestid and tostring.50 The stage names and their order are listed on the architecture page. getstagehistory returns one character per stage, matching the SCOS TC history display:51

Status Letter Status Letter IDLE I SUPERSEDED E PENDING P UNCERTAIN_FAILED N PASSED S UNCERTAIN_PASSED V FAILED F AFFECTED A UNVERIFIED U SCC (empty) UNKNOWN X NOT_APPLICABLE ? TIMEOUT T

The transfer mode for commands can be read and set with gettransfermode and settransfermode (AD or BD).52

docs.title: Telemetry: fetch, subscribe and waiting
docs.text:
fetch <ParameterName> returns a Tcl list with the parameter's properties. Access functions return the name, raw value, extracted value (regardless of validity), engineering value, default value (engineering if it exists, otherwise raw), each value's validity as a bit set, the out-of-limits state (NOMINAL, WARNING, ALARM, SCC), the status consistency state and the time stamp.53 The validity bits are listed on the architecture page.

subscribe <ParameterName> referby <Varname> ?whenever UPDATE|CHANGE? updates a variable whenever the parameter is updated (by a new packet, or by a contributing parameter such as the source of a synthetic parameter or a validity, limit-applicability or calibration-selection parameter) or only when it changes. subscribeset does the same for a list of parameters, and unsubscribe cancels subscriptions.54 waitfor <Varname> ?-until <Expression>? waits until the variable is set and the expression is true. waittime waits for a relative time, watchdog runs an action when a condition on watched variables becomes true, and putlog, openlog and closelog handle the test log.55

# Illustrative TOPE fragment, constructed for this page from the syntax in the EMCS SUM.
# Command and parameter names are invented.
tcsend CMD001 referby vCmd ack {ACCEPT COMPLETE} {PAR1 10 UL RAW}
waitfor vCmd -until {[getcompleted $vCmd]}
putlog "CMD001 stages: [getstagehistory $vCmd]"

subscribe TEMP01 referby vT whenever CHANGE
waitfor vT -until {[isengvaluevalid $vT] && [getengvalue $vT] > 20.0}
putlog "TEMP01 now [getengvalue $vT] ([getoolstate $vT])"

docs.title: Running TOPE
docs.text: In the PACS instrument test set-up of 2004, the router and EGSE gateway were started first, then a gateway for the PACS test equipment interface, then SCOS-2000 from its task launcher (server tasks, then client applications), and finally the EXIF tasks and a TOPE instance from a second launcher. Starting a second procedure in the same TOPE window suspended the first until the second finished. Parallel procedures needed another TOPE window and another EXIF_CHx task.7071 The manual's debugger, TUBA, could step through procedures but had known limits, such as treating several procedures as one sequential flow.68

docs.title: TOPE on the Herschel/Planck CCS
docs.text:
Procedures written for instrument tests were to be reused on the Herschel/Planck CCS, which had its own TOPE implementation ("TOPE/CCS"). Appendix E of the manual lists the differences:69

Topic Instrument EGSE (TOPE/IEGSE) Central checkout (TOPE/CCS) Parallel procedures Cooperative multitasking with one event loop; procedures can share global variables and can miss updates One process per procedure; truly parallel; no shared "spill-over" variables SCOE connection Established automatically Explicit connect and disconnect SCOE commanding No locking attach (an exclusive lock) before the first SCOE command TM update mode whenever UPDATE and whenever CHANGE Packet parameters update only when a source packet arrives; whenever CHANGE not available Features via, mapid, vcid, interlocks, watchdog, openlog/closelog, transfer mode Not supported

The CCS worked only in BD mode.52 A technical note of 2003 proposed how a CCS test script could run a full instrument telecommand sequence while the instrument EGSE supplied the parameter values. The CCS sends a TC packet over the PIPE protocol asking for a named observation. The instrument EGSE expands it with the Herschel Common Science System (HCSS),111 in particular its CUS component, and returns the command IDs, parameter values and delays in housekeeping TM packets.72 The concept was prototyped with MIB files ingested into the PACS SCOS-2000 EGSE and run with TOPE. The note records that the telecommand request ID needed by this scheme was known to SCOS-2000 since version 2.3e, and that the observation request was limited to 242 characters.72

docs.title: The decision for SCOS-2000
docs.text: The Herschel/Planck instrument teams evaluated SCOS-2000 from 3 to 5 November 1999 as a "framework" for a common real-time assessment (RTA) system, and later as an EGSE kernel. PACS collected the missing functions in a "delta" user requirements document in April 2000.28 At a meeting at ESOC on 18 and 19 April 2000, ESOC presented its status, the EGSE elements, the licence and the support and service options.27 The project stated that the choice was entirely the instrument teams' and that it could not provide technical support, hardware, software or funding.29 All instrument groups stated unanimously that they intended to use SCOS-2000 as the basis for their EGSE and RTA systems. The three Herschel instruments agreed a common EGSE development, with requirements frozen around June 2000.31

docs.title: The EGSE-ILT and its integration
docs.text:
The Herschel EGSE for instrument level tests (EGSE-ILT) shared its building blocks among the three Herschel instruments:73

Block Delivered by SCOS-2000 ESA SCOS gateway ESTEC Test equipment interface (TEI) HIFI TM/TC router HIFI Test control PACS CDMS simulator SPIRE OBSM ESA MIB editor ESA 
flowchart LR
  INS["Instrument"] -->|"1553B"| CDMS["CDMS simulator"]
  CDMS --> RT["Router"]
  TE["Test equipment"] --> TEI["TEI"] --> RT
  TC0["Test client"] --> RT
  RT --> EGW["EGSE gateway"] --> SGW["SCOS gateway"] --> S2K["SCOS-2000"]
  MIB[("MIB")] --> S2K
  S2K <--> TCTL["Test control"] <--> HCSS["HCSS"]

The diagram follows the overview figure of the integration plan.73 The plan of 2001 tested the blocks one at a time, each with a MIB that described the TM and TC packets used:74

Test Functions demonstrated Router TM packets from a test client to SCOS-2000, TC packets back, throughput Test equipment interface TM from test equipment to SCOS-2000 and TC to test equipment CDMS simulator TM and TC routing through the simulated command and data management system, its command interface, and (to be confirmed) the time packet protocol Test control Reading housekeeping values from SCOS-2000, sending TCs, test procedures, command mnemonic sequences and autonomy procedures Test control and HCSS Communication between test control, the HCSS and the test client

On-board software maintenance was left as an open item.74 The common EGSE document overview lists the documents of this effort, including the EGSE-ILT and real-time analysis user requirements, the CDMS simulator requirements, the router statement of work and ICDs, the TEI specification and requirements, the test-control statement of work, the Test Technology Activities (TTA-2000) user manual, the MIB-editor requirements and evaluation report, and the OBSM facility requirements.75

docs.title: The ILT packet router
docs.text:
The router at the centre of that diagram is specified in the Herschel EGSE Packet Router ICD (SRON-G/HIFI/ICD/2001-001, issue 1.1 of 23 October 2001, prepared by A. de Jonge and agreed by the EGSE and ICC managers of HIFI, PACS and SPIRE and by the HSC). It distributes PS-ICD telemetry and telecommand packets among SCOS-2000, the test equipment interface computers, the HCSS telemetry ingester and the CDMS simulator during instrument level tests, and the same interface was to serve the HCSS ingestion of raw telemetry in later phases. It runs on any platform with Java and listens on one agreed TCP port.115116117

Every message is a 1-octet messageType, a 4-octet contentLength (at most 1100, TBC) and the content; integers are most significant octet first.120 Twelve message types use three content structures:120122

Type Mnemonic Sent by Content 1 USER_DATA Client or router One complete PS-ICD packet; contentLength = packet length field + 7 2, 3 ADD_CLIENT, DEL_CLIENT Client Subscribe to, or unsubscribe from, a packet address 4, 5 ASK_CLIENT, SHOW_CLIENT Client, router List the subscriptions (with IP address and port, for debugging) 6 NAME_CLIENT Client Must be the first message; a unique client name 7, 8 ADD_BLOCK, DEL_BLOCK Client Block, or unblock, a route given by source name, destination name and packet address 9, 10 ASK_BLOCK, SHOW_BLOCK Client, router List the blocking table 11, 12 ASK_TRAFFIC, SHOW_TRAFFIC Client, router Packet counts per address, source and destination

The packet address is the APID for telemetry and 4096 plus the APID for telecommands, that is the type bit and the APID taken from the 16-bit packet ID (the ICD calls this "masking out the Type and APID fields"); the value 8192 is reserved: it is the wild card of blocking entries and marks "no address" in list replies. The router never looks inside the packet. It forwards a copy of each USER_DATA message to every client that subscribed to its address, unless a blocking entry matches, an entry matching when each of its source name, destination name and address is equal to the message's or empty (address 8192). Replies to ASK_* messages count down in a messageSequenceNumber to 0.121123124

Worked example (illustrative values): one telecommand through the router

A HIFI telecommand to APID 1024 (0x400) starts with the packet ID 0x1C00 (version 0b000, type 1, data field header flag 1). Masking out version and header flag leaves 0x1400 = 4096 + 1024 = 5120, the packet address to which the instrument simulator subscribes. A packet whose length field is 17 (a 24-octet packet) travels as USER_DATA with contentLength 24 = 17 + 7: the header octets are 01 00 00 00 18. The packet values are chosen for illustration; the rules are those of the ICD.121120144

There is no handshake, flow control or security: TCP provides the integrity, unauthorised access must be prevented by an isolated network, and after a router or client crash the client simply reconnects with the same name and repeats its subscriptions, packets in transit being lost. The ICD asks for 5 Mbit/s of free LAN capacity and limits each client to 500 kbit/s averaged over one second (both TBC), and warns that the performance requirements of the ground segment interface requirements may not be met on a loaded platform.119118125

Three generations of EGSE message headers appear in this page's sources:

Protocol Used for Header Addressing Acknowledgements EMCS EGSE router messages (PROBA heritage, EMCS SUM §7) SCOS-2000 EGSE to SCOEs and front ends 20 octets: destination, source, token, SunOS time, template number, spacecraft ID 16-bit system element identifiers Templates 2 and 5 (service 1 subtypes 1-14) Herschel ILT packet router SCOS-2000, test equipment, CDMS simulator, HCSS in instrument level tests 5 octets: message type, content length Packet address (APID, or 4096 + APID) None PIPE (EGSE IRS) CCS to SCOEs, front ends and instrument stations in system tests 10 octets: message ID, VC ID, remaining length, request ID, 0xFADE Separate connections per equipment; APIDs inside the packets ACKTC, ACKRC, TC echo, TC report

The table compares the three documents.56120132

docs.title: Test equipment as PUS application processes
docs.text:
The HIFI TEI TMTC packet ICD of December 2001 shows how test equipment was made to look like on-board software to SCOS-2000. Each TEI unit has an APID in the range 2016 to 2023 and speaks PUS. The TC packet header follows the CCSDS layout, but the ICD (which applies the Herschel/Planck Packet Structure ICD) splits the 14-bit sequence count into a 3-bit source field (always 000 for these packets) and an 11-bit counter maintained per source and APID:76

All TEI units accept (8,4) and (17,1) and generate (1,1), (1,2), (5,4) and (17,2); the other services below are used by particular units (for example (5,1) by the power distribution unit and (21,1) by the scanner):7778

Service (type, subtype) Direction Content (8,4) TC "Perform an activity of a function": function ID, activity ID, structure ID and data (for example set observation ID, set building block ID, switch a power distribution output, set temperatures, move a scanner) (17,1) / (17,2) TC / TM Connection test and link connection report (1,1) / (1,2) TM Acceptance success, and failure with error codes 0 illegal APID, 1 incomplete or illegal length, 2 incorrect checksum, 3 illegal type, 4 illegal subtype, 5 illegal or inconsistent application data (3,25) TM Housekeeping reports, starting with SID, observation ID and building block ID (5,1) / (5,4) TM Event and error/alarm reports (21,1) TM Measurement reports (scanner, network analyser)

See ST[08] function management, ST[17] test and ST[03] housekeeping. Some TEI telemetry carried safety information for SCOS-2000 itself. A status bit in the source unit's report meant that the state was undefined and that "SCOS must not release" commands that increase a bias.79

The TEI APIDs lie inside the range 2016 to 2046 that the Packet Structure ICD reserves for SCOE and EGSE messages, which "may be utilised by several groups in parallel" during unit-level tests and must never address an on-board unit. In system tests the same range was given to the system EGSE: the EGSE Interface Requirement Specification assigns 2016 to the CCS master test processor, 2017 to the CDMU SCOE, 2020 to the TM/TC front end and 2040 to 2044 to the HFI, LFI, HIFI, PACS and SPIRE EGSEs.142143138 The PS-ICD also confirms the PUS version number 0 printed in the TEI headers: it is the only value permitted for Herschel/Planck.144

docs.title: Constraints from the spacecraft level
docs.text:
The spacecraft prime imposed rules on the instrument databases so that they could later be merged. In January 2003 Alcatel asked the instrument teams to limit calibration curve and range set identifiers to 3 digits and command verification stage identifiers to 4, although the Database Import ICD issue 5.1 allowed 4, 4 and 5 digits. It also allocated ranges inside the single "constant packet" of dynamic user-defined constants: system 0000–0099, service module 0100–0199, payload module 0200–0299, then ranges for HIFI, HFI, PACS and LFI. The SPID of the constant packet was to hold 1024 octets.80

As printed

The fax lists HIFI twice (0300–0399 and 0500–0599, both for Herschel) and does not name SPIRE. The second entry may be meant for SPIRE, but the source does not say so. The Planck range 0500–0599 is marked "Not used" with the query "Sorbtion cooler ?", and 0600–1023 is spare for later allocation by Alcatel. The unit of the ranges is not stated. Since they run from 0000 to 1023, octet offsets in the 1024-octet constant packet would fit, but this is the wiki's reading.80

docs.title: Planck LFI: SCOS-2000 in an instrument ground segment
docs.text: The Planck LFI team used SCOS-2000 as the real-time assessment part of its Level 1 software. For the instrument-only tests, the EGSE was based on SCOS 2.3e. The team modified the SCOS-2000 Telemetry Receiver to replay simulated telemetry, and used the Flight Dynamics Interface to stream live packets to its own telemetry handler. From the Planck integration tests onwards, the EGSE was the Herschel/Planck CCS (HPCCS), which used a new protocol, PIPE (Packet Interface Protocol for EGSE), to talk to external equipment (see below). The team then wrote an "LFIGateway" to pass telemetry from the HPCCS to its own systems.812 See Herschel/Planck: SCOS-2000 in a science mission ground segment.

docs.title: The EGSE general requirements
docs.text:
Alcatel Space's EGSE General Requirements Specification (H-P-1-ASPI-SP-0045, issue 3 of June 2002) applies to every EGSE item used in Herschel/Planck system AIT.5 The EGSE must run automated tests, power instruments and modules, supervise the satellite permanently, provide link, simulation and stimulation signals, decommutate telemetry, send and monitor telecommands, manage the 1553 bus, acquire data and issue commands. It must also support test preparation by simulation and offer self-test.5 Its commonality section states that the instrument EGSEs and the ESOC flight control system will both be based on SCOS-2000, and refers to an analysis of which CCS requirements SCOS-2000 supports.8 The equipment includes:9

Group Items System EGSE CCS; TM/TC data front end (DFE); TT&C SCOE; power SCOE (junction unit, solar array simulator, battery simulator, battery conditioning equipment); CDMU SCOE; ACMS SCOE Payload module EGSE CDMU DFE; PLM SCOE Launch interfaces Check Out Terminal Equipment (COTE), spacecraft simulator, cable sets Special equipment OBSW quick loading (to be confirmed), test cabling and adapters, pyro tester, break-out boxes, power distribution unit, data and web server

All SCOEs are connected to the CCS by Ethernet and work in local mode (from their own peripherals) or remote mode (under CCS control), with a manual mode for power instruments.910 The CCS centralises the test-execution user interfaces, but every SCOE keeps a backup interface for safety.6

flowchart TB
  SAT["Herschel / Planck satellite"]
  subgraph SCOES["SCOE / DFE LAN"]
    DFE["TM/TC DFE"]
    TTC["TT&C SCOE"]
    PWR["Power SCOE"]
    CDMU["CDMU SCOE"]
    ACMS["ACMS SCOE"]
    CRYO["Cryo SCOE (Herschel)"]
  end
  CCS["Central Checkout System"]
  IS["Instrument EGSEs (IS LAN)"]
  SAT <--> SCOES
  SCOES <--> CCS
  CCS <--> IS
  DFE <--> NDIU["NDIU link"]
  CCS --> ARCH["Data archive, printers, web server"]

The diagram is a simplified reading of the system-level architecture figure of SP-0045.11 The specification names three user categories: the system administrator, the EGSE operator (who populates the database, writes test sequences and configures the test environment) and the test conductor, who executes or witnesses a test without being an EGSE expert.6

docs.title: Central checkout functions
docs.text:
The CCS is the core of the system EGSE: all testing is prepared, controlled and archived there, and it is the single point of control of the system-level AIV programme. A "CCS lite" with one server instead of two serves the payload module and instrument EGSE. The CCS must be compatible with the two standards that the specification lists as [S2] ESA-PSS-04-105 "TM Packet Standard" and [S3] ESA-PSS-04-106 "TC Packet Standard".123 Those labels do not match the PSS series itself: PSS-04-106 is the Packet Telemetry Standard, the Packet Telecommand Standard is PSS-04-107, and PSS-04-105 is the Radio Frequency and Modulation Standard (see the history of the packet standards).4 Its required functions include:13

  • standard interfaces for data distribution to the instrument EGSEs (without real-time control from them), for the front ends, and for an Internet gateway;
  • pre-transmission checks of telecommands against the satellite database, with operator confirmation for hazardous commands, and a facility to block or veto ESOC commands during system validation tests run from the MOC;
  • a simple test sequence language usable both interactively and in automated sequences, with parallel and nested sequences, debugging, a sequence library, configuration control and automatic logging;
  • a database development environment and a database management system portable between environments;
  • processing of all housekeeping data, automatic verification of TC reception and execution from the satellite database, and support for on-board control procedures;
  • complete archiving of test data in a Test Result Database, time-correlated to 1 s (to be confirmed), with retrieval tools and off-line distribution;
  • support of a mirror site of the Herschel/Planck System DataBase (HPSDB).

The TM/TC DFE connects the CCS to the spacecraft. It acquires telemetry at up to 3.5 Mbps, reconstructs packets from transfer frames and validates them, and can simulate telemetry. It sends telecommands at up to 4 kbps, encapsulating packets in CLTUs, filtering hazardous commands and extracting the CLCW. It also passes telemetry to, and telecommands from, the link of the Network Data Interface Unit (NDIU).142 See TC channel coding and the CLTU. The TT&C SCOE provides the RF links and RF measurements.15

docs.title: PIPE: the CCS protocol for SCOEs and instrument stations
docs.text:
The companion EGSE Interface Requirement Specification (H-P-1-ASPI-IS-0121, issue 4.1 of 14 December 2004, first issued on 7 November 2001) defines how the CCS talks to every SCOE, front end and instrument station (IS): the Packet Interface Protocol for EGSE (PIPE), on 100 Mbit/s Ethernet with TCP/IP, over a SCOE/DFE LAN and a separate IS LAN.126127130 Only the CCS sends telecommands and commands the SCOEs, every SCOE must be fully controllable from the CCS, and the CCS archives all low-rate telemetry, telecommands and other EGSE traffic.128 PIPE carries packets unchanged behind a header and adds remote commanding (RC) and remote monitoring (RM) of the test equipment itself.129

The header layout and field meanings are from §4.1.5; that the packet behind the header is embedded unchanged is stated in §4.1.1.132129

Message ID Kind Direction 0x80 TC: spacecraft telecommand packet CCS to DFE 0x44 RC: SCOE command, a TC(8,4) CCS to SCOE, DFE or IS 0x20 TM: on-board telemetry, and its distribution DFE to CCS; CCS to SCOE, DFE or IS 0x10 RM: periodic (3,25) or asynchronous (5,1) SCOE telemetry SCOE, DFE or IS to CCS 0x11 RM alive packet SCOE, DFE or IS to CCS 0x50, 0x51 ACKRC: RC acceptance success (1,1) or failure (1,2) SCOE, DFE or IS to CCS 0x55, 0x56 ACKTC: TC acceptance success (1,1) or failure (1,2) DFE to CCS 0xA0 TC echo DFE to CCS; CCS to IS 0x57 TC report: success (5,1) or transmission failure (5,4) DFE to CCS

Source: Table 11.133 The CCS is the client and each SCOE, DFE or IS a server that accepts the connection automatically; each must send at least one message (an RM packet or the alive packet) every 60 seconds, and an inconsistent length or synchronisation word in the PIPE header, or a message that cannot be read within 5 seconds drops the connection with an alarm.131 RM packets are PS-ICD telemetry packets whose APID identifies the SCOE (periodic ones every second for the power and PLM SCOEs, every 10 seconds otherwise), and the CCS distributes received telemetry by SPID according to a table defined in the HPSDB.136135

sequenceDiagram
  participant C as CCS
  participant D as TM/TC DFE
  participant S as Spacecraft
  C->>D: 0x80 TC, request ID n
  D-->>C: 0x55 ACKTC success (or 0x56 failure), request ID n, within 5 s
  Note over C: next TC only after the ACKTC
  D->>S: CLTU
  D-->>C: 0xA0 TC echo (CLTU decoded back), request ID 0
  S-->>D: TM frames with CLCW (AD mode)
  D-->>C: 0x57 TC report, request ID n

The flow follows Figure 9 and IFRQT-0161 to -0166: the DFE withholds the ACKTC while its buffer is full, which throttles the CCS, and the TC report is a guaranteed one-to-one final confirmation for every telecommand, sent in AD and BD mode and even after a failed ACKTC.134

Inference

PIPE's acknowledgements play some of the roles of the EMCS ground acknowledgements described above: the ACKTC resembles the GS_Ack (the front end has accepted the command), and the TC report in AD mode, sent after the CLCW check, resembles the ONB_Ack. In BD mode the TC report only confirms acceptance by the front end, so PIPE has no direct counterpart of the UL_Ack. The TC echo, a decoded copy of the transmitted CLTU that the DFE also produces for commands arriving from the MOC through the NDIU and that the CCS forwards to the instrument stations, has no EMCS counterpart. Neither document draws this comparison.57134137

The specification also fixes the APIDs and host names of every EGSE item (2016 CCS, 2017 CDMU SCOE, 2018 ACMS SCOE, 2019 TT&C SCOE, 2020 TM/TC DFE, 2023 battery simulator, 2024 launch power supply and solar array simulator, 2025 PLM SCOE, 2026 Herschel cryo SCOE or cryo COTE, 2028 CDMU DFE, 2029 1553 bus monitor, 2040 to 2044 the instrument EGSEs), synchronises all items by NTP with the CCS as server, requires 150 kbit/s for telemetry from the DFE and to each instrument station and 4 kbit/s for telecommands (plus overhead), and places the EGSE items in the naming convention as subsystem Y with positions 920 to 971 (see Mission tailoring of the MIB).138139140141 The field-level definitions of RC, RM, ACKTC, ACKRC and TC report packets are on the interface documents page.

docs.title: The HPCCS and its database
docs.text:
The Herschel/Planck Central Checkout System (HPCCS) that resulted was developed by Terma (the Netherlands) under an Alcatel Alenia Space Italia subcontract, and is based on SCOS-2000 with additional test functions. The Herschel/Planck System DataBase (HPSDB) was developed by GMV.8283 NLR's account of the attitude control subsystem shows how data flowed into it. The subsystem's test equipment combined the EuroSim real-time simulator with the HPCCS, which commanded and monitored EuroSim through remote messages and commands in the same format as spacecraft TM/TC. A dedicated database therefore had to generate the SCOS-2000 input files. The available SCOS-2000 MS Access database did not fit: it supported a single mission, not two missions with common data, and offered no configuration control at object level. Dutch Space built its operations database in the DOORS requirements tool instead, and exported to the HPSDB, from which SCOS-2000 files were produced for AIT and operations.83 See MIB tooling.

Terma's CCS External ICD (H-P-4-TE-ID-8020, issue 1.8 of 18 January 2006; issue 1.0 was prepared for the CCS PDR in May 2002) names the checkout system's external interfaces: PIPE on the SCOE/DFE LAN (which also carries the TM dumps of the front end) and on the instrument station LAN, a World Wide Web station, and two file interfaces with the HPSDB. Bridge files bring the MIB into the CCS, in the format of the SCOS-2000 import ICD issue 5.1 with explicit exceptions; update files go back, one tab-separated line per telecommand or parameter that a test sequence has validated (time, c or p, name, test sequence name and issue, host), for example 2002.123.20.16.32.43.123 c BATTERY03_ON battest1 12 hp0-s, printed in the ICD with one time field more than its stated format YYYY.DDD.HH.MM.SS.mmm.145146147 The exceptions turn the MIB into a checkout database: a parameter beyond its danger limits starts a test sequence named danger_<parname>, ocp gains delta limits, new tables add calibration selection (cur), parameter and packet groups (grp, grpa, grpk), the equipment list (sco, with host and port) and the distribution of telecommands by APID (tcd) and of telemetry by SPID (tmd) to that equipment, parameter names starting with YZ are reserved for CCS system parameters, and SPIDs 100 to 999 for internal EGSE use, next to the SPIDs up to 100 that the instrument EGSE reserved for its own kernel.14814915015115243 The full list, with the identifier widenings of ECP 1, the logarithmic curves of ECP 3 and the default sub-schedules, is analysed on Mission tailoring of the MIB. The system EGSE specification also required the CCS to host an HPSDB mirror site; GMV's user manual describes such sites as able to change only real (instantiated) objects, with data exchanged with the central site as XML files that the managers carry by hand.13153

The routing tables were filled. A Herschel release note of April 2008 prints the tcd configuration of the flight model database: APIDs 0, 16, 512, 1024, 1152 and 1280 (the CPDU commands, the CDMS, the ACMS and the three instruments) go to TMTCDFE, and the EGSE APIDs to their own equipment, for example 2017 to CDMUSCOE, 2026 to PFM_CRYO and 2042 to 2044 to HHIFIEGSE, HPACSEGSE and HSPIREEGSE. Its tmd configuration sends HIFI, PACS and SPIRE monitoring to the matching instrument EGSE, and CCU and cryo SCOE monitoring to all three.154

Two ways to route a command

The CCS routes by tcd (APID to an equipment name) and sco (equipment name to host and port). The standard MIB's dst table instead gives each APID a route string such as EGSE.TC.0x8800, naming the destination system, the request type and the address of the front end (EMCS system element 0x8800).152112 Neither scheme appears in the other system's documentation, and sco, tcd and tmd did not enter the standard import ICD.155

docs.title: Terma: from SCOS-2000-based CCS to compatible re-implementations
docs.text:
Terma delivered several system-level checkout systems for ESA missions with a CCS based on SCOS-2000, and reused them at instrument level.84 Its 2010 paper explains why it then built a new small system, CMDVS (Commanding Monitoring Data-handling & Visualization System), with Satellite Services BV (SSBV). A SCOS-2000-based system needs a separate EGSE database for the front ends. Commanding front ends with TM and TC packets is awkward and limited by the speed of the SCOS-2000 telecommand chain. Maintaining SCOS-2000 on modern platforms was getting more expensive. Developing a monitoring and control system from scratch had cost about 30 MEUR in the past, and users would not accept a completely new system.8485

The answer was compatibility. CMDVS keeps the CCS test language and the SCOS-2000 MIB interface, which Terma describes as "not perfectly normalized" but well known and well understood.85 By early 2010 it implemented all SCOS-2000 TM and command processing features. Front ends are driven through plugins that expose their APIs directly to the test language instead of through TM/TC packets. Variable packets are fully processed, header generation is fully database driven, all PUS type codes up to 64 bits are supported, and up to 64 verification stages can be configured (SCOS-2000 has no stage after the last completion report).8586 The same plugin technique was moved back into Terma's SCOS-2000-based CCS, whose external interface manager became a generic process with project-specific plugins.87

Terma's current products, CCS5 (multi-user checkout), SCS5 (multi-user operations) and TSC (single user), are full new implementations that keep the SCOS-2000 MIB data model.8897 Terma's 2024 presentation explains the decision. Legacy systems such as SCOS-2000 were becoming uneconomic to maintain, too slow and inflexible for new missions, and onerous to install. Asking users to adopt a completely new data model would require retraining, and Terma was too small to impose industry-wide standards.88

Feature CCS5 / TSC (2024) Source Database SCOS-2000 MIB ICD 6.9 extended (presentation: features of 6.9 to 7.2): unlimited field lengths, several databases loaded and dropped at run time, deduced parameters in TM and TC, little- and big-endian parameters, dynamic housekeeping definitions; TC sequence tables not supported 9789 Automation TOPE on Tcl/Tk 8.6, syntax derived from SCOS-2000 TOPE, with multi-threading, debugger and syntax checker 9792 Standards ECSS PUS-A and PUS-C, CCSDS packets, CFDP, TM frames, CLTU and COP-1, SDLS authentication and encryption, CubeSat Space Protocol 8995 Interfaces EGSE: EDEN and C&C protocols; ground stations: NIS (optionally SLE), Cortex and others 9790 Archive Raw data in segmented binary files, indexes in an RDBMS (MySQL, MariaDB, PostgreSQL; SQLite for TSC) 9793 Performance About 150,000 parameter updates per second, 1,500 packets per second, 500 TC per second with verification (TSC) or 100 (CCS) 91 Test features TM simulation from the MIB definition, TC modelling, SVF mode with simulated time, merging of databases from several suppliers 94 Licence Terma IPR; perpetual licence with one year of warranty 9796

See SDLS, CFDP and SLE.

docs.title: Translating SCOS-2000 databases to other checkout systems
docs.text:
Not every prime contractor used a SCOS-2000-based checkout system. Thales Alenia Space Italia (TAS-I) and Intecs built the SRDB Translator to import a SCOS-2000 MIB into the database of TAS-I's ECHO checkout system. Their paper notes that SCOS-2000 had become a standard for ESA mission control and, in most cases, for EGSE too, so the Satellite Reference Database (SRDB) was almost always based on the SCOS-2000 run-time database.98 The two databases cover similar entities, but a one-to-one table mapping was "almost inapplicable". Each item falls into one of three cases: present in both (converted), present only in the SRDB (handled, ignored or added to ECHO), or needed only by ECHO (supplied separately).99 Examples of the conversion rules:100

Data SCOS-2000 ECHO Action Verification stage Any stage of the execution profile All checks tied to TC uplink Stage not imported Verification window Start time and duration in seconds Maximum time from emission, in ms (start + interval) × 1000 Expected value Raw or engineering Engineering only Raw-value checks discarded Numerical curve identifier Char(10) Integer 1 to 9999 Mapping algorithm; original name kept in the description Raw value radix Decimal, octal or hexadecimal Decimal Converted to decimal Point-pair curve size No limit 2 to 1000 points Shorter curves skipped, extra points dropped Curves per parameter No limit 4 Limit raised to 99

The first version served Galileo GIOVE-B, whose SRDB was a single MS Access 2000 file. An enhanced version served Sentinel-1 and was also used for BepiColombo unit tests of the on-board computer and mass memory. The translator followed ICD issue 6.1, and older BepiColombo databases needed missing columns added before import.101102

BepiColombo database Parameters TM packets TC packets On-board computer (OBC) 3,745 521 399 Solid state mass memory (SSMM) 1,947 1,921 535

The figures come from the paper's Table 3.102 The authors concluded that frequent ICD changes and mission tailoring made such translators costly. They suggested a standard database interface, for example an XML mark-up language.103 See XTCE and ECSS-E-ST-70-31C for standardised alternatives.

docs.title: From TOPE to EGS-CC
docs.text:
ESA uses two flavours of SCOS: SCOS-2000 for operations at ESOC and SCOS-EGSE for EGSE applications at ESTEC, which includes TOPE. With EGS-CC replacing both, repositories of TOPE procedures would in principle have to be rewritten in the EGS-CC automation language.104 GMV and ESA instead connected TOPE to EGS-CC in the ERFEC activity (EGSE reference facility in EGS-CC context), for the Real-Time Bench of ESTEC's Avionics Test Bench (ATB-RTB).104108

In the ATB-RTB, TOPE runs inside a test sequencing subsystem with four parts besides EXIF:106

Component Role TOPE Tcl-based test sequence interpreter; one instance per running sequence TSVR (TOPE Server) Coordination and synchronisation between parallel TOPE instances TEXEC (TOPE Execution Tools) GUI to monitor and control running instances, log viewer, graphical debugger TPREP (TOPE Preparation Tools) Editor and consistency checker for test sequences 
flowchart LR
  subgraph TSEQ["Test sequencing (unchanged)"]
    T["TOPE instances"] --- S["TSVR"]
  end
  subgraph OLD["Before"]
    EXIF["EXIF CORBA servers"] --- K2["SCOS-2000 EGSE"]
  end
  subgraph NEW["After"]
    TAL["TOPE Adaptation Layer<br/>same CORBA IDL"] --- MCM["EGS-CC<br/>Monitoring and Control Model"]
    MIBF[("ASCII MIB files<br/>+ MIB-to-MCM mapping")] --> TAL
  end
  TSEQ -.->|"before"| EXIF
  TSEQ -->|"after"| TAL

The TOPE Adaptation Layer (TAL) replaces EXIF. It implements CORBA servers that comply with the existing TSEQ/SCOS-2000 IDL files, so TSEQ runs unmodified. Inside EGS-CC it uses the monitoring and control access, definition management, messaging and configuration services.108 EGS-CC models the space system as a Monitoring and Control Model (MCM): a hierarchy of monitoring and control elements with activities, events and parameters, independent of TM/TC packets.107 At start-up, TAL reads the ASCII MIB files and a mapping file, generates the EGS-CC conceptual data model from the MIB, and EGS-CC loads it into the MCM. TAL then translates TOPE's commands, parameters and events to MCM activities, parameters and events, and back.109 The approach has two constraints: the ASCII MIB must always be present (the ATB used the EagleEye mission MIB), and new TM/TC defined in the MCM cannot be written back to the MIB.109 TAL is written in Java with JacORB and deployed as OSGi bundles inside an EGS-CC session.110 See ancillary systems, MICONYS and EGS-CC.

The system database faced the same migration. At SESP 2015 Thales Alenia Space presented the System Reference Data Base (SRDB), its adaptation of the Herschel/Planck System Database for the MTG programme. (The acronym is the same as that of the Satellite Reference Database read by the SRDB Translator above; whether the two databases are related is not stated in the available sources.) The SRDB keeps the HPSDB concepts (objects, items and pseudo-items with category flags, physical and logical instantiation, working, reference and archive areas), adds the attachment of former object versions, and was to map its high-level data model onto the EGS-CC product structure and its items onto the other EGS-CC packages, which in 2015 was "still to be done".156157158 Where TAL reads an ASCII MIB at start-up and cannot write new definitions back, the SRDB plan puts the reference database upstream of EGS-CC.109

Inference

Contrasting the two approaches (a MIB converted at run time by TAL, a reference database mapped to the EGS-CC model) is this wiki's reading; the two papers do not refer to each other, and whether the SRDB mapping was completed is not stated in the available sources.

docs.title: GDDS and mission data delivery interface documents
docs.text:
A spacecraft's telemetry is useful to many people who must never touch the mission control system: instrument teams, flight dynamics, science operations centres. ESOC's answer for the missions launched in the 2000s was the Generic Data Disposition System (GDDS), a reusable server that took requests from outside the operations network, retrieved data from the SCOS-2000 archives and delivered them by FTP, on the web, or on CD-ROM and DVD. Each mission configured its own instance, called simply the DDS, and documented it in a Data Delivery Interface Document (DDID).1916

This page describes the GDDS as documented by the common DDID of Rosetta, Mars Express and Venus Express, its XML schema appendix, and the mission papers; then it follows the same conventions into EDDS, whose requirements list GDDS among its predecessors5 and which still accepts its requests and produces its binary format, and into the DDID of Solar Orbiter. Request and response formats of EDDS itself are on EDDS request and data formats.

docs.title: Names
docs.text:
Term Expansion as printed Where GDDS Generic Data Disposition System EDDS glossary; SP-1291; GSAW 2003 and 2005 presentations2191516 GDDS "Generic Data Distribution System" (once, in a remark on SPIDs in the history files) Database Import ICD issue 5.11 DDS Data Disposition System (the RMCS/MEMCS/VMCS component that supports the interface to the science communities) Rosetta/MEX/VEX DDID31 DDS Data Distribution System Mars Express and Venus Express data handling papers1724 DDS Data Dissemination System Solar Orbiter DDID (an instance of the generic EDDS)102 DDID Data Delivery Interface Document EDDS glossary; the DDIDs themselves231 GDDID Generic Data Delivery Interface Document EDDS glossary2 RDDS, MEDDS, VEDDS the Rosetta, Mars Express and Venus Express DDS instances (used in the DDID; not expanded) DDID4263 VDDS Venus Express Data Disposition System, "based on the GDDS" Venus Express paper25

The three words behind "DDS" follow the documents rather than three different systems: the GDDS-era DDID says "disposition", the Mars Express and Venus Express papers say "distribution" (while also calling the underlying software the Generic Data Disposition System), and the EDDS-era Solar Orbiter DDID says "dissemination".311925102

docs.title: The documents
docs.text:
Document Issue and date In the library Rosetta/Mars Express/Venus Express MCS Data Delivery Interface Document, RO-ESC-IF-5003 / MEX-ESC-IF-5003 / VEX-ESC-IF-5003 C2, 2006-02-21 ro-esc-if-5003-ddid-c228 The same DDID as a Rosetta/Mars Express document B5, 2003-03-27 mex-esc-if-5003-b586 DDID Appendix I, Request Dialogue XML Schema C3, 2007-08-21 ro-esc-if-5003-appendix-i-c389 Zender et al., "Spacecraft and Payload Data Handling", in ESA SP-1291 (Mars Express) June 2009 sp-1291-data-handling17 Delhaise et al., "Spacecraft and Payload Data Handling" (Venus Express, SP-1295) not stated vex-delhaise-web24 Solar Orbiter Data Delivery ICD, SOL-ESC-IF-05011 1.2, 2019-06-26 solo-ddid-i1r298 EDDS External User ICD (EUICD), EGOS-GEN-EDDS-ICD-1001 24.0, 2025-01-10 euicd-v259

The generic GDDS documents are referenced but not public: the Generic Data Delivery Interface Document (EGOS-MCS-GDDS-ICD-1003, issue 1.2 of 2004-08-30; the EUICD cites an issue 1.4 of 2008-04-11), the Data Disposition System Software Requirements Document (EGOS-MCS-GDDS-SRD-5720, 1.4), the GDDS-RDM Image Transfer Control Files ICD (EGOS-MCS-GDDS-ICD-1002, 1.1) and the GDDS Operator User Manual (DTOS-INFR-UM-1001, 1.1, cited by SP-1291).341023

The DDID itself records its lineage: it is "broadly based on the Cluster DDID"; drafts A0 to A4 ran from April 1999 to March 2000 (A4 added telemetry delivery by APID); issue B0 (May 2001) answered the review; from B1 (June 2001) it became a common Rosetta/Mars Express document, a separate Mars Express draft being discontinued; B5 (March 2003) followed the December 2002 review; C0 (July 2004) prepared Venus Express; C1 (July 2005) added VMCS throughout; C2 (February 2006) repaired a document corruption that had replaced characters by quotation marks.3729
