docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
Rosetta and Mars Express share a near-identical on-board data management system and on-board software, so ESOC developed most components of their ground data systems jointly; the Venus Express data systems are a delta development of the same system.25 Each mission control system, based on SCOS-2000, kept a mission archive with two parts: a packet archive (historical telemetry, telecommands and derived data) and a file archive (typically flight dynamics and planning files); a SCOS-2000 file generation process could also produce summaries such as command history reports.2127 The DDID calls the repository the MCS Data Archive System (DAS), which is not the long-term archive; the DDS reached it from outside the operational LAN.41

flowchart LR
    subgraph OPS[ESOC operational LAN]
        MCS[SCOS-2000 MCS<br/>packet archive + file archive<br/>= DAS]
    end
    subgraph FE[Front-end LAN]
        DDS[GDDS server<br/>request list, collation]
        WEB[Web interface]
        FTP[FTP server]
        RDM[RDM production<br/>scheduled inside ESOC]
    end
    PI[PIs and other external users]
    MCS <-- "CORBA archive retrievals" --> DDS
    PI -- "XML request file (FTP)" --> FTP --> DDS
    PI -- "web form" --> WEB --> DDS
    DDS -- "SFDU or raw response file" --> FTP --> PI
    DDS -- "online preview (XML)" --> WEB --> PI
    DDS --> RDM -- "CD-ROM / DVD by mail" --> PI
    SO[Standing orders<br/>automatic deliveries] --> DDS

Requests could come from scheduled "standing orders", from the web interface or as request files sent by FTP. All were expressed in the same recursive XML query language, used internally and exposed on the FTP interface, so several filters could be combined. The central DDS server validated the user against its database of authorised users, issued the (relatively low-level) retrievals through a CORBA interface to the MCS, and collated their results into one delivery per request. Web responses were also XML, and online retrieval was meant only for previewing small amounts of data embedded as a byte stream in the XML.212227 The DDS machines sat on ESOC's front-end LAN, reachable from outside, separated by a bridge from the operational LAN that hosted every other MCS machine.39

docs.title: Service requirements
docs.text:
The DDID quotes the user requirements that shaped the system:33343542

Requirement Value Mode Client-server: the DDS responds to requests; one request command per request file What one request can ask for A subset of packets of one data source (APID); one auxiliary file; all auxiliary files of a type in a time range; a catalogue Nominal response Acknowledgement, catalogue entry and data in the same file transfer Latency Start of data within 15 minutes of the DDS receiving the request (load permitting) Online retention 3 months after acquisition (Mars Express); the whole mission for Rosetta Queue At most 12 requested files per user at a time Capacity At least 1000 MB per day in total, split into per-user quotas set with the Project Scientist Quota overrun The whole file is refused; further requests are rejected with an error Sampling Every N-th packet on request; wild cards in catalogue queries Automatic delivery New versions of selected auxiliary files; periodic TM and TC deliveries Off-line Random-access raw data media (RDM), CD-ROM for Mars Express and Venus Express, none for Rosetta; an integer number of days per RDM, default 1; at most 4 RDMs per period; delivered within one month (3 weeks nominal for MEDDS)

The off-line split by day used the on-board generation time of each packet.35 Venus Express recorded science, housekeeping and consolidated auxiliary data on DVDs, one mailed to its science operations centre and one kept at ESOC.26 Mars Express kept all level 1 data for ten years after the end of the mission.20

docs.title: Access
docs.text: Requests went through the web interface or as ASCII (XML) files by FTP, protected by passwords (different for the web and for FTP requests). To avoid partial transfers, FTP in both directions used a two-step upload: write the file under a temporary name, then rename it. The DDS retried a failed delivery a configurable number of times; a user who had neither data nor an error message after 2 hours had to assume failure and resubmit. Delivery went to a node pre-registered for each user, changeable only with the PI's permission; all authorised users could access the auxiliary data, but otherwise users were restricted to their own experiment's data. The DDS had a prime and a backup node.38443940 The DDID also lists host names, addresses and support contacts, which this wiki does not reproduce.

docs.title: The request language
docs.text:
The web forms mapped onto the same XML structure as the FTP files, defined by six XML Schema files in DDID Appendix I.4391

flowchart TD
    MD[MissionDataDef.xsd<br/>MissionFormatType, DataType] --> CO[GDDSCommon.xsd<br/>ReqString, MultiTime, delivery, format, user, request info]
    CO --> MI[GDDSMission.xsd<br/>request, filter, catalogue and event keywords]
    MI --> CA[GDDSCatalogue.xsd<br/>catalogue]
    MI --> RQ[GDDSRequest.xsd<br/>onlineRequest, filter tree]
    RQ --> AK[GDDSAcknowledgement.xsd<br/>onlineAck]

Each arrow is an include.9293959697

docs.title: Request structure
docs.text:
An onlineRequest holds one general element and one or more item elements, and an optional userRequestId attribute echoed in the response. One item only is allowed for web and online deliveries; several are allowed for RDM requests.4396

Element Type Content general/comment string Free text, not processed general/userInfo UserInfoType username, FTPpassword general/destInfo DeliveryType Exactly one of RDM (attributes label, numCopies default 1, maxSpan default 1), FTP (filename, directory relative to the user's default, optional target) or Online (dataResponse as hexBinary, attribute displayAsHex) general/formatInfo FormatInfoType compression (NONE or ZIP), SFDUrequired (boolean), optional missionFormat (RMCS_SPECIAL) general/dataInfo DataInfoType Optional earliestStart: do not submit to the DAS before this time item/dataType DataType TLM, CMH, EVT, AUX item/dataSource ReqString An APID, a super-APID, or a source mnemonic item/catalogueRequest boolean Catalogue instead of data item/keyword (0..n) RequestKeywordValue SampleRate, MaxVolumeSize, TimeType, Application, EventType (LOG, MIB, SOFTWARE, SYSTEM), Severity (INFORMATION, WARNING, ERROR, FATAL ERROR), Workstation, MessageFilter item/onEvent (0..1) EventValue Volume (not supported) item/filter (0..1) FilterExpression A filter tree

The table follows the C3 schema.92939496 Web delivery was allowed for all three methods, FTP requests for RDM and FTP only, and in practice RDM requests were not accepted from outside at all: RDMs were produced by ESOC's own scheduler.44 ZIP compressed the whole response (acknowledgement, catalogue and data) and appended a "Z" to the target file name. Without SFDUrequired the data were delivered "raw", with no acknowledgement or catalogue.45

Schema and document differ

The DDID body (issue C2) lists the data types CAT, AUX, TLM and CMH, whereas the C3 schema enumerates TLM, CMH, EVT and AUX; catalogues are requested with catalogueRequest instead. Appendix I C3 added the event keywords (DCR 417).739490 The body describes the volume keyword as VolumeSize (a byte count, at most 2147483647), the schema as MaxVolumeSize among the request keywords and VolumeSize among the filter keywords.4693

docs.title: Filters
docs.text:
A filter is a tree. A unary node (operation OP_NOT) negates one subtree; a bin node joins a left and a right FilterExpression with OP_AND or OP_OR; a leaf compares one keyword with a value using OP_GT, OP_LT, OP_EQ, OP_GTE or OP_LTE.4796 The filterable keywords are:4893

Keyword Applies to Meaning SourcePktsGenTime TM Spacecraft packet generation time: OBT converted to UTC S2KPktsGenTime TM SCOS-2000 packet generation time, i.e. the archiving time at the MCS; not usable for data in archive files split from the main online archive Type, SubType, P1Val, P2Val TM PUS type, subtype and the two packet identification values (SID); omitted means wildcard UplinkTime, ExecutionTime TC Uplink and execution time (filter on execution time recommended) CreationTime, EventTime (schema only) Name, Release, Issue AUX File name; blank release or issue means latest TimeSpan AUX Validity of flight dynamics attitude files and Mars Express orbit files: all files valid, even for one second, inside the range are returned in a gzipped tar Validity, VolumeSize (schema)

Times use the MultiTime choice of a_dateTime (CCSDS ASCII time code A, YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ, all sub-fields with leading zeros) or a_duration (XML duration).5092

The DDID explains why TC filters on uplink or execution time give results that differ slightly from the times in the returned headers: a SCOS-2000 telecommand has seven times (specified release, uplink and execution times; actual uplink and execution times; packet filing time, the primary key of the TC history; packet creation time, the secondary key initialised to the specified execution time), and the DDS can only retrieve by the two keys.49

A request (illustrative, modelled on the DDID example)

<onlineRequest userRequestId="2004-04-27-hk-pull">
  <general>
    <comment>HK of APID 820, ten-fold decimated, zipped, no SFDU</comment>
    <userInfo><username>MEX_EXAMPLE</username><FTPpassword>...</FTPpassword></userInfo>
    <destInfo><FTP><filename>hk820</filename><directory/></FTP></destInfo>
    <formatInfo><compression>ZIP</compression><SFDUrequired>false</SFDUrequired></formatInfo>
    <dataInfo/>
  </general>
  <item>
    <dataType>TLM</dataType><dataSource>820</dataSource>
    <catalogueRequest>false</catalogueRequest>
    <keyword><SampleRate>10</SampleRate></keyword>
    <filter><bin operation="OP_AND">
      <lhs><leaf operation="OP_GTE"><valuePair><SourcePktsGenTime>
        <a_dateTime>2004-04-27T00:00:00Z</a_dateTime></SourcePktsGenTime></valuePair></leaf></lhs>
      <rhs><leaf operation="OP_LT"><valuePair><SourcePktsGenTime>
        <a_dateTime>2004-04-28T00:00:00Z</a_dateTime></SourcePktsGenTime></valuePair></leaf></rhs>
    </bin></filter>
  </item>
</onlineRequest>
The structure follows the C3 schema and the DDID's own example (APID 1966, sample rate 10); the values here are this wiki's.5196

With SampleRate the DDS took every N-th entry per history file: telemetry came from four data streams (VC 0 and VC 1, real time and playback), so N was applied to each stream and the results merged.46

docs.title: Data streams and ADIDs
docs.text:
Every delivered data set is identified by a data source and a data type, and every data description is registered at ESOC under an eight-character Authority and Description Identifier (ADID): a four-character Control Authority Identifier (EROS, EMEX or EVEX) followed by a four-character data description identifier.7273

Data source Type Content ADID (DDS internal) – RDM directory listing, cumulative index, off-line and on-line catalogues, acknowledgement, volume production information, master and partial catalogues xxxxD001 to xxxxD008 <APID> (decimal) TLM Telemetry of one APID xxxxTnnn <SuperAPID> (negative) TLM Telemetry of a predefined list of APIDs (an instrument) per instrument CMDH CMH Telecommand history packets xxxxC001 CMDPF, CMDPB CMH TC history printout, full and brief xxxxC002, xxxxC003 auxiliary mnemonic AUX One auxiliary file type xxxx + mnemonic

For an APID, nnn is the process ID as two hexadecimal digits followed by the packet category as one: process ID 51 (0x33) and category 4 give EROST334, the ADID of APID 820. Packets of one APID with different SIDs therefore share an ADID.77

The super-APIDs were defined per mission:7374

Mission Super-APID: instrument Rosetta −1 LCC, −2 RPC, −3 OSIRIS, −4 ALICE, −5 MIRO, −6 ROSINA, −7 COSIMA, −8 CONSERT, −9 VIRTIS, −10 GIADA, −11 to −15 RSOC streams (services 1, 3, 5, 6, 12), −16 to −20 RPC streams (services 1, 3, 5, 6, 12) Mars Express −1 HRSC, −2 PFS Venus Express −2 PFS, −3 ASPERA, −9 VIRTIS

Issue B5 had only −1 to −9 for Rosetta; −10 to −20 came later (DCR 316 and 367).8874

docs.title: Auxiliary data per mission
docs.text:
Auxiliary files are delivered unprocessed, exactly as held in the DAS; several files matching one request are wrapped in a Unix tar file. Appendix E of the DDID distinguishes "span valid" files, whose records apply until the next record, from "point valid" ones.61 The data sources of issue C2 are:747576

Group Rosetta Mars Express Venus Express Radio science from the IFMS (RSI) AGC1, AGC2, DOP1, DOP2, RANG, MET_ same same Tracking for flight dynamics D1FD, D2FD, RGFD, MTFD, G1FD, G2FD same same Light time – OWLT OWLT Spacecraft orbit ORHR cruise; ORER, ORFR, ORGR Earth swing-bys; ORMR Mars swing-by; OROR, ORSR, ORHO, ORHS Lutetia and Steins; ORWR, ORPR, ORHW comet ORHM cruise; ORMM, ORMF Mars-centric (ORMF about 800 MB, FTP and RDM only) ORHV cruise; ORVV, ORVF Venus-centric Attitude ATNR, ATPR ATNM ATNV, ATPV, UCAV Events EVTR EVTM, EVTF EVTV, EVTP, EVTF Target environment CCHA, CENV, CKIN, PNAV (NAVCAM) STOM star occultations, VILM lander visibility STOV star occultations, SAAV sun aspect angles Operations requests DOR_, ECF_, FDR_, POR_, PORP, PTR_, PTRP, SOR_, MCR_, MDR_, MPR_, MDAF, MSP_, CONF, SPL_, LTVF DOR_, ECF_, FDR_, POR_, PTR_, SOR_ (OPE and MPS), MCR_, MDR_, MPR_, MDAF DOR_, ECF_, FDR_, POR_, PTRV, SOR_ (OPE and MPS), MCR_, MDR_, MPR_, MDAF, SPL_ Planning products – DMOP, DSOP, RMOP, RSOP, FECS, SECS, FTL_ DMOP, DSOP, RMOP, RSOP, FECS, FTLV, FSCV, TMSV manoeuvre slots Software OASW OASW, FDSW OASW, FDSW

MDAF (the MTL detailed agenda file) cannot be forwarded automatically, only requested.77 The asteroid names tell the history: issue B5 lists Rosetta orbit files for Otawara and Siwa, the targets before the launch delay, together with RFDE, RPI_ and RTI_ reference files; issue C0 replaced them by Lutetia and Steins (DCR 307), and C2 no longer lists the three reference files.8829

docs.title: SFDU packaging
docs.text:
The DDS used the CCSDS Standard Formatted Data Unit (SFDU) concept so that each delivery, and each RDM, describes itself, while users who know the layout can treat the extra headers as spare bytes.36 The building block is the Label-Value-Object (LVO): a 20-octet LABEL, a VALUE of any length and an optional marker.79

Class Category Use in the DDS Z Structure: Exchange Data Unit (EDU) Outer envelope of every product F Structure: Description Data Unit (DDU) Data description registration packages U Structure: Application Data Unit (ADU) One data file plus its catalogue entry R Service: replacement (reference) Points to files elsewhere on an RDM C Service: data administration ADIDNAME= statements I Data: application data object The requested data S Data: supplementary Index and listing files D, E Data: DDR and DED objects Syntactic and semantic descriptions K Data: catalogue attributes Catalogue entries V Data: volume production Acknowledgement, volume information

The CCSDS ADIDs used are CCSD0001 (VALUE contains LVOs), CCSD0002 (ASCII encoded English), CCSD0003 (PVL statements referencing external objects), CCSD0004 (PVL identifying a data description package), CCSD0005 (a DDU), CCSD0006 (PVL) and CCSD0009 (an ADU). All DDS LVOs are version 3 with delimitation B, the length only known once the VALUE has been generated.798052

Note

Appendix F of issue C2 still describes the delimitation parameter for "A" (an eight-character decimal length), while §7.2.2 and the class table specify "B" (binary length) after DCR 032; this page follows §7.2.2.5279

A successful response is one file with three LVOs inside an EDU; an error response has only the first:5263

flowchart TB
    Z["LABEL CCSD Z 0001 - envelope (EDU)"] --> V["LABEL EROS V D005 - acknowledgement (XML)"]
    Z --> K["LABEL EROS K D004 - catalogue entry (XML)"]
    Z --> I["LABEL EROS I Tnnn / C001 / aux - the data"]
    I --> D1["DDS header 1 + packet 1"]
    I --> D2["DDS header 2 + packet 2"]
    I --> DN["... DDS header N + packet N"]

The acknowledgement repeats the request (general), gives ackInfo (actual processing time, hardware, operating system, DDS version, error message, "NO ERROR" when nominal) and one ackItem per data item with the actual delivered volume; the DDID example reports a Sun Blade 100 running SunOS 5.8 and "GDDS 1.2.0".5397 The catalogue entry gives data type, source, ADID and keywords: first and last packet times (by source or SCOS-2000 generation time), sample rate, number of elements, or file name, creation time and version for auxiliary data.5495 Master catalogues (wildcards in both source and type) and partial catalogues (a wildcard in one) listed what was available; for performance the master catalogue for telemetry was disabled (DCR 269), and packet counts in catalogues are empty.62

Errors are reported as ROSETTA DDS ERROR-nn, MEX DDS ERROR-nn or VEX DDS ERROR-nn:78

Group Codes Request specification 01 unrecognised data source; 02 unrecognised data type; 03 illegal source/type combination; 04 no access rights; 05 illegal target file name; 06 and 07 illegal start or end time; 08 start after end; 09 illegal sample rate; 10 illegal amount Processing 50 maximum outstanding files exceeded; 51 no catalogue data; 52 no data packets; 53 timeout; 54 unavailable; 55 resources exceeded; 56 system error; 57 user daily quota; 58 system daily quota; 59 DDS access disabled

A monitoring process timed out requests after a configurable period (default 120 minutes) and deleted new requests once a user had 12 queued.63

docs.title: Telemetry: the DDS packet header
docs.text:
Telemetry is delivered as complete, reassembled, unprocessed source packets in time order, each preceded by an 18-octet DDS packet header, stamped with the Spacecraft Event Time (SCET), the calibrated generation time of the packet's first bit.5556

Octets Field Values 0–7 SCET Sun "MJT": 32-bit seconds since 1970-01-01 00:00 and 32-bit microseconds 8–11 Packet length Octets of the packet that follows 12–13 Ground station ID See below; 0 for time correlation packets (APID 1966, type 190, subtype 40) 14–15 Virtual channel ID 0 = VC 0, 1 = VC 1 16 SLE service Service and delivery mode, see below 17 Time quality 0 good, 1 inaccurate, 2 bad (algorithm on the time correlation page)

The ground station identifiers in issue C2 are:56

ID Station ID Station 0x0D ESA Villafranca 2 0x22 / 0x67 NASA Goldstone (old / new) 0x15 ESA Kourou 0x23 / 0x70 NASA Canberra (old / new) 0x16 NDIULite (for SVTs) 0x24 / 0x6C NASA Madrid (old / new) 0x17 ESA New Norcia 0x7F ESA/ESOC test station 0x18 ESA Cebreros 0x82 NDIU classic (SVTs)

The NASA identifiers changed in November/December 2003; issue B5 still had "TBD" for Madrid and no Cebreros.5687 The SLE service octet combines the delivery mode and the frame selection:56

Real time (RT) Real time flow control (RTFC) Off-line SLC 0 4 8 MC 1 5 9 VC 2 6 10 Bad frames 3 7 11

Inference

The rows correspond to the SLE return services through which the frames reached the MCS: all frames of the space link channel (SLC, as in RAF), a master channel or a virtual channel (as in RCF), and frames that failed decoding; the columns to the SLE delivery modes. The DDID gives only the codes.56

A request is answered in one file sorted by the time keyword used. The DDID example: packets of four SPIDs on APIDs 10 and 23, requested for APID 10, come back as packets 1, 4, 6, 2, 5, 3, i.e. interleaved by generation time regardless of SPID. The SPID, the SCOS-2000 packet ID, is internal to the MCS.57

docs.title: Telecommand history
docs.text:
Raw TC history packets are the encoded telecommands as uplinked, each preceded by a DDS command packet header.58

Octets Field Meaning 0–7 Uplink time Release time from the MCS, later replaced by the ground station's radiation time stamp; release failure time if release failed 8–15 Execution time The user's time tag for commands embedded in service 11 loads, otherwise uplink time plus the one-way light time 16–17 CUV Uplink verification: CLCW-based acceptance of the frame on board 18–21 CAV, CEV (VC 0) Acceptance and execution verification from real-time telemetry 22–25 CAV, CEV (VC 1) The same from playback telemetry 26–29 Packet length Octets of the TC data record 30–37 Command ID Command name in the database 38–45 Parent sequence ID Name of the parent sequence

Note

Issue C2 calls this a "30-octet header" and says the data record starts at octet 30, yet the table continues with the command and sequence names to octet 45 (DCR 037). The EDDS EUICD's description of the GDDS TC header lists all ten fields with their sizes (8, 8, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 4, 8 and 8 octets: 46 in total).5814

Each verification word is 16 bits with exactly one bit set (bit 0 the least significant): bit 0 IDLE, 1 PENDING, 2 PASSED, 3 FAILED, 4 UNVERIFIED, 5 UNKNOWN, 6 TIMED-OUT (CUV only), 7 SCC ONLY, 8 ASSUMED (CUV superseded by a successful later stage). Only PASSED, FAILED and UNVERIFIED are final; an all-zero word means the stage did not apply.59 The printouts CMDPB and CMDPF reproduce the TC History display: name, description, sequence, release and execution times, sub-schedule, service type and subtype, process ID, service 11 and service 13 encapsulation, AD or BD mode, PTV and CEV check states, group, block and interlock flags, source, frame count, sequence counter and one status letter per verification stage (R release to the NCTRS, G ground reception, T uplink, O on-board reception, A acceptance, C completion, for VC 0 and VC 1); the full mode adds one line per editable parameter.60

docs.title: Raw data media
docs.text:
Off-line delivery was entirely controlled by ESOC: every CD-ROM held all data streams of all instruments and all ESOC auxiliary data for its period, plus every data description needed, so each disc was self-contained. Six days were allowed for orbit and attitude data to be consolidated before a write-once master was sent for mastering and reproduction.64

ROOT
├── VOLDESC.SFD            root SFDU (logically includes everything)
├── yymmddnv.IDX/.LST/.LSC cumulative index, directory listing, changed files
├── MEX (or VEX)
│   ├── TLM/<APID dirs>    telemetry, one directory per APID
│   ├── CMH                command history
│   └── AUXF               auxiliary files
├── DATADES
│   ├── TLM_DES  AUX_DES  CMH_DES  DDS_DES
└── SOFTWARE               orbit and attitude access routines

The tree condenses §7.13.1; empty files are present when a source had no data, so a missing file means a manufacturing error.66 Data files are named yyyymmdd-xxxxDDID-nn-i.ccc: RDM generation date, file number, the four-character DDID part of the ADID, RDM set number within the day (hex), index in the set, and .cat or .dat. For example 20040427-0001T334-01-1.dat is APID 820 data on the first RDM of 27 April 2004.67

A CD-ROM held about 650 MB; a day with more than 600 MB continued on a second disc from the split time, and a file could be split anywhere, even inside a record, so it had to be rejoined before use.68 Version control relied on a cumulative index file, yymmddnv.IDX (date, disc number in the day 1 to 9, version A to Z), present on every disc, newest first, with fixed positions: RDM ID (octets 0–7), inclusive start time (9–28), exclusive end time (30–49), disc number (51), discs that day (53), version (55), status DELETED when superseded (57–66), line feed (67).69 The printed and volume label was, for example, 20041212_2_3A for the second of three discs of 12 December 2004, first issue.70

In the SFDU view the root file VOLDESC.SFD is an EDU containing header LVOs (volume production information in PVL: mission, producer, earliest and latest packet, total data quantity, computer, operating system, DDS software version, production time; and class R references to the index, listing and changes files), one DDU per data description (class F holding a class C ADIDNAME= statement and a class R reference), and one ADU per data file (class U holding a class K catalogue entry with RDM_FILENAME and a class R reference).65 ESOC, as Control Authority, registered descriptions in ASCII encoded English; for science telemetry they only name the experiment and its contact, the inner packet formats being the PIs' domain.7181

docs.title: Products of the MCS itself
docs.text:
Appendix K lists packets the MCS assigns or generates on APID 1966, type 190:82

Packet APID Type Subtype Telemetry packet, bad 1966 190 30 Telemetry packet, idle (received) 190 0 Telemetry packet, RICE compressed; time packet (received) 190 (received) Telemetry packet undefined in database 1966 190 38 Transfer frame bad, good, idle 1966 190 20, 21, 29 Time correlation coefficient packet 1966 190 40 Telemetry constants packet (TM Spacon values, generated on request) 1966 190 0

The coefficient packet (gradient, offset and standard deviation as IEEE doubles, generation time in CUC 4+2) is described on the time correlation page.83 Two text products are also delivered: the Lander Telecommand Verification File (LTVF), a listing of the bit patterns of the commands on a manual stack (row, mnemonic, description, source sequence count, PUS version, CRC, packet header and data field), created on request and stored in the directory named by the MISCconfig variable CMD_BIT_PATTERN_STACK_DIR; and the Detailed Agenda File (DAF), the command import format of the Pass, MTL and manual stacks, of which mission timeline DAFs are available to users for traceability.8485

docs.title: From GDDS to EDDS
docs.text:
When ESOC built the EGOS Data Dissemination System, its requirements were derived from three existing subsystems giving access to SCOS-2000 data: TDRS, WebRM and the GDDS.5 A technical note analysed the reuse of TDRS, WebRM, GDDS and MUST (EGOS-MDW-EDDS-TN-1001, 2006), which is not public.3 Backward compatibility was written into EDDS:

  • Requests. The light-weight Request Submitter must convert GDDS requests (as defined in the GDDID) into EDDS requests by XSLT, supporting all requests common to both (EDDS-SR-05683).6 The EUICD documents the mapping (GDDS2EDDS.xsl). Only one item is allowed; the filter must not contain OR nodes inside AND nodes (such subtrees are ignored); MultiTime values must be absolute, except in schedule requests, where the start is a duration relative to execution and the end a duration after the start; a schedule creates ten requests at the given interval in days; RDM, online delivery, SFDUrequired and missionFormat are ignored; and mission and domain can be selected by Mission: and Domain: lines in the comment.911
  • Request types. A TLM item maps to a TM packet request with the APID as data source and a mandatory SourcePktsGenTime range (S2KpktsGenTime is mapped to the same generation time, Type, SubType, P1Val, P2Val allow OP_EQ and negation only); CMH/CMDH maps to a TC packet request on execution time; CMDPB/CMDPF to brief and full TC reports.11
  • Responses. "GDDS_BINARY" is an output format for TM and TC packets from the PARC and for TM packets from HARC and EGS-CC; the SDD names the formatters (PktTmGDDS_BINARYFormatter, PktTcGDDS_BINARYFormatter, PktTcSFDUFormatterHandler "for the backward compatibility with the GDDS"); the EDDS stream client can save TM in GDDS binary; and EDDS-SR-05680 (desirable) asks for the GDDS binary format for archived files and catalogues.1287

The EUICD expresses the GDDS headers in its own extensible binary format: the GDDS TM header (SCET 8, packet length 4, ground station 2, virtual channel 2, SLE service 1, time quality 1 octets) corresponds to EDDS header fields 8, 10, 12, 13, 17 and 18, and the GDDS TC header to fields 9, 10, 23 to 29 and 13. The EDDS TM header field table marks the packet length and the "SleServiceID" as "added for backward compatibility with the GDDS".1413 Its worked example shows two TM packets whose GDDS header reads 4E94 46BE A7B8 D000 | 0000 0050 | 0000 | 0000 | 00 | 00: generation time 0x4E9446BE seconds plus 0xA7B8D000 microseconds, an 80-octet packet, ground station 0, VC 0, SLE service 0 and good time quality.14

Inference

0x4E9446BE is 1318340286 s, i.e. 2011-10-11 13:38 UTC, but the microseconds field 0xA7B8D000 exceeds 999 999, so the example bytes are not a valid time; they are best read as an illustration of the layout only.14

docs.title: Solar Orbiter: the DDID on EDDS
docs.text:
The Solar Orbiter Data Delivery ICD (SOL-ESC-IF-05011) is the mission-specific complement to the generic EDDS ICD and user manual, aligned with the BepiColombo DDID in its last revision.10098 Its structure still follows the GDDS-era DDID (assumptions, interface characteristics, access, detailed specifications, data definition, products), but the content is EDDS:99

Aspect Rosetta/MEX/VEX (GDDS) Solar Orbiter (EDDS) Name of the system Data Disposition System (DDS) Data Dissemination System (DDS), based on EDDS Access Web interface and FTP request files EDDS client application (Java), XML requests by SFTP, user-implemented clients; HTTPS web service Request types Data, catalogue, standing orders Batch and stream services, saved and scheduled requests, FARC subscriptions, user management Sources MCS packet and file archives (DAS) MCS long-term archive: PARC (packets), DARC (parameters), FARC (files) Response formats SFDU or raw; XML acknowledgement and catalogue Binary (files or Google Protocol Buffers), EDDS raw binary, GDDS binary, XML and XML transform, ASCII Packet header 18-octet DDS header SCOS-2000 packet headers (EDDS raw header with no mission fields, or GDDS binary header) Off-line media CD-ROM, DVD none; RAPID files pushed by the Generic File Transfer System (GFTS) Time correlation Coefficient packet type 190/40 Report, couple and coefficient packets type 164/1 to 3 Quotas Per-user daily volume Data type filters (APID, SPID, parameter, file name or type), volume per period, relative time range, access period

Sources for the right column: the DDID's sections 2, 3, 6, 7, 8, 9 and 10.103104105106108 Several GDDS conventions survive in detail:

  • The GDDS binary option is offered as such: a binary header (EUICD §6.1.3) followed by the source packet without SCOS-2000 header. The DDID notes that its "SLE service Id" field, which identifies the SLE service and channel type over which the data were retrieved, is not relevant to end users.106
  • Time and byte order: all times are 4-octet seconds since 1970 plus 4-octet microseconds (leap seconds not counted), the same Sun-style time as the GDDS SCET, and all data are big-endian.106
  • Ground station IDs in the SCOS-2000 header are decimal: 21 Kourou, 22 Perth, 23 New Norcia, 24 Cebreros, 25 Malargüe, 30 Maspalomas, 201 reference test station (ESOC), 202 NDIU Lite, 203 NDIU IFMS.107
  • Time quality keeps the GDDS values 0 good, 1 inaccurate, 2 bad.107
  • Internal packets stay on APID 1966 (SPIDs 66810 to 66999, including the time correlation report, couple and coefficient packets), to be filtered out except for time correlation.108
  • Command history is still available in binary, XML and an ASCII format matching the MCS TC History application, now with Science Kernel custom fields (forced sub-schedule ID, CEV check state for playback, a unique command ID, the service 13 file ID and file attribute).109

Inference

The Solar Orbiter decimal station IDs 21, 23 and 24 equal the GDDS-era hexadecimal 0x15 (Kourou), 0x17 (New Norcia) and 0x18 (Cebreros), so the station numbering appears to have been kept across the two generations. No source states this.10756

The Solar Orbiter DDID's auxiliary file types and file archive, its TM files reconstructed from the service 13 downlink and the RAPID files are discussed on Mission archives; the SCOS-2000 packet header it documents is on EDDS request and data formats.

docs.title: What is not public
docs.text:
• The generic GDDS documents: GDDID, Data Disposition System SRD, GDDS-RDM ITCF ICD and the GDDS Operator User Manual.323
  • DDID Appendix C (PI account details), Appendix H (flight dynamics products), Appendix J (mission planning products, in the MEX and VEX operations concept documents) and the Command Request Interface Document (RO-ESC-IF-0004) that completes the interface with the science communities.3230
  • For Solar Orbiter, the Packetiser ICD (BC-ESC-IF-22002), the Command Source Handler ICD that defines the TC packet body, and the password-protected user details annex.101

docs.title: Herschel/Planck: SCOS-2000 in a science mission ground segment
docs.text:
Herschel (still called FIRST in the documents of 2000) and Planck were two ESA science satellites developed together, with one industrial prime, shared spacecraft units and a common approach to their ground segment. They are the best documented case in this wiki's library of SCOS-2000 used across a whole programme: as the core of the instrument electrical ground support equipment (EGSE) in the instrument teams' laboratories, as the base of the spacecraft Central Checkout System in industry, and as the mission control system at ESOC. The thread that ties these uses together is the SCOS-2000 Mission Information Base. The same ASCII tables had to pass from the instrument teams to the industrial system database, to the checkout system, to the operations centre and into the Herschel science system.1091101123065

This page reconstructs that story from the documents that the Herschel Science Archive kept in its SPIRE instrument folder, from three Herschel documents on ESA's COSMOS web site (the EGSE integration plan, the common EGSE document overview and the operations interface requirements) and from related papers. It covers the decision of April 2000, the operations interface requirements, the system database and naming rules, the MIB tailoring for the Herschel Common Science System (HCSS), the ingestion of SCOS-2000 command history and out-of-limits files, SPIRE's database configuration control, and the experience of the attitude control subsystem team. A second set of documents, copied on 12 November 2026, adds the programme's interface control documents (the Packet Structure and Space/Ground ICDs, the instrument test router, the EGSE interface requirements, the CCS external interfaces and the TC History ICD), the HPSDB user manual, one HPSDB release note, a printed HIFI MIB and a 2015 retrospective by the prime; this page uses them where they show how the MIB moved between the parties, and Herschel/Planck interface documents reads them bit by bit.125138147154158 The Herschel and Planck mission page covers the missions themselves.

At a glance

  • April 2000: at an ESOC meeting all FIRST/Planck instrument groups state their intention to use SCOS-2000 as the basis of their EGSE and real-time analysis; ESA offers the software free of charge under licence, with paid support.614
  • 2001-2003: the Herschel EGSE for instrument level tests is assembled from SCOS-2000, gateways, a router, test control and a MIB editor; the operations interface requirements make the SCOS-2000 Database Import ICD the format of the satellite database.2536
  • 2002-2006: a naming convention and the Herschel/Planck System Database (HPSDB) constrain what instrument MIBs may contain so that they survive the "smooth transition" from instrument to spacecraft level.404447
  • 2003-2008: the HCSS ingests MIBs, telecommand history and out-of-limits files from SCOS-2000 into its own archive.6591
  • 2002-2008: the checkout system reads HPSDB "bridge files" in an extended ICD 5.1 format and returns "update files" listing what each test validated; the HPSDB delivers validated models with release notes, change records and checksums (the library holds one such note, for a delivery to ASED in April 2008).134135149151
  • 2015: the prime presents the HPSDB concept, adapted as a System Reference Data Base for a later programme, as validated by Herschel/Planck.158160
  • Archive: the Herschel MIB releases are listed in the ESA Herschel Science Archive, but this wiki could not copy them (see below).

docs.title: The meeting
docs.text:
On 18-19 April 2000 ESOC hosted a meeting on "SCOS 2000 and FIRST/PLANCK" with the project (ESTEC), ESOC and the instrument groups and their partners (TESRE/CNR, OAT, MPE, RAL, LAL, LABEN, IAS, SRON and KUL).2 The agenda had eleven items:1

# Item Presenter 1 Welcome C. Mazza 2 Introduction P. Estaria 3 SCOS 2000 status J-F. Kaufeler 4 EGSE and supporting elements: router, TPE, Tcl/Tk, WINFOPS/MOIS, database tools J-F. Kaufeler 5 Options for SCOS 2000 systems J-F. Kaufeler 6 Licence agreement and COTS J-F. Kaufeler 7 Service and support J-F. Kaufeler 8 SCOS 2000 delta URD: presentation (PACS) and ESOC comments PACS, ESOC 9 Practical arrangements J-F. Kaufeler 10 Summary and conclusions P. Estaria, J. Dodsworth 11 AOB

The background came from the project's evaluation slides. SCOS-2000 version 0.2 had been evaluated on 3-5 November 1999 by the "RTA CWG" as a "framework" for a common real-time analysis (RTA) system of the FIRST and Planck instruments; the expansion of CWG is not stated in the available sources. Since then the instrument groups had considered a wider role, as an EGSE kernel, and PACS had collected the missing RTA functions and expected EGSE features in a "consolidated" delta URD (user requirements document) dated 4 April 2000, which "cannot be considered consolidated at present".7120

docs.title: What ESOC presented
docs.text:
The ESOC presentation set out the state of SCOS-2000:89

  • Use. Past: SOHO (telemetry only, 1995), Huygens, TeamSat and MTP for Eumetsat (1997). Present: Integral and MSG (successful SVTs), Rosetta (architectural design phase), ERS (first delivery end 1999, migration from SCOS-1), and PROBA (MCS and EGSE). Future: Smart-1, Envisat and XMM (MOC and SOC), both migrating from SCOS-1, Mars Express, the FIRST/Planck MOC and Cryosat and GOCE (listed as "Earth Core Explorer"); "First/Planck EGSE + PIs ??" closed the list.
  • Name. SCOS-2 up to release R1.4 (until 1998), SCOS-2000 from R2.0 (1999), with a new telecommand chain, architectural consolidation, a user interface fully based on ILOG, systematic use of ObjectStore and CORBA for distribution and external interfaces.
  • Releases. R2.0 in September 1999 (Integral SVTs), R2.1 in March 2000 (MSG SVTs), R2.2 in September 2000 as the end of the nominal project. R3.0 (mid-2001) was to port SCOS-2000 to PCs and Linux, separate applications from the operating system and replace ObjectStore; R4.0 (first quarter 2002) was to allow several SCOS-2000 versions on one machine, for constellations, and add higher-level monitoring.

The EGSE elements came from PROBA, where SCOS had served both as checkout facility and mission control system (EMCS). They were a router for TM reception, TC transmission and a SCOS gateway; a procedure automation tool based on the free Tcl/Tk; and database editors based on Oracle.10 The router gives location and data transparency, client management with several clients per connection, and message delivery by asynchronous call-back or synchronous polling. The router on a Windows NT PC (Pentium III) handled 1 Mbit/s of TM input with recording (parallel DMA card), 4 kbit/s of TC (RS422 card), at under 15% CPU, with about 2% CPU per distributed virtual channel. The TCP/IP gateway needed no COTS. The TM/TC front end extracted CCSDS packets from a data stream and built the TC stream; with the ground-space protocol it needed a commercial TC encoder shell (about 10 kEUR).11 The Test Procedure Environment (TPE) linked a SCOE system to the SCOS kernel through parameter and command interface servers, with Tcl/Tk procedures able to get parameters, send commands and read the database.12

ESOC's offer had five software items. Option 1 gave all of them "as is"; option 2 added support and service by TOS-G for items 1-3 and support by TOS-O for items 4-5, with users treated as external customers:13

# Item Basis 1 SCOS-2000 ESOC product 2 Router From PROBA 3 Tcl/Tk procedure automation tool From PROBA 4 Database editors MS Access, from Integral 5 WINFOPS / MOIS MS Access, for procedure preparation and simple tabular automation

docs.title: Licence, costs and support
docs.text:
All software was free of charge but needed a formal, non-exclusive licence stating its purpose; the user had to procure and pay for all hardware and COTS licences.14 The licence text handed out on 19 April 2000 lists the items (SCOS-2000; the PROBA EGSE with router, automation tool and Oracle database; the Integral MS Access database; Winfops/MOIS) and four licence types: documentation only, a time-limited trial, the run-time version, or the source code. ESA keeps ownership, so the software cannot be sold on, and points the licensee to its COTS suppliers at preferential conditions.21 This matches ESA's general practice for "operational software": ESA holds the rights and may grant free, non-exclusive licences to Member State bodies for peaceful use in space research and technology.23

The indicative prices of April 2000:15

Item Price (2000) SCOS-2000 server (Sun Ultra 80) / client (Sun Ultra 10) / basic Sun software set 19 / 10 / 4 kEUR Example: 1 server and 2 clients 51 kEUR Router PC (Windows NT) 4 kEUR SCOS-2000 COTS (ILOG Views, Ctree+, Orbix, ObjectStore, STL): development licences (STL only) 400 EUR per server, plus 400 EUR per year SCOS-2000 COTS: run-time licence 2 200 EUR per client, plus 300 EUR per year Example COTS: 1 server and 3 clients 7.0 kEUR, plus 1.3 kEUR per year Delphi development environment (router, only if developing) 1 kEUR per PC TC transmission shell, only if CCSDS COP-1 is used 10 kEUR per PC SCOS-2000 installation 10 kEUR per site Developer course (20 hours over 4-5 days, hands-on) 4 kEUR per course Consultancy for customisation 14 kEUR per man-month Service (maintenance contract) 35 kEUR per year per user

Support covered the initial phase (installation, training, consultancy). Service assumed an untouched SCOS-2000 kernel and gave a help desk, registered software problem reports (SPRs) fixed in later releases, discussion of change requests (CRQs), updates, and membership of the SCOS-2000 board or user group. Contracts were to be of "Fixed Unit Time" (FUP, for example labour) or firm fixed price (FFP) nature.1622 The minutes clarify that a "user" for service means a single point of contact that may represent a community, and that the first-level help desk is included in the 35 kEUR per year.5

docs.title: The project's position
docs.text: The project stated its limits clearly. ESA's science directorate expects industry to provide the EGSE as part of the spacecraft contract, with a "hands-off" approach, while commonality between flight control and checkout systems is pursued within project constraints (also a goal for Rosetta and Mars Express). Selecting SCOS-2000 as instrument EGSE kernel was "entirely a PI decision". The project could give no technical support, no hardware or software, no money for direct costs (hardware, licences, delta URD developments, support, training) or indirect costs, and no acceptance of responsibility; its coordination of the evaluation ended with the termination of the RTA CWG.1819 The benefits of commonality "have not been quantified".20

docs.title: What was agreed
docs.text:
The minutes record the discussion:3456

  • ESOC called SCOS-2000 stable, mature and reliable, and committed to support it for flight operations and EGSE development. SCOS-2000 is the baseline for MOC operations, and the invitation to tender (ITT) was to say so for the core of the flight control system.
  • The COTS available for Solaris would also be available on Linux (Windows NT under investigation), and ObjectStore would probably be replaced by a cheaper object database.
  • From PROBA: SCOS-2 was the basis; Oracle served as database, extended to the SCOE equipment; the TPE read Oracle at compile time; SCOEs were addressed by APIDs outside the spacecraft range. SCOS-2000 concentrates on an interface to a database that can be any product; the common project database was to come from the prime, and for ESOC the options were Oracle, MS Access (the Integral tool, compatible with SCOS-2000) or custom solutions.
  • ESOC keeps "one product only". Changes are either infrastructure enhancements (ESA funded) or project-specific add-ons, funded by the customer and built either by the customer or by ESOC.
  • The instrument teams worried that no coherent strategy existed for the interface to the prime's checkout equipment, and needed a core option by May 2001 for DPU testing. The three FIRST instruments had agreed a common EGSE, with requirements frozen around June 2000. Interfacing with FINDAS would use the DDS, with the ESOC infrastructure ready between end 2001 and mid-2002.
  • Conclusion: all PI groups "unanimously stated their intention" to use SCOS-2000 as the basis for EGSE and RTA, to be reflected in the ITT interface requirements for database and telemetry.

Two copies of one presentation

The archive holds the ESOC presentation twice, as SCOS2000complete_presentation.pdf and tos-gc_first_planck -presentation+pis_20000418.pdf. The two files differ (different SHA-256 and size) but their extracted text is identical, page for page; this page cites the first.17 Their PDF metadata show the same title, producer, page count (46) and creation time (8 May 2000), with modification times two minutes apart on 10 May 2000, so the difference lies in non-text content.17 The evaluation slides (PT-07671) and the licence text are also archived as separate files.1821

docs.title: The Herschel EGSE for instrument level tests
docs.text:
The decision materialised in the Herschel EGSE for instrument level tests (EGSE-ILT). Its integration plan (SRON-U/HIFI/PL/2001-1, issue 1 of 6 November 2001, identical to draft 4 of 1 July 2001) lists the blocks and who delivered them:2425

Block Delivered by SCOS-2000 ESA SCOS gateway ESTEC Test-equipment interface (TEI) HIFI TM-TC router HIFI Test control PACS CDMS simulator SPIRE OBSM ESA MIB editor ESA

The router, TEI, CDMS simulator and test control tests all start the same way: connect the subsystems and import (or load) the test MIB into SCOS-2000. They then check TM packet reception and content in SCOS-2000 and TC packet transmission to a test client, test equipment or instrument simulator; the last test checks the link between test control and the HCSS.26 On-board software maintenance (OBSM) was still an open item.26

docs.title: The operations interface requirements
docs.text: The Herschel/Planck Operations Interface Requirements Document (OIRD, SCI-PT-RS-07360, issue 2.2, dated "31 September 2003" on its cover, while its change record dates issue 2.2 to 22 May 2003) lists the requirements on spacecraft and payloads needed for operations, and on the deliverables needed at the MOC. It was prepared at ESOC, approved by the project (SCI-PT) and ESOC, and agreed by the prime (ASPI), the project scientists and the instrument PIs; the ESTEC project office controls it.272829 Section 3 derives from the ECSS Packet Utilisation Standard (draft 5.3 of April 2001), and the SCOS-2000 Database Import ICD is an applicable document: it became one in issue 2.0 (July 2001) and was updated to its issue 5.1 (October 2001) in issue 2.2. Requirements marked "P" apply to spacecraft and payloads, "PO" to the spacecraft with possible relevance to payloads, unmarked ones to the spacecraft only.2928

docs.title: Operations concept
docs.text: In routine operations the ground station contact lasts a few hours per day. In that time the ground checks health, dumps the previous day's stored telemetry, uplinks the next day's schedule and corrects problems; science runs autonomously from the schedule. Packet telemetry is expected to ease the ordering of the daily dump, for example status first, then events and command verification reports, then observation data. Operations would use "the same telemetry and telecommand database used in the EGSE".30 Every telecommand is a packet addressed by APID and identified by APID and sequence control, with its function given by PUS type and subtype and its required acknowledgement in a header field. Telemetry is collected in housekeeping, science, telecommand report, event and memory dump packets and stored in the solid-state mass memory until erased by ground.3031

docs.title: PUS services for instruments
docs.text:
The OIRD's table of applicable PUS services for the instruments (see PUS):32

Type Service Instruments 1 Telecommand verification (ST[01]) Mandatory 2 Device command distribution Not applicable 3 Housekeeping and diagnostic data reporting (ST[03]) Mandatory 5 Event reporting (ST[05]) Mandatory 6 Memory management (ST[06]) Mandatory 8 Function management (ST[08]) Optional 9 Time management (ST[09]) Mandatory 11 On-board operations scheduling Not applicable 12 On-board monitoring Not applicable 14 Packet transmission control Mandatory 15 On-board storage and retrieval Not applicable 16 On-board traffic management Not applicable 17 Test (ST[17]) Mandatory 18 OBCP management Optional 19 Event/action Not applicable 21 Science data transfer Mandatory 4, 7, 10, 13, 20, 22 Not used Not applicable

docs.title: Packet rules that shape the MIB
docs.text: Several OIRD requirements decide what the MIB tables can express. APIDs are allocated by the project in the Packet Structure ICD (PSICD; see the APID structure); telemetry from a subsystem uses the same APID as its telecommands where possible; the location of a housekeeping parameter must follow from APID, type, subtype and structure ID (SID); SIDs are unique within an APID and few per APID; housekeeping subcommutation is forbidden and supercommutation allowed only with regular sampling; a parameter has the same structure in every packet; all packets carry a time field (except time and idle packets); and Herschel instrument packets carry a common observation identifier.33 For verification, each telecommand controls its own verification level through the acknowledgement field, acceptance and execution reports carry the failure reason, and reports indicate the command source (ground, mission timeline, OBCP).34 Telemetry must let the ground assess status without the command history, echo the inputs of autonomous processes, use contiguous bits for each parameter and keep the contributing parameters of any synthetic parameter in one packet.35

docs.title: The satellite database
docs.text:
The OIRD makes the database a contractual deliverable:3637

Requirement Content SDBC-1 The prime and the instrument developers deliver a Satellite Database (SDB) with all TM/TC data, command sequences, software parameters and commands; instruments are provided by the PIs SDBC-2 A single common database for system engineering, AIV and operations SDBC-3 Ground checkout and in-orbit content clearly identified SDBC-4 Content complies with the SCOS-2000 Database Import ICD (AD-8) and Annex 2 SDBC-5 to -7 Internally consistent, and consistent with the flight dynamics database and all on-board software SDBC-8 All updates recorded automatically in a configuration control record down to field level SDBC-9 Definitions to write and read parameter values in on-board RAM SDBC-10 to -12 Validated by the prime at system and subsystem level; no irrelevant data; no duplications SDBD-1 Version 0 for the instrument AVM delivery; versions 1 (L-36 months), 2 (L-24 months), 3 (one month before SVT 1, complete with flight values), 4 (one month before SVT 2); a pre-launch update at L-1 month SDBD-2 to -4 Each delivery with a configuration control file down to field level, the spacecraft build standard (EQM or PFM) and the on-board software versions (AOCS, star tracker, CDMS, instruments) SDBD-5 / -6 Delivered "in a set of ORACLE data files"; digital transfer in an agreed file format possible

Annex 2 specifies the configuration control file (SDB version, release date, version of every file, and change tables down to old and new field values, date and initials) and the spacecraft configuration file (model, build standard, on-board software versions).38 Annex 4 delegates database naming to the Herschel/Planck naming convention (H-P-1-ASPI-SP-0141) and fixes procedure names: FCP_AOC_0001 for flight control procedures, CRP_AOC_0001 for contingency recovery procedures (four digits with leading zeros), and TDoyFfNn for timelines (day of year, file number, version).39

docs.title: Naming conventions and the system database
The SPIRE MIB naming convention
docs.text:
SPIRE's naming note (SPIRE-RAL-NOT-001155, issue 1.2, 11 March 2002) applies the Herschel/Planck naming convention to the SPIRE MIB, which it calls the "Mission Implementation Base", delivered to the SCOS-2000 Database Import ICD. Each SCOS-2000 name field gets a pattern:41

Item MIB field(s) Pattern Command packet CCF_CNAME, CDF_CNAME, PTV_CNAME SCiiippp Command parameter CPC_PNAME, CDF_PNAME SPiiippp Command numerical / textual calibration CCA_NUMBR, CCS_NUMBR / PAF_NUMBR, PAS_NUMBR tttnnnrrr (alternative sss) Monitor packet PID_SPID, TPCF_SPID, PLF_SPID tttnnnnppp Monitor parameter PCF_NAME, OCF_NAME, OCP_NAME, PLF_NAME, PTV_PARNAM SMiiippp Numerical, textual, polynomial calibration CAF_NUMBR/CAP_NUMBR, TXF_NUMBR/TXP_NUMBR, MCF_IDENT tttnnnrrr (alternative sss) Numerical / graphical / scrolling display DPF_NUMBE/DPC_NUMBE, GPF_NUMBE/GPC_NUMBE, SPF_NUMBE/SPC_NUMBE SAiiippp / SGiiippp / SLiiippp

Here iii is a theoretical parameter identifier (its first character the subsystem ID, its third the parameter unit ID), nnn a running number, ttt the system element number, rrr the real element number, ppp the position identifier and sss an alternative identifier for calibration curves "if SCOS2000 is incapable of handling 8 character field names". System elements are numbered (OBS 480, DPU 490, DCU 500, MCU 510, SCU 520, EGSE 528, the test facility TFCS 529), real elements count the configurations per model (AVM 100, QM 300, FM 500, FS 700 and so on), and unit IDs are letters such as A (current), K (temperature), V (voltage) or W (power).42

docs.title: The Alcatel limits of January 2003
docs.text:
On 27 January 2003 the prime (fax H-P-ASP-LT-2607) required all instrument teams to restrict their MIBs "in order to support 'smooth transition' from instrument test level to module test level". User-defined constants (UDCs) are MIB parameters whose values SCOS-2000 stores in standard TM packets described in plf.44121

Requirement Reason given Curve identifiers limited to Number(3) The import ICD allows Number(4), but the naming convention's theoretical curve identifier needs the room Range set identifiers limited to Number(3) Same reasoning Command verification stage identifiers limited to Number(4) The ICD allows Number(5) Dynamic user-defined constants in fixed ranges of the unique "constant packet" in plf: system 0000-0099, SVM 0100-0199, PLM 0200-0299, HIFI (Herschel) and HFI (Planck) 0300-0399, PACS and LFI 0400-0499, 0500-0599 labelled HIFI again for Herschel and "not used" for Planck (SPIRE is not named in the list as printed), spare 0600-1023 The constant packet is unique, so allocations must not overlap at integration The SPID of the constant packet supports 1024 octets All levels produce the same archive format, at the cost of disc space at instrument level

docs.title: Identifiers in the checkout system and the EGSE
docs.text:
The checkout system went the other way. Terma's CCS External ICD, whose issue 1.5 of July 2003 introduced the changes labelled ECP 1 and ECP 3, widened calibration curve and range set identifiers from Number(4) to Char(10) and verification stage identifiers from Number(5) to Number(10) in the CCS bridge files, although its field tables still print the range set fields (PRF_NUMBR, PRV_NUMBR, CPC_PRFREF, CSP_PRFREF) as Char(8).133137 It also reserved names and numbers for the test system: no parameter name may begin with YZ (Y being the EGSE subsystem and Z marking system parameters), none with VAR, GVAR or $ (which the OL expression language uses), and SPIDs 100 to 999 are reserved for internal EGSE use.136

Inference

The two rules of 2003 fit together if the short numbers belong to the instrument S2K files and the character identifiers to the CCS files generated by HPSDB: the HPSDB configuration files map S2K curve, stage and range set numbers to naming-convention items (for example SCOS curve 900 to the generic curve 000900).142143 No source states this division of labour explicitly.

The EGSE Interface Requirement Specification placed the test equipment itself in the naming convention. The EGSE subsystem is Y (written 25 in RM packet names, Y being the 25th letter); every EGSE item has a range of positions, from the ACMS SCOE (920-939) and the CCS (940-941) through the front ends, SCOEs and cryo equipment to the instrument EGSEs (HIFI 962-963, PACS 964-965, SPIRE 966-967, HFI 968-969, LFI 970-971). Remote command names are YC, their parameters YP and remote monitoring parameters YM, each followed by a three-character function and the position.131132 Identifiers may contain only digits, the underscore and the upper-case letters other than I, O and Q.131 That is stricter than requirement NMCVT-0100-C as the HCSS note reports it, which forbids those three letters only as leading characters, where the instrument centres used them for their EGSE-ILT parameters.6976

docs.title: HPSDB: MIB files processing (H-P-1-ASP-TN-1060)
docs.text:
The Herschel/Planck System Database (HPSDB), built by GMV for the prime, holds data at element, subsystem, model and generic level. Instantiation keeps consistency: "theoretical" boxes carry default data, "real" boxes the measured values, and logical and physical instantiation build subsystems from elements and multiple real copies of a box. A central site keeps the final data, with mirror sites.112 The prime's technical note H-P-1-ASP-TN-1060 (issue 1, 7 February 2006) documents how the HPSDB ingests and regenerates SCOS-2000 MIB files. In the note, "S2K" means the instrument EGSE "version 2.3eP5 based on SCOS 2000 2.3e" with MIB ICD 5.1, and "CCS" the Central Checkout System with its own MIB ICD.4748 A draft had been annexed to the minutes of a Herschel instruments database meeting at ASED in Munich on 29-30 September 2005 and was finalised to close an ESA action.45

The note lists the constraints that instrument MIBs must respect so that HPSDB returns the same files it was given. Constraints that HPSDB cannot check are printed in bold and are the user's responsibility. It warns that even then CCS and instrument EGSE may behave differently, because CCS has functions without SCOS-2000 equivalent (calibration selection by condition, event limits, critical commands) and because configuration files such as MISCconfig differ.47 The general rules:495051525354

Rule Content G1 Object data model Bridge files are generated from an object plus its generic object, which must be consistent; object identifiers and positions must be supplied G2 Naming convention Character identifiers start with an item-type letter; at subsystem and model level a subsystem letter is prefixed ("Z" for the pseudo-subsystem) and a three-digit position appended ("999" for system); numeric identifiers use subsystem numbers A=00 to Y=25 ("26" pseudo); generic items use letter "G", number "07", position and element "000" G3-G5 Short S2K identifiers S2K curve, verification stage and range set identifiers are too short for instantiation: a specific item is coded Number(3) (curves, range sets) or Number(4) (verification stages); a generic one as 1xxx or 1xxxx, matching generic HPSDB items such as G000xxx000 G6 Enumerated fields Values must be in the ICD set, possibly reduced by the PSICD (allowed type/subtype pairs) or by HPSDB (no octal radix) G7 Commutation HPSDB models packets as lists of parameters, structures and fixed areas, with offsets, repetition counters and supercommutation; a packet is flagged fixed (PLF only), variable (VPD only) or both G8 Default values ICD defaults are forced even when irrelevant, and some are replaced by HPSDB defaults (PID_CHECK, CAF_RADIX/CCA_RADIX) G9 Commonality TM and TC calibration curves can be shared in HPSDB, so the same identifier must not be used for a TM and a TC curve G10 Category flag Each item has an 8-bit flag, one bit per user type (AIT, operations, software, flight dynamics); MIB loading sets "all except FDD" G11 Common fields 64-character mnemonic, 256-character long description and configuration data (last action, user, date, reason, area, source, site, validation and archive dates), not supported by S2K or CCS G12 TC packet header TC headers are generic in HPSDB; TCP, PCPC and PCDF are ignored at loading and must match the generic header referenced by CCF_PKTID; at output they are set from the generic data (PCDF_TCNAME "GX000000") G13 Reserved characters No >, <, quote, double quote or & (XML); short descriptions limited to letters, digits, blank, +, - and _ G14 Radix Unsigned values in decimal or hexadecimal, never octal G15 Range allocation Allocations from the naming convention (PID numbers, UDC locations) must be respected; the note blames a "SCOS limitation" in supporting smooth transition G16 Automatic instantiation The last character of the short description, the APID, the PID and the UDC and MISC parameter positions are computed from the element's position, so users must take care with them G17 Short description Mandatory in HPSDB, filled with the identifier if empty G18 Orphan items Not loaded G19 Sorting Output sorted by the ICD primary key; inputs must be sorted too G20 Derived parameters Expression files delivered with the MIB

The field-by-field part then states for each MIB field how it is loaded, stored and written back. Some points matter for every MIB user:

  • PID and SPID. The ICD allows an n-to-n relation between TM packets (type, subtype, APID, PI1, PI2) and SCOS packets (SPID), "claiming that at any time, only one relation is valid". HPSDB allows only n-to-1 (each TM packet in only one SCOS packet, which several TM packets may share), and AIT asked for 1-to-1. PID_VALID is forced to "Y", PID_TIME to "Y", and PID_DFHSIZE must be equal for all source packets of one SPID.4756 See pid.
  • PIC is generic. The pic table must be the same on every SCOS and CCS system of the programme, so it is never loaded from bridge files and always generated from generic HPSDB data.57
  • PCF_NATUR is set from the HPSDB parameter type and the naming convention, and PCF_CATEG must be "T" for all parameters with PTC 8.55
  • Commands. CCF_HIPRI is computed from the packet header, CCF_ACK is split into four HPSDB fields, and the note asks ESA to clarify how the MCS uses CCF_MAPID, listing the values 0 (high priority), 1 (normal computer), 2 (redundant computer), 5 (reset CROME), 6 (TC only mode) and 32 (TBC).59
  • Not used. Print proformas (PPF, PPC) must not be present; command routing (DST) is not loaded; command sequences (CSF, CSS, SDF) and parameter sets (PST, PSV, CPS, PVS, PSM) are not supported by the CCS ("do not use"), and the CSP section is still "To be written", although HPSDB loads sequences "in order to interface with MOIS for operations".5860
  • CCS-only tables. Conditional calibration (CUR), groups (GRP, GRPA, GRPK), SCOE definitions (SCO), TC and TM distribution to SCOEs (TCD, TMD) and logarithmic curves (LGF) belong to the CCS MIB.61

A TC packet header as the MIB defines it (real data, Solar Orbiter)

Rule G12 and the HCSS rule on pcdf (below) both concern the TC packet header tables. The Solar Orbiter MIB of 2025 shows what such a definition looks like: its header NOM_TC (described as NOM_DH_TC_Packet_Header in tcp) has 13 pcdf rows with bit offsets counted from the start of the packet.123119

The type codes F, A, T, S, K and P are those of the ICD: fixed value, APID, service type, subtype and acknowledgement flags from ccf, and parameters set automatically by the command subsystem.119 The code O used for the source ID is not among the codes listed in ICD issue 7.0. The second header, HPC1_TC, has 7 rows (primary header only, data field header flag 0); 5 318 commands use NOM_TC, 125 use HPC1_TC, 6 NOS2KHDR and 5 NO_HDR.123

docs.title: The HPSDB in use
docs.text:
The processing note says what HPSDB did to MIB files; GMV's user manual (version 2.6, September 2005) and a Herschel release note (issue 9.0, April 2008) show how the files moved. A user zips the SCOS-2000 bridge files of an instrument with configuration files that place them in the object model (elements, subsystem positions, a copy of pid.dat with naming-convention identifiers, and maps from short SCOS curve, stage and range set numbers to generic items) and loads them into the working area; the loader "is not a SCOS bridge file validator". Only the schema manager validates, which moves objects to the reference area and older copies to the archive area.141142139145 Bridge files for the SCOS or the CCS format can then be generated from any box, the manager choosing the user category they are generated for.144 On the checkout side, the CCS writes update files: tab-separated lines naming each telecommand (c) or parameter (p) that a test sequence validated, with time, sequence name and issue and the host, to be read together with the MIB issue in vdf.dat; the user manual's verification file has the same columns with a site instead of a host and is written straight into the reference area.135146

sequenceDiagram
  participant I as Instrument team
  participant H as HPSDB central site
  participant C as CCS at the AIT site
  I->>H: zip of S2K bridge files and configuration files
  H->>H: load into working area, manager validates into reference area
  H->>C: CCS bridge files (zip) with release note and MD5 checksum
  C->>C: import MIB, run test sequences
  C->>H: update files (validated TCs and parameters, sequence and issue)
  H->>H: verification data attached to the items in the reference area

Inference

The loop is this wiki's assembly of the user manual, the CCS External ICD and the release note; no source draws it as one cycle, and how often update files actually travelled back to the HPSDB is not stated in the available sources.146135149

The release note documents one delivery in that loop. The central site (HPSDB 3.3.1.30) delivered the theoretical model HERSCH_FM9, as CCS files filtered for the "AIT User", to ASED in Friedrichshafen for the Herschel IRR, as R_TM_HERSCH_FM9_C_804071709.zip with an MD5 checksum, by e-mail on 9 April 2008.149151152 The note's change record (issues 1.0 of 10 October 2007 to 9.0) lists the DBAMN-H-... items (the abbreviation is not expanded in the note) and the data validation requests behind them: loading new CDMU, ACMS and OBCP software data, new HIFI and SPIRE MIB versions, changes to sco.dat and tcd.dat for the flight-model cryo SCOE, a change of the TC sub-schedule and, in issue 6.0, switching all telecommands to "ground low priority" by default.148 Open non-conformance reports against the instrument EGSE delivery (files not compatible with Windows, extra spaces in cpc.dat, a missing tpcf.dat) show the kind of file-level problems the integration met.150 The model tree, the file naming convention and how it decodes the archive's file names are on the mission page.

Sites never exchanged data automatically. The central site holds all valid objects; mirror sites, one of which the system EGSE specification required at the Central Checkout System, may change only real objects, and managers move XML transfer and log files between sites by hand.140157

docs.title: The HCSS MIB clarification and tailoring note
Purpose
docs.text: The Herschel Common Science System (HCSS) is the common software of the Herschel science ground segment. It uses MIB data to define instrument-related commands and to interpret downlink data for the Quick Look Assessment and Interactive Analysis subsystems. The MIB is produced by an external MIB editor as ASCII files, and the HCSS MIB ingestion software reads and checks them.65 The HCSS MIB Clarification and Tailoring Note (HSC/DOC/0300, issue 1.5, 21 December 2004, approved by the HSC and the PACS, HIFI and SPIRE teams) completes the interface defined by the Database Import ICD (issue 5.2) and the naming convention (issue 2.1): it clarifies their ambiguities, adds Herschel constraints and lists the checks.626466

docs.title: Clarifications of the import ICD
docs.text:
Point ICD section Clarification 4.1.1 §2.3 A line ends with the operating system's terminator (LF on Unix, CR+LF on Windows); one line per record; N fields need N-1 tabs; trailing fields ignored by SCOS-2000 (grey in the ICD) may be omitted, so at least T-G fields 4.1.2 §2.4 Mandatory fields must hold a value of the right type; numeric ones must not be null or blank 4.1.3 §3.3 Non-mandatory fields without default get 0, 0.0 or an empty string 4.1.4 §3.3 The separator is always present, the value may be empty (text from ESOC's DCR-286) 4.1.5 §3.3.2.3.2 An out-of-limit is raised only below the low or above the high limit, for soft and hard limits 4.1.6 §3.3.2.5.1 PLF_OFFBY/PLF_OFFBI count from the end of the SCOS-2000 packet header, which equals the start of the TM source packet with the generic packetiser (DCR 309) 4.1.7 §3.3.2.5.1 Bit 0 of PLF_OFFBI is the most significant bit (DCR 308) 4.1.8 §2 Floating point numbers use a decimal point, not a comma

The table summarises the note's clarification table.68 See plf and monitoring checks.

The terms used: "short name" means CCF_CNAME, CPC_PNAME and PCF_NAME; "short description" means CCF_DESCR, CPC_DESCR, PCF_DESCR and PID_DESCR; "long description" means CCF_DESCR2.67 Of the naming requirements, only NMCVT-0100-C (identifiers; it forbids I, O and Q as leading characters) and NMCVT-7600-C (descriptions: English letters, digits, space, +, -, _; meaningful; understandable abbreviations; short description not empty) affect ingestion.69

docs.title: Herschel constraints for the final interface
docs.text:
For the final pre-launch interface the note requires:7071

  • all tables of the ICD in one directory, plus synthetic parameter definitions in a synthetic subdirectory; everything else ignored;
  • an extra command durations table (command short name, duration) for the HCSS Common Uplink System (CUS), which computes the duration of command sets;
  • vdf ignored; constant parameters (PCF_NATUR = "C") ignored;
  • the SPID as the only way to locate a parameter in a fixed packet, a packet being identified by type, subtype, APID and SID, assuming "a unique SPID for each and every packet type";
  • no PID_PI1_VAL greater than zero where PIC_PI1_OFF is -1 (no SID needed);
  • at least 4 pcdf rows (VERSION, TYPE, DHFLAG, APID) for each command's packet header, except pseudo commands whose names begin with "Z", which contradicts the ICD's statement that PCDF_TCNAME is unique;
  • CDF_CNAME plus CDF_PNAME unique, with repeated groups for repeated values;
  • command sequences (CSF, CSS, SDF, CSP) and parameter sets (PST, PSV, CPS, PVS) ignored;
  • in txp, TXP_FROM not above TXP_TO and no overlapping ranges;
  • short descriptions matching [a-zA-Z0-9_]+, and the first character of the short name plus the short description unique for commands, command parameters and monitoring parameters (the APID plus PID_DESCR for packets): unique "per instrument".

For release 0.2 of the HCSS the note was stricter: only raw parameters (PCF_NATUR = "R") considered, synthetic ones ignored; OCF_CODIN only "R" or "I"; variable packets (vpd) ignored; and a command parameter with CPC_CATEG "N" treated as raw, otherwise as engineering, with engineering parameters not allowed raw defaults. The semantic checks used the monitoring tables pcf, cap, txp, ocf, ocp, pid, pic and plf, the commanding tables pcdf, ccf, cpc and cdf, and the calibration tables ccs, paf and pas.7273

docs.title: The checks
docs.text:
The note lists 34 numbered checks, one of which (7.0.6) was removed. Most raise an error:7475

Group Checks Files and syntax Expected file names (7.0.1); field count per line (7.0.3, lenient for trailing grey fields); empty numeric fields only an informative message (7.0.4); wrong numeric type a warning with a null value (7.0.5) Uniqueness ICD unique keys (7.0.2, to be implemented), temporarily PCF_NAME, OCF_NAME, CPC_PNAME and CCF_CNAME (7.0.18-7.0.21); descriptions per 5.3.1-5.3.5 (7.0.22-7.0.26) Monitoring Non-raw PCF_NATUR a warning, length -1 (7.0.7); no calibration found a warning (7.0.8); status parameter (PCF_CATEG "S") without PCF_CURTX (7.0.15); unknown PCF_CATEG (7.0.16); PID_INTER set for a packet other than (3,25) (7.0.34) Packets SID rule (7.0.12); SPID in plf missing in pid (7.0.14); synthetic and variable packet validity (7.0.10-7.0.11, to be implemented) Commanding Compliance with the Common Uplink System (7.0.9); at least 4 pcdf rows (7.0.13); CPC_INTER only "R" or "E" (7.0.17); CPC_RADIX only D, H or O (7.0.33) Calibration TXP order and overlap (7.0.27-7.0.28); exactly one cca for a calibrated command parameter, with ccs points (7.0.29-7.0.30); ccs values consistent with format and radix (7.0.31); default engineering values consistent with the decalibration curve (7.0.32)

Check 7.0.13 asks for "more than 4" pcdf rows, while the rule it refers to (5.2.7) asks for at least 4; the note does not resolve the difference.7471

docs.title: Comments, answers and the SPID problem
docs.text:
The note also preserves the e-mail exchanges behind it. The HSC asked that the naming convention allow underscores in short descriptions, because they store readable names such as DPU_START_AUT_FUN for the mnemonic PC004380, and because the CUS scripting language cannot use + or -. It pointed out that the leading characters I, O and Q were reserved by the instrument centres for HIFI, PACS and SPIRE EGSE-ILT parameters, while H, P and S lead instrument-related mnemonics.76 ESOC's SCOS team answered on 5 December 2002 and raised document change requests: non-mandatory fields without default are implicitly null; separators are always present (DCR 286); PLF offsets count from the end of the SCOS-2000 packet header (DCR 309); bit 0 is the most significant bit (DCR 308, whose own wording says "most significant byte"). Two odd structures stay: soft and hard limits as separate ocp records, inherited from previous control systems, and the PID_VALID flag that selects which record of a key is valid; ESOC had no intention to change either.77

The best documented problem is SPID uniqueness. In September 2002 PACS reported that all its telecommand verification packets had SPID 10006, because SCOS-2000 did not allow a range of SPIDs for packet type 1. That contradicted the ICD rule that the SPID uniquely defines a packet structure, and SCOS-2000 used PCF_VALID to decide which plf location applied, which PACS called an abuse of a field meant for the validity of a value. ESOC replied that the verifier "listens" only to a predefined list of SPIDs for report-based verification. Rosetta had already allowed any SPID for service 1 packets and Cryosat a range of SPIDs, and the useful Rosetta and Cryosat changes to the verifier and the on-board queue model were planned for S2K R3.1: a function reads all SPIDs of service type 1 from pid.dat and adds them to the TM cache filter.78 See command verification in the MIB.

docs.title: The Herschel rules against a modern MIB
docs.text:
How do the Herschel constraints look against today's public flight MIB? The Solar Orbiter release of 16 September 2025 answers some of them directly:123

Herschel constraint Solar Orbiter 2025 Unique SPID per packet type (5.2.5); the PACS case of one SPID for all TC verification packets 1 809 service 1 packet definitions with 1 809 distinct SPIDs across 31 APIDs; no SPID appears in more than one pid row. pic makes the failure code part of the identification for TM(1,2) and TM(1,8) (PIC_PI1_OFF 20, PIC_PI1_WID 16), so each failure code has its own SPID: 29 for (1,1), 274 for (1,2), 29 for (1,7) and 1 477 for (1,8) PID_INTER only for (3,25) packets (7.0.34) PID_INTER is empty in all 11 150 pid rows Only raw parameters ingested (v0.2) 125 161 raw, 1 582 dynamic OL and 2 saved synthetic parameters OCF_CODIN only R or I (v0.2) R 1 668, I 2 037, and A 1 633 No octal radix (HPSDB G14; HCSS allows D, H, O) CPC_RADIX: D 3 155, H 2 195, empty 1 805; no O Short descriptions [a-zA-Z0-9_]+ (5.3.1) 68 789 of 126 745 PCF_DESCR and 4 602 of 5 454 CCF_DESCR contain other characters such as spaces "Z" marks pseudo commands (5.2.7) 5 441 of 5 454 CCF_CNAME begin with "Z" Status parameters need PCF_CURTX (7.0.15) 5 of 26 538 parameters with PCF_CATEG "S" have none No overlapping TXP ranges (5.2.13) One overlap: a duplicated row in curve CYCT0002TM Unique CDF_CNAME + CDF_PNAME (5.2.9) No duplicate pair

The PIC_PI1_OFF offset is counted in bytes from the start of the TM source packet.122 Each SPID can be opened in the explorer, for example the TM(1,1) packet of APID 161.

Inference

The Herschel rules were constraints of one consumer, the HCSS, and of one programme's naming convention. The comparison does not mean that Solar Orbiter's MIB is wrong. It shows which rules were local (the meaning of "Z", the character set, raw-only ingestion) and that the SPID limitation reported in 2002 is absent from a recent MIB.

SQL used (Herschel rules against Solar Orbiter) 
-- solo-2025-09-16.sqlite (MIB__20250916M25925PFMS001_SOL)
SELECT count(*), count(DISTINCT PID_SPID), count(DISTINCT PID_APID)
  FROM pid WHERE PID_TYPE = '1';                          -- 1809 | 1809 | 31
SELECT PID_STYPE, count(*), count(DISTINCT PID_SPID)
  FROM pid WHERE PID_TYPE = '1' GROUP BY 1;               -- 1:29 2:274 7:29 8:1477
SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT PID_SPID FROM pid
  GROUP BY PID_SPID HAVING count(*) > 1);                 -- 0
SELECT * FROM pic WHERE PIC_TYPE = '1';                    -- (1,2) and (1,8): 20 | 16
SELECT count(*) FROM pid WHERE trim(coalesce(PID_INTER,'')) <> '';   -- 0
SELECT PCF_NATUR, count(*) FROM pcf GROUP BY 1;            -- R 125161, D 1582, S 2
SELECT OCF_CODIN, count(*) FROM ocf GROUP BY 1;            -- A 1633, I 2037, R 1668
SELECT CPC_RADIX, count(*) FROM cpc GROUP BY 1;            -- '' 1805, D 3155, H 2195
-- char(94) is the caret, which negates the GLOB character class (any other character)
SELECT count(*), sum(PCF_DESCR GLOB '*[' || char(94) || 'A-Za-z0-9_]*') FROM pcf;  -- 126745 | 68789
SELECT count(*), sum(CCF_DESCR GLOB '*[' || char(94) || 'A-Za-z0-9_]*') FROM ccf;  -- 5454 | 4602
SELECT substr(CCF_CNAME,1,1), count(*) FROM ccf GROUP BY 1;         -- Z 5441, ...
SELECT PCF_CATEG, count(*),
       sum(PCF_CURTX IS NULL OR PCF_CURTX = '') FROM pcf GROUP BY 1; -- S: 26538 | 5
SELECT a.TXP_NUMBR FROM txp a JOIN txp b ON a.TXP_NUMBR = b.TXP_NUMBR
   AND a.rowid < b.rowid
   AND CAST(a.TXP_FROM AS REAL) <= CAST(b.TXP_TO AS REAL)
   AND CAST(b.TXP_FROM AS REAL) <= CAST(a.TXP_TO AS REAL);          -- CYCT0002TM
SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT CDF_CNAME, CDF_PNAME FROM cdf
  WHERE coalesce(CDF_PNAME,'') <> '' GROUP BY 1,2 HAVING count(*) > 1);  -- 0
SELECT * FROM pcdf ORDER BY PCDF_TCNAME, CAST(PCDF_BIT AS INT);
