  FOP --> MCS
  DISP["Displays<br/>(EUD, ODDE)"] --> MCS
  CCB["Configuration control<br/>(CCB, change requests)"] -.-> ODB
  CCB -.-> FOP

The chain is this wiki's summary. Each element is described, with its source, in the sections below.103102432787

docs.title: What has to be prepared
docs.text:
ESA's paper on the next-generation Mission Operations Preparation Environment lists the data definitions that its EGS-CC based preparation environment was to support, and for which ESOC product each is needed: MICONYS-CC (the mission control system suite), GSMC-CC (ground station monitoring and control) or SIMULUS (simulators).34

Data definition What it is MICONYS-CC GSMC-CC SIMULUS Monitoring and Control Model The EGS-CC M&C model that configures the EGS-CC kernel x x x TM/TC packets Packet definitions for the EGS-CC packet encoder/decoder x x ESA ground station M&C ICD definitions Variable lists, transient variables, tasks and other interface structures x On-board M&C services (PUS) PUS-based monitoring and control services x x User defined displays Displays running in the EGS-CC user interface x x x Synthetic parameters Derived parameters x x Expressions Expressions in the EGS-CC script language x x Activity lists Lists of activities x Ground station subsystem interface definitions Interface to the station subsystems x Flight control procedures Manual flight control procedures x Scripts Scripts in the EGS-CC based script language x x Automation procedures (Java) Native EGS-CC automation procedures x Automation procedures (DSL) Automation procedures in a domain-specific language x x Automation schedule templates Schedules for automated execution x x Mission planning rules Planning rule definitions x FCT documentation Generation of flight control team documents x FCT preparation activity planning Reports of activities in the MCM tree x Ground station main menu Tailored station M&C menu with its actions x Problem and requirements tracking Requirements with cross-references to procedures and validation data x x Simulator preparation data For example simulator scripts x

4

Future extensions could cover mission-specific on-board control procedures, flight operations plan requirements, timelines, diagnostic rules, tracking of tailoring-data validation, and verification and validation data.4 For comparison, a SCOS-2000 MIB holds packets in pid and plf, parameters in pcf, synthetic parameters, displays and command sequences.114 See the MIB data model.

INTEGRAL's flight operations plan names the operational tools that its flight control team kept under control: the flight operations plan itself, the Operational Database (ODB), the On-Board Software Maintenance System (OBSMS), the simulator, the mission control system (IMCS) and the flight dynamics system.101104 Most of them appear as boxes in ESA's 2003 picture of an SCOS-2000-based MCS, where a satellite database import feeds the INTEGRAL ODB, which in turn feeds the INTEGRAL Monitoring and Control System.108

docs.title: Requirements upstream
docs.text: Operations preparation starts before the spacecraft is built: what the ground can do later depends on what the space segment is required to provide. Two ESA documents in the library show how such requirements are now written.

docs.title: The Generic OIRD
docs.text:
Operability requirements are an early input to spacecraft development. Most ESA missions write them in an Operations Interface Requirements Document (OIRD), either standalone or inside the System Requirements Document, tightly coupled with the CCSDS and ECSS standards. ESA's 2019 presentation lists the problems: each mission had its own OIRD derived from previous ones, lessons learnt did not always propagate, the documents looked more different than they were, they had evolved independently of PUS-C and the OBCP standard, and the variability hampered product orientation both on board and in the mission control system.41

In June 2016 SAVOIR entrusted ESOC with establishing a Generic OIRD (GOIRD) that would form the baseline specification for future missions and allow compatible on-board software libraries. Mission OIRDs are to be created from it with only mission-specific deltas, plus the sizing of PUS-C services such as mission timeline capacity.41

flowchart LR
  G["Generic OIRD<br/>(functional + PUS-C requirements)"] --> M["Mission-specific OIRD"]
  P["Mission and project<br/>requirements"] --> M
  M --> ITT["ITT"]
  F["Feedback from new projects<br/>and flying missions"] -.-> G

4344

The GOIRD is not a replacement for mission OIRDs. Missions must take all GOIRD requirements, apply truly mission-specific changes (constants, sizing of PUS-C services, de-scoping of what does not apply), trace every change, and must not copy and paste from previous mission OIRDs.43

Aspect Generic OIRD 1.0 Structure Part I: on-board functional requirements, linked to ECSS-E-ST-70-11C (space segment operability). Part II: PUS-C requirements, tailoring ECSS-E-ST-70-41C, with ECSS-E-ST-70-01C (OBCP) Delivery A PDF document with three Excel files as its core: functional requirements, PUS-C requirements and a change log tracking all changes since Draft A Scope Robotic missions with an avionics-like subsystem in mind Functional groups General, modes, operations/mission phases, spacecraft control, telecommands, authentication (Earth observation only), telemetry, timing, in-flight testing, general autonomy, FDIR, safe mode, and subsystems (attitude control and navigation, on-board processors and software, data storage and file system, power, thermal, TT&C, payloads, mechanisms) Functional format Kept in DOORS: ID, requirement and notes, relationship to ECSS-E-ST-70-11C (unchanged, new or modified) with clause, justification of modifications, mission-family flag (interplanetary, astronomy, Earth observation); a second module lists the operability requirements tailored out PUS-C format DOORS, against the original standard, with an applicability flag (unchanged, modified, deleted, new) and a justification per change; exportable as full tailored standard or deltas only Status Released July 2019; already used for the Copernicus high-priority candidate missions, ERO/Mars Sample Return and HERA

42454644

Why not use PUS-C as it is? The presentation counts 20 services with 33 subservices but no mapping to an architecture; 316 TCs and TM reports if all subservices are implemented, of which only 88 are mandatory (this wiki's own tally of ECSS-E-ST-70-41C Annex C, in the PUS message type catalogue, finds 318 message types, 81 of them in minimum capability sets; how the presentation counted is not stated); and 382 "shall be declared when specifying" statements, so that two untailored implementations would end up with very different interfaces. Some functions that ESOC missions need are missing (critical event log or system log, file transfer, backup mission timeline), as are some lessons from previous OIRDs.46 The PUS-C part of the GOIRD therefore consists of these classes of requirement:47

Class Content Share of the GOIRD PUS-C requirements Services, subtypes and capabilities selection One common set of services, subservices, TC/TM packet types and capabilities for all future ESA missions, so that the satellite interface is fairly mission-independent about 60% Additional observables Parameters added to most services, because PUS-C relies on on-demand reports and mandates few housekeeping parameters about 2% New capabilities Critical event log / system log, parameter extraction from housekeeping, backup MTL, file-based operations; high-level requirements only, interfaces left open, to be raised as change requests to the standard about 19% Avionics architecture A few services centralised (for example service 11, the mission timeline); services 1, 3, 5, 6 (if applicable) and 17 mandated in all packetised units less than 1% Clarifications and refinements Lessons learnt from previous missions and OIRDs about 12% Changes to the standard Kept to the absolute minimum, never changing defined TC/TM interfaces, each justified (typos, omissions, strong operational needs) less than 1%

The presentation warns that PUS-C leaves key low-level aspects unstandardised, such as the number of bytes used to encode certain packet fields, which matters for interoperability; it asks for coordination among PUS-C library implementers. The OBCP standard is not tailored, and a few extra requirements for service 18 sit in the PUS-C part.48 The concluding slide sets out a common requirement set to reduce variability and cost. As a long-term vision it asks whether PUS-C library developers could collaborate and whether interoperable implementations with a generic TM/TC ICD are possible, and it proposes further harmonisation of other elements such as procedures and databases.49 For the services named above see ST[01], ST[03], ST[05], ST[06], ST[11], ST[17] and ST[18]; for the differences between PUS versions see PUS-A vs PUS-C.

docs.title: Ground inputs to the on-board data architecture (PE-TN-ESA-GS-405)
docs.text:
A technical note from ESA's Earth Observation programme, first issued in November 2014 and at issue 2 revision 6 of 26 March 2026, states what the ground segment needs from the on-board data architecture so that payload data can be analysed, simulated and processed efficiently. Its change record shows it being refined for BIOMASS, TRUTHS, FORUM, Harmony and NGGM.50 It explicitly does not apply to TT&C/S-band links. It also covers missions that use CFDP on top of the Space Packet Protocol, noting that CFDP is new to Earth-observation missions and that their payload downlink differs from space science: many short passes, through stations usually procured as a service rather than operated by the flight operations segment.51 The note's working assumptions include routing from on-board source to ground sink on the primary header or the CFDP file name, unmodified commercial CCSDS ground equipment, the Level-1 processor as end consumer, and preferably fully open-loop payload downlink.51

Its glossary separates the data kinds that a database designer has to keep apart:52

Term Meaning in the note Observation data (OBS) Instrument output, as Space Packets, when the stimuli are the mission's targets Calibration data (CAL) Instrument output when the stimuli are internal or external calibration targets Ancillary data (ANC) Space Packets generated on board, mostly by software, in support of observations: navigation, temperature, timing, configuration; "instrument ancillary" or "platform ancillary" by origin Auxiliary data (AUX) Files needed by ground processing but not part of the payload data (for example orbit files, calibration coefficients) Housekeeping telemetry (HKTM) Data for monitoring and control in the mission control centre; a separate stream not used in payload processing Payload Data Observation, calibration and instrument ancillary data; excludes instrument HKTM and platform ancillary data RAW / Level 0 Concatenated packets as received, with no header (RAW); ground-segment header plus concatenated packets (Level 0)

The requirements, numbered by topic, are summarised below.

Group Requirements (paraphrased) Data categories R-001: payload data is categorised as observation, internal calibration, external calibration or instrument ancillary Identification R-010: every payload packet carries a logical stream identifier, the APID, and end-to-end routing relies exclusively on it; an APID is unique on the satellite even across RF bands, virtual channels or files. R-020: each packet type needing distinct ground processing or routing gets its own APID, including separate APIDs per calibration type, observation mode and test mode. R-030/R-040/R-050: platform and instrument ancillary parameters go in dedicated packets, and ancillary packets from different sources (for example navigation and thermal) have different APIDs Secondary header R-110/R-120: a common, CCSDS-compliant secondary header with a time stamp; the PUS-C secondary header is allowed but service type and subtype must not be used to discriminate data types. R-130: the time field uses the PUS-C time format (PTC 9 or 10) Packet content R-140: every packet is self-contained, so no round-robin or slice-based subcommutation. R-150: PUS structure IDs (SIDs) are to be avoided for payload data, because a given APID always has the same structure. R-160: no padding Navigation R-200 to R-270: position, velocity and time (PVT), attitude quaternions and time-correlation parameters go in a platform packet called NAVATT; PVT in an Earth-fixed frame, attitude in an inertial frame, both at configurable minimum rates (PVT by default 1 Hz, the GNSS PPS) Storage R-300/R-310: ancillary packets available for downlink whatever the instrument state. R-320/R-321: any payload or platform-ancillary data type can be allocated from ground to any packet store Data link R-400: avoid the AOS insertion zone. R-410: recorded payload packets downlinked with the virtual channel packet service of TM, AOS or USLP. R-420: payload and platform ancillary data on virtual channels separate from TT&C. R-450: with several physical channels, each packet store is downlinked over one channel only Files R-500 to R-595: data types in separate files, unique file names that identify type and instance, configurable destination (CFDP destination IDs per data type), configurable priority by type and age, repeat and complete re-downlink, file sizes chosen against link outages, open-loop (CFDP class 1) as a goal Operations and downlink R-600/R-610: time-tagged and position-tagged schedules. R-700: everything stored can be downlinked at any time. R-710: only complete packet sequences per the segmentation flags. R-720: autonomous downlink control around acquisition and loss of signal

5354555657585960

These rules also shape the ground database. Under R-020 and R-150 each APID has one fixed structure and maps to one Level-0 product, and under R-010 routing relies on the APID alone.5455 The Solar Orbiter MIB, from a science mission outside the note's scope, shows the opposite choice for its science telemetry. Solar Orbiter's 11-bit APID is a 7-bit process ID plus a 4-bit packet category, category 12 being reserved for its science service 21.116 In the September 2025 release, the 45 on-board science APIDs carry 334 packet definitions. 328 of them are TM(21,3), (21,5) or (21,6), which are told apart by an additional identification field: the pic table puts PI1 for these three subtypes at byte 16, 8 bits wide (317 definitions have a non-zero PI1 value; the other 6 are TM(21,7), which has no PI1). 35 of the 45 APIDs carry more than one definition, up to 45 on APID 1548.117

Inference

In the note's terms, Solar Orbiter's science packets use a structure identifier inside the packet to select the layout, which R-150 asks Earth-observation payloads to avoid. The note does not discuss Solar Orbiter, and nothing here says that either design is wrong for its mission; the comparison only shows what the requirement changes in a ground database.

docs.title: From the manufacturer's database to the ODB
docs.text: On INTEGRAL, the ODB was derived from the Satellite Database (SDB) that the satellite manufacturer delivered before launch. The SDB was not maintained afterwards: during the routine phase all changes went directly into the ODB.103 The two spacecraft analysts of the flight control team maintained it; every modification needed the Spacecraft Operations Manager's (SOM) approval, after which the analysts updated every system that used the ODB: the IMCS, the FOP generation tool and the OBSMS.10399 Change requests could come from the flight control team, the science ground segment or the instrument teams; requests from the science side were first verified at science-ground-segment level and, if needed, went to the Configuration Control Board.103

docs.title: HPSDB and SRDB: a database with views
docs.text:
Thales Alenia Space's 2015 presentation traces its system reference database from Herschel/Planck to MTG and towards EGS-CC. The Herschel/Planck System Data Base (HPSDB) answered two ESA requirements: commonality between the two spacecraft and between the users of the database, and smooth transition, the reuse of validated data from one programme phase to the next up to operations. Commonality was achieved by physical instantiation and category flags, smooth transition by logical instantiation and category flags. The SRDB adapted HPSDB for MTG; its one major conceptual change is that an object can be attached to a former version of another, where HPSDB could attach only the most recent one.27 How HPSDB processed SCOS-2000 MIB files is described on Mission tailoring of the MIB and MIB tooling.

The model has three kinds of element. An object is a node of the product tree at element, subsystem or model level, such as a reaction wheel, the AOCS or the spacecraft. An item is a database entry belonging to an object: a TM packet, a TM parameter, a curve, a synthetic parameter, a group or a constant. A pseudo-item is a sub-record inside an item, for example one entry in a packet's list of parameters, with its own category flag, parameter reference, byte offset and bit offset.282931 Item identifiers have a core part with a type letter and an instantiation part that prefixes it:28

Prefix of the core identifier Item type Example from the slides A TM packet A001 C Curve C001, instantiated RWC001 D Synthetic parameter D001, instantiated AZZZD001 G Group G001 K Constant K001, instantiated A101K001 M TM parameter M001, instantiated A101M001

283138

Category flags select the users of each item and pseudo-item (AIT, OPS, SW in the example). The manager sees everything. In the slide's example the AIT view of the reaction wheel contains packet A001, parameter M001 without its OPS-only pseudo-item, M002 and the curve; the OPS view omits the packet, which is flagged for AIT and software only; the software view contains only the packet. The main constraint is that every view must be consistent.29

Mechanism What it does Physical instantiation A defined object (reaction wheel RW) has realised instances with serial numbers (RW001 ...). An instance can physically delete, modify or add items: RW001 drops packet A001, modifies M002 and adds curve RW001C002 Logical instantiation A higher-level object places lower-level objects at positions: the AOCS places reaction wheels at A101 and A102 and a gyro at A200, giving A101M001, A102M001, A200M001. The higher level can logically delete, modify or define items, and its own items sit at a pseudo-position (AZZZ), for example a synthetic parameter D001 = A101M002 + A102M002 Combined instantiation Element, subsystem and model levels (RW, AOCS, HERSCHEL) each have defined and realised parts; in the slide's example a constant K001 is overridden physically at the realised element (RW001), logically at the subsystem level (AOCS) and physically at the realised model (HERSCHEL001) Generic object A GENERIC object at pseudo-position STD holds items visible from every object, such as STDK001 Configurable levels The number of logical levels is configurable Resources A parameter can be declared valid only when a resource item is in a given state, for example M001 valid if relay resource R001 is closed; a mapping at module level binds A101R001 to the PCDU's relay status A200M001, and the exported operational files carry the validity condition Groups Group items collect items, also across positions: the AOCS group G001 = A101G001 + A102G001 + A200A001, so AZZZG001 holds the members of both wheel groups plus the gyro's packet XML views A flat view lists every instantiated item of an object; a full view keeps the generic, definition and attachment structure (OBJ_GN, OBJ_DF, OBJ_ATTACH)

30313235363839

Editing follows a check-out/check-in cycle across three areas. An object is checked out from the reference area into a working area, modified there, and checked back in; the previous reference version then moves to the archive area.33

stateDiagram-v2
  direction LR
  RA: Reference area (current version)
  WA: Working area (copy being edited)
  AA: Archive area (previous versions)
  RA --> WA: check-out
  WA --> WA: modification
  WA --> RA: check-in
  RA --> AA: archive of the replaced version

33

Every check-in increments an environment counter and can carry a label. By default an inheriting object follows the latest version of its parent (automatic propagation). A forced attachment pins it to an environment counter or label, so that two objects inheriting from the same parent can see different versions of it until the default attachment is reset.34 This is the SRDB feature that HPSDB lacked. For EGS-CC, the high-level model (objects and instantiation) was expected to map onto the EGS-CC product structure, and the low-level model (items and pseudo-items) onto other EGS-CC packages through conversion algorithms; in 2015 this mapping was "still to be done".3740 MTG had also added resources, an owner flag and lists of aliases.40

docs.title: How a delivered MIB identifies itself
docs.text: Whatever tool builds the database, the SCOS-2000 import names each delivery in the vdf table. The ICD says the last imported record sets the internal version name, which SCOS-2000 shows to users and checks, for example, when a saved stack file is loaded against the database that produced it; release and issue numbers support version management.110 The Solar Orbiter release of 16 September 2025 has one record, 25925PFM with comment 20250916-CSW3.1.2_MAS7.33, release 25925 and issue 733. The SWA instrument database instead keeps all 70 versions it went through, from SWA_00.2 ("Received from MSSL") to SWA_6.3.4 of 29 November 2021; 26 of the dated releases fall in 2016 and 23 in 2017, more than in any other year.118119 Both are discussed further on The Solar Orbiter MIB and SWA.

docs.title: Flight procedures under configuration control: INTEGRAL
docs.text:
INTEGRAL's flight operations plan (FOP, issue 2.0 of February 2003) is the reference for all flight operations. Its mission rules say that the FOP's timelines and flight procedures, nominal and contingency, are to be used after separation, that FOP procedures override all other derived procedures, and that deviations need the permission of the Flight Director or SOM during LEOP and of the SOM or a nominated representative thereafter.100 The flight control team prepares and maintains the FOP under the SOM, who alone approves modifications (parts that concern the interface to the science ground segment also need its representatives' approval); changes that could affect mission performance are coordinated with the Project Scientist.102

A procedure is written by the responsible spacecraft operations engineer (SOE), tested by that engineer and by another SOE or analyst, usually on the satellite simulator, and approved by the SOM. Only then is it given to the controllers (SPACONs), who may execute approved procedures only.102 The FOP lists the validation levels; the two not relevant in the routine phase are marked deleted in the source:102

Level Validation step 1 The spacecraft or instrument manufacturer verifies the inputs given in the user manual (in the routine phase the manufacturer is normally no longer involved) 2 The SOE visually inspects the procedure when generating it 3 Generation with FOPGEN checks the parameters implicitly, because FOPGEN accesses the actual database 4 The SOE tests the procedure on the simulator if necessary (not systematically) 6 SPACONs may run procedures on the control system against the simulator: this verifies the command sequence and the telemetry parameters named in the procedure, but not the logic 8 Throughout, the SOEs keep a verification matrix of which procedure was tested in which context 
flowchart LR
  UM["User manual inputs<br/>(manufacturer)"] --> GEN["SOE writes procedure<br/>with FOPGEN (reads ODB)"]
  GEN --> INS["Visual inspection"]
  INS --> SIM["Test on simulator<br/>(SOE + second SOE/analyst)"]
  SIM --> APP{"SOM approval"}
  APP -- approved --> SPC["SPACONs execute<br/>approved procedures only"]
  SIM -.-> VM["Verification matrix"]

102

docs.title: MOIS and ASTRAL-Prepare
docs.text:
RHEA's MOIS, presented in 2023 as ASTRAL-Prepare, is a long-standing preparation product that RHEA says has supported over 100 spacecraft. It authors manual, semi-automated and automated procedures, checks the TM and TC they use against different spacecraft database versions, validates them, and publishes them to a flight operations manual or to operations languages for automation; it also manages spacecraft databases. Procedures can be edited in synchronised tabular, flowchart and script views; configuration management, role-based access and an approval workflow govern releases.15

Its framework classifies configuration data into data types, whose instances are data items. The files and metadata that make up a data type are managed as a group, as a single configuration item. Each data type has common properties (name, description, type) used for search across the whole data set, specific properties, and four mandatory methods: consistency checks, query, generate products and publish, which the framework calls when it checks or publishes the entire data set, for example a FOP release.16 Data types and editors already existed for OBCPs, mission planning rules, PLUTO scripts (see ECSS-E-ST-70-32C), Writer procedures and Word documents, and SCOS-2000 synthetic-parameter scripts.16

The established SCOS-2000 procedure format is the Writer: a per-procedure database with a forms-based editor that uses MS Excel for visualisation, plus a flowchart view. RHEA finds it comfortable for mostly linear procedures because a form can show many attributes, such as calibration curves, while scripting does better with loops, branching and complex expressions. Some ESOC missions automated routine operations with Writer procedures and the MOIS Scheduler, with an event monitor starting contingency recovery procedures on known out-of-limit events.25

docs.title: PME and the Extensible Procedure Model
docs.text:
RHEA's newer Procedure Model Editor (PME) distinguishes two uses of a procedure. A product-generating procedure is a design document that may be detailed enough to generate EGS-CC activity lists, SCOS-2000 MIB sequences or code in an operations language (OBCPs in OL, Tcl/TOPE automation, SPELL). A plain sequence is linear and carries no logic or guidance for the operator, which is why RHEA wants to start from a richer procedure. An executable procedure is run directly by ASTRAL-Automate instead of being submitted to a control system.18

Procedures must be reviewable by non-programmers in textual, flowchart and tabular views, so RHEA starts from a model rather than a language: the Extensible Procedure Model (XPM).18

flowchart TB
  P["Procedure (one file)"] --> S["Steps<br/>start and end point, optional precondition,<br/>confirmation part"]
  S --> ST["Statements"]
  ST --> B["Branching<br/>SelectCase, ForEach, For, While, If"]
  ST --> C["Control<br/>Synchronise, set variable, prompt, log"]
  ST --> E["Execution<br/>ExcuteActivity/TC, CheckState, WaitForState,<br/>WaitForEvent, ExpectPacket, SetMontoring"]

The statement names are given as printed in the paper ("ExcuteActivity", "SetMontoring").19

The minimal XPM is an interface that every structured procedure implements: verifiable steps, executable statements and basic branching. It is enough for flowcharts and for export to activity lists or SCOS-2000 sequences, but execution needs a language extension.19 RHEA defines a domain-specific language (PDSL) with Xtext, whose grammar is derived from the EMF model so that the model is also the abstract syntax tree. Steps have pre- and post-conditions; activities are called asynchronously and can be synchronised on completion; otherwise execution is single-threaded. Boolean and arithmetic expressions are delegated to a scripting language (Groovy, Python possible), and the generated Groovy carries annotations so that breakpoints and variables can be inspected in the PDSL itself.20 The flowchart editor is built with Sirius; text and flowchart can be edited in parallel, and several flowcharts of different granularity can describe one procedure.21 The PME currently supports two DSLs, one for AIT test procedures and one for ESOC flight control procedures, sharing flowcharts, queries and relational checks against the mission model.20

flowchart LR
  subgraph Prepare["ASTRAL-Prepare"]
    ED["PME editor<br/>(RCP or web)"]
    WR["Writer editor"]
  end
  DS["Procedure Data Server<br/>(DA-Service API)"]
  subgraph AS["Procedure Automation Server"]
    RUN["Runner<br/>(CTL-Service API)"]
    CMD["Commander<br/>(EXE-Service API)"]
  end
  ED -->|queries| DS
  DS -->|EGS-CC adapter| TDM["EGS-CC TDM"]
  ED -->|upload procedure set| RUN
  ED -->|debug run, sendTC and checkTM| CMD
  SCH["ASTRAL-Schedule"] --> RUN
  SCH --> WAS["Writer Automation Server"]
  SUP["Web Supervisor"] --> RUN
  RUN -.-> CMD
  CMD -->|EGS-CC adapter| EGSCC["EGS-CC"]
  CMD -.->|S2K adapter possible| S2K["SCOS-2000"]

2223

The editor reaches the mission model only through the Procedure Data Server, whose EGS-CC adapter returns simple objects from TDM queries; a SCOS-2000 adapter is conceivable but not required, since the MME imports the MIB and the SCOS-2000 automation server needs no MIB access. The Automation Server splits into the Runner, which executes procedures server-side without a user interface, and the Commander, which performs atomic actions such as sending a TC or checking TM.22 The Scheduler, used at ESOC for years to run Writer procedures with SCOS-2000, gained a second connector so that one plan can mix Writer and PME procedures.23

RHEA describes three transition steps:242526

  1. Conversion. Writer procedures can be converted to PDSL on import, whether or not the mission moves to EGS-CC; the MIB is converted to the EGS-CC TDM with the MME's MIB importer.
  2. Phase-in on SCOS-2000. Writer and PME procedures coexist in the data set and in the schedule, so a team can keep a Writer-only plan and, in parallel, a plan where validated PME procedures replace their Writer counterparts. For SCOS-2000 the PME generates command sequences, and it runs on Windows and Linux, whereas Writer is Windows/Office based.
  3. Move to EGS-CC. The move is complete when the MIB is converted to the TDM. PME procedures need no conversion. A database analyst imports into a local workspace backed by SVN, runs a consistency check of the whole procedure set against the new TDM, and checks in only if it passes.

For scale: the September 2025 Solar Orbiter MIB holds 3,404 command sequences with 13,879 elements, of which 12,629 are commands and 1,250 nested sequences; there are no textual-comment elements.120 This is the linear, logic-free product RHEA describes;18 see Command sequences and parameter sets.

docs.title: Objectives and layers
docs.text:
ESA's answer to the proliferation of preparation tools is a light, data-type-agnostic framework with generic services, extended by plug-ins for specific data types. Its stated objectives are to streamline tailoring and reduce operator effort, to host all preparation applications in one consistent environment, to harmonise the tools of spacecraft and ground station operations teams, and to bring advanced features such as configuration management to all operations artefacts. A secondary objective is to support the transition from SCOS-2000 to EGS-CC.12

The framework, the Operations Preparation Environment (OPEN; the 2019 paper calls it the "OPEN Preparation Environment"), has two layers.178

flowchart TB
  subgraph Products
    OM["OPEN-M<br/>mission operations<br/>(MICONYS-CC, ESOC)"]
    OS["OPEN-S<br/>ground stations<br/>(GSMC-CC, ESOC)"]
    OD["OPEN-D<br/>EGS-CC system<br/>configuration"]
    MME["MME<br/>Mission Model Editor<br/>(phase C/D, ESTEC)"]
  end
  CC["OPEN-CC layer<br/>EGS-CC aware generic functions"]
  O["OPEN layer<br/>version control, scripting, consistency checking,<br/>model visualisation<br/>(agnostic of EGS-CC except<br/>the configuration item concept)"]
  E["Eclipse RCP, EMF, OSGi"]
  Products --> CC --> O --> E

8106

Extensions can be added to both layers, but EGS-CC-specific extensions only to OPEN-CC.8 OPEN's functions fall into three groups: managed data (the supported definitions), data management services (version and access control, consistency checking such as dependencies between data sets, merge and compare, baselines, reports, change logs, delta and complete import/export) and editors and browsers.5 Format-specific services, such as importing an S2K MIB, are dedicated extensions.5

Topic What the sources say Implementation Java on OSGi and Eclipse RCP; every function a distinct plug-in; managed data held as EMF models and stored and exchanged through a distributed version control system Deployment Desktop applications on several operating systems including Windows; offline editing, with sporadic TCP/IP connections to a central repository when online Data model The EGS-CC Conceptual Data Model (CDM) and its LDM library, shipped with the EGS-CC binaries rather than with OPEN; any EMF-compatible model or CDM extension can be loaded "with a few assumptions" Model visualisation Views to navigate CDM types, sub-types and references, replacing the HTML EGS-CC reference manual for the data model Shared repositories OPEN-M, OPEN-S, OPEN-D and MME can work on the same repositories, so FCT tailoring data can be checked against the EGS-CC system configuration without the FCT editing it SCOS-2000 migration OPEN-M includes a converter from SCOS-2000 MIB 6.9 to the CDM; ESA calls the EGS-CC model "semantically richer", so the migration is possible; validation used data from BepiColombo, ExoMars TGO, Gaia, JUICE and the Sentinels External deliveries The MICONYS-CC environment was to import legacy MIB data both to migrate missions and to accept MIB-format deliveries from external organisations FOP editor Planned as a re-engineering of MOIS Writer as an OPEN-CC extension Licence ESA Community License with weak copyleft; proprietary extensions allowed; redistribution outside ESA Member States needs ESA Technology Transfer Board authorisation Status (Feb. 2019) Development since 2017 with more than six companies in one agile team; JUICE and Sentinels flight control engineers using alpha versions with flying-mission data; goal: OPEN-M fit for operational use by 2020; next: display editors, constellations, EGS-CC system configuration

69101131314

ESA presents OPEN as a way to "raise the software stack", like Eclipse RCP below it, so that implementers of EGS-CC tailoring tools need not reimplement basic functions and can share framework maintenance.12 How ESOC's missions will move their MIBs into OPEN-M, in three categories, is described on Ancillary systems, MICONYS and the move to EGS-CC.

docs.title: The Mission Model Editor
docs.text: The MME, developed by RHEA and now part of EGS-CC, edits data of the EGS-CC Technical Data Model (TDM). It adds a presentation layer that arranges packets, parameters and procedures in a Mission Model tree and hides the TDM's M&C elements, mappers, mapped implementations and file-backed configuration items. It imposes one M&C element per configuration item file, so that a sub-tree is an independent, replaceable set of files that different organisations can work on in parallel. Its TM Parameter Editor maps directly to TDM engineering parameters. Because the MME extends OPEN, it inherits OPEN's SCOS-2000 MIB importer.17

docs.title: Telemetry definitions on the fly: dynamic housekeeping
The problem
docs.text:
An on-board data pool can hold tens or hundreds of thousands of parameters from many suppliers. During AIT and on-board software validation, engineers often define new housekeeping packets on board with PUS service 3 commands, picking only the parameters they need. A central checkout system that recognises packets only from its database then cannot identify these packets unless someone has already written matching static definitions.61

The SCOS-2000 import ICD states the conventional rule: SCOS-2000 has no service-specific processing of service 3, every received packet must be defined in the database before generation is enabled, and the efficient ESA practice is to create the packet definition first and generate the service 3 commands from it in the database manager, not in the kernel.109 Terma's CCS5 reverses the direction and derives the database entry from the command.63

docs.title: The service 3 commands used
docs.text:
Message Name Application data TC(3,1), TC(3,2) Define new housekeeping / diagnostic parameter report SID; collection interval in units of the default housekeeping scheduling rate (DIAG_MIN_INTERV); counters and the list of on-board parameter IDs (with NFA, NREP and NPAR2 for super-commutated groups) TC(3,3), TC(3,4) Clear housekeeping / diagnostic definitions A list of SIDs TC(3,5) Enable housekeeping parameter report generation Not detailed in the paper; the operator sends it after the definition is in place TM(3,25), TM(3,26) Housekeeping / diagnostic parameter report SID followed by parameter samples, possibly super-commutated

626365

SID, APID and subtype together identify a report definition, so the definition commands carry enough information for the ground to create and delete its own packet definitions.62

docs.title: How CCS5 does it
docs.text:
CCS5 reads a SCOS-2000-compatible MIB and runs Tcl-based TOPE procedures (see TOPE). At session start it loads the MIB tables into memory, where TOPE can read all tables and write some; it can merge several MIBs, marking each record's origin in a "Source" field.63 The core of the DYNHK component is a TOPE script, DynHkMonitor.tcl, running on the CCS server console.63

sequenceDiagram
  participant Op as Test operator
  participant OBC as On-board computer
  participant Dyn as DynHkMonitor (TOPE)
  participant CCS as CCS server, clients, IFMGR
  Op->>OBC: TC(3,1) or TC(3,2) define report
  OBC-->>Op: service 1 completion report
  Dyn->>Dyn: derive PID and VPD records, allocate new SPID
  Dyn->>CCS: publish definition with the CCS5 remote command (atomic)
  Op->>OBC: TC(3,5) enable report generation
  OBC-->>CCS: TM(3,25) or TM(3,26), processed like a static packet
  Op->>OBC: later TC(3,3) or TC(3,4) clear
  Dyn->>CCS: set PID_VALID false (packet becomes unknown)

63

Redefining a SID disables the old definition and creates a new one with a new SPID, so SPIDs and TPSDs are never reused within a session. Dynamic records stay in memory and vanish when the MIB is reloaded; they are tagged with Source = DYNHK and can be saved and merged in the next session, which is optional because it depends on whether the on-board software keeps its dynamic definitions over a reboot.63 Packets that arrive after their definition is cleared are archived as unknown, but variable-packet samples already archived remain accessible.6366

docs.title: Mapping PUS to MIB tables
docs.text:
CCS5 identifies packets as SCOS-2000 does: APID from the primary header, type and subtype from the data field header, the pic record giving the position of PI1 and PI2, the pid record giving the SPID, and finally plf or vpd for the layout.64112 Because the definition command lists parameter IDs without offsets, DYNHK uses vpd, which packs parameters one after another and also allows variable-length strings.64 It needs two settings that PUS does not supply: a schedulingRate to convert the collection interval into milliseconds for parameter expiry, and a mapping from TC APID to TM APID, since the report does not necessarily come from the APID that received the command. The pic records for the new packets must exist in advance, because the MIB does not reference the SID directly.6465

Table and field DYNHK value PID_TYPE, PID_STYPE 3; 25 for housekeeping or 26 for diagnostic PID_APID From the TC-to-TM APID setting PID_PI1_VAL, PID_PI2_VAL From the SID, split according to pic (or all in PI1) PID_SPID Counter from a user-configurable offset, clear of static SPIDs, incremented per definition PID_DESCR Generated, for example Dyn HK <SID value> PID_TPSD Equal to the SPID PID_DFHSIZE Derived from pic: start reference for the variable parameters PID_TIME Y (on-board time assumed in the header) PID_INTER From the collection interval PID_CHECK 1 (packet error control assumed present) PID_VALID Set to false on TC(3,3) or TC(3,4) VPD_TPSD, VPD_POS, VPD_NAME TPSD; positions 1 to NPAR; the pcf name whose PCF_PID equals the parameter ID in the TC Super-commutation (NFA = 1) An extra group-repeater row: VPD_NAME = REPEATER, VPD_GRPSIZE = NPAR2, VPD_FIXREP = NREP

65

The ICD defines VPD_GRPSIZE as the number of following records repeated by a counter and VPD_FIXREP as a fixed repetition count carried by a dummy parameter that is defined in pcf but not present in the packet, which is how DYNHK's REPEATER row works.115

docs.title: Worked example: a Solar Orbiter definition seen through DYNHK
docs.text:
Solar Orbiter does the opposite of DYNHK: its MIB already contains the reports together with predefined commands that create them (see ST[03] §9.5). This makes it possible to check DYNHK's rules against a real, static definition. The command ZCA2Z05B "Define HK: AOCS Dynamics FAST" is a TC(3,1) to APID 188 whose application data consists only of fixed areas, so these bytes are real MIB data:121

Resolving the eight IDs through PCF_PID gives the vpd rows DYNHK would write, and packing them back-to-back after the 16 header octets and the SID reproduces exactly the byte offsets of the real fixed layout of SPID 29530:121

VPD_POS (derived) Parameter ID VPD_NAME (from pcf) PTC/PFC Size (octets) Offset in the real plf 1 0B201C1C NCAG6VN0 GyrStarOutputEstRateEst 7/24 24 17 2 0B201950 NCAG4NP0 ErrGenErrAngErr 7/24 24 41 3 0B201C1B NCAG6VL0 GyrStarOutputEstQuat 7/32 32 65 4 0B20143B NCAT1AG0 RW1_RATE 5/1 4 97 5 0B201459 NCAT1B10 RW2_RATE 5/1 4 101 6 0B201477 NCAT1BK0 RW3_RATE 5/1 4 105 7 0B201495 NCAT1C40 RW4_RATE 5/1 4 109 8 0B201C29 NCAG6VZ0 WsEstTrqFricEST 7/16 16 113

The pid record DYNHK would create can be set beside the real one:12165113

Field DYNHK rule applied (illustrative) Real Solar Orbiter record PID_TYPE / PID_STYPE 3 / 25 3 / 25 PID_APID TM APID mapped from TC APID 188 180 PID_PI1_VAL / PID_PI2_VAL 77 / 0 77 / 0 PID_SPID next free number above the offset 29530 PID_DESCR "Dyn HK 77" "AOCS Dynamics FAST" PID_TPSD equal to the SPID -1 (fixed packet, laid out in plf) PID_DFHSIZE from pic 16 PID_TIME Y Y PID_INTER from 48 cycles and schedulingRate empty PID_CHECK 1 0

The real plf layout has 24 records: the SID decoded as parameter NCD030A1, the eight block parameters, and 15 overlapping records that decode the octet strings into components such as NCAD6VN1 at byte 17.121

Inference

A DYNHK-style definition of this packet would decode the eight blocks but not the 15 component parameters, which exist only in the hand-made static layout; the octet strings would stay raw. For PID_DFHSIZE the paper says only that it is derived from pic; reading the ICD, variable parameters starting after the 1-octet SID would need a value of 17 rather than the 16 of the fixed packet. Neither point is stated in the sources.

The TC-to-TM APID setting is a real issue on Solar Orbiter. Its APID is a 7-bit process ID plus a 4-bit packet category, telecommands always use category 12, and housekeeping reports use category 2 (high-priority TM), 4 (routine), 5 (functional cyclic) or 8 (diagnostic).116 Matching each of the 138 TC(3,1) and TC(3,2) commands that fix their SID in a fixed area to the report with the same SID and process ID gives:122

Process ID TC APID (cat. 12) TM APID: SID range (TC(3,1) → TM(3,25)) TM APID: SID range (TC(3,2) → TM(3,26)) 10 172 162 (cat. 2): 2-14; 164 (cat. 4): 77-92 168 (cat. 8): 193-194 11 188 178 (cat. 2): 2-18; 180 (cat. 4): 77-97 184 (cat. 8): 193-229 12 204 194 (cat. 2): 2; 196 (cat. 4): 77 200 (cat. 8): 193-199 13 220 210 (cat. 2): 3-17; 212 (cat. 4): 77-78 216 (cat. 8): 195-255 14 236 226 (cat. 2): 6-15; 228 (cat. 4): 77-81; 229 (cat. 5): 188-191 232 (cat. 8): 193-197 16 268 258 (cat. 2): 1-4; 260 (cat. 4): 79 264 (cat. 8): 193-194

Every one of the 138 commands matched exactly one report packet. The other 21 definition commands take the SID as a parameter (editable or fixed) and could not be matched this way.122

Inference

On Solar Orbiter the report APID depends on the SID range as well as on the command APID: one TC APID feeds up to three housekeeping APIDs and one diagnostic APID. A single TC-to-TM APID mapping, as the paper describes it, would therefore not be enough; the rule would have to include the SID range or the report subtype. The paper does not discuss such a case.

Terma's conclusion is that a flexible data model was essential: since CCS5 could already patch some MIB tables without reloading, the C++ changes for pid and vpd were small. The authors envisaged a display to pick data-pool parameters and send the TCs automatically, and support for the many new service 3 subservices of PUS-C.66

docs.title: Command verification beyond the database
docs.text:
Terma's paper on advanced telecommand verification starts from SCOS-2000, which it calls representative. Verification there is defined in the MIB rather than hard-coded, with global settings such as propagation delay and permitted jitter, and offers three methods:67

Method How it works Strength and weakness (per the paper) Expected TM value Open a window after the command and require the first sample after it opens to have the expected value Fully general, no special packets, works without PUS; but no explicit link to the command that caused the change Service 1 reports Expect TM(1,x) reports for each stage within a time range Practically unambiguous per command; ambiguity possible if the source sequence counter wraps during verification (seen on one science mission with a reduced counter range); costs downlink bandwidth; needs PUS Status consistency check (SCC) Treat any change of a parameter as an error unless a command that changes it was sent, within a window Called "change on command only" (COCOMO) in other systems

SCOS-2000 also tracks tricky cases such as a second command expecting a different value while the first is still pending; the first is then "superseded".67 The MIB side of this is described on Command verification in the MIB and Monitoring checks.

docs.title: Limitations the paper identifies
docs.text:
• Only one type of verification per stage. To check a TM parameter as well as receiving TM(1,7) or TM(1,8) at completion, several missions "borrowed" the last progress stage; an extra finalisation stage would have been cleaner.68
  • The verifier model is encapsulated in C++ and CORBA, so customisation means recompilation and reinstallation; long maintenance had made it complicated.68
  • SCOS-2000 shifts verification timeouts for time-tagged service 11 commands to their execution time, but missions also delete, time-shift and enable or disable stored commands, for example by sub-schedule ID, and the paper knows of no ESA mission that followed PUS exactly here, so following these changes on ground is mission-specific and costly.68

The Solar Orbiter MIB shows how one mission works within the model. It defines 16 acceptance stages by report, 23 completion stages by report and 167 completion stages by parameter, and no start or progress stage. No command has more than one completion stage, so none combines a completion report with a parameter check, and the progress-stage workaround is not used. Status consistency checks (OCP_TYPE = C) exist on 15 parameters, all of them counters (error, reject, reset, stored-packet and other counts) such as NDSD0046 "DST-A WD Reset Counter", and none of the 15 appears in a verification expression. 5,304 of the 5,454 commands name a default sub-schedule (CCF_SUBSCHEDID), using 17 distinct values (1, 2, 4 to 8 and 101 to 110).123

Inference

With no command expected to change them, these 15 counters behave like the paper's COCOMO case: any change is reported. The interpretation of the sub-schedule values (for example as one range for platform and one for instruments) is not stated in the available sources.

docs.title: The CCS5 approach: a scriptable verifier
docs.text:
Because a checkout product must adapt quickly to on-board software and space-ground ICD changes found during AIT, Terma kept most SCOS-2000-like verification in C++ but made mission-specific behaviour scriptable in TOPE.69

  • TC cache. A list, visible in the user interface, of recent commands under verification. It has a configured size above which completed commands are dropped, but grows (with a warning) to keep every incomplete command. The paper sizes it as (timeout + propagation delay) × command rate: for a 30 s timeout, 10 s delay and 100 commands per second, (30 + 10) × 100 = 4,000 entries, a few megabytes.70
  • Command IDs and properties. Each command has a system-wide unique ID that includes the workstation ID in its upper 4 bits. Properties such as id, raw, apid, generationTime, executionTime, mapid and bypass are archived at every verification stage, some indexed for SQL queries, and read or written with tcprop <id> <property> ?value?.70
  • Mission timeline. tcsend ZP_00003 executiontime 12345678.0 subscheduleid 4 checks {SPTV DPTV CEV} (the paper's example) creates a carrier command from a template and postpones verification. tcsubscribe filters sent commands by properties, for example all service 11 commands, so that a script can update the ground timeline model with ::utope::mtldelete, ::utope::mtldisablerelease, ::utope::mtlenablerelease, ::utope::mtlreset and ::utope::timeshift; the verifier follows the modified times.71
  • Cyclic commands. A cyclicRepeats property (a count, or -1 for infinite) is decremented on each repetition; the command leaves the cache only at 0. updatecommand <id> <stage> <state> forces a stage closed or reopened: setting it to IDLE resets it and setting it to PENDING reopens the same window and conditions.72
stateDiagram-v2
  direction LR
  [*] --> PENDING: command released, window opens
  PENDING --> Completed: verification conditions met or window closes
  Completed --> IDLE: updatecommand stage IDLE (script)
  IDLE --> PENDING: updatecommand stage PENDING (orbit position reached)
  Completed --> [*]: cyclicRepeats reaches 0

The two script-driven transitions are those of the paper; the other states are simplified for this diagram.72

A modelled command (isModelled true, via tcsend ... model or tcmodel) is processed, verified and archived like a real one but discarded at the moment of transmission. The paper's uses are system validation tests where the MCS commands and the CCS listens, hot-redundant CCS servers that must take over verification, and commands sent by other EGSE elements such as a CFDP front end. Command sequences could be modelled in TOPE; OBCPs and event-action responses might need an external tool such as MOIS or APEX, an operational simulator or an emulator, each with an efficient API.73 The paper warns against over-engineering: false timeouts confuse operators, network jitter rules out millisecond windows, and modelling a fixed inter-command delay with a ground timer accumulates drift from cycle to cycle.74

In hindsight the authors would have scripted even more of the verifier. They criticise PUS as so loosely defined and tailorable that ground applications cannot be moved between missions, and they worried that EGS-CC, then about to start development, might prolong PUS without a plan to replace it.75

docs.title: Monitoring the EGSE itself as telemetry
docs.text:
Vitrociset's Health Monitoring system (HM) treats the checkout infrastructure as a monitored system. It reports operating-system resources (disk, memory, CPU), process status, point-to-point connections and time synchronisation of the EGSE machines, and models every monitored entity as a TM parameter in the SCOS-2000 MIB inside ad hoc TM packets, so the data appears on normal SCOS-2000 displays and in procedures.7679

It is built on Java's JMX MBean technology, which the paper describes as tooling for distributed, modular management and monitoring of devices, applications and networks, and follows its three levels:77

JMX level HM component Role Instrumentation MBean plug-ins Make a resource (application, service, device, OS component) manageable; emit notifications Agent MBean server with services and at least one connector (RMI) Runs on the monitored machine, or on a mediation element when the resource has no Java environment Manager Management client, handler, interpreter Talks to agents through connectors, exposes their view, collects notifications 
flowchart LR
  subgraph EGSE["EGSE hosts"]
    A1["HM Agent<br/>(plug-ins: disk, memory,<br/>CPU, process, TCP, NTP)"]
    A2["HM Agent"]
  end
  A1 -->|RMI| MGR["HM Manager<br/>(launched with SCOS-2000)"]
  A2 -->|RMI| MGR
  MAP["XML: object Id to<br/>MIB parameter name"] --> MGR
  MGR -->|"TM packets via EXIF (CORBA)"| S2K["SCOS-2000 TM chain:<br/>processing, archiving, displays"]

787980

Each agent mounts its plug-ins at start-up from an XML file of containers and managed objects (in the VEGA example a resource sampler with disk, memory, CPU and process objects, a TCP monitor and an NTP sampler). A second XML file maps object IDs to MIB parameter names; on the VEGA launcher EGSE, client disk usage went to HM_32_01, free memory to HM_16_01, CPU to HM_FL_01 and process or connection status to HM_1_01 and similar.80 The manager injects the packets through the EXIF interface, with a port to the newer SMF module foreseen, and the paper shows SCOS-2000 mimic displays of the VEGA EGSE status built from these parameters. Deployment needs only the XML configuration and the matching MIB entries.7981

Inference

The parameter names appear to encode the value type: HM_32_ for disk, HM_16_ for memory, HM_FL_ for CPU load and NTP, HM_1_ for statuses. The paper gives the mapping but not the naming rule.

docs.title: Displays and user interfaces: the EGOS User Desktop
docs.text:
The EGOS User Desktop (EUD) is ESA's framework for rich-client user interfaces in ground data systems, in mission operation since 2013. It was motivated by obsolescence, removal of COTS dependencies and cost reduction through reuse, with goals of open-source technology, Linux and Windows support, shared implementations and a harmonised look and feel.8283 It is written in Java on Eclipse RCP, uses only open-source software, and integrates user-interface components called displays, which are RCP views or editors; standard RCP views run unchanged, and an extended view base class adds EUD facilities.84

Layer (slide 10) Content Custom EUD application Application-specific displays, interfaces and configuration, with back-end-specific adapters Generic displays Parameter displays (alphanumeric, scrolling parameter, graph, XY graph, MIMIC, matrix), live and history message displays, action executor, system control and system explorer (slide 6 counts 11 commonly used displays) EUD interfaces IEudParameter, IEudMessage, IEudScriptEngine, IEudSystemControl, IPersistentStorage, ISessionManager, matched to back-end parameter, message, scripting, system control, storage and session services Core Core and utility libraries, UI widgets and composites, display management, session management Eclipse framework RCP, EMF, GEF, GMF, BIRT

8485

By 2014 most ESOC ground-system user interfaces were EUD based: it replaced the GUIs of SCOS-2000, SIMSAT, NIS and FARC and underpinned new systems (ARES, GSMC, FIDES, GSSC, MPSF), with MATIS and SPMON in development and GFTS, DARC and DABYS planned. Its telemetry desktop was in operation for Gaia, and the slides show an Offline Display Development Environment (ODDE).86 One listed benefit matters most for operations preparation: display definition files are cross-compatible between ODDE, the MCS, SIMSAT, ARES and GSMC. The lessons were that consolidating functionality across domains took much effort, agile development was crucial and adapters for legacy systems can be tedious; a web version based on Eclipse RAP and use in EGS-CC were planned.87 For display definitions in the MIB see Display definitions in the MIB.

docs.title: Operations preparation in practice: CHEOPS
docs.text:
CHEOPS, ESA's first small-class mission (launched 18 December 2019), is operated by its consortium: a Mission Operations Centre (MOC) at INTA's CEIT near Madrid and a Science Operations Centre (SOC) in Geneva. The 2025 paper describes a ground segment automated so that routine operations need no staff outside working hours, with 3 to 4 people at the SOC and 5 at the MOC.8897

The MOC control system is SCOS-2000 version 5.4.2, configured through environment variables and the MIB, which defines every TC and TM packet. A Python module library gives automation access to the MCS, and GMV's Flyplan orchestrates all automated MCS and flight-dynamics activities, with Jython scripts and a data-driven monitorCHEOPS activity that watches directories for input files.9189

sequenceDiagram
  participant SOC as SOC (MPS)
  participant GFTS as GFTS
  participant FP as Flyplan (monitorCHEOPS)
  participant FDS as FDS (Autofocus)
  participant MCS as SCOS-2000 MCS
  SOC->>GFTS: Activity Plan (XML) and StarMaps via FTP
  GFTS->>FP: files in watched folder
  FP->>FDS: ATTSIM attitude simulation, CONCHECK Sun exclusion check
  FDS-->>MCS: constraint report (only on success)
  FP->>MCS: Python script checks the report and runs CommandBuilder
  MCS->>MCS: activities to TCs via rule file, SSF stack file, uplink duration
  MCS-->>SOC: Conversion Report via GFTS
  FP->>MCS: assign SSF to next pass long enough for uplink

89909192

The CommandBuilder is the preparation step that turns plans into commands. It maps each activity of the Activity Plan to one or more TCs through a configuration rule file and writes an SSF file, an ASCII file that "can be read by any standard SCOS-2000 using the MIB". It also estimates the uplink duration and writes a conversion report.91 The same tool turns the ground-station availability file into TC stacks that open and close the MCS-station link and start and stop recorded-TM downlinks, one pass folder per pass.92

Inference

Because the SSF stack files are generated against the MIB, they belong to one database version. The SCOS-2000 ICD says the vdf version name is used to ensure that a saved stack is loaded with the database version that generated it; whether CHEOPS relies on this check is not stated.11091

During each of the 4 to 6 daily passes, Python scripts restart SCOS-2000 tasks as needed, load the pass TCs into one of two Auto Stack instances, read TM values through SMON from the packet archive (PARC, on MySQL), read and set MISC variables, switch to AD mode so that missing TCs are retransmitted (see COP-1), and run manufacturer health-check procedures written in Python. The on-board time is a free-running oscillator, so the SCOS-2000 time-correlation feature updates the linear OBT coefficients when accuracy degrades (see Time correlation).93 After the pass, the SCOS-2000 TM Processor splits the station file per virtual channel, the TM Replayer ingests recorded housekeeping into PARC, gaps are found from jumps in the virtual-channel frame counter (see TM SDLP), and RGTgenerator and the CHEOPS-specific HKTMreporter produce TC and TM reports; a colour-coded PDF summary is e-mailed to the operators.94 The SOC decodes science and housekeeping TM "according to the spacecraft's MIB" as well.95 A Simulus 5.4 / SIMSAT simulator validated operational procedures, and MUST/WebMUST, fed with SCOS-2000 RAPID files, complements SCOS-2000 for trend analysis.96 For PARC see Mission archives.

docs.title: Configuration control: the INTEGRAL model
docs.text:
INTEGRAL (launched 17 October 2002) split its ground segment into an operational part (stations, MOC at ESOC, communications) and a science part (ISOC at ESTEC, ISDC at Versoix).98 Its configuration control has a ground-segment Configuration Control Board (CCB) chaired by the Project Scientist with the SOM, the ISOC and ISDC operations managers, the Project Science Coordinator and the MOC QA manager, plus local CCBs per centre.101105 The CCB acts on change requests against an agreed list of configuration items, recorded in a common tool, without necessarily meeting; it does not handle time-critical issues and has no contractual power.105

flowchart LR
  REQ["Change request<br/>(FCT, SGS, instrument team)"] --> Q{"Affects an agreed<br/>configuration item<br/>or another centre?"}
  Q -- no --> LOC["Local configuration control<br/>(at the MOC: SOM approval)"]
  Q -- yes --> CCB["GS CCB<br/>(chair: Project Scientist)"]
  CCB --> IMP["Implementation"]
  LOC --> IMP
  IMP --> VAL["Validation and confirmation<br/>of operational readiness"]

105102103

On the space segment the MOC controls the spacecraft configuration: only approved FOP procedures are applied, FOP and ODB changes follow their configuration control concepts and need SOM approval, the timeline must be based on the latest EPOS and approved, and on-board software and parameters are tracked with the OBSMS and the ODB.101 Instrument configuration is shared: ISDC evaluates performance, ISOC approves changes and passes them to the MOC as an observation plan (POS) or a parameter change request, and the MOC converts instrument tables and software images into uplink commands with the OBSM function of the IMCS. The ISGRI table, updated every revolution, had its own interface based on Task Parameter Files processed directly by the IMCS.101

The configuration items fall into four areas: ground-segment set-up at interfaces (the INTEGRAL File Transfer System, communication lines, ports and firewalls, interface hardware), operational tools shared between centres, operational products and documentation. Products such as procedures and the database can be changed locally, except for data of interest to other centres.106 The database fields under CCB control are listed below with, as this wiki's reading, the SCOS-2000 MIB tables that hold the same information:

INTEGRAL CCB item (FOP Vol. 1 §1.4.3.3.2) Corresponding MIB tables (inference) Instrument TM parameters: calibration curves caf/cap, mcf, lgf Instrument TM parameters: aliases txf/txp (the ICD calls textual calibrations alias sets)111 Instrument TM parameters: out of limits ocf/ocp Instrument TM parameters: packet structure pid, pic, plf, vpd, tpcf Instrument TM parameters: new parameters pcf Instrument TC parameters: default values cpc (CPC_DEFVAL), cdf Instrument TC parameters: calibration curves cca/ccs, paf/pas Event designators and related sequences Sequences possibly in csf/css; event designators have no MIB counterpart named in the sources Instrument flight procedures affecting science products; instrument OBS images, DPE CSSW images, instrument tables Outside the MIB tables (FOP, OBSMS, instrument tables)

106

Inference

The right-hand column maps INTEGRAL's wording onto SCOS-2000 MIB tables. The FOP names the fields but not the tables, and the INTEGRAL ODB format is not described in the available sources; ESA's 2003 slide only shows the ODB between the satellite database import and the IMCS.108

The flight control team behind this was small: the SOM; five engineers (subsystem operations of spacecraft and instruments, on-board software maintenance, mission-planning support, flight-dynamics real-time operations); two analysts (database maintenance, operations-tools maintenance, support to mission planning); six SPACONs for routine shift operations; and one mission-planning engineer.99 Reporting closed the loop: shift reports, revolution reports, and weekly, monthly and annual reports (the annual one with trend analysis), plus an anomaly notification within one hour and a later anomaly report.107

The table groups the sources by theme; it is this wiki's synthesis, not a statement made by any one of them, and it does not imply that every mission followed the same path.

docs.title: Not stated in the available sources
docs.text:
• The format of the INTEGRAL ODB and of FOPGEN's output, and the expansion of FOPGEN, EPOS, POS and CSSW.
  • The conference and year of the Kazmirchuk, Armitage and Troso papers (none of the texts states them), and the version of SCOS-2000 used by the Vitrociset HM system. Kazmirchuk calls the 2016 PUS-C "published last year", which points to 2017,66 and the source URLs on the library pages file his paper under the same ESA indico event (180) as the SESP 2017 Trifin paper, and Armitage's under the same event (93) as the SESP 2015 Thales Alenia Space slides. Neither observation is a statement of the venue.
  • The width of the CCS5 command ID (only that the workstation ID occupies its upper 4 bits).
  • The format of the CHEOPS SSF file and the content of the CommandBuilder rule file.
  • Whether OPEN-M's SCOS-2000 converter handles MIB issues other than 6.9, and how individual MIB tables map to the EGS-CC CDM or TDM.
  • The expansion of SAVOIR, and the content of the GOIRD spreadsheets themselves.
  • Which missions, if any, apply PE-TN-ESA-GS-405 outside Earth observation.

SQL used

All queries ran read-only (sqlite3 -readonly) on solo-2025-09-16.sqlite unless stated.

-- Science packets (category 12) and their identification
-- (APID < 1792 excludes process IDs 112-127, which the SolO ICD assigns to EGSE)
SELECT count(DISTINCT PID_APID), count(*), sum(CAST(PID_PI1_VAL AS int) <> 0)
  FROM pid WHERE CAST(PID_APID AS int) & 15 = 12 AND CAST(PID_APID AS int) < 1792;  -- 45 | 334 | 317
SELECT PID_STYPE, count(*) FROM pid WHERE CAST(PID_APID AS int) & 15 = 12
  AND CAST(PID_APID AS int) < 1792 GROUP BY 1;            -- 3: 105, 5: 72, 6: 151, 7: 6
SELECT * FROM pic WHERE PIC_TYPE = '21';
SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT PID_APID, count(*) n FROM pid
  WHERE CAST(PID_APID AS int) & 15 = 12 AND CAST(PID_APID AS int) < 1792
  GROUP BY 1 HAVING n > 1);                                                         -- 35

-- Database version records (also on swa-idb.sqlite)
SELECT * FROM vdf;

-- Sequences
SELECT count(*) FROM csf;  SELECT CSS_TYPE, count(*) FROM css GROUP BY 1;

-- The DYNHK worked example
SELECT * FROM ccf WHERE CCF_CNAME = 'ZCA2Z05B';
SELECT * FROM cdf WHERE CDF_CNAME = 'ZCA2Z05B' ORDER BY CAST(CDF_BIT AS int);
SELECT PCF_NAME, PCF_DESCR, PCF_PTC, PCF_PFC FROM pcf WHERE PCF_PID = '186653724';  -- etc.
SELECT * FROM pid WHERE PID_SPID = '29530';
SELECT * FROM pic WHERE PIC_TYPE = '3';
SELECT PLF_NAME, PLF_OFFBY, PLF_OFFBI FROM plf WHERE PLF_SPID = '29530'
  ORDER BY CAST(PLF_OFFBY AS int);

-- TC APID to TM APID: a short Python script (python3 -I, sqlite3 module) read every
-- ccf row with CCF_TYPE = 3 and CCF_STYPE in (1, 2), took the first cdf element when it is a
-- fixed area ('A') as the SID, and looked up
SELECT PID_APID, PID_SPID FROM pid
  WHERE PID_TYPE = '3' AND PID_STYPE = :st AND CAST(PID_PI1_VAL AS int) = :sid;
-- keeping rows whose APID >> 4 equals the command's APID >> 4 (same process ID).

-- Verification and status consistency
SELECT CVS_TYPE, CVS_SOURCE, count(*) FROM cvs GROUP BY 1, 2;
SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT p.CVP_TASK, sum(s.CVS_TYPE = 'C') c FROM cvp p
  JOIN cvs s ON s.CVS_ID = p.CVP_CVSID WHERE p.CVP_TYPE = 'C' GROUP BY p.CVP_TASK) WHERE c > 1;  -- 0
SELECT OCP_NAME FROM ocp WHERE OCP_TYPE = 'C';
SELECT count(*) FROM cve WHERE CVE_PARNAM IN (SELECT PCF_NAME FROM pcf WHERE PCF_USCON = 'Y');  -- 0
SELECT CCF_SUBSCHEDID, count(*) FROM ccf GROUP BY 1;
